rationale: The index trial enrolled only 4 patients (ORR 0%), too few to test efficacy in VHL-associated ccRCC (NCT03108066). In sporadic ccRCC, PT2385 at or above the 800 mg BID phase 2 dose lowered erythropoietin, dissociated HIF-2 complexes in metastases and suppressed HIF-2 target genes (PMID:31727677), with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:29257710). Engagement was therefore adequate, but it was shown in sporadic ccRCC rather than VHL disease, and it was published after the trial began. Belzutifan, on the same target, is approved for VHL, so the target matters, which argues against F2. Exposure varied widely (PMID:37864646) and may have limited activity, but this is not shown in VHL. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping.

The index trial NCT02992977 was a Phase 1 safety and dose-finding study of the AutoSynVax vaccine with QS-21 adjuvant. It enrolled 3 subjects, and its primary outcomes were adverse events and a recommended dose, not efficacy. It was terminated 'to enable development of an enhanced version of the vaccine' and posted no results. This was not an efficacy test or an efficacy failure of QS-21, so it is coded F9, with a business or reformulation decision (F8) as secondary. QS-21 has no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human pillar data on exposure, engagement or pathway in colorectal cancer. Prior trials, such as the colorectal and pancreatic vaccine trial NCT00006387, posted no immunogenicity results.

The index trial NCT02992977 was a Phase 1 safety and tolerability study of the AutoSynVax vaccine, with QS-21 as its adjuvant. Its primary outcomes were adverse events and a recommended dose. It enrolled 3 patients, posted no results, and was terminated 'to enable development of an enhanced version of the vaccine.' That is a strategic or formulation decision, not a failed efficacy readout, and the trial was never an efficacy test of QS-21. No primary target is recorded. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. The only posted Phase 1 results (NCT00003224) report safety alone. F8 is a secondary code because the stop reflects a development choice rather than a negative result.

QS-21 is a vaccine adjuvant with no recorded molecular target. The index trial NCT03673020 enrolled 3 patients in a Phase 1a study whose primary outcome was safety (treatment-emergent AEs), and it posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of QS-21. Elsewhere in ovarian cancer, QS-21 (OPT-821) served as the control arm in PMID:31653510. There, adding the antigen vaccine produced modest immunogenicity but no PFS or OS benefit. In PMID:35779095, vaccine plus OPT-821 elicited antibody responses to 3 or more antigens in 68% of patients, an adjuvant pathway effect, yet response did not track with survival. No direct exposure or engagement data exist. The stop is best read as not an efficacy failure of QS-21; otherwise it is indeterminate.

Topical TV-45070 (4%, 8% ointment) did not separate from placebo on knee pain in NCT02068599. The only human engagement evidence is oral XEN402 400 mg BID reducing induced pain in 4 inherited erythromelalgia patients (PMID:22035805). That is a different route, dose and compartment, so it does not show the ointment reached or blocked Nav1.7 at knee nociceptors. The topical PK study (NCT02215941) posted no results, and topical use also failed in PHN (NCT02365636). The bundle lists bupivacaine, a sodium-channel blocker on the same target, as FDA-approved for osteoarthritis, which fits F1b (the molecule or formulation, not the target). Bupivacaine is non-selective, so whether the target matters stays indeterminate (U).

The topical XPF-002 ointment showed no separation from placebo on the primary pain endpoint in PHN (-0.94 vs -0.97, NCT01195636). A repeat topical PHN trial also failed (NCT02365636). The bundle has no human skin or nerve exposure or Nav1.7 engagement data for the topical formulation. The only engagement evidence is oral 400 mg BID dosing in 4 patients with inherited erythromelalgia (PMID:22035805). That is a different route, dose and disease, and it was published after the index trial started. Lidocaine, listed on the same target, is FDA-approved for PHN, which supports F1b. Sources point to a responder subgroup (R1150W carriers, PMID:28266963), supporting F3. PMID:37366590 suggests Nav1.7 is not a key driver of PHN pain, but without engagement data this cannot establish F2.

The index trial NCT02215941 is a Phase 1 pharmacokinetic and safety study of TV-45070 ointment in healthy volunteers. Its only primary outcome is plasma concentration, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). No results were posted, so human exposure at topical doses is not shown. The oral XEN402 pilot in inherited erythromelalgia (PMID:22035805) claimed target engagement from reduced induced pain. That was a different route and dose, a 4-patient pilot with no formal endpoint, so it does not support inference for the topical ointment. The topical Phase 2 trials in knee osteoarthritis and postherpetic neuralgia missed their endpoints (NCT02068599, NCT02365636), and so did an earlier PHN trial (NCT01195636). None measured engagement, so those failures are indeterminate (U).

Calmangafodipir is meant to work as a MnSOD mimetic, but no target is recorded and I found no human data on it reaching nerve tissue, its SOD-mimetic activity or oxidative-stress biomarkers. In POLAR-M (NCT03654729) it missed the endpoint at both doses (RR 1.38 and 1.10). POLAR-A (NCT04034355) did worse: neuropathy was significantly more common on drug (RR 1.52, p=0.028). Both trials ended early after a US FDA clinical hold over unexpected serious hypersensitivity reactions (3.6% on drug vs 0.8% on placebo), so drug-specific toxicity also helped end the program (F6, secondary). One paper proposes that manganese from the drug and platinum from oxaliplatin interact (redox) to make neuropathy worse, but this is only a hypothesis. Without engagement data, the evidence can't tell a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the primary code is U.

The biliary trial NCT04784520 was stopped because its PFS primary endpoint fell short. No results or explanation were posted. Phase 1 (NCT03994484, PMC11868595) showed plasma exposure rising with dose from 100 to 800 mg, so exposure counts as adequate. No human data show RET occupancy, kinase inhibition or a downstream biomarker change, so engagement and pathway are no_human_data. In RET-fusion NSCLC (NCT05117658), the response rate was 26.8%. That was a single-arm result in another disease and not clearly a met pivotal endpoint, so it cannot support inferred engagement. The biliary population probably was not selected for RET alterations, but no source blames patient selection. Nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

The index phase 2 ORR trial (NCT05117658) has no posted results or stated stop reason. The only human data are single-dose plasma PK at 200 mg in healthy volunteers (PMID:39876990). These show systemic exposure, but nothing ties that exposure to sufficient RET inhibition or to the index dose. The bundle has no RET occupancy, phospho-RET or pathway biomarker data, and no phase 1 results (NCT03994484). Two other RET inhibitors, selpercatinib and pralsetinib, are FDA-approved in NSCLC, so the target is validated in this disease. With no pillar evidence that HA121-28 engaged RET adequately, this points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). A sister program in biliary cancer also stopped for futility (NCT04784520). The evidence is thin, and U also applies.

Frexalimab missed its primary endpoint in Sjögren's (NCT04572841). Week-12 ESSDAI change was -5.29 on drug vs -5.60 on placebo. The healthy-volunteer Phase 1 (NCT05845996) posted no PK/PD results, and the sources I found contain no human data on CD40L occupancy, exposure or biomarkers in Sjögren's patients. In relapsing MS, frexalimab cut new Gd+ lesions by 89% and lowered CXCL13 and NfL (NCT04879628, NEJM). That shows the drug is active in humans, but MS is a different disease and tissue compartment, and I could not confirm the Sjögren's dose was comparable, so engagement is not inferred here. The very large placebo response (F7) and dazodalibep, another anti-CD40L drug in Phase 3 for Sjögren's (F1b), are possible explanations. Neither source attributes the failure to them, so the result is indeterminate.

AG-86893 is a topical multikinase (VEGFR/PDGFR/FGFR) inhibitor eye drop. In NCT03533244, the 0.1% and 0.3% doses reduced conjunctival hyperemia more than vehicle at Day 28 (-0.33 and -0.35 vs -0.06), but neither difference was significant (p=0.290 and p=0.218). The arms were small (18–22 per arm). No serious AEs were reported, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No human data were found on ocular tissue drug levels, kinase inhibition or a downstream biomarker. No Phase 1 results or sponsor explanation were found, and the sponsor's pipeline listing shows only the inactive Phase 2. No drug on the same target has succeeded in pterygium: nintedanib reached Phase 3 but has no reported success. With no engagement data, an undertested drug cannot be told apart from an irrelevant target. The small trial with a numerically favourable trend suggests it may have been underpowered (F7, secondary).

The index trial, NCT02706730, was a safety extension study. It was stopped after the Phase 3 trial 104-201506 (AVERTS-1) failed. I found no human data on dexamethasone levels in inner-ear fluid, glucocorticoid receptor engagement in the inner ear, or a downstream biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The sources blame the trial. AVERTS-1 had an unexpectedly high placebo response: vertigo fell 58% with OTO-104 versus 55% with placebo. The investigators linked this to patients who had already had intratympanic steroid injections. The sister Phase 3, AVERTS-2 (104-201508), met its primary endpoint at the same 12 mg dose, which argues against a mechanism that simply does not work. A later third study also failed. Because engagement data are absent, U is a secondary code.

The index trial, NCT04964258, was a Phase 1 safety study in 80 healthy volunteers. Its only primary outcome was the number of participants with treatment-emergent adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of TAK-105. Across 7 single doses and 2 multiple doses, adverse events were similar to placebo, with no deaths and isolated serious events. No sign of dose-limiting toxicity appears. The bundle records no target, disease, pharmacokinetic, target engagement or biomarker data. One web search turned up no information on TAK-105's mechanism or why it was stopped. All three pillars therefore have no human data. Because the index trial was not a failed efficacy readout, the code is F9. If a reason is needed, U also applies.

The index FIH Phase 1/2 trial (NCT04622774) reported 0% ORR at 6.0 mg/kg in the NSCLC (n=13) and TNBC (n=6) expansion cohorts. The bundle has no human PK, ADAM9 binding or pathway biomarker data, so all pillars are no_human_data. However, PMID:41166694 states that IMGC936's maytansinoid-payload ocular toxicity (blurred vision, keratopathy) was dose-limiting in the first-in-human study and 'likely constrained its clinical activity.' The sponsor kept ADAM9 as a target with a new topoisomerase-1 payload ADC (MGC028). This points to a tolerability-capped dose rather than an invalid target, so F1a. Molecule-specific (payload) toxicity is secondary (F6). Engagement was never measured, so U also applies.

The index Ph1/2 trial NCT04622774 produced 0% ORR in its NSCLC (n=13) and TNBC (n=6) expansion cohorts at 6.0 mg/kg. The bundle has no human PK, ADAM9 occupancy or pathway data. PMID:41166694 states that IMGC936 hit dose-limiting ocular adverse events (blurred vision, keratopathy) in the first-in-human study. It says this toxicity 'likely constrained its clinical activity', which implies the dose was capped below what was needed. The ADAM9 target was then carried forward with a different payload (MGC028, topoisomerase-1 inhibitor), so the sponsor treated the problem as the molecule and payload, not the target. That supports F1a, with F6 as secondary for payload-specific toxicity. Confidence is medium because the dose-limitation conclusion is inferred and no engagement was measured.

Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers, published before the index trial, found dose-proportional plasma PK and inhibition of ex vivo LPS-induced TNF, IL-1β and PGE2 production. These p38 readouts tracked plasma levels, with TNF IC50 values in the low ng/mL range. This counts as adequate systemic exposure and engagement, but it was not shown in LMNA-DCM patients or in heart tissue. No human cardiac pathway marker was measured. NT-proBNP fell in the uncontrolled Phase 2 trial (PMID:36515663) but showed no significant difference from placebo in REALM-DCM (PMID:38979608). At the full 400 mg BID dose, with no safety issues, the 6MWT difference was 4.9 m (p=0.82), and the trial stopped for futility. The likeliest reading is that p38α inhibition does not drive symptoms in LMNA-DCM as tested (F2). Confidence is only medium because cardiac engagement was never shown.

Array's 2014 protocol says the drug reached plasma exposure in AS patients comparable to healthy volunteers. Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (Koch 2007 abstract, before the index trial) showed dose-dependent ex vivo inhibition of LPS-induced TNF, IL-1β and PGE2. That is human p38 engagement plus a downstream pathway effect, though it was not measured in AS patients. No tolerability cap is reported, and the same drug met endpoints in OA pain (NCT01366014) and dental pain. NCT00811499 stopped at 25 of 130 planned patients with no reason and no results, so the failure is poorly documented. F2 (target not driving AS) is the most direct reading. F7 (trial terminated early and could not answer) is also possible, and confidence is low.

Healthy-volunteer Phase 1 studies (around 2008, before the index trial; NCT00790049) measured both drug levels in plasma and the drug's effect on p38. Doses of 25–200 mg twice daily or 400 mg once daily blocked p38-driven cytokine release in whole blood stimulated outside the body. TNF fell 55–100%, IL-1β 65–90% and PGE2 70–95%, with a clear dose-response. Taking those doses as comparable to the index-trial dose, exposure, engagement and pathway effect look adequate systemically. Engagement was never measured in heart tissue or in patients with LMNA-related cardiomyopathy. The Phase 3 trial NCT03439514 was stopped for futility, not safety. It found no difference in walk distance (p=0.818), and NT-proBNP did not change significantly (p=0.17). The open-label Phase 2 signal (NCT02057341) did not replicate. This points to p38α inhibition not driving the disease (F2). Because no heart-tissue engagement data exist, the target versus molecule question is not fully settled.

DHP1401 is a jujube seed extract with no defined molecular target, and the bundle has no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects. The only pharmacokinetic work measured spinosin in beagle dogs (PMID:31654856). The DRAMA Phase IIb trial gave 500 or 1000 mg/day with background donepezil and missed its primary ADAS-cog endpoint (NCT03055741, PMID:35275529). Only the mild-AD subgroup on high dose and secondary endpoints (MMSE, K-TMT-e) showed benefit, so F3 is listed as a secondary code. No dose limit from tolerability was reported. With engagement unknown, it is not possible to tell whether the drug never engaged a target or whether the mechanism does not matter, so the code is U. No web searches were run, so this rests on the bundle alone.

disease: mature T-cell and NK-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma
rationale: The index trial NCT00838565 is a Phase 1 safety and PK study of PF-04236921 in rheumatoid arthritis. It involves neither paclitaxel nor lymphoma and is not an efficacy test of this drug, so the code is F9. Paclitaxel's pillars are inferred_adequate: it is approved in breast, ovarian, NSCLC and pancreatic cancer on the same tubulin mechanism. Plasma exposure was also characterized directly (PMID:39080018). No engagement data exist in T/NK lymphoma. The closest relevant trial, NCT01555853 (Abraxane in relapsed lymphoma), stopped because the drug did not show activity. That supports F2 as a secondary code: the mechanism was engaged, yet there was no benefit in this lymphoma setting.

The index trial NCT03165955 was a Phase 1 PK study of oral paclitaxel (Oraxol) in breast cancer, not an efficacy test. It reported plasma exposure (AUC ~3400 ng*h/mL, Cmax ~360 ng/mL) and had no failed efficacy endpoint, so F9 applies. Exposure is adequate from plasma PK, and PMID:34085761 shows tumor uptake of an oral formulation in patients. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because paclitaxel is FDA-approved through tubulin in several systemic cancers. No human engagement data exist in Hodgkin lymphoma specifically. Separately, NCT01555853 (nab-paclitaxel in Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma) stopped because the drug showed no activity, which is a secondary F2 signal for this disease.

In the index trial, NCT03551496 (SAVAL), a paclitaxel-eluting nitinol stent placed below the knee did no better than balloon angioplasty (PTA) on 12-month patency (68% vs 76%). It also missed its safety non-inferiority endpoint. I found no human data on paclitaxel levels in the arterial wall, on tubulin engagement, or on any antiproliferative biomarker for this device. The bundle lists no other drug on the same target in this disease, so F1b cannot be supported. The editorial only refers vaguely to drug-eluting stent successes in other vessels, which is too thin to infer engagement. It names several possible causes without settling on one: the drug, the stent, the protocol, the hard below-the-knee setting, or unusually good PTA results. Calcification was also imbalanced between arms (57% vs 41%). With engagement unknown, the cause cannot be determined.

The index trial NCT00838565 is a Phase 1 safety and PK study of PF-04236921 in rheumatoid arthritis. It does not test paclitaxel's efficacy, and its primary endpoints are AEs, anti-drug antibodies and PK, so it is not an efficacy failure of this drug (F9). The tubulin pillars are inferred adequate because paclitaxel is approved in several systemic cancers at comparable doses. It also showed a 25% response rate in relapsed NHL, which included 7 mantle cell patients (PMID:9029021). No engagement data in mantle cell lymphoma itself is shown. Separately, NCT01555853 (Abraxane in recurrent lymphoma) was halted after Phase 1 because the drug showed no activity, which could suggest F2 for the lymphoma program.

The index trial NCT00838565 is a Phase 1 safety and PK study of PF-04236921 in rheumatoid arthritis. It did not test paclitaxel and did not enroll follicular lymphoma patients. It was completed with only AE, anti-drug antibody and PK endpoints, so it was not an efficacy test of this drug (F9). For paclitaxel itself, human plasma exposure is documented (PMID:39080018). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because paclitaxel holds FDA approvals in several cancers through the same tubulin target in tumor cells. No engagement was measured in follicular lymphoma. Separately, a lymphoma trial was halted for lack of activity (NCT01555853), but that is not the index trial.

In MELODY-1 (NCT05201170, n=575), PL9643 missed its co-primary endpoints on the unadjusted analysis. Palatin reports that pain, the symptom co-primary, reached significance only after adjusting for age and gender, and that the sign co-primary (conjunctival lissamine green staining) and the secondary sign endpoints failed. The drug was well tolerated, so toxicity did not end the program. I found no human data on ocular drug levels, MC1R/MC5R binding or a downstream anti-inflammatory biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. After the readout, the company said it would look for a collaboration partner, which suggests money and partnering also shaped the halt (possible F8). The mixed results after statistical adjustment suggest possible design problems (F7).

In R/R AML patients in the index trial, tamnorzatinib reached near-maximal Axl/Mer inhibition at 6 mg, alone and with venetoclax (PMID:41385448). Measurable target inhibition implies the drug reached its site of action. No DLTs occurred up to 10 mg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. This engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, so it was not available before the trial started. Despite adequate engagement, Part D gave 0/22 CR/CRh and the trial stopped on protocol-defined futility (NCT03176277). Only a few responses were seen in the venetoclax-resistant subgroup. Gilteritinib's approval in AML rests mainly on FLT3 and does not point to a molecule problem here. The best reading is that Axl/Mer inhibition does not drive R/R AML as tested (F2).

In the index trial NCT03176277 (R/R acute leukemias/MDS), tamnorzatinib was well tolerated at 3–10 mg with no DLTs, so dose was not limited. Near-maximal Axl/Mer inhibition was shown at 6 mg alone and with venetoclax (PMID:41385448), so exposure and engagement were adequate. That evidence comes from R/R AML patients, not specifically MDS, and was published after the index start. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Despite adequate target inhibition, Part D gave 0/22 CR/CRh and the trial stopped for protocol-defined futility. This points to Axl/Mer inhibition not driving clinical benefit in this setting. Gilteritinib's AML approval does not support F1b, because this drug's engagement was adequate.

In GOLDEN (NCT03815825; PMID:42718940), subcutaneous sefaxersen lowered plasma factor B by 63–69% at steady state in GA patients. This is substantial target knockdown, consistent with the Phase 1 data (PMID:39893955, PMID:42713733). Yet GA growth did not slow significantly (−11.5% and −3.8%), and the higher dose did worse, so there was no dose–response. Alternative-pathway activity fell only 22–34%, so pathway inhibition was partial. The bundle has no ocular or retinal complement measurements, so exposure at the site of action is unshown. Safety matched placebo, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Systemic factor B lowering does not appear to drive GA progression as tested (F2). Incomplete pathway or ocular inhibition remains a possible alternative explanation (F1a). Engagement in GA was shown only in the index trial itself.

The index trial NCT04900428 of intranasal STI-2099 was stopped at interim analysis because 'drops not working on new variants'. The only binding and neutralization evidence (PMID:36109550) is in vitro and in hamsters, against WA-1, Alpha and Beta strains, and does not count as human evidence. No human exposure or pathway data appear in the bundle. The sponsor's stated reason points to loss of neutralizing activity against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants, which means the antibody failed to engage its viral target. The mechanism of antibody neutralization was therefore not properly tested, which supports F1a. Confidence is low because engagement was not measured directly in humans. U is listed as a secondary code.

The index early Phase 1 trial NCT03893019 (CD20 CAR-T in melanoma, n=9) was terminated because 'the risk-benefit assessment was not as expected'. It posted no results, and the bundle contains no PubMed abstracts. No human data show CAR-T expansion or persistence, depletion of CD20+ cells in melanoma patients, or any downstream effect. The lymphoma trial NCT03664635 completed but its outcomes are not shown in the bundle. Rituximab's approval in cutaneous B-cell lymphoma is a different disease, not a melanoma subtype, so F1b does not apply. The vague stop reason does not separate toxicity from lack of efficacy. With engagement having no human data, nothing distinguishes a molecule that failed to engage from an irrelevant target.

In index trial NCT02014363, ETS6103 (a tramadol formulation) at both doses produced only about a 6-point MADRS drop versus 11.4 for amitriptyline, so the primary endpoint was not met. Tramadol repeatedly met pivotal analgesic endpoints through central mu-opioid (OPRM1) agonism (NCT00643383, NCT00736853, NCT01112267), and it is approved for chronic pain. On that basis exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. Opioid miosis in patients (PMID:37765034) and plasma PK (PMID:32538291) support this, though ETS6103 dose comparability is not shown. No MDD engagement data exist. The likely reading is that the mechanism does not deliver antidepressant benefit as tested (F2). However, the trial used only an active comparator with no placebo arm, which limits interpretation (F7).

Dalteparin acts systemically by potentiating antithrombin. Human studies show plasma anti-Xa and anti-IIa activity, prolonged aPTT/TT and TFPI release at therapeutic doses (PMID:8585003, PMID:17063975, PMID:27536434, PMID:28375032, PMID:16616629). It is also approved for VTE. So exposure, engagement and pathway were adequate, and this evidence predates the 2008 index trial. No engagement data come from diabetic foot ulcer patients, and nothing suggests tolerability limited the dose. In NCT00662831, ≥50% ulcer area reduction was identical: 66% dalteparin vs 66% placebo. With the anticoagulant mechanism engaged and no benefit, the target/mechanism does not appear to drive ulcer healing as tested (F2). Bemiparin has not succeeded in this indication, so F1b does not apply.

None of the sources report human lung or airway antibody levels, or any measure of in vivo neutralisation, for inhaled IBIO123, so exposure and engagement have no human data. In the sister trial in severe COVID-19 (NCT05303376, SSRN preprint), IBIO123 met its primary endpoint, cutting viral load more than placebo by day 5. That is a downstream pathway effect in the same disease. The index trial (NCT05298813, PMID:37619584) missed its viral-load endpoint, with only a numerical drop of −0.29 log10 copies/mL. The investigators give two reasons. First, phase 2 stopped before reaching planned enrolment because COVID-19 cases declined, so the trial was underpowered. Second, 89% of participants already had SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, which may have blunted any effect. The primary code is trial execution (F7), with patient population (F3) as secondary.

In NCT04129944, no single intra-articular dose of UBX0101 (0.5–4 mg) did better than placebo on WOMAC-A pain at week 12, and the program was dropped in August 2020. I found no human measure of MDM2 engagement: no data on p53 or p21 induction, senescent-cell clearance, or drug levels in the joint. The Phase 1 study (NCT03513016, ACR abstract) only reported unquantified 'modulation' of synovial-fluid SASP markers. That is too thin to count as pathway evidence. An outside commentary suggested that a short joint residence time and a single dose may not have killed enough senescent cells, which would point to F1a. Others blamed a strong saline-injection placebo response, which would point to F7. Neither explanation is supported by measured data. Because engagement has no human data, the failure is indeterminate (U).

ETX-810 is a prodrug of PEA. In healthy-volunteer SAD/MAD studies (up to 1000 mg BID, the dose used in Phase 2), the 10-K reports about 3x higher plasma PEA exposure than supplement PEA, so systemic exposure is shown. No human source reports PPARα engagement or a downstream biomarker, in healthy volunteers or in patients. Both Phase 2a trials missed their endpoints, LSRP (NCT04778592, p=0.45) and DPNP (NCT04688671). The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Eliem stopped the program after the LSRP readout but gave no mechanistic explanation. With engagement unmeasured, the data can't tell a drug that never engaged PPARα apart from a target that doesn't drive radicular pain, so the code is U.

ETX-018810 (ETX-810) is a prodrug of palmitoylethanolamide (PEA). Eliem's 10-K says single- and multiple-dose studies in 80 healthy volunteers showed better plasma PK and greater PEA exposure. That supports exposure, though the filing gives no tissue levels. No human source measured PPAR-alpha activation or a downstream biomarker. In NCT04688671, pain on the PI-NRS fell slightly less on drug (-1.79) than on placebo (-1.91), and a parallel trial in sciatica (NCT04778592) also failed. The sponsor said the trial was well run, patients were appropriately selected and the placebo response was as expected, and it saw no path forward in this disease. Without engagement data, the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not drive the disease, so the code is U. F2 is a possible secondary code.

The index trial NCT04119947 was a single-ascending-dose study in healthy subjects with a safety/tolerability primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of SY-009. The program then advanced to a T2DM MAD study (NCT04345107) and a Phase 2 trial (NCT05426018). Plasma levels were below quantitation (PMID:37981049), which fits a gut-acting SGLT1 inhibitor, but luminal exposure and direct target binding were not measured. The expected intestinal SGLT1 pathway effects were shown in T2DM patients: lower postprandial glucose, insulin and GIP, and higher GLP-1 (PMID:37981049), plus bile acid changes (PMID:39936104). GI adverse events were reported, but no dose was capped. No failed efficacy readout is shown.

The bundle does not record a target for CN1. Neither the index trial (NCT04880564, 7 patients, CN1 at 0.5–3 mg/kg every 3 weeks plus CN401) nor the Phase 1 trial (NCT04418141) posted results, and my searches found no human pharmacokinetic, occupancy or biomarker data. All three pillars therefore have no human data. The sponsor gave two reasons for stopping: it saw no benefit from treatment, and the company's landscape had changed. That second reason points partly to a business decision (F8), but the main stated reason is lack of efficacy. With no engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Confidence is low because the evidence is very thin.

The index trial NCT02891070 was a non-inferiority comparison of the aprotinin-containing fibrin sealant (Tisseel) against an active comparator sealant (DuraSeal). It compared no-CSF-leak rates (76/89 vs 87/95), giving a difference of -9.29 [-21.11, 2.54]. Non-inferiority appears not demonstrated, although the margin is not stated. This is a missed non-inferiority margin against an active product, not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human measurement of local plasmin inhibition by aprotinin. The sealant met endpoints in vascular and hepatic hemostasis (NCT00892957, NCT01244425), but that benefit cannot be attributed to aprotinin's target over fibrinogen/thrombin. The pillars are therefore no_human_data. An earlier dural Phase 2 (NCT00681824) also showed no difference from standard of care.

SJP002 is a Samjin eye drop for dry eye. It has no recorded target, and a third-party database suggests, without confirming, that it may be rebamipide mofetil. Its Phase 1 trial (NCT02924155) studied systemic exposure and tolerability in healthy volunteers but posted no results. The Phase 2 index trial (NCT03723811), with fluorescein corneal staining as its endpoint, also posted no results. My searches found no publications, PK/PD data, biomarker results or sponsor explanation of why the program failed. No other drug on the same target appears in the bundle. With engagement data absent, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in dry eye, so the code is indeterminate (U).

Phase 1 studies (NCT01510782, NCT01751776; PMID:29127458, 30113724, 33047859) showed dose-related plasma exposure, >90% CD40 receptor occupancy and >90% inhibition of CD40L-induced CD54 upregulation at 120–240 mg, the doses used in the index trial. These measurements were in healthy volunteers only, not lupus nephritis patients. Tolerability did not cap dosing. Despite this, CRR at week 52 showed no dose-response and every arm was numerically below placebo (NCT02770170). The maintenance trial also failed (NCT03385564, PMID:40104960). The mechanism was engaged but gave no renal benefit, which fits F2. Secondary codes: authors cite an unexpectedly high placebo response (PMID:37192040, F7). Post hoc analyses suggest benefit in patients with glomerular monocytes (PMID:39648337, F3).

Exposure was dose-dependent and adequate (NCT01751776 PK). At 120 mg SC, CD40 receptor occupancy and CD54 inhibition exceeded 90% in healthy volunteers. The single-dose data come from NCT01510782, registered before the index trial (PMID:29127458), and multiple-dose data from Part 1 (PMID:30113724). In RA patients, Part 2 moved the CD40-pathway markers expected from the mechanism: IL-6, MMP-3, RANKL, rheumatoid factor and activated B cells all fell (PMID:30902820). RA-specific occupancy was not reported, so engagement_in_disease is false. Despite this, ACR20 at week 12 was 68.2% vs 45.5% (p=0.064), missing the primary endpoint. This points to target insufficiency (F2), supported by the later lupus nephritis failures (NCT02770170). The small trial, high placebo response and an ambitious effect assumption suggest an F7 contribution.

The index trial (NCT00909857, PMID:24713413) tested superiority of EV/DNG over an active comparator, EE/LNG, which acts on the same estrogen receptor plus progestin mechanism. Both arms considerably reduced dysmenorrheic pain days (-4.6 vs -4.2; P=0.34), so it missed a head-to-head superiority claim and did not show the drug lacked efficacy. Exposure and pathway are shown in humans: plasma E2 rose and FSH/LH and bone markers fell with 2 mg EV (PMID:24845171, PMID:28169916). Engagement is inferred_adequate because EV/DNG met contraceptive (NCT01638910) and pelvic pain/headache (NCT00778609, NCT00754065) endpoints. The active-comparator design could not isolate absolute efficacy (secondary F7).

The index phase 2a trial NCT01818544 had only safety and tolerability primary endpoints, and it met them: 1 mg once daily was well tolerated (PMID:30917927). It was therefore not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Trough plasma levels plateaued by week 2, showing exposure. HNE activity in blood after zymosan challenge fell significantly in bronchiectasis patients, showing engagement in the disease, but this was only published after the trial. Sputum inflammatory and tissue-damage biomarkers were unchanged apart from a small rise in IL-8, so the pathway effect in the lung was not shown. Lung function and quality of life did not change over 28 days. The authors call for longer studies, pointing to duration (F4) and a short exploratory design (F7).

In NCT04391894, ECF843, a topical recombinant lubricin, did not beat vehicle on SANDE symptom scores or corneal staining at any dose. The BID arm did worse than vehicle on symptoms. I found no human data for any pillar: no tear or ocular-surface lubricin levels, no measure of restored boundary lubrication, and no downstream biomarker. The sponsor gave no reason for stopping. A 2023 paper compared ECF843 structurally and functionally with a different full-length rhPRG4, which it describes as clinically effective in dry eye. That hints the problem may be this molecule rather than the target. However, rhPRG4 is not approved and has not met a pivotal endpoint, so F1b cannot be confirmed. Nothing in the evidence separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so this is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT04559971 was a completed first-in-human, single-ascending-dose safety/PK/PD study in healthy volunteers, with an adverse-event primary endpoint. It was not an efficacy test, so this is not an efficacy failure (F9). PMID:37497888 reports dose-related plasma exposure. Hepcidin rose dose-dependently and serum iron and TSAT fell for up to 56 days, with no serious AEs. TMPRSS6 transcript knockdown was not measured directly; engagement is rated adequate only from the hepcidin rise, which follows directly from TMPRSS6 silencing. The program continued into thalassemia/MDS (NCT04718844) and polycythemia vera (NCT05499013). These data are from healthy volunteers only and were published after the index trial started.

The index bunionectomy trial NCT04855240 missed its primary endpoint for both regimens: AUC0-24 NRS pain at 400 mg Q6H gave p=0.17 and 1600 mg QD gave p=0.84 versus placebo. Serious AEs were low, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle records no primary target, no posted Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts, and no same-target comparators. There is therefore no human exposure, engagement or pathway evidence. The osteoarthritis trial NCT05008835 was terminated for business reasons and is not assessable. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism irrelevant to acute postoperative pain, so the failure is indeterminate.

ACP-044 (ebaresdax) is a redox modulator meant to speed up the breakdown of peroxynitrite. Its only support before the trial came from animal studies (Acadia 10-K). In the bunionectomy trial NCT04855240, neither dose separated from placebo: the 400 mg every-6-hours arm showed only a trend (p=0.17) and the 1600 mg once-daily arm had no effect. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement (e.g., markers of peroxynitrite or nitroxidative stress), or a downstream pathway effect. Acadia then stopped development in acute and chronic pain based on the final data. The osteoarthritis trial NCT05008835 was ended for business reasons. Nothing in the evidence shows whether the drug failed to engage its target or whether the target doesn't drive pain, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT02365610, PMID:33998885) of 800 mg CBDV twice daily missed its primary endpoint: focal seizures fell 40.5% on drug and 37.7% on placebo. GW blamed an unusually large placebo response. It said the response was much larger than in published studies of other treatments in similar patients, so the trial could not separate the arms (F7). No human data on TRPV1 engagement or downstream biomarkers turned up. Pharmacokinetic results from Part A (NCT02369471) and the Phase 1 trial (NCT01918735) were never posted. The TRPV1 activity rests on in vitro work (PMID:25029033), and even that paper suggests TRPV1 may not drive CBDV's antiepileptic effect. No other TRPV1 drug has worked in epilepsy. Because engagement is unknown, U is a secondary code. The company then shifted CBDV to autism.

The index Phase 3 trial (NCT03058783) gave IGA success of 42.04% for IDP-124 vs 32.73% for vehicle, not significant. Its twin Phase 3 trial (NCT03002571) used the same design and disease and met its primary endpoint (42.95% vs 27.96%). So the pillars are inferred_adequate from clinical efficacy at the same dose, in the same disease and skin compartment. Tacrolimus, on the same calcineurin target, is approved for atopic eczema, which supports the target. The drug's response rate was nearly identical across the two trials. The miss came from a higher vehicle response and the limited power of the 216 vs 110 comparison, which points to trial execution or power (F7) rather than mechanism. No direct biomarker data or tolerability limits appear in the bundle.

The index trial NCT01551381 was a safety, PK and PD study whose primary outcome was platelet aggregation, not clinical efficacy. It was terminated because an interim review judged the selected dose too high for diabetics, a dose-selection issue rather than an efficacy readout. In healthy volunteers (PMID:22815050), exposure was linear and complete platelet aggregation inhibition occurred at 0.125 mg/kg and above (>90% above 20 ng/ml), so engagement and pathway effects were adequate at low doses. The dose cut therefore did not cap engagement. Diabetic-patient data are in vitro only (PMID:23943337), so engagement was not shown in vivo in this disease. The program continued to a completed Phase 3 in diabetic kidney disease (NCT04881123). This is not an efficacy failure.

In the index Phase 1 study in mCRPC (NCT03926013; PMID:36948922), JNJ-081 was escalated to 60 µg/kg SC. Cytokine release syndrome at higher doses produced dose-limiting toxicities and was only partly mitigated by SC dosing and step-up priming. Anti-drug antibodies developed in 19 of 39 patients, which suggests exposure was compromised. Evidence of T-cell redirection was weak: only transient PSA declines above 30 µg/kg and no radiographic responses. So engagement and pathway effects were partial at tolerable doses, and the mechanism was not adequately tested (F1a). CRS is on-target toxicity (F5) and immunogenicity is molecule-specific (F6). The bundle gives no explicit stop reason, so confidence is low.

The index trial ENVISION (NCT05275205) had a descriptive safety primary endpoint, TEAEs versus aflibercept, with no clear excess of harm. It was not an efficacy test, so the program did not stop on a failed efficacy readout of this trial. The related DME trial ASPIRE (NCT06011798) narrowly missed non-inferiority against anti-VEGF control (3.7 vs 5.1 letters), which also falls under F9. The bundle has no human data on ocular exposure, BCL-xL engagement, or senescent-cell clearance; the phase 1 trial and PMID:38321220 report only safety. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, it would be indeterminate (U), because engagement was never measured.

The index trial NCT04461600 had no responses: 0 of 10 patients at 4 mg and 0 of 3 at 6 mg. The sponsor gave no scientific reason for stopping. In the Phase 1 solid-tumor study (NCT01292655, ASCO 2018, Ayala 10-K), plasma levels rose in line with dose (linear PK) and tracked suppression of the Notch marker HES1 in whole blood. This was reported before the index trial, at the 4 mg and 6 mg weekly doses later used in Phase 2. So the drug reached the blood and engaged its target there. However, the read-out was a blood-based downstream marker, the size of the effect was not given, and nothing was measured in TNBC tumor tissue. Activity was also minimal in ACC (NCT03691207). No other drug on this target has succeeded in breast cancer. The most likely explanation is that inhibiting Notch did not drive tumor response in this group, but confidence is limited because engagement was never shown inside tumors.

Engagement was shown in humans. In the mCRPC trial (NCT02711956; AACR 2017, Clin Cancer Res 2020), ZEN-3694 lowered BET target genes in whole blood, including MYC, in a dose- and exposure-dependent way. The effect plateaued at doses of 96 mg or more. In the TNBC index trial (NCT03901469, ASCO 2022), the combination dose chosen for Phase 2 was 48 mg ZEN-3694 plus talazoparib. Paired tumor biopsies at that dose showed robust changes in BET-dependent and HRR transcripts. That dose is below the blood plateau, and thrombocytopenia caused the DLTs. Still, the tumor data show engagement, so I did not mark the dose as limited. Despite this, clinical benefit was 32.4%, and post-TROP2-ADC Cohort A had 0% ORR. Interim futility then stopped Cohorts A and B. The mechanism was engaged but gave no meaningful benefit, so F2. F3 is secondary because Cohort A was a heavily pretreated post-ADC group.

The index CARDEA trial (NCT04345614) missed its primary endpoint narrowly (p≈0.098), but all trends favoured Auxora. Median recovery was 7 vs 10 days, deaths 18/141 vs 27/140, and SAEs 34/141 vs 49/140. This looks like an underpowered near-miss rather than a clear null. The follow-on critical COVID pneumonia trial (NCT04661540) was terminated because too few new COVID-19 patients were being hospitalised, so the program ended on feasibility grounds. No human exposure or target-engagement data exist in pneumonia. The only pharmacodynamic data is a descriptive IL-2 reduction of 55.5% in 4 acute pancreatitis patients (NCT03709342), too thin to rate a pillar. Engagement therefore remains unshown, and U also applies.

The investigators stopped CARDEA (NCT04345614) early because COVID-19 hospitalizations were falling and standard-of-care drugs that regulators had prohibited in the trial were being used more often. The result missed significance but leaned toward the drug: time to recovery was 7 vs 10 days (p=0.098), with fewer deaths and fewer serious adverse events on Auxora. The follow-up trial (NCT04661540) was also stopped because too few patients were being hospitalized. So the main problem is trial execution and power (F7). The only human engagement evidence comes from acute pancreatitis patients (NCT03709342): an ex vivo test of IL-2 release from blood cells showed only about 55–57% inhibition, which is partial. No engagement data come from COVID patients, so engagement in COVID is unproven (secondary F1a). The open-label IL-6 reduction mentioned in the protocol is not a mechanism-specific pathway readout.

Index trial NCT02927457 tested topical 1% GSK2646264 in 11 CLE patients, with each patient's two lesions randomized to drug or placebo. Plasma exposure was low, as intended. The urticaria study (PMID:34020509) says the cream penetrates human skin. Engagement is unclear: skin pSYK and total SYK did not change, but the authors say that assay is unreliable in biopsies, so it neither shows nor rules out engagement. Interferon genes such as CXCL10 and OAS1, and dermal T cells and dendritic cells, fell only modestly, and RCLASI activity scores were unchanged. The authors blame the low baseline disease activity and a sample size too small for formal statistics, caused by poor recruitment. So the trial could not answer the question (F7). Because engagement was never shown, a target that does not matter cannot be told apart from a drug that never engaged it (U).

In healthy volunteers (PMID:28012176, NCT02616445), emestedastat reached CSF at 9-fold its IC50. At ≥10 mg, the urinary THF/THE ratio fell, indicating maximal hepatic 11β-HSD1 inhibition, and ACTH rose, the expected pathway response. XanaCIDD tested 10 mg (PMID:42464916). Engagement was shown only peripherally and in healthy subjects, not in the brain or in MDD patients. The primary cognitive endpoint showed no benefit (p=0.17, favouring placebo). The drug also failed earlier in Alzheimer's disease (NCT02727699). This supports the reading that brain cortisol reduction by this mechanism does not improve cognition as tested. The cognitive composite improved markedly in both arms, suggesting practice or placebo effects that limited sensitivity (F7). A late MADRS trend is not a primary win.

Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (PMID:29134633, published 2018; trial predates the 2016 index start) showed inhaled AZD1419 engaged TLR9 in the lung, inducing interferon responses at all doses, with no tolerization. In the asthma Phase 2a (PMID:32809843), AZD1419 induced a Th1/IFN response with sustained reduction of type 2 inflammation markers, so engagement and pathway were shown in patients. Doses of 1-8 mg were below the 15.4 mg MTD and were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Despite this, time to loss of asthma control was not improved (HR 1.05, p=0.57; NCT02898662), and no secondary clinical endpoint improved. The mechanism was engaged but did not drive the clinical outcome as tested.

In the index phase I (NCT02004106), exposure was roughly dose-proportional at 6-40 mg, with target-mediated disposition. An MTD of 30 mg q2w was set (PMID:42127887). IL-2Rβγ engagement and pathway effects were clear in patients. CD8+ T cells and NK cells expanded in blood but Tregs did not, sCD25 and cytokines rose, and tumor biopsies showed more proliferating and perforin+ CD8+ cells (PMID:41545306). Despite this, there were no objective responses, and activity stayed limited with atezolizumab (PMID:41252574). With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, this fits F2. As a minor caveat, PK modeling suggests the expanding IL2R+ cells consume the drug and may limit tumor uptake (PMID:29463551). High anti-drug antibody incidence (PMID:38319672) could also have reduced exposure, so F1a is secondary. Engagement data were published after the index trial started.

The index trial, NCT02208284, was a single-dose safety study in 16 healthy volunteers. Its endpoints were adverse events, lab tests, vital signs and ECG, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). Amin et al. 2019 (Sci Transl Med) report that in healthy adults, 1500 mg/day for 14 days lowered liver fat on MRI-PDFF and improved liver function markers. That supports exposure and a downstream pathway effect. No direct measure of DGAT2 inhibition in humans was found, and nothing was tested in patients with the program's disease. Pfizer replaced PF-06427878 with ervogastat (PF-06865571), which was designed to fix 'metabolic liabilities' of the earlier compound. This points to molecule-specific problems rather than a failed efficacy readout (secondary F6).

In two phase 1 trials (NCT03166631, NCT04138823), BI 891065 was tolerable and neither study reached an MTD, with few DLTs, so dose was not capped. PMID:41408891 reports reduced cIAP1 levels in PBMCs and tumor biopsies from patients with advanced solid tumors. This shows tumor-tissue exposure and target engagement in the program's population. That evidence was published in 2025, after the index trial started. The bundle shows no downstream pathway biomarker such as NF-κB activation, cytokines or caspase activity, so pathway is no_human_data. Despite engagement, there were no objective responses alone or with ezabenlimab. The trials ended early because efficacy was insufficiently promising, not for safety. Engagement without clinical benefit points to the mechanism not driving these tumors as tested. The degree of cIAP1 reduction is not quantified, so confidence is medium.

Cyclo(His-Pro) plus zinc (CycloZ) has no recorded molecular target. The proposed mechanism, raising NAD+ and changing Sirt1 deacetylase activity, comes only from mouse studies (PMID:37098411). I found no human data on drug levels, target engagement or pathway biomarkers, and no Phase 1 results were posted. In the index trial NCT02784275, HbA1c fell slightly more on drug than on placebo, but the differences were small and no p-values were posted. The arms were small (about 13 patients each), so the trial may have been underpowered. That is why F7 is listed as a secondary code. An earlier trial, NCT00878605, was stopped because it could not enroll enough patients. Without engagement evidence, nothing here separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03710707 was a Phase 1b study whose primary outcomes were all safety measures (AEs, labs, vitals, ECG, neuro exam). It was not an efficacy test of DNL201. PMID:35675433 reports robust CSF penetration in healthy volunteers and PD patients. It also reports LRRK2 inhibition (pS935/pT73 Rab10) and altered downstream lysosomal biomarkers, with the drug well tolerated at engaging doses. The authors concluded these data warrant further development of LRRK2 inhibitors. This engagement evidence was published in 2022, after the index trial started in 2018. The bundle gives no efficacy failure and no stated stop reason. Discontinuation at Phase 1 is not explained by a failed readout, so F9 applies.

RP103 was tested in mitochondrial disease because it was thought to raise glutathione and fix redox imbalance (protocol). Plasma exposure is well documented in cystinosis (NCT00872729, NCT01000961, PMID:22195601). That suggests systemic exposure. However, cystine depletion works through a different mechanism, so it does not show the redox/glutathione mechanism was engaged. I found no human data from mitochondrial patients on glutathione, thiol redox state or tissue drug levels. The base study NCT02023866 missed on NPMDS (p values 0.08 to 1.0), and the sponsor ended the program for lack of efficacy. Reviews suggest the dose may need careful titration, but nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter. So the code is U.

The trial was registered as stopped for 'business reasons', but PMID:39984821 states a planned Week-24 interim analysis judged liver-fat reductions (19–26% relative vs placebo) insufficient to continue. Histologic MASH resolution was not significant at any dose (NCT04583423). The drug was well tolerated up to 300 mg, so the dose was not capped. The Phase 1 trials (NCT02708576, NCT03298464) posted no results, so there are no human exposure or engagement data. The modest MRI-PDFF effect suggests weak pathway activation. The FGF21 pathway is described as having demonstrated efficacy in MASH, and other FGFR1c/KLB agonists (efruxifermin, pegozafermin, efimosfermin) reached Phase 3, implicating this molecule rather than the target. The bundle does not show those drugs meeting pivotal endpoints, hence low confidence and U as secondary.

The index trial NCT04226274 was a 12-week Phase 1 safety study in McArdle disease. Its only primary outcome was adverse events, and it posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of mavodelpar (F9). The program most plausibly ended after the Phase 2b in primary mitochondrial myopathy failed (NCT04535609; drug arm improved less than placebo on 12MWT), which also led to termination of the extension study (NCT05267574). The bundle reports no PK or target-engagement data. The only human pathway evidence comes from PMM biopsies (PMID:42151205, published 2026, after the index trial started): modest fatty-acid pathway upregulation and no consistent mitochondrial change. There are no McArdle data, so the mechanism there is indeterminate (U).

The index Phase 2b trial NCT04535609 missed its primary endpoint: 12MWT change was 26.75 m on mavodelpar vs 30.89 m on placebo. This led to termination of the extension study NCT05267574 for futility. The Phase 1b trial in PMM patients (NCT03862846; published as PMID:42151205, after the index trial started) collected PK but reported no values. Muscle transcriptomics (n=6) showed modest upregulation of fatty acid-metabolism pathways, consistent with PPARδ target engagement in patients' muscle. Muscle biopsies (n=10) showed no consistent change in mitochondrial function. With engagement shown, the drug produced no clinical benefit, which suggests PPARδ agonism does not drive PMM as tested (F2). The engagement evidence is modest and based on very few patients, so under-engagement (F1a) cannot be excluded.

disease: disorder of fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis
rationale: The index FAOD trial NCT03833128 was an open-label Phase 1b safety study with adverse events as its only primary outcome. It completed with no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of mavodelpar. The program's efficacy failure came in primary mitochondrial myopathy: the Phase 2b NCT04535609 missed its 12MWT endpoint, and the extension NCT05267574 was terminated for futility. In PMM, PK/PD were collected but not reported. Muscle biopsies showed no consistent mitochondrial change and only modest transcriptomic upregulation of fatty-acid pathways (n=6) (PMID:42151205). The bundle has no exposure or engagement data in FAOD patients. If the FAOD stop is read as an efficacy failure, engagement is unmeasured and the case is indeterminate (U). PMID:31891000 concerns sotatercept and is irrelevant.

In index trial NCT00604890, no dose of topical API 31510 (ubidecarenone) did better than placebo: complete response was 5–9 per 44–47 patients on active cream versus 9/45 on placebo. The drug has no defined molecular target, and I found no human data on how much drug reached basal cell carcinoma tissue, whether it engaged its proposed mechanism (shifting tumour cell metabolism), or whether any biomarker moved. Related topical BPM31510 studies were safety studies without published pharmacodynamic data (NCT00652080, epidermolysis bullosa Phase 1). The IV Phase 1 study (NCT01957735) used a different formulation and route, and its pharmacodynamic results could not be retrieved. Tolerability did not limit the dose. No sponsor explanation for the failure was found. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter here, so the code is U.

BPM31510IV is an intravenous CoQ10 nanodispersion meant to shift tumour metabolism toward oxidative phosphorylation. It has no defined molecular target. In the Phase Ia/b solid-tumour study (NCT01957735, PMC12727275), plasma CoQ10 rose with dose to more than 200 times normal, so systemic exposure was adequate. The 110 mg/kg dose used in the index trial was the Phase 1 MTD (JCO 2020 abstract). None of the sources shows engagement (tumour mitochondrial CoQ10, or tumour lactate or OxPhos changes) in humans. The pancreatic omics analysis (JCO 2024) only links exploratory biomarkers to outcome. NCT02650804 produced no responses, and neither sponsor nor investigators gave a reason for the failure. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The phase 1 study (NCT01610479, PMID:30511200) reached the plasma exposure it was aiming for, which is why exposure is rated adequate. Inhibition of dUTPase, the primary target, was never measured in humans: the investigators say they did not run a pharmacodynamic assessment. The only human biomarker data show a rise in uracil, which reflects DPD inhibition, an off-mechanism effect (PMID:24452393, PMID:34951129). In the index trial (NCT02855125), progression-free survival was not better with TAS-114 plus S-1 (HR 1.16), although tumour response rate was higher (19.7% vs 10.3%). The TAS-114 arm also had more serious adverse events and deaths, and the gastric cancer program was stopped after these results. Because dUTPase engagement was never shown, the evidence cannot tell a drug that failed to engage its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Rexlemestrocel-L is an allogeneic mesenchymal precursor cell therapy with no defined molecular target. No human data were found on cell retention, cell persistence, receptor engagement or a mechanistic biomarker. In DREAM-HF (NCT02032004), the primary endpoint, recurrent decompensated HF-MACE, showed no benefit (median 27.5 vs 29.7 months). Mesoblast instead emphasised secondary findings: fewer cardiovascular deaths, myocardial infarctions and strokes; a 12-month improvement in LVEF; and a hypothesis that the cells work through an anti-inflammatory effect, best suited to patients with inflammation. These findings point toward subgroup or endpoint explanations (F3/F4), but they are post hoc. Because engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates a mechanism that was never engaged from one that does not matter. The code is therefore U.

SCAI-001 is a low-concentration nanoparticle cyclosporine eye drop (0.01%/0.02%). The index trial (NCT05733624) compared it head-to-head with Restasis (cyclosporine 0.05%), an active comparator. The primary endpoint is classified 'not met' only because there was no between-group difference: tear volume rose in all arms. The publication concludes efficacy and safety were comparable to Restasis (PMID:42804440). Conjunctival staining improved more with the 0.01% dose at weeks 4 and 8. So this was not an efficacy failure of the drug against placebo; it is a lack of superiority over an active drug. The bundle has no pharmacokinetic or target-engagement data. No stop reason is given, so a business-driven discontinuation is possible but not shown.

Neurexan is a homeopathic combination that includes Passiflora incarnata. No molecular target is recorded, and the bundle has no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects. In the index trial (NCT01703819), an exploratory study in healthy volunteers under acute experimental stress, tension and nervousness did not differ from placebo (p=0.77 and p=0.57). The open-label companion study (NCT01703832) was also negative. A later fMRI study (NCT02602275) reported less amygdala activation, but it started after the index trial and does not show target engagement. Because engagement is no_human_data, nothing here separates a drug that never engaged a target from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The trial was small and exploratory, so F7 is a possible secondary code. I ran no web searches; this judgment rests on the bundle alone.

Neurexan is a multi-component preparation with Avena sativa flowering top as one ingredient. It has no recorded molecular target, and the bundle has no human data on exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker. The index trial in healthy volunteers under acute stress missed both primary endpoints, tension and nervousness (p=0.77 and p=0.57, NCT01703819). The open-label companion study also missed both (NCT01703832). An fMRI study reported lower amygdala activation (NCT02602275), but this is an exploratory brain-imaging result, not engagement of a defined target. No serious adverse events occurred, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No same-target comparator drug and no stated reason for failure are available. With engagement undefined and unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Neurexan is a homeopathic combination product, and coffea arabica is one of its ingredients. No molecular target is recorded for it, and no exposure, engagement or pathway data exist in humans, so none of the three pillars can be assessed. I ran no web searches; the target-free homeopathic mechanism means no such data would be expected. In the index trial NCT01703819, Neurexan did no better than placebo on tension or nervousness. The open-label companion trial NCT01703832 also missed. A later fMRI study, NCT02602275, reported mixed exploratory brain-imaging effects, but these do not show target engagement. The sponsor kept developing the product (insomnia trial NCT06278077) and gave no reason for the failure. Nothing here separates a product that never engaged anything from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02570854 posted no results, and the bundle has no other trials, publications or approvals for this drug. A review lists the CSJ137 hemodialysis study as having only 'unpublished data'. The only evidence that the anti-BMP6 antibody lowered hepcidin and raised serum iron comes from monkeys, in a Novartis patent, and animal data does not count here. No human data was found on drug levels, BMP6 neutralization, hepcidin suppression or iron and hemoglobin response, and no reason for stopping was found. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

MM-II is a suspension of large, empty liposomes injected into the knee. It works as a physical lubricant meant to reduce joint friction, so it has no molecular target. I found no human data on the three pillars: exposure, target engagement, or pathway effect. Examples would be persistence of the liposomes in the joint or a change in a friction or cartilage biomarker. The sponsor's cartilage-protective evidence comes from OA models, which don't count as human data. In the index trial (NCT04506463, PMID:40280230), the primary endpoint was missed. For the 3 mL dose, p=0.085 after adjustment for multiple comparisons. The dose response was not monotonic, and placebo responses were high. The sponsor reports benefit for 3 mL on secondary endpoints and plans further development, including Fast Track designation. Engagement can't be assessed, so the failure is coded U, with trial design (F7) as a possible secondary factor.

In the index Phase 2a crossover trial NCT05660850, 14-day cough frequency was nearly the same on GDC-6599 and placebo (12.61 vs 13.21 coughs/h). There were no serious adverse events, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. A Phase 1 SAD/MAD study in healthy volunteers measured PK and pharmacodynamics (registry onderzoekmetmensen), but I found no published human PK, target-engagement or downstream biomarker results, such as AITC- or cinnamaldehyde-evoked dermal blood flow. The only target-engagement data are from rodents (PMID:38431835). No other TRPA1 drug has succeeded in this disease, and no source says why the program failed. Without human engagement data, a drug that never engaged TRPA1 cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive cough, so the cause is indeterminate.

In the index crossover trial (NCT05660850), cough frequency at Day 14 was almost the same on GDC-6599 and on placebo (12.61 vs 13.21 coughs/hour). The protocol says the Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study (GA43010, about 81 subjects) measured TRPA1 inhibition with an AITC skin blood-flow challenge. However, the PK/PD results and the dose rationale are blacked out, and no published human results were found. Target engagement shown in PMID:38431835 comes only from rodents. The bundle has no human data on exposure, occupancy or inhibition, or on any downstream biomarker. It also has no sponsor statement on why the trial failed and no other TRPA1 drug for comparison. So it cannot separate a drug that never engaged TRPA1 from a target that does not drive cough. Code U.

The 'colorectal carcinoma' label looks like a misreading of the abbreviation CRC, which here means chronic refractory cough. The index trial (NCT05660850) missed its primary endpoint: Day-14 cough frequency was 12.61/h on GDC-6599 vs 13.21/h on placebo. The phase 2 protocol says TRPA1 inhibition was tested in the Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study (GA43010) with an AITC skin challenge, but the result was cut off in what I could retrieve. I found no human plasma exposure, target-inhibition or biomarker numbers, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. Strong target engagement is shown only in rodents (PMID:38431835), which does not count. There were no serious adverse events, so tolerability did not limit the dose. Engagement therefore has no human data, and the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

The index Phase 2a crossover trial (NCT05660850) missed its primary endpoint. At Day 14, cough frequency was 12.61/h on GDC-6599 versus 13.21/h on placebo, and there were no serious adverse events. The target-engagement evidence I found is from animals only: a guinea pig cinnamaldehyde cough model and an AITC dermal blood-flow model (PMID:38431835, MedKoo). The Phase 1 study (GA43010; PMID:38309485) was a safety and dose-escalation study. I found no human pharmacokinetics at the site of action, no human cinnamaldehyde or AITC challenge data, and no downstream biomarker results. Roche's Phase 1 lay summary could not be retrieved. No other TRPA1 drug has succeeded in chronic cough, and I found no stated reason from the sponsor. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged TRPA1 apart from a target that does not matter.

The index trial (NCT02423408), using 140 mg TNX-201, missed its primary endpoint: 21/75 patients were pain free at 2 hours on drug versus 20/72 on placebo. The Phase 1 single ascending dose study (NCT02290379, per a Tonix press release) showed plasma levels of (R)-isometheptene rising with dose, highest at 140 mg. That supports systemic exposure, though the sources never say what level would be enough. No human data on imidazoline (NISCH) receptor engagement or a downstream biomarker turned up; Tonix's mechanism data were non-clinical only. No other drug on this target is in the bundle, and the sponsor gave no reason for the failure beyond reporting the missed endpoints. Because engagement was never measured, nothing separates a drug that didn't engage from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is indeterminate (U).

In the SHINE trial (NCT01457846), AZD4547 80 mg twice daily did worse than paclitaxel on PFS in gastric cancer selected for FGFR2 amplification or polysomy by FISH (1.8 vs 3.5 months). Phase 1 trials (NCT00979134, NCT01213160) gave plasma PK at this dose, and it was tolerable. Serum phosphate, an on-target marker of FGFR1 inhibition in the kidney, rose significantly in lung cancer patients (PMID:28615371). That shows systemic engagement, but only outside gastric cancer and only after SHINE started. No tumour pathway biopsies were taken. The investigators blamed patient selection: FGFR2 amplification varied widely within tumours and matched FGFR2 mRNA expression poorly. So FISH picked many patients whose tumours were not FGFR2-driven. This points to F3, with F2 as a secondary possibility.

UP-NEXT (NCT05329545) never produced its own efficacy readout. FDA put it on partial clinical hold over serious bleeding events, five of them fatal. The sponsor then wound it down after the separate UPLIFT trial in platinum-resistant disease missed its primary endpoint: ORR was 15.6% (95% CI 10.0–22.7%) against a threshold of 12% for the lower bound of the CI. Phase 1 data (NCT03319628) give only tolerability, an MTD of 43 mg/m2, and a trend toward more responses with higher NaPi2b expression. No human data were found on drug levels in tumour, payload delivery, or a pathway biomarker. With engagement unmeasured, the data cannot show whether the target does not matter or the molecule fell short, so the code is U. The secondary codes are F6, for bleeding toxicity, and F9, because the index trial was stopped without an efficacy test.

ADC Therapeutics stopped ADCT-901, a KAAG1-targeted PBD antibody-drug conjugate, in January 2024 after the dose-escalation part of NCT04972981 in solid tumors. It gave two reasons: limited signs of efficacy and a wish to move capital to higher-priority programs. No results were posted, and I found no human data on exposure, KAAG1 binding or tumor uptake, or downstream pathway effects. I also found no dose-limiting toxicity that capped the dose, and no other KAAG1 drug to compare against. With no evidence on engagement, a molecule that failed to engage KAAG1 cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive these tumors. The code is therefore U. F8 is listed as secondary because the company also gave capital reallocation as a reason.

SHP639 (TAK-639) is a topical 9-amino-acid CNP analog meant to activate NPR-B in the trabecular meshwork. The first-in-human trial, NCT03131167, enrolled patients with ocular hypertension or early primary open-angle glaucoma. It was well tolerated up to 0.6% twice daily, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Systemic exposure was minimal. No human aqueous humor levels, NPR-B engagement or cGMP biomarker data were reported; aqueous exposure was measured only in rabbits and dogs. Pressure in the eye fell only marginally, in the 0.6% twice-daily cohort alone, and placebo values in that cohort varied widely. The authors said further studies would clarify how well the drug penetrates to the front chamber of the eye. Without human engagement data, poor penetration of the drug cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F1a is a possible alternative.

SHP639/TAK-639 is a topical CNP analogue designed to activate NPR-B in the trabecular meshwork. The published report of the first-in-human trial in OHT/POAG patients (NCT03131167; Martin 2020) found the drug well tolerated up to 0.6% BID, with little or no systemic exposure. Aqueous-humor drug levels, NPR-B activation and cGMP were not measured in humans, so both exposure and engagement have no human data. IOP is the downstream pathway readout, and it fell only marginally, in a single cohort (0.6% BID). The study ended before the 0.6% TID/QID cohorts, and no reason was given for stopping. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Nothing separates poor delivery or engagement from an ineffective mechanism, so the code is U. F1a is listed as secondary because the drug may not have reached the eye tissue at a high enough level.

The index trial NCT03665285 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation and expansion study (8–1600 mg) whose only primary outcome was the count of participants with TEAEs. It had no comparator and was classified as not an efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of NC318. Nearly all participants had TEAEs, with no clear dose-related excess of deaths or serious AEs and no MTD-driven cap shown, so dose_limited is false. The bundle contains no pharmacokinetic, Siglec-15 engagement or pathway biomarker data, no other trials, no same-target comparators and no publications. If this is read as an efficacy failure, nothing separates non-engagement from target irrelevance, which would make it U.

In the index trial (NCT00838708; PMID 21818506), SRD174 cream, a topical form of nalmefene, did not reduce atopic dermatitis itch compared with vehicle. The drug and vehicle scores were 210.7 and 212.1. The only human engagement data in the bundle are brain mu-opioid receptor occupancy after 20 mg oral doses in healthy volunteers (PMID:15956985, PMID:26483076). Those data do not apply to a cream acting on peripheral receptors in the skin. No skin drug levels, peripheral receptor occupancy or itch-pathway biomarker data were found in humans. The investigators questioned whether peripheral opioid receptors are a valid target. Even so, nothing separates poor skin delivery or engagement from an irrelevant target, so the cause is indeterminate (U). The dose was not capped by tolerability.

PET in healthy subjects showed 87–100% central μ-opioid receptor occupancy after 20 mg oral nalmefene (PMID:15956985, 2005, before the index trial), supported by PK/occupancy modelling (PMID:26483076). Pathway is inferred from sister Phase 3 trials in the same disease and dose that reduced heavy drinking days (NCT00811720, NCT00812461, NCT02364947/PMID:31298784). The index trial NCT00811941 was mainly a 52-week safety study: AE and withdrawal endpoints were primary, and the bundle classifies its endpoint class as not_efficacy. Its HDD and TAC comparisons missed (p=0.16 and p=0.23) against a large placebo improvement (−8.9 HDD) in a small placebo arm (n=110, 3:1 randomization). So this was not a decisive efficacy failure of the drug (F9). High placebo response and limited power also apply (F7).

The index trial NCT02561962 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study whose primary endpoints were only DLTs and TEAEs. No efficacy, PK, BCMA engagement or pathway data are posted, and there are no PubMed abstracts. DLTs rose at Dose G (3/4 participants), which set the tolerable dose. Nothing shows engagement required a higher dose, so dose_limited is false. BCMA is clinically validated in myeloma: belantamab mafodotin, an ADC of the same modality, and idecabtagene vicleucel are FDA-approved. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). However, this trial was not an efficacy test (F9), and toxicity may have contributed (F6). No stop reason is given, so the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT04352114 was a Phase 1 study in healthy participants. Its only primary outcome was drug-related serious adverse events, so it was a safety study, not an efficacy test of this APLNR agonist peptide. No results were posted, no stop reason is stated, and no PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators are in the bundle. A follow-on Phase 1 in HFrEF (NCT04840914) completed without posted results. There is no human evidence on exposure, target engagement or pathway effect. Nothing shows an efficacy failure, toxicity or a business decision. The best-supported code is F9 (not an efficacy test). U is a secondary code because engagement is entirely unknown.

Exposure: linear, dose-proportional plasma PK in healthy volunteers (PMID:29856004). Engagement and pathway: CXCR2 blockade reversibly lowered blood neutrophils (PMID:26182832). It cut sputum neutrophils in bronchiectasis (ratio 0.31, NCT01255592). In asthma patients it reduced sputum, blood and bronchial-tissue neutrophils (NCT01890148, PMID:28549850), but that asthma evidence came after the index trial started (2014 vs 2012). Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, no dose reduced severe exacerbations; rates were numerically higher (NCT01704495). The authors question the role of CXCR2-mediated neutrophil recruitment in exacerbations (PMID:27574788), which supports F2. Later subgroup clustering work (PMID:41177856) hints at responder subsets, hence secondary F3.

Healthy-volunteer PK showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:29856004). CXCR2 blockade was shown functionally in humans: it reversibly lowered blood neutrophils at 100 mg BID (PMID:26182832), and it lowered sputum, blood and bronchial-tissue neutrophils in asthma (NCT01890148) and sputum neutrophils in bronchiectasis (NCT01255592). All of this predates the index trial. The recommended combination dose was 80 mg BID (NCT02499328). There is no PDAC or intratumoral engagement data. Combined with durvalumab in metastatic PDAC, the ORR was only 5.6%, with 4/12 DLTs (NCT02583477). This points to a mechanism that was engaged but gave no benefit (F2). Confidence is low because the trial was a small single-arm study (F7) with notable toxicity (F6). The later prostate trial stopped because production of the drug was discontinued (NCT03177187).

The index trial NCT04661839 was a Phase 1 safety and PK study in 28 healthy adults, with primary outcomes limited to adverse events and PK. It was not an efficacy test of COVID-HIGIV, so the stop was not an efficacy failure (F9). Plasma anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibody exposure rose roughly dose-proportionally across 100, 200 and 400 mg/kg (AUC0-last about 2962, 6679 and 11723 h*AU/mL), so exposure is shown in humans. No human neutralization or viral-load data are in the bundle; the efficacy evidence is in mice only (PMID:36680164). Engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. Tolerability did not cap the dose: there were no drug-related SAEs or infusion discontinuations. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping.

Exposure: the Phase 1 vitrectomy study (NCT01229410) found brimonidine in human vitreous, with peak levels of 137 ng/mL for the 400 µg implant and 34.9 ng/mL for 200 µg. That study began in 2010, after the index trial (2008), and no source says these levels were enough. Engagement: no human evidence of retinal alpha-2 receptor engagement or of a downstream neuroprotective biomarker. The approved uses (glaucoma, rosacea, ocular redness) act on other compartments, so engagement cannot be inferred from them. In the index trial (NCT00658619), lesion growth was only numerically smaller on the implant. Later trials gave mixed results: benefit only in larger lesions (PMID:32134802, F3); a significant 24-month result in NCT02087085; and BEACON stopped early because GA grew slowly (PMID:36906177, F7). Since engagement is unknown, the code is U.

EUROCONDOR (NCT01726075) missed its primary endpoint, mfERG implicit time change, in the whole population (PMID:30389750). In the 34.7% of patients with pre-existing retinal neurodysfunction, implicit time worsened on placebo but stayed stable on brimonidine. The authors call screening for neurodysfunction critical to identify the patients who might benefit. Baseline data showed many enrolled patients had no neurodegeneration (PMID:28663190). Together this attributes the failure to patient selection and heterogeneity. Retinal levels after topical dosing and direct receptor engagement were not measured in humans; vitreous PK exists only for the intravitreal implant (NCT01229410).
