However, topical brimonidine dilated retinal arterioles and venules in mild DR (PMID:31112610), showing a retinal pathway effect in this disease. Remaining uncertainty about retinal engagement leaves U as a secondary code.

In the index trial NCT00972374 (n=44), a ≥15-letter BCVA gain occurred in 6.7% on each implant dose vs 0% on sham. No statistical comparison was posted, so no benefit was shown. Exposure is demonstrated: NCT01229410 measured dose-dependent vitreous brimonidine with the same 200/400 µg implant (34.9 and 137 ng/mL), though only after the index trial started. Engagement was not measured. It is inferred_adequate because the same intravitreal implant met its primary GA lesion-growth endpoint in NCT02087085 (p=0.047): same retinal compartment, comparable dose, but a later, marginal and terminated trial. No retinal pathway biomarker exists, and nothing comes from RRD patients. The program likely failed because the mechanism does not drive visual recovery. The very small sample (F7) also limited the readout. Confidence is low.

OCU-300, a topical brimonidine nanoemulsion, missed both primary endpoints in ocular GVHD (NCT03591874). VBR change was -17.62 vs -13.96 for placebo, and VAS change was -1.8 vs -2.6. No target engagement data exist in oGVHD patients. However, topical ocular brimonidine met a redness endpoint in ocular hyperemia (NCT01959230, FDA-approved). That success came through the same alpha2 receptors in conjunctival vessels on the ocular surface, so exposure, engagement and the vasoconstrictive pathway are inferred adequate, though the OCU-300 concentration is not given. A sibling dry-eye phase 3 trial also failed (NCT03785340). Together these suggest alpha2 agonism does not drive oGVHD or dry-eye disease as tested. The small, unbalanced index trial (21 vs 12 evaluable) adds possible underpowering (F7).

The index trial NCT03591874 tested topical brimonidine nanoemulsion (OCU-300) in ocular GVHD and missed both primaries. VBR change was -17.62 vs -13.96 for placebo, and the discomfort VAS was numerically worse (-1.8 vs -2.6). Engagement of ADRA2A in this disease was never measured. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because topical ocular brimonidine met its redness endpoint in ocular hyperemia (NCT01959230, approved): same target, same ocular-surface vascular compartment, with vasoconstriction as the mechanism (PMID:24802713). The OCU-300 concentration is not in the bundle, so dose comparability is uncertain. A sister nanoemulsion also failed in dry eye (NCT03785340). The trial was small and terminated, with 21 vs 12 analyzed, so F7 also applies.

The index trial NCT04969939 met its Part 2b primary efficacy endpoint. NNC0165-1875 1.0 mg plus semaglutide gave -5.55% body weight change versus -3.06% for placebo plus semaglutide (difference -2.15 points, p=0.0437, superiority). This was not an efficacy failure of the drug, so the code is F9. The bundle has no human PK, NPY2R engagement or pathway biomarker data; the Phase 1 trial NCT03707990 posted no results and there are no abstracts. All pillars are therefore no_human_data. Part 1 showed more TEAEs with NNC0165-1875 (56 and 71 events versus 37), but no source says tolerability or business reasons ended the program. Why development stopped despite the positive readout cannot be determined from the bundle, hence U as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT02737007 was a 100 μg IV [14C] microdose PK study in six healthy volunteers. It was not an efficacy test of this drug, so F9 applies. PMID:29168205 says the study was run to support a Go/No-Go decision. Half-life was about 17 h, but combining the human microdose PK with preclinical PfATP4 pharmacodynamic data gave projections that did not support development for a single-dose cure. That projection points to insufficient predicted exposure relative to PD needs, which fits F1a as a secondary code. This exposure judgement rests on modelling rather than measurement at therapeutic doses. The bundle has no human target-engagement or pathway data, and no data in malaria patients.

The index trial NCT02740270 was a first-in-human dose-escalation study. Its primary endpoint was DLT incidence, so it was not an efficacy test. No DLTs occurred with single agent up to 1500 mg q3w, and the combination reached 750 mg plus spartalizumab with 6% DLTs (PMID:34389618). Dose was therefore not capped by tolerability. Population PK in patients plus an ex vivo IL-2 release target-engagement marker supported the projected biologically active dose of 350 mg (PMID:35731955), suggesting engagement was likely reached in patients. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. Single-agent activity was minimal (stable disease only), consistent with a weak mechanism (secondary F2). However, the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping.

Cleveland BioLabs' July 2015 press release reported a Phase 1 trial in 56 healthy volunteers, published before the index trial began in December 2015. Single doses of 0.5–4 µg (MTD 4 µg) caused rapid, dose-dependent rises in plasma cytokines. For a TLR2/6 agonist, this is the direct readout that the receptor was activated. Neutrophil counts (ANC) also rose with dose for about 20 hours. These are reported functional proxies; the release did not give cytokine magnitudes or measure receptor binding. The sponsor said the drug showed 'the expected pharmacological profile'. Adverse events were mild to moderate, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No plasma PK was reported, and engagement was never shown in chemotherapy patients. The 23-patient pilot index trial NCT02778763 posted no results, and no stated reason for stopping was found. So this reads as a mechanism that engaged but gave no durable benefit (F2). The small trial (F7) and missing data (U) keep confidence low.

The Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study in 56 healthy volunteers was reported in July 2015, before the index trial began in December 2015. Single doses of 0.5–4 µg caused rapid, dose-dependent rises in plasma G-CSF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10 and IFN-α, plus a dose-dependent rise in neutrophil counts lasting about 20 hours. That shows the drug activated TLR2 and the expected downstream pathway, though only in healthy volunteers. PK was collected but no numbers were published, so exposure is scored no_human_data. The sponsor found 4 µg tolerable (the MTD), with mild, mechanism-related adverse events. In the breast cancer chemotherapy trial NCT02778763, 'the efficacy hypothesis... was not confirmed.' Since engagement was shown, the mechanism did not protect against neutropenia: F2. The trial's small size (23 patients, a pilot) adds an F7 secondary.

Amlisimod (SDP-4) is a silk-derived protein hydrolysate described as an anti-inflammatory wetting agent. No molecular target is recorded. The sources contain no human measurement of exposure, engagement or a pathway biomarker. PMID:39218389 says this was the first use of SDP-4 in humans, so no Phase 1 pharmacodynamic data exist. In NCT03889886, no dose beat vehicle on SANDE symptom scores. TBUT (tear break-up time, a dry-eye sign) improved at the 1% dose on some days. The investigators attributed better symptom relief to patients with more severe baseline symptoms, which points to patient selection. However, the follow-up trial NCT04535947, run in patients with moderate symptoms, also failed. With engagement having no human data, nothing separates an inactive molecule from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U, with F3 as a possible secondary.

ICON-1 is an intravitreal immunoconjugate meant to bind tissue factor and deplete TF-expressing neovascular cells. In the index trial EMERGE (NCT02358889), ICON-1 alone gained 0.3 BCVA letters versus 7.6 with ranibizumab, and adding it to ranibizumab gave no extra benefit. I found no human data on drug levels in the eye, TF binding or depletion, or a downstream biomarker. The sponsor said CNV lesions shrank, but that was in open-label reports, not a measured pharmacodynamic effect. The only depletion evidence is a pig study (PMID:28738417), which does not count. The follow-on trial NCT03452527 was terminated for business reasons. No other TF-targeted drug is in the bundle. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

The index trial NCT03954067 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of the intratumoral oncolytic virus ASP9801 in advanced solid tumors. Its primary endpoints were safety only (DLTs, AEs, labs, vitals, ECGs). It completed, with no stated stop reason and no posted results. The bundle has no other trials, no PubMed abstracts, no recorded target and no comparator drugs. There is no human evidence on viral exposure in tumors, target engagement or pathway effects. Nothing shows why the program stopped, so a non-engaging drug cannot be told apart from an irrelevant mechanism, toxicity, or a business decision. Engagement is no_human_data, so the code is U.

The bundle has no direct human PK, FDPS-engagement or bone-turnover data. A twin Phase 3 of the same IV regimen in the same disease (NCT03530345) met its 12-week pain endpoint (difference -1.07, p=0.011), so the pillars are inferred to have held. This is an inference from efficacy, not direct measurement. The index trial (NCT03560986) was terminated for an unspecified sponsor decision. Only about 99 of 267 enrolled patients were analysed in Treatment Period A, and placebo showed a large response (-1.71). The discordant twin readouts, early termination and high placebo response point to a trial that could not answer the question. A non-causal target remains possible. The program is now restarting in CRPS type I (NCT07210515), and the sources give no stated cause, so confidence is low.

THR-687 is a pan-RGD integrin antagonist given by intravitreal injection. In the INTEGRAL trial (NCT05063734), Part A tested 1.2 mg and 2.0 mg and missed its key efficacy endpoints, so the drug was dropped. The Phase 1 trial (PMID:36247818) reported only safety, early gains in vision (BCVA) and retinal thickness (CST) with no control group, and plasma levels, which were undetectable by day 7. No human data were found on drug levels in the vitreous or retina, integrin occupancy, or a downstream biomarker. The PK paper (PMID:34302261) covers animals only. No other drug on this target has succeeded in DME, so F1b does not apply. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the failure. Because engagement is unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

In NCT02611466 / PMID:31356878, ASP7962 100 mg BID did no better than placebo on WOMAC pain, while naproxen separated from placebo, so the trial could detect a drug effect. No human TrkA engagement, occupancy or pathway biomarker data were found, and the Phase 1 trials (NCT01981928, NCT02136316) posted no results. The dose was set from preclinical toxicity data and Phase 1 safety, not human tolerability limits, so dose_limited is false. The accompanying editorial says target engagement was never confirmed and suggests ASP7962's lower TrkA affinity may have limited blockade. Intra-articular GZ389988 showed a small benefit in Phase 2, but that was not a pivotal success. So F1b and F1a are only possibilities. With engagement unmeasured, the failure is indeterminate.

The index Phase 2 trial NCT05525520 (EP547 100 mg QD, cholestatic pruritus in PBC/PSC) missed its primary endpoint. Worst Itch NRS change at week 6 was -1.75 on drug vs -2.20 on placebo (p=0.46). The only other trial, Phase 1 NCT04510090, posted adverse-event data only. It shows good tolerability up to 675 mg single and 225 mg multiple doses, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The excerpt contains no PK values, MRGPRX4 occupancy or pathway biomarker data. The bundle has no other MRGPRX4 drugs and no PubMed evidence. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not drive cholestatic itch, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT05525520), EP547 100 mg once daily did no better than placebo on worst itch at Week 6 (LSMD 0.46, p=0.46). In Phase 1 (NCT04510090), single doses up to 675 mg and repeat doses up to 225 mg were well tolerated. Plasma levels rose in line with dose, so systemic exposure counts as adequate and tolerability did not cap the dose. However, the sources show no human measure of MRGPRX4 blockade: no receptor occupancy, no blocking of itch provoked by bile acids or bilirubin, and no downstream biomarker. No other drug on this target has succeeded, and neither the sponsor nor Incyte gave a reason for stopping. The bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not drive this itch, so the answer is indeterminate (U).

The IVR delivered up to 1.05 mg/day anastrozole, and human studies reached predefined ATZ exposure levels (PMID:31174438). Engagement was not measured at IVR doses. It is inferred from the approved breast cancer use: 1 mg oral, systemic aromatase, comparable dose. At that dose, estradiol suppression reached the maximum measurable or about 87% (PMID:7949201, PMID:10912575). A 1998 endometriosis case report showed E2 halved with clinical response (PMID:9548162). The index trial had assay sensitivity, since the leuprorelin control separated from placebo (-3.77 vs -2.29). ATZ arms showed no dose-response and no gain over placebo (NCT02203331), pointing to the mechanism as tested. Uncertainty remains: no premenopausal or IVR-specific pharmacodynamic data exist, so inadequate suppression cannot be excluded.

Exposure is adequate: Phase 1 studies (PMID:33569494, NCT03907280) showed dose-proportional pharmacokinetics in plasma, with about 40% of the inhaled dose reaching the systemic circulation, and patient pharmacokinetics matched healthy volunteers (PMID:34385272). No human study measured airway ENaC inhibition (for example by nasal potential difference) or mucociliary clearance. The 200 µg twice-daily dose was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The trial stopped at a pre-defined futility rule (NCT04059094, PMID:34385272). The ETD001 paper (PMID:38851923) argues from sheep dose-response data that clinical doses were too low, which would point to F1a. That is animal data, so it cannot support an inadequate rating. With no human engagement evidence, an under-dosed drug cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The SAGA trial (NCT02777931) missed its primary ADHD-RS endpoint (-14.2 vs -12.1). The sponsor pointed to signals at the highest dose, on the inattention subscale and in responder analyses. Human data cover only PK and tolerability in adolescents (NCT02286817, PMID:29339723), and the company said the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier, but no CSF levels were given. No human data show mGluR occupancy, receptor activation or a downstream biomarker. Follow-up Phase 2 trials in mGluR+ (NCT03265119) and mGluR-negative (NCT03609619) children both failed, which weakens the idea that selecting patients by genotype explains it. No other mGluR activator has succeeded in ADHD. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In patients with advanced solid tumors (PMID:33514524, NCT03099109), LY3321367 concentrations rose in proportion to dose, and no dose-limiting toxicities occurred, so the dose was not capped. PK/PD modeling indicated 100% TIM-3 target engagement at doses of 600 mg or more, and the RP2D was 1,200/600 mg. CD8 infiltration increased in about half of paired biopsies, a pathway effect, though only in part of the patients. Despite this, antitumor activity was modest: ORR 0% in anti-PD-1-refractory NSCLC and 4% in combination cohorts. This points to TIM-3 blockade not driving benefit as tested (F2). The engagement data were published in 2021, after the index trial began. The index trial (NCT02791334) is an anti-PD-L1 DLT study, not an efficacy test of this drug (F9 secondary).

The index trial NCT02679729 was a first-in-human single-ascending-dose safety and PK study in healthy volunteers. It met its purpose: no SAEs, well tolerated up to 1692 µg, and inhaled bioavailability about 3%. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 is primary. In the later CF study NCT02950805, a single 600 µg dose inhibited nasal ENaC by nasal potential difference, so engagement was shown in the disease, but after the index trial started. Mucociliary clearance did not improve, so the pathway pillar was not met (PMID:35227647). The authors blame testing only a single dose. PMID:38851923 argues clinical doses were too low for sustained lung action, implying under-dosing (F1a) or wrong duration (F4). This was dose selection, not a tolerability cap.

The index trial NCT02679729 was a first-in-human single-ascending-dose safety and PK study in healthy subjects. Doses up to 1692 µg were well tolerated with no SAEs, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). The efficacy signal came from Phase Ib NCT02950805, which started after the index trial. In CF patients, a single 600 µg dose inhibited ENaC as measured by nasal potential difference, which the authors call target engagement, but mucociliary clearance did not improve (PMID:35227647). Engagement was adequate while the pathway was inadequate, which suggests F2. The authors blame the single dose (F4). PMID:38851923 argues from sheep data that clinical doses were too low (F1a). Tolerability did not cap the dose.

No direct pillar measurements are in the bundle. The pillars are inferred adequate because the same foam met clinical endpoints in the same disease, plaque psoriasis: Phase 2 NCT01700985 (52.2% vs 0%, p<0.0001, before the index trial) and twin Phase 3 NCT02368210 (25.3% vs 3.9%, p<0.001). Later Phase 3 NCT02742441 also met its endpoint (30.7% vs 7.4%). The index trial NCT02367911 (n=144) numerically favoured active (18.3% vs 9.6%, p≈0.13) but missed significance. With a higher vehicle response and a small sample, it was most plausibly underpowered or a chance miss rather than a mechanism or molecule failure. GR agonism is validated in psoriasis by many approved corticosteroids. No safety signal was seen.

The index trial NCT05586152 failed its Part 2 efficacy endpoint. Eye dryness VAS fell by 15.5 with INV-102 0.7% BID and by 21.2 with vehicle, so vehicle did numerically better. That arm had only 15 patients, so F7 (small trial) is a possible secondary code. INV-102 has no recorded target. Sources describe it only as treating ocular conditions caused by DNA damage. The bundle has no human data on drug levels in the eye, target binding or downstream biomarkers. A PK population was added to the analysis plan, but no PK results were found. No other drug on the same target and no sponsor explanation for the failure turned up. The sponsor kept going with a further dry eye Phase 2 (NCT06370039). With no engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT04672083 was a Phase 1 single-dose safety study of CPT31 (0.01–0.24 mg/kg) in healthy volunteers. Its only primary outcome was adverse events, and none occurred in any cohort or placebo. It was not an efficacy test, so no efficacy failure is shown. The bundle has no pharmacokinetic, target-engagement (e.g., gp41 binding) or viral-load data, no other trials, no publications and no comparator drugs. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data. Why the program stopped cannot be determined from the bundle; U applies as a secondary code.

Engagement is undetermined, so this is coded U. Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (NCT02699372, PMID:41639230) found ralmitaront well tolerated up to 300 mg, with dose-limiting effects only at 450 mg. The index trial used up to 300 mg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No human brain-penetration, TAAR1 occupancy or biomarker data turned up. The schizophrenia [18F]DOPA PET study (NCT06880328) has no posted results, and the published DOPA PET data are from mice (PMID:40098750). In vitro comparisons and reviews suggest the molecule may be the problem: lower TAAR1 efficacy than ulotaront, slower binding and no 5-HT1A activity. But no other TAAR1 drug has met a pivotal endpoint in schizophrenia; ulotaront reached Phase 3 with no approval. So F1b is only suggestive. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter.

In the healthy-volunteer Phase 1 studies (PMID:39120583, NCT03361540), ASP8302 had linear PK and was tolerated up to 140–150 mg. It also produced a dose-dependent, M3-mediated increase in salivary secretion from 100 mg onward. That functional readout counts as engagement for a positive modulator, so exposure, engagement and pathway are rated adequate at the 100 mg dose used in the index trial. The index trial missed its primary endpoint, change in post-void residual volume (p=0.96). Benefit was confined to males: Qmax and detrusor pressure at Qmax rose, and incontinence fell (PMID:35419807). The authors point to patients selected by non-urodynamic clinical criteria and to inconsistent PVR measurement versus BVE. This supports a wrong population (F3), with endpoint (F4) and design (F7) contributing. CHRM3 antagonists approved for overactive bladder act in the opposite direction, so they are not comparators.

The index trial (NCT04370236) was stopped for futility. Disease progression was numerically worse on the drug (10/39 vs 6/38 on placebo), as were deaths (4 vs 1). I found no human data on plasma exposure, soluble TNF neutralisation or inflammatory biomarker changes in COVID-19 patients. The only human pharmacodynamic data come from Alzheimer's disease: CSF proteomics from the phase 1b study (NCT03943264), published in 2025, and plasma pTau217 and GFAP from the phase 2 study (NCT05318976). Both are downstream brain biomarkers in another disease, published after the index trial started, and they do not show soluble TNF being neutralised in the lung or blood. No other selective soluble TNF inhibitor has succeeded in COVID-19. So nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that does not matter here: U.

In SANDMAN (NCT03603678, PMID:34531274), patients got a single 100 µg nasal dose. Responder rates were 6.3% on drug and 6.7% on placebo, and the sponsor stopped the trial early for futility. No human data were found on drug delivery to the pharyngeal mucosa, TASK-1/3 channel blockade, or genioglossus muscle activation. The paper says the drug is known to work only in an animal model. The authors call the trial 'non-informative from a mechanistic point of view' and list the missing drug-delivery data as a limitation. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Bayer moved on to a chemically altered follow-up compound, BAY2586116 (NCT04236440). With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The small, early-stopped trial adds F7.

None of the sources report human serum or tissue PK or neutralizing titers for BGB-DXP593. The phase 1 trials (NCT04532294, NCT04669262) posted safety data only. The protocol's claim that lung levels stay above the IC99 is a model projection, not a measurement, and the abstract's efficacy evidence comes from animal models. The downstream marker, viral RNA, did not fall in nasopharyngeal swabs at any dose (NCT04551898). In saliva it fell only at 5 and 15 mg/kg, not at 30 mg/kg, so there was no dose response (PMID:36820098). The investigators suggest swab technical problems may explain the negative primary endpoint, which points to F7. Without engagement data, the sources can't tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that failed, so the code is U. Neither the bundle nor the searched pages show another drug on the same target succeeding, so F1b can't be assigned.

OPC-64005 is a triple monoamine reuptake inhibitor (NET/DAT/SERT). In NCT04244253, the 20 mg dose missed MADRS at week 6 (difference -1.1, p=0.288); the small 10 mg arm was numerically better. The bundle holds no Phase 1 data or PubMed abstracts on exposure, transporter occupancy or pathway markers. ADHD efficacy (NCT03324581) suggests some CNS NET/DAT activity. However, that trial's dose is not given, and it does not show SERT engagement, so engagement cannot be inferred as adequate. Other drugs on these same transporters are approved for MDD (bupropion, desvenlafaxine, citalopram), so the target class is validated in this disease. That points to a molecule-level shortfall (F1b), though it cannot be separated from indeterminacy (U) on this thin bundle.

The index trial NCT03579030 was a Phase 1 safety and PK/PD study in healthy adults. Its primary outcome was the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of RTA 1701. It posted no results and gave no stop reason. The bundle has no other trials, no PubMed abstracts and no other RORC drugs, so there is no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway. The program's halt cannot be tied to an efficacy failure, which supports F9. If the stop is read as a failed program, the mechanism question is indeterminate (U), because engagement is no_human_data. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

The index trial NCT02788721 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study in healthy female volunteers, with an adverse-event primary endpoint. It was not an efficacy test of GLPG2451, so the program did not stop on a failed efficacy readout (F9). No results were posted for it, for NCT03214614, or for the CF combination study NCT03540524, so the bundle has no human exposure, CFTR potentiation or pathway (e.g. sweat chloride) data. Only in vitro potentiator activity is reported (PMID:30416447, PMID:33399458). Several approved CFTR modulators exist, but no pillar evidence for this molecule is shown. If treated as an efficacy question, the answer would be indeterminate (U). The bundle states no reason for stopping.

QBECO is a microbial immunotherapy made from inactivated E. coli. It has no recorded molecular target, and the bundle contains no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects. In the index trial (NCT01809275, PMID:31380382), mean CDAI fell by 68 points on QBECO versus 31 on placebo, with no significance reported. The authors called it a proof-of-concept study and said larger trials are needed. A response signal appeared only in TNF-inhibitor-naive patients (64% vs 26%), and exploratory immune biomarkers were linked to response, which points toward patient-selection issues (F3). The small trial (n=68) may also have been underpowered (F7). The follow-up Phase 2 (NCT03472690) ended on a corporate decision after its lead-in portion. Since engagement was never measured, the cause of failure cannot be determined.

The index trial NCT01973114 (published as PMID:41324607) tested intratympanic latanoprost 0.0005% against placebo. It found no difference in speech discrimination in noise at day 14, and no secondary endpoint differed. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not limit the dose. No source has human data on inner-ear (perilymph) drug levels, FP-receptor engagement in the cochlea or vestibule, or a pathway biomarker such as change in endolymphatic hydrops. The only support for the mechanism comes from animal studies (PMID:25131393, PMID:23611671). The positive 2005 pilot (PMID:16143197) was a clinical result, not evidence of engagement. The glaucoma approval works through the eye, a different tissue, so engagement in the inner ear cannot be inferred from it. The sources give no reason for the failure, so a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

ZL-3101 (Fugan) is a topical ointment made from extracts of two Chinese herbs. No molecular target is recorded for it. In the Phase IIa trial (NCT03134352, 295 Chinese patients with mild to moderate subacute eczema), it was safe and well tolerated but showed no difference from placebo in EASI change at day 21. Zai Lab then stopped the program. I found no human data on skin drug levels, target engagement or biomarkers, and no other drug on the same target to compare against. The sponsor gave no explanation beyond the efficacy miss. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Nothing in the evidence separates poor delivery or engagement from an ineffective mechanism, so the failure code is U (indeterminate).

MERKLIN 2 (NCT04393753) tested domatinostat with avelumab in 19 Merkel cell carcinoma patients who had progressed on anti-PD-(L)1 therapy. It posted no results, and none of the pages I found gave the outcome or a reason for stopping. The Phase 1 trial in blood cancers (PMID:30347469) says it measured pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, but its abstract reports no plasma levels, HDAC inhibition, histone acetylation or other biomarker data. It found no maximum tolerated dose and chose a 400 mg/day dose, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Searches turned up no human evidence of target engagement, no company explanation and no published results. Other approved HDAC inhibitors were in T-cell lymphomas, not Merkel cell carcinoma. With no engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

VERU-944 (zuclomiphene) went straight into Phase 2 without published Phase 1 PK or PD data, so exposure has no human data. Veru's interim release reports that in the index trial (NCT03646162) the 50 mg dose produced estrogenic activity that differed from both 10 mg and placebo (p<0.0001). That is evidence of ER-agonist engagement in prostate cancer patients on ADT. But the biomarker is not named, it was measured in the index trial itself rather than beforehand, and it was reported only by the sponsor. Even so, 50 mg cut hot flashes by -42.2% versus -46.6% on placebo. The company left the placebo arm out of its efficacy claims and compared only to baseline and to 10 mg. ER agonism did not beat placebo here, so the primary code is F2. The very large placebo response makes F7 a secondary code. Confidence is low because the engagement evidence is weak.

VERU-944 (zuclomiphene, cis-clomiphene) is a weak ER agonist. It was tested at 10 and 50 mg against placebo for hot flashes caused by androgen deprivation therapy (NCT03646162). At 6 weeks, hot flashes fell 19.7% on 10 mg, 42.2% on 50 mg and 46.6% on placebo, so neither dose beat placebo. No source gives human exposure, estrogen-receptor engagement or pharmacodynamic markers such as SHBG, LH or FSH for zuclomiphene. The bundle has no other trials of this drug and no other drugs on the same target in this disease. The company's 10-K reported only a within-arm drop from baseline on 50 mg. The large placebo response suggests a trial-design problem (F7), but with no engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

The topical JAK1/3 inhibitor ATI-502 index trial (NCT03759340) was terminated by sponsor decision. The only posted result is a single-arm SALT change of -15.72% (n=8), with no comparator. A scalp-biopsy drug-level study exists (NCT03315689), but the bundle reports no results from it, and there is no human target-engagement or pathway biomarker data. Oral JAK1/JAK3 inhibitors (baricitinib, ritlecitinib, deuruxolitinib) are FDA-approved for alopecia areata, so the target is validated in this disease. Without any pillar evidence that this topical molecule engaged JAK1/3 in the follicle, the failure points to the molecule or its delivery, not the target (F1b). Mouse efficacy (PMID:36203601) does not count as human evidence. Engagement remains unmeasured, so U is a secondary code.

Index trial NCT03468855 was a single-arm study of topical ATI-50002 0.46% in 34 patients. Facial depigmentation changed by +2.0 ±8.41 at week 24, with no repigmentation signal. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. NCT03315689 measured scalp drug levels, but no results are shown. Topical ruxolitinib, which shares the JAK1 target, is FDA-approved for vitiligo, and MH004 reached phase 3 in vitiligo. That suggests JAK1 inhibition in skin can work in this disease, pointing to the molecule (formulation or skin penetration) rather than the target, although adequate engagement was never shown. The small, uncontrolled design with no success criterion limits interpretation (F7). The program was later ended by sponsor decision across indications (NCT03759340).

The index trial, topical ATI-502 0.46% in AA/AU/AT (NCT03759340), was terminated by sponsor decision. It produced only a small single-arm SALT change (-15.72%, n=8). The earlier vehicle-controlled trial (NCT03354637) missed its primary endpoint, with vehicle doing better than both ATI-50002 doses. A scalp-biopsy drug-level study exists (NCT03315689), but the bundle reports no values. So there is no human evidence of exposure, engagement or pathway effect. Other JAK1/JAK3 inhibitors (baricitinib, ritlecitinib, deuruxolitinib) are FDA-approved in alopecia areata, which validates the target. The failure therefore points to this molecule or its topical delivery rather than the mechanism. U is a secondary code because engagement was never measured.

The index trial (NCT03759340) was terminated by sponsor decision. It had a single-arm SALT change of -15.7% (n=8). This came after the randomized AA trial NCT03354637 failed for futility, with vehicle beating both doses of topical ATI-50002. NCT03315689 measured drug levels in scalp biopsies of AU/AT patients, but the bundle reports no values. There is no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway. JAK1/JAK3-directed inhibitors (baricitinib, deuruxolitinib, ritlecitinib) are FDA-approved for alopecia areata, of which AU is a subtype, so the target is validated. The failure therefore most plausibly lies with this molecule and its topical delivery, not the target. U also applies because engagement was never shown.

The index SOLITAIRE-U trial (NCT02210325, PMID:31196813) was an open-label non-inferiority comparison against active ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Eradication was 80% vs 84% (difference -4.0%, 95% CI -13.6 to 5.5), so it missed only the -10% non-inferiority margin, which is an F9 situation. Human plasma exposure is documented (PMID:21282444). Antibacterial engagement is inferred_adequate: the phase 2 gonorrhea trial reported 100% culture cure (NCT01591447, PMID:26089222), and both CABP phase 3 trials met non-inferiority (NCT01756339, NCT01968733). Wider development ended in part over safety and regulatory concerns tied to structural similarity to telithromycin (PMID:31644280), and pediatric work stopped as 'development not proceeding' (NCT02605122). Molecule-specific toxicity (F6) is therefore listed as secondary.

No primary target is recorded for solithromycin in NASH, and the proposed mechanism (anti-inflammatory macrolide) has no human target-engagement or pathway data. No hepatic exposure data were found either, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the small open-label NCT02510599, an interim readout of 6 patients showed a mean NAS reduction of 1.3 and ALT falls. Cempra then suspended NASH development, calling the efficacy 'unclear'. This is an uncontrolled, underpowered design (F7). At the same time, the FDA review flagged hepatotoxicity from solithromycin itself, with ALT elevations above 3×ULN in the COPD and NASH trials (F6). Nothing in the evidence separates a drug that never engaged a target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the primary code is U.

In healthy subjects, ACT-774312 showed dose-proportional plasma PK. It achieved full (>90% Emax) CRTH2 blockade in a whole-blood internalization assay at 50 mg BID, and was well tolerated up to 1000 mg, so the dose was not limited (PMID:30589994). This supports adequate exposure and engagement, but only in healthy volunteers, and the paper was published in 2019, after the index trial began in Oct 2018. No downstream pathway biomarker or disease-population data are in the bundle. The index trial enrolled only 10 patients, and the analysis included 5 on drug versus 2 on placebo (NCT03688555). That is far too small to test efficacy, so the trial could not answer the question. The point estimate favoured placebo (p=0.062), which hints at a target-level failure (F2), but this is unreliable at this size.

In adults, the first-in-human trial (NCT02264613; PMID:34301750) showed dose-dependent PK and dose-related rises in serum MIC-1, a p53-activation biomarker, at a tolerable RP2D of 3.1 mg/kg. The pediatric study (PMID:42189874) showed 30–50-fold MIC-1 increases. Together these indicate on-target MDM2/MDMX inhibition and p53 pathway activation, though not in lung cancer patients. The index chemoprotection trial (NCT04022876) was stopped with a favorable safety profile because the between-group difference was insufficient. A later breast cancer chemoprotection trial (NCT05622058) saw grade 4 neutropenia in all four patients enrolled. This suggests that p53-mediated myeloprotection does not deliver clinical benefit as tested (F2). The stop reason's reference to the targeted sample size also hints that the trial was underpowered (F7).

The index trial tested ALRN-6924 as a chemoprotectant in SCLC/NSCLC. The idea was that p53 activation in normal marrow would protect it from chemotherapy. The adult first-in-human trial showed dose-dependent PK and a dose-related rise in serum MIC-1, a p53 activation biomarker, at doses up to the 3.1 mg/kg RP2D (PMID:34301750). The pediatric study showed 30–50-fold MIC-1 increases (PMID:42189874). So exposure, engagement and pathway activation are shown in humans, though not in lung cancer patients, and the data were published only after the index trial began. The drug was tolerable, yet there was no meaningful separation on the composite myelosuppression endpoint (NCT04022876). A similar failure occurred in breast cancer (NCT05622058). This points to the mechanism not delivering chemoprotection. The small sample size is a secondary factor.

The index trial tested ALRN-6924 as chemoprotection in lung cancer, not as an AML antileukemic. In adults it showed dose-dependent PK and raised serum MIC-1, a p53-activation biomarker, at a tolerable MTD/RP2D of 3.1 mg/kg (PMID:34301750). Pediatric data showed MIC-1 rising 30–50-fold (PMID:42189874). So exposure, on-target p53 activation and pathway were adequate, and the dose was not tolerability-capped. These data came from solid-tumor patients, not AML or chemoprotection patients, and were published after the index trial started. Despite this, the arms did not differ on the composite chemoprotection endpoint (NCT04022876). The breast cancer chemoprotection trial also failed, with grade 4 neutropenia (NCT05622058). This points to the mechanism not delivering. The small targeted sample size suggests a possible power limitation (F7).

In the randomized Phase 2 trial NCT02873338, adding dociparstat did not raise the CR rate in the posted results: control 14/26, 0.125 mg/kg 8/25, 0.25 mg/kg 11/24. None of the sources I found report human target engagement: no plasma CXCL12, PF4 or HMGB1 neutralization, no blast mobilization, and no pharmacokinetic link to marrow levels. The pilot trials (NCT02056782, NCT02995655) reported only clinical outcomes such as platelet recovery and CR. The investigators' 2019 ASCO abstract analyzed only evaluable patients, not intent-to-treat, and called the high-dose results encouraging. That gap between their reading and the posted counts points to a small exploratory design (F7). Because there is no evidence that the drug engaged its target, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug or the mechanism, so the code is U.

Santen's documents identify STN1013600 as an ursodeoxycholic acid eye drop for presbyopia. In the Phase 2a OPSIS trial (NCT05665387), neither 0.1% nor 0.3% beat vehicle on near visual acuity at Month 2 (DCNVA change 4.1 and 4.3 vs 4.4 letters). There were no serious adverse events, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Santen's 2024 update says only that the primary and secondary endpoints were not met. My one search found no human data on drug levels in the lens, target engagement or a lens biomarker, and no other drug on the same target. Nothing separates a drug that never reached or engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Inhaled levofloxacin (MP-376) acts on bacteria in the airway. In CF patients with Pseudomonas, the Phase 2 trial NCT00677365 (PMID:21471106, registered and run before the index trial started in 2010) showed a dose-dependent fall in sputum PA density (-0.96 log10 CFU/g at 240 mg BID), an 8.7% FEV1 gain and less use of other anti-PA antibiotics. Engagement and pathway are therefore adequate in this disease. Exposure is inferred from those effects. The Phase 3 NCT01270347 also met a non-inferiority FEV1 comparison against tobramycin. The index trial NCT01180634 missed only its clinical endpoint, time to exacerbation over a short window of about 59 days (HR 1.33, p=0.07, trend favouring drug). The endpoint and duration, plus limited power, look more likely to blame than the mechanism. No source states the reason.

CK0802 is an allogeneic cord-blood Treg cell product with no defined molecular target. The index trial, NCT04468971, was a small phase 1 safety study with 15 patients per arm. Its 2023 Blood Advances report called the cells safe. Results were mixed: Bayesian estimates favoured the 100M dose (98.6% probability of benefit for survival) but not the 300M dose (7 of 13 deaths were in that arm). No human data show the cells' immunosuppressive effect (engagement) or a downstream biomarker change. HLA chimerism was undetectable in blood at days 3 to 28, so the cells' persistence is unclear, but the investigators did not call exposure inadequate. The sponsor then moved to GVHD (NCT07576699). Nothing separates a product that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter. Underpowered design (F7) and a safety-focused primary (F9) also apply.

CK0802 is an allogeneic cord-blood Treg product with no recorded molecular target. The index Phase 1 trial (NCT04468971; 45 patients; placebo vs 100M vs 300M cells) found no grade ≥3 toxicity. HLA chimerism testing on days 3–28 found no donor cells in peripheral blood. That shows the cells did not persist in blood, but it says nothing about engagement in tissue. No occupancy, cytokine or other pathway evidence was found. The sponsor reported the readout as encouraging, with an 89.7% probability of benefit for being alive and extubated at day 28 at 100M cells. The 300M arm started sicker, so the arms were unbalanced. The program then moved to GVHD and aplastic anemia, but no reason for leaving COVID was stated. Engagement data are missing, so the code is U. F7 (small, unbalanced trial) and F8 (business reasons) are possible secondary codes.

The index trial NCT03431974 enrolled only 19 patients on low-dose oral aminopterin and missed both primary endpoints (PASI75 3/11 vs 1/8, p=0.43; sPGA 1/11 vs 1/8). Oral bioavailability was complete in leukemia patients at 2 mg/m2 twice weekly (PMID:16299240), so plasma exposure is shown, though at a different dose and in another disease. The bundle has no human DHFR engagement or pathway biomarker data at the psoriasis dose. Methotrexate, which also inhibits DHFR, is FDA-approved for psoriasis, so the target is valid. That points to a molecule or dose problem rather than the target. The small sample size makes F7 (underpowered trial) a strong secondary explanation. The 1950s–60s psoriasis papers are titles only.

In resistant hypertension, XXB750 gave dose-dependent plasma exposure and raised plasma and urine cGMP at 30–240 mg (PMID:41563174), so exposure and engagement were shown in humans. These data were published after the index trial started. In HF patients (NCT06142383, PMID:41912806), cGMP paradoxically fell and NT-proBNP rose, so the pathway failed in this disease. The DMC stopped the trial early for excess death or worsening HF on XXB750 (25% vs 0% placebo). Serious AEs were also higher on drug. Harm, not just lack of efficacy, ended the program, and it is opposite to what NPR1 agonism predicts. Nesiritide, an approved NPR1 agonist in HF, suggests a molecule-specific paradoxical effect (F6), with F5 and F1b possible.

In the index trial (NCT05562934, PMID:41563174), patients with resistant hypertension showed dose-dependent increases in XXB750 plasma concentrations (exposure). Plasma and urine cGMP, the second messenger of NPR1 guanylyl cyclase, also rose dose-dependently, which shows engagement and the proximal pathway effect in this disease. Even so, 24h SBP did not fall at any dose (p=0.5651), and the authors call this paradoxical. Urinary sodium did not change and renin rose, suggesting a counter-regulatory response. Anti-drug antibodies did not explain the result, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Engagement evidence in patients comes from the index trial itself, so it was not available beforehand. The heart failure program also failed to lower NT-proBNP (NCT06142383). With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, NPR1 agonism does not lower BP here.

Laromestrocel is an allogeneic MSC product with no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human data on exposure (cell persistence or homing) or on target engagement. In frail patients, PMID:41747733 reports a dose-dependent decrease in soluble TIE2, a pathway-level biomarker, so a proximal effect was shown in this disease. The registered primary endpoint, 6MWT change at 180 days, missed: 41.3 m, p=0.0635. The authors describe the effect as dose- and time-dependent, with 63.4 m (p=0.0077) at month 9. The miss is therefore best explained by endpoint timing or duration (F4). Limited power around a borderline 6-month result is a secondary contributor (F7). No tolerability limit is reported (NCT02065245).

LAT8881 is a peptide with no recorded primary target. The index trial NCT04153409 enrolled 21 people and showed no significant effect on pain at any timepoint (2 h p=0.149). I found no human evidence of exposure, engagement or pathway effect: no PK, occupancy or biomarker data in the bundle or in search results. The sponsor's protocol says no established pharmacological models of migraine exist, so the case for migraine rested on nonclinical studies. Patsnap lists the drug as discontinued at Phase 2 but gives no stated reason. NCT05298306 shows only safety and pain outcomes for an IV dose in another indication. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from an irrelevant mechanism. The small crossover trial was also likely underpowered (F7, secondary).

Lung drug levels were never measured directly, and plasma levels were kept low on purpose. Still, lung exposure and engagement are supported in asthma patients. The Phase 1 trial (NCT03652038) showed dose-dependent FeNO drops at 500 µg or more, reported Sept 2019, before the index trial began. Phase 1 Part C showed lower pSTAT and FeNO in moderate-to-severe asthma. The sponsor said 1500 µg engaged the JAK mechanism, and FeNO fell in the index trial too. Yet the late asthmatic response did not change at either dose (p=0.881 and 0.575; NCT04150341), which the sponsor called inconsistent with expectations. With the target engaged and the pathway moving but no clinical effect, the best fit is F2. The program was paused to refine the formulation, which leaves some chance that lung delivery was not enough (secondary F1a).

Human PK showed sustained plasma exposure with a half-life over 50 h (PMID:14597974). Target engagement of TF/FVIIa was shown by dose-dependent PT prolongation and ETP reduction (PMID:14597974, PMID:14717968). The pathway effect, suppressed thrombin generation (F1+2), was shown in endotoxemia, PCI and ACS patients (PMID:14717968, PMID:12821239, PMID:17599602). All of this was published before the index trial, but no engagement data in COVID-19 are in the bundle. In ASPEN-COVID-19, rNAPc2 did not reduce D-dimer more than active heparin (p=0.47) and did not raise bleeding (NCT04655586, PMID:37381988). The mechanism was adequately engaged, yet TF inhibition gave no benefit over heparin. Secondary codes: small open-label active-comparator design with a highly variable biomarker endpoint (F7), and a numerically greater effect only in mildly ill patients (F3).

The index trial NCT02344017 was a Phase 1/2 safety and PK dose escalation in mCRPC, not an efficacy test. PMID:30194031 reports that AUC rose only up to 300 mg and fell after repeated dosing from 200 mg upward. The authors state the molecule's pharmacokinetic properties prevented further development, so adequate exposure is lacking. Testosterone fell, showing qualitative CYP17A1 engagement in patients, but sufficiency was not shown. Only 13% of patients had a >50% PSA decline. The drug was well tolerated up to 500 mg BID, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. Abiraterone and several AR antagonists are approved in prostate cancer, which points to the molecule rather than the targets (F1b). The non-efficacy index trial supports F9.

The index trial, NCT03998514, was a Phase 1a/1b study with safety as its primary endpoint, and it met that endpoint: no serious adverse events. In the 4-week Phase 1b exploratory analysis, 25 mg CB4211 cut ALT by 25% and AST by 17% versus placebo, but liver fat fell the same amount in the drug and placebo groups (-5.03% vs -4.88%). CB4211 is a mitochondrial-derived peptide analog with no recorded molecular target, and no human PK, occupancy or engagement data were published, so all three pillars are no_human_data. CohBar's SEC filings say development stopped because the Phase 1b formulation was not suitable and efforts to improve it failed, followed by a strategic review and a merger that dropped CohBar's candidates. This was not an efficacy failure (F9); the stop was partly for business reasons (F8).

E2730 inhibits GAT1 (SLC6A1), a target in the brain. NCT03603639 enrolled 6 patients and tested 40 and 120 mg. Neither dose suppressed the photoparoxysmal response (SPR) compared with placebo, and the trial was stopped for efficacy reasons. The only human pharmacology I found is plasma PK in healthy volunteers, summarised in the protocol: rapid absorption at 20–120 mg in studies NCT03054194 and NCT03451890. I found no human data on CSF levels or brain penetration, GAT1 occupancy, or a GABA biomarker. The biomarker work in PMID:39302665 was done in rats. No other GAT1 drug appears in the bundle. Because there is no human engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged GAT1 apart from a target that doesn't matter here. The very small trial, which may not have been able to answer the question, is a secondary concern (F7).

MIV-711 is a potent, selective cathepsin K inhibitor (Ki 0.98 nM). In healthy humans, single doses of 20–600 mg gave plasma exposure and dose-dependently reduced serum CTX-I, a cathepsin K–generated bone-resorption product, by up to 79% at trough (PMID:29743078). This counts as adequate exposure, engagement and pathway effect, though only in healthy volunteers, not OA patients, and published after the index trial began. It was well tolerated, with no dose cap (NCT03037489). Despite this, 100 and 200 mg over 26 weeks did not reduce knee pain versus placebo (difference -0.08, p=0.41; NCT02705625). Cathepsin K inhibition did not relieve symptomatic knee OA as tested. Other agents on this target (balicatib, odanacatib) went no further than phase 2.

Ritonavir is used here only as a CYP3A4/P-gp pharmacokinetic booster for oral docetaxel (ModraDoc006), so the index trial was not an efficacy test of ritonavir. Phase Ib work in mCRPC measured ritonavir and docetaxel exposure. Ritonavir 200 mg raised docetaxel AUC to or above IV levels, and PSA falls of 50% or more were seen (PMID:33709626, PMID:33744986), so the boosting mechanism held. The phase 2 trial against active IV docetaxel (NCT04028388) found no significant rPFS difference (9.5 vs 11.1 months; HR CI 0.56–2.65). Response and PSA rates were similar, tolerability was better, and the authors call the regimen effective (PMID:38518534). The superiority test was small and wide-CI, so the trial could not separate the arms (F7).

The index trial NCT04529811 is a Phase 1 safety and PK study of new rifaximin formulations in healthy volunteers, with an adverse-event primary outcome. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. The actual PSC efficacy signal came from the open-label pilot (NCT01695174/PMID:24914504). Rifaximin 550 mg BID, a dose comparable to approved use, produced no change in ALP, other biochemistry or quality of life. Plasma exposure is negligible by design (PMID:7836025), but gut-luminal antibacterial action is inferred adequate from the met IBS endpoints (NCT00724126, NCT00731679, NCT01543178) and the hepatic encephalopathy approval. Methane eradication was also shown (NCT01638429). This supports F2: gut-microbial modulation by rifaximin does not drive PSC. Engagement was not measured in PSC patients.

The index trial NCT04992546 was a Phase 2a safety, tolerability and PK study of topical SAR444727 5% BID in mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis. Its primary outcomes were descriptive safety counts (TEAEs, PCSAs, application-site events), with no TESAEs and no deaths. It was therefore not an efficacy test, and no failed efficacy readout is shown. The bundle has no human data on skin exposure, BTK occupancy or downstream biomarkers. BTK occupancy and local efficacy appear only in preclinical work (PMID:34326199). The bundle gives no reason for discontinuation. If the stop reflected undisclosed lack of benefit, the bundle could not separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter (U).

The index trial NCT02748642 was a Phase 1 safety, PK and immunogenicity study with only safety and ADA primary endpoints, so it was not an efficacy test of BITS7201A. That makes F9 the primary code. PMID:30616547 reports IgG-like plasma PK with no dose-limiting AEs, so systemic exposure was shown. It reports no target-engagement or pathway biomarker, such as free IL-13/IL-17 or downstream markers. ADA incidence was high (53% single-dose, 94% multiple-dose). The mild-asthma cohort was terminated after one patient, and the bundle gives no stated reason. Engagement has no human data and no efficacy readout exists, so U is the secondary code.

In the first-in-human study, TEV-48574 plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose. In a multiple-dose part run in asthma patients (200 mg up to 2300/1600 mg every 2 weeks), free TL1A in blood fell quickly and stayed down, with no dose limit from tolerability. Teva reported this as confirmed target engagement, but only in 2024, after the index trial started. No downstream airway biomarker was reported. In NCT04545385, systemic TL1A blockade in T2-low/non-T2 severe asthma gave no benefit (loss of asthma control 17/33 vs 13/32 on placebo) and the trial stopped for futility. The same drug worked in UC and Crohn's disease (NCT05499130, PMID:42726749). So the drug works on the target, but TL1A does not appear to drive this asthma population. Lung TL1A levels were not measured, and patient selection (F3) is a possible secondary cause.

Sacubitril/valsartan gave valsartan exposure equivalent to valsartan 320 mg. It raised renin and angiotensin II in healthy volunteers, showing AT1 blockade (PMID:19934029, published before the index trial). Clear dose-dependent BP lowering (NCT01193101) and HFrEF outcome benefit (NCT01035255) support engagement and pathway at doses up to 200 mg. No HCM-specific engagement data exist. Despite this, peak VO2 was unchanged in non-obstructive HCM (NCT04164732, p=0.55). SILICOFCM likewise showed no effect on exercise capacity, structure or biomarkers (PMID:38800948). AT1 antagonism therefore does not improve exercise capacity in established HCM. Valsartan did slow remodeling in early-stage sarcomeric HCM (PMID:34556856) but not in subclinical carriers (PMID:37672268). This hints at stage or subgroup and endpoint factors (F3/F4).

Valsartan exposure is shown in humans, including in HF patients (PMID:19934029, PMID:12409989). AT1 blockade was shown in healthy volunteers by rises in renin and angiotensin II (PMID:19934029, published before the index trial). The pathway effect is shown by dose-dependent BP lowering (NCT01193101) and by PARADIGM-HF efficacy in HFrEF (NCT01035255). No engagement data exist in men with erectile dysfunction. The index trial randomized only 27 men in a Phase 3 design against enalapril, an active RAS blocker. Its estimate was imprecise (difference +2.9 IIEF points favouring LCZ696, CI -3.3 to 9.0, p=0.34). The trial was clearly underpowered to answer the question, so the primary code is F7. An open-label study did show IIEF gains (PMID:37984637). F2 is possible but is not separable from F7 with this bundle.

The only source is the index Phase 1/2 trial NCT04282018. An RDFE was identified only for the tislelizumab combination in solid tumors (Part D: 160 and 320 mg). Part E expansion ORR was 0% at both doses (n=9, n=5). No RDFE was reported for monotherapy or for the zanubrutinib combination in hematologic malignancies. The bundle has no human PK, PI3Kδ engagement or pathway biomarker data. There are no other trials, no same-target comparators and no publications. Toxicity was frequent (many grade ≥3 and serious TEAEs), but nothing shows tolerability capped the dose below an engaging level. Because engagement is no_human_data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

NCT04282018 was a Phase 1/2 dose-finding study. A recommended dose for expansion was set only for BGB-10188 plus tislelizumab in solid tumours (160 and 320 mg). The Part E expansion cohorts were very small (n=9 and n=5) and both had 0% ORR. No dose for expansion was reported for monotherapy or for the zanubrutinib combination. Target engagement is shown only in preclinical work (pAKT inhibition and Treg reduction in mice; PMC11415975). The protocol planned pharmacodynamic biomarkers of PI3Kδ inhibition, but I found no published human PK, pAKT or Treg results. A 2024 phase 1a abstract exists, but I could not see any data from it. The sponsor gave no stated reason for stopping. Because engagement has no human data, I cannot tell whether the drug never hit PI3Kδ or the mechanism simply doesn't work in solid tumours. The very small expansion cohorts point to F7 as a secondary code.

In the first-in-human trial NCT04336098 (ESMO 2021 abstract, published before the index trial began), SRF617's pharmacokinetics were linear and tracked target occupancy. At the 1400 mg Q2W recommended dose it was well tolerated and kept full CD39 occupancy for the whole dosing interval. So exposure and engagement were adequate, and tolerability did not cap the dose. The patients had mixed solid tumors, so engagement was not shown specifically in prostate cancer. The company said in a 2020 press release that the drug showed pharmacodynamic activity, but no biopsy data on CD39 ATPase inhibition were reported, so pathway has no human data. In the index trial NCT05177770 (mCRPC, combined with etrumadenant and zimberelimab), 0 of 15 patients responded. Fully engaging the target without any response points most to F2. The trial was small and was stopped for 'strategic reasons' (F8/F7).

Index trial NCT00558467 showed no tic effect: YGTSS total tic change -7.16 vs -7.17, p=0.996. PMID:22407510 concludes there was no evidence pramipexole suppresses tics. The pillars are inferred adequate because pramipexole met efficacy endpoints through central D2/D3 agonism in RLS and PD (NCT00654498, NCT01968460; PMID:28096656). PET in PD patients showed receptor occupancy and prolactin suppression (PMID:27408789). That PET evidence comes from PD patients, was published after the index trial, and the pediatric dose used is not shown. Tolerability did not cap the dose (no serious AEs on pramipexole). Aripiprazole's approval in Tourette rests on a functionally opposite, antagonist-like action, so it does not imply this agonist hypothesis should work. The dopamine-agonist hypothesis for tics appears not to hold.

In the index Phase 1 escalation (NCT03894618; PMID:40042547), Cmax and AUC rose with dose, showing plasma exposure, but half-life was only about 20 h. No DLTs occurred up to 24 mg/kg, so the dose was not limited. Patients showed pharmacodynamic signs of OX40 engagement: dose-dependent egress of CD4+OX40+ cells and more Ki67+ CD4/CD8 memory cells. These support engagement and pathway in the disease setting, though only in blood and only published after the trial started. Efficacy was minimal (1 iPR in 46 evaluable patients). The authors attribute this mainly to disease characteristics and prior PD-1/L1 treatment (61% of patients), pointing to population. Alternatives they raise are PD-1 arm neutralization by circulating inhibitors and ADA, or poor tumor penetration (F1a). Mechanism irrelevance (F2) is also possible. PD-L1 engagement was never measured.

The index trial NCT03194776 tested LLG783 at 6 mg/kg IV in 46 patients. It missed its walking endpoint, and the LLG783 arm did numerically worse than placebo: change in maximum walking distance at week 16 was 19.1 m vs 36.8 m (p=0.26). Safety was similar between arms, so tolerability did not cap the dose. LLG783's target is unclear. Only a third-party drug database (Patsnap Synapse) lists it as an LDLR antagonist, and the mechanism sections of the posted protocol are redacted. I found no human pharmacokinetic, target-engagement or biomarker data, no Phase 1 results, no publications and no sponsor statement on why the program stopped. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for PRAX-114. There are no Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts, and the index trial NCT04832425 posted no results. Other GABA-A positive modulators on the same target are FDA-approved for depression: zuranolone for MDD and PPD, and brexanolone for PPD. That suggests the mechanism can work in MDD. With no evidence that PRAX-114 engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U remains plausible because engagement was never measured. The later PTSD trial NCT05260541 ended for portfolio reasons, which does not inform the MDD failure. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

Stage 1 of the index trial (PMID:29500276) reported PK, LINE-1 demethylation in PBMCs, and promoter demethylation with gene re-expression in paired tumor biopsies and ascites in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer at the 30 mg/m2 dose carried into stage 2. PMID:33289590 also showed tumor demethylation after treatment. So exposure, engagement and pathway were shown in this disease. The dose was cut from 45 mg/m2 for myelosuppression, but demethylation was still seen at 30 mg/m2, so dosing was not limiting. Stage 2 missed its PFS primary endpoint (114 vs 64 days, p=0.065), despite better 6-month PFS. The mechanism was engaged without significant benefit, which supports F2. The authors call for predictive markers to select patients (PMID:31831561), so F3 is secondary.

The index trial NCT05920408 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation combination study with nivolumab. Its primary outcomes were safety, DLTs, tolerability and preliminary activity. It enrolled only 6 patients and posted no results. The sponsor stopped it because of the 'challenge for EXS21546 to reach suitable therapeutic index'. That points to a molecule-specific limit, where tolerable doses could not deliver adequate A2A blockade, rather than evidence that the target does not matter. So the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a, dose-limited). The earlier PK/PD study NCT04727138 posted no exposure or occupancy data, and the bundle has no PubMed or same-target evidence. Every pillar is therefore no_human_data. No efficacy readout occurred (F9), and given how thin the bundle is, U also applies.

In the platform trial NCT04225715, the arms adding the PD-L1 LNA antisense (RO7191863) to siRNA + NUC gave no clear benefit. Combo 7 had 0% HBsAg loss at FUW24, and Combo 8 had 6.7% with a CI spanning zero (-2.2 to 15.7). The bundle contains no human evidence on hepatic exposure, PD-L1 transcript knockdown, or downstream immune or pathway markers for this drug. It has no Phase 1 results and no abstracts. Other PD-L1 drugs succeeded only in oncology indications, not chronic HBV, so F1b does not apply. With engagement having no human data, the bundle cannot separate a molecule that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in HBV.

In healthy volunteers (PMID:38407540, PMID:36195338), LYS006 gave dose-proportional plasma exposure and >90% predose inhibition of LTB4 production in blood and skin blister cells at 20 mg b.i.d. and above. There was no dose-limiting toxicity, so the dose was not capped. The index UC trial (NCT04074590) used 20 mg and showed no benefit (remission 8.95% vs 12.24% placebo). No downstream pathway marker or colonic engagement was measured in UC patients, and the engagement data were published only in 2024. The drug also failed in acne (NCT03497897) and hidradenitis suppurativa (NCT03827798) despite adequate engagement, which points to LTA4H/LTB4 not driving these diseases. The trial was small and terminated for strategic reasons (F7 secondary).

In healthy volunteers, LYS006 had dose-proportional plasma exposure, with drug measured in skin biopsy and blister fluid (PMID:36195338). It gave >90% predose inhibition of LTB4 production in blood and skin blister cells at 20 mg BID and above (PMID:38407540). There was no dose-limiting toxicity up to 80 mg BID, so the index dose of 20 mg BID was not capped. Despite this engagement, inflammatory lesions at week 12 were essentially unchanged versus placebo (GMR 0.93, NCT03497897). Downstream pathway effects in acne patients were not measured, and the engagement data were from healthy volunteers and published after the index trial. Parallel failures in hidradenitis suppurativa (NCT03827798) and ulcerative colitis (NCT04074590) support the view that LTA4H/LTB4 does not drive these neutrophilic diseases as tested.

The NOSTRA III trial (NCT02794168) missed its primary endpoint, 6-month eGOS. Exposure: in the Phase IIa study of TBI patients (PMID:24831445), VAS203 metabolites were found in brain microdialysate. No source measured NOS1 or NOS2 inhibition in humans, such as NO metabolite levels. The intracranial brain markers (ICP, CPP and brain metabolism) did not change, so the brain pathway pillar is inadequate. In healthy volunteers, the drug caused renal vasoconstriction (PMID:30666700). That shows systemic NOS inhibition, but it is not evidence of engagement of the brain NOS1/NOS2 targets. The sponsor pointed to timing, citing a post-hoc benefit when infusion began within 12 hours, which suggests F4/F3. Because engagement is unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01843894 was a Phase 1/2 study of topical RU-101 in severe dry eye. Its only primary outcome was ocular adverse events, and its endpoint is classified not_efficacy. No results, failure readout or stop reason are posted, so the trial was not an efficacy test of the drug, which fits F9. The bundle has no human data on ocular-surface exposure, engagement or pathway effects for albumin replacement in dry eye. The IV Phase 1 trials (NCT04384523, NCT05249374) cover a different route and disease and report only safety. If an efficacy failure were assumed, the mechanism would be indeterminate (U). The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

Donepezil is FDA-approved for Alzheimer disease through central AChE inhibition. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate for the same CNS target at comparable doses. The bundle has no direct AChE inhibition or biomarker data in Down syndrome; PMID:15701773 is a title-only DS pharmacokinetics report. The index extension (NCT00675025) was terminated because sufficient efficacy was not met, with no safety concern, and VABS-II changes were similar in prior-donepezil and prior-placebo arms. Earlier small studies in non-demented DS (PMID:14561111) showed no benefit beyond a possible language effect. Benefit was suggested only in DS with Alzheimer dementia (PMID:12117361), which hints at a population issue (F3). Overall, cholinergic enhancement does not appear to drive cognitive dysfunction in children with DS as tested.

PDA-002 is a placenta-derived adherent cell therapy with no defined molecular target. The sources describe it only as anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory. The index DPN trial (NCT02552277) used change in epidermal nerve fiber density as its primary endpoint but posted no results, and no stated reason for stopping was found. The Phase 1 trial (NCT01859117) reported only safety, with no dose-limiting toxicities up to 100×10^6 cells. It gave no cell persistence, tissue exposure, or pharmacodynamic data. The DFU Phase 2 (NCT02264288) was ended for business reasons. No human evidence of exposure, engagement, or pathway effect was found, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The code is U.

PDA-002 is a placenta-derived MSC-like cell product with no defined molecular target. The index trial NCT02552277 was a small (n=26) exploratory study in diabetic peripheral neuropathy, despite the 'diabetic kidney disease' label, using epidermal nerve fiber density as its primary endpoint. It posted no results, and no stop reason or sponsor explanation was found. The Phase 1 trial NCT01859117 measured only safety, and showed no dose-limiting toxicities up to 100×10^6 cells. NCT02264288, in diabetic foot ulcers, ended for business reasons. No human data on cell persistence, engagement or pathway markers was found. Nothing separates a product that failed to act from a mechanism that does not matter here, so the code is U. The small exploratory design also suggests F7.

The index trial NCT02531178 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study in 8 RA patients. It had no efficacy endpoint, so the program did not stop on a failed efficacy readout (F9). PMID:30156758 states the stop reason: most subjects developed antidrug antibodies (97% single-dose, 83% multiple-dose). Higher ADA titers shortened half-life and lowered exposure, and 'because of the high incidence of ADA-mediated drug clearance, ABBV-257 is no longer being developed.' Exposure was therefore compromised, which supports F1a as secondary. Immunogenicity is a molecule-specific liability, which supports F6 as secondary. No human TNF-α or IL-17A engagement data or pathway biomarkers are reported. The one serious adverse event was judged unrelated to treatment.

The index trial NCT00751205 (PMID:24105751) tested oral acetyl-L-carnitine, 1,000 mg every 3 days, for preventing sagopilone-induced neuropathy in patients with ovarian cancer or castration-resistant prostate cancer. It did not lower overall neuropathy incidence. No target is recorded, and no human data on tissue levels, engagement or pathway markers were found at this dose, in this setting or anywhere else. A healthy-volunteer study (PMID:41243468) did report low oral bioavailability, but at different doses and published later. Grade ≥3 neuropathy was lower only in the ovarian cancer subgroup, which hints at a subgroup effect (secondary F3). Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U. No sponsor explanation for stopping was found.

In the index trial (NCT00751205, PMID:24105751), acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC) was given to prevent nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy) caused by the chemotherapy drug sagopilone. It did not lower the overall rate of neuropathy compared with placebo. No molecular target is recorded for ALC, and no human data show that it reached the nerves, engaged a target or changed a neuroprotective biomarker at the trial dose. One healthy-volunteer study (PMID:41243468) reports that oral ALC is poorly absorbed, but it gives no pillar evidence at this dose. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. F3 is secondary because only ovarian cancer patients had less grade ≥3 neuropathy. The search found no explanation of the failure from the sponsor or investigators.

Acetyl-L-carnitine has no recorded molecular target, and the bundle has no human evidence for any pillar at the dose used (1,000 mg every 3 days), such as nerve-tissue exposure or a mechanistic biomarker. The one human pharmacokinetic study (PMID:41243468) found low oral bioavailability: a 1.5 g dose raised peak plasma levels only modestly, and that was in healthy volunteers. This hints that exposure may have been low, but it does not show the tissue level the mechanism would need. The index trial (NCT00751205, PMID:24105751) missed its primary endpoint of overall neuropathy incidence. Grade 3 or worse neuropathy was lower only in the ovarian cancer subgroup, which suggests a possible population effect (F3). With engagement unknown, the failure cannot be attributed. No web searches were run, so this rests on the bundle alone.

The index trial NCT02914990 was a Phase 1 safety and PK study of BPI-15086 in EGFR T790M-positive NSCLC. Its primary endpoint was adverse events, and no results, PubMed abstracts or other trials are in the bundle. There is no human evidence on exposure, EGFR engagement or downstream pathway effects for this drug. Other EGFR inhibitors, including osimertinib and lazertinib (third-generation T790M-active agents), afatinib, erlotinib and gefitinib, are FDA-approved in NSCLC, so the target is validated in this disease. This points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b), since no pillar evidence shows adequate engagement. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test, F9 also applies. The bundle is very thin.

The index trial NCT01526330 was a Phase 1/2 single intradiscal dose study. Its primary outcome was safety and tolerability over 12 weeks, and it is classified not_efficacy. No results were posted, so it was not an efficacy test of YH14618. The later Phase 2 trial NCT02320019, which had a patient-reported endpoint, also has no posted results. The bundle has no human exposure, TGFB1 engagement or pathway data, and no abstracts. If the program is instead judged as an efficacy failure, it is indeterminate (U), because engagement was never shown. SB-01, which acts on the same target, reached Phase 3 but did not succeed in the bundle, so F1b does not apply.

SUN-131 is Senju's corticosteroid transdermal patch (1.5% TDS) for chalazion. In the Phase 3 index trial NCT03248440, complete response by Day 15 was 32/132 on SUN-131 vs 28/131 on placebo (p=0.579), and there were no serious adverse events, so tolerability did not limit the dose. The Phase 2 trial NCT02338648 posted no results. No human data were found on drug levels in eyelid tissue, glucocorticoid receptor engagement, or anti-inflammatory biomarkers. AdisInsight lists the drug only as still in Phase III, and no sponsor statement on why it failed was found. No other glucocorticoid receptor drug has an approval in chalazion specifically. So the evidence cannot tell apart a patch that delivered too little drug to the lesion from a mechanism that does not work in this setting.

The index trial NCT03004846 enrolled only Part A (n=8). Its primary outcomes were descriptive safety and plasma PK (0 SAEs, no application-site reactions), and the Part B efficacy endpoints (TPSS, PGA, PASI) were never reported. It was therefore not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Elsewhere, the earlier plaque test (NCT02548052/PMID:29150844) is listed, but its abstract gives no results. PMID:39396455 attributes GSK2981278's clinical failure to a poor pharmacokinetic profile, but its support is in vitro metabolic instability and animal bioavailability, which do not count as human evidence. This hints at F1a. No human skin exposure, RORγt engagement or IL-17 pathway data are shown, so a target-versus-molecule judgement is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT03182413 tested THN102 (modafinil plus low-dose flecainide) for sustained attention in 20 healthy volunteers under total sleep deprivation. It was completed, with no results posted and no stated stop reason. It was not an efficacy test in amphetamine abuse, and the bundle shows no failed readout. The pillars are inferred_adequate: modafinil is FDA-approved for narcolepsy and obstructive sleep apnea, acting through central DAT inhibition and wake promotion at comparable doses (PMID:25080137, PMID:38467484). That approval implies brain exposure and engagement, but no direct measurement exists in stimulant-use patients. THN102 was being developed for narcolepsy (PMID:29635319), so the amphetamine-abuse label does not match this healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic study. F9 applies. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT03182413 is a Phase 1 study of THN102 (modafinil plus low-dose flecainide, PMID:29635319) in healthy volunteers under total sleep deprivation. It posted no results and gave no stop reason, so it was not an efficacy test in primary biliary cholangitis. No failed readout is shown. Modafinil's approvals for narcolepsy and OSA support inferring CNS exposure, DAT engagement and the wake-promoting pathway at comparable doses (PMID:38467484). No engagement data come from PBC patients; the PBC fatigue trial NCT00943176 has no results. Nothing in the bundle attributes the stop to efficacy, toxicity or design, so F9 fits best. The bundle is thin and the link between the index trial and PBC is unclear.

No direct human DAT occupancy or CSF data are in the bundle. However, modafinil at 200 mg/day is approved and effective for narcolepsy and hypersomnia through the same CNS target compartment (PMID:25080137, PMID:38467484). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate at the index dose of 200 mg/day. Tolerability did not cap the dose: toxicity was comparable, with only more grade ≤2 nausea. Despite this, the MOTIF trial showed no significant benefit on docetaxel-related fatigue (P=0.15; PMID:24337761, NCT00917748). That suggests DAT inhibition does not meaningfully relieve this fatigue. Secondary codes: the authors note only a modest trend and call for larger, longer trials, implying underpowering (F7). Prior benefit was reported in a severe-fatigue subgroup (F3).

The index trial (NCT00917748, PMID:24337761) gave modafinil 200 mg/day for docetaxel-related fatigue in mostly prostate cancer patients and missed its primary endpoint (MDASI fatigue AUC, P=0.15). The bundle has no direct human exposure, DAT occupancy or biomarker data. However, modafinil is approved for narcolepsy, hypersomnia and OSA via central DAT inhibition at about 200 mg (PMID:25080137, PMID:38467484). That success in the same CNS compartment at a comparable dose makes all three pillars inferred_adequate. Tolerability was comparable to placebo, so the dose was not limited. The lack of benefit therefore points to the mechanism not relieving chemotherapy-related fatigue as tested (F2). The authors note a modest trend and call for larger, longer trials, suggesting possible underpowering (F7).
