In healthy volunteers, [11C]raclopride PET showed brain penetration and concentration-dependent striatal D2/D3 occupancy that plateaued at about 40% (PMID:25248987, published 2015, before the index start in 2017). The authors interpret this as saturable binding to a receptor subpopulation underlying the drug's stabilizer mechanism, not as insufficient engagement. Prolactin rose linearly with plasma level (PMID:25248987, PMID:14973308), showing pituitary D2 pathway effect. Single doses up to 150 mg were well tolerated; there is no evidence the index dose was capped. Engagement was never shown in stroke patients, and the index trial (NCT04127669) posted no results or stated reason. Taking engagement as adequate, the mechanism appears not to drive post-stroke residual symptoms (F2). If ~40% occupancy is judged partial, F1a would apply instead. Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01567683 is a vehicle-controlled safety and tolerability study of a new topical 0.09% imiquimod formulation in healthy subjects. It is not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Topical imiquimod engages TLR7 in human skin: healthy-volunteer challenge studies show TLR7-driven inflammation with IL-6 and MxA induction (PMID:29768709, PMID:32043302, PMID:37545524). Approved efficacy in genital warts (NCT00674739, NCT00735462) supports inferred skin exposure. This engagement evidence is not from DIPG patients and was published after 2012. The separate DIPG vaccine-adjuvant trial NCT01400672 was terminated for 'Treatment ineffective; Extreme toxicity', which suggests possible toxicity (F6). The bundle cannot attribute that toxicity to imiquimod rather than the vaccine.

The index trial NCT01567683 was a Phase 1 vehicle-controlled safety and tolerability study of a new 0.09% topical imiquimod formulation in healthy subjects. It was not an efficacy test in neurofibromatosis type 1, and it posted no results or failure. Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate because topical imiquimod met pivotal endpoints through TLR7 in skin (genital warts NCT00674739 and NCT00735462; approvals for actinic keratosis and basal cell carcinoma). In healthy-volunteer skin, topical imiquimod produced TLR7-driven IRF and NF-κB responses (MxA, IL-6, immune cell influx) (PMID:29768709, PMID:32043302, PMID:37545524), so the pathway pillar holds. The bundle has no engagement data in NF1 patients; the NF1 trial NCT00865644 posted no outcome. The stop is therefore not an efficacy failure of the drug.

In the index Phase 1 (NCT02955251; PMID:33608377), exposure rose roughly dose-proportionally from 0.4 to 3.6 mg/kg. The MTD was not reached, so dose was not limited by tolerability. CD40 receptor occupancy exceeded 90% on peripheral B-cells from 0.8 mg/kg in patients with advanced solid tumors, so engagement was adequate. However, there were no consistent changes in intratumoral CD8+ T-cells, PD-L1+ cells or immune gene expression, so the pathway pillar was inadequate. The best response was stable disease (36% at the RP2D). Engagement data were published in 2021, after the index trial started. Tumor-dependent activation may not mirror peripheral occupancy. The abstract hints at a link with mesothelin expression, which is why F3 is listed as secondary.

The index trial (NCT05679479; PMID:40222976) randomized only 108 patients. Its primary 28-day mortality endpoint showed a large numerical reduction (1.96% vs 7.69%) but missed significance (P=0.17) because events were few. The 56-day mortality secondary endpoint was significant, and the authors call the results promising. This reads as an underpowered trial, not an inactive drug. Exposure was shown in humans: phase 1 PK and lung biodistribution (PMID:34001849). Engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred adequate because DEFLECT (NCT04586153; PMID:36717539) met its mortality endpoint in COVID-19 at 0.12 mg/kg, a comparable dose. DEFLECT also showed lower viral load and IL-8/IL-4 at 0.2–0.3 mg/kg. Tolerability did not limit the dose.

The first-in-human abstract for NCT04881045 (ASCO 2023) covered 18 patients with solid tumours given 150–2400 mg subcutaneously. Drug exposure was measured but did not rise in proportion to dose. In blood, the drug occupied more than 95% of PD-L1 and more than 70% of CD47. Its predicted downstream effect also appeared: IFNγ, TNFα, CXCL9/10 and CCL3/4 rose with dose. Despite this, only 1 of 18 patients responded (ORR 5.6%). At the top dose, 2 of 3 patients had dose-limiting grade 4 drops in blood counts (neutropenia and thrombocytopenia), which fits a CD47-related effect. Occupancy was already high at lower doses, so tolerability did not cap engagement. Pfizer gave no reason for stopping, and this evidence was published after the trial began. Occupancy was measured only in blood, not in tumour tissue. Best fit: the mechanism was engaged and gave no benefit (F2).

The index Phase III trial (Probio-SK-005, NCT02819960) tested a probiotic mixture of BB-12 and LGG. It missed its primary endpoint: grade 3/4 diarrhea was 7.9% on probiotic vs 11.8% on placebo (p=0.38). Earlier, the pilot trial had shown a non-significant trend toward benefit. The proposed mechanism is lower intestinal beta-glucuronidase activity, but the pages I found report no human data on gut colonization, enzyme inhibition or a downstream biomarker. So engagement is no_human_data, and nothing separates a probiotic that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter. That makes the primary code U. A later pooled analysis reported benefit in patients with a colostomy, so F3 (subgroup) is a secondary code.

The published phase III paper on NCT02819960 tested BB-12 plus LGG (Probio-Tec) and missed its primary endpoint: grade 3/4 diarrhea was 7.9% on the probiotic vs 11.8% on placebo (p=0.38). The investigators measured none of the proposed mechanism in this trial: no gut colonization, no microbiome profile, no stool beta-glucuronidase activity, and no adherence check. The only other human data are fecal acetate (SCFA) levels from NCT03755765 in an antibiotic-diarrhea setting, which showed no clear difference, and that is not the same pathway. So there is no evidence on target engagement, and nothing separates a probiotic that never acted from a mechanism that does not matter. Secondary codes: the placebo arm had fewer grade 3/4 events than expected (11.8% vs the 25% assumed), which suggests F7, and benefit appeared only in a colostomy subgroup, which suggests F3.

The index trial NCT04147715 is a Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study. Its primary outcomes are safety, plasma PK, food effect and a drug-drug interaction with dolutegravir. It was not an efficacy test of S-648414, so F9 applies. Plasma PK was measured, but no target is recorded and nothing shows the concentrations needed at a site of action, so exposure adequacy cannot be judged. No engagement or pathway data appear. Tolerability was good up to 1000 mg single dose, with no SAEs or discontinuations, so the dose was not limited. The bundle has no stop reason, other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators, so why the program ended is indeterminate beyond this (secondary U).

The phase 1 trial of PCA062 (NCT02375958) tested doses from 0.4 to 5.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks. The MTD was 3.6 mg/kg, and the dose-limiting toxicity was thrombocytopenia, attributed to the DM1 payload rather than to P-cadherin. Serum exposure rose in proportion to dose and no antidrug antibodies formed, so the authors called exposure adequate. No human data were found on tumor drug uptake, P-cadherin binding or internalization, or a downstream biomarker. Only 1 of 47 patients had a partial response, and tumor P-cadherin level did not predict response. Novartis stopped development for limited activity at the MTD. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that failed to engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, hence U. A dose ceiling set by payload toxicity (F1a) is possible but not shown.

The index prophylaxis trial NCT05201794 was terminated for 'portfolio reprioritization', explicitly not for safety. Its primary endpoint favored the drug numerically: 2/265 and 2/266 infections versus 6/265 on placebo. With so few events the result was not significant (p≈0.14), so the trial could not show efficacy either way rather than showing a clear failure. In humans, PMID:42572208 reports plasma PK across Phase 1 studies and a controlled human DENV-3 challenge study (NCT05048875, registered before the index trial). That study showed antiviral activity on viral RNA, with a concentration-dependent Emax relationship. This supports exposure and engagement, though the magnitude at the index doses is not stated. The bundle shows a business stop, with underpowering (F7) as a secondary contributor.

VE800, a defined bacterial consortium given after vancomycin pretreatment and combined with nivolumab, produced almost no responses in NCT04208958: ORR was 1/20 in gastric cancer, 0/20 in melanoma and 0/14 in colorectal cancer. Safety was acceptable, with only one VE800-related serious AE, so toxicity did not end the program. The bundle contains no human data on bacterial colonization or engraftment (exposure), on immune activation such as CD8 T-cell tumor infiltration (engagement), or on any downstream pathway marker. There are no other trials, no publications and no comparator drugs. Nothing separates a consortium that failed to colonize or activate immunity from a mechanism that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate.

In the index trial (NCT04402957, 61 patients), the primary endpoint was a tie: 28/30 on LSALT versus 28/31 on placebo were alive and free of respiratory failure or dialysis at day 28. The Phase 1 trial (NCT03772678) reported only safety at 1–5 mg; the company said the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. I found no human data on drug levels in lung or kidney, binding to DPEP1, or a downstream biomarker. The 5 mg daily IV dose in the index trial was the top Phase 1 dose. The company says the results validated DPEP1, but that claim is not supported by pillar data. Very few patients in either arm had the outcome, which suggests the trial was underpowered (F7). Because engagement was never measured, the code is U.

The Phase 1 trial (NCT03772678) only looked at safety and pharmacokinetics (PK) up to 5 mg/day, and the bundle has no PK values. I found no human data on DPEP1 binding, neutrophil adhesion blockade or levels in lung or kidney tissue. In the index trial (NCT04402957; PMID:38490660), serum CXCL10 fell with LSALT (p=0.02). That is a non-specific inflammatory marker, not a pathway readout tied to DPEP1. The primary endpoint showed no difference: 28/30 LSALT vs 28/31 placebo. The event rate was very low in a 61-patient COVID-19 trial, so the trial was underpowered for its hard outcome (secondary F7). The sponsor called the result validation and moved to AKI (NCT05879432). Engagement data are missing, so nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a target that does not matter. Code U.

S42909 (Servier/Ilkos) has no single recorded target. The protocol for NCT03077165 describes a pleiotropic anti-leukocyte-adhesion/endothelial mechanism (E-selectin/VCAM-1 expression, NADPH oxidase), but only from in vitro and animal data. Human data cover only plasma PK. Oral bioavailability is low but was improved with a new formulation. Steady state was reached at 600–1800 mg, and repeated doses up to 1200 mg were tolerated (diarrhoea at higher doses). Plasma exposure was therefore shown, but no source reports human adhesion-molecule, oxidative-stress or other PD markers. The phase 2a showed no dose-response in ulcer-area reduction, and no failure explanation was found. Engagement has no human data, so a non-engaging drug can't be separated from an irrelevant mechanism: U.

S42909 is a Servier vascular NADPH oxidase inhibitor. The index trial NCT03077165 compared six groups and found no dose-response in ulcer area reduction at week 4. Group C reduced area least (-31%) and group A most (-53%). The protocol says pharmacokinetic samples and oxidative-stress biomarkers were collected, but I found no published human results. The only pharmacology data are from an animal wound model (PMID 27249648), which does not count. No human data show NADPH oxidase inhibition or a downstream biomarker change. No other drug on this target has succeeded in this disease. No toxicity limited the dose, and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Because there is no engagement evidence, this is indeterminate (U).

The Phase 1b PULSE trial (NCT03849599) gave PRV-300 to UC patients. Its safety primary endpoint was met: the drug was well tolerated and only 7.1% discontinued for adverse events, so the dose was not capped (PMID:42896861). Colonic biopsies showed a greater but non-significant downregulation of TLR3 expression, which the authors call exploratory evidence of target engagement in UC. Engagement is therefore rated adequate, though the evidence is weak. The pathway pillar failed: the UC gene-expression signature was unchanged. Mayo score and endoscopy showed no benefit. PK results were not reported in the abstract. The authors conclude the results challenge a pivotal role of TLR3 in UC pathogenesis, supporting F2. F9 is secondary because the index trial was safety-primary and met that endpoint.

In healthy volunteers, BOS161721 at 1-240 mg showed linear PK with a half-life of 80-87 days (exposure). It suppressed IL-21-induced pSTAT3 dose-dependently, with a threshold at doses of 10 mg or more (engagement), and dose-dependently reversed IL-21-driven downregulation of BATF, IL6, LAG3 and SOCS3 (pathway) (PMID:31664766, NCT03036865). This Phase 1 trial was registered before the index trial began. The Phase 2 dose of 120 mg sits well above the engagement threshold, and the Phase 1b dose escalation showed no dose-limiting toxicity. Even so, SRI-4 at Day 210 did not differ from placebo (40/75 vs 19/37, p=0.84; NCT03371251). With adequate engagement and no tolerability limit, IL-21 neutralization does not appear to drive SLE as tested. Confidence is medium because engagement was not shown in SLE patients within the bundle.

The index trial NCT04377945 (JM-010 in Parkinson's dyskinesia) was terminated for stated 'business reasons' with no results posted, so there was no failed efficacy readout. The open-label extension NCT05516875 was also ended by business decision, explicitly not for safety. Exposure is adequate: human plasma PK is well characterised (PMID:9399013) and PET shows brain penetration (PMID:16402287). Engagement is inferred_adequate from migraine efficacy (NCT02745392) and modelled high 5-HT1B/1D occupancy (PMID:25488888). This inference is weaker for the central dyskinesia compartment. Central pathway effects in healthy volunteers, namely reduced motor cortical excitability and a growth hormone rise, support adequacy (PMID:9748054, PMID:10840172). No engagement data exist in dyskinesia patients.

The index trial NCT03466203 was a Phase 1 safety and tolerability study in obese volunteers. Its only primary outcome was adverse events, it posted no results, and it gave no stop reason. It was therefore not an efficacy test of LLF580/efimosfermin, so no efficacy failure is shown. The bundle contains no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. The NASH Phase 2 NCT04880031 also had safety-only primary outcomes, and its quote reports tolerability without biomarker data. Development then moved to MASH, with Phase 3 trials (e.g. NCT07221227) underway, but the bundle gives no stated business rationale for leaving obesity. If the obesity stop is treated as an efficacy question, it is indeterminate (U) because engagement data are absent.

The index trial NCT02649608 was an uncontrolled Phase 1 ascending-dose safety, tolerability and PK study in 15 Parkinson patients, not a controlled efficacy test. It completed with no stated stop reason, and no serious AEs or deaths were reported. Plasma PK was measured, but there is no brain penetration, receptor occupancy or pathway biomarker data for this CNS target. Open-label 'ON' responses (onset about 20–40 min, duration about 200–400 min) cannot be read as a placebo-controlled efficacy result. Other D1/D2 agonists are approved in Parkinson disease, but the bundle never shows an efficacy failure or gives a reason for stopping. F9 is primary; U is secondary because engagement has no human data.

In SARA-INT (NCT03452488), 400MW gait speed did not differ from placebo in the full analysis set. The publication (PMID:40026058) states that COVID-19 caused loss of 55% of on-site end-of-treatment efficacy assessments, reducing power. The 350 mg bid arm still improved gait speed by 0.07 m/s (full set, NS) and 0.09 m/s (per-protocol, p=0.008), with effects in higher-risk subgroups. Phase 1 PK (PMID:37057316) shows systemic exposure at 350–450 mg bid, well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. No human MAS receptor engagement or pathway biomarker data exist; myoglobin/CK-MB fell only at 450 mg bid. The positive COVID trial (NCT04472728) involves a different tissue compartment. Primary F7 (underpowered), with U because engagement is unmeasured.

ZPL-5212372 is a topical 1% ointment that blocks the HRH4 receptor. In index trial NCT02795832, it missed its primary endpoint: by observed case, EASI fell 34% on drug and 34% on placebo (p=0.50). No skin drug levels, H4 receptor occupancy or downstream biomarker data in humans turned up. The protocol plans to measure plasma PK and trough levels, but no results for them were found. The inhaled first-in-human trial (NCT01415102) posted no results. Other H4 antagonists (adriforant, JNJ-39758979, LEO 152020) also stopped at Phase 2, so none validates the target. That means a drug that never engaged H4 can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. Secondary F7: the trial was small and the placebo arm had heavy dropout (only 7 of 10 observed by Day 15), so results depended on how missing data were imputed.

CSJ148 combines LJP538 (anti-gB) and LJP539 (anti-pentamer). The first-in-human study and the Phase 2 paper show typical IgG1 pharmacokinetics, and trough levels in HCT patients stayed above the targeted efficacious concentrations, so exposure was adequate. No source measured target engagement in humans, such as serum neutralizing titers against HCMV or binding to viral glycoproteins. Viral load showed only non-significant trends, so the pathway pillar has no clear evidence either way. In NCT02268526 the drug missed its primary endpoint (RR 0.89, CI 0.61–1.31). Trough level did not track with the need for preemptive therapy. The authors point to a small trial and baseline imbalances between arms as possible confounders. Because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that failed to engage apart from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U.

LJP539 is an antibody against the HCMV pentameric complex and was given as part of CSJ148. Serum PK was dose-proportional and typical of IgG1, both in healthy volunteers (PMID:26926639) and in transplant patients in the phase 2 paper, so systemic exposure was adequate. No source measured engagement in humans, such as serum neutralizing titres or virus-bound antibody. The pathway evidence is only non-significant trends in viral load and pre-emptive therapy. NCT02268526 missed its primary endpoint (RR 0.89). The investigators pointed to more acute GVHD and unrelated-donor grafts in the CSJ148 arm, the small size of the trial, and severe T-cell deficiency that antibodies may not overcome. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02448914 was not an efficacy test of entacapone, let alone in methamphetamine dependence. It was a Phase 1 pharmacokinetic comparison of two levodopa/carbidopa(/entacapone) infusion gels in 11 Parkinson patients. Its levodopa AUC endpoint was analysed with a significant ratio (1.38, p<0.0001) and there were no serious AEs. In humans, entacapone reaches plasma, inhibits COMT and raises levodopa exposure (PMID:24925090, PMID:21927836, PMID:36309950). These data come from healthy volunteers and Parkinson disease, not methamphetamine users, and the bundle has no human data on central COMT engagement. The only methamphetamine study, the pilot NCT02058966, posted descriptive subjective-effect data without a stated failure. Nothing in the bundle shows an efficacy failure, so the code is F9.

The index trial's protocol and SAP (NCT04207801) say the first-in-human study in healthy volunteers, completed before the index trial, showed suitable PK and 'optimal IL-17 inhibition' at 600 mg BID, with IL-17 inhibition tracking drug levels. INDUS-2 compared 400 and 600 mg BID with placebo. Its posted PASI-75 rates were 18/30 and 19/30 against 8/30, which looks positive if Arm-3 was placebo, but the arms are unlabelled. INDUS-3 (NCT04855721) met its primary endpoint at 400 mg BID and missed it at the lower doses. Aurigene stopped development because the effect size was smaller than IL-17 antibodies and TYK2 inhibitors, not because the drug failed or caused safety problems. That makes this a competitive/commercial stop (F8). No engagement data come from psoriasis patients themselves.

In NCT04137289, BI 905711 was escalated to 4.8 mg/kg Q2W with no DLTs and no MTD reached, so the dose was not tolerability-capped. PK/PD showed linear dose exposure and at least 2-fold activation of plasma caspase 3/7 in GI cancer patients (PMID:41987415). This apoptotic pathway marker indicates TRAILR2 agonism in this disease; engagement is judged from that marker, since receptor occupancy was not measured directly. Despite this, there were zero confirmed responses across 110 patients, only 22% stable disease, and median PFS of about 7 weeks. The combination study (NCT05087992) also gave no responses. Other TRAILR2 agonists (conatumumab, tigatuzumab, dulanermin) never succeeded in these diseases, so F1b does not apply. The authors note that preclinical TRAILR2 activity has failed to translate to the clinic. This points to the mechanism not driving clinical benefit (F2).

In GI cancer patients, BI 905711 showed linear dose-proportional exposure. Plasma caspase 3/7 rose at least 2-fold, an apoptotic pathway readout consistent with TRAILR2 agonism (PMID:41987415). Direct receptor binding was not measured, so engagement is judged adequate from this downstream activation. Doses went up to 4.8 mg/kg with no DLTs and no MTD reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, there were 0 objective responses across all dose levels, PFS was about 6-7 weeks, and only 22% had stable disease (NCT04137289). The combination with FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab also gave no responses (NCT05087992). The authors note limited clinical activity and difficulty translating preclinical TRAILR2-agonist activity, and no other TRAILR2 agonist in these diseases has gone beyond phase 2. This points to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested. The pharmacodynamic data were published after the index trial started.

CSB-001 is topical oremepermin alfa, a deleted-variant hepatocyte growth factor that activates c-Met. In the index trial (NCT04909450), complete corneal healing was 38.9% with drug vs 31.4% with vehicle, a non-significant difference, and there was no excess toxicity. I found no human data on corneal or tear drug levels, c-Met activation or downstream biomarkers. No Phase 1 results were posted, there are no PubMed abstracts, and no other c-Met agonist is listed for comparison. A trade profile says the drug failed in neurotrophic keratitis and the company moved to limbal stem cell deficiency (NCT06452316) and corneal scars (NCT06257355), but the sources give no reason for the failure. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT04731922, was a first-in-human single- and multiple-dose study of subcutaneous TAK-510 in healthy adults. Its primary endpoints were safety only (vital signs, ECG, lab values, side effects), so it did not test efficacy. Takeda's trial page says the drug was meant for nausea and vomiting. The plasma drug-level results were registered but withheld for confidentiality, so there is no human exposure data. No human data on NPY2R binding or downstream biomarkers was found, and there are no papers or company statements explaining the stop. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F9 also applies because the index trial was not an efficacy test.

Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (PMID:40087848) showed linear PK, near-100% BTK occupancy at doses ≥2 mg (>80% at 24 h), and 55–89% inhibition of basophil activation. Engagement and pathway effect were therefore adequate at the index doses (2 and 4 mg). This was shown only in healthy volunteers and published after the index trial started. The index trial (NCT03605251, PMID:37217273) missed ACR20 (78.9% vs 60.0%, p=0.053), with only numerical gains. Despite near-complete engagement, the benefit was modest, so the mechanism is probably not a strong driver of RA (F2). The high placebo response and small trial (n=91) may have contributed (F7). Bleeding events, consistent with on-target platelet effects, clouded the risk-benefit (F5).

JTA-004 combines plasma proteins, hyaluronic acid and clonidine and has no single recorded target. No human data were found on exposure, target engagement or pathway markers such as intra-articular levels or synovial biomarkers. In the index Phase II/III (NCT02740231), the chosen formulation lowered WOMAC pain numerically but not significantly more than hylan G-F 20 (p=0.141); only 35–39 patients per arm were analysed against an active comparator, which points to a possible power problem (F7). The later Phase III also failed against both placebo and hylan G-F 20, with all arms performing about the same. Bone Therapeutics cited only a post-hoc subgroup signal (F3). With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In NCT02037893 every arm showed a large 1-hour pain drop: placebo -4.9, benzocaine -4.6, antipyrine -5.0, combination -4.3, with about 22-30 per arm. A placebo response this large, with no separation between any arms, means the small trial could not discriminate an analgesic effect. Its design could not answer the question (F7). The bundle has no human data on benzocaine reaching or blocking sodium channels in middle-ear or tympanic nerve tissue. Topical sensory and analgesic effects are shown only in oral and skin tissue (PMID:16583593, PMID:25880000, PMID:32852421), a different compartment. So engagement is no_human_data and U also applies. A later Phase 3 otic trial (NCT03116737) suggests the mechanism was not abandoned. Confidence is low because no source states why the trial failed.

The index trial NCT02908620 compared two benzocaine spray formulations in healthy volunteers: CTY-5339-A against CTY-5339-CB. It contained no placebo arm. Both arms produced measurable anesthesia, about 16-18 min on pin prick and 45-51 min on heat threshold. The primary endpoint was superiority of one formulation over the other, and it missed (p=0.322 and p=0.134). That is a formulation-versus-active-comparator test, not a test of whether benzocaine works, so the result is not an efficacy failure of the drug. Sodium-channel engagement and nerve block are inferred from benzocaine beating placebo on toothache pain (PMID:16583593), from raised sensory thresholds (PMID:25880000, PMID:32852421), and from the anesthesia seen in both index arms. Secondary F7: small n=18-20 per arm with wide confidence intervals.

The index trial NCT02908620 compared two benzocaine spray formulations (CTY-5339-A vs CTY-5339-CB) head-to-head for superiority in healthy volunteers. It had no placebo arm. Both arms produced measurable anesthesia: pin-prick duration was about 17 vs 16 min and heat-threshold duration about 45 vs 51 min. The missed endpoint therefore reflects no difference between formulations, not a lack of benzocaine activity. Peripheral sodium-channel block is supported by the anesthesia seen in both arms. Earlier human studies add support: benzocaine beat placebo for toothache (PMID:16583593), raised sensory thresholds in pain patients (PMID:25880000), and gave pin-prick anesthesia comparable to other agents (PMID:17694218). Because the trial was not an efficacy test of the drug itself, it is coded F9.

In the index HCC Phase 1 (NCT01942083; PMID:29898591), patients tolerated the drug well, no MTD was reached, and no one had an objective response (median PFS 1.4 months). The trial ended with the stated reason 'Company decision'. In the first-in-human trial (PMID:29511132), drug levels in plasma reached the micromolar range at 250 mg, the same dose recommended for HCC, so exposure counts as adequate. That paper also says no pharmacodynamic data were collected: the PBMC pSTAT3 assay was never used. I found no human evidence of STAT3 inhibition or of a downstream biomarker change. The HCC authors call for STAT3 biomarkers. No other STAT3 drug has succeeded in HCC, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement was never measured, the cause cannot be determined.

I found no human evidence that BI 706321 engaged RIPK2. The Phase 1 trials (NCT03971695, NCT04241458, NCT04714073, NCT05183360) posted plasma PK and safety only. The first-in-human protocol planned biomarker pharmacodynamics, but I found no published results. Exposure is coded inadequate only because the schema has no 'not assessed' value. There are plasma levels, but no gut-tissue levels and no stated level needed for the target. The 8 mg dose was not capped by tolerability. In the index trial (NCT04978493, n=49), the SES-CD change numerically favoured placebo plus ustekinumab. Baseline SES-CD was 2.1 points higher in the drug arm. The sponsor gave only 'Company decision' as the reason for stopping. No other RIPK2 drug has succeeded in Crohn's. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. F7 is secondary because the trial was small and the arms were unbalanced at baseline.

INM-755 is a topical cannabinol cream, and the index trial NCT04908215 enrolled only 19 patients. InMed reported that plasma CBN levels were in the picogram/mL range, which shows how little drug reached the bloodstream but says nothing about whether the cream reached or activated CB1/CB2 receptors in the skin. I found no skin drug levels, receptor engagement or downstream biomarker data in humans. The suction-blister study (PMID:39084539) in healthy volunteers measured wound healing, not target engagement. InMed said the non-wound itch result was not significant partly because the control cream itself relieved itch, and the CEO pointed to trial challenges including COVID disruption, so trial design (F7) is a secondary code. With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the primary code is U. InMed then said it would seek a partner rather than continue alone.

INM-755 is a topical cannabinol cream tested in a small Phase 2 epidermolysis bullosa trial (NCT04908215, n=19). The sponsor reported that the non-wound itch result was not statistically significant and blamed this partly on a strong anti-itch effect from the control cream (vehicle). Plasma CBN levels were in the picogram/mL range, which is expected for a skin-applied drug. The bundle has no skin drug levels and no human evidence of CB1/CB2 receptor engagement or of a downstream biomarker. The healthy-volunteer suction blister study (PMID:39084539) measured wound healing, not target engagement. No other drug on this target has succeeded in this disease. Engagement is no_human_data, so the code is U. F7 is secondary because the active control cream and small sample size limited what the trial could show.

The index trial, NCT02739373, was a Phase 1 PK/safety/PD study in healthy volunteers. It had no efficacy endpoint and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). An ACS abstract reports that once-daily dosing in healthy volunteers saturated peripheral PD-L1 at low plasma levels, so exposure and engagement were adequate. That evidence comes from healthy volunteers only and was published after the trial. No downstream pathway marker is reported. The sources say the short half-life made daily dosing necessary, which limited how practical the drug was. BMS then moved to a second-generation peptide, BMS-986238, which points to a molecule-optimization or business decision rather than a failed efficacy readout (F8 secondary).

A mechanistic substudy of 32 patients with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis inside the index trial (PMID:30844425, published 2019, after the 2015 start) showed immune engagement: reduced basophil activation, blunted seasonal IgE, fewer IL-4+ Th2 and Tfh cells, and induction of Tregs, Bregs and IgG4. That supports adequate engagement and pathway effect in the disease. Full-population primary CSMS results were never posted (NCT02560948). A second Phase 3 (NCT03724240) followed, which suggests the first did not succeed. With engagement adequate and no benefit shown at the primary endpoint, F2 fits the rules. The bundle never states why the trial failed, and the substudy subset did show a CSMS benefit, so trial execution or seasonal factors (F7) may explain it. Confidence is low.

The index trial of CYT107 in refractory NTM lung disease (NCT04154826) was terminated after 8 patients for 'non convincing results', with no results posted. In humans, rhIL-7 produced T-cell cycling, bcl-2 upregulation and sustained CD4+/CD8+ expansion (PMID:18573906, published 2008, before the index trial). It also raised blood lymphocytes and CD4+ counts in PML patients (PMID:35072281), so IL-7R engagement and the downstream pathway are shown systemically. Neither was measured in NTM patients, and the index dose is not shown. With engagement shown yet no convincing benefit, the most direct reading is that T-cell expansion does not drive NTM clearance (F2). The very small terminated trial limits what it could answer (F7). Confidence is low.

First-in-human rhIL-7 studies (PMID:18573906, 2008, before the 2020 index start) showed in vivo T-cell cycling, bcl-2 upregulation and sustained CD4+/CD8+ expansion. This is direct IL7R engagement and pathway activity, and it implies adequate systemic exposure, although no plasma PK is in the bundle. The PML cohort (PMID:35072281) also showed lymphocyte rises. None of these data come from NTM patients. The refractory NTM trial (NCT04154826) stopped after 8 patients for 'non convincing results', with no results posted. So the mechanism was engaged but did not convert sputum cultures, which fits F2. The very small, early-terminated trial means the question was answered weakly (F7). Thin evidence gives low confidence.

The index trial NCT03821038 tested IV bolus CYT107 in sepsis. It was terminated after 21 patients because of a 'PK issue detected after bolus IV route administration', with no results posted. Exposure by this route is therefore judged inadequate, and the mechanism was never properly tested. This is not a clinical efficacy failure, hence F9 as secondary. With non-IV dosing in other populations, rhIL-7 clearly engaged IL7R in humans: T-cell cycling, bcl-2 upregulation and sustained CD4/CD8 expansion (PMID:18573906, published before the index trial), and lymphocyte increases in PML (PMID:35072281). In sepsis, the earlier NCT02640807 posted immune-reconstitution counts without analysis, and controls responded similarly. PMID:23053510 is ex vivo only, so engagement in sepsis patients is not established.

The index phase 3 trial of pulsed iNO at 45 µg/kg IBW/h in fibrotic ILD on oxygen showed no MVPA benefit (difference 5.5 min/d, P=0.265). Secondary outcomes and a pulmonary-hypertension-probability subgroup also showed nothing. The therapy was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped (PMID:39141673). No direct sGC engagement or hemodynamic data appear in the bundle. Engagement is inferred from inhaled NO meeting its efficacy endpoint in neonatal pulmonary hypertension through pulmonary-vascular sGC (NCT00005776), but that dose differs from the index regimen. A 1995 case report (PMID:7598271) suggests iNO improved oxygenation in a fibrosis patient. The mechanism appears engaged without clinical benefit, consistent with the PAH futility (NCT02725372). The actigraphy endpoint was novel (secondary F4). Confidence is low.

The bundle has no direct human measurement of exposure, sGC activation or a downstream biomarker in preterm infants. All three pillars are instead inferred_adequate. Inhaled NO showed a statistically significant benefit in newborn respiratory failure/PPHN (NCT00005776), acting on the same sGC target in the same lung compartment, so the pathway must have held there. Despite this, survival without BPD at 36 weeks was not improved (80/229 vs 70/222, p=0.427; NCT00931632). Another BPD trial was worse with prolonged iNO (NCT00515281). Reviews call iNO 'less than a silver bullet' and its 'death knell' for BPD prevention (PMID:25266344, PMID:29467517). Together this indicates the mechanism does not drive BPD prevention. A review notes efficacy varies by population and disease stage (PMID:31372499), supporting F3 as secondary.

The index trial NCT02824003 (n=15) was a mechanistic MRS study of hepatic glycogen and lipid content, not an efficacy test. Its missed endpoint, no change in glycogen, was framed as a reassuring finding (PMID:30765435). Human PK was characterized (PMID:28132162). Target engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred from dose-dependent fasting glucose and HbA1c reductions in T2D patients, with the primary endpoint met in NCT02583919 and confirmed in PMID:39008234. So the drug worked on its stated endpoint. The concerns raised were rises in hepatic lipid and transaminases, consistent with on-target GCGR antagonism, which suggests a safety/benefit issue (secondary F5). The bundle does not state why development stopped.

Oral doxercalciferol (2.5–7.5 mcg/day) showed no separation from placebo on PASI-50 at week 12, with about 20% responders in every arm and no dose response (NCT00601107). Its FDA approval for secondary hyperparathyroidism implies systemic exposure and parathyroid VDR engagement (inferred_adequate exposure). The bundle shows no skin VDR engagement or pathway marker in psoriasis, and dose comparability is not shown, so engagement is no_human_data. Other VDR agonists, topical calcipotriene and calcitriol, are FDA-approved for psoriasis. The target is therefore validated in this disease, which points to this molecule, its oral route or its skin exposure rather than the target (F1b). Without engagement data, U also applies. No hypercalcemia or dose-capping evidence is shown.

EDP2939 is an oral microbial extracellular vesicle that acts on the small intestine. The bundle records no molecular target for it. The index trial, NCT05682222, was a KLH/imiquimod immune-challenge study in healthy volunteers and has no posted results. A secondary source reports results only for the sister product EDP1815, which had no effect on the KLH challenge. No human exposure, engagement or pathway biomarker data for EDP2939 were found. Evelo stopped developing EDP2939 after its Phase 2 trial in moderate psoriasis missed the PASI-50 primary endpoint at week 16. The company gave no mechanistic explanation. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug never engaged its target or whether the mechanism does not matter in this disease, so the code is U.

The bundle contains only the index trial NCT05831670, a completed Phase 2 study in ulcerative colitis with a Week 8 modified Mayo clinical response primary endpoint. It has no posted results, no stated stop reason and no recorded target. There are no Phase 1 results, no other trials, no same-target comparator drugs and no PubMed abstracts. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in UC, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

CSL346 at 8 or 16 mg/kg q4w did not lower UACR versus placebo (p=0.485 and p=0.750; NCT04419467, PMID:39150859). Subgroups and tubular injury biomarkers showed no effect either. The Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study in healthy volunteers (protocol) showed dose-proportional plasma PK and good tolerability up to 20 mg/kg IV, so systemic exposure was adequate and the dose was not capped. However, no source I could access reports human free VEGF-B suppression, target binding or a downstream pathway marker. The trial paper says pharmacodynamics were measured, but the full text was blocked. A later review only speculates about poor intrarenal engagement. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so U.

Exposure is adequate: plasma PK was dose-proportional with a long half-life, and exposure was preserved in CKD (PMID:28180234, PMID:28933798). Engagement and pathway are adequate: tecarfarin lowered vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X to the same degree as warfarin at matched INR, with dose-dependent INR rises and no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:28180234, PMID:36622539). In AF patients, the phase 2 study NCT00431782 (registered 2006, before the index trial) kept INR in range, with TTR 71.4% (PMID:19738136). The index trial NCT00691470 tested whether TTR beat warfarin, which acts by the same mechanism. With engagement clearly adequate, a miss reflects no added benefit from the mechanism as tested. No results are posted, so trial execution (F7) cannot be excluded. Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT00691470 compared tecarfarin with warfarin on time in therapeutic INR range. It is classified not_efficacy, has no stated stop reason and no posted results, so the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout against placebo. The pillars are shown in healthy volunteers. Exposure was dose-proportional (PMID:28180234) and preserved in CKD (PMID:28933798). Engagement is shown by lowered vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X, similar to warfarin at matched INR. Pathway is shown by a dose-dependent INR rise at 10-20 mg (PMID:28180234, PMID:36622539). None of this was in patients with the program's diseases, and it was published after 2008. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The index trial was not an efficacy test of the drug's mechanism: F9.

The index trial NCT00691470 compared tecarfarin with warfarin on percent time in therapeutic INR range. This is a quality-of-anticoagulation comparison against an active VKA, classified not_efficacy, and no results or stop reason were posted. It was therefore not an efficacy test of the drug in myocardial infarction (F9). The pillars hold in healthy volunteers. Exposure is dose-proportional with a long half-life (PMID:28180234; PMID:28933798, which also included CKD patients). Engagement and pathway are shown by dose-dependent INR rise and reduced factors II, VII, IX and X, similar to warfarin, and doses were titratable and well tolerated (PMID:28180234, PMID:36622539). No engagement data come from patients with this disease. The human PK/PD data were published after the index trial started in 2008.

The index trial NCT00691470 compared tecarfarin with warfarin on percent time in INR therapeutic range. That is an anticoagulation-quality endpoint, classified not_efficacy, rather than a clinical efficacy test, and no results or failure reason are posted. The human pillars hold. Exposure was dose-proportional (PMID:28180234, PMID:28933798). VKOR antagonism, shown as INR rises and factor II/VII/IX/X reductions comparable to warfarin, was demonstrated in healthy volunteers with titratable dosing and good tolerability (PMID:28180234, PMID:36622539). However, this engagement was not shown in atrial flutter or atrial fibrillation patients in the bundle; NCT00431782 posted no results. The engagement evidence was also published after the 2008 index start. This is best coded F9: not an efficacy failure of the drug's mechanism.

CVXL-0107 (naftazone) is described only as a 'glutamate release inhibitor', with no molecular target given. The 2018 MDS abstract for NCT02641054 (n=16, crossover, 40 mg four times daily) found no effect on the MDS-UPDRS III or AIMS AUCs (p=0.85 and p=0.57). It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Only plasma PK was reported: CVXL-0107 peaked at a median of 141 min versus 20 min for levodopa. There are no CNS exposure, engagement or biomarker data. The investigators guessed the cause was the wrong dose and/or mismatched PK timing during the challenge test, which points toward F1a or a design problem (F7), but neither was shown. Because engagement is no_human_data, U applies.

In NCT03226444/PMID:35942530, topical lacripep at 22 or 44 μM did not significantly change total corneal fluorescein staining or eye dryness score at day 28. There are no human measurements of tear or tissue drug levels, of SDC1 binding or engagement, or of a downstream biomarker, so the pillars cannot be judged. A post hoc subgroup with severe dryness at baseline (score ≥60) improved, which points toward patient selection (F3, secondary). The authors also say dosing and concentration are still being worked out, which leaves open whether exposure was enough. No other drug on the same target is available for comparison. The company has since moved lacripep to neurotrophic keratitis (NCT07568730). Without engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT03226444; PMID:35942530), topical Lacripep at 22 or 44 μM did not significantly change total corneal staining or the eye dryness score at day 28. Gains appeared only in a post hoc subgroup with more severe symptoms and on some regional measures. The search turned up no human data on Lacripep levels at the ocular surface, on SDC1 binding or engagement, or on a downstream biomarker. The investigators said work on 'appropriate dosing and concentration' was ongoing, and the sponsor pointed to the subgroup benefit, which hints at both a dose question and a population (F3) question. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The sponsor has since moved to neurotrophic keratitis (NCT07568730).

The index trial NCT02025803 is a Phase 1 safety, MTD and DLT study of the investigational agent TAS-114 combined with capecitabine in mixed advanced solid tumors. It is not an efficacy test of capecitabine in melanoma, and it reports no efficacy readout or failure. Capecitabine is FDA-approved in breast, gastric, esophageal and pancreatic cancers through TYMS inhibition via its systemic metabolite 5-FU. Exposure and engagement are therefore inferred_adequate. Human PK/PD work in solid tumors shows metabolite exposure and TS-activity modulation (PMID:33386926, PMID:32382808), but nothing shows engagement in melanoma. The melanoma label reflects trial tagging, not a failed melanoma efficacy test, so F9 applies.

The index trial NCT01651780 was an open-label comparison of bivalirudin against an active anticoagulant (UFH) during TAVR. Its posted analyses were framed as non-inferiority/equivalence. Major bleeding (RR 0.77 [0.48, 1.23]) and NACE (RR 0.89) were numerically lower with bivalirudin, with no excess harm. This is a procedural-anticoagulant comparison, not a test of thrombin inhibition as a treatment for aortic stenosis, so it is not an efficacy failure of the drug. Pillars held in humans before the trial started: dose-linear plasma exposure in PCI patients (PMID:12087346), and concentration-dependent ACT/aPTT prolongation in volunteers (PMID:22130240, PMID:22659624). Reduced thrombin-generation markers were shown in infants (PMID:17663736), and the drug succeeded in ACS (NCT01087723). No engagement data come from TAVR patients.

In the index phase 1 trial in R/R AML (NCT04580121; PMID:40746940), RO7283420 at doses of 1 mg or more produced significant T-cell activation and expansion in peripheral blood and bone marrow. This shows CD3/HLA-A2-WT1 engagement and a downstream pathway effect in patients. An MTD was defined (1/3/12 mg q3w), but the pharmacodynamic effects appeared below it, so the dose was not capped under engagement. Even so, CR/CRi was only about 7%. Escalation was stopped for limited efficacy and no exposure-bone marrow response relationship, which suggests the mechanism, as tested, does not drive meaningful response. Blast reduction was linked to baseline immune phenotype (fewer Tregs, more non-exhausted CD8+ T cells), which points to patient heterogeneity (F3) as a contributor. The engagement data were published after the trial started.

In patients with advanced solid tumors, BMS-986178 showed measurable PK and OX40 receptor occupancy. Occupancy of 20–50% was linked to maximal T-cell effector enhancement, and drug treatment raised peripheral CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation (PMID:31573956). Exposure, engagement and pathway were therefore shown in the disease, though only from this trial's own data, published after it started. The MTD was not reached, so dose was not limited (PMID:33148673). Monotherapy gave no responses, and combinations gave 0–13% ORR, with no efficacy signal above nivolumab/ipilimumab (PMID:33148673). With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, F2 fits best. The index trial's primary endpoints were safety only, so F9 is a secondary code.

In the first-in-human study (PMID:38243906), PK at the RP2D/MTD of 243 µg/kg was characterised (T1/2 about 12 h), so plasma exposure is adequate. Every patient had transient lymphocyte redistribution (lymphopenia), a functional IL-2Rβγ signalling response, so engagement is treated as adequate. The dose was not capped below that level; the RP2D was well tolerated. The intended CD8+/NK expansion is not reported in the bundle, so pathway is no_human_data. Engagement was shown in mixed solid tumors, not specifically melanoma, and published after the index trial started. With 0/28 responders at both doses (NCT05578872), the βγ-biased IL-2 mechanism gave no monotherapy benefit in pretreated melanoma. Prior or residual checkpoint therapy (PMID:38702147) suggests a population issue. Evidence is thin.

EDP1867 is a gamma-irradiated, non-colonizing strain of Veillonella parvula with no recorded molecular target. Its anti-inflammatory activity was shown only in mice (PMID:35185874). In the Phase 1b trial (NCT04927195; n=52), it was safe and well tolerated at all doses, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Evelo dropped the program because the 15 atopic dermatitis patients on the lower dose who had analyzable week-8 data showed no clear clinical benefit. No source reports human pharmacodynamic data such as cytokine or immune biomarker changes, or any engagement evidence. That leaves no way to tell whether the drug failed to act or the mechanism does not matter in this disease, so the code is U. A small, short, uncontrolled-like cohort adds F7 as a secondary code.

Sildenafil is FDA-approved for pulmonary hypertension through PDE5 inhibition in the pulmonary vasculature with systemic oral dosing. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate. This rests on the assumption that INSTAGE used a comparable dose, which the bundle does not state. No PDE5 engagement or biomarker data in IPF patients appear in the bundle. In INSTAGE (NCT02802345), adding sildenafil to nintedanib did not improve SGRQ (difference -0.52, p=0.72). Tolerability did not limit the dose; serious AEs and deaths were similar between arms. A parallel trial adding sildenafil to pirfenidone (NCT02951429) also failed on disease progression. The authors conclude sildenafil adds no benefit in IPF (PMID:31191729). The PDE5 mechanism does not drive IPF outcomes as tested.

Sildenafil is FDA-approved for pulmonary hypertension, so PDE5 engagement in the pulmonary vasculature at comparable oral doses is inferred adequate. Therapeutic plasma exposure was shown in PAH patients (PMID:21219411). Pulmonary artery pressure fell in humans (PMID:11468204 in healthy volunteers; PMID:16388195 in PH patients), which supports the pathway pillar. None of this was shown in PH secondary to systolic heart failure, the index population. The index trial NCT01913847 has unknown status, no posted results and no stated stop reason, so the failure itself is weakly documented. With the mechanism inferred engaged, F2 is the default reading. A trial that never reported (F7) remains plausible, and the thin bundle makes confidence low.

In the index trial NCT03364335, sildenafil was given at only 1–4 mg, combined with leucine with or without metformin. The results were mixed and small: weight changed by about 1.5–2% against placebo, and placebo-arm weight rose. The bundle and the search found no human data at these doses on sildenafil plasma levels, PDE5 inhibition, cGMP, or any downstream biomarker. Approved uses (erectile dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension) rely on 20–100 mg doses, which are not comparable, so those approvals cannot support an inferred_adequate rating. The earlier NAFLD trial (NCT02546609 / apt.14674) did not separate from placebo overall. No source gives the sponsor's reason for stopping. Because engagement is unknown, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

NS-0200 combines leucine 1.1 g, metformin 0.5 g and sildenafil at 0.5 or 1.0 mg twice daily. The intended mechanism was synergy on Sirt1/AMPK, not classical PDE5 blockade. In NCT02546609, neither dose lowered liver fat compared with placebo. I found no human data on sildenafil exposure, PDE5 inhibition or cGMP at these doses. The approved ED and PAH doses are 20–100 mg, so those approvals cannot stand in as evidence of engagement at 0.5–1 mg. Very low engagement seems likely at these doses, but nothing measured it, so F1a is not shown. In the published analysis, the high dose cut liver fat only in the high-ALT subgroup, which suggests F3 as a possible secondary code. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

Sildenafil is FDA-approved for pulmonary hypertension via PDE5 inhibition in the pulmonary vasculature. That approval implies exposure and engagement were adequate at comparable doses. Human hemodynamic effects, lower pulmonary artery pressure, are shown in PMID:11468204 and PMID:16388195, and the PAH plasma exposure is described in PMID:21219411. None of this was measured in IPF patients. In INSTAGE (NCT02802345), adding sildenafil to nintedanib did not improve SGRQ (difference -0.52, p=0.72). The authors conclude it adds no benefit and is not recommended (PMID:31191729). The pirfenidone+sildenafil trial in patients with IPF and pulmonary hypertension also failed (NCT02951429). The mechanism was engaged but does not drive IPF outcomes. A right-heart-dysfunction subgroup analysis (PMID:31365829) hints at F3.

Micronized dHACM is an amniotic tissue product with no defined molecular target. I found no human data on its exposure, engagement or pathway effects, either in tendon or anywhere else. NCT03414255 posted no results. In its April 2021 release, MiMedx said it would not pursue a BLA for Achilles tendonitis and might test the product in a 'more well-defined subset of patients', which loosely points to patient selection (F3) or trial limitations (F7). The same product also failed in plantar fasciitis and in knee OA (NCT03485157: VAS change about equal to saline), and a later Phase 2B (NCT05796765) was terminated. Because engagement was never shown, nothing separates an inactive product from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

dHACM has no defined molecular target. I found no human data on intra-articular exposure, engagement or a pathway biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In NCT03485157, VAS (-35.1 vs -34.2) and WOMAC (-20.6 vs -19.6) improved by about the same amount in both arms. MiMedx linked the miss to large placebo responses. It said the pre-interim cohort separated significantly on WOMAC at 3 and 6 months, but the post-interim cohort responded strongly to saline as well. That points to trial execution and placebo response (F7), with a possible cohort effect (F3). The Phase 2B follow-up, NCT05796765, was stopped by the sponsor without results. Because engagement was never measured, this could equally be indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT03834662 was a 19-patient Phase 1 in solid tumours whose primary endpoint was treatment-emergent adverse events. It was not an efficacy test, and no failed readout is shown, so F9 applies. In the myelofibrosis Phase Ib (NCT03895112; PMID:37439808), no dose-limiting toxicity occurred at three dose levels. AVID200 potently suppressed plasma TGFβ1 (engagement, which also implies systemic exposure) and pSMAD2 in MF cells (pathway). Clinical benefit was modest: 2 of 21 patients met IWG-MRT response criteria, though platelet counts rose in 81%. That suggests the target may not drive MF strongly as monotherapy (secondary F2). The engagement data were published in 2023, after the index trial started in 2019.

The index trial NCT04749368 tests the BRII-835 (siRNA) plus BRII-179 combination; interferon alfa appears only as a component or backbone. It achieved 0% sustained HBsAg loss across cohorts. So it was not an efficacy test of interferon alfa itself. The interferon pillars are well established in humans. Serum exposure and 2'-5'OAS or neopterin induction were shown in volunteers (PMID:30179597, PMID:34907578, PMID:10868311). HBV DNA and HBeAg clearance occurred in HBV patients in controlled trials (PMID:1993497, PMID:8314499, PMID:2774373). Pegylated interferon alfa-2a is FDA-approved for HBV. The negative functional-cure readout reflects the combination regimen rather than failure of IFNAR engagement. A secondary F2 reading applies if the outcome is attributed to interferon: the mechanism was engaged but did not produce sustained HBsAg loss here.

In the first-in-human PSMAxCD3 bispecific study (NCT05441501), mean exposure rose with dose to 180 mg. However, anti-drug antibodies developed in 56.8% of participants and the authors say they impacted PK, so exposure was compromised (PMID:41493473). No direct measure of PSMA or CD3 target engagement or tumor T-cell activity was reported. CRS (51%, grade 1-2) hints at T-cell activation but is not quantified engagement. Clinical activity was minimal: one confirmed PSA50 response. The study was terminated for lack of activity, neurologic toxicities (10% neuropathies), high CRS rates and ADAs impacting PK. Compromised exposure is primary (F1a). Molecule-specific neurotoxicity (F6) and on-target CRS (F5) contributed.

In the first-in-human study (NCT05441501; PMID:41493473), 39 mCRPC patients received 0.1–180 mg. Cmax and AUC rose with dose, but anti-drug antibodies developed in 56.8% and the authors say these impacted PK, so sustained exposure was compromised. No direct target-engagement measure was reported. CRS in 51% suggests T-cell activation, but that is indirect. The expected downstream effect largely failed: only one confirmed PSA50 response. The study was terminated for lack of activity, neurologic toxicity (neuropathies in 10%), high CRS rates and ADA-driven PK loss. The mechanism was therefore not adequately tested (F1a), with molecule-specific and on-target toxicity contributing. Note that the bundle lists KLK2 as the target, while the abstract describes a PSMAxCD3 antibody.

AC-701 is a topical small molecule from TWi Biotechnology. A database lists it as an IL-1α/IL-8 inhibitor, and the literature describes it as having antibiotic and anti-inflammatory activity. Its Phase 2 prophylaxis trial in EGFR-inhibitor rash (NCT04239846) finished without posted results. The sponsor gave no reason for stopping. I found no human data on skin exposure, on whether the drug hit IL-1α/IL-8, or on downstream biomarkers. There are no Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts and no other drugs on the same target in the bundle. Without engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

CER-001 raised plasma apoA-I dose-dependently and mobilized unesterified cholesterol into HDL from 2 mg/kg in healthy volunteers, with no dose-limiting toxicity up to 45 mg/kg (PMID:28213743). At 3 mg/kg in carotid atherosclerosis patients it localized to plaque and raised cholesterol efflux capacity by 13.8% (PMID:27263077). FHA patients showed a 44% efflux increase (PMID:25561459). So exposure, engagement and pathway held in humans, though not shown in ACS patients and only published after the 2011 index start. CHI-SQUARE showed no atheroma regression at any dose (PMID:24780501). A post hoc high-plaque-burden subgroup signal (PMID:28567351) failed prospective confirmation in CARAT (NCT02484378, PMID:30046828), and the FHA Phase 3 stopped for futility (NCT02697136). This points to apoA-I infusion not driving plaque regression as tested.

CER-001 is an apoA-I replacement. In FHA patients at 8 mg/kg (PMID:25561459, published before the index trial started), plasma apoA-I and HDL-c rose after infusion, and cholesterol efflux increased by 44%. Healthy volunteers also showed dose-related apoA-I increases and cholesterol mobilisation (PMID:28213743), and PET showed plaque uptake (PMID:27263077). Exposure, engagement and pathway were therefore shown in this disease. Despite this, the randomized index trial showed no significant change in carotid MVWA versus placebo (p=0.185). This matches negative imaging results in ACS (NCT01201837, NCT02484378), so raising apoA-I does not appear to drive vessel-wall regression as tested. The index trial was small (27 analyzed) and lasted only 24 weeks, which leaves possible underpowering or timing problems (F7/F4), but the sources do not explicitly blame these.

BNO 1016 is a multi-component herbal extract with no defined target. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data; the only mechanistic evidence is from rats (PMID:35045922). Efficacy in acute rhinosinusitis (NCT01146860) cannot stand in for these pillars because no shared target or compartment is defined. In the CRS index trial (PMID:28214913), the primary MSS endpoint was not superior to placebo. The authors attribute this to patient heterogeneity: post-hoc analyses showed significant benefit in specialist-diagnosed patients with baseline MSS >9 and disease lasting over a year. This supports F3, though the subgroup finding is post-hoc. Because engagement is unknown, U also applies. A later CRS trial (NCT02746042) has no reported outcome.

Pharmacodynamic data from patients with relapsed or refractory AML in the index trial (ASH 2019) show GSPT1 loss that increased with dose. GSPT1 neared the assay floor at doses of 1.2 mg and above. At 2.4 mg and above, it fell by more than 90% in T cells in 19 of 29 patients and in blasts in 11 of 29. Downstream integrated-stress-response markers (ATF3, DDIT3), cleaved caspase 3 and CD34+ blast reduction followed, so engagement and pathway effect were shown in this disease. Those data appeared after the trial started in 2016. Hypotension during blast clearance was dose-limiting, but doses of 3.0–3.6 mg already reached deep degradation, so the dose was not capped below what engagement needed. Single-agent responses were rare. NCT02848001 stopped for lack of efficacy and NCT04336982 for business reasons. That points to F2: target engaged, yet little clinical benefit. On-target toxicity is a secondary contributor (F5).

Patients with relapsed or refractory AML in the index trial NCT02848001 showed dose-dependent GSPT1 degradation. At 2.4 mg and above on the Days 1-5 schedule, GSPT1 fell by more than 90% in T cells and circulating blasts. Patients whose GSPT1 stayed low had longer blast suppression, and the investigators reported on-target activity. Hypotension linked to IL-1b release was a dose-limiting toxicity. Even so, deep degradation was reached at tolerated doses, so tolerability did not cap engagement. The trial still stopped for lack of efficacy. That fits a target that was engaged but did not give enough benefit (F2). On-target toxicity adds to this (F5). Caveats: all of the engagement data come from AML patients, not MDS, and were published in 2019, after the trial began.

Plasma PK of subcutaneous sepranolone was measured in 26 healthy women, and the doses were set from those results (PMID:28319848). For engagement, a 2015 human study in healthy women (Bengtsson et al.) found that isoallopregnanolone blocked allopregnanolone-induced sedation and slowing of eye movements. This is functional evidence of GABAA antagonism, but it was not measured in PMDD patients and may not match the index doses, so the engagement call is weak; if it is discounted, U applies. Safety was good and no dose cap was reported. Both treatment arms and placebo improved a lot on the patient-reported DRSP score (PMID:34597899). The sponsor said the missed endpoint was due to an unexpectedly high placebo effect and pointed to a positive post hoc 9-day analysis, which suggests the trial could not answer the question (F7).

The index trial NCT05727800 is a first-in-human Phase 1 study of VX-668 in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Its only primary outcome is safety and tolerability (AEs/SAEs, Day 1–20). It completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results. Because it was not designed as an efficacy test, its readout cannot be an efficacy failure of the drug, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects. It has no other trials, no PubMed abstracts and no same-target comparators. Why the program stopped therefore cannot be determined, so U is a secondary code. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

ASP0598 was an Astellas topical otic solution, listed by a third-party database as an HB-EGF modulator. It was tested at microgram doses in chronic tympanic membrane perforation. The index trial, NCT04305184, was a small SAD/MAD study whose primary measures were safety only, and it was terminated for lack of efficacy. There were no serious AEs, so toxicity did not cap the dose. Astellas reported only that it discontinued the program. No human data were found on drug levels at the eardrum, on target engagement, or on downstream effects, and no other drug on the same target served as a comparator. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not drive healing, so the failure is indeterminate.

The index MDS trial (NCT05209152, PMID:39461095) treated only 7 patients, at 120 and 240 mg/m2 IV weekly. There were no DLTs and no responses, with only brief blast reductions. The sponsor ended it for reasons it called unrelated to safety. Plasma PK (Cmax, AUC) was measured in the first-in-human trial NCT02675452, which supports systemic exposure. However, no source shows MCL1 engagement in humans, such as disruption of MCL1–BAK/BIM binding, or a downstream apoptosis biomarker. The pharmacodynamic data are from knock-in mice only (PMID:30254093). Separately, the venetoclax combination trial (NCT03797261) was stopped for safety. With engagement unmeasured and the trial small and stopped by the sponsor, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged MCL1 apart from a target that doesn't drive the disease, so the code is U. A business decision or the trial's small size may also apply.

The index trial NCT05209152 was a 7-patient Phase 1 dose-exploration study with safety-only primary endpoints (0 DLTs). It was terminated by 'sponsor decision, unrelated to safety', so it was not an efficacy test of tapotoclax and no efficacy readout failed (F9). The bundle gives no business rationale beyond that, so F8 is only possible. The first-in-human trial NCT02675452 registered PK endpoints, but no values or target-engagement data are shown. MCL1 engagement or pathway evidence exists only in mouse and in vitro work (PMID:30254093, PMID:35273915), so in human terms engagement is no_human_data (U). The venetoclax combination trial NCT03797261 stopped for safety, which may have shaped the sponsor's decision.

Calcium carbonate acts locally by neutralizing gastric acid. No target pillar was measured directly at the index dose, so all three pillars are inferred_adequate. The drug is FDA-approved for GERD, and calcium-carbonate-containing products met a symptomatic GERD endpoint (NCT01869491) and lowered esophageal acid exposure (NCT01872897). In the index heartburn-meal proof-of-concept trial (NCT01037452), almost nobody in any arm was heartburn-free: combination 0/30, PPI alone 2/30, antacid alone 1/30, placebo 0/30. Because even the active comparators failed to separate from placebo, the challenge model and its stringent 'no heartburn' binary endpoint appear unable to detect known acid-suppressive activity. That points to a design or endpoint problem rather than mechanism failure. The sources do not state a reason.

The index trial NCT03507686 (GEMINI) was an open-label, single-arm safety study of bilateral sequential dosing. Its outcomes were descriptive and it had no comparative efficacy analysis (PMID:38970425). It was therefore not an efficacy test of the drug, which fits F9. The program-level efficacy failure came from the Phase 3 trial (PMID:37814062), which missed its BCVA endpoint. The authors pointed to entry criteria (more preserved retina), surgical technique and endpoints, which supports F3 as a secondary code. The bundle has no human measurement of REP1 transgene expression, Rab prenylation or a downstream biomarker. Small Phase 2 trials gave mixed BCVA results and showed continued atrophy (PMID:31465092, PMID:36581191). Engagement therefore has no human data, so U also applies.

Magnesium hydroxide is a locally acting antacid with no recorded molecular target. The bundle lists an FDA approval for esophagitis (2009) and no pharmacodynamic data. Acid-neutralizing exposure and engagement are therefore inferred_adequate from that approval, which is assumed to work through the same luminal mechanism. In the index proof-of-concept heartburn-meal model (NCT01037452), almost no participant in any arm reached the stringent 'no heartburn' endpoint: combination 0/30, PPI alone 2/30, antacid alone 1/30, placebo 0/30. Even the lansoprazole reference arm did not separate from placebo. This suggests the model and endpoint lacked assay sensitivity, a trial-design problem, rather than showing the mechanism is irrelevant. No source states the reason directly, so confidence is low.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT04282668) of TAS1440, alone and with ATRA, in relapsed or refractory AML was terminated with no posted results. The stated reasons were a changing treatment landscape, poor enrolment and little likelihood of meaningful clinical benefit. No human PK, PD or target-engagement data for TAS1440 turned up in the bundle or the web searches; the only TAS1440 data found were preclinical (SCLC cell lines). No other KDM1A inhibitor has succeeded in AML, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Enrolment problems (F7) and the competitive landscape (F8) are secondary.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT03494231 of HLX06 (anti-KDR antibody) in advanced solid tumors enrolled only 5 patients and was terminated for lack of efficacy. It posted no results. The bundle contains no pharmacokinetic, receptor occupancy or VEGFR2 pathway biomarker data in humans, no other trials of this drug, no same-target comparator drugs and no PubMed abstracts. Because engagement is no_human_data, nothing separates a molecule that failed to engage KDR from a mechanism that did not deliver benefit in this setting. The very small enrollment also suggests the trial could not meaningfully test efficacy. Indeterminate.

NCT03494231 was a first-in-human dose-escalation trial of the anti-VEGFR2 antibody HLX06 in advanced solid tumours. It enrolled only 5 patients and was terminated for 'lack of efficacy', with no results posted. The searches turned up no human data on PK, VEGFR2 occupancy, or pathway markers such as VEGF-A or sVEGFR2. They also found no publication or sponsor explanation, beyond databases listing the drug as discontinued. The informed consent form notes that ramucirumab (Cyramza), another VEGFR2 antibody, is approved in several solid tumours, so the target can work. That makes a molecule-specific failure (F1b) plausible. But with engagement not measured and a vague 'solid tumour' population, the evidence cannot separate a drug that failed to engage from a stop for other reasons. Indeterminate.

Rabeprazole 10–20 mg potently suppressed gastric acid in healthy volunteers (median 24h pH 5–6; ~73–78% time pH>4; PMID:9915106), published well before the index trial. Plasma exposure is documented (PMID:16487225). Efficacy in GERD and ulcer prevention through the same proton pump at comparable doses (NCT00911534, NCT00770913, NCT01397448) also supports engagement. Acid suppression was not measured in FD patients. The trial tested 10–40 mg without tolerability limits; serious AEs were similar to placebo. It missed complete symptom relief (22–29% vs 17.5%; NCT01089543, PMID:23957383). Only 20 mg improved satisfactory relief, with no dose-response and no effect of FD subtype. This points to acid not driving FD symptoms as tested (F2). Choice of a stringent endpoint is a possible contributor (F4).

OP0201 is an intranasal surfactant spray (DPPC with cholesteryl palmitate as a spreading agent) meant to improve Eustachian tube function. It has no molecular target. No source gives human data on whether the drug reached the Eustachian tube or changed its function, such as tube opening or middle-ear pressure. So all three pillars have no human data. In the small exploratory Phase 2a trial (NCT03818815), both primary endpoints missed, though the Day-12 effusion endpoint trended toward the drug (56% vs 38%, p=0.07). That points to a possibly underpowered trial (F7). The sponsor called the results encouraging but announced the same day that it had hired advisors to explore strategic options, which suggests a business-driven stop (F8). Nothing separates poor delivery from an ineffective mechanism, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT04452006, was a first-in-human safety, PK and PD study in healthy volunteers. The sponsor stopped it after an interim analysis without giving a reason, and no results were posted. The bundle lists no target for ACT-541478. Idorsia's 2020–2021 pipeline documents describe it only as a Phase 1 CNS compound and do not give its mechanism. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or biomarkers, and no published explanation for the stop. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter (or from a safety or business reason), the code is U.

The trial was stopped for pharmacodynamic reasons. M4112 inhibited IDO1 ex vivo at all doses in solid-tumor patients, but plasma kynurenine returned to or exceeded baseline after day 15, with no significant steady-state reduction (NCT03306420, PMID:32843490). The abstract indicates target plasma exposure was achieved, so exposure is rated adequate. Sustained in vivo inhibition of the enzymes, measured as lowering of their product kynurenine, was not shown, so engagement and the pathway effect are inadequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose: there was one DLT at 800 mg BID and neither MTD nor RP2D was reached. The IDO1/TDO2 mechanism was therefore never adequately tested. This engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, not from earlier work.

STSG-0002 is a gene therapy for chronic HBV with no recorded target. The index trial (NCT05760703) and a sister Phase 2 trial (NCT05760781) were both terminated with only 9 enrolled because preliminary effectiveness did not meet expectations. Neither trial posted results. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts and no same-target comparators. There is therefore no human evidence on exposure, transgene expression or target engagement, or on HBV biomarker effects such as HBsAg or HBV DNA lowering. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index Phase 1/2 trial NCT04060342 of GB1275, a CD11b (ITGAM) positive modulator, given alone or with pembrolizumab across advanced solid tumors, was terminated because no clear benefit was seen as monotherapy or in combination. The bundle has no posted results, no PK or exposure data, and no human measures of CD11b engagement or downstream myeloid/pathway biomarkers. There are no other trials, no other same-target drugs and no PubMed abstracts. Nothing distinguishes a drug that failed to engage CD11b from a target that does not drive tumor response. Indeterminate.

NCT04060342 (KEYNOTE-A36) was stopped because GB1275 showed no clear benefit, alone or with pembrolizumab. Exposure: SITC/ASCO 2020–21 abstracts report exposure rising with dose from 100 to 1200 mg BID, with no dose-limiting toxicities, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Engagement: I found no human measure of CD11b binding, occupancy or activation. Pathway: TIL counts rose in both regimens, and a 2023 Cancer Cell paper using phase I tumour tissue reports STING/STAT1 activation in tumour-associated macrophages. Both findings appeared after the trial started and only qualitatively. Because direct engagement was never measured, the rules point to U. The pathway signals lean toward F2 (target engaged but did not drive disease), so I list it as secondary. Confidence is low.

The NCT04847674 protocol describes TEV-53275 as an anti-IL-5 IgG4 with an extended half-life, not an anti-IL-15. The IL15 target in the bundle looks like a labelling error. In the Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (50–1800 mg), exposure rose in proportion to dose and blood eosinophils fell in a dose- and time-dependent way, lasting for months. That supports exposure, and pathway response as a stand-in for engagement. Free IL-5 was planned as a measure but not reported, and there are no engagement data from asthma patients. The index trial stopped early 'for strategic reasons' with about 25 patients per arm. Its FEV1 confidence intervals were roughly ±0.2 L, so it could not answer the question. That makes underpowering from early termination (F7) the most direct reason, with business (F8) and a possible target-level null (F2) as secondary codes.

Human PET with [11C]T-773 showed dose- and plasma concentration-dependent striatal PDE10A occupancy, up to 72% (PMID:27423256). This demonstrates brain penetration and engagement in healthy volunteers, published before the index start. The sources say engagement was verified (PMID:32598478). TAK-063 also changed ketamine-induced fMRI BOLD and EEG signals in healthy humans (PMID:31773211, PMID:32598478). It was well tolerated up to 1000 mg, so the dose was not limited (PMID:27572830).
