In the stuttering trial, the MLGSSS change was -7.0 vs -5.5 on placebo with no benefit (NCT05583955). The mechanism was engaged without clinical effect, consistent with F2. However, the index dose is not in the bundle and no engagement data exist in stuttering patients. The small, highly variable trial (n=62) also leaves F7 possible, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT03243760 was a Phase 1 safety and PK dose-escalation study in healthy subjects and moderate COPD patients. It had no efficacy endpoint and posted no results. It was terminated before the repeat-dose parts because those doses would be studied with a new formulation. That is a formulation and program decision, not a failed efficacy readout, so F9 applies. The follow-on Phase 1 NCT03235726, with the inhalation powder, completed and lists PK outcomes, but no exposure values appear in the bundle. No primary target is recorded, and the bundle has no engagement or pathway biomarker data, PubMed abstracts, or same-target comparators. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data, so U is secondary if the stop were read as a failure.

The index trial NCT02573740 was terminated for 'insufficient target engagement of ABT-957', with a CSF SBDP-145 pharmacodynamic endpoint and no posted results. Later abstracts say the trials were stopped because CNS concentrations were too low to produce a pharmacodynamic effect (PMID:32840034) and because neurons were not adequately exposed to the drug (PMID:33615187). Brain exposure, and therefore calpain engagement, was inadequate, so the calpain hypothesis in AD was never properly tested: F1a. The stop reason cites 'preclinical data', so it is unclear how much of this was measured in humans; hence medium confidence. No pathway data were posted. Tolerability is not cited as the cap. The earlier trial NCT02220738 stopped for slow enrollment.

The index trial NCT05154890 was a Phase 1/2 multiple ascending dose study in CBS-deficient homocystinuria. Its only primary outcome was treatment-emergent adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of pegtarviliase. It was terminated for an unspecified 'Sponsor Decision' with no posted results. The bundle has no other trials, no Phase 1 results, no same-target comparators and no PubMed abstracts. Exposure, engagement (e.g., homocysteine lowering or cystathionine changes) and pathway effects therefore have no human data. The best-supported code is F9, because this was not an efficacy failure. U applies secondarily, since nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a business-driven stop. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT02987829 is a Phase 1/2A dose-escalation study whose only primary outcome is DLT count by dose level (1 DLT at 320 mg, 0 at 280 mg). It is classified not_efficacy, so it was not an efficacy test of TRC253. The bundle contains no human PK, AR occupancy, or PSA/AR-signaling biomarker data. The only engagement evidence is preclinical (PMID:33649102), which does not count. Dose was not shown to be capped below an engaging level: 280 mg was tolerated, with a single DLT at 320 mg. No other trials or a stated stop reason explain the discontinuation. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, engagement is no_human_data and the cause would be indeterminate (U). Approved AR antagonists show the target is valid in this disease.

The index trial NCT02987829 is a Phase 1/2a dose-escalation study. Its only primary outcome was the DLT count by dose level: 1 DLT at 320 mg and none at 280 mg, where 51 patients were treated, so 280 mg appears to be the expansion dose. It was classified as not an efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of TRC253, and the readout cannot be called an efficacy failure. The bundle has no human PK, AR engagement or PSA/pathway data, and no abstracts or other trials. All pillars are therefore no_human_data. Approved AR antagonists such as enzalutamide and apalutamide validate the target, but nothing explains why development stopped. U is secondary because the reason is indeterminate.

The PsA trial (NCT05715125) was stopped without an efficacy readout. In its Phase 1 SAD/MAD study in healthy volunteers, published before the index trial began, VTX958 covered TYK2 IC50 and IC90 for up to 24 hours. It also produced dose-dependent suppression of TYK2-mediated genes after an IFNα challenge, plus ex vivo IFNγ effects. This makes exposure, engagement and pathway adequate. In the psoriasis Phase 2 (NCT05655299), the 225 and 300 mg BID doses met PASI75 and the key secondary endpoints, and the sponsor said target exposure was reached. However, it judged the size of the effect below its internal target in a 'highly competitive' market and ended both the psoriasis and PsA trials. That is a portfolio decision, so F8. The modest benefit despite adequate engagement (F2) and the PsA trial never testing efficacy (F9) are secondary codes.

The Phase 1 dose escalation of ASP1235, an anti-FLT3 ADC, in R/R AML (NCT02864290) was terminated for lack of efficacy. Only 6 of 43 patients reached composite CR (PMID:40209615). The bundle reports no human PK levels, FLT3 binding or occupancy, or downstream biomarker data, so all pillars are no_human_data. Preclinical data showed only marginal activity (PMID:36537913) and do not count. FLT3 is clinically validated in AML: gilteritinib, midostaurin and quizartinib are approved. This favors a molecule-level failure (F1b). However, those drugs are kinase inhibitors, whereas this ADC uses a different cytotoxic surface-targeting mechanism, so the case remains largely indeterminate (U). Frequent ocular toxicity (53%, 16% grade ≥3) may also have contributed, but no dose cap is stated.

The index Phase 1 SAD/MAD trial of the GFRAL agonist AMG 171 in obesity (NCT04199351) was terminated because Amgen judged that the totality of the data did not support continuation. The sponsor stated that no safety concerns were identified. Posted results cover only TEAE counts: there were no SAEs and no discontinuations due to adverse events, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle contains no human pharmacokinetic, target engagement (GFRAL activation) or downstream biomarker data. It also has no other trials, no other drugs on the same target and no publications. Without engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage GFRAL from a target that does not drive weight loss in obesity, so the failure is indeterminate.

AMG 171 is a GDF15-Fc fusion protein that acts as a GFRAL agonist. Its only trial, the Phase 1 SAD/MAD study NCT04199351 in obesity, was terminated. Amgen said 'the totality of the data' did not support going on and that there were no safety concerns, so neither toxicity nor a tolerability cap on the dose explains the stop. The posted results cover adverse events only. The protocol planned to measure PK, GDF15 levels and body weight, but no human PK, receptor engagement or weight data could be found. Recent reviews list the program only as halted early with no results. No other GFRAL agonist has succeeded in obesity; the reviews call LY3463251's weight loss modest. With no engagement evidence, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged GFRAL apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

ACE-083 was injected directly into the target muscle. Its follistatin-based myostatin/activin trap produced robust, significant muscle growth in humans: in healthy volunteers (PMID:29486514, NCT02257489), in FSHD at 240 mg/muscle (TMV +16.4% in biceps, +9.5% in tibialis anterior; contractile volume up; PMID:35428982, NCT02927080) and in CMT (PMID:35545446). Engagement is not measured directly; it is judged adequate from this clear pharmacodynamic effect. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The PD/safety primary endpoint was met, but the sources report no consistent functional or patient-reported benefit over up to 12 months, and the program was stopped on those functional endpoints (NCT03943290). The mechanism was engaged, yet muscle growth did not translate into function, so this is F2. The proximal effect versus clinical endpoint gap also supports F4.

ACE-083 was injected directly into the target muscle. Ligand binding was not assayed directly; the pillars rest on the muscle response. In the CMT index trial it produced the intended local hypertrophy: total muscle volume +13.5% vs placebo (p=0.01), plus gains in contractile volume and ankle dorsiflexion strength (NCT03124459, PMID:35545446). A healthy-volunteer Phase 1 registered in 2014 showed the same dose-related volume gains (NCT02257489, PMID:29486514). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, the 6-minute walk, 10-m walk/run and QoL did not improve, and the program was stopped for lack of functional benefit. The FSHD trials showed the same pattern (NCT02927080, PMID:35428982). Local myostatin/activin blockade engaged its mechanism, but the added muscle bulk does not drive function in CMT.

The index trial NCT03482037 is a Phase 1/2 study in neurogenic detrusor overactivity after spinal cord injury. Its only primary outcome is the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events at Day 28, and it is classified as a not_efficacy endpoint. No results were posted, and the bundle has no other trials, Phase 1 data, same-target comparators or publications. Nothing in the bundle shows human exposure, HTR1A engagement or a pathway effect. The index trial was a safety study rather than a failed efficacy test, so F9 fits best. If the program did stop for lack of efficacy, the cause is indeterminate (U) because engagement is no_human_data. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

DF277, a glucocorticoid receptor agonist, met its endpoint as monotherapy in otic eczema (NCT01996748), the same target and ear-canal compartment. Its combination with DF289 also met endpoints in otitis media (NCT01395966, NCT01404611). The pillars are therefore inferred adequate, though no direct human target-engagement data exist. The index trial (NCT03196973) tested the combination; DF277 alone served as a component-contribution arm. Therapeutic cure was numerically highest for the combination (61%), then DF289 (54%) and DF277 (44%). No statistical test is posted, so the primary endpoint cannot be judged and a clear efficacy failure of DF277 is not shown. The cure endpoint is largely microbiological, which a steroid would not be expected to drive. The bundle gives no stop reason, so confidence is low.

The first-in-human trial NCT04809805 enrolled 5 SLFN12/PDE3A-coexpressing patients. It was terminated because a therapeutic window could not be achieved. Grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 3 of 5 patients. PMID:39437010 explicitly calls this an on-target effect, driven by high PDE3A expression in platelets. The drug's long half-life (>360 h) caused accumulation, and the highest doses on both schedules were intolerable, so no MTD was set. Alternative schedules were not predicted to help. There were no objective responses. Tumor exposure, PDE3A-SLFN12 complex formation and downstream effects were never measured in tumors. The dose was capped below any demonstrated engagement level, so the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a secondary). The sources attribute termination to on-target toxicity precluding efficacy (F5).

In the first-in-human trial (NCT04809805; PMID:39437010), plasma PK was measured and showed a very long half-life (>360 h) with accumulation, so systemic exposure was achieved. Grade 3-4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 3 of 5 patients. The authors call it a mechanism-based, on-target effect, driven by high PDE3A expression in platelets and megakaryocytes. The highest doses on both schedules were intolerable, no MTD was set, and no objective responses were seen. Complex formation or pathway effects in tumor were never measured. The sources state that on-target toxicity precluded a therapeutic window and ended the trial, which supports F5. Because tolerability capped the dose before tumor engagement could be shown as adequate, F1a also applies.

The index trial NCT02432664 was a Phase 1 safety, PK and PD study in healthy male volunteers. Its primary endpoint was adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated after the second Part II cohort because of 'complex PK results', with no safety concerns stated. No results were posted. The bundle lists no target, no PD or engagement data, no other trials and no literature. So exposure, engagement and pathway are all no_human_data. The stop was a PK/formulation decision, not an efficacy failure, which supports F9. An exposure problem (F1a) is plausible but not shown, and nothing separates molecule from target (U).

In the FORT trial (NCT03041116, PMID:33200489), 300 mg three times daily did no better than placebo on PKAN-ADL (p=0.91). The trial drew only sparse whole-blood drug levels. I found no human data on brain or CSF drug levels, brain CoA or phosphopantothenate restoration, or any downstream biomarker. Evidence of brain delivery and CoA incorporation comes only from monkeys, mice and cell models (PMID:29522513). PMID:28567317 is a single uncontrolled case report. The investigators themselves name poor blood-brain barrier crossing, and so too little engagement in the brain, as one possible explanation. They do not show it, and the drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects. Because human engagement is unmeasured, the sources cannot tell a drug that never reached its target apart from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U. F1a stays possible.

The index trial NCT01850420 tested IMC-1, a famciclovir + celecoxib combination aimed at suspected herpes virus reactivation, not celecoxib alone. Its published report (PMID:28260944) states the 16-week primary pain endpoint was met: pain fell significantly versus placebo, with gains on PGIC, FIQ-R and fatigue. So this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. Exposure is shown in humans by plasma and CSF pharmacokinetics (PMID:37246720, PMID:36318604). Engagement is shown in healthy volunteers, where in vivo COX-2 activity was lowered versus placebo (NCT02502006), but that trial started after the index trial and was not in fibromyalgia patients. The pathway pillar is inferred from met analgesic endpoints in acute pain (NCT01062113) and the approvals. Program stoppage is unexplained in the bundle.

The index trial NCT01850420 tested IMC-1, a celecoxib-containing combination, in fibromyalgia and myofascial pain. No results or stop reason are posted. Exposure is shown in humans (PMID:37246720, PMID:36318604). Healthy-volunteer data show COX-2 activity lowered versus placebo ex vivo and in vivo (NCT02502006), but this trial started after the index trial. Engagement is also inferred adequate because celecoxib met efficacy endpoints in acute pain (NCT01062113, NCT03554772, PMID:34252915) and is approved for osteoarthritis, the same peripheral COX-2 mechanism. Celecoxib lowered TNF-α and IL-1β in myofascial pain (PMID:38770602), yet pain relief was inferior to the comparator. A rat model suggests COX-2 does not maintain muscle hyperalgesia (PMID:31693705). This fits F2. The combination design and missing results lower confidence.

NCT03799003, a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of the GITR (TNFRSF18) agonist antibody ASP1951, given alone and with pembrolizumab in advanced solid tumors, was terminated for lack of efficacy. No results were posted. The PK endpoints were registered, but the bundle holds no human data on exposure, GITR engagement (e.g., receptor occupancy) or downstream pathway effects (e.g., Treg depletion, effector T-cell activation). The bundle also has no other trials, no Phase 1 results, no other drugs on the same target and no publications. It therefore cannot separate a drug that never engaged GITR from a target that does not drive tumor control. No dose limitation is shown. With engagement lacking human data, the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index Phase 1 trial NCT03799003 tested ASP1951 alone and with pembrolizumab. It was terminated for lack of efficacy, and no results were posted. The only engagement data found are preclinical. The SITC 2018 abstract reports agonist activity in cell assays and primary T cells, which does not count as human evidence. I found no human pharmacokinetics, GITR occupancy, regulatory T-cell or other pharmacodynamic data, and no published trial results. The bundle lists no other GITR agonist that succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Nothing reports dose-limiting tolerability. Because human engagement is missing, nothing separates a molecule that failed to engage GITR from a GITR mechanism that does not drive tumor response. The result is indeterminate.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT03188523 in treatment-naive HIV-1 patients showed plasma HIV-1 RNA reductions of about 1 log10 at 168 h after a single dose (LS mean -1.06 at 100 mg, -0.95 at 240 mg; posterior mean differences vs placebo -1.03 and -0.92). This is a clear antiviral (pathway) effect in the program disease. No serious AEs or discontinuations occurred. The readout therefore does not look like an efficacy failure. No stop reason is given. The bundle records no target, PK, or engagement data, other trials, or publications, so why the program stopped cannot be determined. F9 is the best fit, with U as an alternative given how thin the evidence is.

The phase 1 study (PMID:24297683) showed plasma exposure at or above 32 mg/m2 exceeded the preclinical antitumor threshold, with no MTD reached, so dose was not tolerability-capped. It also reported lymphocyte and platelet decreases as a BCL2-targeted effect. BCL2 knockdown was never measured directly. Engagement is inferred adequate because PNT2258 met its ORR endpoint (53.8%) in relapsed/refractory NHL (NCT01733238), the same target in malignant B cells. In Richter transformation (NCT02378038), 0 of 5 patients responded. With engagement plausible, this points to BCL2 silencing being insufficient in this aggressive disease. However, the trial was terminated at n=5 with no stated reason, which limits inference (F7).

Exposure looks adequate. In the Phase 1 trial (PMID:24297683), plasma exposure at doses of 32 mg/m2 or more exceeded the level that worked in preclinical xenografts, and no maximum tolerated dose was found, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Engagement has no human data: none of the sources measured BCL2 transcript or protein knockdown in tumour or blood. Falling lymphocyte and platelet counts are a non-specific surrogate, not evidence of BCL2 suppression. The Wolverine trial (NCT02226965) was stopped because its response rate (11%) fell short of expectations, not because it crossed a futility boundary. Partway through, the trial narrowed enrolment after heavily pretreated patients progressed rapidly (possible F3). No BCL2 drug in the bundle has succeeded in DLBCL, which rules out F1b. Nothing in the sources separates a drug that never engaged BCL2 from a target that does not drive the disease, so the code is U.

The index trial protocol describes RO7123520 as an anti-cadherin-11 monoclonal antibody, not a multispecific antibody, given as an add-on to MTX and anti-TNF therapy in RA patients who had an inadequate response to TNF inhibitors. The TNF target listed in the bundle seems to come from the background anti-TNF therapy. In NCT03001219, the 810 mg arm did no better than placebo on ACR50 at week 12 (11.1% vs 16.2%), and the trial was stopped for lack of efficacy. No posted ADA was detected. The protocol cites only preclinical pharmacology and PK. My searches found no human data on exposure, Cad-11 engagement or downstream biomarkers. No other Cad-11 drug has succeeded in RA, so F1b does not apply. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive RA, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT05917470 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoint was dose-limiting toxicities. No DLTs occurred at any dose from 40 mg QD to 1200 mg QD or 300 mg BID, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The sponsor stopped all ONCT-534 trials in September 2024 without giving an efficacy reason, so this was not an efficacy test of the drug. The bundle has no PK, AR-engagement or PSA/pathway data, so all pillars are no_human_data. Approved AR inhibitors (enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide) validate the target, but nothing here separates a molecule problem from a business decision. Hence F9, with U and a possible commercial stop (F8) as secondary codes.

The index trial NCT04068259 was a single-ascending-dose safety study in 24 healthy subjects, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because 'PK data from first 3 cohorts does not support study continuation', and the sponsor stated there were no safety concerns. This is human evidence that exposure was inadequate, so dose was not capped by tolerability. The pharmacokinetic profile, not the GPR84 target, ended the program, and the mechanism was never tested. No engagement or pathway data, other trials, same-target drugs or publications are in the bundle. F9 also applies because no efficacy readout occurred. Confidence is medium: the stop reason is explicit, but the PK data themselves were not posted.

Phase 1 trials posted dose-proportional plasma PK in healthy, obese and T2DM subjects (NCT02055547, NCT01982630), so exposure is adequate. The bundle shows no direct GLP1R or GCGR engagement readout; the ISR/glucose pharmacodynamic data are truncated. In the index trial (NCT02492763), 300 μg modestly beat placebo on A1C (-0.61), 180 μg did not, and both were numerically weaker than liraglutide 1.8 mg in the same trial. Heart rate rose about 7 bpm, more than with liraglutide. Liraglutide and other approved GLP1R agonists work in T2DM, which points to the molecule rather than the target. Heart rate rise may be a limiting on-target liability. No stop reason is stated, and there are no PubMed abstracts.

VSJ-110 (CFTRact-K267) is an eye drop that activates CFTR, a chloride channel. In the index trial (NCT04622345), patients were given an allergen challenge. Itching and redness scores were small and inconsistent and not clearly better than placebo. Serious adverse events: none on drug, one on placebo, so toxicity did not end the program. The only evidence of tear-fluid drug levels and CFTR activation comes from mice (escholarship). The human ocular surface potential difference paper set up the method in untreated healthy volunteers and did not test this drug. No source reports human drug levels, CFTR activation, or a downstream biomarker, and no source explains the failure. Vanda has moved on to dry eye trials (NCT06296966, NCT07179055). The bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged CFTR from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

Ace-ER is meant to replace the sialic acid that defective GNE fails to make. The Phase 2 trial (PMID:27854209) found serum sialic acid rose with dose, but the drug acts in skeletal muscle. NCT01517880 was set up to measure whether muscle sialylation was restored, yet no human muscle sialic acid or sialylation result turned up in the bundle or my searches. I hit the search limit before I could open the Phase 2 full text or the trade-press report. So muscle exposure, engagement and pathway effect are all unproven. The Phase 3 trial (NCT02377921, PMID:31036580) missed its primary endpoint (p=0.54) and its key secondary endpoints. Ultragenyx then stopped development without giving a mechanistic reason. Small Japanese trials showed non-significant trends (PMID:37125562, 37568154). Nothing here tells a drug that never restored muscle sialylation apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Ace-ER is meant to replace the sialic acid (SA) that GNE myopathy patients cannot make. The Phase 2 trial showed serum SA rising with dose (PMID:27854209), but that only shows systemic exposure. The site of action is skeletal muscle, and no source we found measured SA levels or restored sialylation in human muscle. So exposure at the tissue, engagement and the downstream pathway all lack human data. At 6 g/day, the Phase 3 index trial (NCT02377921) and its extension (NCT02736188) missed their primary endpoints. The investigators noted that Phase 3 patients were less impaired at baseline and more genetically varied than Phase 2 patients, which points to population differences (F3/F7). Nothing here separates a drug that never reached muscle from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index Phase 1/2 trial (NCT03375047) had a descriptive safety primary endpoint, so it was not formally an efficacy test. MRT5005 was generally tolerated, with febrile and hypersensitivity reactions, but showed no consistent FEV1 benefit (PMID:37121795). The bundle has no human data on lung CFTR mRNA delivery, CFTR protein expression, or chloride-transport biomarkers, so exposure, engagement and pathway are unmeasured. Nothing separates poor LNP delivery from an ineffective replacement approach, so the code is U. F9 applies because the trial was safety-focused. F1b is possible because CFTR modulators are approved for CF, but their mechanism differs from mRNA replacement. No tolerability cap on dose is shown. Confidence is low because the evidence is thin.

Index trial NCT04171843, an allogeneic BCMA CAR-T dose escalation with or without nirogacestat in relapsed/refractory myeloma, was terminated for lack of sufficient therapeutic effect. No results were posted, and the bundle has no Phase 1 or PubMed data. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. Several other BCMA-directed agents are FDA-approved for plasma cell myeloma in the bundle (idecabtagene vicleucel, teclistamab, belantamab mafodotin), and these show the target is valid in this disease. With BCMA validated and no evidence that PBCAR269A engaged adequately, the failure is attributed to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U is listed as secondary because no engagement data exist to confirm this directly.

In the index trial (NCT02743780), one week of the MTD, MGV354 0.1%, lowered IOP no more than vehicle: -0.6 vs -1.1 mmHg. No human source measured drug levels in the outflow tissue, sGC activation or cGMP. The only sign that the drug acted on its target was conjunctival hyperemia, which the authors call consistent with its pharmacology (PMID:29802818). That reaction happens in the surface blood vessels, not at the site of action. Hyperemia also set the MTD, so tolerability may have capped the dose. But nothing shows the dose fell short of what engagement needed, so dose_limited is false and F1a is only secondary. The sponsor checked whether human metabolism differed from animals and found it did not explain the failure (PMID:32662714). So the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter: U.

No human data show MGV354 reaching the outflow tissues, raising cGMP there or activating sGC, so engagement is no_human_data. At the maximum tolerated dose of 0.1%, the drug did not lower IOP more than placebo (-0.6 vs -1.1 mmHg; NCT02743780, PMID:29802818). Patients got ocular hyperemia, which the authors call consistent with the drug's pharmacology. That suggests some sGC activity in the conjunctival blood vessels, not in the trabecular outflow pathway. The cGMP increases and IOP lowering were shown only in animal and lab studies (IOVS). A follow-up study (PMID:32662714) found no species differences in metabolism and could not explain the failure. Nothing here tells a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Hyperemia limited the maximum tolerated dose, but no source shows this kept the dose below what engagement needed. F1a is listed only as a possibility.

AP611074 (teslexivir, BTA074) is a topical drug meant to block the HPV6/11 E1–E2 protein interaction. The sponsor called the Phase 1/2 index trial NCT01532102 positive, citing smaller wart surface area, but no results were posted. The larger Phase 2 trial NCT02724254 (CT4, 218 patients) missed its primary endpoint: 30.6% complete clearance vs 23.3% on placebo. The only signals were non-significant trends in women and in patients with large warts. The sources contain no human evidence that the drug reached the wart tissue, blocked E1–E2, or lowered viral DNA or transcripts. The index trial only measured drug levels in plasma. With engagement untested, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The subgroup trends give a weak F3.

AP611074 (teslexivir, BTA074) is a topical gel meant to inhibit the HPV E1/E2 proteins. In the 218-patient Phase 2 trial (NCT02724254), the drug missed its primary endpoint: 30.6% of patients fully cleared their warts by week 16 on drug versus 23.3% on placebo. Safety was similar to placebo, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Plasma levels were listed as an outcome in the index trial (NCT01532102), but no results were posted. The sources found give no human data on drug levels in wart tissue, E1/E2 inhibition, or viral DNA or load reduction. The sponsor reported trends in women and in patients with large warts, neither significant, so F3 is secondary only. With no engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

EMB-001 combines metyrapone with oxazepam. Oral oxazepam is nearly completely absorbed, with ~93% bioavailability and stable steady-state levels (PMID:3197746, PMID:300541), so exposure is adequate. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate: oxazepam is FDA-approved for anxiety and alcohol dependence through the same CNS GABA-A target. At 30 mg it also produced measurable CNS effects in healthy volunteers (memory impairment, ERP changes; PMID:8473719, PMID:8515824). Dose comparability with the low oxazepam dose in EMB-001 (20 mg/day in PMID:22236504) is uncertain. Engagement was not shown in cocaine-use patients. The index trial missed its abstinence endpoint (2/41 vs 0/41, p=0.092; NCT04501874). Very low event rates in a small trial suggest limited power (F7). Confidence is low.

The index first-in-human trial (NCT03809624) stopped for lack of a meaningful efficacy signal. PMID:41724817 reports an MTD of 0.3 mg/kg Q3W, frequent hepatic AEs (17 grade ≥3) and low ORR (3.7% monotherapy, 13.9% combination). It concludes that low responses plus hepatic safety signals do not support further development. The bundle has no human PK, PD-L1 occupancy, 4-1BB agonism or downstream biomarker data. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore no_human_data. Nothing shows the MTD fell below the dose needed for engagement, and no same-target comparator succeeded. A drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. Hepatotoxicity contributed to the stop; the bundle does not say whether it was on- or off-target. The sister trial NCT04009460 ended for business reasons.

The first-in-human trial NCT03809624 / PMID:41724817 gave 0.001–3 mg/kg. Response rates were low: 3.7% alone and 13.9% with pembrolizumab. Liver toxicity set the combination MTD at 0.3 mg/kg Q3W. The program stopped for low efficacy plus the liver safety signal. No human data were found for PK, PD-L1 receptor occupancy, 4-1BB activation or downstream biomarkers. PD-L1 occupancy and CD8 T-cell expansion were measured only in mouse surrogate studies (ResearchGate abstract). Immune-related liver toxicity fits on-target 4-1BB agonism (F5, secondary), but no evidence shows that engagement fell short at the doses that were tolerated. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its targets from a mechanism that does not work. No other drug on these targets is in the bundle.

The index trial NCT04909723 was a Phase 1/2 safety, tolerability and pharmacodynamics study in healthy volunteers and enteric hyperoxaluria patients. Its primary outcome was treatment-related adverse events, which is not an efficacy endpoint. It was terminated for an unspecified sponsor decision, and no results were posted. The bundle contains no other trials, no Phase 1 results, no same-target drugs and no publications. So exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human data. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test of the drug, F9 fits most directly. If it were treated as a failed program, the absence of any engagement data would make it indeterminate (U). Nothing shows business reasons or toxicity. Confidence is low given how thin the bundle is.

The index trial NCT04909723 was a Phase 1/2 safety, tolerability and pharmacodynamics study in healthy volunteers and enteric hyperoxaluria patients. Its primary outcome was treatment-related adverse events, not efficacy. It was terminated by an unspecified sponsor decision, with no results posted. So it was not an efficacy test of the drug, which points to F9. The bundle has no other trials, no Phase 1 results, no same-target comparators and no PubMed abstracts. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human evidence, and the underlying reason the program stopped cannot be determined (secondary U). Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

GC5131 is GC Pharma's hyperimmune globulin, made from the plasma of people who recovered from COVID-19. The index trial was NCT04555148, an open-label Phase 2a dose-response study in 63 patients, and it posted no results. I found no human data on GC5131 itself showing its neutralizing antibody levels or how well it neutralized the virus in recipients. The only human biomarker data come from a compassionate-use series of 6 critically ill patients given 10 g (PMC8473256). In them, viral load (Ct values) did not fall faster after the infusion, and the authors judged the drug ineffective in that setting. Korea's drug regulator (MFDS) turned down conditional approval and asked for more clinical trial data. GC Pharma then withdrew its application and did not say whether it would run a Phase 2b or Phase 3 trial. Because engagement has no human data, nothing here tells a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. F7 is secondary because the trial was small and open-label.

The bundle has no direct target-engagement or pathway data in NSCLC or squamous carcinoma. Plasma exposure is documented by human PK (PMID:10430061). Brain exposure and DNA-alkylating activity are inferred_adequate because temozolomide is FDA-approved for glioblastoma, the same CNS compartment as the index endpoint (brain metastasis prevention). Despite this, maintenance TMZ showed no benefit: brain metastases 4/22 vs 3/23 with observation (p=0.70; NCT00632203), with the point estimate unfavourable. That points to the mechanism not preventing NSCLC brain metastases as tested (F2). However, the trial was small and terminated with no stated reason, so underpowering (F7) cannot be excluded. MGMT-dependent sensitivity confined to subsets (PMID:24319345) suggests possible selection issues (F3). Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01294735 was a completed Phase 1 dose-finding study of MK-4827 (niraparib) given with temozolomide in advanced solid tumors, glioblastoma and melanoma. Its only primary endpoint was DLTs in cycle 1, it posted no results, and it gave no stop reason. It was not an efficacy test of temozolomide, and it did not enroll meningioma patients specifically. The pillars are inferred from temozolomide's approval in glioblastoma at standard doses. No target is recorded, and meningioma tissue exposure is not shown in humans, so these inferences are weak. A review notes temozolomide has limited efficacy in recurrent meningioma (PMID:27123883), but that is not a readout of this program. The best-supported code is F9: no efficacy failure of the drug.

Phase 1 data show dose-proportional plasma exposure, and before the index trial a single TAK-448 bolus raised testosterone 1.3–2-fold in healthy men, so KISS1R was engaged (PMID:24762108). At index-range microgram doses (0.1–3 µg), MVT-602 produced dose-dependent LH rises in women (PMID:37925096, PMID:33196464). Yet in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, repeated weekly or twice-weekly dosing did not raise total or free testosterone (NCT02369796). A similar trial in older low-testosterone men also failed (NCT02381288). Engagement was never shown in patients with the program's disease. The doses may have been suboptimal in men, or patient selection may explain the result (secondary F1a/F3). The arms had n=3 each. The sources give no explicit cause, so confidence is low.

Index trial NCT01132404 was a small (n=9) safety/PK/testosterone-lowering study. It was terminated because the sponsor was developing a new formulation, not because of an efficacy readout, so it was not an efficacy failure. Pillars held in humans: exposure was dose-proportional (PMID:24762108). KISS1R agonism produced an early testosterone rise followed by sustained suppression to castration levels in healthy men. In prostate cancer patients, testosterone fell below 20 ng/dL in 4 of 5 at 12–24 mg depot, and PSA dropped by more than 50% at 24 mg (PMID:24762108). LH rises with MVT-602 confirm receptor engagement (PMID:33196464, PMID:37925096). This engagement evidence was published in 2014, after the index trial started. Later futility in hypogonadism trials concerns other indications.

The index trial NCT01085331 never reached its randomized PFS part. The sponsor stated that the randomized phase was not recommended because of the MTD reached with FOLFIRI, 45 mg/day pimasertib (PMID:25989270: 'dose escalation... limited by toxicity'). That is far below the monotherapy RP2D of 60 mg bid (120 mg/day). At that RP2D, pERK suppression in PBMCs was sustained only at higher doses or with bid dosing (PMID:33170484, PMID:33211315). Plasma exposure was characterized (NCT01713036). Engagement at the capped combination dose is therefore judged inadequate, and no tumour pathway data exist in CRC. The mechanism was not properly tested because tolerability capped the dose. The limiting toxicities were MEK class effects (diarrhoea, rash), so F5 is listed as secondary.

The index trial (NCT01936363, PMID:31870556) gave pimasertib in both arms and tested whether adding the PI3K inhibitor SAR245409 was superior. It was not an efficacy test of pimasertib itself. ORR was similar (9.4–12.5% vs 12.1%), and the authors read the single-agent activity as encouraging. The study was stopped early for low ORR and high discontinuation, and the authors note it was limited by small numbers. Pimasertib's pillars held in solid-tumour patients at the dose used: plasma exposure (NCT01713036, PMID:33170484) and dose-dependent, sustained pERK inhibition in PBMCs (PMID:33170484, PMID:33211315). It also met its primary PFS endpoint in NRAS-mutant melanoma (NCT01693068). Engagement was not shown in ovarian cancer. Class toxicities (diarrhoea, skin and ocular events) and poor tolerability of the combination (PMID:30425349) likely contributed to discontinuation.

The first-in-human trial NCT00982865 (registered 2007, before the index trial; reported in PMID:33170484) showed adequate plasma exposure. It also showed rapid pERK suppression, sustained with BID dosing, at doses comparable to those in the index safety run-in (up to 120 mg QD and 60–75 mg BID). PMID:30585255 confirms pERK downregulation. The drug met a PFS endpoint in NRAS-mutant melanoma (NCT01693068), so MEK inhibition was clinically active. Even so, adding it to gemcitabine did not improve PFS in unselected pancreatic adenocarcinoma (NCT01016483: 3.75 vs 2.83 months). Engagement was not measured in pancreatic patients. Trametinib's listed pancreatic approval is probably confined to a subset, so a selection issue (F3) is possible. MEK inhibition does not appear to drive benefit in unselected disease.

The index AML trial NCT00957580 was terminated for limited anti-leukemic effects in the Part 1 run-in. Human plasma PK is documented (PMID:33170484, NCT01713036). In the first-in-human solid-tumor trial NCT00982865, which started before the index trial, pimasertib substantially and sustainedly reduced pERK in PBMCs at pharmacologically active doses (PMID:33170484, PMID:33211315), so engagement is adequate. It also produced responses and met a PFS endpoint in NRAS melanoma (NCT01693068). The run-in reached DLTs but did not show tolerability capping engagement. PMID:26657199 reports PD in hematologic patients, but the bundle gives no abstract, so engagement in AML blasts is unshown. Engaged MEK inhibition without anti-leukemic activity suggests MEK1/2 does not drive AML as tested. Confidence is medium because marrow engagement is unverified.

The index trial NCT02729298 was a first-in-human Phase 1 dose-escalation study in solid tumors. Its primary endpoint was DLTs and adverse events, not efficacy, and it posted no results. It was therefore not an efficacy test of dubermatinib in AML. The bundle contains no human PK, AXL occupancy or pathway biomarker data; the AML evidence is preclinical (PMID:33268594, PMID:36612026). The CLL trial NCT03572634 ended for feasibility reasons, not efficacy. The decitabine combination study (PMID:40557912) reported modest activity and acceptable tolerability but no engagement measures. With all pillars lacking human data, the mechanism's relevance cannot be judged, so U applies as a secondary code.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT02952989) was terminated for its overall benefit/risk profile. The publication (PMID:34288257) states that thromboembolic events (grades 2-5 in 16% of part A patients, recurring in part C despite prophylactic LMWH) led to study termination. Pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional, and pharmacodynamic inhibition of glycoprotein fucosylation was shown in patients with advanced solid tumors. That engagement evidence was published in 2021, after the trial started in 2017. Preliminary antitumor activity was seen, including one complete response in head and neck cancer. The MTD of 10 g/day was not shown to sit below the level needed for engagement. The program ended on toxicity, not on lack of efficacy. The bundle does not establish whether the thrombosis is on-target (fucosylation-related, F5) or molecule-specific (F6).

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT02952989) was terminated for 'overall benefit/risk profile'. PMID:34288257 states that thromboembolic events (grades 2-5 in 16% of part A patients, and one in seven in part C despite prophylactic LMWH) led to study termination. Exposure was adequate: pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional with an MTD of 10 g daily. Engagement was shown as pharmacodynamic inhibition of glycoprotein fucosylation in tumor patients, but this was published only after the trial started. No downstream pathway marker is reported. The program ended because of toxicity, not an efficacy readout. The bundle does not say whether the thrombosis came from systemic defucosylation, which would make it on-target. So F6 is primary, with F5 as a plausible alternative.

The index trial NCT01840085 was an open-label, single-arm Phase 3 study. Its primary outcome was the proportion of subjects with treatment-related adverse events, so it was a safety study, not an efficacy test of DSC127. It was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results, so the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, MAS1 engagement or pathway data. The Phase 2 DFU trial (PMID:22672145) reported faster healing (median 8.5 vs 22 weeks, p=0.04) but not whether its primary endpoint was met. Its benefit cannot establish the pillars because it is in the same disease. The reason the program stopped is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT02061878 was a 12-subject Phase 1 mechanistic study of beta-amyloid/ApoE kinetics in healthy volunteers, registered under Alzheimer's disease. It was not an efficacy test of bexarotene in thyroid cancer, so no efficacy failure is shown; no stop reason or results are posted. Exposure is shown in humans: plasma and tumor drug levels with intratumoral biomarker changes in NSCLC (PMID:17363535). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from the CTCL approval via systemic RXR agonism, supported by rapid TSH suppression in healthy subjects (PMID:17062760). Thyroid cancer data are limited to a small pilot (NCT00718770, PMID:22142826, PMID:25778496) without target-engagement measurements in this disease.

Index Phase 1 NCT04633148 (UniCAR02-T plus a PSMA target module) stopped because 'biological activity was very limited' despite good tolerability, so dose was not capped. No results, PK, CAR-T expansion or PSMA-engagement data are posted, and the bundle has no abstracts. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data. PSMA (FOLH1) is clinically validated in prostate cancer: lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan is FDA-approved, and several other PSMA agents reached Phase 3. That points to the molecule or modality rather than the target. However, those agents are radioligands, not immune-cell depleters, so the inference is weak. The sister AML trial NCT04230265 stopped for business reasons. U is listed as secondary because engagement was never shown.

The sponsor terminated NCT02431260 for PK variability. PMID:31527168 reports a short half-life (2.24 h) and very high interpatient variability in oral clearance (CV 142%) for INCB054329. It also reports that exposure-dependent thrombocytopenia limited the target inhibition that could be safely maintained. So exposure was inadequate and tolerability capped the dose below sustained engagement (dose_limited). No human pathway biomarker data are reported. The index trial was a safety/dose-escalation study, not an efficacy test (F9 secondary). The program shifted to the backup BET inhibitor INCB057643, which had a more favorable PK profile. The mechanism was never properly tested with this molecule (F1a).

The trial (NCT01931566) tested 0.8 mg/day sustained-release pioglitazone, a small fraction of the diabetes dose. There was no phase 2 dose-finding. The dose was chosen from preclinical work on mitochondria and from an fMRI study in healthy elderly people (NCT01456117), which found a hippocampal BOLD signal. That signal is a non-specific CNS effect, not a measure of PPARγ engagement or brain drug levels. I found no human data on CSF or brain exposure, receptor engagement, or a PPARγ pathway biomarker at this dose. Later authors suggest the low dose and limited brain penetration may explain the lack of benefit, but this was never measured. The sponsor gave only 'lack of efficacy' as the reason. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U, with F1a (under-dosing) plausible but unproven.

The index trial NCT01456117 is a Phase 1 BOLD-fMRI brain hemodynamics study in healthy elderly volunteers. It has no efficacy endpoint in type 1 diabetes and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of pioglitazone in the program disease (F9). Pillars are inferred_adequate: pioglitazone is approved for T2DM and met HbA1c endpoints through systemic PPARG agonism at 15-45 mg (NCT00722371, NCT04885712). No direct engagement measure appears in T1DM patients. In T1DM itself, a modest HbA1c gain was reported (PMID:17543413). A small pilot (NCT00545857, PMID:24379032) showed no beta-cell preservation despite this presumed engagement, consistent with a secondary F2.

The index trial NCT01456117 was a completed Phase 1 study of brain BOLD fMRI hemodynamics in healthy elderly volunteers. It was not an efficacy test in pneumonitis, posted no results and gave no stop reason, so it is not an efficacy failure (F9). Plasma exposure at 45 mg is documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:26051874). PPARG engagement is inferred_adequate: pioglitazone met HbA1c endpoints in type 2 diabetes before 2011 (NCT00722371) and later (NCT04885712), though that is not the lung or brain compartment. Pathway effects shown in diabetes patients, not healthy volunteers, include improved insulin and beta-cell sensitivity (NCT00511108, PMID:28847910). No engagement data exist in pneumonitis.

AG013 is a Lactococcus lactis mouth rinse that secretes hTFF1. The index Phase 2 trial (NCT03234465) was terminated for futility: duration of severe oral mucositis was 19.6 vs 20.6 days (US) and 17.2 vs 15.3 days (Europe), with more SAEs on drug (43 vs 25). The only evidence of local bacterial and hTFF1 presence at the oral mucosa comes from hamster PK/PD studies (PMID:20542722), which do not count as human data. The Phase 1 trial (NCT00938080) posted no PK or biomarker results. No other TFF1 drugs are in the bundle. Without human evidence of mucosal hTFF1 delivery or pathway effect, nothing separates non-delivery from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U.

Novartis stopped the IPF trial NCT05497284 after enrolling 46 people, about half its target. FVC % predicted fell more on LTP001 6 mg (-3.1) than on placebo (-1.1); the slope difference was -2.6 [-6.9, 1.3], so the drug did not beat placebo. None of the sources has human evidence on the pillars: no lung or plasma exposure data, no SMURF1 engagement, no BMP/SMAD biomarker result. No other SMURF1 drug exists to compare against. Novartis said there were no safety concerns. It also noted that LTP001 sits outside its core therapy areas, which suggests a portfolio reason (F8). The trial was stopped early and too small to answer the question (F7). The PAH trials were also terminated without usable efficacy analyses. Because engagement is unknown, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT04495920, was a small (n=12) early-phase test run by CAGE Bio Inc. It measured the residual antimicrobial activity of one topical test product using the ASTM E2752 method. It finished as planned, posted no results and gave no failure or stop reason. It did not test ethanol's efficacy in pancreatic cystic neoplasms, so this does not look like a failed efficacy readout for the program disease. In the disease-specific trial, NCT02158039, ethanol ablation shrank cysts by 80% or more, or ablated them completely, in 12 of 23 patients. Six of 23 patients had serious adverse events. Ethanol has no defined molecular target, so none of the three pillars was measured in humans. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, the answer would be indeterminate (U).

TOL-3021 (BHT-3021) is a plasmid that encodes proinsulin, meant to induce tolerance to it. In the Phase 1 trial in type 1 diabetes patients (NCT00453375; Roep 2013, published before the index trial), proinsulin-reactive CD8+ T cells fell selectively in the BHT-3021 arm (P<0.006). That shows antigen-specific engagement in this disease. C-peptide preservation in that trial was only exploratory. No human data on exposure (plasmid expression levels) were found. In NCT03895437, C-peptide AUC did not differ from placebo (p=0.368), and the DSMB stopped the trial for futility. So engagement was shown, yet the pathway and clinical effect did not follow, which points to F2. Confidence is low because the engagement marker is a peripheral T-cell frequency and the program has no Phase 2 biomarker data. The sources give no other explanation for the failure.

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation of the UniCAR02-T plus TMpPSMA target module (NCT04633148) was terminated. The sponsor states the product was well tolerated but showed very limited biological activity, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no posted results, PK, target-engagement or biomarker data for TMpPSMA, so all three pillars are no_human_data. PSMA (FOLH1) is a validated target in this disease: lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan is FDA-approved, and many PSMA agents reached Phase 3. That points to the molecule or platform rather than the target, supporting F1b. The modalities differ (radioligand versus redirected CAR-T) and no engagement data exist, so U also applies. Confidence is low.

drug: carbomer homopolymer type c (allyl pentaerythritol crosslinked)
rationale: 1146A is an intranasal carbomer 980 gel meant to trap common cold viruses physically on the nasal surface. It has no molecular target. The protocol for NCT03005067 says the concentration was chosen from in vitro virus-trapping data only, and that safety had been shown in rats. The search found no human data on how long the gel stays on the nasal lining, whether it reduces virus levels, or on any biomarker. The primary endpoint, average nasal symptom score over days 1-4, was not met (p=0.516). Nothing in the sources separates a drug that failed to trap virus in people from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

HST-001 (Hair Stimulating Complex) is a mix of growth factors (KGF, VEGF, follistatin) with no single recorded target. No human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects turned up. The sponsor did not report the index Phase 1b/2a trial (NCT04435847, 36 men) as a failure. Histogen said HST-001 separated from placebo on the week-18 primary endpoint (total hair count at the vertex), but the press release does not say whether that result was statistically significant. At week 26 the company reported a statistically significant gain in total hair count, said the drug was safe, and said it was planning a next US study. No efficacy or safety reason for stopping was found. That points to business or strategic reasons (F8), with F9 as a secondary code since the readout was not an efficacy failure. Confidence is low because no source we found states why the program stopped.

The bundle has no direct human measure of NQO1 engagement or of muscle exposure. The only PK data are from healthy volunteers at 90 mg/day, far below the DMD dose (PMID:15374359). The pillars are inferred because DELOS met its PEF%p endpoint in DMD patients not taking glucocorticoids at 900 mg/day (NCT01027884, PMID:25907158), the dose used in SIDEROS. SIDEROS (NCT02814019) enrolled glucocorticoid users and stopped for futility on FVC%p. The DELPHI post-hoc analysis found a smaller idebenone effect in steroid users and raised possible steroid-mediated suppression or a ceiling effect (PMID:23129412). This points to the population as the main explanation. DELOS reported similar effects with prior steroid use, so a target that does not matter (F2) or an indeterminate cause cannot be excluded.

DS-7080a is an intravitreal antibody that activates ROBO4. The index trial, NCT02530918, was a first-in-human Phase 1 study in nAMD and DME. It set 4.0 mg as the maximum tolerated dose, and the drug was generally well tolerated. Central subfield thickness did not change significantly on DS-7080a alone, and individual patients varied, some improving and some worsening. The published report and preprint give no human ocular drug levels, no measure of ROBO4 binding or activation, and no pathway biomarker. The sponsor gave no stated reason for stopping, and no other drug on ROBO4 is in the bundle. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

OBI-999 is a Globo H-targeting MMAE antibody-drug conjugate. NCT04084366 showed 0% ORR at every dose and in every cohort and was stopped for lack of therapeutic potential. PMID:36701651 reports plasma pharmacokinetics (nonlinear, lower clearance at higher doses), but no tumor-tissue drug levels. It also reports no measure of Globo H binding, ADC internalization or payload delivery, and no downstream pathway biomarker. Neutropenia (a payload effect) capped the dose at an MTD of 1.2 mg/kg. The bundle does not show this cap fell below the level engagement needed, so dose_limited is false. No other Globo H agent appears in the bundle. With engagement having no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter.

OBI-999 is an MMAE antibody-drug conjugate aimed at Globo H. In dose escalation, grade 4 neutropenia at 1.6 mg/kg set the maximum tolerated dose at 1.2 mg/kg, and that dose was used in the expansion cohorts (PMID:36701651). No patient in any cohort had an objective response (NCT04084366). The investigators' expansion paper did not measure target binding, internalization or a downstream biomarker. It blamed the lack of responses on suboptimal systemic exposure at the tolerated dose and inefficient antigen binding. So exposure is rated inadequate and dose_limited is true, both based on the investigators' judgement rather than a direct measurement. That fits F1a: the mechanism was not properly tested. Engagement was never measured directly, so U also applies. Tumour Globo H levels (H-score) did not track tumour shrinkage, and the authors also cited complex tumour biology, so F3 is secondary.

The index trial NCT05081388 was a Phase 1/2 safety study of REGN14256 with or without imdevimab. It was terminated for 'Sponsor Decision' after enrolling 25 participants. Its primary outcomes were mainly safety measures (TEAEs, ISRs, hypersensitivity) plus descriptive viral load, with no statistical efficacy comparison. The posted results show no safety signal. The trial was therefore not an adequate efficacy test of the drug, and no efficacy failure is shown. The bundle has no human data on exposure, viral target engagement or pathway effects. It also has no other trials, no Phase 1 results and no abstracts. Why the sponsor stopped the program, whether for business reasons or viral variant escape, is not documented here. Engagement remains unknown (U), and the tiny enrollment limits what the trial can show (F7).

In the VANCE trial (NCT02578641), adding baltaleucel-T, an autologous EBV-specific CTL product, after gemcitabine-carboplatin did not improve overall survival (25 vs 24.9 months, HR 1.19). Delivery was adequate: cells were made for 94% of patients in the cell-therapy arm, 80.5% got at least two infusions, the median dose was 4.5×10^8 cells/m², and side effects were mild. The sources I found give no human evidence of target engagement for this product in NPC, such as CTL expansion or persistence, tumor homing, killing of EBV-antigen-expressing cells, or a drop in plasma EBV DNA. They also give no sponsor explanation that separates poor engagement from a mechanism that doesn't matter. Many patients went on to checkpoint inhibitors afterward (e.g. 72% at US sites), which could have blurred the OS comparison (F7, secondary). The bundle has no other drug on the same target, so F1b cannot be judged. Primary code: indeterminate (U).

In the phase 1 AURELIO-03 trial (NCT04234113), patients with mixed advanced solid tumors received subcutaneous nanrilkefusp alfa. The 2022 interim pharmacodynamic data showed NK cells fully activated even at low doses and CD8+ T cells maximally activated at 9–12 µg/kg, with no relevant effect on regulatory T cells. On that basis 12 µg/kg was chosen as the combination dose. The index trial used 9–12 µg/kg, so engagement and immune pathway activation were adequate at the doses tested. Tolerability did not cap the dose: dose-limiting toxicities appeared only at 15 µg/kg. Even so, ORR with cetuximab in CRC was 0%, and the pembrolizumab combinations were also futile (NCT05256381). So IL-2/IL-15Rβγ stimulation does not drive response here (F2). Caveats: the index trial was small (n=16), and engagement was not measured in CRC patients specifically.

In the first-in-human trial NCT02516553, a revised dosing schedule (Schedule C) reached plasma levels the authors call sufficient to fully dislodge BRD-NUT from chromatin (PMID:35444289). It also produced sustained, pronounced pharmacodynamic modulation of HEXIM1, an established BET engagement marker (PMID:29491412), and of HIST2H2BF in patient samples. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore look adequate in cancer patients, but this was published after the trial started. Despite this, the authors say monotherapy benefit of BET inhibition is limited and turn to combination therapy, which supports F2. DLTs were frequent and platelet toxicity shaped the schedule, so on-target toxicity (F5) is a secondary code. The index trial was a DLT-based dose-finding study rather than an efficacy test (F9).

The index trial NCT04843319 was a dose-finding study whose primary endpoint was the proportion of men reaching castrate testosterone (<50 ng/dL) by day 28. This is the direct pharmacodynamic readout of GnRHR antagonism. It was terminated because 'end points were not achieved at current dose level', meaning testosterone suppression, the pathway effect, was inadequate at the dose tested. No results were posted, so exposure is unmeasured. Other GnRHR antagonists, degarelix, abarelix and relugolix, are FDA-approved for prostate cancer on the same mechanism and endpoint. That points to the molecule or its dose and formulation, not the target. Inadequate engagement also fits F1a. Confidence is medium because the bundle has no quantitative data.

TER-101 is a topical inhibitor of cPLA2α, an enzyme that drives inflammation. In the index Phase 2a trial (NCT04753034), the 2.75% ointment did not beat vehicle (EASI change -47.4% vs -42.1%). According to the protocol, an earlier Phase 1/2a study of the 1% ointment measured only blood levels (low absorption in AD patients) and found no clear efficacy signal. The 2.75% strength was chosen based on animal and lab studies. No human source reports drug levels in skin, cPLA2α inhibition, or a downstream marker moving, such as lower eicosanoid (prostaglandin or leukotriene) levels. No other cPLA2 drug appears in the bundle, and the sponsor gave no reason for the failure. So I cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage its target or the target does not matter in AD: U.

mRNA-2416 is intratumorally injected mRNA encoding OX40L, so the drug was delivered directly to its site of action. On-treatment tumor biopsies in patients showed increased OX40L protein (engagement, i.e. target expression achieved), plus elevated PD-L1 and proinflammatory responses (pathway) (PMID:40515479). These data were published after the index trial started. MTD was not reached, there were no DLTs, and doses went up to 8 mg, so the dose was not capped by tolerability (NCT03323398). Despite proof of mechanism, ORR was 0% in nearly all arms and 7.7% in the ovarian expansion cohort with durvalumab, and the trial was stopped because efficacy endpoints were not met. Delivering OX40L in this setting did not translate into clinical benefit.

Exposure: dose-proportional plasma exposure to conjugated and free camptothecin at the 15 mg/m2 biweekly MTD (PMID:23397498). Camptothecin was detected in 9/9 gastric/esophageal tumors (PMID:27001839). Engagement and pathway: tumor TOP1, CAIX, Ki-67 and VEGF decreased after dosing (PMID:24768630, PMID:27001839, PMID:23980155), and gammaH2AX rose (PMID:41145467). These data come from other solid tumors, not RCC, though most predate the index start. The index trial used the same RP2D, which was well tolerated with no DLTs (PMID:27457310). It showed no PFS benefit versus SOC (3.7 vs 3.9 months, P=0.831) and no new safety signal (PMID:28950297, NCT02187302). With the mechanism engaged, the TOP1/HIF mechanism did not deliver benefit in refractory mRCC. Confidence is medium because engagement in RCC itself was not measured.

At the 15 mg/m2 biweekly MTD, plasma exposure to conjugated and free camptothecin was dose-proportional (PMID:23397498). CPT was detected in human tumors after dosing (PMID:27001839). The sources describe inhibition of the target in human tumors, with TOP1 and CaIX/Ki-67 falling in tumor biopsies (PMID:23980155, PMID:24768630, PMID:27001839) and γH2AX rising (PMID:41145467). This evidence comes from mixed solid tumors and gastroesophageal cancer, not specifically NSCLC, and was all published after the index trial started in 2011. Despite adequate pillars, OS in NCT01380769 was worse than best supportive care (6.3 vs 11.9 months). That points to TOP1 inhibition by this agent not driving benefit in pretreated NSCLC. The unusually long control-arm survival raises possible design or imbalance issues, but the bundle does not state this.

The only source is the index Phase 1 trial NCT03971825 of CC-92252 in healthy volunteers and psoriasis patients. It was terminated because it 'did not meet progression criteria' and posted no results. The bundle records no primary target, no pharmacokinetic, receptor occupancy or biomarker data, no other trials of the drug, no other drugs on the same target, and no publications. With no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway, nothing separates a molecule that failed to engage its target from a target that does not matter in psoriasis. The failure is therefore indeterminate (U).

CC-92252 (DEL106) is an IL-2 mutein Fc fusion that preferentially binds IL-2Rα and is meant to expand regulatory T cells (Tregs). The index trial NCT03971825 was terminated because it did not meet progression criteria. A 2023 PMC review reports the drug was safe and well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In both healthy volunteers and psoriasis skin lesions, Treg expansion was selective but modest (at most 2-fold), with no clinical improvement trend over placebo. Mechanistic studies found it to be a weak partial agonist, with only a subset of Tregs responding. That means engagement and the downstream Treg effect were partial, so the mechanism was not fully tested (F1a). The bundle has no data on drug levels. These findings were published after the trial began.

In NCT02641002 (0.1–4.0 mg/kg), serum exposure was dose-dependent. However, anti-drug antibodies appeared at all doses and became more frequent over time. The investigators state that the study stopped in dose escalation for lack of monotherapy activity and because of ADAs (PMID:34981142). This points to compromised exposure, with the mechanism not properly tested. The ADA effect on exposure was not quantified, so this call is weak. No human CD47 occupancy or pathway (phagocytosis) data exist; target engagement evidence is preclinical only (PMID:34247273). MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Other CD47 agents (e.g., magrolimab) reached phase 3, but the bundle shows none succeeding, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, U is also plausible.

In NCT02641002, 28 patients with AML or MDS received CC-90002 at 0.1–4 mg/kg. No objective responses occurred, and no MTD or non-tolerated dose was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Serum exposure rose with dose, but anti-drug antibodies appeared at every dose level and became more common over time. The paper's PK became linear only at ≥15 mg/kg, which suggests the target was saturated only at that level. The index doses were therefore far below it. The only occupancy data showed 100% CD47 saturation on red blood cells, which soak up the drug and do not show binding on leukemic blasts. There were no pathway biomarkers. Reviews say the trial ended for lack of activity plus anti-drug antibodies. The mechanism was likely never properly tested, so F1a, with U if the exposure evidence is judged insufficient. F1b does not apply because no same-target drug in the bundle succeeded in MDS.

The only source is the Phase 1 dose-escalation trial NCT03119467 in relapsed or refractory lymphoma. Its primary endpoint was MTD, and it was terminated after 21 patients with the stated reason 'stopped after reviewing PK and safety results' (classified pk_pd_or_formulation). No results were posted. There are no other trials, no abstracts, no target-engagement or pathway data, and no other ORAI1 drugs in the bundle. The stop reason points to a pharmacokinetic or exposure problem, perhaps combined with tolerability, rather than a test of the ORAI1 mechanism. So the mechanism was likely never properly tested (F1a). The PK finding is not described, which makes this inference weak. U applies because engagement is undocumented, and F6 because safety contributed.

No target, Phase 1 or PubMed data are in the bundle. All three pillars are inferred_adequate only because topical otic DF289 alone met clinical endpoints in pediatric acute otitis media (NCT01395966, NCT01404611). There, median time to cessation of otorrhea was about 7 days on DF289 versus 22 days on DF277, a similar ear compartment. In the index AOE trial (NCT03196973), cure rates were 61% for the combination, 54% for DF289 and 44% for DF277, with no statistical comparison posted. The primary endpoint is therefore not assessable. The trial mainly tested whether adding DF277 helped, not DF289's own efficacy, and DF289 was numerically better than DF277. A drug efficacy failure is not shown. Small arm sizes may also have limited the trial's power.

Flufirvitide-3 is an inhaled 16-amino-acid peptide from the HA2 fusion region, meant to block hemagglutinin-mediated fusion. In the index challenge trial (NCT02423577), it did not reduce viral shedding: 51/53 on FF-3 vs 22/26 on placebo (RR 1.14, p=0.14). No serious adverse events were reported, so toxicity is not shown as the reason. Neither Phase 1 trial (NCT01313962, NCT01990846) posted PK results. My searches found no human data on airway drug levels, fusion inhibition or any viral biomarker; the only efficacy evidence is in vitro and in ferrets, which does not count. No other drug on the same target is in the bundle. With engagement having no human data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

IW-3718 is a gastric-retentive form of colesevelam. It is meant to bind bile acids that reflux into the stomach, so the site of action is the stomach and the refluxate. No human data were found on gastric drug levels, bile-acid binding in gastric or oesophageal refluxate, or less bile reflux. The protocol describes this mechanism as theorized. Colesevelam's approvals (LDL, HbA1c) rest on bile-acid binding in the intestine, a different compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred from them. The Phase 2b trial (NCT02637557, PMID:32092310) showed only a modest effect at the top dose. Both Phase 3 trials then showed no difference from placebo (NCT03561883 p=0.56; NCT03561090 p=0.63), and Ironwood stopped the program. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

UNR844 is a lipoic acid prodrug meant to break disulfide bonds between lens proteins and so restore lens elasticity. None of the sources gives human data on drug levels in the aqueous humor or lens, on disulfide reduction, or on any measure of lens elasticity or accommodation. The case for aqueous delivery rests on animal work cited in the index trial's protocol. The phase 2a (PMID:33514891) DCNVA gain did not hold up. In NCT03809611 the drug missed superiority, and in NCT04806503 all four doses (5–30 mg/mL) matched placebo, with no dose response and no tolerability limit. Novartis stopped the program because the trial showed no significant dose response. With no engagement data, the sources cannot tell a drug that never reached or acted on the lens from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U. Placebo arms improved notably, about −0.11 logMAR at Month 3 here, so F7 is a possible secondary.

PMID:39983024 reports for both phase 1 studies (NCT04158583 monotherapy, NCT04642365 with atezolizumab) that serum RG6292 levels rose dose-proportionally (exposure). Peripheral Tregs were depleted in a sustained, dose-dependent way, and intratumoral Treg reduction of ≥50% was seen at 35–100 mg (engagement and pathway, in solid-tumor patients). The drug was well tolerated, with an MTD of 165 mg, and the proposed RP2D of 70 mg was used in Part 2, so dose was not limited. Despite Treg depletion consistent with the mechanism, only three partial responses occurred, and Part 2 ORR was 0%. The authors judged efficacy insufficient. The mechanism was engaged but did not produce benefit. Engagement data were published in 2025, after the index trial started.

In solid-tumor patients, serum RG6292 levels rose dose-proportionally, so exposure was adequate. Engagement was adequate: sustained, dose-dependent depletion of peripheral Tregs. The pathway pillar was also adequate: intratumoral Treg reduction of at least 50% at 35–100 mg, consistent with the mode of action (PMID:39983024). The maximum tolerated dose (165 mg) was reached and the recommended phase II dose was 70 mg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Clinical activity was minimal: three partial responses in combination, and ORR 0% in Part 2 of NCT04642365. The authors judged efficacy insufficient alone or with atezolizumab, and the sponsor cited low likelihood of efficacy. Treg depletion therefore did not drive antitumor benefit as tested (F2). Recruitment challenges were a secondary factor (F7). The engagement data were published in 2025, after the index trial started.

Exposure was adequate: plasma Cmax and AUC rose dose-proportionally (PMID:21385886, PMID:21285985). Engagement was adequate: at the 60 mg three-times-weekly dose used in the index trial, PBMC histone H3 acetylation rose with dose and Cmax in solid-tumor patients, and HDAC inhibition was 'consistently observed' (PMID:21385886, PMID:21586629). This was published years before the index trial started. However, in the heme/AML Phase 1, acetylation did not rise in step with plasma levels (PMID:28841236). So engagement was not shown in AML, which leaves some F1a doubt. No downstream pathway marker was reported. PRIMULA showed identical median OS (9.95 months, p=0.83) despite an encouraging single-arm Phase 2 (NCT03151408, PMID:38499457, PMID:30760466). HDAC inhibition added to azacitidine does not appear to drive benefit.

The sources contain no human data on whether zuretinol acetate (QLT091001) reached the retina or replaced the 11-cis-retinal chromophore. They report no ocular drug levels and no direct measure of rhodopsin regeneration. Open-label Phase 1b studies in RPE65/LRAT LCA and RP (NCT01014052, PLoS One) found some patients with better visual fields or acuity. Those studies had no control group and did not meet a pivotal endpoint, so they cannot support an inferred_adequate rating. In the 43-patient Phase 2a index trial (NCT01999764), QLT's 10-K reported only trends toward faster dark adaptation and glare recovery, and no clear effect on low-luminance, low-contrast acuity. A small proof-of-concept trial may simply have been underpowered (F7). Because there is no engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In SOLAR (NCT01285401), patients took 14,007 IU/day of vitamin D3 alongside interferon beta-1a. Blood levels of vitamin D (serum 25(OH)D) rose, so exposure was adequate. However, no source measured VDR activation in immune cells or any immune biomarker downstream of VDR, so engagement and pathway are no_human_data. The sources mainly blame the trial itself. Recruitment was difficult, the primary endpoint was changed to NEDA-3, and only about two-thirds of the planned patients enrolled. Exploratory MRI results suggested fewer new lesions (PMID 31594857), which points to an underpowered trial rather than a clean negative. Even so, with no engagement data, the evidence cannot separate a drug that did not engage its target from a target that does not matter (U). F4 is also possible because of the MRI signal.

In NCT02980224, OmegaD softgels (an omega-3 plus vitamin D combination) missed both primaries: TBUT change 1.45 vs 1.23 and OSDI change -13.39 vs -15.04, with placebo numerically better on symptoms. Systemic exposure is supported indirectly: colecalciferol raises serum 25(OH)D in osteoporosis trials (NCT00692913, NCT01437111) and is approved for vitamin D deficiency. The index trial dose is not given, so this is labelled inferred_adequate. The bundle has no human evidence of VDR engagement or downstream pathway effects at the ocular surface, in dry eye patients or anyone else. The large placebo improvement may have limited assay sensitivity. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged ocular VDR from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01808482 was a first-in-human safety/PK/PD study. It was terminated without results after GSK confirmed misrepresentation of the preclinical data supporting the MS rationale. It was neither an efficacy readout nor an efficacy failure, so the code is F9. In the later healthy-volunteer study (NCT02293161, PMID:30161291), exposure was shown and engagement was strong: >95% receptor occupancy through day 22 at 2.0 mg/kg. The pathway effect was also shown, with maximal inhibition of IL-7-mediated STAT5 phosphorylation. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers and only after the index trial began. High anti-drug antibody rates were noted (PMID:33755713) but were not cited as the stop reason.

Phase 1 studies in patients with mixed solid tumours, published 2002–2003 before the index trial, showed that plasma CA4P/CA4 exposure rose linearly with dose. DCE-MRI showed tumour blood flow fell significantly at about 60 mg/m2, the dose class used in FALCON. A phase 1 trial with bevacizumab (NCT00395434) showed sustained drops in tumour perfusion. No direct human tubulin-binding assay exists, so I scored engagement as adequate based on this mechanism-specific vascular shutdown, which is a judgement call. Even so, adding the drug to chemotherapy plus bevacizumab did not improve PFS (8.6 vs 9.3 months), and dose was not limited by tolerability. So the vascular-disruption mechanism did not add benefit in NSCLC (F2). If tubulin binding itself is required as engagement evidence, the code would be U. No study shows engagement specifically in NSCLC patients.

Phase 1 studies in patients with solid tumours, published in 2002–2003, measured plasma pharmacokinetics. Their DCE-MRI scans showed tumour blood flow falling at about 60 mg/m2, which is the vascular-disruption effect the mechanism predicts (pathway adequate). No source measured tubulin binding directly. I rated engagement inferred_adequate because a related regimen met its endpoint in ovarian cancer: GOG 186I (NCT01305213) reported that adding fosbretabulin to bevacizumab improved progression-free survival. That inference is weak because the benefit came in combination, not with fosbretabulin alone. No study measured engagement in neuroendocrine tumour patients. In the index trial (NCT02132468, n=18, single arm) chromogranin A improved in only 1 patient, 5-HIAA in 2 of 13 and serotonin in 0 of 12. This fits F2: the vasculature was disrupted, yet hormone markers did not respond. The trial was tiny and had no success threshold (F7). No source states why the program stopped.

In the index trial (NCT00771810), 300 µg/kg TXA127 did no better than placebo on cycles with platelets below 50,000 (21.5% vs 20.0%). The 100 µg/kg arm showed a numerical drop to 11.7%, but the trial was small (n=34) and reported no significant benefit, which suggests underpowering (F7). A Phase I pharmacokinetic study of Ang-(1-7) exists, but the pages I retrieved gave no plasma levels. I found no human evidence of MAS1 receptor occupancy or a proximal MAS1 biomarker. The Springer paper on the index trial reports platelet pharmacodynamics, but platelets are the clinical endpoint itself, not a separate engagement marker. With engagement unmeasured and no MAS1 agonist on the same target to compare against, I cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.
