Later thrombocytopenia studies stopped with no results (NCT01121120) or for recruitment problems (NCT01362036).

None of the sources I found show talfirastide reaching or engaging MAS1 in humans. There are no PK, receptor-binding or proximal MAS1 biomarker data. The only 'pharmacodynamic' readout the investigators report is platelet count, which is the clinical outcome itself, not evidence of target engagement. The index trial NCT00771810 was very small (about 10 to 12 patients per arm). The 100 µg/kg arm showed a trend (Grade 4 thrombocytopenia 0% vs 6% of cycles, p=0.07), but 300 µg/kg was no better than placebo. That non-monotonic pattern, together with the low power, points to a trial that could not answer the question (F7). Without engagement data, though, the sources cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter. So the code is U.

Glatiramer acetate has no recorded molecular target. It met clinical relapse endpoints in RRMS (NCT01067521, NCT04121221), a closely related CNS demyelinating disease, at standard subcutaneous doses. So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate for its immunomodulatory mechanism. In MS patients it induced Th2-polarized T-cell responses (PMID:10749576, published before the index trial) and reduced microglial activation (PMID:22160466). No engagement data exist in optic neuritis patients. In the index trial (NCT00856635), RNFL thinning at month 6 was identical between arms, so the mechanism did not protect the axons after acute optic neuritis. However, the trial was very small (13 per arm analyzed), and the 6-month structural endpoint may not suit a slow-acting immunomodulator. That makes F7 and F4 plausible contributors, though no source states the reason for failure.

The index trial NCT01465529 had safety and local tolerability of multiple inhaled doses as its only primary outcome, and its endpoint class is not_efficacy. It was not an efficacy test of OligoG, so its completion is not an efficacy failure. No results were posted and no stop reason was given. For the pillars, PMID:26833139 (2016, after the index start) reports effective lung deposition in CF patients and altered CF sputum viscoelasticity, a functional effect. Mucin binding was shown only by modeling and ex vivo, so human target engagement is not directly shown. The phase 2b trials (PMID:33421446) are mentioned, but their efficacy outcomes are not in the bundle.

In SPRING (NCT02669849), a single 9 mg dose of VX-210 applied extradurally showed no gain in UEMS over placebo (p=0.75). The trial stopped when it met its pre-defined interim futility rule (PMID:33559524). The only human PK is serum, which showed low and variable systemic exposure (PMID:21381984). That does not tell us whether the drug reached the spinal cord. Nobody measured spinal cord or CSF drug levels, Rho inactivation, or any downstream biomarker in humans. The publication says the 9 mg dose was chosen to maximize target engagement, but that is a rationale, not a measurement. Spinal cord penetration and Rho inactivation were shown only in rodents (PMID:19061375), and no other Rho-targeting drug is in the bundle. So the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter. That makes the code U. F7 is secondary because the authors point to trial design as the area to improve.

The index trial NCT01796171 was a single-arm Phase 1/2 dose-finding study. Its primary outcomes are participant counts with no prespecified threshold or comparator, so it was not an efficacy test that could fail. Lilotomab served as the cold CD37 pre-dosing antibody for 177Lu-lilotomab satetraxetan. SPECT/CT dosimetry in NHL/FL patients showed tumor uptake (exposure and engagement; PMID:27493270). Pre-dosing lowered red marrow dose, showing CD37 engagement (PMID:29470615). FDG-PET reductions tracked tumor dose of at least 200 cGy (pathway; PMID:35486292, PMID:33196921). These data were published after the 2012 start. Clinical activity was shown: ORR 65% in FL (PMID:32877524) and 38.9% in Part B (PMID:41754790). The bundle gives no efficacy failure or stated stop reason, so F9 applies.

The index trial NCT02961283 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study of ASN003, a BRAF/PI3K inhibitor. It was terminated after 24 patients with the stated reason 'reformulation'. No results were posted, and the bundle has no other trials, PK/PD data, publications or same-target comparators. There was no efficacy readout, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). The reformulation reason hints at a pharmacokinetic or formulation problem, possibly inadequate exposure (F1a). However, no exposure, engagement or pathway data are shown in humans. If the stop is read as a failure, the result is indeterminate (U). The bundle is very thin.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT04053062 (n=12, toxicity primary endpoint) was suspended 'due to efficacy evaluation' and posted no results. The bundle has no PubMed abstracts and no human data on CAR-T expansion or persistence, PSMA-cell depletion or downstream biomarkers. Every pillar is therefore no_human_data. Another PSMA (FOLH1)-directed agent, lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan, is FDA-approved in prostate cancer, so PSMA-targeted depletion can work in this disease. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). However, the bundle cannot show whether this CAR-T failed to expand or engage, so U also applies and confidence is low.

The index trial NCT02517359 was a Phase 1 single and repeat dose safety/PK/PD study in healthy volunteers, smokers and asthma patients, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because preset pharmacokinetic stopping criteria were met at lower doses than expected. That points to a PK/exposure-margin cap, not a failed efficacy readout. No results, PD data (the sputum biomarkers) or target information are posted. The bundle has no other trials and no abstracts, so exposure at the site of action, engagement and pathway effect are all unshown in humans. Whether the exposure cap fell below the dose needed for engagement is unknown. That uncertainty is why F1a and U are listed only as secondary codes.

The index trial NCT01166061 had a safety and tolerability primary outcome for multiple intradermal injections (endpoint class not_efficacy). It completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of Grass-SPIRE. The program's later trials (NCT01385800, an exposure-unit study with patient-reported endpoints, and NCT02161107) give no classified efficacy outcome in the bundle. No target is recorded. There are no Phase 1 results, PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators, so exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human data. If the program did stop for efficacy elsewhere, the bundle cannot separate non-engagement from an irrelevant mechanism, so U applies secondarily. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

None of the sources gives human data on whether GCS-100 reached or engaged galectin-3. There are no galectin-3 binding, occupancy or downstream biomarker measurements. The earlier Phase 2a trial (NCT01843790) met its eGFR endpoint at 1.5 mg/m2, according to a company press release. The Phase 2b index trial (NCT02312050) never had an efficacy readout. La Jolla dropped GCS-100 during Phase 2b because FDA said this complex mixture needed better characterization before late-stage development. The company called the timeline for that analytical work highly uncertain and moved its resources to other programs. It stated the decision was unrelated to safety. So this was a regulatory/CMC (manufacturing and characterization) and business stop, not a failed efficacy test. F8 is primary and F9 secondary.

The index trial NCT01671774 was a 29-patient Phase 1 study of the anti-CLDN18.2 antibody IMAB362 combined with zoledronic acid and IL-2. Its primary endpoints were safety and immune-cell profile, and it posted no results and no stop reason. It was not an efficacy test of zoledronic acid, so the stoppage is not shown to be an efficacy failure (F9). Systemic exposure is inferred from approved efficacy in bone diseases (NCT01522521, NCT00799266). Those results reflect FDPS inhibition in osteoclasts, not in the immune or tumor compartment used in gastric cancer. No human engagement or pathway data (e.g., Vγ9Vδ2 T-cell expansion) appear in the bundle, which leaves the mechanism untested here (U secondary).

Index trial NCT02504008 (AXS-02, CRPS-1) posted no results and gave no stop reason, so the bundle does not document the readout itself. Exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate: zoledronic acid met efficacy endpoints through FDPS inhibition in bone in osteoporosis (NCT01522521, NCT00799266) and bone metastases (PMID:11283917). Pathway is adequate, since bone-resorption markers fell dose-dependently in published human data predating the index trial (PMID:12412821, PMID:27482615). No engagement data exist in CRPS patients, and the AXS-02 dose and formulation in the index trial are not shown to be comparable to the approved regimens. Only retrospective CRPS case series suggest benefit (PMID:37094194). Taking the program's failure as given, the most direct reading is that FDPS inhibition did not deliver benefit in CRPS (F2). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

JNJ-67864238 (PTG-200) is an oral peptide built to stay in the gut. In the Phase 2 Crohn's trial NCT04102111, CDAI improved less on drug than on placebo (-124.6 vs -153.2, p=0.288), and the trial stopped for futility. The healthy-volunteer Phase 1 reported only that PK/PD was 'consistent with' gut-restricted design. I found no human data on intestinal tissue levels, IL-23R occupancy, or pathway markers such as pSTAT3 or IL-17/22. Protagonist's 10-K said Janssen dropped PTG-200 in favour of PN-235 (icotrokinra) for its 'superior potency' and PK/PD. That hints the molecule was the problem (F1b), but icotrokinra has no pivotal Crohn's success in the bundle and PTG-200's engagement was never measured. So the cause is indeterminate.

The trial missed its primary endpoint, ACR20 at week 12, with no dose response (placebo 48.4%, 5 mg 49.2%, 20 mg 42.4%, 40 mg 57.7%; NCT05460832). No source measured mitochondrial complex I (MT-ND1) inhibition or drug levels in humans, so exposure and engagement have no human data. The sponsor reports, without published data, that RA patients showed shifts in GDF15 and FGF21, which are markers of mitochondrial function, plus better bone-turnover balance. That counts as weak pathway evidence. The sponsor blames the endpoint rather than the drug: it says leramistat works on bone and tissue repair, and that bone erosions, disability and fatigue improved significantly while ACR20, an inflammation measure, did not. This points to F4. U is listed as secondary because engagement itself was never shown.

ALG-010133 is an S-antigen transport-inhibiting oligonucleotide polymer (STOPS). It is meant to lower HBsAg, and HBsAg is also the readout that would show it engaged its target. In the index Phase 1 (NCT04485663), Aligos reported no meaningful HBsAg reduction in CHB patients at the projected efficacious dose of 400 mg. That dose was modelled, not measured, to give liver exposure above 3x the EC90 for HBsAg inhibition, so exposure is only an estimate. Tolerability did not cap the dose: no dose-limiting safety findings were seen. Higher doses were limited by feasibility, not safety, because the maximum feasible dose was 600 mg, and that dose was judged very unlikely to reach the 1 log10 HBsAg reduction Aligos required. The mechanism was therefore not shown to be engaged in patients. The bundle cannot separate a failed molecule from a mechanism that does not work, hence U as a secondary code.

The index BCRL trial (NCT04243837) had a safety/tolerability primary endpoint, not an efficacy endpoint. It was terminated because the 'primary objective/endpoint has been established' and the sponsor chose not to pursue the indication further, so this was not an efficacy failure (F9). The stop looks strategic (F8 secondary). Phase 1 data show dose-proportional plasma exposure with no MTD up to 1000 mg BID (PMID:34779583), so exposure was adequate. No target is recorded and the bundle has no human engagement or pathway data in lymphedema. The later IPF efficacy (PMID:42085224) is in a different tissue compartment and was published after the index trial, so it does not establish engagement here.

Phase 1 showed dose-proportional plasma PK, well tolerated to 1000 mg BID with no MTD (PMID:34779583), so systemic exposure at 750 mg BID was adequate. No direct target or biomarker data exist, and no target is recorded. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because deupirfenidone slowed FVC decline in IPF (same lung antifibrotic mechanism, comparable 1650–2475 mg/day dosing) in ELEVATE-IPF (NCT05321420, PMID:42085224). That evidence came after the index trial. In PASC, 6MWT improved equally in both arms (p=0.70). The authors note the anticipated progressive fibrosis largely did not materialize, and patients recovered regardless of treatment (PMID:40692836). The antifibrotic mechanism did not drive outcome in this population, which also points to population mismatch (F3). Tolerability did not cap the dose.

Deupirfenidone has no defined molecular target. Phase 1 data showed dose-proportional plasma exposure with no maximum tolerated dose up to 1000 mg BID (PMID:34779583), so exposure was adequate. No human target-engagement or pathway biomarker data exist, in long COVID or anywhere else. ELEVATE-IPF later met its FVC endpoint (PMID:42085224), but that was a different, fibrotic disease, it used higher doses (550/825 mg TID), and it came after the index trial, so it cannot support inferred engagement here. The index trial missed its 6MWT endpoint (p=0.698), and both arms improved substantially. The sponsor reported no treatment effect and did not attribute the failure to dose or to the mechanism. Nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U. The large placebo-arm improvement suggests possible design issues (F7).

The index trial NCT04229303 was a Phase 1 SAD/MAD/crossover safety study of inhaled ZP-059 (voriconazole) in healthy and asthmatic subjects. Its only primary outcome was TEAE counts. It reported no serious or severe TEAEs, so it was not an efficacy test and did not fail on efficacy. Systemic voriconazole is FDA-approved for candidiasis and fusariosis, so antifungal engagement is inferred adequate. Human CSF levels above the minimal fungicidal concentration were reported in PMID:9207418. A retrospective series in cryptococcal meningitis suggests benefit (PMID:26100526). The cryptococcal meningitis trial NCT04072640 has unknown status. The bundle shows no efficacy failure and no stated reason for stopping, so this is F9.

No pillar was measured in PH-COPD patients. All three are inferred adequate because the same inhaled treprostinil, acting on IP receptors in the pulmonary vasculature, is approved for PH due to lung disease (2021). It also met its primary endpoints in IPF (NCT04708782, NCT05255991) at comparable doses. In the index trial (NCT03496623), 6MWD change was the same on drug and placebo (-4.47 vs -5.14 m). Deaths (5/66 vs 0/58) and serious AEs were higher on drug, and a review notes PAH vasodilators may impair gas exchange in COPD (PMID:37487524). The mechanism, though engaged, did not help this unselected population. Sources suggest benefit may be confined to severe PH or an RV phenotype (PMID:41002645), supporting F3 as secondary.

The index trial NCT00848107 was an open-label extension. It was stopped because the randomized parent trial NCT00775463 missed its digital ulcer endpoint (net ulcer burden p=0.20). No human PTGIR engagement or biomarker data at the oral dose in systemic sclerosis appear in the bundle; the SSc PK study NCT00848939 posted no results. Engagement is inferred adequate because oral treprostinil met a hard endpoint in PAH (NCT01560624) through the same systemic vascular IP receptor. Local iontophoresis raised digital blood flow in SSc patients (PMID:24458011), but that was after the index trial started and by another route. Tolerability-limited oral dosing (PMID:29609511) and poor tolerability in SSc (PMID:34718447) leave open some F1a possibility. The bundle is thin.

Oral treprostinil diethanolamine failed on net ulcer burden at week 20 in SSc digital ulcers (NCT00775463, p=0.20), and the extension was stopped for futility (NCT00848107). Oral UT-15C gives measurable plasma exposure (PMID:23188123). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate: the same oral formulation met a hard clinical-worsening endpoint in PAH (NCT01560624) through systemic vascular PTGIR agonism. That trial started after the index, and the vascular bed differs (pulmonary vs digital). Local iontophoretic treprostinil raised digital skin blood flow in SSc patients (PMID:24458011), but that was a different route and was published after the index trial started. The SSc PK study (NCT00848939) posted no results. No tolerability cap is shown. The best-supported reading is that the mechanism did not translate to ulcer healing. A baseline ulcer-count imbalance (median 2 vs 1) is a possible design issue, but no source cites it.

VSL#3 is a multistrain probiotic with no defined molecular target, so engagement cannot be judged and no human target-engagement data exist. Exposure: two studies found the VSL#3 strains in the stool of healthy and IBD subjects, though colonization was only transient (PMID:12485746, PMID:11108019). I rated this inferred_adequate as the closest fit, but strictly it is direct evidence of gut presence, not a clinical-efficacy inference. Pathway: in the MHE trial, ammonia tracked response but did not differ between groups (PMID:25266207). The text I retrieved of the index paper says only that ammonia fell in some patients, not whether it differed from placebo. The index trial (NCT01110447, n=130) showed a non-significant trend on its primary endpoint (HR 0.65, P=.12) but significant cuts in HE hospitalizations, which suggests it was underpowered (F7). Since engagement is unknown, the primary code is U.

In the index trial (NCT01325337), scalp bimatoprost did not clearly beat vehicle on hair count or self-assessment, while minoxidil did. The female trial (NCT01325350) failed the same way. Exposure: plasma levels were measurable in alopecia patients (NCT01189279). Scalp biopsies, taken later (NCT02848300, PMID:42631654), showed tissue concentrations at least 10-fold above those effective in isolated follicles, although the formulations may differ from the index trial. Engagement was not measured, but is inferred adequate: PTGFR agonism by the same topical drug met efficacy endpoints in eyelash and eyebrow follicles (NCT00907426, NCT01698554, NCT01765764). With exposure and inferred engagement in place and no dose-response in the index trial, PTGFR agonism does not appear to drive scalp hair regrowth in androgenetic alopecia.

In the index Phase 1 (NCT05013554), SAR443216 was dosed from 18 to 900 µg with dose-dependent PK and no MTD reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:42705861). In patients, it induced serum proinflammatory cytokines and raised T-cell activation markers in PBMCs; the authors read this as target engagement. However, there was no clear trend in T-cell abundance or activation (the abstract is truncated, likely referring to tumor) and no objective responses. This fits engagement without clinical benefit (F2). Tumor-site exposure and HER2-side engagement were not shown, so inadequate intratumoral engagement (F1a) cannot be excluded. The engagement evidence was published after the index trial started, and the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT05574166 was a Phase 1 single/multiple ascending dose safety and PK study of SP-8356 in healthy males. It was terminated after Part 1 only because exposures were low, so definitive safety conclusions could not be made at the targeted exposure levels. This is direct human evidence that plasma exposure was inadequate. The bundle has no engagement or pathway data for BSG inhibition. Tolerability did not cap the dose; the limit was pharmacokinetic or formulation-related. The mechanism was never properly tested, which supports F1a. F9 is secondary because this was not an efficacy test of the drug. Confidence is medium because the bundle is thin: one trial, no posted results, no publications.

In the index trial, PF-06687234 was detected at a low concentration in only one colonic biopsy, and the authors say efficacious tissue concentrations may not have been reached at 20 mg (PMID:41684726). Tissue exposure at the colonic site of action was therefore inadequate. No engagement or pathway biomarker data exist in humans. The healthy-volunteer Phase 1 was terminated over the risk of further dosing (NCT02711462), which suggests tolerability limited the dose. The trial was small (n=20) and stopped for futility, with the sponsor citing a change in strategy (NCT03269695). Because of that, the trial design and business reasons are secondary contributors. The mechanism was not properly tested.

Bosentan's plasma exposure and ET-receptor binding are shown in healthy adults. Target-mediated disposition with ET-1 displacement appears in PMID:28401480, PK in PMID:23738582. A pathway effect is also shown: reduced PVR in hypoxic pulmonary hypertension (PMID:19188550, 2009). None of this was shown in neonates with PPHN. The index trial NCT01389856 enrolled only 21 analysed patients (13 vs 8) on background iNO. It was terminated for regulatory PIP timeline reasons, not for futility or safety. The placebo arm had 0% treatment failure, and all p-values were far from significance. The truncated, tiny trial could not answer the question. F2 is possible but cannot be separated, given no engagement data in newborns.

The index trial (NCT01360853, PMID:26091808) gave 1800 mg/m2 IV rigosertib with gemcitabine and missed overall survival (HR 1.24). A Phase 1 trial of the same combination (NCT01125891, Clin Cancer Res 2012) measured plasma levels in pancreatic cancer patients at this dose (mean Cmax ~214 µg/mL). Gemcitabine did not change those levels. That supports plasma exposure only. No tumor drug levels were reported. No human measurement of PLK1 inhibition or of downstream markers (phospho-CDC25C, cyclin B1) turned up. Those markers were studied only in xenografts (PMID:19029951). A CETSA paper notes that PLK1 as the drug's mechanism has been disputed. Other PLK1 drugs in this disease reached only Phase 2, so F1b does not apply. Dose was not tolerability-limited. Engagement is unmeasured, so the cause is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT01165905 was a small Phase 1 safety study of 24-hour rigosertib infusion with gemcitabine in advanced solid tumors. Its primary outcomes were adverse events and laboratory parameters, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug in plasma cell myeloma or any other disease. No efficacy failure is shown. The only myeloma-related trial, NCT00861510, posted no results. The bundle has no human PLK1 engagement or pathway biomarker data. PMID:40439508 reports pharmacokinetics only, not as target-sufficient exposure. Rigosertib's later failures in MDS and pancreatic cancer (e.g., NCT01360853) cannot separate poor engagement from target irrelevance, so U is a secondary code.

The index trial, NCT02030639, is a [14C]-rigosertib mass-balance/ADME study in 6 healthy volunteers. Its endpoints are radioactivity recovery and plasma concentrations, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug and cannot be a failed efficacy readout (F9). The bundle shows no human PLK1 engagement or pathway data in mantle cell lymphoma. The MCL-relevant trial NCT00861510 has no posted results. MCL mechanistic data (PMID:19198627) are in vitro only and point to PI3K/cyclin D1 translation rather than PLK1. PMID:40439508 mentions PK monitoring in RDEB-SCC patients but gives no quantitative exposure. If the program's halt were treated as a mechanism question, it would be indeterminate (U). The broader program failed in phase 3 MDS (NCT01241500, NCT02562443).

In INSPIRE (NCT02562443), median overall survival was 6.4 months on rigosertib versus 6.3 months on physician's choice. The earlier phase 3 ONTIME trial (NCT01241500) had also missed its survival endpoint. No source shows in humans that rigosertib reached or inhibited PLK1. Even its target is disputed: the sources describe it as a Ras-effector inhibitor (PMID:29144985) or a microtubule destabilizer (PMID:28985505). The only human signal is lower AKT2 phosphorylation in marrow CD34+ cells from a few patients who responded (PMID:21924492). That is a PI3K-pathway marker, not PLK1, and it was seen only in responders. Plasma PK was collected but never judged against a level needed to engage the target. Other PLK1 drugs have not succeeded in MDS. With engagement unknown, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug or the target, so the code is U. INSPIRE enrolled the post-HMA subgroup picked out after ONTIME, which supports F3 as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT02030639 is a [14C]-rigosertib mass-balance and excretion study in 6 healthy volunteers. Its endpoints are radioactivity recovery and plasma concentrations, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug, and its completion is not an efficacy failure (F9). The bundle has no human PLK1 engagement or pathway data in hairy cell leukemia or elsewhere. The NIH lymphoid pilot (NCT00861510), which included hairy cell leukemia, posted no results. PMID:40439508 reports only qualitative PK absorption in RDEB-SCC. The wider program failed in MDS phase 3 (NCT01241500, NCT02562443), but nothing separates non-engagement from target irrelevance, so U is secondary.

In the ONTIME trial (NCT01241500, PMID:26968357), IV rigosertib at 1800 mg/24 h did not improve overall survival in higher-risk MDS/CMML after hypomethylating-agent failure (HR 0.87, p=0.33). I found no human measurement of PLK1 inhibition, occupancy or a downstream pathway marker. The phase 1 trials posted only safety results. A sponsor patent makes a vague claim of a 'pharmacodynamically effective drug level' for the oral formulation, with no data behind it. The drug's mechanism is itself disputed: an unbiased cell-based target-engagement study (CETSA-MS) found no direct binding to PLK1. That is in vitro, so it does not count as human evidence. No other PLK1 drug has succeeded in this disease (volasertib did not get past phase 3 in AML), so F1b does not apply. With engagement unknown, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02030639 is a [14C]-rigosertib mass-balance and excretion study in 6 healthy volunteers. Its endpoints are radioactivity recovery and plasma concentrations, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. That fits F9. The only Waldenstrom-relevant trial is the phase 1 lymphoid pilot NCT00861510, which has no reported outcome in the bundle. Human plasma exposure is documented: PMID:40439508 reports drug absorption exceeding that seen in prior patient populations. No human evidence of PLK1 engagement or a downstream pathway effect appears, in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia or elsewhere. The phase 3 survival failures in MDS (NCT01241500, NCT02562443) do not establish engagement. Any efficacy interpretation would therefore be indeterminate (U).

MDT-10013 is a Medtronic strip implanted at the surgical site after bunionectomy. The bundle does not record its target or active agent. In the index trial NCT02077140, no dose of 1, 2 or 3 strips clearly beat standard of care on SPI-48 (191.97–252.29 vs 215.35), and no statistical comparison was reported. There were no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Patsnap lists the program as discontinued at Phase 2, and an open-label knee-replacement (TKA) study looked at systemic exposure. No human PK, local tissue level, target engagement or biomarker data were found, and no sponsor statement explains why the program ended. With engagement unknown, the failure is indeterminate.

Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (PMID 27706798, published 2016, before the index trial started in 2017) showed target engagement and pathway effect. NI-0101 blocked TLR4 functionally and stopped ex vivo and in vivo LPS-induced cytokine release and CRP rise. The engagement data come from healthy volunteers, not RA patients. In the RA phase 2 (NCT03241108), drug levels stayed above the targeted 10,000 ng/mL threshold in most patients, and tolerability did not limit the dose. Even so, no efficacy endpoint differed from placebo, and subgroup analyses found no responding population. The investigators concluded that blocking TLR4 alone does not improve RA. This fits F2: the target was engaged but does not drive the disease as tested. They also suggested broader or earlier inhibition might be needed, which adds a possible F3 element.

The index trial NCT03334786 was not an efficacy test. Its primary outcomes were vital signs, oral cavity examination and adverse events after a single clinic dose. It enrolled only 3 patients and was terminated because 'Development of Current Formulation has Ceased', which points to formulation or development reasons rather than a failed readout. No results were posted. The companion Phase 2 cramp trials in motor neuron disease (NCT03196375) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (NCT03254199) were also terminated by the sponsor without results. The bundle has no human exposure, TRPA1/TRPV1 engagement or pathway data, so nothing distinguishes a mechanism problem from a molecule problem. Hence U is secondary.

Fondaparinux has complete subcutaneous bioavailability and linear plasma PK in humans (PMID:12383039). It shows anti-Xa activity, which reflects antithrombin-mediated factor Xa inhibition, in human blood and in patients (PMID:14706599, PMID:34414464). It met hard thrombotic endpoints in VTE (PMID:15172900, NCT00843492), so the anticoagulant pathway is inferred adequate in the same plasma compartment. No AF-specific engagement data were shown. The index trial (NCT00911300) compared fondaparinux against active UFH/VKA during cardioversion. Composite events were 3/174 vs 2/170 (p=1.0), essentially equivalent outcomes against an effective active comparator. This is not evidence that the drug lacks efficacy. The trial was also far too small to discriminate such rare events, so a design limitation applies as well.

Exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate, not measured. Imatinib is approved for PDGFR-driven skin and blood diseases (dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, hypereosinophilic syndrome), so PDGFR inhibition is presumed at standard doses. The index dose is not given. No human target-engagement or pathway biomarker data in SSc exist in the bundle; PMID:22691216 is in vitro only. Index NCT00613171 was single-arm and descriptive. Only 13 of 27 participants reached week 48, all had AEs and 5 had SAEs. A parallel SSc trial, NCT01545427, was terminated for frequent early adverse events and poor tolerability. Tolerability, not a clear efficacy miss, appears to have ended the program; an extension cohort showed mRSS improvement (PMID:25152211). The uncontrolled, high-dropout design also could not answer the efficacy question (F7). Confidence is low.

NCT05170269 is the PreCyssion trial. It was open-label and single-arm, enrolled 48 of a planned 66 patients, and listed 'Sponsor decision' as its stop reason. The published report says it stopped early for futility: maternal-fetal transmission came close to the rate in a calculated historical control group, and transmission did not differ by when CMVIG was started or how often it was given. The bundle has no human data on whether the drug reached its site of action or engaged its target. There are no measurements of anti-CMV IgG or neutralizing titres in mothers, placenta or fetus, and no pathway biomarkers. So the evidence cannot separate inadequate neutralization at this dose from a mechanism that does not prevent transmission. The single-arm design with a historical comparator (F7) adds uncertainty.

The sponsor's stop reason for NCT05355753 states that high levels of BRD9 degradation did not produce sufficient efficacy in heavily pre-treated synovial sarcoma and SMARCB1-null patients. PMID:41285423 reports dose-dependent increases in human exposure and a robust pharmacodynamic response (BRD9 degradation) in these patients, so exposure and engagement were adequate in the disease population. That evidence was published in 2025, after the index trial started. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. Since the target was engaged without benefit, BRD9 degradation as monotherapy does not appear to drive clinical response (F2). Cardiac toxicities also hindered monotherapy advancement (secondary F6), but they are not described as capping the dose below engagement.

The sponsor's stop reason for NCT05355753 says high levels of BRD9 degradation did not produce sufficient efficacy in heavily pre-treated synovial sarcoma and SMARCB1-null patients. PMID:41285423 reports dose-dependent increases in human exposure and a robust pharmacodynamic (degradation) response in these patients, so exposure and engagement were adequate in the disease population. That evidence was published in 2025, after the 2022 trial start. No downstream pathway biomarker is described. Efficacy was only modest, so BRD9 degradation alone does not drive clinical benefit in this late-line setting (F2). Cardiac toxicities also held back monotherapy development; whether they are on- or off-target is unstated (secondary F6). Dose was not shown to be capped below the level needed for engagement.

In NCT02059642, metadoxine ER 1400 mg did not beat placebo on CAARS:O-SV (LS mean difference -2.10, p=0.136). The bundle has human pharmacokinetic studies (NCT01933997, PMID:17335665) but no human data on brain penetration, 5-HT2B occupancy or a downstream biomarker. The 5-HT2B evidence found is a rat stomach-fundus bioassay, which does not count as human data. Earlier positive Phase 2 results (PMID:23290324) and a benefit seen only in the predominantly inattentive subgroup (PMID:23933905) led to the inattentive-type population in the index trial, which still failed, so F3 is a secondary code. No other 5-HT2B drug has succeeded in ADHD, so F1b does not apply. Press coverage reports the readout as a plain efficacy miss and gives no mechanistic explanation. Because target engagement is unknown, the code is U.

The bundle has no direct human HTR2B occupancy, CSF exposure or pathway biomarker data. Only plasma PK (PMID:17335665, NCT01933997) and safety (NCT00995085) are shown. Pillars are inferred_adequate because the extended-release drug met its primary CAARS endpoint in adult ADHD (NCT01243242, p=0.0093), a CNS indication using the same compartment and a comparable dose, before the index trial began. That inference is weak: the Phase 3 ADHD trial (NCT02059642) did not replicate it. The index FXS trial posted no results and gave no stop reason. No tolerability limit is shown. Taken together this leans to F2, with U as the alternative if the ADHD signal is discounted.

drug: recombinant methionyl human brain-derived neurotrophic factor
rationale: The index trial NCT04129775 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study whose registered primary outcomes were safety measures (TEAEs, otoscopy, audiometry). Efficacy speech-in-noise outcomes were exploratory only. The paper (PMID:42479273) reports good tolerability and a numerical responder advantage at 0.3 mg, with no PGIC improvement. This was not a primary efficacy test, so it was not an efficacy failure. No human data show cochlear exposure, TrkB engagement or a pathway biomarker. Plasma BDNF matched endogenous levels, which speaks to systemic safety, not exposure at the site of action. ALS intrathecal CSF levels (PMID:11464953) come from a different compartment and route. Had this counted as an efficacy readout, the case would be indeterminate (U). The bundle states no reason for stopping.

Plasma exposure of tiotropium Respimat 5 µg in CF matched COPD levels (PMID:25380193, PMID:25161072). M3 engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because the same 5 µg dose met FEV1 endpoints in asthma and COPD through the same airway target (NCT01172808, NCT01431274). The CF phase 2 trial also showed dose-dependent bronchodilation (NCT00737100, PMID:25188297), so the pathway pillar held in this disease. The drug was well tolerated, with no dose cap. The phase 3 trial missed its endpoints with only small gains (1.64% AUC, 1.40% trough; NCT01179347). The pooled analysis showed a modest 2.6% benefit (PMID:25819269). Muscarinic blockade was engaged but contributes little to CF airflow obstruction. Inconsistency between the phase 2 and phase 3 results suggests a secondary trial-variance (F7) element.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT03507452) was a safety and dose-escalation study. The published report (PMID:41270699) shows no DLTs, but the MTD could not be determined because 45.7% of patients developed neutralizing antidrug antibodies, which led to treatment discontinuations. There were no objective responses, only stable disease. Neutralizing ADAs point to a molecule-specific immunogenicity problem that likely curtailed drug exposure and repeat dosing, so the mechanism was not adequately tested. No human target-engagement data (e.g., tumor uptake or dosimetry) or pathway data are reported; tumor uptake evidence is preclinical only (PMID:31064781). Classed as F1a on that basis, with F6 (immunogenicity) and U as alternatives. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

In NCT04487860, none of the four AS012 regimens beat placebo on the change in VASI score at Week 24 (all p>0.29). There were no serious adverse events, so tolerability did not cap the dose. AS012 has no recorded target, no Phase 1 or PK/PD results and no publications. My web searches turned up only registry and database entries (Patsnap lists the drug as an inactive small molecule from Aché and Sun Pharma). The protocol PDF came back as unreadable binary, so I could not check it for mechanism or PK data. There is no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway effect. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in vitiligo, so the code is indeterminate (U).

Phase 1 studies, including a multiple-ascending-dose study in SLE (NCT03933943, registered 2019), showed serum exposure and nonlinear PK consistent with near-saturated target binding. Higher doses gave high BTLA receptor occupancy on B cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and were well tolerated (PMID:41549797). In the index trial, 450 mg every 2 weeks kept occupancy near saturation at all post-randomisation time points (PMID:42540177). Even so, remission of arthritis/rash was 11.9% on drug vs 20.9% on placebo, and the trial stopped for futility (NCT05123586). Tolerability did not cap the dose. No downstream agonist-signalling biomarker is reported, so the pathway pillar is unshown and confidence is medium. With engagement adequate, the most direct reading is that BTLA agonism does not drive clinical benefit in SLE as tested.

ADPS is a Taro Pharmaceuticals topical product with no target recorded. In its Phase 2 acne trial (NCT02935036), it did no better than placebo on any of the three primary endpoints. Inflammatory lesions fell 60.8% vs 62.2% on placebo (p=0.59), non-inflammatory lesions 49.9% vs 52.7% (p=0.29), and IGA success was 13.0% vs 10.6% (p=0.69). The placebo response was high, but the sources never say this undermined the trial. No other trials, Phase 1 results or human data on skin exposure, target engagement or biomarkers could be found. The PubMed abstracts in the bundle are about unrelated things that share the 'ADPS' acronym. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never reached or engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in acne, so the result is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT03150771 is a Phase 1 PK, safety and tolerability study in schizophrenia. All its primary outcomes are AEs, labs, ECGs, EPS and injection-site measures, so it was not an efficacy test of aripiprazole. The 'amphetamine abuse' program label does not match this trial, which had no failed efficacy readout. Exposure is shown in plasma by PK in NCT00102479 and NCT01870999. D2 occupancy was measured by [11C]raclopride PET in schizophrenia (PMID:35840763), and a review notes >90% occupancy at clinical doses (PMID:28412910). The pathway pillar is inferred from met efficacy endpoints in schizophrenia (NCT01663532, NCT00705783). The only amphetamine-related human evidence is a lab study showing attenuated d-amphetamine effects (PMID:16540264); it contains no target-engagement data.

The open-label extension NCT02736149 was stopped because the parent LIBERTY trial, NCT02664558, failed: PVR at 150 mg three times daily rose more on ubenimex than on placebo. The lymphedema trial NCT02700529 also failed. Eiger's 10-K says neither the overall population nor key subgroups improved, no safety signals were found, and development was discontinued. The bundle's only human PK is a single 30 mg dose in healthy volunteers (PMID:27062789), not the dose used in the PAH trials. Neither the bundle nor the searches turned up human data on LTA4H inhibition or LTB4 lowering in PAH patients. The Japanese lung-cancer approval works through a different, broad aminopeptidase/immune mechanism, so pillar adequacy cannot be inferred from it. Engagement has no human data, so U.

In ULTRA (NCT02700529), skin thickness, limb volume and bioimpedance did not improve over placebo, and there were no safety signals. Eiger planned no further clinical work and gave no mechanistic reason for the failure. The ubenimex PAH trial (NCT02664558) also failed. The only human pharmacokinetic data are a 30 mg healthy-volunteer bioequivalence study (PMID:27062789), which says nothing about lymphedema tissue or the ULTRA dose. The only human target-engagement evidence is a 2019 colorectal cancer study, published after ULTRA started, in which bestatin lowered serum LTB4. Its dose, comparability and size of effect are unclear, and it was not done in lymphedema. There are no LTB4 or LTA4H data from lymphedema patients, so a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive the disease. F2 is possible only if engagement is assumed.

The index trial NCT04265456 was a Phase 1 safety and tolerability study of pregabalin plus acetaminophen in healthy volunteers. Its primary outcomes were adverse events and drowsiness/dizziness, so it was not an efficacy test in cannabis dependence or any other disease. The pillars are inferred_adequate: pregabalin met efficacy endpoints through α2δ in CNS indications (epilepsy NCT00524030, PMID:12771254; fibromyalgia NCT00830167; PHN NCT01270828) at comparable doses (300–600 mg/day). No target engagement was shown in cannabis-dependent patients. NCT01511640, a lab self-administration study, found no reduction in cannabis puffs but measured behaviour, not engagement. The program continued into the Phase 2 bunionectomy trial NCT04495283, which met its primary endpoint. The stop is therefore not an efficacy failure: F9.

No pillar was measured directly in PGTC patients. Pregabalin met seizure-reduction endpoints in focal epilepsy through the same α2δ target in the CNS at 150–600 mg/day, with a clear dose-response (PMID:12771254, NCT00524030, NCT01389596; FDA-approved). This makes exposure, engagement and pathway inferred_adequate at the doses used in the index trial: 300 and 600 mg/day, or 5–14 mg/kg/day. Tolerability did not cap the dose; SAEs were 2/72–75 per arm. Even so, NCT01747915 showed essentially no difference from placebo at either dose (p=0.81 and p=0.89). The engaged mechanism therefore does not appear to drive primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Seizure-type specificity, efficacy in focal but not generalized epilepsy, is a secondary population/subtype reading (F3).

The index trial NCT02349607 was a healthy-volunteer evoked-pain study of PF-05089771, with pregabalin almost certainly serving as the active analgesic comparator. It had no posted results, no stop reason, and did not enrol nicotine-dependent patients. It was therefore not an efficacy test of pregabalin in nicotine dependence. Pillars are inferred_adequate: pregabalin met CNS efficacy endpoints through α2δ binding at comparable doses in focal epilepsy (PMID:12771254, NCT00524030) and in fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain (NCT00830167, PMID:28967801). The bundle has no engagement data in nicotine dependence. The 'failure' reflects how the index trial was mapped to this program, not a failed drug readout.

OMT-28 is a synthetic analog of 17,18-EEQ (an omega-3 epoxyeicosanoid). It has no defined molecular target, and its proposed mechanism covers Ca2+ handling, mitochondrial function and anti-inflammatory effects. The Phase 1 study (NCT03078738) is described only as showing 'favorable pharmacokinetics' (PMID:32685659), which supports plasma exposure. No human evidence of target engagement or a pathway biomarker was found in AF or in healthy volunteers. No PROMISE-AF (NCT03906799) results or stated failure reason were found. The sponsor later moved to primary mitochondrial disease and reported a positive open-label Phase 2a, but that is a different disease and tissue setting with no defined target, so engagement in AF cannot be inferred. Because engagement is no_human_data, the code is U.

DE-120 is Santen's intravitreal dual VEGFR/PDGFR kinase inhibitor. The index trial, NCT02022501, was an open-label, dose-escalating Phase I/II safety study with 10 patients. It measured plasma drug levels, but no results were posted, and it was classified as not an efficacy test (hence F9 as a secondary code). The Phase 2 trial NCT02401945 (DE-120 alone and with aflibercept) also has no posted results. My searches found no human data on retinal or vitreous drug levels, target binding, or downstream markers. A 2018 review says only that Santen stopped development in 2017 and gives no reason. Engagement is no_human_data, and nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01169675 is a Phase 1 dose-escalation of afatinib combined with pemetrexed in solid tumours. Its only primary endpoint was afatinib dose-limiting toxicity, so it was not an efficacy test of pemetrexed, and no efficacy readout failed. Pemetrexed plasma exposure is documented by consistent pharmacokinetics across 500-900 mg/m2 (PMID:19118069). TYMS engagement and the downstream pathway effect are inferred from approved efficacy in NSCLC and mesothelioma (PMID:21301589) and from responses in relapsed CNS lymphoma (PMID:35898888). That inference rests on systemic exposure at comparable doses. No engagement data exist in leukemia patients, and the bundle contains no leukemia efficacy trial of this drug.

The index trial NCT00732992 was a 12-patient Phase 1 safety study of sunitinib plus pemetrexed in advanced solid malignancies. Its only primary endpoint was adverse events: there were 0 dose-limiting toxicities in either sunitinib cohort, and no stop reason was given. It was therefore not an efficacy test of pemetrexed, and no efficacy failure occurred. Plasma exposure is documented by PK across 500–900 mg/m2 (PMID:19118069). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because pemetrexed is FDA-approved for mesothelioma and NSCLC through the same DHFR/GART/TYMS mechanism at comparable systemic doses. No engagement data exist in childhood malignancy. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The program's halt is not attributable to a failed efficacy readout.

The index trial NCT01169675 is a completed Phase 1 dose-escalation of afatinib plus pemetrexed in advanced solid tumours. Its only primary endpoint is DLT counts across afatinib schedules. It was not an efficacy test of pemetrexed, and certainly not in myelodysplastic syndrome, so no efficacy failure is shown. Exposure is adequate: human PK was consistent across 500–900 mg/m2 (PMID:19118069). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate from the FDA approvals in NSCLC and mesothelioma, which act through the same DHFR/GART/TYMS antifolate mechanism. Dose-related neutropenia shows the drug acts on the marrow (PMID:34181276, PMID:35048355). No engagement data exist in MDS patients. The bundle shows no business or safety reason for ending an MDS program.

In ALTISSIMO (NCT03953079), median time to rescue was 5 months for GB-102 1 mg and 4 months for 2 mg; the aflibercept arm never reached a median. The sources contain no human data on intravitreal sunitinib levels or VEGFR occupancy or inhibition. The only human human evidence is that retinal thickness (CST) was controlled about as well as with aflibercept. That is an indirect, mechanism-consistent sign. It is graded inferred_adequate only loosely, because it does not meet this rubric's definition. Graybug linked the failure to the formulation: microparticles dispersed, the 2 mg arm was stopped for safety, and it planned new formulations. Durability could be an exposure or formulation problem (F1a) or a molecule-specific problem (F6). Neither is measured, so the code is U.

In the index mCRPC study (NCT02607228; PMID:35816286), plasma AUCtau and Cmax did not rise across 2–9 mg doses, and PK varied widely between patients. The BET pharmacodynamic markers (HEXIM1 induction, CCR2 inhibition) rose only at the higher monotherapy doses and also varied widely, so exposure and target engagement look partial and inconsistent. These data came from mCRPC patients but were published after the trial began. Dose was not tolerability-capped: there were no monotherapy DLTs up to 9 mg. Efficacy was limited (24-week nonprogression 25%), and the Phase 2 expansion was never run. Because the mechanism was not adequately tested, the failure is best classed as F1a. No other BET inhibitor in the bundle succeeded in prostate cancer.

The index trial NCT02983604 was terminated after Phase 1b dose escalation (4–9 mg with fulvestrant or exemestane). The Phase 2 PFS portion was never run, so no efficacy readout exists. The only human PK/PD evidence is PMID:35816286, covering mCRPC and the solid tumor study 1599 (NCT02392611). It shows no dose-proportional increase in AUC or Cmax across 2–9 mg and high interpatient variability. The PD biomarkers (HEXIM1 induction, CCR2 inhibition) rose only at higher monotherapy doses. Exposure and engagement therefore look inadequate or unreliable. No engagement data exist in breast cancer, and the data were published after the index trial started. Because the index trial was not a real efficacy test, confidence is low.

In the index trial NCT02607228, PMID:35816286 reports that GS-5829 plasma exposure (AUCtau, Cmax) did not rise with dose from 2 to 9 mg. The same paper reports high interpatient PK/PD variability. The pharmacodynamic markers of BET engagement (HEXIM1 induction, CCR2 inhibition) rose only at higher monotherapy doses. Engagement was therefore measured in mCRPC patients, but it was partial and inconsistent. The data were published in 2022, after the index trial started. Efficacy was limited, with a 25% nonprogression rate at week 24. Tolerability did not cap the dose: few DLTs occurred and no MTD was stated. The authors highlight the lack of dose-proportional exposure. Inadequate exposure and engagement mean the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). No other BRD4 inhibitor has succeeded in this disease.

The index trial, NCT03478319, was a Phase 1 safety study in healthy volunteers and did not test efficacy. Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up human data on ACE-2494's exposure, binding to myostatin or activin, or downstream biomarker effects. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data. According to BioCentury, Acceleron stopped the program in April 2019 because antidrug antibodies appeared often in the healthy volunteers. Acceleron's own press release confirms the stop. The text I could retrieve from it gave no reason, so the reason rests on BioCentury. Antidrug antibodies are a problem with this specific molecule's immunogenicity, not with the target, so the best fit is F6, molecule-specific toxicity or liability. The mechanism was never tested for efficacy, so U is a secondary code. Confidence is medium because the reason comes from a single trade-press report and no primary data were found.

LY3202626 crossed the blood-brain barrier freely in humans and cut CSF Aβ1-42 by about 73% at 6 mg QD (PMID:35243208). The phase 1 study that generated this enrolled AD patients and started in 2014, before the index trial (NCT02323334). In NAVIGATE-AD the 3 and 12 mg doses gave 70-90% BACE inhibition, were well tolerated and were not dose-capped (PMID:34113788). Aβ plaque burden fell (PMID:36641610), yet tau PET did not change (p=0.418, p=0.231) and cognition and function showed no meaningful benefit. The trial was stopped for futility (NCT02791191). With the target robustly engaged, BACE1 inhibition does not drive the disease as tested. Every other BACE inhibitor in the bundle also stalled. Early termination, with only 47 completers, limited power on the primary endpoint (secondary F7).

The only human pillar data come from a single-ascending-dose study in healthy men (PMID:34019711). It showed linear PK and 'indications' of receptor engagement (glucose control, lowered bone resorption). However, dose-dependent nausea and vomiting made doses of 20 μg and above intolerable, which capped exposure. No engagement data exist in T2D patients, and that study was published after the index trial began. The index Phase 2 (NCT03230786) posted no results and no stop reason. Pramlintide, on the same target, is FDA-approved for T2D, so the target is validated. A tolerability-limited dose ceiling is therefore the best-supported explanation. Target irrelevance (F2) is less likely. The bundle is thin and does not show the actual readout.

Udonitrectag (MT8/REC 0/0559) is a small peptidomimetic of NGF that binds TrkA. In NCT04276558, none of the three doses (0.5–5 µg/day) healed the cornea better than vehicle at week 8, and the response did not rise with dose. I found no human data on ocular drug levels, TrkA engagement, or downstream biomarkers. The protocol included PK sampling, but no results were published. The sponsor's summary says only that there was no clinical benefit and that the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Cenegermin, a recombinant NGF that acts on the same TrkA target, has worked clinically in neurotrophic keratitis (Frontiers and FBL reviews). That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Because engagement was never measured, U also applies.

This was not an efficacy failure. In the posted results for NCT05201079, the primary outcome counts patients who had a recurrence, so lower numbers are better: 4/37 recurred on MBK-01 vs 9/40 on fidaxomicin. The superiority test (p=0.228) reads as 'not met', but the published trial was a non-inferiority comparison, and MBK-01 met it (11% vs 23%, P=.01). In patients who already had recurrent CDI, recurrence was 19% vs 62%. The sponsor describes the Phase 3 ICD-01 results as showing MBK-01 is effective and safe. The bundle shows no program failure, so this is coded F9. The drug is a whole faecal microbiota product with no defined molecular target, and none of the sources measure engraftment or another pharmacodynamic marker, so all three pillars are no_human_data.

NP001 has no defined molecular target. Its proximal action on inflammatory monocytes was shown in ALS patients. A single-dose Phase 1 (NCT01091142, registered before the index trial; PMID:25192333) found a dose-dependent fall in monocyte CD16. In the index trial, LPS and IL-18 fell with treatment (PMID:25884010, PMID:36428474). The drug was well tolerated, and no plasma PK is in the bundle. The index trial missed ALSFRS-R slope overall (p=0.55). Benefit was confined post hoc to patients with high CRP or inflammation (PMID:25884010, PMID:28384752). The CRP-enriched Phase 2B also failed, again with only age and progression-rate subgroup signals (PMID:35098554, PMID:41463070). The sources attribute this to ALS heterogeneity and an inflammatory subset, so F3. F2 is secondary because the mechanism was engaged without overall benefit.

BBT-401 is a Pellino-1 inhibitor meant to stay in the gut. In healthy volunteers (NCT03482648) it showed no systemic exposure and was tolerated up to 1600 mg/day, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In the index Phase 2a trial (NCT04596293), BBT-401 matched placebo (54.5% vs 63.6% response). The sponsor said a new formulation improved drug detection in colon tissue compared with the earlier low-dose cohort (NCT03800420), which counts as exposure evidence. Biomarker (PD) samples were planned, but no human data were found on Pellino-1 engagement or on downstream TLR/NF-kB or cytokine effects. No other drug on this target exists for comparison. Because nothing separates a drug that never engaged Pellino-1 from a target that does not matter in UC, the failure is indeterminate (U).

BMS-986288 is a masked, non-fucosylated anti-CTLA-4 antibody meant to be activated in tumors. In the index trial NCT03994601, objective response rate in Cohort 2C was 0 across all three subcohorts. The bundle has no human PK, tumor exposure, intratumoral unmasking or CTLA-4 occupancy data. PMID:41837748 reports reduced peripheral immune responses in patients, which is the intended effect of masking. That is not evidence of engagement or pathway activity at the tumor. DLTs were infrequent and no tolerability cap on dose is stated. Insufficient unmasking (F1a) cannot be separated from a mechanism that fails in this unselected population. Because engagement is no_human_data, the failure is indeterminate.

In index trial NCT03994601, a Phase 1/2 study in advanced solid tumors, BICR objective response rate in Cohort 2C was 0% across all three cohorts (n=50). The bundle has no human PK, tumor CTLA-4 binding or intratumoral pharmacodynamic data. PMID:41837748 reports only reduced peripheral immune activity in patients, which this masked, non-fucosylated antibody was designed to produce, not proof of tumor engagement. The same abstract states that ipilimumab, acting on the same CTLA-4 target, has shown clinical benefit across multiple solid tumor types. That points to the molecule, possibly inadequate unmasking or activity in tumor, rather than the target, consistent with F1b. Without any engagement data the failure remains partly indeterminate (U). No stated stop reason; evidence is thin.

The index trial NCT02661542 was a single-arm phase 1/2a dose-escalation and expansion study. Its primary endpoint was a descriptive TEAE count with no comparator, so it was not an efficacy test that could fail. PMID:36882377 reports a phase 2 dose of 90 mg/m2 and calls the drug well tolerated. It also reports confirmed partial responses in gemcitabine-refractory biliary and urothelial tumors, with longer PFS in BAP1/PBRM1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma. The bundle has no human data on exposure at the target site, POLA1/POLB engagement, or pathway biomarkers, and it gives no reason for stopping. U is listed as secondary because the mechanism's pillars are untested in humans.

The 2022 paper pooling all four studies, including the index trial NCT03568071, reports good serum exposure up to 10 mg/kg IV and 320 mg SC every two weeks. Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. Binding to IL-17C was shown indirectly in patients with atopic dermatitis: total serum IL-17C rose from undetectable to steady levels. This was published after the index trial started. No skin drug levels or downstream skin biomarkers were reported in humans. The ex vivo data in PMID:31793105 do not count. Results were flat across endpoints with no dose response. The authors conclude IL-17C is unlikely to be an effective target in atopic dermatitis, which points to F2. Because engagement is indirect and free IL-17C was never measured, confidence is medium. The large placebo response is only a minor issue.

In HBV patients, emtricitabine showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and rapid HBV DNA suppression, up to -3.3 log10 at 2 months, without dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:12019083, published 2002, before the index trial). So exposure, polymerase engagement and the antiviral effect were shown in this disease. The index trial (NCT00737568) tested whether adding FTC to TDF beat TDF alone in lamivudine-resistant HBV. TDF alone already gave 89.4% suppression, versus 86.3% for the combination (p=0.43). Similar results came from adefovir-experienced patients (PMID:20600025) and NCT00524173. Emtricitabine was active, but adding it to a near-maximally effective drug gave no clinical benefit. The ceiling effect left little room for a superiority result, a design limitation (F7).

In GA patients, single intravitreal doses of 1–20 mg were well tolerated and gave dose-proportional exposure in serum and aqueous humor, so exposure was adequate and the dose was not capped by tolerability (PMID:40538770). Engagement inside the eye could not be confirmed because active (reduced) IL-33 was below the assay's detection limit in every aqueous sample. The aqueous PD biomarkers (CCL2, CXCL10, IL-6, ICAM-1) did not move, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. The authors note that aqueous humor may not reflect IL-33 activity in the retina. Development was stopped because no pathway effect was shown. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter: U.

NaPi-IIb is an intestinal transporter. Plasma levels in haemodialysis patients matched those in healthy volunteers, but no source measured gut drug levels or transporter inhibition in humans, so exposure and engagement have no human data. Downstream markers did not move. In the healthy-volunteer dose-escalation studies, serum phosphate and urinary phosphate excretion did not change with dose. In NCT03305471/PMID:33732982, DS-2330b 400 mg three times daily lowered serum phosphate by 2.2 mg/dl versus 1.9 mg/dl on placebo, which is not clinically meaningful. The authors suggest sevelamer may have reduced DS-2330b bioavailability, but nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a target that does not matter. Other NaPi-IIb inhibitors (ASP3325, EOS789) also failed, which leans towards F2 but does not prove it. Tolerability was not limiting, so the code is U.

In healthy volunteers (PMID:36942507), IV ASP1128 up to 100 mg/day gave roughly dose-proportional plasma exposure. From ≥10 mg it caused rapid, dose-related upregulation of six PPARδ target genes lasting >24 h, which shows engagement and a proximal pathway effect. It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The index trial (NCT03941483, PMID:37441472) used 100 mg daily for 3 days, at the top of that range, and found no benefit: AKI 24.6% vs 21.0% placebo, with no gain on moderate/severe AKI or MAKE. Engagement was not measured in kidney tissue or in cardiac-surgery patients, and the phase 1 data were published after the index trial started. Even so, adequate engagement with no clinical effect points to the mechanism not driving post-surgical AKI.

Zinpentraxin alfa replaces pentraxin-2. In pulmonary fibrosis and IPF patients, IV dosing raised circulating pentraxin-2 2–13-fold, dose-dependently, reaching physiologic or higher levels (PMID:23380438, PMID:26869678); I treat this as adequate exposure and target replacement. A downstream effect followed: fibrocytes fell 30–50% in PF patients (PMID:23380438). All of this was published before the index trial started. The 10 mg/kg dose was well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicities (NCT01254409), so dose was not capped. The adequately sized Phase 3 (NCT04552899) showed no FVC benefit (p=0.54). Post hoc analysis attributed the Phase 2 signal (NCT02550873) to two placebo outliers (PMID:38354066, PMID:40255293). The mechanism appears not to drive IPF progression. F7 is secondary because the underpowered Phase 2 produced a false positive.

The Phase 1 trial in healthy volunteers (NCT03645746, PMID:38099276) gave single IV doses up to 3000 mg. Tolerability was similar to placebo, so the dose was not capped, and plasma PK showed target-mediated disposition. That shows systemic exposure and suggests the antibody bound GFRα3, but nobody measured GFRα3 occupancy, artemin signaling or any downstream biomarker, in volunteers or in OA patients. In the Phase 2 trial, neither 100 mg nor 1000 mg Q4W beat placebo on WOMAC pain (p=0.30 and p=0.69), and the higher dose did no better. The investigators did not settle on a cause: they point to possible mouse–human differences in GFRα3 biology and to differences in experimental setup. With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a target that does not matter, so this is U. F2 is listed only as a possibility. My searches did not reach the paper's full text.

Novartis ran a brain H3 receptor PET study with [11C]MK-8278 in healthy volunteers in 2016 (HRA summary). The index protocol says the 5 mg dose was chosen from that PET study and the first-in-human PK/PD model (NCT02334449) to give more than 80% receptor occupancy for about 10 hours in 90% of subjects. The actual PET numbers are redacted, so engagement is rated adequate only on the sponsor's statement, and only in healthy volunteers. No human pathway biomarker was found. NCT03141086 was ended early for business reasons after enrolling 24 patients. Sleep latency was numerically better on drug (6.76 vs 4.12 min; difference 1.7 min, p=0.13), but the trial had too little power to settle the question. F2 is possible; the business stop (F8) also applies.

GRANITE-1 (NCT00879333) tested everolimus 10 mg daily against placebo and missed its OS endpoint (5.39 vs 4.34 months; HR 0.90, not significant). No target-engagement data in gastric cancer patients are in the bundle. However, the same 10 mg systemic dose is FDA-approved for RCC (approved before the index trial started), breast cancer and pNET through mTOR inhibition in tumour tissue, so exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. A human window study in NSCLC showed dose-dependent pS6 and metabolic modulation (PMID:25673697), supporting the pathway pillar. The dose was not reported as capped. The likely reason is that mTOR monotherapy does not drive survival in unselected gastric cancer. Preclinical papers on ERK feedback resistance (PMID:32444897) and a possible 4E-BP1-defined sensitive subset (PMID:23340172) suggest a secondary population/selection explanation (F3).

The index trial NCT01079143 compared everolimus (Certican) with cyclosporine in de novo renal transplant recipients. Fibrosis progression from M3 to M12 in EMT+ patients was similar between arms (12/26 vs 16/32). Engagement was not measured in this trial. It is inferred adequate because everolimus is FDA-approved for transplant rejection, acting on mTOR at comparable transplant doses in the same kind of patient. PMID:25673697 also shows dose-dependent pS6 and S6 modulation in human tumor tissue, though in another disease. Other bundle sources (PMID:20486905, PMID:33741847) show renal-function benefit only from sparing calcineurin inhibitors. With mTOR inhibition presumably achieved, the anti-fibrotic/EMT hypothesis did not hold, which fits F2. The small EMT+ comparison may also have been underpowered (F7).

Single-arm phase 2 of everolimus in bortezomib-refractory MCL gave an ORR of 8.6% (NCT00702052). No MCL pharmacodynamic data appear in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because everolimus at the same systemic oral dose met efficacy endpoints via mTOR in approved cancers (kidney, breast, PNET). Dose-dependent pS6 and S6 reduction was also shown in NSCLC tumours (PMID:25673697), but that report postdates the index trial. With the mechanism likely engaged, the low response suggests mTOR inhibition alone does not drive this refractory MCL population. Preclinical work points to compensatory AKT rephosphorylation and autophagy as resistance (PMID:22879389, PMID:23079699), and the sources cite MCL heterogeneity (PMID:35237397). Neither the inference nor the bundle is strong, so confidence is low.

Everolimus 10 mg/day, the dose used in PILLAR-2, met efficacy endpoints leading to approvals in kidney cancer (2009), breast cancer and PNET through systemic mTOR inhibition. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate. PMID:25673697 also shows dose-dependent pS6 and S6 reduction in human tumours at 10 mg. No engagement was measured in DLBCL patients. Adjuvant everolimus gave no DFS benefit over placebo (HR 0.92, p=0.276; NCT00790036). AE-driven discontinuation was higher with everolimus (30% vs 12%), but the dose was not capped. The authors attribute the failure to the setting: giving it after complete response rather than with R-CHOP (PMID:29253068). Relapsed-DLBCL activity in PMID:23144193 supports F4 (timing/disease stage) as a secondary code.

Index trial NCT02914613 was a Phase 1b/2 safety and exploratory study. Its primary outcomes were descriptive ocular safety counts plus CRT change, with no statistical comparison, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). The eyedrops were well tolerated, and CRT change was variable, with exploratory 'responders' (PMID:36239675). Posterior-segment drug levels and target engagement were shown only in animals (PMID:29853477); the bundle has no human retinal exposure or αvβ3 engagement data. The later DR trial NCT05409235 missed DRSS improvement versus vehicle. Even so, nothing separates poor topical delivery to the retina from an irrelevant target. That makes U the secondary code if the program failure is considered.

In NCT05409235, the share of patients with a ≥2-step DRSS improvement at week 24 was the same on both nesvategrast doses (about 12%) as on vehicle (13%). OcuTerra's topline release says the drug was safe but missed its primary and key secondary endpoints, gives no mechanistic reason for the failure, and says the company is evaluating strategic alternatives. No source has human data on drug levels in the retina or vitreous, integrin occupancy or inhibition, or a downstream pathway marker after topical dosing. Retinal distribution is claimed only from the drug's design. The Phase 1b (PMID:36239675) reported variable retinal thickness changes with 'activity' in a subset of patients, which is not a target-engagement measure. No other drug on this target has succeeded in DR, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never reached its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

NPC-09 is extended-release aceneuramic acid (sialic acid replacement for GNE deficiency). The index Phase 3 (NCT04671472) enrolled only 14 patients (10 SA-ER vs 4 placebo). The primary UEC score difference (2.51 kg, 95% CI -1.72 to 6.74) favoured drug but was not significant. The authors describe a reproducible trend toward slowing and no safety concerns (PMID:37568154). A trial this small and imbalanced could not resolve the effect, which points to a design or power limitation rather than a demonstrated lack of efficacy. A Phase 1 PK study exists (NCT01236898), but no human exposure, sialylation or pathway data appear in the bundle. All pillars are therefore no_human_data, and U applies as a secondary code.

Plasma exposure of ranolazine with metformin in T2DM is documented (PMID:27128216). Engagement and pathway are not measured directly. They are inferred_adequate because ranolazine met HbA1c endpoints in T2DM through the same target as monotherapy (NCT01472185, -0.56%) and as add-on to glimepiride (NCT01494987, -0.51%). The phase 2 add-on study (NCT01163721, -0.53%) predates the index trial. Only the metformin add-on trial (NCT01555164) missed, with a -0.11% difference. So the mechanism works in T2DM and the failure is confined to the metformin-background population, possibly a context or interaction effect. No source states the cause, and the index-trial dose is not shown. Trial-level noise (placebo arm fell 0.20%) is a secondary possibility.

NCT02598960 was a phase 1/2a study with safety-only primary endpoints, so it was not a formal efficacy test (F9 secondary). The program still showed no compelling clinical activity. PMID:36863094 reports robust peripheral pharmacodynamic activity in patients with solid tumors at the tested doses: T- and NK-cell proliferation and activation, plus proinflammatory cytokines. This shows GITR engagement and peripheral pathway activation in the disease. However, tumor tissue showed no significant change in CD8A, PD-L1 or T/NK functional genes. Tumor drug exposure was not measured. The authors attribute the lack of activity to absent intratumoral activation in unselected patients. This supports a mechanism that, as tested, does not drive anti-tumor benefit (F2). Possible tissue-level under-engagement (F1a) or selection effects (F3) are secondary codes.

Systemic exposure at 450 mg IV was characterized in healthy volunteers, with full target binding and roughly 53–66% depletion of circulating LAG-3+ cells (PMID:36088650, NCT03965533). In the UC index trial, blood LAG-3+ cells fell only to 51% of baseline, and LAG-3+ cells in the colonic mucosa were not reduced at all. Colon transcriptomics showed no difference from placebo. The authors concluded there was 'no pharmacological effect' in the target tissue (PMID:37323059). So depletion at the site of disease was not achieved, and the mechanism was not properly tested. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Earlier psoriasis data showed skin depletion (PMID:33113155), but that does not establish colonic engagement. More UC flares on drug did not drive the stop.

The phase 1b trial in active UC patients (NCT03860896, PMID:35014040) gave GB004 120 mg QD. It showed higher colonic than plasma concentrations, meaning tissue exposure was reached. Exploratory pharmacodynamic analyses demonstrated target engagement, but this was not quantified. That trial was registered before the index trial started. The index phase 2 trial (NCT04556383) used higher doses, 480 mg QD and BID, and showed no benefit in clinical remission at week 12 (15.4% and 22.5% vs 17.9% placebo). It was terminated for lack of treatment benefit. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Downstream pathway or barrier biomarkers are not reported in the bundle. With engagement apparently achieved in-disease at lower doses, the failure points to EGLN1 inhibition/HIF-1α stabilisation not driving UC remission. The engagement evidence is exploratory, so confidence is medium.

The drug is a topical thrombin/fibrin sealant that converts fibrinogen (FGA/FGB/FGG) to fibrin at the surgical site. It met hemostasis endpoints in several surgical trials applied topically at comparable product doses (NCT00684047, NCT00892957, NCT00977925, NCT01166243). So fibrin formation (exposure, engagement, pathway) is inferred adequate, though not shown in ovarian surgery patients. The index pilot (NCT00544310, n=25, adhesion prevention after ovarian surgery) has unknown status, no posted results and no stated stop reason. If it failed, the likeliest reading is that fibrin formation does not prevent adhesions as tested (F2). The small, exploratory, unreported pilot may simply have been unable to answer the question (F7). The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

The drug is BIOSTAT BIOLOGX, a fibrin sealant (human thrombin plus fibrinogen) injected into the disc. In the Phase 3 trial NCT01011816, 33.5% of patients on the drug met the composite success endpoint at 26 weeks versus 39.3% on saline (p=0.52). The sponsor said only that the drug's benefit could not be told apart from saline's, and gave no reason. The sources found contain no human data showing fibrin formed or stayed in the disc, sealed the annular fissures, or moved any biomarker. The pilot study reported only clinical outcomes. The drug's approved hemostasis uses act at a different tissue site and outcome, so they cannot support inferred adequacy here. The fibrinogen 'same-target' comparator is the same product, not a success. With no engagement data, a sealant that never worked in the disc cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02891070 compared Tisseel with DuraSeal, an active sealant, in a non-inferiority design. Non-inferiority was not shown: difference -9.29% [-21.11, 2.54]. This is a missed non-inferiority margin against an active comparator, not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure, so the code is F9. No pillar was measured directly. The same product (FS VH S/D 500 S-apr) met topical hemostasis endpoints in NCT00892957 and NCT01244425. Other human-thrombin fibrin sealants met CSF-leak endpoints (NCT02457546, NCT02309645). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, although no dura-specific measurement exists. An earlier phase 2 dural trial (NCT00681824) showed no gain over standard care, which hints at a weak mechanism (F2) in dural sealing.

XF-73 has no recorded molecular target. Its 'engagement' is direct antibacterial action on nasal S. aureus. In the index trial in healthy carriers (NCT02282605), complete eradication at 48 h post-dose by broth enrichment was no better than placebo (3/27, 1/12 vs 4/24). The arms were small, with no SAEs. A later Phase 2 in surgical patients (NCT03915470) met its primary endpoint: nasal S. aureus fell by about 2.8 log CFU vs 0.5 on placebo. That result implies the drug reached and acted on its nasal target compartment. The pillars are therefore inferred adequate, but only from evidence that postdates the index trial. The failure looks attributable to a stringent eradication endpoint and timing rather than inactivity. Small arms add an underpowering element. No source states the reason, so confidence is low.

XF-73 has no recorded molecular target; for this antimicrobial the proximal effect is bacterial kill. The index trial (NCT02282605) used a stringent endpoint: complete apparent eradication of nasal S. aureus by broth enrichment 48 h after the last dose. It found no difference from placebo (3/27, 1/12 vs 4/24) in a small sample. The later Phase 2 trial (NCT03915470) met its primary endpoint: S. aureus fell by about 2.8 log CFU/mL on drug versus 0.5 on placebo in colonised surgical patients. So exposure and engagement are inferred adequate and the proximal effect is shown in this disease, though only after the index trial. The miss most plausibly reflects the endpoint and timing chosen (durable eradication) plus a small, underpowered trial. No source states the reason, so confidence is low.

Topical aprepitant 10 mg/g gel missed its VAS endpoint versus vehicle (19.7 vs 21.2, p=0.58; NCT01963793). In PMID:28853492 both sides fell by more than 50% (-35.2 vs -38.1) in a split-sided design, and the authors call for parallel-group trials. This is a large vehicle response and a design that could not answer the question. No skin levels, NK1R occupancy or pathway data exist for the topical gel. The skin ERK1/2 changes in PMID:31442331 followed oral dosing and were published after the index trial started. Oral success in CINV (NCT00952341) is a CNS effect, not a comparable compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred. Oral 80 mg also failed in chronic prurigo (PMID:30653242).
