Whether the target matters therefore remains indeterminate (U).

Carbomer 980 (1146A) is a nasal gel meant to act as a physical barrier, and no molecular target is recorded for it. The healthy-volunteer study in PMID:31004286 tested only how well the nose tolerated the gel. No human data show that the gel stayed on the nasal mucosa, blocked viruses from reaching the lining cells, or lowered viral load or inflammatory markers. The index trial NCT03005067 found no difference from placebo on ANSS1-4 (p=0.516) or on any secondary endpoint. The gel was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited by side effects. The sponsor's statistical analysis plan itself notes that little clinical data support barrier sprays. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a barrier that never worked from a mechanism that does not matter in colds, so the code is U.

CLBS03 is a therapy made from the patient's own expanded polyclonal regulatory T cells (Tregs), and it has no recorded molecular target. In the index trial NCT02691247, neither dose preserved C-peptide better than placebo at week 52 (change of -0.29 low dose, -0.39 high dose, -0.27 placebo). Safety was similar across arms, so tolerability did not limit the dose. Exposure counts as adequate: the forerunner Phase 1 trial (Bluestone 2015) in adults with recent-onset type 1 diabetes found that infused Tregs persisted in the blood. However, no source shows the cells engaged their mechanism in humans, such as suppressing islet-directed autoimmunity, or that a downstream immune biomarker moved. The sponsor gave no explanation for the failure. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a therapy that never worked in the body from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

No molecular target is recorded, and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or target-linked biomarker data. The PK studies (NCT02029066, NCT02559934) posted no results. Post-hoc immunohistochemistry in AK skin (PMID:33458860, 2021) is uncontrolled and not tied to a defined target. The index Phase 3 (NCT01493921; PMID:29530340) missed complete clearance (32% vs 17%, OR 2.14, p=0.111) but met 75% partial clearance (OR 4.36, p<0.001). The authors attribute the weak separation to a high vehicle response, which they link to diagnostic uncertainty (not all lesions histologically confirmed) and occlusive dressing. These are design and execution issues, so F7 is primary. Because engagement is unmeasured, U also applies.

Daptomycin is FDA-approved for Gram-positive and MRSA infections, including skin infections, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. It acted on the same bacterial target, although bone penetration in osteomyelitis was not measured. In the index pediatric AHO trial (NCT01922011, PMID:32639465), Day-5 clinical improvement was 78% vs 83% with active comparator (difference -6.1, CI -19.4 to 7.4). The difference was not significant, but the lower bound crossed the prespecified 15% non-inferiority margin. The trial missed only a non-inferiority margin against an active drug, so this is F9. The authors also cite a nonvalidated protocol design and too few MRSA cases to evaluate (F7). PMID:38497326 suggests pediatric label dosing may give suboptimal exposure, but only from simulation.

BLAST (NCT00739466) tested IV liposomal alendronate (LABR-312) at PCI. The overall cohort showed no difference in 6-month in-stent late loss, and there were no safety concerns. Investigators report that the drug 'effectively modulates monocyte behavior' in these patients, published in 2013 after the trial started (PMID:23351827), so I treated engagement and pathway as adequate. The benefit was confined to prespecified proinflammatory, diabetic and high-monocyte subgroups, and the authors attribute the result to patient inflammatory state. That points to population heterogeneity (F3). The follow-up BLADE-PCI trial in diabetic patients was also negative at all doses (PMID:35305955). This suggests monocyte modulation may not drive restenosis even in the enriched subgroup, so F2 is secondary. No PK or exposure data for LABR-312 are in the bundle.

In the index study (PMID:29354707, NCT01493271), 200 mg BID RO5093151 given to POAG/OHT patients produced high, sustained systemic 11βHSD1 inhibition: urinary THF/THE fell from 0.9 to 0.18 by day 7. Engagement was therefore adequate and shown in the disease population, but only from this same trial, not before it. Ocular distribution was shown only in rabbits, so human ocular exposure has no human data. No downstream ocular pathway marker was reported. IOP change did not differ from placebo (-2.7 vs -2.9 mmHg). The authors conclude that despite high inhibition, the target did not produce a meaningful IOP effect, which supports F2. The short 7-day treatment is a possible secondary timing issue.

In the glaucoma study (NCT01493271), 200 mg twice daily, the same dose as the top arm of index trial NCT00823680, gave high, sustained 11β-HSD1 inhibition. The urinary THF/THE ratio fell from 0.9 to 0.18. At that dose the drug also lowered liver fat in NAFLD (NCT01277094, PMID 24795254). So exposure and engagement were adequate and not capped by tolerability. However, this evidence comes from non-diabetic patients and was published after the index trial started. No glucose-pathway marker was found for T2D. In the 28-day T2D trial (Heise 2014), HbA1c showed only trends and body weight fell slightly. Despite strong enzyme inhibition, glucose did not clearly improve, which points to the target not driving glycaemia (F2). The short 4-week duration also weakened the test.

disease: respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants
rationale: The cause of this failure can't be determined. AeroFact is bovactant surfactant given as an aerosol during nCPAP. It has no molecular target, and the protocol says PK studies are not applicable. No human data show how much aerosolized drug reached the lungs or what it did there. In NCT03969992, fewer AeroFact infants than nCPAP-alone infants needed intubation or instilled surfactant (21/68 low dose and 26/70 high dose vs 45/89), but the difference was not significant (p=0.19). The earlier open-label study had only historical controls (PMID 34112722 page). Instilled bovactant is licensed (PMID:28913327). That fits a delivery problem (F1b-like), and an underpowered trial is also possible (F7). Without data on lung deposition, U is the code. The program did not actually stop: the Phase 3 trial NCT06776783 is recruiting.

The index trial NCT02352558 is a Phase 1 study of BBI608 (napabucasin) in adults with refractory hematologic malignancies. Bortezomib appears only as a combination partner. The primary endpoint was BBI608 safety and DLTs, so it was not an efficacy test of bortezomib, and the trial completed without a stated failure. The pillars are inferred_adequate: bortezomib is FDA-approved for mantle cell lymphoma and myeloma through PSMB5 inhibition in the systemic compartment at standard 1.3 mg/m2 dosing. NCT00985959 posted a 69.8% response rate at that dose. The bundle shows no engagement data in pediatric lymphoma, and nothing shows tolerability capped the dose.

Z-100 is a non-specific immunomodulator made from an M. tuberculosis extract, and no molecular target is recorded for it. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway (biomarker) effects. The dose history pointed in opposite directions: in phase II, tumour response improved with dose up to 40 µg (PMID 16926224), but in phase III, 0.2 µg gave better survival than 40 µg (PMID 16360199). The earlier placebo-controlled phase III narrowly missed on 5-year overall survival (HR 0.65, P=0.07), with signals in subgroups (PMID 24569914). That subgroup pattern is why the index trial NCT02247232 was run, and it suggests a possible patient-selection issue (F3). I found no published results for the index trial, and no reason given for stopping. NCT03476018 was designed to show pharmacological action, but it has no results. Without any engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In KALAHARI Part B (NCT04527107), THR-149 gave a BCVA change of -0.2 letters versus +3.5 for aflibercept at month 3, and Oxurion then filed for bankruptcy. Tolerability did not limit the dose: the drug was safe at all doses, so dose_limited is false. The only human data come from the phase 1 study (PMID:34940810), which reported safety, BCVA and CST but no vitreous drug levels, no plasma kallikrein inhibition and no pathway biomarker. CST did not improve and imaging showed no meaningful change, but this is a clinical signal, not a pillar measurement. The evidence for target engagement comes from rat and rabbit studies only (PMID:34677569, PMID:34302260), which do not count. No other drug on this target has succeeded in DME. With no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The protocol for NCT03028870 describes V120083 as a selective TRPV1 antagonist and calls this study its first efficacy trial. At Week 4, pain was 4.2 on 30 mg and 4.3 on 60 mg versus 4.4 on placebo. Naproxen reached 3.6, so the trial could detect an analgesic effect, which argues against a design failure. The sources I found give no human data on drug levels, TRPV1 engagement (for example, blocking capsaicin- or heat-evoked responses, or a rise in body temperature) or any downstream biomarker. Nothing shows the dose was limited by side effects. No other TRPV1 drug in the bundle succeeded in knee OA, and no sponsor explanation for stopping was found. Because engagement is unknown, I can't tell whether the drug never engaged TRPV1 or whether TRPV1 doesn't drive OA pain. Result: indeterminate.

The index trial, NCT04082325, was a single-ascending-dose study in healthy men that measured safety, PK and mass balance. It was not an efficacy test, and it has no posted results. A PET study of brain uptake (NCT04538014, with an [11C]-Lu AF88434 tracer) was completed, but no uptake, occupancy or PDE1B inhibition data are public. According to Alzforum, a planned Phase 2 trial in negative symptoms of schizophrenia was discontinued in August 2020, and Lundbeck dropped the drug from its pipeline at the end of 2020. No reason is given and no efficacy readout is reported. With no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F9 is a secondary code because the index trial was not an efficacy trial.

AD313 is atomoxetine combined with dronabinol. NCT05101122 was a small open-label dose-escalation study. At the top dose (80/10 mg) the primary AHI4% endpoint did not fall from baseline (median 28.6 vs 26.6). The published paper found that the 80/5 mg dose did lower AHI, hypoxic burden and ODI against baseline, but not against atomoxetine alone. The authors point to numerous side effects, dropouts (15 down to 10 patients) and the study's exploratory, open-label design. No human data were found on drug exposure at the site of action, target occupancy (noradrenergic or cannabinoid receptors), or a mechanistic biomarker. That leaves no way to tell whether the drug failed to engage its targets or the mechanism doesn't matter, so the code is U. Tolerability (F6) and design limits (F7) are secondary.

The index trial NCT01595997 was a small intradermal study with a local-tolerability primary endpoint (classified not_efficacy), so it was not an efficacy test. PMID:26738450 reports that intradermal DLX105 in psoriasis produced a 33% local PASI decrease versus 12% on placebo (P=0.001). This was accompanied by reductions in K16, Ki67, epidermal thickness and IL-17, TNF-α, IL-23 and IFN-γ mRNA, so the pathway was shown in patients. Exposure and engagement are inferred from these downstream effects rather than measured directly. The engagement evidence was published in 2016, after the index trial started in 2012. Only the separate topical gel arm missed clinical efficacy, which the authors attribute to limited penetration. The index readout was not an efficacy failure of the drug.

Suramin has no recorded primary target. The proposed chemosensitizing mechanism, telomerase inhibition, has only in vitro and mouse data (PMID:25425294). Exposure was adequate: earlier NSCLC trials (NCT00066768, NCT00006929) used dosing nomograms that kept plasma levels in the intended non-cytotoxic 10–50 μM range, and that range was reached in 90% of treatments. However, none of these sources reports human evidence of target engagement or a pathway biomarker. The index trial (NCT01038752) was stopped after enrolling 14 patients, gave no reason, and posted no progression-free survival data. So the readout cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The code is U. F7 is a secondary code because the trial was too small to answer the question.

Exposure is adequate for plasma only. In SAT-1 (PMID:28695149), a 20 mg/kg dose gave children with autism blood suramin levels of about 12 µM at 2 days, with a half-life of about 15 days. The same paper says suramin cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so the drug did not reach brain tissue. No human study measured P2Y1 or P2Y2 receptor blockade. The plasma metabolomic shifts in purine pathways seen in SAT-1 (5 treated children) are not specific to these receptors, so the pathway pillar is also unsupported. In the index trial (NCT06058962/PMID:37932739), 10 mg/kg improved the core-symptom score numerically but not significantly, and 20 mg/kg did no better than placebo. The sponsor pointed to subgroup signals: younger children and those with milder symptoms. Because nothing shows whether the drug engaged its target, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug or the mechanism, so the code is U.

The index trial tested rasagiline 1 mg/day in MSA-P, the approved PD dose. It showed no difference in UMSARS progression (-0.60, p=0.70; NCT00977665, PMID:25498732). Engagement was measured directly: 11C-deprenyl PET in healthy volunteers showed complete brain MAO-B blockade after 10 days of 1 mg (PMID:16204711, 2005, before the index trial). Plasma exposure is well characterized (PMID:30218626) and peripheral MAO-B inhibition was dose dependent (PMID:29159774). Pathway is inferred adequate because 1 mg met PD efficacy endpoints through brain MAO-B (NCT01556165, NCT02337725, NCT01479530). Engagement was never measured in MSA patients. The tolerability-limited dose was not an issue. The mechanism was engaged at an adequate dose, yet disease progression did not change, so MAO-B inhibition does not modify MSA as tested.

In NCT01154985, neither EPA-E dose (1800 or 2700 mg/day) improved histology (p=0.57), and placebo lowered ALT more than either dose. No molecular target is recorded. The bundle has no human data on liver EPA levels, target engagement or plasma EPA levels in this trial. Triglycerides, the only pathway marker, fell only modestly and only at 2700 mg/day (P=.04). The investigators (Sanyal 2014) said the dose may not have been high enough, since the TG effect was smaller than in trials using the approved 4 g/day (NCT01047683, NCT01047501, PMID:27418543). Tolerability did not cap the dose, and nobody measured engagement. So the bundle cannot tell an under-dosed drug apart from a mechanism that does not matter in NASH. Code U, with F1a as a secondary possibility.

In healthy volunteers, plasma exposure and engagement were shown: ex vivo LTB4 production was inhibited dose-dependently with low-nM IC50, and simulated LTB4 inhibition exceeded 90% (PMID:29517132, PMID:31793171). Endogenous urinary and plasma LTE4 fell by more than 80% (PMID:34546534, PMID:32450304). Urinary LTE4 was also significantly reduced in CAD patients (NCT03317002). All of this predates FLAIR. The drug was well tolerated across doses, with no dose capping. FLAIR (NCT04492722) tested three doses on top of dapagliflozin. UACR changes were similar across arms (0.77–0.81 vs 0.84 placebo), and the trial was terminated for lack of efficacy with no safety concerns. With leukotriene suppression well established, FLAP inhibition does not appear to lower albuminuria in proteinuric CKD. Engagement was not shown in CKD patients themselves, which lowers confidence.

Topical bromfenac reaches ocular tissue in humans: aqueous humor concentrations were measured (PMID:17720067, NCT01387464). COX engagement was not measured directly, since aqueous PGE2 data were uninterpretable. It is inferred adequate because bromfenac ophthalmic solution met ocular inflammation endpoints after cataract surgery (NCT00704418, NCT00853970, NCT01367249, NCT01576952). Those trials used the same COX targets, the same topical ocular route and comparable concentrations, and most were completed before the index trial started. In the index trial (NCT01212471), 0.06% and 0.03% showed no OSDI benefit over placebo, with no dose-response. No tolerability cap was shown. No engagement evidence exists in dry eye patients (NCT00758784 was single-arm and descriptive). The likeliest reading is that COX inhibition does not drive dry eye symptoms as tested.

L-glutamine has no recorded molecular target. The index trial, Emmaus's Phase 1 diverticulosis study NCT05106101, enrolled only 9 patients, finished, and posted no results. The sponsor gave no reason for ending the program. No source found shows human exposure, engagement or pathway data in the colon or in diverticulosis. Success in sickle cell disease (NCT01179217) cannot support an inferred_adequate rating, because that involves a different tissue and mechanism. Without any evidence of engagement, a drug that never acted cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. A 9-patient open-label trial counting diverticula on colonoscopy is also a weak test of efficacy (secondary code F7).

In the index trial, NCT01087658 (Sanofi GLUTOX, open-label Phase 3), patients with colorectal cancer received oral glutamine plus calcium-magnesium or calcium-magnesium alone. Sanofi's summary reports no significant difference in time to first grade 2–4 peripheral sensory neuropathy. Glutamine has no recorded molecular target. No source gives human data on glutamine levels in plasma or nerve tissue, on target engagement, or on a downstream biomarker during oxaliplatin therapy. The sickle cell approval (NCT01179217) works in red blood cells, not peripheral nerves, so it cannot stand in for the engagement pillar. A separate Phase 2 trial (GELUPO) also found glutamine ineffective. No source says why the program failed. Nothing separates a drug that never reached its site of action from a mechanism that does not protect nerves, so the code is U.

AXA1125 is a multi-amino-acid mixture that includes glutamine and has no defined target. The sources contain no human data on its exposure or engagement. In NCT05152849 (PMID:37223439), the primary mechanistic endpoint did not move: τPCr, a 31P-MRS measure of muscle mitochondrial recovery. I scored the pathway pillar inadequate on that basis. The secondary fatigue score (CFQ-11) did improve significantly (p=0.0039). The sponsor treated the readout as positive, got FDA clearance for a Phase 2b/3 trial, and refocused the company on long COVID. It never ran that trial: it had laid off 85% of staff and later stalled for lack of resources. The program therefore ended for business reasons rather than an outright efficacy failure (F8). Because engagement was never measured, the mechanistic question is unresolved (U).

Sanofi's results summary for the index trial (NCT01087658/OXALI_L_03768) reports 200 patients randomised to calcium-magnesium with or without glutamine 10 g three times a day. Time to grade 2–4 peripheral sensory neuropathy did not differ: median 162 days with glutamine vs 174 days without. Secondary endpoints were also negative, and the summary gives no reason for the failure. No primary target is recorded for this drug. Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up human data on plasma or nerve-tissue glutamine levels, engagement of a target, or a pathway biomarker in this setting. The sickle cell approval (NCT01179217) works through a different tissue and mechanism, so it cannot stand in for engagement here. Nothing separates inadequate exposure from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03989440 was a first-in-human Phase 1/2 study whose primary outcomes were safety and PK only (PMID:37479373). It was not designed as an efficacy test; upper-extremity motor score was only a secondary objective. Intrathecal dosing up to 200 mg gave dose-dependent CSF exposure (Cmax about 412,000 ng/mL), so exposure is adequate. The bundle has no human measure of binding or neutralization of the Nogo/MAG/OMgp ligands, and no downstream biomarker, so engagement and pathway are no_human_data. Supporting efficacy evidence is from animals only (PMID:32375169). Tolerability did not cap the dose. The primary code is F9. U is secondary, because the bundle cannot separate absent engagement from an irrelevant target.

The index trial NCT05325775 was a 2-week dose-ranging PK and safety study in 49 women with menopausal vasomotor symptoms. Its primary outcomes were descriptive (Cmax, AUC, half-life, AE counts), with no efficacy comparison, so it was not an efficacy test of osanetant (F9). Plasma PK rose dose-dependently, but no CNS or tissue exposure, TACR3 occupancy, or downstream biomarker results (e.g., LH or hormones) appear in the bundle, so all pillars lack adequate human evidence. Tolerability did not cap the dose: one SAE at 200 mg and no discontinuations. The related prostate cancer trial NCT05607342 was terminated because the drug program was discontinued, which points to a business or portfolio stop (F8) rather than an efficacy failure.

In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, MK-5442 produced dose-dependent plasma exposure and transient PTH pulses lasting over 3.5 h, showing CaSR antagonism at the parathyroid (PMID:23436611, PMID:25166719). The expected pathway effects followed: bone formation markers (P1NP, BSAP) rose, and dose-related hypercalcemia occurred. Yet lumbar spine aBMD did not differ from placebo at any dose (NCT00960934). In the post-bisphosphonate trial, BMD declined (NCT00996801, PMID:26556736), and the authors concluded MK-5442 is not viable for osteoporosis. The target was engaged, but the calcilytic PTH-pulse mechanism did not yield an anabolic BMD benefit; resorption markers also rose. Dose-related hypercalcemia (73% at 15 mg) is an on-target toxicity that further limited the program. Engagement data published after the 2009 index start.

The index trial, NCT06284798, was a small Phase 1 study in healthy men (n=11). Its only primary endpoint was the number of treatment-emergent adverse events, so it did not test efficacy, and no results are posted. A GlobalData listing says NNC0650-0013 is in Phase 1 for type 2 diabetes, but neither the bundle nor the search names a target. The search found no human data on drug exposure, target binding or biomarkers, and no sponsor statement on why the program stopped. Because engagement is no_human_data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, the code is U. F9 is listed as secondary because the index trial was not an efficacy test.

Topical nebivolol 0.5% and 1% suspension failed non-inferiority to timolol 0.5% (NCT04910100). IOP was about 2-3 mmHg higher at every timepoint, so nebivolol was clearly less effective, not just narrowly outside the margin. Beta-1 blockade by nebivolol is documented only after oral dosing for systemic targets (PMID:9049578, PMID:2455841), which is a different compartment from the eye. Ocular aqueous humor exposure and IOP effects come only from rabbit studies, which also cite low ocular bioavailability of the suspension (PMID:36839727, PMID:39195385). The bundle has no human data on ocular exposure or engagement. Beta-blockers including the beta-1-selective betaxolol are FDA-approved for glaucoma, so the target class works and the topical molecule or formulation is the likely failure point (F1b). Because the trial missed a non-inferiority margin against an active drug, F9 is listed as secondary.

STP is a stain-control excipient in experimental potassium nitrate dentifrices with no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway. In NCT03267511, all four arms reduced MLSI stain at 8 weeks (about -0.3 to -0.5), and neither test product differed from its reference product (p=0.65, p=0.57). It is unclear whether the comparison was meant to show superiority or comparability against reference dentifrices that may contain similar stain-removal agents, so this may not have been an efficacy test of STP itself (F9 possible). There are no other trials, abstracts or same-target drugs. Nothing separates a non-engaging agent from an irrelevant mechanism, so the failure is indeterminate.

NCT03267511 was a GSK proof-of-principle study of experimental low-abrasive 5% KNO3/NaF dentifrices against marketed reference pastes. STP was not the variable being tested. At 5%, it was in both Test Product 2 and Reference Product 2, which differed mainly in silica abrasive (1% spherical vs 16% abrasive). The other pair had no STP at all. Neither comparison showed a difference in MLSI stain change, but that says nothing about whether STP works. The trial was not an efficacy test of this drug, so F9 applies. STP has no recorded molecular target, and the bundle and my search found no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. If the trial were treated as a test of STP, the answer would be indeterminate (U).

SEARCH (NCT00901901) added erlotinib to sorafenib and missed its OS endpoint (289 vs 259 days). Toxicity did not cap the dose: serious AEs were similar between arms. Plasma exposure at 150 mg/day is documented in patients (PMID:20479691). Engagement and pathway were never measured in HCC. Both are inferred adequate because erlotinib is FDA-approved for NSCLC and pancreatic cancer through EGFR inhibition in tumour tissue at comparable doses (100–150 mg; NCT00925769). With the mechanism plausibly engaged, adding EGFR blockade gave no benefit. A review lists erlotinib among agents with no meaningful HCC benefit and cites tumour heterogeneity (PMID:32434345), so F3 is secondary. The network meta-analysis showed no gain over sorafenib alone (PMID:29234637). Confidence is medium because engagement is inferred.

Erlotinib had no responses in recurrent pediatric ependymoma (ORR 0% vs 16.7% for etoposide), and the trial stopped for futility at interim with no safety concerns (NCT01032070, PMID:27287856). Exposure looks adequate: pediatric PK at 85 mg/m2 matched earlier pediatric data. In adults with NSCLC brain metastases, CSF levels (about 5% penetration) were above the cellular IC50 (PMID:20479691). Tolerability did not cap the dose. No human source shows EGFR inhibition, phospho-EGFR lowering or a downstream biomarker change in ependymoma tissue. The only tumor-tissue EGFR data found were in adult glioma, not this disease. No other EGFR drug has succeeded in ependymoma, so F1b does not apply. The sources do not say why it failed beyond lack of activity, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter: U.

Index trial NCT01627613 (PMID:28750677) found no difference in EVLWI between inhaled AP301 and placebo. The drug was well tolerated, and the 125 mg nebulizer dose was below the phase 1 maximum, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The first-in-human study (PMID:24515273) measured only plasma levels, which were very low; that is read as the drug staying in the lung, but no lung or alveolar levels were measured. No human measure of ENaC activation or alveolar fluid clearance was found; ENaC activation is shown only in animal cells and in vitro (PMID:23313096, PMID:26254591). The investigators point to a mixed patient population, an underpowered trial, and a possible benefit limited to patients with SOFA scores of 11 or more. Because engagement was never measured in humans, the failure cannot be attributed, so the code is U.

MK-8291 has no recorded target. The bundle contains only the index crossover trial NCT02336555 in 35 PHN patients with allodynia. The difference in pain change versus placebo was -0.452 (95% CI -1.076 to 0.172, p=0.075) and missed significance. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, target engagement or biomarker data, no other trials of this drug, no same-target comparators and no publications. Tolerability did not appear limiting (1/34 serious AEs). The small sample suggests the trial may have been underpowered, but no source states this. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate.

NCT04612062 was the first-in-human study of CEE321, a topical 'soft' pan-JAK inhibitor, in healthy volunteers and atopic dermatitis patients. No results were posted. Novartis dropped the program, citing an unfavorable benefit-risk profile, and gave no details. The only engagement evidence I found is ex vivo human skin biomarker inhibition and minipig skin levels, which don't count as human data. No human skin exposure, JAK engagement or biomarker data were found, so all three pillars are no_human_data. A topical JAK1/2 inhibitor, ruxolitinib cream, is approved for atopic dermatitis, which suggests the JAK target works in this disease and points toward the molecule (F1b), for example too little drug reaching the skin. With no pillar data, the case stays largely indeterminate (U).

Target engagement was shown in humans, but in HCV-cured fibrosis patients (NCT03420768), not in NASH. In that trial, liver biopsies at week 12 showed HSP47 mRNA reduced in 71% of patients at 90 mg, versus 13% on placebo. Median HSP47 protein fell about 10% on drug and rose 23.5% on placebo. Plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose. The authors say this showed target engagement, and it was presented in 2020, before the index trial began. Fibrosis histology in that trial did not differ significantly from placebo, so no downstream pathway effect is established. The same 45 and 90 mg doses in NASH cirrhosis (NCT04267393) did worse than placebo on fibrosis (12.2% and 7.1% vs 20.5%). Most likely the mechanism does not drive fibrosis regression as tested (F2). The 12-week treatment period may also have been too short (F4). The protein knockdown was modest, which weakens this verdict.

In the index trial (NCT03420768, HCV patients after cure with advanced fibrosis), liver biopsies at week 12 showed lower HSP47 mRNA and protein on drug than on placebo. The investigators called this target engagement. Engagement was therefore shown in this disease, but only in the paper published after the trial. The knockdown was modest: median mRNA change was −1.2% at 45 mg and −5.9% at 90 mg, versus +13.7% on placebo. The authors said maximal engagement may not have shown in the biopsies. I found no reported human result for downstream collagen markers, so pathway is no_human_data. Fibrosis did not improve meaningfully more than on placebo. The authors suggested testing patients with active fibrogenesis (F3). However, the NASH cirrhosis trial (NCT04267393) was stopped for futility, which supports the target not driving the disease as tested (F2). The index trial was also small (F7).

The index trial NCT03538301 (JUNIPER) had a descriptive safety primary endpoint: discontinuations due to TEAEs were 1/42 placebo, 3/41 at 45 mg and 4/40 at 90 mg, and serious AEs were not higher on drug. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human evidence of HSP47 knockdown, lung exposure or a collagen pathway biomarker. The Phase 1 studies (NCT03142165) posted no PD results, and PMID:31332587 reports only negative anti-drug antibody results. The liver fibrosis trials NCT03420768 and NCT04267393 also failed without engagement data. Benefit appears only in rat models (PMID:34109242). If this is treated as an efficacy failure, U applies, because nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

The Phase 1 study in type 2 diabetes patients with atherosclerosis or CV risk (NCT03654313, PMID:36688371) showed exposure: nonlinear PK consistent with target-mediated disposition, supporting monthly dosing. It also showed engagement: dose-dependent suppression of free soluble LOX-1 by 72–83% at 90–250 mg monthly. The drug was well tolerated, with no dose cap, and this preceded the index trial. No downstream pathway biomarker (e.g., inflammatory or oxLDL markers) was reported. In NCT04610892, post-MI patients received 150/400 mg, at or above the engaging doses, yet non-calcified plaque volume did not change versus placebo (p=0.685). With LOX-1 engaged and no benefit, the evidence suggests LOX-1 blockade does not drive plaque regression as tested.

In the Phase 1 trial in type 2 diabetes patients (NCT03654313, PMID:36688371), MEDI6570 showed nonlinear pharmacokinetics consistent with target-mediated disposition. It also lowered soluble LOX-1 dose-dependently, by 72-83% at 90-250 mg monthly, which is comparable to the 150/400 mg index doses. It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. That supports adequate exposure and engagement, though not in post-MI coronary patients. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Despite this engagement, the index trial (NCT04610892) showed no reduction in non-calcified plaque volume at any dose (pooled p=0.685), with no dose-response. Engaging LOX-1 therefore did not modify coronary plaque, which points to the target not driving the disease as tested.

Peptron said PT320 (NCT04269642) missed its primary endpoint, MDS-UPDRS part 3 (p=0.7355), but would keep developing the drug because of secondary outcomes. Earlier trials gave the same exenatide dose, 2 mg weekly, to PD patients. In those trials exenatide reached the CSF (about 2% of serum), so exposure is counted as adequate. Neuron-derived exosomes showed changes in insulin/Akt signalling (pathway), but that is a downstream marker, not a measure of the drug binding brain GLP1R. The diabetes approval reflects peripheral action, so it cannot support inferred engagement in the brain. The PD3 investigators (PMID:39919773) could not rule out that CNS exenatide levels were too low. Brain engagement is unmeasured, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter: U.

In the first-in-human study (NCT02923349, PMID:36316061), patients with advanced solid tumors received 7–1400 mg. No maximum tolerated dose was reached and only one dose-limiting toxicity occurred, so the dose was not capped. Pharmacokinetics were assessed, and OX40 receptor occupancy stayed above 90% at doses of 200 mg or more, so exposure and engagement were adequate in patients. Engagement was published only after the trial began. Pathway effects were absent: no peripheral T-cell proliferation or activation, no reduction in circulating Tregs, and no consistent intratumoral changes. Clinical activity was minimal (1 partial response among 87 patients). Full target occupancy without immune or clinical effect supports F2. The index trial's primary endpoint was safety, not efficacy, and the combination study's Phase 2 was not conducted (NCT03241173), so F9 also applies.

In the index trial, NCT02387125, lapretolimod (GLA-SE) was mainly the adjuvant in G305, part of the CMB305 prime-boost vaccine, plus an optional G100 arm. The trial was a Phase 1b safety and immunogenicity study of the regimen, not a test of TLR4 agonism alone, so the futility stop reflects the vaccine, not this drug (F9). No human TLR4 binding or plasma levels were measured. For an agonist, downstream activation is the best available proxy for engagement. Intratumoral G100 in Merkel cell carcinoma (NCT02035657) raised immune-gene activation and CD4+/CD8+ T-cell infiltration in injected tumors. CMB305 raised NY-ESO-1 antibodies (62.9% of patients) and T cells (47.4%) in the index-trial cancers, yet clinical benefit did not follow (secondary F2). That evidence was published after the index trial started.

Phase 1 studies (PMID:42875830) showed RGH-706 reached measurable, roughly dose-proportional plasma levels and was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited by side effects. No human MCHR1 receptor occupancy was reported. Occupancy was measured only ex vivo in mice (PMID:41567076). Downstream appetite and intake measures showed only trends, mostly at the lower doses (2.5–7.5 mg), which is not a clear dose-dependent effect. Richter dropped the drug for PWS hyperphagia based on preliminary Phase 2 data and gave no mechanistic explanation. Results for NCT05322096 have not been posted. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged MCHR1 from a target that does not matter in PWS, so the code is U.

Inhaled iloprost is approved for pulmonary hypertension and met a pivotal PVR endpoint (NCT01469169). In PH patients, inhaled 5 µg produced measurable plasma levels and roughly 35–38% PVR reduction (PMID:14555558). IP-receptor engagement is therefore inferred adequate in the same lung vascular compartment at comparable inhaled doses. Platelet cAMP rose and aggregation was inhibited in humans (PMID:2423342). No engagement data come from COVID-19 patients; titles only suggest oxygenation benefit (PMID:35279981, PMID:34289888). The 40-patient index trial (NCT04445246) posted no results, and the only linked paper calls it ongoing (PMID:34529182). With engagement plausibly adequate and no demonstrated benefit before the program stopped, F2 is the default. However, the small size and missing results leave trial-related causes (F7) open. Confidence is low.

Ramelteon is FDA-approved for insomnia. CNS MT1/MT2 agonism produced dose-dependent sleep-latency reductions and sedation in humans (PMID:16309958, PMID:21955196, PMID:17389558), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Caveat: the index trial used sublingual 0.1–0.8 mg, and the bundle has no SL pharmacokinetic data showing exposure comparable to oral 8 mg. That uncertainty leaves U as a secondary code. In bipolar depression, no dose separated from placebo on MADRS (NCT01467700). Two companion trials also failed: maintenance relapse (NCT01467713, PMID:28662460) and an acute MADRS trial stopped for futility (NCT01677182). Adjunctive use in MDD also failed (NCT00642694). No tolerability limit was shown. The stated business-decision stop followed consistently null readouts, which points to a melatonergic mechanism that does not drive bipolar mood.

Ramelteon is approved for insomnia, acting through central MT1/MT2 agonism. Polysomnographic sleep-latency effects (PMID:16309958, PMID:21955196) and sedation in volunteers (PMID:17389558) imply CNS exposure, engagement and pathway effects. These pillars are therefore inferred_adequate; no receptor-level measurement exists in mood-disorder patients. The index sublingual trial (NCT01467700) showed no MADRS separation at 0.1, 0.4 or 0.8 mg, with no dose trend. Two other bipolar trials also failed (NCT01467713, NCT01677182; the latter for futility). An oral ramelteon MDD study had fewer remitters on drug than placebo (NCT00642694). The 'business decision' followed failed readouts, so F8 does not apply. Dose comparability between the SL and approved oral 8 mg doses is not shown in the bundle, which lowers confidence.

In the index trial (NCT01677182), sublingual ramelteon at 0.1 and 0.4 mg did not separate from placebo on MADRS (p=0.783 and 0.329), and the trial was stopped for futility. The sister bipolar trials (NCT01467700, NCT01467713/PMID:28662460) also failed. Oral 8 mg ramelteon works for insomnia through MT1/MT2 (PMID:16309958), so the receptors are druggable in the brain. But the bipolar program used a different formulation at much lower doses. Nothing found links SL exposure to the oral dose or measures receptor engagement or circadian markers (e.g., melatonin phase) in bipolar patients. That leaves 'inferred adequate' unsupported. Because of this, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter here. F2 is listed as a possible secondary code if SL exposure matched the oral dose.

The index trial NCT04086238 is a Phase 1 food-effect pharmacokinetic study of oral decitabine/tetrahydrouridine in healthy adults. Its endpoints are absorption and plasma concentration, so it was not an efficacy test and cannot be a failed efficacy readout (F9). The pillars hold systemically in humans. Oral decitabine with a cytidine deaminase inhibitor gave exposure comparable to IV and DNMT1 downregulation in healthy volunteers (PMID:37417197). It also gave equivalent LINE-1 demethylation and clinical responses in MDS/CMML (NCT02103478, PMID:32285126, PMID:38135371). No engagement data in pancreatic adenocarcinoma appear in the bundle. Nothing indicates the program stopped because of an efficacy failure.

Fiztasovimab is an antibody against CMV glycoprotein B. In the Phase 1 study in healthy men (PMID:34989174), serum levels rose in proportion to dose, and the half-life was about 26–33 days. The Phase 2 doses were chosen from simulations meant to keep trough levels above a neutralizing target of 19 µg/mL. Those levels were not actually measured in patients, so exposure is labelled inferred_adequate as a judgement call rather than in the narrow sense defined above. No human data on engagement exist, such as serum neutralizing activity or blocking of virus spread between cells. The investigators said serum antibody levels were not analysed in detail. In NCT04225923 / PMID:40072882, CMV infection was no lower than with placebo, with only a non-significant trend toward less CMV disease. Nothing shows whether the drug failed to engage its target or whether the mechanism does not work, so the code is U.

IMM-124E is an oral hyperimmune bovine colostrum whose antibodies bind bacterial LPS (protocol). In the index trial in NASH patients (NCT02316717), the sponsor reported that serum LPS fell significantly more than with placebo: 64% vs 34% of patients had a ≥15% drop. That is target-ligand lowering in this disease, but it was measured in the index trial itself, not before it. Downstream effects were partial. Only the high dose produced a significant drop in CK18 (a marker of liver-cell death). ALT/AST changes were not significant, and hepatic fat was no better than placebo (-0.90 to -1.55% vs -1.85%). The drug works in the gut, and no human data measure levels there. Because the dose was well tolerated and LPS was lowered without clinical benefit, F2 fits best. However, the LPS result is a modest responder analysis, so engagement is only moderately convincing. Also, 'pathway' is graded inferred_adequate on partial biomarker data, not as defined.

Riliprubart had a long half-life and dose-dependent PK in healthy volunteers. It produced clear dose-related inhibition of classical complement pathway activity (Wieslab CP and CH50 assays, with defined IC90) without tolerability limits (PMID:36661084, PMID:39171350). Exposure-response modelling in cold agglutinin disease patients also supported >90% efficacy (PMID:40308078). Engagement was therefore adequate in humans, though it was not shown in ITP patients, and the dated publications post-date the index trial's start. Despite this, durable platelet response was 0/8 in naive patients and 1/4 in switchers (NCT04669600). This suggests classical-complement C1s inhibition does not drive platelet loss in ITP as tested. No other C1s drug has succeeded in ITP. The tiny open-label trial limits certainty.

The index trial NCT04030195 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study. Its primary outcomes were MTD (not reached, reported as NA) and dose-limiting toxicities (1 DLT at dose level 1, none at dose levels 2 or 3). It was not an efficacy test of PBCAR20A, so F9 is primary. The bundle has no human data on CAR-T expansion or persistence, CD20 engagement, or B-cell depletion, so the pillars cannot be judged (U as secondary). Other CD20 agents are approved in this or related diseases, including ofatumumab in CLL. With no engagement evidence for PBCAR20A, this gives a possible F1b secondary. No stated stop reason or abstracts explain why the program ended.

In the index trial (NCT02355028), topical LHA510 did not reduce the need for ranibizumab rescue: 25/33 patients needed it versus 25/37 on vehicle (PMID:35247334). The Phase 1 trial (NCT02076919) posted only safety results. The evidence for good drug levels in the retina and choroid, and for efficacy, comes only from rabbits and rodents (PMID:29400470; AJO full text). No human data show that the eye drop reached the choroid, inhibited VEGFR2 there, or moved a biomarker. The investigators note that earlier topical TKIs failed because too little drug reached the eye, which makes poor delivery a plausible cause (secondary F1a), but this was never measured for LHA510. No KDR kinase inhibitor is approved for wet AMD. Reversible corneal haze occurred in 21 of 46 patients but did not clearly cap the dose. The evidence cannot separate a drug that never reached its target from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT02355028), topical 2% acrizanib did not reduce the need for Lucentis retreatment compared with vehicle (25/33 vs 25/37). The investigators' paper (AJO 2022) says insufficient exposure at the target tissue is the most likely reason. They measured only plasma, where levels were extremely low (about 0.2 ng/mL), not drug levels in the retina or choroid. No human data show VEGFR2 inhibition or a downstream biomarker change. Good ocular exposure was seen only in rabbits and rodents. The Phase 1 trial (NCT02076919) reported safety only. The investigators believe the mechanism was never properly tested because too little drug reached the back of the eye, which points to F1a. This is their inference rather than a measurement, so confidence is medium and U is listed as a secondary code. No other VEGFR2 drug has succeeded in wet AMD, so F1b does not apply.

Merck ended both Phase 2 trials (NCT04663321 and NCT05602727) and dropped the program after an unblinded review linked MK-1942 to liver toxicity. Abnormal liver tests in several participants triggered that review. This is a molecule-specific safety stop (F6). The JCP paper reports that a Phase 1 PET study in healthy volunteers put 10 mg at about 40% mGluR2 occupancy. That is the target level, but it was taken from monkey data. Phase 2 doses of 10 mg up to 20 mg bid gave plasma levels matching Phase 1, so exposure and engagement look adequate. Engagement was never measured in depressed patients, and there is no human pathway biomarker. Even so, MADRS showed no benefit and numerically favoured placebo (secondary F2). Enrolment stopped at about 70% of target, and a high early placebo response (PMID:42684061) limits interpretation (secondary F7).

MK-1942 is an mGluR2 negative allosteric modulator (PMID:42894266). A Phase 1 PET study in healthy volunteers found that a single 10 mg dose should give about 40% receptor occupancy. Investigators treated ≥40% as the level for maximal effect, based on glutamate-cycling data in monkeys. So brain exposure and engagement were shown in humans at about the index doses (5 and 15 mg), but only in healthy volunteers, not in people with Alzheimer's. No human downstream biomarker was found. In the index trial (NCT05602727), ADAS-Cog11 at week 12 did not separate from placebo at either dose, and the 5 mg arm was numerically worse. The depression trial (NCT04663321) also failed. Both point to the mechanism not driving the disease (F2). The early-terminated trial had only about 20–25 patients per arm, so it was underpowered (F7). The occupancy paper is still unpublished ('submitted'), so its timing relative to the index trial is uncertain.

IXT-m200 is an anti-methamphetamine antibody that sequesters the drug in plasma. Exposure was adequate: IgG-like PK, 17-19 d half-life, vascular confinement, and no MTD reached up to 20 mg/kg (PMID:25484042). Engagement was shown in methamphetamine-dependent patients before the index trial (NCT03336866, 2018). Plasma METH AUC and Cmax rose markedly and dose-dependently after challenge, consistent with binding. No downstream pathway measure, such as reduced brain METH or subjective effects, appears in the bundle. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. In the index trial (NCT05034874), abstinence was 5.9% versus 4.3% on placebo, and the trial stopped for futility. That points to a mechanism that does not drive abstinence as tested (F2). The sponsor also cited dropout and an insufficient sample size (F7).

CorMedix gave about 5.4 g/day of deferiprone (CRMD001) for 8 days, a dose in the range of its approved uses, to test whether chelating catalytic iron protects the kidneys from contrast injury (NCT01146925). Plasma levels are well documented in healthy volunteers and in people with impaired kidneys, so systemic exposure counts as adequate (PMID:27276421, PMID:25052529, NCT01989455). No human study I found measured whether the drug lowered catalytic or labile iron in plasma, urine or kidney. None showed a downstream marker such as reduced oxidative stress moving as expected in this setting. No results were posted, and the sponsor never published a topline readout or explained why it stopped, even after getting an FDA Special Protocol Assessment for a Phase 3 trial in 2011. Because target engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Deferiprone's intended action in PD is chelation of excess nigral iron. In PD patients, FAIR-PARK (PMID:25943368, published 2015, before the index trial started in 2016) showed reduced substantia nigra iron on R2* MRI. FAIRPARK-II (PMID:36449420, 15 mg/kg twice daily) confirmed a greater nigrostriatal iron decrease than placebo. Together these show brain exposure and target engagement in the disease, and no dose cap from tolerability. Yet the index dose-ranging trial (NCT02728843) showed no MDS-UPDRS III benefit at any dose. The larger FAIRPARK-II trial showed faster worsening on deferiprone. Deferiprone also accelerated cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease (PMID:39495531). With iron lowered and no benefit, the iron-chelation mechanism does not appear to drive PD progression as tested. Index-trial doses may be somewhat lower than FAIRPARK-II, hence medium confidence.

Deferiprone crosses the blood-brain barrier. Two PKAN studies showed it lowered globus pallidus iron on T2*/R2* MRI at 15 mg/kg twice daily, the same 30 mg/kg/day dose used in the index trial. One of these (PMID:21557313) was published in 2011, before the index trial started; the other is PMID:24661465. So exposure and engagement were adequate, in this disease and before the index trial. No downstream pathway marker, such as oxidative stress, was measured in PKAN. Even so, the index trial NCT01741532 missed both co-primary endpoints (BAD p=0.076; PGI-I p=0.73). Long-term studies also found that iron reduction did not track clinical change (PMID:35956138). Lowering brain iron therefore did not translate into clinical benefit (F2). Authors also point to disease stage, treatment duration and dosing regimen (PMID:21557313, PMID:35956138), so F4 is secondary. Tolerability did not cap the dose (NCT02174848).

The index trial NCT00530127 had a safety/tolerability primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. Per PMID:25112865, 20 mg/kg/day was well tolerated, which met the safety objective. Engagement in FRDA patients was shown before the trial: 20–30 mg/kg/day lowered dentate-nucleus iron (R2*) (PMID:17379741, 2007). Left ventricular mass index fell at 20–40 mg/kg, a downstream effect. Efficacy readouts were secondary and uninformative because the placebo arm did not deteriorate (F7). A possible benefit appeared only in the less-severe subgroup (F3). Higher doses worsened ataxia and the 60 mg/kg arm was stopped, consistent with over-chelation harming iron-dependent enzymes (PMID:18558000; F5). Engagement was already shown at the tolerated dose, so dose_limited is false.

In the index trial (NCT03631407), vicriviroc 150 or 250 mg plus pembrolizumab gave an ORR of 5% in both arms of MSS CRC. Dose-limiting toxicity was low (0 and 2), so the dose was not capped by tolerability. CCR5 engagement is inferred_adequate: vicriviroc met its HIV efficacy endpoint (VICTOR-E1, PMID:20064072/NCT00243230) with exposure-response (PMID:20071999), so systemic CCR5 blockade must have held there. Doses of 150-250 mg were tolerated with exposures up to 5x the HIV therapeutic level (PMID:20350942). However, no tumor penetration, intratumoral engagement or pathway biomarker is shown in CRC. This supports F2 (CCR5 blockade does not rescue PD-1 response in MSS CRC) only weakly; U is plausible. The single-arm design without a comparator limits interpretation.

Index trial NCT03631407 (PMID:38942693) gave vicriviroc 150 or 250 mg plus pembrolizumab in MSS CRC. ORR was 5% in both arms, and toxicity was manageable. The 150 mg dose had no DLTs, so the dose was not capped. No CCR5 occupancy or pathway biomarker was measured in CRC. Engagement is therefore inferred from HIV, where vicriviroc met its efficacy endpoint through CCR5 blockade (VICTOR-E1, PMID:20064072/NCT00243230) with a PK–response relationship (PMID:20071999). The CRC doses gave exposures equal to or above HIV therapeutic levels (PMID:20350942). However, tumour-microenvironment CCR5 is not the same compartment as circulating CD4 cells, so the inference is weak. The study was single-arm-like with no comparator. U remains plausible.

In the index MGD trial (NCT01633788), no dose of this topical androgen did better than vehicle on meibum quality: 46.3% responders on 0.1% vs 42.9% on vehicle. The Phase 3 protocol (NCT02815293) mentions a Phase 1 safety/PK study (195263-001) in postmenopausal women, but gives no data on drug levels at the eyelid glands, AR engagement or AR pathway biomarkers. No source gives a tolerability limit on dose; all strengths were described as well tolerated. Allergan then moved to evaporative dry eye based on symptom and TBUT signals, including a low-TBUT subgroup, so patient selection may also play a part (F3). Those Phase 3 trials were stopped without a stated reason. With no engagement data, an undertested mechanism can't be told apart from an irrelevant one.

The index trial NCT02221037 tested inhaled GSK2862277 26 mg in oesophagectomy patients. It stopped when protocol-defined stopping criteria were met, and PVPI was essentially unchanged versus placebo (small n, wide SDs). The Phase 1 trial NCT01818024 measured PK/PD in healthy volunteers but posted no results. PMID:26178412 reports only tolerability and pre-existing anti-drug antibody findings, with no exposure, TNFR1 occupancy or pathway data. Tengonermin acts on the TNF axis in lung cancer, not as a TNFR1 antagonist in ARDS, so it cannot support F1b. With engagement unmeasured in humans, the bundle cannot separate a drug that failed to engage from a target that does not drive the disease. Hence U. The trial was small (n=35) and terminated early, so F7 also applies.

The published paper on the index trial (NCT02221037, EJA 2020) reports that nebulised GSK2862277 at 26 mg reached the lungs at pharmacologically relevant concentrations, measured in epithelial lining fluid. That covers exposure. In these oesophagectomy patients, BAL free soluble TNFR1 fell significantly, which shows the drug engaged its target. MIP-1α and total protein also fell, so the downstream pathway moved. This evidence appeared after the trial started. Even so, PVPI did not change in either arm, unlike earlier trials in this population. The placebo group never developed the expected lung leak, so the model gave the drug no injury to prevent, and the trial was stopped at an interim when protocol stopping criteria were met. Trial design or model failure (F7) is the main explanation. The target simply not mattering (F2) is possible but was not cleanly tested.

Febuxostat 80 mg gives robust plasma exposure (Cmax ~2.7–3.7 mg/L, far above the urate-production IC50 of 0.11 mg/L; PMID:32386239, PMID:25997544). Xanthine oxidase inhibition, read out as serum and urinary urate lowering, is shown in humans at 80 mg, including the pre-index 2011 study PMID:21654267. It is also shown in gout trials meeting urate endpoints (NCT02139046, NCT02128490) and in NCT01077284, plus the 2009 gout approval. Urate was not reported in hypertensive patients in the index trial, so engagement in this disease is not shown. Despite adequate systemic XO inhibition at 80 mg, 24-h SBP change did not differ from placebo (−0.3 mmHg, CI −3.9 to 3.4; NCT01496469). The tight CI points to the mechanism not lowering blood pressure in this population.

Plasma PK is characterized in bipolar I patients and is unaffected by disease (PMID:27436172). PET in healthy adults showed striatal DAT occupancy of 34-40% at 100 mg and 60-65% at 250 mg, with small extracellular dopamine changes (PMID:21035624). Engagement and pathway are also supported by efficacy at 150-250 mg in approved sleep indications acting through the same CNS target, with dose-dependent wakefulness effects (PMID:22039290, PMID:16393442). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, the 150 mg adjunctive arm missed its primary endpoint (p=0.13; NCT01072630), as did NCT01305408; only NCT01072929 was positive. The extension was stopped for an efficacy-related business decision (NCT01121536). This points to DAT-mediated activity not driving bipolar depression benefit. Heterogeneous background mood stabilizers (PMID:26330288) and the early-dropped 200 mg arm (PMID:25933099) are secondary factors.

Plasma exposure was well characterized, including in bipolar I patients (PMID:27436172). In healthy adults, PET showed dose-dependent striatal DAT occupancy of about 34-40% at 100 mg and 60-65% at 250 mg, with modest extracellular dopamine changes (PMID:21035624). Wakefulness effects and the approved sleep indications at similar doses support the pathway. Even so, the index trial missed its primary endpoint (difference -2.1, p=0.13). A third trial, NCT01305408, also missed, and only NCT01072929 met its endpoint. The extension NCT01121536 was ended by a business decision tied to efficacy. This suggests DAT inhibition at these doses does not reliably treat bipolar depression. A case report argues the doses were too low (PMID:37459498), but no tolerability cap is shown. Inconsistent results and a large placebo response also raise design or execution concerns (F7).

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of the iron chelator VLX600 in refractory solid tumors (NCT02222363) was terminated for slow recruitment and lack of efficacy after several dose steps. It posted no results. The bundle contains no human pharmacokinetic, target-engagement (iron chelation) or pathway biomarker data, no other trials, and no publications. No MTD or dose-limiting toxicity is reported, so tolerability capping the dose cannot be established. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate. Slow recruitment (an operational issue) is a secondary contributor (F7). The evidence is very thin.

VLX600 is an iron chelator meant to inhibit mitochondrial respiration. Its only trial, the first-in-human dose-escalation study NCT02222363 (Mody et al. 2018), measured pharmacokinetics, but the available abstract gives no exposure values. The pages I found show no human measurement of iron chelation or of mitochondrial respiration being inhibited, and no pharmacodynamic biomarker. So none of the three pillars can be judged. The study closed early because of slow recruitment, after dose steps had been cut back following a grade 3 pulmonary embolism. It never found a maximum tolerated dose or a recommended phase 2 dose. Tolerability did not formally cap the dose, and no patient had an objective response. Because target engagement is unknown and the trial stopped before escalation finished, the code is U, with trial execution (F7) as a secondary code.

The index Phase 1/2 trial of lenalidomide plus sunitinib in RCC (NCT00975806) was terminated because the MTD, 10 mg lenalidomide with 37.5 mg sunitinib, was judged 'sub-optimal as efficacious treatment for renal cell carcinoma'. No Phase 2 response data were posted. So tolerability of the combination capped the dose below what the investigators considered necessary, and the mechanism was never properly tested. Lenalidomide combinations in myeloma reached 25 mg (NCT00560391, NCT00603447). Human plasma PK is well characterized (PMID:28724202, PMID:30672004), so exposure is adequate. The bundle has no CRBN engagement or pathway biomarker data in RCC patients. Engagement is rated inadequate because of the dose cap.

The index trial NCT01732861 was a completed Phase 1 safety study of CC-292 plus lenalidomide in CLL/SLL. Its only primary outcome was adverse events, it gave no stop reason, and it posted no results. It was not an efficacy test of lenalidomide, and its CLL population does not match the labelled program disease, childhood ependymoma. Plasma exposure is documented in patients, including CLL (PMID:30672004, PMID:28724202), and CSF penetrance has been studied (PMID:23600765). CRBN engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from FDA approvals in MCL, FL, MZL and MDS, and from a met endpoint in CLL (NCT00751296). No engagement data exist in ependymoma. Because the index trial did not test efficacy, the code is F9.

The index trial NCT01732861 is a 20-patient Phase 1 safety study of CC-292 plus lenalidomide in CLL/SLL. Its only primary endpoint is adverse events, it completed with no stop reason, and it posted no results. It was not an efficacy test of lenalidomide, and it does not concern the listed program disease, medulloblastoma. Plasma exposure in patients, including CLL, is characterised by population PK (PMID:30672004, PMID:28724202). CRBN engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred adequate because lenalidomide is FDA-approved in B-cell lymphomas (mantle cell, follicular, marginal zone) and met its primary endpoint in CLL (NCT00751296, 72% overall response). Nothing in the bundle shows an efficacy failure, so F9 applies.

Plasma exposure is well characterised in patients (PMID:28724202, PMID:30672004). CRBN engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because lenalidomide met efficacy endpoints through CRBN in myeloma and lymphoma at comparable doses (~25 mg). In prostate cancer patients, lenalidomide shifted cytokines and anti-prostate antibodies (PMID:21748755) and reduced MDSCs (PMID:25617965), so the immunomodulatory pathway was engaged. Monotherapy activity was only modest (PMID:24238760). In the index trial, adding lenalidomide to docetaxel/prednisone worsened overall survival (HR 1.53, p=0.0017) and raised serious AEs (283 vs 176) (NCT00988208). With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, the mechanism does not drive CRPC outcomes as tested. Excess toxicity, plausibly CRBN-mediated myelosuppression, likely contributed to the survival detriment (F5).

The index trial NCT01732861 is a 20-patient Phase 1 safety study of CC-292 plus lenalidomide in CLL/SLL. Its only primary outcome is adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of lenalidomide. It completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results. The listed program disease (craniopharyngioma) does not match the index trial. Plasma exposure is documented in patients, including CLL (PMID:30672004, PMID:28724202). CRBN engagement and pathway effects were never measured directly in the bundle. Both are inferred adequate because lenalidomide is approved in B-cell lymphomas (MCL, FL, MZL) and met its primary response endpoint in CLL (NCT00751296) at comparable doses. No efficacy failure is shown, hence F9.

The index trial NCT03577028 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study. Its only primary endpoint was dose-limiting toxicities, and it was classified as not_efficacy. It was terminated by an unspecified sponsor decision not to proceed to expansion, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. DLTs occurred across priming schedules, but the bundle does not show that toxicity drove the stop. The bundle contains no human PK, T-cell engagement or PSA/biomarker data, so all three pillars are no_human_data and the mechanism remains untested (U). PMID:33203731 describes HPN424 as PSMA-targeting, which conflicts with the listed KLK2 target. Other prostate T-cell engagers (pasritamig, xaluritamig) reached Phase 3 but are not approved, so F1b does not apply.

The first-in-human study showed dose-proportional plasma exposure, with a half-life of 2–3 h, which suits once-daily dosing (PMID:27063928). The drug also improved glucose in that study and lowered post-prandial glucose in a 14-day Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) trial (PMID:29320575). That gives some evidence for systemic exposure and a downstream effect. No source measured target engagement directly: there is no receptor occupancy data (the receptor for unacylated ghrelin is undefined), no evidence the drug reached the brain or hypothalamus, and no proof that acylated-ghrelin signalling was antagonised. In ZEPHYR (NCT03790865), neither dose separated from placebo on the HQ-CT hyperphagia score, and Millendo stopped development. Nothing in the bundle tells apart a drug that failed to engage its central target from a target that does not drive hyperphagia, so the code is U.

Exposure: the Phase 1 study NCT01401543 measured plasma AUC of about 500 ng·h/mL at the 5 mg dose used in the index trial. AR agonism was shown in humans at the same doses (1, 5 and 15 mg). In the JCEM 2021 trial of androgen-deficient prostate cancer survivors, lean mass rose and fat mass and alkaline phosphatase fell with dose, and Phase 1 work reported PSA suppression. These are strong signs of activity, but they are downstream readouts, not direct binding data. That trial also measured erectile function, which did not improve, matching the index result: adding the drug to tadalafil was no better than tadalafil alone (p=0.5). The 5 mg monotherapy arm got worse on the erectile function score (-0.97). So the drug engaged AR systemically, but AR agonism did not help erections. Caveats: engagement was not measured in ED patients or in penile tissue, and all of this was published after the index trial (2010). The secondary F3 code is tentative: these patients were not testosterone deficient, though no source blames patient selection.

In sepsis patients, BMS-936559 at 900 mg gave full PD-L1 receptor occupancy for 28 days. That trial also showed a sustained, dose-related rise in monocyte HLA-DR, a downstream immune effect (PMID:30747773, published 2019, before the index trial). This counts as human engagement and exposure, though not in esophageal cancer. Pathway is marked inferred_adequate on that HLA-DR signal; strictly it is a measured effect in another disease, not inference from efficacy. The index trial (NCT04460066) has unknown status, no stated stop reason and no posted results. Its dose is not shown, so the bundle cannot confirm an actual efficacy failure. No same-target drug is approved in esophageal cancer here. F2 is tentative; incomplete execution (F7) is possible.

The index trial, NCT04880564, was a Phase I/II study of CN401 combined with CN1. It enrolled only 7 patients and was terminated without posting results. The sponsor gave two reasons for stopping: no benefit from the drug, and a change in the company's landscape. A Patsnap listing describes CN401 as a PI3Kγ/δ inhibitor. However, the bundle contains no human data on exposure, target engagement (for example, PI3K pathway inhibition) or downstream biomarkers. It has no Phase 1 results or publications either. The bundle shows no other drug on this target succeeding, so F1b cannot be supported. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the primary code is U. The partly business-driven reason for stopping supports F8 as a secondary code. The tiny enrollment, below what the trial needed to answer its question, supports F7.

The bundle has no human PK, SF3B1 engagement or on-treatment splicing biomarker data. PMID:34172893 reports only pre-treatment aberrant TMEM14C transcripts as a response predictor, plus transfusion independence in a SF3B1-mutant subset (subset benefit, hence F3 as secondary). In the expansion (PMID:40651101), thrombocytopenia forced a dose reduction from 10 mg to 5 mg BID, with frequent dose adjustments and atrial fibrillation. The authors attribute the low RBC-TI rate to insufficient efficacy at the doses tested and call for further dosing exploration. This hints at a dose cap (F1a as secondary), but no engagement data show the dose fell short. The index trial was stopped for futility (NCT02841540). With engagement unmeasured, an unengaged drug cannot be separated from an irrelevant target, so the primary code is U.

In the escalation part of NCT02841540 (PMID:34172893), patients with MDS, CMML or AML showed predictable PK. Splicing markers in their peripheral blood changed with dose from 2 mg up to 30 mg. Aberrantly spliced TMEM14C, a downstream SF3B1 target, went down. Even so, there were no IWG complete or partial responses. In the SF3B1-mutant lower-risk MDS expansion (PMID:40651101), the 10 mg BID dose was cut to 5 mg BID for thrombocytopenia, and few patients became transfusion independent. The sponsor stopped the trial for futility. Splicing still changed at doses at or below 5 mg BID, so engagement was shown and the target does not seem to drive benefit as tested (F2). The authors' remark about 'insufficient efficacy at dose levels tested' and the benefit limited to a biomarker subset support F1a and F3 as secondary codes. All engagement data came from the index trial itself.

Wave stopped PRECISION-HD1 (NCT03225833), which tested rovanersen against SNP1 in HD patients, in March 2021 because the drug did not lower mutant huntingtin (mHTT) in CSF. In the sister trial of WVE-120102, the 32 mg dose gave a non-significant 9.9% median CSF mHTT drop versus 0.8% on placebo, with no dose response. Wave said the PRECISION-HD1 data it had reviewed were similar. Wave also judged that higher doses were unlikely to give the exposure needed for meaningful depletion. CSF NfL did not change. So target engagement in patients was shown to be inadequate, meaning the mechanism was never properly tested (F1a). Tolerability did not cap the dose. No published human data show rovanersen exposure directly, and the exposure statement is about WVE-120102. Other HTT-lowering drugs have not succeeded, so F1b does not apply.

The index trial NCT03137758 was a Phase 1 safety and dose-escalation study whose primary endpoint was toxicity. It was terminated to reformulate the drug and cut pill burden before higher doses were tested, so it was not a failed efficacy readout. The follow-on Phase 1 trial NCT04677855 was stopped as a business decision for insufficient enrollment. There is no human PK, target engagement or biomarker evidence; plumbagin has no recorded primary target, and all mechanistic data are in vitro or animal. Preclinical papers note poor solubility and bioavailability (PMID:28746182, PMID:35047632), which fits the formulation problem but is not human exposure evidence. Because the mechanism was never tested in humans, the case is also indeterminate (U), and execution or enrollment problems (F7) contributed.

The best explanation is F2: the drug hit CSF1R in patients, but this produced little clinical benefit. In the index trial's own patients (NCT02829723), conference abstracts show BLZ945, alone or with spartalizumab, raised plasma CSF-1 and lowered intermediate and nonclassical monocytes at every dose and schedule. Tumor biopsies showed macrophage gene signatures falling and T-cell inflammation signatures rising. These are the expected engagement and pathway effects, reported as on-target. The data come from the index trial itself, published in 2020, so they did not exist before it started. Dose was not reported as the limit. Efficacy was still limited: glioblastoma PFS6 was 15–22%. Investigators suggested the drug may work less well in non-mesenchymal glioblastoma, which supports F3 as a secondary code. Brain drug levels were not measured directly in humans. No stop reason was posted.

The index Phase 1 trial of orludodstat in myeloid malignancies (NCT03404726) was terminated for lack of sufficient clinical benefit. It posted no results: no PK, DHODH inhibition or pyrimidine-pathway biomarker data such as plasma dihydroorotate. There are no other trials of this drug and no other DHODH drugs in this disease to compare against. The only abstract (PMID:42818329) reports in vitro structural and resistance screening, which does not count as human evidence. All three pillars therefore lack human data. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged DHODH from a target that does not drive the disease, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

NCT03404726 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of BAY2402234 in myeloid malignancies. It was terminated for 'lack of sufficient clinical benefit' and no results were ever posted. The searches turned up only preclinical evidence: plasma DHO lowering and differentiation in mouse xenografts (Leukemia 2019) and preclinical AACR abstracts. No human PK, plasma DHO biomarker, DHODH inhibition or differentiation data were published. The bundle shows no other DHODH inhibitor succeeding in AML, and no tolerability cap is documented. With all three pillars at no_human_data, the bundle can't tell a drug that never engaged DHODH apart from a target that doesn't drive the disease, so the code is U.

For a T-cell therapy, I treated engagement as the infused virus-specific T cells persisting and expanding in the patient. In the open-label phase 2 in allo-HCT patients, many treated for BK virus-associated hemorrhagic cystitis (PMID:36628536), the infused cells were detected for up to 12 weeks in 69% of patients. Circulating BK-specific T cells rose in 37.5% (9/24) of BKV-infected patients, so engagement was only partial. In the randomized kidney-transplant trial (NCT04605484), BK viremia fell more than with placebo, and the fall tracked a rise in BK-specific T cells. That supports the pathway pillar, but in another population. In the placebo-controlled index trial (NCT04390113), time to resolution of hematuria was the same in both arms (HR 0.92). All three phase 3 studies stopped for futility with no safety concerns, and the sponsor called the outcome unexpected. This suggests the cells engaged but BK-directed T cells do not speed hematuria resolution. The index trial measured no pillars, so confidence is low.

Posoleucel is an off-the-shelf multivirus-specific T-cell product, so 'engagement' here means the infused cells persisting and acting against BK virus. Human data exist. In the phase 2 trial in kidney transplant patients with BK viremia (NCT04605484), cells were still detectable up to 12 weeks after infusion, and a 2023 ASN abstract reported persisting BK-reactive T cells alongside lower BK viremia. The phase 2 prevention data (ASH 2022) showed functional virus-specific T cells expanding as viral loads fell. That makes engagement adequate, but only from abstracts and press releases, all published after the index trial started. The pathway grade does not fit the 'inferred_adequate' definition: no efficacy endpoint was met elsewhere, and I based it on viral-load declines without a clear placebo-controlled comparison. In the index hemorrhagic cystitis trial, the treated arm did no better than placebo (HR 0.92). Two of the other three phase 3 trials (NCT05305040, NCT05179057) also stopped for futility, and no safety concerns were noted. This fits F2: the mechanism as tested gave no clinical benefit. Confidence is low because the engagement data are thin.

Posoleucel is a third-party multivirus-specific T-cell product, so the 'target' is the viral antigens. In the uncontrolled 2017 Phase 2 study (Tzannou, JCO; PMID 28783452), epitope tracking showed functional donor VSTs persisting for up to 12 weeks in post-transplant patients, including 7 with adenovirus. I took this as evidence of exposure and engagement before the index trial, though it was not quantified at the level of the adenovirus subgroup. The adenovirus response rate in that study was 71%. However, in the randomised NCT05179057, viral clearance was the same on drug and placebo (11/25 vs 9/21; OR 0.98), and the DSMB stopped the trial for futility with no safety concerns. This suggests the earlier uncontrolled responses reflected natural recovery or standard care. The parallel Phase 3 trials (NCT05305040, NCT04390113) were also futile. The small, early-terminated sample adds an F7 element.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT03253185 (SC-007, advanced colorectal and gastric cancer, n=7) was terminated for a 'Benefit/Risk Imbalance' and posted no results. The bundle records no primary target and has no PK, target engagement or pathway data. There are no other trials, no same-target comparators and no publications. The stop reason was classified as safety/tolerability, which hints at molecule-specific toxicity (F6). However, it is unclear whether the imbalance came from toxicity, lack of activity, or both. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a molecule that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the failure is indeterminate (U). Confidence is low given the thin bundle.

SC-007 is an antibody-drug conjugate from Stemcentrx, not a small molecule, and its target was never disclosed. The index trial NCT03253185 was a Phase 1 dose-finding study in colorectal and gastric cancer. It was stopped after 7 patients for a 'benefit/risk imbalance', and ADC Review reports that dose-limiting toxicities drove the decision. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement, or pathway effects, so the mechanism was never tested. Toxicity ended the program rather than a failed efficacy readout. It cannot be determined whether the toxicity came from the target itself (F5) or from the molecule or its payload (F6). I chose F6 because toxicity was the stated cause, and listed U as secondary because there is no engagement evidence.

Rufinamide showed no separation from placebo on HAMA or any other scale at week 8 in GAD (NCT00595231). The bundle has no direct human CNS occupancy or sodium-channel biomarker data. Engagement is therefore inferred, not measured: the drug met efficacy endpoints in epilepsy (LGS, NCT01146951; partial seizures, PMID:20887365, PMID:20061123), so in the same CNS compartment it must have reached and blocked neuronal sodium channels. Healthy-volunteer PK confirms systemic exposure (PMID:9604126). The GAD dose is not reported, so dose comparability is uncertain. Tolerability was similar to placebo, so the dose was not capped. The likeliest reading is that sodium-channel blockade does not drive GAD as tested. Confidence is low because the inference is thin; U is the alternative.

The index trial NCT05609825 was a Phase 1 safety study in healthy participants and people with hypertriglyceridemia.
