Its primary outcome was TEAEs/SAEs, so it was not an efficacy test (hence secondary F9). It was terminated because of a 'change in risk/benefit ratio', with no further detail. No results were posted, and the bundle has no other trials, PubMed abstracts, or same-target comparators. There is no human evidence on exposure, APOC3 knockdown, or triglyceride lowering. The stated reason does not separate toxicity, strategic or commercial reprioritization, or inadequate pharmacology. With engagement lacking human data and nothing distinguishing these explanations, the failure is indeterminate (U).

Adding sorafenib to mFOLFOX6 did not improve PFS (9.1 vs 8.7 months, HR 0.884, p=0.23; NCT00865709). Plasma PK in CRC patients at 400 mg bid is documented (PMID:22615057, PMID:22089297). Engagement and pathway were not measured in CRC. They are only inferred adequate from the FDA approval in another malignancy at the same dose. Other drugs on the same targets are approved in colorectal cancer: fruquintinib and ramucirumab (KDR), and encorafenib (BRAF). This points to the molecule rather than the target. PMID:22089297 notes high protein binding and limited free drug as a possible cause of sorafenib's borderline activity. No direct pillar evidence shows adequate engagement in CRC. F2 is possible if the inferred engagement is accepted. The bundle is thin.

In the maintenance trial NCT00791778, sorafenib did not improve PFS over placebo (386 vs 478 days; HR 1.09, p=0.655). At 400 mg BID, plasma exposure is substantial (Cmax ~21 μM; PMID:24309512). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate: sorafenib is approved for HCC and RCC through RAF/VEGFR inhibition (PMID:31029219), so the mechanism must have held there at this dose. No engagement data exist in ovarian cancer patients. PMID:22089297 notes that high protein binding may limit free drug, but it does not show engagement was inadequate. A topotecan combination in ovarian cancer was also futile (NCT00526799). RAF-pathway successes in ovarian cancer (dabrafenib, avutometinib) are in mutation-selected subtypes, which suggests patient selection matters (F3 secondary).

In the index trial NCT04494256 (ALSpire), intrathecal BIIB105 produced statistically significant, sustained drops in ATXN2 protein in the CSF of ALS patients. That shows the drug reached the CNS and knocked down its target in this disease. The evidence came from the index trial itself, not from earlier work. The sources did not report the size of the reduction. Plasma neurofilament light, the neurodegeneration marker, did not fall, and function, breathing and strength did not improve over 6 months of placebo control or 40+ weeks of follow-up. No subgroup benefited. Neither sponsor said tolerability capped the dose. Biogen read the lack of NfL change as evidence the disease was not slowed, so ATXN2 lowering failed as tested (F2).

The index crossover trial (NCT00744978, PMID:24247022) used varenicline 1 mg twice daily, the full approved smoking-cessation dose, and showed no ADAS-Cog benefit (p=0.39). In smokers, PET at that same dose showed alpha4beta2 occupancy across brain regions plus suppressed nicotine-induced striatal dopamine release (PMID:31096265), so engagement and pathway effect are adequate. In Parkinson disease, doses of 0.25-1 mg gave 60-70% occupancy (PMID:33977560). Brain exposure is inferred from the approval for nicotine dependence via the same CNS target. GI adverse events occurred but did not cap the dose. Engagement was never measured in Alzheimer patients, and the direct data postdate the index trial. Agonism of this target therefore did not improve cognition. The short 6-week crossover in 66 patients is a minor design caveat.

The index trial was an open-label safety extension, terminated because all three antecedent adjunctive MDD trials failed (PMID:29912786). The Phase 3 trials NCT01436162 and NCT01436149 and the dose-ranging NCT01435759 found no MADRS separation from placebo, with no dose-response up to 70 mg. No receptor occupancy was measured. Engagement and exposure are inferred adequate because the same 20–70 mg doses met efficacy endpoints in ADHD and BED through central DAT/NET (NCT00763971, NCT01718483). Plasma d-amphetamine and sympathomimetic effects are documented (PMID:27935735, PMID:28936175), and pulse rose in the index trial. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the mechanism engaged, the lack of antidepressant benefit points to a target that does not drive adjunctive MDD response. F9 is secondary because the index trial was not itself an efficacy test.

In the FTIH study in healthy volunteers (NCT03984812), clearance of GSK3732394 was faster than expected. PK/PD fell below projections: the top dose of 80 mg reached a mean trough CD4 receptor occupancy of only about 25% on Day 7 (PMID:36191080). PK/PD modelling showed that even the maximum planned doses could not reach the desired therapeutic profile, so the study was terminated after SAD cohort 3. Tolerability did not cap the dose; adverse events were mostly mild injection-site reactions. Exposure and engagement were therefore inadequate, and the mechanism (multi-specific HIV entry inhibition, PMID:31375580) was never tested in HIV patients. No pathway or viral-load data exist in humans.

Aliskiren's pillars are well shown in humans before the 2009 index start. It has dose-dependent plasma exposure and suppresses PRA, Ang I and Ang II (up to 89%), with aldosterone falling (PMID:11799102). PRA is suppressed for 24 h at 300 mg in diabetic patients (PMID:17048976; PMID:21659626). At 300 mg it clearly lowers blood pressure in hypertension (NCT00706134, approved use). PMID:26882043 notes maximal renal renin blockade needs more than 300 mg, but systemic RAS suppression was substantial. No engagement data come from CAD patients. In NCT00853827, 300 mg did not significantly slow atheroma progression (PAV p≈0.08). This fits other null aliskiren outcome trials (NCT00549757, NCT00894387, NCT00853658), so renin inhibition does not drive the outcome. The numerical trend suggests limited power (F7).

STARS (NCT02790034) tested 10 and 20 mg/day and missed its primary endpoint, waking apnea reduction (p=0.64 and p=0.20). Newron ended the program without giving a mechanistic reason; it said only that further analyses were pending. The only human evidence is plasma PK in healthy volunteers (PMID:17542349). That does not show the drug reached the brain, and the 5-HT1A target is in the CNS. A ScienceDirect topic snippet says sarizotan was studied with PET ligands in volunteers, but I found no occupancy values. Rat data suggest free brain levels may sit below 5-HT1A affinity (PMID:25796190), but animal data do not count. No other 5-HT1A drug has succeeded in Rett. With no human data on engagement, the failure is indeterminate.

The index phase 2a trial was stopped for futility, with remission at 1/16, 2/16 and 3/16 on drug versus 4/17 on placebo (NCT02895100). The sponsor's publication (PMID:34474038) says a blinded third-party reread of the endoscopy videos showed clinical efficacy and histologic remission. That points to a problem with endpoint assessment (F7). In humans, plasma exposure and blood target engagement rose with dose. However, receptor occupancy in peripheral blood was below 100% at the effective doses, i.e. partial. Gut-tissue engagement and T-cell trafficking effects were shown only in mice, so pathway has no human data. Vedolizumab is approved in UC on the same target, so the target is validated and the molecule may be the problem (F1b). Partial occupancy also supports F1a.

NCT01514864 tested dasatinib 140 mg in NSCLC with DDR2 mutations or inactivating BRAF mutations. It enrolled 19 patients and was stopped for lack of efficacy and slow accrual, and no ORR values were posted. I found no human evidence that dasatinib engaged DDR2 or SRC in lung tumours. The NSCLC trial built to measure tumour target modulation (NCT00858403) stopped after 7 patients without usable data. The phospho-SRC biomarker work (PMID:18301894) is preclinical. Dasatinib's success in CML runs through BCR-ABL in leukaemia cells, a different target and tissue, so engagement here cannot be inferred from it. A review (PMC5952024) points to toxicity, citing the related trial NCT01491633, where grade 3 or worse toxicities and pleural effusions were seen. That makes F6 secondary, with slow accrual (F7) as another factor. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

The index trial NCT00764309 was a single-arm safety study in scleroderma pulmonary fibrosis. All of its primary outcomes were descriptive safety counts (AEs, SAEs, discontinuations, lab toxicity) with no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Exposure at 100 mg is documented in humans (PMID:37679434, PMID:38931339). Engagement is inferred from CML approval and efficacy through ABL1 (NCT01593254), and from reduced SFK phosphorylation in patient platelets (PMID:31683623). No engagement or fibrosis pathway data exist in scleroderma patients. Tolerability was notable: 13/31 discontinued for AEs, including 2 for drug-related pleural effusion. This is listed as secondary F6, although the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping.

The trial registry (NCT02980705) identifies SUNPG1622 as tildrakizumab, an antibody against IL-23 p19, so the recorded 'small molecule' modality looks wrong. I found no human occupancy or biomarker data in axial SpA. However, tildrakizumab is approved for plaque psoriasis (PMID 37162744) at a lower dose (100 mg every 12 weeks, from memory, not the sources) than the 200 mg every 4 weeks used here. So exposure, binding of systemic IL-23 and pathway effects can be inferred as adequate, though this rests on success in skin, not axial tissue. Ankylosing spondylitis is not psoriasis, so engagement was not shown in this disease. Even so, the drug did numerically worse than placebo on ASAS20 (74.0% vs 80.4%), with no subgroup effect. The study was stopped after the week-24 interim analysis. Blocking IL-23 does not appear to drive benefit in AS. The very high placebo response (80%) is a secondary design concern.

In NCT05630937, the trial of the TTK/MPS1 inhibitor stopped at the first futility analysis because none of the 14 evaluable Phase II patients had a response (0 CR, 0 PR; 3 stable disease, 11 progressive disease). In Phase I, the MTD was set at 100 mg/m2 per week because of neutropenia and thrombocytopenia dose-limiting toxicities at 135 mg/m2. The sources I found give no human data on drug exposure (pharmacokinetics), MPS1 inhibition, or a pathway marker such as spindle checkpoint override or aneuploidy in tumour. They report only clinical activity (2 partial responses in Phase I) and AFP decreases. Neutropenia fits an antimitotic effect but is not a target-engagement measure. Nothing shows engagement was adequate or inadequate. No other TTK drug has succeeded in HCC. So the failure is indeterminate (U).

Index trial NCT05954143 enrolled 11 patients and saw 0 responders in both arms (n=4 each evaluable) before it was terminated by sponsor decision. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, HER2 engagement or pathway data for BDC-1001. The first-in-human trial NCT04278144 posted no results and no abstracts are provided. HER2 is clearly a validated driver in breast cancer: trastuzumab, pertuzumab, T-DM1, T-DXd, margetuximab, lapatinib, neratinib and tucatinib are all approved. So the target matters, and with no evidence that this molecule engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule (F1b). The trial was tiny and stopped early for an unstated sponsor reason, so it was underpowered (F7). Evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

Posaconazole acts on T. cruzi CYP51 (PMID:27977118). Human plasma exposure is documented (NCT01777763), and absorption was checked in the CHAGASAZOL trial (PMID:24827034, NCT01162967). Target engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred from a functional effect in Chagas patients: almost all became T. cruzi PCR-negative on treatment beyond day 14. Most relapsed afterwards (80-92% PCR-positive vs 38% on benznidazole). The index trial similarly showed 15.6% vs 10% placebo PCR response, against 86.7% for benznidazole. The drug suppressed the parasite but did not eradicate it. CYP51 inhibition therefore appears insufficient for sterile cure (PMID:32557280 calls the trials unsuccessful). Duration and follow-up questions (PMID:28683978) are a secondary consideration. The CHAGASAZOL results were published after the index trial started.

The index trial NCT04893551 was a Phase 1b dose-escalation study. Its primary endpoints were safety and PK, and efficacy was only exploratory. It ended by sponsor decision after all planned dose levels were completed, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. PMID:40696160 reports dose-proportional PK with steady state by the second dose. Pharmacodynamic data in PROC patients showed reduced tumour AXL protein and fibrosis-related gene signatures, with EMT reversal in 2 patients. These data were published after the index trial started. Tolerability was good, with no drug-related grade 3 or higher events, so the dose was not limited. There were no objective responses; the authors suggest testing AXL inhibition in other indications. This hints at F2, but that is secondary.

In the index trial (NCT03225846), Huntington's patients on WVE-120102 showed no statistically significant drop in CSF mutant HTT versus placebo at doses up to 32 mg monthly. Patients given 32 mg had a median reduction of 9.9% (p=0.74). An earlier interim analysis had reported a 12.4% reduction, which is modest. Wave said CSF drug levels correlated with mHTT lowering, but its PK modelling showed further dose escalation was unlikely to reach the levels needed for robust knockdown. Its former CMO said not enough drug reached the target. The 32 mg dose was also poorly tolerated: 9/13 patients had serious TEAEs and 6/13 withdrew. So the drug did not reach or engage its target well enough, and the mechanism was never properly tested.

REX-001 is an autologous bone marrow mononuclear cell product with no recorded molecular target. Neither the bundle nor my search turned up any human evidence of cell delivery, engraftment, a paracrine or angiogenic biomarker response, or perfusion change. The only mechanistic data come from mice (PMID:33363160), and animal data don't count. In SALAMANDER (NCT03174522), the IDMC stopped the trial for futility: response was 28.6% with REX-001 vs 27.3% with placebo, and secondary endpoint data were not available (PMID:42119725). The investigators point to trial design, endpoint selection and funding problems, so F7 is a secondary code. Without any engagement or pathway evidence, a product that never acted can't be told apart from a mechanism that doesn't work in CLTI, so the code is U.

The only trial in the bundle is a Phase 1 single- and multiple-ascending-dose study in healthy volunteers (NCT04323124). It tested doses up to 4000 mg and several formulations, with and without polymer. The sponsor terminated it because it 'did not demonstrate sufficient pharmacological effect' and said the stop was not safety-related. The posted results show no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. This sponsor statement is the only human evidence on pharmacology. It indicates that target engagement or pharmacodynamic effect was inadequate, so the mechanism was never properly tested. No PK, target, disease-population or pathway data appear in the bundle, and no other drugs, trials or abstracts are given. Confidence is medium because the sponsor states the reason but gives no detail.

KITE-585, an anti-BCMA CAR-T, was stopped for lack of efficacy (NCT03318861). It produced only 1 partial response among 14 infused patients and had no DLTs across doses from 3×10^7 to 1×10^9 cells, so tolerability did not cap the dose. CAR-T blood levels were measured (PMID:34249462), but the abstract is truncated before any expansion data, so exposure and engagement are not shown. Mild, infrequent CRS (21%, grade 1–2 only) hints at weak activity but is not direct evidence. Other BCMA-directed drugs succeeded in the same disease: idecabtagene vicleucel, teclistamab and belantamab are FDA-approved. That points to this molecule rather than the target. F1b is primary. F1a (likely poor expansion) is plausible but not shown in the bundle.

In the index Phase 1 trial (NCT03770494), LY3405105 showed sustained plasma exposure with QD dosing (t½ 15–19 h). CDK7 target occupancy in skin and peripheral blood of patients with advanced solid tumors was dose-dependent and reached near-maximal occupancy (~75%) at ≥15 mg QD (PMID:37531083). That level sits below the 20 mg QD MTD, so tolerability did not cap engagement. Despite this, there were no CR/PR responses, only stable disease, and development stopped for lack of efficacy. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Engagement was measured in surrogate tissues, not tumor, and plateaued at only ~75%. So inadequate tumor engagement (F1a) remains a possibility. Engagement data were published after the trial started.

In the index Phase 1 trial (NCT03770494, PMID:37531083), LY3405105 showed sustained plasma exposure with QD dosing (half-life 15-19 h). CDK7 occupancy in skin and peripheral blood was dose-dependent and reached a near-maximal plateau of ~75% at >=15 mg QD, below the 20 mg QD MTD. The dose was therefore not capped below engagement. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Despite this engagement in cancer patients, there were no objective responses, only stable disease, and the sponsor stopped for insufficient efficacy. This points to CDK7 inhibition as monotherapy not driving tumor response in this unselected solid-tumor population. Confidence is medium: occupancy was measured in surrogate tissues, not tumor, and was ~75% rather than complete.

NCT02666846 is a small Phase 1 UVB pain-model study in healthy volunteers comparing several topical NSAID formulations. SPR300 is presumed to contain methyl salicylate, though the bundle does not confirm this. It gave numerically higher heat-pain tolerance (0.39 vs -0.01 °C) and less erythema (12 vs 67 flux units) than placebo. No failure or stop reason is stated. The drug is already FDA-approved topically for knee osteoarthritis and injury, so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Human percutaneous absorption is documented (PMID:3780827), and further Phase 3 topical trials continued (NCT00970658, NCT07475663). This was a formulation and pain-model study, not a failed efficacy readout that ended a program. Its small cohorts (n=8–20) also limit any interpretation.

Fesoterodine is approved for overactive bladder (2008). It met efficacy endpoints there through M2/M3 antagonism in the lower urinary tract at the same 4 and 8 mg doses (NCT00611026, dose-response in PMID:20723260). It also increased cystometric capacity in pediatric neurogenic bladder (NCT01557244). Exposure, engagement and the detrusor pathway are therefore inferred adequate, and plasma exposure is dose-proportional (PMID:19000553). The index trial in stress urinary incontinence (NCT01042236) used those doses in a crossover design, and opening urethral pressure did not change versus placebo (p=0.49 and p=0.59, with tight confidence intervals). Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the mechanism engaged, the null result indicates that muscarinic antagonism does not raise urethral closure pressure. Engagement was not measured in this disease itself, so confidence is medium.

drug: human natural killer cell line nk-92
rationale: The index trial, NCT00900809, was a 7-patient Phase 1 safety and maximum-tolerated-dose study of NK-92, a natural killer cell line with no defined molecular target. A 2017 report (Boyiadzis et al., Cytotherapy) describes it as giving responses in some patients without severe toxicity. That report was only seen as cited in later review pages. None of the sources show human evidence that the cells persisted, homed to the leukemia or killed AML cells in vivo. A follow-up publication found that exosomes from the patients' AML cells suppressed NK-92 killing in the lab. That is a possible reason for weak activity, but it is not human engagement evidence. Because the trial was a safety study and not a test of efficacy, F9 is listed as a secondary code. Neither the sponsor nor the investigators gave a reason for stopping.

The index first-in-human trial NCT02335814 in relapsed/refractory AML was terminated after dose escalation by sponsor decision, with no posted results. The bundle contains no human PK, target engagement (e.g., pSTAT5 or pRB inhibition) or pathway data. Only preclinical xenograft PD is available (PMID:24526162, PMID:25487917), and animal data do not count. Other FLT3 inhibitors (gilteritinib, midostaurin, quizartinib) are FDA-approved in AML, so FLT3 is a validated target in this disease. With no evidence that FLX925 engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Because no efficacy readout or stated reason is shown, a business decision cannot be excluded and the case remains largely indeterminate (U).

ATA188 is an allogeneic EBV-specific T-cell therapy. Its Phase 2 part of EMBOLD (NCT03283826) missed its primary endpoint of confirmed disability improvement: 6% on ATA188 versus a 16% placebo rate. It also failed to move fluid and imaging biomarkers. Atara said no treatment benefit was observed and stopped the study, while still believing EBV plays a role in MS. The sources I found give no human data on how long the infused cells lasted in the body, on clearance of EBV-infected B cells, or on any proximal pathway marker. Because of that, I can't tell whether the cells never engaged their target or whether targeting EBV doesn't help this disease, so the code is U. F2 is listed as a secondary code because the sponsor did not suggest any delivery or dose problem.

ATA188 is an allogeneic T-cell therapy against EBV. In EMBOLD (NCT03283826), the primary endpoint of confirmed disability improvement was missed: 6% improved on ATA188 versus 16% on placebo. Reports also say the drug had no effect on fluid or imaging biomarkers, so the pathway pillar is marked inadequate. None of the sources gave human data on whether the cells persisted or killed their targets, meaning the EBV-infected B cells (no persistence, no depletion of infected cells). So the bundle cannot tell a therapy that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not drive progressive MS. That makes the code U. Atara pointed to a placebo improvement rate far above expectations (16% versus an expected 4–6%), so F7 is a secondary code.

disease: metastatic malignant neoplasm in the brain
rationale: In the index trial NCT00820222, CNS metastasis as first relapse was 8 vs 12 events (OR 0.65, p=0.36). Lapatinib's breast cancer approval supports systemic engagement, but not engagement in the CNS compartment. The bundle has no usable human brain-metastasis evidence: PMID:24667724 (CSF levels in 2 patients) is title-only, and NCT00863122 measured extra-axial schwannoma tissue levels. No target engagement or pathway readout was shown in brain metastases. Tucatinib, which also targets ERBB2, is FDA-approved for brain metastases. That points to the molecule (likely CNS penetration) rather than the target, so F1b applies. With only 20 events in about 500 patients, the trial was likely underpowered (F7). Engagement in the brain is unmeasured, so U also applies.

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of the ATR inhibitor ATG-018 (NCT05338346, n=22, advanced solid tumors and hematological malignancies) was terminated for 'lack of efficacy of study compound'. It posted no results. The bundle has no other trials, no PK, target-engagement or pathway biomarker data (e.g., pChk1 or γH2AX), no PubMed abstracts and no comparator ATR inhibitors. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage ATR from a target that does not drive these unselected tumors. Tolerability limits are not shown either. The failure is therefore indeterminate.

NCT05338346, a first-in-human dose-escalation trial of the ATR inhibitor ATG-018 in all-comer solid tumours and blood cancers, was terminated for 'lack of efficacy of study compound'. No results were posted. Antengene's 2023 interim update gave only stable disease in 7 of 12 evaluable patients at low dose levels. It reported no human PK, ATR target-inhibition or pharmacodynamic biomarker data. The PD-biomarker work presented at SITC 2022 was preclinical, done ex vivo on human blood cells. No other drug on the same target is in the bundle, and the sponsor gave no further explanation. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the code is U.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT03379584 of the CD48-directed ADC SGN-CD48A in multiple myeloma was terminated after 14 patients 'due to overall benefit/risk profile'. It posted no results, and the bundle contains no other trials, no Phase 1 pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic data, no PubMed abstracts and no same-target comparators. There is no human evidence on exposure, CD48 engagement or downstream depletion. The stop reason could reflect toxicity (possible F6, which would fit an ADC payload) or a lack of activity, but the bundle does not separate these. Because engagement has no human data, the failure is indeterminate (U).

In the first-in-human trial (NCT03449030; PMID:36738333), plasma exposure rose with dose from 0.032 to 0.25 mg/kg. Dose-limiting toxicities after cycle 2 at 0.19 and 0.25 mg/kg (grade 4–5 hepatic failure, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia) set the RP2D at 0.064 mg/kg. That is far below the 0.76 mg/kg active dose in xenografts (PMID:32788205). The authors state the RP2D 'was considered insufficient to derive clinical benefit,' and the stop reason cites insufficient benefit at the RP2D. No human tumor uptake, target engagement or payload pharmacodynamic data were reported. Tolerability capped the dose below the level needed, so the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). Hepatic toxicity, likely payload-related, contributes (F6).

In the first-in-human trial, plasma exposure rose with dose (0.032–0.25 mg/kg), but no target engagement or tumor pharmacodynamic data were reported in humans (PMID:36738333). Dose-limiting toxicities appeared after cycle 2 at 0.19–0.25 mg/kg, including fatal and grade 4 hepatic failure and severe cytopenias. These capped the RP2D at 0.064 mg/kg, about tenfold below the 0.76 mg/kg dose active in preclinical xenografts (PMID:32788205). The authors and the registry state the RP2D was insufficient to derive clinical benefit, and development stopped (NCT03449030). The mechanism was therefore not tested at an adequate dose: F1a, dose_limited. Molecule-specific toxicity from the payload (hepatic failure) drove the dose cap, so F6 is secondary.

In the index first-in-human trial (NCT05397171), AZD8853 was tested in MSS colorectal cancer and urothelial carcinoma. It showed linear pharmacokinetics with a 5–10 day half-life, so plasma exposure was achieved. Target engagement fell short: suppression of free serum GDF15 was transient and not sustained at doses up to 3000 mg every 3 weeks. Downstream effects were absent, with no ctDNA clearance, no dose-dependent peripheral T-cell changes and no body-weight trend (PMID:40354065). There were no DLTs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No objective responses were seen, and the trial stopped after dose escalation on risk-benefit grounds. Because target neutralization was not sustained, the GDF15 mechanism was not properly tested, which supports F1a.

In the index trial NCT05397171, AZD8853 showed linear PK with a half-life of 5–10 days, so exposure was adequate (PMID:40354065). Engagement was inadequate: suppression of free serum GDF15 was only transient and not sustained, even at 3000 mg Q3W. Engagement was measured in the patients themselves (mostly MSS colorectal cancer), but only within the index trial. Pathway effects were absent: no dose-dependent change in peripheral T cells, no ctDNA clearance, and no body-weight trend. There were no DLTs and no treatment-related SAEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. With no objective responses and target suppression not sustained, the mechanism was never properly tested, and the study ended after dose escalation.

Exposure: plasma levels were therapeutically monitored, and myocardial uptake correlated with plasma levels (PMID:24117487, PMID:28692346). CPT1B inhibition was never measured directly. Engagement is inferred_adequate because a 2010 placebo-controlled RCT in symptomatic nonobstructive HCM at 100 mg improved myocardial PCr/ATP (adequate pathway), diastolic filling and peak VO2 (PMID:20921440). That trial was in the same disease and preceded the index start. The open-label index trial (NCT02862600) in HCM with moderate-to-severe heart failure showed no VO2max change at 16 weeks (-0.2 ml/kg/min, n=15 of 35) and stopped for lack of efficacy. This fits F2. A different, sicker population (F3) and the small, uncontrolled, terminated design (F7) may also explain it. The sources state no reason, so confidence is low.

The index TEAM trial (NCT01028222) was not an efficacy failure. The posted counts show only ORR 11/42 vs 3/13 with no comparison, but the final publication (PMID:28327988) reports ORR 26.2% (95% CI 13.9–42.0%), enough to reject the null of ORR ≤10%, so the primary endpoint was met. The DTIC comparator arm was dropped because few KIT-mutated melanomas were found. Responses clustered in exon 11 and L576P mutations, pointing to subgroup-confined benefit. No target-engagement data exist in melanoma. The pillars are inferred adequate because the same 400 mg twice-daily regimen met efficacy endpoints through ABL1 in CML (NCT01275196, NCT01254188). Tolerability did not cap the dose.

AUTO2, an APRIL-based CAR T targeting BCMA and TACI, was terminated in the index trial NCT03287804 because preliminary efficacy was judged insufficient: 4/11 infused patients responded. No DLTs occurred, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The bundle has no human data on CAR T expansion or persistence, BCMA/TACI target engagement, or downstream biomarkers. Other BCMA-directed agents, including idecabtagene vicleucel (a CAR T), teclistamab and belantamab mafodotin, are FDA-approved in plasma cell myeloma. This points to the molecule (the APRIL-ligand binder design) rather than the target, with no pillar evidence that AUTO2 engaged adequately. U is secondary because engagement was never measured.

The HARMONY Phase 1 trial (NCT05153408) of BLU-701 in EGFR-mutant NSCLC was terminated for lack of efficacy after enrolling 20 patients. No results were posted, and the bundle contains no other trials, no Phase 1 PK/PD results and no abstracts. So exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human data. EGFR as a target clearly drives EGFR-mutant NSCLC: osimertinib, lazertinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib and dacomitinib are approved for this disease. That points to a molecule-specific failure (F1b) rather than an invalid target. The caveat is that BLU-701 was aimed at C797S resistance mutations, a subtype where no comparator is shown to succeed. U therefore remains a plausible alternative. Evidence is thin.

Index trial NCT04882176 is a Phase 1/2 study of LM-061 in advanced tumours. It enrolled 18 participants, had safety, DLT and MTD primary endpoints, and was terminated for 'not meeting expected endpoints'. The companion Phase 1 trial NCT04737122 was also terminated for failure to achieve expected outcomes. Neither trial posted results. The bundle records no target, no pharmacokinetic, occupancy or biomarker data, no PubMed abstracts, and no other drugs on the same target. With engagement having no human data, nothing separates a molecule that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter. The failure is therefore indeterminate (U), with low confidence given how thin the bundle is.

LM-061 is an oral HPK1 (MAP4K1) inhibitor. Two small early-phase trials in advanced tumours were terminated early. The index trial NCT04882176 (n=18) gave the reason as not meeting expected endpoints, and NCT04737122 gave failure to achieve expected outcomes. Neither posted results. My searches found no human PK, target-engagement data (such as pSLP76 inhibition) or downstream biomarker data for LM-061. The only extra detail was a trial-tracker note that enrollment was cut and the trial terminated. No other HPK1 drug has succeeded in this setting, so F1b does not apply. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the drug failed to engage HPK1 or whether the target does not matter, so the cause is indeterminate.

Ambrisentan, a systemic oral ETA antagonist, has measured human plasma exposure (PMID:18832294, PMID:19552747). It met efficacy endpoints in PAH at 5-10 mg (PMID:16053970, NCT01178073; FDA-approved), with haemodynamic effects in the lung. ETA engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate at comparable doses, though not measured in IPF tissue. ARTEMIS-IPF (NCT00768300) was stopped for lack of efficacy, and outcomes were worse on drug (HR 1.74 for death or progression; more SAEs). The bundle shows no tolerability cap on dose. Bosentan and macitentan also failed in IPF (PMID:29341047), pointing to the target, not the molecule. ETA antagonism does not drive IPF progression. Harm suggests possible on-target detriment (F5).

The index trial NCT05694741 was a first-in-human single ascending dose study (5–150 mg) in healthy participants, with a safety primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. PMID:41015846 reports good tolerability (nausea only at 150 mg, a GLP-1RA class effect) and roughly dose-proportional plasma AUC with a short half-life (1.95–7.58 h). Systemic exposure was therefore shown. No human receptor engagement or glycaemic or insulin biomarker data are given; the nausea is suggestive but was not measured as engagement. The sponsor stopped because the overall profile lacked differentiation versus current standard of care. That is a competitive/portfolio decision, not a failed efficacy readout. Hence F8, with F9 also applying.

The index trial NCT05694741 was a first-in-human single ascending dose safety/PK study (5–150 mg) in healthy participants, with adverse events as the primary endpoint. It was not an efficacy test. PMID:41015846 reports good tolerability (nausea at 150 mg, a GLP-1RA class effect) and approximately dose-proportional plasma exposure with a half-life of 1.95–7.58 h. No human receptor engagement or glucose/insulin pathway biomarker data are shown. Termination was attributed to insufficient differentiation versus the current standard of care, a strategic or competitive judgment rather than a failed efficacy readout. Hence F9 is the primary code, with a commercial component (F8). The bundle does not show which data drove the differentiation judgment.

Phase 1 in healthy men (PMID:32946574, 2020, before the index start) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and a dose-dependent, reversible LH and testosterone reduction of about 70%, near maximal at 15 mg. The authors call this proof of central NK3R antagonism, so exposure, engagement (functional) and pathway are rated adequate. This was not shown in postmenopausal women with VMS. The index trial NCT04278872 enrolled only 13 patients and stopped because no safe and efficacious dose was identified. Its primary endpoint is not assessable, and no serious AEs were reported. With engagement shown, F2 fits the rules best. However, the tiny terminated trial could not really answer the question (F7), and the index doses are not reported in the bundle, so confidence is low.

In a single ascending dose Phase 1 in healthy men (PMID:32946574, published before the index trial started in Nov 2020), SJX-653 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure. It produced a dose-dependent, reversible reduction of LH (up to 70%) and testosterone, near-maximal from 15 mg. The authors call this proof of central NK3R antagonism, so engagement and pathway are treated as adequate. That evidence comes from healthy men, not postmenopausal women with vasomotor symptoms. The index trial (NCT04278872) enrolled only 13 patients, the primary endpoint was not assessable, and it was terminated because no safe, efficacious dose was identified. No serious adverse events occurred. This points to lack of benefit despite engagement (F2). The tiny, truncated trial leaves the answer uncertain (F7). The bundle is thin.

Temsirolimus engaged mTOR in humans before the index trial. PBMC p70S6K inhibition at 25–250 mg in RCC patients (PMID:12912932) and pS6 inhibition in paired tumour biopsies at 25 mg weekly (PMID:17031397) show this. Dose-dependent pathway inhibition was also seen in other studies (PMID:21690471, PMID:35112552). RCC approval supports adequacy. None of this engagement evidence comes from NSCLC. In the combination phase 1 (NCT00838539), the temsirolimus MTD was 50 mg, above the approved 25 mg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In HER2-mutant NSCLC, adding temsirolimus to neratinib gave only modest responses (6/43 vs 0/17). There was no prespecified comparison, and the primary endpoint is not assessable. Mechanism engaged with limited benefit suggests F2. Because the readout was not clearly negative, F9 is possible. Confidence is low.

Index Phase 1/2 trial NCT02606123 was terminated at the end of Phase 1 because of an excessive pill burden (18 capsules/day). PMID:34843005 states the study stopped before reaching the MTD because of poor oral bioavailability. PMID:32259077 attributes termination to poor pharmacokinetics and reports glucuronidation that reduces potency. Exposure was therefore inadequate. No direct human engagement data on the AR N-terminal domain are shown. Pathway evidence was weak: six patients had PSA declines, none meeting response criteria. The mechanism was not properly tested, so the code is F1a. Other AR inhibitors (enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide) are approved in prostate cancer, but they bind the ligand-binding domain rather than the NTD, so F1b is secondary.

The index Phase 1/2 trial (NCT02606123) was terminated at the end of Phase 1 because of an excessive pill burden of 18 capsules/day. This is a formulation or PK problem specific to the molecule. Part II, the PSA efficacy readout, was never run, and no PK, engagement or biomarker results were posted, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The AR target is clinically validated in prostate cancer: enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide, bicalutamide and flutamide are all approved. Nothing shows ralaniten engaged AR adequately. The failure therefore points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Secondary codes: F1a, since the pill burden implies adequate exposure was impractical, and F9, since the drug never received an efficacy test.

In NCT04847141, subcutaneous C19-IG20% at 1 g or 2 g did not stop asymptomatic infected people from developing symptoms, and the DSMB ended the trial early for futility. The published paper reports no serum antibody levels after dosing, so exposure has no human data. The doses held only 200–400 mg of polyclonal IgG. Investigators noted that casirivimab/imdevimab delivers 1.2 g of specific antibody. Dose was capped by the 10 mL volume that can be tolerated subcutaneously. Nasopharyngeal viral load did not change versus placebo, unlike with the monoclonals. Plasma collected before the variants neutralized alpha and delta 2–3-fold less well. The investigators blame insufficient dose and neutralizing capacity, so the mechanism was probably not adequately tested. Engagement was never measured directly, which leaves this close to U.

Dicerna's 2016 release says paired tumor biopsies from the DCR-MYC-101 solid-tumor trial (NCT02110563) showed the drug reached tumors and destroyed MYC mRNA through RNAi in every patient tested. The level of MYC knockdown, however, was below what the company targeted. That shows delivery to the tumor, but engagement was not enough. In the HCC trial (NCT02314052), doses up to 0.85 mg/kg were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by tolerability, and no mRECIST responses were seen. The engagement data came from other tumor types, not HCC, and were reported in 2016, after the index trial began in January 2015. No downstream pathway marker was reported. Because MYC was never adequately knocked down, the mechanism was not properly tested. The company was also shifting resources to its GalXC platform, so business reasons played a part (F8 secondary).

The index trial NCT00914277 was a small single-dose Phase 2 study in 24 men, measuring how long penile rigidity lasted. It finished, but no results were posted and the sources give no reason for stopping. My searches found only animal data and tests on strips of human penile tissue in the lab (PMID:22444253), which do not count as human evidence. No human data were found on plasma or tissue drug levels, ROCK inhibition, or downstream markers such as MYPT phosphorylation. No other ROCK inhibitor has an erectile dysfunction result to compare against. The later angina trial (NCT03236311) was stopped for slow recruitment and could not be assessed. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the first-in-human trial (NCT01417546, PMID:30131389), NHS-IL12 was given to patients with solid tumors including malignant mesenchymal tumors, with PK measured up to the 16.8 µg/kg MTD. IL-12 receptor agonism was shown functionally: a time-dependent rise in IFNγ, NK/NKT activation and increased tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, with dose-dependent immune activation (PMID:37234190). This evidence was published after the index trial started in 2017. In the index trial (NCT02994953, PMID:37236636), the MTD was not reached and the 16.8 µg/kg recommended dose was given with avelumab, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, there were 0/16 responses in the expansion cohort and pre-specified futility was met. The mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, so F2. The small single-arm two-stage design adds F7.

Plasma exposure was characterized in cancer patients (PMID:24727324, PMID:28643374). Peripheral pathway effects were clear, with dose-dependent CD34+ mobilization up to 18-fold (PMID:24727324, PMID:29212254). The only direct receptor-occupancy data come from AML at 10–20 mg (PMID:30319961). There, only 4 of 9 patients showed a ≥50% fall in CXCR4 signal, which the authors called incomplete blockade, and they planned 30 mg to reach full occupancy. The phase 1 MTD was capped at 20 mg by grade 3 neutrophilia at 30 mg (PMID:24727324), although 40 mg was later tolerated with durvalumab (PMID:32219196). No engagement data exist in RCC tumors, and none predate the index trial. The RCC PFS failure (NCT01391130) therefore likely reflects an inadequately tested mechanism. The evidence is indirect.

Plasma exposure in cancer patients was characterized, and the dose-dependent CD34+ mobilization (up to 18-fold) shows the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis was blocked systemically, peaking at about 20 mg/day (PMID:24727324, PMID:28643374, PMID:29212254). The phase 1 MTD was capped at 20 mg/day by grade 3 neutrophil increases. The only direct receptor-occupancy data, from AML published after the index trial started, showed incomplete CXCR4 occupancy at 10–20 mg, prompting escalation to 30 mg (PMID:30319961). 40 mg was later tolerated with durvalumab (PMID:32219196). No engagement was shown in SCLC tumors. The index PFS HR was 1.06 (NCT01439568). This suggests inadequate engagement, but the robust pathway effect leaves target irrelevance (F2) plausible.

drug: autologous endothelial progenitor cells transfected with human eNOS
rationale: Index trial NCT03001414 was terminated for low enrollment after 12 evaluable patients. Its 6MWD primary endpoint was not met (difference 13.7 m, p=0.42, wide CI). The bundle contains no human data on cell engraftment, eNOS expression or NO pathway biomarkers. The phase 1 trial NCT00469027 posted no results, the AMI trial NCT00936819 has no outcome, there are no PubMed abstracts, and no other drug acts through this mechanism. Engagement is therefore no_human_data, and nothing separates a therapy that never delivered its mechanism from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The tiny, underpowered, prematurely stopped trial also fits F7 (trial design or execution) as a secondary explanation.

In the first-in-human study (NCT02659631, PMID:35493516), patients reached measurable plasma exposure, with cytokine peaks and CRS correlating with Cmax. That shows systemic CD3-driven T-cell activation but no tumor P-cadherin engagement or T-cell killing in humans. Cytokine release syndrome was the dose-limiting toxicity at 400 ng/kg IV, so escalation stopped there and SC and IV-prime schedules were tried instead. The study was terminated for limited antitumor activity. Tolerability, through an on-target CRS mechanism, capped the dose before any tumor-level engagement was shown. The QSP model's efficacious trimer concentration was never confirmed in patients (PMID:31119428), and only mouse data support the mechanism (PMID:29067496). The mechanism was therefore likely not adequately tested. Evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

The index Phase 1/2a trial NCT03094169 was terminated for lack of efficacy. In the Phase 2a expansion at 220 mg/m^2, 23 of 24 patients had progressive disease and 1 had a complete response. Dose escalation found DLTs in 2/7 patients at 270 mg/m^2, so 220 mg/m^2 was carried forward. The bundle does not show that this tolerability ceiling sat below the level needed for engagement. The bundle holds no human PK, EGFR engagement or pathway biomarker data. It has no other trials of this drug, no Phase 1 results and no comparator EGFR drugs. Nothing therefore separates an ADC that failed to engage or deliver its payload from a target or mechanism that does not drive these tumours, so the failure is indeterminate.

In the index trial NCT03094169, AVID100 (an anti-EGFR antibody conjugated to the toxin DM1) failed in the Phase 2a expansion: 23 of 24 patients had progressive disease and 1 had a complete response. The trial was terminated for lack of efficacy. The Phase 1a data in the AACR 2019 abstract report plasma exposure at the recommended Phase 2 dose (220 mg/m2) that was above the levels predicted from preclinical work and comparable to cetuximab and T-DM1, so exposure counts as adequate. That dose was set because 270 mg/m2 exceeded the maximum tolerated dose. Since 220 mg/m2 already gave the predicted exposure, tolerability did not cap the dose. None of the sources report human evidence of EGFR engagement, payload delivery to tumours, or a downstream biomarker. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage its target from a mechanism that does not work here, so the code is indeterminate (U).

Phase 1 in advanced solid tumors (NCT01946074, PMID:34315767) showed measurable PK and biomarker evidence of binding to both VEGF and DLL4. The RP2D was set on tolerability, with hypertension and GI perforation (including a death) consistent with the anti-angiogenic mechanism. This evidence was published in 2021, after the index trial started, and came from mixed solid tumors rather than mCRC. In the index trial (NCT03368859, PMID:35920133), dilpacimab+FOLFIRI did worse than bevacizumab+FOLFIRI: PFS 3.78 vs 7.36 months, HR 3.57; more deaths (12/34 vs 6/32) and serious AEs; a fatal intestinal perforation. The authors conclude it was not well tolerated and gave no benefit. Mechanism-type toxicity plus added DLL4 blockade offset efficacy (F5). Lack of benefit despite engagement also supports F2.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT05486208 was terminated for lack of an efficacy signal in atopic dermatitis participants. Its only posted outcome is descriptive safety: TEAEs with no SAEs or deaths up to 1000 mg IV, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no target recorded and no PK, target engagement or pathway biomarker data. It also has no other trials, no same-target comparators and no publications. Nothing separates a molecule that failed to engage from a target irrelevant to atopic dermatitis, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

Synapse lists LY3844583 as an anti-GITR antibody (described as an inhibitor) from Lilly. The index Phase 1 trial NCT05486208 (SAD/MAD in healthy volunteers, then Part C at 1000 mg IV Q2W in atopic dermatitis) was stopped for lack of an efficacy signal in AD. Its posted results cover only safety: no SAEs, and the AE rate was similar to placebo, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The searches found no human PK, receptor occupancy, Treg/GITR engagement or downstream biomarker data. They also found no other GITR drug that worked in AD. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a target that does not drive AD. Code: U.

The index trial NCT03119077 was a first-in-human single ascending dose study measuring safety and PK (AUC, Cmax) in the context of polycystic ovary syndrome. It was terminated early with the stated reason 'lower drug exposure'. Human plasma exposure was therefore shown to be insufficient, so the mechanism was never properly tested. That points to F1a. The bundle has no target, engagement, or pathway data, and no other trials or publications. Because this was not an efficacy readout of the drug, F9 also applies as a secondary code. Confidence is medium: the stop reason is explicit, but the bundle is otherwise very thin.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: In the first-in-human study (PMID:33245172; NCT01159522), the drug showed linear plasma pharmacokinetics up to an MTD of 24 mg/m2. The index trial used 12–24 mg/m2, so plasma exposure counts as adequate. Neither the bundle nor the search turned up any human data on target engagement (TRAP1 inhibition, or tubulin/vascular disruption, which is how the abstract describes SCB01A) or on a downstream biomarker. The index trial (NCT03020823) treated only 10 patients, none responded, and the sponsor withdrew it without giving a scientific reason. The earlier head and neck trial (NCT02488629) also ended early. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The tiny trial size means F7 is a possible secondary explanation.

NCT04875806 (Phase 1/2 dose escalation of NC762, 0.5–20 mg/kg) was terminated for 'limited activity in Phase 1', and the sponsor prioritized a B7-H4 ADC program instead. The bundle contains no pharmacokinetic, receptor occupancy, B7-H4 engagement or downstream immune biomarker data. It reports no other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target drugs. The posted adverse events (deaths largely attributable to advanced cancer) do not show that tolerability capped the dose, since escalation reached 20 mg/kg. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot distinguish a molecule that failed to engage from a B7-H4 blockade mechanism that lacks antitumor activity, so the code is U. Portfolio reprioritization (F8) contributed to the stop, but the stated driver was limited activity.

NCT04875806 escalated NC762 to 20 mg/kg every two weeks with no dose-limiting toxicities, so tolerability did not cap the dose. It was stopped for 'limited activity' and because the sponsor chose to prioritize a B7-H4 ADC. The protocol planned to measure PK and tumor B7-H4 downregulation, but I found no published human exposure, occupancy or B7-H4 engagement data. The SITC 2022 release reports only nonspecific NK/myeloid cell shifts and cytokine increases. These are not mechanism-specific evidence of target engagement. No other anti-B7-H4 drug in the bundle succeeded. Without human engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The strategic switch to the ADC adds partial F8.

Icatibant 30 mg SC gives robust plasma exposure in humans (PMID:27128215). The same 30 mg dose met its primary endpoint in hereditary angioedema (NCT00912093; FDA approval 2011). HAE is bradykinin/B2-mediated subcutaneous and submucosal swelling, the same target and tissue compartment as ACE-inhibitor angioedema, so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Human studies also show icatibant blocks B2-mediated vascular effects (PMID:9054837, PMID:8846415). No direct engagement was measured in ACEi-angioedema patients. The index trial in this population (NCT01919801) showed no effect on time to discharge criteria (median 4.03 vs 4.00 days, p=0.633). Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the mechanism engaged at an effective dose, B2 antagonism did not drive clinical resolution of RAAS-blocker angioedema as tested.

In Part A of the index Phase 2a/b trial (NCT04417036), inhaled PEG-ADM was well tolerated, but neither dose (960 or 1920 μg) gave any meaningful benefit. Ventilator-free survival at day 28 was 52% and 67%, against 65% on placebo. Bayer then dropped Part B and stated the decision was not about safety. The only human pharmacology I found is unpublished Phase 1 data ('data on file'): a longer half-life and blood-pressure lowering after IV dosing. The inhaled form was designed to avoid that blood-pressure effect. I found no human data on drug levels in the lung, CALCRL/RAMP receptor activation, or endothelial barrier biomarkers with the inhaled form in ARDS. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in ARDS, so the code is U.

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation trial NCT04430348 (six dose levels, 22 patients with advanced solid tumors) was terminated for 'absence of immunological response'. That is a downstream pharmacodynamic readout failing to move, so pathway is rated inadequate. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, receptor-binding or occupancy data for TNFRSF25. The posted results show adverse events in nearly all patients and many deaths, but nothing shows the dose was capped by tolerability. There are no other trials, no other drugs on this target and no publications. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot separate an antibody that failed to agonize TNFRSF25 adequately (F1a) from a target whose agonism does not produce the expected immune response. The code is therefore indeterminate (U).

NCT04430348 was a first-in-human dose-escalation trial of the TNFRSF25 agonist antibody PTX-35. It ran six dose levels in 22 patients and stopped because of 'absence of immunological response'. The protocol planned to measure the drug's PK and its effect on NK, CD4 and CD8 T-cell expansion, but no human PK, receptor-occupancy or binding data were published. The stop reason indicates the downstream immune pathway did not move, so pathway is inadequate. Without engagement data, it is unclear whether the antibody failed to agonize TNFRSF25 in patients (a molecule problem, F1a) or whether TNFRSF25 costimulation simply does not drive anti-tumor immunity. No dose limit from tolerability was reported. The program is now listed as discontinued. Code U, with F1a possible.

The sponsor's stop reason for the index trial NCT04931862 reports robust, sustained reductions in poly(GP) in C9orf72 ALS/FTD patients. Poly(GP) is the dipeptide-repeat product of the targeted repeat-containing transcripts, and its lowering supports CNS exposure, target knockdown and the expected pathway effect in this disease. Despite this, there was no clinical benefit at 24 weeks, and poly(GP) lowering did not track with functional stabilization. The mechanism was therefore tested and did not translate clinically (F2). The engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself; earlier data were preclinical only (PMID:35592494). No toxicity limited dosing; the OLE NCT05683860 reported no SAEs. A 24-week window may be short for ALS function, hence secondary F4. No quantitative values are posted.

In the index trial NCT04931862, run in C9orf72 ALS/FTD patients, WVE-004 produced robust, sustained reductions in poly(GP). Poly(GP) is the dipeptide-repeat product of the targeted repeat-containing transcript, so this shows CNS exposure and target engagement in the disease population. That evidence came from the index trial itself, not before it. The sponsor stated there was no clinical benefit at 24 weeks and that poly(GP) reductions were not associated with functional stabilization, so development was stopped; the extension NCT05683860 was also terminated. No downstream functional biomarker in humans is reported. Mouse data (PMID:35592494) do not count. No tolerability cap is shown. Engaged target with no clinical effect fits F2: lowering the repeat transcript did not drive benefit as tested.

GSK3494245, a Leishmania proteasome inhibitor for visceral leishmaniasis, was tested only in a single-ascending-dose healthy-volunteer study (NCT04504435). No efficacy readout occurred. Its half-life was short (about 1–2.3 h), and two participants hit the Cmax stopping criterion. Sponsors stated that predicted efficacious doses could not be reached within safe exposure under a once- or twice-daily target product profile (NCT04504435 stop reason; PMID:42127151). Exposure was therefore inadequate and the dose was capped by a safety-based Cmax limit. Engagement of the parasite target and the pathway effect were never measured in humans. The mechanism was not tested, so the code is F1a.

In the first-in-human index trial (NCT02437916), AMG 228 was escalated to 1200 mg Q3W with no DLTs, so dose was not limited by tolerability. Serum exposure was roughly dose-proportional, with target-mediated disposition. Doses above 360 mg gave trough coverage for 95% GITR occupancy. GITR coverage was confirmed in peripheral blood and in tumor biopsies from patients with advanced solid tumors, so engagement was adequate in this disease. However, there was no T-cell activation (the expected pathway effect) and no anti-tumor activity (PMID:30253804). Engagement was adequate but produced neither the downstream effect nor clinical benefit, so GITR agonism as tested does not drive tumor response: F2. The engagement data come from the index trial itself.

In the index trial (NCT00947882), single low doses of degarelix (10–30 mg) did not significantly improve IPSS over placebo. Differences were about 1–1.4 points (p≈0.09), with no clear dose-response. The approach relied on brief testosterone lowering, which the explorative study NCT00527488 tested at 32–64 mg, but I found no published testosterone, LH or prostate-volume results from it or from the index trial. Proof that degarelix engages GNRHR (LH and testosterone suppression; PMID:16967346, PMID:17096678) comes from healthy men and from prostate cancer patients on far higher doses (120–320 mg). So it can't be inferred at 10–30 mg in BPH. No sponsor explanation was found. The modest trend leaves open that the trial was underpowered (F7), but no source says so. Overall indeterminate.

The index trial NCT03289455 was a single-arm dose-escalation study with safety primaries and no prespecified efficacy threshold, so it was not an efficacy test that failed. It reported no DLTs at any dose and MRD-negative CR/CRi in 13/15 patients. That elimination of CD19/CD22+ blasts in paediatric ALL is the basis for rating engagement and pathway adequate. No CAR-T expansion or pharmacokinetic data are given, so exposure is no_human_data. The bundle states no stop reason for the ALL program. The sister DLBCL study NCT03287817 was ended for competitive-landscape reasons despite no DLTs, which points to a business decision. F8 is listed as secondary.

The only trial, NCT03539484 (Phase 1 dose escalation of a CD3xCEACAM5 bispecific, 65–1800 mcg Q3W, n=26), was terminated because of a 'change in benefit-risk ratio, driven by high incidence GI toxicity in absence of clinically significant anti-tumor efficacy.' DLTs occurred at 800 and 1800 mcg, and every participant had adverse events. The bundle has no human exposure, target-occupancy, T-cell activation or pathway data. Toxicity outweighing efficacy is the stated reason, so this is classed as toxicity-driven failure. GI toxicity from a CEA-directed T-cell engager plausibly reflects on-target effects (F5), but the bundle does not say whether it was on-target or molecule-specific (F6). The thin data and missing engagement evidence leave the role of the mechanism itself indeterminate (U).

The Phase 1 dose escalation of RO7172508 (65–1800 mcg IV Q3W) in CEA-positive solid tumors, NCT03539484, was terminated for a changed benefit-risk ratio. The stated driver was a high incidence of GI toxicity with no clinically significant anti-tumor efficacy. The bundle has no human PK, CEACAM5/CD3 engagement or pathway biomarker data, no PubMed abstracts and no other same-target drugs. So the pillars are all no_human_data. Toxicity is the stated reason the program ended, which supports a toxicity code. F6 is chosen because the bundle does not say whether the GI toxicity was on-target (CEACAM5 in normal gut) or molecule-specific. F5 is plausible but unshown. Efficacy was never adequately tested, so U also applies.

The index trial NCT03693989 compared PRO-145 (difluprednate) with an active steroid, Prednefrin. Its primary outcome was visual acuity, and the result was no significant difference (0.91 vs 0.87 logMAR, p=0.065). That reads as comparability with an effective active drug, not a failure of the drug's efficacy. No pillar was measured directly, so all three are inferred. Difluprednate 0.05% met clinical endpoints through ocular NR3C1 agonism: it was approved for uveitis, met non-inferiority in NCT01201798, and beat vehicle on post-surgical anterior chamber cell clearing in NCT03426267. In pediatric cataract surgery it was similar to prednisolone (NCT01124045, PMID:27367745). The active-comparator design with a visual acuity endpoint could not show superiority (F7).

No human pillar measurements are in the bundle; rabbit receptor-binding data (PMID:21182429) do not count. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Topical 0.05% difluprednate met clinician-scale efficacy endpoints for anterior uveitis (NCT01201798) and post-surgical inflammation (NCT03426267) through glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1) agonism in ocular tissue. In dry eye, the 4-week patient-reported VAS discomfort score showed no separation from vehicle (NCT01276223). That fits F2 by rule. However, loteprednol, which acts on the same target, is approved for dry eye. So the target plausibly matters, and endpoint choice, short duration or noisy design (F7) may explain the miss. The bundle states no reason for the failure, so confidence is low.

The bundle holds only the index Phase 1 trial NCT04025216 of CART-TnMUC1 across TnMUC1-positive solid tumors and myeloma. It was terminated after 16 patients because the sponsor judged the risk/benefit unfavorable, and no results were posted. The bundle has no human data on CAR-T expansion or persistence (exposure), on TnMUC1-positive cell depletion (engagement), or on any downstream effect. There are no other trials, no same-target comparator drugs and no publications. The unfavorable risk/benefit statement does not say whether toxicity or lack of efficacy drove the stop. Nothing separates a product that failed to engage from a target that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

The bundle contains only the index Phase 1 trial NCT04025216 of CART-TnMUC1 across several TnMUC1-positive cancers. It was terminated after enrolling 16 patients because the sponsor judged the risk/benefit unfavorable, and no results were posted. The bundle has no human data on CAR-T expansion or persistence (exposure), on TnMUC1 target cell depletion (engagement), or on downstream effects. It has no other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators. Nothing in the bundle separates a product that failed to expand or engage from a target that does not drive disease. Nothing documents toxicity either. Engagement is no_human_data, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index topical multiple-ascending-dose study in healthy volunteers (NCT02778477) was terminated because a preliminary analysis 'failed to indicate any meaningful pharmacodynamic response.' That is the only human evidence in the bundle. It shows the drug did not produce the intended PD effect at the doses tested, so engagement and pathway are treated as inadequate. The mechanism was therefore not properly tested (F1a). The bundle has no target, no exposure or skin-penetration data, no results, other trials or publications. It cannot show whether the PD readout measured engagement or a downstream effect, or whether poor exposure was the cause. No tolerability cap is shown. U is listed as a secondary code because the bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

The index topical multiple-ascending-dose study in healthy volunteers (NCT02778477) was terminated because a preliminary analysis 'failed to indicate any meaningful pharmacodynamic response.' No disease was tested, so this was not a test of whether the target drives disease. It reads as the molecule failing to produce its proximal pharmacological effect in humans at the doses given, which leaves the mechanism untested (F1a). The target is unrecorded and no exposure, PK, results or publications are in the bundle. So it cannot be shown whether the gap was poor skin penetration, inadequate engagement or a missing downstream effect. U is a plausible alternative, and confidence is low.

The index trial was a Phase 1 dose escalation (NCT03604445) that set the MTD at 2.8 mg/kg every 3 weeks. All patients at 3.6 mg/kg had DLTs. Paired tumour biopsies showed decreased Axin2 expression, which the authors read as target inhibition (PMID:39617530). That is pathway evidence in cancer patients at tolerated doses, and it implies engagement. PK was measured, but no values are reported. The best response was stable disease in 38%. The authors state that minimal efficacy plus a narrow therapeutic range led to termination. This supports F2: the pathway was modulated without antitumour benefit. F5 is secondary because the narrow therapeutic index likely reflects Wnt on-target effects (diarrhea, raised C-telopeptide). Confidence is low because the biopsy data were partial and the trial was not designed as an efficacy test.

AL-704 (JNJ-54257099) is a liver-targeted uridine nucleotide prodrug that inhibits HCV NS5B polymerase. Only preclinical data on it were found (EASL 2016). The first-in-human trial NCT02510248 was terminated after enrolling 42 people. It gave no reason for stopping and posted no results. I found no human data on its PK, intrahepatic triphosphate levels, or HCV RNA decline, so all three pillars are no_human_data. There was also no failed efficacy readout. Janssen's lead nucleotide was AL-335, and in 2017 the company left HCV for strategic reasons in a crowded market, which suggests a business or portfolio decision (F8 as a secondary code). No source states this was the reason for dropping AL-704 specifically. With engagement unknown, the code is U.

P-321 is a topical ENaC blocker. In the index trial NCT02831387 (0.017%, n=47, terminated early), dry eye symptoms did not improve versus placebo (p=0.749). I found no human evidence of target engagement or pathway effect, such as ENaC inhibition or an increase in tear volume. The companion pharmacodynamic study NCT02824913, which was meant to measure tear meniscus volume, enrolled only 1 subject and posted no data. The Phase 1 study NCT02242032 posted no results. ENaC inhibition and the tear-volume increase were shown only in cells and animals (IOVS abstract), and those data do not count here. No other drug on this target is in the bundle. No reason for stopping is stated, and Shire licensed the drug after the readout. Because engagement has no human data, the code is U. The trial was small and terminated early, so F7 is a possible secondary code.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT02614131 was terminated because 'new data suggests that insufficient target engagement would be achieved for efficacy.' Engagement is therefore inadequate by the sponsor's own judgment, so the mechanism was never properly tested (F1a). PMID:30741684 reports serum PK and suppression of plasma soluble Aβ40/42 in healthy subjects, and in 4 AD patients on 25 mg weekly, fitted by a TMDD model. CSF samples were collected to assess blood-brain barrier penetration, but no results are given, so CNS exposure is unshown. These data come from the index trial itself and were published in 2019, after it started. No related SAEs occurred, so no tolerability cap is evident. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported.

The index trial (NCT03225105) was a Phase 1 dose escalation of M3541 with palliative RT. It was terminated because the PK/PD properties precluded further development. PMID:35150356 reports that M3541 total plasma levels did not increase with dose (50–300 mg). It also found no relationship between dose and the phosphorylated/total ATM ratio. Exposure and target engagement were therefore shown to be inadequate, and the ATM-inhibition mechanism was never properly tested. Tolerability was acceptable (one DLT, no grade ≥4 TEAEs), so the dose was not capped by toxicity. No pathway biomarker was shown to move. No other ATM drugs appear in the bundle. This is F1a: the molecule could not deliver adequate exposure or engagement.

NCT04242147 was terminated without a stated reason or posted results. The SITC 2023 abstract on 39 solid-tumour patients reports the expected IL-15 pharmacodynamics: potent expansion of peripheral NK and CD8 T cells and a Ki67 peak on days 2–3. So the IL-15 (IL2RB) arm engaged its target and moved its pathway in this disease population at tolerated doses. The Q2W MTD was 200 µg/kg, with DLTs of CRS and pneumonitis, but the PD effects were already present below that cap. PD-L1 occupancy and tumour-site delivery were not reported. No efficacy data or reason for stopping was found, so calling this an F2 (mechanism engaged, no benefit) is a weak inference. U or a portfolio decision after Sanofi bought Kadmon (F8) are also possible. The dates suggest the PD data came after the listed index start.

Exposure: in the monotherapy Phase 1 (NCT03634982), plasma levels rose with dose and stayed within the range predicted to be active. Engagement and pathway: pERK fell in blood cells and in paired tumor biopsies from KRAS-mutant NSCLC patients (JTO 2019, before the index trial). Weekly troughs sat near the EC50, which is partial coverage, but these sources treat it as enough. SHP2 binding was never measured directly; engagement is inferred from pathway inhibition. The index combination trial (NCT05054725, 200 mg D1D2) gave an 11/43 response rate with no clear added benefit, and the sponsor gave no reason. Development stopped after review of the full data, weighed against prioritising RMC-6236. The SHERPA dose cap (PMID:42114409) applies to a different combination.

The index trial (NCT00909857, PMID:24713413) was a superiority test of E2V/DNG against an active PGR-agonist comparator (EE/LNG). Both arms reduced dysmenorrheic pain days considerably and similarly (-4.6 vs -4.2, P=0.34), so the drug was active and the miss reflects failure to beat an active drug of the same class. Dienogest's PK is well characterized (PMID:36718548). Dose-dependent ovulation inhibition, estradiol suppression and endometrial thinning in humans were shown (PMID:22128200). DNG beat placebo in primary dysmenorrhea (PMID:31727415, published after the index trial) and in endometriosis pain (NCT01822080). It also beat EE/LNG on pelvic pain and headache (NCT00778609). The failure therefore lies in the comparator design rather than in drug efficacy or the mechanism.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: In the first-in-human study (PMID:33245172, NCT01159522), the maximum tolerated dose was 24 mg/m2. Plasma exposure rose linearly with dose, and patients in the index trial got 12–24 mg/m2, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. No source has human data on tubulin binding, mitotic arrest, or vascular disruption (for example tumor perfusion imaging). The phase 1 paper reports drug levels and tumor responses only. The index trial NCT03020823 enrolled just 10 patients, had no objective responses, and was ended by the sponsor without a stated reason. An earlier phase 2 trial in the same disease (NCT02488629) also stopped early after 5 patients. Nothing here tells apart a drug that failed to engage its target from a mechanism that does not work in this cancer. Small, early-terminated trials may also have played a part.

ATL001 is an autologous clonal neoantigen-reactive T-cell (cNeT) product. Its index trial, THETIS (NCT03997474), and the sister trial CHIRON (NCT04032847) were both stopped by the sponsor. Exposure is the weak pillar. Early cNeT doses were low (median 14.2M cells in the first patients, SITC 2021). The sponsor's CMO linked the lack of new responses to limited cNeT persistence, and the sponsor then added enhanced conditioning (Cohort C) to improve engraftment. No source shows engagement in humans, such as tumour killing or neoantigen-specific activity, or any pathway biomarker moving. The program ended in September 2024 because the sponsor said the data missed its goals for commercial viability. So the mechanism was likely never properly tested (F1a). Commercial framing (F8) is secondary.

The index trial NCT04032847 was a Phase 1/2 study whose only primary outcome was descriptive TEAE counts, so it was not an efficacy test of ATL001. It was terminated for an unspecified 'Sponsor decision'. There were no treatment-related deaths. Related grade ≥3 events were attributed mostly to lymphodepletion and IL-2 rather than ATL001, so toxicity does not clearly explain the stop. The sister melanoma trial NCT03997474 was also stopped by sponsor decision with only safety endpoints, which suggests a program-level business decision, though the bundle does not confirm this. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement, or pathway data and no PubMed abstracts, so mechanism adequacy cannot be judged. The evidence is thin, hence low confidence.

Rocapuldencel-T is an autologous tumor-RNA/CD40L-electroporated dendritic cell vaccine with no single molecular target. In the Phase 3 ADAPT trial (NCT01582672; PMID:32034074), immune responses were detected in 70% of treated mRCC patients, and the drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Yet OS did not improve (HR 1.10), and PFS and ORR were no better than sunitinib-based standard of care. The trial was terminated for lack of efficacy. The Phase 2 showed CD8+ effector/memory T-cell expansion correlating with OS (PMID:25901286), but that was published after the index start. Immune activation occurred without clinical benefit, which fits F2: the mechanism, as tested, does not drive outcome. Survival correlated with immune-response magnitude and baseline Tregs, suggesting a possible subgroup effect (F3).

The index Phase 1/2 trial NCT05219578 had safety and DLT primary endpoints, not efficacy. The sponsor terminated it after two dose groups (7 patients). The stated reason notes the drug was well tolerated, with no DLTs or grade 3/4 AEs, but that RTX-224 cleared rapidly (within 10 minutes). This points to inadequate systemic exposure, a PK problem, rather than toxicity or lack of benefit. No engagement or pathway data were posted, and there are no other trials, publications or same-target comparators in the bundle. The mechanism was therefore never properly tested, which supports F1a on the exposure pillar. F9 applies secondarily because the trial was not an efficacy test of the drug. Confidence is medium because the evidence is a single stop-reason statement.

Exposure is shown in SCLC patients: plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose and was absorbed quickly (PMID:31260835), so it is rated adequate. The paper names PD as a secondary endpoint, but I could not open its full text, and none of the pages I reached report any human measure of KDM1A inhibition or a downstream biomarker. Engagement and pathway are therefore no_human_data. Toxicity limited dosing (3/3 DLTs at 3 mg daily; thrombocytopenia; encephalopathy). The study stopped for poor disease control plus a high adverse-event rate (NCT02034123). The AML and MDS trials stopped for the same risk-benefit reason (NCT02177812, NCT02929498). No other KDM1A inhibitor has succeeded in SCLC, so F1b does not apply. Nothing here separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Toxicity is a secondary factor.

The first-in-human SCLC trial (NCT02034123, PMID:31260835) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure. Dose-limiting grade 4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 3 of 3 patients at 3 mg daily. The investigators called the thrombocytopenia an on-target effect, which suggests KDM1A was engaged in blood-forming tissue. They also reported that the intermittent schedule did not reach the exposure tied to target engagement in preclinical models, and that dose-limiting thrombocytopenia kept the desired exposure from being achieved. No tumour biomarker result was found showing the pathway effect. On-target toxicity therefore capped the dose below what engagement needed, so the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). The low tolerated dose also fits efficacy offset by on-target toxicity (F5). The AML and MDS trials stopped for similar risk-benefit reasons. These reasons come from text fragments, not the full paper.

Engagement was judged adequate and the code is F2, but the evidence is indirect. LSD1 inhibition was not measured directly. In NCT02177812 (PMID:34927529), drug exposure in relapsed/refractory AML matched the SCLC study, where exposure rose in proportion to dose (PMID:31260835). On treatment, CD11b+ cells rose and CD71+ cells fell, which the authors cite as evidence of target engagement. Because these differentiation markers shifted in only a small subset of patients, the pathway pillar was rated inadequate. No clinical responses occurred. Toxicity was substantial: hemorrhage in 24 patients, SAEs in 37 of 41 and 13 withdrawals. Dose was escalated to 20 mg with one dose-limiting toxicity, so it was not capped. The program was stopped for poor risk-benefit with no benefit despite partial target effects (F2). Toxicity is a secondary code (F5), and partial differentiation leaves F1a possible.

Flubentylosin's target is the worm endosymbiont Wolbachia. In the index trial (NCT04913610), Wolbachia depletion in live female worms, a direct engagement readout, was essentially absent: 0–6% of worms were Wolbachia-free versus 2.6% with albendazole alone. Engagement was therefore measured in patients and found inadequate. Phase 1 (PMID:37428804) showed plasma exposure with a half-life under 4 h. It set 400 mg for 14 days as the maximum tolerated dose because of transaminase elevations at 1000 mg. The dose was chosen from preclinical modelling (PMID:30867321), and tolerability capped any escalation. Tissue exposure at the worm and downstream effects were not measured. The stated termination reason was strategic (F8 secondary), but the readout showed the mechanism was not achieved.

Artefenomel has no defined molecular target; its peroxide alkylation is stochastic (PMID:31626733), so direct engagement data are absent.
