Parasite killing was shown in humans (PRR48 >10,000 at 500 mg, NCT02453581/PMID:27272721) and as faster clearance in patients (PMID:36597076), but 500 mg monotherapy already recrudesced. In the index single-dose trial with ferroquine, no arm reached the target ACPR28; efficacy rose with Day-7 artefenomel and ferroquine concentrations (PMID:34011358). This indicates single-dose exposure was insufficient. Formulation exposure was problematic (PMID:30902103), and vomiting was common. Artefenomel's contribution was not demonstrated in phase 2a (PMID:36597076), and in vitro quinoline antagonism is reported (PMID:40894733). Low efficacy in kelch13-mutant Vietnamese patients and young children adds a population component (F3).

The cause can't be determined. In the first-in-human study in healthy volunteers (PMID:31138568), ASN100 had linear serum PK with a half-life of about 3 weeks, no dose-limiting toxicity up to 8,000 mg, and only 'detectable' penetration into lung epithelial lining fluid. So systemic exposure was adequate, but how much drug reached the lung is unclear. Serum taken from dosed volunteers still neutralized the toxins in the lab up to day 58. That shows the antibody stayed functional, not that it bound toxins in the lung during infection. No study measured engagement or a downstream biomarker in ventilated patients. The index trial NCT02940626 stopped for futility (5 vs 7 pneumonia cases, p=0.547). The sponsor said it was too early to know why. Nothing separates a drug that didn't engage from a target that doesn't matter.

In healthy volunteers, ASN100 up to 8,000 mg had linear serum PK, a half-life of about 3 weeks, detectable lung ELF penetration, and ex vivo serum toxin-neutralizing potency maintained to day 58, with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:31138568). This supports exposure and functional engagement, but only in serum of healthy subjects, published after the index trial started. No downstream pathway data exist in patients. The index trial stopped at a pre-planned futility interim: S. aureus pneumonia 5 vs 7 (p=0.547), with numerically more deaths on drug (NCT02940626). This suggests toxin neutralization did not prevent pneumonia as tested. The low event rate and many censored or indeterminate cases leave the trial underpowered (F7). Lung engagement is unproven, so confidence is low.

The index Phase 1/2a trial (NCT03576131) was a dose-escalation safety study with descriptive DLT and TEAE endpoints, terminated by sponsor decision. PMID:42175632 reports activation of the apoptotic pathway in patients (plasma cCK18 rose, ctDNA fell, PERCIST metabolic responses), which supports DR5 engagement and pathway effect in tumor patients. No direct occupancy measure was reported, so engagement is inferred from these downstream markers. There were frequent grade ≥3 liver transaminase elevations and diarrhea, DLTs at 1–3 mg/kg, and no objective responses. Nonclinical work showed direct hepatocyte killing; the authors conclude tumor specificity was insufficient for an acceptable therapeutic index. That points to on-target (DR5) hepatotoxicity offsetting modest activity. Molecule-specific features (hexamerization, dual epitope) contributed, hence F6 as secondary.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT04502706) was terminated by sponsor decision with no posted results. The publication from that trial (PMID:37206279) reports that receptor occupancy in NHL patients was highly variable. It also reports much lower affinity for SIRPα variant 2 than variant 1, so phagocytosis was variant-dependent. Target engagement was therefore inconsistent and inadequate in part of the population, and the mechanism was not properly tested. PK was reported but its adequacy was not characterized, and pathway evidence is in vitro only. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. No other SIRPα agent succeeded in NHL. The stop is framed as a sponsor decision and the primary endpoint was safety, so commercial reasons (F8) may also apply.

The bundle has no direct nasal-tissue exposure or engagement data for the spray. All three pillars are inferred_adequate: the same nasal spray met its primary rTNSS endpoint in SAR in an earlier phase 2 (NCT01277341). Oral bepotastine met an endpoint in perennial allergic rhinitis (NCT01861522) and suppressed histamine wheal-and-flare in healthy volunteers (PMID:15347340). H1 antagonism is a validated mechanism in allergic rhinitis, with many approved drugs, including nasal azelastine. In the index trial all doses beat placebo numerically by 0.36–0.49 TNSS points, similar to the prior positive trial. Against an SD of about 2.2 with roughly 122 per arm, the trial was likely underpowered for a modest effect. This points to a design or variability failure rather than a target failure. The sources do not state the reason, so confidence is low.

Oral bepotastine reached adequate plasma exposure in humans (PMID:24105252). It significantly suppressed histamine-induced wheal-and-flare in healthy volunteers at 10 mg BID (PMID:15347340, 2004, before the index trial), which shows peripheral H1 engagement and functional effect. The index pediatric PAR trial (NCT01425632) showed small, non-significant separation from placebo, with no safety signal. A repeat confirmatory trial of the same drug in the same pediatric PAR population met its primary endpoint (NCT01861522, PMID:26364765). Oral bepotastine was also effective in adult PAR (PMID:32735704), and many H1 antagonists are approved for allergic rhinitis. The mechanism and molecule therefore work in this disease. The index miss most plausibly reflects trial sensitivity or execution (assay sensitivity, placebo response, power), though no source states the cause.

Tapentadol ER met its primary endpoint in painful diabetic neuropathy (NCT01041859) and is FDA-approved there and in chronic pain. That approval covers the same MOR/NET targets and CNS compartment at comparable doses, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Healthy-volunteer studies also show central effects (PMID:35776835, PMID:34427941). No pillar was measured in PHN patients. In the small index trial (60 vs 31), mixed DPN/PHN patients in both arms improved by exactly 2.6 NRS points, a high placebo response. A parallel Japanese chronic-pain study (NCT01124604) failed the same way (-3.0 vs -2.9), although the drug works elsewhere. This points to a trial unable to separate drug from placebo rather than a failed mechanism. No source states the reason, so confidence is low.

Active-metabolite exposure in SCD adults matched healthy subjects (NCT01178099, PMID:23171128). Platelet reactivity fell on every assay, so engagement in this disease was published in 2013, before DOVE began. Pediatric dose-ranging (NCT01476696, PMID:25493452) reached ≥30–56% platelet inhibition, which the authors called clinically relevant, and DOVE titrated dose to that pharmacodynamic target (PMID:26402148). Pathway markers moved as predicted: platelet-monocyte aggregates, soluble tissue factor and ADP-stimulated P-selectin/GPIIb-IIIa all decreased (PMID:24368019, PMID:25140584). DOVE was adequately enrolled (341) yet missed its VOC-rate endpoint (RR 0.83, p=0.117) and was terminated for lack of efficacy. The bundle shows no other P2Y12 success in SCD. Mechanism tested and not disease-driving as tested.

Plerixafor's systemic exposure and CXCR4 antagonism are well characterized in humans. PK/PD studies show dose-linear plasma levels and dose-dependent CD34+ mobilization (PMID:18628138, PMID:12855591, PMID:15900288). Engagement is inferred adequate because the drug met mobilization endpoints through the same systemic CXCR4 mechanism (NCT01288573, NCT02221492). That mobilization of stem cells toward injury is the rationale for MRG-001 in wounds (PMID:31073167, rat data only). No engagement or biomarker data exist in surgical wound patients. The index abdominoplasty trial (NCT05844527, n=10) posted no results and no stop reason, so attributing the failure to the target is weakly supported. The tiny size suggests the trial could not answer the question (F7). A separate diabetic wound trial stopped for safety (NCT02790957).

No direct human PK, receptor or biomarker data in PWS. The pillars are inferred adequate because the same 3.0 mg GLP1R dose met weight endpoints in general obesity (NCT01272219, NCT00781937, pre-index) and in pediatric obesity (NCT02918279, BMI SDS -0.22 vs placebo). Patients were dosed to 3.0 mg or the maximum tolerated dose, and no tolerability cap is shown. In PWS, BMI SDS change did not differ from placebo at 16 or 52 weeks in children or adolescents (NCT02527200, PMID:36181471). This points to GLP1R agonism not overcoming PWS obesity as tested. Secondary codes: hyperphagia scores improved only in adolescents (F3), and the trial was small with large placebo-arm declines under a structured diet program (F7; PMID:36638011).

The index adolescent trial (NCT03008460) was an active-comparator non-inferiority test against Klean-Prep. Successful preparation was 71.4% vs 79.0%, a difference of -7.61 [-18.45, 3.24]. It missed only the non-inferiority margin, with no safety signal (SAEs 4/124 vs 3/117), so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug. No molecular target is recorded. The osmotic bowel-cleansing action is inferred adequate because the same preparation met cleansing endpoints before the index trial: superiority to PEG in adults (NCT00856843), non-inferiority in adults (NCT02321462), and non-inferiority in pediatric subjects (NCT02819323, 2016). No source gives the reason the program stopped.

The index trial NCT02092116 was a single-arm pilot. Its primary outcomes were descriptive (Part A adverse events; Part B mean reservoir change of total HIV DNA -39.7%), with no prespecified success criterion, so it was not an efficacy test that failed. Pillars held in HIV patients at 5 mg/m2. Lymphocyte H3 acetylation rose 3.7-7.7 fold (engagement). Cell-associated HIV RNA and plasma HIV RNA increased, showing latency reversal (pathway) (PMID:26379282, Part A of this trial). Plasma PK was characterized in BCN02 (PMID:33367767). This HIV engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, so it postdates the start. Earlier oncology data showed acetylation in patients (PMID:15466934, PMID:23757352). Dosing was tolerable (grade 1-2 only). F2 is secondary if the lack of a durable cure is counted as a failure.

VanGogh (NCT00753675, PMID:25538178) found no PFS benefit for vandetanib 300 mg alone or 100 mg plus gemcitabine versus gemcitabine (P=0.18). Toxicity did not differ between arms, so the dose was not capped. Plasma exposure at 300 mg is documented in humans (PMID:22206795). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate: the same 300 mg oral dose met efficacy and won approval in medullary thyroid cancer (NCT01661179, NCT00923247), a systemic tumour compartment. That inference rests mainly on RET. EGFR and VEGFR engagement in biliary tumours was never measured, which leaves residual U-type uncertainty. No same-target drug succeeded in biliary cancer, so F1b does not apply. The likeliest reading is that these targets do not drive advanced biliary tract cancer.

Index trial NCT00862836 combined vandetanib 100 mg/d with PLD in recurrent ovarian cancer and was stopped for lack of efficacy. In ovarian cancer patients on 300 mg monotherapy (NCT00445549/PMID:20068097), paired biopsies showed reduced EGFR phosphorylation. VEGFR2 phosphorylation was not consistently inhibited, and DCE-MRI and plasma VEGF were unchanged, so the anti-angiogenic mechanism was not engaged. The index used a third of that dose and still needed vandetanib dose reductions in 36%, with toxicity judged possibly intolerable (PMID:24005613). Under this dose cap, the KDR mechanism was not properly tested. EGFR engagement without benefit (also 100 mg in PMID:24709487) partly supports F2.

In NCT01877915, rivaroxaban did not reduce death, MI or stroke in heart failure with coronary disease (HR 0.94, p=0.27). Bleeding was not in excess, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Plasma exposure and anti-Xa inhibition are documented in humans (NCT03864406, PMID:17100983, PMID:35504629). No engagement data from heart failure patients are in the bundle. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same low-dose, plasma-compartment factor Xa inhibition met hard cardiovascular endpoints in acute coronary syndrome (NCT00809965, 2008, before the index trial) and in coronary and peripheral artery disease (NCT01776424, NCT02504216). The target was therefore engaged at a dose that works in coronary disease. Thrombin-driven events apparently do not drive outcomes in this post-decompensation heart failure population, which supports F2. F3 (population) is a secondary consideration.

MARINER (NCT02111564) tested rivaroxaban 10/7.5 mg for post-discharge VTE prophylaxis in medically ill patients, including respiratory failure. It missed its primary endpoint (HR 0.76 [0.52-1.09], p=0.136). Exposure was shown by PK in healthy volunteers and DVT patients (NCT03864406, NCT00786422). Engagement was shown directly by anti-Factor Xa activity in orthopaedic patients (NCT01094886, 2010) and pathway by thrombin-antithrombin suppression after PCI (NCT01442792). At the same 10 mg dose, the drug met a VTE endpoint (NCT02064439) and is approved for VTE, so the mechanism held at this dose. None of this was measured in respiratory-failure patients. The engaged mechanism gave no significant benefit in this population: F2. The favourable point estimate with a low event rate suggests an underpowered trial (F7), but the bundle does not state this.

Exposure is adequate: plasma PK was shown in humans (NCT03864406, PMID:35504629). Engagement is inferred_adequate. Rivaroxaban 10 mg, the index dose, met a VTE prevention endpoint (NCT02064439) through plasma FXa, and is FDA-approved for VTE. Direct FXa inhibition and PT/aPTT prolongation are documented in humans (PMID:17100983, PMID:35504629), though not in COVID-19 patients. The index trial was terminated early for enrollment challenges. Only 41 events accrued (22 vs 19, HR 1.16 [0.63, 2.15]), so it could not answer the question. Thrombotic event rates in COVID outpatients are very low (PMID:40096722). A secondary reading is F2: the phase 2 COVID trial NCT04504032 also stopped for futility, suggesting FXa inhibition does not alter outpatient COVID-19 outcomes.

Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional plasma eslicarbazepine and substantial CSF levels in humans (NCT00900237, PMID:21680153). Sodium-channel engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because ESL met epilepsy efficacy endpoints through the same Nav-channel mechanism at 800–1200 mg (NCT00957047, NCT00957684, NCT00957372, NCT00866775; FDA approval). Exposure-related serum sodium and seizure-frequency effects support the pathway (PMID:29732549), and PR prolongation indicates functional channel block (PMID:21415284). The index trial in painful diabetic neuropathy used 800–1600 mg, which tolerability did not cap, and no dose beat placebo (NCT01129960). The parallel post-herpetic neuralgia Phase 3 also failed (NCT01124097). This suggests the mechanism does not deliver analgesia in this disease. No engagement was shown in neuropathy patients.

Exposure was adequate: eslicarbazepine reached high plasma and CSF levels in humans (NCT00900237, PMID:21680153). Engagement and pathway were not measured directly but are inferred adequate. ESL met epilepsy efficacy endpoints and is FDA-approved through the same sodium-channel blockade at 800–1600 mg, the doses used in the index trial. Exposure tracked serum sodium and seizure response (PMID:29732549). Tolerability did not cap the dose: 3000–3600 mg was tolerated (NCT01879332). No dose separated from placebo on PHN pain (NCT01124097), and the parallel diabetic neuropathy Phase 3 also failed (NCT01129960). This points to the mechanism not driving neuropathic pain as tested. Topical lidocaine succeeded in PHN, but it acts peripherally, so F1b is only secondary.

Ticagrelor 90 mg bd strongly engages P2Y12. Human pharmacodynamic data show high inhibition of platelet aggregation and low PRU/VASP versus clopidogrel in coronary patients (NCT00642811, NCT01118325, PMID:38597172, PMID:24154787), registered before EUCLID began. The same dose met hard-outcome endpoints in PEGASUS, THALES and THEMIS (NCT01225562, NCT03354429, NCT01991795). In PAD, ticagrelor reduced white thrombus (PMID:29550045), but no platelet-function data in PAD patients appear in the bundle. Despite this, EUCLID (NCT01732822) showed no superiority over clopidogrel on CV death/MI/stroke (HR 1.02). More intense inhibition of an already-targeted mechanism added no benefit in PAD. Secondary F3: PAD patients with prior MI did benefit in PEGASUS (PMID:27046162).

Ticagrelor reached measurable plasma levels in pediatric SCD, with dose-dependent PRU inhibition (NCT02214121, PMID:30187935, PMID:30972696). HESTIA3 (NCT03615924) missed its VOC endpoint (RR 1.06, p=0.76). In that trial median platelet inhibition was only 34.9% predose and 55.7% at 2 h (PMID:35849650). This is partial P2Y12 blockade, far below the near-complete inhibition seen with adult ACS dosing (PMID:38597172). The trial itself aimed for greater inhibition than earlier studies (PMID:31446143). Bleeding was similar between arms, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The mechanism was therefore not fully tested. HESTIA2 adults (45 mg bid) also showed no benefit (PMID:30443999), which leaves F2, a target that does not drive VOC, as a plausible alternative.

Index trial NCT01362348 tested topical pazopanib eye drops (10 mg/mL QID). By Day 29, central retinal thickness (CRT) had risen by 37.9 µm and visual acuity changed by 0.07 letters (PMID:24896137). The other eye-drop trials (NCT00612456, NCT01134055, PMID:25432081) also showed no change in retinal thickness or lesions, so the expected downstream effect was absent; we rate pathway inadequate. In humans, only plasma levels were measured. No human data exist on drug levels in the retina or choroid, VEGFR inhibition there, or receptor occupancy. Only animal work (PMID:31763044) points to a delivery problem: posterior-eye drug levels were much lower in rabbits and monkeys than in rats, and the authors suggest this could explain the clinical failures. Animal data do not count here. Because nothing in humans separates poor delivery from an ineffective mechanism, the code is U. F1a is secondary, since poor delivery is the likely explanation. No tolerability cap on dose was found.

The index single-arm trial in relapsed transitional cell carcinoma had 1 response in 30 patients (NCT00722553). Human plasma PK at the 30 mg/m2 weekly MTD is characterized (PMID:19474785, PMID:19652067). DHFR engagement is inferred_adequate: at comparable doses pralatrexate met response endpoints in PTCL (NCT02013362, NCT03349333; PMID:19652067), so this intracellular, ubiquitous tumor target was reached there. Inference across tumor types is weak, because uptake depends on the folate carrier in each tumor. Bladder tumor engagement and pathway markers were never measured. The drug was similarly inactive in NSCLC, breast cancer and B-cell lymphoma, which suggests DHFR inhibition by this agent does not drive response outside T-cell malignancies. No toxicity cap or design problem is cited. U is plausible given that no direct engagement data exist in this disease.

The index single-arm phase 2 in previously treated breast cancer produced 1 response in 22 patients (NCT01118624). Human plasma PK exists in lymphoma patients (PMID:19474785). However, the bundle has no human measure of DHFR inhibition or a downstream folate-pathway marker in breast tumors. Activity in PTCL (NCT03349333, NCT02013362) comes from a different tissue compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred for solid tumors. Methotrexate, another DHFR inhibitor, is FDA-approved for breast cancer, which points to a molecule-specific shortfall rather than an irrelevant target, so the code is F1b. Similar near-zero activity in bladder cancer and NSCLC (NCT00722553, NCT00606502) is consistent with poor solid-tumor activity. Because engagement data are absent, U also applies, and the thin evidence keeps confidence low.

Exposure is adequate: in NSCLC patients, serum pralatrexate rose dose-dependently up to 230 mg/m2, and 190 mg/m2 was chosen as the phase 2 dose (PMID:21841501). The same study saw 10% responses. Mucositis limited the dose, but nothing shows engagement fell short at the phase 2 dose. DHFR engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because pralatrexate met response endpoints in PTCL (NCT02013362, NCT03349333; PMID:19652067, PMID:23008944). The index trial (NCT00606502) gave OS 6.7 vs 7.0 months against active erlotinib, HR 0.84 with a CI crossing 1. So the engaged mechanism gave no superior benefit (F2). A secondary F7 applies: a 201-patient phase 2 superiority test against an active drug could hardly show a modest effect.

INFORMS (NCT00731692, PMID:26827074) missed its primary endpoint with fingolimod 0.5 mg in PPMS (HR 0.95, p=0.544). No direct human occupancy or lymphocyte data appear in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 0.5 mg dose, acting systemically on S1PR1, met a relapse-rate endpoint in RRMS (NCT01633112, p=0.0138 vs glatiramer). PMID:26827074 also states the drug is effective in relapse-onset MS. Within PPMS, treatment reduced slowly expanding lesions (PMID:37823722), and relapses occurred after withdrawal (PMID:27159986), which suggests biological activity. The dose was not capped by tolerability. With the mechanism engaged yet no slowing of disability progression, the most direct reading is that S1PR1-mediated lymphocyte sequestration does not drive progression in PPMS as tested.

The index trial, NCT04927572, tested FMX114, a topical gel combining tofacitinib and fingolimod. Each of 21 patients had one lesion treated with FMX114 and a comparable lesion treated with vehicle. At week 4, ADSI fell 61% with FMX114 versus 51% with vehicle, which was not significant. None of the sources show skin drug levels, S1PR1 engagement or a pathway biomarker for topical fingolimod in humans. The sponsor said the gel had limited systemic exposure. Fingolimod's oral efficacy in MS doesn't transfer, because both the route and the tissue differ. The large vehicle response in a tiny trial (F7) and the sponsor's later claim that more severe disease responded better (F3) may have contributed. Neither separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Fingolimod 0.5 mg, the dose used in FORCIDP (NCT01625182, PMID:30001923), is FDA-approved for MS and beat comparators there (NCT00289978, NCT00355134, NCT01633112). That benefit comes through the same S1PR1 mechanism, systemic lymphocyte sequestration, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate. PMID:29694732 also links fingolimod-P blood levels to lymphocyte lowering. The bundle shows no engagement measured in CIDP patients and no dose limitation by tolerability. Despite that, the CIDP trial was flat (HR 1.0 [0.6, 1.7], p=0.98). A spontaneous autoimmune polyneuropathy mouse model was also negative (PMID:29618748, animal data). Together these point to S1PR1-mediated lymphocyte trapping not driving CIDP as tested. Confidence is medium because engagement is inferred rather than measured.

The index trial NCT04631354 was a Phase 1 lung-deposition study of radiolabelled inhaled S-770108 in 12 healthy volunteers. Its primary outcome was total lung deposition, a formulation and device scintigraphy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of pirfenidone. No results were posted and no stop reason is given. The program's labelled disease (precancerous condition, from the NF1 plexiform neurofibroma trial NCT00053937) has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data in the bundle. No primary target is recorded, and IPF approval is a different tissue, so none of the pillars can be inferred adequate. Because the index trial was not an efficacy readout, F9 applies.

The index trial NCT01596400 was a Phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study of Sancuso and IV granisetron in adolescents. Its primary outcome was plasma concentration, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug, and no failure is shown. Exposure is adequate: therapeutic plasma granisetron levels were documented in patients (PMID:27186139, PMID:26812081). Receptor engagement and the pathway effect were not measured directly. Both are inferred adequate because granisetron met CINV efficacy endpoints through 5-HT3 antagonism at comparable doses (NCT02106494, PMID:10408847, PMID:26921245). A separate breast cancer trial (NCT01649258) was terminated for lack of efficacy but is not the index trial.

Primary code F1a: the dose and treatment length probably did not engage the target well enough. In NCT02971007, oral MAT2203 at 200 and 400 mg/day for 5 days cleared the fungus in only 36% and 32% of women, against 84% on fluconazole. Clinical cure was 52–55% versus 75%. No plasma or vaginal drug levels were reported, though PK was a tertiary objective. The sponsor blamed the low dose and short course. It noted that higher doses given for longer worked in the NIH mucocutaneous candidiasis study (NCT02629419), and EnACT (NCT04031833) later used high oral doses successfully. Tolerability did not cap the dose: there were no serious AEs and side effects were mild GI. The trial was a safety-primary proof of concept and not powered against fluconazole (F7). Engagement is judged inadequate from the poor fungal clearance and the sponsor's explanation, not from a direct measurement, so U also applies.

The index trial NCT05597462 is a Phase 1 study of DFD-29's effect on microbial flora (CFU counts, MIC90) in healthy adults, registered under rosacea. It is a safety and resistance study, not an efficacy test of minocycline in autism or any disease, so F9 applies. DFD-29 met its rosacea Phase 3 endpoints (NCT05296629, NCT05343455). For autism, the bundle has no human CNS exposure, microglial engagement or pathway data. The ASD crossover proof-of-concept (NCT04031755, PMID:38102393) found no clinical change, and its authors could not separate an ineffective drug from an underpowered study. In small vessel disease, MINERVA showed no effect on the microglial PET signal (PMID:38629936). Any judgment on the autism mechanism would therefore be indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT02250859 is a 12-subject Phase 1 pharmacokinetic and local-tolerability study of a minocycline formulation in acne volunteers. Its endpoints are AEs, irritation, Cmax, Tmax and AUC, and it posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug, which makes F9 primary. For alcohol dependence, the only human study is NCT02187211, with no results posted. The bundle has no CNS exposure, target engagement or pathway data in alcohol-dependent patients, and no target is recorded. PMID:20838775 shows only attenuated amphetamine reward in healthy volunteers, and PMID:42444989 is mouse data. Efficacy in acne and rosacea (NCT02815280, NCT03142451) involves a different compartment and mechanism. The alcohol program is therefore indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT05597462 is a Phase 1 study of DFD-29 in healthy adults. Its endpoints are skin microbial colony counts and MIC90 shifts over 16 weeks, a microbiological safety study supporting the rosacea program. It was not an efficacy test of minocycline. The same DFD-29 formulation met its Phase 3 rosacea endpoints (NCT05296629, NCT05343455). For fragile X, the bundle shows plasma MMP-9 activity lowered by minocycline in FXS patients (PMID:23824974, 2013) and ERP normalisation (PMID:23981511). No human brain or CSF exposure data appear in the bundle. An acute-dose EEG study showed no gamma-power change (NCT02998151). The program's stop therefore does not reflect an efficacy failure in this index trial.

The index trial NCT03646188 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation safety study of doxorubicin-loaded microneedle arrays (25–200 µg) in BCC, with DLT as the primary endpoint. No DLTs occurred at any dose, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The trial was terminated because 'application of arrays was inconsistent', which was classified as a PK/formulation problem. This means local drug delivery to the tumour was unreliable, so the TOP2A mechanism was never properly tested in skin. No human tissue exposure, engagement or pathway data are shown for this route. Systemic doxorubicin approvals and the case reports of systemic cisplatin/doxorubicin in BCC (PMID:3703526, PMID:8427483) involve a different compartment and dose, so they do not support inferring adequacy. The trial was also not an efficacy test (F9), and it had operational problems (F7).

The index trial NCT00854061 compared T-Pred (tobramycin/prednisolone) with Pred Forte in cataract surgery patients. Its primary outcome was the aqueous humor concentration of prednisolone acetate, a descriptive pharmacokinetic comparison of the steroid component with no statistical analysis posted. The trial was classified as not_efficacy and its primary endpoint as not_assessable. It therefore was not an efficacy test of tobramycin, and no efficacy failure occurred. No stop reason is stated. The bundle has no human target-engagement data for tobramycin in this context. PMID:6801986 shows subconjunctivally injected tobramycin reaches therapeutic aqueous levels, but that is a different route and dose. Serious AEs were balanced at 1/162 per arm. F9 applies.

Index trial NCT05472090 tested TNX-102 SL 5.6 mg for long-COVID multi-site pain. Pain NRS change was -2.2 on drug vs -2.0 on placebo, with no safety signal. Human PK studies show effective sublingual systemic exposure and dose proportionality at 2.8–5.6 mg (PMID:41749492, PMID:41948806). The bundle has no direct HTR2A occupancy or biomarker data. However, the same 5.6 mg dose met pain endpoints in fibromyalgia (NCT04172831, NCT05273749; FDA approval 2025), a centrally mediated pain condition. Engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate. The NCT04172831 fibromyalgia result predates the index trial. With the mechanism plausibly engaged, the lack of benefit suggests it does not drive long-COVID pain as tested. The small sample (n=63) leaves some possibility that the trial was underpowered.

In the index trial NCT01323374, carbidopa was a peripheral DDC-inhibiting adjunct to droxidopa, the agent whose noradrenergic mechanism was being tested for fibromyalgia pain. No results were posted and no primary outcome is classified, so the bundle does not show a failed readout of carbidopa's own mechanism. Peripheral DDC inhibition is inferred adequate because levodopa/carbidopa met endpoints in Parkinson's disease (NCT00357994, NCT00974974, NCT00880620). Supporting this, higher carbidopa doses raised levodopa AUC in healthy volunteers (NCT03055936). No engagement data exist in fibromyalgia. A similar droxidopa+carbidopa trial in ADHD (NCT00983814) also missed. If the trial is read as testing the combination, F2 applies. Confidence is low because there are no results and no stated reason.

The index trial NCT00983814 tested droxidopa, a norepinephrine prodrug, in adult ADHD. Carbidopa was co-administered as a peripheral DDC blocker to raise prodrug availability, so the efficacy question concerned droxidopa rather than DDC inhibition itself. That is why F9 is primary. Carbidopa's peripheral DDC engagement is inferred adequate from its Parkinson efficacy trials (NCT00357994, NCT00880620, NCT00974974). It is also supported by a dose-dependent rise in levodopa AUC with carbidopa in healthy volunteers (NCT03055936). Engagement was never shown in ADHD patients. The double-blind phase randomized only 6 vs 5 participants, and AISRS change was identical (-17 vs -17). The trial was therefore badly underpowered to answer the question (F7). No safety signal was seen.

RX-10100 (clavulanic acid, 5–15 mg twice daily) has no recorded molecular target. The proposed mechanism through Munc18-1/Rab4 rests only on cell-line data (PMID:21964384). I found no human evidence of CNS exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker at the antidepressant doses. The only human brain data are an MRS glutamate correlation in cocaine use disorder at 500–1000 mg/day (NCT04411914). That is a different disease, a dose roughly 30–100 times higher, and it was measured after the index trial. In the index trial overall MADRS change was close to placebo, with a benefit only in the severe-depression subgroup (PMID:22203317). The larger follow-up trial (NCT01273376) failed, and the sponsor's advisor blamed a high placebo response. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Inhaled AZLI (75 mg, airway compartment) is approved in CF, where it improved FEV1 and respiratory symptoms and reduced sputum bacterial density (NCT00757237, PMID:20672296). Exposure, antibacterial engagement and the pathway effect are therefore inferred adequate, though not measured in bronchiectasis. The index trial NCT01313624 missed QOL-B respiratory symptoms (p=0.68). The sister trial NCT01314716 reached p=0.011 but with an effect below the 8-point minimal important difference, and AZLI was judged ineffective overall (PMID:25323621). Post hoc analyses confine benefit to patients with high bacterial load or high bronchitic symptoms (PMID:31109172, PMID:32265309). Sources also cite treatment-response heterogeneity and a large placebo effect (PMID:34675045, PMID:40892817), pointing to patient selection rather than lack of engagement.

Kurobe's vancomycin 1.1% ophthalmic ointment failed to beat placebo on clinical resolution at day 8 in NCT02432807 (71/83 vs 59/76, p=0.22). Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up human data on tear or conjunctival vancomycin levels, bacterial eradication or any other pharmacodynamic measure for this ocular formulation. Vancomycin's approvals are for systemic or gut infections, a different tissue compartment, so engagement cannot be counted as inferred_adequate. The placebo arm resolved at about 78% because acute bacterial conjunctivitis often clears on its own. That suggests the trial had little room to show a difference (F7), but no source says this. Because engagement is no_human_data, the failure is indeterminate. No stated reason for stopping was found.

Exposure at the lung site was shown in CF patients: inhaled AeroVanc kept sputum Cmin above the usual MRSA MIC for 24 h, with no serious toxicity (PMID:31964790, NCT01537666). Engagement here means MRSA killing. In the Phase 2 CF trial (NCT01746095) sputum MRSA density did not change at 32 mg; 64 mg showed only about a 0.8-log apparent separation, with no p-values. So engagement in CF patients, shown before the index trial, was weak and unconfirmed. In vitro, vancomycin needs ≥1000 µg/mL to eradicate CF-pathogen biofilms (PMID:31136714), far above the sputum levels reached. The mechanism was likely not adequately tested, and the index trial missed its FEV1 endpoint (p=0.325). IV approvals do not support inference because the compartment differs. Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT04358081 enrolled only 20 patients (5–7 per arm) with no statistical comparison, so its primary endpoint could not be assessed. It could not answer the efficacy question (F7). Azithromycin has no defined COVID-19 target. Plasma exposure at comparable doses is documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:35598114). Lysosomal accumulation is only a theoretical argument (PMID:32389720). The bundle has no human evidence of antiviral or immunomodulatory target engagement or pathway effect in COVID-19. The program was abandoned on external evidence of no benefit: the futility stop in NCT04332107 (~50% symptom-free in both arms), the stops in NCT04344444 and NCT04335552, and the review PMID:36387723. With engagement untested, those null results cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter (U secondary).

The index trial NCT02168946 (Vabomere vs best available therapy in CRE infections) was a small (n=77) descriptive study with no statistical comparison. Numbers favoured Vabomere: cUTI/AP success 4/12 vs 2/4, Day-28 mortality 4/18 vs 4/9, cIAI cure 2/2 vs 0/2. Harm was not excessive. It was not a failed efficacy test of the drug. The same combination met its non-inferiority primary endpoint in cUTI/AP (NCT02166476) and gained FDA approval for cUTI. All three pillars are therefore inferred adequate in that systemic infection setting. No direct PK or PD data are posted, and the supporting cUTI trial began after the index trial started. The trial's small size and descriptive design (F7) also meant it could not answer a comparative question.

In the index trial NCT03250624, topical CD5024 0.3% did not beat placebo on EASI change (-2.64 vs -2.36, p=0.632). The bundle names no molecular target, and there is no human evidence of skin exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker for ivermectin in atopic dermatitis. The 1% cream worked in rosacea (NCT01493687, NCT01494467), but that mechanism is thought to involve Demodex mites and inflammation. Rosacea is a different disease and the dose was higher, so engagement cannot be inferred to have held in atopic dermatitis. The same cream also failed in acne (NCT03034460). No sponsor explanation for the failure was found. With engagement unknown and nothing to tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the answer is U.

No target is recorded, so all pillars are inferred. The same CD5024 1% cream, applied to facial skin, met its pivotal endpoints in papulopustular rosacea (NCT01493687, NCT01494467, NCT01493947). In treated rosacea patients it lowered Demodex density and normalized skin transcriptomic dysregulation (PMID:40220854). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate at this dose and in this tissue, though not shown in acne. In the index trial (NCT03034460) the active arm was numerically worse than vehicle (10.1 vs 8.9 lesions, p=0.158). The adapalene/BPO reference arm separated clearly (p=0.002), so the trial could detect an effect. The mechanism that works in rosacea appears not to drive acne. A similar null result was seen in atopic dermatitis (NCT03250624). There is no tolerability limit.

The index trial (NCT02156063, G-CSF/NT100 in unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss) has unknown status, no posted results and no stated reason for stopping. Systemic exposure to filgrastim in humans is well documented (PMID:11677930, PMID:32820861). CSF3R engagement is inferred adequate from approved efficacy in neutropenia, a systemic compartment, at comparable doses. The pathway pillar holds: there is a dose-dependent ANC rise and CD34+ mobilization (PMID:20019087, PMID:25837839), and the stroke trial confirmed the expected PD (PMID:23963331). Engagement was not shown in women with RPL or in endometrial or decidual tissue, and the index trial's dose is not given. The best-supported reading is that CSF3R agonism did not drive pregnancy outcome. The bundle is very thin, so confidence is low.

Filgrastim's systemic exposure and CSF3R agonism are well documented in humans before the 2013 index trial. Healthy-volunteer PK/PD studies (PMID:11677930, PMID:20019087, PMID:25837839, PMID:32820861) show serum levels and a dose-dependent rise in neutrophil count, and receptor binding is equivalent across products. No tolerability cap appears (PMID:9327037). The drug also met efficacy endpoints in neutropenia. Yet Thrive-IVF (NCT01864356), measuring ongoing pregnancy in women with repeated IVF failure, has no posted results and gives no stop reason. No endometrial exposure or engagement data exist for these patients, and the dose and route used are not shown. The pattern of systemic engagement without benefit fits F2, as with stroke (PMID:23963331), but the tissue-level gap leaves U plausible. Confidence is low.

Inhaled mannitol is an osmotic mucoactive agent with no recorded molecular target. Its airway action is inferred adequate because the same inhaled formulation met an FEV1 endpoint in CF (NCT02134353), leading to approval. A review reports that mannitol improves mucus clearance in non-CF bronchiectasis (PMID:26634006), so the pathway effect is shown in this disease, though only in a 2015 publication, after the index trial started. The index trial missed its exacerbation-rate endpoint (RR 0.92, NCT00669331). A post hoc analysis confined the exacerbation benefit to highly symptomatic patients (PMID:32097051). Other sources stress heterogeneous treatment response, a large placebo effect and limited generalizability of trial populations (PMID:34675045, PMID:26856192). Together these point to patient selection as the main reason for failure.

SURF-100 is a topical eye drop. The sources contain no human data on ocular-surface drug levels, IMPDH inhibition or biomarkers after ocular dosing. The IMPDH inhibition shown in blood cells after oral dosing (PMID:11156363, PMID:35570339) does not carry over to topical ocular use. In the index trial (NCT04734197), the vehicle arm had a very high UNC DEMS responder rate (80.9%). Neither approved active control separated from vehicle (cyclosporine 72.3%, lifitegrast 57.4%), and MPA 0.1% alone was numerically highest (90.0%). That pattern points mainly to a trial unable to tell treatments apart: high vehicle response and doubtful assay sensitivity (F7). With no engagement data, the reading stays uncertain (U secondary). The search found no sponsor statement explaining why the program failed.

The index trial NCT03248479 tested magrolimab (anti-CD47) alone or with azacitidine in AML and MDS. Azacitidine was the backbone, not the investigational agent. The trial stopped for futility of magrolimab in the ENHANCE trial, so it was not an efficacy test of azacitidine. Pillars for azacitidine: exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate from its FDA approval in MDS through DNMT1 inhibition in the same compartment. PMID:26296092 (2015, before the index start) shows exposure-correlated global DNA hypomethylation in MDS and AML patients. No engagement data exist in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, the program disease, but the stop does not reflect DNMT1 failing there. Code F9.

The index trial NCT03248479 tested magrolimab, alone or added to azacitidine, in AML/MDS. It was terminated for futility based on the planned analysis of magrolimab's ENHANCE trial, so it was not an efficacy test of azacitidine. Azacitidine was the standard backbone, and its posted CR rates (~30–37% in treatment-naive MDS/AML) are consistent with known activity. Azacitidine is FDA-approved in MDS, so exposure and DNMT1 engagement are inferred adequate at the standard dose. PMID:26296092 shows exposure-correlated global DNA hypomethylation in MDS/AML patients, so pathway is adequate. No engagement data exist in prolymphocytic leukemia. The stop reflects magrolimab's failure, not azacitidine's.

The index trial NCT03248479 tested magrolimab alone or with azacitidine, which served as the standard backbone. It was stopped for futility after the ENHANCE analysis of magrolimab plus azacitidine versus azacitidine, so it was not an efficacy test of azacitidine. Azacitidine's pillars hold in myeloid disease. CC-486 exposure correlated with reduced global DNA methylation, and responders showed greater hypomethylation (PMID:26296092, published before the index start). Demethylation was also measured in E1905 (PMID:24663049). Azacitidine is approved in MDS. No engagement data exist in small intestine lymphoma, so engagement_in_disease is false. The 'before index' flag reflects the MDS/AML evidence only. The stop reflects magrolimab's failure, not azacitidine's.

Alteplase (PLAT) met clinical and physiological endpoints by intravascular fibrinolysis in stroke (NCT02930837) and pulmonary embolism (NCT01513759, NCT04248868). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate for a vascular target, though no fibrinolysis biomarkers were measured in COVID-19 patients. The index trial NCT04640194 had 104 patients split across several small arms (20/20/22 in Part 1; 17/8 and 12/5 in Part 2). Every hazard ratio for clinical improvement had a wide CI crossing 1, while point estimates favored alteplase (high dose HR 1.75 [0.73, 4.15]) and deaths were numerically fewer (6/20 vs 9/22). The trial looks underpowered to answer the question (F7) rather than showing that the mechanism fails (F2 secondary). No source states a reason for stopping, so confidence is low.

In the four-arm Phase 2 trial NCT03684772 (PMID:36177541), facial actinic keratosis was treated with topical gel: 0.125% digoxin plus 0.125% furosemide, either drug alone, or placebo. The gel did not improve clinical scores or the trial's pharmacodynamic (biopsy and skin-swab) markers, so I rated the pathway pillar inadequate. No source measured furosemide levels in skin or showed that it engaged its target (the ion transporter it blocks) in human skin. The investigators gave two explanations they could not tell apart: either the concentration or treatment time was too low, or HPV matters too little in actinic keratosis for this antiviral approach to work. No other drug on the same target has succeeded in this disease. With engagement unmeasured and both explanations still open, the code is U.

The index trial (NCT03334240) tested topical ionic contra-viral therapy (ICVT), a digoxin plus furosemide combination meant to block potassium influx in keratinocytes. That target is a skin ion co-transporter, not the kidney transporter SLC12A1 listed for the drug. The trial was terminated for lack of effect at interim analysis. No human data show local drug levels in lesions, co-transporter inhibition or potassium flux changes in skin. The first-in-human study (NCT02106260) found no systemic exposure. A Phase 2 cutaneous wart trial (NCT02333643) met its endpoint and lowered HPV load, but two Phase 3 wart trials (NCT02971891, NCT03259620) failed. That weakens any inferred engagement, and the combination confounds attribution to furosemide. Genital mucosa also differs from keratinized skin. No source explains the failure, so the code is indeterminate.

Sargramostim is an approved GM-CSF receptor agonist for neutropenia and radiation-induced myelosuppression (PMID:31021662). Those clinical benefits imply systemic exposure and receptor engagement in humans, so both pillars are inferred_adequate. In Alzheimer's patients it changed innate immune markers as expected (PMID:33778150), supporting the pathway pillar. Tolerability did not cap the dose. In the outpatient COVID-19 index trial (NCT04707664), ER visit, hospitalization or death occurred in 21/301 on drug vs 16/299 on placebo, so no benefit. Other COVID trials were also negative or mixed. NCT04642950 missed its primary endpoint. NCT04411680 improved oxygenation without reducing intubation, a proximal-only effect that supports F4 as secondary. The mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, pointing to F2. No in-disease target engagement data exist.

Index trial NCT04642950 tested inhaled sargramostim in moderate COVID-19 pneumonia and missed its primary endpoint, days to 2-category improvement (9 vs 8). The publication (PMID:37729076) reports that serum CCL17 rose with sargramostim, a downstream pathway marker shown in patients with this disease. That implies engagement, but receptor binding and lung exposure were not measured directly, and this evidence was published after the index trial. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The authors attribute the null result to concomitant corticosteroids: in a post hoc analysis, benefit appeared only when the cumulative steroid dose was ≤500 mg. That points to population and treatment-context heterogeneity (F3). Alternatives remain: the mechanism may not drive disease (F2), or the trial was small and confounded (F7). An open-label trial at the same inhaled dose (PMID:36458916) improved oxygenation.

In the index trial (NCT01126177, PMID:24937476), inhaled IFN-β boosted innate immunity in blood and sputum biomarkers in asthma patients. That shows lung exposure, receptor engagement and pathway activation in this disease, measured during the index trial itself. Morning PEF recovery also improved. The primary ACQ endpoint was missed overall because asthma symptoms did not worsen meaningfully, a low-signal population. Benefit was confined to the Step 4-5 difficult-to-treat subgroup (P=0.004), and the authors called for adequately powered trials in that population. The follow-up INEXAS trial in severe asthma (NCT02491684, PMID:33091192) confirmed the pharmacodynamic effect. It was stopped early for an unexpectedly low exacerbation rate, so trial design and event rate also contributed. The mechanism was engaged, so failure is mainly attributed to patient selection and heterogeneity.

The index trial NCT03119701 tested FP-1201-lyo 10 µg against placebo for preventing multi-organ failure after RAAA surgery. It was terminated on IDMC recommendation because of unexpectedly high concomitant corticosteroid use. With only 27 vs 11 patients analysed, day-30 mortality did not differ (OR 1.30, p=0.78). The stated reason is an execution problem: confounding co-medication in a tiny sample, so the trial could not answer the question. That makes F7 primary. In healthy volunteers and MS patients, IFN beta-1a produced dose-dependent neopterin, MX1 and 2'5'OAS induction and NK-cell changes, shown before 2017 (NCT04183491, PMID:21680782, PMID:12799025, PMID:34536787). Engagement and pathway effects were never shown in RAAA patients. The same formulation also failed in ARDS (NCT02622724), which supports secondary F2.

The index trial of IV FP-1201-lyo 10 μg in ARDS (NCT02622724) showed no benefit on VFDsurv (10 vs 8.5 days, p=0.82) or mortality. Systemic IFNAR agonism by IFN beta-1a is well characterised in humans before 2015. PK was reported (PMID:10210923). Dose-dependent rises in neopterin, 2'5'-OAS and MX1 were shown in healthy volunteers and MS patients (PMID:21680782, PMID:34536787, NCT04183491), with NK-cell trafficking effects (PMID:12799025). The drug is also approved in MS through the same receptor. No engagement data were shown in ARDS patients, and there was no tolerability cap. With systemic engagement adequate but no clinical effect, the evidence points to the mechanism not driving ARDS outcomes. A possible corticosteroid interaction is hinted only by a sister trial halted for concomitant steroid use (NCT03119701), so the population confounder is secondary.

In the index trial (NCT01746420), a single injection of rhPDGF-BB into the tendon at 0.45 to 3.0 mg did no better than placebo on VAS pain, DASH, PRTEE or grip strength. The 3.0 mg arm actually did numerically worse. I found no human data showing that the drug reached tendon tissue, activated PDGFR there, or moved a downstream biomarker. The sponsor patent's pharmacokinetic data after injection into the tendon seem to come from animals (doses are in µg/kg), so they don't count here. Becaplermin's approval for skin ulcers is topical and acts on a different tissue, so it can't stand in for engagement in tendon. No other PDGFR agonist has succeeded in this disease. No source gives a reason for the failure. With engagement unknown, the outcome can't be explained, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02631538 was a Phase 2 safety study of belimumab plus rituximab co-administration. Its primary outcomes were descriptive SAE and AESI counts, with no efficacy comparison, so it was not an efficacy test of rituximab (F9). The safety counts show no clear excess. In primary Sjögren's patients, earlier studies showed dramatic B-cell depletion in blood and salivary gland (PMID:17330280, 2007) and rapid peripheral B-cell depletion (PMID:16142737, 2005). This supports adequate exposure and engagement in this disease before the index trial. Serum IgG stayed stable (PMID:16142737), so the downstream pathway marker was unchanged. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

NCT02197169 (TARGET-I) was a small phase 1b trial. It randomised about 27 patients with recurrent glioblastoma to the oncolytic adenovirus DNX-2401 alone or DNX-2401 plus systemic interferon gamma-1b. A review (PMC7912718) reports that interferon gamma was poorly tolerated and gave no clinical benefit over DNX-2401 alone. No source shows, in humans, that the drug reached the brain tumour, engaged IFNGR1/IFNGR2 there, or produced a pathway effect, such as interferon-stimulated gene induction or MHC upregulation in tumour tissue. Nothing shows the dose was capped below what engagement needed. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The secondary codes are F6, because poor tolerability contributed, and F7, because this was a small add-on design.

Receptor engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because interferon γ-1b is FDA-approved for osteopetrosis (NCT00004402) through the same systemic IFNGR agonism at comparable dosing, about 50 mcg/m2 subcutaneously three times weekly (PMID:24576196, PMID:25335475). The index trial's dose escalation was tolerated (serious AEs 1/47), so dose was not limiting. The hypothesized pathway, a rise in frataxin, failed: there was no change in buccal or whole-blood frataxin (PMID:30911578), and the pilot showed only small, inconsistent tissue changes unrelated to FARS (PMID:25335475). The FARS-mNeuro primary endpoint was not met (p=0.54, NCT02415127). The IFN-γ→frataxin mechanism did not hold in patients, supporting F2. The authors' suggestion that longer studies might show benefit adds a minor F4.

The index trial NCT00754650 enrolled only 2 chemo-naive CLL patients at 15 mg/kg. The primary bone marrow response was reported only descriptively (median -20% infiltration), with no serious AEs, so the endpoint was not assessable. The trial could not answer the efficacy question; this is an execution or accrual failure, not a demonstrated lack of benefit. Systemic VEGFA neutralization at comparable doses is inferred adequate: bevacizumab is approved in multiple solid tumors, and human data show free VEGF-A lowering (PMID:32466535, PMID:28106709). No engagement data exist in CLL. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Because the readout was uninformative, F7 fits best. F2 cannot be supported without an interpretable efficacy result.

The index trial used the approved MS regimen of 300 mg IV every 4 weeks and missed its primary endpoint: seizure frequency changed -14.4% vs placebo, p=0.51 (NCT03283371, PMID:34521687). In MS patients, the bundle shows adequate plasma exposure and α4-integrin saturation at this dose (PMID:31355324, PMID:32019876, PMID:34690914). It also shows the pathway effect, with reduced CSF leukocytes (PMID:34943468). MS efficacy through the same peripheral-trafficking mechanism was shown in trials registered before the index trial (NCT00027300, NCT01440101). No engagement data come from epilepsy patients, and there was no tolerability limit. With engagement adequate and no benefit, the mechanism appears not to drive drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The authors note the trial lacked precision to exclude an important effect, so F7 is secondary.

Natalizumab 300 mg IV gives saturating α4-integrin occupancy, raised lymphocyte counts and reduced CNS leukocyte trafficking in MS patients (PMID:31355324, PMID:32019876, PMID:34690914, PMID:34943468). Its MS and Crohn approvals act on the same peripheral leukocyte target, so the pillars held at comparable doses. Pediatric PK/PD work (NCT01884935) was registered before the index trial. Engagement was not measured in stroke patients. Infarct growth was unchanged in NCT01955707 (ratio 1.09, p=0.779). ACTION II (NCT02730455, PMID:32591475) at 300 and 600 mg found clinical outcomes worse than placebo, with no dose limitation. Mouse models showed that blocking leukocyte infiltration did not reduce infarct size (PMID:24743435, PMID:31522409). α4-integrin blockade does not appear to drive stroke outcome.

Human PK is linear with adequate plasma exposure at standard doses (PMID:19262560, PMID:30229926). Engagement was not measured in nephrotic patients, but it is inferred adequate because abatacept met efficacy endpoints through systemic CD80/CD86 blockade (e.g. NCT01860976), and CD86 occupancy is measurable in humans (PMID:35383117). In the index trial, renal response was 0% with abatacept vs 7.7% with placebo, with no signal. The bundle points to the target rather than the molecule. A prospective study found no remission with abatacept or the higher-affinity belatacept and no podocyte B7-1 expression in biopsies (PMID:26701979). This undermines the CD80-podocyte hypothesis (PMID:29340321). Secondary: the trial was underpowered (36 enrolled vs 90 planned) and the planned CD80-guided patient selection was not shown.

Exposure is adequate: linear PK, with ~10 mg/kg IV giving trough levels at or above the 10 μg/mL plateau (PMID:19262560, PMID:30229926). Engagement is inferred_adequate: the same CD80/CD86 blockade in systemic immune cells met endpoints in RA and PsA at comparable doses (NCT01142726, NCT01860976). No receptor occupancy was measured in lupus nephritis. Pathway is adequate: in the earlier LN trial, abatacept improved anti-dsDNA, C3 and C4 and reduced proteinuria (PMID:24504810, NCT00430677). Reanalyses blamed the complete-response definition (PMID:22806274, PMID:23529285), which supports F4 as secondary. However, the large confirmatory index trial still showed no difference (35.1% vs 33.5%, p=0.73), so costimulation blockade does not drive renal response as tested.

Abatacept's systemic CD80/CD86 blockade is proven by approvals and pivotal wins in RA and PsA (NCT01142726, NCT01860976) at ~10 mg/kg, with plateau exposure (PMID:30229926) and measured CD86 occupancy (PMID:35383117). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate for the systemic compartment. The podocyte compartment was not measured. In one MCD patient (PMID:25239302, pre-index), urinary CD80 became undetectable after abatacept, weak in-disease engagement evidence. The index trial showed no renal response (0% vs 7.7%). Biopsy data found no podocyte B7-1 induction (PMID:26697986), suggesting the target does not drive the disease as tested (F2). The mixed FSGS/MCD population and CD80-uria heterogeneity (F3), and 36 enrolled against 90 planned (PMID:29340321; F7), also apply.

The index trial of weekly SC abatacept 125 mg missed ESSDAI at Day 169 (-3.2 vs -3.7, p=0.44) and its key secondaries (NCT02915159, PMID:33168545). The same dose gives Cmin ≥10 µg/mL, the plateau of response in RA (PMID:30229926). Linear PK is shown in humans (PMID:19262560), so exposure is adequate. Engagement was not measured in pSS, but is inferred adequate because the same systemic CD80/86 blockade at this dose met endpoints in psoriatic arthritis, RA and JIA (NCT01860976, NCT01142726, NCT01835470). In pSS patients, abatacept lowered IgG, IgA and IgM-RF and pathogenic cell subsets; the authors call this 'biological activity' without clinical benefit. CD80/86 costimulation blockade therefore does not drive pSS disease activity as tested. Glandular B-cell effects were absent (PMID:28390747).

The index trial NCT04472494 was terminated for slow accrual after 61 participants. Its primary endpoint (IMV or death by Day 28: 30.0% vs 31.6%, OR 1.07, CI 0.26–4.49) was far too imprecise to answer the question. Human PK shows linear, sustained plasma exposure (PMID:19262560, PMID:30229926). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate: abatacept met efficacy endpoints in systemic T-cell costimulation diseases (NCT01860976, NCT01142726). CD86 occupancy was also measured in other patients (PMID:35383117), though not in COVID-19. The larger ACTIV-1 trial reported evidence of abatacept benefit in hospitalized COVID-19 (PMID:38977241, PMID:36203544). So this readout does not show the target is irrelevant. The failure reflects an underpowered, prematurely stopped trial.

Systemic CD80/CD86 blockade is inferred adequate: abatacept met efficacy endpoints at ~10 mg/kg in PsA and JIA (NCT01860976, NCT01835470), and RA exposure-response shows a plateau at this exposure (PMID:30229926). No podocyte or kidney engagement was shown in FSGS. The rationale rested on podocyte B7-1 expression. Early responses occurred in B7-1-positive patients (PMID:24670178). Later sources found no podocyte B7-1 in FSGS biopsies and no response (PMID:26701979), and suggested efficacy depends on B7-1 status (PMID:25432003). This points to patient selection or target heterogeneity, or a target that does not drive the disease. The index trial enrolled 36 against a planned 90 and had wide CIs (NCT02592798, PMID:29340321), so it was underpowered.

No ROP-specific engagement data are shown; PMID:22672259 on serum VEGF in a ranibizumab-treated infant is title only. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because intravitreal ranibizumab met efficacy endpoints for VEGF-A-driven retinal disease at comparable intraocular doses (NCT00687804, NCT01976312, NCT01840410). In RAINBOW (NCT02375971), 0.2 mg gave 80.0% treatment success vs 66.2% for laser, with nominal p=0.0254, but the OR CI (0.993–4.82) narrowly included 1. The extension (NCT02640664) also favored ranibizumab without significance. Aflibercept is FDA-approved for ROP, so the target is valid. This was a borderline statistical miss consistent with insufficient power rather than mechanism failure (F7), and arguably near-success (F9). The bundle gives no stated reason, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT00741338 was a 7-patient immune tolerance induction study. Azathioprine served as part of an immunosuppressive regimen meant to prevent antibody responses to laronidase enzyme replacement therapy. It was not an efficacy test of azathioprine against MPS I itself; the endpoint was classified not_efficacy (tolerance achieved in 0/3 and 1/3 participants). Pillars are inferred_adequate because azathioprine is FDA-approved for transplantation and rheumatic disorders through the same systemic immunosuppressive mechanism. The bundle does not confirm that the doses were comparable, and nothing shows engagement measured in MPS I patients. The very small, cohort-based design (F7) also limits interpretation. No stated stop reason.

PROTECT (NCT02145182) missed its primary endpoint: delayed graft function 35.9% vs 41.7%, OR 0.81, p=0.40. Nothing in the bundle shows C5 blockade in deceased-donor transplant recipients. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because systemic anti-C5 dosing met efficacy endpoints in aHUS, a complement-driven kidney injury, before the index trial began (NCT00844545, NCT01194973). Measured pharmacodynamics elsewhere show complete terminal complement inhibition and lowered sC5b-9 (PMID:25833956, 34795626, 34803867). No tolerability ceiling appears, and safety was balanced between arms. With the mechanism engaged, the absence of benefit suggests terminal complement does not drive delayed graft function as tested. A follow-on DGF trial stopped on the PROTECT result (NCT01919346). No sources attribute the failure to population or design.

In the index Phase 3 trial in severe GBS (NCT04752566, PMID:38987228), eculizumab given with IVIg reduced serum free C5 by 99.99% from 1 h after dosing through week 5. This is direct, near-complete target engagement in GBS patients, but it was reported with the index results, not before them. The trial still missed its primary endpoint (HR 0.9, p=0.89) and was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. The pathway pillar is inferred adequate: the same regimen gave complete terminal complement inhibition and efficacy in gMG and NMOSD (PMID:34795626, PMID:34803867, NCT01892345). sC5b-9 is not elevated in GBS (PMID:36936980), and a review points to upstream C1q rather than C5 (PMID:42788065). Terminal complement therefore appears not to drive recovery in GBS as tested.

PROTECT (NCT02145182) missed its DGF endpoint (35.9% vs 41.7%, p=0.40) with no safety excess. Eculizumab neutralizes plasma C5, a systemic target. Complete terminal complement inhibition at approved doses is documented directly: free C5 below 0.5 µg/ml in gMG and NMOSD (PMID:34795626, PMID:34803867), and free C5 lowered 99.99% in GBS (PMID:38987228). Classical-pathway blockade was also shown in transplant-rejection patients (PMID:28647502, published after the index start). Pathway is inferred adequate: sC5b-9 fell in aHUS (PMID:25833956), and the drug met efficacy endpoints in aHUS, PNH and NMOSD through plasma C5. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The related AMR-prevention trial also failed (NCT01399593). With the target engaged and no benefit, the evidence points to C5 not driving DGF as tested.

No direct PK, IL-1 binding or biomarker data in gout patients. Pillars are inferred adequate because rilonacept 160 mg weekly with a 320 mg loading dose met gout-flare prevention endpoints in gout patients (PMID:22223180, PMID:22549879, PMID:23485476, PMID:25028379) and succeeded in CAPS and pericarditis (NCT03737110, PMID:22096352). Canakinumab is approved in gout, so IL-1 is a valid target. The index trial gave a single 320 mg SC dose for an established acute flare. Pain at 24-72 h did not separate from indomethacin, rilonacept monotherapy was slower, and groups were similar by 72 h (PMID:23375025). This points to a timing/setting mismatch (F4). The add-on-to-active-NSAID design likely limited detectable benefit (F7). The sources do not state the cause explicitly, so confidence is low.

Index trial NCT01945086 used the approved psoriasis doses (45 and 90 mg) and showed no separation from placebo on EASI at week 12 (-37.5% placebo vs -38.6% and -39.4%). There were no serious AEs, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. Exposure, IL-12/23 p40 engagement and pathway effect are inferred adequate. At the same doses, in the same tissue compartment (skin), ustekinumab met pivotal endpoints in psoriasis before the index trial started (NCT00747344, NCT01008995, NCT01090427), so the pillars must have held there. No engagement data in atopic dermatitis appear in the bundle. The likely conclusion is that p40-mediated signalling does not drive atopic eczema. The large placebo response (~38%) may have reduced assay sensitivity, so F7 is listed as secondary.

No pillar was measured directly in axial SpA. However, the same 45/90 mg SC doses met ACR20 in psoriatic arthritis (NCT01009086, NCT01077362), a related musculoskeletal disease acting through IL-12/23p40 blockade. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. PK is comparable across indications (PMID:35442011). In nr-axSpA, ASAS20 at week 24 was 47.6% on placebo versus 55.4% and 49.4% on drug (NCT02407223). The sister radiographic axSpA trial also failed at both doses (NCT02437162), which prompted termination of this trial and NCT02438787. Safety was unremarkable and the dose was not capped. Real-world data show no response in axial SpA despite peripheral responses (PMID:32981373), consistent with IL-12/23 not driving axial disease.

In the open-label PBC study, ustekinumab 90 mg SC (weeks 0 and 4, then q8w) reached steady-state serum concentrations by week 12, so systemic exposure was adequate (PMID:26597786). Target engagement and pathway effects were not measured in PBC. Both are inferred_adequate: the same 90 mg regimen neutralizing circulating IL-12/23 p40 met pivotal endpoints in psoriatic arthritis (NCT01009086, NCT01077362) and psoriasis, and related doses succeeded in Crohn disease (NCT01369329, NCT01369342). The psoriasis approval predates the index trial. Tolerability was good, with no dose cap. Despite this, no patient achieved an ALP response; the median ALP reduction was only 12% (NCT01389973). This points to IL-12/23 not driving cholestasis in UDCA-refractory PBC. No same-target drug succeeded in PBC.

Ustekinumab neutralizes systemic IL-12/23 p40. It met pivotal endpoints in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (NCT00747344, NCT01009086, NCT01369329, NCT01369342, NCT02407236) at comparable doses, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. The bundle shows no direct target-engagement biomarker in SLE patients. Tolerability did not limit the dose: SAEs were similar to placebo. Despite a positive phase 2a SRI-4 result (NCT02349061; PMID:37807057), the phase 3 index trial was stopped for futility at interim analysis, with SRI-4 numerically favouring placebo (56.0% vs 43.9%) (NCT03517722). An adequately engaged IL-12/23 blockade therefore did not drive benefit in SLE as tested. SLE heterogeneity is a possible contributor, but the bundle does not state it.

The index trial NCT05890118 is a Phase 1 PK study of oral RaniPill ustekinumab in healthy volunteers, with Cmax/Tmax/AUC endpoints. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Exposure, engagement and pathway are not measured in Sjogren patients. They are inferred adequate because subcutaneous/IV ustekinumab met pivotal endpoints through systemic IL-12/23 p40 neutralization in Crohn's, psoriatic arthritis and psoriasis (NCT01369342, NCT01009086, NCT00747344). Biosimilar PK studies confirm systemic exposure (PMID:37212315, PMID:37483071). The only Sjogren data is an 8-patient pilot (NCT04093531) showing a negligible ESSPRI change of -0.125. That suggests the target may not matter in this disease (F2), but the pilot is too small to be conclusive (F7).

The index trial (NCT03981744; PMID:37652554) gave ~6 mg/kg IV, then 90 mg SC every 8 weeks. This is the same regimen that met pivotal endpoints in Crohn disease (UNITI-1/2, IM-UNITI) and ulcerative colitis (NCT02407236). Ustekinumab also succeeded in psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis by neutralizing systemic IL-12/23p40. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, although none was measured in myositis patients. The drug was safe and well tolerated, with no dose limitation. Despite this, IMACS TIS minimal improvement was 64.0% vs 61.5% on placebo (p=0.94), suggesting p40 blockade does not drive PM/DM. The high placebo response in a small trial (n=51) is a possible contributing design issue (F7).

The index trial NCT05890118 is a Phase 1 PK study of oral ustekinumab via RaniPill in healthy volunteers, with Cmax/Tmax/AUC endpoints. It is not an efficacy test of ustekinumab in ichthyosis, so F9 applies. Plasma exposure of subcutaneous ustekinumab is well characterized (PMID:37212315, PMID:37483071). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from the psoriasis efficacy approvals (NCT00747344, NCT01008995), which act through the same IL-12/23 p40 target in skin. In ichthyosis itself, an open-label study gave a modest, variable TISS reduction (NCT04549792). A Netherton case series showed no significant benefit and no change in IL-17 immunostaining (PMID:36419401). These hint at a weak mechanism in ichthyosis (secondary F2), but no engagement was measured in ichthyosis patients.

Ustekinumab was dosed at 180 mg then 90 mg q8w SC (PMID:25034562), equal to or above the doses that met pivotal endpoints. These include psoriasis (45 mg; NCT00747344), PsA (45/90 mg; NCT01009086) and Crohn's disease (NCT01369342), all via IL-12/23 p40. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. No direct engagement was measured in sarcoidosis. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limiting. FVC did not improve versus placebo (numerically worse), and no secondary endpoint improved. Case reports of ustekinumab-induced or aggravated sarcoidosis (PMID:32178618, PMID:35644583) further argue that IL-12/23 does not drive the disease as tested. The post-hoc transcriptome analysis cites marked molecular heterogeneity across phenotypes (PMID:28205212), supporting secondary F3.

In NCT01917006, no onabotulinumtoxinA dose changed IELT versus placebo (p=0.26–0.86), with no dose-response. Serious AEs were 0 in every arm, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Engagement is inferred_adequate rather than measured here: the drug is approved for skeletal-muscle chemodenervation indications (cervical dystonia, blepharospasm) through SNAP25 cleavage. Healthy-volunteer M-wave data show 70–80% paralysis at low doses (PMID:9222189), but nothing shows engagement in PE patients or in the bulbospongiosus, and dose comparability is unverified. The rationale was hypothesis-only (PMID:19683401), and later open-label signals are weak (PMID:40399413), suggesting the mechanism does not drive PE. Very small arms (n=5–8; F7) and a stated business termination (F8) also apply, so confidence is low.

In NOVA (NCT03779841, PMID:38661602), neither dose cut post-operative AF compared with placebo, and the higher 250 U dose showed no effect. I found no human evidence that the toxin given into the epicardial fat pads blocked autonomic cholinergic signalling: no heart-rate-variability, vagal-response or denervation measurements. The pages I searched report none either. Approvals in muscle and gland disorders involve different tissues and doses, so they do not establish engagement in the heart. A related trial (PMID:30414840) and a meta-analysis (PMID:38343481) were also negative, but neither measured engagement. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that failed to engage from an autonomic target that does not matter, so the code is U. AbbVie pointed to subgroup benefit (older CABG-only patients; F3), and the authors called the trial hypothesis-generating and asked for an adequately powered trial (F7).

Dysport 300 U and 500 U, given by local injection, did not beat placebo on daily NPRS at Week 8 in hallux abducto valgus (NCT03569098). Placebo improved by 2.04 points versus 1.71 and 2.40 on drug. No SNAP25 or denervation measure was taken in HAV. However, the same toxin met efficacy endpoints through local SNAP25 cleavage at comparable unit doses: approved for cervical dystonia, where 500 U is the standard dose (PMID:25414799), and for cerebral palsy, plus glabellar-line trials (NCT01333397, NCT03736928). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose (one serious AE). The drug also failed repeatedly in other musculoskeletal pain trials (NCT01518257, NCT02230956, NCT03137407, NCT03825315). This suggests the mechanism does not drive HAV pain.

The index trial NCT04102501 tested RT001, a different investigational agent, against placebo in Friedreich ataxia. It is not a trial of botulinum toxin type A, a SNAP25-cleaving protein with many local-injection approvals. Its missed peak VO2 endpoint (p=0.5858) therefore says nothing about this drug's efficacy through SNAP25. The bundle holds no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for botulinum toxin in Friedreich ataxia. The only related source is a case series noting toxin use for foot deformity in this disease (PMID:15662315), with no controlled efficacy data. The failure is best coded as not an efficacy test of this drug (F9). If the attribution were taken at face value, the absent engagement data would make it indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01209689 tested IV tocilizumab 4 or 8 mg/kg in anti-TNF-inadequate AS. ASAS20 was 12.7% vs 14.3% for placebo, and the program was terminated for lack of efficacy. No AS-specific pharmacodynamic data are in the bundle. However, the same systemic IL-6R blockade at the same IV doses met clinical endpoints in RA (NCT00773461, NCT01007435) and in JIA (NCT00642460, NCT00988221), and the drug is approved for GCA. So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Healthy-volunteer data show sIL-6R/CRP and neutrophil pharmacodynamic effects (PMID:35354411, PMID:28796316). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Sarilumab on the same target reached phase 3 in AS without approval. IL-6R blockade engaged but gave no benefit, so IL-6 does not appear to drive AS signs and symptoms.

Index trial NCT02888080 (300 mg) missed: FVC %pred change -1.90 vs placebo +0.52, so no trend toward benefit. Engagement with circulating IL-1β was shown directly in humans, as rises in total IL-1β complex in gout and SJIA (PMID:24122883, PMID:27119439, PMID:19364880), all published before the index start. Dose-dependent hsCRP/IL-6 lowering at up to 300 mg shows the pathway effect (PMID:28855077, PMID:24122883). Lung tissue exposure was not measured. It is inferred from clinical efficacy at comparable doses in tissue-based IL-1β diseases (gout, SJIA, CAPS). Engagement was never shown in sarcoidosis patients. With adequate systemic engagement and no benefit, IL-1β blockade appears not to drive pulmonary sarcoidosis as tested. The small n=40 trial limits certainty (F7).

Canakinumab clearly binds circulating IL-1β in humans. Total serum IL-1β rose and CRP/SAA fell in gout, SJIA and CAPS (PMID:24122883, 27119439, 19364880), so systemic exposure and engagement are established. For Alzheimer's the target sits in the brain, though. The index trial NCT04795466 listed total IL-1β in serum and CSF as a target-engagement marker, but the pages I retrieved showed no values, and I found no CSF drug levels or evidence of central engagement. Systemic approvals do not cover the CNS compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred. The trial was small (34 enrolled, 10 vs 16 analysed), the sponsor ended it without saying why, and NTB showed no difference (p=0.64). Nothing separates a drug that never engaged centrally from a target that does not matter, so the code is U; F7 is secondary because of the small size.

In the index trial (NCT03484923), canakinumab plus spartalizumab gave a 4.7% ORR in previously treated melanoma, no better than the other combination arms. In humans, systemic exposure and IL-1β binding are directly shown: total IL-1β complex rises after dosing, and IL-1β production is normalized (PMID:24122883, PMID:19364880, PMID:27119439). Downstream pathway markers also moved: dose-dependent hsCRP and IL-6 falls in CANTOS (PMID:28855077) and in T2DM (PMID:25240532). Efficacy across seven approved IL-1β-driven diseases supports adequate systemic neutralization. No dose limitation is evident. Engagement was never measured in melanoma or in tumour tissue, which lowers confidence. Even so, a well-engaged IL-1β blockade added no antitumour benefit to PD-1 blockade. This points to the mechanism not driving response in this setting (F2).

In T2DM patients, canakinumab exposure was dose-proportional (PMID:25240532). Target binding was measured directly as rising total IL-1β complex in gout and CAPS (PMID:24122883, PMID:19364880), the latter with RA data (PMID:18534016) available near the index start. Approvals in systemic IL-1β-driven diseases at similar 150 mg doses corroborate this. Pathway: hsCRP and IL-6 fell dose-dependently in T2DM (PMID:25240532, PMID:27737744). Tolerability was good with no dose cap (PMID:24884602). Despite this, HbA1c fell only 0.06–0.18% versus placebo, with no dose response. Beta-cell and insulin-secretion measures did not change (PMID:24075453, NCT01068860, NCT00995930), and the trial stopped for futility (NCT00900146). The IL-1β mechanism, though engaged, does not meaningfully drive glycaemia in T2DM.

No OA-knee PK or target data are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate because canakinumab met pain and flare endpoints in gout, also IL-1β-driven joint inflammation (NCT01029652, NCT01080131). Gout patients showed IL-1β binding and CRP lowering (PMID:24122883), and CAPS/RA data published before 2010 showed binding (PMID:19364880, PMID:18534016).
