In the index trial a single intra-articular dose (up to 600 mg, well tolerated) gave no pain benefit. However, the naproxen active control also failed to separate from placebo (VAS -27.6 vs -26.5; WOMAC -4.5 vs -4.0) against a large placebo response, so the trial lacked assay sensitivity. Hence F7 primary, with F2 secondary (IL-1β may not drive OA pain). CANTOS joint-replacement signals are exploratory (PMID:32744862).

Canakinumab is a systemic anti-IL-1β antibody. Several sources measured exposure, target binding and pathway effects directly in humans. PK was dose-proportional, and total IL-1β complexes rose after dosing, showing binding to circulating IL-1β (PMID:24122883, PMID:19364880, PMID:27119439). CRP and SAA fell dose-dependently, including in T2DM and atherosclerosis patients (PMID:25240532, PMID:28855077). Most of this evidence predates the 2013 index start. No engagement data were collected in AAA patients, and the index dose is not shown in the bundle. In NCT02007252, AAA growth did not differ from placebo (12-month 2.54 vs 2.58 mm/yr, p=0.48), and the trial stopped for futility. So IL-1β neutralization did not slow aneurysm growth. The small, ad hoc-terminated trial adds some design uncertainty (F7).

Canakinumab's systemic exposure and IL-1β binding are shown in patients: dose-proportional PK, rising total IL-1β complexes and an in vivo Kd in gout, CAPS and T2DM (PMID:24122883, PMID:19364880, PMID:25240532). CRP fell in RA in 2008 (PMID:18534016), before the index trial. In atherosclerosis patients (CANTOS), hsCRP and IL-6 fell 26-43% dose-dependently (PMID:28855077, published after the index start). No engagement data exist in PAD itself. Despite adequate pillars, MRI vessel wall area did not improve: ratio 1.06 [0.97, 1.15], p=0.284, numerically worse than placebo (NCT01731990). A carotid/aortic imaging trial also failed (NCT00995930). The index trial was small (n=21 analysed) with an exploratory imaging endpoint, and CANTOS showed some MACE reduction (NCT01327846), so underpowering or the endpoint choice may have contributed.

The single 10 mg/kg IV canakinumab dose did not separate from placebo on NEI corneal staining at Week 4 (0.12 vs 0.26; NCT01250171). Safety was clean. The same 10 mg/kg IV dose gave dose-proportional plasma exposure, bound circulating IL-1β and lowered CRP/hsCRP in RA and T2DM, published before 2010 (PMID:18534016, PMID:25240532, PMID:24122883, PMID:19364880). Canakinumab also met efficacy endpoints in systemic IL-1β diseases (CAPS, SJIA). So systemic IL-1β neutralization held and engagement is inferred adequate. However, no tear or ocular-surface drug levels or IL-1β engagement were measured in dry eye patients. Local penetration therefore remains unverified, which leaves U as a possibility. The bundle names no other cause, so F2 is assigned with low confidence.

Exposure was dose-proportional in T2DM patients (PMID:25240532). Engagement is inferred adequate: canakinumab binds circulating IL-1β (PMID:24122883, PMID:19364880) and met efficacy endpoints through systemic IL-1β at comparable 150 mg doses in CAPS and gout (NCT01362608, NCT00819585). Pathway was adequate: hsCRP fell dose-dependently in T2DM (PMID:25240532) and in CANTOS (PMID:28855077). No tolerability cap is shown. Despite this, aortic distensibility was unchanged and the plaque trends were not significant in T2DM/IGT patients (NCT00995930). Glycemic endpoints also failed (NCT00900146, NCT01068860). This suggests IL-1β does not drive these outcomes as tested. CANTOS later showed a MACE benefit in atherosclerosis (NCT01327846), so imaging surrogates may have been insensitive (F4). Engagement was not measured in prediabetes, and that evidence postdates the index trial.

Canakinumab neutralizes circulating IL-1β, a systemic target. Plasma exposure and binding (rise in total IL-1β complex) were shown in patients with gout, SJIA and CAPS (PMID:24122883, PMID:27119439, PMID:19364880), all published before the index trial started. Dose-dependent hsCRP and IL-6 lowering is documented (PMID:28855077). The drug met efficacy endpoints in several IL-1β-driven diseases (NCT00889863, NCT01029652). In sickle cell patients, canakinumab lowered inflammatory markers (PMID:39568425), but direct engagement was not measured in this disease. Despite this, daily pain VAS did not separate from placebo (difference -0.07, p=0.55; NCT02961218), and tolerability was not limiting. Reading: IL-1β blockade does not drive SCD pain as tested. PMID:39568425 suggests organ-damage endpoints rather than vaso-occlusion measures, so F4 is secondary.

Canakinumab's systemic exposure and binding to circulating IL-1β (rising total IL-1β complex) are shown in humans with gout, SJIA and CAPS (PMID:24122883, 27119439, 19364880; CAPS data published 2009, before the index trial). CRP, SAA and hsCRP fall dose-dependently (PMID:24122883, 25240532, 28855077, 18534016). No engagement data exist in PMR itself. The index trial (NCT01364389) gave 3 mg/kg IV, comparable to effective doses, with no tolerability limit. PMR-AS fell 64.5% versus 91.9% with prednisone, and the sponsor stopped because the effect did not match steroids. IL-1β blockade therefore appears insufficient to drive PMR. Caveats are the tiny arms (n=3), the active comparator and the 2-week horizon (F7/F4).

Canakinumab neutralizes circulating (systemic) IL-1β. Before the index trial, human data showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:25240532, 24122883) and direct target binding, seen as increases in total IL-1β complex (PMID:24122883, 27119439, 19364880). Dose-dependent CRP and IL-6 lowering confirmed the pathway effect (PMID:28855077, 25240532). Efficacy in IL-1β-driven diseases (NCT00889863, NCT01029652) further supports adequate engagement. In COVID-19, a small case-control study reported falling inflammatory markers (PMID:33385581), but this is pathway evidence published after the index trial started, not direct engagement data. No tolerability cap is shown; serious adverse events and deaths were not in excess. Despite this, NCT04362813 showed no benefit on survival without invasive ventilation (OR 1.39, p=0.29). IL-1β neutralization, as tested, did not drive outcomes in COVID-19 pneumonia.

Canakinumab neutralizes circulating IL-1β, a systemic target. In other diseases its human PK and target binding are well characterized: total IL-1β complex rises after dosing and CRP, SAA and IL-6 fall (PMID:24122883, PMID:27119439, PMID:19364880, PMID:28855077). It met efficacy endpoints and is approved in CAPS, SJIA and gout, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. The bundle has no engagement data in COVID-19 CRS patients beyond one case report (PMID:32983123). The index trial (NCT04362813) missed its primary endpoint of survival without mechanical ventilation (OR 1.39, p=0.29) and showed no tolerability problem. This points to IL-1β blockade not driving outcomes in COVID-19 CRS. A secondary concern is the high placebo event-free rate (86%), which may have limited power.

The index ORCHARRD trial (NCT01014208, PMID:28029326) tested ofatumumab-DHAP against rituximab-DHAP, an active comparator on the same CD20 target, for superiority. Outcomes were equivalent: PFS HR 1.12, OS HR 0.90. CD20 depletion is a validated mechanism in DLBCL through rituximab, so this is not an efficacy failure of the mechanism. The drug simply was not better than the standard anti-CD20. Engagement is shown in humans: dose-dependent B-cell depletion in MS (PMID:29695594, PMID:35233753) and CD20 loss with C3d deposition on CLL cells (PMID:39774793). Exposure is inferred adequate from Phase 3 PFS wins in CLL at 1000 mg IV (NCT00824265, NCT00748189), the dose used in the index trial. No DLBCL-specific engagement data are in the bundle. Secondary F2: the proposed added mechanism gave no incremental benefit.

CCH is injected locally to lyse collagen. It met efficacy endpoints in collagenous fascial and fibrous tissue: Dupuytren's cords (NCT00528606, NCT02193828), Peyronie plaque (NCT01221597, NCT01221623) and cellulite septae. NCT04236635 showed histologic change in injected tissue. Local exposure and collagen engagement are therefore inferred adequate, though not measured in plantar fascia. The index trial (NCT06169319) posted no results and gave no stop reason. A sister plantar fibromatosis trial also missed its pain endpoint (NCT05152173). No tolerability cap or other same-target drug appears. The most direct reading is that collagen lysis does not relieve the pain of plantar fasciitis, a degenerative rather than contractile fibrotic condition. Confidence is low because the index data and dose are absent.

In TOSCA-5 (NCT01753180), collagenase (MZ-004) was injected into the lesion before attempting a guidewire crossing of chronic total occlusions (CTOs). Overall crossing was 74% vs 63% with placebo (p=0.52), so the primary endpoint was not met. Crossing with a soft-tip wire was significantly higher on drug (0/17/29%, p=0.03). The investigators called the drug safe and supported a pivotal trial. No source measured, in humans, how much drug stayed in the plaque or how much collagen it broke down inside a coronary CTO. Plaque digestion was shown only in rabbits. The Dupuytren and Peyronie approvals cannot stand in for this, because they involve a different tissue compartment. The engagement evidence is therefore missing, so the code is U. The trial was small, with 76 patients, and the soft-wire signal may point to an underpowered design (F7).

Locally injected collagenase met pivotal endpoints at 0.58 mg in Dupuytren contracture and Peyronie disease (NCT01221597, NCT01221623; FDA approvals). This lets us infer adequate collagen lysis in injected fibrotic tissue at the dose used in shoulder trials (0.58 mg, PMID:32764872). Human histology also showed tissue change after injection (NCT04236635). The inference rests on palmar and penile tissue, not the shoulder capsule. Earlier shoulder trials showed only small, uncertain gains in range of motion over placebo or exercise (NCT02006719, NCT01483963). The index trial showed no ASES difference (41.35 vs 41.16, p=0.659). Large improvement in both arms, consistent with the condition resolving on its own, may have masked any benefit (PMID:32764872). Overall, capsular collagen lysis did not translate into clinical benefit.

Albiglutide's plasma PK is well characterized: half-life about 6–8 days and dose-dependent exposure (PMID:19187286, PMID:18812476). GLP1R engagement is inferred adequate because the same 30 mg weekly systemic dose met HbA1c endpoints in T2D Phase 3 trials before the index trial (NCT00849017, NCT00849056). It was not measured in heart-failure patients. In NCT01357850, 30 mg was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Yet myocardial glucose use, myocardial efficiency, LVEF and 6-minute walk did not change (PMID:27039125). The expected myocardial metabolic effect did not follow. A modest peak VO2 gain was attributed to possibly noncardiac effects. GLP1R agonism does not appear to drive HFrEF as tested. The small PET subgroups (n=4–11) limit power.

Albiglutide 30–50 mg weekly, the index dose, met HbA1c endpoints in multiple T2D Phase 3 trials (NCT00849017, NCT00849056, NCT00838903) and is approved for T2D. That shows systemic exposure, GLP1R engagement and a glycemic pathway effect, so these pillars are inferred_adequate. Earlier PK/PD studies showed dose-dependent glucose lowering (PMID:18812476, PMID:19863477). No direct GLP1R engagement measure exists in T1D patients. In new-onset T1D, one year of albiglutide did not preserve stimulated C-peptide (posterior difference 0.12 nmol/L, low probability of a ≥0.2 nmol/L difference), apart from a transient week-28 peak C-peptide difference (PMID:32219329). Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the mechanism engaged at the approved dose and no benefit, GLP1R agonism does not appear to drive beta-cell preservation in T1D.

The index trial (NCT01480596; PMID:29661905) used 10 mg/kg IV, the approved SLE dose. It missed QMG at week 24 (-1.84, p=0.256) and all secondary endpoints, with no tolerability limit. Human PK at 10 mg/kg is well characterised (PMID:31953740, PMID:27536436). B-cell reductions in SLE patients show the downstream pathway effect (PMID:19714604, PMID:31953740). Engagement is inferred adequate because belimumab met pivotal endpoints in SLE and lupus nephritis via systemic BLyS neutralisation at comparable doses (NCT01345253, NCT01484496, NCT01639339). The bundle has no engagement or B-cell data in MG patients; AChR antibodies fell in both arms. A mechanism engaged at the approved dose without benefit points to F2. The small trial (n=40) leaves underpowering as a possible contributor (F7).

The program disease label appears to be a mislabel. The index trial NCT03271047 tested nivolumab+binimetinib with or without ipilimumab in MSS RAS-mutant colorectal cancer. ORR was 7.4% with ipilimumab versus 0% without, so the primary endpoint was missed. No CTLA4 engagement or pathway data exist in CRC patients. However, ipilimumab is FDA-approved in melanoma, NSCLC, mesothelioma and esophageal cancer through the same systemic T-cell CTLA4 mechanism at comparable doses (PMID:35835722). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, and dual blockade shows pharmacodynamic immune activation (PMID:42838943). Phase 1b DLTs (2/11) did not cap the dose. The failure suggests CTLA4 blockade does not drive benefit in this immunologically cold MSS subtype (secondary F3).

The index trial NCT03130959 (nivolumab ± ipilimumab in pediatric high-grade CNS tumors) reported only descriptive endpoints. It found no DLTs in the safety lead-in, so the dose was not capped. Outcomes were poor: median OS was 10.78 months with nivolumab+ipilimumab versus 11.66 with nivolumab alone, and median PFS was about 1.2–4.6 months. No statistical comparison was made. The bundle has no CTLA4 engagement data in this disease. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because ipilimumab is FDA-approved through systemic CTLA4 blockade in several cancers before 2017, including a pediatric indication and brain metastases. Adding ipilimumab gave no apparent benefit, which points to the target not driving these tumors (F2). Because the endpoints were descriptive and the trial was classified as not an efficacy test, F9 also applies.

The index trial NCT01148615 was a small Phase 1 study of IV aflibercept with docetaxel in Chinese solid-tumor patients. Its only primary endpoint was cycle-1 dose-limiting toxicity. It completed, gave no stop reason and posted no efficacy results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. The pillars are inferred_adequate: systemic aflibercept met its PFS endpoint with FOLFIRI in metastatic colorectal cancer (NCT01661270) through the same VEGF/PlGF target in the systemic compartment. Plasma free-VEGF lowering in humans is also reported (PMID:28106709). None of this evidence comes from childhood cancer, and all of it postdates the index trial. Nothing shows the dose was capped by tolerability.

Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Intravitreal aflibercept 2 mg, the same dose and intraocular compartment against VEGF, met pivotal endpoints in wet AMD, CRVO and DME (NCT00637377, NCT00943072, NCT01363440). Case series in NVG show NVI regression (PMID:26016631, PMID:40020147). In the index trial (n=54), the week-1 IOP change favoured aflibercept (-8.5 vs -4.9 mmHg), but the difference was not significant (p=0.064; CI -10.2 to 0.3). The sham response was large and variability was high. The single-arm follow-up NCT03639675 met its IOP endpoint (-8.3 mmHg, p=0.0004). This pattern points to a small, underpowered trial with a noisy, early surrogate endpoint rather than an inert mechanism. No source states the reason directly, so this is inferred.

Vitreous PK showed high ocriplasmin activity after intravitreal injection (NCT01159665). The same 125 µg intravitreal dose met VMA-resolution endpoints in MIVI-TRUST and later phase 3 trials (NCT00781859, NCT00798317, NCT01429441), so engagement and the vitreolytic pathway are inferred adequate in the vitreous compartment. In wet AMD, VMA release at Day 28 was 24.3% vs 12.0%, similar to the drug-arm rate in the pivotal trials, but not significant (p=0.262; small 25-patient sham arm). At month 12 there was more VMA release, more PVD and fewer anti-VEGF injections, yet no visual acuity benefit (PMID:25435217). Releasing the adhesion did not translate into clinical benefit in AMD (F2). Secondary codes: the trial was underpowered (F7), and real-world data link concomitant macular pathology to treatment failure (F3; PMID:28681138).

Ocriplasmin reached the vitreous in humans, with high vitreous activity levels shown by PK (NCT01159665). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate. The same intravitreal 125 µg dose met Phase 3 VMA-resolution endpoints through proteolysis of vitreoretinal fibronectin and laminin (NCT00781859, NCT00798317, NCT01429441, NCT01889251; PMID:25582211). The index trial in NPDR used 0.0625 and 0.125 mg and produced zero total PVD in every arm (NCT02681809). This mirrors the failed total-PVD endpoint in the paediatric trial (NCT00986362) and suggests the mechanism does not induce total PVD in this setting. The trial was terminated early for slow recruitment, so it was small (F7 secondary). The complete absence of events in the drug arms still argues against a power problem alone. No engagement data exist in NPDR.

In the phase 1 study (PMID:20048182), mean troughs exceeded biologically relevant target levels at all doses, which shows exposure. Serum VEGF-A rose 1.5–3.5x, consistent with receptor blockade, and tumor perfusion fell in 69% of patients, which supports engagement and pathway. PK was also confirmed at 8–10 mg/kg (NCT01682135, NCT01005355). The same mechanism with docetaxel improved survival in NSCLC (NCT01168973), and the drug met endpoints in gastric and colorectal cancer, so engagement is also inferred adequate there. Dose was not capped by tolerability. Despite this, ROSE/TRIO-012 missed PFS (HR 0.88, p=0.077), and two other breast trials (NCT01234402, NCT01427933) also failed. VEGFR2 blockade does not meaningfully drive HER2-negative breast cancer outcomes. Engagement was not shown specifically in breast cancer patients.

Ramucirumab 8 mg/kg q2w monotherapy in recurrent, largely platinum-resistant ovarian cancer gave PFS-6 25% and ORR 5%; the predetermined efficacy endpoints were not met (NCT00721162, PMID:25016924). Target engagement was shown in these patients: VEGF-A and PlGF rose and sVEGFR-2 fell after infusion (PMID:25016924). This was published after the index trial started. The Phase 1 study reported troughs above biologically relevant levels, dose-independent VEGF-A rises and reduced tumor perfusion in 69% of patients (PMID:20048182). The same dose met its endpoints in gastric cancer (NCT00917384, NCT01170663). The dose was not limited by tolerability. VEGFR-2 blockade alone therefore engaged the target but did not deliver adequate benefit in this population. A heavily pretreated, platinum-resistant population may have contributed (F3).

Adult phase 1 data show trough levels above biologically relevant targets at all doses, with a 1.5–3.5x serum VEGF-A rise (receptor blockade) and decreased tumor perfusion in 69% of patients (PMID:20048182). Ovarian PD showed increased VEGF-A and PlGF and decreased sVEGFR-2 (PMID:25016924). PK was confirmed in NCT01682135. Multiple phase 3 wins at 8 mg/kg (NCT01170663, NCT01168973, NCT01183780, NCT02435433) confirm the mechanism is engaged systemically. No dose cap by tolerability. Engagement was not measured in synovial sarcoma patients. In CAMPFIRE, adding ramucirumab to gem/docetaxel gave no PFS benefit (2.10 vs 2.03 mo, HR 2.62) and the trial met futility (NCT04145700). This points to VEGFR2 blockade not driving benefit here. The trial was small (n=23), so F7 is secondary.

The index trial NCT02586051 was a 24-patient Phase 1 desensitization study in hypersensitized ESRD patients. Its only primary outcome was the percentage with adverse events. It completed, gave no stop reason and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of obinutuzumab. Exposure is shown by dose-dependent serum levels and population PK (PMID:23046388, PMID:25353187, PMID:31050355). Engagement is shown by complete B-cell depletion after the first infusion (PMID:23046388, published 2013, before the index trial) in lymphoma, not ESRD. Pathway is inferred_adequate from efficacy through CD20 B-cell depletion in lupus nephritis (NCT02550652) and CLL (NCT01010061). The bundle shows no efficacy failure, so the code is F9. Confidence is medium because no results or stop reason were posted.

Siltuximab reached adequate serum exposure across diseases including myeloma (PMID:31482226, PMID:25784388). Direct IL-6 binding was not measured in humans. Engagement is inferred_adequate because the drug met its endpoint in multicentric Castleman disease at 11 mg/kg q3w, the same systemic IL-6 target (NCT01024036, approved 2014). The pathway pillar held: PK/PD data from NCT00412321, including multiple myeloma patients, show CRP suppressed below 1 mg/L at that regimen (PMID:25784388, PMID:22828917). No such data exist for smoldering myeloma itself. Despite this, one-year PFS was 84.5% vs 74.4% and missed the threshold (NCT01484275), consistent with the null siltuximab+VMP myeloma trial (NCT00911859). IL-6 neutralization therefore does not drive progression as tested. A small trial (n=85) leaves possible underpowering.

Siltuximab 15 mg/kg q4w did not reduce RBC transfusions in lower-risk MDS (12% vs 3.8%, p=0.271). The trial was stopped at the futility analysis with no safety concerns (NCT01513317, PMID:24888488). IL-6 is a systemic soluble target. PK is well characterized (PMID:31482226). PK/PD modeling and observed data show sustained CRP suppression at 11 mg/kg q3w and 15 mg/kg q4w across diseases (PMID:25784388, PMID:20179212, PMID:22828917). Engagement is inferred adequate because the same dosing met the efficacy endpoint in multicentric Castleman disease (NCT01024036). No engagement or CRP data in MDS patients appear in the bundle. Adequate IL-6 blockade without benefit points to F2. The authors suggest selecting patients with elevated IL-6 or less iron overload, which supports F3 as secondary.

The index trial gave secukinumab 10 mg/kg IV and showed no ACQ benefit (difference -0.166, p=0.54; NCT01478360). No asthma PK or IL-17A engagement data appear in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 10 mg/kg IV dose met ASAS20 in ankylosing spondylitis before the index trial (NCT00809159). Secukinumab also succeeded in psoriasis, with downstream BD-2 normalization (NCT00941031, NCT01358578, PMID:27502297). However, airway tissue was not shown, and secukinumab did not attenuate ozone-induced airway neutrophilia in healthy volunteers (PMID:23277522). No other IL-17A agent has succeeded in asthma. The sponsor cited possible changes to population, endpoints or antibody (F3). The trial was small and terminated (F7).

The index trial gave 2×10 mg/kg IV secukinumab, the same IV dose that met ASAS20 in ankylosing spondylitis (NCT00809159, PMID:26699169). Systemic IL-17A neutralization also produced efficacy in psoriasis and PsA (NCT01358578, NCT01392326), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate. No direct engagement data in Crohn's patients exist, and that inference postdates the index start. Despite this, CDAI worsened versus placebo (PMID:22595313): the AUC analysis favoured placebo, and patients with high inflammatory markers did worse. Infections, including fungal ones, were more frequent on drug. Sources suggest IL-17A blockade alone is ineffective, or even protective-role-removing, in Crohn's (PMID:23998727, PMID:31198577). The target does not drive the disease as tested; on-target harm is a possible contributor (F5).

Secukinumab 300 mg, the dose used in SELUNE, met pivotal endpoints through systemic neutralization of soluble IL-17A in psoriasis, PsA and AS (NCT01358578, NCT01365455, NCT01392326, NCT01358175), with linear PK (PMID:28273356, PMID:40839197) and normalized IL-17A-driven biomarkers such as BD-2 (PMID:27502297). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate; none was measured in lupus nephritis. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. CRR at week 52 was numerically lower on drug (25.9% vs 38.6%) and no secondary endpoint differed, prompting termination for futility (NCT04181762, PMID:41092316). No subgroup, endpoint or design explanation is offered. The data suggest IL-17A blockade does not drive lupus nephritis as tested.

No target-engagement or biomarker data in lichen planus patients are in the bundle. Secukinumab 300 mg Q4W met endpoints in psoriasis (NCT01365455, NCT01358578), the same skin compartment at the same dose. Skin IL-17A pathway markers normalised there (PMID:27502297). So all three pillars are inferred_adequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose. In PRELUDE (NCT04300296, PMID:38735684), no lichen planus cohort met proof-of-concept, and the authors conclude IL-17A blockade was not effective (PMID:38715466). Case reports of lichen planus triggered by secukinumab (PMID:36628552, 37220295, 27726180) further suggest IL-17A does not drive this disease, hence F2. Secondary: responses differed by subtype, numerically favouring LPP and MLP (F3). Cohorts were small and placebo response in CLP was high (58%) (F7).

The bundle has no ocular-surface, tear or target-engagement data in dry eye. Engagement is inferred: the index trial gave a single 10 mg/kg IV dose. The same IV dose met ASAS20 in the ankylosing spondylitis proof-of-concept trial (NCT00809159), registered before the index trial, and secukinumab met endpoints in psoriasis (NCT00941031, NCT01071252). There, IL-17A-driven tissue biomarkers normalised (PMID:27502297), so systemic and tissue IL-17A neutralisation held at comparable exposure (PMID:28273356). Even so, NEI-CSS change at week 4 matched placebo (0.23 vs 0.26). This suggests IL-17A does not drive corneal staining in dry eye as tested. The secukinumab ocular programme in uveitis also failed (PMID:23290985). Caveats: the ocular-surface compartment is untested, and the trial was small, single-dose and only 4 weeks long.

The index trial is the extension of SHIELD (NCT00995709). SHIELD showed no reduction in ocular exacerbations at 300 mg SC q2w or q4w (PMID:23290985). Sister uveitis trials also failed (NCT01095250, NCT01032915). No exposure or IL-17A engagement data exist for Behçet's patients. Pillars are inferred adequate because the same 300 mg SC dose met pivotal endpoints through systemic IL-17A neutralization in psoriasis and AS (NCT01365455, NCT01358175, PMID:28273356). This points to IL-17A not driving Behçet's uveitis (F2). Paradoxical Behçet's flares on IL-17A blockade support this (PMID:39896301). Benefit appears confined to mucocutaneous-articular phenotypes (PMID:32381569, PMID:41703603), supporting F3. Higher IV doses outperformed 300 mg SC in uveitis (PMID:25638011), raising a possible dose question (F1a).

Secukinumab 150/300 mg, the doses used in NCT02008890, met large psoriasis endpoints (NCT01358578, NCT01365455, NCT01071252). Exposure is shown by PK (PMID:28273356). Skin IL-17A pathway effects (BD-2 and antimicrobial peptides normalized; histology response) are shown in psoriasis (PMID:27502297, NCT01537432). Skin-compartment engagement is therefore inferred adequate, though it was never measured in palmoplantar pustulosis. Even so, the index trial gave only marginal benefit: ppPASI75 was 26.6% on 300 mg vs 14.1% on placebo (p=0.04), and 150 mg did not separate. Reports of paradoxical PPP induced by IL-17 blockade (PMID:32293563) also suggest IL-17A is not a dominant driver of PPP. The 300 mg arm was nominally significant, so F9 also applies in part.

ENDURE (NCT01032915) used SC 150–300 mg regimens and showed no effect on recurrence. No IL-17A engagement or ocular exposure was measured in uveitis. Systemic neutralization is inferred adequate because the same SC doses met pivotal endpoints in psoriasis and AS (NCT01358578, NCT01365455, NCT01358175). That inference spans a different tissue compartment, which weakens it. SHIELD in Behçet's uveitis (NCT00995709) and INSURE also failed (PMID:23290985). PMID:32673565 offers a mechanistic reason: IL-17A loss does not reduce Th17 pathogenicity in uveitis. Behçet's flares on secukinumab fit this (PMID:31198577). A secondary F1a concern remains: high-dose IV gave better uveitis responses than 300 mg SC (PMID:25638011), so SC exposure may have been insufficient.

No pillar is measured directly. All three are inferred_adequate because secukinumab, at comparable doses through IL-17A, met pivotal endpoints in the index trial's own populations: psoriatic arthritis (NCT01392326) and ankylosing spondylitis (NCT01358175). These were registered before the index trial and led to approvals, including enthesitis-related JIA (PMID:35961761). Real-world data also show enthesitis improving on secukinumab (PMID:36089612). In NCT02771210, resolution of Achilles enthesitis was numerically higher (42% vs 31%, OR 1.63, CI 0.87–3.08). The miss reflects a substantial placebo response and limited power for a single-site clinician endpoint. A target that does not drive enthesitis is less consistent with the bundle, so F2 is secondary. The sources state no reason for the failure, so confidence is low.

In the index trial NCT03098030, adding dinutuximab to irinotecan gave no OS benefit in relapsed SCLC (6.9 vs 7.0 months). Safety was similar, and no stop reason or toxicity signal was given. The bundle has no SCLC-specific exposure, GD2 engagement or pharmacodynamic data. Dinutuximab is FDA-approved in neuroblastoma (NCT00026312), where it binds GD2 on tumor cells. Studies in neuroblastoma patients show antibody levels and GD2-specific ADCC/CDC (PMID:26785755, PMID:30336605), though these used ch14.18/CHO. So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from another GD2-positive tumor, which suggests GD2-directed ADCC does not drive benefit in SCLC as tested. Confidence is low: SCLC tumor GD2 expression and engagement are not shown, so U remains plausible.

The index trial NCT03055195 used mepolizumab 100 mg SC and stopped at a prespecified interim futility analysis. IGA 0/1 responders were 2/18 vs 0/16 on placebo, with no safety concerns. At this dose, systemic exposure and IL-5 neutralisation are well shown in humans. SC bioavailability is about 74%, and 99 mg gives about 90% of maximal eosinophil suppression (PMID:26445140, PMID:27128231). Blood eosinophils fall by about 78% long term (PMID:30359681). The same 100 mg dose met pivotal endpoints in asthma, and mepolizumab also met pivotal endpoints in HES and EGPA. Engagement was not measured in atopic dermatitis patients. With adequate IL-5 blockade and eosinophil depletion but no clinical benefit, IL-5/eosinophils appear not to drive atopic dermatitis as tested. The small trial (n=34) and early stop are a secondary design consideration.

The program disease label appears to mean microsatellite-stable (MSS) RAS-mutant colorectal cancer. In the index trial (NCT03271047), nivolumab plus binimetinib, with or without ipilimumab, gave ORRs of 0% and 7.4%. Phase 1b DLTs were few, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Nivolumab is FDA-approved through PD-1 blockade in many cancers, including Lynch syndrome (MSI-H colorectal cancer), at comparable systemic doses. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate; PK in NCT00836888 supports exposure. No engagement data exist in MSS patients. PD-1 blockade, even combined with MEK inhibition, did not produce responses in MSS colorectal cancer, so the mechanism does not drive this subtype as tested (F2). Benefit confined to MSI-H colorectal cancer also supports subtype selection (F3).

The index trial NCT01624246 was a 12-patient Phase 1 pharmacokinetic study of ceftaroline-avibactam in augmented renal clearance. Its primary outcomes were plasma PK parameters, so it was not an efficacy test and no failure is shown. Plasma exposure is well characterized (PMID:30380060, PMID:27431215). One human case report shows CSF penetration of 2.4–7.6%, with CSF levels above the MIC and clinical success (PMID:32461749). That report postdates the index trial and is a single case. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate from approved efficacy in pneumonia and skin infection (NCT00621504, NCT01499277). These are a different tissue compartment, so they do not establish efficacy in meningitis. A CSF penetration study (NCT02806882) exists but posted no results.

Lurasidone 20 and 60 mg missed ABC-Irritability versus placebo in pediatric autism (NCT01911442, PMID:26659550). Placebo improvement was large (-7.5), and CGI-I was positive only at 20 mg. Pediatric PK showed exposure similar to adults (PMID:26631428). Engagement was never measured in autism. It is only inferred from pediatric schizophrenia and bipolar depression wins at 20-80 mg (NCT01911429, NCT02046369). The PET data (PMID:24073841, published after the index trial started) suggest ≥65% D2 occupancy needs 80-160 mg and blood levels >70 ng/mL, so 20-60 mg may have under-engaged. Aripiprazole, also a D2 drug, is FDA-approved for autism irritability, which argues against the target being irrelevant. The most likely explanation is molecule or dose specific (F1b), with high placebo response (F7) as an alternative. Confidence is low.

Searches found no human data on exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker for trimethoprim against Plasmodium, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The index trial NCT01746199 (MACOMBA, PMID:23945130) tested daily co-trimoxazole for superiority against an active comparator, SP intermittent preventive treatment. It was not tested against placebo. The published report (PubMed 34407273) found only 13 placental infections in total: 5 in the co-trimoxazole arm and 8 in the SP arm. The difference numerically favoured co-trimoxazole but was not conclusive. The authors still supported its use because it was safe and women took it reliably. So the trial missed because of few events and limited power against an active drug, not because the drug clearly failed. Without engagement data, U is a secondary code.

Pasireotide LAR reached steady-state plasma exposure in GEP NET patients at 20–60 mg, with on-target metabolic effects such as hyperglycemia (PMID:23765178). In humans it engaged SSTRs strongly: dose-dependent GH suppression of 79–96% (PMID:22573933, PMID:16003295 before index start) and GH/IGF-1 control in acromegaly (PMID:24800725, NCT00600886). Tumor-level engagement in carcinoid patients was not shown, and tumor markers (CgA, NSE) showed no dose-response in a later NET study (PMID:28721067). The index trial (NCT00690430) compared it against octreotide LAR, which acts on the same mechanism, and found no symptom-control advantage (20.9% vs 26.7%). The likely explanation is that its broader SSTR1/3/5 agonism adds nothing over SSTR2 agonism for refractory carcinoid symptoms. The mechanism was engaged, but the added receptor profile does not drive benefit.

Pasireotide LAR gave dose-proportional plasma exposure at 20–60 mg (PMID:24800725, PMID:23765178). It suppressed pituitary GH in healthy volunteers and acromegaly patients (PMID:22573933, PMID:16003295). It met pivotal endpoints in acromegaly at comparable LAR doses (NCT00600886, NCT01137682), so SSTR engagement in pituitary adenoma tissue is inferred adequate. That engagement was not measured in non-functioning adenomas. In the index single-arm trial (NCT01283542) only 16.7% of 12 analysed patients reached ≥20% tumor shrinkage, and no other NFPA study advanced (NCT00929669 enrolled 2). The mechanism therefore appears not to drive meaningful tumor shrinkage in NFPA. The small uncontrolled design (F7) and possible SSTR-subtype heterogeneity (F3) also limit interpretation. Neither is stated in the sources.

Adding pasireotide LAR to everolimus gave no PFS benefit (HR 0.991, NCT01374451). Exposure is adequate: dose-proportional plasma troughs in GEP-NET patients at LAR 20–60 mg (PMID:23765178). Engagement is inferred adequate. The drug met pivotal endpoints in acromegaly at comparable LAR doses (NCT00600886, NCT01137682), with GH/IGF-1 suppression (PMID:24800725, PMID:22573933). On-target effects also appeared in NET patients: hyperglycemia (PMID:23765178) and IGF-1 falling with concentration (PMID:28721067). Both NET publications postdate the index start. Tumor markers (CgA, NSE) showed no dose-response (PMID:28721067), and no tolerability cap applied at MTD 120 mg. With systemic SSTR agonism shown, the extra SSTR agonism added nothing beyond everolimus in PNET, so the mechanism does not drive the outcome as tested.

The index trial tested a single 1.5 mg s.c. pasireotide dose in cluster headache and missed its primary endpoint: 30-min headache response 10/20 vs 9/20 on placebo, p=0.698 (NCT02619617). It stopped after cohort 1 with no safety signal, so dose was not limited. Plasma exposure is dose-proportional. Systemic SSTR engagement is shown in humans before the index trial: 79-96% GH suppression at 200-1200 µg (PMID:22573933, PMID:34741720). Efficacy in acromegaly and Cushing's at lower doses supports this (NCT00600886, NCT01374906). No headache-relevant pathway biomarker or CNS/trigeminal penetration data exist, and engagement was never shown in cluster headache patients. Given adequate systemic engagement, F2 is most likely. U remains plausible because target-site engagement is unshown.

Cabazitaxel met OS endpoints in prostate cancer at 20–25 mg/m² (NCT01308580), so systemic exposure and tubulin engagement are inferred adequate at those doses. Tumour microtubule-bundling evidence exists only in prostate patients and was published in 2020 (PMID:32478682). In the index GASTANA trial (NCT01497964, PMID:25486878), febrile neutropenia and prolonged neutropenia at 20 and 25 mg/m² forced dosing down to 15 mg/m², below the approved range. Response was 1 PR in 16 patients. Tolerability therefore capped the dose, and the mechanism was not tested at an adequate dose. Docetaxel, which acts on the same target, is approved in gastric cancer, which points to the molecule (F1b). Activity at 20 mg/m² was modest elsewhere and hinted at a HER2 subgroup (PMID:29285668, PMID:32641434).

Cabazitaxel lost clearly to topotecan in relapsed SCLC (median PFS 1.4 vs 3.0 months, HR 2.17; NCT01500720). The cause was lack of activity, not an underpowered or noisy trial. The drug is FDA-approved (2010) in prostate cancer through the same tubulin target at comparable systemic doses, with phase 3 OS success (NCT01308580). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Systemic plasma exposure is documented (PMID:37925350). Tumour microtubule bundling was shown in prostate cancer biopsies (PMID:32478682), but no engagement data exist in SCLC patients. No dose capping by tolerability is reported in the index trial. With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, tubulin-targeted cabazitaxel does not drive response in relapsed SCLC as tested (F2).

Ruxolitinib has dose-proportional systemic exposure. Healthy-volunteer studies showed whole-blood pSTAT3 inhibition tracking plasma levels, published 2011 before the index trial (PMID:21257798). It is approved in myelofibrosis at 10–20 mg BID with spleen responses (NCT01392443, NCT01348490), so the systemic JAK1/2 pathway effect is inferred_adequate at the index dose of 15 mg BID. The dose was not capped: 20 mg BID was well tolerated in the run-in (PMID:30123970). Engagement was not measured in colorectal cancer. Despite this, OS did not improve in the high-CRP inflammation substudy (HR 1.04, stopped for futility), the population the mechanism targeted. This points to JAK-STAT inflammation not driving outcome in refractory CRC. Substudy 2 (HR 0.77) was stopped early by the sponsor, which limits its interpretability (F7).

Ruxolitinib cream 1.5% BID, the same topical formulation and dose, met primary efficacy endpoints in atopic dermatitis (NCT03011892, PMID:41037525), vitiligo (NCT03099304) and psoriasis (NCT00778700) and is FDA-approved for AD and vitiligo. Exposure, JAK1/2 engagement and pathway effect in skin are therefore inferred adequate, though none were measured in lichen sclerosus. No dose limitation: there were no serious AEs on drug. The index trial (NCT05593445) showed no itch benefit: ITCH4 was 35.7% on drug vs 40.0% on vehicle, p=0.74. This suggests JAK1/2 inhibition does not drive lichen sclerosus itch as tested, despite a case report (PMID:38443119). The high vehicle response raises a possible design issue (F7). No same-target drug is approved in lichen sclerosus; delgocitinib is in phase 3 only.

Ruxolitinib has dose-proportional plasma exposure. Whole-blood pSTAT3 inhibition tracked plasma concentration in healthy volunteers, published 2011, before the 2014 index start (PMID:21257798, PMID:20699411). JAK2 engagement in the hematopoietic compartment is also supported by myelofibrosis efficacy (NCT01392443, approval). In transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, ruxolitinib significantly reduced spleen volume, a pathway effect consistent with suppressing ineffective erythropoiesis (PMID:34520107, which also cites a prior adult study). Despite this, the index trial (NCT02049450) produced only a -5.9% ±22% change in transfusion volume. JAK1/2 inhibition therefore does not reduce transfusion need in this disease, so F2. F4 is possible because a proximal effect (spleen) was shown without clinical benefit. Direct engagement was not measured in thalassemia patients.

Ruxolitinib 5 mg BID failed the hard composite in COVID-19 cytokine storm (OR 0.91, p=0.769; NCT04362137). Baricitinib, another JAK1/2 inhibitor, is FDA-approved for COVID-19, so the target can work in this disease. Exposure is dose-proportional (PMID:21257798). pSTAT3 inhibition tracked plasma concentration in healthy volunteers, but no engagement was measured in COVID patients. The index dose was low: only modest pSTAT3 inhibition was seen at 15 mg BID (PMID:36369506), and pSTAT reduction was variable in GVHD (PMID:38401793). Engagement at 5 mg BID was therefore likely partial. The failure is best read as the molecule and dose rather than the target (F1b), with possible under-engagement (F1a). The bundle is thin.

The index trial of ruxolitinib 5 mg BID in COVID-19 cytokine storm showed no benefit on death, ventilation or ICU (OR 0.91, p=0.769; NCT04362137). Oral exposure is dose-proportional, and plasma levels correlated with pSTAT3 inhibition in healthy volunteers (PMID:21257798, published 2011, before the index start; also PMID:34694880). Engagement and pathway are rated inferred_adequate: 5 mg dosing gave significant spleen reduction in myelofibrosis (NCT01348490), and the drug met endpoints in GVHD (NCT02953678). No JAK-STAT engagement was measured in COVID patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With systemic JAK1/2 inhibition plausibly achieved, the failure points to the mechanism not driving outcomes in COVID-associated hyperinflammation. Confidence is medium because the low 5 mg dose and the absence of in-disease pharmacodynamic data leave some uncertainty.

The randomized phase 2 trial of axitinib vs placebo in advanced HCC (NCT01210495) missed its OS endpoint (12.7 vs 9.7 mo, HR 0.907, p=0.29). Exposure in patients is documented (NCT00726752). Before the index trial, engagement was shown: exposure-dependent sVEGFR2 lowering (PMID:20180805) and ≥50% falls in DCE-MRI Ktrans at the clinical dose (PMID:16027440). In HCC patients, two-week perfusion drops and AFP declines followed (PMID:25565269, PMID:27033332). Axitinib also met its endpoint in RCC (NCT00678392). With the mechanism engaged and no survival benefit, the code is F2. F1b is excluded because engagement was adequate, even though other VEGFR drugs succeeded in HCC. The phase 2 authors called for biomarker-selected populations, so F3 is secondary.

The index trial NCT03316131 was a small crossover PK/PD study of verinurad plus febuxostat with dapagliflozin in asymptomatic hyperuricemia. Its primary outcomes were verinurad and metabolite PK and urinary uric acid excretion, reported descriptively without hypothesis testing. It was not an efficacy test of dapagliflozin, so it was not an efficacy failure (F9). Dapagliflozin's exposure is well characterised (NCT01525238, NCT02582840). SGLT2 engagement is shown by dose-related glucosuria (PMID:27291448), and the downstream effect by HbA1c lowering across many met Phase 3 trials (e.g., NCT00736879) and FDA approvals. The bundle shows no engagement data in hyperuricemia patients. The only uric acid data are in T2DM and were published after the index trial (PMID:38220410). No toxicity limited dosing.

For an antibiotic, engaging the target means killing bacteria at the site of infection. In the published IASIS index trial (NCT01969799), inhaled amikacin-fosfomycin given on top of IV antibiotics led to significantly fewer positive tracheal cultures on Days 3 and 7 than placebo. That shows the drug reached the airway and acted microbiologically in ventilated Gram-negative pneumonia patients. Exposure is rated adequate only by inference from this effect: the pages found give no fosfomycin airway concentrations. The clinical endpoints did not move: CPIS change was -0.76 vs -0.88, and mortality was 24% vs 17%. Commentaries describe the result as disappointing, with clinical outcomes similar despite lower bacterial burden. So an adjunctive inhaled mechanism that clearly engaged did not give clinical benefit (F2). CPIS as the endpoint may also have played a part (F4). This evidence was published after the trial started.

Plasma exposure in hematologic malignancies was measured in NCT00150462. Proteasome inhibition of up to 85% at 15 mg/m2 was shown in myeloma patients (PMID:23364621), before the index trial started. The pathway pillar is inferred from carfilzomib meeting pivotal PFS endpoints in myeloma (NCT01080391, NCT01568866) through the same target, systemic compartment and comparable doses. The index trial (NCT02303821, pediatric relapsed ALL) reached the 20/56 mg/m2 dose without a tolerability cap. Even so, complete remission rates after induction were low (14.8% B-cell, 13.6% T-cell). This suggests proteasome inhibition does not drive response in this setting. Caveats: the trial was single-arm with no prespecified threshold, it studied ALL rather than PLL, and the PLL trial NCT01212380 posted no outcomes. No engagement was shown in PLL or ALL.

Plasma exposure was characterised in hematologic malignancies (NCT00150462). Proteasome inhibition up to 85% at 15 mg/m2 was measured in myeloma patients (PMID:23364621, 2013), before the index trial started. Pathway is inferred_adequate because carfilzomib met PFS endpoints in myeloma at comparable or lower doses (NCT01080391, NCT01568866). The index trial (NCT02303821, pediatric relapsed ALL) escalated to 20/56 mg/m2 with chemotherapy, so the dose was not capped below engagement. Phase 2 CR rates were only about 14%, suggesting the proteasome mechanism did not add clear benefit in leukemia. No engagement data exist in CLL or ALL; the CLL trial NCT01212380 posted no results. The index trial was single-arm with no prespecified success threshold, so F9/F7 also apply. Confidence is low.

No direct human occupancy or biomarker data exist for perampanel's AMPA-receptor action. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate: the same brain AMPA target at 8–12 mg met pivotal endpoints in partial-onset seizures (NCT00699972, NCT00699582, NCT01618695) and PGTC seizures (NCT01393743), with exposure-response shown (PMID:23772853, PMID:29171002). In LGS (NCT02834793), drop-seizure reduction was numerically larger (-23% vs -4.5%) but not significant (p=0.107). With engagement inferred adequate, F2 applies: AMPA antagonism did not significantly reduce LGS drop seizures, and a case report notes paradoxical atonic worsening (PMID:37485229). The trial was terminated by sponsor decision with only 70 core-phase patients analysed, so underpowering (F7) is plausible, but no source states this.

In PHN (NCT00592774), perampanel showed small, inconsistent pain changes versus placebo across cohorts, with no reported significance. No PK, receptor occupancy or biomarker data in neuralgia patients appear in the bundle. Engagement of central AMPA receptors is inferred_adequate from epilepsy, where 8–12 mg met pivotal endpoints (NCT00699972, NCT00699582, NCT01618695, NCT01393743) with exposure-dependent efficacy (PMID:23772853, PMID:29171002). Those trials started after the index trial, and the PHN doses are not shown, so comparability is uncertain. The best-supported reading is that AMPA antagonism did not relieve PHN pain (F2). Small cohorts of 22–53 limit power (F7). The PHN trial was titled a dose-tolerability titration study, but the bundle shows no tolerability cap. Confidence is low because of the unknown dose and indirect engagement evidence.

In the DREAM study (NCT02222207, PMID:30341774), topical regorafenib eye drops did not improve BCVA (+1.2 letters at week 4, -2.4 at week 12), and 20 patients needed ranibizumab rescue. The program was terminated because efficacy was lower than current treatments. Post hoc analyses attributed this most likely to insufficient exposure at the back of the eye. PMID:31763044 explains why: posterior-segment drug levels after instillation were far lower in rabbits and monkeys than in rats. Systemic oncology efficacy is a different compartment, so it cannot be used to infer ocular engagement. Ocular engagement was never measured in humans. VEGFR-pathway drugs work in nAMD (secondary F1b), but no approved comparator appears in the bundle. The sources state the reason directly: exposure, not the target.

In ADHD the targets are central adrenergic receptors, reached by norepinephrine made from droxidopa in the brain. The bundle has no human evidence of CNS exposure, receptor engagement or a central biomarker at the ADHD doses. PMID:7834959 reports a non-significant rise in ventricular-fluid monoamines in neurological patients who were also taking L-DOPA, which is not adequate evidence. Droxidopa's approval for orthostatic hypotension (PMID:11710796) rests on peripheral vascular receptors, a different compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred. The index trial (NCT00983814) was an open-label run-in followed by a randomized withdrawal with only 6 vs 5 patients. Both arms changed by -17 on the AISRS. The sponsor reported strong open-label activity but gave no reason for stopping. A drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U, with an underpowered trial design (F7) as secondary.

Plasma exposure is documented (NCT01710033, PMID:27137149). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because tofacitinib met remission endpoints in ulcerative colitis, the same JAK target in gut mucosa, at a comparable dose (10 mg BID; NCT01465763, NCT01458951, NCT00787202). Peripheral pSTAT5 inhibition in transplant patients (PMID:22960764) was published after the index trial and not in Crohn's. At week 4 the index trial showed no separation from a 44% placebo response at doses up to 15 mg BID, with no tolerability cap (NCT00615199). A later induction trial also failed (NCT01393626), and maintenance was only marginal (NCT01393899). This points to F2. The high placebo response and small arms (F7) also apply, and upadacitinib's approval in Crohn's suggests a molecule-specific contribution (F1b).

A biomarker substudy of the dry eye Phase 1/2 trial (NCT00784719) gave patients the same topical doses used in the index trial (0.003–0.005%). After 8 weeks, conjunctival HLA-DR expression, a marker downstream of JAK signalling, fell to 67–71% of baseline on tofacitinib versus 133% on vehicle, and tear inflammatory cytokines also dropped. No direct engagement measure (such as pSTAT) or ocular drug level was reported, so engagement is rated adequate only because of this downstream effect at the site of action. The drop in HLA-DR did not track clinical signs. Even so, corneal staining in NCT01135511 was identical to vehicle (-3.0 vs -3.0/-3.1) and tolerability was good. This points to JAK1/3 inhibition not driving the corneal staining endpoint (F2). The evidence was published in 2012, after the index trial started. Because engagement was not measured directly, U is listed as a secondary code.

The index AML/MDS monotherapy trial (NCT01880437) was terminated with no stated reason and no response data posted. At 150 mg/d, plasma exposure reached a Cmax of about 3.6–7 µM with no MTD (NCT00607724, PMID:21300762). GLI1 was down-modulated in skin and in mCRPC tumors (PMID:21300762, PMID:27826729). Engagement is inferred_adequate because vismodegib met its efficacy endpoint in BCC through SMO at the same dose (NCT00833417), though not in marrow. In AML patients, a downstream GLI1/UGT1A reduction appeared only in a later combination trial (PMID:36951168). Glasdegib, on the same target, is approved in AML, which raises F1b, but the bundle shows no tolerability cap. The likeliest reading is that SMO inhibition alone does not drive AML. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

Vismodegib 150 mg/day, the approved BCC dose (NCT00833417), was used in MYLIE (NCT02593760; PMID:30249277), where PK in myelofibrosis was characterized. Plasma exposure at this dose was established in solid tumors (NCT00607724). Phase 1 data showed GLI1 down-modulation in skin, and 150 mg was chosen for maximal concentration and PD response (PMID:21300762). Tumor Gli1 suppression was also shown in mCRPC (PMID:27826729; NCT02115828). Engagement was never measured in myelofibrosis marrow. Added to ruxolitinib, vismodegib gave 3/10 spleen responses, no fibrosis improvement and no anemia responses. The added benefit over ruxolitinib was unconvincing, suggesting Hedgehog inhibition does not drive myelofibrosis as tested. The trial was a single-arm study of 10 patients with no comparator, which limits inference (F7).

Enzalutamide 160 mg daily gave no overall survival benefit in advanced HCC versus placebo (HR 1.15; NCT02528643, PMID:34351608). AR engagement was never measured in HCC. It is inferred adequate because the same 160 mg dose of this systemic AR antagonist met overall survival endpoints in prostate cancer (NCT00974311, NCT01212991). The dose was not tolerability-capped: the phase 1 MTD was 240 mg (NCT00510718), and the HCC phase Ib at 160 mg had no DLTs but also no single-agent activity (PMID:32548867). Most consistent is that AR blockade does not drive advanced HCC as tested (F2). Preclinical work notes nuclear AR overexpression in only about 37% of tumours and AKT-mTOR feedback (PMID:29220539). That suggests the unselected population may also have contributed (F3).

FCM has no recorded target; its mechanism is iron repletion. Human PK studies show dose-dependent serum iron exposure and rises in ferritin, TSAT and reticulocytes (PMID:20648928, PMID:29357079, PMID:31937462). In the index trial, iron indices improved versus placebo in iron-deficient fibromyalgia patients (PMID:29149437), so engagement was shown in this disease, though only within the index trial itself. The primary responder endpoint missed (30/39 vs 26/39). The placebo response was high (67%) in a small trial of about 80 patients, while continuous FIQR, BPI and fatigue scores favoured FCM and the authors call it beneficial. This points to a design and power problem with a dichotomous endpoint, not an absent mechanism. An open-label study also reported benefit (PMID:37975360). Tolerability was good, so dose was not limited.

The index trial NCT00537511 was a Phase I/II dose-finding study of pomalidomide with cisplatin/etoposide in small cell carcinoma. Its primary endpoint was the MTD, which was met and reported as 4 mg. The trial was terminated for administrative reasons, not for lack of efficacy, so this was not an efficacy test (F9). The stop looks like a sponsor decision, so F8 is a possible secondary code. Exposure is robust in humans (PMID:25556560). CRBN engagement and the pathway effect are inferred_adequate because 4 mg met a PFS endpoint in myeloma (NCT01311687, PMID:41178491). That inference crosses tissue compartments and no SCLC biomarker data exist. Tolerability did not cap the dose below the approved level.

Exposure looks adequate. Pomalidomide was given at the paediatric RP2D of 2.6 mg/m2, and paediatric population PK matched adult PK and rose with dose (Nature Pediatr Res; FDA review). In adults with CNS lymphoma, CSF levels were about 17–19% of plasma levels, though this was measured in only one patient (Blood 2018). However, no source measures cereblon engagement or its downstream effects (such as Ikaros/Aiolos degradation or immune changes) in medulloblastoma or any paediatric brain tumour. Medulloblastoma had 0% response or long-term stable disease (NCT03257631, PMID:34168987), and the investigators gave no mechanistic explanation; they only suggested trying molecularly selected tumours or combinations. Success in myeloma does not carry over to a CNS solid tumour. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't drive the disease, so the code is U.

The index Phase I/II trial NCT00537511 was a dose-finding study with cisplatin/etoposide in SCLC. Its primary endpoint, the MTD, was met (4 mg), and it was terminated 'for administrative reasons'. It was not an efficacy test of pomalidomide, so it is not an efficacy failure (F9). The administrative stop suggests a sponsor or business decision (F8 secondary). Exposure at 4 mg is robust in humans (PMID:25556560). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because 4 mg met PFS endpoints in myeloma via CRBN (NCT01311687, NCT00833833). That evidence came after the index trial started and was not shown in SCLC. The dose was not capped below the myeloma-effective dose.

The phase 3 index trial (NCT01178281) tested 0.5 mg/day, an eighth of the 4 mg dose that is effective in myeloma (NCT01311687). The bundle has no human CRBN-engagement or pathway data at that dose, so efficacy cannot be inferred from myeloma. Exposure across 0.5-10 mg is documented (PMID:25556560). The dose was capped by tolerability: 3 mg/day was poorly tolerated in myelofibrosis (PMID:23890523). In myelofibrosis, 2 mg gave higher response rates than 0.5 mg (OR 2.62; PMID:27774990), and full PK/PD effect needs higher doses (PMID:41178491). This points to an under-dosed test of the mechanism. Responses were confined to JAK2V617F-positive patients with small spleens, or TET2-mutated patients (PMID:22081489, PMID:27774990), so subgroup selection (F3) also applies. With no direct engagement data, the evidence is thin and U also applies.

The index trial was an open-label safety extension, terminated because the parent RUBATO DB trial (NCT03153137) showed no peak VO2 benefit with macitentan 10 mg. Exposure at 10 mg is documented in patients (PMID:28378883). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate: the same 10 mg dose met hard and haemodynamic endpoints through pulmonary vascular endothelin blockade in PAH (NCT00660179), CTEPH (NCT02021292) and LVAD-related PH (NCT02554903), with concentration-dependent PVR lowering (PMID:29501590). No target or pathway data were shown in Fontan patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose; no new safety signals were seen. Endothelin blockade therefore appears not to drive exercise capacity in Fontan circulation (F2). F9 is secondary because the index trial itself was not an efficacy test.

In NCT01499251 (PMID:34693288), doses up to 300 mg were well tolerated. There were no dose-limiting toxicities, and plasma exposure rose with dose without a plateau, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The target sits in brain tumour tissue, but the investigators state that it is not known whether macitentan crosses the blood-brain barrier in humans. In the ancillary tumour-biomarker study, ET-A/ET-B phosphorylation, pMAPK and pAKT were too variable to interpret, and that study stopped at 6 patients. That leaves no human evidence of tissue exposure, engagement or pathway effect. The sponsor stopped because the exploratory efficacy signal was weaker than the mouse data (PMID:26106074) had suggested. The trial was small and not powered for efficacy (F7). Nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

In the MUSIC trial (NCT00903331, PMID:23682110), macitentan 10 mg was well tolerated over a median 14.5 months, so the dose was not capped. It showed no effect on FVC (median change -0.20 L in both arms) or on time to worsening or death. Plasma exposure at 10 mg is well characterised in patients (PMID:28378883), and phase I/II data show raised plasma ET-1, consistent with receptor blockade (PMID:20730702). No target engagement was measured in IPF patients. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 10 mg dose met hard and haemodynamic endpoints in PAH via lung endothelin receptors (NCT00660179, PMID:29501590; also NCT02021292). Bosentan and ambrisentan also failed in IPF (PMID:29341047). Endothelin antagonism therefore appears not to drive IPF progression.

The index GAD trial (NCT00730691) tested 2.5, 5 and 10 mg; none separated from placebo, while duloxetine did, so assay sensitivity held. A healthy-volunteer PET study (PMID:23428337) showed brain exposure, but SERT occupancy was dose-dependent, ranging from 2% at 2.5 mg to 97% at 60 mg. The half-occupancy dose was 8.5 mg, and the authors state 20-30 mg is needed for clinically relevant occupancy. No 5-HT1A occupancy was seen even at 30 mg. So index doses gave sub-therapeutic engagement. In MDD, efficacy was more consistent at 15-20 mg (NCT01140906, PMID:36708956). The PET data were published after the trial started and were not in GAD patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Same-target drugs (amitriptyline, buspirone) are approved in anxiety, which supports F1b as secondary.

Index trial NCT02327013 tested 10 and 20 mg/day, the approved MDD doses. Neither separated from placebo on AISRS (p=0.97, p=0.60). Engagement is shown in humans: PET in healthy controls found dose-dependent SERT occupancy up to 97%, with 20–30 mg judged clinically relevant (PMID:23428337). Efficacy at 10–20 mg in MDD (NCT01140906, NCT02389816) also implies CNS engagement, so engagement is at least inferred_adequate. On the pathway side, plasma 5-HT fell markedly by day 14 (NCT01299805), and 5-HT1A occupancy was negligible. All of this evidence predates the index trial but comes from healthy volunteers or MDD, not ADHD patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the serotonergic mechanism engaged and no benefit, F2 fits. The authors also cite placebo response and non-adherence (PMID:30843450), supporting F7 as secondary.

Suvorexant met sleep efficacy endpoints in insomnia (NCT01097616, NCT01097629, NCT00792298) and in insomnia with Alzheimer's (NCT02750306). These trials act through the same central orexin receptors at comparable doses, including the 15 mg elderly dose used in the index trial, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Human orexin-receptor occupancy thresholds were also derived for suvorexant (PMID:28663311). No engagement was measured in delirium patients. In the index trial, 15 mg for up to 7 days lowered delirium incidence numerically but not significantly (16.8% vs 26.5%, p=0.13; NCT04571944, PMID:39150711). This supports F2. The trial was small (n=203) with a wide CI, so underpowering (F7) is plausible, but the sources do not state it.

sGC engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same 0.5–2.5 mg TID regimen met 6MWD endpoints through pulmonary vascular sGC in PAH (NCT00810693) and CTEPH (NCT00855465). Pathway effects were shown in humans: dose-dependent falls in PVR and PAP, including in ILD-associated PH (PMID:19129292) and COPD-PH (NCT00640315), all before the index trial. Even so, RISE-IIP gave no significant benefit (6MWD +21.5 m, p=0.21), and the iDMC stopped it for excess mortality and SAEs on riociguat (PMID:33744088; 27/73 vs 17/74). Vasodilation in group 3 PH does not drive benefit here (F2). The harm may be on-target (F5). A post hoc look implicated CPFE and disease burden but found no link to treatment assignment (F3, weak).

RISE-SSc (NCT02283762) titrated riociguat to 2.5 mg TID, the dose that met pivotal endpoints in PAH and CTEPH (NCT00810693, NCT00855465). Plasma exposure is documented (NCT00640315, PMID:18519919). sGC engagement was not measured directly, so it is inferred_adequate from that systemic efficacy at the same dose. Pathway is adequate: dose-dependent haemodynamic and blood-pressure effects in patients (PMID:19129292, PMID:20530034). Engagement was not shown in SSc patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, mRSS was not improved at p<0.05 (difference -2.34, p=0.08; PMID:32299845), pointing to sGC stimulation not driving skin fibrosis as tested. The authors cite secondary signals (FVC, Raynaud's) warranting further trials, so a powering limitation (F7) is a secondary explanation.

The index trial NCT01926847 was a small (n=23) single-dose Phase 2 safety, PK and pharmacodynamic study of digital blood flow, classified not_efficacy. It posted no results and gave no stop reason, so the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout. Plasma exposure is well characterised in humans (PMID:18519919, NCT00640315). sGC engagement is inferred adequate because riociguat met pivotal endpoints in PAH and CTEPH through the same vascular smooth-muscle target at comparable doses (NCT00810693, NCT00855465). Systemic vasodilation, with falls in blood pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance, is documented and non-selective (PMID:19129292), supporting the pathway pillar. No data in Raynaud patients are shown. If the program instead failed on efficacy, F2 would apply, but the bundle is thin.

In Rio-CF (NCT02170025, PMID:34419414), riociguat at 0.5 then 1.0 mg tid, below the approved 2.5 mg tid, did not lower sweat chloride or improve FEV1. Plasma exposure at 1 mg is documented in humans (NCT00640315), and vascular sGC effects (hemodynamics, blood pressure) are shown in healthy volunteers and PH patients (PMID:18519919, PMID:19129292). However, no source measured cGMP or sGC engagement in airway or sweat-gland epithelium, and nobody measured it in CF patients. PH efficacy works through vascular smooth muscle at higher doses, so engagement cannot be inferred for the CF tissue. Headache was the only notable AE, and no source says tolerability capped the dose. The authors gave two reasons for stopping: lack of efficacy and the changing CF landscape (minor F8). The bundle cannot tell inadequate engagement apart from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U.

Index trial NCT01787552 was a single-arm Phase Ib/II dose-finding study of sonidegib 400 mg plus ruxolitinib (INC424). Its primary outcomes were DLTs and the descriptive rate of ≥35% spleen volume reduction (44.4% at Week 24), with no prespecified success threshold. It was classified not_efficacy, so it was not an efficacy failure of sonidegib. Without a ruxolitinib-alone control, sonidegib's contribution cannot be isolated. Plasma exposure is shown in patients (PMID:24523439, PMID:26898300). Exposure-dependent GLI1 mRNA suppression appeared in skin and tumor in the first-in-human trial (NCT00880308, PMID:24523439). Prostate tissue showed a 63-fold GLI1 drop (PMID:29262631), and the BCC trial met its endpoint (NCT01327053). None of this engagement evidence comes from myelofibrosis patients. Only a few creatine kinase DLTs occurred, so the dose was not tolerability-limited.

The index trial NCT01487785 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of sonidegib plus gemcitabine whose only primary endpoint was DLT incidence. It posted no results and no efficacy readout, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Plasma exposure in patients is well characterised (PMID:24523439, PMID:26898300). Exposure-dependent GLI1 mRNA suppression was seen in skin and tumor biopsies in the first-in-human study (NCT00880308, PMID:24523439). A 63-fold tumor GLI1 reduction was seen in prostate cancer (PMID:29262631). Engagement is inferred adequate from the BCC efficacy and approval (NCT01327053). No engagement data exist in pancreatic cancer patients. No stated stop reason or tolerability cap is shown in the bundle.

Sonidegib reached plasma exposure across 100–3000 mg (PMID:26898300, PMID:24523439). It suppressed GLI1 in an exposure-dependent way in skin and tumor (PMID:24523439) and more than 60-fold in prostate tissue (PMID:29262631). It met its endpoint in BCC at 200 and 800 mg (NCT01327053). So SMO engagement and pathway suppression were adequate at the 400/800 mg doses used in the index trial, though this was not shown in AML patients. Despite this, monotherapy gave 0 CR and 1 CRi in 70 relapsed/refractory acute leukemia patients (NCT01826214). Azacitidine combination data also note limited responses, as with other hedgehog inhibitors (PMID:37042080). Glasdegib's AML approval suggests the setting may matter, hence the F3 secondary code. Mainly, SMO inhibition does not drive relapsed/refractory leukemia as tested.

In myelofibrosis (including post-PV/ET MF), the index single-arm trial NCT00931762 had an ORR of 2.9%, with no termination reason given. Systemic exposure is dose-proportional (PMID:32809242). Histone acetylation rose in blood, tissue and blasts (PMID:24429877, PMID:32809242), but only in other diseases and only in reports published after 2009. Engagement and pathway are also inferred adequate from efficacy in myeloma (NCT01083602, NCT02290431; approval 2015) through the same systemic HDAC target. An investigator trial reported 36% ORR but frequent discontinuation for perceived ineffectiveness and an ill-defined optimal dose (PMID:27930945), so dosing or schedule is a possible contributor. Overall, with engagement inferred adequate, there was minimal clinical benefit in MF, which fits F2. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT00670553 was a 7-patient Phase 1 dose-finding study of panobinostat with radiotherapy. Its primary endpoint was DLT/MTD, it completed, and it posted no results. It was not an efficacy test of the drug, so F9 applies. Plasma exposure in humans is shown (PMID:32809242, NCT02717455). Histone acetylation was confirmed in blood, fat pad and tumor samples from patients with aerodigestive tumors, including head and neck cancer (PMID:24429877). That evidence was published in 2014, after the index trial started in 2008. The pathway pillar is inferred from the myeloma approval and the met endpoint in NCT01083602, though that is a different tissue compartment. No stated stop reason or efficacy failure appears in the bundle for this program.

The index trial NCT00567879 (panobinostat plus trastuzumab in HER2+ MBC) stopped for insufficient clinical benefit at doses similar to the 20–30 mg regimens used elsewhere. Human exposure is dose-proportional (PMID:32809242, NCT02717455). Histone acetylation, a pharmacodynamic marker of target engagement, rose in blood, fat pad and solid-tumor biopsies at 30 mg (PMID:24429877) and in AML blasts (PMID:32809242). Pathway is inferred adequate from myeloma efficacy through HDAC inhibition (NCT01083602, NCT02290431). No engagement data exist in breast cancer, and none was published before 2008. Tolerability capped dosing near 20 mg (PMID:26774555), and preclinical data suggest solid tumors need sustained exposure (PMID:23299388). That makes F1a a plausible secondary code, though inadequacy is not shown in humans.

Single-agent panobinostat in mCRPC gave a 24-week PFS rate of only 11.4% (NCT00667862). Human pharmacology is established elsewhere. PK was dose-proportional (PMID:32809242), and histone acetylation rose in blood, fat pad and solid-tumour biopsies (PMID:24429877) and in leukaemic blasts (PMID:32809242). Pathway is inferred_adequate from efficacy in myeloma via the same HDAC mechanism (NCT01083602, NCT02290431). None of this engagement evidence came from prostate cancer, and all of it was published after the index trial started. In CRPC, panobinostat helped only when paired with bicalutamide (PMID:30224345). That points to HDAC inhibition alone not driving the disease (F2). Preclinical data suggest clinically achievable exposure may be too short for solid tumours (PMID:23299388), so F1a remains possible.

Plasma exposure rose with dose in MDS/CMML patients (PMID:28905323). No CMML engagement data exist. Histone acetylation rose in AML blasts (PMID:32809242) and in blood and tumor (PMID:24429877), and myeloma efficacy at 20 mg (NCT01083602, NCT02290431) supports inferred adequacy; all of this postdates the 2009 index start. In NCT00946647/PMID:28546581, PAN+AZA roughly doubled composite CR (27.5% vs 14.3%) but gave no OS or time-to-progression benefit. Grade 3/4 AEs (97.4% vs 81%) and on-treatment deaths (13.2% vs 4.8%) were higher. The authors call for dose or schedule optimization to improve risk/benefit. The response signal was therefore offset by class-typical HDAC-inhibitor toxicity (F5). The small trial had no formal test (F7), and the lack of survival gain is consistent with F2.

Index NCT00931762 single-arm ORR was 2.9% (1/35), and no termination reason was given. Plasma exposure is documented and dose-proportional (PMID:32809242). Histone acetylation, a pharmacodynamic readout, rose in blood, tissue and blasts (PMID:24429877, PMID:32809242), but these data are from other diseases and were published after the index trial started. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from the systemic HDAC-inhibitor efficacy in myeloma at comparable doses (NCT01083602, NCT02290431; 2015 approval). With the mechanism engaged, the near-null response points to HDAC inhibition not driving myelofibrosis as tested (F2). Investigators had reported activity at lower doses over prolonged duration, with thrombocytopenia as the dose-limiting toxicity and frequent discontinuation (PMID:23330839, PMID:27930945). That suggests schedule or duration as contributors (F4). The bundle does not show the index dose, so confidence is low.

Brain exposure and D2/5-HT2A engagement were measured by PET in humans. In schizophrenia, D2 occupancy was 64% at 1 mg and 80% at 4 mg, with dose-related 5-HT2A occupancy (PMID:31847007, NCT01854944). In healthy volunteers, D2 occupancy reached 77-88% at higher doses, and 2 mg/day was predicted efficacious (PMID:33196868). This evidence predates the index trial but is not from BPD patients. Pathway is inferred adequate: 2-3 mg/day met efficacy endpoints in schizophrenia and MDD through the same CNS targets (NCT01396421, NCT01360645, NCT01668797). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, the index trial showed no separation on ZAN-BPD (p=0.24, NCT04100096; PMID:39558901), so the mechanism does not appear to drive BPD as tested. Placebo response was robust, and signals at other time points (PMID:35049469, PMID:39558901) point to possible design issues (F7).

Exposure and D2/5-HT2A engagement were measured directly. PET in schizophrenia patients (NCT01854944, registered 2013; PMID:31847007) showed about 80% D2 occupancy at 4 mg/day, and healthy-volunteer PET (PMID:33196868) supports efficacious occupancy at ≥2 mg. Neither was done in bipolar patients. Pathway is inferred_adequate because the same 2–4 mg doses met efficacy endpoints in schizophrenia (NCT01396421, NCT01668797). The index mania trial missed its YMRS endpoint (p=0.10), as did the sister study. The sources attribute the failure to the patient sample: efficacy appeared in patients with impaired insight (mostly EU) but not in those with good insight (mostly US), and they say future samples must be more severe (PMID:33691517). They also call the titration too modest, a design issue (F7). Dose was not capped by tolerability.

PET shows brain penetration and dose-dependent striatal D2 occupancy: 64–80% at 1–4 mg/day in schizophrenia patients (NCT01854944, registered 2013; PMID:31847007) and up to 77–88% in healthy volunteers (PMID:33196868). Occupancy is projected at >80% at 2 mg/day (PMID:40157325). 5-HT2A occupancy was robust, but 5-HT1A occupancy was negligible. Pathway is inferred_adequate from approved efficacy at 2–3 mg in MDD and schizophrenia (NCT01360645, NCT01396421, NCT02196506). These are the same doses tested in the PTSD index trial (NCT04174170), where neither dose separated from sertraline+placebo (p=0.52, 0.66). The positive phase 2 combination signal (NCT03033069) did not replicate. A large sertraline+placebo response (−17.6) may have contributed (F7), but the bundle does not state this. No engagement data exist in PTSD patients.

Brexpiprazole missed ABC-I at week 8 (diff -1.22, p=0.46; NCT04174365, PMID:39970021). PET showed dose-dependent D2 (64–80%) and 5-HT2A occupancy in schizophrenia patients (NCT01854944, registered 2013; PMID:31847007) and up to 88% in healthy volunteers (PMID:33196868). Engagement is therefore adequate, but not shown in ASD. Pathway is inferred_adequate from efficacy in adult and adolescent schizophrenia (NCT01396421, NCT03198078). Tolerability did not cap the dose: no serious AEs. By the rules this fits F2. However, aripiprazole is approved for ASD irritability through the same D2 partial agonism, so the target matters. A large placebo response (-8.9) in a small trial points to design or assay sensitivity (F7). No source states the cause, so confidence is low.

Adjunctive brexpiprazole showed no separation from placebo on CAARS-O:SV in stimulant-treated adult ADHD (NCT01074294; p=0.58). Human PET showed dose-dependent D2 occupancy of 64–80% and robust 5-HT2A occupancy in schizophrenia (NCT01854944, PMID:31847007). It also showed 77–88% striatal D2/D3 occupancy in healthy volunteers (PMID:33196868; NCT00805454 was registered in 2008, before the index trial). Pathway is inferred_adequate because the drug met efficacy endpoints in schizophrenia and MDD through the same CNS targets at comparable doses (NCT01396421, NCT01360645, NCT01668797). Engagement was not measured in ADHD patients. Tolerability was comparable to placebo, so the dose was not capped. The target mechanism therefore did not improve core ADHD symptoms. A post-hoc trend in prior stimulant non-responders and the authors' criticism of 2:1 randomization support F3 and F7 as secondary codes (PMID:35977005).

Brain exposure and D2/5-HT2A engagement were measured directly by PET. In schizophrenia patients, D2 occupancy was 64–80% at 1–4 mg (NCT01854944, registered 2013; PMID:31847007). In healthy volunteers it reached 77–88% at higher single doses (PMID:33196868). There is no occupancy data in bipolar mania, so engagement_in_disease is false. The downstream pathway is inferred adequate because the drug met efficacy endpoints in schizophrenia through the same CNS D2 mechanism (NCT01396421, NCT01668797). No dose-limiting toxicity was seen in the index trial. Despite adequate engagement, both mania trials missed YMRS (NCT03257865 p=0.10; NCT03259555 p=0.88). This points to the mechanism, at this partial-agonist profile, not driving acute mania as tested. Large placebo responses (~-10.7 points) suggest a possible trial-sensitivity contribution.

Plasma exposure at 20–30 mg BID is characterized in humans (PMID:24962564). PDE4 engagement was not measured directly in AS.
