It is inferred adequate because the same 30 mg BID dose met ACR20 endpoints in psoriatic arthritis (NCT01172938, NCT01212757, NCT01212770, NCT01307423), a systemic, joint/enthesis-related compartment. Pathway effects were shown in AS patients: bone biomarkers RANKL and sclerostin moved in the pilot (PMID:22984171), and plasma proteomic changes appeared in the Phase 3 (PMID:31953524). Despite this, ASAS20 was flat versus placebo at both doses (NCT01583374, PMID:33589554), and tolerability was consistent with the known profile. This supports PDE4 inhibition not driving axial disease. A secondary F1a concern: apremilast 30 mg gave only partial, transient TNFα inhibition in healthy subjects (PMID:33382916).

RESOLVE (NCT02436668, PMID:33539945) gave ibrutinib 560 mg, the dose that met efficacy endpoints through BTK inhibition in mantle cell lymphoma (NCT01236391) and cGVHD (NCT02195869) before the index trial started. Systemic exposure and BTK engagement are therefore inferred adequate. PDAC-specific stromal or mast-cell engagement and pathway biomarkers were never measured in patients; the rationale was murine only (PMID:25878147). PFS was significantly worse and OS unchanged. The ibrutinib arm also received lower cumulative chemotherapy doses. A durvalumab combination was likewise inactive in pancreatic cancer (PMID:31230047, NCT02403271). The best-supported reading is that BTK-mediated stromal modulation does not drive PDAC outcomes as tested. Confidence is medium because tumor-compartment engagement is inferred, not shown.

The bundle has no direct BTK occupancy or biomarker data in myeloma. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because ibrutinib met response endpoints through BTK at 560–840 mg in MCL, CLL and MZL (NCT01236391, NCT01744691, NCT01980628), the same systemic compartment and comparable doses. Even so, myeloma activity was modest. Monotherapy or dex cohorts in NCT01478581 gave a clinical benefit rate of only 0–12/43. Combinations (NCT01962792, NCT02902965) reported descriptive results without clear added benefit. The index pom/dex combination (NCT02548962) stopped after Phase 1, with 4/11 responders and heavy serious-AE burden, by unspecified sponsor decision. This suggests BTK is not a strong driver in myeloma. Business reasons are possible (NCT03015792 was unfunded). Confidence is low.

In RESOLVE (NCT02436668), adding ibrutinib to gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel worsened PFS (HR 1.525) and did not improve OS. The bundle has no BTK occupancy or tumour-microenvironment biomarker data in pancreatic cancer. Systemic exposure and BTK engagement are inferred adequate from efficacy and approvals in MCL (NCT01236391) and chronic GVHD (NCT02195869), an immune-cell-driven indication, using standard oral doses. Human plasma PK data also exist (PMID:33740218). No tolerability cap is shown. A separate pancreatic and solid-tumour combination, ibrutinib plus durvalumab (NCT02403271), was also essentially inactive (ORR 2/105). The most direct reading is that BTK inhibition does not drive pancreatic adenocarcinoma as tested (F2). The inference does rest on a different cellular compartment (stromal cells versus malignant B cells), so U applies secondarily.

Index single-arm Ph2 of ibrutinib plus venetoclax in T-PLL gave an ORR of 7.1% (1/14) (NCT03873493). The bundle has no BTK pillar data in T-PLL. BTK exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because systemic ibrutinib met efficacy endpoints in BTK-driven B-cell diseases at comparable doses (NCT01236391, NCT01744691, NCT02195869). The drug likely hit BTK, but BTK/B-cell receptor signaling does not drive this T-cell leukemia. The alternative T-cell kinase rationale (ITK) showed only partial occupancy (mean 50%, range 15-80%) and minimal activity in T-cell lymphoma (PMID:29669753), so F1a applies secondarily. The venetoclax combination and small sample size further confound attribution.

Ibrutinib 420 mg plus standard of care did not improve survival without respiratory failure at day 28 versus placebo (86.4% vs 79.2%, p=0.599; NCT04375397). Exposure, engagement and pathway were not measured in COVID-19 patients. They are rated inferred_adequate because the same 420 mg dose met a clinical efficacy endpoint in chronic GVHD (NCT02195869, PMID:34102349), which also works through BTK in systemic immune cells. The dose was not limited by tolerability: serious AEs were 4/22 vs 3/24. So BTK inhibition was plausibly achieved without clinical benefit (F2). The trial was very small (n=46) with a wide confidence interval, so it may have been underpowered (F7). No other BTK inhibitor in the bundle succeeded in COVID-19.

Tasimelteon met clinical endpoints through central MT1/MT2 agonism in Non-24 (NCT01163032, NCT01430754; FDA approval at 20 mg) and jet lag (NCT03373201). Brain exposure and receptor engagement are therefore inferred adequate. Pathway is also inferred adequate: entrainment was measured by melatonin and cortisol rhythms (PMID:34152055), and phase II work showed melatonin-rhythm resetting (PMID:19579175). Plasma exposure at 20 mg is documented (PMID:30412929). Tolerability was good and nothing shows the dose was capped. Despite this, the index MDD trial showed a negligible HAM-D difference (-8.19 vs -7.83). The likely reading is that melatonergic agonism does not drive depressive symptoms as tested; PMID:19579175 had already questioned efficacy beyond circadian-related symptoms. The bundle shows no engagement data in MDD patients.

Index trial NCT02957851 (ProtoTOP, PMID:33044394) missed its primary endpoint, average pain intensity at day 7. Inhaled 30–60% N2O plainly reaches the human CNS: it shifts heart-rate variability, alters evoked potentials and raises cortisol (PMID:19000603, 7095448, 3364667). The bundle has no human measure of NMDA receptor engagement or of a downstream pathway marker, and the drug has no approval elsewhere from which engagement could be inferred. Evoked pain and PGIC did improve (PMID:33044394). A post hoc analysis then found significant benefit on average pain confined to patients taking opioids, which the authors describe as a responder population (PMID:35050957). That points to patient selection (F3). Because engagement is unmeasured, the bundle remains largely indeterminate (U). Choice of endpoint (F4) may also have contributed.

The index trial NCT02957851 tested EMONO, a 50% N2O/50% O2 mixture, in peripheral neuropathic pain. The proposed mechanism is NMDA blockade by N2O. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway biomarker data. The primary endpoint, average pain at 7 days, was not met. Evoked pain (secondary) and PGIC (exploratory) improved and stayed improved for 4 weeks (PMID:33044394). A post hoc analysis found benefit on average pain, NPSI and responder rates only in patients taking concomitant opioids, and named them a specific responder population (PMID:35050957). Because the sources point to benefit confined to a subgroup, F3 fits best. With engagement unmeasured, the failure remains partly indeterminate (U). Confidence is low given the post hoc basis and thin bundle.

Nasal CO2 has no defined molecular target. No human data show tissue exposure or target engagement. In the nasal allergen challenge study (PMID:21703101), patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) had less reflex secretion and no histamine rise, so a downstream effect moved. A later Capnia protocol (NCT02381795) reports the index study C215 (NCT00688441, n=453, twice daily): the 14-day reflective TNSS missed (2.0 vs 1.7, p=0.144). In the same trial, instantaneous TNSS improved after the first dose at 30 min (p=0.0001) and at 6 h. That fits single-dose results (PMID:18028997). The drug acted acutely, but the endpoint, a symptom score averaged over 14 days with fixed dosing, missed it. The sponsor then switched to as-needed dosing scored per episode (NCT00917020, PMID:28705451). Hence F4 rather than U. No source states the reason directly.

Helium has no molecular target. It acts physically by lowering inspired gas density. That action was shown in COPD patients before the index trial: lower airway resistance, intrinsic PEEP and trapped gas (PMID:12851764), and lower PaCO2 and work of breathing (PMID:3996069). In the index trial itself (PMID:27736154), heliox improved pH, PaCO2, respiratory rate and encephalopathy faster than air/O2. So exposure, engagement and pathway all held in this disease. Yet NIV failure was essentially identical (14.7% vs 14.5%, P=0.97). The trial was stopped early because the overall event rate was lower than assumed (NCT01155310), which limited power (F7). The proximal physiological gain did not translate into fewer intubations or deaths, so the mechanism does not appear to drive this outcome.

The index LUME-Meso phase III used nintedanib 200 mg BID, the recommended dose, not a tolerability-capped one. It showed no PFS benefit (HR 1.01) despite a positive phase II (HR 0.56, mostly in epithelioid disease) (NCT01907100, PMID:28892431). In advanced solid-tumour patients, published before 2013, PK was dose-linear (PMID:20028771, PMID:27093880). Soluble VEGFR2 and CD117+ progenitors fell significantly (PMID:20688946), and DCE-MRI showed reduced tumour blood flow (PMID:20028771). Antiangiogenic activity at this dose also yielded PFS benefits in NSCLC, ovarian and colorectal cancer (NCT00805194, NCT01015118, NCT02149108). Engagement was not measured in mesothelioma itself. With an adequately engaged mechanism and no confirmed benefit, plus modest monotherapy activity (PMID:37301693), angiokinase inhibition does not appear to drive mesothelioma outcomes. The phase II subgroup signal suggests possible heterogeneity (F3).

The index trial was an exploratory 2:1 randomised comparison against active sunitinib. It was not powered for comparison and its p-values are descriptive only (PMID:26448178). Efficacy was equivalent: PFS-9 was 43.1% vs 45.2%, median PFS 8.4 months in both arms, OS 20.4 vs 21.2 months. The authors called the efficacy promising and tolerability favourable, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug. Pillars: plasma PK at 200 mg bid was dose-linear and measured in RCC patients (PMID:20028771, PMID:23625328). Soluble VEGFR2 fell and DCE-MRI showed reduced tumour blood flow in mixed solid tumours (PMID:20688946, PMID:20028771). Engagement is inferred from met phase 3 PFS endpoints in NSCLC, ovarian and colorectal cancer (NCT00805194, NCT01015118, NCT02149108). No stop reason is given for RCC, so a business decision is possible but not shown.

Nintedanib 200 mg BID, the MTD in HCC with no cycle-1 DLTs (NCT00987935, PMID:27627050), gave TTP 2.73 vs 3.71 months for sorafenib (HR 1.36, CI crossing 1). NCT01004003 also showed no advantage. Exposure: dose-linear plasma PK in cancer patients, higher in hepatic impairment (PMID:20028771, 27093880, 29106740). Pathway: reduced tumour blood flow on DCE-MRI and lower sVEGFR2/CD117 progenitors at 150–250 mg BID in solid tumours (PMID:20028771, 20688946). Engagement is inferred_adequate because 200 mg BID met PFS in NSCLC (NCT00805194). No engagement data in HCC itself. Lenvatinib (and comparator sorafenib) work in HCC, so a molecule-level shortfall (F1b) remains plausible. The small randomized phase 2 against an active same-class drug also limits interpretation (F7).

The index single-arm Phase 2 in relapsed/refractory Hodgkin lymphoma (NCT01393106) gave an ORR of only 20%, below its endpoint. The bundle has no direct human PK, PI3Kδ inhibition or pathway biomarker data in Hodgkin patients. However, idelalisib met efficacy endpoints through PI3Kδ in hematologic B-cell malignancies at 150 mg BID: iNHL ORR 57% (NCT01282424, PMID:24450858) and CLL PFS benefit (NCT01539512, NCT01569295), with these results available before or around the index start. So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate, though not shown in Hodgkin disease. No tolerability cap is shown for the index trial. Selective PI3Kδ inhibition therefore appears not to drive relapsed classical Hodgkin lymphoma enough to give meaningful monotherapy responses. Isolated responses occurred (PMID:30191811).

The index trial NCT02457598 was a phase 1 dose-escalation study of tirabrutinib combinations. Idelalisib was only a partner drug, given at reduced doses (50 mg BID or 100 mg QD). It stopped because the combinations, though well tolerated, showed 'no efficacy advantage'. It was not an efficacy test of idelalisib in MCL: only about 2 MCL patients received idelalisib combinations. Pillars are inferred_adequate because idelalisib met pivotal endpoints through PI3Kδ in B-cell malignancies (NCT01539512, NCT01282424). It also showed single-agent activity in MCL (ORR 40%, PMID:24615778). However, the bundle contains no direct PK/PD data in MCL. The trial's small, fragmented subgroups also limit interpretation (F7).

In the phase 1 trial in patients with advanced solid tumors (PMID:18245542, published 2008, before the 2009 index start), IV belinostat showed linear plasma PK. It produced dose-dependent histone H4 hyperacetylation in PBMCs, sustained 4-24 h, at the 1000 mg/m2 MTD. Downstream effects followed: caspase-cleaved cytokeratin-18 and IL-6 increases. Further PD evidence came from PMID:25189481 and PMID:25483416, and single-agent efficacy in PTCL (NCT00865969) supports activity. Engagement was not measured in cancer of unknown primary patients. Adding belinostat to carboplatin/paclitaxel gave no PFS gain (5.4 vs 5.3 months) and more serious AEs (22/42 vs 10/44) (NCT00873119). Pan-HDAC inhibition therefore appears not to drive benefit in this setting. The small randomized phase 2 size is a secondary limitation.

Index trial NCT02471118 (knee OA, OARSI/OMERACT response at week 16) posted no results, and no OA-specific exposure, TNF-neutralization or biomarker data appear in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate. Systemic subcutaneous adalimumab met clinical endpoints through TNF neutralization in joint diseases at standard doses: RA radiographic progression (NCT00870467), peripheral SpA (NCT01064856), enthesitis-related arthritis (NCT01166282) and axial SpA (NCT00939003). An earlier randomized trial in refractory hand OA was also negative versus placebo (PMID:24817417). This suggests TNF does not drive OA pain or function as tested. No tolerability limit is shown. The index trial's focus on inflammation hints at a patient-selection question (F3), but the bundle does not show this.

Plasma exposure is well characterised and dose-proportional (PMID:26879594, NCT02578316). Engagement is inferred_adequate: lenvatinib met efficacy endpoints through VEGFR/FGFR in RCC (NCT01136733), HCC and endometrial cancer at comparable systemic doses. Pediatric 14 mg/m2 was the RP2D, with on-target hypertension DLTs (PMID:34562750). Pathway biomarkers moved in humans: CEC/CEP decreased (PMID:21372218, PMID:26500236) and FGF19/23 rose (PMID:34108184), all before the 2020 index start. None was measured in osteosarcoma. OLIE (NCT04154189, PMID:39418029) missed its PFS primary endpoint (HR 0.54, CI 0.27–1.08, 6.5 vs 5.5 months). Single-agent osteosarcoma activity was also modest (PMID:34562750). This supports F2. The small trial (n=81) with a sizeable but non-significant HR suggests possible underpowering (F7).

Lenvatinib 20 mg plus pembrolizumab missed both PFS (HR 0.90) and OS (HR 1.14) in first-line cisplatin- or platinum-ineligible urothelial carcinoma (NCT03898180, PMID:37778952). Exposure is well characterised: dose-proportional PK (PMID:21372218, PMID:26879594). Pathway effects were shown in humans: circulating endothelial cells fell, VEGF and FGF19/23 rose, and VEGF-driven hypertension appeared (PMID:21372218, PMID:26500236, PMID:34108184). Engagement is inferred_adequate because the same dose and combination met efficacy endpoints in RCC and endometrial cancer, leading to approvals (NCT02501096, NCT01136733). No engagement data exist in urothelial carcinoma itself. So VEGFR/FGFR inhibition added to PD-1 blockade does not appear to drive benefit in this disease. Grade 3-5 adverse events were roughly doubled (51% vs 27%), giving an unfavourable benefit-risk balance.

The index trial NCT03753763 had a descriptive safety primary outcome (TEAEs/SAEs, 32 vs 17 patients, no formal efficacy comparison), so it was not an efficacy test of safinamide in MSA (F9). Pillars: human PK was linear with good exposure (PMID:15082032, PMID:27713822). Plasma MAO-B inhibition was measured in healthy volunteers, with an ED50 of 87.5 µg/kg/day, far below the therapeutic dose (PMID:12897643, PMID:15082032). These data predate the trial but come from healthy volunteers, not MSA patients. The pathway pillar is inferred adequate from PD efficacy through brain MAO-B (NCT00627640, NCT03881371). Tolerability did not cap the dose; supratherapeutic doses of 300-350 mg were tolerated (PMID:22948897, PMID:21850574).

Human PET in healthy volunteers (PMID:17708779, 2008, before the index trial) showed brain 5-HT2A receptors near-saturated at 10–20 mg. PMID:42677352 confirms concentration-dependent occupancy up to 100%. The index doses of 20 and 34 mg therefore engaged the target, so exposure and engagement were adequate despite the QT-related cap at 34 mg. Pathway is inferred adequate because the same doses met clinical endpoints in Parkinson disease psychosis (NCT01174004, FDA approval) and dementia-related psychosis (NCT02035553, NCT03325556). In SERENE neither dose separated from placebo on CMAI (NCT02992132), pointing to 5-HT2A not driving agitation as tested. Secondary codes: the trial was small with a large placebo response and baseline imbalance (F7). Post hoc data suggest agitation benefit only in psychosis responders (PMID:32729631; F3).

Human PET in healthy volunteers, published 2008 before the index trial, showed single doses of 10–20 mg near-saturated cortical 5-HT2A receptors (PMID:17708779; occupancy up to 100%, PMID:42677352). Human PK was dose-proportional (PMID:17473118). The QT-related 34 mg cap (PMID:42208178) sits above the saturating dose, so the dose was not limiting. Pathway is inferred adequate because the drug met its endpoint in Parkinson disease psychosis through the same CNS target at comparable doses (NCT01174004). Despite full engagement, adjunctive pimavanserin missed PANSS total (NCT02970292, p=0.094), and the negative-symptom Phase 3 also failed (NCT04531982). This is consistent with weak evidence for selective 5-HT2A blockade in schizophrenia (PMID:26044978). The target does not drive the disease as tested.

Human PK shows systemic exposure to the active neprilysin inhibitor LBQ657 (PMID:19934029, PMID:28527109). Dose-dependent plasma cGMP rises in healthy volunteers, a pathway readout, were published before the index trial (PMID:19934029). Engagement is inferred adequate because the drug met hard outcomes in HFrEF (NCT01035255) through the same systemic target at comparable doses (up to 200 mg BID). No direct engagement data exist in HCM. Tolerability did not cap the dose: few serious AEs and no deaths at 200 mg. The index trial missed peak VO2 (p=0.55). The independent SILICOFCM trial in non-obstructive HCM also showed no effect on VO2, structure or biomarkers (PMID:38800948). This points to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested.

Sacubitril reached plasma exposure in humans, and its active moiety LBQ657 raised plasma cGMP in healthy volunteers (PMID:19934029), which shows neprilysin inhibition and a downstream pathway effect. In HFrEF, the same systemic target at a comparable dose met a hard outcome endpoint (NCT01035255), so engagement is inferred adequate. No neprilysin engagement was measured in men with erectile dysfunction. In the index trial, sacubitril/valsartan did not improve IIEF-15 versus active enalapril (difference 2.9, p=0.34). Within the bundle this points to the mechanism not driving erectile function as tested (F2). The trial was very small (n=27) with a wide CI, so it may have been underpowered (F7). No source states the reason, so confidence is low.

Fish oil (MLF 541) has no recorded molecular target. Neither the bundle nor my search turned up any human measurement of EPA or DHA uptake into plasma or cell membranes, or of a defined target being engaged, at the doses used in the index trial. In NCT00798447 (PMID:25609264), pro-inflammatory markers did not differ meaningfully between groups. Only lipid measures (free fatty acids, triglycerides, HDL) differed, so the expected anti-inflammatory effect was not shown. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter here, so the code is U. The investigators said adequately powered trials are still needed, which points to an underpowered study of 99 patients (secondary code F7).

Crisaborole 2% failed PGA success in psoriasis (17.4% vs 13.6%, CI includes zero; NCT01300052). Topical roflumilast, acting on the same PDE4 target, is FDA-approved for psoriasis, so the target is validated there. Crisaborole's skin PDE4 engagement is only inferred from atopic dermatitis efficacy at the same 2% dose (NCT02118766, NCT02118792). Lesional biomarker normalization was also shown only in AD (NCT03233529, PMID:37054814). Systemic exposure was measured in psoriasis patients (PMID:32433779), but the bundle has no tissue-level, engagement or biomarker data in psoriatic plaques. This points to the molecule (its potency or plaque penetration) rather than the target. The small, 2:1 trial (n=68) with a wide CI also limited its power (secondary F7).

The index Phase 2 trial of SP160412 (chlorphenamine) in sunburn pain was terminated for lack of efficacy (NCT03332524) and posted no results. The bundle has no engagement data in sunburn. Chlorphenamine is approved for allergic rhinitis and the common cold through H1 inverse agonism, and human PK shows systemic exposure at 4 mg doses (PMID:8688987). That makes exposure, engagement and pathway inferred_adequate for systemic HRH1, assuming a comparable dose and route. The SP160412 formulation and dose are not shown, so this inference is uncertain. With the target plausibly engaged and no benefit, the likeliest reading is that H1 signalling does not drive sunburn pain as measured. No toxicity, population or design explanation is given.

Human plasma exposure to selexipag and its active metabolite ACT-333679 is well characterised and dose-proportional up to 1,600 µg bid (PMID:25277144, PMID:27885399). Engagement and pathway effects were not measured directly in Raynaud's. They are inferred_adequate because selexipag met a hard outcome endpoint in PAH via the IP receptor in vascular smooth muscle at similarly individualised doses (NCT01106014, PMID:28556581). In the SSc-RP trial, 91.7% of selexipag patients had prostacyclin-associated AEs, consistent with on-target pharmacology. Most patients reached ≤800 µg bid. Attack frequency still did not fall and numerically favoured placebo, with no effect on RCS or attack duration (PMID:29193819). This points to the mechanism not reducing RP attacks as tested. The small trial (n=74) is a possible secondary limitation.

Plasma exposure to selexipag and its active metabolite is well characterised in humans (PMID:25277144, PMID:28556581). IP receptor engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same 200–1600 µg bid individual-titration regimen met its hard outcome endpoint in PAH, the same target and pulmonary vascular compartment (NCT01106014). In CTEPH, Japanese trials showed PVR and cardiac index improvement (PMID:34824052; PMID:32879152, a phase 2 registered before the index trial), so the pathway effect can occur in this disease. SELECT, at maximum tolerated doses, showed no PVR effect (ratio 0.95, p=0.412) and stopped for futility (NCT03689244, PMID:39326918). This points to the mechanism not driving benefit in this population. The mixed post-PEA/BPA and inoperable patients, and the discordance with the Japanese results, suggest population heterogeneity (F3).

Tipiracil (TYMP inhibitor) is given as part of TAS-102 to protect trifluridine from degradation. Engagement is not measured directly, but at the same oral systemic dose TAS-102 met overall-survival endpoints in refractory colorectal (NCT01607957, NCT01955837) and gastric cancer (NCT02500043). That makes TP inhibition, and the resulting trifluridine exposure, inferred adequate. Plasma FTD/TPI exposure in patients was measured and tracked with neutropenia (PMID:31912801). No pillar data exist in SCLC, and no dose limitation is shown. The index SCLC trial stopped when an ad hoc interim analysis showed a PFS imbalance against topotecan/amrubicin, with no safety signal (NCT01904253). This fits a mechanism that was engaged but gave no benefit in this disease. The small (n=18) ad hoc analysis adds a design caveat (F7).

No direct human PK, occupancy or biomarker data appear in the bundle. Lifitegrast topical ophthalmic solution later met efficacy endpoints in dry eye (OPUS-3 NCT02284516; OPUS-1 staining NCT01421498) and was approved in 2016. That is the same target (LFA-1) and the same ocular-surface compartment at a comparable 5% concentration, so the pillars are inferred adequate. That evidence postdates the 2009 index trial, and engagement was not shown in allergic conjunctivitis. In the index trial NCT00882687, all three concentrations failed on itching and redness after conjunctival allergen challenge, with no dose trend. Itching at Day 14 was numerically worse at 5%. Tolerability did not cap the dose (no serious AEs on drug). This suggests LFA-1 antagonism does not drive the acute allergic response. The small arms (n=15 each) limit power (F7).

No direct Kv-channel engagement data exist in humans. However, amifampridine met pivotal endpoints in LEMS (NCT01377922, NCT02970162; FDA-approved) through the same presynaptic NMJ potassium-channel mechanism at comparable titrated doses. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. In AChR-MG, an open-label study showed RNS decrement improvement, but it was published after the index trial (PMID:36052140). Despite this, the index MuSK-MG trial showed no MG-ADL benefit (p=0.22), and a separate AChR-MG RCT also failed (PMID:41945880). This suggests that boosting acetylcholine release does not meaningfully drive MG outcomes as tested (F2). Secondary codes: low baseline MG-ADL scores and a withdrawal design; the follow-on study cited lack of appropriate MG-ADL data (NCT03579966) (F7). A small AChR subgroup trend favoured the drug (F3).

Amifampridine met pivotal endpoints in LEMS (NCT01377922, NCT02970162) through the same presynaptic Kv blockade at the neuromuscular junction at comparable doses, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. PK in humans is documented (PMID:25692017). No CMS-specific engagement data exist. The index crossover withdrawal trial enrolled 16 patients. SGI worsening was larger after switching to placebo (-1.75 vs -0.13), but the difference was not significant (p=0.085). CMS is genetically heterogeneous, and case series show 3,4-DAP benefit confined to particular subtypes such as COLQ, VAMP1, CHRNE, DOK7 and slow-channel (PMID:22088788, 38833907, 27634344). This points to patient heterogeneity diluting the effect, compounded by a small, likely underpowered trial. No source explicitly states the cause of failure.

NCT03567291 was an open-label safety extension, terminated because its parent placebo-controlled trials (NCT03452943, NCT03571256; PMID:34609495, 34661664) missed YGTSS-TTS at up to 48 mg/day. No direct VMAT2 occupancy or biomarker data exist in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate: at comparable doses the drug met efficacy endpoints in HD chorea and tardive dyskinesia (NCT01795859, NCT02291861, NCT02195700) through the same striatal VMAT2 mechanism. Healthy-volunteer PK confirms systemic exposure (PMID:33038289, 32155315). Tolerability did not cap dosing (PMID:37772282). With engagement inferred, the failure fits F2: VMAT2 inhibition did not reduce pediatric tics versus placebo. The large placebo responses (-8.4 vs -9.1) and the uncontrolled open-label signal (PMID:27917309) suggest F7, though no source states this.

The index trial NCT04200352 was an open-label safety extension terminated because its parent study NCT03813238 missed its primary endpoint (MD-CRS Part II, p=0.335). The real failure is the parent's lack of efficacy in dyskinetic cerebral palsy. No human VMAT2 occupancy or biomarker data appear in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate: the drug met clinician-scale endpoints in HD chorea (NCT01795859) and tardive dyskinesia (NCT02195700, NCT02291861), which act through the same CNS target at comparable doses. Healthy-volunteer PK confirms systemic exposure (PMID:33038289). No tolerability cap is shown. VMAT2 inhibition, though engaged, did not improve dyskinetic CP, so the mechanism appears not to drive the disease as tested (F2). It also failed in Tourette syndrome (NCT03452943, NCT03571256).

In NCT03954106, defibrotide was given at the approved VOD dose (6.25 mg/kg), so plasma exposure can be inferred as adequate. The trial was single-arm and compared against historical data. It was stopped after an unplanned interim look: 51% of patients had any-grade neurotoxicity, against a futility threshold of 64%. The protocol planned PK and biomarker analyses before and after dosing, but the published report (Blood Adv 2023) gives no data on adenosine receptor, plasmin or endothelial-marker engagement. It only describes a modest effect versus ZUMA-1. The drug's mechanism is poorly defined, and its prevention trials in VOD and GvHD (NCT02851407, NCT03339297) also failed. Without engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its targets from a mechanism that doesn't matter here, so the code is U. The uncontrolled design and unplanned interim analysis add an F7 element.

The bundle has no direct human pharmacodynamic data for defibrotide (no occupancy, fibrinolytic or endothelial biomarkers). The bundle shows FDA approval for hepatic veno-occlusive disease (2016), which implies systemic exposure and endothelial target engagement at standard dosing. On that basis, exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate. A comparable dose in GvHD is assumed but not shown. In the open-label index trial NCT03339297, aGvHD B-D incidence by Day +100 was 38.4% vs 47.1%, with no significant difference. This suggests the endothelial-protective mechanism does not meaningfully prevent aGvHD as tested. The prevention trial NCT02851407 in VOD also failed. The modest numerical benefit in an open-label, roughly 150-patient trial leaves possible underpowering (F7). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial compared IV iron isomaltoside with oral iron in IBD patients with iron deficiency anaemia, using Hb change at week 8 as the endpoint. No results are posted, so the bundle does not show a failure. Exposure in IBD is documented by first-order PK (PMID:22419860). Iron repletion (ferritin normalisation) and Hb rise ≥2 g/dL were shown in IBD patients (PMID:27326766). PHOSPHARE-IBD (PMID:36343979) also found FDI corrected IDA in IBD. The drug met Hb endpoints in several other IDA trials (NCT02130063, NCT02940886) and was FDA-approved for IDA in 2020. All three pillars therefore held. This was most likely an active-comparator readout, not a failure of the drug's mechanism, so F9 applies. Confidence is medium because the index result is missing.

The index trial NCT03971357 enrolled only 19 patients and was terminated because outcome variance was substantially greater than the statistical plan anticipated. Corneal clearing was 42±45% with netarsudil vs 43±49% with placebo, and no analysis was posted, so the trial could not answer the question. This is a design and execution failure. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred from topical ocular ROCK inhibition meeting IOP endpoints in glaucoma (NCT02558374, NCT03233308; outflow facility increase in PMID:29469601). That is an anterior-segment compartment related to, but not the same as, the corneal endothelium. A later Fuchs trial (NCT04498169, started after the index) showed within-group CCT reduction, consistent with pathway activity in this disease. Engagement was not measured directly in Fuchs patients.

EVO100 is a locally applied vaginal pH-modulating gel with no protein target. Its proximal effect was measured in healthy women in NCT02693418, where vaginal pH fell by about 0.5–0.76 units over 6–12 hours versus near zero with placebo. Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate because the same gel, in the same compartment at a comparable dose, met its contraceptive endpoints (NCT01306331, NCT03243305). The phase 2B/3 trial also met its chlamydia endpoint (NCT03107377, PMID:33705748). Yet in the larger index trial, study success was 684/906 with EVO100 versus 696/913 with placebo, so no benefit. This fits a mechanism that does not reliably prevent infection as tested (F2). The bundle gives no stated reason, so trial execution or user adherence (F7) cannot be excluded.

EVO100 is a topical vaginal acidifying gel with no recorded molecular target. Its intended effect is lowering vaginal pH. A Phase 1 study in healthy women (NCT02693418) showed a dose-related pH reduction versus placebo or no intervention, about -0.6 to -0.76 at 6-12 h, so the pathway was adequate and exposure and engagement are inferred. The same gel met endpoints in contraception (NCT01306331, NCT03243305) and in the Phase 2b/3 chlamydia prevention trial (NCT03107377). In the Phase 3 index trial (NCT04553068), study success was essentially identical between arms (684/906 vs 696/913). The mechanism appears engaged, yet it gave no reproducible protection, which fits F2. The inconsistency with the earlier positive trial suggests that signal was not robust (F7). The bundle offers no stated explanation.

EVO100 is a vaginal acidifying gel with no recorded protein target; its mechanism is lowering vaginal pH. Phase 1 NCT02693418 (2016, healthy women) showed that pH fell after a single dose (about -0.5 to -0.76 units at 6–12 h vs placebo), so local exposure and the acidification effect are shown in humans, before the index trial but not in infected patients. Contraceptive Phase 3 trials (NCT01306331, NCT03243305) also met their endpoints. Downstream pathogen-level effects were not measured. The Phase 2b/3 trial NCT03107377 met its chlamydia endpoint, but the larger index trial NCT04553068 showed no difference in study success (684/906 vs 696/913). With acidification achieved, this suggests the mechanism does not prevent infection, or that the earlier positive result was not reproducible. Adherence and design issues are possible but are not documented in the bundle.

The index trial NCT03967964 was a Phase 1 pharmacokinetic study of a vaginal testosterone/DHEA delivery system in hormone deficiency. It had PK primary endpoints and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of prasterone. The program's actual synovial sarcoma trial, NCT02683148, was terminated for futility ('did not show any positive effects') but posted no data. The bundle has no human evidence of AR or ESR1 engagement, tumour exposure or pathway effects in sarcoma. The vaginal atrophy approval (NCT02013544, NCT01256684) reflects local vaginal tissue action and does not carry over to systemic or tumour targets. If the sarcoma failure is the true question, it is indeterminate (U).

The index trial, NCT04274907 (venetoclax plus pembrolizumab in NSCLC), enrolled 2 patients and was terminated for 'Company Decision' with no results, so there was no efficacy readout. Sibling solid-tumour trials stopped the same way: NCT04274933 for 'Company Decision' and NCT04422210 for 'strategic prioritisation… no benefit-risk impact'. This points to a business or portfolio stop (F8) rather than a drug failure (F9). In prostate cancer itself, the enzalutamide combination (PMID:41315064) found sub-optimal venetoclax plasma levels. Its peripheral-blood pharmacodynamics showed BCL-2 changes, published after the index trial started. Only 1/10 patients had a PSA50 response. Any prostate efficacy shortfall would therefore point to inadequate exposure (F1a), not an untested target. The bundle is thin.

The index trial (NCT02015637, PMID:30985632) compared a single oral 900 mg dose of delafloxacin with active ceftriaxone. It missed only the prespecified -10% non-inferiority margin (85.1% vs 91.0% cure; CI -13.18 to 1.36). This fits F9. Plasma exposure at 900 mg was shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:26581327). Engagement of the bacterial target is inferred from efficacy in skin infection and pneumonia (NCT01811732, NCT01984684, NCT02679573), though those trials used multi-day regimens against different pathogens. Failures were concentrated in isolates with delafloxacin MIC ≥0.008 μg/mL (64.6% vs 0.6% failure). Benefit was therefore confined to low-MIC strains (F3), and the single dose may have given insufficient exposure relative to higher-MIC gonococci (F1a). No stop reason was stated.

In a 2012 lymphoma study (PMID:22965964), pacritinib reached pharmacologically active concentrations and inhibited JAK2 signaling at all doses, which shows human exposure and engagement before the index trial. Pathway is inferred_adequate: the drug met spleen-volume endpoints in myelofibrosis (NCT01773187; approval) at 200 mg BID (NCT04884191), the same dose used in COVID-19. Engagement was never measured in COVID patients. The index trial was null on IMV/ECMO or death (26/99 vs 25/101; NCT04404361), and toxicity did not limit the dose. Baricitinib (JAK1/2) succeeded in COVID-19, while pacritinib lacks JAK1 activity (PMID:42213484). This suggests JAK2-selective inhibition does not drive the outcome here (F2). A trend in the elevated-IL-6 subgroup (PMID:36469321) and early enrollment closure support F3 and F7 as secondary codes.

The index MCL trial (NCT01739309) was single-arm, with n=28 and a DCR of 71.4%. It had no prespecified threshold or comparator, so it could not show success or failure. The bundle gives no stop reason. The PMID:32381571 title reports clinical activity in R/R MCL. Exposure and engagement are shown in humans: in the first-in-human study (PMID:27217383, NCT01394016), plasma levels rose with dose and pharmacodynamic effects appeared in tumors and keratinocytes at the 200 mg Q12H MTD. Pathway is inferred adequate from efficacy in breast cancer (NCT02102490, 2017 approval). Engagement was not shown in MCL patients. Because the design could not answer the efficacy question, F7 is primary. F2 is secondary, applying only if the program was in fact judged ineffective. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index single-arm Phase 2 trial (NCT03790111), testing telotristat 500 mg with first-line chemotherapy, stopped after failing the prespecified 6-month PFS threshold: only 12 of 53 patients were responders. TPH1 inhibition at 250–500 mg was shown in humans with carcinoid syndrome. Urinary 5-HIAA fell (NCT02063659) and bowel movements improved (NCT01677910), and the drug was approved for that disease. So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate systemically at comparable doses. However, no serotonin or tumour biomarker was measured in biliary tract cancer patients, and the rationale rests only on preclinical data (PMID:39223878). The best-supported reading is that the TPH1/serotonin mechanism does not drive BTC as tested. Tumour-compartment engagement remains unverified, hence low confidence.

The index UC trial NCT01456052 had only a descriptive safety primary endpoint: TEAE counts of placebo 3/10, low dose 9/24 and high dose 10/24. It was not an efficacy test, so it cannot count as a failed efficacy readout (F9). TPH1 pillars are inferred only from carcinoid syndrome. There, telotristat met clinical endpoints: bowel movement frequency in TELESTAR (NCT01677910) and urinary 5-HIAA lowering versus placebo (NCT02063659). It was also FDA approved, which supports systemic and gut exposure, engagement and pathway effect at 250–500 mg doses. No engagement or biomarker data exist in UC patients. The carcinoid evidence postdates the index start (2012). The bundle gives no stated reason for discontinuing the UC program.

ATLAS (NCT03397394) gave the approved 600 mg BID dose and produced 0/95 responses with median PFS 1.8 months, with no difference by HRD status (PMID:34030643). Exposure and engagement were measured in humans before the trial: Phase 1 PK/PD showed about 90% PARP inhibition in PBLs and tumor tissue (PMID:27128213), with high PARP inhibition also reported in PMID:27002934, though not in urothelial patients. Pathway is inferred_adequate because the same dose met efficacy endpoints in ovarian and prostate cancer (NCT01968213, NCT02975934). The mechanism was engaged but produced no single-agent benefit in unselected UC, so the code is F2. A DRD-selected maintenance trial showed a PFS signal (PMID:35960902), which suggests patient selection may matter, so F3 is secondary.

In glioma, flucytosine (Toca FC) is a prodrug converted to 5-FU by vector-delivered cytosine deaminase (Toca 511). The index Toca 5 trial (NCT02414165) ended on sponsor decision with no results posted. Cryptococcal meningitis efficacy (PMID:449951) implies CNS penetration, but it acts through a fungal enzyme, not the vector-expressed target, so it cannot support inferred adequacy. The glioma Phase 1s (NCT01156584, NCT01470794, NCT01985256, NCT02015819) report only DLT and feasibility counts. The bundle shows no human data on intratumoral 5-FU conversion or a downstream effect. No same-target comparator exists. Because engagement is unmeasured and nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant mechanism, the failure is indeterminate.

Valbenazine met pivotal endpoints at 40–80 mg in tardive dyskinesia (NCT02274558, NCT03176771) and Huntington chorea (NCT04102579), acting on the same CNS VMAT2 target. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. PMID:39757283 estimates 85–90% VMAT2 occupancy at 80 mg, but that relationship comes from non-human primates. No engagement data exist in Tourette patients; the pediatric PK/PD trial NCT02256475 posted no results. No dose cap from tolerability is shown. Repeated Tourette trials in adults and children missed YGTSS endpoints (NCT02581865, NCT02679079, NCT03325010), and the randomized-withdrawal index trial stopped for futility (NCT03530293). Together these point to VMAT2 inhibition at these doses not driving tic benefit. The secondary F7 reflects that the index trial's primary endpoint could not be assessed (NA medians in both arms).

Single-arm phase 2 in T-cell lymphoma: 4/18 regressive responses (NCT00798096). Human PK shows rapid conversion to R406 with dose-proportional systemic exposure (PMID:23190017). SYK engagement was never measured in this bundle. It is inferred_adequate because fostamatinib met efficacy endpoints through systemic SYK inhibition in ITP (NCT02076399, NCT04132050; FDA approval) and RA (NCT00665925, NCT01197534) at 100-150 mg doses, with an exposure-response relationship (PMID:25280085). However, the index dose is not shown. The inference also crosses compartments, from immune effector cells to malignant T cells, and no engagement was shown in lymphoma tissue. A non-driver SYK target (F2) is the most supported reading. Drug-level indeterminacy (U) and a small, uncontrolled design (F7) remain plausible.

Index trial gave ORR 2/21 at 100mg BID and 0/47 at 200mg BID (NCT01499303, PMID:26707592). Plasma R406 exposure is well characterized (PMID:23190017). No direct SYK occupancy or BCR-pathway biomarker data exist in DLBCL. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because the same SYK inhibition at 100mg BID met efficacy endpoints in RA and ITP (NCT00665925, NCT01197534, NCT02076399). This is an inference across different tissues. The 200mg BID dose was the phase 1-selected dose and was 'generally well tolerated', so the dose was not capped. The earlier 22% DLBCL response (PMID:19965662) was not reproduced. The pattern suggests SYK is not a driver in relapsed DLBCL as tested. Clinical benefit occurred only in GCB/intermediate cases, never ABC, which points to heterogeneity (secondary F3).

The index trial tested 9 mg ITI-007 for dementia agitation and stopped for futility (CMAI-C aggressive -1.0 vs -2.3 placebo). Healthy-volunteer PET published in 2015, before the index trial, showed rapid brain entry. At a comparable 10 mg dose it showed >80% cortical 5-HT2A occupancy (PMID:25843749). So the 5-HT2A mechanism was engaged, yet there was no benefit, which points to F2. However, D2 occupancy at that dose was only ~12%, versus about 39% at the efficacious 40-60 mg doses (PMID:30449883). The D2 component was therefore barely tested, and brexpiprazole, which acts on D2, is approved for Alzheimer's agitation; hence F1a as secondary. The bundle shows no engagement data in dementia patients (NCT02078310 posted no results) and no pathway biomarker.

Exposure is adequate: linear PK at 1 mg in humans (PMID:28398597). Engagement was not measured directly but is inferred_adequate, because the same 0.92 mg dose met pivotal UC endpoints through S1PR1 in the gut (NCT02435992). Pathway is adequate: marked B- and T-cell reductions in Crohn patients in STEPSTONE (NCT02531113, PMID:38568396) and in MS (PMID:32737072). The index trial failed (29.8% vs 30.5%). Its identical twin, NCT03440372, met the same endpoint with a similar drug-arm rate (31.3%) but placebo at 20.8%. This points to a high placebo response in the index trial rather than an absent drug effect. The maintenance trial was borderline (p=0.054), and the program was terminated for business reasons (F8). F2 remains possible if the true effect is modest.

Siponimod's S1PR1 functional antagonism was shown in humans. Healthy-volunteer studies showed a profound lymphocyte reduction (PMID:22646698, 2012; IV regimen designed for ICH, PMID:31926605), and the drug is approved for MS via the same peripheral lymphocyte mechanism (NCT01665144). In the ICH patients themselves, T and B cells fell markedly by day 3 and monocyte TNF signaling was suppressed (PMID:42501052, PMID:41646803), so engagement and pathway held in the disease. Despite this, perihematomal edema at day 14 was unchanged (ratio 1.05, p=0.585; NCT03338998), even though siponimod reduced edema in mice (PMID:31558140). Peripheral immunomodulation therefore did not drive edema as tested; higher monocyte TNF signaling even tracked with better outcome. The trial was very small (n=27 analyzed), so F7 also applies.

Plasma exposure is well characterised in humans (PMID:35620290, PMID:26519230). Engagement of S1PR1 is shown as profound, dose-related lymphocyte sequestration in healthy volunteers, published in 2012, before the index trial started (PMID:22646698, PMID:31926605). Efficacy in MS at 2 mg confirms the mechanism holds clinically (NCT01665144, NCT00879658). The index trial tested 0.5, 2 and 10 mg, spanning and exceeding the approved dose, with no tolerability cap. It found no MMT-24 benefit versus placebo and was stopped for futility (NCT02029274). Engagement was not measured in dermatomyositis patients. This supports F2: lymphocyte trafficking modulation did not improve the disease as tested. Arms of only 3–4 patients limit the inference (secondary F7).

Siponimod's systemic exposure is well characterised in humans (PMID:35620290, PMID:31926605). S1PR1 engagement was shown in healthy volunteers in 2012, before the index trial: profound, reversible lymphocyte sequestration (PMID:22646698). Efficacy in MS at 2 mg (NCT01665144, NCT00879658) also supports engagement. Doses up to 10 mg were tolerated (PMID:26519230), so the dose was not capped. No engagement data exist in dermatomyositis or polymyositis patients. The index trial (NCT02029274) stopped for futility: there was no MMT-24 benefit at 0.5, 2 or 10 mg, with numerically worse change at higher doses. This points to S1PR1-mediated lymphocyte trafficking not driving myositis as tested. The tiny groups (n=3–4) and the terminated polymyositis trials (NCT01801917, NCT01148810) limit certainty (F7).

Adding acalabrutinib to pembrolizumab gave no response gain in NSCLC (4/28 vs 4/31; NCT02448303). Exposure and BTK engagement are well documented in humans at 100 mg doses: about 99% peripheral B-cell occupancy in healthy volunteers (PMID:28882879), and 95-97% trough occupancy with BCR/NFkB pathway suppression in CLL (PMID:31876911, PMID:32054731, PMID:32202637). This evidence comes from blood or B cells, not NSCLC tumor or myeloid compartments, and was not obtained in this disease. The same null result with pembrolizumab in urothelial, head and neck, pancreatic and ovarian cancer (NCT02351739, NCT02454179, NCT02362048, NCT02537444) suggests BTK inhibition does not drive solid-tumor response as tested. Medium confidence because tumor-compartment engagement was never measured.

Acalabrutinib achieves reliable plasma exposure. It produces near-complete peripheral BTK occupancy: about 99% at 100 mg in healthy volunteers (PMID:28882879) and over 95% at trough in CLL (PMID:32054731, PMID:31876911). It also inhibits downstream BCR/NFκB signalling (PMID:32202637). No dose-limiting toxicities occurred (PMID:26641137). No occupancy was measured in ovarian cancer patients or tumour tissue, but systemic BTK engagement is well established. In NCT02537444, monotherapy responses were 1/35 and combination with pembrolizumab 3/33. The same pattern of essentially no added activity appeared in pancreatic, NSCLC, head and neck, and urothelial trials (NCT02362048, NCT02448303, NCT02454179, NCT02351739). This suggests BTK inhibition does not drive solid-tumour response as tested, rather than a failure to engage the target.

Acalabrutinib achieved robust systemic exposure and near-complete BTK occupancy in humans: about 99% in peripheral B cells after 100 mg in healthy volunteers (PMID:28882879) and over 95% trough occupancy in CLL (PMID:32054731, PMID:31876911). In CLL it also produced downstream BCR/NFκB pathway inhibition (PMID:32202637), and it is approved for B-cell malignancies. None of this was measured in RA patients, and the cited publications appeared after the index trial started. In the index trial (NCT02387762), DAS28-CRP at week 4 was numerically worse with drug (5.40) than placebo (5.05). There were no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement adequate, this points to BTK inhibition not driving RA as tested. The trial was small (n=31) and short (4 weeks), so F7 also applies. No BTK inhibitor has succeeded in RA in this bundle.

Acalabrutinib achieved robust plasma exposure and near-complete BTK occupancy in humans: about 99% in healthy volunteers (PMID:28882879) and over 95% trough in patients (PMID:31876911, PMID:34269152). Downstream BCR/NFκB signaling was inhibited in CLL (PMID:32054731, PMID:32202637), with no dose-limiting toxicity. These data come from healthy volunteers and hematologic patients, not pancreatic cancer, and were published after the index start. In NCT02362048, monotherapy produced 0/29 responses and the pembrolizumab combination 3/27. Parallel solid-tumor trials also showed no benefit from adding acalabrutinib (NCT02537444, NCT02448303, NCT02454179, NCT02351739). This points to BTK inhibition not driving pancreatic cancer as tested. No same-target drug succeeded in pancreatic cancer, so F1b does not apply.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The index trial used acalabrutinib 100 mg BID. At this dose BTK occupancy is near-complete: about 99% in healthy volunteers and 95–97% at trough in CLL (PMID:28882879, PMID:32054731, PMID:31876911). The CLL phase 1/2 PK/PD study NCT02029443 began before the index trial. Occupancy was never measured in HNSCC patients or on tumor myeloid cells. The proposed myeloid-reprogramming pathway effect was only a non-conclusive CD45+ infiltration trend in 2 combination-arm patients (PMID:34862248). Even with adequate systemic engagement, adding acalabrutinib gave no ORR benefit over pembrolizumab (5/30 vs 7/37), and the trial was terminated for lack of clinical benefit. The same null result appeared in bladder, NSCLC, pancreatic and ovarian trials, pointing to the mechanism rather than the molecule. Serious AEs were higher with the combination (25/37 vs 12/39), a secondary concern.

Acalabrutinib at its approved dose gives about 95-99% BTK occupancy in healthy volunteers and CLL patients (PMID:28882879, PMID:32054731, PMID:31876911), with CLL PK/PD work registered before the index trial (NCT02029443). Exposure and engagement are therefore adequate, though not measured in urothelial patients. In the index trial, MDSC suppression, the proposed pathway effect, was not shown overall: MDSCs fell in only one patient and did not track response (PMID:32757302). Adding acalabrutinib did not improve ORR, PFS or OS over pembrolizumab (NCT02351739). The same null result recurred in NSCLC, head and neck, ovarian and pancreatic cancer, suggesting BTK inhibition does not add to PD-1 blockade in solid tumors. Commentary suggests biomarker-based patient selection (PMID:32757318), so F3 is secondary.

Acalabrutinib reaches plasma and engages BTK in humans. In healthy volunteers, 100 mg gives about 99% peripheral B-cell occupancy (PMID:28882879). In CLL, 100 mg BID gives about 97% trough occupancy with downstream BCR/NF-kB inhibition (PMID:31876911, 32054731, 32202637). These data were published before the index trial began in June 2020. Exposure via NG tube was comparable (PMID:36029150). Tolerability did not limit the dose. Engagement was not shown in COVID-19 patients: PMID:32503877 has no abstract. Despite this target coverage, both randomized COVID-19 trials missed their endpoints, with the drug arm numerically worse (NCT04346199: 83.1% vs 90.9%; NCT04380688: 80.6% vs 83.9%). Other BTK inhibitors in COVID-19 also stopped at phase 2. BTK inhibition does not appear to drive outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19.

The CARE index trial (NCT01970371) randomized only 37 mMITT patients. The primary ACM/SDRC outcome strongly favored plazomicin (23.5% vs 50%), but the 95% CI (-0.7 to 51.2) narrowly crossed zero. This reads as an underpowered trial, not a drug that lacks activity. Exposure was adequate: plazomicin met its AUC/MIC PD target in all 15 CARE patients with BSI or HABP/VABP, and microbiological response was 86.7% (PMID:31254273). Population PK supports plasma exposure across these patients (PMID:30670433). Engagement is inferred adequate because plazomicin met its cUTI endpoint in Phase 3 and was approved (NCT02486627). The in-disease evidence was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:21911572).

In ER+ post-AI metastatic breast cancer, abiraterone plus prednisone, alone or with exemestane, did not improve PFS versus exemestane (HR 1.14 and 0.96; NCT01381874). At the standard 1000 mg dose, plasma exposure rose with dose and CYP17A1 inhibition was clear in humans: testosterone and DHEAS fell to near the quantification limit (PMID:25117615, NCT01186484), and tissue androgens fell (NCT00924469). This was shown only in prostate cancer, before the index trial, which followed the 2011 approval (NCT00638690). With a systemic adrenal target engaged and no tolerability cap, androgen-synthesis blockade failed to drive benefit. Preclinical work suggests abiraterone has ER-agonist activity that may blunt efficacy (PMID:29991699, PMID:27083183), but this is not shown in humans. Breast-specific estrogen lowering was not measured.

In NCT01284634, none of the cannabidiol doses (200, 400 or 800 mg/day) changed liver triglycerides relative to placebo after 8 weeks, and no serious adverse events occurred. The bundle and my searches found no human evidence of CB1 occupancy or modulation, liver drug levels, or a downstream biomarker change. The human PK data on cannabidiol (PMID:29540584, PMID:30286443) come from other doses and populations, and none measures the liver or the target. The epilepsy approvals cannot stand in for engagement, because they do not work through liver CB1. No other CB1 drug succeeded in fatty liver disease; rimonabant reached phase 3 only. The trial was very small (5–7 participants per arm) with a wide spread of results, so F7 is secondary. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here.

In the index trial NCT04421456, adjunctive CBD at 300 or 1000 mg did no better than placebo on PANSS-T or any other primary endpoint (p>0.4). The sponsor stopped the trial early for a business decision, so only about 20 patients per arm were analysed. The bundle has no human data on CB1 occupancy, CB1 modulation or a downstream CB1 marker. Evidence that CB1 is engaged comes only from in vitro work (Laprairie 2015). The epilepsy approvals cannot stand in for engagement, because the sources do not tie CBD's effect in epilepsy, or its antipsychotic-like effects in animals, to CB1 (PMID:39305939). A single-dose fMRI study in psychosis (PMID:31994476) shows CBD acts on the brain but not on this target. With engagement unknown, the failure is U. The small, early-stopped trial also fits F7.

Canopy Growth ran the index trial (NCT04577612). It gave single oral doses of 150, 300 or 600 mg CBD before a 10% CO2 breathing challenge, and fear, panic symptoms and heart rate were no different from placebo. In panic disorder patients, 300 mg CBD added to exposure therapy also did not help (PMID:35561538, PMID:38044339). None of the sources show, in humans, brain CBD levels, CB1 occupancy or modulation, or a change in an endocannabinoid biomarker. The epilepsy approvals do not let us infer engagement, because no source says those seizure effects come through CB1. So engagement is no_human_data, and nothing separates 'CBD never engaged CB1 adequately' from 'the mechanism does not drive fear'. The code is U.

The index trial (NCT01898520) tested Sativex/nabiximols for pediatric cerebral palsy spasticity on a 0-10 NRS endpoint. It posted no results and gave no stated reason. The same product met an identical spasticity NRS endpoint in MS (NCT00681538, p=0.0002; registered 2008, before the index trial). That supports inferring that exposure, engagement and pathway held in the CNS for this symptom mechanism. No pediatric CP pharmacokinetic or engagement data are in the bundle, and dose comparability in children is unverified. Pediatric CBD exposure was dose-proportional in Dravet (PMID:29540584), but that was a different formulation. No tolerability cap is shown. A failure despite the inferred mechanism points most directly to F2. U and F7 (small trial, n=72) remain plausible, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT03573518 (topical BTX 1503, 2.5–5%) registered only descriptive safety (TEAEs at Day 84) as its primary outcome. It reported no deaths or serious AEs and posted no efficacy comparison, so the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout. The index trial was not an efficacy test, hence F9. For pillars, there are no human skin-level exposure, CNR1 engagement or sebum/inflammation biomarker data for topical CBD. Acne mechanism evidence is in vitro only (PMID:25061872, PMID:35982758) and does not count. Oral CBD's epilepsy approvals involve a different route and tissue compartment (PMID:29540584), so pillars cannot be inferred as adequate. If an unshown efficacy miss drove the stop, U would apply because engagement has no human data.

The index trial, NCT01217112 (Jadoon et al., Diabetes Care 2016), was a small pilot study with about 12 people per arm. It gave CBD (GWP42003) alone, THCV (GWP42004) alone, or the two combined, and none of the arms changed HDL compared with placebo (all p>0.4). Neither the bundle nor my search turned up any human evidence that CBD occupies or blocks CB1 (CNR1), or moves a CB1-linked biomarker, at any dose. The CBD exposure data in PMID:29540584 come from the epilepsy program, where CBD works through mechanisms other than CB1. So the approved uses do not let us infer that CB1 was engaged. The related CBD liver-fat trial NCT01284634 was also negative. Rimonabant, which acts on the same target, never reached approval in this disease. Engagement is unknown, so the failure code is U. The trial's exploratory pilot design (F7) also limits what it can show.

The index trial NCT04615949 was terminated because recruitment became unfeasible as COVID-19 changed (vaccination, natural immunity, milder variants). Only 90 patients were randomized, with 3 vs 2 composite events (p=0.68). The trial could not answer the efficacy question, so this is a design/execution failure rather than a test of the mechanism. Systemic exposure is dose-proportional in humans (PMID:29540584). There are no human data on CNR1 engagement or on an anti-inflammatory pathway effect in COVID-19; the small pilot's cytokine changes were mixed (PMID:40170643). The epilepsy approvals (e.g., NCT02224703) involve a different, CNS compartment and cannot be used to infer engagement here. If the readout is treated as informative, the mechanism question remains indeterminate (U).

Elagolix PK and dose-dependent suppression of LH, FSH and estradiol were shown in healthy premenopausal women before the index trial (PMID:19033369, PMID:28323948). The drug also met pivotal endpoints in endometriosis and fibroids (NCT01620528, NCT02654054). In PCOS patients in the index trial, LH AUC fell significantly versus placebo in every dose group, and estradiol and testosterone were consistently reduced (PMID:37398623). Engagement and pathway are therefore adequate in this disease, although that evidence came only from the index trial itself. Across 25 mg BID to 300 mg, menstrual cycle normalization was not improved (0–5.6% vs 7.7% placebo; NCT03951077). Tolerability did not limit dosing. Suppressing GnRHR/LH did not restore ovulatory cycles, so the mechanism does not drive the endpoint as tested.

The sponsor blamed the trial, not the drug. Array said placebo response was higher than expected and varied by region: South American placebo ACR20 was 60.9%, versus 34.6% in Eastern Europe, where the drug showed trends toward benefit (ACR20 p=0.115, DAS28 p=0.067). So F7 is primary. Before the trial (2006), healthy-volunteer data showed linear plasma exposure. Ex vivo, the drug blocked IL-1β by 50% to over 95% and also blocked TNFα once plasma levels passed 50 ng/mL. This cytokine read-out is the main evidence for both engagement and pathway effect. Whether the 10–20 mg BID RA doses reached that level, and whether target was hit in RA patients, is not reported. Cancer studies later confirmed target inhibition (PMID:28152546). F2 is secondary: engagement looked adequate but overall benefit was missing.

The disease label appears garbled; the index trial (NCT03271047) tested binimetinib with nivolumab ± ipilimumab in MSS RAS-mutant mCRC. ORR was 0% and 7.4%, with few DLTs in phase 1b, so the dose was not capped. The phase 1 study (NCT00959127/PMID:28152546, registered 2009, with KRAS-mutant CRC expansion cohorts) showed dose-proportional exposure and target inhibition in serum and skin at 45 mg BID. Tumor pERK/DUSP6 fell in melanoma biopsies (PMID:30956763, 31395751). MErCuRIC showed engagement in RAS-mutant CRC (PMID:40211189). Melanoma approval (NCT01763164) confirms the MEK pathway was active at this dose. Despite adequate engagement, MEK inhibition with checkpoint blockade produced no meaningful responses, consistent with prior null CRC results (NCT01927341).

Glasdegib 100 mg QD gave measurable plasma exposure in MF patients (PMID:30849661). Hedgehog engagement was shown in other populations: >80% skin GLI1 downregulation at 80-320 mg in solid tumors (PMID:25388167) and marked GLI1 suppression at 25-100 mg in heme malignancies (PMID:28556364). The same 100 mg dose produced an approval-level OS benefit in AML (NCT01546038, PMID:32885274). Tolerability did not cap the dose (MTD 320 mg). Yet in the ruxolitinib-pretreated MF lead-in (NCT02226172), no patient reached ≥35% SVR at week 24, and symptom and anemia responses were sparse (PMID:30849661). This points to SMO inhibition not driving MF as tested (F2). No engagement data from MF patients themselves was shown. The randomized cohort was never run and no termination reason was stated (F7 possible).

In the index trial NCT00678535 (n=904), adding cetuximab to capecitabine/cisplatin gave no PFS benefit: 4.4 vs 5.6 months, HR 1.09, p=0.32. It also brought more serious AEs. Cetuximab holds FDA approvals in several EGFR-driven solid tumors. At the standard 400/250 mg/m2 weekly dosing used in human studies (PMID:22615057, PMID:30811063), anti-EGFR efficacy therefore implies adequate systemic exposure and EGFR engagement, so all three pillars are inferred_adequate. PMID:30811063 also shows plasma exposure in HNSCC with a soluble-EGFR change. No engagement data exist in gastric cancer patients, and nothing shows the dose was limited by tolerability. The best explanation is F2: EGFR blockade does not drive unselected esophagogastric cancer. Preclinical data suggest only an EGFR-amplified subset responds (PMID:24141978), which supports F3 as secondary.

Cetuximab is FDA-approved in several EGFR-driven solid tumours (anal, nasopharyngeal, salivary gland and others) through systemic tumour EGFR blockade at standard dosing. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. PK and soluble-EGFR changes are also shown in HNSCC patients (PMID:30811063). No prostate-specific human engagement data exist, and preclinical work notes low EGFR expression in prostate cancer (PMID:30320363) and no added effect in DU145 cells (PMID:34321039). In the index trial NCT00661492, median TTP was 4.9 vs 6.6 months with no statistical comparison, unlabeled arms and more serious AEs in the larger arm. No benefit appeared. This suggests EGFR does not drive AIPC as tested. The non-assessable design (F7) is a secondary contributor.

No study in the bundle measured target engagement directly. Rifamycin SV-MMX is a colon-targeted antibiotic: 87% of an oral dose is excreted unchanged in feces. At 400 mg b.i.d. it met its endpoint in traveler's diarrhea (NCT01142089, NCT01208922), which acts through the same bacterial target in the gut lumen at a similar dose, so I treat all three pillars as inferred_adequate. In the index trial (NCT01847664), day-10 treatment success was 62.2% on RIF-800, 49.4% on RIF-1800 and 47.5% on placebo (P=0.06). Investigators reported the clearest benefit at day 3; placebo patients caught up by day 10. Patients whose attack had lasted longer also did better on drug. So the published report points to endpoint timing in a self-limiting disease (F4). Secondary codes: a responsive subgroup (F3) and possibly little role for antibiotics in this disease (F2).

The index ITP trial (NCT01054443) tested 0.5–1.0 mg. Week-6 response was 0–20% with no dose trend (p=0.431). It was terminated because 'a higher dose was necessary to elicit an efficacy effect.' Tolerability was not the limit: there was only one SAE. Platelet PK/PD effects were shown in healthy subjects (PMID:27209291). Efficacy in chronic liver disease (NCT02389621) used 3 mg daily (PMID:31055790), several-fold above the ITP doses. So the doses tested did not adequately engage MPL in ITP patients, and no engagement data in ITP exist. The target is valid: eltrombopag, romiplostim and avatrombopag are approved for ITP. That supports F1a, with F1b as a secondary code. The companion ITP study (NCT01129024) then stopped for a business decision rather than another efficacy readout.

The index trial NCT01978938 was an active-controlled non-inferiority test against levofloxacin. Responders were 180/298 vs 202/302, a difference of -6.5% (CI -14.1 to 1.2), so it missed only the NI margin, which fits F9. The later cUTI trial NCT03032510 was also numerically inferior to ertapenem. Plasma exposure was dose-proportional in healthy volunteers (PMID:30150464). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because eravacycline met cIAI cure endpoints at 1 mg/kg q12h (NCT01844856, NCT02784704), although that is a different compartment. Biliary/fecal elimination is the major excretion route (PMID:30559132), but urinary exposure in cUTI patients is not shown. So the bundle cannot separate inadequate urinary exposure from true relative inferiority, hence U as secondary.

Pitolisant 40 mg gave high (84%) brain H3 receptor occupancy by PET in healthy volunteers (PMID:32293706). The index trial used a comparable 36 mg dose. The PET paper appeared in 2020, after the index trial started, so engagement_before_index rests on the earlier narcolepsy Phase 3 program (NCT01067222, NCT01638403, NCT01800045). That program and the 2019 FDA approval show the CNS H3R mechanism worked at similar doses, so exposure, engagement and pathway held there; photosensitivity suppression in epilepsy also showed central pharmacodynamics (PMID:23665640). In T1D, the glucagon response to hypoglycemia did not improve (7.5 vs 13.1 pg/mL placebo). The sponsor stopped the trial on 'scientific data' (NCT04026750), suggesting the mechanism does not drive counterregulation. Tiny enrollment (n=5) and high screen failure limit the conclusion (F7).

In healthy volunteers, PET showed high (84%) brain H3 occupancy after 40 mg pitolisant (PMID:32293706), comparable to the 36 mg dose used in NCT04026750. Plasma exposure is characterised (PMID:26879827). The narcolepsy approval (pivotal NCT01800045) implies the central H3 pathway effect holds at these doses. Engagement was never shown in T1D, and the PET data were published after the index trial started; pre-index support comes only from the narcolepsy efficacy. The trial was stopped citing 'scientific data collected during the trial' plus a high screen-fail rate. The glucagon response to hypoglycemia did not favour drug (7.5 vs 13.1 pg/mL), suggesting the target did not drive the expected counterregulatory benefit (F2). However, with n=5 the trial was underpowered and operationally compromised (F7), so confidence is low.

In the index trial NCT01601236 (n=34), percent eGFR change at week 36 for Acthar 8 U and 16 U overlapped with placebo, and no statistical test was reported. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, MC2R engagement (e.g., cortisol response) or pathway data at these doses, in diabetic nephropathy or elsewhere. Approvals in FSGS and membranous nephropathy exist, but the bundle gives no doses. So comparability to the 8/16 U arms cannot be shown, and inferred adequacy is not justified. Nothing separates inadequate engagement from target irrelevance, so the code is U. The very small, unbalanced arms (10/7/16) and the absence of formal testing mean the trial could hardly answer the question (secondary F7). No other MC2R drugs or PubMed evidence relevant to diabetic kidney disease are in the bundle.

Human plasma exposure is documented: rapid absorption and a 5–11 h half-life (PMID:29191916). Engagement in humans was shown only in CLL, as phospho-AKT inhibition in tumor cells (PMID:29191916, published 2018, after the index trial began in 2013). The drug met efficacy endpoints in CLL/SLL and iNHL through PI3Kδ/γ in leukocytes at 25 mg BID (NCT02004522, NCT01882803, PMID:30094870). That supports inferred adequacy for systemic immune-cell engagement, although the RA doses and any synovial or RA-specific PD are not in the bundle. No RA results were posted for NCT01851707, and no stop reason is given. Arthritis models were positive (PMID:24244039), but no RA-patient engagement data exist. F2 is the most likely code, with low confidence; U remains plausible.

The index trial NCT03037203 had a safety/tolerability primary endpoint (TEAEs leading to discontinuation), so it was not an efficacy test. That endpoint was descriptive, and tolerability matched the known profile. No pillar was measured directly. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 75–300 mg doses met MWT/ESS endpoints in narcolepsy and OSA through the same CNS DAT/NET mechanism (NCT01485770, NCT01681121, NCT02348632, NCT06103825). In PD, MWT improved dose-dependently (+5.05 min at 300 mg, nominal P=0.0098). ESS did not separate because placebo response was large (−4.78 vs −4.82 to −5.72) (PMID:34191352). This suggests high placebo response, a small 4-week crossover design, and a subjective-endpoint issue rather than mechanism failure.

AM-101 was intratympanic esketamine gel meant to block NMDA receptors in the cochlea. Its Phase 3 trial TACTT2 (NCT01803646) missed both primary endpoints (TLQ p=0.32, TFI p=0.63). No source gives human perilymph or cochlear drug levels, NMDA receptor engagement, or an auditory-nerve biomarker. The only human pharmacology finding is trace plasma levels, showing minimal systemic exposure. The cochlear mechanism evidence is from animals (PMID:25871611). Esketamine's success in depression (NCT01640080 and others) involved a different tissue compartment (the brain) and a different route, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. Earlier Phase 2 signals appeared only in subgroups (PMID:24603353), and the sponsor shifted its focus to the otitis media and severe-tinnitus subgroups, which suggests F3. With no human engagement data, the code is U.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Index single-arm HNSCC trial (NCT00768664) of dacomitinib 45 mg gave an ORR of 12.5% with no stated success threshold, and the program went no further. The bundle has no human target-engagement or pharmacodynamic data in HNSCC. Plasma PK in healthy volunteers is documented (PMID:23760812). At the same 45 mg dose, the drug met PFS endpoints through EGFR inhibition in NSCLC (NCT01774721, NCT00769067), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. That inference is weak because the NSCLC benefit was in EGFR-mutant tumours, not EGFR-overexpressing HNSCC. The bundle shows no other EGFR drug succeeding in HNSCC, so F1b does not apply. F2 is the best fit, but the thin data leave an indeterminate (U) reading possible.

The index trial NCT04537806 was ended early by an 'internal company decision' after enrolling 29 patients. Its primary endpoint was a tie: 23.1% of patients in each arm were alive and free of respiratory failure at Day 28. Plasma exposure at the 90 µg/kg/h dose is documented in humans (Cmax about 90 ng/mL, PMID:35869362). The drug's approval for postpartum depression (NCT02942004, NCT02614547) depends on GABA-A modulation in the brain. That is not the same tissue compartment as the proposed effect on lung and immune cells in ARDS, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. No human data on engagement or immune/inflammatory biomarkers in ARDS was found. Engagement therefore has no human data, and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The small, terminated trial also limits what it can show (F7).

In the index trial (NCT04537806, n=26 analyzed), 23.1% of patients in each arm were alive and free of respiratory failure at Day 28 (p=1.0). Sage gave only an 'internal company decision' as the reason for stopping. Plasma exposure at the 90 µg/kg/h infusion rate is documented (PMID:35869362, Cmax about 90 ng/mL). The protocol rested only on preclinical evidence and proposed several mechanisms through GABA-A receptors in the lung and immune cells. PPD efficacy (NCT02614547, NCT02942004) shows GABA-A engagement in the brain, which is a different tissue compartment, so it does not support inferred engagement for ARDS. No human data on engagement or on inflammatory or airway biomarkers were found for COVID-19. The very small trial (F7) also could not answer the question, so the failure is indeterminate.

Topical trifarotene, an RARγ agonist, met pivotal endpoints in acne at 50 µg/g (NCT02556788, NCT02566369; FDA approved 2019). That shows skin exposure, RARγ engagement and a downstream effect in the same compartment (topically treated skin) at a dose lower than the 100–200 µg/g tested in lamellar ichthyosis. All three pillars are therefore inferred_adequate. No direct engagement data exist in LI patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose: there were no serious AEs, and PMID:32017149 reports no safety concerns up to 100 µg/g. The index trial stopped for futility with 0/15, 2/17 and 0/17 resolutions versus vehicle, suggesting RARγ agonism does not resolve LI as tested. The small arms and the strict 'resolution' endpoint leave some design uncertainty (F7).

In relapsed/refractory Hodgkin lymphoma (NCT01217229), single-agent pexidartinib gave 1 PR in 20 patients and a median PFS of 56 days. Tolerability was acceptable (1/20 serious AEs), so the dose was not capped. At 1000 mg/day, human data show adequate plasma and tumor-tissue exposure (Cmax 8090 ng/mL; 5500 ng/g in tumor). CSF1R engagement and pathway effects were also shown: plasma CSF1 rose and CD14dim/CD16+ monocytes fell (PMID:26449250, PMID:32943455). Tissue macrophage modulation was seen in sarcoma (PMID:34321280), and the drug succeeded in CSF1-driven TGCT (NCT02371369). This engagement evidence comes from other diseases and was published after the index trial began. No CSF1R agent has succeeded in Hodgkin lymphoma. CSF1R inhibition engaged but did not drive benefit in this disease.

At 600–1000 mg/day, pexidartinib reached high plasma levels and tumor tissue levels (Cmax 8090 ng/mL; tumor 5500 ng/g) in glioblastoma patients (PMID:26449250, NCT01349036), with population PK in solid tumors (PMID:33043474). Target engagement was shown by a rise in plasma CSF1 and a fall in CD14dim/CD16+ monocytes (PMID:26449250, PMID:32943455). Tumor M2 macrophages fell in sarcoma (PMID:34321280). Engagement is also inferred from the TGCT approval (NCT02371369). None of this was in colorectal cancer. Despite engagement, monotherapy activity in solid tumors was minimal: 1 PR in 8 in the index trial (NCT02734433) and none in NCT01004861. This points to CSF1R not driving tumor control. However, the index trial was a tiny Asian dose-cohort study, not a CRC-specific efficacy test (F9/F7).

At 1000 mg/day (an index-trial dose), human exposure was shown: plasma Cmax ~8 µg/mL and tumor tissue levels of 5500 ng/g (PMID:26449250). Engagement and pathway were shown by a rise in plasma CSF1 and depletion of CD16+ monocytes (PMID:26449250, PMID:32943455). The drug also met a pivotal endpoint in TGCT through the same target (NCT02371369). None of this was measured in pancreatic cancer patients. With CSF1R engaged, single-agent activity was minimal across solid tumors: in NCT02734433, 1 PR in 8 evaluable patients, alongside failures in GBM and Hodgkin lymphoma (NCT01349036, NCT01217229). This points to the target not driving these tumors. The index trial was a small Asian safety/PK bridging study, not a pancreatic efficacy test, so F9 is also possible. The bundle is thin.

In the index trial, 1000 mg/day was well tolerated. Plasma Cmax was about 8,000 ng/mL (NCT01349036), and tumor tissue reached a median 5,500 ng/g, so the drug crossed the blood-tumor barrier (PMID:26449250). Target engagement in GBM patients was shown by a rise in plasma CSF1 and a fall in CD14dim/CD16+ monocytes, consistent with CSF1R blockade; pediatric data show the same markers (PMID:32943455). These data were published after the index trial started. Even so, PFS6 was 8.6% with no responses. The newly diagnosed GBM combination trial also failed despite pharmacodynamic modulation (NCT01790503, PMID:39734810).
