The 'business decision' stop followed a clear efficacy failure, so F8 does not apply. CSF1R inhibition does not drive GBM as tested. Intratumoral macrophage effects were not reported, so confidence is medium.

In the R/R FLT3-ITD AML trial NCT01349049, doses ≥3000 mg gave trough plasma that produced about 95% inhibition of FLT3 phosphorylation. Exposure plateaued, and no maximum tolerated dose was reached, so the dose was not tolerability-capped (PMID:32330242). CSF1R engagement and pathway effects were shown in humans at ≤1000 mg: plasma CSF1 rose and CD16+ monocytes fell (PMID:26449250, PMID:32943455). Efficacy in TGCT was also confirmed (NCT02371369). Despite adequate engagement, only about 11% composite CR and a median OS of 112 days resulted, so the mechanism alone did not drive meaningful benefit. Non-responders carried co-mutations (NRAS, TP53, CCND3), which suggests heterogeneity contributed (PMID:34103301). The engagement data were published after the trial started. The trial was single-arm with no formal success threshold.

Golimumab (200 mg load, then 100 mg every 4 weeks SC) did not improve week-16 FVC versus placebo in pulmonary sarcoidosis (NCT00955279, PMID:25034562). It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. No direct TNF engagement was measured in sarcoidosis. Engagement is inferred adequate because the same systemic TNF neutralization at comparable or lower SC doses met endpoints in UC, PsA and AS (NCT00487539, PMID:23735746, NCT02181673, NCT02186873). Human plasma PK is shown (PMID:19940229). Post hoc whole-blood transcriptomics found treatment-associated gene changes, published after the index trial. They also found marked molecular heterogeneity across sarcoidosis phenotypes (PMID:28205212), and skin endpoints trended positive. This supports F2, the TNF target not driving pulmonary disease as tested, with secondary F3 for heterogeneity.

The index trial NCT01850420 (IMC-1 = famciclovir + celecoxib, 143 fibromyalgia patients, 16 weeks) is reported in PMID:28260944 as having significantly reduced pain versus placebo, its registered primary outcome, with secondary benefits and good tolerability. The index readout was therefore not an efficacy failure. A follow-on Phase 2 (NCT04748705) was run, but the bundle gives no outcome for it. Exposure is adequate: penciclovir plasma levels are documented in humans (PMID:8059539, PMID:8162668). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate from approved antiviral efficacy against herpes viruses at comparable doses (PMID:8667538, NCT01281007). That engagement evidence comes from herpes, not fibromyalgia. Nothing in the bundle shows a failure attributable to the drug.

Index trial NCT02138786 gave selinexor 60 mg (the RP2D) and stopped at interim analysis for lack of efficacy: ORR 4%, 1 PR in 25. The same dose met efficacy endpoints in myeloma (NCT02336815, NCT03110562) and supported a DLBCL approval, so exposure and engagement in malignant B cells are inferred adequate. In the phase 1 NHL trial (NCT01607892/PMID:28468797), which included Richter patients, tumour biopsies showed nuclear retention of XPO1 cargos (p53, PTEN) and reduced Bcl-2, c-Myc and Ki67, so the pathway moved in humans. The bundle has no Richter-specific biopsy data. With the target engaged and essentially no activity, XPO1 inhibition alone does not drive response in Richter transformation (F2). 11 of 25 patients were not evaluable, which limits interpretation (F7).

Human plasma PK at clinical doses is documented (NCT01896505, NCT02323880). XPO1 engagement and pathway effect were not measured in melanoma, but are inferred adequate. Selinexor at about 60 mg met efficacy endpoints through XPO1 in myeloma (NCT02336815, NCT03110562) and in solid-tumor liposarcoma (NCT02606461). PMID:29299164 supports the 60 mg dose for target occupancy. The index trial (NCT04768881) used selinexor plus pembrolizumab in checkpoint-resistant melanoma. ORR was 33% and 17% in tiny arms, and the trial was terminated for insufficient anti-melanoma signal. With the mechanism presumably engaged, XPO1 inhibition did not overcome checkpoint resistance, so F2 is primary. F3 is secondary: the phase 1b reported ORR 70% in treatment-naive patients versus 7% after prior anti-PD-1 (PMID:39524469), suggesting benefit confined to a population the index trial did not enroll.

Plasma exposure of alpelisib is characterized in humans (PMID:29401002, PMID:24617631). Engagement was not measured in colorectal cancer. It is inferred adequate because alpelisib at 300 mg met a PFS endpoint in PIK3CA-mutant breast cancer (NCT02437318), the same dose used in the index triplet. Tumor engagement and pathway effects were also shown in breast cancer patients (PMID:33947692, PMID:25877889), and on-target hyperglycemia supports pathway activity (PMID:35178031). In NCT01719380, adding alpelisib to encorafenib plus cetuximab gave median PFS of 4.9 vs 4.2 months, with no meaningful benefit and more serious AEs. This suggests PI3Kα inhibition does not add benefit in BRAF-mutant CRC as tested. The Phase 2 comparison was descriptive only, so a design limitation (F7) also applies. Neither the 1.5-year registration gap nor any pre-2012 engagement data is shown.

Human plasma exposure of alpelisib is well characterized (PMID:29401002, PMID:24617631). Engagement is inferred adequate: alpelisib met its PFS endpoint in PIK3CA-mutant breast cancer (NCT02437318), so PI3Kα inhibition in tumor tissue held at comparable doses. Tumor mRNA profiling also showed PIK3CA engagement with the same LJM716 partner (PMID:33947692), and on-target hyperglycemia confirms the pathway effect (PMID:35178031). No engagement or results were reported in ESCC, and the index Phase 1b/2 trial (NCT01822613) posted nothing. With the mechanism engaged and no further development in ESCC, the target appears not to drive this disease as tested. Two alternatives remain possible: tolerability limits of the LJM716 combination (alpelisib MTD 250 mg in PMID:33947692) and the lack of PIK3CA selection. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT02051751 was a Phase 1 safety study of alpelisib plus paclitaxel in breast and head-and-neck cancer. Its primary endpoints were DLTs and adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test in uveal melanoma, which supports F9. The uveal melanoma evidence comes from NCT02273219 (PMID:34771668, published after the index trial started). There, alpelisib with sotrastaurin gave dose-proportional plasma exposure in uveal melanoma patients. Pharmacodynamic pAKT data showed only 'modest' target inhibition, which did not correlate with response. No objective responses occurred and median PFS was 8 weeks. Preclinically, alpelisib alone had minimal activity in uveal melanoma cells (PMID:24563540). Partial engagement in uveal melanoma, rather than lack of efficacy at the target, is the secondary explanation (F1a, possibly F2). The breast cancer efficacy shown in NCT02437318 does not transfer to this setting.

In the phase 1b trial NCT01735968 (PMID:35524239), alpelisib reached its MTD of 350 mg QD with imatinib. That dose is at or above the 300 mg breast-cancer dose. The combination showed only 2.9% PR and a median PFS of 2 months, and was judged insufficiently active. Exposure is adequate: human PK is characterized at these doses (PMID:30588709, PMID:24617631). Engagement is inferred_adequate because alpelisib met its PFS endpoint through PIK3CA in breast cancer (NCT02437318). PMID:33947692 also showed on-treatment PI3K pathway modulation. On-target hyperglycemia occurred in the GIST trial, but GIST tumor engagement was never measured. The dose was not tolerability-capped, so PI3Kα inhibition added to imatinib appears not to drive refractory GIST. Secondary F3: GIST was not selected by PIK3CA status, and a PIK3CA-mutant GIST case responded (PMID:35917491).

Plasma exposure was characterized in healthy volunteers (PMID:37282507), and gepants inhibit CGRP responses at therapeutic plasma concentrations (PMID:39198753). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate: rimegepant 75 mg met pivotal endpoints in migraine (NCT03235479, NCT03237845, NCT03461757, NCT03732638, NCT05399459). That is the same CGRP receptor in the peripheral trigeminal system, comparable to TMD. No engagement was measured in TMD patients. In NCT05262517, SPID-2 and SPID-24 were essentially null versus placebo (difference -0.15), so CGRP antagonism did not relieve acute TMD pain as tested (F2). However, the trial was terminated early for strategic reasons with only 71 participants analyzed, so underpowering (F7) and a business stop (F8) also apply.

In the index trial (NCT00817635), LCI699 lowered BP only about 2.6–4.3 mmHg more than placebo, versus about 10 mmHg for eplerenone. Exposure is inferred from the Cushing approval trials (NCT02180217, NCT02697734). A primary aldosteronism trial that started before the index (NCT00732771) showed aldosterone fell 68% at 0.5 mg, so aldosterone-synthase inhibition occurred in a hypertensive population. Poor CYP11B1/CYP11B2 selectivity blunted ACTH-stimulated cortisol; the cortisol-based MTD was about 1.3 mg (NCT00817414). PMID:26540564 states this limited further hypertension studies and prompted selective CYP11B2 inhibitors. The program therefore ended on a molecule-specific selectivity liability, which also capped dosing (F1a); the cortisol effect is on-target for the listed CYP11B1 target (F5).

At the 1.5 mg dose used in BATON-CRC, the pillars held in humans. PK was dose-proportional, plasma VEGF-A rose and sVEGFR-2 fell dose-dependently, and DCE-MRI showed reduced tumor perfusion (PMID:21976547, PMID:23679664). The same dose met PFS endpoints in RCC (NCT01030783, NCT02627963). These biomarker data come from mixed solid tumors, not specifically CRC. The index trial was a superiority test against bevacizumab, an active anti-VEGF comparator on the same pathway. Efficacy was comparable (PFS 9.4 vs 10.7 months, HR 1.09) and the study was discontinued only because superiority was not shown at the interim futility analysis (PMID:27401244). This is not evidence that the drug lacked activity or that VEGF signalling does not matter in CRC. A post hoc low-NRP-1 subgroup signal was reported.

The index trial (NCT03806127, PMID:35975404) tested vibegron 75 mg daily for 12 weeks in women with IBS. API responders were identical to placebo (27/66 vs 27/63; difference -1.9). Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. No ADRB3 engagement or gut biomarker data in humans are in the bundle. However, the same systemic oral drug met its pivotal endpoints in overactive bladder (NCT03492281, NCT03902080; dose-dependent efficacy in NCT01314872) and is FDA-approved there. This allows exposure, engagement and pathway to be inferred adequate for a peripheral smooth-muscle beta-3 target at a comparable dose. The inference is weakened because bladder and gut are different tissues. A properly dosed, engaged agonist gave no pain benefit, which suggests beta-3 agonism does not drive IBS pain as tested.

Artesunate has no defined SARS-CoV-2 target, and no human engagement data were found. Plasma exposure at oral malaria doses is documented (PMID:9840605). However, PMID:32786284 says the in vitro antiviral EC50 (~13 µM) is reached only after IV dosing, which raises doubt about exposure at oral doses. The Phase 2 trial (NCT04475107) missed virological clearance. In the Phase 3 index trial (NCT05084911), the primary endpoint missed with 0/690 vs 1/697 hospitalisations, and all nine secondary endpoints, including viral load, failed. The IDMC said severe cases had dropped because of Omicron and vaccination, so the trial had almost no events to compare (F7). The unchanged viral load shows no antiviral effect, but nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT01074138; PMID:23314737), oral KX2-391 at 40 mg BID gave a median Cmax of 61 ng/mL. The authors state that ≥142 ng/mL, a threshold taken from preclinical work, is needed for tubulin polymerization inhibition, and they planned higher once-daily dosing. Human exposure was therefore below the level needed for the tubulin mechanism. Target engagement was never measured in humans. Downstream effects were weak: PSA response 10%, and bone turnover markers fell in only a minority. The trial stopped for futility (24-week PFS 8%). The authors blame underexposure, not tolerability caps. Other tubulin agents (docetaxel, cabazitaxel) are approved in prostate cancer, which supports F1b. The topical AK approval is not a comparable compartment or dose.

Zanubrutinib reached adequate plasma exposure and showed complete, sustained BTK occupancy in PBMCs and lymph nodes in B-cell malignancy patients at 320 mg/day (PMID:32207333, PMID:32985902, PMID:34159878), published before the index trial began. Pathway is inferred adequate from pivotal efficacy through BTK in CLL/MCL (NCT03734016, NCT03206970), though BTK-driven pathway effects in COVID-relevant myeloid cells were not measured. Engagement was never shown in COVID-19 patients. In NCT04382586, respiratory failure-free survival (27/30 vs 28/33, p=0.41) and time to room air (HR 0.92) showed no benefit. No other BTK inhibitor progressed beyond phase 2 in COVID-19. The most direct reading is that BTK inhibition does not drive outcome in hospitalized COVID-19. The small trial (n=63) with high control-arm survival limited power (F7).

Samidorphan reached plasma exposure (PMID:25456560). It also functionally antagonised mu receptors in humans: added to buprenorphine, it dose-dependently reduced pupillometric and subjective opioid effects in opioid-experienced adults, with 1:1 giving maximal blockade (PMID:25518754). That was not shown in MDD patients, and the dose was not tolerability-capped. FORWARD-4 missed its week-5 MADRS endpoint (-1.8, p=0.109) amid a large stage-1 placebo response. The sponsor reports significance at end of treatment and in pooled analyses (effect size 0.22) (PMID:30374191). FORWARD-5 was positive, FORWARD-3 was negative, and the phase 2 results were mixed. The sources attribute the miss to endpoint timing and the sequential-parallel design rather than lack of engagement. The effect is small and inconsistent, which leaves some F2 signal.

Oral samidorphan reached dose-proportional plasma exposure in humans (PMID:25456560). It produced dose-dependent blockade of buprenorphine opioid effects (pupillometry, euphoria, drug liking) in opioid-experienced adults (PMID:25518754, PMID:30102427), which shows functional mu-receptor engagement in humans. Pathway is inferred_adequate: at 5–20 mg it met weight-mitigation endpoints via central opioid antagonism (PMID:30845818, NCT02694328, NCT03187769). None of this engagement evidence came from BED patients, and all of it postdates the 2010 index trial. In the BED proof-of-concept, there was no separation from placebo amid a large placebo response. The authors note a failed trial cannot be excluded, but the null result is consistent with other opioid antagonists in bulimia (PMID:23381803). This points to the target not driving binge eating (F2), with F7 secondary. The registered primary endpoint was safety only (NCT01098435), hence F9 secondary.

Oral samidorphan was rapidly absorbed with dose-proportional plasma exposure in humans (PMID:25456560). In opioid-experienced adults, samidorphan produced dose-dependent blockade of buprenorphine's pupillary and subjective effects (PMID:25518754, PMID:30102427), showing human MOR engagement and a functional effect. That evidence came from non-alcohol populations and was obtained after the index trial began. In the index trial (NCT00981617), the primary endpoint (PSNHDD) was missed. However, heavy drinking days fell dose-dependently (-41% at 10 mg, p<0.001), and craving and patient global response improved. The authors attribute the discrepancy to the choice of endpoint and the need for patient-relevant outcomes (PMID:30055046). This fits a wrong-endpoint failure rather than an inactive mechanism. No dose limitation was evident.

No human exposure, engagement or pathway data exist for melanoma. All three pillars are inferred_adequate because capmatinib is FDA-approved in MET-altered NSCLC (NCT02414139: ORR 40.6–67.9%) through MET inhibition in systemic tumor tissue at 400 mg BID, a dose shown tolerable in other trials (PMID:31853265). The bundle does not state the dose used in LOGIC 2. In the genomically assigned capmatinib + encorafenib/binimetinib arm, ORR was 0% (n=13). The authors conclude that adding a third agent at progression lacked meaningful efficacy and that other targets are needed (PMID:40106536), so MET does not drive resistance as tested. The arm was small and uncontrolled (F7). Preclinical data show MET amplification did not predict sensitivity (PMID:26673799), suggesting a selection problem (F3).

Capmatinib 400 mg BID plus spartalizumab gave an ORR of 9.4% versus 10% for spartalizumab alone in sorafenib-pretreated HCC that was not selected for MET (NCT02795429, PMID:38617599). The combination was tolerable at the RP2D, so the dose was not capped. No direct engagement data in humans are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate: at the same 400 mg BID tablet dose, capmatinib met response endpoints and was approved in MET-altered NSCLC (NCT02414139). In MET-high HCC, single-agent capmatinib gave a 30% ORR, including durable responses (PMID:31853265, NCT01737827). Benefit therefore appears confined to the MET-dysregulated subset, and preclinical work stresses selection by MET amplification (PMID:40991144). Primary code is wrong population (F3), with secondary F2 because MET inhibition does not drive unselected HCC.

In Phase Ib of NCT01870726, neither capmatinib nor buparlisib reached its target exposure when the two were given together. Capmatinib AUC was 0.73-fold and buparlisib AUC 0.38-fold of single-agent values, probably from a drug-drug interaction. Because of this, no RP2D was declared, and investigators said the low exposure may explain the lack of efficacy (PMID:31776899). The planned surgical arm to measure drug levels and pharmacodynamics in tumour tissue was never run, so there are no human data on tumour levels, MET inhibition or pathway effects in GBM. The Phase II capmatinib-alone arm (n=10, MET-amplified) stopped for limited activity, with no PD data. The authors also blamed molecular selection based on archival tissue (F3). Intracranial responses in MET exon 14 NSCLC show some CNS activity, but that does not establish engagement in GBM.

Triheptanoin has no protein target. Its mechanism is anaplerotic fuel supply via heptanoate and C5 ketones. Plasma heptanoate exposure is well characterized (PMID:33789001, PMID:35908210), and C5 ketones crossed into CSF in a patient case (PMID:15781190). Five-carbon ketosis was measured in G1D patients (PMID:37268656), and EEG spike-wave reduction occurred in 13/14 G1D patients in an earlier Phase 1 study (NCT02018315), so the proximal effect was shown in this disease. Dose was not tolerability-capped; GI adverse events were mild and caused only 2 discontinuations. Despite this, the randomized Phase 3 showed no reduction in movement disorders (p=0.27; NCT02960217, PMID:38725190), the Phase 2 seizure trial also failed (NCT01993186), and the extension was halted for lack of efficacy (NCT02599961). Anaplerosis does not appear to drive the clinical phenotype as tested.

Lurbinectedin is a DNA minor-groove binder with no recorded protein target. Its plasma PK and the dose–myelosuppression link were described in solid tumours (PMID:24563480, PMID:33914350), but no source measures target engagement or a pathway biomarker in humans, either in leukaemia or elsewhere. The index phase 1 trial in AML/MDS (NCT01314599, published in PMC6386594) found the drug tolerable up to 5 mg on days 1 and 8 and up to 3 mg on days 1–3. Blasts fell transiently in 79% of patients, but there were no complete remissions and no lasting responses (overall response rate 7%). The investigators pointed to the very high-risk, heavily pretreated population and suggested MLL-rearranged or lower-risk subsets for future study, which is weak support for F3. Because engagement has no human data, the result is indeterminate (U).

Topical voclosporin ophthalmic solution missed the STT ≥10 mm responder endpoint at all three doses (NCT04147650; ORs about 2, p 0.09–0.28, wide CIs). The bundle has no ocular-tissue exposure, calcineurin-engagement or tear or inflammatory biomarker data for the eye drop. The phase 1 ocular study (NCT00851734) and tolerability study (NCT03597139) posted no PK or PD. Human calcineurin inhibition is shown only after oral dosing, a systemic compartment (PMID:23736966, PMID:24243422). The lupus nephritis approval (NCT03021499) therefore cannot support inferred engagement at the ocular surface. Cyclosporine, on the same target, is FDA-approved for dry eye, so the molecule or formulation rather than the target is implicated (F1b). Low event rates suggest the trial was also underpowered (F7).

Oral voclosporin acts on a systemic target, calcineurin in T cells. Its human plasma PK and dose-related calcineurin inhibition were measured in healthy volunteers (PMID:23736966) and in renal transplant patients (PMID:24243422), but those reports were published after the index trial started in 2011. Pathway is inferred adequate: voclosporin prevented transplant rejection (PMID:21943027) and met its pivotal lupus nephritis endpoint (NCT03021499), leading to approval. Engagement was never measured in uveitis patients. No index results are posted and the bundle gives no stated reason for failure. Earlier LUMINATE trials reportedly showed efficacy (PMID:20571806). This points to the mechanism failing to deliver benefit on vitreous haze rather than inadequate engagement. Trial-design issues are possible but undocumented, so confidence is low.

Human PK at 75 mg is documented (NCT01605916). The Phase 1 PK/PD study showed ERK phosphorylation inhibition in PBMCs at all doses and a 79% pERK reduction in tumor biopsies, with Ki-67 falls in some patients (PMID:18390968), so engagement and pathway effect are adequate. MEK engagement also yields clinical benefit in NF1 (PMID:39762421). In uveal melanoma, the later 2022 intermittent-dosing study confirmed at least partial pathway inhibition in tumor (PMID:36249046), but this postdates the index trial. Despite engagement, adding selumetinib to dacarbazine did not improve PFS (HR 0.78, p=0.32; NCT01974752), consistent with PDX data showing no additive DTIC effect (PMID:29774094). PMID:36249046 attributes limited efficacy at 75 mg BID to incomplete or compensated pathway inhibition, supporting F1a as secondary.

Index trial NCT01843062 tested selumetinib 75 mg BD with adjuvant RAI in differentiated thyroid cancer. Complete remission was 40.0% vs 38.5% (p=0.82). Exposure is shown by dose-proportional plasma PK (NCT01605916). Engagement is shown by about 79% pERK reduction in tumour biopsies and PBMC inhibition at all doses in a phase 1 study published before the index trial (PMID:18390968), and by significant pERK lowering in NF1 biopsies at the approved dose (PMID:39762421). Pathway: MEK inhibition restored radioiodine uptake in thyroid cancer lesions (PMID:28117292). That was only in a subset of RAI-refractory patients, and pERK was never measured in thyroid patients. With engagement adequate and no added remission, the mechanism did not improve RAI outcomes as tested, so F2. Benefit confined to a responsive subset suggests F3 as secondary.

SUMIT (NCT01974752) used selumetinib 75 mg BID Hyd-sulfate, the MTD defined in PMID:20179232. Human PK and PD at that dose were adequate. PBMC ERK phosphorylation inhibition tracked plasma concentration (Emax ~91%). Paired tumor biopsies in advanced cancer patients showed a 79% pERK reduction, and some had Ki-67 inhibition (PMID:18390968). Both studies were published before 2014. Engagement was confirmed again in NF1 tumor biopsies (PMID:39762421). The dose was the MTD, and the sources do not show it capped below the level engagement needed. Despite MEK engagement, adding selumetinib to dacarbazine did not improve PFS (HR 0.78, p=0.32). The same pattern repeated in other tumor types (NCT00936221, NCT01750281), supporting F2. Approved MEK inhibitors in other molecular subsets suggest population may also matter (F3).

The index trial NCT03358576 compared sulopenem head-to-head with active ertapenem in cIAI. Clinical success was high in both arms (85.5% vs 90.2%). The primary endpoint was classified not met, which reads as missing a non-inferiority margin against an active drug, not a lack of antibacterial activity. The bundle does not state the margin, so this is inferred. Sulopenem met endpoints and was approved for uUTI (NCT05584657, NCT03354598; PMID:39907459), but that is a different tissue compartment (urine), so it cannot infer adequacy here. The bundle has no human PK, tissue-level or target data for intra-abdominal infection. Higher serious AEs (25 vs 12) were noted, but no source blames toxicity for the stop.

The index COVID-19 trial (NCT04801836) has unknown status, no posted results and no stated stop reason. Estetrol's systemic ER agonism is inferred adequate in humans. It met pivotal efficacy endpoints for vasomotor symptoms at 15–20 mg (NCT04209543, NCT04090957) and for contraception (NCT02817828, NCT02817841), all before the index trial started. Systemic exposure is also supported by PK data (NCT02720224). No ER engagement or biomarker data exist in COVID-19 patients. No tolerability cap is shown. Given inferred-adequate engagement and no evidence of design or population problems, the most supported reading is that ER agonism does not drive COVID-19 recovery as tested. Confidence is low because the bundle shows no index results, doses or publications.

Index trial PRESERVE 1 (NCT04607668) met both myeloprotection co-primary endpoints: DSN 0.1 vs 1.3 days and severe neutropenia aRR 0.04, both p<0.001. It was a myelosuppression test, not a failure of the drug's intended efficacy. Engagement was shown in healthy-volunteer bone marrow aspirates, with near-100% HSPC G1 arrest at 192 mg/m2 (PMID:33595690, NCT02243150). Exposure was characterized in patients (PMID:36180417). The pathway effect, neutrophil protection, held in CRC. However, ORR (41.6% vs 57.1%) and PFS (10.3 vs 13.1 months) were significantly worse with trilaciclib, and deaths were higher (49 vs 26) (PMID:39579142). This harm is plausibly an on-target CDK4/6 effect, hence secondary F5. The sponsor's stated stop reason is unspecified.

Plasma exposure is dose-proportional in humans (PMID:33125516, PMID:34086190). sGC engagement was not directly measured. It is inferred adequate because vericiguat at a target dose of 10 mg met a hard-outcome endpoint in HFrEF (NCT02861534), acting on the same systemic target. Pathway is also inferred: NT-proBNP fell in an exposure-dependent way in HFrEF (PMID:34086190, PMID:26547357). The index trial tested doses up to 10 and 15 mg, which were tolerated, so the dose was not capped. KCCQ physical limitation showed no benefit (NCT03547583). The earlier HFpEF trial also found no NT-proBNP or left atrial volume effect (NCT01951638). With a comparable dose engaging the target in HFrEF, the lack of benefit suggests sGC stimulation does not drive HFpEF symptoms as tested. Engagement was never shown in HFpEF patients.

The index kidney-transplant trial (NCT02439957), which enrolled 6 patients, was stopped because of the results of another brincidofovir study, the SUPPRESS HCT Phase 3. The trial itself did not fail on efficacy. Exposure is shown in humans: oral dosing gave dose-proportional plasma levels (PMID:22391537). In CMV patients, the 100 mg twice-weekly dose suppressed CMV, first in Phase 2 (NCT00942305, before the index trial) and again in SUPPRESS. There, fewer CMV infections occurred while on treatment, and CMV DNAemia was lower through week 24, so engagement and pathway effects held. SUPPRESS still missed its week-24 endpoint. CMV infections rebounded after prophylaxis stopped at week 14, and there were more deaths and more GVHD and corticosteroid use, which the company said may reflect drug GI toxicity mistaken for GVHD. The drug's own toxicity offset its efficacy (F6). Stopping prophylaxis too early (F4) also contributed.

Avacopan showed dose-dependent PK and ≥94% blockade of C5a-induced neutrophil CD11b upregulation at 30 mg BID in healthy volunteers (PMID:27768695, published 2016, after the index start). Its efficacy in ANCA vasculitis (NCT02994927, approval) supports adequate systemic C5aR1 engagement and pathway effect there. No engagement data exist in IgAN patients, and tolerability did not limit dosing. The index trial (NCT02384317) was a 7-patient, open-label, single-arm pilot. UPCR slope fell numerically (run-in +15.3 vs treatment −23.9 mg/g/week), but the confidence interval was enormous (−133.6 to 128.7, p=0.965). The trial could not answer the efficacy question, so design and power are the most direct explanation (F7). F2, a target not driving IgAN, cannot be excluded.

In the Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study (PMID:27768695, published 2016, before the index trial), avacopan showed dose-dependent PK and was well tolerated up to 100 mg. At 30 mg twice daily it blocked C5a-induced neutrophil CD11b upregulation by ≥94% all day, which the authors call essentially complete target coverage. The same 30 mg regimen met the pivotal endpoint in ANCA vasculitis (NCT02994927), so the systemic C5aR1 pathway effect is inferred adequate. AURORA (NCT03852472) tested 10 and 30 mg and missed HiSCR at both doses: 30 mg gave 35.1% vs 30.8% on placebo (p=0.45). Safety was similar across arms, so no dose limit. Engagement was not measured in HS patients or skin. Even so, near-complete C5aR1 blockade without benefit points to C5aR1 not driving HS as tested.

The index trial tested avacopan 30 mg BID, the same regimen shown in a 2016 Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (PMID:27768695) to have dose-dependent PK and to block C5a-induced neutrophil CD11b upregulation by ≥94% all day, i.e. essentially complete C5aR1 coverage. That was published before the index trial began. The same dose met pivotal endpoints in ANCA vasculitis (NCT02994927), so the downstream pathway in kidney disease is inferred adequate. Engagement was not measured in C3G patients. Tolerability was comparable to placebo, so dose was not limited. Despite this, the histologic index, UPCR and eGFR did not differ from placebo (NCT03301467, PMID:39392695). This suggests C5aR1 blockade does not drive C3G as tested. The authors call other effects variable and needing further evaluation, so endpoint or timing (F4) is a minor secondary code.

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT01975701) gave infigratinib 125 mg, the maximum tolerated dose (PMID:27870574). Median PFS was 1.7 months and the 6-month PFS rate was 16%. A later Phase 0 trial in recurrent high-grade glioma (NCT04424966) used the same 125 mg dose. Unbound drug in the non-enhancing tumour region averaged 3.5 nM (4.4 nM in enhancing tumour). The prespecified target was 5 nM, five times the biochemical IC50. The investigators concluded that tumour exposure was sub-optimal, so exposure is inadequate. No human data on target occupancy or pathway biomarkers exist, and this exposure evidence came after the index trial started. The mechanism was likely not properly tested (F1a). Investigators also reported lasting disease control only in patients with specific FGFR point mutations or fusions, which points to patient selection (F3).

In PBC (NCT01904058), maralixibat 10 and 20 mg did not beat placebo on ItchRO. Both arms improved sharply (about -26 vs -23), and the publication (PMID:30859149) says a large placebo effect may have confounded the pruritus assessment. That points to trial design, F7. The bundle has no engagement or bile-acid data from PBC patients. Engagement is inferred_adequate because the drug met pruritus and bile-acid endpoints through the same gut IBAT target in PFIC (NCT03905330, approved) and ALGS (NCT02160782, NCT02057692). It also lowered serum bile acids in adults with PSC (NCT02061540), but that trial started after the index trial. GI adverse events were frequent, yet no dose cap is shown. F2 is secondary, since IBAT inhibition may simply not help PBC pruritus.

The index trial NCT04524390 in post-Kasai biliary atresia showed no bilirubin benefit at Week 26 (-0.39 mg/dL, p=0.74). Safety was similar between arms, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No BA-specific engagement data appear in the bundle. Maralixibat acts on ileal IBAT in the gut, and it met efficacy endpoints in ALGS (sBA, NCT02160782) and PFIC (pruritus, NCT03905330), leading to FDA approvals. It also lowered sBA in PSC (NCT02061540) and the ALGS extension (NCT02047318). All of this predates the index trial, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. The target was engaged yet bilirubin did not improve, which suggests IBAT inhibition does not drive post-Kasai outcomes as tested. Odevixibat on the same target is not approved in BA. The case series (PMID:42666930) reports pruritus relief only.

The index trial NCT02061540 was a single-arm, open-label safety and proof-of-concept study. It met its primary objective: fasting serum bile acids fell by 14.8 µmol/L (p=0.0043). Pruritus also improved, most strongly in patients with more severe itch at baseline (PMID:37184523). The authors concluded the results support further study. This was not a failed efficacy readout, so the code is F9. Exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate because the same IBAT-inhibiting mechanism in the gut met pivotal endpoints in PFIC (NCT03905330) and ALGS (NCT02160782), leading to FDA approvals. Pathway is adequate because bile acids were lowered in PSC patients. The bundle gives no stated reason for not continuing in PSC.

Direct ROCK2 engagement was never measured. Belumosudil met efficacy endpoints in cGVHD at 200 mg QD/BID (NCT02841995, NCT03640481; FDA approval), a T-cell-driven disease, so exposure and engagement are inferred adequate at doses the index trial matched or exceeded (200-600 mg/day). Pathway effects were shown in humans: ex vivo IL-17/IL-21 suppression in healthy volunteers (PMID:25385601), and IL-17/IL-23 reduction with IL-10 increase in psoriasis patients from trials registered in 2014 (PMID:28389592). Doses up to 600 mg/day were tolerated, so dose was not limited by tolerability (NCT02852967, PMID:35881051). Despite this, PASI75 showed no dose response and no arm beat placebo (10.9% vs 16.7%). ROCK2 inhibition appears insufficient to drive clinical benefit in plaque psoriasis.

The SSc trial used 200 mg QD/BID, the same doses at which belumosudil met response endpoints in cGVHD (NCT02841995, NCT03640481; FDA approval), so exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. In healthy volunteers, oral KD025 cut T-cell IL-21/IL-17 secretion by 90%/60% (PMID:25385601). In SSc tissue, STAT3/TGF-β fell and FOXP3 rose, with trends toward lower fibrosis biomarkers on drug (PMID:40088930), but this was published after the index trial began. Even so, CRISS response showed no signal (QD 6/11, BID 3/12 vs placebo 7/12), and BID ran numerically below placebo, which points to the mechanism not driving dcSSc as tested. Secondary F7: the trial stopped early for slow enrollment with high placebo response and few patients (NCT03919799, NCT04680975).

Belumosudil showed no FVC benefit over best supportive care at week 24 in IPF (NCT02688647; -115.8 vs -71.2 mL). Systemic exposure in humans is documented (PMID:35881051, NCT03907540). ROCK2 engagement is inferred from cGVHD efficacy (NCT02841995, NCT03640481). This inference is limited because cGVHD acts mainly in the immune compartment rather than lung fibroblasts. A downstream pathway effect was shown before the index trial: healthy-volunteer T cells had IL-21/IL-17 suppression via STAT3 (PMID:25385601, 2014). Tissue pathway modulation appeared in systemic sclerosis (PMID:40088930). No lung or IPF-specific engagement data exist. The drug was tolerable and dosing was not capped. Overall the evidence points to ROCK2 inhibition not driving IPF progression as tested. The unmeasured lung engagement leaves some indeterminacy.

PEGASUS (NCT03533257), a 24-week, 95-patient phase 2a, missed its global composite of cognition, function and hippocampal volume (p=0.37). Exposure and engagement were not measured in Alzheimer disease. They are inferred adequate because AMX0035 met its ALSFRS-R endpoint in ALS, a CNS disease (NCT03127514). Phenylbutyrate also raised blood histone acetylation in ALS patients (PMID:18688762, published 2009). In the AD trial, CSF biomarkers moved versus placebo: p-tau181, total tau, neurogranin, FABP3, YKL-40 and Aβ42/40 (PMID:39131742). So a disease-biology effect was shown without clinical benefit over a short 24-week trial, which points to endpoint or duration (F4). The treatment arm was more impaired at baseline, a design confounder (F7). The link to target relevance (F2) remains possible. Confidence is low because the stated reason for stopping is absent.

The index trial of oral difelikefalin added to topical corticosteroids showed no meaningful benefit over corticosteroids alone (NCT05387707). No receptor occupancy or biomarker data exist in atopic dermatitis. Pillars are inferred from efficacy elsewhere. IV difelikefalin repeatedly met itch endpoints in uremic pruritus (NCT02858726, NCT04711603, NCT05885737, PMID:35511180), and oral 1 mg met in CKD pruritus (NCT03617536). These act through the same peripheral kappa-opioid receptor compartment. This suggests the mechanism was engaged and the target does not drive atopic dermatitis itch as tested. Caveat: CKD patients clear the drug far more slowly; plasma half-life is 38 h on hemodialysis versus 2.6 h in healthy subjects (PMID:37369955). So oral exposure in atopic dermatitis patients with normal kidneys may not have been comparable. Hence low confidence, with U as an alternative.

The index OLE (NCT03836716) was a safety study, terminated only because ORARIALS-01 (NCT03491462, PMID:38782015) missed CAFS at 1200 mg/day (0.51 vs 0.49, p=0.62). Exposure was adequate: in ALS patients the drug showed dose-linear serum PK, CSF levels rose with dose, and it crossed the BBB (PMID:18551622). The pivotal dose was well tolerated, so it was not capped. The bundle has no direct human HSF1/HSP70 biomarker data. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because arimoclomol met its primary endpoint in Niemann-Pick C (NCT02612129), a CNS disease, via the same mechanism. The bundle does not give the NPC dose, which weakens this inference. With an adequately dosed, brain-penetrant drug failing, HSP co-induction does not appear to drive ALS progression as tested.

Arimoclomol at 1200 mg/day missed the IBMFRS primary endpoint (NCT02753530, PMID:37739573). Thigh qMRI also showed no drug effect (PMID:40018748). Dose-linear plasma exposure was shown in ALS (PMID:18551622). The drug met its efficacy endpoint in NPC (NCT02612129), so systemic exposure is inferred adequate. That inference does not extend to engagement in muscle, which is a different tissue compartment. The pilot IBM trial measured HSP70 in muscle biopsies, but the pages I found do not report the result (PMID:27009270; ScienceDirect abstract). The NPC HSP70 changes in blood cells come from a patent on another disease. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Nothing shows heat-shock activation in IBM muscle, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. That makes the code U.

Deucravacitinib reached systemic exposure and showed dose-dependent inhibition of IL-12/IL-23 and type I IFN signalling in healthy volunteers (NCT02534636, registered before the index trial; PMID:36325947). IL-23/Th17 pathway biomarkers fell dose-dependently in psoriasis at 3–12 mg doses (PMID:34767869, PMID:39283417), and the drug is approved in psoriasis (NCT03611751). LATTICE-CD used 3–6 mg BID, comparable or higher doses, and was well tolerated. Clinical remission still did not beat placebo; only endoscopic response at 3 mg was nominally significant. UC trials also failed (NCT03934216, NCT04613518). Ex vivo IBD tissue data suggest TYK2 blockade mainly hits IL-10/IFN-β, possibly paradoxically (PMID:37855324, PMID:40320905). Engagement was never measured in Crohn patients. The high placebo response reported in PMID:40355364 adds an F7 element.

In humans, deucravacitinib dose-dependently inhibited IL-12 and type I IFN signalling in healthy volunteers (PMID:36325947). It lowered IL-23/Th17 and IFN pathway biomarkers in psoriasis skin and serum and in PsA patients (PMID:34767869, 39283417, 38770592). It also met pivotal psoriasis endpoints (NCT03611751), all at doses at or below the 6 mg BID used in LATTICE-UC. Colonic tissue exposure was never measured, so exposure is inferred. The index trial was flat (14.8% vs 16.3%). A higher 12 mg BID dose also failed in UC (NCT04613518), and a Crohn's trial failed too (PMID:40355364). This argues against under-dosing and points to TYK2 not driving UC. Ex vivo data on IL-10 antagonism offer a mechanistic explanation (PMID:37855324, 40320905). High placebo response was also noted (F7).

In the index AA trial, SALT change at week 24 was no better than placebo at 6 mg QD or 6 mg BID (NCT05556265, PMID:41905775). The trial was terminated for strategic reasons after database lock, but the readout itself failed, so F8 does not apply. Deucravacitinib engaged TYK2 in humans at these doses: dose-dependent inhibition of IL-12 and type I IFN pathways in healthy volunteers (PMID:36325947). It also normalized IL-23 and IFN skin and serum biomarkers in psoriasis at ≥3 mg BID (PMID:34767869, PMID:39283417), and won approval for psoriasis at 6 mg. There is no target-engagement data in AA itself. Dose was not tolerability-capped. Selective TYK2 inhibition appears not to drive AA as tested. Brepocitinib, a dual TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor, has no reported success in the bundle, so F1b is not supported.

Plasma PK was characterized in humans (NCT00908908, PMID:26362045), which also showed microtubule bundling in PBMCs and tumor cells. Eribulin met OS/PFS endpoints in breast cancer and sarcoma at the same dose (NCT01327885, NCT02225470, PMID:24161305), so tubulin engagement in tumor tissue is inferred_adequate. The index trial NCT01454934 compared eribulin against active physician's-choice chemotherapy, including docetaxel and vinorelbine, which act on the same target and are approved in NSCLC. OS was identical (9.5 vs 9.5 months; HR 1.16, p=0.13). The drug was active but not superior to same-class comparators, so this is not an efficacy failure of the mechanism. That fits F9 rather than a non-engaging drug or an irrelevant target. F2 is secondary for lack of incremental benefit.

MERIDIAN (NCT04579666) missed its CAFS primary endpoint (p=0.72) and its secondary endpoints. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In plasma, systemic C3 inhibition is well established: PNH data show high exposure and changes in LDH and hemoglobin (PMID:39612158, PMID:33464651), and C3G data show C3 rising and sC5b-9 falling (PMID:38025230). But the proposed site of action in ALS is the spinal cord, the CNS and the neuromuscular junction. The bundle has no human data on CNS or CSF penetration of this large PEGylated peptide, no C3 or C3-fragment biomarker measured in ALS patients, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. Approvals in PNH, C3G and geographic atrophy involve other compartments (blood, kidney, intravitreal injection into the eye). A 2026 mouse study (PMID:42492371) suggests systemic C3 inhibition may not reach the relevant sites, but animal data do not count. So nothing here separates a drug that did not engage its target in ALS from a target that does not matter, and the code is U. F2 is listed as a secondary possibility only.

Plasma exposure in HFrEF patients was documented: peak concentrations at end-infusion, plus acute LV volume reductions that tracked concentration (PMID:29217757, NCT02388464). No in vivo human cardiolipin or mitochondrial engagement was measured; ex vivo failing-heart tissue data (PMID:31061916) do not count. Engagement is inferred_adequate because of the 2025 Barth syndrome approval, a cardiolipin and mitochondrial cardiomyopathy, together with case-level cardiac benefit (PMID:42415111). The bundle does not show the approval endpoint or dose, so this inference is weak. In the index trial neither 4 mg nor 40 mg improved LVESV versus placebo at 4 weeks, and there was no dose response. This suggests the mechanism does not drive HFrEF remodeling as tested. An animal HFpEF study similarly found improved bioenergetics without functional benefit (PMID:41596703). If the Barth inference is rejected, U applies. The short 4-week duration may also have contributed (F4).

Elamipretide is a mitochondria-targeting peptide with no recorded molecular target. In the index trial (NCT02693119; PMID:37923251) it was given as a 1% eye drop to 12 LHON patients. BCVA in treated eyes did not differ from vehicle eyes, and OCT RNFL/ganglion-cell thickness did not change. The only positive findings were post hoc (central visual field mean deviation). No human measurement shows that topical drug reached the retina or optic nerve, or that it engaged mitochondria or moved a mitochondrial biomarker there. The Barth syndrome approval used systemic subcutaneous dosing in a different tissue, so engagement cannot be inferred for this program. A single-centre trial of 12 patients with a safety primary endpoint also limits interpretation (F7). Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Index NCT02245620 (n=41, elderly) missed its primary endpoint. Muscle ATPmax change was 0.09 vs 0.06 mM/s at Day 7, which is within the variability. That is a pathway marker that did not move. Plasma PK exists (PMID:29217757, heart failure), but there are no human muscle-tissue levels. No target (cardiolipin) engagement measure exists in humans. The Barth syndrome approval cannot support inferred engagement: the Barth Phase 3 NCT03098797 missed its primary endpoints, and the route, dose and duration differ from this short IV regimen. Other trials also failed (NCT02805790, NCT02788747). With no engagement data, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The small, short trial (F7) may also have contributed. No toxicity limited the dose.

Elamipretide is described as binding cardiolipin, but no source shows it engaging that target in humans. There are no occupancy or binding measurements. In the index trial NCT02245620, the published analysis (Roshanravan, PLoS One 2021) reports that a single 2-hour infusion raised in vivo muscle ATPmax over placebo. The posted registry data show only small differences relative to the variability, and no effect at Day 7, so the pathway evidence is weak and not sustained. The authors also note a disconnect: muscle endurance did not improve even when ATPmax rose. Plasma PK exists only from other populations (PMID:29217757). With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. F4 and F2 are possible secondary codes.

No human PK, RARγ engagement or biomarker data exist in MO. The pillars are inferred_adequate because palovarotene met its Phase 3 endpoint in FOP (NCT03312634, reduced new heterotopic ossification; FDA-approved). That effect works through RARγ agonism suppressing chondrogenic and endochondral bone formation, at a chronic 5 mg dose comparable to the 5.0 mg MO arm. Yet in NCT03442985 neither 2.5 nor 5.0 mg reduced the annualized rate of new osteochondromas versus placebo (RR 3.04 and 1.44, both non-significant), so the mechanism did not translate into benefit in MO. Secondary F7: the trial was terminated early, few participants were analyzed (16–23 per arm), and the placebo event rate was very low, which limits power.

No human PK, target-engagement or biomarker data in the bundle. Oteseconazole, a fungal CYP51 inhibitor, met complete cure in toenail onychomycosis, a dermatophyte (Trichophyton) infection of keratinized tissue, at comparable oral doses (NCT02267356, PMID:32421854). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, but that trial started after the index. In the index tinea pedis trial (NCT01891305), cure numerically favored the drug in all arms (2/12, 1/12, 3/14 vs 0/12 placebo), with no statistical analysis and about 12 patients per arm. The trial was too small to answer the question, and a strict composite cure at Day 42 may also be too early (F4). There were no serious AEs, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. The program moved on to onychomycosis and VVC.

In the index trial (NCT01339689), ganaxolone did not separate from placebo on CAPS at week 6 (54.05 vs 60.64, large SDs). No PTSD-specific occupancy or biomarker data exist. Brain GABAA engagement is inferred from efficacy in CNS disease through the same receptors: the CDKL5 Phase 3 met its primary endpoint (NCT03572933), and status epilepticus trials showed seizure cessation (NCT03350035, NCT04391569). IV ganaxolone also produced dose-dependent CNS pharmacodynamic effects (BIS/qEEG) in healthy volunteers (PMID:38231434). Dose comparability with the PTSD regimen is not shown in the bundle. All of this evidence postdates the index trial. Rodent PTSD-model benefit (PMID:25309317) did not translate. Most likely the mechanism does not drive PTSD as tested. The modest size and absent statistics leave some design uncertainty.

The index open-label extension (NCT02519439) was terminated because the double-blind Phase 3 in drug-resistant focal seizures (NCT01963208) missed its primary endpoint (-21% vs -10%, p=0.18). No focal-epilepsy engagement data exist. Pillars are only inferred from the CDKL5 Phase 3 success (NCT03572933, same GABA-A target and CNS compartment, doses not shown as comparable). A healthy-volunteer IV study showed plasma exposure and sedation/BIS effects (PMID:38231434), but that is a different route and population. Other GABA-A modulators (benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, cenobamate) are approved for epilepsy or focal epilepsy. That argues the target matters and points to ganaxolone's molecule or dose rather than the mechanism, hence F1b. F2 and F7 (modest effect, possibly underpowered cohort) remain plausible.

Plasma exposure and dose-dependent central pharmacodynamic effects (bispectral index, qEEG) were shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:38231434). Engagement is inferred adequate because oral ganaxolone met its pivotal seizure endpoint in CDKL5 deficiency disorder (NCT03572933; FDA approval 2022), acting on the same CNS GABAA target in a related developmental epileptic encephalopathy. Neither came before the index trial or in PCDH19 patients. In the Violet trial (NCT03865732), ganaxolone gave a large numerical seizure reduction (median -61.5% vs -24.0% placebo) but missed significance with only 10 vs 11 analysed. This points to an underpowered small trial rather than a clear target failure. No sponsor statement explains the stop, so F2 (mechanism not driving PCDH19 seizures) remains possible.

The index crossover trial missed CGI-I (3.4 vs 3.5, p=0.45) and all secondary endpoints (NCT01725152, PMID:28764646). No target-engagement data exist in FXS. However, oral ganaxolone met its pivotal endpoint and was approved for CDKL5 seizures (NCT03572933), acting on brain GABAA receptors. Engagement and exposure are therefore inferred adequate at comparable pediatric doses. IV PD effects in healthy volunteers (PMID:38231434) and increased CNS AEs in the FXS trial support this. The dose was not capped by tolerability. Only post-hoc trends in high-anxiety and low-IQ subgroups were seen, so F3 is secondary. The engagement inference rests on later evidence from another disease, not data collected before the index trial.

No molecular target is recorded, and the bundle has no direct human exposure or engagement measurement. Exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate because AMX0035 met its efficacy endpoint in ALS (NCT03127514), a CNS disease, through the same hypothesized ER-stress/mitochondrial mechanism at a comparable dose. In the AD trial PEGASUS (NCT03533257, PMID:39131742), CSF biomarkers differed between groups: p-tau181, total tau, neurogranin, FABP3 and YKL-40 fell and the Aβ42/40 ratio changed. The 24-week global composite endpoint still did not differ (p=0.37). So a biomarker effect was seen in AD without short-term clinical benefit (F4). Two design limits also apply: the treated arm had worse baseline cognition, and the small 24-week phase 2a trial was underpowered (F7).

The index trial NCT02259231 was a small, single-arm, dose-escalation study of omaveloxolone added to ipilimumab or nivolumab. ORR was reported only descriptively, with no comparator or response threshold, so the primary endpoint is not assessable. Responses occurred, but the drug's contribution cannot be separated from the checkpoint inhibitors. The trial could not answer the efficacy question (F7), and it was arguably not an efficacy test of omaveloxolone itself (F9). In melanoma/NSCLC patients (NCT02029729, PMID:28919776), exposure was dose-proportional, with a trend toward dose-dependent Nrf2 target-gene induction in PBMCs. Engagement is inferred adequate from Friedreich ataxia efficacy at 150 mg, but that is a different tissue compartment (NCT02255435, PMID:30656180). No stop reason is given, and no business reason is shown.

The index trial NCT02128113 tested topical omaveloxolone eye drops (0.5% and 1%) against vehicle and did not reduce corneal endothelial cell loss after cataract surgery (p=0.45 overall). The 1% dose did no better than 0.5%. I found no human data on drug levels in the eye, Nrf2 target gene induction in the cornea or aqueous humor, or any downstream eye biomarker. The only eye evidence I found was preclinical (Review of Ophthalmology; PMC4731949). Human Nrf2 activity was shown only with oral dosing, in Friedreich ataxia (PMID:30656180, NCT02255435) and solid tumors (PMID:28919776). That success is a different tissue and route, so it cannot stand in for engagement in the eye. The sister eye trial NCT02065375 also failed. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the drug failed to engage its target or the target does not matter here, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT02142959), omaveloxolone lotion was applied to the skin at 0.5% and 3%. In healthy volunteers (Phase 1 NCT02029716), the same lotion at 0.5–3%, applied twice daily for up to 28 days, raised NQO1 protein significantly in skin biopsies when spread over 100–500 cm². NQO1 is the classic Nrf2 target gene, so this shows the drug reached the skin and switched on Nrf2 there, while staying almost undetectable in plasma. These Phase 1 results were already in the index protocol, and the dose was not limited by side effects. Even so, neither strength improved radiation dermatitis grade over vehicle. Turning on Nrf2 in the skin does not seem to prevent radiation dermatitis in this setting (F2). One caveat: engagement was only shown in healthy volunteers, not in irradiated patients, and its size was reported only as statistically significant.

Omaveloxolone gave dose-proportional plasma exposure in humans (PMID:31118567, PMID:28919776). Nrf2 target-gene induction was seen in PBMCs, as a trend, in cancer patients (PMID:28919776). Nrf2 pathway markers (ferritin, GGT) moved at 80–160 mg in Friedreich ataxia (PMID:30656180). The drug met its pivotal mFARS endpoint at 150 mg in Friedreich ataxia (NCT02255435), so engagement at comparable doses is inferred adequate. The index trial (doses up to 160 mg) showed no effect on peak workload (p=0.73). No dose-limiting toxicity was reported. Caveats: no engagement data in mitochondrial myopathy, and none before the index trial. Dose arms had only about 6 patients each over 12 weeks, and the same endpoint also failed in Friedreich ataxia Part 1, so underpowering and endpoint choice may have contributed.

Omaveloxolone lotion was tested in the index trial (NCT02142959) at 0.5% and 3%. Neither strength reduced the time-averaged CTCAE radiation dermatitis grade compared with vehicle: the LS mean differences were -0.1 and 0. In the healthy-volunteer Phase 1 (NCT02029716, BMC Dermatology 2015), the same lotion strengths (0.5–3%) were well tolerated, with low systemic exposure. Skin biopsies from that study showed significant induction of the Nrf2 target gene NQO1, which shows the drug acted on its target, and the pathway responded, in the skin where it was applied. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Engagement was shown only in healthy skin, not in irradiated patients, so the evidence rests on healthy volunteers. Activating Nrf2 adequately in the skin did not prevent radiation dermatitis, which points to the target or mechanism not driving the disease as tested (F2).

In the index trial (NCT02065375), topical omaveloxolone eye drops did not clear anterior chamber cells better than placebo, and placebo did significantly better on ocular pain. The available human Nrf2 engagement data all come from the oral drug: target-gene mRNA in blood cells (PMID:28919776) and ferritin/GGT changes in Friedreich ataxia (PMID:30656180). The site of action here is the anterior eye. No source reports ocular drug levels or Nrf2 activation in the eye after topical dosing. The Friedreich ataxia approval used a different route and tissue compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. The sister ocular trial (NCT02128113) also failed. No source gives a reason for the failure, so the code is indeterminate (U).

Zilucoplan 0.3 mg/kg daily SC, the dose used in the index trial, met its pivotal endpoint in generalized myasthenia gravis (NCT04115293; approved 2023). That success came through systemic C5 inhibition, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate at the same dose. The IMNM publication states there was no CK benefit 'despite target engagement based on mode of action' in IMNM patients (PMID:36923454). However, it reports no quantitative engagement measure, and it was published after the trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Reviewers conclude that C5 inhibition failed to show efficacy despite the complement hypothesis (PMID:40809544). This points to terminal complement not driving IMNM as tested. A secondary caveat is the small, short trial (n=27, 8 weeks, CK endpoint).

In the ACCORD zilucoplan sub-protocol (NCT04590586), median time to recovery was 14.0 vs 15.0 days, so the primary endpoint was not met. No COVID-specific engagement or biomarker data appear in the bundle. Zilucoplan 0.3 mg/kg met efficacy endpoints in gMG (NCT03315130, NCT04115293, PMID:37059508) through systemic plasma C5 inhibition. It also lowered LDH in treatment-naive PNH (NCT03078582). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate in the same compartment, and this was known before the index trial. With no tolerability limit, the failure points to terminal complement not driving COVID-19 recovery as tested (F2). The small adaptive screening-stage arm (PMID:32736596) adds possible underpowering (F7).

The index trial NCT02124746 is a single-arm, long-term safety extension. Its primary outcome is descriptive adverse-event incidence, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). Exposure is adequate: stable predose plasma levels in PV/ET (PMID:28622623) and characterized PK (PMID:29024542). Engagement is inferred_adequate because momelotinib met JAK1/2-driven endpoints in myelofibrosis at comparable doses (NCT04173494, NCT01969838; approved 2023). Pathway effects were shown in MF: IL-6 decline and JAK2V617F allele-burden reduction (PMID:27634203, PMID:23459451). The actual ET efficacy study, NCT01998828, was terminated for limited efficacy (ORR 5.1%, no ET responders; PMID:28622623). That suggests the mechanism was engaged without benefit in ET (secondary F2). No engagement was measured in ET patients.

The index trial NCT02101021 was terminated after the lead-in, and the randomized OS phase was never reported. Its publication (PMID:30105668) says PK analyses showed momelotinib concentrations were too low for TBK1 inhibition, the preclinical rationale in PDAC. It concludes that no OS or PFS benefit was apparent 'in context of suboptimal engagement of the target TBK1.' Tolerability did not cap the dose: MTD was not reached at 200 mg BID. JAK1/2 activity is supported by myelofibrosis efficacy (NCT04173494, NCT01969838), but that is a different tissue compartment, so it cannot be carried over to pancreatic tumor. No pathway data in PDAC were reported. The sources attribute the failure to inadequate exposure and engagement, so the mechanism was not properly tested.

Index trial NCT02206763 was a Phase 1 safety/DLT study of erlotinib plus momelotinib in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. It terminated after 11 patients with no stated reason and no posted results, so there was no efficacy readout. Plasma exposure is documented in humans (PMID:29024542, PMID:38634429). JAK1/2 activity is clinically validated in myelofibrosis (NCT01969838, NCT04173494), but that is a hematopoietic compartment, not NSCLC tumor. The bundle has no human evidence of JAK1/2 engagement or pathway modulation in lung tumor. PMID:30105668 shows inadequate TBK1 exposure in pancreatic cancer, but TBK1 is not a listed primary target. With engagement unmeasured and no reason for stopping given, the cause is indeterminate. F9 is secondary because the index trial was not an efficacy test.

The index trial NCT02124746 was a single-arm, long-term safety extension. Its primary outcome was adverse-event incidence, with no efficacy comparison, so it was not an efficacy test of momelotinib in polycythemia vera. Exposure is shown in humans (PMID:29024542). JAK1/2 engagement and pathway effect are inferred_adequate: momelotinib met pivotal endpoints in myelofibrosis at comparable doses (NCT01969838, NCT04173494) and is FDA-approved there, through the same targets in the same hematopoietic compartment. No engagement data specific to polycythemia vera exist. The dedicated PV/ET trial NCT01998828 terminated without a stated reason or results, so the bundle shows no efficacy failure in PV.

The index trial, NCT01831804, was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study of topical daprodustat in healthy volunteers and diabetic foot ulcer patients. All its primary endpoints were safety and PK, and wound measures were only exploratory, so it was not an efficacy test. Topical dosing was well tolerated and gave sporadic or unquantifiable plasma levels, as intended. No wound-tissue drug levels, local HIF stabilization or HIF target-gene biomarkers were reported, so all three pillars lack human data at the site of action. Wound improvements were weak but consistent, and small, variable control arms limited interpretation (PMID:30720931). The authors said healing needs longer, purpose-built studies. No stated stop reason was found. If this is treated as an efficacy readout, the code would be U (engagement unknown).

The index trial NCT02135848 (PAD, 300 mg acute and 15 mg chronic) had only descriptive safety primary outcomes (AEs, ECGs, vitals, labs) and is classified not_efficacy. It was not an efficacy test that failed, so F9 applies. Systemic exposure is shown in humans (PMID:26643993, NCT02243306). Dose-dependent EPO, VEGF and reticulocyte rises at 50–100 mg show the pathway moved (PMID:26643993, PMID:26827289). Engagement is inferred_adequate because daprodustat met hemoglobin endpoints in CKD anemia (NCT03409107) and was approved. No engagement data exist in PAD patients, and published PD evidence postdates the 2010 start. Doses were not tolerability-capped at 300 mg; 500 mg was poorly tolerated (PMID:28419747). No stop reason or efficacy readout is reported.

ASCEND-Fe (NCT03457701) was a 15-patient mechanistic crossover comparing fractional oral iron absorption with daprodustat versus rhEPO (20.64% vs 20.62%). It was an exploratory biomarker comparison, not an efficacy test of the drug, so missing it is not an efficacy failure. Daprodustat met hemoglobin endpoints in CKD anemia, including pivotal trials (NCT03409107, PMID:34739194, PMID:34739196), and is FDA-approved. In CKD patients, before the index trial, it produced dose-dependent EPO rises, hepcidin falls and hemoglobin gains (PMID:26827289; PMID:30746141), so exposure, engagement and pathway were adequate. Plasma exposure is documented in dialysis patients (NCT02243306). Tolerability did not cap the dose: 500 mg was poorly tolerated, but effective doses are far lower. The small sample also limited power (F7).

The index trial NCT03239522 is a 6-subject radiolabeled ADME/mass-balance study in healthy volunteers. It has PK-only endpoints and is not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Plasma exposure was shown directly. Engagement was not measured directly but is inferred adequate from the approved anemia indication and its met Hgb endpoints (NCT03409107), which use the same systemic PHD target. Pathway markers moved in humans: EPO, VEGF and reticulocytes rose dose-dependently (PMID:26643993, PMID:26827289). The tendon/muscle-injury experimental-medicine study (NCT02231190, PMID:30424786) used high-dose daprodustat in healthy volunteers. It reduced circulating damage markers but did not lessen functional deficits, which hints at F2. No tendon-disease patients were studied.

Index trial NCT01920594 (300 mg load + 100 mg QD in thoracic aortic aneurysm repair) missed its exploratory CSF S100B and GFAP endpoints. Both markers trended higher on drug (p=0.08, p=0.20), and deaths were 6/27 vs 2/28. Dose-proportional plasma exposure, plus EPO, VEGF and reticulocyte rises at 100 mg in healthy volunteers (NCT02348372, registered 2011; PMID:26643993), show systemic HIF-PH engagement and pathway activation at the index dose. Dose-dependent EPO and Hgb responses in CKD (PMID:26827289, PMID:30746141) and the anemia approval support this. Spinal cord or CSF drug levels and engagement in surgical patients were never shown. The best-supported reading is that systemic HIF stabilization did not protect against ischemic injury. The mortality imbalance (F6) and the small sample (F7) are possible contributors.

Etrasimod 2 mg gives dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:38345530). It produces dose-dependent peripheral lymphocyte reductions of 41–69% in healthy volunteers (PMID:38345530, PMID:40529495) and lymph-node T-cell sequestration in Crohn's patients (PMID:41828664). These are the expected S1PR1 pathway effects. Engagement is inferred_adequate because 2 mg met pivotal endpoints in UC through the same systemic lymphocyte-trafficking mechanism (NCT03945188, NCT03996369). No AD-specific engagement data exist, although on-target cardiac conduction effects appeared in the index trial. At the same 2 mg dose, the index trial was stopped for futility (IGA 3.3% vs 7.1%, NCT05732454). This followed an earlier failed phase 2 in AD at 1 and 2 mg (NCT04162769), with no tolerability cap. The S1PR1 mechanism appears not to drive AD.

In healthy volunteers, etrasimod 2–3 mg gave dose-proportional plasma exposure and dose-dependent lymphocyte reductions of 41–69%, the S1P1-mediated trafficking effect (PMID:38345530, PMID:40529495). The same systemic mechanism at 2 mg met pivotal endpoints in UC, including Phase 2 before the index start (NCT02447302, NCT03945188, NCT03996369). Engagement was not measured in AA patients, and the 3 mg dose was tolerated without dose capping. In the AA trial, 2 mg and 3 mg missed SALT %CFB at Week 24 (p=0.26 and p=0.059), with numerical benefit only (NCT04556734, PMID:40145547). This points to S1P1-driven lymphocyte sequestration not providing meaningful benefit in AA as tested. The small trial (80 randomized, wide CIs) and a suggested benefit in less extensive disease (PMID:40418069) support F7 and F3 as secondary codes.

The index trial NCT00805818 (INTREPID) had a registered primary endpoint of AE/SAE incidence versus placebo, a safety endpoint rather than an efficacy test. No results were posted, and the only linked publication is a post hoc cEEG analysis (PMID:30624278). Plasma PK was characterized in healthy volunteers (PMID:28522374), but the bundle has no human CNS exposure, target engagement or pathway data in TBI, and no primary target is recorded. The Rett approval (NCT04181723) involved a different disease and oral dosing, with no shared target established, so it cannot support an inference of adequacy. The later mTBI trial NCT02100150 terminated without a stated reason. The index trial was not an efficacy failure (F9). Mechanistically the case is indeterminate (U).

Phase 1 showed good oral bioavailability and an MTD of 30 mg/day (PMID:31338688). Zuranolone met efficacy endpoints in MDD and PPD (NCT03000530, NCT02978326, NCT04442490, NCT04442503) through central GABAA modulation at comparable doses, so CNS exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. EEG low-beta increases (PMID:37366077) support pathway activation, but only in healthy volunteers and published after the index trial. No engagement was measured in essential tremor patients. In NCT02978781, randomized Part B showed no difference from placebo (p=0.91). Part B had only 4 participants per arm, and the open-label Part C trend was borderline (p=0.053). The mechanism, engaged, gave no benefit on tremor, but the tiny trial limits interpretation (F7).

Phase 1 PK shows oral bioavailability and linear exposure (PMID:31338688, PMID:37366077). A 30 mg dose raised EEG low-beta power, consistent with GABAA activation (PMID:37366077). Engagement is also inferred from efficacy in PPD and MDD via the same CNS GABAA target (NCT02978326, NCT04442503, NCT04442490). Zuranolone improved PSG sleep efficiency in a healthy-volunteer insomnia model (NCT03284931, PMID:34352138), so the hypnotic pathway effect holds. The index trial (NCT03771664) was terminated by internal company decision at 87 participants. Baseline sleep efficiency was imbalanced (placebo 67.7% vs drug 73.7%). The difference favoured the drug (+3.2, CI -1.2 to 7.7, p=0.15). This points to an underpowered, truncated trial rather than a disproven mechanism. The sponsor gave no stated reason, so confidence is low.

In RADIANT (NCT02733432; PMID:30893271), topical CD101 (3% gel or 6% ointment applied in the vagina) had lower day-28 cure rates than oral fluconazole. Clinical cure was 35% and 30% vs 52.6%, and mycological cure was 45% and 40% vs 57.9%. Cidara then dropped the vulvovaginal candidiasis program. I found no human measurement of drug levels in vaginal tissue or fluid, or of glucan synthase inhibition or a biomarker in that tissue. The claim that vaginal levels would exceed the fungal MIC is a projection from lab data only (PMID:28158577). Intravenous rezafungin worked against invasive candidiasis (PMID:32955088, NCT03667690), but that was a different body compartment, formulation and dose, so I did not infer engagement from it. A topical formulation that delivered too little drug (F1a) cannot be separated from a mechanism that does not help here, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03445013 was a Phase 1 PK/PD and safety study in psoriasis. Its primary outcome was plasma hMAP3 concentration, it posted no results, and no stop reason is given. It was not an efficacy test of the drug, so F9 fits best. No primary target is recorded, and the bundle has no human evidence on skin exposure, engagement or pathway effects in psoriasis. Efficacy in molluscum (NCT04535531) and tinea pedis (PMID:30124729) rests on antimicrobial nitric oxide effects in different diseases, so it cannot support an inferred_adequate rating here. Why the psoriasis program stopped cannot be determined; U is listed as secondary. PMID:11041316 concerns an unrelated compound (SB206,553) and is irrelevant.

The index trial (NCT02653417) gave low doses (5–20 mg), meant to act as a selective ER modulator on the hypothalamus. It showed no benefit: hot-flash reductions matched the large placebo response, and the sponsor gave no reason beyond its own decision. The human engagement data come from much higher doses. Uterine ER occupancy was 83–92% at 200–500 mg, CSF/plasma ratio was about 0.1–0.2% (PMID:32661909), and FES-PET tumour uptake fell 89% at 200–400 mg (PMID:32912274). None of this covers hypothalamic ER at 5–20 mg. The breast cancer approval works through antagonism in tumour tissue at 345–400 mg, so it cannot show adequacy here. In the earlier trial only the 10 mg dose separated from placebo (PMID:27575546), which hints at a high placebo response or underpowering. Engagement is unknown, so the code is U.

Probenecid is a pharmacokinetic booster (OAT1/OAT3 inhibitor) co-formulated with oral sulopenem-etzadroxil. The index trial NCT03358576 compared a sulopenem regimen against active ertapenem in cIAI (85.5% vs 90.2% clinical success). The bundle gives rates only, not the margin, but this pattern fits a missed non-inferiority comparison against an active drug. It tested the antibiotic sulopenem, not probenecid's mechanism, so it was not an efficacy test of this drug. Target engagement in humans is clear: furosemide renal clearance fell from 96 to 33 mL/min (NCT05365451). Beta-lactam exposure rose (PMID:34081957, PMID:31521742; earlier, PMID:6490225). These data come from healthy volunteers, not patients with this disease. The same combination later met its primary endpoint in uUTI (NCT05584657).

The index trial (NCT02775916) missed its ESSPRI endpoint: net difference -0.69 with a CI spanning zero. It was small (20 vs 10), and the drug was tolerated without SAE excess. No engagement data in Sjögren's patients appear in the bundle. Healthy-volunteer PK shows systemic plasma exposure (PMID:30215545). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from APDS (NCT02435173, approved 2023). There, leniolisib met its endpoints on lymphoproliferation and naive B cells through PI3Kδ in circulating immune cells, though the bundle does not show the doses were comparable. Other PI3Kδ inhibitors in Sjögren's (seletalisib, parsaclisib) did not advance past phase 2. This suggests the target as tested does not drive the disease (F2). The small, likely underpowered trial is a secondary factor (F7).

The index trial NCT01256762 (imetelstat plus paclitaxel in metastatic breast cancer) posted no results and gave no stop reason. Human target engagement exists only outside breast cancer. In PMID:27350411, published in 2016 after the index start, 285 mg/m2 inhibited intratumoral telomerase by 95% in the one evaluable patient and suppressed PBMC telomerase for at least 8 days. Hematologic efficacy and approval (NCT01243073; MDS approval) support engagement in marrow. No breast-tumor engagement, no downstream human biomarker such as telomere shortening, and no dose limitation in breast cancer are shown. Breast support is preclinical only (PMID:16707619, PMID:19509275). With engagement shown elsewhere and no benefit, F2 is the best fit. Confidence is low because breast-specific data are absent, so U also applies.

Imetelstat 9.4 mg/kg maintenance did not improve PFS in advanced NSCLC (HR 0.844, P=0.446) (PMID:25467017). Human target engagement was shown directly: 95% intratumoral telomerase inhibition in a solid tumor and sustained PBMC telomerase inhibition at 285 mg/m2, a comparable dose (PMID:27350411). This was shown in pediatric CNS tumors, not lung cancer, and published after the index trial began. The drug is also clinically active in ET/PV and approved in MDS through TERT, though that is a hematologic compartment. Telomere-shortening pathway data in lung tumors are absent. With engagement shown, the failure points to TERT inhibition not driving benefit as tested (F2). The exploratory short-telomere subgroup trend suggests possible patient selection issues (F3).

Givinostat is FDA-approved for DMD (2024) through the same HDAC targets in the same skeletal-muscle compartment at comparable weight-based doses, and it improved muscle histology in DMD (NCT01761292). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, though none was measured in BMD. In BMD the fibrosis biopsy endpoint was not met (p=0.83; NCT03238235), yet MRI fat fraction favoured givinostat (p=0.0149 whole thigh, p=0.0022 quadriceps). The authors read this as a possible signal of slowed progression (PMID:36793492), which points to the endpoint choice and duration (F4). Trial problems also apply (F7): placebo patients had more severe disease at baseline, and only 4 per arm entered the posted primary analysis. F2 cannot be excluded.

The index NASH trial NCT03551522 was terminated for 'unexpected histological findings'. The PSC trial NCT04024813 was also stopped as a precaution because of these findings, so a molecule-specific safety signal ended the program. Serious AEs rose with dose (1/53, 3/51, 5/50 vs 0/27 on placebo). No human PK or engagement data exist in NASH. However, seladelpar met liver-acting PBC efficacy endpoints at 5–10 mg, a dose within the index range of 10–50 mg (NCT02609048, NCT02955602, NCT03602560, NCT04620733, PMID:35367282). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, and this PBC evidence predates the index trial. Despite this, MRI-PDFF did not improve vs placebo at any dose, which supports F2 as a secondary code.

The HoFH index trial (NCT02472535; 13 patients, 12-week LDL-C endpoint) posted no results and gave no stop reason. No PK, target-engagement or biomarker data in HoFH appear in the bundle. Hepatic PPARD engagement is inferred from PBC, where seladelpar met surrogate efficacy endpoints with dose-dependent ALP reductions (NCT02609048, NCT02955602, PMID:35367282) and pivotal endpoints (NCT03602560, NCT04620733) leading to approval. This is the same hepatic compartment, though dose comparability to the HoFH trial is unknown. All of that evidence postdates the index start. No other PPARD agonist succeeded in HoFH. The default reading is that PPARD agonism did not lower LDL-C meaningfully in HoFH, but the bundle is thin, so confidence is low and U remains plausible.

The final report of the C3G studies (PMID:36423588, covering index NCT03459443) states that optimal systemic danicopan concentrations were not achieved. Alternative pathway (AP) inhibition was incomplete and not sustained, likely because of PK/PD limitations in C3G, and this led to lack of efficacy. The authors conclude that complete, sustained AP inhibition is required. The earlier proof-of-mechanism study (NCT03124368) showed essentially no change in serum C3 (+0.11 g/L). Safety was favorable, so the dose was not tolerability-capped. In PNH, danicopan met endpoints (NCT04469465), with near-complete AP inhibition at approved doses (PMID:41757870). That does not carry over to C3G, where the sources directly show engagement was inadequate. The mechanism was not properly tested.

In healthy males, a PET study (PMID:36515395) found high NET occupancy and moderate (~45%) DAT/SERT occupancy at 400 mg/day, the top dose in the index trial. This was published in 2023, after the index trial started, and was not done in BED patients. The same 200–400 mg doses met primary endpoints in adult ADHD (NCT03605680, NCT03605836, NCT02547428), so the central pathway effect is inferred adequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose.
