Despite this, neither dose beat placebo on binge-eating days in NCT05113953 (p=0.19, p=0.85), with a large placebo response. Lisdexamfetamine is approved for BED, but this drug engaged its targets, so F1b does not apply. The likely reason is that this transporter-inhibition profile does not drive binge eating as tested.

A PET study in healthy men (PMID:36515395, published 2023, after the index trial started in 2021) showed high NET occupancy and moderate DAT/SERT occupancy at 400 mg/day. That shows brain exposure and target engagement. Centanafadine also met its primary endpoints in ADHD (NCT02547428, NCT03605680, NCT03605836) through the same CNS transporters, so the downstream pathway effect is inferred adequate. Despite this, the single-arm index trial (NCT05066724) produced 0% continuous abstinence (2% by CO confirmation). Bupropion is approved for nicotine dependence, but F1b does not fit because engagement was shown. Most likely this NET-dominant mechanism does not drive cessation as tested. The small uncontrolled design is a minor caveat (F7).

The index trial gave the recommended monotherapy dose, 480 mg twice daily on a 4-days-on/3-days-off schedule. At that dose, the first-in-human study showed adequate plasma levels and robust target modulation in solid tumors (PMID:29066505). STAKT in breast cancer showed dose-dependent falls in pPRAS40 and pGSK3β (engagement) and in pS6 and Ki67 (pathway) (PMID:31836609). This evidence predates the index trial, but none comes from NHL patients. In R/R B-cell NHL, monotherapy gave only modest response rates (FL 18.8%, MZL 33.3%, MCL 30%). The sources call antitumor activity limited, so an engaged AKT target did not drive enough benefit (F2). Secondary codes: responders were enriched for PTEN deficiency, and the authors suggest biomarker selection (F3). The trial ended early with 30 of 272 planned patients, limiting interpretation (F7).

No target is recorded and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for selenium sulfide (AZR-MD-001). The PubMed abstracts are rodent toxicology or unrelated. The index trial (NCT03972501) analysed only 7 patients per arm for the MGD endpoints. MGS and MGYLS changes numerically favoured active over vehicle, with wide overlapping spreads and no significance reported. A larger Phase 2 in MGD (NCT03652051) met its primary endpoint (MGYLS 4.2 vs 2.4). The program then continued into further Phase 2/3 trials (NCT04314362, NCT04391959, NCT06329791). This makes a tiny, underpowered trial the most direct explanation (F7), rather than a mechanism failure. Because engagement is unmeasured, U also applies.

At 200 mg b.i.d., the dose used in NCT04154787, iptacopan saturates plasma factor B. Phase 1 shows the highest alternative-pathway inhibition and EC90 for Wieslab, Bb and sC5b-9 (PMID:41701988), and TMDD modelling supports saturation (PMID:39856537). In IgAN and C3G patients, Bb, Wieslab and sC5b-9 fell, with proteinuria benefit (PMID:37914086, PMID:38106570, NCT04578834). Engagement was never measured in membranous nephropathy. Even so, proteinuria barely moved on iptacopan (UPCR ratio 0.88 at Day 169) and the drug was not superior to rituximab. This suggests factor B/alternative-pathway inhibition does not drive membranous nephropathy as tested (F2). The trial was small (n=37), terminated by the sponsor and used an active comparator, which limits interpretation (F7).

In the phase 1 trial (NCT03918980; PMID:33834628), healthy and atopic subjects showed rapid absorption. Blood BTK occupancy was above 95% at 30 mg or more, and near complete with 10 mg or more once daily on repeat dosing. Basophil CD63 and skin prick responses were nearly fully inhibited at 50–100 mg, with no dose-limiting toxicity. The drug also met efficacy endpoints in mast cell-driven CSU across a wide dose range (NCT03926611, NCT05030311, NCT05032157), confirming functional engagement. Despite this, the asthma trial showed no FEV1 benefit (difference 0.030 L, p=0.66). This suggests BTK inhibition does not drive airflow limitation in asthma as tested. Engagement was not shown in asthma patients. The trial was small and terminated early by company decision (F7 secondary).

The index trial (NCT00611130, 3 g/d) showed no difference in end-of-trial abstinence (7/92 vs 5/94). Its publication (PMID:23575810) reports that post hoc urine vigabatrin levels suggested 40–60% of the vigabatrin arm were non-adherent, and states this may have obscured efficacy. That is an execution problem that also left exposure inadequate in much of the arm. GABA-T engagement in humans is supported by platelet GABA-T inhibition (PMID:2757907) and by CSF data in epilepsy (PMID:2767013), all published before the index trial. Efficacy in infantile spasms (PMID:11673582) supports engagement by inference. No engagement or pathway data exist in cocaine-dependent patients. An earlier positive single-site trial (PMID:19651710) did not replicate, and a later cocaine/alcohol trial stopped for futility (NCT01335867).

Index MDD trial NCT01034995 posted no results, and none of the sources give a reason for the failure. Crinecerfont clearly engaged CRF1 in humans, but only at the pituitary in CAH patients: ACTH and 17-OHP fell (NCT03525886, NCT04045145, JCEM 2023). This evidence came years after the index trial. The anterior pituitary lies outside the blood-brain barrier, while the antidepressant hypothesis relies on CRF1 sites in the brain beyond the hypothalamus (PMID:24569014). So the CAH success does not show brain exposure or occupancy. I found no human CSF, PET-occupancy or central biomarker data, and no MDD dose information. Because brain target engagement is unknown, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not drive depression.

Target engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same 80 mg dose met efficacy endpoints in PBC through the same PPARα/δ hepatic mechanism (FDA approval; PMID:42007495). Pathway effects were clear in the index prediabetic patients (PMID:21816979): triglycerides fell 24.8%, HDL rose, and HOMA-IR, fasting glucose, fructosamine and GGT all decreased. Despite this, 2-h OGTT glucose was not reduced (P=0.18). The mechanism was engaged without the expected benefit on glucose tolerance, so F2. The trial was a small (n=47), short (35-day) pilot, and secondary measures improved, so endpoint or duration (F4) and underpowering (F7) may also contribute. The sources do not explicitly blame either. No tolerability limit was reported.

The index T2DM trial (NCT01261494) tested 80 mg against HbA1c at 12 weeks and posted no results. Exposure is adequate: population PK pooled 17 trials, and 80 mg gives a saturating ALP response in PBC (PMID:42007495). Engagement is inferred adequate because the drug is approved for PBC at 80 mg through the same PPARα/δ agonism with systemic exposure. Pathway effects at 80 mg appeared in metabolic patients: lower triglycerides and higher HDL (NCT01271751), and a modest gain in insulin sensitivity (NCT01271777). Even so, 2-h glucose was not reduced in prediabetes (NCT01275469). No tolerability cap was reported. The glycaemic mechanism appears insufficient, so F2. Confidence is low because the index trial has no posted results and the bundle shows no engagement in T2DM itself.

Human plasma PK across 17 trials is shown (PMID:42007495). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because elafibranor 80 mg met efficacy endpoints and was approved in PBC (ALP/bilirubin response) via PPARα/δ in the liver. That dose is below the 120 mg used in the index trial. Pathway effects consistent with PPARα agonism were shown at 80 mg: triglycerides fell, HDL rose (NCT01271751), and insulin sensitivity improved (NCT01271777). There was no tolerability cap, and the index trial reported no safety issues. Despite this, NASH resolution was not met (p=0.066) and the long-term outcome HR was 0.95 (NCT02704403). The phase 2b trial also missed (NCT01694849). The PPARα/δ mechanism at this exposure does not appear to drive clinically meaningful NASH benefit. No NASH-specific engagement data are in the bundle.

No direct receptor occupancy data exist. Elafibranor 80 mg is approved in PBC through hepatic PPAR agonism at the same dose (PMID:42007495), so exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate. In the index population (S2, prediabetic abdominally obese), 80 mg moved PPARα pathway markers: TG -24.8%, HDL +9.3%, LDL down, GGT down. It also lowered HOMA-IR, fasting glucose and fructosamine (PMID:21816979). The clamp study showed improved insulin sensitivity (NCT01271777). Yet the 5-week 2-h OGTT glucose endpoint was not met (P=0.18), with no safety issues. This reads as the mechanism not moving the tested glycemic endpoint (F2). The short duration and the choice of exploratory endpoint may also have contributed (F4). Pathway evidence was published in 2011, after the index trial started in 2009.

The index eyebrow AA trial of delgocitinib 30 mg/g ointment (NCT03325296) stopped for futility. The prior scalp AA phase 2a trial with the same ointment (NCT02561585, PMID:35230488) found no SALT difference from vehicle (p=0.92/0.97). Its authors attribute the failure to the ointment's inability to penetrate deeply enough into the scalp dermis to reach the hair follicle, i.e. inadequate tissue exposure. That is a stated inference, not a measured penetration result. Success in hand eczema and atopic dermatitis (NCT04872101, NCT03725722) reflects superficial epidermal exposure, a different compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred for follicles. Systemic JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, ritlecitinib, deuruxolitinib) are approved in AA, so the target is valid and the formulation is what failed (F1b secondary).

The index trial NCT03958955 of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g in DLE was terminated for recruitment challenges after enrolling only 27 patients. Target-lesion IGA 0/1 was 3 with delgocitinib vs 6 with vehicle (p=0.45). Pillars are inferred_adequate, not measured: the same 20 mg/g cream met clinical endpoints in chronic hand eczema and atopic dermatitis (NCT03683719, NCT03725722, NCT04871711, NCT04872101; PMID:35084738, PMID:42483929). That benefit acted through the same JAK targets in the same skin compartment, so cutaneous exposure and engagement must have held there. No engagement data exist in DLE patients. The sources attribute termination to recruitment, so the small, truncated trial could not answer the question (F7). The numerically unfavorable result also allows that JAK inhibition at this topical dose does not drive DLE (F2).

In a healthy-volunteer study published in 2017, before the index trial, rilzabrutinib showed good oral exposure and BTK occupancy above 90% in PBMCs at 300–900 mg/day (PMID:28636208). The index trial (NCT05104892, PMID:41936356) used 800 and 1200 mg/day, comparable or higher doses. The same doses met clinical endpoints in ITP (NCT04562766, approved) and in mast-cell-driven CSU at 1200 mg/day (NCT05107115, PMID:40266575). From those successes, the pathway pillar is inferred adequate for systemic immune cells. No asthma-specific engagement or airway biomarker data appear in the bundle. Tolerability did not cap the divided doses used. LOAC events fell numerically but not significantly, so the BTK mechanism appears not to drive loss of asthma control as tested. The small 800 mg cohort (32 vs 32) adds a possible power limitation.

In healthy volunteers, rilzabrutinib was rapidly absorbed and achieved >90% sustained BTK occupancy in PBMCs at 300–900 mg/day (PMID:28636208, published 2017, before the index trial). The pathway pillar is inferred adequate: the same regimens produced efficacy in ITP (NCT04562766, approved) and in skin mast-cell-driven CSU at 400 mg TID (NCT05107115, PMID:40266575). The index trial tested 400 mg BID and TID, which were tolerated; GI intolerance occurred only at a single 1200 mg dose (PMID:35301810). Yet EASI change did not separate from placebo in either cohort (p=0.62, p=0.67; NCT05018806), so BTK inhibition does not appear to drive atopic dermatitis. No engagement was shown in AD patients. Secondary F7: placebo response was high (~45% EASI reduction) and the cohorts were small.

In healthy volunteers, rilzabrutinib was rapidly absorbed and gave >90% sustained PBMC BTK occupancy at 300–900 mg/day (PMID:28636208, published 2017, before the index start). The index dose of 400 mg BID sits in that range and was well tolerated. Only a 1200 mg single dose caused GI intolerance (PMID:35301810), so the dose was not capped. The pathway pillar is inferred from the ITP Phase 3 success via BTK (NCT04562766). No occupancy or biomarker data in pemphigus patients are in the bundle. PEGASUS missed complete remission (24% vs 18%, p=0.45) despite engagement, pointing to F2. The authors note an amended corticosteroid endpoint, excluded remote observations and a supportive prespecified sensitivity analysis (PMID:38493933), so endpoint and design issues (F7/F4) remain secondary possibilities.

The index trial tested topical brepocitinib cream. No dose separated from vehicle on Week-12 PASI (NCT03850483, PMID:36972293). The bundle has no human skin-level, engagement or biomarker data for the cream in psoriatic plaques. The target is validated in psoriasis. Oral brepocitinib met PASI endpoints (NCT02969018, PMID:32311398) and lowered lesional IL-17/IL-23 transcripts (PMID:31972249, PMID:29266308). Deucravacitinib (TYK2) is approved for psoriasis. Because oral dosing is a different exposure route, it does not show the cream engaged. The cream did work in atopic dermatitis (NCT03903822, PMID:35986699), but the bundle shows nothing for psoriatic skin. The failure is therefore best read as a formulation or delivery problem rather than the target: F1b, with possible inadequate local exposure (F1a).

Oral brepocitinib gave dose-proportional plasma exposure in healthy volunteers and patients (PMID:29266308, PMID:36045513, PMID:38332554). Target engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because 30-60 mg QD met systemic efficacy endpoints through JAK1/TYK2 in psoriasis (NCT02969018), PsA (NCT03963401, PMID:37194394) and dermatomyositis (NCT05437263). Those doses are comparable to the 15-45 mg used in the SLE index trial. In psoriasis patients, IP-10 and hsCRP fell on drug (PMID:29266308), published before the index trial started; no engagement data exist in SLE. The index trial showed no dose separating from placebo on SRI-4 (NCT03845517), with no tolerability cap. This points to F2. The high placebo response (64.6%) may also have limited the trial's ability to detect benefit (F7).

A human PET study (PMID:20018493, 2010, before the index trial) showed dose-dependent brain NK1 receptor occupancy up to 93% at 100 mg/d. Plasma levels at 50 mg/d exceeded those predicted for maximal occupancy. Later trials used 85 mg bid (PMID:35644931), so exposure and engagement were adequate, though shown only in healthy volunteers and not in atopic dermatitis. Pathway is inferred_adequate from efficacy in motion sickness via the same target (NCT04327661, NCT05903924; FDA approval). No pathway biomarker was measured in AD. Despite this, the index trial EPIONE (NCT03568331) showed no itch separation (-3.6 vs -3.5), consistent with two prior phase 2 misses (NCT02004041, NCT02651714). NK1 antagonism does not appear to drive AD pruritus. EPIONE2 was later terminated for business reasons (NCT04140695).

Human PET in healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent brain NK1 occupancy, reaching 93% at 100 mg, with modeled trough occupancy above 80% at doses over 30 mg/day. This demonstrates brain exposure and adequate engagement, though not in alcohol-dependent patients, and was published in 2010, after the index trial began (PMID:20018493). In detoxified alcoholics, LY686017 suppressed craving and blunted cortisol responses (PMID:18276852, NCT00310427), so pathway effects were shown in this disease. No dose limitation is evident, with no serious AEs in either arm. Despite this, the 190-patient Phase 2 trial showed only small, likely non-significant reductions in heavy drinking days versus placebo (NCT00805441). The index dose is not stated in the bundle. Engagement held, so NK1 antagonism does not appear to drive drinking outcomes.

In healthy volunteers, rusfertide showed dose-dependent plasma exposure (PMID:38785334, PMID:39546273). It also produced dose-dependent falls in serum iron and transferrin saturation, the direct functional readout of ferroportin blockade, and with repeat dosing lowered hemoglobin and hematocrit (PMID:39888264). The same systemic mechanism met its endpoint in polycythemia vera (NCT04057040) and led to approval there. So exposure, engagement and pathway are supported, but only in healthy volunteers and PV, not in thalassemia patients. All of this was published after the index trial started. The beta-thalassemia trial (NCT03802201) posted no results and gave no stop reason, and no tolerability cap is shown. The most consistent reading is that ferroportin inhibition did not deliver anemia benefit in thalassemia as tested. Confidence is low because the readout itself is absent from the bundle.

The index trial NCT04373265 was a small Phase 1 combination study with pembrolizumab whose only primary outcome was dose-limiting toxicity. It completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of relacorilant. Human pillars are supported elsewhere. Plasma PK and GR antagonism (blocking prednisone effects) were shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:28967708, 2018, before the index trial). GR-regulated transcript changes were seen in solid-tumor patients (PMID:35583817). The drug also met a Phase 3 endpoint in Cushing syndrome (NCT03697109). No engagement data exist in adrenocortical carcinoma, and no tolerability cap is shown. The bundle gives no evidence of an efficacy failure or of the reason the program was not continued.

No direct human PK, occupancy or biomarker data are in the bundle. However, oveporexton at 1–2 mg BID produced large MWT gains in NT1 (NCT05687903, NCT06470828, NCT06505031) through the same brain OX2R target, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate at doses comparable to the NT2 trial. In NT2 (NCT05687916), 2 mg BID gave no MWT benefit (diff −0.24 min, p=0.989), and 2/5 mg gave a nonsignificant 2.4 min. Tolerability was clean, so dose was not limited. This suggests OX2R agonism does not drive wakefulness in NT2 as it does in orexin-deficient NT1 (PMID:41844849). The small arms (~20 each) and wide CIs leave some underpowering (F7).

The index trial (34 Chinese patients, enrolled from July 2020) matches PMID:39986946. Confirmed ORR was 14.7% (95% CI 5.0-31.1%). Benefit was confined to PD-L1-positive tumours (ORR 40% vs 0%; PFS 7.4 vs 1.5 months), and the authors call the activity encouraging, especially in PD-L1-positive disease. No human PD-L1 occupancy data appear in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 1200 mg q3w dose met efficacy endpoints through PD-L1 in other tumours (PMID:37672694, NCT01903993, NCT02108652). In thymic carcinoma itself, atezolizumab plus chemotherapy met its ORR endpoint in MARBLE (PMID:40049197), and Japan approved it for this disease (PMID:41504991). So the monotherapy readout reflects patient selection rather than a failed mechanism. It may not have been a true efficacy failure (F9).

The index trial NCT03312530 was a phase 1/2 safety-led study. Its primary endpoints were AE rates and descriptive ORR, with no prespecified statistical comparison and no control arm. It was classified not_efficacy and not_assessable, so it was not an efficacy test of atezolizumab. Adding atezolizumab gave ORR 26.7% versus 31.3% for cobimetinib+venetoclax, but arms were small (n=15–16) and uncontrolled (F7 secondary). The bundle has no direct PK, occupancy or biomarker data in myeloma. Pillars are inferred_adequate because atezolizumab at 1200 mg q3w met efficacy endpoints through systemic PD-L1 blockade in NSCLC, urothelial cancer and ASPS (NCT01903993, NCT02108652, NCT02031458, PMID:37672694). That is a different tissue context, so engagement in myeloma itself was not shown.

The index trial NCT05315713 enrolled only 8 participants, all in a Phase 1b arm of SC mosunetuzumab plus IV tiragolumab. No atezolizumab-containing arm is shown as treated. The Phase 2 ORR was never reported, and the trial was terminated for an unspecified sponsor decision. It therefore was not an efficacy test of atezolizumab in follicular lymphoma (F9), and it could not answer the question (F7). The bundle has no direct PD-L1 engagement data in FL. Pillars are inferred adequate because atezolizumab at 1200 mg q3w met efficacy endpoints through PD-L1 blockade in NSCLC, urothelial carcinoma and ASPS (NCT01903993, NCT02951767, PMID:37672694). PMID:35031227 reports the 1200 mg RP2D in FL. No tolerability cap is shown.

Brodalumab 210 mg Q2W, the dose in the index trial, had human PK (PMID:27128833). Phase Ib RA data showed IL-17RA receptor occupancy and signaling inhibition on circulating leukocytes (PMID:24286136, NCT00771030, registered before the index). It produced near-complete psoriasis clearance at 210 mg (PMID:22455412, NCT01708603) and suppressed IL-17-inducible genes there (PMID:41077515), so the pathway is inferred adequate. Engagement was never measured in asthma patients. In asthma, the first Phase 2 showed no effect across 140–280 mg (NCT01199289, PMID:24200404). The index trial then enriched for the nominal high-reversibility subgroup and was stopped for futility (ACQ difference -0.05, p=0.52; NCT01902290). With the target engaged and no tolerability cap, IL-17RA signaling does not appear to drive asthma control; the subgroup hypothesis (F3) also failed.

In RA patients, brodalumab produced IL-17RA receptor occupancy and inhibition of receptor signaling (PMID:24286136; NCT00771030, registered 2008 with PD endpoints). It met efficacy endpoints in psoriasis at 140–210 mg with suppression of IL-17-inducible genes (NCT00975637, PMID:22455412, PMID:41077515). The Crohn's trial used equal or higher doses (210–700 mg), so exposure and pathway are inferred adequate. No engagement was measured in Crohn's patients. In the index trial there was no meaningful remission benefit, and the study was stopped for worsening Crohn's disease in active arms (NCT01150890, PMID:27481309, NCT01199302). A review attributes this to a protective role of IL-17 in the gut: secukinumab also failed and also worsened Crohn's (PMID:34179741). This points to the target not driving the disease (F2), with on-target harm as a secondary code (F5).

Exposure and IL-5 engagement were not measured directly in EoE. Both are inferred adequate because the same IV doses (up to 3 mg/kg) met pivotal endpoints in eosinophilic asthma (NCT01285323, NCT01287039, NCT01270464). In the index trial, the pathway effect in diseased tissue was clear: peak esophageal eosinophils fell 59-67% versus 24% on placebo, p<0.0001 at all doses (NCT00538434, PMID:22206777). Yet the physician's global assessment did not differ from placebo. The authors state that symptom improvement was not associated with eosinophil changes, which suggests IL-5/eosinophil depletion does not drive symptoms as tested (F2). A later network meta-analysis notes histologic improvement does not guarantee patient-important benefit (PMID:42901296). The large placebo improvement (F7) and a possible endpoint or duration mismatch (F4) also contribute.

The index trial NCT03320707 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK/PD study in healthy participants, with adverse-event primary endpoints. It was not an efficacy test of daratumumab in prostate cancer, so F9 applies. In prostate cancer itself, the presurgical study PMID:36948506 showed daratumumab reached the tissue and engaged CD38: CD38+ T, NK and myeloid cells fell in prostate tumors, bone marrow and blood. However, no T-cell infiltration was induced, PSA did not change, and there were no pathologic complete remissions. This suggests the target was engaged without antitumor benefit, supporting F2 as a secondary code. That engagement evidence was published in 2023, after the index trial started in 2017. Efficacy in myeloma (NCT02076009, NCT02136134) confirms the drug is active through CD38.

The index extension (NCT01118728) was terminated for lack of efficacy after the ALIGN dose-ranging trial (NCT01061723; PMID:24550171) missed ASAS20 at every dose, including 150 mg qw and 200 mg q2w. Those are the regimens that met ACR20 in RA (PMID:24297381; NCT01061736; NCT01709578), so exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. Modelled receptor occupancy in RA exceeded 90% at 150 and 200 mg q2w (PMID:33314148). In AS patients, higher doses significantly lowered hs-CRP, showing IL-6 pathway blockade in this disease. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The authors conclude that IL-6Rα blockade is not effective in AS, so the target does not drive the disease as tested. No other IL-6R drug has succeeded in AS in the bundle.

At the 200 mg q2w dose used in NCT01900431, RA studies showed >90–98% IL-6Rα occupancy and sustained CRP suppression (PMID:33314148, PMID:24297381), with efficacy in RA and PMR (NCT01061736, NCT01709578, PMID:40105153). These data come from other diseases; no ocular or uveitis-specific engagement was measured. In this small trial (n=58, 20 placebo), the primary endpoint missed on central reading (46.1% vs 30.0%, p=0.235, OR 2.1, wide CI). The investigator-read VH endpoint (p=0.037), BCVA gain (p=0.033) and the subgroup with VH ≥2 (p=0.026) were positive (PMID:30316888). Few central-read patients had meaningful baseline haze. The likeliest reason for the miss is limited power and endpoint assessment rather than an inert mechanism; patient selection is a secondary contributor.

Target engagement was not measured directly in COVID-19. It is inferred adequate because sarilumab met efficacy endpoints in RA at comparable systemic doses (NCT01061736, NCT01709578), with >90% IL-6Rα occupancy there (PMID:33314148). The pathway effect held in this disease: CRP fell about 77% versus 20% on placebo in COVID-19 patients (NCT04315298, p<0.0001). Yet the clinical endpoints in critical, ventilated patients failed (NCT04315298, NCT04327388). The same target is validated in COVID-19: tocilizumab is FDA-approved, and a meta-analysis shows mortality benefit for both IL-6R blockers only when combined with corticosteroids, with possible harm used alone (PMID:36936570). This points to population and co-treatment context, and plausibly disease stage or timing (PMID:32789663), not an irrelevant target. The 800 mg cohort was tiny (n=31), so it was underpowered.

In NCT00918203, adding olaratumab to paclitaxel/carboplatin did not change median PFS (19.1 vs 19.0 weeks), and the publication also reports no OS gain. Phase 1 trials (NCT00768391, NCT01199822) showed systemic exposure that rose with dose (Cmax about 900–1160 µg/mL at 15–20 mg/kg) with no dose-limiting toxicities, so tolerability did not cap the dose. However, none of the sources show human PDGFRα occupancy, receptor phosphorylation inhibition or a downstream biomarker change. NCT02783599 measured only PDGF/PDGFR gene expression in sarcoma tissue, and the results were noisy. The sarcoma signal (NCT01185964) is not a confirmed efficacy result: the Phase 3 trial NCT02451943 failed, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. Investigators noted that PDGFR is rarely expressed on NSCLC tumor cells, though it is common in stroma. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Olaratumab 15 mg/kg plus mitoxantrone/prednisone did not improve PFS in post-docetaxel mCRPC (HR 1.29; NCT01204710, PMID:30573277). Plasma exposure at 15–20 mg/kg was shown (Cmax ~900–1160 µg/mL; NCT01199822) with no DLTs, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. No receptor occupancy or pathway biomarker was measured in prostate cancer. Engagement is inferred only from the STS phase 2 at the same dose, which met its endpoint and supported approval (NCT01185964). That inference is weak because the confirmatory STS phase 3 failed (NCT02451943), so U remains plausible. Preclinical data suggest bone-marrow transactivation of PDGFRα may escape antibody blockade (PMID:17234763). Authors suggest patient selection and earlier disease, citing a high-CTC subgroup (F3).

Exposure was adequate: in the first-in-human study (NCT00768391), trough serum levels at 20 mg/kg every two weeks stayed above the concentration that worked in preclinical xenograft models. The index trial used comparable doses (20 mg/kg loading, then 15 mg/kg) with no DLTs, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. No source I found shows that olaratumab occupied PDGFRα or inhibited its signalling in human tumour. The tumour biomarker study (NCT02783599) only reported widely scattered changes in PDGFR and PDGF ligand gene expression, which do not show engagement. Engagement can't be inferred from efficacy either: the sarcoma Phase 3 (NCT02451943) failed, and the earlier Phase 2 signal (NCT01185964) came from a loose alpha of 0.2. Overall survival in the index trial was no better (HR 1.054). Without engagement data, the cause can't be determined.

Phase 1 trials (NCT01199822, NCT02377752) show high plasma olaratumab exposure at 10–20 mg/kg without DLTs, so dose was not capped. No receptor occupancy or PDGFRA signaling data exist in humans. NCT02783599 measured only tumor gene expression, which is uninformative. Engagement is inferred from the soft tissue sarcoma Phase 2 that met its endpoint (NCT01185964) and from the 2016 approval, which targets the same tumor compartment. That inference is weak because the confirmatory Phase 3 failed (NCT02451943). The index trial showed no PFS benefit (HR 1.05). Repeated failures in NSCLC, prostate and pancreatic cancer suggest PDGFRA blockade does not drive these tumors. Without direct engagement data, U remains plausible.

The index trial NCT02677116 was a pediatric Phase 1 safety study. Its only primary endpoint was olaratumab DLTs given with chemotherapy, and few DLTs occurred, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Plasma exposure was dose-proportional (Cmax about 600–1160 µg/mL in NCT01199822). The bundle has no receptor occupancy or PDGFRα inhibition data. Tumor gene-expression changes in NCT02783599 were too variable to interpret as engagement or pathway effects. The program-wide stop most plausibly followed the Phase 3 overall-survival miss in soft tissue sarcoma (NCT02451943). With engagement unmeasured, that underlying failure stays indeterminate (U).

Avelumab 10 mg/kg Q2W gave >90% peripheral PD-L1 target occupancy across the dosing interval (NCT02603419, PMID:34477818), with well-characterized PK (PMID:28373007, PMID:31553054). No dose-limiting tolerability was shown. Pathway is inferred adequate because avelumab met efficacy endpoints through PD-L1 blockade in Merkel cell (NCT02155647) and urothelial carcinoma. Occupancy was measured in Hodgkin lymphoma and mixed solid tumors, not gastric cancer, and was published after the index start. Despite adequate engagement, maintenance avelumab did not improve OS (HR 0.91; NCT02625610). Modeling found no treatment effect (PMID:34971492), and third-line monotherapy also failed (PMID:30052729), so PD-L1 monotherapy does not drive benefit here. Sources point to benefit possibly confined to EBV+ or PD-L1-high subsets (PMID:29155997, PMID:40388549, PMID:39649204).

The index trial NCT02718417 (PMID:34363762) stopped for futility, with PFS HR 1.43 and 1.14 versus observation. Avelumab at 10 mg/kg Q2W had well-characterized PK (PMID:28373007, PMID:31553054). Peripheral target occupancy exceeded 90% across doses (NCT02603419, PMID:34477818), but this was measured in Hodgkin lymphoma and mixed solid tumours, not ovarian cancer. The Phase 1a occupancy work was registered in 2013, before the index trial. The pathway pillar is inferred adequate: the same dose met efficacy endpoints in Merkel cell carcinoma (NCT02155647) and urothelial carcinoma, both through the same PD-L1 blockade. No dose limitation was seen. Ovarian activity was modest (ORR 9.6%, PMID:30676622), and JAVELIN Ovarian 200 also failed (PMID:34143970). PD-L1 blockade therefore appears not to drive ovarian cancer as tested. A possible biomarker-selected subset (PMID:36601114) is weak support for F3.

Index trial NCT03750071 tested VXM01 plus avelumab with a safety/tolerability primary endpoint (classified not_efficacy). It reported no results and gave no stop reason, so it was not an efficacy test of avelumab: F9. Peripheral PD-L1 occupancy above 90% at 10 mg/kg was shown in cHL patients (NCT02603419, PMID:34477818; PMID:28373007 published earlier). This is not glioblastoma, and the bundle has no data on brain or tumor penetration. Pathway is inferred_adequate from avelumab's approved efficacy in Merkel cell carcinoma (NCT02155647). Other avelumab trials in glioblastoma showed no apparent OS gain (PMID:34604752) and missed a 6-month PFS threshold (PMID:33067319). This hints the mechanism may not drive this disease (secondary F2), but brain exposure is unproven.

Avelumab had well-characterised PK and achieved >90% PD-L1 target occupancy in peripheral blood across doses in relapsed/refractory cHL (NCT02603419, registered before the index trial; PMID:34477818). Its efficacy approvals (Merkel, urothelial) and cHL responses support inferring that the pathway worked. Tolerability did not cap the dose: there were no new safety concerns and DLTs were rare. Despite this, JAVELIN DLBCL (NCT02951156) gave low ORRs (11%, 0%, 27%), and the authors conclude that PD-L1 inhibitor activity may be limited in R/R DLBCL (PMID:34687398), pointing to the target. Secondary codes: activity confined to the PMBCL/EBV+ subsets (PMID:36906715), and the trial was small with enrollment difficulty and an arm that could not be expanded. Engagement was not measured in DLBCL itself.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT02476123 (mogamulizumab plus nivolumab, solid tumors including renal) posted no results. At the same 1 mg/kg dose, which was tolerated without DLTs (NCT02705105, NCT02444793), plasma exposure was dose-proportional (NCT00355472). Mogamulizumab nearly completely depleted peripheral CCR4+ effector Tregs and reduced intratumoral Tregs in most solid-tumor patients (PMID:32586937). There was no correlation with response. The same combination with nivolumab gave an ORR of 10.5% and 'did not result in enhanced efficacy' (PMID:34753777). Other combinations were also inactive (PMID:31801624). Target engagement and the pathway effect held, yet there was no clinical benefit, so CCR4+ Treg depletion does not drive antitumor efficacy as tested. Renal-specific engagement data are absent, and the engagement evidence was published after the index trial started.

In HAM/TSP patients, mogamulizumab depleted CCR4+ HTLV-1-infected cells. The phase 1-2a (PMID:29414279, registered before the index trial) showed a dose-dependent ~65% proviral load drop and falls in CSF CXCL10 and neopterin, with no dose-limiting toxicity up to 0.3 mg/kg. Infected cells in CSF fell 66% long term (PMID:37093965). In the index phase 3 (NCT03191526; PMID:38430272) at 0.3 mg/kg, proviral load fell ~59% versus placebo, and CSF neopterin and CXCL10 fell significantly. Yet the 24-week Osame motor score showed no difference. The authors suggest benefit may come as long-term prevention of progression, which implicates the short improvement endpoint for a chronic neurodegenerative disease (F4). F2 also applies. F3 is possible: in PMID:37157862 only milder, shorter-duration patients improved.

The index trial NCT01514981 was a single-dose Phase 1 study in 7 asthma patients. Its primary outcomes were adverse events and anti-drug antibodies, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated for an 'administrative decision' and posted no results, so there was no failed efficacy readout (F9). The unspecified sponsor decision fits a business stop (F8, secondary). Exposure is shown by dose-proportional plasma PK (NCT00355472). Engagement is shown by near-complete peripheral eTreg depletion and intratumoral Treg depletion (PMID:32586937, PMID:40180420). Pathway effects appear as falls in HTLV-1 proviral load and CSF markers (PMID:29414279, PMID:38430272). None of this was measured in asthma, and all of it was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

The index phase 1b (NCT02444793; PMID:31801624) combined utomilumab with mogamulizumab 1 mg/kg in advanced solid tumors. It had no DLTs, an ORR of 4.2%, and was stopped for marginal efficacy plus a sponsor reprioritization. Plasma exposure at 1 mg/kg is well characterized (NCT00355472). In solid-tumor patients at this same dose, mogamulizumab caused almost complete depletion of peripheral CCR4+ eTregs and reduced intratumoral Tregs, yet response did not track depletion (PMID:32586937). Those data were published after the index trial started. Combinations with durvalumab, tremelimumab or nivolumab also showed no enhanced efficacy (PMID:32586937, PMID:34753777). So the target was engaged, but CCR4-Treg depletion did not drive antitumor benefit (F2). Sponsor prioritization contributed to stopping (F8).

Dupilumab 300 mg q2w, the dose used in NCT04681729, gives well-characterised serum exposure (PMID:34435584, PMID:35986664). Healthy-volunteer studies published in 2020, before the index trial began, showed lower total IgE and TARC, indicating IL-4Rα blockade (PMID:32348036). The drug is approved in chronic idiopathic urticaria and atopic dermatitis at this dose, so skin-compartment engagement is also inferred adequate (NCT02277743). Engagement was not measured in cold urticaria patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose, and AEs were lower than placebo (PMID:41852856). The primary endpoint was flatly null (negative ice-cube test 40.5% vs 37.5%, OR 1.03), and key secondary endpoints also missed. IL-4/IL-13 signalling does not appear to drive cold-induced mast cell urticaria.

The HS dose (200 mg SC q4w, or 1200 mg IV) exceeded the doses that cleared psoriatic skin (100 mg q8w; NCT02207231, NCT02207244, PMID:26154787). Exposure and IL-23 engagement in skin are therefore inferred_adequate. Downstream IL-17A/F and IL-22 reductions and skin pathway gene changes were measured directly in psoriasis (PMID:39114670). Tolerability did not cap the dose, and serious AEs were not higher on drug. HiSCR was not met at either dose, with no dose response, and the authors conclude the data do not support efficacy (NCT03628924, PMID:37317022). The open-label mode-of-action study found no consistent biomarker–response correlation in HS (PMID:36811949), so IL-23 does not appear to drive HS broadly. Case reports suggest benefit limited to patients with IBD or psoriasis comorbidity (PMID:31389737), supporting secondary F3.

In GCA, guselkumab's GC-free remission at week 28 was 40.0% vs 33.3% on placebo (p=0.638) (NCT04633447). No GCA target-engagement data are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred adequate: the same systemic IL-23p19 neutralization met pivotal endpoints in psoriasis and PsA (NCT02207231, NCT03158285) and in UC (PMID:37659673). Human plasma PK is well characterized (PMID:35470450). Serum IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 fell clearly in psoriasis and PsA (PMID:39114670, PMID:37587493, PMID:38253404), all published or registered before 2020. No tolerability cap is shown. A drug that reliably blocks IL-23 yet gave no GCA benefit points to IL-23 not driving GCA as tested. A small trial (n=53) with a wide CI leaves an underpowering caveat, but no source blames the design.

Exposure was shown by dose-related PK in Phase 1 (PMID:20593411, PMID:24272917). Pathway was adequate: P1NP rose and CTX fell dose-dependently, and BMD increased, in the Phase 1 studies registered and published before the index trial started. Sclerostin binding was not measured directly, so engagement is inferred_adequate: the same 210 mg monthly dose met a hard vertebral fracture endpoint in osteoporosis through the same target in bone (NCT01575834, NCT01631214). No engagement data come from fracture patients. In tibial fractures (NCT00907296), no dose from 70 to 210 mg shortened time to radiographic healing, all p>0.35. The hip fracture trial (NCT01081678) also failed. Tolerability did not cap dosing. Sclerostin inhibition does not appear to speed acute fracture healing as tested.

In healthy volunteers, galcanezumab had linear PK and produced robust, dose-dependent, durable inhibition of capsaicin-induced dermal blood flow, a CGRP-mediated functional readout. Near-maximal inhibition came at doses within the 5-300 mg range tested (PMID:29089894, PMID:26116630, PMID:33740315; NCT01337596 registered 2011). The same doses (120 mg) met efficacy endpoints in migraine (NCT02163993, NCT02614183). Tolerability did not limit dosing. In the knee OA trial, no dose separated from placebo on WOMAC pain, while celecoxib did (-31.3 vs -19.2), which shows the trial could detect an analgesic. It stopped at a prespecified Bayesian interim futility analysis (PMID:30321909). With CGRP neutralization adequate, this points to CGRP not driving OA knee pain as tested. Engagement was not measured in OA patients.

CALLA (NCT03830866) added durvalumab 1500 mg Q4W to chemoradiotherapy and missed its PFS endpoint (HR 0.84, p=0.174). The bundle has no direct human PD-L1 occupancy or pathway data in cervical cancer. Durvalumab is FDA-approved in NSCLC, urothelial, HCC and other cancers through the same systemic anti-PD-L1 mechanism at comparable doses (e.g., PMID:34292792), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. No dose limitation was shown, and no other CD274 drug succeeded in cervical cancer. The pembrolizumab approval in PMID:39730899 is for a PD-1 drug, a different target. PD-L1 blockade with CRT therefore did not improve outcomes as tested. PMID:40500687 notes a biomarker-unselected ITT population, which raises possible patient-selection issues (F3).

Durvalumab plus daratumumab in RRMM produced 0/18 objective responses (NCT03000452). The bundle has no direct PD-L1 occupancy or pathway data in myeloma. Durvalumab is approved in multiple solid tumors (NSCLC, urothelial, HCC, and others; PMID:34292792, NCT01693562) through systemic PD-L1 blockade at standard doses, so exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. Myeloma is a marrow, not solid-tumor, compartment, which weakens this inference. No other PD-L1 agent is shown to have succeeded in myeloma, which rules out F1b, and tolerability did not cap the dose. The most direct reading is that PD-L1 blockade does not drive myeloma control in this setting (F2). The trial was small and short (median about 8 weeks, n=18), and a related myeloma study was placed on a regulatory hold (NCT02716805), so F7 is a secondary code.

FUSION (NCT02775903) added durvalumab 1500 mg Q4W to azacitidine. AML ORR was 31.3% vs 35.4%, OS 13.0 vs 14.4 months, with no new safety signals (PMID:34933333). Population PK in AML/MDS patients showed exposure consistent with solid tumors and supported the 1500 mg Q4W regimen as adequate (PMID:31332669), so exposure is adequate. PD-L1 engagement was not measured in AML. It is inferred adequate because the same systemic dose met efficacy endpoints in approved indications (NSCLC, HCC, urothelial carcinoma, and others). Dose was not limited by tolerability. PD-L1 expression, methylation, SF and TP53 status did not predict response (PMID:34933333, PMID:40546817), so no subgroup explains the result. PD-L1 blockade does not appear to drive benefit in AML as tested. Confidence is medium because engagement is inferred, not measured.

The index trial (NCT02281084) was mainly a CC-486 study in HMA-failure MDS. Its durvalumab plus azacitidine arms were tiny (n=6 and 5), with median treatment of 1.84 months and ORR of 16.7% and 0%. The bundle has no direct PD-L1 occupancy or PK data in MDS. Pillars are inferred adequate because durvalumab, a systemic anti-PD-L1 mAb, met efficacy endpoints and won approvals in NSCLC, urothelial cancer and HCC through the same target at comparable doses (NCT01693562, PMID:34292792). The separate MDS phase 1 of durvalumab ± tremelimumab ± azacitidine was terminated for limited efficacy despite tolerability, with no dose limitation (PMID:40153010). This points to PD-L1 blockade not driving MDS response. The very small, short combination arms also limit interpretability (F7).

Benralizumab 30 mg gives dose-proportional systemic exposure and near-complete blood and tissue eosinophil depletion. EDN and ECP fall, so the pathway also moves, but this was shown in asthma, CRSwNP and children (PMID:20513521, 26775606, 38715387, 38491795, 28109128), not in bronchiectasis. MAHALE (NCT05006573) missed its endpoint (RR 1.14, p=0.59). The publication (PMID:42639375) attributes this to early termination for COVID-related recruitment problems: 100 of the planned patients, not powered, with baseline imbalances favouring more severe disease in the benralizumab arm. It concludes the trial could not answer the question, so F7 is primary. Only 21 patients had eosinophils ≥300, which points to a mis-selected population (F3). A target-irrelevance reading (F2) cannot be excluded.

Benralizumab is an IL-5Rα depleter. Human data published before the 2020 index trial show dose-proportional plasma PK (PMID:28109128). They also show near-complete blood eosinophil depletion with lasting eosinopenia (PMID:20513521) and reductions in the downstream granule proteins EDN and ECP (PMID:26775606). Later work shows tissue eosinophils depleted to zero in nasal polyps (PMID:38715387), and phase 3 asthma efficacy (NCT01914757, NCT01928771) confirms the mechanism works at 30 mg. No engagement data come from atopic dermatitis patients or skin, and no tolerability cap is shown. In NCT04605094, IGA 0/1 responders were numerically worse on drug (9.4%) than placebo (17.3%), p=0.080. With engagement and pathway adequate, eosinophil depletion does not appear to drive atopic dermatitis as tested.

In MESSINA (NCT04543409/PMID:38924732), benralizumab 30 mg q4w produced histologic remission (≤6 eos/hpf) in 87.4% vs 6.5% on placebo (p<0.0001). This shows exposure and near-complete esophageal eosinophil depletion in EoE patients. Blood eosinophil depletion and tissue depletion at this dose are also documented elsewhere (PMID:20513521, PMID:38715387). Dysphagia (DSQ) did not improve (p=0.18), and endoscopic scores did not differ. Tolerability did not limit the dose. The mechanism was fully engaged, so the failure indicates that eosinophils do not drive dysphagia in EoE as tested (F2). PMID:35283330 suggests that residual symptoms reflect persistent epithelial or remodeling changes, which supports an endpoint/timing element (F4). In-disease engagement evidence came only after the index trial started.

Benralizumab has dose-proportional PK and near-complete blood and tissue eosinophil depletion in humans (PMID:20513521, PMID:28109128, PMID:38715387). It is approved in asthma, which supports adequate exposure and engagement. In the index trial, engagement and the expected pathway effect held in eosinophilic gastritis/gastroenteritis: histologic response was 5/6 on benralizumab vs 0/6 on placebo (NCT05251909). Symptoms did not follow: SAGED change was -9.59 vs -13.69 on placebo. The sponsor stopped the study citing emerging evidence on the pathology of eosinophilic upper GI disease. The EoE trial showed the same split, with histology met and symptoms (DSQ) missed (NCT04543409). Together this suggests eosinophil depletion does not drive symptoms in this disease (F2). Secondary F7: only 12 patients were randomized, so the trial was underpowered.

Benralizumab has dose-proportional systemic PK and causes near-complete blood eosinophil depletion from low doses in humans (PMID:20513521, PMID:28109128). It also lowers EDN and ECP, showing a pathway effect (PMID:26775606). Tissue eosinophils fell to zero in nasal polyps (PMID:38715387). Its approved asthma efficacy confirms engagement (NCT01914757, NCT01928771). There was no tolerability cap and no new safety concerns. Engagement was not shown in bullous pemphigoid patients specifically. The index trial nonetheless failed futility: responders 11.1% vs 5.3%, p=0.509 (NCT04612790). A case of BP arising during benralizumab therapy (PMID:37122191) also suggests eosinophil depletion does not control the disease. The small evaluable sample (18 vs 19) adds some design uncertainty.

ARROYO (NCT04612725) tested 30 and 60 mg Q4W, at or above the approved asthma dose, and missed ISS7 at Week 12 (p=0.38, p=0.12) with no tolerability cap. In humans, benralizumab showed dose-proportional PK (PMID:28109128). It produced near-complete blood eosinophil depletion (PMID:20513521, PMID:38491795) and complete tissue eosinophil depletion in nasal polyps at 30 mg (PMID:38715387). EDN and ECP were reduced (PMID:26775606), and pivotal asthma endpoints were met (NCT01928771, NCT01914757). Engagement and pathway are therefore adequate. Eosinophil/basophil depletion did not improve itch, suggesting these cells do not drive chronic spontaneous urticaria symptoms as tested. Atopic dermatitis also failed (NCT04605094). Caveat: skin engagement in CSU patients is not shown in the bundle.

The index trial NCT01688739 was a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study whose primary endpoints were adverse events and anti-drug antibodies, so it was not an efficacy test. It completed with no serious AEs and no discontinuations. Erenumab then advanced and met primary endpoints in Phase 2/3 migraine trials (NCT01952574, NCT02066415, NCT02456740, NCT02483585) and was FDA-approved for migraine in 2018. The pillars held. PK was characterised (PMID:28593473, PMID:28736918). Capsaicin-induced dermal blood flow was inhibited by more than 75%, up to a maximum of 89%, in pooled healthy and migraine subjects. This engagement evidence was published after the index trial began. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The program did not fail on efficacy.

The index migraine extension trial (NCT05016661) was terminated because the parent data (NCT04845178) missed the primary and key secondary endpoints. No migraine engagement or biomarker data were posted. SNAP25 engagement and the neuromuscular pathway effect are only inferred from injected-muscle efficacy in glabellar lines (NCT05320393, met; NCT01629875). That is a different indication at much lower doses. Cervical dystonia studies (NCT04849988) report only safety. Another toxin on the same target, botulinum toxin type A, is FDA-approved for migraine, so the target is validated in this disease. That points to a molecule, dose or injection-paradigm issue rather than target failure. No tolerability limit was shown. The bundle has no abstracts or results, so confidence is low.

Fremanezumab showed no effect on fibromyalgia pain at either dose: the LS mean differences were 0.1 and 0.0 versus placebo, and the trial stopped for futility at interim (NCT03965091). Plasma exposure is well characterised in humans (PMID:31418911, PMID:29667896). Engagement and pathway were not measured in fibromyalgia, so both are inferred_adequate. The same CGRP neutralisation met pivotal endpoints in migraine before this trial began, at comparable subcutaneous doses (NCT02621931, NCT02629861, NCT03308968), leading to the 2018 approval. A later healthy-volunteer study also showed CSF distribution and target engagement (PMID:42775430). Tolerability did not cap the dose; no maximum tolerated dose was reached (PMID:24366980). The likeliest reading is that CGRP does not drive fibromyalgia pain.

Fremanezumab failed its interim futility analysis in episodic cluster headache (NCT02945046: 675 mg p=0.91; 900/225 mg p=0.13, a numerical trend), and the chronic cluster headache trial (NCT02964338) also failed. Plasma exposure at 675 and 900 mg is documented (PMID:29667896). No MTD was found (PMID:24366980), so dose was not limited. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because the same doses met endpoints in migraine (NCT02621931, NCT02629861). Measured CGRP engagement exists only in healthy volunteers, published after the index trial (PMID:42775430). Galcanezumab, also acting on CGRP, is FDA-approved for cluster headache, so the target is validated. This points to molecule or regimen (F1b). The large placebo response (-5.7 attacks/week) suggests a trial-design contribution (F7).

Lanadelumab targets plasma kallikrein, a systemic target. Human data show dose-dependent plasma exposure, including 300 mg IV PK in NCT04503603. Kallikrein inhibition was shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:24980392), and cHMWK cleavage was reduced toward normal in HAE patients (PMID:28225674, PMID:32407574). Clinical efficacy in HAE followed (NCT02586805). All of this predates the index trial. Engagement was never measured in COVID-19 patients. In the index sub-protocol (NCT04590586), time to recovery was not improved (HR 1.17, p=0.67). A separate phase 2 trial of the same IV 300 mg regimen also showed no benefit on oxygen needs (PMID:41508921). The likeliest reading is that kallikrein inhibition does not drive COVID-19 outcomes (F2). The very small sub-protocol (25 vs 30 patients) leaves it underpowered, so F7 is secondary.

The index trial NCT02855450 was a Phase 1 vehicle-controlled study whose primary outcomes were safety events and VAS ocular tolerability, not efficacy. Tolerability was modestly worse on rhNGF (6/40 drug intolerance; Day 7 VAS p=0.040), but no efficacy endpoint failed, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). Corneal NTRK1 engagement is inferred from NK efficacy (NCT01756456, NCT02227147), but that is a different tissue compartment. The bundle has no human evidence that topical drops reach the retina or optic nerve or engage NTRK1 there, so pillars are no_human_data for glaucoma. No stop reason is given, which leaves the mechanism's relevance indeterminate (U as secondary).

The index trial tested topical rhNGF 20 µg/ml for ocular discomfort after cataract or refractive surgery. It missed both SANDE co-primaries (p=0.974, p=0.399) and corneal staining (p=0.214) (NCT03035864). No pillar was measured in the index trial. The same 20 µg/ml topical corneal dose met healing endpoints in neurotrophic keratitis (NCT01756456, NCT02227147; FDA-approved), and corneal nerve regeneration followed (PMID:37965220). So exposure, NTRK1 engagement and pathway are inferred adequate in the same tissue. Tolerability did not cap the dose: 20–180 µg/ml was tolerated (NCT01744704). Benefit was absent despite this, so NGF agonism does not appear to drive post-surgical discomfort. Dry eye trials met objective tear endpoints but missed SANDE (NCT05133180, NCT05136170), which suggests endpoint sensitivity may also contribute (F4).

Risankizumab 90 mg SC every 4 weeks shortened time to first asthma worsening versus placebo (HR 1.46; NCT02443298, PMID:34706172). Tolerability did not cap the dose: serious AEs were fewer on drug. Exposure is dose-proportional and well characterized (PMID:31054118). Engagement and pathway were not shown in asthma; the sputum biomarker results are truncated in the bundle. Both are inferred adequate because the same systemic IL-23p19 neutralization met efficacy endpoints in psoriasis at 90-180 mg SC (NCT02054481, NCT02684370) and in Crohn disease (NCT03105128), with IL-23/IL-17 pathway suppression shown in psoriasis (PMID:25769911, NCT01577550). The asthma dose exceeded the psoriasis regimen. The mechanism was tested, and IL-23 blockade does not benefit severe asthma; the trend was toward harm.

Risankizumab 18–180 mg SC gave no ASAS40 separation from placebo, and the 180 mg arm was numerically worse (NCT02047110, PMID:29945918). Exposure was dose-proportional across 18–300 mg SC (PMID:31054118, PMID:31257614). Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because comparable doses (150 mg SC) met endpoints in psoriatic arthritis (NCT02719171, PMID:35931879) and psoriasis. Psoriasis lesional skin also showed reduced IL-23/IL-17 pathway gene expression (PMID:25769911). Engagement was not measured in AS patients. Tolerability did not limit dosing. The authors conclude IL-23 may not drive AS pathogenesis (PMID:29945918). Molecular and genetic differences between axial PsA and r-axSpA (PMID:36995469) support a mechanism-in-disease failure, with a possible disease-heterogeneity component.

In NCT03926169/PMID:36892753, HiSCR at week 16 was 46.8% (180 mg) and 43.4% (360 mg) versus 41.5% on placebo, and the study stopped early. Systemic exposure is dose-proportional and well characterised (PMID:31054118). The HS doses, with intensive loading, were at or above the 75-150 mg doses that met psoriasis endpoints in skin (NCT02684370, NCT02684357, NCT03000075). That supports inferred_adequate engagement in the same tissue compartment. Lesional-skin IL-23/IL-17 gene expression fell in psoriasis (PMID:25769911), but nothing was measured in HS. Tolerability was good, so the dose was not limited. The most direct reading is that IL-23 does not drive HS as tested (F2). A later analysis of phenotype-specific response signals (PMID:42660432) hints at subgroup effects (F3).

CHAMPION-ALS (NCT04248465) used the same weight-based q8w IV regimen that gave above-threshold serum levels (>175 µg/mL) and immediate, complete, sustained free C5 suppression (<0.5 µg/mL) in PNH, gMG and NMOSD (PMID:32449174, 36890354, 38356884). The same dosing met clinical endpoints in gMG at the neuromuscular junction (NCT03920293) and in CNS NMOSD (NCT04201262), so the terminal-complement pathway effect is inferred. ALS-specific PK/PD is not shown in the bundle. Tolerability did not cap the dose. ALSFRS-R was numerically worse on drug (PMID:37695623). Zilucoplan, another C5 inhibitor, also failed in ALS. Mouse data, which are supportive only, implicate proximal C3 rather than C5 (PMID:42492371). Together these point to terminal C5 not driving ALS progression.

In the index trial NCT04999020, the TIS40 response at Week 26 was 9/26 on ravulizumab vs 6/12 on placebo (p=0.42); placebo was numerically better. C5 is a serum target. In PNH, gMG and NMOSD, weight-based dosing kept serum levels above the 175 µg/mL threshold and drove free C5 below 0.5 µg/mL immediately, completely and durably (PMID:32449174, published before the index start; PMID:36890354; PMID:38356884). Pathway is inferred adequate: the same systemic C5 blockade met efficacy endpoints in PNH, gMG and NMOSD. No dermatomyositis-specific PK/PD is in the bundle, so confidence is medium. With engagement adequate and no benefit, terminal C5 blockade does not appear to drive dermatomyositis as tested. The small, terminated trial (n=38) limits power (F7, secondary).

The index open-label trial stopped for futility, with Day 29 survival of 57.6% on ravulizumab versus 59.7% on best supportive care (NCT04369469). Ravulizumab's target, C5, is in plasma. At weight-based IV doses, other diseases show therapeutic serum levels and immediate, complete, sustained free C5 suppression below 0.5 µg/mL (PMID:32449174, 36890354, 38356884, 38551806). Dose-dependent LDH falls in PNH (NCT02598583, NCT02605993) confirm the downstream pathway effect, and all of this predates the index trial. A COVID-specific PK/PD paper exists (PMID:33826106), but its results are not shown, so engagement in COVID patients is not demonstrated in the bundle. No tolerability cap is evident. Given established, complete terminal complement blockade with no survival benefit, C5 inhibition does not appear to drive mortality in severe COVID-19 pneumonia.

The index trial NCT01020383 compared caplacizumab with a GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor in high-risk PCI. Its primary outcome was bleeding incidence (TIMI major, minor and minimal), a safety endpoint classified not_efficacy, with no posted results or stated stop reason. So it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Pillars hold in humans: near-complete VWF:RCo suppression in healthy volunteers and iTTP patients (PMID:42456747), PK/PD modeling of VWF:Ag suppression (PMID:34699078), and efficacy in TTP (NCT01151423, NCT02553317). However, this evidence comes from the TTP program and is dated after 2009, not from coronary disease. CAD data are in vitro only, showing higher VWF needs a higher concentration (PMID:21655675). No tolerability dose cap is shown.

In MORPHEUS-CRC (NCT03555149), the atezolizumab + isatuximab arm had an ORR of 0% (n=15), and the arm showed no efficacy signal (PMID:35856081). The trial's formal termination was operational (recruitment), but this arm was completed. At the 10 mg/kg dose, isatuximab exposure matched myeloma trials (PMID:38147137). In other solid tumors, isatuximab nearly cleared CD38+ tumor-infiltrating immune cells (PMID:35987165, PMID:35058326; receptor occupancy in myeloma, PMID:30926770), so engagement was adequate. That evidence comes from solid tumors other than colorectal cancer and was published after the index trial started. The expected immune effect did not follow: Tregs and PD-L1 were not modulated. Similar solid-tumor combinations also failed (NCT03637764, NCT03367819). Together this points to CD38 depletion not driving antitumor benefit; operational termination and small arms are secondary.

ISAKIDS (NCT03860844) gave isatuximab 20 mg/kg with salvage chemotherapy. AML CR/CRi was 61%, below the ≥70% Stage 2 threshold, so the sponsor stopped the study; safety was not the reason (PMID:41180900). Exposure was adequate: pediatric PopPK matched adult exposure and showed no exposure–efficacy relationship (PMID:41331127). Engagement was adequate in humans: CD38 receptor occupancy plateaued at about 80% at 20 mg/kg in myeloma, published in 2019 (PMID:30926770). Pathway was adequate: CD38+ cells were depleted in other settings (PMID:38147137, PMID:35987165, PMID:35058326). No engagement data exist in AML blasts themselves. Adequate engagement with no added benefit supports F2. The trial was single-arm on a chemotherapy backbone with stringent thresholds, so it could not isolate the drug's contribution (F7). Adult T-ALL monotherapy produced a 0% response rate (NCT02999633).

Index trial NCT03367819 (isatuximab 10 mg/kg + cemiplimab) stopped at the Simon stage-1 interim analysis. ORR was 4.2% in mCRPC and 0% in NSCLC. In post-treatment biopsies from these patients, CD38+ tumor-infiltrating immune cells fell from a median of 40% to 3% (PMID:35058326). That shows tissue exposure and target depletion in the disease itself. A similar near-clearance was seen with atezolizumab in other solid tumors (PMID:35987165, NCT03637764). Exposure was likely adequate: the same 10 mg/kg dose works in myeloma (NCT02990338), and PK was assessed in the index trial. However, Tregs and PD-L1 were not consistently modulated, so the hypothesized immune pathway did not follow. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred, so tolerability did not cap the dose. CD38 depletion was achieved without clinical benefit, so the mechanism does not drive these tumors as tested. The engagement data were published after the trial started.

In the index trial (NCT03367819), isatuximab 10 mg/kg plus cemiplimab cut median CD38+ tumor-infiltrating immune cells in mCRPC/NSCLC biopsies from 40% to 3% (PMID:35058326). Target engagement and tissue exposure were therefore shown directly in this disease, at the dose approved in myeloma (NCT02990338). There were no DLTs, so the dose was not capped. The expected downstream effect did not follow: PD-L1 and Treg levels in the tumor microenvironment showed no consistent change. Clinical benefit was absent (ORR 4.2% mCRPC, 0% NSCLC), and the trial stopped at a Simon-stage interim. The same pattern appeared with atezolizumab in four other solid tumors (PMID:35987165, NCT03637764). CD38 depletion was achieved but does not drive anti-tumor immunity in these cancers, which supports F2. The in-disease engagement data were published after the index trial started.

The index episodic cluster headache trial missed its primary endpoint: weekly attacks fell by 4.0 on eptinezumab vs 4.6 on placebo (p=0.50, NCT04688775). Plasma exposure is characterized (PMID:32155317). CGRP engagement was never measured directly, but is inferred from migraine efficacy with the same systemic CGRP-ligand mechanism (NCT02559895, NCT02974153, NCT04418765). That inference may not carry over, because cluster headache may need different CGRP blockade, and no engagement was shown in cluster headache patients. Galcanezumab, which binds the same target, is FDA-approved for cluster headache, so the target is validated there. This favors a molecule- or regimen-specific failure (F1b) over target irrelevance (F2). The large placebo response suggests a design issue (F7). The bundle states no reason, so confidence is low.

The sponsor terminated NCT03810313 for excess intraocular inflammation, retinal vasculitis and retinal vascular occlusion with q4w dosing beyond the loading doses. The sister BRVO trial NCT03802630 was stopped for the same reason despite meeting non-inferiority. PMID:36724241 attributes these events to molecule-specific immunogenicity (scFv format, bacterial-shared epitope, ADA immune complexes), which is off-target and not VEGF-mediated. Efficacy-wise, brolucizumab only narrowly missed non-inferiority versus aflibercept (p=0.173), so this was not a failure of VEGF inhibition (F9). Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate from approvals and met endpoints in AMD and DME with the same intravitreal 6 mg dose. CSFT reduction in AMD (PMID:26906165) supports the pathway pillar.

At 5 mg/kg, the dose used in the index trial, crizanlizumab reached expected serum levels and gave near-complete, sustained P-selectin inhibition in SCD patients (NCT03264989, registered 2017; PMID:36355805, PMID:39497751). These were SCD patients with VOC, not men with priapism specifically. Pathway is inferred_adequate: the same dose met a VOC endpoint in SCD (NCT01895361, PMID:27959701). Dose was not tolerability-limited. The index trial was single-arm with only 36 patients. It showed a median -61.3% change in priapic events but missed significance (p=0.0676), and case reports also describe benefit (PMID:37731262). This looks more like an underpowered, uncontrolled design than proof the mechanism is irrelevant. F2 is possible, but the sources do not explicitly attribute the miss.

The index neoadjuvant umbrella trial NCT04586244 was terminated for a stated 'Business Decision', with no safety concerns. Its primary endpoint was an exploratory biomarker (intratumoral CD8+ change). In the retifanlimab arm this rose by 0.79 log2 fold, p=0.09, but with only n=6, so the trial could not answer the question. No pillar was measured directly in urothelial carcinoma. All three are inferred adequate because retifanlimab at the same 500 mg Q4W dose met efficacy endpoints through PD-1: anal SCC PFS (NCT04472429), Merkel cell ORR (NCT03599713) and NSCLC OS (NCT04205812). It also gave a 37.9% ORR in UC (PMID:38401247). No MTD was reached (PMID:38387109). The stop was a portfolio decision, not an efficacy failure.

Inebilizumab 4 mg/kg plus bendamustine gave an ORR of 63.9% versus 59.7% for rituximab plus bendamustine (p=0.45) in R/R CLL (NCT01466153). The drug was active but not superior to an active anti-B-cell comparator. Exposure was dose-proportional in B-cell malignancies (PMID:30915717). CD19 engagement was measured directly as complete or dose-dependent B-cell depletion in MS and SSc (PMID:29143550, PMID:27267753), though not in CLL patients and only published after the index trial started. Pathway is inferred_adequate from NMOSD efficacy through B-cell depletion (NCT02200770, PMID:35332558). Engaged CD19 depletion added nothing over CD20 depletion in CLL. Caveats: the index doses sat below the 12 mg/kg optimal biologic dose (NCT00983619), and CLL engagement was unmeasured, so confidence is low.

Inebilizumab plus ICE/DHAP gave the same ORR as rituximab plus ICE/DHAP in relapsed/refractory DLBCL (46.2% and 43.6% vs 47.5%, p=0.55; NCT01453205). The trial tested superiority over an active anti-CD20 antibody. Exposure was dose-proportional in B-cell lymphoma, with an MTD of 8 mg/kg, above the 2–4 mg/kg used, so the dose was not tolerability-capped (PMID:30915717). Engagement was strong: complete B-cell depletion in MS (PMID:29143550) and dose-dependent depletion in systemic sclerosis (PMID:27267753), which was registered before the index trial (NCT00946699). The drug also met its endpoint in NMOSD (NCT02200770). Engagement of tumour B cells in DLBCL was never measured, so this rests on peripheral depletion in other diseases. CD19 depletion simply added nothing over rituximab here.

In the phase 1 solid-tumour study (PMID:20371689), R1507 showed slow clearance, no DLTs, and a dose-proportional rise in serum IGF-1, a PD marker of IGF1R blockade. 9 mg/kg weekly was recommended. Engagement is inferred adequate from TED efficacy at comparable doses (NCT01868997, NCT03461211). No tumour-level occupancy was measured, and no data come from NSCLC patients. Both doses taken into the index trial (9 and 16 mg/kg) gave 12-week PFS similar to placebo (16/57 and 21/57 vs 18/57, NCT00760929). No other IGF1R agent in the bundle succeeded in NSCLC. This points to IGF1R blockade plus erlotinib not driving benefit in unselected non-squamous NSCLC. The termination was labelled a business decision, but the readout itself was negative.

The phase 1 healthy-volunteer study (press release, 2014, before the index trial) reported that both IV and SC dosing gave a high, sustained degree of lectin pathway inhibition for at least a week. That counts as adequate exposure and engagement, but only in healthy volunteers. No human evidence on renal or downstream pathway effects in IgAN was found. At the ARTEMIS-IGAN interim analysis, proteinuria fell 21.3% on narsoplimab vs 16.6% on placebo, and the trial was terminated (NCT03608033). Omeros blamed the miss on an unusually large placebo response, which points to trial execution (F7). Because engagement was confirmed systemically, a target that does not drive the disease (F2) remains possible. There was no tolerability limit on dose.

The index safety study (NCT02902809) was terminated because the asthma program stopped after the Phase 3 D2210C00008 readout. Serum exposure in asthma patients is documented (NCT00974675, NCT01592396), and 300 mg Q2W was chosen as near-maximal on FEV1 modelling (PMID:28758192). Engagement is inferred_adequate: the same 300 mg Q2W IL-13 neutralization met pivotal endpoints in atopic dermatitis (NCT03131648, NCT03160885), and the drug was approved there. No direct engagement data in asthma. The airway biomarker study missed its endpoint (NCT02449473). Phase 3 asthma trials found no exacerbation benefit, including the biomarker-positive subgroup (NCT02161757, NCT02194699), and no OCS-sparing effect (NCT02281357, PMID:30442714). This points to IL-13 alone not driving asthma as tested. F9 is secondary because the index trial was not itself an efficacy test.

Systemic exposure to tralokinumab was well characterised and dose-proportional (NCT00974675, NCT00638989). Tralokinumab 300 mg Q2W, the dose used in the UC trial, met its pivotal endpoints in atopic dermatitis (NCT03131648, NCT03160885, NCT03363854). That success implies IL-13 neutralisation and downstream effect, so engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate. This inference crosses tissue compartments (skin to gut), which lowers confidence. IL-13 engagement was never measured in UC patients. Despite this, the primary endpoint was clearly missed (37.5% vs 32.7%, p=0.41), and disease markers showed no consistent change (PMID:25304132). This points to IL-13 not driving UC as tested (F2). The authors also suggest some patients may benefit, citing a higher remission rate (F3).

Systemic exposure is dose-proportional with a long half-life in humans (NCT00974675, PMID:29622380). The bundle shows no direct IL-13 engagement in IPF. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because tralokinumab met pivotal endpoints in atopic dermatitis by neutralizing IL-13 (NCT03131648, NCT03160885, NCT03363854) at 300 mg SC Q2W, a lower exposure than the IPF doses of 400/800 mg IV Q4W. The tissue differs (skin vs lung), which is a caveat. In asthma, lung FEV1 showed a dose-response (PMID:22743678, PMID:28758192). The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. FVC was numerically worse on drug, and periostin-defined subgroups also showed no benefit (PMID:28787186), arguing against a selection explanation. IL-13 neutralization appears not to drive IPF progression as tested.

Plasma exposure at 15 mg/kg IV Q4W is well characterized (PMID:34585515, PMID:40095399). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same dose and the same plasma ANGPTL3 target met LDL-C endpoints in HoFH (NCT03399786, NCT02265952; approval 2021). Pathway: dose-dependent TG lowering was shown in hypertriglyceridemic subjects (PMID:31242752, PMID:33130482). In the index trial, cohort 3 TG fell 37% vs a 19% rise on placebo, but only 5 patients received placebo and variance was huge. The CI spanned zero, and the authors call for larger trials (PMID:36879129). This points to an underpowered trial rather than a disproven mechanism. Responses also differed by genotype: they were limited in LPL-deficient FCS and marked in multifactorial disease (PMID:42742892), supporting subtype heterogeneity.

The index OLE (NCT05918978) was terminated because its parent RCT (NCT05633407) in post-COVID POTS showed no benefit: COMPASS-31 change was -14.4 with efgartigimod vs -16.0 with placebo. FcRn blockade by efgartigimod is well shown in humans at comparable dosing. Total IgG fell about 62-66% (NCT04735432), with rapid IgG and autoantibody lowering in gMG (PMID:31118245), and the drug met efficacy endpoints in gMG and CIDP (NCT03669588, NCT04281472). There was no tolerability cap. IgG lowering was not reported in the POTS patients themselves. Even so, an engaged mechanism that produced no clinical effect implies that IgG-mediated autoimmunity does not drive post-COVID POTS as tested. The index trial itself was a safety extension, not an efficacy test (F9 secondary).

The index trial NCT05810961 in PLA2R+ membranous nephropathy enrolled only 8 patients and was terminated for an unspecified 'sponsor decision' with no posted results. No efficacy readout exists, so it could not answer the question. FcRn engagement and its pathway effect were shown in humans before the index trial. In gMG, 10 mg/kg IV produced rapid total IgG and anti-AChR autoantibody reductions (PMID:31118245), and SC and IV doses lowered total IgG by about 62-66% (NCT04735432). The drug also met efficacy endpoints in gMG and CIDP (NCT03669588, NCT04281472). No engagement data exist in membranous nephropathy itself. Neither a business reason nor an efficacy failure is documented, so a commercial or strategic stop (F8) is possible but unconfirmed.

The index trial is an open-label extension stopped because the pivotal ADDRESS trial (NCT04598451) failed. Remission on minimal prednisone was 35% vs 30% for placebo. FcRn engagement is shown in humans: total IgG fell about 62-66% with SC and IV dosing (NCT04735432), and IgG and anti-AChR autoantibodies dropped rapidly (PMID:31118245, published 2019, before the index trial). Clinical success through the same systemic IgG-lowering mechanism in gMG and CIDP (NCT03669588, NCT04281472) supports adequacy. The bundle shows no pemphigus-specific PD data; NCT03334058 reported safety only. No tolerability cap was reported. With engagement adequate and no benefit, IgG lowering via FcRn did not drive benefit as tested. The 30% placebo remission rate on background steroids may also have limited the trial's ability to show a difference.

The index trial NCT03657043 used dose-dense tisotumab vedotin (0.9–1.2 mg/kg on days 1, 8, 15 of each 28-day cycle) in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer and got a confirmed ORR of about 9% (7/79). The bundle has no direct human tissue factor occupancy or payload-delivery data. However, the same anti-tissue-factor MMAE ADC met efficacy endpoints in cervical cancer (NCT03438396 ORR 23.8%; NCT04697628 OS HR 0.70) at a comparable or lower cumulative dose (2.0 mg/kg Q3W, PMID:30745090). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. DLTs were minimal (1/8), so the dose was not capped. Patients were not selected for tissue factor expression, so disease heterogeneity may also have contributed (F3). Overall, the tissue factor–directed mechanism did not produce meaningful benefit in ovarian cancer.

The index HCC trial (NCT05653427) used the approved recommended phase 2 dose (1050/1400 mg) and was stopped for futility with ORR 0% (n=18). PMID:37776107 reports that at this dose PK was linear, no MTD was reached, 87% of patients exceeded the target exposure threshold, and soluble EGFR and MET were depleted. That supports adequate exposure and engagement in humans and shows the dose was not tolerability-capped. Downstream pathway activity is inferred from clinical efficacy and approval in NSCLC. Engagement was shown only in NSCLC, not HCC, and was published (2024) after the index trial started (December 2022). No other EGFR/MET drug is shown succeeding in HCC itself. Dual EGFR/MET blockade appears not to drive HCC. Confidence is medium because engagement was never measured in HCC.

At the 2.7 mg/kg weekly dose used in the index trial, the drug showed measurable plasma exposure (AUC) in a phase 1 study. It also kept plasma arginine at the lower limit of quantification, with sustained 'therapeutic arginine depletion', and had no dose-limiting toxicities (PMID:34287772). Arginine lowering is confirmed in the ARG1-D trials (NCT03921541, PMID:42404437). In HCC patients, arginine depletion was measured, and its duration correlated with OS (PMID:33856599). However, these reports were published after the index trial started in 2014. Despite well-tolerated, adequate substrate depletion, median TTP was only 6 weeks, with a 21.7% disease control rate. Arginine depletion therefore did not control unselected HCC (F2). The OS advantage in the ASS-negative subgroup points to heterogeneity and patient selection (F3).

The index trial NCT02732184 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study in AML/MDS. Its primary endpoints were MTD/RP2D, it posted no results, and it gave no stop reason, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Systemic exposure and target engagement (plasma arginine depletion) were shown in humans elsewhere: in ARG1-D, a superiority Phase 3 on plasma arginine (NCT03921541, NCT06582524, PMID:42404437), and in solid tumors at 1.7–2.7 mg/kg/week with no DLTs (PMID:34287772). All of this was published after the index trial started, and none was in MDS patients. No downstream or clinical effect in MDS is shown. The bundle contains no evidence of an efficacy failure, so F9 applies, with low confidence.

Linear systemic PK was shown in AD patients (PMID:30779339, NCT00757042). No TSLP neutralization or skin biomarker was measured in AD. Engagement and pathway are inferred from the same antibody meeting pivotal endpoints in asthma and CRSwNP (NCT02054130, NCT03347279, NCT04851964), where it lowered eosinophils and FeNO (NCT03688074, PMID:33368307). Those effects came at 210 mg Q4W, about 90% of maximal effect. The AD trial tested up to 420 mg Q2W without tolerability limits.
