Even so, IGA and EASI75 were flat across all doses (NCT03809663), and an earlier Phase 2a also missed (NCT02525094). This points to TSLP blockade not driving AD as monotherapy. The skin compartment differs from airway, so the inference is imperfect (U secondary). No anti-TSLP drug has succeeded in AD.

In NCT04833855 tezepelumab 210 mg Q4W and 420 mg Q2W showed no UAS7 effect versus placebo (p=0.99, 0.60). The omalizumab arm separated, so the trial could detect benefit. Linear plasma PK is documented (PMID:30779339). TSLP binding was never measured directly. Engagement is inferred adequate because the same systemic dose met endpoints in asthma and CRSwNP (NCT02054130, NCT03347279, NCT04851964). The PK-PD model put 210 mg Q4W at about 90% of maximal effect (PMID:33368307). The index tested up to four times that dose. Pathway markers moved as expected: blood and airway eosinophils, FeNO and IgE (NCT03688074, PMID:35707873, PMID:42409576). No engagement data exist in CSU skin, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Blocking TSLP appears not to drive CSU.

The index trial NCT03310619 was a descriptive phase 1/2 study of CAR-T (JCAR017) combinations. Its primary outcomes were DLTs and complete response rate, with no success threshold. Only 2 patients received relatlimab and/or nivolumab, so it was not an efficacy test of relatlimab (F9); the tiny arm also could not answer the question (F7). All pillars are inferred_adequate: relatlimab met PFS in melanoma via LAG-3 at comparable doses (PMID:37921680). No pillar was measured in DLBCL. In DLBCL, nivolumab plus relatlimab gave 7% ORR with no CRs and no DLTs (NCT02061761, PMID:40030000). That suggests LAG-3/PD-1 blockade does not drive benefit in this disease (F2 secondary).

Plasma exposure was well characterised in healthy volunteers, with linear kinetics at ≥0.3 mg/kg and IV doses up to 1200 mg well tolerated (PMID:36451029, NCT02852824). Engagement was never measured in atopic eczema. It is inferred adequate because spesolimab met its primary endpoint in GPP, a skin disease, through the same IL-36R target at comparable IV dosing (NCT03782792; NCT04399837). It also suppressed IL-36 pathway signatures in GPP skin (PMID:34678325). The index trial at 600 mg IV q4w did not separate from placebo on EASI percent change (-25.6, p=0.149) (NCT03822832). No tolerability cap was seen. IL-36R blockade appears not to drive atopic eczema as tested (F2). The small randomized sample (12 placebo vs 28 analyzed) and wide CI leave some underpowering concern (F7).

Engagement is supported. Sponsor protocols report more than 99% peripheral IL-36R occupancy at doses of at least 1 mg/kg in healthy volunteers, measured with an ex vivo IL-36γ whole-blood assay (≥94% MIP-1β inhibition). The index trial gave 1200 mg IV every 4 weeks, far above that threshold, and was well tolerated (PMID:36451029). Pathway effects are shown in GPP skin (PMID:34678325), and the drug met efficacy endpoints in GPP (NCT03782792). This was measured in blood and skin, not in Crohn's patients or gut tissue, so gut-level engagement is assumed rather than shown. In the index trial, gut biopsy gene deregulation was 0 vs 0 and no fistula benefit was seen. Spesolimab also failed in UC. This points to IL-36R not driving fistulizing CD. The trial was small (n=27), and BI ended the CD program as a portfolio decision (NCT04362254).

Phase 1 PK showed linear, saturating plasma exposure with IV doses up to 1200 mg well tolerated (PMID:36451029). IL-36R engagement was not measured in UC. It is inferred adequate because spesolimab met pivotal endpoints in GPP through the same target (NCT03782792, NCT04399837), and IL-36 pathway signatures fell in GPP skin (PMID:34678325). This inference assumes a systemic IgG1 reaches comparable peripheral tissue, so it is weaker for gut than for skin. UC doses (up to 1200 mg IV q4w) met or exceeded the GPP doses, with no tolerability cap (PMID:35861588). Remission was flat at all doses (NCT03482635), and add-on endoscopic improvement was not better than placebo (NCT03123120). This points to IL-36R not driving UC as tested.

Healthy-volunteer PK showed saturation of target-mediated disposition and linear kinetics at doses of 0.3 mg/kg or more (PMID:36451029), so the 300/900 mg IV doses gave adequate exposure. No PPP engagement data exist. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate: spesolimab met endpoints in GPP through IL-36R in skin (NCT03782792, NCT04399837). In GPP skin it also downregulated IL-36 pathway transcripts (PMID:34678325). No dose limit; tolerability was clean. The index trial (PMID:33661508) failed, and a larger Phase IIb also missed its primary endpoint (NCT04015518, PMID:37731086). This argues that IL-36R is not a strong enough driver in PPP. Authors also cite small sample size, low baseline severity and natural resolution (F7), and benefit confined to non-Asian patients (F3).

The index trial NCT02718911 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of the anti-CSF1R antibody LY3022855 combined with durvalumab or tremelimumab in mixed solid tumors. Its only primary endpoint was the MTD/RP2D of LY3022855, which was reported (100 mg). It was not an efficacy test of tremelimumab in cervical cancer, so the code is F9. Exposure is adequate: the HCC PK analysis shows Cmin above the EC50 for CD8+Ki67+ expansion (PMID:36477555). CTLA4 engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because tremelimumab is FDA-approved in HCC and NSCLC through systemic CTLA4 blockade. Pathway is adequate: ICOS+ T-cell increases, TCR repertoire broadening and CD8 proliferation were shown (PMID:20479064, PMID:24583799, PMID:34292792). Durable responses in a separate cervical cancer study (PMID:39773562) also argue against an efficacy failure.

The index MDS phase 1 trial (NCT02117219) tested durvalumab with tremelimumab, with or without azacitidine, in HMA-failed MDS. It was terminated early for limited efficacy: marrow CR 15%, with tolerable DLT rates (PMID:40153010). Exposure was adequate: tremelimumab PK in HCC put Cmin above the EC50 for CD8+Ki67+ expansion (PMID:36477555). CTLA4 engagement was never measured directly, so it is inferred_adequate from the HCC and NSCLC approvals, which act on the same systemic T-cell target. Pathway effects were shown in humans in other diseases: ICOS+ T-cell rise, TCR repertoire broadening and CD8 proliferation (PMID:20479064, PMID:24583799, PMID:33428583). No engagement data come from MDS, and tolerability did not cap the dose. The mechanism was engaged but gave no meaningful benefit in MDS.

In the index phase 1b trial (NCT02549651), durvalumab plus tremelimumab 1 mg/kg was well tolerated in R/R DLBCL. The safety primary endpoint was met, but antitumor activity was limited (ORR 6.3%, median PFS 7.4 weeks; PMID:33632668). CTLA-4 engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because tremelimumab is approved in HCC and NSCLC at comparable systemic doses through the same peripheral T-cell mechanism. Pathway effects are shown in humans in other cancers: ICOS+ T-cell rise, TCR diversification, and dose-related CD8+Ki67+ expansion (PMID:20479064, PMID:24583799, PMID:36477555, PMID:33428583). No dose limitation appears. With the mechanism engaged, the lack of benefit points to CTLA-4 blockade not driving DLBCL. F9 is secondary because the trial was a safety study that met its primary endpoint.

Rozanolixizumab showed sustained, dose-dependent serum IgG lowering in healthy volunteers (PMID:29093180, PMID:39569616) and in ITP patients (PMID:32886753), all published before the index trial. It met its Phase 3 endpoint in gMG (NCT03971422), so systemic FcRn blockade at comparable doses is clinically active. No IgG data from fibromyalgia patients appear in the bundle. In NCT05643794 (560 mg weekly), BPI-SF interference improved only modestly (-0.54, two-sided p=0.129). The paper says this met a lenient pre-specified one-sided 10% alpha (PMID:42748952), yet the program stopped. With engagement adequate, the most likely reading is that IgG-mediated autoimmunity does not meaningfully drive fibromyalgia symptoms. The small proof-of-concept size and the borderline 'met' result keep F9 and F7 as secondary codes.

Rozanolixizumab produced sustained, dose-dependent serum IgG lowering in healthy volunteers (PMID:29093180, published 2017, before the index trial; PMID:39569616). It also lowered IgG with platelet responses in ITP patients (PMID:32886753). The 7–10 mg/kg dose met the gMG phase 3 endpoint (NCT03971422), so systemic FcRn engagement and the IgG-lowering pathway were adequate at the 10 mg/kg weekly CIDP dose. No IgG data from CIDP patients appear in the bundle. The index trial (NCT03861481) showed no iRODS difference, and the authors attribute this possibly to a high placebo stability rate in a small study (n=34) (PMID:38729747). Efgartigimod's CIDP approval argues against the target being irrelevant, so F7 is primary and F2 secondary.

In asthma patients, lebrikizumab clearly engaged the IL-13 pathway. LAVOLTA I/II showed significant serum periostin, CCL13, CCL17 and IgE reductions (PMID:39781908), and CLAVIER showed falls in FeNO, bronchial CCL26 and SERPINB2 with reduced subepithelial fibrosis (PMID:32909660). Both reports were published after the index trial began. Tolerability did not cap the dose. LAVOLTA II narrowly missed (RR 0.74, p≈0.06), while its replicate LAVOLTA I met (PMID:27616196). Benefit concentrated in periostin-high patients (PMID:26001563). A post hoc reanalysis explicitly attributes the failure to patient selection, showing significant benefit in patients with eosinophils ≥300 and prior exacerbations (PMID:38360213). The modest effect despite full engagement also supports F2. The adolescent trial was terminated by sponsor decision (NCT01875003).

The COPD index trial (NCT02546700) showed no FEV1 benefit in either biomarker-high or biomarker-low patients, and the drug was well tolerated. The bundle has no engagement data in COPD. Engagement is inferred adequate because lebrikizumab met lung-function and exacerbation endpoints in asthma through IL-13 in the same airway compartment at subcutaneous doses of 37.5–250 mg (NCT00930163, NCT01867125/PMID:27616196). The bundle does not give the COPD trial's dose, so dose comparability is assumed, not shown. CLAVIER (PMID:32909660) showed lower FeNO, CCL26 and SERPINB2 in bronchial tissue, so the pathway effect held in asthma airways. In IPF, pharmacodynamic activity was shown without lung benefit (PMID:33008934). Taken together, IL-13 blockade does not appear to drive FEV1 in COPD.

In IPF, lebrikizumab 250 mg SC Q4W alone or with pirfenidone did not slow FVC decline (p=0.456 and p=0.557; NCT01872689). The IPF publication reports that pharmacodynamic biomarkers showed lebrikizumab activity in these patients and concludes IL-13 blockade may not be sufficient for a lung function benefit (PMID:33008934). So engagement and pathway effects were shown in the disease, but only in that 2021 report, after the index trial began. Exposure is inferred adequate: comparable doses improved FEV1 in asthma (NCT00930163, PMID:26001563) and lowered bronchial IL-13 markers (PMID:32909660), and the drug is approved in atopic dermatitis (NCT04146363). Tolerability did not cap the dose. The target does not drive IPF as tested.

The index trial NCT03853317 was terminated for 'not meeting recruitment goal' after enrolling only 9 patients, so it could not properly answer the question (F7). The objective response rate was 0% in checkpoint-refractory Merkel cell carcinoma, and the triplet design muddies attribution to N-803. The pillars are shown in humans. Subcutaneous PK gives prolonged serum exposure (NCT03381586, PMID:29463563). Doses of 6–20 µg/kg produced significant NK and CD8+ T-cell expansion and activation (PMID:30045932, PMID:29463563), published before 2020. No dose-limiting tolerability ceiling was seen (NCT01946789). Engagement was not shown in MCC patients themselves. The earlier MCC trial NCT02465957 was also small and terminated. Given adequate engagement and no responses, F2 is a secondary possibility.

In the index COVID-19 Phase 2 trial (NCT04409509), a single 700 mg IV dose of garadacimab produced no benefit on intubation or death: 22.2% vs 26.2% on placebo (p=0.274), with 11 deaths per arm. In the same patients, PMID:37000214 reports prolonged aPTT and FXIIa-mediated kallikrein activity suppressed to Day 28, stating this showed target engagement. So exposure, engagement and pathway were all shown in the program's disease. Phase 1 data (PMID:34859955, PMID:34811931) showed dose-dependent PK and FXIIa inhibition, but those results were published in 2022, after the index trial began. Tolerability did not limit the dose. With FXIIa inhibited in patients and no clinical benefit, the evidence points to the mechanism not driving severe COVID-19 outcomes.

The index trial LIBerate-HoFH (NCT04034485, PMID:39870096) was an open-label crossover non-inferiority comparison of lerodalcibep with the active drug evolocumab. It missed only the prespecified 6% non-inferiority margin (mean difference 5.4%, 95% CI -0.2 to 11.1). Both drugs were well tolerated. This is not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure, so the code is F9. The pillars are inferred_adequate: in HeFH, lerodalcibep met its LDL-C endpoint against placebo (NCT04797104; LS mean difference -60.5%, p<0.0001) through the same target and plasma compartment at a comparable monthly dose. No direct PCSK9 binding data in HoFH are in the bundle. The HeFH evidence came after the index trial started. Development continues (China trials).

In the index RA trial (NCT04991753), nipocalimab 15 mg/kg Q2W significantly and reversibly reduced serum IgG, ACPA and circulating immune complexes (PMID:38942592), with IgG reductions of about 60–65% (PMID:42084498). This shows exposure, FcRn engagement and the downstream pathway effect in RA patients themselves. These data were published after the index trial started. Even so, DAS28-CRP did not differ significantly from placebo (p=0.224) and CRP was unchanged. A higher 30 mg/kg dose added to certolizumab also gave no benefit (NCT06028438, PMID:41781163). Lowering IgG and autoantibodies therefore does not drive RA activity as tested. Secondary codes: greater benefit in patients with high baseline ACPA (F3), and a small trial of 53 patients with a numerical trend (F7). Dose was not limited by tolerability.

The index trial NCT02806960 was a Phase 1 PK/PD study of nasal glucagon. It was terminated because the device partially clogged with aggregated particles and delivered less than the target dose. It was not an efficacy test of glucagon, so this is F9, with an operational/device secondary (F7). Exposure is adequate: the near-identical successor study NCT02806973 posted clear plasma glucagon Cmax/AUC in diabetic patients. GCGR engagement is inferred_adequate: glucagon is approved for hypoglycemia, and nasal glucagon met rescue endpoints in T1D (NCT01994746, NCT03339453). Pathway is adequate because glucose rose after dosing (NCT03091673, NCT01556594). Tolerability did not cap the dose; the shortfall came from device delivery.

NTCP engagement is shown in humans. High-dose bulevirtide raised total bile acids 35-fold in healthy volunteers (PMID:37089922), and later editorials describe bile acid rise as its pharmacodynamic signature (PMID:42092232). Neither source involves HBV-monoinfected patients, and both postdate the 2012 index start. Exposure and pathway (blockade of viral entry into hepatocytes) are inferred adequate: the same target and compartment produced HDV RNA responses at 2–10 mg (NCT03852719, NCT03546621). Despite this, HBsAg response at week 12 was essentially absent in all arms of NCT02881008, with tolerability acceptable. So the entry-inhibition mechanism did not deliver the HBsAg endpoint in HBV. The short 12-week duration and HBsAg endpoint may also be implicated (F4), though no source states this.

Atacicept is a systemic BAFF/APRIL decoy. Human PK/PD at comparable doses (25–150 mg weekly SC) showed serum exposure and BAFF–atacicept complex formation (PMID:36532058). It produced dose-dependent IgM/IgG/IgA and B-cell reductions in healthy volunteers, RA and SLE (PMID:17473917, PMID:18303125, PMID:18163485, PMID:19395457), mostly published before the April 2008 start, so engagement and pathway were adequate. None of this was shown in MS patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. ATAMS was stopped because relapse/MS activity increased on atacicept versus placebo (NCT00642902, PMID:24613349), which also halted ATON and the extension (PMID:25758472). The sources attribute this to the mechanism, not to failure to engage (PMID:21179612, PMID:25505277): BAFF/APRIL blockade does not benefit, and appears to worsen, MS. That fits F2, with on-target harm (F5) as a secondary code.

Atacicept reached systemic exposure and engaged its ligands in humans. BAFF–atacicept complexes accumulated (PMID:17473917, PMID:18303125, PMID:36532058). The expected pathway effect followed: dose-dependent Ig and B-cell reductions in healthy volunteers, RA, SLE and IgAN (PMID:18163485, PMID:35967104, PMID:27390168), all published or registered before ATAMS began. No MS-specific engagement data are in the bundle. ATAMS (NCT00642902) was stopped because the IDMC saw increased MS disease activity on atacicept versus placebo, although mean Gd-enhancing lesion counts were numerically lower. Related MS and optic neuritis trials were terminated for the same reason (NCT00853762, NCT00624468). This points to a mechanism-driven worsening of disease (possible loss of APRIL-driven regulatory B cells, PMID:27372914) rather than inadequate engagement. The target, as modulated, does not benefit relapsing MS.

In NCT04532931, a small open-label exploratory Phase 2 trial of about 37 patients per arm, artesunate-amodiaquine did not improve Day-7 SARS-CoV-2 clearance over standard of care (38.5% vs 34.2%). The bundle records no target for this repurposed drug. Its anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity is shown only in vitro or in silico, with proposed targets including PLpro, Mpro, RdRp and host-directed effects (PMID:32545799, 33330842, 36453012). Human PK covers plasma levels at malaria doses (PMID:3814460, 18415093). No source shows respiratory-tissue levels reaching antiviral concentrations, target engagement or a viral biomarker effect in humans, and none states why the program stopped. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The underpowered open-label design (F7) is a secondary factor.

Nobelpharma dropped NPC-06 because the Phase 3 trial (NCT05480553, n=51) showed no significant difference from placebo. Exposure is adequate: in the earlier Phase 2 trial in herpes zoster patients (NCT04139330, PMID:38149403), IV doses of 12–18 mg/kg gave plasma phenytoin levels of 10–15 μg/mL, the range linked to pain response. Engagement was never measured directly. I rated it inferred_adequate because phenytoin works in epilepsy through the same sodium channels at these plasma levels, but that is the central nervous system rather than the peripheral nerves involved in zoster pain, so the inference is weak. No pathway biomarker was measured. Assuming the channels were engaged, the failure points to F2. However, the Phase 2 signal came from only 16 patients and that trial was cut short by COVID-19, and the Phase 3 trial was small, so trial size or noise (F7) is a real possibility.

The index trial NCT03512756 tested SM-88, a regimen built on racemetyrosine. It was given with low-dose methoxsalen, phenytoin 50 mg daily and sirolimus. Here phenytoin served as a CYP3A4 inducer, not as a sodium channel (SCN1A/2A/3A/8A) blocker. The trial therefore did not test phenytoin's own mechanism in pancreatic cancer. Survival in the SM-88 arm was worse than in the control arm (14.0 vs 24.1 weeks), but that failure belongs to the combination. The bundle has no human data on phenytoin reaching or blocking sodium channels in pancreatic tumours. The stop was described only as the sponsor's decision. I chose F9 because this was not an efficacy test of phenytoin's targets. U is a secondary code because engagement has no human data.

Tenofovir acts on the HBV reverse transcriptase. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because tenofovir met a virologic endpoint in chronic hepatitis B (NCT01063036): same target, liver compartment and comparable dose (TDF 300 mg). In HDV-coinfected patients, tenofovir-containing ART markedly lowered HBV DNA, but HBsAg stayed elevated (PMID:24599769). That evidence was published after the index trial started. In HIDIT-II (NCT01088659, PMID:30833068), adding TDF to peginterferon gave 48% vs 33% HDV RNA negativity (p=0.12). Suppressing HBV replication does not control HDV, which depends on HBsAg rather than the HBV polymerase. The trial's small size (about 60 patients per arm) may also have limited power.

The index trial NCT01230970 was an exploratory pharmacodynamic window study, with intratumoural hormones and STS activity as endpoints. It was not an efficacy test in breast cancer. It enrolled 2 patients and was terminated because the endometrial cancer trial NCT00910091 failed futility (PFS6 36% vs 54% for megestrol). In ER+ breast cancer patients, exposure was characterised (PMID:25355461) and doses of 5 mg and above gave at least 95% STS inhibition in PBMCs with endocrine suppression, without reaching an MTD (PMID:23797179, published 2013, after the index start). Ki67 and FLT uptake fell (PMID:28795252), and IRIS met its success criterion (PMID:28612226). The breast program was halted by a sponsor decision driven by failure in another disease, with engaged-target non-benefit (F2) shown there.

This doesn't look like an efficacy failure. The index trial, NCT00790374, was a small (n=17) Phase 1 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoint was the change in hormone levels, not clinical benefit. Its results appeared in a 2011 EJC poster (Denmeade et al., found via ResearchGate); this summary comes from Wikipedia's secondary account of it. In men with castration-resistant prostate cancer, irosustat was safe, nearly fully inhibited STS (its target) at three doses, and clearly lowered hormone levels in every patient. So the drug reached its target, engaged it and moved the downstream pathway in this disease. Engagement was shown during this trial, not before it began. No prostate efficacy trial followed. Sponsor trials elsewhere were stopped after the endometrial futility analysis (NCT00910091, NCT01251354, NCT01230970), which points to a portfolio decision rather than a prostate readout failure (low-confidence F8).

A Phase 1 study published in 2006 (Stanway, Clin Cancer Res) treated postmenopausal breast cancer patients with irosustat (STX64). It inhibited STS by a median of 98% in blood lymphocytes and 99% in tumor tissue, even at 5 mg/day. Serum estrone, estradiol, DHEA and androstenediol fell, which is the downstream effect the mechanism predicts. That dose is lower than the 40 mg/day used in endometrial cancer, so exposure, engagement and pathway all count as adequate. These data predate the index trial. Even so, in NCT00910091 (PMID:27870712) irosustat was numerically worse than megestrol acetate: 36.1% vs 54.1% free of progression at 6 months. The investigators concluded it was not active enough to develop further. The index trial NCT01251354 was stopped on that futility result. So STS inhibition alone did not control this disease (F2). Engagement was never measured in endometrial cancer patients.

Sanofi stopped the index trial, NCT00602680, after enrolling 1 patient, citing 'insufficient expected benefit risk'. It posted no results. No other trials or Phase 1 results for this drug are in the bundle. All target-engagement evidence for SSR180711 comes from animals: monkey PET blocking (PMID:18800169) and rodent α7 occupancy (PMID:22108649). Neither counts as human evidence. My searches found no human PK, brain-penetration, receptor-occupancy or biomarker data, and no sponsor explanation beyond the stop reason. No other α7 agonist has succeeded in Alzheimer disease, so F1b does not apply. Because human engagement data are absent, U is the answer. With only 1 patient enrolled, the trial was effectively never run (F7), so it could not test efficacy.

The extension NCT00982150 was stopped because its core trial, ALSTAR (NCT00696332), missed its primary functional endpoint in May 2010. Teva gave little detail about the data. In humans, talampanel was measured in plasma (PMID:12581229, PMID:19961264). It also caused more dizziness and somnolence than placebo, which suggests it acted in the brain, so exposure is classed as inferred_adequate. No source shows human AMPA receptor occupancy or a downstream biomarker change. The healthy-volunteer TMS/EEG study (NCT00057460) posted no results that I could find. Tolerability did not cap the 50 mg t.i.d. dose. No other AMPA antagonist has succeeded in ALS. Because engagement is unknown, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT04446377) missed its day-4 viral load endpoint (−0.47 log10, p=0.35). In C9orf72 ALS patients, apilimod 125 mg BID, the MTD from NCT02594384, gave measurable plasma and CSF drug and raised plasma sGPNMB >2.5-fold, a marker of PIKfyve inhibition (PMID:38606777, NCT05163886). That supports systemic exposure and engagement, though not in COVID-19 patients, only after the index trial started, and the index dose is not stated in the bundle. Pathway is rated inferred_adequate on the same sGPNMB evidence plus the 73% CSF poly(GP) fall in ALS, a disease-specific readout rather than an approved efficacy endpoint. No antiviral benefit followed; PIKfyve inhibition appears not to drive COVID-19 viral clearance in humans. A murine model also worsened (PMID:35962188, animal only). The small analyzed sample (n=78) is a possible limitation.

Plasma exposure was characterised in humans and was dose-proportional (PMID:27136906, PMID:23254770). Engagement was shown in healthy volunteers: pHSP27 fell up to 55% after 15 mg, with a direct PK/PD link (PMID:23215699). Engagement was also shown in FSHD blood and muscle (PMID:33931884). None of this was in atherosclerosis patients, and all was published after the 2008 start. In the index trial the high dose lowered hsCRP by 28% and reduced TBR in active segments (PMID:22974804), so the pathway moved. Yet index-vessel TBR was unchanged (NCT00633022). Later ACS trials, including the phase 3 MACE trial, also failed (NCT00910962, NCT02145468), and arterial TBR was unchanged in COPD (PMID:29566026). p38 inhibition does not appear to drive the disease as tested. The active-segment benefit supports F3/F4 as secondary codes.

Losmapimod reached dose-proportional plasma exposure in healthy volunteers and patients (PMID:27136906, PMID:23254770). Target engagement was shown in humans: pHSP27 fell 44-55% (PMID:23215699, 2013, before the index trial), and engagement was seen in blood and muscle (PMID:33931884). This is partial inhibition, but no source calls it insufficient. Pathway effect: at 7.5 mg BID, the index dose, hsCRP fell 28% and inflamed-segment FDG uptake fell in atherosclerosis patients (PMID:22974804). Engagement was never measured in ACS patients, and the Phase 2 ACS trial showed no hsCRP or troponin change (NCT00910962). The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not capped. In LATITUDE (NCT02145468), MACE was not reduced (HR 1.16), pointing to a target that does not drive outcomes after ACS.

The index COVID-19 Phase 3 (NCT04511819) was terminated after enrolling only 52 patients. The stated reasons were the rapidly evolving treatment landscape and difficulty enrolling, so the trial was too small to answer the efficacy question (p=0.88, wide CI). Exposure and engagement at the index dose (15 mg) were shown in humans before the trial: 15 mg oral reduced pHSP27 by 55% in healthy volunteers (PMID:23215699), and target engagement was seen in blood and muscle in FSHD (PMID:33931884). Pathway: hsCRP fell 28% in atherosclerosis patients (PMID:22974804). No engagement data exist in COVID-19 patients. Repeated failures across inflammatory diseases despite engagement suggest F2 as a secondary code. No dose limitation was seen.

In FSGS, losmapimod PK matched prior studies, so plasma exposure was shown (PMID:32775822). Target engagement at the index doses was shown only outside FSGS. A 15 mg oral dose cut pHSP27 by 55% in healthy volunteers (PMID:23215699, before the index trial). Blood and muscle engagement was seen in FSHD (PMID:33931884, PMID:38959779). Pathway markers moved: hsCRP fell 17% after one dose and 28% at 7.5 mg BID in atherosclerosis (PMID:22974804). Despite adequate exposure and engagement, 0/17 patients met the proteinuria response endpoint at the planned timepoints, and tolerability did not cap the dose. This points to p38 inhibition not driving proteinuria in FSGS (F2). The authors also suggest population heterogeneity may have contributed (F3). Kidney-tissue engagement was never measured.

The index neuropathic pain trial (NCT00969059) posted no results, and the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping. In humans, losmapimod reached dose-proportional plasma exposure without tolerability limits (PMID:27136906, 23215699). It engaged p38: pHSP27 fell 55% at 15 mg in blood (PMID:23215699), and engagement was shown in blood and muscle (PMID:33931884, 38959779). A downstream effect followed, with hsCRP reduced 17–28% (PMID:23215699, 22974804). Across many diseases the drug failed despite this engagement, consistent with p38 not driving the disease as tested (F2). Caveats: no engagement data in nerve or spinal tissue, none in neuropathic pain patients, and none published before 2009. The relevant compartment is therefore unproven, so U is a plausible alternative. Confidence is low.

Index trial NCT02292771 was stopped because it could not recruit in a timely manner. With only 97 women, it tested superiority of retosiban over atosiban, an active comparator on the same target, and found no difference in time to delivery (p=0.38). The underpowered, early-stopped sample cannot answer the efficacy question. The placebo-controlled Phase 3 (NCT02377466) ended when the asset was terminated for portfolio reasons ("Asset terminated by PIB"), with only 23 participants analysed. Plasma PK was measured in preterm-labour women (PMID:28556962). No receptor occupancy data exist. The uterine quiescence and contraction effects were non-significant trends only, so engagement and pathway are not established. The mechanism question therefore remains indeterminate (secondary U).

Balapiravir (R1626) is a prodrug of R1479, which inhibits the viral polymerase. In hepatitis C (PMID:18553458), it was converted efficiently to R1479 and lowered HCV RNA in a dose-dependent way. In the dengue trial (NCT01096576; JID 2013), plasma R1479 levels at 1500 and 3000 mg reached roughly the in vitro EC50, so exposure was adequate. Even so, viremia, NS1 antigenemia, cytokines and the blood transcriptional profile were unchanged, so the drug showed no antiviral effect against dengue in patients. In follow-up work (JVI 2014), the investigators traced the gap mainly to dengue-activated immune cells converting less of the drug into its active triphosphate form, which cut R1479 potency. That mechanism comes from cells in the lab, not from patients. The polymerase was therefore never adequately inhibited (F1a). Engagement was not measured directly, so U also applies.

In NCT03821415 (PMID:33710587), topical estradiol-3-phosphate eye drops (RP101) at 0.05–0.1% did not beat vehicle on Schirmer II. Schirmer scores rose in every arm, and the IntelliGel vehicle improved signs and symptoms by itself. That points to a vehicle-response or trial-design problem (F7, secondary). No source reports estradiol levels in tears, conjunctiva or lacrimal tissue, ocular estrogen-receptor engagement, or an estrogen-responsive marker in the eye. The approved uses are systemic or vaginal, a different tissue compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred from them. The only difference from vehicle was greater inferior corneal staining reduction at the top dose (p=0.046), and that is a clinical sign, not a pathway marker. Because engagement has no human data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

Index trial NCT01189812 (citalopram plus lithium vs placebo; depressive disorders including BPD) showed no difference in S-STS suicidality at week 4 (5.0 vs 4.8). No direct GSK3B or IMPA1 engagement data exist in humans. Lithium is FDA-approved for bipolar disorder, a CNS indication at standard serum levels (PMID:9618695 reports about 0.95 mEq/L), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Human plasma PK is documented (PMID:16927534), and a CSF-lithium study title (PMID:4801624) points to brain exposure. With engagement inferred, the null result suggests the mechanism does not reduce suicidality or depressive symptoms in this mixed population. Secondary F7: a small trial (40 per arm), a short 4-week window, and low baseline scores limited its ability to answer the question. No engagement data in BPD.

Index trial NCT01189812 added lithium to citalopram in a mixed population (MDD, dysthymia, depression NOS, borderline PD). It showed no difference in S-STS suicidality at week 4 (5.0 vs 4.8; n=40 per arm). The bundle has no human GSK3 or IMPase engagement measure in dysthymia. Engagement is inferred adequate because the bundle lists lithium as FDA-approved for bipolar disorder through the same CNS targets, and it met endpoints at low serum levels in MCI (PMID:30947755). Plasma and CSF exposure in humans is documented (PMID:12242603, PMID:4801624). With the mechanism presumed engaged and no benefit, F2 fits. The small, heterogeneous sample, short duration and low baseline suicidality scores also point to design limits (F7) and population heterogeneity (F3). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

Index trial NCT01189812 found no S-STS difference at week 4 (4.8 vs 5.0). No direct human GSK3 or IMPase engagement data are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate because lithium is listed as FDA-approved for bipolar disorder, the same CNS compartment, at standard doses. Human PK is well documented (PMID:12242603, PMID:16927534), and lithium changes CNS function in healthy volunteers (PMID:33127993). No dose limitation was reported, and serious AEs were equal (1/40 per arm). The failure is consistent with the mechanism not reducing suicidality in this population. PMID:34787653 and NCT00883493 also found no lithium benefit in depression-related settings. The trial was small (n=80), short (4 weeks) and diagnostically mixed, so F7 and F3 are possible. No source states the cause.

In NCT00883493, adding lithium to quetiapine XR gave essentially the same 8-week MADRS change as quetiapine alone (24.3 vs 23.7), with similar safety, so there was no tolerability cap. The bundle has no direct GSK3 or IMPase engagement data. Plasma and CSF lithium exposure is documented (PMID:12242603, PMID:4801624), and therapeutic serum levels occur in patients (PMID:9618695). Lithium is listed as FDA-approved for bipolar disorder, the same CNS target compartment at comparable doses. On that basis exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. The failure therefore reads as the mechanism adding no benefit as tested in acute bipolar depression on top of quetiapine. An add-on design against an active antipsychotic (possible ceiling effect) is a secondary consideration, though the sources do not state it.

The index Phase Ib expansion (NCT01171924) had only a safety primary endpoint (number of participants with AEs). It was not an efficacy test, and no efficacy failure is shown. Exposure was adequate: linear PK, Cmax 9.3 mg/L at the 275 mg/m2 MTD (PMID:25107918). HDAC engagement was shown by histone H3 acetylation in skin, PBMC and HNSCC tumor biopsies (PMID:25573383), but EGFR inhibition was only a trend. All of this was published after the index trial started. No downstream pathway readout appears in the bundle. A high rate of DLT-independent discontinuation suggested the IV schedule needed changing (PMID:25573383), and an oral formulation trial was terminated with no stated reason (NCT01702285). That hints at molecule- or formulation-specific tolerability problems, but the stop reason is unstated.

In NCT04347915, clevudine, a repurposed HBV polymerase inhibitor, missed its primary endpoint: the rate of patients testing negative for SARS-CoV-2. A second Phase 2 trial (NCT04891302, CLV-203, 150 mg) also missed its primary endpoint, and Bukwang dropped the COVID-19 program (KoreaBiomed). Human PK and pharmacodynamics exist only for HBV at 10–50 mg (PMID:18363895). I found no human data showing that clevudine reached, bound or inhibited a SARS-CoV-2 target, or moved a pathway biomarker at the COVID doses. The sponsor's report of a viral-load reduction in hypertensive patients is a post-hoc subgroup claim, so F3 is only secondary. With engagement unknown, the evidence cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage or the mechanism does not matter, so the code is U.

Quinidine in AVP-786 acts as a low-dose systemic (hepatic) CYP2D6 inhibitor that boosts deudextromethorphan exposure. No human PK or CYP2D6-inhibition data are in the bundle, but the same combination met clinical endpoints in Alzheimer's agitation: AVP-923 in NCT01584440 and AVP-786-18 in NCT02442765. That works through the same target and compartment at comparable doses, so exposure, engagement and the pathway effect (raised dextromethorphan levels) are inferred adequate. The index adjunctive MDD trial (NCT02153502) posted no results, and the bundle gives no stated reason. Open-label data (PMID:37683231) suggested only modest benefit. The mechanism was plausibly delivered but gave no benefit as tested. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin and has no index results.

Quinidine's role in AVP-786 is CYP2D6 inhibition to boost (deuterated) dextromethorphan. CYP2D6 engagement was not measured directly in the bundle. It is inferred adequate because the non-deuterated DM/quinidine combination (AVP-923) met its primary agitation endpoint in Alzheimer disease (NCT01584440) through the same mechanism. AVP-786 then missed CMAI at both doses (NCT02442778), with only mixed results in NCT02442765. PMID:40490784 notes that AXS-05, another CYP2D6-inhibitor/DM combination, also succeeded. It attributes AVP-786's failure to deuteration lowering dextromethorphan's NMDA potency, a molecule-specific problem rather than a failure of the target. F1b strictly requires engagement not adequate; inferred_adequate is used here as the closest fit. The large placebo response (-16.2) suggests a contribution from trial design (F7).

In AVP-786, quinidine serves as a CYP2D6 inhibitor that raises deudextromethorphan exposure; the hepatic CYP2D6 compartment is the same in every disease. The bundle has no direct human CYP2D6 inhibition data. Engagement is inferred_adequate because AVP-923 met its primary endpoint in Alzheimer agitation (NCT01584440), as did the AVP-786-18 arm in NCT02442765, at comparable low quinidine doses. Even so, the index trial showed no effect on PANSS Marder negative factors (difference 0.2, p=0.768) and stopped for futility (NCT03896945). This repeats an earlier miss in residual schizophrenia (NCT02477670, p=0.073). No tolerability cap is evident, with 2/65 serious AEs. The combined mechanism does not appear to drive negative symptoms. Engagement was never measured in schizophrenia patients.

In AVP-923 (dextromethorphan/quinidine), quinidine acts as a hepatic CYP2D6 inhibitor that boosts dextromethorphan exposure. CYP2D6 inhibition was not measured directly in the bundle. It is inferred adequate because the same combination was FDA-approved for pseudobulbar affect in 2010 (PMID:30615021) and met its primary endpoint in Alzheimer agitation (NCT01584440, started 2012) at comparable 10 mg quinidine doses, so the systemic target and the pathway (raised dextromethorphan) must have held. No engagement data exist in Parkinson disease. The index crossover trial in levodopa-induced dyskinesia (NCT01767129) showed no significant effect (p=0.19) and no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. This supports F2: the mechanism did not reduce dyskinesia as tested. With only 13 analyzed per arm and a point estimate favouring the drug, underpowering (F7) also applies.

In AVP-923 (dextromethorphan/quinidine), quinidine acts as a CYP2D6 inhibitor that raises dextromethorphan exposure. No human CYP2D6-inhibition or PK data appear in the bundle. However, AVP-923 met its primary endpoint for Alzheimer's agitation (NCT01584440), so systemic CYP2D6 inhibition and the resulting dextromethorphan exposure are inferred adequate at comparable quinidine doses. This was not shown in levodopa-induced dyskinesia and not before the index trial. The index crossover trial (NCT01767129) was well tolerated, with no serious AEs, and missed its endpoint (AUC difference -83.4, p=0.19). This suggests the mechanism does not meaningfully reduce dyskinesia as tested (F2). With only 13–14 patients the trial was small and possibly underpowered (F7). No stated stop reason; inference only.

In AVP-786, quinidine acts as a CYP2D6 inhibitor that boosts (deuterated) dextromethorphan. No direct CYP2D6 inhibition data are in the bundle. However, AVP-923 (DM/quinidine) met its primary NPI agitation endpoint in Alzheimer's agitation (NCT01584440), so systemic exposure and CYP2D6 engagement are inferred adequate. The TBI disinhibition trial showed no separation from placebo in either stage (p=0.405 and p=0.921), suggesting the mechanism does not drive this condition as tested. Caveat: PMID:40490784 proposes that deuteration weakened DM's NMDA pharmacology, which is a molecule-level issue outside quinidine's target. The NCT02442778 failure is consistent with that. No engagement was shown in this disease, so confidence is low.

Quinidine in AVP-923 inhibits CYP2D6 to boost dextromethorphan (DM) exposure. In the index MS central neuropathic pain trial (NCT01324232), plasma DM Cmax rose dose-dependently across the 20/30/45 arms in patients. That shows exposure and the expected pathway consequence of CYP2D6 inhibition, though no unboosted comparator was measured. Engagement is inferred adequate because the same combination met its primary endpoint in Alzheimer's agitation (NCT01584440) with the same hepatic CYP2D6 mechanism at comparable dosing. That evidence came after the index trial started. Despite adequate DM levels, pain change showed no association with DM concentration (r=0.0019, p=0.98), and the 45 mg arm did no better than placebo. No tolerability cap is evident, so the boosted-DM mechanism does not relieve this pain.

Quinidine's role in AVP-786/AVP-923 is systemic CYP2D6 inhibition to raise dextromethorphan exposure. No direct human CYP2D6 inhibition or PK data are in the bundle, since no Phase 1 results are posted. However, the combination met a clinician-scale efficacy endpoint in Alzheimer's agitation (NCT01584440, started 2012) and in one AVP-786 arm (NCT02442765), so CYP2D6 engagement at comparable doses is inferred adequate. In TBI disinhibition (NCT03095066) the drug did not separate from placebo (p=0.405; p=0.921), which points to the mechanism not driving this disease as tested. The large placebo response (-18.7) and the small Stage 2 groups suggest the trial had limited power to answer the question (F7). Evidence is indirect, so confidence is low.

Quinidine in AVP-786 serves as a CYP2D6 inhibitor that boosts dextromethorphan exposure. No direct human CYP2D6 inhibition or PK data are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate because AVP-923 met its primary endpoint in Alzheimer's agitation (NCT01584440), and AVP-786-18 beat placebo in one Phase 3 (NCT02442765), via the same hepatic CYP2D6 mechanism at comparable low quinidine doses. In TBI disinhibition (NCT03095066), Stage 1 showed no separation (p=0.405) against a large placebo response (-18.7). Stage 2 was tiny (n=12 vs 15, p=0.921). This suggests the mechanism does not drive this indication. Trial-design weakness (high placebo response, small Stage 2) is a secondary factor. Engagement was never shown in TBI patients.

The index chronic-asthma trial (NCT00404313), reported in PMID:21945511, met its primary endpoint at 100 mg: FEV1 change was 0.20 vs 0.13 L (p=0.004). Several secondary endpoints also improved, so the efficacy readout was not a failure. However, MK-0633 caused dose-dependent ALT/AST elevations. The optional extension periods were terminated, and the authors concluded the benefit-risk ratio did not support clinical use. The program therefore ended on molecule-related hepatotoxicity relative to modest efficacy. The bundle does not establish that this toxicity is on-target, so F5 is listed only as secondary. No human PK, LTB4 or other target-engagement data appear in the bundle. The COPD trial (NCT00418613) missed its endpoint.

In the index trial, MK-0633 100 mg did not improve trough FEV1 more than placebo (p=0.556) and was well tolerated. The only positive result was more patients reporting they felt better on the global evaluation (PMID:20970976). I found no human evidence of drug levels, 5-LO inhibition or leukotriene lowering (LTB4 or urinary LTE4). The only potency figure, an IC50 in human whole blood, comes from a lab test (vendor page) and does not count. The search tool limit ended my searching before I found a sponsor statement on why the program stopped. Zileuton, on the same target, is approved for asthma but not COPD, so F1b does not apply. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Conatumumab showed dose-linear plasma PK with a 13–19 day half-life up to 20 mg/kg. No MTD was reached, so dose was not limited (PMID:20947515, PMID:21161528). The index trial used 3 and 15 mg/kg with no PK interaction with paclitaxel-carboplatin. High DR5 receptor occupancy on monocytes was shown at all doses from 3 mg/kg in solid-tumor patients (PMID:21161528). That evidence is peripheral rather than tumor, not NSCLC-specific, and was published after the index trial started. No human tumor pathway effect was shown: caspase-3 changes did not track response. Despite engagement, PFS was not improved at either dose (NCT00534027, PMID:23370314). Single-agent and combination responses elsewhere were near zero (NCT00630786, NCT00819169), which supports a target that does not drive disease. A squamous-histology interaction and an FCGR3A signal suggest possible subgroup effects (F3).

Index Phase 1b in mantle cell lymphoma posted no results, and the bundle gives no stop reason. Exposure was shown: dose-linear PK, half-life 13–19 days, no MTD reached up to 20 mg/kg (PMID:20947515, PMID:21161528). Engagement was shown as high DR5 receptor occupancy on monocytes at all doses, but only in solid-tumour patients and published after the index start (PMID:21161528). There are no dose-limiting toxicities, so the dose was not capped. Pathway evidence is lacking: tumour caspase-3 changes were not linked to response (PMID:20947515). Across tumour types, conatumumab with adequate occupancy repeatedly gave no benefit (NCT00534027, NCT00819169, NCT00630786). This suggests DR5 agonism does not drive disease as tested. Confidence is low because MCL data are absent.

Exposure was adequate: dose-linear PK, 13–19 day half-life, and no MTD up to 20 mg/kg q2w (PMID:20947515, PMID:21161528). Engagement was shown as high DR5 receptor occupancy on monocytes at all doses in solid-tumor patients (PMID:21161528). That evidence comes from patients without lymphoma and was published after the index trial started in 2008. No tolerability cap was found. Human pathway evidence is lacking: tumor caspase-3 changes did not track response. Despite adequate engagement, conatumumab showed no benefit across combination trials (NCT00534027, NCT00630786, NCT00819169). Other DR5 agonists did not succeed in lymphoma either, so F1b does not apply. This points to a mechanism that does not drive disease (F2). The index trial NCT00791011 posted no results, so the bundle is thin.

The first-in-human trial in B-cell malignancies (NCT00457782; mostly myeloma patients) reported PK data and dose-related Hsp70 induction in blood immune cells (PBMCs). Hsp70 is the standard marker of Hsp90 inhibition, and it rose at doses of 71 mg/m² and above, up to 176 mg/m². In the phase 1 part of the index trial (NCT01063907), Hsp70 rose in all 13 patients at 130–175 mg/m². Tolerability did not limit the dose. At the recommended phase 2 dose, the response rate was 39.2%, about what bortezomib achieves alone (~35%). The investigators said the share of benefit from bortezomib versus KW-2478 was unclear. So Hsp90 was inhibited but added no clear benefit (F2). The single-arm design without a bortezomib-alone control could not separate the two drugs' contributions (F7). Caveat: Hsp70 was measured in blood cells, not myeloma cells.

Exposure in iron-overloaded patients was dose-proportional (PMID:21173101). For a chelator, net iron removal (LIC fall) is the engagement readout. It was weak and dose-dependent: at 24 weeks LIC rose by 3.1 mg/g at 14.5 mg/kg/d and fell by 0.3 mg/g at 29 mg/kg/d (PMID:22251482). At 96 weeks the mean change was -1.75 mg/g (p=0.077) (NCT01186419). The tested doses were therefore too low for adequate iron removal (F1a). Tolerability did not cap them. The program itself ended later, when the pediatric and follow-on trials (NCT01363908, NCT01671111, NCT01604941) were stopped. Their records say treatment was stopped while nonclinical rat findings were evaluated. That makes molecule-specific toxicity the direct reason the program ended (F6).

I found no human evidence that PF-06473871 lowered CTGF mRNA or protein in scar tissue, and no tissue drug levels or downstream biomarker data. The Phase 1 trial (NCT01753791) posted no results. The CTGF-knockdown data I found come from patents and use animal or xenograft models, so they don't count. Earlier Phase 2 results were mixed: NCT01037413 met its endpoint, NCT01037985 did not. In the parent trial B5301001, the 4-injection arm improved the physician POSAS score at week 24 (P=0.022) but the 3-injection arm did not. The authors suggest the effect of revision surgery alone may have swamped the drug effect, which points to a design problem (F7). Even so, with no engagement data, a drug that never engaged can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01548287 was a safety and tolerability study. Its primary endpoint was change in PSG total sleep time, a sleep-disruption safety measure, not a cognitive efficacy test. So 'not met' does not show the drug lacked efficacy (F9). Pillars: a human PET study (NCT01194986, registered 2010, before the index; PMID:23217964) showed brain penetration and dose- and concentration-dependent H3 occupancy of 16–90% in healthy volunteers, the dose range used in the index. This was not shown in AD patients. The dose-dependent TST reduction versus placebo in the index trial fits the wake-promoting effect expected from H3 antagonism (a pathway signal). Later Phase 2 failures in Tourette (NCT01904773) and painful diabetic neuropathy (NCT01928381) despite engagement hint at F2 more broadly.

Human PET in healthy volunteers (NCT01194986, PMID:23217964, before the 2013 index start) showed brain penetration and dose-dependent H3 receptor occupancy of 16–90%, so exposure and engagement were adequate. Engagement was not shown in diabetic neuropathy patients. A dose-dependent fall in total sleep time in NCT01548287 fits central H3 antagonism, which supports the pathway pillar. In the index trial (NCT01928381) AZD5213 plus pregabalin did not separate from pregabalin alone. The pregabalin active control also failed to separate from placebo (p=0.89). PMID:33086238 states that the small, enriched cross-over design could not robustly detect even pregabalin's efficacy, meaning the trial lacked assay sensitivity (F7). With engagement adequate, a target that does not matter here (F2) is also possible.

A human PET study (NCT01194986, PMID:23217964) showed brain H3 receptor occupancy by AZD5213 that rose with dose and plasma concentration, from 16% to 90% over single doses of 0.05–30 mg. This was in healthy volunteers, before the index trial, and the range covers the 0.5–2 mg index doses. The index trial confirmed plasma exposure in adolescents. In NCT01548287, total sleep time fell with dose, consistent with the wake-promoting effect expected from H3 antagonism, which supports the pathway pillar. Despite this, neither dose reduced tics, and 2 mg significantly worsened tic severity versus placebo (p=0.0087, NCT01904773). Engagement was adequate, so H3 antagonism appears not to drive tic reduction. The small crossover design (n≈29) is a minor caveat. Engagement was never measured in Tourette patients.

WIN-901X is a Whanin Pharmaceutical small molecule with no recorded target. Its index trial, NCT01820481, was a placebo-controlled Phase 2 dose-ranging study with three dose levels and a 12-week FEV1 endpoint. The trial completed, but no results were posted. Two web searches found only registry listings. There were no PK or pharmacodynamic data, no publications and no sponsor statement on why the program stopped. No human evidence on exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker exists, and the target itself is unknown. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that does not matter, so the failure cannot be explained (U).

In the two healthy-volunteer phase 1 studies (NCT02099071, NCT02099201), ACT-389949 was well tolerated with good plasma exposure and accumulation (PMID:27730665). It caused dose-dependent, long-lasting FPR2/ALX internalization on leukocytes, so target engagement was shown. Cytokine changes appeared only after the first dose, and steady-state dosing had no effect on neutrophil recruitment in the LPS inhalation challenge. The authors attribute this to receptor desensitization, so the expected pathway effect was not sustained even though the receptor was engaged and dose was not capped. The index trial was a safety study, not a patient efficacy test (F9 secondary). Engagement was shown only in healthy subjects, and it was published after the index trial started.

The index trial, NCT00912392, compared EC chemotherapy with or without Endostar in ED-SCLC and posted no results. It was published by Lu et al. in JTO, but I could not open the full text, so the result and any reason the authors gave for failure are unconfirmed. I found no human evidence that Endostar (the MGGSHHHHH-tagged endostatin) bound KDR or VEGF signalling, such as occupancy, VEGFR2 inhibition or a biomarker change. The early phase 1 PK/PD studies (NCT00004229/NCT00004872, JCO 2002–2003) tested untagged rh-endostatin from another sponsor, and the Endostar PK report snippet does not show exposure at the site of action. No dose limit from tolerability is reported. Other KDR drugs succeeded only in other diseases; none was approved in SCLC, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement has no human data, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug rather than the target: indeterminate.

disease: metastatic malignant neoplasm in the brain
rationale: The index trial, NCT01410370 (Simcere, Endostar plus radiotherapy for brain metastases, ORR primary endpoint), has status unknown, gave no reason for stopping and posted no results. My searches found no human data on Endostar's exposure in the brain or CSF, on KDR/VEGF-pathway engagement, or on a downstream biomarker in patients with brain metastases or anyone else. The only engagement-related data I found came from animal or in vitro work, which does not count. The bundle also shows no regulatory approval or pivotal success in another disease, so no pillar can be called inferred_adequate. Other KDR drugs in this disease (cabozantinib, lenvatinib) reached only phase 3 and show no approval or pivotal win here, so F1b does not apply. With engagement no_human_data and no stated reason for failure, the outcome is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT00976508 was a phase 1 safety and DLT study of figitumumab plus pegvisomant. It was terminated without a stated reason and had no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). The pillars hold at 20 mg/kg. Exposure is shown by PK (NCT00926263, PMID:23400740), and sarcoma PK matched other solid tumours (PMID:20036194). Engagement is shown by lower granulocyte and prostate tumour IGF-1R (PMID:18474873, PMID:22553344). The pathway effect is shown by sustained rises in IGF-1, IGFBP-3 and insulin (PMID:23400740). None of this engagement evidence came from sarcoma patients. In Ewing sarcoma, activity was modest (ORR 14.2%) and confined to subgroups such as patients with high free IGF-1 (PMID:22025154, PMID:22798295), supporting F3 and F2 as secondary codes.

At 20 mg/kg, the maximal feasible dose with no MTD reached (PMID:19745765), plasma exposure was high (NCT00926263, PMID:23400740) and the drug reached prostate tissue (PMID:22553344). Engagement was shown before the index trial: granulocyte IGF-IR fell and IGF-1 accumulated (PMID:18474873, 2008), and IGF-IR-positive CTCs declined (PMID:17575225, 2007). Pathway feedback followed, with sustained rises in IGF-1, IGFBP-3 and insulin (PMID:23400740) and lower tumor IGF-IR (PMID:22553344). No NSCLC-specific engagement data are shown. Despite this engagement, OS was numerically worse (HR 1.18) with more serious AEs (NCT00596830). The second phase 3 also failed (NCT00673049). This points to F2. Toxicity likely offset benefit (F5). Response possibly tied to free IGF-1 suggests a selection issue (F3).

Exposure is adequate. Dose-proportional plasma PK (NCT00926263, PMID:23400740) and prostate tissue drug levels (PMID:22553344) were shown at 20 mg/kg, the dose without an MTD (PMID:19745765). Engagement is adequate and was published before 2010: IGF-IR fell on granulocytes (PMID:18474873), on circulating tumor cells (PMID:17575225) and in tumor tissue (PMID:22553344). Pathway is adequate: sustained compensatory rises in IGF-1 and insulin, plus a trend toward lower downstream signaling. None of this was shown in SCLC. The index trial enrolled only 9 patients, posted no PFS and gave no stated reason, so it could not answer the question (F7). The likely context is the IGF1R program failing despite engagement: two NSCLC phase 3 trials stopped for futility (NCT00596830, NCT00673049). Business closures also appear in the program (NCT00372996), so F8 is possible.

Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional plasma PK at 10–20 mg/kg (NCT00926263, PMID:23400740) and prostate tissue levels about 51 μg/g (PMID:22553344). Engagement was adequate: granulocyte IGF-IR fell at high doses (PMID:18474873, 2008), CTC IGF-IR fell (PMID:17575225, 2007), and tumor IGF-IR dropped in 14/16 patients (PMID:22553344). Pathway was adequate: free IGF-1 rose 8–12-fold, insulin rose, and downstream signaling trended down. None of this engagement was shown in Ewing sarcoma. The index trial used 30 mg/kg, above the 20 mg/kg RP2D, with no MTD reached. It gave only a 14.2% ORR (NCT00560235), consistent with IGF-1R blockade not driving most Ewing tumors. Responses in a minority suggest benefit confined to a subgroup (F3). Futility in phase 3 NSCLC trials of the drug (NCT00596830, NCT00673049) also coincided with the program ending.

The index trial NCT01978327 was a Phase 1 safety, PK and DDI study in healthy volunteers, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because strong CYP3A4 inhibition (simvastatin exposure up 3.6–4.3-fold) gave no rationale to test higher doses (PMID:27719741). This is a molecule-specific liability, so F6 is secondary. Pillars were shown in healthy volunteers. Plasma exposure rose roughly dose-proportionally. PET confirmed blood-brain barrier penetration (whole-brain VT 0.56; PMID:27402093, NCT01924858). Plasma Lp-PLA2 activity was inhibited dose-dependently, with 85.6% trough inhibition after twice-daily dosing, from the earlier single-dose PD study NCT01702467 and the index study. No downstream pathway biomarker and no data in Alzheimer's disease patients are in the bundle. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

INM-176 is a standardized ethanol extract of Angelica gigas with no defined primary target. The suggested mechanisms are acetylcholinesterase inhibition and anti-neuroinflammatory effects, and these come only from mouse and in vitro work (PMID:22846435, PMID:22342662). The index Phase 3 trial (NCT01245530; 24 weeks, ADAS-Cog) posted no results and gave no stated reason for stopping. My searches found no human data on brain penetration, AChE inhibition, or biomarker changes for INM-176. They also found no statement from the sponsor (Whanin) explaining the failure. A 2018 study measured plasma PK of A. gigas coumarins in humans (PMC6100347), but it does not show the drug reached or engaged any target in the brain. Engagement is no_human_data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Emibetuzumab 2000 mg Q2W was given in the index trial. Phase 1 showed linear, dose-proportional PK and no DLTs up to 2000 mg (PMID:27803065, PMID:27422720), and gastric-patient PK matched prior data (PMID:29071414). Exposure is therefore adequate and the dose was not capped by tolerability. The phase 1 report mentions PK/PD analysis, but no human MET engagement or downstream biomarker data appear in the bundle. The index trial showed limited activity: 8-week PFS rate 0.47, no responses, and no MET-outcome association (PMID:29071414). The bundle lists cabozantinib, a MET-targeting drug, as FDA-approved in gastric cancer, so the target is not discredited. Preclinical data suggest this molecule weakly suppresses pMET (PMID:29188469, PMID:28679766), but animal and in vitro data do not count. Hence F1b, with U as an alternative given absent engagement data.

The index trial NCT01280786 was a single-agent Phase 1 study in relapsed or refractory AML. It was published as PMID:26732437 (Hedley 2016). A later review summarises that study as showing good tolerability but no clinical responses. I could not access the full text, and none of the sources I found report human blast or plasma data on copper delivery, FDX1 engagement, ROS induction or mitochondrial membrane potential at the doses tested. The patent planned to measure mitochondrial membrane potential, but no results were found. Tolerability did not cap the dose. No other FDX1 drug has succeeded in AML. The AML evidence for the mechanism is all in vitro or animal work, which does not count. Engagement has no human data, so I cannot tell whether the drug never engaged its target or the target does not matter in AML. Code U.

Human PET showed brain penetration and concentration-dependent GlyT1 occupancy (EC50 ~190 ng/ml, Emax ~92%) in healthy volunteers (PMID:23132267). CSF glycine rose dose-dependently (1.3-fold at 10 mg, 1.7-fold at 30 mg), and the authors judged the mechanism confirmed (PMID:27178435). Index doses of 10 and 20 mg targeted the low-to-medium occupancy the phase 2 linked to optimal efficacy (PMID:24696094, NCT00616798). Bitopertin was well tolerated, so dose was not capped. Despite this, FlashLyte, DayLyte and most SearchLyte trials showed no separation from placebo (PMID:28117049, PMID:27816567). This points to the mechanism not driving negative symptoms as tested (F2). Partial occupancy and an unchanged NMDAR biomarker (mismatch negativity) in patients at 10 mg (PMID:28590364) leave some doubt that engagement was sufficient (F1a).

The OCD index trial (NCT01674361) posted no results, and the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping. Human pillar data come from healthy volunteers. PET showed dose- and concentration-dependent brain GlyT1 occupancy, with Emax ~92% (PMID:23132267). CSF glycine rose dose-dependently, 1.3–2.3-fold at 3–60 mg (PMID:27178435), confirming central exposure, engagement and the proximal glycine effect. Tolerability did not cap the dose; bitopertin was well tolerated in phase 3. No engagement data exist in OCD patients. In schizophrenia, the mismatch-negativity biomarker did not move at 10 mg (PMID:28590364), and most phase 3 trials missed their endpoints. With engagement shown, no benefit points to the GlyT1/NMDA-glycine mechanism not driving OCD as tested (F2). Confidence is low because the index readout itself is not in the bundle.

Human exposure and GlyT1 engagement were shown before the index trial. PET in healthy volunteers found occupancy up to ~92% (PMID:23132267), and CSF glycine rose dose-dependently at 3–60 mg (PMID:27178435), with PK characterized (PMID:26341813). The erythroid pathway effect was shown in humans: a dose-dependent fall in PPIX in EPP (NCT05308472) and dose-dependent changes in erythropoiesis and haemoglobin-synthesis biomarkers in healthy subjects (PMID:40707717). No engagement was shown in beta-thalassemia patients. The index trial (NCT03271541) posted no results, and only the title of PMID:33931857 is available, so the haemoglobin outcome and the stop reason are unshown. Because the mechanism was engaged without a clinical advance in thalassemia, F2 is tentatively assigned, with low confidence given the thin bundle.

The topical HY209 gel did not separate from placebo on EASI improvement in the index trial (PMID:40458407). No human data show that the gel reached GPBAR1 in skin, engaged the receptor, or moved an inflammasome marker. The topical Phase 1 trial (NCT03492398) posted only safety results. The IV pharmacokinetic study (PMID:39670278) covers sepsis dosing and gives plasma levels only. The investigators blame disease heterogeneity: a post hoc plasma-proteomic CRKlow/K2C5 subgroup responded. The sponsor then started a biomarker-guided Phase 2 in a different population. A post hoc subgroup does not show that the target was engaged, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. That makes the code U, with F3 (patient selection) as secondary.

The index trial (NCT00817362; PMID:23580070) gave retaspimycin 300 mg/m² weekly with trastuzumab. There were no DLTs and no confirmed responses, so the trial stopped for futility. Plasma exposure rose with dose (PMID:24045182). In the GIST/sarcoma Phase 1, Hsp70 rose in blood cells in all 7 evaluable patients dosed at 225 mg/m² or more, given twice weekly. That shows a downstream response in a surrogate tissue, not in breast tumour. No source measured Hsp90 binding or HER2 loss in breast cancer patients. The investigators raised possible underdosing, since the drug was well tolerated, but did not show it. This points to F1a. No other Hsp90 inhibitor succeeded in breast cancer, so F1b does not fit. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter. Hence U.

In the index pilot trial (NCT01217112), THCV 5 mg twice daily did not change HDL, the primary endpoint (p=0.668). The published report (Jadoon 2016, Diabetes Care) says THCV lowered fasting plasma glucose, but that is a clinical metabolic signal, not a CB1-specific biomarker. Neither source has human data on CB1 occupancy, plasma or tissue exposure at this dose, or a CB1-linked pathway marker. The healthy-volunteer studies of a single 10 mg dose (fMRI changes, PMID:25542687 and PMID:26362774) and of reduced THC effects (PMID:26577065) suggest central activity only indirectly; they did not measure occupancy and did not involve diabetes. Engagement therefore has no human data, so U applies. Secondary codes: F4, because HDL was probably the wrong endpoint given the glucose signal, and F7, because this was a small, underpowered pilot. There is no stated reason why development stopped.

In the index trial NCT01217112, THCV alone (5 mg twice daily) and both CBD combinations did not change HDL compared with placebo. The published report did find that THCV lowered fasting glucose and changed adiponectin and apolipoprotein A. However, nothing in the bundle measures CB1 occupancy, plasma or tissue THCV levels at this dose, or a CB1-specific biomarker in patients. The only human signals come from small healthy-volunteer studies published after the index trial: fMRI changes at 10 mg and a blunted THC heart-rate response (PMID:25542687, PMID:26577065). Neither measures engagement directly. Mouse data suggest THCV's metabolic effects work differently from CB1 inverse agonists (PMID:23712280). With engagement unmeasured, the bundle can't tell a drug that didn't engage CB1 from a target that doesn't drive HDL, so the code is U. Small arms (n=9 to 13) in a pilot trial point to F7 as a secondary code.

The index trial (NCT01265875) was a 12-patient, single-arm escalating infusion of secretin (0.05–0.8 mcg/kg). It produced no significant change in pain VAS (p=.19–.27), opiate use or quality of life. No PK, occupancy or secretion biomarkers were measured. Engagement and pathway are inferred: in a phase 3 study (PMID:24906040) of patients with acute or recurrent pancreatitis, RG1068 met its diagnostic endpoint, improving duct detection on MRCP through SCTR-driven pancreatic ductal secretion at comparable doses. That study was published in 2014, after the index trial started. No serious tolerability cap is evident. Stimulating SCTR therefore did not relieve chronic pancreatitis pain (F2). However, the tiny uncontrolled design limits any conclusion (F7).

The index trial NCT00741338 was a 7-patient immune tolerance induction study in which cyclosporine served as an immunomodulatory adjunct to laronidase enzyme replacement. Its endpoint, tolerance to laronidase, is classified not_efficacy, so this was not an efficacy test of cyclosporine against MPS I. Tolerance was achieved in 1 of 6 participants. Calcineurin and cyclophilin engagement is inferred adequate from the approval in transplant rejection, which acts through the same systemic T-cell target. PMID:10706056 shows dose-related suppression of CD4+ IL-2 in transplant patients, and PMID:9263387 shows cyclophilin binding in blood. No engagement data exist in MPS I patients. The very small sample (F7) and a tolerance mechanism that may not work in this setting (F2) are possible secondary explanations.

Index trial NCT01109056 tested topical cyclosporine 0.05% emulsion against vehicle for primary pterygium hyperemia. At Week 16 there were 6/56 responders on drug versus 8/57 on vehicle, and severity change was -0.7 versus -0.8. Tolerability was comparable, with 1 serious AE per arm. The bundle has no direct ocular engagement data. The drug is FDA-approved for dry eye, which per the bundle implies efficacy through calcineurin inhibition in the same ocular-surface compartment. Assuming the approved product is this 0.05% emulsion (the bundle does not state the dose), exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Nothing suggests the dose was capped. The calcineurin/T-cell mechanism therefore appears not to drive pterygium hyperemia. Consistent with this, PMID:31271569 found no reduction in recurrence.

NCT03844932 tested ST-0529, an oral cyclosporine formulation, in moderate-to-severe UC. It was stopped at interim analysis because the 9.6% remission difference for 75 mg BID versus placebo was judged insufficient to keep funding. The sponsor explicitly attributed the small margin to an increased placebo response, which is a trial-execution or design explanation, so the primary code is F7. Funding was the proximate trigger (F8). The bundle has no human data on exposure, calcineurin or cyclophilin engagement, or pathway effect for this formulation. IV cyclosporine used in acute severe UC (PMID:33634990, PMID:26343066) is a different route, population and exposure, so it cannot support an inferred pillar. U therefore also applies.

BOSTON-2 (NCT03656926) tested inhaled liposomal cyclosporine (L-CsA-i) on top of standard care and missed its primary endpoint: change in FEV1 at week 48 was -0.096 vs -0.067 L (p=0.66). Exposure was shown in lung transplant patients. Gamma scintigraphy found 33-40% of the dose deposited in the lung, with a peripheral lung dose of 2-3.4 mg (Behr 2009), and blood levels were low. Neurohr 2022 and the phase IIb ERJ trial reported pharmacokinetics only. No source measured calcineurin inhibition, IL-2 suppression or another lung biomarker in humans. There is also no sponsor explanation of the failure. Because engagement and pathway have no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U. Confidence is medium because the gap rests on what the sources leave out.

Phase 1 (PMID:23833302) showed rapid conversion to the active metabolite RPR258063 with dose-proportional exposure at an RP2D of 50 mg/m2 that tolerability did not limit. Vascular-disruption biomarkers (CEC, VEGF, MMP-9) rose post-infusion in a subset of solid-tumour patients, but none were NSCLC patients. Tubulin engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the sarcoma phase 3 (NCT00699517) met its PFS endpoint through the same tubulin and tumour-vasculature mechanism. Adding ombrabulin to taxane/platinum in NSCLC (NCT01263886) gave no reported benefit, which points to the vascular-disrupting mechanism not adding efficacy in this setting. The index trial posted no results and no stated reason, and engagement was never shown in NSCLC, so confidence is low.

In the phase 1 study (PMID:23833302), ombrabulin and its active metabolite showed dose-proportional plasma exposure up to the 50 mg/m2 RP2D, which was not capped below an active level. Tubulin binding was not measured directly. Engagement is inferred_adequate because ombrabulin met its PFS endpoint in the phase 3 soft tissue sarcoma trial (NCT00699517), acting through the same tubulin/tumor-vasculature mechanism. Vascular-disruption biomarkers (CEC, VEGF, MMP-9) rose in a subset of patients (PMID:23833302). There is no engagement evidence in ovarian cancer patients; ovarian support is preclinical only (PMID:17909042). With adequate exposure, the add-on PFS failure in platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer (NCT01332656, no results posted) is best read as the mechanism adding no benefit there. The bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT01021150 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of ombrabulin plus cisplatin with dose-limiting toxicity as its only primary outcome, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Exposure was adequate: PMID:23833302 showed dose-proportional exposure of ombrabulin and its active metabolite in solid-tumor patients. In a subset of patients, circulating endothelial cells, VEGF and MMP-9 rose after infusion. Tubulin engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the Phase 3 sarcoma trial NCT00699517 met its PFS endpoint. These data were published in 2013, after the index trial started in 2010. No tolerability cap below the needed dose was shown.

The index trial NCT03019627 was sponsored by Dompé and tested rhNGF eye drops at 20 µg/mL. That is the same molecule and concentration as cenegermin, which is FDA-approved for neurotrophic keratopathy. In that disease it works through TrkA on the ocular surface (cornea), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate in the same tissue at the same dose. No direct target-engagement data in dry eye patients were found, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Neither SANDE symptom comparison separated from vehicle (frequency p=0.428, severity p=0.974). A later dose-ranging Phase II trial also missed its Schirmer I primary endpoint at week 4. Topical NGF agonism therefore does not appear to drive dry eye symptoms as tested. A symptom endpoint with a large vehicle response may have contributed (F4), but the sources do not say so.

In decompensated HF patients, ularitide 15–30 ng/kg/min IV raised plasma cGMP, the NPR1 second messenger, which shows engagement and implies systemic exposure (PMID:16338265, 2005, before the index trial). It also lowered PCWP and NT-proBNP. Phase 2 SIRIUS II showed dose-dependent haemodynamic effects at the 15 ng/kg/min dose later used in TRUE-AHF (PMID:17074775, PMID:18513512). In TRUE-AHF (NCT01661634, PMID:28402745), ularitide again reduced SBP and NT-proBNP more than placebo, but CV mortality (HR 1.03) and the hierarchical composite were unchanged. Hypotension was managed with dose adjustment, not shown to cap engagement. The mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, so F2. The authors also note that short-term treatment was insufficient (F4).

In the index trial (NCT00838799), 458 patients received radiprodil at 15, 30 or 45 mg three times daily, an active comparator, or placebo for 14 weeks. No radiprodil dose produced a meaningful reduction in pain, and the sponsors gave no mechanistic reason. GluN2B is a CNS/neural target, but I found no human data on brain or CSF drug levels, receptor occupancy, or a downstream biomarker. Receptor occupancy in PMID:32822519 was modelled from in vitro data and plasma PK, not measured. The other engagement evidence is from animals: a monkey PET study that was inconsistent (PMID:30306318) and partial NMDA inhibition in rodents (PMID:26325093). The page I read gave no result for the active comparator, and no other GluN2B drug has succeeded in diabetic neuropathy, so F1b does not apply. The tolerability findings did not cap dosing. With engagement untested, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug or on the target.

No direct human measure of p38α inhibition, occupancy or CSF drug level at the index doses was found. Engagement is graded only from indirect evidence. In REVERSE-SD (NCT03402659; PMID:34044875), 40 mg twice daily significantly lowered CSF total tau and p-tau181, which the authors cite as at least showing target engagement in AD patients. That counts as a pathway signal (published 2021, after the index trial). However, the investigators' prespecified PK-PD analyses tied the clinical miss to the dose being too low. Only patients with trough levels of about 4 ng/mL or more, or in the top quartile, showed trends toward memory benefit. So exposure and engagement were inadequate in most patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose; the dose was simply chosen too low. The small exploratory amyloid PET index trial (NCT02423122) showed no consistent effect at 40 or 125 mg.

The index Phase 2 trial NCT05565092 enrolled only 2 participants. It was terminated by 'sponsor decision to terminate program', and its primary endpoint was safety only, so it was never an efficacy test. In healthy volunteers (NCT04631562, PMID:40134111), tarperprumig showed dose-proportional exposure with 94% bioavailability. It produced complete alternative pathway inhibition (<1% of baseline) at 50 mg SC and above, which covers the 300–600 mg index doses. Tolerability was good, with no serious AEs, so the dose was not limited. Engagement was not shown in sickle cell patients, and these data were published after the index trial started. No efficacy failure is evident. The bundle suggests a sponsor or business decision (F8), though no explicit commercial reason is given.

In the index trial (NCT00707889, PMID:25066269), linifanib plus mFOLFOX6 did not improve PFS over bevacizumab plus mFOLFOX6.
