Grade 3/4 toxicity was higher, and fewer 5-FU cycles were delivered in the linifanib arms. Pooled PK (PMID:24307488) shows plasma exposure in CRC patients, though clearance was 41% faster. The bundle has no human VEGFR or PDGFR engagement or pathway biomarker data; target inhibition was shown only in rats (PMID:22080168). The VEGFR axis is validated in CRC: bevacizumab was the comparator, and ramucirumab, regorafenib and fruquintinib are FDA-approved. This points to a molecule-level shortfall rather than a target failure. Monotherapy in KRAS-mutant CRC was also futile, with an objective response rate of 0 (NCT01365910, PMID:28353122). Molecule-specific toxicity that reduced chemotherapy delivery may have contributed.

The bundle has no direct human PK, receptor-occupancy or VEGFR/PDGFR biomarker data. Engagement is inferred: the NCT00716534 combination met a PFS benefit in NSCLC (HR 0.51), and in the index HCC trial linifanib improved TTP (HR 0.76) and ORR versus sorafenib (PMID:25488963). It also caused grade 3/4 hypertension in the phase 2 study (PMID:22833179). Overall survival nonetheless matched sorafenib (HR 1.046), and the trial missed both superiority and non-inferiority boundaries. Grade 3/4 AEs, serious AEs, discontinuations, interruptions and dose reductions were all significantly more frequent with linifanib. This pattern, antitumor activity offset by class (VEGFR-type) toxicity against an active comparator, best fits F5. F9 applies secondarily because this was an active-comparator non-inferiority test.

In the first-in-human solid-tumor study, exposure was dose-proportional. pAKT was suppressed by ≥90% in platelet-rich plasma at 50 mg, with target modulation from 16 mg. FDG-PET uptake fell >25% in 66% of patients at the 40 mg RP2D (PMID:26787751). Engagement and pathway effect were therefore shown, but in mixed solid tumors, not endometrial cancer. In MAGGIE (NCT01455493, PMID:27603005), 40 mg gave only 6% ORR and 20% 6-month PFS. On-target toxicity was heavy: grade 3/4 hyperglycemia in 46% and rash in 30%. A further 42% of non-diabetic patients needed dose reductions, 23% stopped for adverse events, and 19 patients left before the first tumor assessment. Toxicity offsetting modest activity is the most direct explanation. Responses occurred only in tumors with PI3K-pathway alterations, which suggests a selection issue (F3); limited benefit despite engagement supports F2.

In the phase 1 trial in solid tumors (PMID:26787751), pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional and target modulation occurred at doses of 16 mg or more. Platelet pAKT fell by at least 90% at 50 mg, and FDG-PET uptake fell by more than 25% in 66% of patients at 40 mg. So all three pillars held at the 40 mg dose used in the index trial. This evidence was not shown in RCC patients and was published after the index trial began. In NCT01442090/PMID:26951309, apitolisib gave shorter PFS than everolimus. It also caused far more grade 3-4 hyperglycemia and rash, which were exposure-related, and more discontinuations (31% v 12%). The authors attribute the inferiority to full PI3K/mTOR blockade, which suggests on-target toxicity offset efficacy. PMID:38639108 also notes faster loss of effect. Secondary F2: the added PI3K inhibition gave no benefit over mTORC1 inhibition alone.

In the phase 1 trials (NCT00854152/NCT00854126; PMID:26787751), apitolisib PK was dose-proportional. Platelet-rich-plasma pAKT fell by at least 90% at the MTD, target modulation occurred at 16 mg and above, and FDG-PET uptake dropped more than 25% in 66% of patients at 40 mg. Exposure, engagement and pathway were therefore shown in solid-tumour patients, but not specifically in breast cancer. Severe on-target toxicities (hyperglycemia, rash, pneumonitis) appeared at 40 mg and above. In RCC (NCT01442090), apitolisib was worse than everolimus, with 40% high-grade hyperglycemia. Other PI3K/mTOR drugs are approved in breast cancer, so the target is valid there. The likely cause is a narrow therapeutic window from on-target toxicity. The bundle does not report results for the apitolisib arm of the index trial (NCT01437566), so confidence is low.

Imexon has no recorded protein target; its mechanism is pro-oxidant thiol binding. The 2007 Phase 1 in advanced cancers (PMID:17470869) measured plasma PK (dose-independent clearance, 95-min half-life) and a dose- and AUC-dependent fall in plasma cystine at 750 mg/m2/d. That is human evidence of the thiol-depleting mechanism near the 875 mg/m2 recommended dose, published before the index trial, but not in pancreatic cancer specifically. Tumor ROS or apoptosis effects in humans were not shown. In NCT00637247, adding imexon to gemcitabine gave numerically worse OS (5.2 vs 6.8 months, p=0.2) and more serious AEs. Because engagement was shown yet there was no benefit, the mechanism does not appear to drive pancreatic cancer. The nonspecific target and thin bundle keep confidence low.

Imexon has no recorded protein target. Its mechanism is pro-oxidant thiol binding. In the phase 1 trial in patients with mixed advanced cancers (PMID:17470869, 2007, before the 2008 index start), the drug showed measurable plasma PK. Plasma cystine fell in a dose- and AUC-dependent way, which the authors read as a thiol-depletion biomarker of engagement. An MTD of 875 mg/m2/d was defined, with no sign that the dose was capped below engagement. Tumor ROS or apoptosis was never measured in humans, and engagement was not shown specifically in pancreatic patients. In the index trial NCT00637247, overall survival was numerically worse (5.2 vs 6.8 months, p=0.2) and serious AEs were somewhat more frequent. With systemic thiol depletion shown but no benefit, the mechanism appears not to drive pancreatic cancer as tested. The evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

LEAP (NCT01124786) found no OS difference versus gemcitabine in low-hENT1 patients (HR 0.994). The phase 1 study (PMID:26289594) shows only dose-dependent plasma PK and an MTD/RP2D of 1250 mg/m2, the dose used in the trials. The dose was therefore not capped below a needed level, but no tumour intracellular gemcitabine nucleotide levels or RRM1 inhibition were measured in humans. The same target is validated in this disease: gemcitabine, the parent drug, is FDA-approved for pancreatic cancer. So the failure points to the molecule's premise (hENT1-independent uptake giving an advantage) rather than the target, which fits F1b. The second-line hENT1-negative study also showed no signal (PMID:25278310). The program was terminated after LEAP failed (NCT01641575). The evidence is thin.

FORTIS-M (NCT00707304) missed its overall survival endpoint, with a median of 7.5 months on talactoferrin versus 7.7 months on placebo (p=0.66). Talactoferrin is an oral drug thought to work through the gut and dendritic cells, but it has no recorded molecular target. Blood levels were undetectable after oral dosing (PMID:16193240), so no human data show the drug reaching or binding a defined target. That trial saw IL-18 rise in 10 patients with mixed solid tumours. A small study in NSCLC tumour biopsies, run after FORTIS-M (NCT01528137/PMC6464638), found only a monocyte increase in 2 patients and no clear change in other immune cells, so the pathway pillar is weak. No source explains the failure. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

CASSIOPEIR (NCT01090037) missed its renal composite endpoint at both doses (HR 0.98 and 0.91; PMID:31119846). Exposure was shown in CKD patients at the 120 μg SR dose, with plasma BPS/BPS-314d levels rising with CKD stage (PMID:27681484). Prostacyclin-receptor engagement and its functional effects were shown in humans at comparable doses before the trial: raised platelet cAMP, inhibited platelet aggregation and increased vasodilation/skin blood flow (PMID:7596955, 7506323, 8960377, 9187411, 33583799). This evidence comes from healthy volunteers and diabetics, not non-diabetic CKD. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, the most likely explanation is that it does not drive CKD progression. A post hoc Japanese and early-stage subgroup signal (PMID:33340238) supports F3 as secondary.

Healthy-volunteer studies show plasma exposure (PMID:33583799, 7506323) and IP-receptor engagement and pathway effects. These include raised intraplatelet cAMP (PMID:7596955), inhibited platelet aggregation (PMID:8960377) and skin vasodilation. All predate the index trial, but none was in PAH patients or used the MR formulation. The IP target is validated in PAH: selexipag, treprostinil and iloprost are approved. Immediate-release beraprost itself gave a transient 6MWD benefit (PMID:12821234). The index trial (NCT00989963) had about 11 patients per arm, no placebo arm and very wide SDs, and showed no hemodynamic change. That points to a trial unable to answer the question rather than a non-causal target. The bundle gives no stated reason, so confidence is low.

Plasma exposure of BPS and BPS-314d is documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:33913081, PMID:7506323). IP-receptor engagement markers there were modest: 10-19% platelet aggregation inhibition, a small platelet cAMP rise, and weaker antiplatelet potency than aspirin (PMID:8960377, PMID:7596955, PMID:20124989). No engagement was measured in PAH. In the controlled PAH dose-ranging trial, BPS-MR did not change PVR, cardiac output or PAP at any dose and showed no dose-response (NCT00989963). This is the pathway evidence in disease. Earlier beraprost benefit faded over time (PMID:12821234), and the open-label hemodynamic gains (PMID:19609055) were uncontrolled. Other IP agonists (selexipag, treprostinil, epoprostenol, iloprost) are approved in PAH (PMID:31496830). That points to the molecule falling short, not the target. BEAT missed its primary endpoint (NCT01908699).

Azficel-T is an autologous fibroblast cell therapy with no recorded molecular target. I found no human data on whether the injected cells survived, made extracellular matrix in the vocal fold lamina propria, or moved any biomarker in that tissue. In the small 15-vs-6 trial NCT02120781, placebo did as well as or better than drug: 14/15 vs 5/6 improved mucosal wave, and voice handicap fell 10% on drug vs 29% on placebo. Fibrocell said the trial missed its endpoints against placebo with no safety problems, and gave no mechanistic reason. The published paper reports only within-group gains from baseline. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a failed product from a mechanism that does not matter. The small size and strong placebo response are a possible design factor (F7).

The index trial NCT00799552 is not an efficacy failure as far as the sources show. It ran 28 days in 232 patients, and the sponsor's August 2009 press release says RX-10045 gave dose-dependent, statistically significant improvement on both primary endpoints, signs and symptoms. No results were posted to ClinicalTrials.gov, so this rests only on the sponsor's own claim. That is why confidence is medium, not high. Development went on afterwards, with a second dry-eye trial (NCT01675570) and a cataract-surgery inflammation trial (NCT02329743) that missed its endpoint. My search found no human data on ocular drug levels, CMKLR1 engagement or downstream biomarkers. So all three pillars are no_human_data, and if a later failure were the real cause it would be indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT00724425 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation safety and MTD study in advanced malignancies, not an efficacy test. It and the hematologic Phase 1 trial NCT01193491 were both terminated with the same stated reason: drug exposure of IPI-493 was inferior to that of retaspimycin HCl, the sponsor's other HSP90 inhibitor, so the sponsor chose to focus on retaspimycin. This points to inadequate human exposure, meaning the mechanism was never properly tested with this molecule (F1a). No engagement or pathway data were posted or published. Secondary codes: F9, because there was no efficacy readout, and F8, because the decision was portfolio prioritization. Evidence is limited to the stop statements; no results or abstracts were available.

MK-8723 has no recorded target, and the sources found do not describe its mechanism. In the single-rising-dose study NCT01963260, doses up to 100 mg/kg were well tolerated: there were no serious adverse events and no discontinuations, so tolerability did not cap the dose. None of the 8 ITP patients on drug had a platelet response, but Part 2 was tiny (n=2–3 per dose). Serum AUC was a secondary endpoint, but no PK values, target-engagement or pharmacodynamic data were found. AdisInsight says only that Merck was developing it and that a Phase 1 was completed; it gives no reason for stopping. Because engagement data are missing, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter. The underpowered Part 2 is a possible contributing factor.

Exposure rose proportionally with dose, and HSP70 induction in plasma, PBMCs and tumor biopsies showed target engagement at the RP2D in solid-tumor patients, not NSCLC specifically (PMID:25336693, NCT00878423). Downstream client-protein depletion in tumor was not significant in paired biopsies (PMID:26082332) and only modest in prostate cancer (PMID:31113841), so the pathway pillar is weak. Tolerability set the RP2D, but nothing shows it was below the engagement level. Clinical activity stayed limited across indications (NCT01294202; PMID:31113841). No other HSP90 inhibitor succeeded in NSCLC. The index trial (NCT01712217) posted no results and is classified not_efficacy, so this is a low-confidence F2, with F9 as an alternative.

In the index CRPC trial (NCT01685268; PMID:31113841), onalespib was given at 220 mg/m2 weekly or 120 mg/m2 days 1–2, near the phase 1 RP2Ds of 260 and 160 mg/m2. Phase 1 PK was dose-proportional and HSP70 was induced in plasma and tumor biopsies (PMID:25336693, PMID:26082332), so exposure was adequate. In CRPC patients, HSP72 was significantly upregulated, showing target engagement. However, only a modest decrease in the client proteins AR and GR was seen in tumor biopsies, with transient CTC/AR changes, so the pathway effect was weak. No objective or PSA responses occurred. The authors conclude the biological effect did not translate into clinical activity: HSP90 inhibition does not drive benefit as tested (F2). Incomplete client depletion near diarrhea-limited doses leaves some F1a possibility.

In the index trial, onalespib (150–220 mg/m2 weekly) plus imatinib gave only 19% disease control at 4 months in TKI-resistant GIST (PMID:27156227). Phase 1 in solid tumours showed dose-proportional exposure and target engagement by HSP70 induction in plasma and tumour biopsies at comparable doses (PMID:25336693). Engagement was not shown specifically in GIST patients, and it was published after the index trial started. Downstream client-protein depletion in tumour was not significant (PMID:26082332), and AR/GR fell only modestly (PMID:31113841), so the pathway effect was inadequate. Tolerability was not stated to cap the index doses, although they were below the 260 mg/m2 RP2D. With engagement adequate, the failure best fits F2: HSP90 inhibition did not translate into benefit.

The index phase 3 trial (NCT01097018) of perifosine 50 mg daily plus capecitabine in refractory CRC posted no results. The bundle holds no CRC pharmacodynamic data. Human plasma levels were measured (PMID:11499478) but are not reported. In leukemia, perifosine 100 mg/day, double the CRC dose, gave no appreciable direct Akt inhibition in patient cells, and the authors attribute the failure to insufficient in vivo Akt inhibition (PMID:23443507). Only partial downstream pS6 reduction appears there and in ovarian cancer (PMID:22487539). Myeloma data only associate response with phospho-Akt (PMID:22640031). Engagement therefore looks inadequate, so the mechanism was likely not tested at the CRC dose. This evidence comes from other diseases and was published after the index trial started. No tolerability cap was shown. The positive phase 2 had only 38 patients (PMID:21969495).

The index Phase 3 trial NCT01002248 was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results. The only direct human target-engagement measurement in the bundle (PMID:23443507, NCT00301938) used perifosine 100 mg/day, comparable to the myeloma doses of 50-100 mg (PMID:22640031). It found no appreciable Akt inhibition in patients' mononuclear cells; only reduced pS6 was seen. The authors attributed the lack of efficacy to insufficient Akt inhibition in vivo. In myeloma, response was merely associated with phospho-Akt (PMID:22640031), which does not show engagement. The ovarian study showed pS6 decreases only in responders (PMID:22487539). No human exposure levels are reported in the bundle. Partial or absent engagement suggests the mechanism was not properly tested. Confidence is low because the index stop reason is unknown.

BCI-540 (coluracetam, MKC-231) is a choline-uptake (SLC5A7) enhancer. It was licensed from Mitsubishi Tanabe after missing endpoints in Alzheimer's trials. Its Phase 2 MDD-with-anxiety trial (NCT00621270, 80 mg once daily or three times daily for 6 weeks) never posted results. Secondary sources say the drug has no published human efficacy evidence and that development was discontinued. They mention only vague 'suggestive' phase IIa findings. I found no human data on CSF or brain exposure, SLC5A7 or high-affinity choline uptake engagement, or downstream cholinergic biomarkers. No sponsor statement gives the reason for failure, and no other drug on this target is shown. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

BCI-540 (coluracetam, MKC-231) is a choline-uptake (CHT1/SLC5A7) enhancer. It was tested at 80 mg once or three times daily in the 6-week index trial NCT00621270 and showed no benefit over placebo on HAM-A or HAM-D in the overall population. It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. I found no human data on CNS exposure, choline-transporter engagement or any downstream cholinergic biomarker. That means a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The sponsor reported a signal in a post hoc subgroup with MDD plus GAD, which points to population heterogeneity (secondary F3). The company apparently then shut down. The press release was found only as a forum repost.

In the index trial NCT01091116, intra-articular fasitibant (MEN16132) did not beat placebo on WOMAC pain at any dose (p=0.53). The placebo arm improved strongly and as much as the drug arms (about -103 mm at week 3). In the follow-up trial NCT02205814, only the intermediate dose showed any separation from placebo. My searches found only rat and in vitro studies on B2 blockade in synovial fibroblasts and chondrocytes. I found no human data on drug levels in synovial fluid, B2 receptor occupancy, or downstream biomarkers. The only other B2 antagonist, icatibant, reached Phase 2 in knee OA without success, so F1b does not apply. With no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F7 is a secondary code because the placebo response was large.

In the index trial NCT00664352, Juvidex (M6P at 300 and 600 mmol/L, given intradermally plus topically or topically alone) did not shorten the time to complete wound closure at skin-graft donor sites. It did meet some secondary endpoints, such as better skin appearance. None of the sources found give any human measurement of M6P levels in the skin, binding to IGF2R (the M6P receptor), or blocking of TGF-β1/β2 activation. The earlier trials (NCT00984854, NCT00984516) looked at safety and scarring and posted no results. No sponsor statement explains the miss. Renovo then moved topical Juvidex toward a cosmetic product and planned to sell the program, so business reasons played a part afterwards (F8, secondary). Because engagement has no human data, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug or the target, so it is coded U.

Obatoclax did not significantly improve response rate, progression-free survival or overall survival in extensive-stage SCLC (PMID:24997137). It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not limit the dose. The only human evidence of target activity comes from a single-agent Phase 1 in CLL, which reported Bax/Bak activation in blood cells but no quantitative occupancy or inhibition. That study was in another disease, and I could not confirm the doses were comparable. In SCLC, the Phase 1b biomarker study (PMID:21472138) showed CK18 cell-death markers rising only in responders. The authors blamed suboptimal sampling times, so this is not a usable pathway readout. Preclinical work suggests some of the drug's killing does not go through BCL-2 family proteins (PMID:21368880). Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here. I could not fetch the full papers, so the evidence is thin.

In older AML patients, single-agent obatoclax produced no complete responses (NCT00684918/PMID:25285531). Neurologic DLTs at 30 mg/day capped the 3-hour dose at 20 mg/day. The bundle has no AML pharmacokinetic, occupancy or target-binding data. The only human pharmacodynamic evidence comes from a CLL phase 1 published before the index trial. It showed Bax/Bak activation in blood mononuclear cells and exposure-related apoptosis markers, but no measure of how fully the target was engaged. 'Pathway' is graded inferred_adequate only loosely, from that CLL Bax/Bak signal; it was not shown in AML. No same-target drug in the bundle has succeeded in AML, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement is unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter. The tolerability cap makes F1a possible.

PF-04523655 is an siRNA injected into the eye. The only human pharmacokinetic data come from the Phase 1 wet AMD study (NCT00725686, PMC3420041), which measured low, short-lived drug levels in plasma. No data show drug levels in the retina or vitreous, the site of action. No human study measured RTP801 (DDIT4) knockdown or a downstream biomarker. Evidence of target knockdown comes only from rats and cell lines (PMID:24458146, 22304497). In DEGAS (NCT00701181, PMID:23074206), benefit showed a dose-related trend but the trial stopped early for futility. Doses were not limited by tolerability, as Phase 1 found no dose-limiting toxicities up to 3 mg. The index trial posted no results, and no sponsor statement explains why the program stopped. No other drug on this target exists for comparison. Because target engagement in humans is unmeasured, the code is U.

No human data show that PF-655 knocked down RTP801/DDIT4 in the retina. The Phase 1 study (PMID:22627477) measured only safety and plasma PK; plasma levels after intravitreal injection do not show retinal exposure. Knockdown was shown only in rats, rabbits and cell lines (PMID:24458146, PMID:22304497; IOVS abstract), which do not count. In MONET (NCT00713518/PMID:22683252), PF monotherapy did worse than ranibizumab. The PF+ranibizumab combination was numerically better but not significantly so, and the authors call the study underpowered (F7 secondary). Tolerability did not cap the dose. With no human evidence of engagement, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Human exposure is well characterized (PMID:20386017). Before the index trial started, single doses in healthy volunteers produced dose-dependent ex vivo inhibition of lymphocyte proliferation and IL-2 mRNA (PMID:18688284). At 400 mg, IL-2 mRNA fell 90% (PMID:20386017), so engagement looks adequate, though it was measured only in healthy subjects. In psoriasis patients the same paper reported a 2-week PASI fall of up to 69%, histologic improvement and fewer p40+ dermal cells, a pathway signal. Through the same T-cell mechanism, the drug matched MPA in kidney transplant (PMID:23668931, NCT01064791). No dose cap from tolerability is shown in psoriasis. The index dose-finding trial posted no results and gave no stop reason, so F2 is the best fit but rests on thin evidence.

The index trial NCT00796484 was a Phase 1 safety, MTD and PK study in solid tumors. It posted no results and was terminated by 'sponsor decision', so it was not an efficacy test of XL888 in colorectal cancer (F9). Pillar evidence comes later and from another disease. In melanoma (PMID:29674508, 2018), PBMC HSP70 induction at XL888 doses ≥45 mg shows engagement, which also implies systemic exposure, and intratumoral HSP client proteins were modulated. In CRC, the pembrolizumab combination (NCT03095781, PMID:40079916) showed immune modulation but no direct HSP90 engagement and no objective responses. A business-driven stop (F8) is possible, but the unspecified sponsor decision does not establish it.

The index trial NCT00796484 was a Phase 1 safety, MTD and PK study in solid tumors. It was terminated for an unspecified 'Sponsor decision' and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of XL888 (F9). A business or strategic stop is possible but not documented (F8 secondary). Pillars: no human PK data appear in the bundle. HSP90 engagement was shown in melanoma patients (PMID:29674508, published 2018, long after the 2008 index start): PBMC HSP70 rose at doses of 45 mg or more, and intratumoral client proteins (ERBB3, BAD) were modulated. Engagement was not shown in pancreatic cancer. A pembrolizumab combination in pancreatic and colorectal cancer (NCT03095781) reported only RP2D and safety data.

The ASH 2015 Phase I report for NCT02040506 covered 19 patients with relapsed or refractory AML. It reported pharmacokinetics in all patients, with target-mediated drug disposition below 10 mg/kg. At the MTD of 10 mg/kg weekly, trough CD98 receptor occupancy started at 50 to over 90% and stayed above 90% after 4 to 8 weeks. At 15 and 20 mg/kg, occupancy was above 90% from the first dose. This means exposure and engagement were adequate in AML patients, and the tolerability limit (first-dose DLTs above 10 mg/kg) still allowed near-saturating occupancy, so the dose was not limited. No downstream pathway biomarker was found. The program went no further, which fits a target that does not drive the disease as tested (F2). The reason was not stated and no efficacy data were retrieved, so confidence is only medium.

The index trial NCT02944162 is a small (n=10) Phase 1/2 study. Its only primary outcome is adverse events, and it is classified as not_efficacy. Its status is unknown, with no stop reason and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug and no failed efficacy readout is shown (F9). The bundle has no human data on CAR-NK persistence, exposure, CD33 engagement or blast depletion, and no PubMed abstracts. A later Phase 1 trial (NCT05008575) also has unknown status. Gemtuzumab ozogamicin is approved on CD33, but only for APL. Because engagement is no_human_data, U is listed as a secondary code. The thin evidence keeps confidence low.

In RA patients on methotrexate, spebrutinib 375 mg/day gave a median peripheral BTK occupancy of 83%. It also significantly reduced CXCL13, MIP-1β and CTX-I and shifted B-cell subsets (PMID:31721017), so engagement and pathway were adequate in this disease. That evidence came from the index trial itself, published in 2020; healthy-volunteer occupancy was shown earlier (PMID:23709115). ACR20 at week 4 was 41.7% vs 21.7%, nearly double, but P=0.25 with only 47 patients. The authors call it a small mechanistic study. Adverse events were comparable between arms, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The 4-week, underpowered design could not answer the efficacy question (F7). Lack of benefit despite engagement (F2) and the short duration (F4) are secondary possibilities.

The index trial (NCT01090492) gave a mixed result. 20 mg beat placebo on Raynaud's Condition Score in primary Raynaud's (p=0.0057), but not in secondary Raynaud's (p=0.63), and 4 mg was negative in both strata. Benefit was confined to a subtype, consistent with F3. Plasma exposure at 20 mg was shown in healthy volunteers (Cmax ~1140 ng/mL; NCT02319148), but only after the index trial began. Engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred adequate because PF-00489791 met its UACR endpoint in diabetic nephropathy (NCT01200394), a systemic PDE5 effect, though dose comparability is unclear. The dose-responsive signal in primary Raynaud's also suggests the mechanism was engaged. No pathway biomarker was measured. No tolerability cap was seen. Small arms (n=34–47) may have limited power (F7).

In index trial NCT00599638, adding PF-00489791 to pregabalin gave no benefit over pregabalin alone (difference 0.08, p=0.39). Pregabalin itself beat placebo, so the trial could detect an effect. Outside the bundle, a hypertension trial (NCT00422461; Hypertension journal) showed a systemic effect: plasma cGMP rose and blood pressure fell at 20/40 mg. In NCT01200394, the drug also lowered UACR in diabetic nephropathy. That supports systemic PDE5 inhibition with downstream effects, which points to F2. Confidence is low: no one measured engagement in patients with postherpetic neuralgia or in nerve or spinal tissue. The trial's dose and how much drug reached the nervous system are also unknown, and the engagement data were published after the index trial started.

Xenon was given at anesthetic concentrations (50–70%). Its anesthetic effect is attributed to NMDA antagonism (PMID:23762640). In NCT00919126, registered before the index trial, it met an anesthetic-efficacy endpoint (significantly less propofol needed). Brain uptake is documented (PMID:33458859). Exposure, engagement and the functional CNS effect are therefore inferred adequate, though not measured directly in delirium patients. Even so, xenon did not reduce postoperative delirium versus sevoflurane in HIPELD (9.7% vs 13.6%, P=0.33; NCT01199276/PMID:29397119). A cardiac-surgery RCT gave the same null result (PMID:32005514), and neural injury biomarkers were not reduced either (PMID:34472497). This points to the mechanism not preventing delirium. Secondary F7: delirium incidence in HIPELD was low, which may have limited power.

Intranasal SB-705498 12 mg achieved estimated nasal-tissue TRPV1 occupancy above 80%. In non-allergic rhinitis patients, it markedly reduced capsaicin-provoked symptoms, a 2–4-fold capsaicin potency shift (PMID:23909699; capsaicin challenge NCT00731250, registered 2008, before the index trial). Capsaicin-induced nasal symptoms were also inhibited in allergic rhinitis patients (PMID:21951314). PK supported the dosing regimen and the drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, the index allergen-chamber trial showed no TNSS benefit alone or added to fluticasone (NCT01424397, PMID:23735181). The cold-dry-air NAR trial also failed (NCT01424514, PMID:24472402). The authors explicitly attribute the failure to TRPV1 not driving symptoms (redundancy in symptom pathways) despite engagement.

Index trial NCT02691182 was an open-label extension stopped because the program lacked efficacy. The Phase 3 trials CHIME 1 (NCT02618408, 36 mg p=0.09) and CHIME 2 (NCT02618434, -51.6% vs -54.1% on placebo) both missed. Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up human D2 occupancy, prolactin or other pharmacodynamic data for SPN-810. The only engagement data are in vitro (PMID:30538587) or from mice (PMID:26327279). The Phase 2b result was non-monotonic, with the high dose inactive (PMID:32338106), and tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. Supernus blamed rising variability after the interim analysis, and placebo response was high, which points to a possible trial-design problem (F7). With no human engagement evidence, these data cannot separate a drug that did not engage D2 from a mechanism that does not drive impulsive aggression, so the code is U.

In the first-in-human trial (NCT01168752), plasma levels of Debio 0932 and its active metabolite rose with dose and reached steady state. The drug was well tolerated, and the recommended phase 2 dose was 1000 mg once daily, so the dose was not limited by toxicity. No source shows direct target engagement in humans, such as HSP90 client-protein loss in tumour. The downstream marker, HSP70 induction in blood cells (PBMCs), showed only a trend, and the investigators said its meaning was unclear, so the pathway pillar was not convincingly shown. The NSCLC combination trial (NCT01714037) was terminated, and none of the sources found gives a reason or results. No other HSP90 inhibitor succeeded in NSCLC, so F1b does not apply. With no engagement evidence, the outcome is indeterminate (U). F1a is a possible secondary code because the pharmacodynamic signal was weak.

UISH001 (BTL-UI, from Beech Tree Labs) has no recorded target or mechanism. In the index trial NCT01340066, it showed no benefit over placebo: 61.7% vs 60.6% of participants had at least a 30% drop in leakage events (p=.92). The search found no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects, no PK/PD or biomarker reports, and no sponsor statement on why the program failed. Patsnap lists only that the program was discontinued at Phase 1/2. Since engagement is unknown, the evidence cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The high placebo response might point to trial-design problems (F7), but no source says so.

UISH001 is a Beech Tree Labs small molecule. No target or mechanism is recorded for it (Patsnap lists the target as '-'). In the index trial NCT01340066, the share of patients whose leakage events fell by at least 30% was the same on drug and placebo (61.7% vs 60.6%, p=.92), and the placebo response was high. My search found no human data on exposure, target engagement or pharmacodynamics. There are also no other trials, no other drugs on the same target and no PubMed abstracts. Patsnap lists the program as discontinued. Because no target is known and engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00981240 was a Phase 1 dose escalation with safety and PK endpoints, not an efficacy test. The published report (PMID:24794806) states the sponsor stopped the study before reaching the MTD because drug exposure was unpredictable. Toxicity was not the cause: there were no drug-specific adverse events. Human exposure was therefore unreliable, and no human target engagement (Src/Lyn phosphorylation) or pathway data are shown. STAT5 and Src inhibition appear only in vitro, ex vivo and in animals (PMID:23121564). The mechanism was never properly tested, which fits F1a through inadequate exposure. F9 applies secondarily because the trial was not an efficacy readout, and F6 because the failure was a molecule-specific pharmacokinetic liability.

Plasma exposure rose with dose (25–800 mg, Cmax ~380 ng/mL) and doses were well tolerated with no SAEs (NCT01119846), so dose was not limited. In T2D patients, GSK263 raised total PYY about five-fold, which shows functional GPR119 activation in L-cells (PMID:24699248). The expected incretin and insulin effects did not follow: GLP-1, GIP, insulin, C-peptide, glucagon and glucose were unchanged, both alone and with metformin (NCT01128621). The authors conclude it did not improve glucose control. This fits F2: the target was engaged without glycemic benefit. The index trial was a PK/PD study, not a formal efficacy test (F9). Rat data suggesting low intrinsic activity (PMID:30217957) hint at F1a but are not human evidence. Engagement evidence was published after the index trial started.

The index trial NCT01218204 was an exploratory safety/PK/PD study with descriptive co-primary outcomes and no hypothesis-tested efficacy endpoint. Lipid results are not shown in the bundle, and it was classified not_efficacy, so this was not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). Target engagement was shown in T2D patients, not dyslipidaemia: GSK263 raised post-meal PYY about fivefold at 300 mg BID (PMID:24699248; NCT01119846 and NCT01128621, started 2009). However, GLP-1, GIP, glucose and insulin were unchanged. No tolerability cap was seen; there were no SAEs at 800 mg. If the lipid readout was the reason for stopping, the evidence would point to F2 (target engaged, no benefit), but the bundle does not show that result.

The HCC randomized phase 2 (300 mg weekly plus sorafenib) gave only a modest, non-significant PFS gain (4.0 vs 2.6 months) in 48 evaluable patients (PMID:24977690). Plasma exposure rose with dose in phase 1 (PMID:19237630). In solid-tumour patients, however, XIAP mRNA suppression in blood cells was only 21% at maximum, which is partial knockdown. Robust knockdown (42-100%) was shown only in circulating AML blasts at 350 mg/m² (PMID:20938744), a different disease and compartment. No tumour-tissue or HCC engagement data exist, so the mechanism was likely not adequately tested. The small open-label design also limits conclusions (F7). Because tissue engagement was never measured, U remains plausible.

SK-PC-B70M is a saponin-enriched fraction from the root of Pulsatilla koreana. It has no defined molecular target; Synapse loosely lists it as an 'APP modulator'. The only mechanistic evidence comes from animals and cells: Aβ was lowered in Tg2576 mice (PMID:19401163), and the drug showed antioxidant effects in a mouse model of ALS (PMID:20971081). Neither counts as human evidence. I found no human pharmacokinetics, brain penetration, target engagement or biomarker data. The index Phase 3 trial (NCT01249196) posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in Alzheimer disease, so the code is U.

Exposure was dose-proportional in T2D patients (PMID:20336066), and exposure was confirmed in AleCardio itself (PMID:31468659). Engagement of PPARα and PPARγ and the downstream pathway were shown in T2D patients before the index trial. Treatment produced dose-dependent HbA1c, glucose, insulin-resistance and lipid changes, with balanced α/γ effects (PMID:19515415, PMID:20336066). In AleCardio the 150 µg dose moved HbA1c and adiponectin (PMID:31468659). Despite this, MACE was unchanged (HR 0.96, P=.57) and the DSMB stopped the trial for futility (NCT01042769, PMID:24682069). ALEPREVENT likewise concluded the class holds little promise for CV benefit (PMID:26093872). So the mechanism does not reduce CV events as tested. Expected PPAR class toxicities also added harm without offsetting benefit: renal dysfunction, heart failure, edema and hypoglycemia (PMID:20837369, PMID:26093872), hence secondary F5.

The index trial NCT01668524 was a 12-subject open-label dose-ranging study whose primary outcome was ocular safety and tolerability (hyperemia, irritation, vital signs), classified not_efficacy. It was not an efficacy test of ATS907, so F9 fits best. No results were posted, and the bundle has no Phase 1 results or PubMed data. Exposure, engagement and pathway (e.g., IOP lowering) are all no_human_data, which is why U is listed as a secondary code. Netarsudil, another ROCK inhibitor, is FDA-approved for open-angle glaucoma, so the target is clinically valid. If the program's discontinuation reflects an efficacy problem in NCT01520116, whose outcome is unknown, it would point to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The bundle gives no stated stop reason.

The index trial NCT01668524 was a 12-subject open-label dose-ranging study. Its primary outcome was only ocular safety and tolerability (hyperemia, irritation, vital signs) over 3 weeks, and it is classified not_efficacy. It therefore was not an efficacy test of ATS907, which fits F9. No results are posted for it. The earlier efficacy trial NCT01520116 has unknown status and no outcome. The bundle contains no human data on exposure, ROCK engagement or pathway effect, and no PubMed abstracts. The other ROCK inhibitors listed reached only phase 2, so F1b does not apply. If the program in fact failed on efficacy, the lack of engagement data would make it indeterminate (U). The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

In the Phase 2 RCC trial (PMID:24242861), AS1411 at 40 mg/kg/day by 4-day infusion gave 1 response in 35 patients (2.9%). Toxicity was low, so the dose was not capped. A Phase 1 PK study (NCT00881244, AACR 2007 abstract) measured plasma levels in 13 patients, but the pages I could read give no concentrations against the roughly 5 µM in vitro IC50. I found no human data on nucleolin binding, tumour uptake or a downstream biomarker. PMID:29218153 even questions whether nucleolin drives the drug's activity. The investigators said activity was minimal in unselected patients and pointed to the single responder's mTOR/FGFR2 mutations as a possible predictive biomarker (secondary F3). Since engagement was never measured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The Phase 3 trial (NCT01786395) used 0.15% eye drops twice daily for 52 weeks and missed its primary endpoint, central retinal sensitivity versus placebo. The company still said the drug worked and pointed to VFQ-25 and change from baseline. A post-hoc subanalysis found benefit only in less advanced patients (HFA MD of -15 dB or better), which supports F3 as a secondary code. No source gives human retinal drug levels or a measure of BK-channel (KCNMA1) activation. BK mediation is shown only in vitro (PMID:22219651). The fundus blood-flow increases seen in humans (PMID:11853711, 24868583) are not tied to BK channels. Engagement therefore has no human data, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, and the code is U.

ST101's target is not well defined. Preclinical papers propose several mechanisms: a T-type calcium channel enhancer (PMID:22251222), an inducer of a new APP cleavage (PMID:21416488) and an acetylcholine release agent. All of that evidence comes from animal or in vitro work. No human data on CNS exposure, target engagement or a downstream biomarker were found. Results of the monotherapy index trial (NCT00842673) were never posted or published, and Alzforum lists Alzheimer disease as inactive. The companion add-on trial with donepezil (NCT00842816/PMID:26402011) showed only weak trends with no significant safety concerns, so toxicity was not the reason. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in Alzheimer disease, so the code is U.

Traumeel is a homeopathic combination with no recorded target, so no human exposure, engagement or pathway evidence exists in bursitis. The available human biomarker studies are ex vivo neutrophil assays (PMID:21525811) and a muscle-damage study in healthy subjects (PMID:27478305), and none uses a defined target. The index trial NCT01702233 was designed as a non-inferiority comparison against dexamethasone 8 mg (PMID:25649543). Pain improved in both arms, but less with Traumeel (-18.7 vs -27.2 mm), so the trial apparently missed non-inferiority against an active drug. The margin is not reported. The placebo comparison is not posted, so efficacy against saline is untested here. This fits F9. Because engagement is no_human_data, U also applies.

Traumeel is a homeopathic combination product with no recorded molecular target, so exposure, engagement and pathway cannot be assessed. The bundle has no human target-engagement data, and the ex vivo neutrophil assays (PMID:21525811) do not count. The index trial NCT01702233 used a non-inferiority comparison against dexamethasone 8 mg as its primary analysis (PMID:25649543). Pain VAS improvement favoured dexamethasone (-27.2 vs -18.7, difference 13 mm). This reads as a missed non-inferiority margin against an active drug, which fits F9. However, the margin is not reported and no placebo comparison is posted, so the reading is uncertain. Because engagement has no human data, U also applies. A related knee osteoarthritis trial met its endpoint versus placebo (NCT01887678).

The evidence conflicts, so confidence is low. A 2008 first-in-human abstract (NCT00298675) reported over 50% PARP inhibition in blood cells after one dose and at least 80% after repeated doses. This came from patients with mixed solid tumours, not NSCLC. Later sources say iniparib is not a true PARP inhibitor, and PMID:27841728 calls it inactive against PARP, though that is mouse data. I rated engagement inadequate: the mechanism was probably never tested, which points to F1a. If the blood-cell data are taken at face value, F2 applies instead. Iniparib also failed in NSCLC phase 2 (NCT01086254) and TNBC phase 3 (NCT00938652). Sanofi stopped development in 2013 after the squamous NSCLC phase 3 failed. No pathway biomarker data were found.

The index GOG trial (NCT00687687, PMID:22634397) reported 4 of 17 responses with iniparib plus paclitaxel-carboplatin, short of the 8 needed to proceed to stage two. The bundle contains no human pharmacokinetic, PARP-inhibition or PAR-biomarker data, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Mouse PET data (PMID:27841728) describe iniparib as having no PARP inhibitory activity, which strongly suggests the molecule, not the target, failed. Approved PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib) support F1b as a secondary code. However, animal data cannot set a pillar, and no PARP inhibitor is shown to have succeeded in uterine carcinosarcoma itself; niraparib in uterine sarcoma only reached phase 3 with no outcome given. Under the rules this is U, with F1b likely.

The Phase 3 trial of gemcitabine/carboplatin ± iniparib in mTNBC missed its OS and PFS coprimary endpoints (PMID:25349301). Plasma PK was measured in humans; the drug cleared rapidly, with a half-life under 1 h (PMID:31172407). The bundle has no human data on PARP engagement or pathway effects. A mouse PET study describes iniparib as having no PARP inhibitory activity and shows no reduction in the PARP tracer, unlike olaparib (PMID:27841728). The ovarian cancer authors also describe the activity as attributable to gemcitabine/carboplatin (PMID:36718018). Other PARP inhibitors, olaparib and talazoparib, are FDA-approved in breast cancer and TNBC. This points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The second/third-line subgroup signal is secondary (F3).

Iniparib monotherapy (8 mg/kg IV twice weekly) gave no responses in 12 gBRCA ovarian cancer patients (NCT00677079, PMID:26745694). The doses were tolerable, mostly grade 1-2 AEs, so the dose was not capped. The bundle has no human PK, PARP engagement or pathway data. In mice, iniparib did not reduce PARP-PET signal and is described as having no PARP inhibitory activity (PMID:27841728). Later authors call it only 'thought to have' PARP activity and attribute its combination responses to gemcitabine-carboplatin (PMID:36718018). Other PARP1 inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib) are FDA-approved in ovarian cancer. So the failure reflects the molecule, not the target (F1b). U is secondary because human engagement was never measured.

disease: metastatic malignant neoplasm in the brain
rationale: The index trial (NCT01173497, iniparib plus chemotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer brain metastases) posted no results. I found no human data on iniparib's brain or CSF levels, PARP inhibition, or PAR biomarkers. The sources strongly suggest the drug never truly inhibited PARP. In vitro work (Liu 2012, Clin Cancer Res) shows it modifies cysteine-containing proteins nonselectively and is 'not a bona fide PARP inhibitor'. In mice, PARP PET (PMID:27841728) showed no effect on the tracer signal, and the glioma trial record (NCT00687765) says the mechanism is unclear. These are non-human data, so the engagement pillars stay no_human_data and the primary code is U. F1b is a possible secondary code because other PARP inhibitors such as olaparib and niraparib are in late-stage brain-metastasis trials, although none has been shown to succeed in this disease.

A PET study in AD patients and elderly controls (NCT01701089, registered Sept 2012, before the index start; PMID:27633250) showed brain penetration and near-maximal (~80-90%) brain MAO-B inhibition at 1 mg daily. Both index doses (1 and 5 mg) therefore achieved adequate engagement, and tolerability was placebo-like, so the dose was not limited. Despite this, the 52-week trial missed ADAS-Cog11 and its secondary endpoints (PMID:28550255). No human downstream biomarker (ROS, astrogliosis) was reported. With engagement confirmed, the failure points to MAO-B inhibition not driving cognitive decline in moderate AD. Post hoc benefit in behaviorally impaired patients suggests a possible subgroup effect, so F3 is secondary.

Human PET in Alzheimer's patients and elderly controls (PMID:27633250) shows sembragiline crosses into the brain. At ≥1 mg daily it gives near-maximal (~80-90%) brain MAO-B inhibition, so exposure and engagement were adequate in humans. This evidence comes from a non-smoking population and was published in 2017, well after the 2008 index trial. The bundle does not give the dose used in the smoking trials, so whether they matched the engaging dose is uncertain. No pathway biomarker was reported. The drug was well tolerated (NCT01677754), so dose was not limited. The index trial (NCT00622752) and NCT00738595 posted no results. With the target engaged and no benefit, F2 is the best fit, but the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT00656357 was a small (n=20) inpatient Phase 1/2 safety and interaction study. Its primary outcome was the hemodynamic and subjective effects of cocaine challenge during ascending SYN117 doses. It is classified not_efficacy, with no stop reason and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of nepicastat. The bundle contains no human evidence of exposure, DBH inhibition, or norepinephrine lowering. Only animal data are available: NE reduction and blocked reinstatement in rats (PMID:20736996), no effect on reinstatement in monkeys (PMID:24817036), and in vitro potency (PMID:25641750). If this is treated as an efficacy failure, engagement is no_human_data and the outcome would be indeterminate (U).

Index trial NCT00818129 is a Phase 1 single- and multiple-ascending-dose study in healthy Japanese volunteers. Its endpoints were safety and PK, so it did not test efficacy (F9). AZD7295/A-831 is an HCV NS5A inhibitor. A review (PMC3949698) reports human plasma levels: at 350 mg bid, Ctrough was 145.5 ng/mL, against a genotype 1b replicon EC50 of 7 nM, so systemic exposure looks adequate. That review cites an EASL 2010 multiple-ascending-dose study in genotype 1 and 3 patients, but I could not find any viral-load data on the retrieved pages. Engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. The review says the 1a replicon EC50 was weak and the compound's 'status remains unknown'. No source gives a reason the program stopped.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The index trial (NCT01040832) gave 0.32 mg/kg subcutaneously each week. It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. It showed no benefit: PFS HR 1.1 and the same response rate in both arms. The NSCLC phase 1b paper (PMC11028443, NCT00633529) says 0.32 mg/kg gave maximal blood IL-12, IL-6 and IFN-alpha responses and a maximal lymphocyte effect in an earlier phase 1 in refractory solid tumours. That supports TLR9 engagement and pathway activation at the index dose. The caveats are that these data are 'data on file', were not measured in HNSCC, and the earlier trial's timing is inferred, not dated. No drug levels were reported; exposure is inferred from the systemic cytokine response. Investigators reported no incremental efficacy, so F2 is the best fit. The sponsor later dropped the drug for portfolio reasons and safety concerns with platinum combinations.

In the index trial (NCT00784875), LY2624803 1 mg and 3 mg gave 30 and 37 min total-sleep-time gains versus 23 min on placebo and 51 min on zolpidem. No statistics were posted. Plasma PK was measured in healthy subjects (NCT01236105), but brain penetration, H1/5-HT2A receptor occupancy and any downstream biomarker were never measured in humans. The Japanese transient-insomnia study (NCT01784614) showed dose-dependent WASO reduction. That is a clinical sleep effect, not direct engagement data. Other H1-targeting drugs, doxepin and diphenhydramine, are FDA-approved for insomnia, so the target is validated. With no evidence that this molecule engaged adequately, F1b fits best. The thin bundle also leaves U plausible.

Pagibaximab, an anti-lipoteichoic acid mAb, produced dose-related serum anti-LTA levels (peaks 88–259 µg/mL), a roughly 33-day half-life, and dose-related ex vivo opsonophagocytic killing of S. epidermidis (88–95%) in healthy adults at 3–10 mg/kg (PMID:19268719). That killing correlated with antibody levels, which supports exposure, target binding and the functional effect in humans. The phase 1 trial was registered in 2001, before the index trial. The neonatal PK/PD trials (NCT00631878, NCT00631800) posted no data in the bundle, so engagement in VLBW neonates is not shown. Tolerability was clean. Despite this, the index trial showed no reduction in staphylococcal sepsis (85/792 vs 79/787; NCT00646399), suggesting anti-LTA opsonization does not prevent neonatal staphylococcal sepsis. Confidence is low because engagement is shown only ex vivo in adults.

Anecortave acetate has no recorded molecular target. Its IOP-lowering mechanism is unknown, and the small pilot series themselves say the mechanism still needs to be worked out (PMID:18789793, PMID:20051887). The outflow-facility data come only from sheep (PMID:20212205). I found no human data on drug levels in the target tissue, target engagement or pathway effects. According to the reviews, the roughly 200-patient Phase 2 safety and efficacy study (one injection per patient) gave sustained but small IOP lowering, about 3.8 mmHg at the highest 60 mg dose. Alcon stopped development in July 2009 because the benefit was too small (MDPI review; Glaucoma Today). With engagement unmeasured and no target defined, nothing separates a drug that never engaged a relevant target from a mechanism that matters too little, so the code is U. The later dose-volume trial NCT00788541 was cancelled as a consequence of this decision.

The published report of the index trial, NCT01869959 (Gaich et al., Cell Metab 2013), treated obese patients with type 2 diabetes for 28 days at 3, 10 or 20 mg. It measured plasma exposure. FGF21-pathway markers responded in these patients: adiponectin and β-hydroxybutyrate rose, the share of high-molecular-weight adiponectin increased, and lipids, insulin and body weight improved. These markers show that receptor agonism worked (engagement inferred from pathway readouts; no direct occupancy assay exists for an agonist). Glucose fell only as a non-significant trend. Tolerability did not cap the dose: the 20 mg arm had 1 related serious adverse event. With the mechanism engaged but no glucose benefit, FGF21 agonism appears not to drive glycaemic control as tested (F2). The short 28-day duration is a possible secondary factor (F4). The engagement evidence was published in 2013, after the trial started.

BCT-100 is an arginase, so engagement means plasma arginine depletion. In melanoma and CRPC patients, weekly 2.7 mg/kg gave measured AUC and kept median arginine at the quantification limit with no DLTs (PMID:34287772), so exposure and engagement were adequate and the dose was not capped. The HCC index trial (NCT01092091) used the same dose, and arginine depletion was tracked in these patients (PMID:33856599), but all of this was published after the 2010 start. There was no tumour-level pathway readout. No responses were seen and TTP was 6 weeks. The sources tie the failure to patient selection: ASS-negative tumours had an OS of 35 vs 15 weeks for ASS-positive tumours, and ASS-negativity is proposed as a selection biomarker. This supports F3 with F2 secondary.

The phase 1 trial in melanoma and CRPC (NCT02285101, PMID:34287772) showed measurable PK (AUC about 20,000 h·µg/ml) and plasma arginine depleted to the lower limit of quantification at all doses. That is the target ligand lowered systemically, which counts as adequate engagement. There were no dose-limiting toxicities, so the dose was not capped. These data come from solid-tumour patients, not AML, and were published in 2021, after the index trial started. No human downstream biomarker of blast arginine starvation is in the bundle. The index AML trial (NCT02899286) posted no results and gave no stop reason. With arginine depletion achieved but no AML benefit shown, F2 is the best fit. Preclinical work links resistance to arginine-recycling enzyme expression in blasts (PMID:25710880), so patient-selection heterogeneity (F3) is also possible. The bundle is thin.

In healthy volunteers, 30 mg LY3023703 inhibited ex vivo LPS-stimulated PGE2 synthesis by 91–97%, comparable to celecoxib. It also raised prostacyclin by 115%, consistent with mPGES1 blockade (PMID:26351780, NCT01849055). This was not shown in pain patients, and the data were published after the index trial started. In dental pain (NCT01872910), LY3023703 was numerically worse than placebo (VAS difference +9.0 mm), while celecoxib was clearly effective (-34.6 mm). So despite near-complete PGE2 synthesis inhibition, the mechanism gave no acute analgesia: F2. A secondary concern is hepatotoxicity: one subject had aminotransferases at 10× ULN, and a later trial was terminated for safety findings (NCT01965782). This may also have contributed to stopping the program (F6).

In the index Phase 1 trial (NCT02269735), MK-2640 reached measurable plasma exposure, with clearance saturating at higher doses. It also acted on the insulin receptor: glucose infusion rate rose under clamp in healthy adults and in people with type 1 diabetes, though potency was about 25-fold lower than regular insulin (PMID:30125349). That covers exposure, engagement and pathway. The program's defining hypothesis was glucose-responsive, MRC1-mediated clearance, and it was not confirmed: no glucose-dependent change in clearance was shown, despite some glucose-dependent increase in glucose infusion rate. The concept did not translate even though the target was engaged, so F2. A model-informed strategy supported rapid decision-making (PMID:31889297). This was a PK/PD study rather than a classic efficacy trial, hence F9 as secondary.

Bucindolol reached plasma and blocked beta-adrenoceptors in humans: it blunted exercise tachycardia and lowered exercise PEFR (PMID:2859199, PMID:2868744). In BEST it cut new-onset AF in HFrEF versus placebo, an effect reported before the index trial (PMID:24159564). In GENETIC-AF, 74.9% of bucindolol patients were at target dose, with lower sinus heart rates than baseline-type beta-blockade would predict and little bradycardia, so tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:35243434). The index trial tested superiority against metoprolol, another beta-1 blocker, and showed none (HR 1.02; NCT01970501). The authors attribute the miss to heterogeneity: patients with shorter AF/HF history whose AF did not precede HF benefited (HR 0.54), and they proposed these groups for phase 3 (PMID:31042551). This points to patient selection, with mechanism-level non-superiority as a secondary explanation.

The index trial NCT01640249 was a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose safety study in 18 healthy volunteers (1–40 mg). Its only primary endpoint was adverse events, and none were serious. The registry states it was terminated because of an 'unacceptable pharmacokinetic (PK) profile'. That makes exposure the stated failure: the molecule did not achieve acceptable human PK, so the mechanism was never tested. This supports F1a. Tolerability did not cap the dose. No target is recorded, and the bundle has no engagement or pathway data, no patient trials and no abstracts. The trial was not an efficacy test, so F9 also applies as a secondary code. Confidence is moderate because the bundle does not give PK details.

ASP3652 is a peripherally acting FAAH inhibitor. In healthy volunteers it was readily absorbed, and doses up to 300 mg bid (the top dose in the index trial) produced dose-dependent FAAH inhibition with a parallel rise in plasma anandamide (PMID:32681461; MAD NCT02243657 started 2009, before the index trial). Supratherapeutic single doses up to 1800 mg were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped (PMID:32715381). Engagement was not measured in IC/BPS patients or in bladder tissue. Despite adequate peripheral engagement and pathway effect, the 300 mg dose differed from placebo on pain by only 0.02 (PMID:32734461). A related CP/CPPS trial also stopped for futility (NCT01391338). This points to the target not driving disease. Hunner's-lesion phenotype heterogeneity was suggested as a secondary factor.

ASP3652 is a peripherally acting FAAH inhibitor. In healthy volunteers it reached good plasma exposure, inhibited FAAH dose-dependently and raised plasma anandamide (PMID:32681461, PMID:32456804). The MAD study (NCT02243657) started in 2009, before the index trial, and used 10-300 mg bid, matching the index doses of 25-300 mg bid. It was well tolerated up to 1800 mg single doses (PMID:32715381), so dose was not capped. The index trial stopped for futility on NIH-CPSI; the placebo response was large (-7.3 points) and no arm beat it (PMID:28254462). Micturition outcomes improved, which suggests the drug was active. FAAH inhibition does not appear to relieve CP/CPPS pain. Engagement was not measured in patients, and the high placebo response is a minor contributor.

The index trial NCT01733459 was a non-inferiority comparison of DLBS3233 100 mg with metformin-XR. HOMA-IR improved significantly from baseline in both arms, with comparable changes (-1.03 vs -1.19). The between-group difference was 0.16 with a wide CI (-1.24 to 1.56), so the authors called non-inferiority 'inconclusive' (PMID:39033369). The readout therefore missed only a non-inferiority conclusion against an active drug, not a placebo-controlled efficacy test, which fits F9. The wide CI suggests an imprecise, possibly underpowered trial (F7). DLBS3233 is a botanical fraction with no recorded target, and the bundle has no human exposure or engagement data. The later 3-arm trial (NCT01999686/PMID:37424700) showed no HOMA-IR change, which leaves mechanism adequacy indeterminate (U).

The index Phase 1 trial NCT01352884 posted no results, and the bundle has no human PK, PD-1 occupancy or pathway data for AMP-224. In refractory mCRC (NCT02298946, PMID:31351862), AMP-224 at 10 mg/kg with SBRT and cyclophosphamide was well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicity, so dose was not limited. It produced no objective responses and no clinical benefit. The only biomarker reported was loss of M2 macrophage polarization, which is not a direct PD-1 engagement readout. Other PD-1 agents (berahyaluronidase alfa, dostarlimab) are FDA-approved in colorectal and rectal cancer. Because the target works in this disease and engagement by this molecule was never shown, F1b fits. U applies secondarily, and patient selection (unselected refractory mCRC) may also have contributed (F3).

The index trial NCT00816686 was a Phase 1 safety/PK study in advanced RCC. It enrolled 7 subjects and was terminated because the study drug had to be re-formulated. No results were posted, and there is no efficacy readout of the drug. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data, and no PubMed abstracts. The stoppage was a formulation/development decision, not an efficacy failure, so F9 applies. Other ENPP3 agents (AGS-16C3F, AGS-16M8F, XmAb819) reached at most phase 2 and are not shown to have succeeded, so F1b does not apply. U is listed secondarily because the mechanism's relevance cannot be judged from the bundle.

Phase 1 studies in advanced solid tumours showed dose-linear plasma exposure. At the 150 mg BID RP2D used in NSCLC, inhibition of IGF1R/IR phosphorylation in PBMCs correlated with plasma concentration, and plasma IGF-1 rose as expected (PMID:25212606, PMID:25208878). The erlotinib combination study showed the same pharmacodynamic effects without drug interaction (PMID:26831715). These trials were registered before 2011, but engagement was not shown specifically in NSCLC tumours. Doses were tolerable at the MTD. Despite this, the sister NSCLC trial was inferior to erlotinib alone (PMID:27686971), and the adrenocortical phase 3 failed (NCT00924989). This points to IGF1R/INSR not driving disease as tested. The authors cite the lack of a predictive biomarker, so F3 is secondary. The index trial's own results are not in the bundle.

The index trial NCT01529684 was a 5-patient 14C mass-balance ADME study with only PK endpoints, so it was not an efficacy test of linsitinib (F9). Across the program, the pillars were measured in humans. Plasma exposure was dose-linear (PMID:25208878, PMID:25212606). IGF1R/IR phosphorylation inhibition correlated with plasma levels and was seen in PBMCs at the MTD. Plasma IGF-1 rose, indicating pathway inhibition (PMID:26831715). These data come from mixed solid tumors, not specifically colorectal cancer. Despite this, the colorectal combination trials showed no responses (PMID:25335932, PMID:30139840, NCT01016860), and the adrenocortical phase 3 missed overall survival (NCT00924989). The irinotecan trial report blames multiple negative IGF-1R trials in unselected populations for ending development (PMID:30139840). This supports F2 and F3 as secondary codes.

The Phase 3 trial of linsitinib 150 mg twice daily versus placebo in adrenocortical carcinoma showed no overall survival benefit (HR 0.94) and was unblinded for futility (PMID:25795408). At this recommended Phase 2 dose, Phase 1 studies in patients with solid tumours showed dose-linear pharmacokinetics and steady-state plasma exposure. They also showed inhibition of IGF1R/IR phosphorylation that correlated with plasma concentrations, plus a compensatory rise in plasma IGF-1 consistent with pathway inhibition (PMID:25212606, PMID:25208878, PMID:26831715). Those trials were registered before the index trial started. Engagement was measured in peripheral blood cells, not in adrenocortical tumours, and no tolerability cap on engagement is shown. With the target engaged and the pathway moved but no clinical benefit, IGF1R/IR does not appear to drive this disease as tested.

In Phase 1 solid-tumour patients, linsitinib showed dose-linear plasma exposure. At the MTDs (150 mg BID continuous; 600 mg intermittent), which are the schedules used in the index trial, IGF1R/IR phosphorylation fell in correlation with plasma levels and plasma IGF-1 rose (PMID:25212606, PMID:25208878, PMID:26831715). Engagement and pathway effect were therefore shown, though not in ovarian cancer patients. Those trials were registered in 2007, before the index trial started, but published later. Dose was not capped below engagement. In NCT00889382 neither schedule improved PFS, ORR or OS over paclitaxel alone (PMID:29454514). Linsitinib also failed in adrenocortical carcinoma and EGFR-mutant NSCLC (NCT00924989, PMID:27686971), and no IGF1R agent succeeded in ovarian cancer. This supports a target that does not drive the disease.

Index trial NCT01157377 tested AGN-214868 across a 120-fold dose range (500–60000 ng) in idiopathic OAB. It showed no dose-response and no separation from placebo in micturition episodes at Week 12. Serious adverse events were few and similar to placebo, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no primary target recorded, no Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts and no same-target comparators. There is therefore no human evidence of exposure, engagement or pathway effect. The postherpetic neuralgia trials NCT01129531 and NCT01678924 also failed and give no pillar data. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Senrebotase (AGN-214868), a protein with no recorded target, missed its primary pain endpoint in the index trial NCT01129531. At Week 12, pain change was -1.42 (3.25 μg) and -1.35 (16.25 μg) versus -1.27 for placebo. A follow-up PHN trial at higher doses up to 130 μg (NCT01678924) also failed and was terminated. An overactive bladder trial failed as well, with no dose-response (NCT01157377). The bundle has no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers, and no Phase 1 results or PubMed abstracts. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target irrelevant to PHN pain, so the failure is indeterminate.

AIR645, an inhaled antisense oligonucleotide against IL4R, failed an allergen-challenge FEV1 trial in mild atopic asthma (NCT00941577), with no results posted. Its Phase 1 (NCT00658749) posted no results, and the only abstract (PMID:20799138) is a conference report with no PK or knockdown data. All three pillars therefore have no human data. Another drug on the same target, dupilumab, is shown as FDA-approved for aspirin-induced respiratory disease, an asthma-related subtype, and for COPD. That suggests IL4R blockade can work in airway disease, which points to the molecule rather than the target. Because AIR645's engagement is wholly unmeasured, U remains a plausible alternative. The bundle is thin.

Golotimod (SCV-07) has no recorded primary target. SciClone describes it only loosely as an immunomodulator that may work through STAT3 inhibition and the TLR pathway. In the index trial (NCT00968357), patients took 0.1 or 1.0 mg/kg, and the drug was safe but missed the primary endpoint of a 2-log drop in viral load. Only 3 high-dose patients had a drop of more than 1 log. The sponsor said the trial tracked immune-activation biomarkers but released no data on drug levels, target engagement or those biomarkers, so all three pillars have no human data. The only pharmacology source (PMID:18619817) is a guinea pig study. SciClone stopped HCV development, pointing to the fast-changing HCV treatment landscape (secondary F8). The readout itself was still a failure, and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the primary code is U.

Exposure was adequate: in NSCLC patients, plasma AUC rose roughly in proportion to dose. A downstream vascular-disruption marker also moved: plasma 5-HIAA rose 116–204% at the doses used in phase 3 (PMID:21205086). The index trial and the second-line trial were terminated with no reason given and no results posted (NCT00662597, NCT00738387). Later sources explain the failure: DMXAA's antitumour effect in mice comes through mouse STING, but it does not bind or activate human STING (PMID:29288534 review; InvivoGen; LKT). That evidence comes from in vitro and structural work, not from measurements in patients, and it was published after the index trial started. On that basis I rated engagement inadequate, meaning the mechanism behind the preclinical results was never tested in humans (F1a). Confidence is only medium because no human engagement data exist; hence U as a secondary code.

In the index Phase 2 trial, MADRS showed no separation from placebo at 40 mg or 80 mg (PMID:30626911). For exposure, the Phase 1B study in patients with MDD showed plasma AUC rising with dose, nearly proportionally (PMID:26643541). No source reports CSF or brain levels. NSI-189 has no known molecular target, so engagement could not be measured, and no human pathway biomarker was found. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement unknown, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. A post-hoc analysis found a benefit only in moderately depressed patients (PMID:32722729), which supports F3 as a secondary code.

HP802-247 is a spray of allogeneic keratinocytes and fibroblasts with no recorded molecular target, so there is no receptor occupancy or target-inhibition data. In a Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (NCT01190865), donor cells were still detectable for only 1–2 weeks. That is not evidence of engagement, and no human biomarker shows a pathway effect. The index trial in Mohs surgery wounds (NCT01359735) enrolled only 8 patients, which is too few to test efficacy (F7). The drug's venous leg ulcer Phase 3 trials also failed. The sponsor's root-cause analysis ruled out trial design and pointed to variable quality of the product's cells, which suggests the product rather than the mechanism. However, adequate engagement was never shown or ruled out, so the cause stays indeterminate (U).

HP802-247 is a spray of allogeneic growth-arrested keratinocytes and fibroblasts in fibrin, and no molecular target is recorded. For exposure, the Phase 1 study NCT01190865 found donor-cell DNA in skin biopsy wounds of healthy volunteers: 3/3 at week 1, 1/3 at week 2, none afterwards. No human engagement or pathway biomarker was found, and the pharmacodynamic study NCT02154087 enrolled only one subject. Both Phase 3 trials, NCT01656889 and the index NCT01853384, showed no benefit over vehicle. The sponsor found no fault in trial design or execution. It blamed variable cell quality, meaning keratinocyte phenotype drift from ageing cell banks. That points to a product potency failure (F1a-like), but engagement was never measured, so U is the primary code.

HP802-247 is a spray-on mix of donor (allogeneic) fibroblasts and keratinocytes with no defined molecular target. No human target-engagement or pathway biomarker exists. The Phase 1 study NCT01190865 shows only that donor cells persisted in wounds for about 1–2 weeks. The index Mohs trial (NCT01359735) had 8 patients and could not answer the efficacy question, so F7 applies. Across the program, Phase 2 NCT00852995 was positive but the Phase 3 trials NCT01656889 and NCT01853384 failed, and the PD study NCT02154087 was stopped. Smith & Nephew's root-cause analysis blamed changes in the cells and batch-to-batch variability from aging cell banks. That points to the product, not the mechanism (F1a-like), but it is not human engagement data. So the primary code is U.

In the index Phase 1 trial (NCT01640873), 80 mg and 320 mg of MK-8655 for 16 days did not lower fasting plasma glucose versus placebo (LS mean difference -8.5 mg/dL, p=0.356). The posted oral glucose tolerance test results also showed no clear benefit. The drug was well tolerated, with no discontinuations or serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. My searches found no human data on exposure, receptor engagement, or insulin/incretin biomarkers, and no sponsor statement on why the program stopped. Fasiglifam, which acts on the same target, reached Phase 3, but the bundle does not show that it met a pivotal endpoint. Without engagement evidence, I can't tell whether MK-8655 failed to engage FFAR1 or whether the target doesn't matter. Indeterminate.

The index trial NCT00691808 in age-associated memory impairment registered only descriptive exposure, safety and compliance primary outcomes (days exposed, AEs, withdrawals, compliance). It was classified not_efficacy and its primary endpoint not_assessable, so it was not an efficacy test that failed. Tolerability was good: no serious AEs, only one withdrawal, and AE rates similar to placebo, so the dose was not capped. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, CNS penetration, SLC6A7 (proline transporter) engagement or biomarker data, no other trials of the drug, no other drugs on this target and no publications. Even if an efficacy failure were assumed, nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant target (U). No stop reason is given, so the evidence is thin.

In NCT00759395, 22 patients with anxious MDD took AZD2327 3 mg twice daily or placebo. It missed both primary endpoints: HAM-D p=0.39 and HAM-A p=0.15 (PMID:26728893). Plasma levels of the drug and a metabolite were measured, but delta opioid receptors are in the brain, and no brain or CSF levels were reported. Receptor occupancy could not be measured because no PET tracer for this receptor exists. The investigators used EEG as a stand-in, and it showed only a trend. VEGF fell, but the sources do not tie that to the receptor mechanism. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The trial was a small, underpowered pilot (F7). AZD7268, the other drug on this target, also stopped at Phase 2.

Index NCT01489826 was a dose-escalation trial in solid tumours that measured safety and DLTs. Exposure: in the brain-cancer Phase 1 (NCT01654497/PMID:33615223), systemic exposure rose with dose and dexanabinol reached 'appreciable' CSF levels, so the drug did reach the CNS. The dose was not capped below a needed level, since an RP2D of 28 mg/kg was set and tolerability was acceptable. No source in the bundle or found by search measured NMDA receptor occupancy, target inhibition or a downstream pathway biomarker in humans. The sources give 'limited antitumor activity' (21% stable disease) and no stated reason for stopping. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00920686 missed its primary endpoint (time to rescue medication, p=0.64 vs placebo). NXN-188 also failed in migraine without aura (NCT00959751). Phase 1 PK was studied in healthy volunteers at 2–800 mg (PMID:20171420), but the bundle shows no exposure levels, receptor occupancy, nNOS inhibition or downstream biomarker. Many 5-HT1B/1D agonists (sumatriptan, rizatriptan and others) are approved for migraine. That fits F1b: the target works, and nothing shows this molecule engaged adequately. PMID:29913885 adds that oral PK may be too slow for nNOS inhibition during aura, and that triptan agonism is ineffective when dosed in aura. That raises timing (F4) and trial-difficulty (F7) issues. Engagement is unmeasured, so U also applies.

In the index trial NCT00959751, 600 mg NXN-188 gave 2-hour headache relief in 42/80 patients versus 30/79 on placebo. This difference is not significant (about p=0.07). A sister trial in migraine with aura also missed its primary endpoint (NCT00920686). Human evidence is limited to healthy-volunteer plasma pharmacokinetics at 2–800 mg (PMID:20171420). This shows systemic exposure, but no 5-HT1B/1D receptor occupancy, nNOS inhibition or downstream biomarker was measured in humans. Many 5-HT1B/1D agonists (the triptans and dihydroergotamine) are FDA-approved for migraine, so the target is validated, and nothing shows this molecule engaged it adequately. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The trial was also modest in size with a borderline result (F7), and engagement data are absent (U).

Index trial NCT00945932 (1 mg once daily, 28 days) showed no FEV1 benefit over placebo. The authors call 1 mg 'suboptimal' (PMID:23991670) and note a moderate placebo response. No human PK, receptor-occupancy or cortisol-suppression data appear in the bundle, so exposure and engagement are no_human_data.
