The allergen-challenge trial (NCT00857857, 3 mg, primary met) and adenosine-challenge protection (PMID:25784273) show a proximal airway effect in asthma, so pathway is rated adequate. GR agonism is clinically validated in asthma by many approved inhaled corticosteroids. GW870086X is a partial GR agonist in vitro (PMID:25625944) and also failed in atopic dermatitis while the fluticasone propionate control succeeded (NCT01299610, PMID:25614148). Together this points to the molecule, not the target.

Topical GW870086 0.2% and 2% did not separate from placebo on TIS at Day 22 (p=0.48 and p=0.118). In the same trial, the GR-agonist positive control fluticasone propionate 0.05% did separate (p=0.011), and several GR agonists are approved in atopic eczema. This points to the molecule, not the target. The bundle has no human skin exposure, GR engagement or pathway data. Inhaled efficacy in an asthma allergen challenge (NCT00857857) is a different tissue compartment and route, so it cannot support inferred adequacy. Absence of skin thinning (PMID:25614148) is consistent with weak cutaneous GR activity. The trial was small (n=25) and showed a dose-dependent, non-significant trend, so underpowering (F7) may also have contributed.

I found no human evidence that ADL5747 reached or engaged the delta opioid receptor: no occupancy, PD or biomarker data, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the index trial NCT00979953, the active control (oxycodone CR 20 mg twice daily) also failed to beat placebo (-2.24 vs -2.20 on the NPRS pain scale). That means the trial could not tell an effective drug from an ineffective one. The sponsor blamed a high placebo response, which points to a design or execution failure (F7). ADL5747 was well tolerated at 150 mg twice daily, so the dose was not limited by side effects. Pfizer then ended the partnership, and the PHN trial NCT01058642 was terminated without a stated reason. Because engagement was never measured, whether the target itself matters remains undetermined (U as secondary code).

The index PHN trial, NCT01058642, was a 2-period crossover study testing ADL5747 150 mg twice daily against placebo and pregabalin. It was terminated after enrolling 41 participants. No reason was given and it posted no analyzable efficacy data. In osteoarthritis (NCT00979953), ADL5747 reduced pain less than placebo did. I found no human evidence on any of the three pillars: no measure of CNS or peripheral exposure, delta-opioid receptor occupancy, or a pharmacodynamic biomarker. Secondary sources say only that the drug 'passed phase I' and that the phase 2 pain endpoints were missed. Its delta-opioid effects are shown only in rodents. Because engagement has no human data, a molecule that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The early termination also suggests possible design or execution problems (F7).

The index trial NCT00623870 was a Phase 1 MTD and safety study, not an efficacy test. Its publication (PMID:26459177) reports adequate exposure, with twice-daily dosing raising exposure. In leukemic cells of AML patients it showed p53 stabilization and induction of p53 target genes, and 5 IWG responses among 30 AML patients at the MTD. These data postdate the 2008 start. Liposarcoma (PMID:23084521) and solid-tumor (PMID:26210682) studies also showed p53/p21/MIC-1 pathway activation. So the readout was not an efficacy failure. Development moved to the second-generation nutlin RG7388 (idasanutlin) because tolerability of the needed daily RG7112 dosing was poor (PMID:24812409). This suggests a molecule-specific tolerability limitation (F6 secondary).

The index trial NCT01958970 was a Phase 1/2 dose-finding study with an MTD primary endpoint plus 12-week lean body mass change. It is classified not_efficacy, posted no results and gave no stop reason, so the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout. In men on androgen deprivation (PMID:24971661), AMG 745 exposure rose linearly from 0.3 to 3 mg/kg. At 3 mg/kg, lean body mass rose 2.2% and fat mass fell, a downstream pathway effect in another population. No direct myostatin binding or neutralization was measured, and nothing was shown in hemodialysis patients with protein-energy wasting. Tolerability did not limit the dose. If this counted as an efficacy failure, engagement would be no_human_data and the code would be U.

NCT01098266 tested 0.8 µg/m2 weekly NGR-hTNF with best investigator choice and missed OS (HR 0.94). In Phase 1 studies, plasma PK was measured, and the 0.8 µg/m2 cohort was expanded specifically to show its vascular effect: DCE-MRI found an antivascular response in mixed solid tumours, not mesothelioma. That is a pathway signal. No study directly measured binding to CD13 or TNFR1. Soluble TNF-receptor shedding was not detected at doses of 0.8 µg/m2 or lower. The NGR015 investigators found a PFS benefit only in patients with a short treatment-free interval (rapidly progressing disease), which points to patient selection. Because engagement has no direct human data, U also applies.

Phase 1 studies in mixed solid tumours (NCT00419328, NCT00878111) showed plasma exposure rising with dose. Soluble TNF receptors were shed in plasma, but at higher doses this plateaued (≥25 µg/m² in one study) and did not change across high dose levels. Tumour DCE-MRI changes were not shown to be consistent. None of these sources confirm CD13 or TNFR1 engagement in tumour vessels of NSCLC patients at the low dose used in phase 2. The sponsor described the NSCLC trial (NCT00994097) as showing activity mainly in squamous histology and in patients on maintenance, which points to subgroup or selection effects (F3). Still, there are no tumour-level engagement data, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter. The related phase 3 mesothelioma trial also failed (NCT01098266).

The index trial NCT00989872 was a Phase 1 single ascending-dose study in healthy volunteers. It measured only safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics. It was not an efficacy test of EDP-322, so it was not an efficacy failure. The companion multiple-dose study NCT00990145 was also a healthy-volunteer safety study. Neither trial posted results, so the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. The only abstract, PMID:25182063, reports in vitro MICs against N. gonorrhoeae and notes that human PK/PD remained to be defined. No stated reason for stopping appears. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, engagement would be no_human_data, so U applies secondarily.

The index trial NCT00928343 was a first-in-human single-dose safety and tolerability study in 18 healthy volunteers. It had no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of GLPG0187 (F9). In the later solid-tumor study (NCT01313598, PMID:26792581), continuous IV infusion up to 400 mg/day gave dose-proportional PK with no DLTs, so the dose was not capped. Serum CTX fell at every dose, which the authors read as target engagement. Skin toxicity suggested cutaneous integrin inhibition. These data come from patients and were published after the index trial started. Single-agent treatment produced no tumor responses despite apparent engagement, which points to the mechanism not driving the tumors as tested (secondary F2). Engagement rests on an indirect marker, so confidence is medium.

In the Phase 1 trial in SLE patients (NCT00541749, PMID:22833362), PK was dose-proportional. IFN-regulated gene expression fell rapidly and stayed down at 3–10 mg/kg IV. This shows IFN-α neutralization in disease at doses comparable to the 750 mg IV used in ROSE. IFN-inducible proteins and autoantibodies did not change, so the pathway effect was partial. No dose-limiting toxicity occurred. ROSE (NCT00962832, PMID:26038091) missed BILAG and SRI overall and in ISM-High patients. Exploratory benefit (SRI, flares, steroid use) appeared only in ISM-Low patients, pointing to disease heterogeneity and patient selection (PMID:25861459). The review (PMID:27497254) contrasts ROSE's mandated immunosuppressant withdrawal with sifalimumab's positive Phase 2, suggesting design may also have contributed.

The index trial (NCT02361931, PMID:33504262) randomized only 20 DFU patients. Its primary endpoint, ≥75% closure, favored topical EPO numerically (6/10 vs 1/8, ~p≈0.06), and mean ulcer area was significantly smaller (p=0.023). The authors call topical EPO promising and report no treatment-related AEs. The miss looks like a small, underpowered trial unable to answer the question rather than a clear mechanism failure. No human data show EPO penetration or EPOR engagement in wound tissue. The systemic hematopoietic approvals use a different route and compartment, so they cannot support inferred adequacy. That leaves engagement no_human_data, so U is secondary. No stated stop reason is given.

The index Phase 2 trial NCT01544296 (42 patients, 2-week pain-intensity change) posted no results, and the bundle has no Phase 1 data, other trials or PubMed abstracts. Exposure, Nav1.7 engagement and pathway effects of KHK6188 are therefore all no_human_data. The bundle lists lidocaine, a drug on the same SCN9A target, as FDA-approved for postherpetic neuralgia. That suggests the target can deliver benefit in this disease, pointing to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). However, lidocaine is a non-selective sodium-channel blocker, so its success may not reflect Nav1.7 specifically. The bundle also does not even confirm the readout failed. U is therefore a close alternative, and confidence is low.

Phase 1 abstracts (NCT00955786) show dose-related plasma PK at doses up to 480 mg/m2 and good tolerability. This gives systemic exposure but no tumor drug levels. No human data show nucleolin/rDNA G-quadruplex disruption or rRNA synthesis inhibition. Planned PD measures (FDG-PET, circulating tumor cells) were never reported. The index Phase 2 trial in carcinoid/NET (NCT00780663) posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. The weekly-schedule Phase 1 (NCT00955292) was terminated because it 'presented no advantage', a PK/schedule issue, not toxicity. No other drug on this target is in the bundle. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT01038804; PMID 25547219), YM155 plus docetaxel did no better than docetaxel alone: median PFS was 8.4 vs 10.5 months (HR 1.53, p=0.176). The combination was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Circulating tumor cells were too few to compare. Phase 1 work established plasma PK, but no tumor drug levels were found. No human evidence showed survivin suppression in tumors. In NSCLC, pharmacodynamic markers did not track response (PMID 23857959). Later lab work suggests YM155 acts mainly by generating ROS, with survivin suppression only a secondary effect (PMID 34046628). Preclinical PET data show tumor uptake varies (PMID 30041149). No other survivin-targeting drug has succeeded in breast cancer. Since engagement was never measured in humans, a drug that did not engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01041222 was a first-in-human Phase 1 intrathecal dose-escalation study (0.15–3 mg). Its primary objective was safety, tolerability and PK, not efficacy. PMID:23541756 reports no dose-limiting toxicity and no drug-related serious adverse events, so the trial met its objective. It was not an efficacy failure. The bundle shows no human CSF or tissue exposure data, no SOD1 lowering, and no downstream biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The same target was later validated by tofersen, which is FDA-approved for SOD1-ALS. That suggests the program likely gave way to a different molecule (secondary F1b), but the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping.

The index trial NCT01162889 was a first-in-human single-ascending-dose safety and PK study in healthy volunteers, not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Pillars were shown in healthy subjects. PK was dose-proportional, though clearance was rapid and bioavailability about 30%. A single 60–120 mg IV dose maximally occupied IL-21R on circulating B cells through Day 42 (PMID:23913720). IL-21-induced pSTAT3 inhibition tracked receptor occupancy in dosed volunteers (PMID:23496892). There were no patient data, and this evidence was published after the 2010 start. Escalation was halted partly because more than 75% of subjects developed anti-drug antibodies, and hypersensitivity was dose-limiting at 300 mg SC (PMID:23913720, PMID:26400440). This molecule-specific immunogenicity supports F6 as secondary. It did not cap dosing below the levels that gave full occupancy.

In the index trial NCT00673465, SCH 497079 did not lower 24-hour plasma glucose versus placebo at week 4 (difference -4.4 mg/dL, p=0.53). Metformin, the active control, worked clearly (-53.9 mg/dL), so the assay itself was sensitive. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetics, H3 receptor occupancy or pathway biomarker data. The obesity Phase 2 trial NCT00642993 also missed its weight endpoint, but it shows nothing about target engagement. No other H3 antagonist succeeded in diabetes: pitolisant reached only Phase 1 in type 1 diabetes, so F1b does not apply. No serious adverse events were reported. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged H3 from an H3 mechanism that does not matter in diabetes, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00642993 missed its primary endpoint. Weight change at week 12 was -0.51 kg on SCH 497079 versus -0.92 kg on placebo (p=0.187). The only other trial, NCT00673465 in type 2 diabetes, reported a downstream glucose endpoint that also did not move (p=0.53). It reported no plasma exposure, brain penetration, H3 receptor occupancy or histamine pathway marker. With no human evidence of exposure or engagement, a drug that never engaged H3 cannot be told apart from an H3 mechanism that does not drive weight loss. No other H3 drug succeeded in obesity (betahistine reached only phase 2), so F1b does not apply. Indeterminate.

Cystine was tested as one ingredient of Pantovigar, an oral supplement, given with 2% minoxidil to women with female pattern hair loss (NCT01900041). The trial posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. No molecular target is recorded, and the bundle has no human data on cystine reaching the hair follicle, engaging a target, or moving a biomarker. The two related PubMed papers (PMID:39911983, PMID:36645365) test multi-ingredient supplements and contain no pharmacology data. My one search turned up only a minoxidil trial with no Pantovigar results. Nothing here separates a supplement that never acted from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the failure is indeterminate.

In NCT01900041, Merz tested Pantovigar (an oral keratin-containing supplement) added to 2% minoxidil against minoxidil alone in women with female pattern hair loss. The trial was open-label and randomised. No results were posted and no stop reason was given. The drug has no recorded molecular target. The bundle and my search found no human data on exposure at the hair follicle, on engagement of any target, or on any pathway biomarker. No other drug on the same target is listed. The PubMed abstracts are about keratin biology in general and do not cover this product. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a molecule that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, the code is U.

Aminobenzoic acid (PABA) was tested here as one ingredient of Pantovigar, an oral multi-ingredient hair supplement made by Merz. In the index trial (NCT01900041) it was added to 2% minoxidil in women with female pattern hair loss. The trial was open label and no results were posted. The drug has no recorded target. The bundle has no human data on PABA levels in hair follicles, on target engagement or on any pathway biomarker. The PubMed abstracts cover PABA as a tracer or chemical-biopsy agent, not as a hair-loss treatment. No sponsor statement explains why the program ended. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Index trial NCT00743483 was a small open-label single-arm study (n=9 evaluable, 170 mg TID for 5–6 days). CFA rose by a mean of 6.9 points, which was not significant (p=0.22). For an orally given replacement lipase, target engagement would mean lipolytic activity in the intestinal lumen. I found no human data on luminal enzyme activity, intraduodenal lipolysis or any other proximal marker. A review mentions a Phase 1 study in which adding rhBSSL let Creon doses be lowered, but it gives no data. Sobi's 2009 annual report says only that the endpoint was not met and gives no reason. Engagement is no_human_data, so the result is U. The tiny uncontrolled design suggests F7 as a secondary code. The preterm-infant trials also failed (NCT00659243, NCT01413581).

rhBSSL is an oral enzyme replacement, so it acts in the gut lumen. No human measurement of intraluminal lipase activity or fat hydrolysis appears in the bundle, so engagement is no_human_data. Phase 2 (NCT00659243; PMID 25222806) found better DHA/AA absorption but no change in total fat absorption, so the pathway evidence is mixed. Phase 3 LAIF (NCT01413581) measured no fat absorption. Growth velocity did not differ (difference 0.21 g/kg/day). The investigators said the reason is still unclear. They named two possible causes: better growth in the placebo arm than in phase 2 (F7), and a benefit seen only in SGA infants (F3). They found the product comparable to the phase 2 batch. Nothing here separates poor engagement from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the open-label, single-arm Phase 2 index trial (NCT00743483), 15 cystic fibrosis patients took oral rhBSSL 170 mg three times daily for 5–6 days. Fat absorption (CFA) rose by a mean of 6.9 points (p=0.22), which was not significant. Sobi's 2009 annual report says only that the study's primary objectives were not reached; it gives no reason. No source reports lipase activity in the human gut or any other measure of exposure or engagement. In preterm infants (NCT00659243), the drug improved growth but did not improve total fat absorption, so it cannot stand in for engagement here. The Phase 3 infant trial (NCT01413581) was stopped for futility. With engagement not measured, a drug that never worked can't be told apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter. F7 is listed as secondary because the trial was small, short and uncontrolled.

The index trial NCT01435720 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study of SNS01-T in relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies. Its only primary outcome was safety and tolerability at week 6, and it was classified as a not_efficacy endpoint. It has unknown status, no stated stop reason and no posted results. The bundle has no other trials, Phase 1 results, same-target comparators or PubMed abstracts, so there is no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test, F9 is the most direct code. U is listed as secondary because pillar data are entirely absent and nothing separates non-engagement from target irrelevance. The bundle is very thin.

Exposure was confirmed in all treated kidney recipients, with expected IgG1 PK and low ADA (PMID:29133549). No direct measure of target engagement, such as serum neutralizing activity, appears in the bundle. The 12-week viremia endpoint narrowly missed (45.8% vs 61.4%, P=0.100). However, 24-week viremia (P=0.040), time to viremia (HR 0.53, P=0.009) and CMV disease (3.4% vs 15.8%) all favored the drug, and tolerability was good (PMID:27872061). So the drug was active, and the miss reflects a small Phase 2a trial (n=116) underpowered for the primary endpoint. Patients with above-median exposure did better, and the authors used this to guide future dose selection. That suggests the dose may have been suboptimal (secondary F1a).

Code U: no human data show that cicletanine engaged NOS3. Exposure: healthy-volunteer studies show plasma pharmacokinetics are linear from 50 to 300 mg (PMID:1526688, PMID:1820874, PMID:3416722). Engagement: no human study measured eNOS activation, NO output or cGMP rise in PAH or at the trial doses. In PMID:1965645 the drug left plasma cGMP unchanged at 50–150 mg, but that study did not test eNOS directly. The rise in urinary prostacyclin metabolites (PMID:3867354, PMID:2514674) is a separate pathway, not NOS3 engagement. The index trial (ERS 2012 abstract) missed its endpoint: the combined 300 mg group gained a placebo-adjusted +19.4 m in 6-minute walk distance (p=0.50), and pulmonary vascular resistance did not improve in any clinically relevant way. Nothing in the evidence separates a drug that never engaged eNOS from a target that does not matter in PAH.

PMBL has no single molecular target, so engagement is read as immune activation. In asthmatic children in the index trial itself, PMBL changed peripheral T-cell subsets: more T cells, Tregs, CD8+ and NK cells, and fewer activated CD69+/CD25+ cells (PMID:33472687, published after the index start). In healthy volunteers, salivary IL-23 and antimicrobial peptides rose (PMID:36807710). The index trial missed its primary endpoint, ACT/C-ACT change at 3 months. However, exacerbation number, exacerbation days and time to second and third exacerbation all improved significantly, and the authors conclude PMBL is effective at reducing exacerbations (PMID:29575037). The failure therefore reflects the choice of endpoint (symptom-control score over 3 months) rather than an inert mechanism. No tolerability limit was reported.

In the index trial (NCT00921804, PMID:26922656), AZD8529 40 mg as monotherapy did not separate from placebo on PANSS or CGI. Risperidone did, so the trial itself could detect a drug effect. The searches found no human data on CSF or brain levels, and none on receptor engagement; as a PAM, the drug has no occupancy PET measure. The pathway pillar is marked inadequate only in the sense that the sole functional evidence is weak. A later pilot study (PMID:34667261) used a higher 80 mg dose and found increased striatal and anterior cingulate fMRI activation, but no improvement in cognition or symptoms; this was published after the index trial. The investigators concluded the target alone was not sufficient (F2), but because engagement at 40 mg was never measured, the cause cannot be determined (U).

The index trial NCT02079688 tested topical SB011, a GATA3 DNAzyme, on atopic eczema lesions. It posted no results, its primary outcome is unclassified, and it gives no stop reason. The bundle has no human data on skin exposure, GATA3 knockdown or downstream Th2 markers in lesional skin. The inhaled form SB010 met its late asthmatic response endpoint in asthma (NCT01743768). That was a different tissue compartment (lung) and formulation, so it cannot support inferred adequacy for topical skin delivery. There are no PubMed abstracts, no Phase 1 results and no comparator drugs on GATA3. With engagement no_human_data, the bundle cannot separate a molecule that failed to engage in skin from a target that does not matter in eczema, so the code is U.

Z160 was reformulated to fix poor bioavailability and a food effect. In 2012 Phase 1 work, the sponsor reported reaching the consistent exposure needed to test efficacy. After the trials, the sponsor said both Phase 2 studies (NCT01655849 in lumbosacral radiculopathy, NCT01757873 in postherpetic neuralgia) produced adequate exposure, yet the drug failed to beat placebo on every endpoint, so the program was discontinued. No human evidence of CaV2.2 occupancy or blockade, or of a downstream pain biomarker, was found. Plasma exposure was shown, but without engagement data the sources cannot tell a drug that never blocked the channel apart from a target that does not drive radicular pain. The sponsor's framing points toward F2, but engagement was never measured, so the code is U.

Z160 is a state-dependent CaV2.2 blocker. It missed its primary endpoint in PHN (NCT01757873) and in lumbosacral radiculopathy (NCT01655849). It was safe and well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The sponsor said both trials reached 'adequate exposure', which supports the exposure pillar (plasma), but it showed no data. No human evidence of N-type channel block, occupancy, or a downstream pharmacodynamic marker was found. BioWorld called the failure 'something of a mystery'. A later medicinal-chemistry paper reworked the scaffold for better bioavailability and CNS penetration, which hints at weak points in the molecule, but that is not human data. No drug on this target has succeeded in PHN (cnv-2197944 only reached Phase 2). With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Ironwood's top-line press release says IW-9179, a GC-C agonist peptide, did not meaningfully reduce diabetic gastroparesis symptoms in the exploratory Phase IIa trial (NCT02289846). Ironwood dropped the indication and gave no mechanistic explanation. The only linked paper (PMID:29079987) is a qualitative interview substudy. The functional dyspepsia study (NCT01712412) ended early because of slow enrollment. The 2015 DDW materials I found describe potency and metabolism data that appear to be preclinical. I found no human evidence of GC-C engagement, such as intestinal cGMP or a change in stool or fluid output. No other GC-C agonist in the bundle succeeded in gastroparesis. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged GC-C cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT00858936 (IK-1001, sodium sulfide, in CABG ischemia-reperfusion injury), enrolled only 6 patients. It was terminated as a 'company decision' and posted no results, so there was no real efficacy readout. A sister STEMI trial (NCT01007461) exists, but I found no human pharmacokinetic, target-engagement or biomarker data (for example, blood sulfide levels or troponin effects). The drug also has no recorded molecular target. Nothing in the sources separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter. The unspecified company decision and the tiny enrollment point to business reasons or operational problems (F8/F7), but no source states a reason. Primary code is U.

The index trial NCT02193815 tested a topical 4% solution of a pan-JAK/TYK2 inhibitor in 15 psoriasis patients. Over 12 days it showed no reduction in plaque thickness versus vehicle (ratio 93.2, p=0.35). The bundle has no human data on skin or plasma exposure, target engagement, or pathway biomarkers. The healthy-volunteer study NCT01981681 posted no PK results here. Deucravacitinib, a TYK2 inhibitor, is FDA-approved for psoriasis, so the target class can work in this disease. That points to the molecule or its topical delivery rather than the target (F1b). Because engagement is unmeasured, the failure stays partly indeterminate (U). Tolerability was not limiting: there were no serious AEs.

The index trial, NCT01195207, was a Phase 1 safety study with no posted results. The efficacy readout came from the HRV-16 challenge study NCT01704040 (JACI 2018). In asthmatics, CNTO3157 gave no protection against the drop in FEV1 or against symptoms, and most exacerbations occurred on the drug. In 12 healthy subjects it reduced cold symptoms. My searches found no human data on TLR3 occupancy, ex vivo poly(I:C) inhibition, airway tissue drug levels or a downstream biomarker. Nothing found shows whether the antibody reached its endosomal target in the airway. The symptom signal in healthy volunteers is a small clinical effect, not engagement evidence. The investigators did not attribute the failure to inadequate exposure. No other drug on this target has succeeded in asthma. With engagement unmeasured, the failure is indeterminate.

KYG0395 appears to be Guizhi Fuling Wan, a multi-component Chinese herbal formula. The PMC4887624 paper and the Springer review of Chinese patent medicines both cite this trial in that context. No molecular target is recorded, and no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects turned up. In NCT01588236, neither dose beat placebo at the end of 6 months' treatment (p>0.05). Both follow-up primary endpoints at 9 months were significant (VAS p<0.01, pain days p<0.05), which hints at a delayed effect, so endpoint timing (F4) is possible. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. No reason for stopping the program was found.

The index trial NCT00847197 left LDL-C unchanged versus placebo (difference 0.2%, p=0.926). HDL-C rose only modestly (4.6%, p=0.013). The bundle has no Phase 1 results, PK, receptor-engagement or proximal HCAR2 biomarker data (e.g., free fatty acid suppression), and no PubMed abstracts. So exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human evidence. Nicotinic acid, another HCAR2 agonist, is FDA-approved for familial hypercholesterolemia, a closely related lipid disorder. That points to this molecule rather than the target, with no pillar evidence that MK-1903 engaged adequately, which fits F1b. The bundle is thin, so U also applies: nothing directly separates a non-engaging molecule from an irrelevant mechanism. No safety signal was seen (0 serious AEs).

The index trial NCT00594984 was a Phase I/II combination study with irinotecan-cetuximab. Its primary outcomes were PK, coagulation biomarkers and safety (classified not_efficacy), so it was not an efficacy test of brivanib: F9. On the pillars, exposure is adequate, with linear PK up to 1000 mg/day (PMID:21131369). DCE-MRI showed significant drops in tumor vascularity at 800 mg, a pathway effect (PMID:21131369). Direct receptor engagement was not measured. In the CRC Phase 3 CO.20 (PMID:23690424), brivanib improved PFS and response but not OS. It increased grade ≥3 toxicity, reduced dose intensity and worsened quality of life (PMID:24127364). This suggests benefit offset by toxicity, so F5 is secondary.

Phase 1 (NCT00207103, PMID:21131369) showed exposure rising linearly up to 1000 mg/day. At the 800 mg MTD used in BRISK-PS, DCE-MRI showed significant falls in tumor vascularity and permeability. This is functional evidence of VEGFR engagement, though measured in mixed solid tumors rather than HCC specifically. In the index trial, brivanib produced on-target hypertension and a clear antitumor effect: TTP HR 0.56 and mRECIST ORR 10% vs 2%. Even so, OS was not improved (HR 0.89, P=0.33; PMID:23980090). The first-line trial also failed (NCT00858871). The mechanism was engaged without a survival benefit (F2). The TTP/ORR-versus-OS discordance (PMID:28131794) and possible patient-selection effects (PMID:24516020; adjusted HR 0.81) support F4 and F3 as secondary codes.

Phase 1 (PMID:21131369) showed plasma exposure rising linearly up to the 800 mg/day recommended dose, which was the dose used in the index trial, so exposure is adequate. DCE-MRI showed significant drops in tumour vascularity and permeability at that dose, so the pathway pillar is adequate. No direct human measure of VEGFR2 or FGFR1 engagement was found, such as receptor phosphorylation inhibition. The index randomised discontinuation trial (NCT00633789) found activity only in soft-tissue sarcoma (PFS HR 0.64, P=.09, after the cohort was expanded) and in ovarian cancer. The other tumour types showed little benefit, and FGF2 expression did not predict who would respond. Benefit was therefore limited to some tumour types, which fits F3. Because engagement was never measured directly, U is a secondary code.

In NCT00570752 (PMID:25913664), BMS-582949 100 mg/day did not lower arterial FDG-PET TBR or hs-CRP compared with placebo, while atorvastatin 80 mg did. I found no human data on p38 inhibition, phospho-HSP27, ex vivo TNFα suppression or plasma exposure at this dose. hs-CRP did not fall, but that is a distal marker, not a direct test of engagement. PMID:26359680 says the parent drug had a pH-dependent absorption problem in clinical studies, which BMS later fixed with a prodrug. That hints exposure may have been variable (possible F1a), but it was never measured. No other p38 inhibitor has succeeded in atherosclerosis. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

The index trial NCT00710333 was a 10-patient Phase 1/2 safety study in ear lobe keloid excision. Its only primary outcome was adverse event frequency, classified as not_efficacy, and it posted no results. It was not an efficacy test of avotermin in keloid, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human data on exposure, TGF-beta receptor engagement, or pathway biomarkers: no Phase 1 results and no abstracts. If the program's broader stop is read as an efficacy failure, engagement is unknown and U would apply. The general scar program included the Phase 3 NCT00742443 and a futility-terminated trial, NCT00432328, but the bundle gives no outcome detail for either.

disease: inborn disorder of amino acid metabolism
rationale: The index MMA trial (NCT01141075) was terminated for low enrollment and an 'unclear pharmacologic effect'. The proximal pathway biomarker did not move: median plasma MMA rose rather than fell (196.5 to 280.9 umol/L). No PK or enzyme-restoration data appear for this disease. The readthrough mechanism showed weak or absent engagement in other diseases: 0/10 FVIII/FIX responders in hemophilia (NCT00947193) and an unmet dystrophin endpoint (NCT03648827). PMID:35857082 notes a narrow, bell-shaped effective range. Because the deficient enzyme is genetically causal, unchanged MMA points to insufficient readthrough rather than an irrelevant target. This favours F1a, although engagement in MMA itself was never measured (U). Low enrollment (n=11, descriptive only) adds F7. Confidence is low.

Index NCT02107859 is an open-label safety extension, closed because the pivotal ACT CF trial (NCT02139306) missed ppFEV1 (p=0.53), after the first Phase 3 (NCT00803205) also missed. PMID:26840186 reports Phase 2 CF studies (2005–2007, before the index) showing increased nasal epithelial CFTR protein and improved nasal potential difference in patients. That is engagement and pathway evidence in this disease, though only described as modest and not quantified. Despite this, lung function did not improve, which points to F2. Secondary F3: the first Phase 3 effect was attributed to an interaction with concomitant inhaled tobramycin, yet the tobramycin-free trial still failed. F1a is possible given the narrow, bell-shaped dose response (mouse data, PMID:35857082) and null pharmacodynamics in other indications. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial (NCT00947193) used a target-engagement primary endpoint, plasma FVIII/FIX activity response at Day 14. 0 of 10 hemophilia patients responded at 10/10/20 mg/kg, so engagement (nonsense readthrough restoring factor protein) was measured in this disease and was absent. There were no serious AEs, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Stopping was a sponsor decision, not for safety. Patient fibroblasts in PMID:31197069 showed no FVIII rise with PTC124, and readthrough depended on mutation context, which suggests molecule and subtype limits. Factor replacement products succeed in hemophilia A, but they act by a different modality. The bundle has no human PK or downstream bleeding data. The mechanism was never properly tested, giving F1a.

The index trial NCT00947193 measured the proximal readout of ataluren's mechanism, nonsense readthrough restoring plasma FVIII/FIX activity. At Day 14, 0 of 10 participants responded, so engagement was shown inadequate in patients. There were no serious AEs, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The bundle has no human PK. Restoring FIX clearly treats hemophilia B: replacement factors and gene therapies (nonacog alfa, etranacogene dezaparvovec) are approved. The failure therefore reflects inadequate readthrough by this molecule, not an irrelevant target, which supports F1b as secondary. This fits ataluren's weak pharmacodynamic signals elsewhere: unchanged MMA in NCT01141075, a modest dystrophin change in NCT03648827, and a narrow bell-shaped dose response in PMID:35857082. The sponsor gave no stated reason for termination.

In NCT02647359, oral ataluren did not improve reading speed (p=0.49), and only 11 ataluren and 5 placebo patients were analysed. The only evidence that ataluren raises PAX6 protein comes from mice (PMID:24355924, 28624217) and patient-derived cells (PMID:32125788, 37483273). Those mouse studies mostly gave the drug as eye drops, but the trial gave it by mouth. I found no human data on drug levels in the eye, on PAX6 readthrough, or on any downstream biomarker in aniridia. The dystrophin data come from a different disease and tissue (PMID:24349052), and ataluren met no pivotal endpoint there, so the pillars can't be inferred from it. A later paper describes the trial only as missing its primary endpoint with a positive trend. Nothing tells apart a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter, so U. The very small analysed sample also suggests the trial was underpowered (F7).

NCT01768520 was designed to show that Entelon (grape seed extract, 150 mg twice daily) is non-inferior to celecoxib on change in K-WOMAC. The posted means were almost identical: Entelon -19.38 vs celecoxib -19.26. Placebo had only 30 analyzed patients, so the trial was not built to test superiority over placebo. Only descriptive results are posted, but nothing shows a failed efficacy readout. Patsnap lists the drug as approved for osteoarthritis in Korea, so the program does not appear to have stopped after a failure. The drug has no defined molecular target, and no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects were found. U would apply if this were treated as a failure.

Earlier asthma-patient studies (NCT00679263, MN-221-CL-004/005; PMID:23094708) showed linear plasma PK and dose-related β2-mediated systemic effects: heart rate, hypokalemia and tremor. This is engagement and downstream effect in asthma before the index trial. In the index trial, adjunct IV bedoradrine on top of maximal nebulized albuterol improved dyspnea but not %FEV1 at 3 h, with on-target cardiovascular and metabolic effects (PMID:26324315). Since β2 agonism clearly works in asthma (many approvals), the failure reflects no incremental bronchodilation from extra β2 agonism over standard therapy, i.e. the mechanism as tested adds no benefit. The dyspnea benefit despite the missed FEV1 endpoint supports F4/F7 as secondary codes. Dose was not shown to be tolerability-capped.

The topical cream met a clinician-scale efficacy endpoint (TCS) in a psoriasis plaque test (NCT00875277), acting through the same PDE4 target in skin. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate. Ex vivo human skin explants also showed high dermal levels and raised cAMP (PMID:33188482), but explant data do not count as in-human evidence. PDE4 is validated in atopic dermatitis by approved crisaborole, roflumilast and difamilast, which argues against F2. In the index trial (NCT01037881) arms were small (~25) and variance high: vehicle SD 6.85. Every dose improved numerically (difference -1.3 to -2.0) and none differed from Elidel, which itself only barely separated (p=0.04). This points to an underpowered trial. F1b is secondary because no direct in-human skin engagement data exist in AD.

In the phase 1 study in advanced malignancies (NCT00408434, PMID:22570147), efatutazone exposure was roughly dose-proportional. Adiponectin, a PPARγ-responsive biomarker, rose at all doses. Escalation stopped once maximal PPARγ biomarker impact was reached, before any MTD, and a PK/PD analysis set 0.5 mg BID. That dose was confirmed by PK in NSCLC with carboplatin/paclitaxel (NCT01199055). So engagement and pathway activity held at the doses tested, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, adding the drug to carboplatin/paclitaxel gave worse 18-week PFS than placebo (40.2% vs 63.3%, NCT00806286). The erlotinib combination in NSCLC also failed (NCT01101334). This points to PPARγ agonism not driving NSCLC as tested. Higher PPARγ/RXR expression in patients with disease control hints at a selection issue (F3). Engagement was not shown specifically in NSCLC patients.

Exposure was roughly dose-proportional in humans (PMID:22570147, NCT01199055). Plasma adiponectin, a PPARγ-responsive marker, rose at all doses. Escalation stopped once PPARγ-related biomarkers reached maximal effect, not because of a toxicity cap, which set the 0.5 mg BID RP2D (PMID:22570147; trial NCT00408434 began before the index trial). In mCRC patients on FOLFIRI, adiponectin rose with dose and time at 0.5 mg BID (PMID:24337768). Despite this, adding efatutazone to FOLFIRI did not improve 16-week PFS (59.7% vs 66.7%) and had more deaths and serious AEs (NCT00967616). This fits F2. Possible selection by PPARγ/RXR tumour expression (PMID:22570147) and a positive maintenance-setting trial (NCT00986440) suggest a population or setting issue (F3).

The index trial added arhalofenate 400/600 mg to allopurinol and barely moved serum urate versus placebo (-16.0% and -9.9% vs -9.5%; NCT01399008). Exposure was measured in gout patients (PK/AUC in PMID:27980008). URAT1 engagement was only partial: monotherapy lowered serum urate by just 12.5–16.5% (PMID:26989892), and the urate-lowering effect is described as modest, usable only with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (PMID:29214511). All of this engagement evidence came after the 2011 index trial. Tolerability did not cap the dose; 800 mg was well tolerated. Another URAT1 inhibitor, lesinurad, is FDA-approved for gout alongside an XOI, so the target is valid. The failure points to a weak molecule (F1b) with inadequate engagement (F1a).

The index trial NCT00917293 in tardive dyskinesia was terminated because a 'modified formulation' was being investigated. It posted no results, so the bundle has no efficacy readout. No human target is recorded for MC-1, and nothing in the bundle shows exposure at the site of action, target engagement or pathway biomarker effects in tardive dyskinesia or in any other disease. The CABG program (NCT00402506, MEND-CABG II) found no clinical benefit, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. The Cochrane review describes only small, inconclusive pyridoxal 5-phosphate trials in tardive dyskinesia. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the code is U. F7 is a secondary code because the trial was stopped early for operational and formulation reasons.

The index trial NCT00692159 was a Phase 1 dose-finding study of TRC102 plus pemetrexed in solid tumors. Its primary endpoint was RP2D and safety, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. PMID:23054206 reports dose-proportional exposure and an MTD of 60 mg/m2/d, capped by anemia. A pharmacodynamic assay confirmed TRC102 binding to AP sites at all doses, so engagement held below the cap. Stable disease or better occurred in 60% of evaluable patients. Pathway: the fludarabine combination increased DNA damage on the Comet assay in hematologic malignancies, including one ALCL patient (PMID:29108368, NCT01658319). That evidence was published after the index trial started and is not ALCL-specific. No efficacy failure is shown; the bundle gives no reason the program stopped.

The index trial NCT01728207 tested subcutaneous IMMU-114 and was stopped for insufficient efficacy and slow accrual. The Phase I data, found in an ASH 2015 abstract and a patent, show very low systemic exposure. Serum drug was undetectable (<24 ng/mL) at 200 mg weekly and peaked at only about 40–50 ng/mL at the higher dose levels. Whether the drug bound HLA-DR on tumor or normal cells (occupancy) was never measured. Normal B-cell changes were modest, although circulating CLL cells fell in a few patients and some responses occurred. Two fatal SAEs at DL3 were judged mostly unrelated. Dose was not clearly capped by tolerability. The very low exposure suggests the mechanism was not adequately tested, so F1a is the best fit. Because target engagement was never measured, U also applies. Slow accrual adds a trial-execution factor (F7).

The index trial NCT00929968 is a safety, tolerability and PK study classified as not_efficacy, with no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of VAK694 (F9). No human PK or target-engagement data (free IL-4 neutralization) appear in the bundle. In the immunotherapy-combination trial (NCT01018693/PMID:26531865), anti-IL-4 plus SCIT sustainably reduced allergen-specific IL-4-producing cells (P<.01), a downstream Th2 effect in allergic rhinitis patients. It added no benefit on the skin late-phase response, and the authors called for a larger trial. The later QBX258 asthma success (NCT01479595) is a different product, so it cannot be used to infer VAK694 engagement. Engagement remains undetermined (U secondary).

BGC20-0134 (Pleneva) is an oral structured lipid. BTG described it as designed to rebalance pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines in MS, but no molecular target is recorded. The Phase IIa trial (NCT01037907) used a 5 g dose against placebo. It missed its primary endpoint, new gadolinium-enhancing lesions over 24 weeks, and its secondary endpoints, and was terminated for lack of efficacy. My searches found no human data on exposure, target engagement or cytokine changes, and no other drug on the same target to compare with. With engagement unknown, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease, so the code is U.

The index Phase 3 (NCT01006252) was put on clinical hold and terminated for an excess of possibly treatment-related deaths on the tasisulam arm: 13 deaths, all on tasisulam, mostly in cycle 2 with grade 4 myelosuppression (PMID:24676877). The sources attribute this to unexpectedly low clearance in a subset of patients, causing drug accumulation and high albumin-corrected exposure. That is a molecule-specific pharmacokinetic liability of this highly albumin-bound drug, so F6 is primary. Plasma exposure was measured and targeted in humans (PMID:21456002, NCT00718159). The bundle has no human RBM39 engagement or pathway data, so efficacy failure (OS HR 1.23, p=0.121) cannot be split into non-engagement versus target irrelevance; U is secondary.

In the single-arm breast cancer trial NCT00992225, only 6.1% of patients responded. Plasma exposure was shown: dosing was tailored to a target Cmax based on albumin levels, and pharmacokinetics were characterized in phase 1 and phase 2 trials (NCT00718159; the Kirkwood melanoma paper). The bundle has no human evidence that tasisulam engaged its target. The melanoma paper says the cellular target was still unknown at the time, and nothing shows RBM39 degradation or a downstream biomarker in patients. So it is not possible to tell a drug that never engaged RBM39 apart from a target that does not matter in breast cancer, which makes the code U. Development ended after the phase 3 melanoma trial (NCT01006252) was stopped because of excess treatment-related deaths, and NCT01284335 was then terminated with the program. That supports F6 as a secondary code.

In healthy volunteers, PET showed dose-dependent striatal D2 occupancy (44% at 32 mg single dose; predicted 52–66% at steady state), so the drug reached the brain and engaged its target (PMID:19717284, NCT00480246; registered before 2011). In schizophrenia, 20–30 mg beat placebo on PANSS and caused prolactin rise and EPS (PMID:23059159, PMID:20921890), supporting pathway effects at comparable doses. The index CLARITY trial (NCT01363349) tested a pro-cognitive advantage over risperidone on MCCB. Scores improved similarly in both arms, and the trial was stopped for futility. The phase 2 BACS signal did not replicate. Despite adequate D2 engagement, the claimed cognitive benefit did not materialise, so the mechanism does not drive cognition as tested. The cognition endpoint choice is a secondary factor.

Cat-PAD is a mix of Fel d 1 T-cell epitope peptides with no recorded molecular target. I found no direct human measure of target engagement, such as T-cell tolerance or occupancy. A 2013 review reports that Fel d 1 peptides reduced early- and late-phase skin responses in cat-allergic patients, a downstream pathway signal, so pathway is marked adequate. In the index Phase III (NCT01620762), all arms improved by about the same amount (1.04/1.00 vs 1.05), and the follow-on trial NCT02040844 was also flat. The sponsor blamed a powerful placebo response that did not appear in Phase II and that hid any treatment effect, which points to a trial-design problem (F7). Because engagement is unmeasured, the alternative that the mechanism simply does not work cannot be ruled out (U).

Hyperimmune caprine serum has no defined molecular target, so exposure, engagement and pathway cannot be judged. The serum biomarker shifts (PIIINP, ACTH, α-MSH; PMID:28270187) are exploratory and tied to no specific mechanism. The published index trial (PMID:24067785) states its primary objective was safety and tolerability, which was met with no safety concerns. The efficacy readout was a favourable trend: mRSS fell 1.4 with drug versus a 2.1 rise on placebo, and responders were 50% vs 10% (p=0.062). PIIINP rose significantly. The authors judged that the drug warrants further evaluation. This was therefore not a clear efficacy failure. The trial had 20 patients and was underpowered for efficacy (F7). The bundle gives no reason the program stopped, and with engagement unmeasured, U also applies.

Target engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred from clear glucose lowering in T2D patients. Weighted mean glucose fell 40.8 mg/dL more than placebo at Day 13 (NCT00873821), and HbA1c beat placebo at Week 14 at every dose (NCT00767000, PMID:21994424). In the index trial (NCT00792935), MK-0941 lowered glucose by as much as glimepiride (-43.4 vs -44.2 mg/dL). It gave no hypoglycemia advantage (32/72 vs 37/71), so its superiority endpoints were missed. PMID:21994424 reports the glycemic benefit was not sustained by 30 weeks. It also reports mechanism-consistent hypoglycemia plus rises in triglycerides and blood pressure. Benefit offset by on-target harms (F5) and non-durable efficacy (F2) best explain the stop. The index trial was an active-comparator superiority test (F9).

COR-1 is a cyclic peptide that scavenges anti-β1-adrenergic receptor autoantibodies. It is not an ADRB1 ligand, so approved beta-blockers do not support F1b. The Phase 1 trial in healthy volunteers (PMID:22968742, NCT01043146, registered before the index trial) showed plasma exposure and near-complete ex vivo antibody neutralization at the two highest doses. No engagement or downstream biomarker was shown in patients. The index trial NCT01391507 was a 36-patient pilot with 6–12 per arm. It reported only descriptive LVEF changes with no statistical comparison, and the dose response was not monotonic. It could not answer the efficacy question (F7). The excess of serious AEs at 160 mg (6/12 vs 1/10 on placebo) is a possible safety signal. The bundle gives no explicit reason the program stopped.

In healthy volunteers, TRV027 showed dose-proportional systemic exposure. It lowered blood pressure more in sodium-restricted subjects with elevated plasma renin activity, a renin-dependent effect consistent with functional AT1R antagonism (PMID:23813302). This supports exposure, engagement and pathway in humans, though not in heart-failure patients. That study was published in 2013, after the index trial started in 2010. The index trial (NCT01187836) posted no results. The program's decisive readout, BLAST-AHF (NCT01966601, PMID:28459958), showed no benefit at any of three doses on the composite or any component, with no safety issues. So engaging this biased-ligand mechanism did not translate into clinical benefit in AHF. A post-hoc analysis suggested benefit confined to patients with higher baseline systolic blood pressure (PMID:28986703), supporting F3 as secondary.

Serum exposure of both antibodies was confirmed in healthy volunteers (PMID:26055360) and in all treated transplant patients, with expected IgG1 PK (PMID:29133549). No direct target-engagement measure, such as viral glycoprotein binding or neutralization titers, appears in the bundle. The 120-patient phase 2a trial narrowly missed its 12-week viremia endpoint (45.8% vs 61.4%, P=0.100). Yet it reduced 24-week viremia (P=0.040), delayed time to viremia (HR 0.53) and lowered CMV disease (PMID:27872061). That pattern points to a small, underpowered trial rather than an inactive mechanism. Exposure-response analysis showed patients with higher exposure had less viremia, suggesting the dose may have been suboptimal (secondary F1a). No stop reason is stated, so confidence is low.

Auriclosene is a topical antimicrobial (a stable chlorotaurine) that kills microbes non-specifically and has no defined molecular target. The sources I found include no human data on how much drug reached or stayed in impetigo lesions, and no controlled data showing bacteria were killed beyond vehicle. The Phase 2a (NCT01367314, PMID:21904634) had high response rates but no vehicle arm. The index Phase 2b/3 (NCT01670032) was safe but missed its primary clinical endpoint, and no results were posted. NovaBay said that if the program went forward, lessons from the two studies would lead to an improved protocol and an optimized formulation. That hints at possible formulation or delivery problems, or trial-design problems (F7), but nothing measured tells apart a drug that failed to work in the skin from a mechanism that does not help. So the code is U.

Auriclosene (NVC-422) is a non-specific N-chlorotaurine-analog antimicrobial with no recorded molecular target. The index trial NCT01877694 (BACTOvation, 0.3% ophthalmic solution) finished in 2014–2015, but it posted no results. Its primary endpoint, microbial eradication at day 5, was never reported. PMID:29602567 covers the adenoviral trial, not this one. I found no human data on drug levels in the eye, bacterial killing in the eye, or a biomarker for this formulation. The adenoviral program (NCT01532336) missed every endpoint. A positive Phase 2b in urinary catheters (NCT02130518) used a different compartment and formulation and led to no approval. No sponsor explanation for the conjunctivitis outcome was found. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U.

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT03651557, PMID:39899673; n=105) missed its primary endpoint. Serum NSE at 48–52 h did not differ between either nelonemdaz dose and placebo. Only high-dose MRI fractional anisotropy improved, and 90-day mRS showed a small non-significant shift. No serious adverse events were reported, so tolerability did not cap the dose. My searches found only safety and patent material, the trial protocol, and the stroke trials. I found no human data on brain or CSF exposure, NR2B occupancy or a pathway biomarker for nelonemdaz. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged GRIN2B cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. The small trial, with NSE as a surrogate endpoint, may also have been underpowered (secondary F7).

Serum drug levels in the index trial (NCT01966549, PMID:28753067) reached steady state by Week 16, and the authors said exposure was likely not why it failed, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. No lung drug levels were reported. In the full-text paper, bronchial brushings used as a stand-in for lung tissue showed no sign of target engagement or of downstream IL-17A gene-expression effects. Only a vague systemic signal was described as possibly reflecting engagement. Tested in the lung, both engagement and pathway therefore look inadequate, which points to F1a. The authors themselves concluded that IL-17A is not a dominant driver of COPD, which fits F2. The drug also failed in rheumatoid arthritis (PMID:29093159), so no inferred_adequate credit applies. Confidence is low because the full text was only seen in fragments.

Exposure: in the RA Phase II trial (NCT01909427/PMID:29093159), serum drug levels rose roughly in proportion to dose and fell in the expected range; the target is systemic. Engagement: no human test of IL-17A neutralisation was reported (no free/total IL-17A levels, no ex vivo inhibition). Investigators saw more frequent neutrophil drops and said these only 'possibly' reflect engagement. Pathway: CRP showed a small trend with no dose-response and no significant difference from placebo. Doses up to 200 mg were well tolerated, so the dose was not limited by tolerability. 19.4% of patients developed neutralising antidrug antibodies. No other anti-IL-17A drug has succeeded in RA, so F1b does not apply. Investigators suggest IL-17 is less potent than TNF/IL-6 in RA, which fits F2. But with engagement unmeasured, U is the correct code.

Drug reached CSF in proportion to dose (PMID:18090456). Engagement was only partial. At 100–140 mg, CNS Aβ production fell by only 47–52% after single doses (PMID:19360898), and the drug's 2.5 h half-life makes that effect transient. In AD patients, plasma Aβ fell but CSF Aβ40/42 did not change (PMID:18695053, PMID:20350302). Brain Aβ was raised at autopsy in a treated patient (PMID:25628963). Modelling puts brain levels below IC50 for half the dosing interval (PMID:35606598), and semagacestat is described as a pseudo-inhibitor that did not truly test the Aβ hypothesis (PMID:28978478). So the mechanism was not adequately tested. Cognition and function worsened on drug, with excess serious AEs (NCT00594568). Atrophy tracked γ-secretase inhibition (PMID:26064192), supporting secondary F5 (on-target toxicity).

JVS-100 is a plasmid encoding SDF-1 (CXCL12) given by endomyocardial injection. The only human data in the bundle is the open-label phase 1 dose-escalation study (NCT01082094/PMID:23429605). It reports safety and uncontrolled improvements in 6MWD and quality of life, but no measure of transgene expression, myocardial SDF-1 levels or a downstream pathway biomarker. The index trial NCT01643590 has no posted results or stated reason for stopping. No other CXCL12 drug has succeeded in heart failure (INXN-4001 reached only phase 1), so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot separate a plasmid that failed to express adequately from a target that does not drive heart failure, so the code is U.

Index trial NCT02708186 (n=34, 28 days) missed its primary endpoint on RBD event frequency. PMID:19841476 shows that oral dosing in healthy volunteers was rapidly absorbed and produced vigilance-lowering EEG effects and better sleep consolidation. This points to CNS exposure and a functional effect consistent with the mechanism. However, no human 5-HT2A receptor occupancy or other direct engagement data were found, and nothing was measured in DLB/PDD patients. Axovant called the study exploratory, then dropped the drug as part of a shift from small molecules to gene therapy (Fierce; NCT02871427 was terminated for portfolio reasons). Nothing in the sources separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U, with a small trial (F7) and business factors (F8) as secondary codes.

The index trial NCT02640729 had only safety and extrapyramidal (UPDRS) primary outcomes and is classified not_efficacy, so it was not an efficacy test of nelotanserin. That makes F9 primary. In healthy volunteers the drug was rapidly absorbed and produced CNS EEG and sleep-consolidation effects (PMID:19841476), supporting exposure and a downstream pathway effect. No human receptor-occupancy data exist, and nothing was shown in Lewy body patients. The sister RBD trial NCT02708186 missed its primary endpoint. The open-label extension NCT02871427 was terminated for program changes, a business reason (F8). Because engagement lacks human data, any efficacy failure would be indeterminate (U).

No source reports human data on TT223 exposure, CCKBR/gastrin receptor engagement, or a downstream biomarker. The index Phase 2 trial (NCT00743002) posted no results. Its sponsor press release claimed a 1.13% HbA1c drop 6 months after treatment, but only in a subgroup: the highest-dose patients who finished the study without changing their diabetes therapy. That points to benefit confined to a subset (F3, secondary). The next trial (NCT00853151/PMID:30848033) added TT223 2–3 mg to a GLP-1 agonist and found no added effect on HbA1c or on insulin secretion during mixed-meal tests. Nausea and vomiting were more common with TT223. Engagement has no human data, so nothing shows whether the drug failed to engage its target or the target does not matter. Hence U.

The index Phase 3 trial NCT01208129 (458 enrolled) was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results. Its sister Phase 3 trial NCT01208168 ended the same way. The bundle has no primary target, no Phase 1 pharmacokinetic or engagement data, no PubMed abstracts, and no same-target comparator drugs. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. It is not even shown that the readout was an efficacy failure rather than a business or operational stop. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate (U), and confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01114503 was a safety/tolerability study in Graves' ophthalmopathy. It enrolled 2 patients, had no efficacy endpoint and posted no CD3 saturation data. It was terminated pending 'a better understanding of an efficacious dose' from other studies, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. In type 1 diabetes, human PK and CD3/TCR modulation are documented (PMID:19934031). About 90% CD3ε occupancy with downmodulation was reached at 18–27 mg (PMID:30566758). EBV reactivation stopped escalation at 27 mg (PMID:33145642), but this came after maximal engagement, so the dose was not capped below engagement. The DEFEND phase 3 failures (NCT00678886, NCT01123083) and the futility stop of NCT01222078 drove the dose uncertainty. Engagement was never shown in thyroid eye disease.

DEFEND-1 showed no C-peptide difference. The sponsor's later trials attribute failure to dose: re-dosing was stopped because the Phase 3 dose 'is not effective' (NCT01222078), and the thyroid eye disease study awaited 'an efficacious dose' (NCT01114503). In T1D patients, dose-finding showed only ~60% CD3 occupancy at 9 mg and ~90% occupancy with full TCR modulation only at 18–27 mg (PMID:30566758). Cytokine release and EBV reactivation capped dosing at 27 mg (PMID:33145642), and subcutaneous dosing was also dose-limited (PMID:27023009). An earlier phase 2 dose preserved beta-cell function (PMID:15972866). Teplizumab, on the same target, is approved in T1D, which supports F1b. So the mechanism was not adequately tested.

The index trial, NCT01087645, was a Phase 1 study in healthy men, and its only primary endpoint was adverse events. It did not test efficacy, so F9 applies: this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. No results were posted, and I found no published human pharmacokinetic, target-engagement or biomarker data for NN9925. The drug is an oral GLP-1 analogue that used Merrion's GIPET absorption enhancer (Fierce Pharma). No source says why development stopped; Patsnap lists the status only as 'Pending'. If the stop is treated as an efficacy failure, the evidence leaves it indeterminate (U), because engagement has no human data.

The index trial NCT01288391 is a Phase 1 single-dose study in 15 haemophilia A/B patients. Its primary outcomes are safety measures only (AEs, SAEs, MESIs) plus pharmacokinetics, so it was not an efficacy test of this drug. No results were posted, and the bundle has no other trials, PubMed abstracts, or same-target comparators. There is therefore no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway effect. No stop reason is stated, so a business stop cannot be shown either. Primary code is F9 because no efficacy readout failed. U is listed as secondary because the pillars are entirely unobserved. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT02024932 met its primary endpoint. In Part B, thigh muscle volume changed by 0.0% on BVS857 versus -3.4% on placebo (p=0.0164). This is the anabolic effect IGF1R agonism predicts, so I rated pathway adequate. Safety showed no SAEs or deaths. The bundle has no PK, receptor engagement or IGF signalling data, and no Phase 1 results are posted for NCT01435330. So exposure and engagement are no_human_data. The bundle gives no stop reason and no PubMed abstracts explaining why development ended. The sister burn trial NCT02074995 was terminated for recruitment problems. Because the index readout was not an efficacy failure, F9 applies. Business or other reasons may lie behind the stop, but the bundle does not show them.

TMC649128 is a prodrug of a nucleoside NS5B polymerase inhibitor. The Phase 1b index trial NCT01391117 in genotype 1 HCV patients was stopped because its antiviral activity was too weak to continue. That makes the downstream readout, the drop in HCV RNA, inadequate. No human data on liver triphosphate levels, polymerase inhibition or PK were ever published; the FIH trial NCT01288677 posted no results. So exposure and engagement have no human data. The target itself is validated: the sources note that sofosbuvir, a nucleotide NS5B inhibitor, transformed HCV treatment. That points to a failure of this molecule (likely poor delivery or activation of the active metabolite in the liver), not of the target, so the code is F1b. If the sofosbuvir evidence is set aside, U also applies.

The Phase 3 trial NCT01767155 found no OS difference between AEZS-108 and untargeted doxorubicin (HR 1.06, p=0.54). The drug's claim was GnRHR-mediated delivery of doxorubicin. The only human target evidence is qualitative: receptor-mediated internalization seen in circulating tumor cells of prostate cancer patients (PMID:25278449, published 2014). That is not endometrial cancer, and it was not quantified. The Phase 2 endometrial responses (PMID:24418927) cannot be separated from doxorubicin's own activity. No human PK or tumor-selective accumulation data are in the bundle. Premature ester cleavage by plasma carboxylesterases (PMID:39902544, preclinical) may have made the drug behave like free doxorubicin. Calling this F2 (targeted delivery adds no benefit) is tentative; U also fits.

Hepar-P is a standardised Phyllanthus niruri extract (EPN 797, 4% corilagin and 18% flavonoids) with no defined molecular target. The index trial (NCT01680003) was published as a small 52-patient pilot RCT in biopsy-proven NASH. It gave two capsules three times daily for 48 weeks, with the change in AST/ALT as the primary endpoint. The excerpt I could retrieve did not show the full primary result. No human source reports exposure at the site of action, target engagement or a pathway biomarker, and no target is recorded. A related herb, Phyllanthus urinaria, also failed against placebo in NASH, but that tells us nothing about engagement. With engagement no_human_data, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The pilot size suggests the trial may also have been underpowered (F7).

HSC is a mixture of growth factors made by cells, with no recorded molecular target, so none of the three pillars (exposure, engagement, pathway) can be judged from human data. The index Phase I/II trial in 56 men (NCT01501617) was not a failure. Histogen's preliminary data showed statistically significant gains in total hair count, terminal hairs and hair thickness at 12 weeks, an 86% responder rate, and no toxicity. The program then moved to female pattern hair loss (NCT03662854) and continued as HST-001, which reported positive Phase 1b/2a results. Nothing in the evidence shows a failed efficacy readout, so F9 fits. Results were never posted on ClinicalTrials.gov and come only from the sponsor, so confidence is medium.

Index trial NCT01101594, a dose-escalation study of the hLL1-DOX conjugate in myeloma, was stopped for lack of efficacy and posted no results. The sister trial in NHL and CLL (NCT01585688) was also stopped for futility. I found no human data for the conjugate itself: no pharmacokinetics, no CD74 occupancy and no pathway biomarker. A Phase 1 trial of the unconjugated antibody in myeloma (PMID 24112026) found fast clearance and low trough levels, with a moderate 34% drop in B cells. That was a different molecule, though, and it doesn't show whether the ADC engaged CD74. A review says the conjugate had no responses in Phase 1. No other CD74 drug has succeeded in myeloma, so F1b doesn't apply. Engagement is unknown, so the code is U.

Both hLL1-DOX trials ended early for lack of efficacy and posted no results. These were the index trial NCT01585688 in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), with 13 patients, and NCT01101594 in myeloma. My searches found no human data for the conjugate on pharmacokinetics, CD74 binding or occupancy, internalization, or any downstream biomarker. The only human data I found were for unconjugated milatuzumab (PMID 24112026), a different molecule. No other CD74-targeted drug has succeeded in these diseases, so F1b does not apply. No source says why the drug failed beyond lack of efficacy. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged CD74 from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

Engagement is supported. In the Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, LX1033 significantly lowered plasma and urinary 5-HIAA, the serotonin breakdown product used as the synthesis marker, at all doses (250–750 mg three times daily and 1,000 mg twice daily). That was before the index trial. In the IBS-D index trial NCT01494233, plasma 5-HIAA also fell more than with placebo, most at 500 mg three times daily. The size of the drop is not reported. Plasma or gut drug levels were not found, so exposure is no_human_data. The stool-consistency primary endpoint missed because placebo improved as much as the drug. Lexicon blamed a placebo response it thought early dropouts may have inflated, and the 4-week length, saying 12 weeks is historically needed. The 500 mg three-times-daily arm improved abdominal pain (47% vs 33% responders, p<0.05). The ending fits F4 (endpoint/timing), with F7 (trial design) secondary.

In the index trial (NCT01356914, PMID:26462707), BMS 914392 did not reduce AF burden at any dose. Trough plasma levels in patients were 50–357 ng/mL, matched predictions, and were well above the IKACh IC50 (24 nM) and the canine anti-AF levels (20–60 ng/mL), so exposure counts as adequate. No human measurement of IKACh block, atrial refractory period or another pathway marker was found. The investigators list both 'may not block IKACh in patients' and a target that does not matter in human PAF as possible causes. They also suggest the dose was restricted because of CNS adverse events, but tolerability capping engagement is not shown. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U. The trial was small (n=20).

A0001 (α-tocopherylquinone) is described only as a redox-cycling antioxidant, with no molecular target on record. A healthy-volunteer study showed plasma exposure with food and good tolerability, with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:21343342). No human measurement of target engagement or of an oxidative-stress pathway biomarker was found. The index trial missed its Disposition Index endpoint at 4 weeks, although FARS scores improved with dose (PMID:22744651). The program was then dropped without a stated efficacy reason (curefa.org). Its sister mitochondrial trial was ended for commercial reasons (NCT01074359), which suggests the program may have stopped for business reasons (F8). With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In humans, sulindac sulfide reaches plasma and accumulates in colonic tissue (PMID:33002468, PMID:6539116). COX engagement is shown by a dose-dependent 45-85% fall in systemic eicosanoids and lowered TxB2, but only in healthy volunteers (PMID:3549118, PMID:3884880). The pathway pillar is rated inferred_adequate because celecoxib is approved in FAP on the same target, and sulindac lowered HER-2 in FAP rectal mucosa (PMID:10025882). The index trial (NCT01483144) missed its composite FAP-event endpoint. Its lower-GI event analyses were significant (HR 0.17-0.20), but these were a subset of the overall endpoint. This suggests the composite endpoint diluted an effect confined to the lower GI tract. The bundle does not state the sponsor's explanation, so confidence is low; F2 and F7 are alternatives.

The index Phase 3 trial NCT00718965 and three parallel Phase 3 trials (NCT00729027, NCT00741715, NCT00766688) were all terminated for insufficient efficacy on LDL-C lowering. No results were posted, and the bundle contains no Phase 1 data, no Phase 2 results (NCT00440154 completed without posted results) and no PubMed abstracts. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. Ezetimibe, which acts on the same NPC1L1 target, is FDA-approved for familial hypercholesterolemia, a close subtype in which LDL-C reduction via NPC1L1 inhibition is validated. With no evidence that canosimibe engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U applies secondarily given the absence of any engagement data.

None of the sources measure silibinin binding to or inhibiting its listed target, SLCO1B3, in humans, or report site-of-action drug levels. That leaves exposure and engagement as no_human_data. The downstream antiviral effect does show up in the program disease: IV silibinin at 20 mg/kg/day cut HCV-RNA in liver-transplant patients (PMID:21605016; Springer 2016). In the published report of the index trial (NCT01535092; Hepatology 2013, via natap), HCV-RNA fell during peri-transplant dosing, but no patient reached SVR. The investigators point to the short treatment window (14–21 days before transplant plus 7 days after) and call for longer regimens. That fits F4: a proximal effect was shown, but the duration was too short for the endpoint. The trial was also tiny (n=14, F7). Target engagement itself is unknown (U).

PREOB is an autologous osteoblastic cell therapy with no defined molecular target. The bundle has no human evidence that the implanted cells survived, engrafted or formed bone in the necrotic lesion, and no biomarker data. The phase 2 trial (NCT02890537, PMID:22891449) reported only clinical superiority over bone marrow concentrate. In the index trial (NCT01529008), a DSMB stopped the study for futility at the interim analysis. Responders were 60.9% with PREOB vs 69.2% with placebo (p=0.539), with no difference in safety. The press coverage gives no mechanistic explanation, and the later termination for business reasons concerned only the non-union trial. Since there is no engagement data, a failed cell product cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

PREOB is an autologous osteoblastic cell therapy with no defined molecular target. The trial stopped for futility after an interim analysis by the data monitoring board. Responders were 60.9% with PREOB vs 69.2% with placebo (p=0.539; NCT01529008). PREOB was well tolerated. No source shows in humans that the implanted cells engrafted or survived, or that they formed bone or changed any osteogenic biomarker. The sponsor compared PREOB with its allogeneic ALLOB cells, which it said had stronger bone-forming properties and could be given at a 5-fold higher dose. That suggests the potency or dose may have been too low. But this was not measured in humans, so the bundle cannot tell an ineffective cell product apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The code is therefore U.

In a Phase 1 study of advanced NSCLC patients (PMID:20922800), apricoxib 400 mg/day with erlotinib was well tolerated with no DLT. PK informed the RP2D. Urinary PGE-M, a COX-2 product, fell in 70% of patients, showing engagement and pathway effect in this disease at the index dose. The abstract states the Phase 2 used 400 mg and selected patients on PGE-M change. Even so, the index trial (NCT00652340) showed no time-to-progression benefit (1.8 vs 2.1 months), and the pancreatic trial NCT00709826 also failed. This suggests COX-2 inhibition does not drive NSCLC progression as tested. The PGE-M paper was published in 2011, after the index trial started in 2008. Biomarker-based selection did not rescue efficacy, so F3 is only a minor secondary code.

In the Phase 1 NSCLC study (PMID:20922800), apricoxib reached 400 mg/day with no dose-limiting toxicity. That dose was chosen from pharmacokinetics and urinary PGE-M decreases (70% of patients), which shows COX-2 inhibition with its downstream prostaglandin effect. This evidence comes from lung cancer, not pancreatic cancer, and was published in 2011, after the index trial started in 2008. At that dose, the index trial (NCT00709826) showed no PFS benefit: 3.0 vs 2.8 months. The sister NSCLC trial also failed (NCT00652340). With engagement adequate, the most direct reading is that COX-2 does not drive outcome in this setting. Possible F3: benefit tracked with baseline-elevated, suppressible PGE-M, and the pancreatic trial did not select on it.

The index trial NCT01586468 was a single-centre, 60-patient pilot that started in 2010. Nuvo's press release describes the same design (60 patients, change in TNSS at 3 weeks) and says it met its primary endpoint, so the index trial was not an efficacy failure (F9). The program actually ended after later Phase 2 trials. In the 2015 German trial the placebo response was much larger than in the 2010 pilot and WF10 did not separate from placebo; that points to F7, a high placebo response. In the December 2015 trial WF10 again did not separate from placebo, and Nuvo stopped all WF10 development. WF10 has no defined molecular target, and none of the sources show human exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker, so the mechanism question cannot be settled (U).

NCT03514121 was a Phase 1a/1b study whose endpoints were safety only. It found no DLTs at any dose up to 20 mg/kg Q3W, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The sponsor stopped the study 'for reasons unrelated to safety' and gave no efficacy or business reason. Exposure should be no_human_data, not inadequate: the inadequate value in the exposure field is an error, since no source shows exposure was too low. The ASCO 2019 and ESMO 2019 abstracts and the Five Prime 10-K cover safety, PK and the dose chosen for Phase 1b, but give no receptor occupancy, B7-H4 engagement or downstream biomarker data. A later review says the only published PK result is a 1–2 week half-life and that PD data were not released. No other B7-H4 drug succeeded. With engagement unknown, the failure cannot be explained (U). A business stop (F8) is possible but not documented.

The index trial NCT02329717 missed its primary endpoint: 26.3% of patients were alive at 4.5 months against a 50% target. The authors gave no mechanistic reason for the failure.
