In the first-in-human trial (NCT00554268; Hong 2014), plasma oleandrin rose with dose and tolerability did not cap dosing, so exposure counts as adequate. That trial reached its recommended phase II dose and the drug was well tolerated. No source measured Na/K-ATPase (ATP1A1) inhibition directly in humans. Downstream markers moved only modestly in blood cells (PBMCs): phospho-Akt fell about 10% and pS6 about 35%. That points to partial pathway suppression, not a robust effect. No source measured engagement in pancreatic cancer. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

No results were posted for the index trial NCT01234038 in NSCLC (ISIS 183750 plus carboplatin/paclitaxel; primary endpoint PFS). In humans with other solid tumours, eIF4E was knocked down. A phase I/II colorectal study (PMC6407898) reported lower eIF4E mRNA in peripheral blood and checked tumour eIF4E. The phase 1 study of the same molecule, LY2275796, reported plasma PK that supported dosing and good tolerability up to 1000 mg. A review states that the drug reduced eIF4E expression in clinical studies, but phase II trials showed no tumour responses and development stopped. Engagement therefore looks adequate, though it was shown outside NSCLC and was published after the index trial began. No downstream pathway effect was shown. Lowering eIF4E did not translate into benefit, so this points to F2. Confidence is low because the NSCLC efficacy data are sparse and I could only read search-result excerpts of these papers.

In the index trial (NCT01173471), AZD4017 400 mg BID did not lower IOP more than placebo (p=0.413), and 200 mg OD also failed. The same 400 mg BID dose clearly engaged 11β-HSD1 in humans. Systemic activity fell by 87% (PMID:35113805), and in IIH patients the urinary metabolite ratio, hepatic prednisolone generation and CSF cortisone:cortisol ratio all showed inhibition (PMID:32954315). Downstream metabolic changes in lipids and androgens followed (PMC7765633). This supports F2: the target engaged, but there was no IOP benefit. The caveats are large. Nobody measured engagement in eye tissue or in patients with ocular hypertension, skin 11β-HSD1 was not inhibited ex vivo, and all of this evidence was published after the index trial. The trial was also small, with only 7 patients on 200 mg OD (F7), so tissue-level failure (U/F1a) cannot be ruled out.

NCT02098967 was a Phase 1 safety and PK study, not an efficacy test. It met its objectives: MTDs were defined (200 mg in AML, 110 mg in solid tumors), and the prodrug converted rapidly and nearly completely to idasanutlin with dose-proportional exposure. Exposure-dependent MIC-1 induction showed p53 activation, consistent with MDM2 engagement and pathway effect, in AML and solid-tumor patients (PMID:32020437, PMID:31734832). Engagement was inferred from this pathway marker rather than measured directly. Both papers state development stopped because RO6839921 offered insufficient differentiation in biologic or safety profile over oral idasanutlin. That is a strategic/portfolio decision, not an efficacy failure, so the primary code is F8 with F9 secondary.

Exposure was adequate. Serum neublastin rose with dose, reaching dose-proportional increases in SPRINT (PMID:28746076) and dose-dependent increases in sciatica patients, with a half-life of 40–60 h (PMID:27016000). No source measured GFRα3 or RET engagement in humans, such as receptor phosphorylation or a target-tissue readout. In the first-in-human study, the exploratory pharmacodynamic markers (substance P, MCP-1) showed no significant trends, and nerve-fibre density and sensory testing were unchanged (PMID:25962165). These do not confirm or rule out engagement. Pruritus and feeling hot were frequent, which hints at biological activity, but pruritus showed no dose-response and was never established as an engagement marker. Pain relief was greatest at the lowest dose and showed no dose-response. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. No source states why the program stopped.

In the sciatica studies, serum levels of BG00010 rose with dose and stayed in a consistent range between patients, so systemic exposure was shown (PMID:27016000, PMID:28746076). No source measured GFRα3/RET binding, receptor activation in sensory neurons, or a downstream biomarker. Nerve fibre density and sensory testing did not change in Phase 1 (PMID:25962165). Pruritus and feeling hot were common side effects and may reflect action on the target, but no source presents them as evidence of engagement. They were also not dose-related, and they did not limit dosing, since doses up to 1200 μg/kg were tolerated. In SPRINT (NCT01873404), pain scores showed no dose-response, and the lowest dose did best, which suggests noisy data. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not drive pain. My search found no stated reason for ending the program.

The index trial (NCT00829881) gave 16 adults with ADHD single doses of 50–200 mg. No results were posted, and the sponsor's patent describes the design but reports no CPT efficacy outcome. PMID:25904220 measured only the inactive metabolite 2-PAA, which rose in proportion to dose, and found the drug well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. PMID:37920833 shows heavy first-pass metabolism: parent-drug exposure without an MAO-B inhibitor is tiny, about 0.64 h*ng/mL at 48 mg. That suggests low systemic and brain exposure, but it was not measured in the brain. I found no human H3 receptor occupancy or CNS biomarker data, and no stated reason for stopping. Because engagement has no human data, this is indeterminate (U).

In the index first-in-human study (NCT02004717; PMID:31412935), serum exposure rose with dose up to 20 mg/kg without reaching an MTD, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Activity was minimal: one partial response. Systemic NK-cell and cytokine changes showed Fc-mediated activity, but no tumour-level pathway effect was shown. The 89Zr-DS-8895a PET biodistribution trial (PMID:35404015) found low, low-grade tumour uptake and limited efficacy. The authors state these biodistribution data were key in halting development. Tumour delivery and target engagement were therefore insufficient, and the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). One caveat lowers confidence: imaging was done only at 1–3 mg/kg, below the 20 mg/kg expansion dose.

The first-in-human dose-escalation trial NCT00932126 (1 mg QD to 60 mg BID) was terminated. Its posted results show only a few DLTs at 50–60 mg BID, so tolerability did not clearly cap the dose. Secondary literature found on the web says the program ended because of undesirable pharmacokinetics: poor bioavailability, unfavourable plasma drug levels and no dose-response relationship. A recent review also calls the compound a multidrug transporter (efflux) substrate. No source reports human PAK4 engagement or pathway biomarker data. Because exposure was inadequate, the PAK4 mechanism was never properly tested, which fits F1a. Confidence is medium because these PK statements come from reviews rather than a primary PK report or a sponsor statement.

Replacement therapy: in the index trial, plasma C-peptide rose to 1.8–2.2 nmol/L (low dose) and 5.6–6.8 nmol/L (high dose) in T1D neuropathy patients (PMID:26884473). That supports exposure and ligand replacement, so engagement is judged adequate. No receptor-level data exist, and this evidence comes from the index trial itself. VPT improved 25% versus placebo, which is a functional effect consistent with the mechanism. The primary endpoint, SNCV, rose similarly on drug (1.0 m/s) and placebo (1.2 m/s), and mTCNS was unchanged. The miss therefore reflects the chosen endpoint and its unexpected placebo improvement rather than absent pharmacology. This points to F4, with F7 (placebo response) secondary. The sources do not explicitly state the cause, hence medium confidence.

In the Phase 1 study (PMID:22616628), GSK679586 showed linear PK, which supports exposure. In mild asthmatics it raised serum total IL-13, indicating drug–IL-13 complex formation (engagement). It also cut FeNO dose-dependently, by 44–55% at 10 mg/kg, the index dose (pathway). That engagement evidence was only published in 2013, after the index trial started in 2008. The index trial (NCT00843193; PMID:24582316) was well tolerated at 10 mg/kg but missed ACQ-7, with no FEV1 or exacerbation benefit. Subgroups with high IgE or eosinophils were also negative. So IL-13 neutralization alone did not drive asthma control in severe refractory asthma (F2). The authors leave open benefit in a subpopulation (F3 secondary). No IL-13 drug in the bundle is approved for asthma.

The index trial, NCT01130818, was a first-in-human single-ascending-dose study whose only primary outcome was safety. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 is the primary code. Galapagos reported good safety at 0.5–120 mg and plasma PK that supports once-daily dosing, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. No direct measure of androgen receptor engagement (such as occupancy) was found. Galapagos said its healthy-volunteer proof-of-mechanism study (NCT01538420) showed a biomarker effect similar to oxandrolone, which I count as pathway evidence. Galapagos did not say which biomarker it was or how big the effect was. The company dropped the drug because the data were insufficient to pursue it in cachexia. This was a portfolio decision, not a failed efficacy readout in patients. The secondary code U applies because target versus molecule cannot be told apart.

Theranor sponsored TAO1, a homeopathic dilution (below 10^-24 M) of rabbit antibodies raised against a peptide from human TLR3. Its supporting evidence was a proof-of-concept study in influenza-infected mice. At that dilution, essentially no antibody molecules remain in a dose. The bundle has no human data on exposure, TLR3 engagement or any downstream biomarker. The index trial (NCT01651715) posted no results and gave no stop reason. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the drug failed to engage TLR3 or whether TLR3 does not matter in the common cold, so the code is U. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

The index trial NCT02100839 was a Phase 1/2 SAD/MAD safety study in refractory hypercholesterolemia. Its primary outcomes were counts of treatment-emergent adverse events: 33/37 on AEM-28 vs 10/15 on saline, moderate 7 vs 0, with no serious AEs and no deaths. It was not an efficacy test of the drug, so the program's halt cannot be read as an efficacy failure (F9). The bundle has no human exposure, engagement, or pathway data, no other trials, no PubMed abstracts, and no stated stop reason. Why the program stopped therefore remains indeterminate (U, secondary). No dose-limiting tolerability is evident.

The bundle has no human pillar evidence for siG12D LODER. The Phase 1 trial NCT01188785 posted no results, there are no PubMed abstracts, and the index Phase 2 trial NCT01676259 has unknown status with no posted results or stop reason. Exposure, KRAS transcript knockdown and pathway effects in humans are therefore all unshown. The bundle does list another KRAS-directed drug, daraxonrasib, as FDA-approved in malignant pancreatic neoplasm. That suggests KRAS is a valid target in this disease and points to the molecule or local delivery approach rather than the target (F1b). It is unclear whether the index trial even read out as a failure, and the bundle is very thin, so U also applies and confidence is low.

VF001-DP is a topical vitronectin:IGF-1 chimeric peptide meant to act as an IGF1R agonist. In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT02973893), 157 patients with venous leg ulcers got standard care plus low-dose (28 µg/mL) VF001, high-dose (280 µg/mL) VF001 or placebo. The trial missed all endpoints, and Factor Therapeutics stopped developing the drug. The sponsor said only that the drug does not improve healing. It gave no reason tied to the mechanism. The only earlier human data were from an open-label Phase 2 trial in 53 patients, which reported safety and tolerability. No source gave human evidence of drug levels in wound tissue, IGF1R activation or a downstream pathway biomarker. Without engagement data, we cannot tell whether the drug never engaged its target or whether the target does not drive healing, so the code is U.

MK-7145 is a ROMK (KCNJ1) blocker intended as a natriuretic diuretic (PMID:27437080). In hypertension (NCT01370655, started 2011), 3–6 mg lowered 24h SBP versus placebo (−6.7 and −7.4 mmHg) and versus HCTZ. That is clinical efficacy through the same renal target at a dose comparable to the index 8 mg, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. In renal insufficiency (NCT01558674), 8 mg raised 24h urinary sodium by only 11 mEq versus 109.5 mEq with furosemide, and the trial was terminated for lack of efficacy. Engagement was never measured in renally impaired patients. Reduced tubular delivery in this population (F3) cannot be separated from limited natriuretic capacity of ROMK block. The evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01370655 did not fail. MK-7145 6 mg lowered 24h SBP versus placebo (LS difference -7.4 mmHg [-10.6, -4.1]) and versus HCTZ 25 mg (-5.4 [-9.2, -1.6]). DBP also fell versus both comparators. 6 mg raised day-1 urinary sodium versus placebo (+76.5 mmol/day [49.2, 103.8]), the natriuretic effect expected from ROMK blockade (PMID:27437080). That pathway effect in hypertensive patients implies the target was engaged, although occupancy and PK were not measured directly. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The later futility stop of NCT01558674, with weak natriuresis versus furosemide in renal insufficiency, concerns a different population. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping the hypertension program.

No direct PK or target-engagement measurements in humans are in the bundle. Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate because MK-7145 3–6 mg lowered 24h SBP versus placebo and HCTZ in hypertensive men (NCT01370655). That is the same renal ROMK target at a dose comparable to the 8 mg used in the index trial. In the index trial (NCT01558674), patients with renal insufficiency had a 24h urinary sodium increase of only 11 mEq with MK-7145, against 109.5 mEq with furosemide. The natriuretic pathway effect was therefore inadequate, and the trial was terminated for lack of efficacy. ROMK blockade did not give useful natriuresis in this population. Reduced drug delivery to the tubule in renal impairment cannot be excluded, which is why F3 is secondary and confidence is low.

In healthy volunteers, ipamorelin showed dose-proportional plasma PK and caused GH release at every infusion dose, with a modeled SC50 of 214 nmol/L (PMID:10496658, published 1999, before the index trial). This is functional evidence of GHSR agonism in humans, though measured at the pituitary rather than the gut. No GI motility biomarker or patient engagement data exist, the index-trial doses are not given, and NCT01280344 posted no results. On the available evidence the drug engaged GHSR systemically, yet the program stopped after the Phase 2 GI-recovery trial. That points to the mechanism not driving GI recovery as tested (F2). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin and engagement in the gut compartment is unproven.

In PD patients, piribedil shows linear plasma PK after IV dosing (PMID:15726579). It lowered CSF HVA, indicating central dopamine-receptor stimulation (PMID:1091122, PMID:930747). It also gave consistent motor benefit (PMID:30019007, PMID:1634909), so the pillars hold in this disease and predate the index trial. The index trial (NCT01007864/PMID:24992083) was a switch study against active D2/D3 agonists on the same target. It tested a vigilance reaction-time endpoint, which showed no difference. Yet Epworth sleepiness improved significantly, motor effect was maintained, and CGI favoured piribedil. The miss therefore reflects the chosen objective endpoint rather than a non-engaging drug. The trial was a differentiation study against active drugs, not a test of PD efficacy (F9). The target was engaged but gave no vigilance gain (F2).

The index Phase 2 migraine-prevention trial NCT01184508 was terminated early. Its stated reason was elevation of ALT and AST in some patients, which is molecule-related hepatic toxicity with no evidence linking it to CYSLTR1 or GRM2 pharmacology. At termination the primary endpoint (change in migraine attacks at 12 weeks) trended toward benefit (LS mean difference -1.03, p=0.085) in a small, truncated sample of about 22 per arm at Month 3, so the efficacy question was left unanswered. The bundle contains no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects, and no other trials or comparator drugs. Toxicity ended the program (F6). The mechanism is otherwise indeterminate (U), and early termination left the trial underpowered (F7).

In the index 28-day trial in T2DM (NCT01298518), 2.5 mg BID and 5 mg QD lowered post-meal glucose AUC no more than placebo (-118 and -143 vs -118 mg*hr/dL). I found no human plasma, intestinal, postprandial-triglyceride or other DGAT1 engagement data. Only animal data are available (PMID:29972081), and PMID:23871442 raises concern about poor permeability. A 2023 Pfizer review pooling PF-04620110 Phase 1 safety data (single doses up to 21 mg) says nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea limited the development of DGAT1 inhibitors. This hints that tolerability capped the dose (F5/F1a), but no source states that the dose was capped below what engagement needed. With engagement unmeasured, it stays indeterminate.

The Phase 3 trial NCT01640808 (600 mg/day) missed its recurrence-free survival endpoint (HR 0.90, p=0.35). In humans, the drug reached plasma at levels that rose with dose. But the target tissue is the liver, and in a clinical pharmacology study liver concentrations were below the limit of quantitation (0.050 µg/g) in all 6 patients at 300 mg/day and in 4 of 6 at 600 mg/day. The dose could not go higher: in Phase 1, 4 of 9 patients on 900 mg/day developed high blood pressure, so 900 mg was judged poorly tolerated. The sources report no human data on RAR engagement or on downstream biomarkers. The Phase 2/3 trial (PMID:24728665) suggested benefit only at the higher dose and only after year 2. Because liver exposure was poor and the dose was capped, the mechanism was probably not properly tested (F1a). Confidence is low because no source states these levels were too low or names this as the cause; with no engagement data, U also applies.

The index Phase 3 trial of LACTEOL 340 mg in IBS-D (NCT01358708) was terminated for 'administrative reasons' after only 26 participants. No formal primary analysis was reported. Responder rates were identical (30.8% vs 30.8%), and no serious AEs occurred. So the trial could not test efficacy, and nothing indicates a safety stop. There is no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human data for this product on gut delivery or colonization, engagement, or a pathway biomarker in IBS. Fecal recovery of other L. acidophilus products was poor (PMID:17721765). Other L. acidophilus strains improved IBS symptoms (PMID:32019158, PMID:18274900), but another did not on its primary endpoint (PMID:31952938). These are different strains or products, so F1b does not apply. The mechanism remains untested (U). An unstated business decision is possible (F8).

Nadolol's systemic exposure is well characterized in healthy humans, with dose-proportional plasma levels (PMID:6714285, PMID:3366166). Beta-1/beta-2 blockade was measured directly: large isoprenaline dose-ratios and reduced exercise heart rate at 40 mg (PMID:1676675), and reduced exercise double product (PMID:37871). Downstream effects followed, including falls in heart rate and renin (PMID:37877), and nadolol was clinically effective in angina (PMID:26520). All of this predates the 2014 index trial, but none of it comes from smokers. In NCT01825122, 45/73 on nadolol vs 36/72 on placebo reached ≥70% cigarette reduction, which was not significant. Tolerability did not appear limiting. With beta-blockade presumably achieved, the mechanism did not translate into benefit (F2). Caveats: the bundle gives neither the index dose nor CNS penetration data. The numerical trend in a modest trial also suggests it may have been underpowered (F7).

In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT01269242; 600 or 1,200 mg vs placebo, 148 patients), bindarit missed its primary endpoint, in-segment late loss, but lowered in-stent late loss, a secondary endpoint. None of the sources I found measured drug levels or CCL2/MCP-1 lowering in humans, either in these patients or in healthy volunteers, so exposure, engagement and pathway have no human data. The 1,200 mg dose worked no better than 600 mg, and that does not show whether the target was engaged. The investigators suggested a loading dose or pre-treatment and a more specific patient group. That hints at dosing or design problems (F7) and patient selection (F3), but nothing separates a drug that never engaged CCL2 from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects.

CureXcell is an activated blood-cell (macrophage) product with no target recorded. Its Phase 3 DFU trial (NCT01421966) missed its primary endpoint of complete closure sustained for 4 weeks and also missed all secondary endpoints. The sister venous leg ulcer Phase 3 (NCT02130310) stopped after a futility analysis. The sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation; it said it would analyze the data to understand why the trial failed. I found no human evidence of cell persistence or activity in the wound, of engagement, or of a pathway biomarker moving. No other agent with the same mechanism is shown succeeding. With engagement no_human_data, the evidence cannot separate an inactive product from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

CureXcell is a suspension of activated white blood cells with no defined molecular target. Its Phase 3 trial in diabetic foot ulcers (NCT01421966) missed its primary endpoint of complete wound closure, and it missed every secondary endpoint too. Before that, the venous leg ulcer Phase 3 (NCT02130310) was stopped after a futility analysis. The sponsor said it would analyse the data to understand why the trial failed, but gave no explanation. My searches found no human data on where the cells end up in the wound, how active they are, or any downstream biomarker. The company's claim of good results in more than 5,000 patients in Israel is anecdotal, not pillar evidence. With engagement unmeasured, I can't tell a product that never worked biologically apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00813813 was a Phase I/II study whose primary outcomes were descriptive safety counts: neurological assessment and drug-related TEAEs, with no comparator. It was not an efficacy test, so it cannot count as an efficacy failure. The later Phase 2 trials (NCT01124006, NCT01158924, NCT01182337) were also safety-focused, with no efficacy hypothesis test. The bundle has no human data on intradiscal exposure, BMPR1B engagement or downstream disc biomarkers. The only pharmacology shown is from non-human primates (PMID:21940517). No other BMPR1B agonist succeeded in disc degeneration; dibotermin alfa reached only Phase 2. With no efficacy readout and no engagement data, the reason the program stopped cannot be told from the bundle (U secondary).

The index trial NCT02312011 was a phase 1/2a dose-escalation study whose registered primary outcomes were only safety and tolerability. The publication (PMID:36804094) reports that baliforsen was generally well tolerated up to 600 mg, so the trial met its descriptive aim and was not an efficacy test. The truncated abstract in the bundle gives no human data on muscle tissue drug levels, DMPK transcript knockdown, or splicing biomarkers. The pillars therefore cannot be assessed, and nothing separates inadequate exposure or engagement from target irrelevance, so U applies as a secondary code. Other DMPK-directed agents (delpacibart etedesiran, zeleciment basivarsen) have reached phase 3 but none are approved, so F1b does not apply. The reason for stopping is not stated.

In the index crossover allergen-challenge trial in mild atopic asthmatics, the drug at 100 mg/day substantially inhibited ex vivo stimulated whole-blood LTB4 production, showing exposure and enzyme inhibition. It also lowered sputum LTB4, which is the proximal pathway product in the target tissue. The authors state that target engagement was demonstrated in blood and sputum. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited. Even so, the late asthmatic response did not change (P=0.63), while the montelukast control significantly attenuated it, which validates the model. Engagement was shown in patients but only within the index trial itself, not before it. The mechanism was adequately tested, and LTB4 does not appear to drive the allergen-induced response (PMID:25018015).

Exposure and engagement are adequate. In the healthy-volunteer Phase 1, which the sponsor reported before the AZURE trial (NCT05205070) started, rosnilimab gave a robust PK profile and full PD-1 receptor occupancy at subcutaneous doses of 60 mg or more. PD-1+ conventional T cells fell by about 50%, in step with occupancy, and tetanus-stimulated IFN-gamma dropped by up to about 90%, so the pathway pillar is also adequate. In alopecia areata patients, a blinded interim review found 'proof of mechanism': PD-1-high T cells fell by more than 80%. However, absolute SALT scores did not support the target product profile, and the sponsor dropped alopecia areata, with no tolerability problem noted. The mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, so the code is F2. Confidence is medium because only peripheral blood was measured, with no data from scalp tissue, and the interim review was blinded.

NCT01441986 was a small (n=20) single-dose crossover OGTT study. Its amantadine arm gave 100 mg once, and it posted no results. The target here is pancreatic islet NMDA receptors. Neither the bundle nor my searches show human evidence that amantadine reached the islets, engaged islet NMDA receptors or changed insulin secretion at this dose. Its approved uses (dyskinesia, PMID:30087157; motor cortex effects, PMID:16794570) reflect CNS action at higher, sustained plasma levels, so they don't support an inferred_adequate rating for pancreatic beta cells. Later reports from the same group (Marquard 2015) focus only on dextromethorphan's glucose-lowering effect. The amantadine result is not reported, and no reason for not pursuing it is stated. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged the target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The trial was exploratory, so F7 is secondary.

The index trial, NCT04952519 (TITAN), tested high-dose oral amantadine in hospitalised COVID-19 patients and stopped after its annual analysis showed no efficacy. The published paper registers the time-to-recovery endpoint, but the text retrieved here did not show the results or why the investigators think it failed. Plasma PK (PMID:29777529, 30087157) and evidence of NMDA modulation in the brain (PMID:16794570) come from Parkinson's disease and healthy volunteers. That is CNS dosing for a different mechanism. None of it shows exposure at the site of a COVID-relevant target, such as lung or viral replication sites, or engagement of that target. No viral-load or other pathway biomarker was found in COVID patients. A separate trial in early mild-to-moderate COVID (ene.16045) reported benefit, which it attributed to central effects. So a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, and the code is U.

The index trial NCT01090024 tested 400 mg/day (400 mg QD or 200 mg BID) for 4 weeks on ICS, and missed trough FEV1 (p=0.14–0.45). Its authors suggest the failure may reflect insufficient CRTH2 inhibition at those doses (PMID:28234053). In the same population, NCT01103349 at 400 mg BID (800 mg/day, 6 weeks) met the endpoint (+3.9%), and steroid-naive NCT01092143 also succeeded (PMID:25861737). This points to under-dosing rather than an irrelevant target. No human PK, receptor occupancy or biomarker data appear in the bundle, so 'inadequate' engagement is inferred from cross-trial dose contrast and author attribution, not measured. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Confidence is low; U and the short duration (F7) remain plausible.

In SAR patients in the index trial, BI 671800 produced a dose-related reduction in ex vivo PGD2-mediated eosinophil shape change, which is direct CRTH2 engagement and implies systemic exposure. It also lowered nasal eosinophils at all doses and IL-4/eotaxin at 200 mg, so the pathway moved (PMID:24332218). Clinical benefit was small and not dose-dependent. Only 200 mg reduced TNSS, by 17%, versus 33% for fluticasone; 50 and 400 mg were not significant. With the mechanism engaged, the modest, inconsistent symptom effect points to CRTH2 being a weak driver of SAR symptoms. Asthma results were also mixed (NCT01090024 not met; NCT01092143 and NCT01103349 met). F9 is a secondary code because one dose met the primary endpoint. Engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself, not from before it.

The index trial NCT02003742 was stopped because two other Phase 3 trials (NCT00918983 and NCT00945490) did not beat placebo, and Nymox confirmed the misses. Fexapotide has no defined molecular target. It is described as a pro-apoptotic protein injected into the prostate, and one source says its exact mechanism is unknown. The bundle has no human measurement of drug levels in prostate tissue, no target-engagement data and no proximal apoptosis biomarker. The reviews (PMID:23251763, PMID:29380128) report prostate volume reduction and symptom changes, but these are clinical outcomes, not engagement measures. Because no pillar is measured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter in BPH, so the code is U. F2 is listed as a possible secondary code.

The index trial NCT01775462 had only safety, immunogenicity and PK primary outcomes, and its endpoint class is not_efficacy. It was not designed as an efficacy test of EDI200, so it was not an efficacy failure as registered (F9). Neither it nor the Phase 1 study NCT01564225 posted results, so the bundle shows no human exposure, EDA receptor engagement or downstream (e.g., sweat gland) biomarker data. The only mechanistic evidence is canine: prenatal, not postnatal, dosing improved the phenotype (PMID:31000577). This hints that timing may matter, but it is animal data and does not count. If the program stopped for lack of benefit, nothing separates non-engagement from target irrelevance, so U applies as a secondary code. The bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT00718627 was a Phase 2 safety study of liver cell infusion and portal-vein catheter placement over 7–15 weeks. Its endpoint is classified as not_efficacy, and no results were posted, so it was not an efficacy test of HHLivC. The follow-on Phase 2 NCT01195753 was terminated after 10 patients, with no stated reason and no results. The bundle contains no human data on cell engraftment (exposure), metabolic enzyme activity (engagement), or ammonia/ureagenesis biomarkers (pathway). It also has no PubMed abstracts, no comparator drugs, and no stated stop reason. The best-supported code is F9 (not an efficacy failure). U is listed secondarily because nothing in the bundle shows why the program ended.

In atrial flutter patients (NCT01396226), AZD2927 reached a total plasma level of 1.2 µM, close to the 1.5 µM target. With about 68% protein binding, the unbound level was roughly 0.38 µM, near the 0.35 µM IC50 measured in human atrial myocytes, so exposure was adequate. Left atrial refractory period, the expected downstream effect, did not change, so pathway is inadequate. Block of IKACh in humans was never measured, so engagement is no_human_data. The authors rule out low exposure. They blame species differences: dogs have much more constitutively active IKACh, which suggests the target matters less in humans (F2). However, exposure near the IC50 implies only partial block, and the sources cannot separate weak engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U. Tolerability did not limit the dose, and no serious adverse events were reported.

The bundle has no human pharmacology for BAT8001. Its Phase 1 trial (NCT04189211) posted no results, and there are no PubMed abstracts, so exposure, engagement and pathway are all no_human_data. The index Phase 3 trial (NCT04185649, PFS endpoint) has unknown status, no stated stop reason and no posted results. Other ERBB2-directed drugs, including the ADCs trastuzumab emtansine and trastuzumab deruxtecan, are FDA-approved in HER2-positive breast cancer. The target is therefore validated in this disease, which points to a molecule-specific shortfall (F1b) rather than an irrelevant target. Because nothing in the bundle shows whether BAT8001 engaged adequately, U also applies. The bundle is very thin, so confidence is low.

BAT8001 is a trastuzumab-biosimilar ADC. ERBB2 is clearly validated in HER2+ breast cancer: trastuzumab, trastuzumab emtansine, trastuzumab deruxtecan, pertuzumab and others are approved. For BAT8001 itself, the bundle has no human target-engagement or pathway data. The phase 1 study (PMID:33528890, NCT04189211) reports PK as an objective but gives no values. It set the MTD at 3.6 mg/kg, with thrombocytopenia and transaminase rises as dose-limiting toxicities, and showed 41% objective responses; these are clinical signals, not pillar evidence. The index phase 3 (NCT04185649) posted no results and no stop reason. Since the target succeeds with other drugs, the most likely explanation is the molecule (F1b). Evidence is thin and engagement is unmeasured, so U also applies.

AZX100 is a peptide that mimics phosphorylated HSP20. In the index trial (NCT00811577), neither the 3 mg nor the 10 mg dose improved PSAS or OSAS scar scores over placebo (p=0.56–0.80). Two keloid trials (NCT00825916, NCT00892723) also failed. The only evidence of a pharmacological effect is in vitro: lower CTGF and collagen in keloid fibroblasts at 50 µM. I found no human data on drug levels in the skin, on target engagement, or on downstream biomarkers. No other drug on this target is in the bundle. Afterwards, Capstone stopped developing AZX100 to save cash because it had not found a partner (business reason, secondary F8). With no engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

AZX100 is an HSP20 phosphopeptide mimetic injected into the excision wound. The index keloid trial (NCT00825916, 3 and 10 mg/cm) missed its POSAS endpoint, and so did the lower-dose keloid trial (NCT00892723) and the trocar-site trial (NCT00811577). Evidence that AZX100 lowers CTGF and collagen comes only from keloid fibroblasts in vitro and from a hamster model (PMID:18787533, PMID:20140957). Phase 1 press releases report safety only. I found no human data on skin drug levels, HSP20/cofilin pathway engagement, or CTGF lowering. The sponsor said its doses and schedules 'may not be optimal' and said the subjective POSAS scale was insensitive, which points to possible design limits (F7). Without human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index ED trial (NCT01168817) posted no results, and no source gives a reason the program stopped. The only human pharmacology comes from a 2009 abstract of the heart-failure dose-escalation study (NCT00565565). It showed linear plasma PK with a 14–20 h half-life and clear dose-related systemic vasodilation at 2.5–10 mg (lower PCWP and SVR, higher cardiac index), with good tolerability. That counts as systemic exposure and a downstream pathway effect, but in heart failure, not ED. No source measured sGC engagement (e.g., cGMP) or drug effects in penile tissue in ED patients. Doses and PD from the ED combination study (NCT01110590) are unpublished. The ED supporting data are only from animals and isolated tissue. Engagement is no_human_data, so the code is U.

CLP is a non-absorbed cross-linked polyelectrolyte that acts in the gut lumen; no target is recorded. Phase 1 NCT01598740 (2012, before the 2013 index start) in heart failure patients with CKD showed mean fecal sodium increases of about 635 mg (CLP alone) and 502 mg (with spironolactone). This is a direct sign that the drug reached its luminal site and bound sodium in this disease, so exposure and engagement are rated adequate. No downstream effect in humans (body weight, NT-proBNP, fluid status) is shown. The index trial NCT01736735 has unknown status and no posted results or stated stop reason, and no PubMed abstract concerns this drug. F2 rests only on the engagement evidence plus the program stopping, hence low confidence.

Phase 1 showed rapid absorption and measurable plasma exposure in humans. A 40 mg single dose caused ECG abnormalities, which capped dosing at ≤15 mg (PMID:24126567). At 10 mg in NCT01264692, SiDBP did not differ from placebo, while amlodipine (same L-type target) lowered SiDBP by 16.8 mmHg in the same trial, confirming assay validity and that the target drives BP (PMID:25231512). The only pharmacodynamic signal was cardiac: PR prolongation and second-degree AV block. Vascular L-/T-type blockade sufficient to lower BP was not shown. The dose was limited by conduction effects below an effective level, so the mechanism was not properly tested. This is a molecule failure (F1b), with an on-target conduction liability (F5).

No primary target is recorded for andrographolide, and none of the sources measure engagement or a pathway effect in humans. There are no CNS levels and no pharmacodynamic biomarker. The only human pharmacokinetic data come from healthy volunteers taking an extract and show low, non-linear plasma exposure (PMID:39760215). The HIV phase 1 (PMID:10925397) reported no target engagement. In the index trial (NCT02273635), 44 people were enrolled against 68 planned and took 140 mg twice daily. Brain atrophy measured by SIENA was 0.68%/yr on drug vs 1.07%/yr on placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant. Only a post-hoc measure reached significance. The authors called the trial exploratory and asked for a larger study, so it was small and underpowered (secondary F7). Nothing in the sources tells apart a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Andrographolide has no defined target, and the sources contain no human data on CNS exposure, engagement of a target, or a pathway biomarker in MS. The only human pharmacology is low plasma levels of andrographolide taken as an extract (PMID:39760215) and an HIV Phase 1 stopped early for adverse events (PMID:10925397). In the published index pilot (NCT02273635, PMC7203851), 44 of a planned 68 patients were randomised to 140 mg twice daily. Brain atrophy (the primary endpoint) favoured the drug by 36.5% but missed significance (p=0.08). EDSS was nominally better. With engagement unknown, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The small, under-enrolled exploratory design (F7) also limited what the trial could show.

The index trial NCT01348919 was a small dose-finding phase 1/2 study (n=11). It set an MTD of 1.8 mg/m^2 and reported a descriptive 40% ORR at the MTD (n=5), with no hypothesis test. The bundle contains no human PK, proteasome inhibition or pathway biomarker data. Proteasome inhibition in tumours appears only in xenografts (PMID:18057228). The earlier myeloma phase 2 (NCT01023880) was terminated without stated reason or results. Three other PSMB5 inhibitors (bortezomib, carfilzomib, ixazomib) are FDA-approved in myeloma, so the target is validated. With no pillar evidence that delanzomib engaged adequately, the molecule rather than the target is the likeliest explanation (F1b). The index trial was not a formal efficacy test, so F9 also applies.

Reparixin made no difference in the index trial: 20.0% of patients were insulin independent at day 365 versus 21.2% on placebo (NCT01967888). Plasma exposure in humans is documented by Phase 1 pharmacokinetic data (NCT02001974) and the CSR. Steady-state levels of about 25 µg/mL match concentrations that blocked neutrophil responses in vitro (NCT05496868 protocol), so exposure counts as adequate. No source measured CXCR1/2 occupancy or ex vivo inhibition of neutrophil chemotaxis in humans. The only downstream signal is a smaller rise in neutrophil count after cardiopulmonary bypass in a small trial (n=32) in another setting. Serum CXCL8 was an exploratory endpoint, but no results were found. No sponsor explanation was found, and no other drug on this target has succeeded here. Engagement therefore has no human data, which gives U.

Reparixin is a systemic drug, and Phase 1 trials, including NCT02001974, measured high plasma exposure. No source reports human CXCR1/2 receptor occupancy or inhibition of the target. Human pathway data in the sponsor's investigator brochure are mixed: reparixin did not significantly affect LPS-induced neutrophilia in volunteers, but blunted the neutrophil rise after cardiopulmonary bypass. None of this was measured in islet transplant recipients. The phase 3 trial NCT01817959 missed its primary endpoint, and so did the islet auto-transplant study NCT01967888. The investigators concluded the data do not support a role for CXCR1/2 inhibition. A subgroup induced with antithymocyte globulin showed a trend favouring reparixin (26.7% vs 0%, p=0.09), which is weakly consistent with F3. Because engagement was never shown, a drug that failed to engage cannot be separated from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F2 is listed because the authors blamed the target.

In the index trial NCT05254990, reparixin numerically lowered death/IMV/ECMO (7/160 vs 12/152 on placebo), but the trial was stopped for futility under its protocol. Plasma exposure in humans is documented: in NCT02001974, peak levels after oral dosing reached tens of µg/mL, well above the low-nM in vitro IC50 for CXCR1. However, no source I found shows engagement in humans, such as receptor occupancy, inhibition of neutrophil chemotaxis ex vivo, or a lung neutrophil biomarker, in pneumonia or any other disease. Other trials of the drug did not separate target from molecule either: the earlier COVID Phase 3 NCT04878055 and the ARDS trial NCT05496868 both failed, and no other CXCR1/2 drug has succeeded in pneumonia. Tolerability did not limit the dose. With engagement unknown, the failure cannot be explained, so the code is U.

Reparixin missed its PFS endpoint in the fRida trial (NCT02370238; HR 1.14, p=0.59). In the phase Ib study (NCT02001974, PMID:28539464), tolerability did not cap the dose. That study measured plasma levels in the tens of µg/mL at the selected 1200 mg three-times-daily dose, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. The sources I found contain no human data on receptor occupancy or CXCR1/2 inhibition (for example, a neutrophil CXCL8 assay). The downstream readouts were weak: the phase Ib cancer stem cell (CSC) biomarker analysis was inconclusive. In the window trial (NCT01861054, PMID:31924241), CSCs fell by ≥20% in only 4 of 17 and 9 of 17 patients, and immunofluorescence could not confirm this. The fRida paper (PMID:34476645) gives no reason for the failure. Because engagement is unmeasured, I can't tell a drug that never engaged CXCR1/2 apart from a target that doesn't drive this cancer, so the code is U.

Human plasma pharmacokinetics are documented (NCT02001974). The sponsor's protocol says 1200 mg three times daily gives steady-state unbound levels above the in vitro IC50 of about 1 ng/mL, so I rated exposure adequate. Engagement was never measured in a person who took the drug. The only pharmacodynamic data were concentration-dependent blocking of IL-8-induced NET release when reparixin was added to healthy volunteers' blood in the lab. That is in vitro evidence. No receptor occupancy or downstream biomarker was measured in COVID-19 patients. The open-label phase 2 was positive (NCT04794803), but the phase 3 (NCT04878055) and the index trial (NCT05254990) failed, with only non-significant trends favouring reparixin. The sources give no reason for the failure, so with engagement unmeasured the result is indeterminate (U). The small, early-stopped, underpowered index trial makes F7 a secondary possibility.

The index trial NCT01086462 was an IV [14C] microdose PK study in six healthy men, not an efficacy test, so this is F9. Pillar data come from PMID:23448278, which covers healthy volunteers only and was published in 2013, after the index trial started. Oral bioavailability was low (at most 16%) and exposure rose less than dose-proportionally. The top dose of 1500 mg gave only a mean 74% CCR4 occupancy in the TARC-induced actin polymerisation assay. That is partial engagement, and absorption rather than tolerability capped it. This suggests the molecule could not reliably engage CCR4 (secondary F1a). No downstream pathway or asthma-patient data exist, and no reason for stopping is given.

In mild allergic asthmatics, anti-OX40L did not attenuate early- or late-phase allergen responses (NCT00983658, PMID:24224471). The bundle has no PK or direct OX40L binding or occupancy data. Downstream pharmacology did move in this disease: total IgE fell 17% and sputum eosinophils fell 75% by day 113, though blood eosinophils and airway hyperresponsiveness were unchanged. AEs were similar to placebo, so dose was not tolerability-capped. The authors suggest treatment duration or dose may have been insufficient. A proximal effect without clinical benefit, with duration or dose blamed, fits F4. Because engagement and exposure were never measured, an undertested mechanism (U) cannot be excluded, and target irrelevance (F2) remains possible.

In the index trial NCT00919763, CD2027 3 mcg/g ointment applied twice daily for 4 weeks did not beat vehicle on target-lesion TSS (4.7 vs 4.6 at week 4), and there were no serious adverse events. The bundle and my searches turned up no human data for CD2027 on skin drug levels, VDR engagement or a downstream marker such as cathelicidin induction. There are also no Phase 1 results and no statement from the sponsor about why the program stopped. Other VDR agonists like calcipotriene and calcitriol are approved for psoriasis, a different disease, and none succeeded in atopic eczema, so F1b does not apply. With engagement having no human data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged VDR apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

CSPS is a dentin-tubule occluder with no molecular target. The only occlusion evidence (PMID:24455439, PMID:21207917) is in vitro, so no human pillar is shown. In NCT01691560 (PMID:27295867), 5% CSPS did not beat the 0% CSPS control and was worse on Schiff at week 8. The investigators said the abrasivity-matched placebo, with extra dental silica, may itself have reduced sensitivity, so the comparator was not inert. In the companion trial NCT01831817 (PMID:27295868), 5% CSPS beat fluoride controls but not 0% CSPS, which fits that explanation. A meta-analysis found 5% CSPS better than negative controls, and the sponsor later marketed it. The failure therefore points to the trial design; engagement itself is unmeasured (U secondary).

Calcium sodium phosphosilicate is a bioactive glass with no recorded molecular target, so the sources contain no human measurement of receptor occupancy, enzyme inhibition or a defined pathway biomarker. The index study (NCT01657877) was an exploratory in situ model in which adding 5% CSP to a 1500 ppm SMFP dentifrice did not improve enamel surface microhardness recovery (p=0.26). The published trial concludes that CSPS neither helps nor hinders fluoride remineralization. PMID:30099066 found a modest in situ gain, but no source explains why. Because engagement was never measured, nothing separates a mechanism that does not add to fluoride from a formulation that delivered too little bioavailable calcium. Its sister trials in dentine hypersensitivity (NCT01691560, NCT01831817) also showed no difference from the 0% CSP formulation.

In the PHN crossover trial (NCT01106716, PMID:23438341), a single 25 mg subcutaneous infusion of KAI-1678 was well tolerated but did not reduce pain compared with placebo. Lidocaine did reduce pain, so the trial could detect a response, which argues against a design failure (F7). I found no human data on KAI-1678 levels at nerve tissue, on how much it blocked εPKC binding to its anchoring protein (RACK), or on any downstream biomarker. The only pharmacodynamic data I found were preclinical (AdisInsight). No other εPKC inhibitor has succeeded in neuropathic pain, so F1b does not apply, and tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

KAI-1678 is a peptide that blocks PKCε from binding its anchoring protein (RACK). I found no human data on its exposure at the site of action, its engagement of PKCε, or any pathway biomarker. The index SCI pain trial (NCT01135108) enrolled only 5 subjects and posted no results, so it could not answer the efficacy question; that supports F7 as a secondary code. The published postoperative pain trial (NCT01015235) found the drug was not an analgesic. A postherpetic neuralgia crossover trial (NCT01106716) was also published, but I could not open its full text. Neither source shows target engagement. No other PKCε drug has succeeded in this disease. Because engagement has no human data, the evidence cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged PKCε from a target that does not drive pain after SCI. So the primary code is U.

KAI-1678 is a peptide that blocks εPKC from binding its intracellular receptor. It was given by subcutaneous infusion for postoperative orthopedic pain in the index trial NCT01015235 (published as Moodie 2013, Pain Medicine) and also tested in postherpetic neuralgia (NCT01106716) and spinal cord injury pain (NCT01135108). In the postherpetic neuralgia crossover trial it did not beat placebo, while the lidocaine comparator worked. The pages found had no human data on tissue or nerve exposure, εPKC engagement, or a downstream biomarker. The only engagement support is from animal hyperalgesia models. No other drug on this target has succeeded. Because engagement data are missing, these sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged εPKC apart from a target that doesn't matter for pain. The code is U, with low confidence.

The index trial NCT01298830 was a small (n=11) Phase 1/2 safety study of GLP-1 CellBeads in space-occupying ICH. Its primary outcome was safety, not efficacy. It was terminated because the study medication needed improvement, safety data were judged sufficient, and no further knowledge gain was expected. No results were posted. The bundle has no other trials, no Phase 1 results and no PubMed evidence on exposure, GLP1R engagement or pathway effects in humans. Because it was not an efficacy test of the drug, F9 applies. The formulation-driven stop hints at a delivery problem, but nothing in the bundle shows inadequate exposure. With engagement unmeasured, U is a secondary code. Other GLP1R agonists in ischemic stroke do not bear on this cell-encapsulated product's engagement.

The iDSMB stop reason for index trial NCT02353143 says there was 'meaningful target engagement not translating into any clinical objective response' in relapsed/refractory AML patients, alongside unpredictable liver toxicity. Engagement is therefore treated as adequate in this disease. That engagement implies systemic exposure, although no PK values are posted. It was shown only within the index trial itself. The MTD of 1.7 mg/kg was reached, with dosing up to 2.5 mg/kg, so the dose was not capped below engagement. No downstream blast-depletion or ADCC biomarker data are shown. Engaged but no response fits F2. Liver toxicity contributed to stopping (F6). PMID:28415689 notes heterogeneous NK-cell function in AML patients, which may have limited ADCC (F3).

In the index trial (NCT01124539), AR-67 was given at 7.5 mg/m2/day for 5 days. Only 6 of 30 patients in cohort 1 reached 6-month PFS, and 2 of 13 in cohort 2 reached 2-month PFS. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Human data are plasma PK only: a phase 1 study plus PMID:30820810, which tied exposure to blood-count toxicity. Tumor tissue levels were measured in one NSCLC patient. No human data show brain or GBM drug levels, TOP1 inhibition, or a downstream biomarker. Other TOP1 drugs in GBM (irinotecan, edotecarin) are not shown to have succeeded, so F1b does not apply. The sources give no failure reason. They cannot tell a drug that never reached or engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The solid-tumor Phase 1 trial (NCT00389480, PMID:30820810) measured plasma exposure: a dose-proportional, two-compartment PK model, with Cmax and AUC predicting leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. NCT01202370 reported more than 85% lactone stability. Systemic exposure therefore looks adequate at doses that include the 7.5 mg/m2/day x5 used in the MDS trial. No source measured TOP1 engagement in humans (no TOP1-DNA cleavage complexes, enzyme inhibition, or DNA-damage markers) or a pathway biomarker, in MDS or any other disease. The 2011 ASH abstract on the index trial reports 'acceptable tolerability and preliminary activity' but no response data and no reason for stopping. The index trial status is unknown and no results were posted. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

CMX-2043 is a modified alpha-lipoic acid. No primary target is recorded, and no human PK, target-engagement or kidney pathway biomarker data were found. In the CARIN trial (NCT02103959), none of the three IV doses (2.4, 3.6 or 4.8 mg/kg) reduced contrast-induced AKI compared with placebo (18.6–25.6% across arms; placebo 18.6%). The earlier Phase 2 trial (NCT00984802) reported fewer periprocedural cardiac injury biomarkers at the highest dose. That is a cardiac clinical-biomarker result, not evidence of target engagement in the kidney. The sponsor suggested dosing as a possible limitation but had no data to support it. There were no drug-related serious adverse events, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT00984802, SUPPORT-1, n=142) was a Phase 2a safety study, and it was not an efficacy failure. Its primary safety endpoint was met. In an exploratory analysis, no patient on 2.4 mg/kg had CK-MB rise to 3x the upper limit of normal or more, versus 16% on placebo (P=0.02), and the investigators said this supported further study (PMID 32769849). The sponsor then ran a kidney-injury trial (NCT02103959), reported as positive, and later moved the drug to traumatic brain injury with a new Phase 1 in 2023. No primary target is recorded, and no human target-engagement or pathway-biomarker data were found. So all three pillars are no_human_data. The drug's stalling in coronary disease looks like a strategic shift, not a failed readout.

Topical SBG (a beta-1,3/1,6-glucan meant to activate the Dectin-1/CLEC7A receptor) was compared with placebo on top of best standard wound care in Phase 3 (NCT00804414). Biotec Pharmacon reported that both Phase 3 studies showed the same result: about 30% of target ulcers healed in each arm. No harm was reported. The sponsor stopped work in this indication because earlier positive results (e.g., NCT00288392) did not replicate. No source gives human evidence of drug levels in wound tissue, Dectin-1 engagement, or downstream changes such as macrophage activation or cytokine signals. Nothing in the evidence separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not drive ulcer healing, so the code is U.

Biotec Pharmacon reported that topical SBG failed to beat placebo in the Phase 3 oral mucositis trial (NCT00790322). This followed negative Phase 3 results in diabetic foot ulcer (NCT00804414). None of the sources gives human evidence that SBG engaged Dectin-1/CLEC7A in oral mucosa. A healthy-volunteer study (PMC1809555) found no SBG in serum after oral dosing and an increase in salivary IgA. That IgA rise is a nonspecific immune readout, not a target-engagement measure, and it was not measured in mucositis patients. The company said it was not surprised given the foot-ulcer result, and it then began testing alternative packaging containers, which hints it was looking at product stability. No other Dectin-1 agonist has succeeded in this disease. With engagement untested, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Apatone B is oral vitamin C plus menadione (vitamin K3). No molecular target is recorded for it. The index trial, NCT01272830, posted only within-arm paired t-tests, and its week-13 VAS pain scores were nearly identical between arms (39.7 drug vs 39.1 placebo). It enrolled only 38 patients with analysable data and posted no between-group analysis, so the trial design was weak (secondary F7). I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or a downstream biomarker. The only mechanism work I found was in vitro synovial-fibroblast experiments described in a patent, and lab data do not count. The available sources cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged a target from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease. No sponsor explanation for stopping was found.

Apatone B is an oral combination of vitamin C and vitamin K3 (menadione), and no molecular target is recorded for it. Neither the bundle nor my search turned up any human data on drug levels in tissue, target engagement or downstream biomarkers. In the index trial NCT01272830, pain improved within the Apatone arm (p=0.0063). But by week 13 VAS was the same in both groups (39.7 vs 39.1), and the Apatone arm started with a higher baseline. No between-group analysis was posted and the arms were small (17 vs 21), so the trial looks underpowered (possible F7). No sponsor statement explaining the failure was found. With engagement unknown, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index HCV trial (NCT00790673) posted only adverse-event counts at 1 mg once or twice daily. It posted no viral-load or PK data, and I found no published reason for stopping. In HCC patients (NCT00790218, PMC3556251), CF102 had good oral bioavailability and linear plasma PK at 1–25 mg twice daily, so systemic exposure was shown. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred, so tolerability did not cap the dose. A3AR expression in blood cells (PBMCs) was measured as a baseline predictor of response, not as receptor occupancy or a drug-induced pathway change. The PBMC A3AR biomarker endpoint in NCT00790218 has no data. No human data show target engagement or a pathway effect, in HCV or anywhere else. No other A3AR drug has succeeded in HCV. So whether the drug never engaged or the target does not matter can't be told apart: U.

No web searches were run, so this rests on the bundle alone. In the Phase 2 trial (PMID:22048878), blood levels of TLN-4601 reached their targets at 480 mg/m2/day. However, no human tumour or CSF levels were reported, which a glioblastoma target needs. There is also no human measure of TSPO occupancy, and PMID:20655882 says TSPO binding does not drive the drug's anticancer effect. The pathway markers measured in patients' samples (Raf-1 and pERK) did not change consistently, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited. The index trial stopped after 20 patients for lack of efficacy. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F1a is a possible secondary, since the unchanged biomarkers hint that the mechanism was never properly tested.

The Phase 2 trial in recurrent GBM gave TLN-4601 at 480 mg/m2/day by continuous IV infusion. It stopped after 20 patients for lack of efficacy (NCT00730262; Springer report). Serum PK reached the targeted drug levels, and Phase 1 plasma concentrations of 4.5–7 µM were above the preclinical 2 µM target, so systemic exposure is adequate. Human tumor or brain drug levels were not measured. No source reports TSPO occupancy or any downstream pathway marker in humans; TSPO binding and tumor accumulation were shown only in rodents (PMID:20655882). That same paper found TSPO binding does not drive the drug's anti-tumor effect. The drug was tolerated without dose capping. With no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

No human study measured SREBP binding directly. Exposure is supported: Phase 1 PK work (NCT01725594) reported the desired PK/PD profile. The downstream pathway also responded: triglycerides fell (postprandial by up to 90%) and LDL-C dropped significantly in earlier trials (NCT01912560, NCT01968720). In the index trial (NCT02098278, CAT-2003-203), the 500 mg dose cut fasting triglycerides by a median 40% in multifactorial chylomicronemia and refractory severe hypertriglyceridemia. It gave no meaningful reduction in patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS). Catabasis describes CAT-2003 as working by raising lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity, and FCS patients lack functional LPL. So the benefit was limited to subtypes that are not FCS, which fits F3. GI side effects led to some dose reductions. Catabasis then chose to prioritize CAT-2054 (business reason, F8).

In T2D patients, GSK256073 acutely engaged HCA2. A 2-day trial (NCT01147861, PMID:23701262) showed sustained NEFA and glycerol suppression, lower glucose and better HOMA-IR, without flushing. In the index trial (NCT01376323, PMID:25773496), exposure was sustained, with 2-fold accumulation, and NEFA fell on day 2. By week 6, however, NEFA suppression was lost at three doses and reduced at 50 mg QD despite continued exposure. HbA1c fell at most 0.30% vs placebo (not significant). Safety did not limit dosing. The drug reached and engaged its target, but the receptor mechanism did not give durable glycaemic control, which points to the target biology. Waning functional engagement over time, possibly receptor desensitization, adds an F1a element.

In humans, GSK256073 engaged HCA2 acutely. Over 48 h in T2DM patients (NCT01147861, PMID 23701262) it suppressed NEFA, the proximal biomarker of the mechanism, and single doses in healthy volunteers lowered NEFA and TG. With chronic dosing the effect faded despite sustained exposure: in the 12-week T2DM trial (NCT01376323) NEFA suppression waned, and the authors blamed the missed endpoint on this. In the index dyslipidemia trial (NCT00903617), mean NEFA rose from baseline at weeks 2–8 in all drug arms, so sustained pathway suppression was not shown in this disease. The index trial posted no HDL values or hypothesis test. Sustained engagement was inadequate (tachyphylaxis), so the mechanism was not durably tested. Acute engagement data were published only after the index trial started.

Necuparanib is a heparan sulfate mimetic that acts on many targets and has no single defined target. In the Phase 1 part, drug levels were measurable from 2 mg/kg, and Phase 2 used 5 mg/kg (PMID:29158367). No human measure of target binding exists. Dose escalation was held back by the number of injections, cellulitis and a mild aPTT rise, but no source says the dose was too low to engage the target. A 2018 paper reported that plasma TIMP3 rose significantly in treated patients, which looks like a downstream pathway effect, but it was published after the index trial started. The Phase 2 interim analysis crossed the futility boundary (median OS 10.71 vs 9.99 months, HR 1.12). The sources do not say why it failed. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT00767793 measured safety, tolerability and intraocular pressure (IOP) changes with topical INS117548. No results were posted. The bundle has no other trials of this drug and no PubMed abstracts, so there is no human evidence of ocular exposure, ROCK engagement or a pathway effect. Another ROCK inhibitor, netarsudil, is FDA-approved for open-angle glaucoma, which shows ROCK inhibition can lower IOP in this disease. The failure is therefore more likely attributable to this molecule than to the target (F1b), since no pillar evidence shows INS117548 engaged adequately. The index trial was mainly a safety study, and the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, so F9 is a secondary possibility. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

Albitiazolium is thought to work by blocking choline uptake by the parasite and phosphatidylcholine synthesis, but that evidence is in vitro and in mice only (PMID:22471905). No human study measured target inhibition or a pathway biomarker. The phase 2 trials measured plasma drug levels; children had a lower AUC than adults. The 3-day regimen cured 90% of adults but only 68% of children, and most teenagers on a higher dose needed rescue therapy (PMID:28472957, NCT01445938). The authors offered several possible reasons without choosing one: adult semi-immunity, lower starting parasite counts in adults, and lower exposure in children. With no engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so U. Low exposure (F1a) and population effects (F3) are possible secondary explanations. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose.

The index trial NCT01016366 was a 2-week Phase 2 safety and tolerability study (endpoint class not_efficacy). Its primary goal was met: CEPO was safe and well tolerated, with no immunogenicity (PMID:24515352). Exploratory secondary measures did not differ from placebo, including frataxin, oxidative stress markers and ataxia ratings, so the expected pathway effect (frataxin increase, seen only in vitro in PMID:20456483) was not seen in patients. The bundle has no human PK or target engagement data, and the drug works by an unclear receptor mechanism. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test, F9 applies. Had it been judged on efficacy, U would apply: nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant mechanism.

In NCT01830920, AKI rates were about the same on THR-184 and placebo at every dose (74–79%, P=0.43; PMID 29203473). No human data shows THR-184 engaged its target: there is no BMPR/Smad readout, and the planned KIM-1/NGAL biomarkers were never assayed (PMID:35873578). The Phase 1 studies did measure plasma drug levels. The plasma half-life was only about 5 minutes and Cmax/AUC varied widely. The sponsor names these as confounders and says a longer infusion or a higher dose was needed. Its press release also says the trial found only 'the bottom of the therapeutic window.' So exposure looks inadequate, and the mechanism was probably not properly tested (F1a). This rests on the sponsor's own after-the-fact reading, so confidence is low. U also fits, because engagement was never measured.

The index trial NCT01146886 was a single-dose safety and PK study in healthy volunteers, not an efficacy test, so F9 applies secondarily. In the T2DM multiple-dose study (NCT01282970, PMID:26799632), exposure rose dose-proportionally with a 55-65 h half-life. The urinary THF/THE ratio fell, indicating liver 11β-HSD1 inhibition, and the HPA axis was mildly activated as the mechanism predicts. However, adipose tissue 11β-HSD1 inhibition, which PMID:25445047 calls a key metabolic tissue, was 90% after one dose but only 31% or lower after 14 days. Engagement was therefore inadequate in a key target tissue despite good tolerability up to 200 mg. The mechanism was not properly tested, which fits F1a. This engagement evidence was published after the index trial started.

The index trial, NCT03852459, tested a topical 5% S-ibuprofen gel for delayed-onset muscle soreness. It missed its primary endpoint (SPIDMOVE -33.09 vs -29.09, p=0.43) with no safety issues. All human pillar evidence in the bundle concerns oral dosing. Oral plasma PK is in PMID:9726693. Platelet COX inhibition in healthy volunteers is in PMID:17264714. Oral efficacy in hip osteoarthritis is in PMID:10667832. None of this is comparable to topical delivery, which depends on skin and muscle penetration. The bundle has no data on tissue levels or local COX inhibition for the gel. It therefore cannot separate inadequate local delivery from a lack of mechanism relevance in this model. The large placebo response hints at a trial-design issue (F7), but the sources do not state it.

The index trial tested AP0302, a 5% topical S-ibuprofen gel, for elbow-flexor DOMS. It missed its primary endpoint: SPIDMOVE was -33.09 vs -29.09 on vehicle, p=0.43, with a large vehicle response (NCT03852459). There is human evidence that oral dexibuprofen inhibits COX: platelet COX inhibition at 800 mg/day in PMID:17264714, and efficacy in hip osteoarthritis in PMID:10667832. But these are systemic oral doses. They cannot show that a topical gel delivered enough drug to muscle or tissue to inhibit COX locally, so I did not count them as inferred_adequate. My search found no skin or muscle drug levels, no tissue prostaglandin data, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. With no human data on local engagement, nothing separates poor skin penetration from a target that does not matter in this model, so the code is U. The large vehicle response raises a possible trial-design (F7) issue.

LEO 19123 cream combines calcipotriol with LEO 80122, whose target is not recorded anywhere in the sources. In the index trial NCT00764751, the cream did worse than Dovonex (calcipotriol alone): PASI change -24.8% vs -40.2%, p=0.003. It did not beat vehicle (p=0.07). The sources contain no human pharmacokinetic, target-engagement or biomarker data for LEO 80122, and they give no sponsor explanation for stopping. There are no other drugs on the same target to compare against. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a molecule that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in psoriasis. The answer is indeterminate.

In the GATE trial (NCT00890097, PMID:26310670), topical AL-8309B eye drops at 1.0% and 1.75% did not slow lesion growth in geographic atrophy compared with vehicle. The trial was stopped as ineffective, and no safety problem limited the dose. The only human pharmacokinetic study measured plasma levels in healthy volunteers (PMID:27206141). No study measured drug levels in the retina or retinal pigment epithelium, 5-HT1A engagement in the eye, or a downstream retinal biomarker in humans. The evidence that topical dosing protects the retina comes only from rats (PMID:21087971). Human PET work with oral tandospirone found no measurable 5-HT1A occupancy (PMID:12474116), and that was in the brain, not the eye. A search turned up no human target-engagement data. So the bundle cannot tell apart a drug that never reached or engaged its retinal target from a target that does not matter in this disease.

The index trial, NCT01747941, was a single-dose safety, tolerability and PK study in healthy volunteers. Its only primary outcome was adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test and there was no failed efficacy readout (F9). PF-06305591 is a selective Nav1.8 blocker (IC50 15 nM), but the evidence on it is preclinical only. No human PK, Nav1.8 channel block or pain-model biomarker results were posted or found for the multiple-dose study (NCT01776619), the capsaicin flare study (NCT01797796) or the cold pressor study (NCT01812265). The later academic cold-pain study (NCT05935280) gave the drug by intradermal injection, and its full text could not be retrieved. No reason for stopping was found. Without engagement data, it is unclear whether the drug failed to engage Nav1.8 or the target does not matter, hence the secondary U.

The bundle has no direct human measure of S100A9 engagement or of a pathway biomarker. A plasma assay was validated in cancer patients (PMID:21963277), but no exposure levels are reported. Tasquinimod met radiographic PFS endpoints in mCRPC (phase 3 NCT01234311, HR 0.64; also NCT01732549 and NCT02057666). The pillars are therefore inferred adequate through the same systemic, tumour-microenvironment target, assuming comparable dosing; the doses are not shown in the bundle. In the index basket trial, PFS rates were not significant in any of the HCC, ovarian, RCC or gastric cohorts (NCT01743469). No tolerability cap is shown. This points to the mechanism not driving benefit in these tumour types. Confidence is low because engagement is only inferred across cancers and dose comparability is unverified.

Ivy leaf extract is a herbal mixture with no recorded molecular target, so none of the three pillars can be assessed. The bundle and my search found no human data on drug levels at the site of action, target engagement, or a pathway biomarker. The index trial NCT01127048 (Prospan suppositories in children) has status unknown, posted no results and gave no stop reason. The registry only says the study would continue as a placebo-controlled part after an interim analysis. The PubMed abstracts are open-label or observational efficacy reports (PMID:22532491, PMID:16860549, PMID:32454850) with no pharmacodynamic data. Since engagement has no human data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the answer is U.

The index trial NCT01191996 was an open-label dose-escalation safety study with a primary endpoint of safety and MTD, so it was not an efficacy test. It met its objectives: MTD was not reached, adverse events were mostly mild flu-like symptoms, and 500 µg/week was recommended for Phase 2 (PMID:28607691). Pharmacodynamic evidence in progressive MS patients shows target-pathway activity, including induction of a known PD marker and elevated serum IFN-γ and IFN-γ-associated proteins (PMID:24498172, PMID:28607691). These results were published after the index trial started. No PK data are in the bundle. The follow-on Phase 2 trial NCT02228213 has no classified outcome shown. This is therefore not an efficacy failure: F9.

PET with 11C-MK-8278 showed MK-0249 reaches brain H3 receptors, with about 90% occupancy at clinically feasible doses in healthy volunteers (PMID:24263088). PK/PET data predicted about 85% occupancy at 5 mg in elderly AD patients (PMID:22272611). The OSA index trial used 5–12 mg, so exposure and engagement were adequate, though not measured in OSA patients. This evidence was published after the index trial started in 2008. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. MWT at week 2 did not differ from placebo (13.34 vs 12.79 min, p=0.615), and there was no tolerability cap. Despite high engagement, there was no wakefulness benefit in CPAP-treated OSA, consistent with F2. Pitolisant's OSA outcome is not shown in the bundle.

Brain exposure and H3 engagement were measured in humans. 11C-MK-8278 PET in healthy volunteers showed about 90% H3 receptor occupancy reachable at clinically feasible MK-0249 doses (PMID:24263088). PK/PET modelling projected about 85% occupancy at Cmax even at 5 mg in elderly subjects (PMID:22272611). The index OSA trial used 5–12 mg, with no tolerability cap: no SAEs on drug. Even so, MWT at week 2 did not differ from placebo (13.34 vs 12.79 min, p=0.615; NCT00620659), and the drug also failed in AD (NCT00420420). Engagement data come from healthy volunteers and were published after the index trial started. No pathway biomarker is reported. The trial was terminated without a stated reason, and the modafinil comparator result is not shown, so assay sensitivity is uncertain (secondary F7).

Lemuteporfin is a topical photosensitizer given with red light (PDT) and meant to shrink sebaceous glands in acne. The index trial, NCT01490736, posted no results. Its primary endpoint was change in sebum excretion rate and its secondary endpoints were tissue biomarkers, but none of these were reported. For exposure, a Dermira/QLT patent describes a human study in which the drug was seen in the sebaceous gland by fluorescence in more than 50-70% of biopsies, so I rated exposure adequate, though the evidence is weak. An older report says an earlier formulation did not get through the stratum corneum, citing only mouse data. The searched pages contained no human data on photodynamic damage to the gland, sebum reduction or biomarker changes, and no stated reason the program stopped. With engagement unknown, the failure is indeterminate (U).

In healthy volunteers, JNJ-39758979 had good oral plasma PK (half-life 124-157 h). It caused dose-dependent inhibition of histamine-induced eosinophil shape change, indicating in vivo H4R blockade (PMID:24549371). It also reduced histamine-induced itch at 600 mg (PMID:24817035). No engagement data exist in asthma patients. The index trial (300 mg) missed its FEV1 primary endpoint, with nominal benefit in eosinophilic subgroups (PMID:29682796), which supports F3/F2 as secondary codes. However, the program itself was halted because of drug-induced agranulocytosis in two subjects. The atopic dermatitis trial NCT01497119 was terminated for this reason (PMID:24495018). This is a molecule-specific toxicity, so the primary code is F6.

The index trial NCT01850849 was a Phase 1 safety and PK study. The efficacy test was NCT02219633 in mild-to-moderate AD. PMID:33188482 used dermal open flow microperfusion on human skin explants with the clinical formulation. In barrier-impaired skin, LEO 39652 reached only 33 nM in dermal interstitial fluid, versus 2100 nM for LEO 29102. It produced no cAMP rise, so there was no evidence of target engagement. The authors attribute the lack of clinical efficacy in AD to insufficient drug availability at the target, meaning the mechanism was not properly tested. This evidence comes from ex vivo explants rather than patients, and was published after the index trial. Other topical PDE4 inhibitors (crisaborole, roflumilast, difamilast) are approved in AD, so F1b also applies.

NT-503-3 is an encapsulated cell implant secreting an anti-VEGF binder. The index trial in recurrent CNV due to AMD (NCT02228304) was terminated because rescue injections exceeded the stopping criteria after about half of enrollment. The bundle contains no human data on intraocular drug levels, VEGF neutralization, or downstream effects. It also has no Phase 1 results and no publications. Several other VEGFA neutralizers (aflibercept, ranibizumab, bevacizumab, brolucizumab, faricimab, pegaptanib) are FDA-approved for wet AMD, so the target is validated in this disease.
