Since no pillar evidence shows this implant delivered or engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule or delivery system rather than the target. That fits F1b, with U as a secondary code given the absence of engagement data.

The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, engagement or biomarker data for topical DRM02, and no results were posted for index trial NCT01993420 (n=21) or for the sister psoriasis and rosacea trials (NCT01993433, NCT01993446). The bundle lists other PDE4 inhibitors as FDA-approved for atopic eczema: crisaborole, roflumilast and difamilast. Because the target is validated in this disease and nothing shows DRM02 engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U is listed as secondary because engagement is unmeasured. The very small trial could not answer the question well (F7). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

Topical PDE4B/D inhibitor DRM02 was tested in a small 6-week Phase 2 psoriasis trial (NCT01993433, n=23) with no posted results. Sibling trials in atopic dermatitis and rosacea also have no results. The bundle has no human data on skin exposure, PDE4 engagement or a downstream biomarker. The only pharmacology is in vitro, ex vivo and mouse work (PMID:32479135), which shows modest micromolar IC50s (0.6–14 µM) and does not count as human evidence. Roflumilast, on the same PDE4 target, is FDA-approved for psoriasis. That argues the target matters in this disease, so the failure points to the molecule (F1b) rather than the mechanism. Because engagement was never shown, U remains possible. The evidence is thin.

DRM02 is a topical PDE4 inhibitor. Dermira tested it in three small Phase 2a vehicle-controlled trials (rosacea NCT01993446, atopic dermatitis NCT01993420, psoriasis NCT01993433). None of them posted results. Later reviews say these trials have no published reports. The only pharmacology found comes from mouse skin-inflammation models. No human skin drug levels, PDE4 inhibition or cytokine biomarker data were found. No sponsor statement explains why the program stopped. The other PDE4 drugs listed for rosacea (apremilast, idrebormilast) reached only Phase 2 and are not shown to have succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01393652 was a single-dose escalation study in healthy volunteers. Its primary outcomes were adverse events and pharmacokinetics, with no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. That fits F9. PMID:28603038 (2017, after the index trial started) reports that, in humans, PF-05105679 reversed the cold pain of the cold pressor test without changing core body temperature. This shows adequate exposure and a functional TRPM8 blockade effect, which I treat as engagement and pathway evidence. That evidence comes from healthy volunteers, not from patients with a disease. The bundle gives no stop reason and no dose-limiting tolerability. The program's halt is therefore not explained as an efficacy failure.

The sources do not say what LY3053102 targets. They show only that it was given as a weekly subcutaneous injection and that Lilly later discontinued it. In the index trial NCT02020616, HbA1c changes at 7–200 mg were similar to placebo (−0.22 to −0.75% vs −0.49%), with no dose response, while the active comparator exenatide ER gave −1.43%. That points to a sensitive assay and a drug with no effect. In the Phase 1 study NCT01736241, healthy volunteers tolerated doses up to 405 mg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. That trial posted only adverse-event results, with no PK, PD or target-engagement data, and my web searches found none either. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT02149160, PMID:34559230) gave GRN carriers 300 or 500 mg FRM-0334 daily. The drug was safe but did not raise plasma or CSF progranulin, which was the downstream marker of the mechanism, so pathway is inadequate. Plasma exposure did not rise in proportion to dose. The investigators' abstract says systemic and CSF drug levels stayed below what preclinical work suggested was needed, pointing to too little exposure. Direct HDAC inhibition was not measured in humans, so engagement is no_human_data. The investigators state that the HDAC-inhibition hypothesis was not fully tested. That is a formulation and exposure failure, not a tolerability cap, so the code is F1a.

In the phase 2a index trial (NCT02149160; PMID:34559230), 300 and 500 mg of FRM-0334 were safe but did not raise plasma or CSF progranulin. Plasma and CSF drug levels did not rise in proportion to the dose. They also stayed below the exposures that preclinical work suggested were needed to raise GRN mRNA and progranulin. So exposure was inadequate. No direct HDAC inhibition was measured in humans, so engagement is no_human_data. The downstream progranulin biomarker did not move, so pathway is inadequate. The investigators concluded that low exposure meant the HDAC-inhibition hypothesis was not fully tested. That makes this F1a: the mechanism was not properly tested. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

The index trial NCT01092780 does not show an efficacy failure. Both MK-7288 doses lengthened Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency versus placebo by about 8.1–8.2 minutes (95% CIs roughly 6–10, excluding zero), close to modafinil. Both doses also improved the SDLP driving measure (−0.07 m, CI excluding zero). The trial therefore met its primary efficacy endpoints, so F9 applies. No target is recorded and the bundle has no PK, engagement or pathway data, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Clinical adverse events were more frequent on MK-7288 (30/54 and 37/55 vs 12/52 on placebo). Tolerability or business reasons may explain why the program stopped, but the bundle states neither.

The index trial NCT01092780 does not read as an efficacy failure. In sleep apnea patients, MK-7288 10 and 20 mg improved Maintenance of Wakefulness Test sleep latency over placebo by about 8.1 minutes, with confidence intervals excluding zero. Driving lane deviation (SDLP) also improved, by about -0.07 m, CI excluding zero. Modafinil performed similarly. No target is recorded, and the bundle has no exposure, engagement or pathway data. Clinical adverse events were more frequent on MK-7288 than placebo (30 and 37 vs 12), but no stop reason is given. The bundle does not explain why the program stopped. F9 fits best because the primary endpoints appear to have been met; U is listed as secondary because the reason for discontinuation is undetermined.

The phase 1 index trial (NCT01723475) was a dose-escalation safety study, not a failed efficacy test. It produced PSA responses: >50% declines in 9 SC and 3 cIV patients, including two long-term responders. A sponsor change stopped the cIV cohort early before its MTD was set (PMID:33172323), so the stop looks business-driven (F8). Every SC patient developed neutralizing anti-drug antibodies, causing profound exposure loss and reversal of PSA responses (PMID:37942314). That makes exposure inadequate on that route (F1a). The antibodies were traced to non-tolerant T-cell epitopes in the molecule, a molecule-specific liability (F6). The cIV route produced no anti-drug antibodies. Direct target-engagement data are absent from the bundle; PSA decline supports the pathway pillar.

The index trial NCT00951405 had safety primary endpoints (thrombogenicity, immunogenicity), so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. PMID:23578227 reports the drug was well tolerated, with no related serious adverse events, immunogenic or thromboembolic events, so the primary endpoint was met. Exposure was adequate: PK in patients matched phase 1, with a prolonged half-life of about 15 h. The bundle reports no direct activity, engagement or pathway biomarker data. Exploratory annualized bleeding rate fell at all doses, but with no dose-response. Bleeding also dropped late in the observation period, suggesting design limitations in this small (n=23) uncontrolled-comparison trial (secondary F7). No business or other stop reason is shown.

IDP-107 was an oral drug for moderate-to-severe acne from Dow/Valeant. No target is recorded, and I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or biomarker effects. Neither Phase 2 trial (NCT00666900, NCT01194375) posted results, and there are no publications. Valeant's 2012 10-K says it ended the program and wrote off the $133.4M asset after reviewing the Phase 2 results with key opinion leaders. It gives no specific reason, and it also says it could not find a partner. Engagement is unknown, and nothing here tells apart a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter in acne, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00977522 was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results, and its doses are not given. PET occupancy data in schizophrenia patients (PMID:29499855, from NCT01911676, which started after the index trial) show 76–83% GlyT1 occupancy at 40–60 mg BID, so brain exposure and engagement were adequate. The same study showed a pathway effect, with enhanced LTP in patients. PF-03463275 was well tolerated, so dose was not limiting. At doses chosen for high occupancy, a later randomized trial still showed no clinical benefit on cognition (PMID:37141764). This points to the mechanism not driving benefit (F2). Confidence is low because the index trial's own termination reason and doses are not in the bundle.

In the index allergen-challenge crossover (NCT01890161, reported in PMID:29423947), AXP1275 50 mg daily did not affect the late asthmatic response or blood and sputum eosinophils. Unchanged eosinophils mean the expected downstream effect did not follow. The abstract calls the drug a CCR3 inhibitor, while the listed target is PTGDR2. The authors attribute the poor efficacy to low and variable drug exposure over a short treatment period. No receptor occupancy data are given. Methacholine PC20 improved modestly. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Because the sources blame inadequate exposure, the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). No other PTGDR2 antagonist in the bundle is shown to have succeeded, so F1b does not apply.

Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate: the same 4 mg suprachoroidal CLS-TA met a pivotal BCVA endpoint in uveitic macular edema (NCT02595398), acting through the same target and retinal compartment, and won approval for macular edema. In RVO itself, the Phase 2 Tanzanite trial (NCT02303184, PMID:31047241), which started before the index trial, showed an anatomical pathway effect: central subfield thickness normalised and fewer aflibercept retreatments were needed. Yet SAPPHIRE (NCT02980874) showed no added BCVA gain over aflibercept alone (114/231 vs 127/229, p=0.187), and the sponsor stated there was no additional benefit from adding the corticosteroid. The sister trial (NCT03203447) and the DME combination trial (NCT03126786) were also negative. The add-on mechanism does not improve vision beyond anti-VEGF (F2). The 8-week BCVA endpoint, set against an anatomical effect, is a possible contributor (F4).

The index trial NCT01273337 (RECOVER-Stroke) had safety of intracarotid ALD-401 delivery as its primary outcome, so it is classified as not an efficacy endpoint. PMID:30586746 reports that safety was acceptable: no infusional reactions and no difference in adverse events, with only small asymptomatic MRI diffusion lesions. The 90-day mRS efficacy measure was secondary and showed no difference (P=0.33). Because the primary endpoint was met and the trial was not an efficacy test, F9 fits best. The cell therapy has no recorded target, and the bundle has no human evidence of exposure, engagement or pathway effect. The efficacy miss therefore cannot be attributed to the mechanism or to delivery, which supports U as a secondary code.

Exposure was shown in humans. Scyllo-inositol rose in CSF and brain in AD patients at 250 mg BID (PMID:21917766), and in healthy volunteers at 2000 mg (PMID:27121673). The target-related marker CSF Aβx-42 fell significantly in AD patients at 250 mg (PMID:21917766, published before the index trial started), which I take as adequate engagement. No downstream pathway or functional marker was reported, so pathway is no_human_data. Despite this, the index agitation trial NCT01735630 showed no separation from placebo on NPI-C A+A (-4.3 vs -4.2). The anti-amyloid mechanism, as tested, did not drive agitation or aggression. Higher doses were stopped earlier for infections and deaths, and SAEs were imbalanced in the index trial (17 vs 5), so molecule-specific toxicity is a secondary factor.

Exposure: in mild-moderate AD patients, 250 mg BID raised scyllo-inositol in CSF and brain (PMID:21917766). Healthy volunteers on 2000 mg reached CSF levels matching transgenic-model efficacy (PMID:27121673). Engagement: CSF Aβx-42 fell significantly versus placebo at 250 mg in AD (PMID:21917766, published 2011, before the 2012 index start). This is the best available proxy for the anti-aggregation mechanism, so it is treated as adequate. Higher doses were dropped for infections and deaths, but engagement was shown at the retained 250 mg dose (the dose of the long-term extension, NCT00934050). The index trial dose is not stated in the bundle. Despite this, NPI-C agitation/aggression did not separate from placebo (-4.3 vs -4.2; NCT01735630). The mechanism as tested did not drive the agitation/aggression endpoint, so F2.

In the index trial (NCT00739739), 30 mg and 60 mg of PD-0299685 did not improve the ICSI score or the urinary endpoints. The 60 mg dose gave only a borderline pain reduction (-0.82; 90% CI -1.72 to 0.08), and the authors concluded it 'failed to demonstrate positive proof of concept' (PMID:22818144). Neither the bundle nor the web search turned up human PK, CSF exposure, α2δ-1 binding/occupancy data or a pharmacodynamic biomarker for this drug. No other α2δ ligand has succeeded in interstitial cystitis: pregabalin reached only phase 1 there. That rules out F1b, and since F2 needs adequate engagement, F2 does not apply either. More patients on the drug than on placebo stopped because of adverse events, but nothing shows tolerability capped the dose below what engagement needed. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index Phase 1/2 trial (NCT02191878) had an MTD primary endpoint. PMID:30598500 reports limited antitumor activity: median PFS 2.04 months, OS 7.5 months, no survival gain over historical control. The authors judged further single-agent evaluation unwarranted. The bundle contains no human PK, tumour PLK1 mRNA or protein knockdown, or downstream biomarker data, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The MTD was lowered from 0.75 to 0.6 mg/kg after grade 4 thrombocytopenia, but nothing shows this capped the dose below what engagement required. No other PLK1 drug succeeded in HCC, so F1b does not apply. Nothing separates non-delivery or non-knockdown from PLK1 irrelevance, so the code is U. F9 is secondary because the index trial was a dose-finding study, not an efficacy test.

In NCT01143337, MP-435 at 100 mg twice daily on top of methotrexate gave the same Week-12 ACR20 rate as placebo (39.5% vs 39.5%). At Weeks 4–8 it was numerically ahead, but the trial was small (n=47 per arm). My searches found no human pharmacokinetic, C5aR1 receptor-occupancy or C5a-induced neutrophil biomarker data for MP-435. Secondary sources only say that MP-435, like PMX53, showed little efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis. No other C5aR1 drug in the bundle succeeded in this disease: NNC 0151 reached Phase 2 and avdoralimab Phase 1, so F1b does not apply. Because there is no engagement data, a molecule that never engaged can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The small size and early numerical separation make an underpowered trial (F7) possible.

The index trial NCT01037556 was a phase 1/2 dose-finding study. Its primary outcome was the optimal individualized dose, not efficacy. The published results (PMID:25682597) report responses in 2/10 ALL and 10/31 AML patients at 3–4 g/m2. They also report a measurable post-dose decrease in hypoxic leukemic cells in marrow, and the authors conclude that further evaluation is warranted. So this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. No human PK adequacy or direct activation/engagement measure appears for leukemia. PMID:21744473 suggests human metabolite exposures may fall below the preclinical active levels. PMID:26116659 proposes AKR1C3-based T-ALL selection. The program's discontinuation reason is not shown in the bundle.

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT01354691) missed its endpoint, with ADAS-Cog change of -0.27 vs 0.19 (p=0.67). Cholinesterase inhibition is a validated mechanism in Alzheimer disease: donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine are FDA-approved on the same target. The bundle has no human evidence that ladostigil reached adequate exposure, cholinesterase/MAO-B inhibition or brain penetration at the doses tested; all mechanistic data are from rats or cells (PMID:19625104). PMID:30108930 notes pharmacokinetic limitations of ladostigil and in vivo hydrolysis/deactivation of its carbamate, which points to the molecule rather than the target. The MCI trial (NCT01429623, PMID:31492718) also failed. Because engagement is unmeasured, U is also defensible.

The index trial (NCT01401673) was a 12-patient open-label cough pilot. It was terminated for lack of efficacy and posted no results. Earlier, in 2010, the IN-STEP Phase IIb trial (NCT00794430) missed its primary endpoint in diabetic neuropathic pain. Plasma levels in humans rose with dose (PMID:12953347), but no CSF or brain data exist for this CNS-acting drug. Before the index trial, healthy-volunteer studies showed dose-dependent MAO-A inhibition, measured as lower plasma DHPG (Astruc 2005). No human evidence shows NMDA receptor engagement. That is the antitussive mechanism that matters most, and no engagement data come from cough patients. Doses were not limited by tolerability. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged NMDA from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The small, uncontrolled trial also limits what it could show (F7).

The index trial tested topical digoxin plus furosemide (CLS003 ionic contra-viral therapy) in actinic keratosis, and PMID:36177541 reports no effect. No skin exposure, Na+/K+-ATPase engagement or biomarker data are posted, and the planned biopsy markers have no results. The same topical formulation met its primary endpoint in cutaneous warts (NCT02333643), cutting wart diameter and HPV load versus placebo. That makes exposure and engagement in the skin inferred_adequate, assuming comparable dosing, which the bundle does not state. Given a tested mechanism, failure points to ion-flux and antiviral modulation not driving AK. HPV genital lesions also failed (NCT03334240). There is no stated stop reason and no tolerability cap. Evidence is thin, so U is a plausible alternative.

The index trial NCT03334240 (topical CLS003 ICVT, digoxin plus furosemide, in HPV genital lesions) stopped for lack of effect at interim. No posted results, PK or target-engagement data exist for this disease. The same topical product met its primary endpoint in cutaneous warts (NCT02333643). It reduced wart diameter and HPV load, which predates the index trial. Exposure, Na+/K+-ATPase engagement and the antiviral pathway effect are therefore inferred adequate in HPV-infected skin at a comparable topical regimen. Failure in genital lesions then points to the mechanism not driving clinical benefit in this setting (F2). Differences in population, mucosal tissue or immune status (F3) may also apply, but no source states the reason. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

In the paired-lesion Phase 2a trial NCT01826201, 10% MOL4239 ointment did not clearly beat placebo. The change in lesion severity score was -1.9 with the drug versus -1.5 with placebo. The trial was registered to measure pharmacokinetics, but no posted result or source I found reports skin drug levels, p-STAT3 inhibition or downstream biomarkers in humans. Moleculin's S-1 filing says only that the psoriasis program was stopped for limited efficacy, without separating the molecule from the target. The later topical trial in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (NCT04702503) was a small Phase 1b study in another disease. It reported only lesion responses and was not a pivotal efficacy result, so it cannot support inferred engagement. No other STAT3 drug is shown for psoriasis. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00773890 was terminated for perceived futility. The stated reason is that baseline pain scores in the first 40 patients were too low to show any improvement. That is a design and execution problem: the trial could not answer the efficacy question. It is not evidence that the drug failed. The bundle has no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects. No primary target is recorded, no results were posted, and there are no other trials, Phase 1 results or abstracts. Mechanism adequacy therefore cannot be assessed, and U applies as a secondary code. Confidence is medium because the source states the reason directly, but the bundle is otherwise thin.

Engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself (NCT03612869, AAVance), not from earlier work. In these MPS IIIA patients, heparan sulfate (the disease substrate) in CSF fell by about 23–30% at 6 and 12 months, and CSF GM2/GM3 gangliosides fell by about 40%. The sponsor read this as a specific effect from the brain tissue and called it a positive biological response. The drug's CSF HS effect was only partial, so engagement is rated adequate with some doubt. The bundle has no direct measure of vector or enzyme levels in the brain. In the main cohort, aged 30 months or older, the trial missed its DQ primary endpoint and every key secondary endpoint. Children treated before 30 months showed a 27% slower DQ decline (p=0.037). Lysogene said the results delineate which patients would benefit. This points to patient selection and disease stage (F3, with F4 as secondary).

The index trial NCT01465802 was not an efficacy test of alclometasone against NSCLC. It was a supportive-care study of dacomitinib. Topical alclometasone was given in a small arm (Cohort I Arm C, n=4) as prophylaxis for dacomitinib-induced skin adverse events. The primary endpoints were descriptive rates of dermatologic and GI adverse events, patient-reported outcomes and dacomitinib PK, with no statistical comparison posted. Tumor-directed efficacy of alclometasone via NR3C1 was never assessed. The bundle contains no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for alclometasone, and no other trials or abstracts. The program's NSCLC label is an artifact of its use as an adjunct, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug.

The index Phase 3 trial NCT03403205 met its primary endpoint: dNCC AUEC was higher with ALXN1840 than standard of care in both cohorts (p<0.0001). It was terminated by an unspecified sponsor decision, so this was not an efficacy failure (F9). In Wilson disease patients the drug bound copper, forming tripartite copper-albumin complexes and raising plasma NCC. It also normalized NCCcorrected in the Phase 2 study, published in 2017 before the index start (NCT02273596, PMID:28988934). Copper balance became negative through fecal excretion (PMID:42155004), and the drug limited hepatic copper uptake (PMID:38081365). Liver copper did not fall in NCT04422431. The bundle does not state a business reason, so F8 is only a possible secondary code.

In the index TNBC trial (NCT01639248), serial fresh tumor biopsies at 250 mg daily showed reduced proliferation and microvessel density and increased p53/p73, consistent with preclinical mechanism (PMID:30071865). Hypertension, an on-target VEGFR effect, was common. This shows the drug reached tumor tissue and engaged its Aurora and angiogenic kinase targets, though no direct occupancy or Aurora A phosphorylation assay is reported. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite these tissue effects, the 6-month clinical benefit rate was only 16.7% (2 partial responses), so the mechanism did not drive meaningful single-agent benefit. The authors call for predictive biomarkers, implying benefit may be confined to an unidentified subgroup (F3 secondary). The engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself, published after it started.

In the index FLC trial (NCT02234986), 1 of 35 patients had a partial response. The authors concluded that ENMD-2076 should not be studied further as a single agent, citing no reason beyond lack of activity, and said the drug was well tolerated. In the Phase 1 trial (NCT00658671, Diamond 2011), plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose at doses comparable to the 150–250 mg/day used in FLC. Plasma sVEGFR2 fell significantly, a downstream sign of VEGFR blockade. However, the program's rationale was AURKA, and skin biopsies showed no clear phospho-histone H3 trend. Target engagement was therefore never directly shown in humans, and nothing was measured in FLC patients. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged AURKA apart from a target that does not drive FLC, so the code is U (indeterminate).

In the Phase 1 solid-tumour trial (NCT00658671; PMC3867298), exposure was linear and plasma soluble VEGFR2 fell at every dose level and stayed down. That is direct human evidence that the drug engaged its VEGFR2/KDR target. It was shown across tumour types, not specifically in ovarian cancer, and it was published around the time the index trial started. I found no human evidence of Aurora A engagement in solid tumours. The index trial (NCT01104675) gave a 6-month PFS rate of 22% and a median time to progression of 3.6 months. That matched the Phase 1 result but was modest. Later, in clear cell ovarian cancer (NCT01914510), single-agent ENMD-2076 did not meet the preset efficacy bar. The target was engaged but gave little clinical benefit, so the code is F2. Confidence is low: engagement rests on one biomarker, and Aurora A engagement is unmeasured.

In fibrolamellar carcinoma, the index trial NCT02234986 had 1 partial response in 35 patients. Exposure is adequate: the phase 1 study (PMID:21131552, 2011, before the index trial) showed dose-proportional PK at an MTD/RP2D of 160 mg/m2. Hypertension and neutropenia limited only doses above that. The same study saw plasma sVEGFR2 fall after treatment, a human pharmacodynamic sign of VEGFR2/KDR engagement. That was in mixed solid tumours, not FLC/HCC. No human Aurora A engagement data exist. With KDR engagement shown at the RP2D, the lack of response points to the mechanism not driving FLC. Other KDR inhibitors are approved in classic HCC (lenvatinib, regorafenib, ramucirumab), so a molecule-specific failure (F1b) remains possible. Single-agent activity was also weak in TNBC (NCT01639248).

The index trial NCT01899768 tested inhaled GSK2339345 at 1000 µg in refractory chronic cough and missed its endpoint. Total cough counts went up versus placebo because the drug itself set off coughing just after each dose. With those transient coughs removed, the result was flat (ratio 1.02). The capsaicin and citric acid cough challenges gave inconclusive results. The investigators say outright that their data could not show whether the drug reached its target, the voltage-gated sodium channel. The coughing after dosing shows the drug got to the airway nerves, but it does not show the channel was blocked. Neither Phase 1 trial (NCT01494636, NCT01587716) posted results, and I found no occupancy or biomarker data in humans. With no engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01253499 was a 31-subject Phase 1 multiple-dose study. Its primary outcomes were bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, and safety/tolerability, with no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of TRx0037. It completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results. The bundle has no other trials, no PubMed abstracts, and no same-target comparators. There is no human evidence on exposure, MAPT engagement, or pathway effects. The most direct code is therefore F9 (not an efficacy failure). U is listed as secondary because engagement is no_human_data and nothing in the bundle explains why the program stopped. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional in HCV patients (NCT00445315). Antiviral activity, the direct functional readout of polymerase inhibition, was shown in HCV patients before the index trial: -2.15 log10 HCV RNA at Day 4 with 700 mg (NCT00671671, 2008). Week 4 viral load also fell significantly versus placebo at 200 and 300 mg with pegIFN/RBV (NCT00720434). The Day 11 decline at 450 mg was small (-0.45 log), which suggests the effect does not last. Despite engagement, SVR72 was no better than placebo (41.7%/39.6% vs 45.8%; NCT00987337), so the mechanism as tested gave no cure benefit. Tolerability did not cap the dose. A review attributes most HCV discontinuations of that period to corporate strategy (PMID:25384989), so F8 is secondary. The bundle does not state the cause directly.

DP-b99 is a lipophilic, membrane-activated chelator of zinc. In the Phase 3 MACSI trial (NCT00893867) it was given at 1 mg/kg/day for 4 days, the dose used in Phase 2 (NCT00190047). The trial was stopped for futility because 90-day mRS was the same in both arms. The only human pharmacology found is the Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (PMID:15963088), which reports safety and plasma pharmacokinetics. It has no brain or CSF drug levels, no measure of zinc chelation, and no MMP or other biomarker data. The MMP-9 modulation evidence comes only from preclinical work. No source separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in stroke. Tolerability did not limit the dose, no other drug on the same target has succeeded, and the investigators named no specific cause, so the code is U.

The Phase 3 MACSI trial (NCT00893867, PMID:23391764) was stopped for futility after an interim analysis. The 90-day modified Rankin Scale results were similar on DP-b99 and placebo, with a non-significant trend favoring placebo on recovery to mRS ≤1. The human pharmacology study (PMID:15963088) measured only safety and blood levels in healthy volunteers. No source shows in humans that the drug reached the brain, chelated zinc there, or moved a downstream biomarker. The only engagement data are from cell cultures and brain slices (PMID:19622352), which do not count. There is no human target-engagement evidence and no other drug on the same target, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from zinc chelation not mattering in stroke. Code: U.

The index UC trial (NCT02000453) was an open-label safety study and was terminated after 2 patients. It was not an efficacy failure. GSK ended development because of a statin drug-drug interaction study and safety signals in the parallel SLE trial: liver enzyme elevations and DRESS (PMID:27055521). Both are molecule-specific toxicities. The two UC patients actually showed clinical and endoscopic response and reduced faecal calprotectin (PMID:28790099). Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate because the drug met PASI75 in psoriasis via systemic JAK1 inhibition (NCT01782664), although the SLE interferon biomarker did not move. Tofacitinib and upadacitinib validate JAK inhibition in UC. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test, F9 also applies.

No direct human PK or JAK1 occupancy data are in the bundle. Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate because the same JAK1 inhibitor, at a comparable dose (400 mg), met PASI75 in psoriasis (57% vs 0%, dose-responsive; NCT01782664). That dose falls within the 50–400 mg BID range used in SLE. In the SLE index trial, the prespecified interim showed no effect on interferon transcriptional biomarkers despite 84–92% high baseline expressors. The pathway pillar was therefore inadequate, and futility was declared (PMID:27055521). This supports a mechanism that does not drive SLE as tested. Separately, molecule-specific toxicity contributed to ending the program: liver enzyme elevations and DRESS (PMID:25724932), plus a statin drug-drug interaction cited for terminating development (NCT02000453).

Exposure: dose-proportional plasma PK at 30–50 mg in healthy volunteers (PMID:32361977). Engagement and pathway were not measured directly. They are inferred_adequate because 30/45 mg met the MRI primary endpoint in RRMS, with dose-dependent NfL lowering, through systemic DHODH inhibition (PMID:38662979, NCT03846219). That evidence postdates the index trial start, and none comes from UC patients. The index trial missed its week-10 endpoint (14% vs 14%, p=0.58). Both the sponsor's stop reason and the publication point to concomitant corticosteroids. Steroid-free patients showed 12% vs 4% remission, and week-50 remission and endoscopic healing rose dose-dependently (PMID:39791563). This points to subgroup/population confounding (F3), with endpoint timing (F4) and design (F7) also contributing. Hematuria occurred only at 45 mg and did not cap the dose.

COMPONENT (NCT01010581) missed ACR20 at 13 weeks, with only a numerical advantage. Plasma levels were measured in RA patients, and Phase 1 data show good, dose-proportional absorption (PMID:31621054, PMID:32361977). However, the bundle has no human DHODH inhibition or pathway biomarker data in RA. A possible PK interaction with methotrexate was noted. PMID:31621054 states that leflunomide, a DHODH inhibitor, is approved for RA, so the target is validated in this disease. That points to the molecule or its dosing rather than the target. Later efficacy signals in RRMS (PMID:38662979) and IBD (NCT00820365) come from different doses and diseases, and the RA dose is not given, so engagement cannot be inferred here. Confidence is low.

Phase 1 SAD/MAD showed dose-proportional, well-absorbed systemic exposure at 10–50 mg with good tolerability (PMID:32361977), so exposure is adequate and the dose was not capped. No direct DHODH engagement or pathway biomarker is reported in COVID-19 patients. Engagement is inferred_adequate because the drug met efficacy endpoints through systemic DHODH inhibition at comparable 30–45 mg doses. These were MRI lesion suppression with a dose-dependent NfL fall in RRMS (PMID:38662979, NCT03846219) and IBD response (NCT00820365, before the index trial). Yet the index trial showed no benefit on the need for invasive ventilation: 12 vs 9 patients needed it (NCT04379271). That points to F2. Low event rates suggest limited power (F7). The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

The index Phase 2 sham-controlled trial (NCT00876863, PMID:29582053) missed ADAS-Cog at 24 months. Safety was good. Postmortem analysis of trial patients (PMID:32126838) found NGF expression persisted, but vector spread averaged only ~0.96 mm. At none of 15 injection sites did NGF directly reach the target basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, because spread was limited and stereotactic targeting inaccurate. The authors conclude the mechanism was not tested and plan improved delivery. Phase 1 autopsy reported targeted NGF expression and bioactivity (PMID:24411134), but that was published in 2014, after the index trial started. The trial-cohort autopsy contradicts adequate engagement. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The failure is delivery and engagement, not evidence against the NGF mechanism.

The index trial NCT02215499 is a single-dose Phase 1 study of JZP-386 (a GABA-B agonist), listed under narcolepsy and excessive daytime sleepiness. Its only primary outcome is safety over 3 days, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. No results were posted. The bundle contains no other trials, no Phase 1 PK/PD results, no same-target comparators and no PubMed abstracts. There is therefore no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway effect, and no stated reason the program stopped. The readout cannot be read as an efficacy failure (F9). If an efficacy failure is assumed, the cause is indeterminate (U), because engagement has no human data. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

The index trial NCT00715689 was a Phase 2 safety, PK and PD dose study whose only primary outcome was safety and tolerability. It was not an efficacy test, and it reported good tolerability (PMID:21177789). In adults with GHD, NNC126-0083 gave measurable exposure, and IGF-I rose in a clear dose-dependent, sustained way (SDS from -3.2 up to 4.4), so engagement and pathway held in the program's disease. Earlier healthy-volunteer studies (NCT01034202, PMID:20427496, PMID:20718773) showed the same. In children, an adequate once-weekly IGF-1 profile was not reached at the doses tested (PMID:21724838). The bundle gives no stated reason the program stopped, so no efficacy failure of the drug is shown.

The index trial NCT00936403 was a single-dose safety/PK/PD study with an AE-frequency primary endpoint, not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Exposure and GHR engagement were shown: dose-dependent PK and strong IGF-I/IGFBP-3 rises in healthy volunteers (PMID:20427496, PMID:20718773) and adult GHD (NCT00715689, registered before the index trial; PMID:21177789), with IGF-I SDS reaching up to 4.4. In GHD children, IGF-I rose in all dose groups, but the response subsided at ~3 days and 'a satisfactory once-weekly IGF1 profile was not reached' (PMID:21724838). The weekly pathway profile was therefore inadequate at the doses tested, with no tolerability limit. This PD shortfall, not a clinical efficacy miss, appears to explain discontinuation.

The index trial NCT01453738 had a safety and tolerability primary endpoint (adverse events over 2 years), so it was not an efficacy test of Stempeucel. PMID:27993154 reports intra-articular injection was safe. Efficacy measures (VAS, ICOAP, WOMAC) showed only a non-significant trend at the 25-million-cell dose, and whole-organ MRI showed no change versus baseline or placebo. Adverse events (knee pain, swelling) were more common at higher doses, but doses up to 150 million cells were given, so tolerability did not cap dosing. No target is recorded, and the bundle has no human data on cell persistence, engagement or a proximal mechanistic biomarker. If the readout is treated as an efficacy failure, it is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01591200 is a dose-finding Phase 2 study in alcoholic liver cirrhosis. Its only registered primary outcome is safety at 2 years, it is classified not_efficacy, and no results are posted. The bundle therefore shows no failed efficacy readout, so this was not an efficacy test of the drug. No targets are recorded. There is no human evidence of cell homing, persistence or engagement in liver tissue, and no pathway biomarker data. The only PubMed abstract (PMID:29631634) is an equine study of a different MSC product and does not count. Other Stempeucel trials, such as NCT01453738, also report safety only. If the program is treated as an efficacy failure, engagement is no_human_data, which would make the case indeterminate (U).

In the index trial NCT01157065, AL-78898A (POT-4) lowered central subfield thickness by only 12.1 microns at week 4, against 199.9 microns with Lucentis. The Phase 1 ASaP trial (NCT00473928) escalated single intravitreal doses up to 150 µg and reported only safety and tolerability. I found no human data on drug levels in the vitreous or retina, on C3 inhibition or ocular complement activation products, or on any downstream biomarker. Review articles describe the drug forming a gel depot in the vitreous, but give no pharmacodynamic data. The sponsor gave no reason for stopping, and the GA trial NCT01603043 ended as a management decision. No other C3 inhibitor has succeeded in wet AMD, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement was never measured, I cannot tell a drug that failed to engage apart from a target that does not matter: indeterminate.

The index GA trial NCT01603043 was terminated for 'Management Decision' after 10 patients, with no primary outcome values posted. That makes it a stop with no readout rather than a demonstrated efficacy failure, so F8 or F7 also plausibly apply. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, C3 engagement or complement-pathway data for AL-78898A/POT-4. The wet AMD trial NCT01157065 missed its exploratory endpoint, and the Phase 1 NCT00473928 posted no results. Another C3 inhibitor, pegcetacoplan, is FDA-approved for dry AMD/GA, which supports the target. So the shortfall is attributable to this molecule or program rather than to C3 inhibition (F1b). The evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

The index trial, NCT01898884, was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoints were safety only (adverse events, lab results, vital signs, ECGs). It tested no efficacy, and doses up to 1200 mg single and 900 mg multiple were tolerated without dose-limiting toxicity. Sources report that the drug was rapidly absorbed and had a defined pharmacokinetic profile in healthy volunteers and in people with Friedreich ataxia, so plasma exposure is shown. No human data were found on target engagement or an oxidative-stress biomarker, and no primary target is recorded. CureFA lists the program as discontinued without giving a reason, and the drug changed hands when Shire acquired ViroPharma. Because no efficacy test failed, F9 fits best. The reason the program stopped is unknown (U), and a business decision (F8) is possible.

Indole-3-propionic acid (VP 20629, also called SHP622 or OXIGON) is an antioxidant that scavenges hydroxyl radicals. It has no defined protein target. The index trial NCT01898884 was a Phase 1 safety study in people with Friedreich's ataxia. Doses up to 1200 mg single and 900 mg multiple were well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. FARA says only that healthy-volunteer Phase 1 data showed rapid absorption. It reports no oxidative-stress biomarker, CNS or tissue levels, or any pharmacodynamic data. FARA and the MDPI review say only that the drug showed no efficacy signal and development stopped. Nothing in the sources separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01202214 was a repeat-dose safety/PK study, not an efficacy test (hence F9 secondary). The program-level efficacy readout was the Phase Ib asthma crossover (NCT01424280, PMID:23641215). There, all asthmatics given 750 mg exceeded plasma concentrations predicted to give 96% UT receptor occupancy for at least 3 h, and the drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Occupancy was predicted from PK rather than measured directly. Despite this, GSK1440115 neither bronchodilated nor protected against methacholine bronchospasm, with no exposure–response relationship. The authors conclude acute UT antagonism is unlikely to benefit asthma. PK variability and the short half-life temper the engagement call. Only acute dosing was tested, so F4 is also possible.

The first-in-human trial NCT01332552 in chronically infected HCV patients was terminated 'due to unfavorable human pharmacokinetic properties'. This is the sponsor's own statement that the molecule's human exposure profile was inadequate. No PK values, HCV RNA reductions or other results were posted, so engagement (antiviral activity) and pathway have no human data. No other trials or same-target drugs appear in the bundle. The review PMID:25384989 notes that most HCV discontinuations in 2012–2013 were strategic, but it gives no drug-specific detail. Because the stated cause is a human PK shortfall, the mechanism was never properly tested (F1a). U is listed as secondary because engagement was never measured.

The index trial was not an efficacy failure. In the published report of NCT01008163 (Yoon 2012, J Diabetes Investig), 72 drug-naive type 2 diabetes patients took ginsam, a vinegar extract of Panax ginseng, at 1500, 2000 or 3000 mg/day for 8 weeks. All doses lowered HbA1c, the primary endpoint; 1500 mg cut it by 0.56% versus placebo (P=0.021). No severe adverse events occurred. This is a herbal extract with no defined molecular target, and no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects were found. That is why all three pillars are no_human_data and U is the secondary code. The sources found give no reason why the program did not go past Phase 2. A commercial or regulatory reason is possible but is not documented.

The index trial NCT01518881 was a first-in-human Phase 1 study of TKM-100201 in healthy participants. Its primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, not efficacy against Ebola infection. It was terminated by a corporate decision to reformulate the investigational product, and no results were posted. The bundle contains no failed efficacy readout, so this was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). No human exposure, engagement or pathway data exist in the bundle, and there are no other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators. If an efficacy failure had to be assumed, the evidence could not separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so U is listed as secondary.

The index trial NCT00976261 was a Phase 1 two-part study whose primary outcomes were only safety and tolerability (adverse events, GI effects, labs, ECGs). It was not an efficacy test. No results were posted, and no stop reason or PubMed abstracts exist. A later single-day Phase 1 study (NCT01607385) also posted nothing. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, SGLT1-engagement or glucose-pathway data, so the mechanism cannot be judged. Sotagliflozin, a dual SGLT1/2 inhibitor, is approved for T2D. That makes a molecule-specific failure (F1b) conceivable but unproven. With engagement absent, U also applies. The evidence is very thin.

The index trial NCT00917826 was terminated after enrolling 1 patient, gave no stopping reason and posted no results. The successor industry trial NCT00992732 also stopped at 1 patient. Neither was a real efficacy test, which points to an execution or accrual failure (F7) rather than a negative readout. The bundle has no human PK, HDAC engagement or pathway data for arginine butyrate in lymphoid disease. PMID:21422239 mentions fetal hemoglobin induction, and PMID:20955402 reports sickle-cell ulcer healing. Both are in other tissues, and neither is a measured HDAC endpoint, so they cannot support inferred adequacy. Approved HDAC inhibitors in lymphoma (romidepsin, vorinostat) exist, but no efficacy data from this drug separates target from molecule. U is therefore a secondary code.

The bundle has no human pillar data for CH-4051: no Phase 1 results, no other trials and no abstracts. The index trial NCT01116141 (12-week hACR/ACR20) posted no results and gives no stop reason. Methotrexate, an inhibitor of the same target (DHFR), is FDA-approved for polyarticular arthritis, so DHFR inhibition is a validated mechanism in this disease area. Because the target is validated and nothing shows this molecule engaged DHFR adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The bundle is very thin and the readout details are unknown. U remains plausible as a secondary code, since engagement is entirely unmeasured. Confidence is low.

Patients in NCT01371617 got 160 mg once daily, the recommended phase 2 dose. The phase 1 study (PMID:23575478) showed this dose was tolerable, gave usable blood levels and produced responses in basal cell carcinoma. Exposure is therefore adequate, and the dose was not capped by tolerability. In the 14 myelofibrosis patients, the target-pathway marker GLI1 (mRNA and protein) fell only in some, and the drop was not significant for the group. JAK2V617F burden, fibrosis and cytokines also showed no significant change. So on-target effect in the disease was not shown to be adequate. The basal cell carcinoma responses were in a different tissue, so they do not support inferring engagement in marrow. Infinity ended the program in June 2012. The readout cannot separate weak engagement (F1a) from a target that does not drive the disease (F2), so confidence is low.

In the first-in-human study (NCT00761696, PMID:23575478), patidegib reached plasma levels that supported once-daily dosing (half-life 20–40 h). It was tolerated up to 160 mg QD, so the dose was not capped. Normal-skin biopsies showed GLI1 transcript falling in 74% of patients, and Hh-naive BCC patients responded at doses of at least 130 mg. This shows systemic SMO/Hh pathway inhibition in humans at the dose used in the index trial. Hh engagement was not measured in pancreatic tumour or stroma, and the full PD data appeared in 2013, after the index trial started. The randomized phase 2 (NCT01130142) was stopped at interim analysis because it would not meet its overall-survival endpoint, with no unexpected toxicity. This fits SMO/Hh inhibition not driving metastatic pancreatic cancer as tested.

In NCT02828111, topical patidegib gel did not significantly lower tumour GLI1 mRNA versus vehicle in any arm (pooled p=0.117). The Gorlin trial NCT02762084 likewise showed no significant GLI1 change, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. The bundle has no human data on skin or tumour drug levels, or on SMO engagement, for the topical formulation. SMO inhibition is a validated mechanism in BCC: oral vismodegib and sonidegib are FDA-approved, and oral IPI-926 produced BCC responses (PMID:23575478). This points to the topical molecule and formulation rather than the target, and a review notes an optimal formulation is still needed (PMID:35258366). Very small arms (n=5-6) with high variance also limited the trial's power (F7).

The bundle has no posted results for the index trial NCT01968265 (6 weeks, fructosamine primary endpoint, n=38). The only human target-engagement evidence is Isis's 2014 10-K. It says a healthy-volunteer Phase 1 study found reduced GCCR in liver and fat tissue and was well tolerated, but it gives no numbers. I treat that as tissue knockdown the sponsor considered adequate. It was not shown in diabetic patients, and I found no human data on drug exposure or downstream pathway effects. The program later stalled, and no further diabetes or Cushing's development was reported. Because knockdown appears to have occurred without a benefit that justified continuing, F2 fits best. Confidence is low because the knockdown was never quantified, the trial outcome and sponsor's reason were never published, and no stated reason was found. U is listed as a secondary code.

SAMe is a methyl donor with no defined molecular target, so I could not assess target engagement. The MSI-195 Phase 1 study (PMID:33317621) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure, about 2.8-fold higher than a commercial supplement. Older SAMe salts were reported to raise CSF SAMe (PMID:15989609), so I rated exposure adequate. Pharmaco-EEG changes in healthy volunteers (PMID:16046102 and others) are nonspecific and do not show a mechanism-specific biomarker in MDD. The investigators blamed the failure on enrollment and design: placebo response, baseline score fluctuation and patient characteristics that changed over the course of the trial. Post-hoc subgroups were positive (PMID:30368163, PMID:31812110). These analyses cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U, with F7 and F3 as secondary.

Index trial NCT01754714 was not an efficacy test. Its primary outcome was a descriptive methionine elimination half-life (about 4.3 h in every SAMe arm and in untreated controls), with no statistical comparison and no clinical endpoint, so it is classified not_efficacy and not assessable. That makes F9 the primary code. Plasma exposure to oral SAMe was shown in humans: dose-proportional AUC for MSI-195 (PMID:33317621) and raised plasma SAMe (PMID:15989609). No target is recorded, and the bundle has no human engagement or hepatic pathway evidence in MASLD. Any mechanistic judgment would therefore be indeterminate (U secondary). Tolerability was good, with no dose limitation. No stop reason is given.

Exposure: the Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (PMID:25224876, NCT01738425) found plasma trimebutine levels that rose in proportion to dose up to 1000 mg, so the drug reached the bloodstream. No source measured opioid-receptor engagement or a downstream marker in humans. In the index trial (NCT01926444), no dose beat placebo on pain during colonoscopy. The sponsor said only the mid dose helped and described the dose response as 'U-shaped'. In a follow-up rectal-balloon (barostat) pain study (NCT02276768, Altasciences poster), no dose differed from placebo, and the poster notes high variability. That study is a clinical-type pain outcome, not a measure of target engagement. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In an earlier single-ascending-dose study, RG7713 was measured in CSF, which shows it reached the brain. The 20 mg IV dose was estimated from those CSF levels to occupy about 90% of central V1a receptors for at least 8 hours, with no tolerability limit. Occupancy was not measured directly (no PET) and was only estimated in the SAD study, not in autistic patients. The index trial (NCT01474278) was a small single-dose, exploratory proof-of-mechanism crossover study (n=19). Results were mixed: one eye-tracking measure improved (p=0.047), but the composite score and overall affective speech score did not change. The authors read this as preliminary support for V1a blockade (PMID:27711048), not as a failed efficacy test. The bundle does not say why RG7713 stopped. The sponsor's V1a program continued with balovaptan, which reached Phase 3, but no source here links the two.

ASP3325 blocks the intestinal phosphate transporter NPT-IIb. In healthy volunteers (NCT02500953), it did not change urinary or fecal phosphate excretion at any dose or schedule. In hemodialysis patients (NCT02510274), it did not lower serum phosphate (PMID:29340316). So the pathway pillar is inadequate. However, no source measured drug levels in the gut or direct NPT-IIb inhibition in humans. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The investigators said NPT-IIb's relevance in humans is still uncertain. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the molecule failed to engage the target or the target does not matter, so the code is U. Later papers also point to the small sample, short treatment and lack of a positive control (F7). The other NPT-IIb drugs have not succeeded, so F1b does not apply.

In the index study (NCT02500953) and the ESRD Phase 1b (NCT02510274), reported in PMID:29340316, ASP3325 caused no dose-dependent change in urinary phosphate or fecal phosphorus in healthy subjects, and it did not lower serum phosphate in dialysis patients. That makes the downstream pathway pillar inadequate. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects. Plasma PK was measured, but nobody measured inhibition of the intestinal transporter or drug levels in the gut. Engagement therefore has no human data. The authors say NPT-IIb's relevance in humans is uncertain, and later reviews (PMC6552399) argue that phosphate absorption mostly goes around the transporter, between gut cells (paracellular), which favours F2. But no data separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The only data on AMG 172 come from its first-in-human study in relapsed or refractory ccRCC (NCT01497821, PMID:30915497). That study set the maximum tolerated dose at 1.6 mg/kg, limited mainly by thrombocytopenia and liver injury. Plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose, with low levels of unconjugated antibody and payload, so exposure was adequate. No human source reports CD70 binding, receptor occupancy, tumour uptake or a downstream biomarker. The 'pharmacodynamics' in the paper's title was not described in any accessible text, and the full paper could not be retrieved. Activity was limited: 2 of 37 patients (5.4%) had a partial response. No CD70 drug has succeeded in RCC. Nothing separates poor target engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

Gaboxadol 5 and 10 mg added to escitalopram gave no MADRS benefit over escitalopram alone (diff -0.45, p=0.64; NCT00807248, PMID:22008735). Escitalopram separated from placebo by about 5.6 points, so the trial had assay sensitivity and was well tolerated. Before the index trial, studies in healthy humans showed dose-dependent CNS effects at 10–15 mg: increased slow-wave activity on EEG and MEG, plus hypnotic efficacy in transient-insomnia models (PMID:17552374, 17765013, 22003345, 25195191). This implies brain exposure and extrasynaptic GABA-A engagement at the index dose. No occupancy was measured and nothing came from MDD patients, so engagement is inferred_adequate. The mechanism was engaged without antidepressant benefit, which points to F2. Approved neurosteroid GABA-A modulators act by a different mode.

In healthy humans, gaboxadol 10–15 mg (about 0.2 mg/kg, comparable to NEPTUNE's 0.125–0.24 mg/kg) produced dose-related increases in slow-wave and theta EEG activity and a distinct MEG signature. It also improved sleep in transient-insomnia models (PMID:17552374, 22003345, 25195191, 17765013, 22002961). This implies brain penetration and functional δ-GABAA receptor engagement, though it was shown before the index trial and not in Angelman patients. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not capped. NEPTUNE showed no CGI-I-AS difference (LS mean difference 0, p=0.83; PMID:37639777) despite an exploratory signal in adolescents and adults in STARS (PMID:33443117). Mouse data show region-specific tonic-inhibition deficits, with gaboxadol worsening EEG (PMID:42227760). Together this suggests the mechanism does not drive Angelman symptoms as tested. Age differences and endpoint sensitivity are possible contributors.

In the index phase 1 (NCT01684150), plasma pinometostat rose roughly dose-proportionally to steady state (PMID:29724899), so exposure was adequate. Pharmacodynamic reduction of H3K79 methylation, the direct DOT1L catalytic mark, was shown in leukemia patients and used to pick expansion doses, so engagement was adequate. The MTD was not reached, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. No downstream target-gene data are in the bundle, so pathway is no_human_data. Despite this engagement, single-agent efficacy was modest, with only 2 complete remissions, both in t(11;19). That points to DOT1L inhibition being insufficient to drive benefit in MLL-r leukemia. Benefit confined to one translocation subtype also supports F3. Engagement data were published after the index trial started. Later combination trials ended for drug supply reasons (NCT03724084).

The index trial NCT00960349 was a 14-patient Phase 1 study of cediranib with cisplatin plus capecitabine/S-1 in Japanese gastric cancer patients. Its primary endpoint was safety only, it completed, and it posted no results and no stop reason. It was therefore not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Earlier human data in solid tumours showed adequate plasma exposure and dose- and exposure-related reductions in soluble VEGFR2 and in DCE-MRI iAUC60 (PMID:17634482, NCT00501605). Similar soluble VEGFR2 changes appeared in later studies (PMID:20061136, PMID:26008604). None of this was measured in gastric cancer. Doses up to 45 mg were tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The bundle gives no reason why gastric development stopped.

The SPECTRA trial (NCT05393284, n=114) missed its primary DRSS endpoint and all secondary endpoints in the predefined primary population. Valo then paused OPL-0401 and is looking for a partner, citing a strategic refocus on its Opal platform. That is a secondary commercial factor (F8), but it followed a failed readout. I found no human data on retinal drug levels, ROCK1/2 inhibition, or a downstream biomarker such as pMLC. The only retinal exposure figure is from an animal study (about 200 times the plasma level), which does not count. The drug was well tolerated in about 300 people, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No other ROCK inhibitor has succeeded in this disease. Nothing here separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The SPECTRA trial (NCT05393284, 114 patients) missed its primary DRSS endpoint and its secondary endpoints. Valo then suspended development, citing a strategic refocus on its Opal platform, and is seeking a partner. That business framing is why F8 is listed as a secondary code. The only exposure evidence found is from animals: retinal levels about 200-fold above plasma. That does not count as human data. The sources found mention Phase 1 studies in more than 200 people only as evidence of safety and tolerability. None reports retinal drug levels, ROCK inhibition, or a downstream biomarker in humans. There is also no other ROCK inhibitor in this disease to compare against. Post-hoc signals at certain doses were small. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged ROCK from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The AML/MDS Phase 1 trial (NCT02078609) posted no results, and I found no publication or statement explaining why AML development stopped. The only human data are from the first-in-human myeloma trial (NCT01456689, Raab 2019). It set a maximum tolerated dose of 500 mg once daily and a recommended dose of 300 mg, and reported single-agent activity in myeloma. The abstracts I could reach report no PIM target engagement or pathway biomarker data (e.g. phospho-BAD) in patients. Phospho-BAD was proposed as a biomarker only in preclinical work (Clin Cancer Res 2017), whose authors say no clinical data validate it. No other PIM inhibitor has succeeded in AML (AZD-1208 Phase 1, dapolsertib Phase 2), so F1b does not apply. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01590810 was a Phase 1 single-rising-dose safety and pharmacodynamic study, not a failed efficacy test. MK-8150 lowered central SBP in a clear dose-dependent way versus placebo in healthy men (e.g., -10.4 mmHg at 90 mg, -12.0 mmHg at 120 mg, p<0.0001) and numerically in hypertensive men. There were no AE discontinuations. No molecular target is recorded, so engagement has no human data. PK was measured in NCT01656408. In that multiple-dose study, several participants on MK-8150 (none on placebo) stopped under hemodynamic stopping rules. This hints at excessive mechanism-related hemodynamic effects (possible F5), but no stop reason is stated. The bundle shows no efficacy failure, so the code is F9.

The index trial NCT01590810 was a Phase 1 single-rising-dose safety and pharmacodynamic study, not a failed efficacy test. MK-8150 produced dose-dependent, significant central SBP reductions versus placebo in healthy men (e.g., -10.4 mmHg at 90 mg, -12.0 at 120 mg) and larger reductions in hypertensive men, with no AE discontinuations. The multiple-dose study NCT01656408 measured plasma PK and reported some discontinuations for hemodynamic stopping rules. No target is recorded, so no human engagement data exist. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, and there are no abstracts or same-target comparators. The readout was not an efficacy failure, so F9 applies; why the program stopped is indeterminate.

MK-5757 is an ORL1 (NOP) antagonist. In healthy humans, PET with [18F]MK-0911 showed brain tracer displacement proportional to MK-5757 dose and plasma level. That occupancy was used to choose doses giving sufficient target engagement for the proof-of-concept study (PMID:23238431), so exposure and engagement were adequate. No human pathway biomarker was reported. The occupancy data came from healthy volunteers, not schizophrenia patients, and were published in 2013, after the index trial began in 2008. In the index trial (NCT00848484), BACS composite change did not separate from placebo (0.3 vs 1.5, p=0.277), with no tolerability signal. This points to ORL1 antagonism not improving cognition as tested (F2). The small, 2-week trial leaves some design uncertainty (F7).

The bundle contains no human PK, PDE3 inhibition or downstream biomarker data for K-134, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Cilostazol, on the same PDE3 target, is FDA-approved for PAD/claudication and was the active comparator in the index trial. There, peak walking time rose 46% with cilostazol versus 37% with 100 mg K-134 and 23% with placebo; the primary K-134 vs placebo comparison was non-significant (P=.089) (PMID:22119244). The target is validated in this disease and this molecule underperformed without engagement evidence, which fits F1b. Secondary F7: high placebo response, AE-driven withdrawals, and positive completer and mixed-model analyses suggest the trial was underpowered. Dose was not shown to be tolerability-capped (PMID:21612611).

No human evidence of AZD6714's exposure, glucokinase activation or effect on glucose or insulin was found. The only trial, NCT00886366, was a single-ascending-dose study and posted no results. It stopped because the Part A ascending-dose cohorts hit a predefined stopping criterion, so no doses could be chosen for Part B in type 2 diabetes patients. The registry does not say what the criterion was. It could have been hypoglycaemia, an on-target effect (F5), or an exposure problem that capped the dose (F1a), but neither is shown. Web searches turned up nothing on AZD6714, only papers on the related compound AZD1656. Engagement has no human data, and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT02079649), AL-53817 eye drops did no better than vehicle on Day-7 ocular redness AUC (-4.7 vs -4.5). The Maxidex steroid comparator did work (-8.1), so the trial was able to detect a real effect. There were no serious adverse events, and nothing suggests tolerability limited the dose. The only source naming a target is a former Alcon employee's LinkedIn profile, which lists AL-53817 as a PDE4 inhibitor. I found no human data on drug levels in ocular tissue, PDE4 inhibition, or cAMP and other biomarkers. The nasal Phase 1 (NCT01454505) reported only adverse events and congestion scores. No other PDE4 drug appears in the bundle for this disease. Without engagement data, I can't tell whether the molecule failed to engage its target or whether the mechanism simply doesn't matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01353040 was a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study in healthy volunteers, with adverse events as its primary outcome. It was not an efficacy test of AVI-7287, so F9 applies. PMID:25155593 reports that AVI-6003 (AVI-7287 plus AVI-7288) was safe and well tolerated up to 4.5 mg/kg per component, with no MTD reached. Plasma PK was dose-proportional with a half-life of 2–5 h, so systemic exposure was shown, though the source does not judge it sufficient for antiviral effect. Engagement of Marburg viral mRNA cannot be measured in uninfected humans, so engagement and pathway have no human data. Efficacy evidence was limited to nonhuman primates. The bundle gives no reason why the program stopped.

In the index trial (NCT01561456, PMID 27882820), 25.9% of patients on AXL1717 300–400 mg BID were progression-free at 12 weeks versus 39.0% on docetaxel (not significant, p=0.19). The only human target evidence comes from the Phase I trial (NCT01062620), published in 2015, after the index trial started. There, plasma exposure was measurable, but IGF-1R on granulocytes fell by only about 27% on average, which is partial engagement in a surrogate cell. Free serum IGF-1 rose, a pathway-consistent signal. Tumour IGF-1R engagement in squamous NSCLC was never shown. The Phase II doses were also below the 520–700 mg BID tested in Phase Ib. Because engagement looks partial, the IGF-1R hypothesis was probably not properly tested (F1a). The sponsor also pointed to a second mechanism, which muddies attribution. Confidence is low.

The phase Ia/b trial (NCT01062620, PMID:26161618) characterized PK and reported down-regulation of IGF-1R on granulocytes in treated patients, mostly NSCLC. This is engagement. It also reported a rise in free serum IGF-1, a feedback pathway marker consistent with IGF-1R blockade. Both were reported qualitatively, not quantified, and were published in 2016, after the index trial started. Neutropenia set the RP2D (390 mg BID), but nothing shows that dose was below what engagement needed. The index trial (NCT01561456) posted no results and gave no stop reason. Other IGF-1R agents in NSCLC (figitumumab phase 3, linsitinib, cixutumumab, ganitumab, dalotuzumab) never succeeded, consistent with the target not driving NSCLC. The evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01139723 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoints were DLTs and adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Per PMID:29905898, no DLTs occurred and the MTD was not reached. Monocyte α5β1 receptor occupancy was saturated at 15 mg/kg in solid-tumor patients, which supports adequate exposure and engagement. That evidence was published in 2018, after the trial began. No pathway biomarker is reported. Monotherapy produced no confirmed responses. Combination activity could not be separated from bevacizumab alone. This weakly suggests the target lacks impact despite engagement (secondary F2). The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping.

Exposure was adequate. In the glioma phase 1 trial (PMID:23349317, published in 2013 before the index trial), therapeutic concentrations of the conjugate and of free paclitaxel were measured in resected tumour from patients dosed at ≥200 mg/m2, and plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose. Tubulin engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred as adequate because the drug, at a comparable 600 mg/m2, produced intracranial responses in breast cancer brain metastases (NCT02048059; phase 1 responses in PMID:22203732). That inference is weak, because those were uncontrolled responses rather than a formal efficacy endpoint being met. The dose was not limited by tolerability: 600 mg/m2 was safe and toxicity matched the taxane profile. Even so, response rate and 3-month PFS were missed in every arm (median PFS 1.4 months; PMID:39713041), which points to paclitaxel's mechanism not working in recurrent glioma. If the inference does not hold, the code would be U.

Exposure was adequate. In the phase 1 glioma trial (PMID:23349317), tumours removed at surgery contained therapeutic levels of GRN1005 and free paclitaxel at doses of 200 mg/m2 or more, below the 600 mg/m2 dose used in the index trial. No source in humans measured engagement of tubulin or microtubules, such as mitotic arrest or microtubule stabilization in tumour, and none measured a downstream pathway marker. The phase 2 trial (NCT01967810/PMID:39713041) missed its response-rate and 3-month progression-free survival endpoints. It gives no mechanistic reason for the failure and says only that no further glioma studies are planned. The drug has no approval through this target that would let engagement be inferred. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter in glioma, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01008332 had a safety and tolerability primary outcome only (multiple intradermal injections over 18-22 weeks). It is classified not_efficacy, and no results were posted, so it was not an efficacy test of ToleroMune HDM. That fits F9. Later trials did occur: an exposure-chamber efficacy study (NCT01447784, patient-reported endpoint) and a further tolerability study (NCT01949441). Neither has an outcome classified in the bundle. There is no human evidence of exposure, T-cell tolerance or engagement, or downstream pathway effects, and no PubMed abstracts. If the program's eventual failure stemmed from the efficacy readout, the cause would be indeterminate (U), because engagement has no human data.

drug: allergen extract (Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus or Phleum pratense), aluminium hydroxide-adsorbed
rationale: Allergovac depot is an aluminium-adsorbed allergen extract with no recorded molecular target. My searches found no published human evidence for this product in grass allergy, such as allergen-specific IgG4 induction or IgE or T-cell changes, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the index trial NCT01567306, NPT changes were noisy (SD ~2.2) and overlapped placebo. Only the highest dose, Group 5, trended better (1.385 vs 0.839), and that group also had the most serious AEs (8/25, mostly generalized urticaria). No sponsor statement explains why the program stopped. The short, small, highly variable trial (F7) and toxicity at the top dose (F6) are possible contributors. With engagement unmeasured, U applies.

BTL-TML-HSV is a very low dose of sublingual thimerosal (0.2 µg per dose). Its proposed mechanism is vague: it may prompt the host's immune system to fight the virus. No molecular target is defined, and the bundle has no human data on exposure, engagement or a downstream marker. The index trial NCT01902303 missed its endpoint: 11/23 lesions aborted on drug vs 6/14 on placebo. The earlier NCT01308424 showed a trend that was not significant (p=0.106). The investigators blamed the UV-challenge model, which in a post-hoc analysis appeared to blunt antiviral activity for about 48 hours, and they called for properly designed and powered trials. This points to trial design (F7) and timing (F4). Because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never worked on anything from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

AL-78843 is an undisclosed Alcon small molecule. No target is recorded and it has only one trial. In the index trial NCT02079649, its ocular redness AUC change was -2.8, versus -4.5 for vehicle and -8.1 for Maxidex, so it did no better than vehicle. The active control did work, which means the trial was able to detect an effect. A web search turned up only the registry entry and a pipeline listing. There were no human data on drug exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker, and the sponsor gave no reason for the failure. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a molecule that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

In healthy men, PET with [11C]clorgyline (PMID:19890267) showed CX157 reaching brain and inhibiting MAO-A by 47-72% at 60-80 mg, tracking plasma levels (EC50 19.3 ng/ml). The authors call this robust and used it to set the 60 mg TID index dose, so exposure and engagement are rated adequate. Caveats: inhibition was partial and fully gone by 24 h, it was not measured in MDD patients, and it was published after the index start. No human pathway data were shown (the tyramine study NCT01633437 posted no results). The index trial NCT00739908 had no separation on MADRS (-12.5 vs -12.3), suggesting F2. Secondary codes: signal-detection problems from early improvement and possible bio-types (PMID:28926793) point to F7/F3; partial, transient inhibition leaves F1a possible.

SLC022 is propentofylline, a glial modulator. In the Phase IIa trial NCT00813826 (300 mg three times daily, about 180 patients with postherpetic neuralgia), it did not reduce self-reported pain compared with placebo, and Solace disbanded soon after. None of the sources show human data on spinal or CNS drug levels, glial target engagement or biomarker change. Investigators gave several possible reasons. The drug may not have reached the spinal cord in enough quantity or for long enough, which was never measured. Postherpetic neuralgia may have been the wrong disease. Human microglia responded weakly to propentofylline in vitro, unlike rodent cells, but in vitro data do not count as human evidence. With no human data on engagement, the sources cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The CMV~IMPACT ASH 2014 abstract (Cytovir CMV, NCT01077908) reported no safety problem. Its preliminary analysis suggested fewer CMV reactivations and shorter antiviral treatment with the T cells. But reactivation was lower than predicted, and the 14 gamma-capture patients were left out, so the trial looks underpowered rather than negative. No published efficacy failure or stated stop reason was found. In other studies, Streptamer-selected CMV T cells expanded in patients and lowered CMV DNA by at least 1 log (Frontiers review). PMID:29029297 also showed in vivo expansion with viral clearance. So the transferred cells did take hold and act. These pillar data come from other studies, not from immune measurements in the index trial itself.

Cunermuspir is a copper(I)-niacin supplement (BioCopper1) with no recorded molecular target. I found no human data on copper exposure, tissue copper delivery or target engagement. Its only mechanistic paper (PMID:42792186) used fibroblasts in vitro, and its authors say they cannot attribute the effects to copper. In NCT04737278, platelet ATP, the proposed pathway marker, rose in both arms, with no significant difference versus placebo (p=0.15). Neuromuscular symptoms improved in both arms too, and no between-group test was reported, which points to a large placebo response and a small trial that was poorly analysed (F7, secondary). With engagement unknown, nothing separates a drug that failed to act from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The phase 1 trial (NCT01475006, PMID:31154523) measured only plasma PK. Conjugated-antibody exposure rose in proportion to dose, but nobody measured drug levels in tumor or brain, EGFRvIII binding, or a downstream marker in patients. One snippet cites a modelled efficacious plasma level of 4990 ng/mL, but none of the sources I found say whether the MTD reached it. Grade 4 thrombocytopenia, likely from the DM1 payload, capped the dose at an MTD of 2.0 mg/kg. There is no evidence that this was below what engagement needed, so dose_limited is false. Responses were modest: 2 partial responses and 15 stable disease. No source gives a reason for stopping the program. With engagement unmeasured, the answer is indeterminate (U). Payload toxicity may also have played a part (F6).

GSK457 is a mix of four nutritional agents, one of them oleic acid, that was meant to release gut peptides through GPBAR1 and other gut receptors. In NCT01725126 and PMID:27093610 it did not reduce weight or meaningfully lower glucose in people with type 2 diabetes. The bundle and the full text have no human evidence that the drug engaged its target: GLP-1 and PYY were not measured in humans, and investigators could not measure the components in blood. So nothing separates a drug that never engaged GPBAR1 from a target that does not matter. Investigators blamed the lack of translation mainly on the hard-to-take clinical formulation, possible non-adherence, varied diets and differences between mice and humans.
