Those points support F7 as a secondary code. Two subjects stayed at 30 g because of gastrointestinal side effects, which is too few to count as dose-limited.

GSK2890457 is not a single GPBAR1 agonist. It is a mix of four nutritional agents: fibers (oligofructose, apple pectin), oleic acid and one other component. In humans, no measure of exposure, GPBAR1/TGR5 engagement or gut hormone release (GLP-1, PYY) was reported (NCT01725126, PMID:27093610). The authors said they could not measure the components in blood to confirm adherence, because these substances are common in a normal diet. They blamed the lack of translation from mice mainly on the hard-to-take clinical formulation (a drink plus 12 capsules twice a day, so adherence is uncertain), on variable diet and gut microbiota, and on species differences. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Execution and adherence problems (F7) are a secondary code.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT00634452) of MDX-1401, a CD30-depleting antibody, in relapsed/refractory Hodgkin lymphoma posted no results. The bundle has no other trials, abstracts or approvals for it, so exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human data. Brentuximab vedotin, which acts on the same target (CD30/TNFRSF8), is FDA-approved in Hodgkin lymphoma. That shows CD30 is a valid target in this disease, which points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Nothing shows MDX-1401 engaged CD30 adequately. One caveat: brentuximab is an antibody-drug conjugate, so its success may reflect the attached payload rather than CD30 engagement alone. With such a thin bundle, indeterminate (U) remains a plausible alternative, and confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01311713 was a Phase 1/2 dose-finding study. Its primary endpoints were MTD (reported as NA, not determined) and adverse-event counts. It was terminated without a stated reason, so it was not an efficacy test of CEP-9722 and it is coded F9. In the earlier Phase 1 study (NCT00920595, PMID:24880570) in solid-tumor patients, systemic exposure rose with dose, with high variability. Pharmacodynamic assessment confirmed PARP inhibition, though without a dose response. The combination MTD was set at 750 mg/day for asthenia and weight loss, and there is no evidence this capped the dose below what engagement needed. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. The PD data were published in 2014, after the index trial started in 2011.

Phase 1 NCT02013804 (PMID:31439037), mostly kidney cancer patients, showed linear PK, apparent PD-1 receptor saturation at 10 mg/kg Q2W and above, and no dose-limiting toxicities. PK-RO modelling (PMID:35133489) showed >90% occupancy at the 20 mg/kg Q2W dose used in the index trial. Pathway effects followed: peripheral T-cell proliferation, raised IFNγ and chemokines, and more intratumoral CD8 and IFNG/CXCL9 expression. That phase 1 trial was registered before the index trial started, though results were published later. In NCT02118337 (ccRCC), MEDI0680 plus durvalumab did not beat nivolumab on ORR (16.7% vs 23.8%, p=0.51). PD-1 was engaged, but dual PD-1/PD-L1 blockade added no benefit over PD-1 alone. The small, active-comparator superiority design limits the conclusions (F7/F9).

The index trial NCT01330953 was a first-in-human single-ascending-dose safety study in healthy volunteers. Its only primary endpoint was adverse events, with no serious AEs at any dose, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). PMID:30677788 reports that LY2928057 bound ferroportin and blocked hepcidin interaction. In humans, serum iron, transferrin saturation and hepcidin rose, and in CKD patients serum iron roughly doubled at 600 mg. The CKD trial NCT01991483, which started after the index trial, showed only an inconsistent haemoglobin effect: slower decline at 600 mg but none at 300 or 1000 mg. Despite pathway engagement, clinical benefit was not clear, so F2 is secondary. No stop reason is given in the bundle.

The index trial NCT00749411 was a repeat-dose safety study. Its primary endpoint was the change in pulse rate, not efficacy, and it showed no difference from placebo and no serious AEs. So it was not an efficacy test of darotropium (F9). Elsewhere in COPD patients, GSK233705 produced significant bronchodilation (trough FEV1 improvement). In PMID:22329914 only the 200 µg dose exceeded the 130 mL target, and PMID:22419863 showed an added gain on top of salmeterol. This functional effect implies airway exposure and M3 engagement, which were not measured directly. Bronchodilation, however, waned over 24 h, making the drug unsuitable for once-daily dosing (PMID:22329914). That is a molecule-specific duration limitation rather than a target failure. The engagement evidence was published after the index trial started.

SAR292833 (GRC15300) is a TRPV3 antagonist. Reviews say it failed the 4-week Phase 2 trial in chronic peripheral neuropathic pain (NCT01463397), and Sanofi reported in its 4Q13 results that it had stopped development without giving details. Glenmark said a Phase 1 study was completed, but I found no human data on drug levels, TRPV3 engagement or downstream biomarkers. The structure was never disclosed and no results were posted. No other TRPV3 drug has succeeded clinically, so F1b does not apply. Nothing available separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in neuropathic pain, so the code is U.

NCT05759208 was the first study of OK-101 in humans. No human data were found on ocular drug levels, CMKLR1 engagement, or a pathway biomarker such as goblet cell density. The company's goblet cell and anti-inflammatory mechanism was only proposed. Press releases never say the registered primary endpoints (corneal fluorescein staining and ocular discomfort) were met. Instead they point to secondary symptom and sign results and responder analyses. The 0.1% dose did worse than 0.05%, which hints at an odd dose-response but not at a tolerability limit. The sponsor then moved to neuropathic corneal pain (NCT06637527, NCT07838506) and said the drug worked best in more severe pain, a sign that patient selection may matter (F3). Engagement is no_human_data, so a drug that never engaged CMKLR1 cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter in dry eye. Code: U.

In NCT01756898, oral ASB17061 at 5, 10 or 20 mg did not separate from placebo on IGA response at Day 29. Response rates were about 20% in every arm, with no dose-response. I found no human evidence of exposure, chymase inhibition or a downstream biomarker. The only potency data are in vitro (IC50 0.02 µM), and the drug's other publications are mouse studies. The only other chymase inhibitor in eczema, SUN13834, also stopped in Phase 2, so it does not show the target works. The 2025 preprint from the new licensee calls the drug well tolerated and does not explain the eczema failure, which rules out a dose cap from tolerability. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. That makes the code U.

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation trial NCT00695448 of the pan-PI3K inhibitor GSK1059615 in solid tumours and lymphoma was terminated early. The sponsor explicitly stated it stopped 'due to lack of sufficient exposure following single- and repeat-dosing.' No results, engagement data or biomarker data were posted, and the bundle has no other trials or publications. Exposure is therefore inadequate by the sponsor's own account, so the PI3K mechanism was never properly tested in humans. Engagement and pathway have no human data. Nothing indicates tolerability capped the dose; the limitation was pharmacokinetic or formulation-related. The code is F1a with high confidence because the source states the reason directly.

The index Phase 2a trial of 300 mg vimnerixin (RIST4721) missed both pustule-count endpoints (p=0.24, p=0.804) (NCT03988335). A progressing-disease subgroup did better (PPPASI-50 71% vs 15%, p=0.022) (PMID:34716902), which hints at F3. The bundle has no human PK, CXCR2 occupancy or neutrophil biomarker data. The blister-model study NCT04105959 posted no results and started after the index trial, so the efficacy miss alone is indeterminate (U). The program nevertheless continued into Phase 2b in PPP and a Phase 2 trial in HS. Both were terminated 'due to safety findings in ongoing Phase 2 trials' (NCT05194839, NCT05348681). Toxicity therefore ended the program. Whether that toxicity was on-target is not shown.

The first-in-human study (PMID:23757357) showed that 70 mg/m2 weekly, the dose used in phase 2, reached plasma levels matching active xenograft concentrations. It also showed target inhibition: HSP70 induction in PBMCs, client protein depletion in tumour, and reduced FDG-PET uptake. The RP2D was not described as capped below engagement. Client degradation at this dose was confirmed in breast cancer patients by HER2 PET (PMID:25085789). No gastric-specific pharmacodynamic data exist, and this evidence was published after the index trial began. The index trial (NCT01084330) posted no results. With engagement shown but no benefit, the mechanism likely does not drive unselected gastric cancer. Activity limited to molecular strata elsewhere (NCT01124864, NCT01271920) suggests selection may matter (F3). The bundle is thin.

First-in-human study (NCT00526045/PMID:23757357) reached 70 mg/m2, the dose used in later trials. At that dose, concentrations matched active xenograft levels. It also showed target inhibition: HSP70 induction in PBMCs, client-protein depletion in tumour, and reduced FDG-PET signal. Client-protein (HER2) downregulation was confirmed in breast cancer patients (PMID:25085789). The RP2D was described as tolerable, so the dose was not capped below engagement. Engagement was not shown specifically in NSCLC. In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, single-arm activity was modest (6/35 responses; NCT01124864). The randomized index trial then stopped for futility, with PFS 1.5 vs 2.3 months against chemotherapy (NCT01646125). HSP90 inhibition engaged but gave no benefit, so F2. Activity differed by molecular stratum, so F3 is secondary.

The index trial NCT00708292 was a phase I/Ib dose-finding study. Its primary endpoint was the MTD, with no efficacy success criterion, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). The monotherapy MTD was not reached, and the RP2D was 70 mg/m2 (PMID:25809731). At 70 mg/m2 in solid tumours, exposure matched active xenograft concentrations. PBMC HSP70 induction, tumour client-protein depletion and FDG-PET reduction showed target inhibition and pathway effect (PMID:23757357), so dose was not capped below engagement. That evidence comes from solid tumours, not myeloma, and was published after the index trial started. In myeloma, monotherapy gave no responses, only stable disease (secondary F2). The bortezomib combination was not tolerated (3/5 DLTs), which is molecule/combination toxicity (secondary F6).

In NCT01109381, the lauric acid formulation GT08 cleared H. pylori in only 2 of the 31 participants who finished treatment, and the trial was stopped for poor efficacy. The drug has no recorded molecular target. Neither the bundle nor my one web search found human data on drug levels in the stomach or gastric mucosa, direct antibacterial action on H. pylori in patients, or any biomarker. That leaves exposure, engagement and pathway all at no_human_data. The trial reported no serious adverse events, so tolerability did not limit the dose. No other drug works the same way for comparison. The bundle cannot tell whether the drug failed to reach or kill the bacteria at the site of infection or whether the idea itself does not work, so the result is U.

YH14642 is a herbal water extract of Notoginseng Radix and Rehmanniae Radix Preparata with no defined molecular target. No human data were found on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects. Results for NCT01499225 were never posted, and the only linked publication (PMID:33197289) does not report this drug. However, Yuhan later stated that YH14642 improved probing depths in its double-blind Phase 2 trial. The company then optimized the extraction process to make a successor, YH23537, which needs a lower dose (300 mg matched 1,000 mg of YH14642 in dogs). So the stop does not look like an efficacy failure but like replacement by an improved formulation, which is partly a business decision. Confidence is low because the trial results themselves are unpublished.

Exposure was characterized in patients with HCC and other tumors (two-compartment PopPK). Rises in C4, total bile acid and circulating FGF19 'confirmed effective FGFR4 inhibition' (PMID:35655320). Modeling showed close-to-maximal PD effect across the clinical exposure range, with no clinically relevant exposure-safety relationship (PMID:36131557). So the RP2D of 120 mg was not capped below engagement. Despite this, activity was minimal: 8 objective responses among roughly 160 treated, median TTP 2.6–3.9 months, and 0% ORR in Group 3 (NCT02325739). Adequate engagement without benefit points to F2. The authors call for a 'refined biomarker strategy', and modeling notes large interpatient variability (PMID:35728123), so patient selection (F3) also applies. Engagement data were published after the index trial started.

The index trial NCT00638365 was a single-dose Phase 1/2 study whose primary outcome was safety and tolerability. It was not an efficacy test, and the drug was acceptably tolerated, so the code is F9. Serum PK was reported (half-life 11.9 days), but no airway or sputum drug levels appear in the bundle. No direct measure of PcrV binding or TTSS inhibition in humans was shown, so engagement is no_human_data. Sputum neutrophil elastase and neutrophil counts fell at 10 mg/kg (PMID:24019259), and IL-8 fell in the repeat-dose trial (PMID:29292092), supporting a downstream pathway effect. The later Phase 2 NCT01695343 missed time-to-antibiotics. Without engagement data, that failure cannot be attributed to the molecule or the target, hence secondary U.

The CT.gov record for NCT01521663 describes IPX159 as an extended-release form of nefopam. AdisInsight lists its mechanism as undefined, and the bundle records no primary target. A Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers compared formulations, but no PK, occupancy or biomarker data were published. Impax's 2012 10-K says the Phase IIb trial showed only a modest improvement in RLS symptoms and missed its primary endpoints, and the program was dropped in February 2013. No human evidence covers exposure, engagement or pathway, and the target is undefined, so nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that doesn't matter in RLS. The code is U.

E-101 is a topical solution containing porcine myeloperoxidase (pMPO) and glucose oxidase. The enzymes are meant to make HOCl and singlet oxygen that kill microbes in the surgical wound. In the Phase 3 trial NCT01297959, SSI rates were no better than placebo: 53/241 vs 41/225, p=0.39. The pages found show only in vitro activity (PMC4136076) and animal wound models (Exoxemis ICAAC poster). None reports, in humans, wound bacterial load falling, oxidant generation or how long the enzymes stayed active in the wound. No sponsor explanation of the failure was found, and no other drug works through this mechanism. Engagement is no_human_data, so nothing separates a drug that never worked in the wound from a mechanism that does not prevent SSI. The code is U.

In MITOCARE (NCT01374321), a 6 mg/kg IV bolus of TRO40303 did not reduce infarct size measured by CK or troponin I AUC, or by cardiac MRI. Exposure counts as adequate: the Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (PMID:24507657) showed predictable plasma pharmacokinetics up to 13 mg/kg with good tolerability, and the dose was chosen by scaling up from rats. Engagement does not: no human data show TSPO binding or inhibition of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), and no downstream biomarker was measured. A review (PMC7077531) notes the drug also failed in pigs and in saline-perfused rat hearts. That raises doubt about the molecule but is not human evidence. No other TSPO drug has succeeded in this disease. Nothing here separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01068184 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study in healthy volunteers and COPD patients. Its primary outcomes were safety and PK variables only, so it was not an efficacy test of AZD6553. It was halted because an emerging PK profile could not be reconciled with the drug's known pharmaceutical properties. That points to a PK or formulation problem, not a failed efficacy readout. No results were posted, no target is recorded, and the bundle has no other trials, no abstracts and no data on exposure, engagement or pathway. If this were read as an efficacy failure, the cause would be indeterminate (U).

The index trial, NCT01230645, was a pharmacodynamic translational study in healthy volunteers deliberately infected with RSV. Its primary endpoint was nasal IL8, and its stated aim was to support moving RV568 into patients with respiratory disease. It was not an efficacy test for treating RSV. Intranasal RV568 at 400 µg cut nasal IL8 AUC by 46% versus placebo (p=0.07), a borderline result. It did not change IL6, viral load, infectivity or symptoms, which fits a host-directed anti-inflammatory drug. The sponsors read the result as positive and took the drug into COPD trials (NCT01475292, NCT01867762). I found no human data on drug levels, p38 occupancy or p38 inhibition, so if the outcome were read as an efficacy failure it would be indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01475292 was a 28-day safety and tolerability study (endpoint class not_efficacy), so it was not an efficacy test of RV568. The published 14-day COPD trial (PMID:29074542) reported that inhaled RV568 was well tolerated, with modest improvement in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 and a significant reduction in sputum malondialdehyde. Sputum cell counts did not change, so the pathway evidence is mixed; it is rated adequate only on the malondialdehyde change. The bundle has no human PK data and no direct p38 target-engagement data, so exposure and engagement are no_human_data. Later development (NCT01867762) has no outcome shown. Why the program stopped is not shown. F9 is primary; U is secondary because engagement was never shown.

In healthy volunteers, single 400 and 800 μg doses of AZD1940 produced dose-dependent CNS cannabinoid effects ('high', 'sedated') and CNS/GI adverse events. The authors state this shows the dose range predicted from preclinical data was attained (PMID:23324098). This is taken as evidence of systemic exposure and CB1 agonist activity in humans. Even so, AZD1940 failed to reduce capsaicin pain or hyperalgesia. In the index post-surgical pain trial (NCT00659490) it matched placebo (AUC 355 vs 356), while naproxen separated clearly, so assay sensitivity was intact. This points to peripheral CB1/CB2 agonism not driving acute pain as tested (F2). Caveats: engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers, it was published after the index trial started, and peripheral target engagement was not measured directly, so U is secondary.

In the index trial NCT01326780, topical JNJ-10229570 at 1.2–3.6% had only a small dose trend on total lesion counts at week 12 and did not beat vehicle. No serious adverse events were reported, so tolerability did not limit the dose. The only pharmacology evidence is from cultured human sebocytes and human skin grafted onto SCID mice (PMID:21602033), and non-human data do not count. The bundle and my searches turned up no human data on skin drug levels, MC1R/MC5R occupancy, or sebum reduction. The Phase 1 trials (NCT01492647, NCT01494714) posted no results. No other drug on this target has succeeded in acne. Because engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The full text of the index-trial paper (PMID:37532622) cites a Phase 1 PET receptor-occupancy study, reported only as 'data on file' and not published separately. In it, 100 mg of SYN120, the dose used in NCT02258152, gave more than 95% 5-HT6 occupancy and more than 80% 5-HT2A occupancy over 24 hours. That shows the drug reached the brain and bound both targets. This was Phase 1 work done before the Phase 2a trial, but it was not done in patients with Parkinson disease dementia (PDD). No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Even with both receptors highly occupied, the trial showed no benefit on its primary attention endpoint or any other cognitive measure. This points to dual 5-HT6/5-HT2A blockade not improving cognition in PDD. Pimavanserin's success was in psychosis, not cognition, so F1b does not apply.

KPAX002 combines low-dose methylphenidate with a micronutrient formula meant to support mitochondria. It has no defined molecular target. None of the sources report human exposure, target engagement or a downstream biomarker (such as mitochondrial or metabolic markers) at the trial doses. The published Phase 2 (n=135, NCT01966276) missed its primary CIS endpoint. The authors pointed to subgroups (severe ME/CFS; fatigue with pain) where the effect only approached significance, which fits F3. A patient-advocacy blog blamed a high placebo response, which fits F7. Since engagement has no human data, nothing separates a mechanism that was never tested from one that does not matter, so the code is U.

Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate, not measured. The same OXN PR formulation and other oral oxycodone products met pain endpoints through MOR agonism in the CNS: chronic low back pain (NCT01358526, NCT01685684, NCT01571362) and postoperative pain (NCT01484652). Oxycodone is also approved for chronic pain. Healthy-volunteer MRS showed a brain glutamate change (PMID:34427941), but this was published after the index trial, and no engagement data exist in diabetic polyneuropathy. In the index trial (NCT00944697), adding oxycodone/naloxone to pregabalin gave no SF-MPQ difference versus placebo (47.65 vs 49.56). This fits F2: added MOR agonism did not help as tested. Tapentadol's approval for this disease (PMID:21689507) involves a dual mechanism. The small, high-variance add-on design (n=98) may also have limited the test (F7). No stated reason is given.

Pillars were not measured in Parkinson patients. MOR engagement is inferred adequate because oxycodone/OXN PR met efficacy endpoints through the same CNS mu-opioid target at comparable doses: chronic low back pain (NCT01358526, NCT01685684) and RLS (NCT01112644), plus the approval for chronic pain. PK-PD was shown in humans in 1996 (PMID:8549034). In PANDA (NCT01439100/PMID:26494524) the analgesic difference was -0.6 (p=0.058), with similar adverse events in both arms, so the dose was not capped. The independent OXYDOPA trial in parkinsonian central pain also failed (PMID:38850081). This suggests mu-opioid agonism does not adequately treat PD pain as tested (F2). Secondary codes: the heterogeneity of PD pain types (PMID:26134157) supports F3, and the near-significant result with a sizeable placebo response supports F7.

The index OXN PR trial in bladder pain syndrome (NCT01197261) posted no results and gave no stop reason. Oxycodone exposure is well characterised in humans (NCT01160614, PMID:8549034). Mu-opioid engagement and its CNS effects (pupillometry, respiratory depression, analgesia) are shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:28340145, PMID:41379941). The same OXN PR formulation met pain endpoints through the same central MOR mechanism in chronic low back pain (NCT01358526) and in RLS (NCT01112644), so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Engagement was never measured in IC/BPS patients. With adequate engagement and no benefit, this most likely reflects MOR agonism not relieving bladder pain as tested (F2). Confidence is low because no efficacy data from the index trial appear in the bundle.

Human PK shows dose-proportional exposure, with 600 mg keeping serum levels above target for 8-12 weeks and no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:34437752). In cat-allergic rhinitis patients, published in 2021 before the index trial started, the drug neutralized allergen in serum and nasal fluid. It also lowered nasal type 2 cytokines and basophil responses and improved nasal symptoms after allergen challenge (PMID:33651675). Skin-test reactivity fell and early asthmatic responses were prevented (PMID:35934082, NCT03838731). Despite adequate pillars at the same 600 mg dose, the Phase 3 trial in patients living with cats stopped for lack of efficacy (NCT04981717). This fits F2: neutralizing Fel d 1 does not drive the symptom-medication outcome under natural exposure. F4 is secondary, because the effect was shown in challenge settings but not on the long-term patient-reported endpoint.

The drug neutralizes the cat allergen Fel d 1. Exposure was adequate: linear, dose-proportional PK, and a single 600 mg dose kept serum above target concentration for 8-12 weeks with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:34437752). Engagement and pathway were adequate in cat-allergic rhinitis patients before the index trial: allergen-neutralizing capacity in serum and nasal fluid, suppressed nasal IL-4/5/13 and TARC, and improved TNSS after allergen challenge (PMID:33651675). A phase 2 bronchial-challenge study also met its endpoint (NCT03838731). Yet the 600 mg phase 3 in patients living with cats stopped for lack of efficacy on a 12-week symptom/medication score (NCT04981717). Allergen neutralization did not translate to benefit under chronic natural exposure. The challenge-versus-real-world endpoint gap supports F4 as secondary.

Smilagenin (Cogane) is described as a neurotrophic-factor inducer, but no molecular target is recorded. Phase 1 work (NCT00875316 and a 2009 PK abstract) showed only plasma pharmacokinetics that rose linearly with dose and good tolerability. I found no human data on brain or CSF levels, GDNF or BDNF induction, or any biomarker of engagement. The GDNF/BDNF rise was seen only in mice (PMID:18364399). CONFIDENT-PD (NCT01060878) tested 60, 120 and 180 mg once daily for 28 weeks and missed every endpoint with no trend toward benefit. The sponsor called the trial well conducted, so trial execution (F7) is ruled out, and tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement never measured, a drug that did not engage cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U. Strictly, exposure fits no_human_data better than 'inadequate': plasma levels were measured, but brain penetration (needed for this CNS target) was not shown either way.

F373280 is a panthenyl ester prodrug of DHA (omega-3). It was tested at 1 g/day in NCT01831856, a trial of keeping sinus rhythm after cardioversion in patients with persistent AF and heart failure. It missed its primary endpoint: hazard ratio 1.14, p=0.57, with a numerically shorter time to recurrence than placebo. The bundle has no other trials, no Phase 1 results and no PubMed abstracts. My searches turned up only the protocol, the EU trial registry entry and patents. They describe animal burst-pacing data and give no human PK, plasma or red-cell DHA incorporation, or electrophysiological biomarker data. Pierre Fabre gave no stated reason for stopping. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that failed to deliver DHA from a mechanism that does not work in this setting. So the code is U.

The index trial NCT02427568 was an 18-patient pilot with a 13:5 split. It posted only descriptive STAI-Trait means, and these favoured MDMA (-23.5 vs -8.8), with no statistical test, so it could not answer the efficacy question. It was not a demonstrated failure. No pillar was measured directly. All three are inferred adequate because MDMA at comparable doses (around 125 mg) met pivotal CNS efficacy endpoints in PTSD (NCT03537014, NCT04077437) and in earlier phase 2 trials (NCT01211405, NCT01793610). No engagement evidence exists in anxiety patients. Serious adverse events occurred only at the 12-month follow-up. The trial was underpowered and descriptive, so F7 is primary. F9 is secondary because the readout was not an efficacy failure.

The index trial NCT02238756 was a Phase 1 safety and reactogenicity study of CV8102 alone or mixed with Rabipur in healthy volunteers, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Its published report (PMID:30797640) shows it met its aims. Doses of 25–50 µg were acceptably tolerated and significantly improved rabies neutralising titre kinetics and magnitude, a functional adjuvant (pathway) effect. Escalation stopped at 100 µg because of CRP rises, but effective doses were reached, so the dose was not limited. Direct receptor engagement was not measured. The drug moved on to oncology vaccine trials (PMID:35421231, NCT03291002). Nothing in the bundle shows a failed efficacy readout.

The index trial (NCT00758446) was a small allergen-challenge study with a TNSS endpoint. It posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. I found no human data on drug levels, PDE4 inhibition or anti-inflammatory biomarkers at the doses used in allergic rhinitis. The [11C]rolipram PET occupancy study (NCT01215552) was terminated with an inadequate design and reported no occupancy data. Later ALTO-101 data from 2024 come from healthy volunteers on a transdermal patch and show CNS EEG/cognitive effects. They are not relevant to nasal inflammation and come after the index trial. Other PDE4 inhibitors are approved for atopic eczema and COPD, but not for allergic rhinitis, so F1b does not apply. Engagement has no human data, so nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter here.

In NCT04382651, a single 10 mg/kg IV dose of MAS825 missed the APACHE II primary endpoint (difference 0.98, p=0.33). Binding to IL-1β/IL-18 was not measured directly. However, PMID:37338154 reports large downstream changes in COVID-19 patients: CRP down 51%, IL-6 down 42%, plus lower neutrophils and IFN-γ. The authors call these indicative of IL-1β/IL-18 pathway engagement, so engagement and pathway are rated adequate. These data were published after the trial began, and the bundle has no PK data. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite the mechanism being engaged, the clinical endpoint showed no benefit, so the primary code is F2. F4 is secondary: ICU admissions and oxygen duration trended favorably, which raises the question of whether the composite APACHE endpoint was the right measure.

The index trial, NCT00664703, was a small laboratory proof-of-concept study in 9 adults with ADHD. Sublingual lobeline at 7.5–30 mg modestly improved working memory but did not significantly improve attention. Nausea was a mild, dose-related side effect, but no source says it capped the dose. The Phase 1 studies (NCT00100074, NCT00519259) were registered to measure pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers but posted no results. No human data turned up on VMAT2 occupancy, on how much drug reaches the brain, or on a downstream dopamine biomarker. Lobeline also acts on nicotinic receptors and the dopamine transporter, so the drug may have hit other targets. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged VMAT2 cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter in ADHD, so the code is U. The very small, exploratory trial (F7) also limits what it could show.

The index trial NCT02211469 was a single ascending dose safety, PK and PD study in healthy males. It was not an efficacy test, and no results were posted. PMID:30785748 reports that in clinical trials BMS-986104 had a longer half-life than fingolimod and reduced formation of the phosphate metabolite needed for S1P1 activity. This suggests limited exposure to the active species. The sponsor then designed a successor, BMS-986166, with a shorter half-life and more phosphate formation. No human engagement data (lymphocyte lowering, heart-rate effect) appear in the bundle. The program appears to have been replaced because of molecule-specific PK properties, not an efficacy failure. F1a is a secondary code given the inadequate active-metabolite exposure.

The cause of failure can't be determined. M516102 has no recorded target. Its only known trial is the index trial, NCT00980629 (EudraCT 2008-001685-87), a Phase IIb dose-finding study of itch in atopic dermatitis. No results have been posted for it. The search found no human data on drug levels, target binding or biomarker effects. It also found no sponsor statement on why the program stopped. A 2020 review (Exp Dermatol 10.1111/exd.14145) cites the trial only by its registry entry and gives no results. Without engagement data, the bundle can't tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter for this itch. That makes the code U.

No direct PK, occupancy or biomarker data appear in the bundle. However, the sister RA trial NCT01569152 met ACR20 at Week 12 (68% vs 24%, p<0.001), so exposure, SYK engagement and pathway are inferred adequate in RA. The index trial NCT01651936 was terminated without a stated reason after enrolling 56. Only 13 vs 18 participants were analyzed for the primary endpoint. The point estimate favored MK-8457 (DAS28-CRP difference -0.52) with a wide CI (-1.54 to 0.50). The miss therefore looks like an underpowered, truncated trial rather than a mechanism failure. Serious AEs were imbalanced (5/30 vs 0/26), suggesting safety may have driven termination of the program (F6 secondary). No stop reason or publication confirms either explanation.

Human data for DA-8031 cover only plasma PK and tolerability in healthy men (PMID:28331291, PMID:34103898). Single doses up to 80 mg were well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Brain penetration, SERT occupancy and pathway effects were measured only in rats: 31–84% midbrain occupancy and a rise in serotonin (PMID:24824409). No human PET, platelet serotonin data or PE-patient biomarker were found. The index trial NCT01798667 posted no results and gave no stop reason; a review says results were never reported. Dapoxetine, which acts on the same target, reached phase 3 with positive placebo-controlled trials in PE. That points toward the molecule rather than the target (F1b), but engagement is unmeasured, so U also applies. Confidence is low.

NOVOCART Disc plus is an autologous disc chondrocyte implant with no recorded molecular target. The bundle has only a study protocol (PMID:26920137) and a Phase I safety report from 24 patients (PMC5566491). The safety report found adverse events in the range expected after disc surgery, no rise in inflammatory markers and no imaging abnormalities. Neither paper reports engraftment or survival of the implanted cells, new disc matrix, or any biological readout showing the mechanism worked. The index trial NCT01640457 posted no efficacy results, and no source says why the program stopped. Because there is no human evidence of exposure, engagement or pathway effect, nothing separates a cell product that failed to act from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The TRIADE trial (NCT01318434) of amitifadine at 50 and 100 mg/day missed its primary endpoint, change in MADRS score. Every transporter occupancy and brain-penetration result in the bundle comes from rats (PMID:18538356, PMID:23826879); there is no human PET occupancy, CSF or biomarker data for SERT, NET or DAT. A small earlier trial in MDD (PMID:21925682, 50 mg BID) reported a MADRS benefit, but it was not a pivotal, target-confirming success, and concerns were raised about how it was reported (PMID:22520251), so engagement cannot be inferred from it. Press coverage describes the failure as being 'at low doses', which hints the dose may have been too low (F1a, secondary). That is not shown, though, and the dose was not capped by tolerability. With no human engagement data, the code is indeterminate (U). I could not fetch the full press release text.

Revexepride is a 5-HT4 agonist. In healthy volunteers it reached measurable plasma levels (1 mg: Cmax about 3.9 ng/mL, half-life about 10 h; PMID:25767373), so exposure counts as adequate. No source measured receptor engagement in humans. The downstream motility markers did not move: 0.5 mg three times daily for 4 weeks did not change pH/impedance reflux measures in patients with GERD (nmo.12484), and in a gastroparesis pilot it did not speed gastric emptying (nmo.12736). Because engagement was never measured, the sources cannot tell apart a drug that did not engage its target from a mechanism that does not help these patients, so the code is U. The index trial missed its endpoint at all doses, with no dose-response (NCT01472939). The investigators suggested it is hard to identify the patients who would benefit, which supports F3 as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT00810238 (C-CURE) was a feasibility/safety study. PMID:23583246 reports that it met that aim: dose attained in 75% of patients, uncomplicated delivery in 100%, and no added toxicity. It also showed favourable efficacy signals: LVEF rose from 27.5% to 34.5% versus no change with standard care (p<0.0001), with improved LVESV and 6-minute walk distance. The bundle therefore shows no efficacy failure of the index trial, so F9 fits. The cell therapy has no defined molecular target, and no human data on cell retention, engagement or pathway markers are given. Later commentary calls the field unresolved (PMID:23712104, PMID:24689022). Why the program later stopped in Phase 3 is not shown, so U applies secondarily.

In the index trial NCT01312922, the PNB01 combination (pipamperone plus citalopram) did no better than either citalopram or pipamperone alone: 17 early and sustained responders in every arm, p=1.0. I found no human evidence that low-dose pipamperone (5 mg twice daily) reached or blocked brain 5-HT2A or D4 receptors. The only occupancy data come from dogs (PMID:18753826), and animal data do not count. The phase 2 trial NCT00672659/PMID:21349239 showed only an early MADRS benefit that was gone by week 8. Response was about 10% in all arms, including citalopram, which suggests the trial had little power to show a difference (possible F7). No sponsor statement explaining the failure was found. Because engagement has no human data, the failure is indeterminate.

ORIENTAL (NCT01465464, PMID:28988687) showed no OS benefit for orantinib 200 mg bid plus TACE (HR 1.09) and was stopped for futility. Plasma PK was characterized in HCC patients (PMID:20390419, PMID:24829073). The dose was set by DLTs at 400 mg bid in Child-Pugh B patients, but no data show 200 mg bid was below what engagement needed. No human receptor occupancy or kinase-inhibition data exist. The only PD signal is a plasma PDGF decrease in colorectal cancer (PMID:21567184) and a tentative sVCAM-1 marker. Lenvatinib, acting on the same KDR/FGFR targets, is approved in HCC, which argues against an irrelevant target and points to the molecule. However, the TACE-combination setting differs, so U also applies.

PXL01 is a lactoferrin-derived peptide applied locally around the repaired tendon, and no molecular target is recorded for it. The Phase 1 local tolerability/PK study (NCT00860080) posted no results, and none of the sources report human data on tissue exposure, engagement, or a mechanistic biomarker. The proposed mechanisms (raised PRG4/lubricin, lower inflammatory mediators) come only from rabbit and in vitro work (PMID:23174064, PMID 27658527). The index trial missed its primary endpoint, TAM2 at 12 weeks (p=0.89). The investigators reported benefits only in the per-protocol analysis at 6 months on secondary measures, which hints at a timing or endpoint problem (secondary code F4). Even so, without any engagement evidence, the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Ensereptide (PXL01) is a lactoferrin-derived peptide applied locally to stop adhesions forming around a repaired tendon. No molecular target is recorded for it. The index trial missed its primary endpoint: TAM2 at 12 weeks, 121 vs 108 degrees, p=0.89 (NCT01022242). The Phase 1 trial (NCT00860080) posted no PK results. The only mechanistic evidence comes from rabbits (PMID:23174064 and a lubricin/PRG4 study), which does not count. No human pillar data were found. The investigators reported benefit only in the per-protocol population at later timepoints (excellent/good mobility 61% vs 38%), and still concluded the drug works. With engagement unmeasured and no other drug on the same target, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Veliparib 200 mg BID plus FOLFIRI did not improve PFS in untreated mCRC (HR 0.94; NCT02305758, PMID:30531832). Target engagement was shown in humans before the index trial started. The 2009 phase 0 study found significant PAR inhibition in tumor biopsies at 25–50 mg (PMID:19364967). An irinotecan-combination phase 1 (NCT00576654, PMID:26842236) found tumor PAR reduction at 10–50 mg BID with rises in γH2AX and pNBS1. Topotecan data (PMID:21795476) showed over 75% PAR reduction in tumor plus γH2AX induction. The index dose was well above these levels and was not capped by tolerability. Veliparib also met PFS endpoints in BRCA breast and ovarian cancer (NCT02163694, NCT02470585). The mechanism was therefore engaged but did not add benefit. A biomarker-unselected population (F3) may also have contributed. Engagement was not shown specifically in colorectal patients.

Index NCT01063816 is a Phase 1 dose-escalation (MTD/RP2D) study of veliparib with carboplatin/gemcitabine in advanced solid tumors. It had no efficacy endpoint and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). In humans, plasma exposure and tumor PAR inhibition were shown at 25-50 mg in the 2009 Phase 0 study (PMID:19364967), before the index started. Further tumor/PBMC PAR suppression and γH2AX increases appear in PMID:21795476, 26842236 and 27503200. None of this was measured in DIPG. CNS penetration is shown only in primates (PMID:19526240). The DIPG phase I/II trial stopped for futility (PMID:32009149) without brain-tumor engagement data, so that failure is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01617928 is a 12-patient Phase 1 dose-finding study in Japanese patients with solid tumors. Its primary outcome was MTD/RP2D, so it was not an efficacy test and no failed readout exists. Pillars held in humans before the index trial started. The Phase 0 study showed exposure and significant PAR inhibition in tumor biopsies and PBMCs (PMID:19364967). Later studies showed >75% tumor PAR reduction with γH2AX increases (PMID:21795476, PMID:26842236) and ≥50% PBMC PAR inhibition at 50–500 mg (PMID:28387939). In peritoneal carcinomatosis itself, only γH2AX in circulating tumor cells was shown (PMID:25355929); target engagement was not measured there. Veliparib met PFS endpoints in Phase 3 ovarian/primary peritoneal cancer (NCT02470585) and BRCA breast cancer (NCT02163694). The ovarian trial was terminated as a 'business decision', supporting F8 as a secondary code.

In the index trial (NCT00813098), week-4 pain/discomfort relief was similar across arms (high dose 23/43, low dose 18/44, placebo 20/47). PMID:21684281, reporting this same trial in IBS patients, shows a dose-dependent fall in urinary 5-HIAA, a marker of TPH inhibition. This indicates the drug reached its target and engaged it, and it improved stool consistency. Both doses were well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Pain relief was significant only at week 1. The authors tie symptom relief to the extent of 5-HIAA reduction and suggest the marker could identify responders. That points to a heterogeneous population in which only a subset benefits (F3). The alternative is that TPH1 inhibition does not drive IBS pain overall (F2). The engagement data come from the index trial itself, so they did not precede it.

HMPL-004 is a multi-component botanical extract and has no recorded molecular target. The index Phase 3 trial (NCT01805791) was stopped for futility: remission at week 8 was 9/57 at 2400 mg, 7/58 at 1800 mg and 9/52 on placebo. The maintenance trial (NCT01882764) was stopped because of it. The earlier Phase 2 signal (PMID:23044768, NCT00659802) did not replicate. The only human PK found was andrographolide absorption in healthy volunteers given a different product (Kang Jang). No human data show tissue exposure, target engagement (TNF-α, IL-1β or NF-κB inhibition) or a biomarker change. Mechanistic support is animal and in vitro only (PMID:23292349). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Nothing separates poor engagement from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the first-in-human study (NCT02189174; PMID:30073466), PK modeling indicated pharmacologically active concentrations only at the top dose of 100 mg, so exposure was adequate at that dose. No target-engagement or pathway biomarker was measured in humans. At 100 mg, 27% of patients had DLTs and all had grade ≥3 toxicity: rash, hyperglycemia, stomatitis and diarrhea, which are class-typical PI3K effects. The MTD was never defined and no objective responses occurred. The authors attribute termination to poor tolerability and limited activity. They note the difficulty of achieving a therapeutic index when inhibiting all class I PI3K isoforms, which points to on-target toxicity offsetting efficacy (F5). Tolerability also capped dosing at the threshold of activity, so the mechanism was arguably not fully tested (F1a).

Exposure was shown: Phase 1 studies measured plasma levels at 1–2 mg (Cmax about 4 ng/mL, half-life about 11 h; PMID:25767373, PMID:27729771), and the target (gut 5-HT4) is reached from plasma. There is no published human measure of 5-HT4 engagement. The only pathway claim is that revexepride sped gastric emptying in healthy people, and the sponsor cited this as 'Shire, unpublished data'. In GERD, the index trial (0.5 mg three times daily) showed no change in reflux parameters (PMID:25530111). It was also stopped early for slow recruitment, so it was underpowered (F7 secondary). The 0.1–2 mg regurgitation trial NCT01472939 found no dose-response either. No other 5-HT4 agonist succeeded in GERD. Nothing in the bundle tells a drug that never engaged apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

AGN-207281 has no recorded target, and one search found no published mechanism, pharmacokinetics or target-engagement data. In the index trial (NCT01215786), the drug lowered intraocular pressure (IOP) by about 4 mmHg at Day 14, compared with about 1–2 mmHg on placebo. The 0.5% timolol comparator lowered it by about 6 mmHg at hours 0 and 2. A likely reason for stopping is that the drug was less effective than the standard treatment, but no source says so. No safety signal was reported. With the target unknown and no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway, nothing separates poor engagement from a modest mechanism. The code is therefore U.

In the index trial NCT00914186, TS-022 topical lotion at 0.005%, 0.010% and 0.020% did no better than vehicle on pruritus VAS, IGA, EASI or Skindex-29. The highest dose looked numerically worse than vehicle. There were no serious adverse events, so tolerability did not limit the dose. No primary target is recorded. The search found no human data on skin exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers, and no sponsor statement explaining the failure. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts and no other drugs on the same target. With engagement no_human_data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In RA patients in the index trial, ISIS-CRPRx lowered hs-CRP in a dose-dependent way, by 76.7% at 400 mg versus 14.4% on placebo (P=0.0015). That is direct, substantial target knockdown in the program's disease, which also implies the drug reached the liver. It was well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicity. Even so, ACR20 did not differ from placebo at Day 36 or Day 92 (PMID:25885521). This points to CRP lowering not driving RA disease activity. The engagement data came from the index trial itself, not before it. Caveats: the registered primary endpoint was safety only, ACR20 was exploratory, and arms were small (n≈12-14), so F9 and F7 also apply (NCT01414101).

Human target engagement was shown in rheumatoid arthritis, not AF. In NCT01414101/PMID:25885521, ISIS-CRPRx lowered hs-CRP dose-dependently (-76.7% at 400 mg vs -14.4% placebo, P=0.0015) and was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. This hepatic knockdown also implies adequate exposure at the liver. That trial was registered before the AF index trial began. No downstream pathway marker was reported, and ACR20 was unchanged in RA. The AF index trial NCT01710852 enrolled only 7 patients and posted no results, so it could not test whether CRP lowering reduces AF burden. Trial size and execution (F7) best explain the uninformative readout. If a true null occurred despite engagement, F2 would also apply. The bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT01353027 is a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose safety study in healthy volunteers. Its primary endpoint was adverse events, not efficacy, so it was not an efficacy test of AVI-7539. PMID:25155593 reports that AVI-6002 (AVI-7537 plus AVI-7539) was safe and well tolerated up to 4.5 mg/kg per component with no MTD, and showed dose-proportional plasma PK (half-life 2–5 h), which supports systemic exposure. Engagement of Ebola viral mRNA and any antiviral effect cannot be measured in uninfected humans, so the bundle has no human data for either. The bundle does not show why the program stopped. Because there was no efficacy readout, F9 applies; if this were read as a failure, the evidence would be indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01279590 was a Phase 2 safety and tolerability study of PPD10558 against atorvastatin in statin-intolerant patients. Its primary outcome was discontinuation due to statin-associated myalgia, and it is classified not_efficacy, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug's lipid-lowering. No results were posted, and the bundle has no Phase 1 data, PK, HMGCR engagement or LDL biomarker data, and no PubMed abstracts, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Other HMGCR inhibitors (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin and others) are approved, which validates the target. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, so why the program ended cannot be determined beyond this. U is a secondary code because engagement is unknown.

FX-322 combines CHIR99021, a GSK3 inhibitor, with valproic acid, an HDAC inhibitor. In the index trial (NCT04120116), FX-322 showed no benefit over placebo, and the placebo arm improved more (41% vs 19% on word recognition). For exposure, the drug's two components were measured in human perilymph after intratympanic dosing in cochlear implant subjects (Otol Neurotol 2021), so they reached the inner ear. No human data show GSK3 or HDAC inhibition, a progenitor or Wnt biomarker, or hair cell regeneration. The sponsor blamed an unexpected placebo response and study bias (F7) and later tried to narrow the population (F3). Its next single-dose trial (FX-322-112), redesigned with multiple baseline hearing tests, also showed no effect. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug never engaged its targets or the mechanism does not work, so the code is U.

The published report of NCT01727778 (Haematologica) shows plasma exposure that rose in proportion to dose (Cmax about 75 µg/mL at 6 mg/kg; half-life about 7 h). It also shows PAT-SM6 bound to circulating myeloma cells in patients after dosing, but in only 2 patients and without quantification, so engagement is called adequate only weakly. No pathway biomarker was reported, such as apoptosis or myeloma-cell depletion. The highest dose was not limited by tolerability (no maximum tolerated dose was reached). There were no responses: 4 of 12 patients had stable disease, which the authors called modest activity. So the program shows binding without benefit (F2). Caveat: the index trial was a 12-patient safety study whose primary endpoint was adverse events, not an efficacy test (F9/F7). Engagement data were published after the trial started.

The index trial NCT01727778 was a 12-patient Phase 1 study in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Its only primary outcome was adverse-event frequency over 14 days, so it was a safety study, not an efficacy test of PAT-SM6. It was completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results. The bundle has no other trials, no PubMed abstracts and no same-target comparators, and gives no human data on exposure, HSPA5 engagement or downstream pathway effects. Nothing shows an efficacy failure, so F9 is the closest fit. Because engagement is entirely unmeasured, why the program stopped is indeterminate (U secondary). Confidence is low given how thin the bundle is.

The index Phase I/II trial NCT01957059 (9 enrolled, 6MWT primary endpoint) was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results. The bundle contains no other trials, no Phase 1 results and no PubMed abstracts for BMN-053. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data, and there is no evidence of dystrophin restoration in patients. Other antisense oligonucleotides on the same DMD target are FDA-approved for Duchenne: golodirsen, viltolarsen, casimersen and eteplirsen. Because the target is validated in this disease and this molecule shows no engagement evidence, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). This rests only on the target-level comparison in the bundle, so U remains a plausible alternative. The bundle is very thin, so confidence is low.

drug: peripheral blood stem/progenitor cells, autologous, cd34+, g-csf mobilized
rationale: The index trial, NCT04990427, gave intra-renal-artery autologous CD34+ cells (CLBS201/LSTA201) to six patients with diabetic kidney disease. It was open-label with no control arm. The sponsor had set increased GFR in advance as the criterion for going on. The cells were safe, but kidney function did not improve consistently. This drug has no recorded molecular target. No source showed in humans that the cells reached or stayed in the kidney, engraftment, effects on the small blood vessels of the kidney, or any biomarker change. So the data cannot tell apart cells that never acted from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease (U). The company said more development would need much larger studies and money, and would continue only if it found a partner (F8). Six uncontrolled patients make this a weak test of efficacy (F7).

In the index trial (NCT00698828), neither 20 nor 40 μg/kg of the drug improved 6-minute walk distance over placebo; placebo gained 28.5 m. SUN11031 has the same structure as human ghrelin. Human studies, published before 2008 and run in healthy subjects rather than COPD patients, show ghrelin causes dose-dependent GH release, which is evidence that it activates GHSR. No SUN11031-specific PK, GH or IGF-1 data at the subcutaneous trial doses were found. The investigators' conference abstract (title only) reports better lean body mass in COPD cachexia, which suggests a proximal anabolic effect but no functional gain. I have read only the titles of the sponsor's paper and abstract, not their contents. Coded F2 (engagement present, no clinical benefit). F4 (endpoint) and F7 (high placebo response) are secondary. Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT02231671 is an open-label ADME and absolute bioavailability study of the prodrug ALS-008176. Its endpoints are bioavailability and mass balance, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Program-level evidence (PMID:37467213) shows dose-proportional plasma ALS-008112 exposure in infants. However, there was no reduction in viral load or symptoms versus placebo in hospitalized infants, despite antiviral activity reported earlier in an adult challenge study. The bundle has no direct human target-engagement measure. Dose-related reversible neutropenia was observed and may have contributed to stopping (secondary F6). The bundle does not show that this toxicity capped dosing below an effective level.

In the index trial, NCT00979953, ADL5859 lowered pain less than placebo did (-1.77 vs -2.20 NPRS). I found no human data on exposure, delta-opioid receptor occupancy or a downstream biomarker. Phase 1 posted no results, and published reviews say only that the drug passed phase 1. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that failed to engage apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Adolor blamed an unusually high placebo response, and the oxycodone CR arm (-2.24) did no better than placebo. That suggests the trial could not detect a working painkiller, so F7 is a secondary code. The program stopped after phase 2 failures in several indications, and Pfizer then ended its partnership with Adolor.

Topical phentolamine 1% did not lower IOP versus vehicle at day 15 (-2.30 vs -2.18 mmHg, p=0.89; NCT03960866). No direct exposure, occupancy or IOP-pathway biomarker was measured in glaucoma patients. The same ocular alpha-1 antagonism met clinical endpoints at comparable topical doses (0.75–1%): reversal of mydriasis (NCT04024891, NCT04620213) and presbyopia (NCT05646719, NCT04675151; later FDA approval). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate in the anterior segment. However, that evidence came from other diseases and postdated the index trial's start. Because engagement was plausible yet IOP did not change, alpha-1 blockade does not appear to drive IOP lowering as tested (F2). The trial was small (n=39), so F7 is secondary.

Exposure and C1q engagement were shown in humans in other diseases: effective serum C1q inhibition in GBS (PMID:40000167, NCT04035135) and full serum/CSF saturation in Huntington's (PMID:41787606). No dose-limiting toxicity was reported. In the small single-arm wAIHA trial (NCT04691570, n=6–7), hemolysis markers did not improve by Day 71: LDH +7.8, haptoglobin +1.0, bilirubin rose, and the hemoglobin gain was modest at 1.3 g/dL. This suggests classical complement blockade does not meaningfully drive warm AIHA hemolysis. Caveats: no C1q engagement or complement pathway data in wAIHA patients, and the trial was a tiny descriptive study, not a powered efficacy test (F7/F9). Confidence is therefore low.

The index trial NCT00639249 registered only safety and tolerability as its primary outcome, and that was met: both 1 and 3 mg/d were safe and well tolerated (PMID:25270629). It was therefore not a formal efficacy test, which fits F9. The exploratory NIHSS change was not significant. A post hoc benefit in moderate-to-severe patients at 3 mg/d led the authors to call for studies in that population, so F3 is secondary. Tracer-dose [11C]SA4503 PET shows the molecule enters the human brain (PMID:17240168). However, no receptor occupancy, exposure or pathway data exist at the therapeutic doses, and none in stroke patients. Engagement is therefore no_human_data, and U is secondary.

In the index Phase 1 trial (NCT01338831), LFA102 at 3–60 mg/kg every 4 weeks in PRLR-positive MBC/mCRPC showed no antitumor activity. Tolerability did not cap the dose: the MTD was not reached and grade 3/4 related AEs occurred in 4% of patients. A rise in serum prolactin gave PD evidence of PRLR blockade in patients. However, the authors conclude that dosing intervals that were too long and insufficient LFA102 exposure may explain the lack of efficacy (PMID:27091421). The commentary PMID:27107001 likewise calls the trial negative but informative on PK/PD. Exposure, and therefore sustained engagement at the tumor, was inadequate, so the mechanism was not properly tested. Downstream tumor pathway effects were not shown in the bundle.

The index trial NCT01140061 was a topical patch safety/PK study with no efficacy endpoint. It showed low plasma Cmax (about 5–12 nM) and was well tolerated, with no dose limitation. No skin drug levels, PDE4 inhibition or cAMP/cytokine biomarker data appear in the bundle, so engagement at the site of action is unknown. The follow-on efficacy study NCT01235728 showed minimal separation from vehicle (TLS -47.4% vs -42.7%). Oral MK-0873 failed in COPD (NCT00132730), so engagement cannot be inferred from another indication. Topical roflumilast, which acts on the same PDE4 target, is FDA-approved for psoriasis. This points to the molecule or formulation rather than the target, and no pillar evidence shows this drug engaged adequately in skin. F9 applies because the index trial itself was not an efficacy test.

The index trial, NCT01462851, was a first-in-human pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic study in healthy volunteers, not a test of clinical efficacy. Its results were reported in AAIC 2013 abstract P1-351 (Bell et al.). The drug was well tolerated at single doses of 25-325 mg. It lowered plasma Aβ40 and Aβ42 in an exposure-related way, with the effect peaking at 250 mg, so it did engage BACE1 outside the brain. But this plasma effect did not carry over into the CSF, so amyloid production in the brain was not reduced. That points to poor central exposure or engagement, and tolerability did not limit the dose. The central mechanism was therefore never properly tested, and this most likely explains why the program stopped at Phase 1. No sponsor statement on discontinuation was found.

The trial's statistical analysis plan for NCT02265510 says the study was stopped early for lack of efficacy. The full Phase 1/2 publication measured drug levels and target effect in patients with advanced blood cancers. It reports that JAK1 inhibition was confirmed at every dose level, shown by blocking IL-6–stimulated pSTAT3, and that the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. So tolerability did not cap the dose. Exposure and engagement are adequate, and engagement was shown in the program's own patients. That evidence was published only in 2022, after the index trial began. No downstream biomarker was reported. Clinical activity was minimal: 0/6 AML responders in Phase 2. The authors conclude that JAK1 inhibition is unlikely to help these patients, which fits F2. Small, uncontrolled cohorts add an F7 element.

MGCD290 is meant to inhibit the fungal enzyme Hos2 and was given as one 540 mg dose with 150 mg fluconazole. In NCT01497223, therapeutic cure at day 28 was no better than with fluconazole alone (p=0.879), and no secondary endpoint differed. The only support for the mechanism comes from lab and mouse studies. No source reports human drug levels in vaginal tissue, Hos2 inhibition in Candida, or any biomarker change, so exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human data. The sponsor only said it was disappointed and gave no reason for the failure. Its rationale was reversing azole resistance, but most VVC responds to fluconazole alone, which leaves little room for an add-on to show benefit. That points to a possible population problem (F3), but no source says so.

AV2-DM is a topical antiviral spray with no recorded molecular target. Neither the bundle nor the search turned up any human evidence of exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker. No results were posted for the index Phase 2 trial (NCT01654822). A later Phase 3 trial in HPV-associated cervical lesions found no significant difference from placebo: 89.4% vs 91.6% lesion regression on visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and 51.9% vs 34.4% HPV clearance. The investigators blamed low statistical power, because enrollment fell short of the planned sample size and many patients were lost to follow-up. That points to a trial-design problem (F7) as a secondary factor. Because there is no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that doesn't work, so the primary code is U.

The IDMC stopped the index trial NCT02699385 for lack of efficacy after only 10 enrolled. Domperidone acts on a peripheral D2 target (gut, chemoreceptor trigger zone). Human plasma exposure at 10 mg is documented (PMID:35396924). D2 engagement shows as regular hyperprolactinemia in humans (PMID:7413230, PMID:1465520), and a pathway effect as increased antroduodenal motility (PMID:6941408). All of this was published long before the index trial, but in healthy subjects or other patients, not gastroenteritis. Despite engagement, efficacy in pediatric AGE vomiting is weak: domperidone was inferior to ondansetron at 24 h (PMID:31700742, PMID:35991241), and a review says ondansetron alone has evidence-based efficacy (PMID:18829050). This supports F2. The tiny enrollment adds a design caveat (F7).

The first-in-human trial NCT01447732 (PMID:27457707) reported only plasma PK. Exposure rose in proportion to dose, and the half-life was short, 34–70 hours. Infusion reactions and transaminase rises capped the dose at an MTD of 0.3 mg/kg. The trial measured no tumour drug levels, no binding to the sialylated glycoconjugate target and no ADCC/pharmacodynamic biomarker. Nothing shows whether 0.3 mg/kg was enough for engagement, so dose_limited cannot be called true. There were no responses, and the study was stopped for lack of efficacy. The authors also cited cardiac, hepatic and infusion-related toxicity as making the benefit-risk unfavourable, so F6 is secondary. With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

The index trial NCT01954615 was a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose safety, PK and PD study in healthy males, not an efficacy test. That alone fits F9. Its published results (PMID:25331625) show the oral di-ester prodrug ACT-281959 (formulation F1) gave poor exposure to the active moiety ACT-246475. Cmax was less than dose-proportional, at only 13.8 pmol/mL at 1,000 mg. Peak platelet inhibition was only 31%, so P2Y12 engagement and its functional readout stayed partial. Tolerability did not cap the dose: all doses up to 1,000 mg were well tolerated. Exploratory formulations (F2, and ACT-246475 itself) raised bioavailability and antiplatelet effect. This suggests the prodrug formulation, not the target, was the limitation. No patient data exist, and the engagement data were published after the trial started.

AMR-001 is an autologous CD34+ cell product with no defined molecular target. None of the sources measures whether the cells were retained or engrafted in the myocardium, or any marker of target engagement such as an angiogenic biomarker. The only earlier human signal is a Phase 1 result: infarct-region perfusion improved at doses of at least 10 million cells. That is a clinical efficacy endpoint, not evidence for any of the three pillars. In PreSERVE-AMI (NCT01495364, PMID:27821724), perfusion did not differ from control, and both groups improved from baseline. The authors pointed to dose-dependent benefit after adjusting for ischemia time and focused on safety and bioactivity, which suggests a possible design or power problem. Since no source shows whether the cells engaged, a non-engaging product can't be told apart from an inert mechanism, so the code is U.

Engagement was shown in humans. The first-in-human study (PMID:25109413, NCT01035645) found dose-proportional PK, sustained drug-bound IL-18, and prolonged ex vivo inhibition of IL-18-induced IFN-γ production. The 3 mg/kg dose was chosen by PBPK modeling to give rapid, high engagement. In the index DGF trial (NCT02723786, PMID:33684160), IL18–drug complexes were detected and total IL-18 rose, confirming engagement in patients. Downstream IFN-γ-induced chemokines declined or stayed unchanged in most patients, a partial pathway signal. Despite this, 4/7 patients had DGF, above the 50% standard-of-care rate, and the trial stopped for lack of efficacy. This points to IL-18 not driving DGF as tested (F2). The tiny single-arm, early-stopped design adds some uncertainty (F7). No dose limitation was reported.

Phase 1 (PMID:25109413, 2014, before index start) showed dose-proportional plasma PK, sustained drug-bound IL-18, and prolonged ex vivo inhibition of IL-18-induced IFN-γ. In the index DGF trial (PMID:33684160), 3 mg/kg was chosen by PBPK modeling to give rapid, high target engagement. IL18–drug complexes and higher total IL-18 confirmed binding in transplant patients. IFN-γ-induced chemokines declined or stayed flat in most patients, so the pathway evidence in this disease is only partial. Despite this, 4/7 patients had DGF, above the 50% standard-of-care rate. Neutralizing IL-18 did not prevent DGF, which points to the mechanism (F2). The study was single-arm, n=7 and stopped early, so it is also a weak test (F7). Separately, IL-18 blockade failed in T2DM (PMID:26930607) and atopic dermatitis (NCT05999799).

Index trial NCT02723786 gave 3 mg/kg IV, a dose chosen by PBPK modelling to give rapid, high IL18 engagement. In transplant patients (PMID:33684160), IL18–drug complexes were detected and total IL18 rose from half-life prolongation, showing engagement. IFN-γ-induced chemokines declined or stayed flat in most patients, so the pathway signal in this disease is only partial. Earlier healthy-volunteer data (PMID:25109413, 2014) showed sustained drug-bound IL18 and ex vivo inhibition of IL18-induced IFN-γ across 0.008–10 mg/kg. Despite this, 4/7 patients (57%) had DGF, above the 50% background rate, and tolerability did not cap the dose. So IL18 neutralization did not prevent DGF. The single-arm trial was very small and ended early, so trial design is secondary.

No human evidence was found for exposure, receptor occupancy or NK2 pathway effects (for example, blocking NKA-induced motility) for ibodutant. The bundle and searches contain only in vitro or animal pharmacology (PMID:19218528, PMID:26758701). Phase 2 NCT00761007 failed overall. NCT01303224 showed benefit only in a prespecified female subgroup at 10 mg (PMID:27196574). Phase 3 trials enrolling only women then failed: in NCT02107196, 35.7% vs 34.7% responded, and index trial NCT02120027 had OR 0.986 and was terminated for futility. Tolerability did not cap the dose, since 10 mg was well tolerated, but no higher dose was tested in women. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from an NK2 target that does not drive IBS-D, so the code is U. The phase 2 benefit seen only in women, which phase 3 did not reproduce, points to F3 as a secondary code.

In the 12-week Phase 2 trial (NCT00668070, PMID:24530600), ASP9831 at 50 or 100 mg twice daily did not change ALT, AST or NASH biomarkers. A Hepatology review notes that circulating TNF-α, adiponectin and keratin-18 were also unchanged, so the downstream pathway pillar counts as inadequate. The Phase 1 work only set a 'therapeutic window' and tested the two doses in patients. I found no published human data on drug levels in plasma or liver, on PDE4 inhibition (for example, ex vivo LPS-stimulated TNF-α suppression in whole blood) or on cAMP. Without that, nothing separates a drug that never engaged PDE4 from a target that does not drive NASH. Tolerability did not cap the dose (adverse events were mostly mild GI effects). Other PDE4 drugs have not succeeded in NASH, so F1b does not apply.

NCT02181699 was a first-in-human dose-escalation study of KHK2823, an afucosylated anti-CD123 IgG1 meant to deplete CD123+ cells. It was terminated for 'Failed treatment response' and posted no results. The sources found contain no human PK, no data on CD123 occupancy on blasts, and no in-vivo depletion data. The ASH 2015 and EHA 2016 abstracts show only that KHK2823 bound to patient AML/MDS cells in the lab (ex vivo) and in other preclinical work, which does not count as human evidence. No other drug on this target has succeeded in AML: talacotuzumab, flotetuzumab and the CAR-T products did not get there, and the approvals are in BPDCN. So F1b does not apply. With no engagement data, the sources cannot tell apart a molecule that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in AML, so the code is U.

KHK2823 is a non-fucosylated anti-CD123 antibody meant to deplete cells by ADCC. Its first-in-human Phase 1 trial in AML and MDS, NCT02181699, was terminated for 'failed treatment response', and no results were posted. The only pharmacodynamic data found are preclinical: binding to AML and MDS cells taken from patients, measured in the lab, and depletion of CD123-positive cells in monkeys. I found no human data on drug exposure, CD123-positive cell depletion or other biomarkers. A 2021 review notes only the termination. In MDS, no other drug on this target is shown here as approved or as having met a pivotal endpoint (tagraxofusp and talacotuzumab reached Phase 2). That makes F1b weak. With no human evidence of engagement, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

KHK2823 is a non-fucosylated anti-CD123 antibody meant to deplete CD123-positive cells. Its first-in-human trial in AML/MDS, NCT02181699 (n=39), stopped for 'Failed treatment response'. The trial planned to measure PK and CD123+ cell pharmacodynamics, but no results were posted. My searches found only preclinical data: the ASH 2015 abstract on binding and monkey results, and trial listings showing the program was discontinued. I found no human data on drug levels, CD123 binding or CD123+ cell depletion, and no sponsor explanation beyond the stop reason. The bundle lists no other CD123 drug that succeeded in AML/MDS. With no evidence of engagement, I can't tell whether the drug failed to engage CD123 or whether depleting CD123 cells doesn't help, so the code is U.

The index Phase 3 trial NCT00709865 had only a safety and tolerability primary outcome, classified not_efficacy, and posted no results. It was not an efficacy test of tonapofylline, so F9 applies. The companion Phase 2 trial NCT00745316 was terminated for 'Company Decision', which suggests a business stop (F8 secondary). Human plasma exposure was well characterized and dose-proportional (PMID:20926751, PMID:21888869). No direct A1 receptor occupancy was measured. However, the expected downstream effect, natriuresis without kaliuresis and with renal function preserved, was shown in heart failure patients (PMID:17692744) and in severe renal impairment (PMID:21888869). Tolerability did not limit the dose.

The index Phase 3 trial NCT00709865 had a safety and tolerability primary outcome, not efficacy, and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). Exposure was adequate: PK was linear and predictable in HF patients and healthy subjects (PMID:20926754, PMID:20926751). No receptor occupancy was measured, so engagement has no direct human data. The pathway effect, natriuresis without loss of renal function, was shown in HF patients at IV doses up to 1 mg/kg and oral doses of 3–225 mg (PMID:20926754, PMID:17692744, PMID:21888869). A seizure at 3 mg/kg capped the IV dose, but natriuresis occurred at lower doses. The parallel oral Phase 2 trial NCT00745316 was terminated by company decision, which suggests a business-driven stop (F8).

None of the sources report human ROCK occupancy, kinase inhibition or ocular drug levels for SNJ-1656/RKI983. The only human effects are modest IOP drops: about 2–3 mmHg in healthy volunteers (PMID:18332309), and about 3–3.5 mmHg at peak and 2 mmHg at trough versus placebo in POAG/OHT (PMID:25783615, PMC6188806). Conjunctival hyperemia was frequent, which fits ROCK-driven vasodilation, so it may be an on-target effect. Results of the index trial against latanoprost (NCT00846989) were never posted, and no stop reason is given. Other ROCK inhibitors (ripasudil, netarsudil) went through Phase 3 trials in the same disease (PMC12030167). That points to the molecule rather than the target, but none of the cited pages states that they were approved. Without engagement data, U is still possible, so confidence is low.

The index trial, NCT01200784, was Medice's DONATO dose-finding study. No results were posted, and a review says they were never published, so the bundle has no evidence that it failed. The same sponsor then took modified-release nicotinamide into the Phase 3 NOPHOS trial, which suggests the Phase 2 readout was not a negative efficacy result. No human data measured exposure or binding to the proposed intestinal NaPi2b transporter. The downstream effect, lower serum phosphate, was shown in hemodialysis patients before the index trial (PMID:18385391), and again in NOPHOS through 24 weeks. In NOPHOS the effect was gone by week 52, adherence was poor, and new safety signals appeared: thrombocytopenia, pruritus, anaemia, diarrhoea and herpes zoster (gfac206). Those, not a failed Phase 2, are the likely reasons the program stalled.

The index trial NCT01214603 had a descriptive safety primary endpoint, but its publication (PMID:26735141) reports AML-patient data. PK matched Phase 1. β-catenin levels indicated an on-target GSK3 effect, yet no complete or partial remissions occurred, and the authors conclude single-agent LY2090314 has limited clinical benefit. This points to engagement without benefit (F2). The engagement evidence in AML comes from the index trial itself, so it was not available before the index started. F9 also applies because the trial was not formally an efficacy test. F1a is possible: the MTD was capped at 40 mg by DLTs, and the β-catenin rise at 40 mg was only transient (PMID:26403509), so the depth of engagement may have been limited.

C3BS-CQR-1 is an autologous cardiopoietic cell therapy with no defined molecular target. None of the sources give human data on cell retention or engraftment, target engagement, or a pathway biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In CHART-1 (NCT01768702) the hierarchical composite primary endpoint was neutral (Mann-Whitney estimator 0.54). Post-hoc analyses found benefit on the primary composite in patients with baseline LVEDV of 200-370 mL, and reverse remodelling (PMID:28560782). The investigators linked these results to patient selection by heart failure severity and called for further study in that subgroup. That fits F3 (benefit confined to a subgroup). U is listed as secondary because engagement was never measured.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT01082562 (BMS-844421, a PCSK9 antisense oligonucleotide, in hypercholesterolemia) was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results. Its primary outcome included PCSK9 concentrations, but none were reported. The bundle contains no other trials, no Phase 1 results, no PubMed abstracts and no comparator PCSK9 drugs. With no human evidence on exposure, PCSK9 knockdown or LDL lowering, nothing distinguishes a molecule that failed to engage from a target that does not matter. The bundle also does not show whether the program stopped for toxicity or business reasons. Engagement is no_human_data, so the code is indeterminate (U).

The index trial (NCT01918865) narrowly missed its week-27 HbA1c endpoint (-0.44%, P=0.074). Hepatic PTP1B knockdown and drug exposure were not measured in humans in the bundle. Downstream effects did move in T2D patients at 200 mg weekly: leptin fell, adiponectin rose and weight dropped 2.6 kg (PMID:29439147). The glycemic effect appeared late: HbA1c was significantly reduced at week 36 (-0.69%, P=0.034), along with fructosamine and glycated albumin. The authors frame this as a prolonged, delayed effect.
