That points to endpoint timing rather than an inert mechanism. The small 2:1 trial (n=92) may also have been underpowered (F7). Engagement data are absent, so confidence is low. No tolerability limit was reported.

The index trial NCT01150812 was a single ascending dose safety study of the thrombin (F2) inhibitor AZD8165 in healthy men, with safety variables as its primary outcome. It was not an efficacy test. It was terminated because 'pharmacodynamic stopping criteria were met after the first dosing group.' This most plausibly means thrombin inhibition reached or exceeded the predefined threshold at the first dose, so engagement was shown in humans, though no numbers were posted. That suggests an on-target PD or tolerability ceiling (secondary F5) rather than failed engagement. There is no posted PK, no data in patients, no other trials and no literature, so the bundle is very thin.

Exposure was shown before the index trial: dose-proportional plasma levels in healthy volunteers (PMID:16397282, PMID:16411387). Engagement was also shown: anti-FXa activity tracked concentration in volunteers, stable CAD patients and PCI patients, reaching 65–691 ng/mL (PMID:17178269, PMID:17502577). Pathway effects followed: clotting times prolonged, ETP fell, and prothrombin F1+2 fell more than with UFH (PMID:16411387, PMID:17502577). Engagement was not shown in ACS patients specifically, so engagement_in_disease is false. In TAO, the dose chosen at interim (0.080 mg/kg bolus then 0.140 mg/kg/h) gave no reduction in death/MI versus UFH+eptifibatide (RR 0.99). Results were consistent across subgroups, and bleeding doubled (PMID:23995608). The target was engaged but FXa inhibition added no benefit over the active comparator. On-target bleeding (F5) is secondary.

In the index trial (NCT02236195, PMID:30570744), mocetinostat exposure was lower than anticipated. Toxicities caused treatment interruptions in 82% and dose reductions in 29%, with a median of only 46 days on treatment. The authors state that this reduced exposure may have contributed to the modest activity (1 PR among 9 evaluable patients). Phase 1 data in solid-tumour patients (PMID:18421048, PMID:18519775) showed dose-dependent HDAC inhibition in peripheral WBCs, with some histone acetylation. However, this was surrogate tissue, not urothelial carcinoma, and was not measured at the reduced exposures seen in the index trial. Because tolerability capped exposure, the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). The small evaluable sample (9 of 15 planned) adds a trial-execution limitation (F7).

Iferanserin is an intra-anal ointment that blocks the HTR2A receptor. I found no human data on whether it reached the anal tissue, bound HTR2A there, or moved any downstream biomarker. The Phase IIb trial (PMID:22244049) reported less bleeding and itching, but those are clinical outcomes, not target-engagement data. In the Phase 3 trial (NCT01355874), neither the 7-day nor the 14-day arm beat placebo on the primary endpoint or the secondary endpoints. Side effects matched placebo, so tolerability did not limit the dose. Ventrus called the result a surprise and gave no mechanistic explanation. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter in hemorrhoids, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT00804687, PMID:23791513) missed its objective primary endpoint, nasal patency measured by acoustic rhinometry (p=0.06), while the pseudoephedrine control did separate from placebo. JNJ-39220675 did significantly improve subjective nasal symptom scores (TNSS). The only receptor-occupancy evidence is a baboon PET study showing about 90% brain H3 blockade (PMID:22614669, PMC3456925). Animal data do not count, and no human PK, occupancy or nasal H3 engagement data were found. Insomnia (17.3%) hints that the drug acted centrally, but it is not a measured engagement marker. No other H3 antagonist has succeeded in allergic rhinitis, so F1b does not apply. With human engagement unknown, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter. The split between the objective and subjective endpoints is a possible secondary explanation (F4).

The index trial NCT01165736 was a microdose pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers at a dose stated to have no pharmacological activity. It was not an efficacy test, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). Per PMID:26895021, human microdose PK fed into a PBPK model, which predicted lower multiples of Nav1.7 IC50 for PF-05186462 than for PF-05089771 at the same oral doses. PF-05089771 was therefore selected and PF-05186462 was dropped. That predicted shortfall in exposure, based on human PK, supports a secondary F1a. However, it rests on modelling, not on measured exposure at therapeutic doses. No human target engagement or pathway data exist for this compound.

In relapsed/refractory myeloma, the phase 1 trial NCT00552396 (registered 2007, before the 2009 index start) reported PK matching predictions. It showed full KIR2D occupancy across the dosing cycle, with no DLT and no MTD reached (PMID:23033266). IPH2101 also enhanced ex vivo NK cytotoxicity against MM, though no responses were seen. In AML, occupancy above 90% was sustained at 1–3 mg/kg, with rises in TNF-α, MIP-1β and NK CD69 (PMID:23002117). Full occupancy was confirmed again with lenalidomide (PMID:25999435). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, single-agent responses were 1/27 in the index trial and 0/30 in smoldering MM (NCT01222286). The engaged mechanism did not produce benefit, so F2.

The index trial, NCT00731445, was Zeria's Phase I/II dose-escalation study of oral Z-208 in advanced HCC. It was completed, but no results were posted and the bundle records no primary target. My searches found no publications, conference abstracts or sponsor statements on Z-208's exposure, target engagement, biomarkers or why the program stopped. No other trials or other drugs on the same target are in the bundle. Engagement is therefore no_human_data. Nothing here separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter in HCC, so the code is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01165736 was a healthy-volunteer microdose PK study of four Nav1.7 inhibitors. It used a dose chosen to have no pharmacological activity, so it was not an efficacy test of PF-05241328 (F9). PMID:26895021 reports that PBPK modelling from the human microdose PK predicted lower multiples of Nav1.7 IC50 for PF-05241328 than for PF-05089771 at the same oral doses. PF-05089771 was therefore selected to go forward. This is a modelled human-PK judgment that exposure would be relatively insufficient, which supports secondary F1a. The bundle has no human target engagement or pathway data.

In the first-in-human proof-of-concept trial (NCT01316237), oral GS-6620 gave poor plasma exposure, lower than in dogs. The sources attribute this to the 3'-isobutyryl ester being metabolised extensively in the intestine, which also caused large PK/PD variability (PMID:24419340). Antiviral activity was only a 'potential' and needed high doses, with high intra- and inter-patient variability (PMID:24419349, PMID:23547794). The sources blame absorption, not tolerability, so the dose was not capped by toxicity. Direct NS5B engagement was never measured, and the inconsistent HCV RNA responses do not establish adequate engagement. The failure is a molecule-level pharmacokinetic problem, so the polymerase mechanism was not properly tested. Code F1a.

The index trial NCT01582347 was a 7-day Phase 2 transfer of patients from Subutex/Suboxone to RBP-6300 (buprenorphine hemiadipate). It posted no results and gives no stop reason. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, other trials or PubMed abstracts, so exposure, OPRM1 engagement and pathway effects are all undocumented in humans. Buprenorphine itself, which acts on the same target (OPRM1 partial agonist), is FDA-approved for opiate dependence, as are methadone and naltrexone. With no pillar evidence for this formulation, the target is validated and the problem points to this molecule or formulation (F1b). U applies equally because engagement data are absent. The transfer design may also not have been an efficacy test of the drug (F9). The bundle is thin.

ZYGK1 is a glucokinase activator from Zydus, according to its annual reports. The index trial was a single ascending dose study in healthy volunteers (NCT01472809). It was suspended with the stated reason "Not achieved the objective till 4 mg single dose". The sponsor did not say what that objective was. It could have been a target exposure level or a glucose-lowering effect. No pharmacokinetic, glucokinase engagement or glucose biomarker data were posted or published. The trial was suspended for safety reasons, so tolerability does not seem to have capped the dose. The stop reason hints that exposure or effect fell short at the doses tested, which would point to F1a. But with no human pillar data, engagement is no_human_data, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01359852 was a microdose PET-ligand study of [11C]JNJ-42491293 in healthy volunteers. Its endpoints were biodistribution, dosimetry, brain uptake and safety, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). PMID:36928556 reports that human, macaque and rat PET imaging showed the tracer entered the brain but appeared to bind an unidentified non-mGlu2 site. Marmoset blocking with AZD8529 showed no competition, in line with the earlier human findings. Selective mGlu2 engagement was therefore not supported, which explains why the tracer was abandoned (secondary F1a-like). No pathway data in humans or in any patient population were shown.

The index trial NCT00886782 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study in advanced solid tumors. It enrolled 11 patients at 25, 50 and 100 mg, and its primary endpoints were all safety measures (DLTs, AEs, deaths, lab abnormalities). It had no comparator and no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of BMS-863233. It was terminated with no stated reason. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, CDC7 engagement or pathway data, and no other trials, publications or same-target drugs to compare against. One DLT and more SAEs occurred at 100 mg, but the bundle does not show that tolerability capped the dose. Because engagement is unmeasured, the failure would also be indeterminate (U) if treated as an efficacy readout.

The index trial NCT01137006 was a Phase 1 3+3 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoints were MTD and safety, not efficacy. It met its objectives. No DLTs were seen, so the dose was not tolerability-capped, and a provisional MTD of 20 mg/kg q2w was set on serum concentration and safety data. That suggests adequate systemic exposure, although sufficiency is not stated explicitly. One complete response and a 41% disease control rate were reported, and the authors called for further study (PMID:27797971). No TYRP1 engagement or downstream biomarker data are in the bundle, and no reason for stopping is given. This was not an efficacy failure (F9). If it is viewed as a failure, it is indeterminate (U).

The index trial, NCT01028404, was a Phase 1 trial whose primary outcomes were adverse events and safety. It did not test efficacy, and no results were posted. Reviews say Novo Nordisk stopped NN1952, an oral prandial insulin made with Merrion's GIPET absorption technology, because its interactions with food intake were unacceptable. A secondary review table reports higher serum insulin exposure than subcutaneous insulin, but a bio-efficacy of only about 0.7% and no dose response. That points to oral absorption that was unreliable and food-dependent. It does not show a failure of insulin-receptor agonism. The sources reviewed give no direct measure of receptor engagement or glucose-lowering pharmacodynamics. So the primary code is F9 (not an efficacy test), with F1a as secondary for the formulation's exposure problem.

NOVOCART 3D plus is an autologous chondrocyte implant on a scaffold. It has no molecular target, so no source reports exposure, occupancy or pathway biomarkers for it. The sponsor's lay summary of the 5-year results of NCT01656902 says knee function improved in both arms, with no relevant difference between the implant and the active microfracture comparator. The only signal was a higher share of patients improving in sports activity. The sponsor gives no reason for stopping the program. The positive results in PMID:38501741 come from a non-randomized matched-pair analysis, and the MRI study PMID:40778441 does not separate the arms. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the implant fell short or whether microfracture was simply as good, so the failure is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT01637142 was a healthy-volunteer absolute bioavailability and microtracer PK study (PMID:25382826), not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Plasma exposure was shown: oral bioavailability 0.68 with complete conversion to LY404039. Central pharmacological activity was shown as rises in CSF monoamine metabolites at 40 mg BID (PMID:21847569), so pathway and CNS exposure count as adequate. Engagement evidence is weak. The ketamine pharmacoBOLD signal was reduced only at 160 mg (PMID:29564482), and 320 mg/d failed to suppress it, with the authors suggesting a higher dose may be needed (PMID:32403118). That points to possibly inadequate engagement, consistent with F1a as a secondary code. Tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:22544017).

NCT01221831 (FIESTA) was an open-label Phase 2 dose-finding study in 396 women. It was not a placebo-controlled efficacy test. It compared estetrol (E4) combined with drospirenone (DRSP) or levonorgestrel (LNG); P2 is most likely LNG. The published results (PMID 27153745) concluded that 15 mg E4/DRSP gave the most favourable bleeding pattern and cycle control. The LNG arms had more absent withdrawal bleeding (14.0–18.5% vs 3.5–3.8% by cycle 6). The P2 arm was dropped because the combination with the better cycle-control profile was selected, not because the drug failed an efficacy endpoint. I found no human data on the progestin's exposure, receptor engagement or pathway effects; a related ovulation-inhibition study is cited but I did not review its results. Hence F9, with U as a secondary code.

In healthy women of reproductive age, PGL2001 (E2MATE) at 4 mg/week reduced endometrial STS activity by 91%, and by 96% with NETA. The effect persisted a month after stopping, and functional STS biomarkers in the endometrium changed (PMID:24604234). This shows tissue exposure, target engagement and a pathway effect in humans. That evidence comes from healthy volunteers, not endometriosis patients, and was published in 2014, after the index trial started in 2012. The index proof-of-concept trial (NCT01631981) completed with no posted results and no stated reason for stopping. With engagement adequate and no evidence of dose limitation or toxicity, the most likely reading is that local STS inhibition does not relieve endometriosis pain (F2). Confidence is low because the readout and the index dose are not shown.

The index trial NCT01578070 was a Phase I/IIa study in healthy volunteers. Its registered primary outcome was descriptive safety (AEs, SAEs, SUSARs), so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. The publication (PMID:25218298) reports no safety or tolerability concerns, meaning the primary objective was met. Secondary immunogenicity results were mixed. There was no adjuvant effect on anti-HIB antibodies, which the authors set against large baseline titre variation. IFN-γ ELISpot responses did increase. No molecular target is recorded, so the exposure, engagement and pathway pillars cannot be assessed. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping. Because the index readout was not an efficacy failure, F9 is the best fit, with U and F7 as secondary codes.

In the first-in-human study (NCT01324830), MTDs were 120 mg (Schedule A) and 150 mg (Schedule B). Dose-limiting toxicities were haematologic and gastrointestinal. PK showed high inter-subject variability, and markers of MEK or Aurora kinase inhibition showed no clear relationship with exposure. The authors state that development was halted because drug exposure at the MTD was insufficient to achieve relevant MEK inhibition (PMID:26650227). Tolerability therefore capped the dose below the level needed for adequate engagement in solid-tumour patients, so the mechanism was never properly tested. Exposure, engagement and pathway were all inadequate, and dose_limited is true. Engagement was measured in patients, but only within the index trial itself, not beforehand.

The index trial was the first-in-human dose escalation (NCT02262455), and its results were published by Tao et al. in Clin Cancer Res 2019. They report pharmacokinetics across 8 dose cohorts, up to 8 mg/kg every 2 weeks. STM 434 had the expected effect of activin A blockade in patients, including those with granulosa cell tumors: FSH fell in most patients, and lean body mass and 6-minute walk distance increased. Activin A binding itself was not measured directly, so engagement is rated adequate on this functional evidence. There were no objective responses. The common bleeding events (epistaxis 34%, gingival bleeding 22%) were attributed to off-target BMP9 inhibition. The authors stopped development because of the safety profile and the lack of clear efficacy. So off-target toxicity (F6) is primary, and target engaged without antitumor benefit (F2) is secondary.

SCM-CGH is a clonal mesenchymal stem cell therapy from SCM Lifescience. It has no defined molecular target. The index Phase 2 trial (NCT04189432) has unknown status and no posted results, and the bundle contains no PubMed abstracts and no Phase 1 data. My search found no human evidence on cell persistence or homing, immunomodulatory engagement, or a downstream biomarker. It also found no sponsor statement explaining why the program stopped. Engagement is no_human_data, and nothing separates a product that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter in steroid-refractory cGVHD, so U applies.

In the first-in-human Phase I/II trial in post-chemotherapy mCRPC (NCT01352208/PMID:24771350, n=13), plasma exposure was shown: absorption was rapid, the half-life was 16–35 h and exposure rose with dose. There was no dose-limiting toxicity. Tumour drug levels and AKR1C3 enzyme inhibition were never measured. Serum endocrine biomarkers, which include AKR1C3's androgen substrates and products, did not change. Circulating tumour cell counts and PSA/radiological responses did not change either. So there is no human evidence that the enzyme was blocked, and the program stopped because there was no activity. This points to F1a (mechanism not properly tested), but confidence is low. Serum androgens in castrated men are a weak readout of enzyme activity inside the tumour, so an untested target (U) cannot be ruled out. A later review suggested the drug may only work in combination, because tumours have other routes to DHT (PMC4520654), which hints at F2.

ASP9521 is an AKR1C3 inhibitor tested in the first-in-human Phase I/II trial NCT01352208 (PMID:24771350) in men with mCRPC after chemotherapy. Plasma levels rose in proportion to dose and the drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects. No study measured AKR1C3 inhibition directly in humans or drug levels inside tumours. The bundle reports that 'endocrine biomarker levels' did not change, which counts as a failed downstream pathway effect. That result cannot show whether the drug never inhibited intratumoural AKR1C3 or whether AKR1C3 does not drive this disease. Mouse xenograft data showed testosterone suppression inside tumours, but animal data do not count. The trial ended for lack of clinical activity, so the code is U, with possible F1a.

The index trial (NCT01204099, PX-866 plus docetaxel in NSCLC/SCCHN) posted no results, and no reason for stopping is stated. In the first-in-human study (PMID:22693357) in advanced solid tumors, PK was dose-proportional and platelet pAKT-Ser473 inhibition was seen at the continuous-schedule MTD. Diarrhea capped the dose, but there is no evidence that engagement at the MTD was insufficient. That pAKT evidence is a surrogate in mixed solid tumors, not this disease, and was published after the index trial began. Elsewhere, single-agent activity was modest (PMID:31056399). With the pathway apparently engaged but little clinical benefit, F2 is the best fit. Confidence is low: the bundle is thin, there is no tumor-tissue or index-disease engagement data, and the magnitude of inhibition was not quantified.

In the PhagoBurn trial (NCT02116010; Jault et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2019), the PP1131 phage cocktail lost potency after GMP manufacturing. Patients received about 1×10^2 PFU/mL per day instead of the planned 1×10^6, so the dose was roughly 10,000-fold too low. Bacterial burden fell more slowly than with silver sulfadiazine (HR 0.29), and the trial was stopped in January 2017 for insufficient efficacy. An ancillary study found that bacteria from patients whose treatment failed resisted low phage doses. That points to too little drug reaching and acting on the target bacteria, a manufacturing failure rather than a tolerability cap. The investigators called for higher phage concentrations and phagograms, which suggests patient selection by strain susceptibility also mattered. The mechanism was therefore not properly tested.

The index trial NCT03191903 tested Cingal (hyaluronic acid plus triamcinolone hexacetonide) for superiority over triamcinolone hexacetonide (TH). TH was the active comparator, so the trial was not an efficacy test of TH. TH reduced WOMAC pain by about 45 points, similar to Cingal. NCT03390036 showed the same pattern. Intra-articular TH gave sustained synovial exposure, and endogenous hydrocortisone suppression tracked steroid levels (PMID:3948470), which supports exposure and a pathway effect. Engagement is inferred_adequate because TH relieved knee OA pain through week 24 (PMID:29081706). The missed comparison reflects a combination product failing to beat its own steroid component, not a failure of TH. This fits F9.

The Phase IIb field study (TH005, NCT02150343) missed its primary endpoint. At weeks 50–52, the combined score was 1.40–1.69 on drug and 1.56 on placebo. Circassia attributed the miss to a strong placebo response, which also matched its earlier cat-allergy failure. The drug groups' combined scores fell 35–44%, while placebo fell 39%. Circassia then stopped all allergy investment, so the trial design and placebo response (F7) is the reason the sources give. The searches found no human measurement of HDM-SPIRE exposure, T-cell tolerance or a regulatory T-cell biomarker. The mechanistic shift away from Th2 cells described in the review is reported for SPIREs as a class, not for this drug. Engagement therefore has no human data, and an indeterminate (U) reading also applies. An earlier Phase II chamber study did report symptom benefit.

The index trial NCT01272830 tested Apatone B, a vitamin C plus K3 combination, against postoperative synovitis after joint replacement. No molecular target is recorded. The bundle and my one search found no human data on how much drug reached the joint, whether it engaged a target, or whether a pathway biomarker changed in synovitis. Only paired t-tests within each arm were posted. Pain scores at week 13 were almost the same in both arms (39.7 vs 39.1), and there was no comparison between groups. The arms were small (17 and 21) and started at uneven baseline pain, which points to design weakness (F7). No source explains why the program stopped. Because engagement is unknown, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter.

The index trial NCT03680105 was a completed Phase 1 safety and tolerability study of RJX in healthy volunteers, registered under critical limb ischemia. It was not an efficacy test. It reported only mild or moderate TEAEs, with no ECG or neurological findings, so no efficacy failure occurred (F9). No molecular target is recorded, so engagement has no human data. Exposure is inferred from the approved scurvy indication. A pathway effect in humans is shown: 1 g IV ascorbic acid improved flow-mediated dilatation in previously preeclamptic women (PMID:11268269), but not in PAD (NCT00491751). The preeclampsia trial NCT03451266 posted no results. Mechanistically, why the program did not proceed is indeterminate (U).

Apatone B is an oral mix of vitamins C and K3 (menadione). No molecular target is recorded for it, and neither the bundle nor my search turned up any human data on tissue or synovial drug levels, target engagement or a downstream biomarker in patients with osteolysis or synovitis after joint replacement. The index trial (NCT01272830) was small (17 vs 21 analysed) and posted only within-arm tests. Pain scores at week 13 were almost the same in both arms (39.7 vs 39.1), and the treatment arm started with more pain (57 vs 46.8 at baseline). No between-group analysis was posted and no sponsor explanation was found. Since engagement is no_human_data, a drug that never acted on its target can't be told apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U. Weak design and execution (F7) is a possible secondary factor.

The index trial NCT01299727 was an open-label safety extension of the intrathecal (IDDD) dose-escalation study NCT01155778. Its primary outcomes were descriptive safety counts (TEAEs, labs, ECG, antibodies), and it ended for 'completion of follow-up period'. It was not an efficacy test, and no efficacy readout failed: no deaths, no drug-related serious TEAEs, no serum or CSF anti-drug antibodies. The bundle has no human CSF exposure, heparan sulfate reduction or clinical data for rhHNS. Evidence of brain delivery and substrate lowering comes only from dogs and mice (PMID:21550404, PMID:36306823). SOBI003 human data (PMID:35835061) concern a different molecule. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, engagement would be unknown, giving U.

Arasertaconazole is a topical azole that inhibits fungal CYP51 (Patsnap). I found no human data on vaginal drug levels, CYP51 inhibition or a pathway biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In NCT01144286, global cure was numerically higher at every dose (48.7–53.8%) than on placebo (31.7%), but the dose-response test missed significance (p=0.063). No serious adverse events occurred, so the dose was not limited by tolerability. Other fungal CYP51 inhibitors (oteseconazole, and fluconazole as comparator; PMC10869335) work in VVC. That points to this molecule or formulation not delivering enough effect, rather than the target failing (F1b). The near-significant trend at n≈57 per arm also suggests the trial was underpowered (F7). Ferrer reported clinical and mycological benefit in an earlier Phase 2 but gave no reason for stopping.

ALS-2158 is a nucleotide prodrug meant to inhibit the HCV NS5B polymerase. In the 7-day viral kinetic part of NCT01554085, patients with genotype 1 HCV took up to 900 mg. It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects, but antiviral activity was too low to go on. HCV RNA decline is the direct functional readout of polymerase inhibition, and it was not enough. That means the drug did not inhibit its target adequately in patients. No plasma or intracellular triphosphate levels were found. ALS-2200, a sister nucleotide prodrug aimed at the same polymerase and run in parallel by the same sponsors, produced about a 4-log viral decline. That points to a problem with this molecule, not the target (secondary F1b), although ALS-2200's result was not a pivotal success.

Human exposure is established, with linear PK and a 500 mg 5-on/2-off schedule (PMID:18381947, PMID:23400739). Engagement is shown in other diseases. Plasma FGF23 rose and sVEGFR2 fell (PMID:21976540, PMID:24691021, PMID:25149706), tumour pFGFR fell (PMID:21976540), and urothelial pFGFR3 was inhibited (PMID:27932416). Pathway effects followed: dose-dependent reductions in tumour blood flow and perfusion (PMID:21976540, PMID:34251745). The index scirrhous gastric trial (NCT01576380) enrolled only 11 patients and posted no results. No gastric-specific engagement data exist. Dovitinib broadly lacked single-agent activity despite engagement, so F2 is the best-supported code. Confidence is low: the readout is unshown, the trial was tiny (F7), and the company ceased development (NCT01484041, NCT01732107), suggesting F8.

In the index trial (NCT00790426, PMID:25457633), dovitinib 500 mg 5-on/2-off gave ORR 0% in FGFR3-mutant and 3.2% in wild-type advanced UC. It was generally well tolerated. At the same dose in bladder cancer patients, it reached pharmacodynamically active urothelial tissue concentrations and reduced pFGFR3 staining (PMID:27932416, NCT01732107). That evidence came after the index trial started. FGF23 rises confirmed systemic FGFR inhibition in other diseases (PMID:21976540, PMID:24691021). With engagement shown, this reads as F2: no benefit despite FGFR engagement. Patient selection is also blamed (PMID:27932416). Erdafitinib's approval in urothelial carcinoma suggests dovitinib's FGFR inhibition, measured only semi-quantitatively, may have been weaker than a selective inhibitor's. That weakens confidence in F2.

The index trial (NCT01232296) was a randomized comparison against sorafenib. Median OS was 33 weeks on dovitinib versus 39.4 weeks on sorafenib, so no benefit was shown. Exposure is documented by human PK (PMID:18381947, PMID:23400739). At the 500 mg 5-on/2-off dose, VEGFR and FGFR engagement markers moved: PlGF rose, sVEGFR2 fell and FGF23 rose (PMID:24691021, PMID:21976540, PMID:25149706). Tumor pFGFR inhibition was also shown (PMID:27932416). In HCC itself, plasma VEGFR-blockade markers and reduced intratumoral perfusion were shown (PMID:34251745), though this was published after the index start. Despite adequate engagement, dovitinib added nothing over sorafenib, which acts on the same VEGFR pathway. Poor tolerability in HCC, with dose reductions in 83% of patients and on-target hypertension (PMID:34251745), likely eroded any benefit.

Dovitinib at 500 mg 5-on/2-off, the index-trial regimen, engaged FGFR in humans with other cancers. It reduced pFGFR3 in urothelial tissue at pharmacodynamically active concentrations (PMID:27932416). It raised FGF23, a marker of FGFR inhibition (PMID:24691021, PMID:21976540), and reduced pFGFR in a melanoma biopsy. These data were published after the index trial started (2010), and none were collected in myeloma patients. In relapsed/refractory myeloma, the index trial (NCT01058434, PMID:25402977) produced no objective responses, including in t(4;14)/FGFR3-driven patients. FGFR3 inhibition by itself therefore did not drive benefit as tested (F2). Stable disease was more frequent in t(4;14)-positive patients (61.5% vs 34.6%), which points to possible subgroup confinement (F3).

The index trial (NCT01379534, PMID:25981814) gave dovitinib 500 mg on a 5-days-on/2-days-off schedule. Neither group reached the 18-week PFS threshold: 31.8% FGFR2-mutated, 29.0% wild-type, with no difference by mutation status. At this dose, other studies show human target engagement. Exposure was characterized (PMID:23400739). FGF23 rose and PlGF/sVEGFR2 shifted, consistent with FGFR and VEGFR inhibition (PMID:24691021, PMID:21976540, PMID:25149706). Tissue pFGFR3 fell at pharmacodynamically active concentrations (PMID:27932416). Tumor perfusion dropped (PMID:21976540, PMID:34251745). The melanoma PD data were published before the index trial started. No engagement data come from endometrial cancer patients, so confidence is medium. Lenvatinib is approved in endometrial cancer, but engagement here appears adequate, which argues against a molecule-specific (F1b) failure. The FGFR/VEGFR mechanism, as tested, did not drive benefit.

In SPI2 (NCT02936037), 12.0% of patients on MD1003 improved versus 9.2% on placebo, which was not significant. The stated 'business' stop reason followed this failed readout. The sources show high plasma biotin levels at 300 mg/day (Cmax about 1100 ng/mL). However, I found no human data on CNS or CSF biotin levels, activation of the targets ACACA/ACACB (acetyl-CoA carboxylase), or a downstream myelin or energy biomarker. A small open-label biomarker study (PMC7882156) measured plasma neurofilament light chain and brain and spinal cord volume, not mechanism-specific endpoints. The investigators said the earlier positive MS-SPI result was probably a type 1 error, which suggests the mechanism does not work rather than the drug failing to engage it. Without engagement data, the two explanations cannot be separated, so the code is U.

ALF-5755 is a recombinant REG3A replacement protein. According to PMID:26983031, a Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers showed good tolerability and a good pharmacokinetic profile. No actual plasma or liver drug levels were reported, and there were no measurements of target activity or downstream pathway markers in humans. In the Phase 2a trial (NCT01318525, n=57), neither the primary endpoint (prothrombin rate slope over 72 hours) nor transplant-free survival differed from placebo in the intention-to-treat analysis. Investigators reported a modest benefit in a per-protocol analysis of the HBV/autoimmune hepatitis subgroup, which suggests patient heterogeneity may have played a role (F3, secondary). Because there is no human evidence of engagement, the bundle cannot tell apart a drug that never acted on its target from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease, so the primary code is U.

In Sanofi's results summary for the index trial NCT01266525, no dose (0.5, 2 or 5 mg/day for 24 weeks) separated from placebo on the primary endpoint, ADAS-Cog. Only an unadjusted secondary ADCS-ADL result at 5 mg reached nominal significance. I found no human data on H3 receptor occupancy, brain or CSF drug levels, or a downstream biomarker. Plasma PK was sampled, but the summary reports only the donepezil interaction. Dose-related insomnia and muscle spasms hint at central activity, but nobody linked them to how much of the target was engaged. Sanofi gave no reason for stopping. Other H3 drugs in Alzheimer disease never got past Phase 2, so F1b does not apply. Since engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. All of the efficacy data came from animals (PMID:22542742).

The index trial NCT00677053 was a dose-ranging phase 2 study whose primary endpoint was TIMI major bleeding, a safety endpoint classified as not_efficacy. It was not an efficacy test. PMID:24671450 reports no significant or dose-dependent rise in TIMI major bleeding, a dose response on the modified ISTH bleeding scale, and cardiovascular events similar to placebo ('no evidence for efficacy'), but the trial was not powered for efficacy. The bundle has no human PK, anti-Xa activity or other biomarker data, so exposure, engagement and pathway are no_human_data. Other FXa inhibitors in ACS (rivaroxaban, otamixaban) are shown only as reaching phase 3, with no approval shown, so F1b is not supported. If this is read as an efficacy failure, U applies.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Lifileucel is a polyclonal autologous TIL product with no defined molecular target, so the pillars cannot be measured in the usual way. In the HNSCC trial (NCT03083873/PMID:40854613), overall ORR was 11%, with 0% in cohort 3. The full text reports no link between infused cell number or phenotype and response. Post-infusion T-cell persistence was available for only two responders, so it could not be correlated with outcome. No HNSCC data show tumor homing, persistence or antitumor activity at the cohort level. The melanoma approval (NCT02360579) used patient-specific TIL against a different tumor, so it does not show engagement in HNSCC. The investigators did not know why responses failed and pointed to HNSCC genomic heterogeneity (a weak F3). With no engagement data, the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT02132754 was a first-in-human dose escalation with safety primary endpoints (DLTs, AEs, discontinuations). It met its objectives: the MTD was not reached and 900 mg Q3W was tolerable, with one DLT (PMID:33355238). It was not an efficacy test, so F9. Pharmacodynamics showed dose-dependent loss of GITR availability on circulating T cells in solid-tumor patients, so engagement was adequate. That implies systemic exposure, although plasma PK was not reported. This evidence was published in 2021, after the trial began. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Monotherapy produced no responses, and the responses with pembrolizumab were confined to ICI-naïve melanoma. That pattern is consistent with the GITR mechanism adding little despite engagement (secondary F2). No stop reason is given.

Index Phase 3 trial NCT02089425 (acute pain from ankle sprain/strain, SPID 0-72h) was terminated after an interim futility analysis, with no results posted. The bundle has no Phase 1 data, no other trials and no PubMed abstracts for K-103, so exposure, COX-1/COX-2 engagement and pathway effects are undocumented in humans. Other drugs on the same target are listed for injury, and methyl salicylate is shown as FDA-approved for injury. That suggests COX inhibition can relieve injury pain, pointing to a problem with this molecule or formulation rather than the target, so F1b fits. Because engagement was never shown, this cannot be separated with certainty from an indeterminate failure (U). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT02196636 was a Phase 1 study in 37 healthy male volunteers. Its only primary outcome was adverse event incidence, so it was a safety and tolerability study, not an efficacy test of RO6806127. No results were posted, and no target, disease, other trials, same-target drugs or publications appear in the bundle. There is no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway, and no stated reason why development stopped. The readout was therefore not an efficacy failure (F9). If the program is judged on mechanism, it is indeterminate (U), because engagement has no human data. The bundle is extremely thin, so confidence is low.

In a human LPS challenge (NCT01937338, started before the index trial), inhaled AZD7624 cut sputum TNF-α by 85% and neutrophils by 57%. This shows lung exposure, p38 engagement and the expected downstream anti-inflammatory effect, despite sub-pharmacological systemic levels (PMID:29549158, PMID:29628759). This engagement was shown in healthy volunteers, not in COPD patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose: serious AEs were balanced and there were no Phase 1 SAEs (NCT01817855). In COPD, exacerbations were not reduced (HR 1.39, p=0.24; NCT02238483), and the authors conclude p38 inhibition failed to show benefit. No other p38 inhibitor in the bundle succeeded in COPD. This supports a target/mechanism failure (F2) rather than a failure to engage.

The bundle records no target for GRT6010 and contains no Phase 1 results, PK, occupancy or biomarker data, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Index trial NCT01485094 was terminated for futility after an unblinded interim analysis. Ongoing pain change was -2.30 for GRT6010 versus -2.55 for placebo. The active comparator pregabalin also failed to separate from placebo (-2.33), with only 19 patients per arm over 7 days. This suggests limited assay sensitivity and a high placebo response, so F7 is a secondary code. Because nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, the primary code is U.

In sickle cell disease (NCT00040677; Blood 2008), oral senicapoc at 10 mg/day blocked the KCNN4 (Gardos) channel in red blood cells. Hemoglobin rose and markers of red-cell destruction fell, so systemic exposure and target blockade in humans are shown. That evidence comes from another disease and cell type, but the index trial (NCT00861185) used a higher maintenance dose of 40 mg/day. No airway or mast-cell biomarker was measured in asthma, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Icagen reported no improvement on any FEV1 endpoint and stopped developing the drug. The allergen-challenge study (NCT00861211) had been called positive. Calling engagement adequate depends on carrying the red-cell result over to airway cells, so confidence is low and U is a reasonable alternative.

KL7016 is an oral small molecule from Yungjin Pharm/KT&G with no recorded target. Its only listed trial is the Phase 2 dry eye study NCT02092207, which ran for 12 weeks with corneal staining as the primary endpoint. That trial was completed in 2014 and posted no results. The searches found no human pharmacokinetic, target engagement or biomarker data, and no sponsor statement on why the program stopped. Without a known target or any engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in dry eye, so the failure cannot be classified (U).

No molecular target is recorded for birch triterpenes. The bundle has no human data on skin exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers in actinic keratosis. In the index trial (NCT00786994; Pflugfelder 2015), the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. It still did no better than petrolatum placebo. Response was 22/47 and 17/39 on drug vs 19/46 on placebo (p=0.60 and p=0.83). The drug's success in wound healing and epidermolysis bullosa (e.g. NCT03068780) involves a different, wound-healing mechanism. It cannot support an inferred antitumour engagement in actinic keratosis. Nothing in the bundle tells apart a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter here, so the code is U.

In the single-arm Phase 2 index trial (NCT01149681, PMID:25768401), plitidepsin at 5 mg/m2 on days 1 and 15 every 4 weeks gave 1 response in 11 patients. Patients tolerated it well, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The investigators called the activity modest and stopped single-agent work in myelofibrosis. They gave no mechanistic reason. The only evidence of drug binding to eEF1A2 or modulating p27 comes from lab or cell studies (the eEF1A2 binding paper, and preclinical work in PMID:25768401). The sources report no human drug levels, eEF1A2 engagement, or pathway biomarker (p27, JAK2 allele burden) in patients. No other drug on this target has succeeded in myelofibrosis. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a molecule that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index Phase 3 (NCT04784559) was terminated for recruitment failure at 205 patients. Neither dose separated from control on time to oxygen withdrawal (2.5 mg HR 1.06, p=0.88; 1.5 mg p=0.06). NEREIDA (NCT05705167) also stopped for poor accrual. The bundle has no human measure of eEF1A engagement or lung exposure; lung distribution and target-mediated antiviral activity are preclinical (PMID:33495306, PMID:35012962). Viral load fell in the uncontrolled Phase 1 (NCT04382066, PMID:34075384), but natural decline cannot be excluded, so pathway is unproven. The myeloma PFS benefit (NCT01102426) used a higher dose in a different tissue, so it cannot support inference. Recruitment-driven termination makes F7 primary; U is secondary because the engagement evidence is absent.

The index trial NCT00935662 was a single-ascending-dose safety study in healthy men, not an efficacy test, so F9 also applies. The only mechanistic evidence is PMID:26218540, a 2015 paper published after the index trial started. In abdominally obese volunteers, AZD8329 acutely inhibited 11β-HSD1 activity in adipose tissue, which shows the drug reached the tissue. However, that inhibition was lost after 7-9 days of repeat dosing (tachyphylaxis). Sustained target engagement was therefore inadequate, and the mechanism was never properly tested with chronic dosing. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported, and no results were posted for the repeat-dose trials NCT01207089 and NCT01225939. Loss of engagement, rather than a target that does not matter, is the failure the bundle supports.

In the index solid-tumor Phase 1 (NCT01358903), 89Zr-RG7356 PET showed tumor targeting at doses ≥200 mg q2w, so the drug reached tumor tissue and bound CD44 (PMID:27507056). In AML patients (NCT01641250), supraproportional PK showed target-mediated disposition, which was saturated at ≥1200 mg. The MTD was not reached, so dose was not limited, and 2400 mg q2w was recommended (PMID:27081038). However, blood and tissue analyses showed no dose- or schedule-dependent biological activity, so the pathway pillar failed. Clinical activity was modest in both settings: 21% stable disease in solid tumors, and one CRi and one PR in AML. Engaging CD44 thus did not translate into benefit. The index trial was itself a safety/MTD study rather than an efficacy test, hence the secondary F9.

The index trial NCT01483924 had a descriptive safety primary endpoint: the number of patients with adverse events over 12 weeks. Rates were similar across placebo (4/12) and Apo805K1 10–100 mg (5–7/12), with one serious AE at 30 mg. No efficacy endpoint was assessed, so this readout was not an efficacy test of the drug and does not show an efficacy failure (F9). The bundle records no primary target, Phase 1 results, PK, target-engagement or biomarker data, related drugs, or publications. All pillars are therefore no_human_data. If the program stopped for lack of efficacy, nothing here separates non-engagement from an irrelevant mechanism (U, secondary). Evidence is very thin.

NCT01288430 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation trial (0.6–5.85 mg/m²) with NSCLC expansion cohorts at 4.5 mg/m². No patient in any cohort had an objective response, and the sponsor ended the trial without giving a reason. My searches found no human PK, HSP90 inhibition or HSP70-induction data for DS-2248. The only sources were a JTO meeting summary describing the trial design and a mouse/in vitro study (TCR), and neither counts as human evidence. Posted adverse events do not show that tolerability capped the dose. No other HSP90 drug in the bundle succeeded in this disease. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Adefovir's antiviral activity in chronic HBV patients is well documented. Plasma PMEA exposure at 10 mg is dose-proportional (PMID:16869815). Viral polymerase engagement is shown by HBV DNA declines in patients (about -2.3 log at 10 mg, PMID:31838002; PMID:21993835), and the 2005 literature already treated adefovir as effective (PMID:15897532). The index trial (NCT00410202) compared active combination regimens in lamivudine-resistant HBV: ETV+ADV versus ETV alone versus ADV+LVD. Adefovir was in both the test and comparator arms. ETV+ADV was numerically better (25.4% vs 16.4% and 19.7%) but missed superiority, with wide CIs. This was a test of regimen superiority against active drugs, not an efficacy test of adefovir itself. The modest response rates and wide CIs suggest limited power (F7).

Lapuleucel-T (DN24-02) is a vaccine made from the patient's own antigen-presenting cells loaded with a HER2 antigen. In NeuACT (NCT01353222), patients with HER2+ urothelial cancer got all three infusions, and product potency was checked at each one. The ASCO 2016 abstract reports HER2-specific T-cell proliferation, IFN-γ ELISPOT responses and antibody responses that lasted more than a year. That counts as target engagement shown in the program's own disease, but it was published after the trial started in 2011. Even so, overall survival (HR 1.14 in the posted results; 0.96 at the interim) and distant relapse-free survival did not improve. So the HER2 immune response was induced but gave no clinical benefit (F2). The sponsor stopped the trial early for 'administrative reasons' at 142 of a planned 180 patients, which limits power (F7, secondary). The pathway pillar is a judgement call: the durable T-cell response was read as the downstream signal, not a separately measured biomarker.

No direct human measure of TOP2A engagement is in the bundle. Pixantrone holds a conditional EU approval for monotherapy in relapsed/refractory aggressive B-NHL, citing the PIX301 registration trial (PMID:27093976, PMID:32194699). Antitumor activity is also shown in DLBCL in PMID:23946328 and PMID:37161912. So the pillars are inferred adequate at comparable doses. In the index trial (NCT01321541), pixantrone+rituximab gave a median PFS of 7.3 months versus 6.3 for gemcitabine+rituximab, which missed the primary endpoint. The mechanism added no benefit beyond an active comparator in this population. Real-world data report limited efficacy in refractory patients and stress patient selection (PMID:32194699), so F3 is a secondary code. Confidence is low because the bundle gives no stated cause.

The bundle has no direct human PK, receptor occupancy or SSTR4 biomarker data; Phase 1 trials posted no results and there are no abstracts. Pillars are inferred because the same 600 mg dose met its primary pain endpoint in the CPMP diabetic neuropathic pain trial (NCT04707157; posterior difference -1.56). That benefit acts through the same peripheral SSTR4 analgesic mechanism, so exposure and engagement must have held there. In OA (NCT04627038) and chronic low back pain (NCT04874636), 600 mg was well tolerated but gave no separation from placebo. This suggests SSTR4 agonism does not drive nociceptive OA pain. Confidence is low: the DPNP signal comes from a small, early-terminated trial, and a later DPNP trial at lower doses failed (NCT06074562). If that inference is rejected, U applies.

In the chronic low back pain index trial (NCT04874636), 600 mg LY3556050 showed no separation from placebo (posterior difference 0.08). The osteoarthritis arm (NCT04627038) also failed. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, SSTR4 occupancy or biomarker data. The phase 1 trials posted no results and there are no abstracts. A diabetic neuropathic pain trial (NCT04707157) met its Bayesian primary endpoint, but it was terminated early. A later dose-ranging trial in the same disease failed (NCT06074562). That isolated positive result is too fragile to infer adequate engagement. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged SSTR4 from a target that does not drive this pain, so the code is U. F2 is listed as possible if the neuropathic signal is taken at face value.

I found no direct human measure of SSTR4 occupancy, pharmacodynamics or a biomarker for mazisotine. The later protocol says PD parameters are not evaluated. Engagement is inferred only from the sister trial NP03 (NCT04707157), which ran at the same 600 mg BID dose in diabetic neuropathic pain. NP03 met its Bayesian primary endpoint, with an effect size of 0.75. The NP03 result was not available before the index trial started. At that same dose, the drug matched placebo in chronic low back pain (NCT04874636) and in osteoarthritis (NCT04627038). This suggests that SSTR4 agonism does not drive nociceptive or mixed pain, so F2. Confidence is low because NP03 was stopped early and a larger DPNP trial (NCT06074562, 50–400 mg) failed. That makes the inference weak, so U is also plausible.

The index trial, NCT01900041, tested Pantovigar (a multivitamin product that contains thiamine) added to 2% minoxidil, against 2% minoxidil alone, in women with female pattern hair loss. It was completed, but no results were posted, and the search found no publication of its outcome. No molecular target is recorded for thiamine in hair loss. The bundle has no human data on thiamine levels in the scalp or hair follicle, on target engagement, or on a downstream hair-follicle biomarker. PMID:37182050 and PMID:37818523 are uncontrolled studies of a different multi-ingredient serum and show nothing about engagement. No source explains why the program stopped. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, the code is U.

The index trial NCT06242535 tested GLY-LOW, a supplement mix of alpha-lipoic acid, pyridoxamine, nicotinamide, piperine and thiamine meant to lower methylglyoxal. It was a single-arm, open-label pilot with no placebo. It planned 40 women but enrolled 13, and it has no posted results or stated reason for stopping. No human target is recorded. The bundle and search show no human data on exposure, target engagement such as methylglyoxal or AGE lowering, or a pathway biomarker at these doses. A related GLYLO trial (NCT06813261) lists methylglyoxal as an outcome, but no results were found. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. F7 also applies because the uncontrolled, under-enrolled design could not test efficacy.

The index trial, NCT03380507 (hydrocortisone, vitamin C and thiamine in septic shock, Qatar), was stopped for futility and lost funding. It posted no results and published no explanation. None of the sources measured the target directly in humans, such as pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) activity. Exposure is undocumented: no thiamine levels were posted. The downstream marker, lactate, did not change overall in Donnino's septic-shock RCT (NCT01070810), or at day 2 after cardiac arrest (NCT02974257). It did fall in a prespecified subgroup of thiamine-deficient patients (35% of the cohort). This suggests that any benefit was limited to deficient patients (secondary F3). The trial was also small, single-centre and lost its funding (secondary F7). Because engagement is unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate inadequate engagement from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Saracatinib had dose-proportional plasma exposure and accumulated in solid-tumour patients (PMID:20805299, PMID:22415795). Tumour biopsies showed reduced Src activity at doses up to the 175 mg MTD, which became the phase 2 dose (PMID:20805299). Engagement was shown in mixed solid tumours, not ovarian cancer specifically. Src-pathway readouts moved dose-dependently: sCTX fell 88% in healthy men (PMID:19775203), and betaCTX fell about 71% in patients with bone metastases (NCT00558272). Despite this, adding saracatinib to carboplatin/paclitaxel did not improve response (47/88 vs 45/87) and increased serious AEs (NCT00610714). It also failed with weekly paclitaxel in platinum-resistant disease (PMID:25070546). Src inhibition does not appear to drive ovarian cancer as tested. Later preclinical work cites MAPK bypass and the need for biomarker selection (PMID:29435137), so F3 is secondary.

Human phase 1 data show dose-proportional exposure, with plasma concentrations above biologically active levels at the 27 mg/m2 RP2D on the days 1/4/8/11 schedule (PMID:25393368). Markers of CDK activity fell in skin biopsies across the dose range, with antiproliferative effects at 28 mg/m2 (PMID:21325451). PD activity occurred below the QTc dose-limiting toxicity, so the dose was not capped. This engagement was shown only in surrogate tissue of solid-tumor patients, not in myeloma, and was published after the index trial began. The index myeloma trial (NCT01183949) posted no results and no stop reason. With engagement apparently adequate yet no clinical advance, F2 is most consistent, but the bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

In the index trial (NCT01208233, PMID:26738812), PF-03049423 6 mg once daily was well tolerated but missed the primary endpoint: the share of patients with mRS 0-2 at Day 90 was 42.6% on drug vs 46.2% on placebo. No other outcome measure showed an efficacy signal. Tolerability did not cap the dose, and only a few more patients on drug had low blood pressure. My searches found no human data on brain or CSF drug levels, PDE5 inhibition, or cGMP or other biomarker changes. The only claim that the drug is 'brain penetrant' comes from vendor and preclinical pages, and those don't count as human evidence. No other PDE5 inhibitor has succeeded in stroke. So the bundle can't tell apart a drug that never reached or engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter in stroke recovery, which gives U.

Plasma exposures were measured and judged adequate (PMID:31205187, PMID:31688451). The only direct engagement data are a PET study in healthy volunteers (NCT01918202/PMID:28122201). It started after the index trial and showed only partial striatal PDE10A occupancy: 14-37% at 10 mg and 45-63% at 20 mg single doses. The index trial used 5 and 15 mg BID, which by those data would give mostly partial occupancy, and 5 mg less still. No occupancy was measured in schizophrenia patients, and the bundle reports no pathway readout. The authors conclude the PDE10A hypothesis is refuted (F2 as secondary). However, the measured partial occupancy at comparable doses means the mechanism may not have been adequately tested.

The index OLE (NCT02342548) was terminated because the parent trial NCT02197130 missed its primary endpoint, with Total Motor Score not separating from placebo at 5 or 20 mg BID. NCT01806896 also failed. The only human engagement data are PET occupancy in healthy volunteers (NCT01918202, PMID:28122201), registered before the index trial. These show brain penetration but only partial striatal PDE10A occupancy: 14-37% at 10 mg and about 45-63% at a single 20 mg dose, with half-maximal occupancy at 93 ng/mL. No occupancy or downstream biomarker was shown in HD patients, and no pathway data are posted. Partial engagement means the mechanism may not have been adequately tested (F1a). Tolerability did not visibly cap the dose. Confidence is low because no source states what occupancy would be sufficient.

Index NCT03760666 (R/R AML, n=17, safety primary) was terminated for 'no efficacy observed' and COVID-19 site shutdowns. Older human data show plasma exposure with dose-related AUC (PMID:2369734). In cancer patients, lymphocyte DHODH activity became undetectable within 15 min and stayed low for up to a week. Plasma uridine fell 40–85% at ≥600 mg/m2 (PMID:2164443). So engagement and pathway effect were shown in humans before the index trial, but not in AML, and dose comparability to the index regimen is not shown in the bundle. Despite this, no AML benefit was seen, which points to F2. The small, COVID-disrupted trial with a non-efficacy primary endpoint adds F7. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

In the index trial (NCT04575038), brequinar 100 mg did not reduce viral load versus placebo; at Days 4 and 8 placebo declines were larger. Human data from 1990 oncology studies show plasma exposure (PMID:2369734). Lymphocyte DHODH activity became undetectable after IV doses of 15–2250 mg/m2 (PMID:2164443), so engagement counts as adequate, though only in cancer patients and not in COVID-19. The pathway readout, plasma uridine depletion, appeared only at ≥600 mg/m2, far above the index dose. Salvage pathways can offset DHODH inhibition (PMID:36041646), which prompted the later dipyridamole combination (NCT05166876). Engaging DHODH alone gave no antiviral benefit, so this is coded F2. Pyrimidine depletion may not have been reached at the index dose, which leaves F1a possible. The evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

In the index trial NCT03512756, SM-88 920 mg missed its overall survival (OS) endpoint. Median OS was 14.0 weeks on SM-88 versus 24.1 weeks on physician's choice, so survival favoured the control arm. The separate Precision Promise arm was also stopped for futility on OS, and TYME then ended pancreatic development. No source shows human data on tissue exposure, tyrosine hydroxylase inhibition or a downstream pathway marker. The first-in-human study (PMID:30929156) and the phase 2/3 abstract report only safety and clinical outcomes. No other drug on this target has succeeded in this disease, so F1b does not apply. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug never engaged its target or the mechanism does not matter. That makes the code U. A breast cancer trial was also stopped for lack of efficacy (NCT04720664).

The index trial tested THVD-201, tolterodine 2 mg plus pilocarpine 9 mg, against tolterodine alone. Its co-primary endpoints were daily micturitions and dry-mouth incidence at 12 weeks. PMID:31009289 matches this design and reports both endpoints met: micturition change was non-inferior (difference -0.26, 95% CI -0.79 to 0.27) and dry mouth was lower (30.0% vs 42.9%, p=0.009). Pilocarpine's role was to offset anticholinergic dry mouth, not to treat OAB. The earlier OAB study (PMID:24666884, 2014) showed salivary flow preserved with the combination, so engagement and pathway were demonstrated in OAB patients before the index trial. The readout was not an efficacy failure, so the code is F9. The bundle gives no stated stop reason; a business decision is possible but not shown.

The CHARM trial (NCT02864953) tested 8.6 mg IV glibenclamide given over 72 h and missed its primary endpoint (mRS common OR 1.17, p=0.42). The sponsor stopped it early, before unblinding, because of slow COVID-era enrolment and strategic reasons. The investigators say the trial was underpowered to reach definitive conclusions, so trial execution (F7) is the main cause. The bundle has no direct human measure of SUR1 binding or drug levels in the brain, so engagement is no_human_data. However, in the phase 2 GAMES-RP trial in stroke patients, the drug lowered plasma hypoxanthine, a marker linked to edema (PMID:35700741, published 2022, after CHARM started), so the pathway pillar holds. Post hoc results suggest benefit in some subgroups, such as smaller lesion volume or patients who also had thrombectomy (F3).

The listed disease (gas gangrene) does not match the bundle; the index trial tested IV glyburide in large hemispheric infarction with malignant edema. It missed the composite mRS 0-4 without craniectomy endpoint (OR 0.87, p=0.77; PMID:27567243). No receptor-level SUR1 engagement or brain/plasma PK is shown, and the T2D approval acts on a different tissue compartment, so it does not support an inferred engagement. However, in the index trial's own patients, the drug reduced midline shift, MMP-9, net water uptake, hypoxanthine and edema-attributed deaths (PMID:30446594, 31537189, 29789393, 35700741). That is a disease-proximal pathway effect not carried through to function. Enrolment stopped early for funding, leaving the trial underpowered (F7). Age ≤70 and infarct-topography subgroups suggested benefit (F3).

The index CHARM trial (NCT02864953) missed its 90-day mRS endpoint (OR 1.17, p=0.415) and was stopped early for operational and strategic reasons. The bundle has no human data on brain exposure or direct SUR1 engagement. The T2D approval works through pancreatic SUR1, a different tissue compartment, so it cannot support inferred engagement. In patients with this disease, post hoc analyses of GAMES-RP showed IV glibenclamide reduced net water uptake, midline shift, MMP-9 and hypoxanthine (PMID:31537189, 29789393, 35700741). Yet the GAMES-RP primary endpoint was not met (NCT01794182). So a proximal edema effect occurred without clinical benefit (F4). Benefit seen only in patients aged ≤70 (PMID:29789393) suggests F3. Early termination with reduced analyzed numbers suggests F7.

The sources did not show whether IV glyburide engaged SUR1-TRPM4 in human brain tissue. No study measured brain or CSF drug levels, channel occupancy or a target biomarker in traumatic brain injury. The hypoxanthine pharmacodynamic marker came from a stroke trial (PMID:35700741), and that program also failed (NCT02864953), so engagement cannot be inferred from it. The earlier pilot, PMID:31354055 (14 patients with contusions), showed only non-significant MRI trends. The index trial (NCT03954041) was stopped early, and Biogen pulled out because of operational and strategic factors, not efficacy or safety. Its biomarker-type primary endpoint, contusion volume, was not met (p=0.38) with small, uneven arms. Nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target. Secondary codes are F7 (underpowered, early termination) and F8 (business stop).

AP301 (solnatide) is an inhaled peptide meant to activate ENaC. In the first-in-human study (PMID:24515273), plasma levels were very low and lung levels were never measured, so exposure at the alveolar site is not shown. No human study measured ENaC activation or alveolar fluid clearance; the ENaC data are in vitro or animal only (PMID:26254591, PMID:23313096). In the index trial (NCT01627613, PMID:28750677), lung water (EVLWI) did not change overall, so the downstream marker did not move. The bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged ENaC from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. An exploratory post-hoc finding in patients with SOFA ≥11 led the investigators to suggest patient selection, so F3 is secondary. Note that NCT07030595, NCT06933472, NCT06100627 and PMID:38453435 concern a different drug with the same code, a phosphate binder.

The bundle has no direct human PK, NK1 receptor occupancy or biomarker data. At the same 1 and 5 mg doses, serlopitant met pruritus endpoints through the same NK1R mechanism in chronic pruritus (NCT01951274, registered 2013, before the index) and psoriatic itch (NCT03343639). It also met the primary endpoint in overactive bladder (PMID:20639026). So exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate, and tolerability was good with no dose cap. In atopic dermatitis (NCT02975206), both doses gave WI-NRS changes only slightly better than placebo (-2.25 and -2.32 vs -2.01). This suggests NK1R/substance P does not drive AD itch as tested. A large placebo response may also have contributed (F7). Repeated failures in prurigo nodularis and chronic pruritus of unknown origin support a limited role for the mechanism.

The bundle has no human PK, NK1 receptor occupancy or biomarker data for serlopitant. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate: 5 mg met itch endpoints in chronic pruritus (NCT01951274), psoriasis pruritus (NCT03343639) and a PN phase 2 (PMID:30894279), so the target was presumably engaged at the index dose. Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. Even so, both PN phase 3 trials missed the primary endpoint (NCT03546816: 26.5% vs 20.3%, p=0.229; NCT03677401: 25.9% vs 19.0%), as did the atopic dermatitis and CPUO trials. This suggests NK1 antagonism gives at most a small antipruritic effect in PN, too small for a 4-point WI-NRS responder endpoint. Development was then abandoned (NCT03540160). Confidence is low because the engagement evidence is indirect.

The bundle has no direct human occupancy or biomarker data for serlopitant. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 1 mg and 5 mg doses met itch endpoints through NK1 antagonism in chronic pruritus (NCT01951274, which began before the index trial) and psoriatic pruritus (NCT03343639). Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped (PMID:20639026). In atopic dermatitis itch (NCT02975206), both doses gave WI-NRS changes close to placebo (-2.25 and -2.32 vs -2.01). Prurigo nodularis Phase 3 trials (NCT03546816, NCT03677401) and chronic pruritus of unknown origin (NCT03841331) also failed. This points to NK1 not meaningfully driving itch in these populations (F2). Heterogeneity across itch subtypes may contribute (F3), and development was later stopped for business reasons (NCT03540160).

In this program, methoxsalen was one part of SM-88: racemetyrosine given with MPS (methoxsalen, phenytoin and sirolimus). It was not tested as a single drug. No primary target is recorded. In the index trial NCT03512756, overall survival in Part 2 was worse with SM-88 than with physician's choice (14.0 vs 24.1 weeks). TYME stopped SM-88 in pancreatic cancer in January 2022 after the Precision Promise arm was also ended for futility on overall survival. I found no human data on exposure at the site of action, target engagement or a pathway biomarker for methoxsalen or SM-88 in this setting. The only human data are on methoxsalen kinetics and UVA phototoxicity in PUVA use. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Palifosfamide is ifosfamide's active DNA-alkylating metabolite. Neither the bundle nor my search turned up any human measure of target engagement, such as DNA crosslink formation, pharmacodynamic biomarkers or published PK/PD at 150 mg/m2/d. PICASSO III (NCT01168791, PMID:27621408) missed its PFS endpoint (HR 0.86, P=.19) and showed no OS benefit. The combination did cause more grade 3-4 toxicity and febrile neutropenia, and PMID:28841543 reports a higher response rate. That points to some biological activity but does not measure engagement. PMID:28841543 also raises STS trial-design issues, including heterogeneity and an unexpectedly good doxorubicin control arm (F7, secondary). Without engagement data, nothing separates inadequate engagement from a mechanism that adds nothing to doxorubicin, so the code is U.

Palifosfamide is a DNA-alkylating agent and the active metabolite of ifosfamide. No human target was recorded for it. I found no human pharmacokinetic data at the site of action, no DNA crosslink or pharmacodynamic data, and no biomarker data in the bundle or my searches. In PICASSO III (NCT01168791, PMID:27621408), palifosfamide 150 mg/m2/d added to doxorubicin did not improve PFS (HR 0.86, P=.19) or OS. It did increase grade 3–4 toxicity, including febrile neutropenia, which suggests the drug was biologically active but does not count as engagement evidence. The sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation; press reports say only that the primary endpoint was missed. PMID:28841543 points to trial design issues and a stronger-than-expected control arm, so F7 is a possible secondary code. Because engagement has no human data, the code is U.

The index trial NCT01912404 enrolled only 5 patients and was terminated because systemic drug levels might exceed the exposures covered by toxicology studies. Its survival endpoint was never assessable, so this was a molecule-specific exposure and safety-margin stop, not an efficacy failure. Exposure in severe liver disease was high: 25 and 50 mg gave comparable plasma levels in acutely decompensated cirrhosis (PMID:30302038). That study also showed caspase-dependent cleaved keratin M30 falling early. Target engagement and lowering of ALT and caspase biomarkers were shown in NASH and cirrhosis (PMID:31870950, PMID:31887369, NCT02077374) and ALT lowering in HCV (PMID:17654603). None of this was in alcoholic hepatitis specifically, and the engagement data were published after 2013. The trial could not answer the efficacy question (F9/F7).

The index trial in post-transplant HCV fibrosis/cirrhosis showed no difference in ≥1-stage Ishak fibrosis reduction (25/41 vs 14/23, p=0.73). Exposure held: PK in decompensated cirrhosis showed adequate plasma levels at 25–50 mg (PMID:30302038). Engagement held: caspase and cytokeratin biomarkers fell in NASH cirrhosis, NASH fibrosis and ACLF patients, and the authors explicitly cite target engagement (PMID:31870950, PMID:31887369, PMID:30302038; cCK18 trend in NCT02230670). Pathway held: ALT/AST fell (PMID:17654603, NCT02077374). Despite this, fibrosis and HVPG did not improve, and fibrosis possibly worsened through alternative cell-death routes. This points to the mechanism not driving the disease (F2). Effects confined to the high-HVPG subgroup suggest F3. Most engagement data postdate the index start.

The index trial in post-transplant HCV fibrosis missed its endpoint: Ishak ≥1-stage improvement 25/41 vs 14/23, p=0.73 (NCT02138253). Across liver-disease patients, emricasan reached adequate plasma levels at ≥25 mg bid (PMID:30302038). It lowered ALT/AST in HCV patients as early as 2007 (PMID:17654603) and in NASH (NCT02077374). It also lowered caspase and cytokeratin biomarkers (PMID:31870950, PMID:30302038, NCT02230670). The authors state histology and HVPG did not improve 'despite target engagement' (PMID:31887369, PMID:31870950). They suggest caspase inhibition may redirect cells to alternative cell death and so worsen fibrosis, which implicates the mechanism. A small HVPG effect confined to compensated, high-HVPG subgroups gives secondary F3 (NCT02230683, PMID:31870950). No dose limitation in chronic disease.

In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT00555919/PMID:23788750), patients took lonaprisan 25 or 100 mg. No patient had a complete or partial response, and the trial missed its clinical-benefit target of at least 35%. The paper says pharmacokinetics were measured, but the snippets I could reach give no exposure values, and the full text would not load. I found no human data on progesterone receptor binding or occupancy, no PR-pathway biomarkers, and nothing showing that adverse events limited the dose. The only mechanism evidence is from cell lines (PMID:21138753) and animals (PMID:11150172). None of the other PR antagonists (onapristone, mifepristone) succeeded in this disease. The approved drug, megestrol, switches the receptor on rather than blocking it, so F1b does not apply. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter here.

The index trial NCT02630004 (MUCOMEL) tested a 3% melatonin mucoadhesive oral gel in 84 patients. The published report says there was only a non-significant trend toward lower incidence and shorter duration of severe oral mucositis. A later secondary analysis found no significant reduction in grade 3 mucositis (oral p=0.78). The sources found no human data on melatonin levels in the oral mucosa, MT1/MT2 receptor engagement, or any downstream marker such as antioxidant or apoptosis effects. The only mechanism data come from mice (PMID:37681910). No other drug on this target has succeeded in this disease. Because engagement has no human data, I can't tell whether the drug failed to engage or the target doesn't matter, so the code is U. The trial was small, and the authors asked for a phase 3, so underpowering (F7) may also have played a part.

The reason this program stopped can't be determined from the evidence found. The myelofibrosis index trial (NCT04218071) finished with 17 patients, but it posted no results, and searches found no publication or sponsor statement explaining the outcome. The Phase 1 solid-tumour study (NCT03678883; Clin Cancer Res 2024) measured elraglusib in plasma after IV dosing, so systemic exposure was shown. The searches found no direct human measure of GSK-3β binding or inhibition, and no human downstream pathway marker. That means no receptor occupancy, no kinase inhibition and no substrate phosphorylation data, in myelofibrosis or anywhere else. A cytokine-profile abstract links cytokines to survival but does not show the mechanism working. No other GSK-3β drug has succeeded in this disease. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter. Code: U.

NCT01337154 was stopped at interim analysis because its PFS endpoint would not be met. No sponsor explanation of the failure was found. The only human target-engagement evidence comes from AML/MDS patients in NCT02807558 (Syros, 2017). In that trial the dosing reached the expected plasma exposure, and DHRS3 induction, a direct RARα target gene, showed the receptor was engaged. That evidence came after the index trial started, was not gathered in NSCLC, and does not show RARα activity inside lung tumours. Nothing suggests tolerability capped the dose. With systemic RARα activation shown in humans, the most likely explanation is that RARα agonism added to chemotherapy does not drive NSCLC outcomes (F2). Tumour-level engagement is unknown, so U remains plausible and confidence is low.

Phase 1 data in healthy volunteers show leriglitazone crosses the BBB and reaches CNS concentrations needed for PPARγ engagement (PMID:38549500). The same phase 1 showed CNS target engagement (adiponectin rise) and inflammatory biomarker changes in plasma and CSF (PMID:34078742). Engagement was never measured in FRDA patients, and these data were published only after the index trial began. In FRAMES (NCT03917225, PMID:36524101), the spinal cord area primary endpoint was not met (p=0.61). Dentate iron accumulation was lower on drug (p=0.05) and tNAA/mIns differed only numerically. This points to a mechanism that did not move the chosen outcome. The 48-week imaging endpoint and small sample (n=39) may also have limited the test (F4/F7). Edema did not cap dosing.

Human plasma PK was dose-proportional and well tolerated up to 200 mg/day (PMID:22676397). Tracer-dose 11C-preladenant entered human brain (PMID:28280214), so the dose was not tolerability-capped. No human A2A occupancy or pathway data exist for therapeutic doses; NHP modeling suggested less sustained occupancy than tozadenant (PMID:25082853). In the index trial the active control rasagiline also failed to separate from placebo (-0.3 h, NS), as it did in the monotherapy trial. The authors say this makes the results hard to interpret (PMID:26523919, PMID:28490648), pointing to a trial unable to answer the question. Istradefylline, on the same target, is approved for PD, so a molecule-specific failure (F1b) remains possible. With engagement unmeasured, the cause is partly indeterminate.

The index oncology trial (NCT03099161, n=10) stopped because 'data did not support study endpoints'. It had no DLTs, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Human plasma exposure is shown, with dose-related PK up to 100 mg (PMID:22676397, 22167566). No human A2A receptor occupancy or immune and adenosine-pathway biomarker data exist for therapeutic preladenant in tumors or anywhere else. Occupancy was only modelled from monkey PET (PMID:25082853), and the 11C-preladenant PET studies use tracer doses (PMID:28280214). The Parkinson's phase 3 failures (NCT01155466, NCT01227265) give no inferred engagement. No other A2A drug in the bundle succeeded in cancer. With engagement unmeasured, never-engaged cannot be separated from irrelevant target, so the code is U. The trial was also very small.

The index trial (NCT03099161) was a tiny Phase 1b oncology trial (n=10) that stopped because 'the data did not support study endpoints'. It had no DLTs, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Plasma exposure in humans is documented in healthy-volunteer SAD/MAD studies, with dose-related exposure up to 100 mg (PMID:22676397). No human A2A receptor occupancy data exist for therapeutic preladenant: the occupancy figures are predictions from monkey PET (PMID:25082853), and the human [11C]preladenant studies used it as a tracer, not as a drug (PMID:28280214). No adenosine-pathway or immune biomarker data from the tumor setting were found. Nothing tells a drug that never engaged apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The trial's small size points secondarily to F7.

In NCT01097707, IPSS change at 1–25 mg was no better than placebo, and the published report says total prostate volume (the proof-of-concept endpoint), Qmax and PSA also did not change. The only human pharmacology is a single-dose study in healthy men (PMID:27136911). It modelled testosterone suppression, which the authors say comes from lost selectivity at high doses.
