They recommend a biomarker-selected population, supporting F3. F2 also applies for the unselected population.

In the CADA DIA trial (NCT03412006, PMID:33367744), fulacimstat 25 mg twice daily was well tolerated. Mean plasma trough levels were about 9 times what was predicted for minimal therapeutic activity, so exposure looks adequate. The dose was not limited by tolerability. However, chymase engagement was never measured in people: no chymase-activity readout and no change in a chymase-dependent marker such as tissue angiotensin II. Pillar 2 (target engagement) therefore rests only on predictions from animal and in vitro data. The heart-attack trial (NCT02976467) also failed, so it gives no inferred engagement. With no human engagement data, nothing separates inadequate chymase inhibition from chymase not mattering in DKD. The investigators conclude the target is not relevant, but that conclusion is not backed by engagement data, so the code is U.

In CHIARA MIA 2 (NCT02976467; PMID:32375104), the 25 mg twice-daily dose was well tolerated. Mean trough plasma levels were about tenfold above those predicted to be needed, so plasma exposure was adequate. In CHIARA MIA 1 (PMID:30452784), exposures were in the predicted therapeutic range. None of the sources I found measured whether the drug actually blocked chymase in heart tissue in dosed patients, or whether a downstream marker such as angiotensin II moved. The kidney-allograft study only added the drug to biopsy tissue ex vivo, which is not evidence from dosed humans. One source suggests heavy background ACE inhibitor or ARB use may explain the lack of effect, but that comment comes from the diabetic kidney disease trial. Because there is no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Romilkimab binds circulating IL-4 and IL-13, so plasma exposure is the relevant measure, and PK was sampled. In the earlier phase 1b/2a trial in IPF patients (NCT01529853/TDR11326), it lowered TARC (CCL17), a chemokine induced directly by IL-4/IL-13, in a dose-related way. In the index trial, TARC fell in both arms vs placebo (-147 QW, -77 Q2W vs +132 ng/L; p=0.003 and 0.02), which the investigators said confirmed target engagement. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The same drug also met its endpoint in systemic sclerosis (NCT02921971). Yet FVC decline was unchanged at either dose (PMID:30337444). The mechanism was engaged, so IL-4/IL-13 neutralisation does not appear to drive IPF progression.

In mRCC patients, plasma levels of the ADC, total antibody and cys-mcMMAF payload were measured at 1.8 mg/kg every 3 weeks (onco.13628), so systemic exposure is shown. No human study measured target engagement, such as ADC uptake into tumour, payload levels in tumour or a downstream pharmacodynamic marker. Tumour ENPP3 expression was high (median H-score 255). The investigators said this high expression does not explain the lack of effect. Keratopathy, an off-target toxicity driven by macropinocytosis (PMID:29382707), forced the dose down from the 3.6 mg/kg MTD to 1.8 mg/kg (PMID:29848572). That might have limited activity, but no source shows 1.8 mg/kg was below the dose engagement needed, and durable responses were seen at that dose. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell an under-engaging molecule apart from an ineffective mechanism, so the code is U.

Engagement of SGLT1/2 was not measured directly in PCOS. It is inferred adequate because licogliflozin met weight-loss endpoints in obesity at comparable total daily doses (150 mg qd; 50 mg bid/tid) in NCT02470403, NCT03100058 and PMID:32187881. NCT01915849 also showed reduced glucose absorption in T2DM before the index trial. In the PCOS trial the expected pathway effect was strong: peak insulin fell about 70% (P<.001), and DHEAS fell 24%. Yet free testosterone, the primary endpoint, was unchanged (ratio 0.88, p=0.353; PMID:34263971). The mechanism engaged without moving the primary androgen endpoint. The very short 2-week duration and small n (29) also limit the readout, hence secondary F4/F7.

In the index trial NCT03831191, LY3375880 at 50, 150 and 600 mg every 4 weeks did no better than placebo on vIGA-AD 0/1 (about 5% vs 9.5%), and the study was stopped for futility at an interim analysis. A secondary-source summary of the trial reports typical antibody plasma PK in patients (half-life about 20 days), so systemic exposure looks adequate. However, I found no human data on torudokimab engaging IL-33 (no free or total IL-33 measurement) or moving a downstream biomarker. The only engagement evidence is in vitro and in mice (PMID:34408465). Other anti-IL-33 antibodies, such as itepekimab, saturated IL-33 in serum and also failed in AD, and authors suggest IL-33 may not drive AD (F2 secondary). Still, torudokimab's own engagement is unmeasured, so the code is U. The 600 mg top dose was not capped by tolerability.

In the published report of the myeloma index trial (NCT03068351), 24 relapsed/refractory patients were treated. CD11b in blood monocytes fell steadily through dosing at every dose level (0.30–0.65 mg/kg). This marker reflects BRD4 being displaced from a super-enhancer, so it counts as evidence of on-target activity in patients with this disease. Dose escalation set a recommended dose of 0.65 mg/kg. Thrombocytopenia occurred, but the marker moved even at the lowest dose, so tolerability did not cap the dose below what engagement needed. Still, responses were rare and brief (clinical benefit rate 20.8%). The solid tumour trial (NCT01987362) also reported favourable drug exposure and target engagement. The mechanism worked as expected but brought little benefit, which fits F2. Cytopenias, an expected effect of this drug class, are a secondary factor (F5). One limit: the marker was measured in blood cells, not in myeloma cells. A related trial (NCT03292172) was later stopped for portfolio reasons.

The index trial NCT01987362 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study in advanced solid tumors. Its primary endpoints were DLTs, MTD and adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of RO6870810. No results were posted. The bundle has no human data on exposure, BET target engagement or pathway biomarkers, either in AML (NCT02308761, no results) or elsewhere, so a mechanistic failure cannot be judged (U). One sibling trial, NCT03292172, was terminated for portfolio prioritization, which suggests business reasons contributed to stopping the program (F8). No other BET inhibitor in the bundle is approved or has met a pivotal endpoint in AML. The bundle is thin.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT02308761; Roboz 2021, PMID 33586590) enrolled 32 patients with relapsed/refractory AML or HMA-refractory MDS. The authors reported favorable pharmacokinetics and evidence of target engagement: CD11b, an established BET-inhibitor pharmacodynamic marker, fell in peripheral blood cells at drug levels above 120 ng/mL. A maximum tolerated dose was set, but the bundle does not show that toxicity stopped the drug from reaching levels that engage the target. Even so, activity was minimal. One AML patient reached complete remission only after leaving the study, 11 had stable disease, and no MDS response was reported. Other trials of the drug (venetoclax combination, atezolizumab combination) also showed on-target effects with infrequent, short-lived responses, which points to F2. Later trials were stopped for portfolio prioritization (NCT03292172). The engagement data were published after the index trial started.

In the index trial NCT03255096 (Blood Adv 2021), patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL had sustained drops in monocyte CD11b. The authors treat this as evidence of pharmacodynamic activity and target engagement. The first-in-human study NCT01987362 found linear PK and the same CD11b effect, but it was published after the index trial began. The combination was not inactive: 38.5% of patients responded and 20.5% had a complete response. However, tolerability limited the dose. Dose-limiting toxicities were diarrhea, febrile neutropenia and high bilirubin, and the triplet's maximum tolerated dose fell to 0.45 mg/kg. These are BET class (on-target) effects, and the authors said they would need to be addressed before further development. They also called for better predictors of response. The related trial NCT03292172 ended for portfolio prioritization, so business reasons may have contributed.

In patients with diabetic nephropathy, PMID:29385323 reports nonlinear, target-mediated pharmacokinetics, showing exposure. Epiregulin and TGF-α levels rose, which the authors call consistent with target engagement. Doses were well tolerated up to 750 mg IV, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, proteinuria and albuminuria did not fall significantly. Only the 50 mg arm reached nominal one-sided significance, with no dose-response (NCT01774981). Disease biomarkers (MCP-1, synaptopodin, transferrin) were unchanged, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. A later pain-program model predicted about 92% engagement at similar doses (PMID:40266472). The best reading is that EREG/TGF-α neutralization does not drive proteinuria in DKD as tested. The engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself, so it was not available before it started. Very small arms (n=6–11) add an F7 element.

Fepixnebart 750→500 mg Q2W showed no pain benefit in OA (posterior difference -0.03 [-0.77, 0.70], NCT04456686). Exposure was characterized in the phase 2 patients themselves. PK/PD modeling of epiregulin in the OA, DPNP and CLBP trials predicted a median 92% target engagement, which the authors called adequate to test the analgesic hypothesis (PMID:40266472). Before the index trial, nonlinear PK and rising epiregulin/TGF-α levels had already shown engagement in healthy volunteers and diabetic nephropathy patients, with good tolerability up to 750 mg (PMID:29385323). The dose was not capped by tolerability. The sister pain trials also failed (NCT04476108, NCT04529096). No downstream pain-pathway biomarker was reported. With engagement high and no benefit, the EREG/TGF-α mechanism does not appear to drive OA pain.

Plasma exposure was shown with nonlinear, target-mediated PK in healthy subjects and diabetic nephropathy patients, and epiregulin/TGF-α rose, consistent with engagement (PMID:29385323, published before the index trial). A population PK/PD analysis that used data from the index DPNP trial itself predicted a median 92% target engagement at the Phase 2 regimen and judged the dose adequate (PMID:40266472, published after the index trial). Single doses up to 750 mg were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped (NCT01545583). No downstream pain-pathway biomarker was reported. Despite adequate engagement, NRS pain did not separate from placebo (NCT04476108). The parallel osteoarthritis and low-back-pain trials also failed (NCT04456686, NCT04529096). Together these indicate EREG/TGFA neutralization does not drive the pain as tested.

Fepixnebart showed nonlinear, target-mediated PK and dose-related rises in epiregulin/TGF-α (ligand capture) at up to 750 mg in healthy subjects and diabetic nephropathy patients, without dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:29385323, NCT01545583). A population PK/PD analysis of the phase 2 pain studies, including chronic low back pain, predicted median epiregulin target engagement of 92% with the 750/500 mg regimen and called it adequate to test analgesia (PMID:40266472). This in-disease evidence was published after the index trial started. No downstream pain-pathway biomarker was reported. Despite adequate engagement, NRS pain was not improved in CLBP (NCT04529096), osteoarthritis (NCT04456686) or DPNP (NCT04476108). This points to the EREG/TGF-α mechanism not driving chronic pain as tested.

In the CLBP index trial, the drug (750 mg then 500 mg Q2W) showed no benefit over placebo on NRS pain (NCT04529096). Exposure and engagement were shown in humans. Nonlinear PK with target-mediated disposition and rising epiregulin and TGF-α levels were seen in healthy subjects and diabetic nephropathy patients (PMID:29385323). A population PK/PD model built on epiregulin data from the CLBP, OA and DPNP phase 2 studies predicted about 92% target engagement and judged the regimen adequate (PMID:40266472). That patient-level analysis was published after the index trial started. No pain-pathway biomarker was reported. Tolerability did not cap dosing (NCT01545583). Consistent nulls in OA and DPNP (NCT04456686, NCT04476108) suggest EREG/TGFα neutralization does not drive chronic pain.

Index NCT04732494 missed its ORR endpoint (30.6% vs 20.6%, p=0.21), with no overall survival gain (HR 0.92; PMID:42901884). In the first-in-human study AdvanTIG-105 (NCT04047862; PMID:37857528), exposure rose in proportion to dose. TIGIT receptor occupancy on CD8+, CD4+ and regulatory T cells in blood was complete at every dose from 50 to 1800 mg, so the 900 mg dose was well above saturation. The index trial's own protocol cited these occupancy data before the trial began. Patients were mixed solid tumours, not specifically ESCC. Tumour-tissue occupancy and downstream pathway markers were not found, and no dose was capped by tolerability. Ociperlimab also failed in NSCLC trials (NCT04746924, NCT05014815), pointing to the target rather than the molecule (F2). An exploratory signal in inflamed tumours supports F3 as secondary.

In the first-in-human trial AdvanTIG-105 (NCT04047862, PMID:37857528), 32 patients with various solid tumours received ociperlimab. The maximum tolerated dose was not reached, and the trial set the 900 mg every-3-weeks dose later used in the index trial. According to the sponsor's protocol, TIGIT on circulating CD8+, CD4+ and regulatory T cells was 100% occupied at every dose tested, so engagement counts as adequate. This was shown only in blood, not in tumour, and not specifically in HCC patients. The sources found do not establish that it was published before the index trial began. No human downstream biomarker data were found. In the index trial (NCT04948697, PMID:42047833), adding ociperlimab did not raise response rate (37.1% vs 40.6%). The same pattern of no added benefit appeared in NSCLC trials (NCT04746924, NCT05014815). This points to TIGIT blockade not driving the disease as tested.

In the AdvanTIG-105 phase 1 (NCT04047862, PMID:37857528, PMC full text), ociperlimab exposure rose roughly in proportion to dose. TIGIT receptor occupancy on peripheral CD8+ T cells was complete and sustained at every dose, including the 900 mg RP2D used in the index trial. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred, so dose was not capped. The patients had advanced solid tumours, not SCLC. The full paper was published in 2023, after the index trial started; earlier conference data were not checked. No Treg or other downstream pathway result was found. In NCT04952597, adding ociperlimab gave no PFS gain over tislelizumab alone (12.6 vs 13.2 months). The add-on also failed in NSCLC (NCT04746924, NCT05014815) and ESCC (NCT04732494). With the target engaged and no benefit, F2 fits: TIGIT blockade does not drive outcome in this setting.

The index trial NCT05267054 had only descriptive primary endpoints: safety and the RP2D, set at 900 mg Q3W in both arms. It was not an efficacy test of ociperlimab, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human pillar data. PK was a secondary endpoint in the Phase 1 trial (PMID:37857528), but no results are shown. Engagement data (TIGIT blockade, Treg depletion) come only from preclinical models (PMID:35273608). The cervical cancer ORR (NCT04693234) came from a combination with tislelizumab and cannot be attributed to TIGIT, so it does not support inferred_adequate. Toxicity did not limit the dose: the MTD was not reached and there were no DLTs. The wider program failures (NCT04746924) leave target versus molecule unresolved, hence U as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT01971515 is a first-in-human Phase 1 dose-escalation study. Its primary endpoints are DLTs and adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of rupitasertib, and no results are posted. The bundle has no other trials, no approvals and no same-target comparators. The only abstract (PMID:27186432) is preclinical: potent p70S6K/Akt inhibition, pS6 suppression and blood-brain barrier penetration in rodents. Animal data do not count, so all three pillars lack human data. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, so business, toxicity or mechanistic causes cannot be told apart. F9 is primary because the index trial was not an efficacy readout. U is secondary because engagement in humans is unknown.

The index trial mainly tests CX-2009, with pacmilimab only as a combination partner. No results or stop reason are posted. Exposure was adequate: plasma PK supported 10 mg/kg (PMID:32681519), 89Zr-PET showed tumor uptake in all patients (PMID:34253583), and no MTD was reached (PMID:34301809). Tumor PD-L1 occupancy was only model-predicted, and no pathway biomarker was reported in humans, so engagement is unshown, including in breast cancer. Atezolizumab, on the same target, is approved in breast cancer. A working target plus no evidence that this masked prodrug engaged it adequately fits F1b. Low confidence: pacmilimab was not the main agent tested (F9), and other trials ended by sponsor decision (NCT03013491, NCT03993379).

In the low-risk amendment (f) arm of NCT04634409, bebtelovimab 175 mg lowered day-7 persistently high viral load from 19.8% (placebo) to 12.0%. The OR of 0.56 was not significant (p=0.097). The effect size resembles that of bamlanivimab monotherapy (OR 0.44, significant against a 27.7% placebo rate), so the low event rate in low-risk patients and the small arms point to an underpowered comparison (F7). The bundle has no human PK, serum neutralization or binding data; neutralization is shown only in vitro (PMID:35568025, PMID:33972947). Engagement is therefore unmeasured, which leaves room for U. Other anti-spike mAbs succeeded in NCT04427501. Real-world hospitalization data were non-significant (PMID:36438619), and the EUA was withdrawn (PMID:36651898), but the bundle does not give the reason.

In NCT02097277, 12 weeks of pegbelfermin (1–20 mg daily, 20 mg weekly) produced no HbA1c change versus placebo, with no tolerability limit. At comparable doses (10 mg QD, 20 mg QW), pegbelfermin clearly engaged FGFR1/KLB signalling in humans. Hepatic fat fell significantly in NASH (NCT02413372). Secondary bile acids fell in NASH patients and in overweight/obese adults (PMID:34977519). FALCON trials showed improved fibrosis and injury biomarkers (PMID:37088457, PMID:37088458). This indicates the agonist was functionally active, yet glycaemia did not move. That suggests FGF21 agonism does not drive glucose control in T2D as tested. Caveats: no T2D-specific engagement data are in the bundle (the PMID:30520566 abstract is absent), and the engagement evidence postdates the index trial, so confidence is medium.

The bundle has no human exposure data. In NASH patients, the earlier Phase 2a trial (NCT02413372, started 2015) showed significant hepatic fat fraction reduction. Pooled data show rises in adiponectin, a classic FGF21-receptor pharmacodynamic marker, and lower PRO-C3 (PMID:40104016). Engagement and pathway are therefore treated as shown, though not by direct receptor measures. In FALCON 1, responses were numerically higher (24–31% vs 14%), but the trend-test primary failed for lack of dose response (PMID:37088457). This points partly to analysis design (F7). FALCON 2 in cirrhosis showed no fibrosis benefit (NCT03486912, PMID:37088458). Despite engagement, no clear histologic fibrosis benefit followed, so F2 is primary. Tolerability was acceptable, so dose was not limiting.

Index trial NCT02291237 missed peak VO2 (LS diff -0.55, p=0.416), with balanced serious AEs and no stated stop reason, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No HCM-specific exposure, engagement or biomarker data are in the bundle. However, eleclazine met its primary endpoint of QTcF shortening (-8.5 ms, p=0.0087) in LQT3 (NCT02300558). That is a late-INa (Nav1.5) block effect in the same cardiac compartment, so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Dose comparability is not shown, so the inference is weak. The LQT2 results (NCT02365506) and the ICD/arrhythmia trial (NCT02104583) were null. Late-INa inhibition appears not to drive exercise capacity in HCM as tested. Confidence is low because engagement was never measured in HCM patients.

Index trial NCT02104583 (3 and 6 mg) showed no reduction in appropriate ICD interventions; the 3 mg rate ratio leaned the wrong way (1.52). No PK or direct target-engagement data are posted. Human evidence of late-sodium-current block comes from LQT3 patients, where eleclazine met its QTc-shortening primary endpoint (NCT02300558, -8.5 ms). This implies cardiac target engagement and a functional effect, so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. However, the doses are not shown, that trial started after the index trial, and the population is a different disease. The HCM trial (NCT02291237) was also negative despite engagement. F2 is favoured, but small cohorts with wide CIs (F7) and the lack of in-disease engagement data (U) temper confidence.

In NCT03928184 (OA-11), a 0.07 mg intra-articular dose did not reduce pain more than vehicle at week 12 (PMID:39808286). Two other Phase 3 trials also missed their primary endpoints (NCT04385303, NCT05603754). Phase 2 results were mixed (NCT03122860, NCT02536833). In humans, only plasma levels were measured, and these were mostly below quantification (PMID:37902943; the Phase 1 paper). No source reports drug levels in synovial fluid or cartilage, CLK2 or DYRK1A inhibition, or Wnt-pathway biomarker changes in patients. The Phase 1 trial collected COMP, P1NP and β-CTX, but no shift in them was found. No other drug on this target gives a comparison. The sources do not separate a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The post-hoc benefit seen only in KL grade 2 patients (PMID:39808288) supports F3 as a secondary code.

Lorecivivint is injected into the knee joint. No source reports drug levels in synovial fluid or cartilage. Plasma levels were below quantification in the first-in-human study (NCT02095548) and in PMID:37902943. That is expected for a locally injected drug, so it says nothing about exposure at the joint. No human data show CLK2 or DYRK1A inhibition or Wnt modulation. In Phase 1, serum biomarker changes were 'inconclusive', which at best is weak evidence of a pathway effect. Pain results were inconsistent: NCT03122860 was mixed, while NCT02536833, the index trial, NCT04385303 and NCT05603754 all missed. The sponsor later bet on milder disease (STAT), which hints at patient selection (F3), but this is untested. Because engagement is unknown, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter. Hence U.

In the index trial (NCT00994214), 0% of patients at any dose from 1 to 6 mg reached GH ≤2.5 ng/mL with normalised IGF-1. The sponsor stated the data did not support the expected GH/IGF-1 inhibition, so the downstream pathway effect was inadequate in humans. The bundle has no human PK, receptor occupancy or engagement data; the potency evidence is in vitro only (PMID:16625841, PMID:33433890). The SSTR2 target is validated in acromegaly: octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide and paltusotine are FDA-approved for it. This points to the molecule rather than the target. The carcinoid program (NCT01018953) was stopped on the same data. U is secondary because engagement was never measured.

The index carcinoid syndrome trial was stopped early with 8 patients enrolled. The stated reason was that preliminary data from the acromegaly study NCT00994214 did not show the expected GH and IGF-1 suppression: 0% of patients in any arm reached the control endpoints. GH suppression is the proximal human pharmacodynamic readout of SSTR2/D2 agonism in vitro (PMID:16625841). Its absence in patients shows the drug did not functionally engage its targets, so engagement and pathway are inadequate. No human exposure data are given. Other SSTR2 agonists, lanreotide and octreotide, are FDA-approved for carcinoid syndrome. The failure therefore points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b), with inadequate engagement (F1a) as a secondary code. The only carcinoid-relevant evidence is in vitro (PMID:30939452).

The index trial NCT05682170 (ZN-d5 plus ZN-c3 in AML) was a Phase 1/2 study whose primary outcomes were DLTs and adverse events. It was terminated for an unspecified 'sponsor decision' with no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test and no efficacy readout failed. The bundle has no human exposure, BCL2 engagement or pathway data: no Phase 1 results were posted (NCT04500587, NCT04854174) and there are no PubMed abstracts. Other ZN-d5 trials were also stopped by sponsor decision or have no results (NCT05127811, NCT05199337), which hints at a portfolio or business decision (F8), but the bundle does not show this explicitly. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, the code would be U because engagement is unknown.

In NCT04734197 the vehicle arm had an 80.9% UNC DEMS responder rate. This was higher than SURF-100 (65.4%), betamethasone 0.01% (71.4%), and even the approved dry-eye comparators cyclosporine (72.3%) and lifitegrast (57.4%). That pattern points to a vehicle response so high the trial could not separate active drugs, a design or assay-sensitivity failure. The sister trial NCT04734210 (SURF-200) showed the same pattern, with vehicle 65.2% above both active doses. Ocular exposure and engagement of betamethasone are only inferred: the SURF-201 eye drop met its anterior-chamber-inflammation endpoint after cataract surgery (NCT04324359), but that trial's concentration is not shown. There is no human ocular-surface biomarker for this disease, and the bundle gives no stated reason the program stopped.

First-in-human work sampled CSF and reported excellent brain penetration with good tolerability up to 160 mg (PMID:34240455, NCT02769065), so exposure was adequate. No receptor-occupancy data exist; qEEG changes appeared only at 40-160 mg. In the index PD trial at 7.5 mg (NCT04334317), the gait primary endpoint (stride time variability) was unchanged. However, the secondary cognitive composite improved (P=.01; PMID:39761063), with an exposure-response plateau at 5-7.5 mg (PMID:40711392). Engagement is therefore inferred from a clinical effect in this same disease at the same dose, published only after the trial. The cognitive effect did not translate to the gait endpoint over 6 weeks. Gait gains were confined to attention responders (F3). The M1-to-gait link may simply be weak (F2).

PERISCOPE-ALZ (NCT03518073) missed iADRS at both 1400 and 5600 mg; secondary clinical endpoints were also negative (PMID:38386949). Serum PK was linear with ~20-day half-life, but no CSF or brain exposure data are in the bundle. Target engagement in AD patients is suggested by a dose-dependent rise in plasma tau (NCT03019536, PMID:37849628) and in plasma p-tau181/total tau in the index trial. However, tau PET, MRI volume and NfL were unchanged, so the downstream pathway did not move. Doses reached 5600 mg without dose-limiting toxicity. Engagement is only peripheral, so central engagement remains unproven and U is a plausible alternative. Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT02933606 (150–600 mg b.i.d.) used the early aqueous suspension. PMID:41014090 reports that this formulation had solubility-limited absorption and a significant food effect, which prompted a dispersible tablet with better bioavailability. With the tablet at 900 mg b.i.d., the Phase 2b ATTUNE trial (NCT04951076, PMID:39647171) met its CAPS-5 primary endpoint in PTSD. Target engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers (qEEG nicotine-shift assay); no engagement or pathway data were shown in PTSD patients. The index failure is best explained by inadequate exposure from the formulation, so the mechanism was not properly tested. The PTSD program did not stop after this readout but continued with the reformulated drug.

The index agitation trial (2018, n=38, 5 days) posted no results. PMID:41014090 reports α7 nAChR engagement via a nicotine-shift qEEG assay, but only in healthy volunteers and only in a 2026 publication. The same source says the early aqueous suspension had solubility-limited absorption and a significant food effect, which prompted a higher-bioavailability tablet. The 2018 index trial predates the tablet trials, so it likely used the suspension; the bundle does not state this. The 2016 PTSD suspension-era trial failed (NCT02933606), while the later tablet trial met its endpoint (NCT04951076). That pattern points to an exposure limitation (F1a). The mechanism may also simply not drive agitation (F2), and the trial was small (F7). Evidence is thin.

The first-in-human study (NCT03564691, PMID:34598945) in advanced solid tumors evaluated pharmacokinetics and reported dose-related target engagement. There were no dose-limiting toxicities and no MTD was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. This evidence was published before the index trial started, but it came from mixed solid tumors, not specifically ovarian carcinoma. No downstream pathway biomarker was clearly shown; the IFN-gamma association was exploratory only. In the index trial (NCT05446870), adding MK-4830 to pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy did not improve ctDNA change at Week 7 (posterior probability 38.75%, not favouring MK-4830). With engagement shown and no dose limitation, the failure is best read as ILT4 antagonism not adding benefit in this disease as tested (F2). Confidence is medium because engagement was not measured in ovarian patients.

TRILOGY 2 (NCT03361501) missed its primary endpoint. CaPre lowered median triglycerides by 30.4%, but placebo lowered them by 17.9%, leaving a 12.4% placebo-corrected difference (p=0.19). TRILOGY 1 (NCT03398005) also failed, and Acasti blamed an unusually large placebo response (27.5%). After TRILOGY 2, the CEO also pointed to the cholesterol-lowering drugs patients were taking alongside the study drug as a possible cause. When the two trials were pooled, CaPre beat placebo by only 10.9% (PMID:34989797). The sources blame trial design and execution, so the primary code is F7. No target is recorded, and the bundle has no human evidence on exposure (e.g. plasma EPA/DHA levels), engagement or pathway. That means a drug that never worked can't be told apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so U is listed as a secondary code.

Exposure was dose-proportional in humans (NCT04646044) and comparable across trials (PMID:37651676). In mixed solid tumors, tumor biopsies showed IL2 receptor pathway engagement, increased effector genes and immune-cell expansion, with peripheral lymphocyte rises at the 0.006 mg/kg RP2D (PMID:30988166, PMID:31043381). That evidence predates the index trial, but none of it comes specifically from bladder cancer. Despite this, clinical benefit was absent across the program: melanoma phase 3 (NCT03635983), RCC (NCT03729245) and a low ORR in cisplatin-ineligible urothelial cancer (NCT03785925). The sponsor ended the program after three negative studies (NCT04969861). The index trial was truncated at 114 patients with no statistical analysis, so on its own it could not answer the question (F7).

Exposure is shown by dose-proportional PK (NCT04646044) and comparable PK across trials (PMID:37651676). Engagement and pathway effects were published before the index start: tumor biopsies showed IL2 receptor pathway engagement, CD8/NK expansion with limited Treg increase, and peripheral ALC rises at the 0.006 mg/kg RP2D (PMID:30988166, PMID:31043381). These data come from mixed solid tumors, not specifically bladder. Despite this, combination trials failed: melanoma (NCT03635983), RCC (NCT03729245) and urothelial PIVOT-10 (NCT03785925, ORR ~18%). Nektar ended the program after three negative studies (NCT04969861), so the mechanism did not add benefit. The index trial was truncated at 114 patients with only descriptive, numerically favourable pCR and EFS. It could not answer its question, hence F7 as a secondary code.

Human PK was dose-proportional (NCT04646044) and comparable across trials (PMID:37651676). The first-in-human study showed IL-2 receptor pathway engagement in tumor biopsies plus peripheral immune expansion at the RP2D of 0.006 mg/kg (PMID:30988166). PIVOT-02, which included RCC patients, showed increased intratumoral CD8+ infiltration and activation (PMID:32439653). The phase 3 used the same dose, which was not tolerability-capped. Despite this, BEMPEG plus nivolumab gave a lower ORR than TKI and no OS gain in ccRCC (NCT03729245, PMID:38838287). It also failed against nivolumab alone in melanoma (NCT03635983). Engagement and pathway were intact but brought no clinical benefit, so the CD122-biased IL-2 mechanism as tested does not add benefit. Sponsor stopped after three negative studies.

Human PK was measured, and exposure in PIVOT IO 001 was comparable to PIVOT-02 (PMID:37651676, NCT04646044). Engagement was shown in the first-in-human study: tumor transcriptional analysis showed IL2 receptor pathway engagement and immune cell expansion with limited Treg increase (PMID:30988166, NCT02869295). In melanoma patients, PIVOT-02 showed polyfunctional CD8+/CD4+ responses (PMID:34255535), and the index trial reproduced the lymphocyte changes (PMID:37651676). The dose (0.006 mg/kg) was chosen on safety and pharmacodynamic grounds, not capped below engagement. Despite adequate pillars, adding bempegaldesleukin to nivolumab gave no benefit: ORR was worse and PFS and OS were unchanged (NCT03635983). The CD122-biased IL-2 mechanism, as tested, does not add to PD-1 blockade. Engagement predates the index start only through trial registration; publication was later.

Exposure was shown by dose-proportional human PK (NCT04646044) and by PIVOT IO 001, where PK and lymphocyte changes matched PIVOT-02 (PMID:37651676). In the first-in-human solid-tumour study (NCT02869295, registered before the index trial), tumour biopsies showed IL2 receptor pathway engagement, effector gene induction and CD8/NK expansion at the 0.006 mg/kg RP2D, with limited Treg increase (PMID:30988166). This engagement was shown in mixed solid tumours, not specifically NSCLC. The index NSCLC trial was descriptive: ORR 13/60 at 0.006 mg/kg with pembrolizumab, with no clear added benefit. Nektar then ended the whole program after three negative randomized studies (NCT04969861; NCT03635983; NCT03729245). The target was engaged at tolerable doses, yet there was no benefit, so the mechanism did not drive disease as tested.

PROPEL-36 (NCT04969861) enrolled one patient. It was stopped because Nektar ended the program after three negative studies, so it never tested efficacy in HNSCC (hence F9 as secondary). The program-level failure followed adequate pillars in solid-tumor patients, though none with HNSCC. PK rose with dose (NCT04646044). The first-in-human trial showed IL2-pathway engagement in tumor biopsies, CD8/NK expansion with limited Treg increase, and an RP2D set on PD markers rather than toxicity (PMID:30988166, PMID:31043381). PIVOT IO 001 confirmed comparable PK and lymphocyte-count changes, yet ORR, PFS and OS were not better than nivolumab alone (PMID:37651676, NCT03635983). RCC was also negative (NCT03729245). The mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, so F2 is primary.

The index trial NCT03335540 (ADVISE) was a biomarker feasibility study. Its primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with a qualified baseline biopsy whose biomarker analysis was completed within 12 business days to allocate an I-O combination (PMID:40389374). It was not an efficacy test of cabiralizumab, and 87% of eligible patients were allocated. So this is not an efficacy failure (F9). For context, PMID:34140403 (NCT03502330), which included 13 RCC patients, reported pharmacodynamic activity with MCSF rising after therapy. This is consistent with CSF1R blockade, but it was published after the index trial started. No PK or downstream pathway data are given. Dose escalation reached a 4 mg/kg recommended dose without a tolerability cap (NCT02526017).

The index trial NCT03335540 was an adaptive biomarker-matching study whose primary outcome was the number of participants with a qualified baseline tumor biopsy. It was not an efficacy test of cabiralizumab, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). On the pillars, no PK data are shown. Engagement is supported by increased MCSF after therapy and the reported 'pharmacodynamic activity' (PMID:34140403), though that was mostly in melanoma/RCC (1 NSCLC patient) and was published after the index start. The cabiralizumab dose (RD 4 mg/kg) was not capped by tolerability (NCT02526017). Pathway effects were not shown. Separately, cabiralizumab failed elsewhere: no PFS benefit in pancreatic cancer (NCT03336216).

In NCT03336216, no cabiralizumab arm improved PFS over investigator-choice chemotherapy; cabiralizumab plus nivolumab was worse (HR 1.47). The only human target-engagement evidence is a rise in M-CSF after therapy at cabiralizumab 4 mg/kg Q2W, which PMID:34140403 calls pharmacodynamic activity. That was in melanoma, RCC and NSCLC, not pancreatic cancer, and was published after the index trial started. The 4 mg/kg Q2W dose was set as the recommended dose in NCT02526017 without a tolerability cap. No PK, tumor macrophage depletion or downstream pathway data appear in the bundle. Engagement at a comparable dose without benefit points to the mechanism not driving the disease (F2). Confidence is low because engagement evidence is indirect and from other diseases.

The index trial NCT02627274 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study with safety, MTD and PK primary endpoints. It reached an MTD and showed PK plus dose-independent IL-2R pharmacodynamics: NK cells up 13-fold and CD8 T cells up 3.5-fold, without Treg skewing (PMID:38630781). In RCC (NCT03063762, PMID:41956546), FAP-IL2v combinations gave ORR 25% (doublet) and 47% (triplet), with NK and T-cell expansion and increased tumor infiltration in paired biopsies, so the pillars held in this disease. That evidence was published after the index trial began. The sponsor stated development was discontinued for portfolio prioritization, not for safety, efficacy or quality (NCT03386721). This is a commercial stop, and the index trial was not an efficacy failure.

In the index melanoma trial (NCT03875079, PMID:39895413), FAP-IL2v PK matched monotherapy and the drug preferentially expanded NK and CD8 T cells, consistent with IL-2Rβγ agonism. Similar dose-independent NK/CD8 expansion was seen in solid tumors (PMID:38630781) and intratumorally in HNSCC (PMID:39422604, PMID:41956546). Despite adequate engagement at 10 mg, within the tolerated range, responses were 6.7% in CPI-experienced patients (90% of the cohort), and further exploration was precluded for lack of activity. This fits a mechanism that does not drive benefit as tested (F2). The CPI-experienced population may also matter, since 2/8 CPI-naïve patients responded (F3). Program-wide discontinuation was attributed to portfolio prioritization (NCT03386721; F8). Disease-specific engagement evidence came from the index trial itself.

Ampion is a low-molecular-weight filtrate of human serum albumin. Its main ingredient, DA-DKP, is described only as an immunomodulator, and no molecular target is recorded. No source gives human data on intra-articular drug levels, target engagement or a pathway biomarker. In the index trial NCT02024529, pain change was identical in both arms (-0.81 vs -0.81, p=0.97). Phase 3 results were inconsistent. NCT02242435, NCT02556710 and NCT03988023 failed. NCT03182686 met its endpoint against a small saline arm, and Phase 2 NCT01839331 was positive. Because both arms improved by the same amount, a strong saline/placebo response may be involved (F7 as a secondary code), but no source attributes the failure to that. With no engagement evidence, a drug that never acted on its mechanism cannot be told apart from an ineffective mechanism, so the code is U.

Ampion has no recorded molecular target. The bundle and searches turned up no human data on its exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers in COVID-19 or in any other disease. Mixed results in knee osteoarthritis cannot support an inferred_adequate call because the target is undefined. In the index trial AP-017 (NCT04839965), 5/21 patients on Ampion and 5/15 on placebo reached the primary endpoint, with no statistical analysis. The sponsor said the interim analysis was for sample size re-estimation. It then stopped enrollment because enrollment was slow and COVID-19 treatment and regulatory approvals had changed, which points to trial execution (F7) and business reasons (F8) rather than a stated futility finding. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U.

Human PET studies in healthy volunteers showed brain penetration with high, sustained SV2A occupancy (>90%) and the intended 10-15% GABAA occupancy (PMID:33241213). Simultaneous PET-ASL showed occupancy of 57-98% with a dose- and concentration-dependent fall in cerebral blood flow (PMID:40655962), a downstream effect. These PET studies guided dose selection for the 2015 Phase 2a, before the index trial started. Doses up to 400 mg BID were tested. Withdrawals rose at the top dose, but the dose was not capped below the occupancy target. Despite this, the Phase 2b (NCT03373383) and Phase 3 (NCT03739840) both missed, and Phase 3 effects were near zero. Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers. The Phase 2a signal in a highly resistant inpatient population, the population heterogeneity and the placebo response are possible contributors.

The index trial NCT02854631 had only a descriptive safety primary outcome (TEAEs, SAEs, discontinuations), with no formal efficacy comparison, so it was not an efficacy test of selonsertib (F9). Pillars: dose-proportional plasma PK with pharmacologically relevant exposure in healthy subjects (PMID:32333325). Dose-dependent hepatic phospho-p38 reduction showed engagement and a pathway effect, but only in NASH (PMID:32147362), published after the index trial started and never shown in alcoholic hepatitis. In the index trial, the selonsertib arm had more SAEs (50% vs 40%), more drug discontinuations (18% vs 7.7%) and more deaths (14/50 vs 9/52). This imbalance may have contributed to stopping (F6, secondary), but no source states that reason.

Phase 1 showed dose-proportional PK and pharmacologically relevant exposures against a whole-blood EC50 of 56 ng/mL (PMID:32333325). Selonsertib dose-dependently reduced hepatic phospho-p38 at 6/18 mg in NASH (PMID:32147362). A plasma proteome signature of ASK1 inhibition was seen in DKD patients in MOSAIC (PMID:40375085). All of this was published after the index trial started. The index trial authors blame the eGFR endpoint: an unanticipated drug-induced inhibition of creatinine secretion confounded eGFR at week 48, and post hoc 4–48-week slopes suggested benefit at 18 mg (PMID:31506292). GCP issues at two sites add an execution component. The follow-up MOSAIC trial, which corrected for this, still missed (NCT04026165, PMID:39018154), supporting F2. Proteome effects concentrated in a subgroup support F3.

Phase 1 showed dose-proportional PK, with exposures above the whole-blood EC50 (56 ng/mL) judged pharmacologically relevant (PMID:32333325). In the STELLAR trials, selonsertib produced dose-dependent reductions in hepatic phospho-p38 in NASH patients, read as ASK1 pathway engagement in the target tissue (PMID:32147362). The magnitude of inhibition is not quantified, so engagement is treated as adequate with some uncertainty. Adverse events were similar to placebo and the 18 mg dose was not tolerability-capped. Despite this, there was no effect on fibrosis, liver biochemistry, non-invasive fibrosis tests or clinical events (NCT03053050, NCT03053063), and combinations also failed (NCT03449446). ASK1 inhibition does not appear to drive fibrosis regression in NASH. The engagement evidence was published after the index trial started.

In ARROW (NCT02234141; PMID:34425071), no selonsertib dose (2, 6 or 18 mg) reduced PVR versus placebo, and there was no dose trend. Exposure was adequate: Phase 1 showed dose-proportional plasma PK, and PD data suggested pharmacologically relevant exposures across the dose range (PMID:32333325). Engagement was shown in humans at the same 6 and 18 mg doses in NASH, where selonsertib dose-dependently reduced hepatic phospho-p38, a direct readout of ASK1 activity (PMID:32147362). That evidence comes from liver in another disease, not PAH lung or vasculature, and was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With ASK1 apparently engaged and no benefit in PAH or any other indication, the evidence points to the target not driving PAH as tested. Confidence is medium because engagement was never shown in PAH tissue.

Pillars hold. Human PET showed CNS penetration and projected NET occupancy above 75% at doses over 4 mg (PMID:25522383, before the index trial). In nOH patients at a median dose of 10 mg, plasma NE rose 71% and DHPG fell 22%, consistent with NET inhibition (PMID:33782836). The Phase 2 trial (NCT02705755, registered 2016) showed a seated BP rise in its randomized part (PMID:34657222). Despite this, SEQUOIA (NCT03750552) and REDWOOD (NCT03829657) missed their primary endpoints in a mixed PD/MSA/PAF population. A prespecified MSA subgroup, which has relatively spared peripheral neurons, trended toward benefit (15% vs 40% treatment failure, p=0.11) and met secondary endpoints (PMID:42475649). This points to population heterogeneity. Otherwise the mechanism did not drive benefit across nOH as tested (F2).

Human PET in healthy males (PMID:25522383) showed CNS penetration, with NET plasma EC50 1.21 ng/mL and projected steady-state NET occupancy above 75% at doses over 4 mg. The index trial's 5 and 20 mg doses therefore sit in the high-occupancy range, and popPK including the ADHD trial supports over 75% NET inhibition at 10 mg (PMID:32856281). A pathway marker moved in humans: plasma NE rose and DHPG fell in nOH patients (PMID:33782836), though this is peripheral. No dose limitation; there were no serious AEs on drug. Yet AISRS change matched placebo at both doses (NCT01458340). Engagement data come from healthy volunteers and were published after the index start. Approved NET drugs (atomoxetine) argue against target irrelevance in ADHD, but adequate engagement precludes F1b. F2 by rule, medium confidence.

CLG561 is an intravitreal anti-properdin Fab, so its target is in the eye. In the first-in-human study (NCT01835015; ARVO 2016 abstract), doses of 0.1–10 mg were measured only in serum. Serum drug levels were low, and neither serum properdin nor systemic complement activity changed. The study took no vitreous or aqueous samples, so it gives no human evidence on drug levels, properdin neutralisation or alternative-pathway suppression in the eye. In the Phase 2 trial (NCT02515942), CLG561 alone showed a non-significant trend (−0.29 mm² vs sham, p=0.10), and the combination with LFG316 had no effect. Neither the sponsor nor the reviews gave a reason for the failure. With no data on ocular engagement, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. A small trial of about 36 patients per arm suggests it was underpowered (F7, secondary).

The index trial NCT01598077 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study with a DLT primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. It met its objective: the MTD was not reached and the RDE was set at 40 mg/kg QW (PMID:28899363). Exposure at the RDE exceeded the preclinical minimum effective concentration, and exposure rose with dose in Japanese patients (PMID:27942917). Down-modulation of phospho-HER3 was seen in paired tumor samples, which supports engagement and proximal pathway effect. That evidence came from a mixed tumor population, was not specific to ESCC, and was published in 2017, after the index trial began. Clinical activity was minimal: one unconfirmed PR in 54 patients. This suggests HER3 blockade alone did not drive benefit (secondary F2). No stated stop reason appears in the bundle.

In the healthy-volunteer SAD/MAD study (NCT04106297), Galapagos reported good PK and a dose-dependent ex vivo shift in blood: TNFα fell and IL-10 rose, the dual effect expected from SIK2/3 inhibition. No direct occupancy or kinase-inhibition data exist, so engagement is inferred from this functional readout. These data appeared in the 2020 annual report, after the index trial had started. In UC (NCT04577794), the drug improved objective measures: endoscopic improvement in 7/18 vs 1/9 on placebo, plus histology and fecal calprotectin. Transcriptional changes in patients matched those seen in ex vivo biopsies (PMID:42728025). The 6-week total Mayo score, however, was the same as placebo (-2.6 in both arms per the posted results; the sponsor reported -2.7 vs -2.6). The trial was small (31 patients) and short. The drug was discontinued in March 2022, with no reason given for UC specifically.

LADYBUG (NCT04577781) showed no effect on DAS28-CRP (-1.29 vs -1.24, p=0.885), and GLPG3970 also missed its primary endpoints in UC (NCT04577794) and Sjögren's (NCT04700280). No human measure of SIK2/3 inhibition, occupancy or exposure at the site of action turned up in the bundle. The only Phase 1 human data are Galapagos reports of 'encouraging' PK and PD (ex vivo blood cytokine readouts) in healthy volunteers, and the excerpt I saw was cut off. Treatment-responsive transcript changes in UC patients (PMID:42728025) are downstream pathway evidence from another disease, not RA. The sponsor gave no reason for the failure and moved on to follow-up compounds. Because there is no direct engagement evidence, I can't tell an inadequately engaging molecule apart from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

In the Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study (NCT04106297), Galapagos reported good PK. Blood drawn from dosed volunteers and stimulated ex vivo showed TNFα falling and IL-10 rising with dose. That is the expected SIK2/3 effect, reported in 2020, before the index trial started. This is a functional proxy, not a direct measure of kinase inhibition, and it was never shown in Sjögren's patients. The sponsor terminated the index trial (NCT04700280) early with only 8 vs 5 patients evaluable for ESSDAI (p=0.617), so it could not answer the question. Galapagos dropped GLPG3970 in March 2022 after no signal in RA (NCT04577781) and a null primary endpoint in UC (NCT04577794), turning to next-generation SIK inhibitors. This suggests the mechanism was engaged but gave little benefit (F2). No reason specific to Sjögren's was stated.

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional with once-daily PK (PMID:38988035). Three healthy-volunteer studies using a ketamine challenge (NCT03771586, NCT03770780, NCT03844906) found that SAGE-718 changed ketamine's effects on EEG and resting fMRI brain activity. Sage presented this before 2022 as functional CNS target engagement of the NMDA receptor, and it was well tolerated with no dose cap. That is indirect functional evidence, not occupancy, and it was not shown in PD patients. PRECEDENT (NCT05318937) showed no effect: the WAIS-IV Coding difference was 0.0, p=0.99, and exploratory endpoints did not move either. Sage pointed to PD's distinctive pathophysiology and stopped PD development. This fits F2: NMDA PAM activity does not drive PD cognitive impairment as tested. Because engagement is only functional evidence, U is listed as secondary.

Mitiperstat 5 mg showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:30618054, PMID:39495467). It inhibited MPO in healthy volunteers (>50%, PMID:32770730) and gave a 75% placebo-adjusted reduction in MPO activity at the same 5 mg dose in HFpEF patients (NCT03756285, PMID:37072105), all before the index trial. Engagement was not measured in COPD patients or lung tissue, and no downstream pathway biomarker is shown. The COPD trial (NCT05492877, PMID:42562590) showed no effect on CompEx, exacerbations, FEV1 or symptoms, with numerically more pneumonia. Parallel failures in HFpEF Phase 3 (NCT04986202) and MASH (PMID:41108609) at the same dose support that MPO inhibition does not drive these diseases. Dose was not tolerability-capped below engagement.

Exposure was dose-proportional with a long half-life in humans (PMID:30618054, PMID:32770730). Target engagement was measured directly in HFpEF patients in SATELLITE (NCT03756285, PMID:37072105): 5 mg gave a 75% placebo-adjusted reduction in MPO activity. That trial started in 2018, before the index trial. Healthy-volunteer data show more than 50% MPO inhibition at low nM concentrations (PMID:32770730). A downstream proteomic biomarker profile was reduced in HFpEF patients (PMID:37140510). Tolerability did not cap dosing; rash appeared mainly at 15 mg and above. Despite this, neither 2.5 mg nor 5 mg improved KCCQ-TSS or 6MWD at 16 weeks (NCT04986202). Similar null results in MASH and COPD (PMID:41108609, NCT05492877) support the conclusion that MPO inhibition does not drive the disease as tested.

Mitiperstat 5 mg gives dose-proportional plasma exposure with a long half-life (PMID:39495467, PMID:30618054). At the same 5 mg dose, MPO activity fell by 75% versus placebo in HFpEF patients (NCT03756285, PMID:37072105), and healthy volunteers showed more than 50% inhibition at low nM concentrations (PMID:32770730). That engagement evidence predates the index trial. Engagement was not reported in MASH patients or in liver tissue. In the index trial (NCT05638737, PMID:41108609), 5 mg was well tolerated, yet ALT, Pro-C3 and all other MASH biomarkers were unchanged; the authors concluded there was no proof of concept. Rash at 15–45 mg did not cap the dose below the level needed for engagement. With systemic MPO inhibition adequate and no effect, MPO inhibition appears not to drive MASH as tested. The negative HFpEF Phase 3 (NCT04986202) fits this.

The index trial was not an efficacy failure of itepekimab. Itepekimab 300 mg monotherapy met the primary endpoint, reducing loss of asthma control vs placebo (22% vs 41%, OR 0.42, p=0.02), and improved FEV1, control and quality of life (NCT03387852, PMID:34706171). Only the combination with dupilumab missed (p=0.07). The pillars held in asthma patients. Phase 1 MAD trials, registered before the index trial (NCT02999711, PMID:34523807), showed linear PK, a rise in total IL-33 (target binding) and durable eosinophil lowering. Serum target saturation at 300 mg was later confirmed (PMID:39077906). The bundle does not state why asthma development stopped while COPD advanced. A strategic or commercial reason (F8) is plausible but not shown.

In AD patients from both terminated Phase 2 trials (NCT03736967, NCT03738423), itepekimab showed linear, dose-proportional PK. Total IL-33 data showed saturated serum target binding at 300 mg q2w/q4w, and blood eosinophils decreased (PMID:39077906). Exposure, engagement and pathway were therefore measured directly in disease, though only in serum, not skin. The AD engagement data came from the index trials themselves; earlier engagement evidence was from healthy volunteers and asthma patients (PMID:34523807). The drug was well tolerated, with no dose cap. The same dose worked in asthma (NCT03387852) and in one COPD Phase 3 (NCT04701983). Despite this, EASI change did not separate meaningfully from placebo, and the authors conclude IL-33 may not be a key driver of AD. The target does not drive the disease as tested.

The index trial NCT02295332 was a first-in-human healthy-volunteer study with a safety-only primary outcome, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). That trial showed dose-dependent Lip10 accumulation, confirming cathepsin S engagement (PMID:28769925), and PK was characterised (PMID:33576513). The engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, so it does not predate it. In celiac disease (NCT02679014/PMID:39739628), downstream effects appeared: fewer gliadin-specific T cells, lower intestinal permeability and fewer circulating B and T cells. Target engagement itself was not directly measured there. That trial was underpowered because the gluten-challenge response was weak (F7). The authors still concluded that CTSS inhibition may not be effective (F2), consistent with the Sjögren's failure despite engagement (NCT02701985).

Plasma exposure in humans was characterized by PK modelling (PMID:33576513). First-in-human dosing produced a dose-dependent Lip10 accumulation in antigen-presenting cells, confirming cathepsin S engagement (NCT02295332, PMID:28769925); this was published in 2017, after the index trial started. In the pSS index trial at 100 mg twice daily, soluble biomarkers indicated target engagement in patients (PMID:36864622). Downstream immune effects were weak: B- and T-cell decreases were modest and non-significant. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. ESSDAI response did not differ from placebo (42.1% vs 37.8%, p=0.80), and no secondary clinical endpoint showed benefit. With engagement shown, cathepsin S inhibition appears not to drive pSS disease activity as tested; the celiac study was similarly negative (PMID:39739628).

The index trial NCT06062602 is an early-phase intratumoral microdosing substudy of TAK-676 in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Its primary endpoint is tissue IHC/ISH biomarkers measured 4 hours to 4 days after injection. It is not an efficacy test of fluorouracil in chronic dacryocystitis, or of fluorouracil at all, so F9 applies. In chronic dacryocystitis, PMID:39257076 found that intraoperative 5-FU did not improve endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy outcomes. That study gives no human measure of local exposure, TYMS engagement or pathway effect; its cellular assays are not human pillar data. PMID:27138786 reports plasma PK only in nasopharyngeal cancer, not in lacrimal or nasal tissue. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, engagement is no_human_data, so U would apply.

In the first-in-human study (NCT02462525, PMID:31969330), ABBV-838 showed roughly dose-proportional plasma exposure up to 6.0 mg/kg. The MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no human data on SLAMF7 binding, payload delivery or a pathway biomarker. Efficacy was very limited (ORR 10.7%), and the sponsor made a 'No Go' decision. Another SLAMF7 drug, elotuzumab, is FDA-approved in multiple myeloma, which suggests the target is relevant. That points to the molecule (its epitope or ADC design) rather than the target, so F1b is primary. Engagement was never measured, however, so the call is weak and U also applies. Elotuzumab also acts through a different mechanism (immune-mediated killing rather than payload delivery).

The index umbrella neoadjuvant trial (NCT04586244) gave verzistobart (400 mg Q2W, with retifanlimab and INCAGN02385) to only one patient. Its primary CD8+ biomarker endpoint was analyzed only in the retifanlimab monotherapy arm (n=6, p=0.0925). The trial was terminated for a stated business decision with no safety concerns, so it was not an efficacy test of verzistobart (F9), with a commercial stop (F8). The phase 1 study (PMID:40631773) listed PK and pharmacodynamics as objectives but reported no occupancy or biomarker data. It reported no DLTs and no MTD, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. All pillars lack human data (U secondary). The triplet also failed in HNSCC (NCT05287113), but that does not resolve target versus molecule.

The index trial NCT01071837 posted no results, but several bundle sources describe it as a success. PMID:29453321 says it 'prolonged patient survival' and was 'successfully used', PMID:25850884 says it 'has shown clinical efficacy', and PMID:31679112 reports better quality of life with asunercept plus re-irradiation. Development then continued (NCT02853565, NCT05447195), so the index readout was not shown to be an efficacy failure: F9. Only serum PK is documented (PMID:22446296, PMID:34911992), with no brain or tumor levels, no measured CD95L neutralization and no pathway biomarker. Dosing was well tolerated. A later asunercept arm in the N2M2 umbrella trial missed PFS-6 (PMID:40913172), but that trial is not the index.

Serum E6011 rose dose-dependently and serum total fractalkine rose with it. The sources call this confirmation of target engagement, shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:30575978) and in Crohn patients at 2–15 mg/kg in NCT02039063 (PMID:33599356), a study registered before the index trial. The index trial used 10 mg/kg, which was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. The index trial closed at 25 of 40 planned patients because COVID-19 slowed enrollment. CR100 was 33.3% vs 23.1%, with a wide CI. The authors attribute the inconclusive result to the small sample size and call for further studies (PMID:41323523). That points to F7. F2 is possible given the failures in RA (NCT02960438, NCT02960490), but this readout cannot separate the two.

Serum E6011 exposure rose dose-dependently in healthy volunteers, Crohn's and RA patients. Engagement was shown by a rise in serum total fractalkine, which the healthy-volunteer study states confirms target engagement (PMID:30575978). The Crohn's study saw the same rise at 2–15 mg/kg every two weeks (PMID:33599356), a range comparable to the PBC doses of 10–15 mg/kg. No engagement was measured in PBC patients, and no downstream pathway marker was reported. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. ALP did not move at any dose versus placebo, and the trial stopped for lack of efficacy at interim (PMID:40226574). The mechanism appears not to drive PBC as tested. The authors also suggest that advanced histology (83% Stage 4) contributed, a population/stage factor (F3).

In RA patients, serum E6011 rose dose-dependently (PMID:28681650), so exposure was adequate. Target engagement was shown in humans by a rise in serum total fractalkine, both in healthy volunteers (PMID:30575978; NCT01731275, registered before the index trial) and in Crohn's disease (PMID:33599356). It was not shown in RA. The bundle has no downstream pathway biomarker. The index trial missed ACR20 at week 12, but the 200 mg and 400/200 mg arms reached significance at week 24. Benefit was larger in patients with a high baseline proportion of CD16+ monocytes (PMID:33038062). The sources point to evaluation timing, dose and subgroup; the biologic-IR trial also found effect clearer at higher troughs (PMID:33427546). Because engagement was not shown in RA, F4's biomarker condition is only partly met, so F2 and F3 are listed as secondary.

NCT04505839 was a first-in-human dose-escalation trial with a safety primary endpoint (DLTs), not an efficacy test. Basroparib was well tolerated, and the trial set 360 mg as the MTD/RP2D. Plasma exposure rose less than proportionally with dose up to 300 mg, so systemic exposure was shown. The sponsor collected axin and β-catenin immunohistochemistry, but the pages I could retrieve report no target-engagement or pathway results. Of 17 evaluable patients, 4 had stable disease, and those 4 had higher drug exposure. The investigators concluded the drug warranted further investigation. No stop reason is given. Engagement has no human data, so nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter: U. F9 could also apply, because this was a safety trial.

The index trial NCT03419403 was not an efficacy test of corticosteroids against glioblastoma. It was a supportive-care study comparing steroid regimens, with or without vasoconstrictor and cold compress, for managing ocular side effects of depatuxizumab mafodotin. Its primary endpoint was the percentage of participants needing a change in ocular side-effect management. The trial was terminated because development of depatuxizumab mafodotin in glioblastoma stopped for lack of survival benefit, a failure of the partner drug, not of the steroids. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for this drug at the index doses, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Code F9: the stop was not an efficacy failure of this drug.

Phase 1 studies showed linear, dose-proportional systemic PK with a half-life of about 3 weeks across 1–30 mg (PMID:26449617), so plasma exposure was adequate for a systemic NGF neutralizer. No direct NGF-binding or pathway biomarker was measured. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same doses (up to 10 mg SC Q4wk) met the primary dose-response endpoint in diabetic neuropathic pain (PMID:25008392), a small trial truncated by clinical hold. In chronic low back pain, all regimens up to 10 mg were flat against placebo, and secondary endpoints agreed (PMID:27101815). This suggests NGF blockade did not drive benefit in this population. A placebo effect was noted, so a trial-design contribution (F7) is possible. Confidence is low because the inference rests on one small, truncated trial.

NCT03627065 was a single-arm, open-label study of 10 patients. It gave parsaclisib at 1 mg once daily for 12 weeks (per the protocol). No patient had a ≥1-point change in salivary gland ultrasound score. The only human target-engagement data come from lymphoma patients in CITADEL-101 (NCT02018861). There, ex vivo pAKT inhibition showed that trough levels at 20 mg once daily were above the IC90, 20 times the Sjögren dose. No pharmacokinetic, pAKT or B-cell biomarker data exist at 1 mg or in Sjögren's patients. The 1–2.5 mg AIHA study (NCT03538041) reported only descriptive responses and no formal efficacy endpoint, so it cannot support inferred engagement. Nobody stated why the program stopped. The trial was tiny, uncontrolled and short, with an imaging endpoint, so it could not show whether the drug failed to engage its target or the target does not matter.

Human brain PET in healthy volunteers (NCT02497235, registered 2015, before the index trial) showed CH24H occupancy of 64–96% at 2 h across 50–600 mg (PMID:37770111). This establishes brain exposure and engagement. Multiple dosing at 100–400 mg QD lowered plasma 24HC by 47–63% (PMID:35001412). Pathway is inferred adequate because soticlestat met its seizure-frequency primary endpoint in pediatric DEE (NCT03650452), acting on the same brain target at comparable doses. Engagement was not shown in Dup15q patients specifically; the DEE PK/PD modelling (PMID:38445548) does not cover them. Tolerability did not cap dosing below high occupancy. In ARCADE (NCT03694275), Dup15q seizures rose by a median of 11.7%, so the mechanism appears not to drive seizures here. The trial was a tiny uncontrolled pilot (n=8), which limits the conclusion.

In healthy volunteers, human PET showed soticlestat reached the brain and occupied CH24H at 64-96% at 2 h across 50-600 mg (NCT02497235, PMID:37770111; registered 2015, before the 2019 index start). Plasma 24HC fell dose-dependently, by 47-63% at steady state (PMID:35001412, PMID:33837574). The CRPS regimen of 100-300 mg BID matched the modeled optimal dosing (PMID:37212649), and tolerability did not cap the dose. Engagement was not measured in CRPS patients. Despite adequate engagement, pain NPS did not improve versus placebo (difference -0.34, P=.57), and secondary endpoints were also null (PMID:36538782, NCT03990649). This points to CH24H inhibition not driving CRPS pain (F2). The small proof-of-concept size (n=24) limits power (F7 secondary).

Human brain PET in NCT02497235 (registered 2015, before the index trial) showed CH24H occupancy of 64-96% at 2 h for single 50-600 mg doses (PMID:37770111). This establishes brain exposure and engagement. Multiple dosing at 100-400 mg lowered plasma 24HC by 47-63% (PMID:35001412; PMID:33837574), so the pathway pillar held. PK/occupancy/PD modeling extended these findings to DEE patients (PMID:38445548, published later). Despite this, the single-arm ARCADE pilot (NCT03694275) showed median motor seizure change of +11.7% in Dup15q and -23.6% in CDD. Phase 3 trials in Dravet and LGS also failed (NCT04940624, NCT04938427). This points to the mechanism not driving seizures as tested. The subtype divergence and the small uncontrolled design are secondary contributors.

Phase 1 trials (NCT03817424; Karnell 2021, published before the index trial began in 2022) showed daxdilimab depleted plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), the cells that carry its target, in patients with autoimmune disease. Depletion in blood was dose-dependent. In cutaneous lupus skin, median pDC density fell 87–99% at 50–150 mg every 4 weeks, and skin type I interferon activity fell with it. The alopecia trial gave 300 mg every 4 weeks, a higher dose, with no serious AEs, so tolerability did not limit the dose. Even so, SALT fell only 12.6% (±35) at week 24 in this open-label study (NCT05368103). Engagement was never measured in alopecia areata patients. The best-supported reading is that pDC depletion does not drive alopecia areata as tested. The SLE trial (NCT04925934) also failed despite engagement.

The index LN trial (NCT05540665) was terminated by unspecified sponsor decision after 19 patients, with no CRR values posted, so it gave no interpretable efficacy readout. Human SLE data cited in PMID:40364448 show daxdilimab PK, pDC and IFNα biomarker changes, and an IFN gene-signature reduction at 150 mg (larger than the model predicted). This supports exposure, engagement and pathway effect, though in SLE, not LN, and published after the index trial started. Despite this, the adequately sized SLE Phase 2 missed BICLA (NCT04925934), alopecia areata also failed (NCT05368103), and sibling trials were stopped for sponsor or business reasons (NCT05591222, NCT05430854). The pattern fits a target that does not drive disease (F2), with commercial or underpowered-trial elements for the LN study itself.

The index trial NCT04925934 clearly failed: BICLA at week 48 was 29/69 and 27/69 on daxdilimab vs 25/64 on placebo (p=0.75, 0.99). Human pillar evidence comes only from a 2025 modelling paper (PMID:40364448). It used daxdilimab trial PK, pDC (the depleted target cells) and IFNα biomarker data, implying measured exposure and target-cell engagement, apparently in SLE. Even so, maximum IFN gene-signature reduction was modest (~25%), well below anifrolumab, so the pathway effect looks partial. No dose limitation is shown. Engagement adequacy is inferred, not quantified, and was published after the index trial started. Lack of efficacy in alopecia areata (NCT05368103) is consistent with a mechanism that does not drive disease. F2 is favoured over U, with low confidence.

Human pillar evidence exists, but only from cutaneous lupus (CLE), not COVID-19 lung injury. In the Phase 1 CLE trial (NCT03817424), subcutaneous VIB7734 depleted pDCs in blood and skin, with a 97.6% median drop in skin pDCs, and lowered local type I interferon responses. Sponsor interim data showing this were released in May 2020, before the index trial started in August 2020. PMID:40364448 also notes pDC and IFNα biomarker changes at 150 mg. So engagement counts as adequate and no tolerability cap was reported. Even so, the 10-patient COVID trial NCT04526912 stopped for efficacy futility, which points to F2 (pDC depletion does not drive COVID lung injury as tested). Confidence is low: pDC depletion was never measured in lung or in COVID patients, the COVID dose is not stated, and with n=10 the trial was tiny, so F7 also applies.

Daxdilimab (VIB7734) is an afucosylated anti-ILT7 antibody. In Phase 1 studies in autoimmune patients (NCT03817424; Karnell et al., Sci Transl Med 2021), it rapidly and potently depleted plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), the cells it targets. It also lowered type I interferon responses in skin and blood (PMID:40364448). So exposure, engagement and pathway effects are shown in humans, though only in autoimmune patients. Nothing shows engagement in COVID-19, and these data were published after the index trial started in August 2020. The 10-patient COVID-19 trial NCT04526912 stopped for futility. That fits pDC depletion not changing COVID-19 acute lung injury (F2). However, the trial was very small and posted no results, so trial design or execution (F7) is possible. Confidence is low.

In healthy volunteers, the phase 1 study (NCT03554993; PMID:35982464, PMID:35691544) showed linear plasma PK, measured MK2 binding in PBMCs and sustained ex vivo TNF inhibition. Engagement was therefore shown, though only outside AS. Doses were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. In the index AS trial (NCT04947579; PMID:42167889), ASAS20 at both doses was indistinguishable from placebo (48.8% vs 51.2%/56.1%). MRI inflammation showed trends, but serum pro-inflammatory cytokines were minimally inhibited. That leaves the downstream effect in patients weak. The authors conclude MK2 inhibition was insufficient for clinical benefit, consistent with the mechanism not driving AS as tested. Because the in-disease pathway signal was poor, F1a (inadequate engagement in patients) remains possible.

The index trial NCT00920660 is a single-dose pharmacodynamic study (ex vivo LPS-induced TNF-alpha) in healthy volunteers. It was not an efficacy test of SRT2104 in ulcerative colitis, so F9 applies. The program's actual UC readout (NCT01453491/PMID:26595549) showed dose-dependent exposure, with colonic levels 140-160x plasma, so exposure was adequate. Clinical activity was minimal, and fecal calprotectin stayed about 4-fold above normal. No human measure of SIRT1 activation or engagement exists in the bundle. Lipid changes in elderly volunteers (PMID:23284689) are nonspecific, and there was no dose limitation (PMID:22616762). For the UC failure itself, nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant target, so U is secondary.

In the Phase 1 trials (NCT02618967, NCT03156023), rozibafusp alfa showed dose-related dual-target engagement. ICOSL receptor occupancy exceeded 90% at 210 mg and above q2w, and maximal naive B-cell reduction, the BAFF pathway readout, occurred at 70 mg and above (PMID:37150935, PMID:35899378). Tolerability did not limit the dose. These data, registered before the index trial, informed its dose selection. However, engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers and RA patients, not in SLE. In NCT04058028, SRI-4 response did not separate from placebo, with placebo at 60% and the 420 mg arm at 73%. The adequately engaged dual ICOSL/BAFF mechanism therefore gave no clear benefit as tested. Belimumab's approval in SLE does not support F1b, because engagement was adequate. The high placebo response and small arms point to possible design limits (F7).

The index trial NCT03285178 had only safety primary endpoints (TEAE counts across 2–18 mg and placebo arms) and was classified not_efficacy and not_assessable, so it was not an efficacy test of olinciguat. No stopping reason is given. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement (for example cGMP) or pathway data: the Phase 1 trials (NCT02572349, NCT02792998) posted no results, and the only abstract is from mouse models (PMID:33864386), which does not count. The 18 mg arm showed more TEAEs, but only 2 of 24 discontinued, so the dose was not shown to be tolerability-capped. With engagement no_human_data, any efficacy interpretation would be indeterminate, hence U as secondary. The achalasia trial (NCT02931565) ended for enrollment reasons and adds nothing on pillars.

Exposure: Phase 1 data (NCT01577758, PMID:27178743) showed roughly dose-proportional plasma exposure at the 1.8 mg/kg MTD. The Phase 2 paper says exposure held throughout each cycle. No source measured drug uptake in the tumour, GCC binding or internalisation, or a payload marker in patients. Engagement therefore has no human data. Only 2 of 36 patients responded (both in the intermediate-GCC group), and the stage 1 interim analysis did not support going on to stage 2. The registry gives 'business decision' as the stop reason, but the readout itself failed. Grade 4 neutropenia set the MTD, but no source says this dose was too low to engage the target. Preclinical work (PMID:32788205) points to the payload or molecule rather than GCC, but it is animal data only. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In NCT03238781, neither AMG 301 dose (210 mg Q4W or 420 mg Q2W) beat placebo on monthly migraine days (p≈0.65), and tolerability was good, so dose was not capped by side effects. I found no human pharmacodynamic data for AMG 301: no receptor occupancy, no blocking of maxadilan-induced skin blood flow, and no biomarker. The Phase 2 paper cites only rat data on trigeminal nociception and says the role of PACAP isoforms and receptors needs more study. A PAC1 biomarker using maxadilan skin injections was first tested in humans only after the trial and has not been applied to AMG 301. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged PAC1 apart from a target that does not matter in migraine. F2 is possible but unproven.

PG2 is a polysaccharide mixture from Astragalus root with no recorded molecular target. The bundle and the search found no human data on exposure, target binding or a mechanism-linked biomarker at the 500 mg dose. In the index trial (NCT03314805; PMID:39465324), the change in fatigue score did not differ between PG2 and placebo. Benefit appeared only in a premenopausal subgroup, so F3 is secondary. The abstract does not report the grade 3/4 neutropenia endpoint. A neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio finding in lung cancer comes from a different setting and is not evidence that a target was engaged. Without any engagement data, a drug that never acted cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

PG2 is a crude polysaccharide extract from astragalus root. It has no defined molecular target, and no human PK, brain-penetration or target-engagement data were found. The index trial (NCT01325233; published as PMID 28361971) randomized 61 patients with ICH to 500 mg IV PG2 or placebo. Outcomes at day 84 were numerically better with PG2 but not significant (good GOS 69.0% vs 48.4%, p=0.2; good mRS 62.1% vs 45.2%, p=0.3). The proposed anti-inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) and S100B did not change, so pathway is inadequate. Because engagement cannot be judged, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter. The authors called the small single-centre study preliminary, and it was likely underpowered (F7 secondary).

The index trial NCT02999100 was a Phase 1 pharmacokinetic and safety comparison of inhaled versus IM/IV oxytocin in postpartum women. Its condition was postpartum hemorrhage, not prosopagnosia, and it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated because plasma oxytocin could not be reliably measured regardless of route, including approved IM dosing. That points to an assay or PK-method problem, not a drug efficacy failure, so the code is F9. For the CNS program, PMID:28629540 reports CSF accumulation after intranasal dosing in humans and dose-dependent amygdala modulation.
