The index trial gave 20 mg/kg, the recommended Phase 2 dose, and tolerability did not limit the dose (no MTD was reached). Engagement was never shown in COVID-19 patients, whose Ang-2 levels are high. No downstream marker (e.g., Tie2 signalling or vascular leak) was measured. Ventilator-free days were identical (median 28 vs 28), and the trial stopped for futility at an interim look after 95 patients (PMID:35991210). On the available evidence, Ang-2 blockade did not drive outcomes in this population. The trial was small and stopped early (F7). Confidence is low because engagement was inferred from cancer patients.

The index trial, AVATAR (NCT03941444), was reported by the sponsor as meeting its primary RSBQ endpoint and its secondary endpoints. That was not an efficacy failure, so F9 applies. One caveat: NeurologyLive describes it as a 'new primary end point', meaning the endpoint was changed after the trial was registered. The later failure in the program came from the pediatric trial (NCT04304482), not the index trial. On the pillars, the only receptor-occupancy evidence is mouse PET (PMID:34433831), and Rett efficacy evidence is from mouse models (PMID:31704481). I found no human data on CSF or brain exposure, SIGMAR1 occupancy, or a mechanism-specific biomarker. The sponsor's mention of biomarker changes is vague. If the program is treated as a failure, the cause is indeterminate (U).

Healthy-volunteer PK/PD (NCT02654002, PMID:36573450) showed exposure-dependent FGF19 rise and C4/bile acid suppression, with intestinal FXR activation plateauing above 30 mg; the index trial used 100 mg. In PSC patients, the phase 2 study (NCT02943460, PMID:30661255, published 2019, before the index trial) showed C4 and bile acid reductions plus significant ALP, GGT and ALT reductions at 100 mg, sustained over 96 weeks (PMID:35934287). Pruritus was present but did not cap the dose. Despite adequate engagement and pathway effects, PRIMIS stopped for futility: fibrosis progression was 30.8% vs 32.8% on placebo (NCT03890120, PMID:41173015). The FXR mechanism did not alter fibrosis progression in PSC as tested. Biochemical response not translating to histology supports F4 as secondary.

Phase 1 PK (PMID:32008115) shows dose-proportional plasma exposure at the recommended 200–300 mg bid, with an MTD of 300 mg bid. No direct target-engagement or pathway biomarker exists in humans. Engagement is inferred_adequate only because donafenib showed efficacy in HCC (PMID:34664852; NCT02645981) and met its endpoint early in thyroid cancer (NCT03602495), both through the same systemic kinase targets. Other drugs on the same target (fruquintinib, ramucirumab via KDR; encorafenib via BRAF) are approved in colorectal cancer, so the VEGFR/RAF mechanism does drive CRC. That points to a molecule-specific shortfall (F1b) rather than a target failure, though F2 cannot be excluded. The index trial posted no results or stated reason, so the bundle is thin.

The index trial (NCT04080752, PMID:40215570) used 135 mg daily and showed no separation from placebo on HDRS-17 or HAM-A. Human plasma exposure was dose-proportional up to 90 mg in the single-dose study (PMID:37165642). OX1R occupancy was not measured in humans. The cited 93–98.5% occupancy was extrapolated from rat ex vivo binding and plasma levels, so engagement counts as no_human_data. In healthy volunteers who react to CO2 challenge, 90 mg reduced CO2-induced fear about as much as alprazolam (PMID:32895369). That is a functional central effect, which counts toward the pathway pillar, but nothing was measured in MDD patients. The sponsors gave no reason for the failure. Because engagement is not measured directly, the code is U. F2 is plausible given the extrapolated high occupancy and the CO2 effect.

BI 764198 missed its primary endpoint in hospitalised COVID-19 patients (83.1% vs 87.5% alive and free of mechanical ventilation). The Data Monitoring Committee stopped the trial early for lack of efficacy and an imbalance in deaths (PMID:37024277). The Phase 1 studies show only that plasma levels rose roughly in proportion to dose and that the drug was well tolerated (PMID:40455255, PMID:40402558). The only potency data come from in vitro patch-clamp assays (IC50 14.4 nM). I found no human evidence that the drug reached lung tissue, engaged TRPC6 or moved a downstream biomarker, either in COVID-19 patients or in healthy volunteers. The later FSGS proteinuria result (NCT05213624) is a different disease, kidney podocytes rather than lung, and came after the COVID trial, so it cannot be used to infer engagement here. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that did not engage from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Metyrapone's CYP11B1 inhibition is well documented in humans at gram-level doses. It significantly lowered plasma cortisol (PMID:16814663). It raised ACTH and 11-deoxycortisol (PMID:15163445) and increased precursor neuroactive steroids (PMID:9807647). In cocaine-dependent patients, 2.25 g produced a robust ACTH rise, published in 2001, before the index trial (PMID:11282257). Tolerability did not cap dosing (PMID:15820533, PMID:22236504). Despite this, EMB-001 did not show superiority on continuous abstinence (2/41 vs 0/41, p=0.092; NCT04501874). This points to the cortisol-synthesis mechanism not driving cocaine abstinence as tested. Near-zero abstinence in both arms and the small sample suggest limited power (F7 secondary). No source explicitly states the reason the program stopped.

In patients with advanced solid tumours (NCT03478995), GX-I7 showed dose-dependent Cmax and AUC. It also produced dose-dependent expansion of CD8+/CD4+ T cells and lymphocytes, with an EC50 of 0.066 ng/mL, plus more tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes on biopsy (PMID:40490502, PMID:41127361). Direct receptor occupancy was not measured, so engagement is judged from these strong agonist-driven pharmacodynamic effects. Engagement was not shown specifically in TNBC. Dose was not capped by tolerability: only one DLT occurred, at 1200 µg/kg (NCT04332653). Despite this, the pembrolizumab combination in TNBC and other tumours gave a low ORR of 0–13% (NCT04332653). The index trial (NCT03752723) posted no results. This points to IL-7R-driven T-cell expansion not delivering clinical benefit as tested. The bundle is thin and the trials were single-arm and uncontrolled, hence F7 as secondary and low confidence.

Phase 1 work (NCT05431634; PMID:39604226) showed dose-proportional systemic exposure. It also showed maximal TYK2 pathway inhibition: pSTAT1 suppression and dose-dependent reduction of type I IFN genes and SIGLEC1, with a strong PK/PD relationship. In psoriasis, the drug achieved continuous target inhibition and clear efficacy at 40 mg BID with no dose-limiting safety findings (NCT05600036; PMID:40659116). Engagement was not shown in uveitis patients, and ocular tissue levels were not reported. The index NIU trial (NCT05953688) was stopped at interim for futility. With systemic TYK2 engagement established and tolerability not limiting, the failure points to TYK2 inhibition not driving NIU as tested. No other TYK2 drug has succeeded in uveitis, so F1b does not apply. Confidence is medium because the bundle has no disease- or eye-specific engagement data.

In healthy volunteers, the Phase 1 studies (NCT05431634; PMID:39604226) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and maximal TYK2 pathway inhibition, measured as pSTAT1, Type I IFN genes and SIGLEC1, with a strong PK/PD relationship. In psoriasis, STRIDE (NCT05600036; PMID:40659116) showed continuous target inhibition and dose-dependent efficacy with no dose-limiting toxicity. These studies were registered before the uveitis trial started. No engagement was measured in uveitis patients. The index trial was terminated on interim efficacy that did not meet the sponsor's criteria. That points to TYK2 inhibition not being sufficient in non-infectious uveitis as tested (F2). Brepocitinib has not been approved for uveitis, so F1b does not apply. The small interim readout (n=36) leaves F7 possible.

Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (NCT05431634, PMID:39604226) showed dose-proportional systemic exposure, maximal pSTAT1 inhibition, and dose-dependent suppression of type I IFN genes and SIGLEC1, with a strong PK/PD relationship. Psoriasis phase 2 (NCT05600036, PMID:40659116) showed continuous target inhibition and clear efficacy, with no dose-limiting safety findings. The phase 1 work was registered before the index trial began. Engagement was never shown in uveitis patients, and ocular-tissue penetration is unmeasured. The index NIU trial (NCT05953688) was a small, two-dose comparison without placebo, terminated at interim for futility. With TYK2 well engaged systemically, the failure points to TYK2 not driving NIU as tested (F2). The small, uncontrolled design may also have limited interpretability (F7). Brepocitinib is not approved, so F1b does not apply.

The index phase 1b trial (NCT02549651, PMID:33632668) met its safety primary endpoint, but antitumor activity of durvalumab plus danvatirsen was limited (ORR 6.3%). The bundle shows no measured STAT3 knockdown in DLBCL tumor tissue or in DLBCL patients. PMID:30446007 assessed only peripheral immune cells, with a non-significant trend. The only engagement signal is a truncated 'STAT3 expression tended to decrease' in Japanese solid-tumor patients, published after the index trial (PMID:36270753). That is not a quantitative or disease-specific measure. Plasma PK was reported, but tumor-tissue exposure was not. Dosing reached the 3 mg/kg MTD/RP2D and was not capped below engagement (NCT01839604). With engagement unshown, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged from an irrelevant target, so the code is U. F9 is secondary because the index trial was a safety study that met its primary endpoint.

In the SLE phase 1b (NCT03724916; PMID:38453421), PK was measured and engagement was shown in patients: median CD38 occupancy up to 88.4% on NK cells, with up to 90% NK depletion at 135 mg. The drug was well tolerated, with no grade ≥3 events, so dose was not capped. Healthy-volunteer data (NCT02219256, PMID:32045493) also showed plasmablast and NK depletion. The downstream pathway barely moved: IgG and autoantibodies fell <20%. SLEDAI-2K and CLASI responder rates did not differ from placebo. Engaging CD38 therefore did not translate into benefit as tested (F2). A trend toward skin response in patients with baseline CLASI >10 suggests a subgroup (F3). The trial was small and safety-powered, with 23 enrolled (F7).

Exposure in cirrhosis patients at 1–3 mg BID was dose-proportional (PMID:37889522). Target engagement was shown in healthy volunteers: plasma cGMP rose and blood pressure fell (PMID:38789635; trials registered 2016–17). The drug met UACR endpoints in CKD and diabetic kidney disease (NCT04736628, NCT04750577), supporting systemic engagement. In Child-Pugh A cirrhosis, 2–3 mg BID reduced portal-systemic shunt fraction dose-dependently (PMID:37889522, PMID:38869987), a pathway effect in this disease. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, HVPG reduction versus placebo at 24 weeks was non-significant, and the confidence intervals included zero (NCT05161481), which fits F2. The trend was dose-dependent, the arms had about 27 patients, and the intervals were wide, so an underpowered trial (F7) is a secondary explanation. Related trials were terminated by company decision.

The index ASPEN-05 trial (NCT04755244) was a Phase 1 safety run-in (primary endpoint DLTs). It enrolled 14 patients, posted no results and was terminated only because it 'never moved forward to Phase 2'. The sister MDS study (NCT04417517) ended the same way. No efficacy readout in AML is shown, so this was not an efficacy test of the drug. The termination pattern suggests a sponsor or portfolio decision, but the bundle does not state business reasons. Engagement is adequate in other diseases: PK plus ≥85% complete CD47 occupancy at 10–15 mg/kg in NHL and solid tumours (PMID:40207726, PMID:34793719). It was not shown in AML, and no downstream pathway biomarker is reported. No dose limitation was evident: no MTD was reached in NHL.

Phase 1 studies in MS and solid-tumour patients showed complete peripheral cellular SEMA4D saturation at serum levels of 0.3 μg/mL or below, lasting at least 155 days at 20 mg/kg, with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:28642891, PMID:26446947). These trials were registered before SIGNAL. SIGNAL (NCT02481674) missed its coprimary endpoints (CGIC and cognitive tests) despite good tolerability. The authors cite positive FDG-PET and volumetric MRI findings, plus post hoc early-manifest subgroup results, as rationale for a phase 3 trial (PMID:35941373). These point secondarily to endpoint or population issues (F4/F3). However, brain or CSF exposure and central engagement in HD patients are not shown in the bundle, so the F2 call rests only on peripheral occupancy. Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT04886063 was an open-label safety extension. It was stopped only because its parent trial, LIFT-AD (NCT04488419, PMID:41393340), missed the GST primary endpoint and all secondary endpoints at 40 mg. Plasma exposure was dose-proportional in Phase 1 (PMID:35180125). The same study reported qEEG gamma induction and P300 latency normalization in 7 AD subjects as indirect evidence of brain activity. However, no human measure of HGF/MET binding or MET activation exists in the bundle. The P300 primary outcome of the Phase 2 trial (NCT04491006) shows only baseline values. Dosing was not capped by tolerability. Without direct engagement data, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged MET from a mechanism that does not matter. F2 is possible if the neurophysiology markers are accepted as engagement.

FX-322 (CHIR99021 plus valproic acid) was given by injection through the eardrum. In cochlear-implant patients (NCT03300687), drug was measured in human perilymph, and levels in the high-frequency region of the cochlea were projected to be pharmacologically active. That supports exposure, though only at the cochlear base. No source shows human evidence of GSK3 inhibition, Wnt/β-catenin activation or progenitor activation/hair-cell regeneration in the cochlea. The only early human signal was word-recognition gains in a few people in the small Phase 1b study (NCT03616223). The Phase 2b index trial missed its primary endpoint (14.7% vs 11.1% responders, p=0.525), and the sponsor stopped the program without giving a mechanistic explanation. With engagement unmeasured and no other drug on this target to compare against, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03616223 (Phase 1/2, n=23) had a descriptive safety primary outcome, TEAEs through Day 90. These occurred in 6/7 low-dose, 7/8 high-dose and 5/8 pooled placebo participants, with no deaths or serious AEs. It was classified as not an efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of FX-322, and no tolerability problem appears. The bundle has no human data on intracochlear exposure, GSK3 inhibition or Wnt pathway activation, and no other trials of the drug. The PubMed abstracts are in vitro or animal studies only. If the program's stop were read as an efficacy failure, engagement would be no_human_data and the cause indeterminate (U).

Intranasal GSK2245035 at 20 ng produced clear local and systemic IP-10 increases, an IFN-pathway readout, in healthy volunteers and allergic rhinitis patients (PMID:26044169, PMID:28681506, NCT01607372). This was published before the index trial began. Higher doses (80–100 ng) caused cytokine-release AEs, but the sources treat 20 ng as giving clear target engagement. In the index trial in mild allergic asthma, the authors report target engagement was observed (PMID:33166307). Even so, the late asthmatic response was not attenuated (posterior probabilities 0.385 and 0.303), and type 2 biomarkers (eosinophils, IL-5, FeNO) showed no treatment effect (NCT02833974). With engagement achieved, TLR7-driven IFN induction did not modify allergen-induced asthmatic responses, which points to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested.

ASP8062 30 mg showed no separation from placebo on pain NRS at week 8 (LSM diff 0.06, p=0.59; NCT03092726). Phase 1 data show dose-proportional plasma exposure, ~2-fold accumulation and CSF detection (PMID:31926000). Single 35/70 mg doses produced dose-dependent slow-wave sleep increases and GH release, which the authors read as CNS penetration and enhanced GABAergic activity (PMID:33433644). For a positive allosteric modulator this functional readout is the practical engagement measure, so I graded engagement adequate. PMID:36925215 also states clinical exposures produced pharmacodynamic effects. All of this is from healthy volunteers and was published after the 2017 index start. Sodium oxybate, a GABAB agonist, reportedly helped FM (PMID:31647906) but was not approved. Mechanism engaged, no benefit: F2. Confidence medium because 30 mg sits below the 35–70 mg pharmacodynamic doses.

The index trial NCT04653467 was a Phase 1 single- and multiple-dose study in healthy adults. Its only primary outcome was safety and tolerability (TEAEs, SAEs, discontinuations), so it was not an efficacy test of GLPG4399. It completed with no stated stop reason and no posted results. The bundle has no other trials, no PK, target-engagement or biomarker data, no other SIK3 drugs and no publications. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data. The failure cannot be attributed to the drug or the target, and the halt is best coded F9, with U secondary. Nothing in the bundle shows why development stopped, which may have been strategic, so confidence is low.

Phase 1 data in healthy volunteers (PMID:40520205; NCT03054402, NCT03493269) show good oral plasma exposure. A PK-based model projected about 80% IRAK4 occupancy at 120 mg BID, the maximum feasible dose. That cap came from under-proportional absorption, not tolerability, so dose_limited is false. The same paper cites distinct pharmacodynamic effects in a proof-of-mechanism study (likely NCT05003089, registered before the index trial). These support engagement and pathway effect, though only in healthy volunteers, never in atopic dermatitis patients, and occupancy was modelled rather than measured. At this dose the index trial showed no benefit (EASI-75 32.3% vs 37.4% placebo). This suggests IRAK4 inhibition does not drive atopic dermatitis as tested. The small trial and high placebo response add F7 as a secondary code. Confidence is low because the PD data are not detailed in the bundle.

BLUEPRINT (NCT04693195) tested 200 mg twice daily for 4 weeks and missed its WI-NRS itch endpoint. The sponsor then stopped all work on pruritic conditions. The first-in-human study (PMID:42578597) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure that was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. No human study measured P2X3 occupancy or a biomarker directly. Engagement is inferred because the same 200 mg twice-daily dose significantly cut cough frequency in SOOTHE (NCT04678206), which also works through P2X3 on peripheral sensory nerves. That inference assumes vagal airway afferents are comparable to the skin's itch-sensing nerves, which limits confidence. With the target engaged but no effect on itch, P2X3 likely does not drive atopic dermatitis itch, so F2. U applies if that inference is rejected.

The index trial NCT01774851 was stopped by the DSMB for futility: median PFS was 9.6 weeks with MM-111 vs 23.3 weeks with paclitaxel plus trastuzumab alone. The Phase 1 trials (NCT00911898, NCT01097460, NCT01304784) report tolerability only: MM-111 with trastuzumab and paclitaxel was well tolerated up to 20 mg/kg weekly, so tolerability did not limit the dose. The Phase 1 biomarker analysis looked only at baseline HER2, HER3 and heregulin expression in archived tissue. It could not separate MM-111's contribution from trastuzumab's and gave no human data on drug levels in tumour, receptor occupancy or HER3 signalling. Review sources say only that the trial was halted for lack of efficacy. With no engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. F1b is a weak secondary: trastuzumab works on HER2 in this disease, but MM-111's intended added effect was HER3 blockade.

The index trial NCT00911898 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study. Its only primary endpoint was MTD, posted as NA, so it was not an efficacy test of MM-111. The bundle has no human PK, target-engagement (ERBB2/ERBB3 binding) or pathway (pErbB3) data; the only mechanistic evidence is preclinical (PMID:22248472, PMID:23943608). The related Phase 2 in HER2+ gastroesophageal cancer (NCT01774851) stopped for futility with worse PFS and no safety signals, but it shows nothing about engagement. Many ERBB2-targeted drugs are approved in breast cancer, which hints at a molecule-level problem (F1b). Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter (U). Confidence is low.

The data monitoring committee stopped NCT01774851 early for lack of efficacy. Median PFS was 9.6 weeks with MM-111 versus 23.3 weeks without it, and there were no safety signals. The Phase 1 trials (NCT00911898, NCT01097460, NCT01304784) report MTD, safety and PK in their designs, but none of the sources found shows human evidence of HER3/HRG pathway blockade: no occupancy, no pHER3 suppression and no biomarker change. Engagement is therefore no_human_data, so the code is U. The investigators suggested that heregulin expression was lower than expected in the enrolled patients, which may have contributed to the result. That points to patient selection (F3), but they framed it as speculation. ERBB2 agents (trastuzumab, zanidatamab) work in this disease, but MM-111's distinct HER3 mechanism was never shown to be engaged, so F1b is only a weak secondary code.

The index trial, NCT01304784, was a Phase 1 safety study. Its abstract says MM-111 was safe and feasible with standard HER2 regimens up to 20 mg/kg weekly or 40 mg/kg every 3 weeks. The program then stopped for futility in the Phase 2 gastroesophageal trial (NCT01774851): median PFS was 9.6 weeks on MM-111 vs 23.3 weeks on control, with no safety signals. The human data on record are plasma PK, tolerability and archived-tumor biomarker levels (HER2, HER3, heregulin) linked to outcome. Inhibition of HER3 phosphorylation was shown only in preclinical models. I found no tumor drug levels, target binding or signaling-inhibition data in patients. The biomarker abstract says MM-111's contribution could not be separated from trastuzumab's. With engagement unmeasured, the failure is indeterminate.

HTD1801 (berberine ursodeoxycholate) has no recorded primary target, so no pillar can be measured against a defined target. In the index open-label PBC trial (NCT04604652), patients with an inadequate response to standard therapy took 1000 mg BID and ALP fell by only 7.7% (one-sided p=0.077). The same dose lowered ALP in PSC (NCT03333928), HbA1c in T2DM (NCT06411275) and LDL cholesterol (PMID:33183320), but no common target or tissue compartment links these to PBC, so inferred adequacy can't be claimed. My search found no human PK, target-engagement or biomarker data in PBC, and no sponsor statement on why the program failed. Because engagement is no_human_data, a drug that never engaged can't be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter in PBC.

In the index trial NCT02279719, amcasertib plus sorafenib gave an objective response rate of 0%, against 9.7% for sorafenib alone. Phase Ib showed no DLTs at the 100 mg recommended Phase II dose, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The phase 1 abstracts I found (ASCO 2014, 2015 and 2017) call amcasertib a multi-kinase 'stemness' inhibitor acting through Nanog. They report no human PK at the site of action, no STK33 inhibition and no pharmacodynamic biomarker change. Nanog was used only to select patients in a colorectal cancer extension study. No other drug on STK33 has succeeded, and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Engagement has no human data, so the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter. The code is U. The small, open-label randomized phase II also limits what the trial could show.

Exposure: the first-in-human trial (NCT01781455; ASCO 2014 abstract) gave doses from 10 to 450 mg once daily and reported that plasma levels rose with dose, which supports systemic exposure. Engagement: amcasertib has no single defined target. It is described as a multi-kinase 'stemness kinase' inhibitor acting on Nanog. I found no human data on kinase inhibition, Nanog lowering or a downstream biomarker. Nanog suppression appears only in cell lines (PMID:37891391). The index trial (NCT02432690) stopped after 13 patients with no stated reason and posted no primary results. No other drug on the same target exists to compare against. The bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT02232633, was a single-arm Phase 2 study in hepatobiliary cancer measuring disease control rate. It posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. The Phase 1 dose-escalation study (NCT01781455) gave 10–450 mg daily to patients with solid tumors. The pages found describe the drug as a multi-kinase 'stemness' inhibitor said to suppress Nanog. They show no human data on drug levels, STK33 or kinase inhibition, or Nanog or other biomarker changes. The drug did no better in hepatocellular carcinoma (0% response rate with sorafenib, NCT02279719). No other drug on the same target is in the bundle, and no source explains why the program failed. With no human engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02259595 is a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study of HPN-07 with or without NAC in hearing loss. Its primary outcome is adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of NAC (F9). In the actual HCM program, the HALT-HCM pilot (NCT01537926, PMID:29540445) found small effect sizes on hypertrophy and fibrosis. Plasma PK of NAC is documented (PMID:3803419). Glutathione rises were shown only in other diseases and tissues (PMID:39756697, NCT01427517). No human data show myocardial oxidative-stress lowering or downstream pathway change in HCM. An unengaged drug therefore cannot be separated from an irrelevant mechanism (secondary U). Evidence for efficacy comes only from animal models (PMID:16487852, PMID:19255346).

No molecular target is recorded. Human PK shows systemic exposure after oral dosing, with about 6–12% bioavailability (PMID:3803419, PMID:34833436). The mucolytic and antioxidant mechanism has been shown to work in humans. NAC met a sputum-viscosity superiority endpoint in respiratory mucus disease (NCT03843541) and holds a COPD approval. It also raised glutathione in patients (PMID:39756697, NCT01427517). Engagement and pathway are therefore inferred_adequate in the airway compartment, though the index trial's dose and route are not shown. Despite this, objective cough counts in common cold were numerically worse with NAC than placebo (NCT02379637). A related acute rhinosinusitis trial also failed (NCT04123405). This suggests the mechanism does not drive cough in acute viral infection. Confidence is low because no target-specific engagement data exist, which leaves U as an alternative.

No molecular target is recorded; the mechanism is mucolysis. Human plasma PK exists (PMID:3803419, PMID:34833436), with low oral bioavailability. No sinus-tissue or nasal-mucus data in humans; the nasal mucus effect is in vitro only (PMID:9932596). Engagement is inferred_adequate: NAC is FDA-approved for COPD as a mucolytic and met a sputum-viscosity endpoint at 600 mg BID in respiratory tract disease (NCT03843541), the contiguous airway-mucus compartment at comparable doses. In NCT04123405, all three doses (600–2400 mg) were numerically worse than placebo, with no dose response and no tolerability cap. An earlier subacute sinusitis RCT was also negative (PMID:28122105). This suggests mucolysis does not drive symptom resolution in acute rhinosinusitis. Because there is no direct engagement evidence in sinus tissue, U remains plausible.

The index trial NCT01109381 was a small, single-arm, open-label test of GT08 (omeprazole 40 mg, NAC 1.2–2 g and lauric acid daily). Only 2 of 31 patients cleared H. pylori, and the trial was stopped for poor efficacy. NAC has no recorded molecular target. Here its intended action was to break down biofilm and mucus in the stomach. No source shows, in humans, NAC levels in gastric mucus, biofilm disruption, or a lower bacterial load in this disease. Systemic NAC data (oral bioavailability 6–10%, PMID:3803419; brain glutathione rise, NCT01427517) do not apply to a gastric target. No other drug on the same target is listed. Without engagement data, we cannot tell whether the drug failed to act or the mechanism does not matter, so the code is U.

In the phase 1 solid-tumour study, published in 2018 before the index trial, M7824 saturated peripheral PD-L1 and sequestered plasma TGFβ1-3 throughout dosing at >1 mg/kg, with no MTD reached (PMID:29298798). This is adequate engagement, though not shown specifically in NSCLC. 89Zr-PET later showed tumour-specific uptake in NSCLC (PMID:41462000). The 1200 mg dose was chosen by modelling (PMID:37165943). Yet against pembrolizumab, PFS was 7.0 vs 11.1 months and OS 21.1 vs 22.1 months (NCT03631706). Exposure did not predict tumour dynamics in NSCLC (PMID:38087967). The stage III NSCLC trial was stopped for futility (NCT03840902). Adding a TGF-β trap gave no benefit, and sources suggest TGF-β is not the dominant barrier (PMID:42336657). More serious AEs, including on-target bleeding (PMID:36066618), suggest partial toxicity offset.

The phase 1 trial (PMID:29298798) showed that M7824 saturated peripheral PD-L1 and sequestered plasma TGFβ1-3 at doses >1 mg/kg. The MTD was not reached, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. This evidence predates the index trial but comes from mixed solid tumors, not TNBC. Tumor uptake was later shown by 89Zr-PET (PMID:41462000). No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. The index TNBC trial (n=11) stopped because the sponsor judged the probability of success too low, and its primary endpoint was not assessable (F7 secondary). That judgement fits program-wide failures with adequate engagement (NCT03631706, NCT04066491, NCT03840902). PMID:42336657 attributes the inconsistent benefit to TGF-β not being the dominant barrier and to a need for population selection, which supports F2 with F3.

No human pharmacokinetic, receptor-occupancy or direct engagement data were found for TC-6499. However, there is functional evidence that the mechanism acted on the gut. In Phase 1, the drug increased GI motility (vomiting and/or diarrhoea), per the HRA summary. In the index trial NCT01149200, a 4-week, single-site study of 24 IBS-C patients, TC-6499 beat placebo on spontaneous bowel movements per week, an objective downstream effect. It missed only the subjective primary endpoint, global symptom relief. So a proximal or functional effect was shown in this disease, but the patient-reported endpoint failed in a very small exploratory trial. That points to F4, with F7 (underpowered) as a secondary code. The sponsor did not directly state why the program stopped. The later gastroparesis study (NCT02187094) also missed its primary endpoint.

Index trial NCT02187094 tested single doses of TC-6499 (simpinicline), a nicotinic receptor agonist, in diabetic gastroparesis. Targacept reported that it missed its primary endpoint: change in gastric emptying half-time on the 13C breath test versus placebo. The bundle and search results contain no human data on drug exposure, nicotinic receptor engagement, or any downstream biomarker. No posted Phase 1 results or PubMed abstracts were found, and the IBS-C trial (NCT01149200) has no results. No other drug on the same target is listed, so F1b does not apply. Because nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index FCS trial (NCT03360747) was single-arm with n=3. Fasting TG fell 33% on average (SD ±32), reported descriptively with no statistical test, so the trial could not answer the efficacy question. In other populations, vupanorsen showed plasma exposure, dose-dependent ANGPTL3 lowering (56% at the same 20 mg weekly dose; up to 95% at higher doses) and TG reductions (PMID:32860031, PMID:35369705, PMID:37002654, PMID:38949758). However, ANGPTL3 lowering was not shown in FCS patients, and the published evidence appeared after the index trial started. The 20 mg weekly dose fell short of the a priori 75% ANGPTL3 target (PMID:37170423). The bundle gives no stated stop reason. The modest TG effect in FCS may also mean the mechanism adds little in this disease (F2).

The index trial NCT03514420 was an open-label, single-arm proof-of-concept study in only 4 FPLD patients. It was not a controlled efficacy test. Its primary biomarker moved favourably: fasting TG fell 59.9%. Exposure is adequate: plasma PK was characterised in humans (PMID:37002654, PMID:38949758). Engagement is adequate and was shown in FPLD itself, with ANGPTL3 down 54.7%. The pathway pillar is adequate (TG -59.9%, VLDL-C -53.5%; PMID:34865644). This is consistent with the significant TG and ANGPTL3 reductions at the same 20 mg QW dose in NCT03371355 (PMID:32860031). The disease-specific engagement data come from the index trial itself, so they postdate its start. No efficacy failure is shown, and the bundle gives no reason for stopping. Hence F9, with F7 for the n=4 uncontrolled design.

The index trial NCT02749630 was a Phase 1b safety study with an adverse-event primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. PMID:36732049 reports acceptable safety and exposure, IL-22 serum biomarkers and colonic IL-22-responsive genes induced, and favorable exploratory remission (5/18 vs 0/6). That is not an efficacy failure. Exposure, engagement (REG3A, on-target skin effects) and pathway activation were shown in healthy volunteers and UC patients (PMID:29952004, PMID:36732049, PMID:39694207). None of this was in chronic skin ulcer patients; the diabetic foot ulcer trial NCT02833389 posted no data. Dose-limiting skin AEs occurred only at 90 µg/kg every 2 weeks, above doses already engaging the target. Separately, the UC Phase 2 (NCT03558152) failed despite engagement, supporting F2 as secondary.

The index extension study (NCT03650413) was terminated because the parent Phase 2 trial NCT03558152 showed low efficacy. In that trial, remission was 9–12% across 30–90 µg/kg arms versus 9% on placebo and 26% on vedolizumab (PMID:39694207). Exposure was dose-proportional in UC patients (PMID:36732049, PMID:37864000). In the Phase 1b study (NCT02749630, registered 2016), IL-22-responsive genes in colon biopsies and serum biomarkers were induced, confirming IL-22R pathway activation in the colonic epithelium of UC patients. Phase 2 showed dose-dependent REG3A/CRP increases and on-target skin AEs. The dose-limiting toxicity occurred only at 90 µg/kg every 2 weeks. The Phase 2 regimen still achieved dose-dependent engagement, so the dose was not capped below engagement. With engagement and pathway effect adequate and no benefit, IL-22 agonism does not drive UC as tested.

Efmarodocokin alfa (IL-22Fc agonist) had dose-proportional systemic exposure. Healthy-volunteer and UC studies showed dose-dependent increases in the IL-22R biomarkers REG3A, SAA and CRP, and induction of colonic IL-22 genes (PMID:29952004, PMID:36732049, PMID:39694207, PMID:37864000). In the index COVID-19 trial, the authors state that biomarkers demonstrated the drug was pharmacologically active in patients (PMID:36519984). Yet time to recovery was not improved (HR 1.15, p=0.36) and key secondaries showed no benefit (NCT04386616). There was no tolerability cap at the tested dose and no new safety signal. The trial was adequately sized (n=396), with no subgroup or design attribution. With engagement and pathway activation shown, the failure points to IL-22 agonism not driving recovery in severe COVID-19 pneumonia. In-disease engagement data came only from the index trial itself. Lung tissue levels were not shown.

In the index trial NCT02709109, VX-371 at 85 µg twice daily did not improve ppFEV1, with or without hypertonic saline. I found no human data on lung exposure, ENaC block (for example, nasal potential difference) or mucociliary clearance. The healthy-volunteer clearance study NCT01793649 was terminated and posted no results. The 14-day CF study NCT02343445 showed only that the drug was well tolerated, with no FEV1 effect. The PCD result in NCT02871778 was only nominal, so it does not support an inferred_adequate rating. PMID:38851923 suggests the clinical doses were too low, which points toward F1a, but that comes from a sheep model and does not count as human evidence. The sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U.

The index Phase 1b psoriasis trial (NCT04119557) had a safety primary endpoint (related SAEs). PMID:39455575 reports that REZPEG was safe and well tolerated with consistent PK at 10–24 µg/kg Q2W, meeting its primary objectives, so this was not an efficacy test that failed. Exposure was shown by dose-proportional PK. Engagement and pathway effects were shown by dose-dependent 12–17-fold selective CD25bright Treg expansion in healthy volunteers and SLE patients (PMID:35517914; NCT04133116, NCT03556007, registered before the index trial). Treg expansion specifically in psoriasis patients is not shown in the bundle. Psoriasis efficacy is not reported while AD efficacy is highlighted, so a weak psoriasis signal leading to deprioritization (F2) is possible but not shown.

Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers and SLE patients (NCT04133116, NCT03556007; PMID:35517914) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure, a long half-life and dose-dependent, selective 12–17-fold expansion of CD25bright Tregs, with no dose-limiting toxicity. Systemic exposure, engagement and the proximal pathway effect were therefore adequate, though shown outside UC. Those trials were registered before the index trial started. The UC index trial (NCT04677179) was terminated for enrollment futility with very small arms (14 placebo patients) and wide confidence intervals, so it could not answer the efficacy question. That makes F7 primary. The lack of any signal at the high dose, together with the failed SLE Phase 2 (NCT04433585), also supports F2: Treg expansion did not translate into benefit.

In the phase 1 SAD and MAD studies (NCT04133116; NCT03556007, which enrolled SLE patients and was registered in 2018 before the index trial), NKTR-358 showed dose-proportional PK with a long half-life. It produced dose-dependent, selective, sustained 12–17-fold increases in CD25bright Tregs without changes in conventional T cells, and was well tolerated with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:35517914). Exposure, engagement (IL-2R agonism read out by selective Treg expansion) and the pathway effect were therefore adequate in SLE. Even so, NCT04433585 showed no dose-response or separation from placebo on the SLEDAI-2K primary endpoint at any dose. Ulcerative colitis also failed (NCT04677179). Treg expansion via this mechanism did not translate into SLE benefit, supporting F2. The full results were published only in 2022, after the index trial started.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: In Phase 1 (NCT01222637/PMID:29464112), tomuzotuximab showed dose-proportional PK similar to cetuximab, with no MTD reached, so dosing was not limited. Frequent skin toxicity (73%) and hypomagnesaemia (39%) are classic on-target EGFR-blockade effects in humans, supporting engagement. These data came from mixed solid tumours, not specifically HNSCC. The bundle has no human evidence that the glyco-engineered ADCC enhancement translated into a pathway effect. The index trial (NCT02052960/PMID:34482179) tested superiority over cetuximab, an active EGFR comparator, and PFS was identical (HR 1.000, p=0.86). With EGFR engaged and dose not capped, the added Fc-enhanced mechanism produced no clinical benefit over standard EGFR blockade in this setting. This fits a mechanism that does not drive improved outcome, not a molecule that failed to engage.

Gatipotuzumab missed its primary endpoint in NCT01899599/PMID:34920291. Median PFS was 3.5 vs 3.5 months (HR 0.96), with no subgroup benefit, and the drug was well tolerated. The Phase 1 trial (NCT01222624, Fiedler 2016) found no maximum tolerated dose, and the 1700 mg Q3W dose used in the index trial reached the target plasma trough of at least 50 µg/mL in 80% of patients. I rate exposure adequate on plasma levels only, since no tumour drug levels were reported. The sources contain no human data on binding to TA-MUC1 in tumours, ADCC activity, or downstream biomarkers, and the sponsors gave no mechanistic reason for the failure. Without engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Phase 1 (NCT03676322, PMID:34414672) showed dose-proportional PK and exposure-dependent inhibition of ex vivo TLR7/8-stimulated cytokines. PK/PD modelling (PMID:35390178) chose 50/100 mg BID for COVID-19, with near-complete target coverage at 100 mg. In COVID-19 patients from this trial, enpatoran lowered NFKBIZ and altered neutrophil counts (PMID:40397760), but that disease-specific evidence was published after the index start. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The primary endpoint (time to recovery) was missed. The authors attribute this to placebo patients recovering faster than anticipated (median about 3.4 days), so the trial could hardly discriminate (PMID:37873555). Deterioration secondaries favoured drug and the authors point to hyperinflammatory patients (F3). F2 remains plausible given adequate engagement.

No human PET occupancy or pathway data were found. The PRD paper only mentions the 60–80% occupancy generally needed, not a measurement for KW-6356. Exposure and engagement are rated inferred_adequate because the Phase 2b adjunct trial in PD (NCT03703570) met its primary endpoint, showing the drug works through the A2A receptor in the striatum. That inference is loose because it comes from the same disease, not another one. In the index monotherapy trial (NCT02939391, PMID:37948832), both doses beat placebo numerically at every visit, but the trial was small and the result was not significant. Kyowa Kirin said it dropped KW-6356 for non-clinical reasons, describing it as effective as monotherapy and as an add-on. So the stop was a business decision, not a failed mechanism (F8). The index trial being underpowered (F7) is a secondary factor.

In the index NSCLC trial (PMID:34552864), citarinostat plus nivolumab reached an MTD of 360 mg. DLTs occurred at 480 mg. Patients showed increases in tubulin and histone acetylation, the HDAC6 substrate readout, so engagement was shown in disease. In the paclitaxel study (PMID:35070991; NCT02551185), PK was linear to 360 mg and PBMC tubulin acetylation peaked at that dose. Together these support adequate exposure and engagement at the dose used. The acetylation was described as transient and was measured in surrogate blood cells, not tumor, so partial engagement (F1a) remains possible. No downstream immune or pathway biomarker was reported. The program was halted for lack of efficacy despite this engagement. The trial was a small single-arm dose-escalation study, which limits any conclusion about efficacy (F7).

In the index gMG trial (NCT05218096; PMID:42043793), pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data showed that vemircopan, at the doses tested, cut mean serum alternative pathway (AP) hemolytic activity to below 10% within 2 hours of the first dose. Reports of the trial describe this as substantial AP inhibition and confirmed target engagement, measured in patients with this disease. That supports exposure, engagement and pathway all being adequate. Even so, response rates on vemircopan (57% at both doses) did not beat placebo (64%), and no secondary endpoint differed. The trial was stopped because it missed the minimal efficacy threshold. So, as tested, blocking factor D and the AP did not drive benefit in AChR-Ab+ gMG (F2). The 8-week trial was small, with only 14 patients on the 120 mg dose, so F7 is a secondary code. The engagement data came from the index trial itself, not before it.

In PNH patients, vemircopan 120–180 mg BID raised Hgb by about 3.3–3.6 g/dL in treatment-naive and eculizumab-switch cohorts, so the primary endpoint was technically met (PMID:41124654). This shows some alternative-pathway inhibition in the disease. However, the trial was terminated for suboptimal, inconsistent control of intravascular hemolysis: 82 breakthrough IVH events in 25 of 29 participants, and more BTH and LDH >2x ULN excursions than with ravulizumab (NCT04170023). This points to incomplete or inconsistent factor D blockade, so the mechanism was not adequately tested. No human PK or factor D inhibition data appear in the bundle. Tolerability did not cap the dose. F9 is secondary because the primary Hgb endpoint was met.

In NCT02605967, spartalizumab 400 mg Q4W lost to chemotherapy on PFS (1.9 vs 5.6 months). Human engagement at the same 400 mg dose is shown only outside NPC: PD-1 occupancy rose on peripheral T cells and activated CD8+ T cells increased (PMID:40010764, published 2025, after the index trial began). On-treatment CD8+ infiltration was seen in tumour biopsies (PMID:32179633). No MTD was reached and there were no DLTs, so the dose was not capped. The bundle reports no PK values, so exposure is no_human_data. With engagement adequate, F2 fits: PD-1 blockade alone did not beat chemotherapy as tested. Nivolumab's listed NPC approval argues against the target being irrelevant, so F1b is noted. Confidence is low because the engagement data come from another disease and are qualitative.

Human PK shows dose-proportional systemic exposure across 100–900 mg with a ~20 h half-life (PMID:41014112). No direct GR occupancy or engagement biomarker is reported. In healthy men, 600 mg attenuated olanzapine-induced weight gain and blunted insulin, HOMA-IR and transaminase rises (NCT03877562, PMID:34369902). This is a pharmacodynamic signal suggesting the target was engaged at the index dose, but it comes from healthy volunteers, not patients. In obese patients with established antipsychotic-associated weight gain, 600 mg did not change weight at 12 weeks (NCT03818256), and 600 and 900 mg did not at 26 weeks (NCT04524403). GR modulation may prevent acute weight gain but not reverse established obesity (F2/F4). Because engagement is only inferred from healthy volunteers, U remains plausible.

In the index trial, NCT02427464, the drug missed its primary endpoint (pain change -1.80 vs -1.57 on placebo). A later Phase 3 trial, NCT04469270, also missed. None of the sources measure HGF expression in muscle or nerve in humans, or a downstream biomarker. The Phase III paper describes only a short-lived, mostly local HGF rise, so engagement counts as no_human_data and no other HGF drug gives a comparison. First, VM202 plasmid DNA found in placebo samples raised fears of a drug mix-up. After its review, Helixmith said there was no mix-up. It blamed the pain measure and how the trial was run (F7), pointing to the positive 3-1B extension. NCT04469270 then failed as well, so the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter: U.

The index trial NCT05450198 was a completed Phase 1 multiple-rising-dose study whose only primary endpoints were adverse events and discontinuations. It was not an efficacy test, and its results show no efficacy failure or limiting toxicity (2/54 serious AEs). In healthy volunteers, PK was dose-proportional and MK-6194 produced dose-dependent, selective Treg expansion up to about 5-fold (PMID:40139976, PMID:42752454), so exposure, engagement and pathway were shown, though not in atopic dermatitis patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle gives no stated reason for ending atopic dermatitis development. The sibling programs NCT06113328 and NCT06161116 were terminated for business reasons, which suggests a portfolio decision rather than a failed atopic dermatitis readout.

The index UC trial NCT04924114 was a Phase 1 study whose only primary endpoints were adverse events and AE-related discontinuations. No efficacy outcome was posted, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Tolerability was acceptable: few discontinuations and no deaths. In healthy volunteers, PK was dose-proportional, and dose-dependent, selective Treg activation and expansion reached about 5-fold with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:40139976, PMID:42752454). This shows exposure, engagement and pathway, but not in UC patients, and the publications postdate the index start. Later Phase 2 trials in vitiligo and SLE were terminated for 'Business Reasons' (NCT06113328, NCT06161116), suggesting a portfolio decision rather than a UC efficacy failure.

In the MS multiple-ascending-dose study (NCT02601885, registered 2016, published PMID:36093738), elezanumab up to 1800 mg IV gave dose-proportional plasma exposure and dose-dependent CSF levels, with 0.1–0.4% penetration, typical for mAbs. CSF free RGMa fell by >40%, with an apparent maximal effect at 1800 mg, and CSF IL-10 rose with exposure, supporting pathway modulation. The index trial used 400 and 1800 mg monthly, was well tolerated (no dose cap) and showed no ORS benefit. The relapsing trial (NCT03737851) also missed, consistent with a mechanism that does not drive MS disability as tested. Residual doubt: >40% is only partial CSF neutralization, and penetration was low, so under-engagement (F1a) cannot be fully excluded.

The index trial NCT00972725 was not an efficacy test of chloroquine against HIV disease. It was a small (n=28) descriptive immunogenicity and safety study testing whether a single chloroquine dose modifies CD8+ T-cell responses to the GSK732461 HIV candidate vaccine. Results are descriptive counts (1/13 vs 3/13 CD8+ responders) with no statistical comparison, and the primary endpoint was classified not_efficacy and not_assessable. No stop reason or safety signal was recorded (0 SAEs). The bundle has no human data on chloroquine exposure, target engagement or pathway effects in HIV, and no primary target is recorded. The related trial NCT00819390 posted no results. The trial therefore does not represent an efficacy failure of the drug.

Index trial NCT04344951 was a small (n=29), open-label, non-randomised Phase 2 study. It stopped for 'no clinical efficacy' and posted no results. The bundle records no defined molecular target. The only antiviral evidence is in vitro and in hACE2 mice (PMID:33639976), which does not count. My searches found no human data showing chloroquine reached antiviral levels in the lung, blocked endosomal acidification, or lowered SARS-CoV-2 viral load in patients at the doses used. The Norwegian viral-kinetics RCT studied hydroxychloroquine, a different drug, so it does not settle chloroquine's pillars. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter in COVID-19, so the code is U. The uncontrolled design and small size also limit what the trial can show (F7, secondary).

HIMALAYA (NCT05237284, PMID:42716044) tested oral SAR443820 20 mg BID versus placebo and missed its ALSFRS-R primary endpoint (LS mean difference -0.41, p=0.53). Part B CAFS was also negative (p=0.18). The drug is described as CNS-penetrant. A healthy-volunteer study (PMID:38010108, NCT05795907) reports brain penetration and target engagement, which supports exposure and engagement, though the bundle gives only the title and no levels. Engagement was not shown in ALS patients. The publication postdates the index trial's start. No proximal pathway biomarker was reported in ALS. In MS, serum neurofilament light did not move (NCT05630547). No dose limitation is evident. With the RIPK1 mechanism engaged yet no benefit, F2 fits best. Confidence is moderated because the engagement magnitude is not visible in the bundle.

EDP1815 is a gut-restricted, non-colonizing bacterial strain with no defined molecular target. No human measure of target engagement exists, and by design it has no systemic exposure (PMID:37215725). The best pathway evidence is the KLH challenge study in healthy volunteers. It reported anti-inflammatory imaging trends, but a Leiden thesis says the humoral and skin-challenge results were not statistically significant, so the pathway pillar is weak or inadequate. The parent AD trial NCT05121480 missed EASI-50, with placebo numerically better than all active arms. Evelo blamed an 'unusually high placebo response' for cohorts 1–3. Cohort 4 also failed, and Evelo dropped EDP1815 in AD. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U, with trial design/execution (F7) as secondary.

EDP1815 is a gut-restricted, non-live preparation of Prevotella histicola. It has no defined molecular target, and there is no systemic exposure (PMID:37215725), so the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. The sponsor mentioned cytokine biomarker improvements, but did not quantify them. In the index trial NCT04603027, the primary endpoint (percent change in PASI) was not met; all credible intervals included zero. Only the secondary PASI-50 endpoint reached significance (PMID:38813388). Evelo called the results positive and said it was moving toward registration studies, and the program later stalled amid company-level setbacks: the NCT05121480 atopic dermatitis trial failed, and the company began exploring strategic alternatives. With engagement unmeasurable, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. F8 is listed as possible because the stop may have been driven partly by business reasons.

Receptor engagement was never measured directly. Pathway evidence: a 2020 Phase 1b in ET patients given 45 or 60 mg reported a 'clear PK/PD relationship', and Sage's 10-K names EEG beta power as the functional biomarker. KINETIC (NCT04305275/PMID:38357797) met its endpoint at 60 mg in ET with GABAergic AEs (somnolence, dizziness), so engagement is inferred adequate. That is same-disease evidence, not another-disease efficacy as the label strictly requires. In KINETIC 2 (NCT05173012), no dose beat placebo at Day 91 and the 60 mg arm got numerically worse. Placebo response was high (-2.53 vs -1.24 in KINETIC). Only 13 of 33 on 60 mg were analysed, which hints at tolerability attrition. No one stated a mechanism. Primary F2; F7/F5 secondary.

XT-150 is an IL-10v plasmid injected into the joint. In NCT04124042, neither dose beat placebo on WOMAC pain at Day 180, and placebo did slightly better. The facet-joint trial NCT05196919 also failed. The sources I found have no human data showing the plasmid was expressed: no IL-10v levels in synovial fluid or tissue, and no change in downstream cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6). The OARSI 2021 abstract supports its dose choice with the Phase 1 studies and the preclinical MABEL estimate. The ACR 2023 abstract only reports a post hoc benefit of two doses over one and does not explain the failure. No other IL-10 drug is in the bundle. With engagement unmeasured, the sources cannot tell apart a drug that was never expressed from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

XT-150 is a plasmid meant to make cells in the joint produce an IL-10 variant. In the index trial, NCT05196919, neither dose reduced facet-joint pain more than placebo (p=1.00 and p=0.99). The knee osteoarthritis Phase 2 trial, NCT04124042, also failed. The index trial's analysis plan (SAP) says IL-10 protein and plasmid DNA levels would be measured, but I found no published results. No source shows human evidence of transgene expression, IL-10 levels in the joint, or any change in downstream inflammatory markers. Efficacy claims come only from dogs and horses, which do not count. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With no human engagement data, nothing separates a drug that failed to express IL-10 from a target that does not matter for this pain. The code is therefore U.

XT-150, an IL-10 gene therapy, missed its VAS pain endpoint in facet joint pain (NCT05196919). Both doses were numerically worse than placebo, and placebo response was large (-42 points). An earlier Phase 2 in knee osteoarthritis also failed, again numerically favouring placebo (NCT04124042). The Phase 1 trials posted no results (NCT03282149, NCT03477487). The bundle contains no human data on transgene expression, local IL-10 levels or downstream anti-inflammatory biomarkers. No other IL-10 drugs and no PubMed abstracts are included. Tolerability was clean, so the dose was not capped. Because engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates absent expression from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U. The high placebo response and heavy missing data at Day 270 point to F7 as a secondary factor.

NCT02479802 was a 13-patient, open-label, single-arm pilot with no comparator, so its primary efficacy result cannot be judged. In the published paper (Springer, 2021), plasma albumin rose from 42.7 to 49.45 mg/mL with exchange, a sign of exposure and target replacement in ALS patients. Albumin's fatty-acid binding and the lipid peroxidation marker 8-isoPGF2α both changed after each session, so a pathway effect was seen. These effects were transient and were published only after the trial started. ALSFRS-R and FVC kept declining. The authors say the study was not powered for efficacy and its results are preliminary. The follow-on single-arm study NCT02872142 was also only descriptive. Design limits explain the failure best (F7). An ineffective mechanism (F2) is possible but untested.

The index trial NCT01843894 tested topical RU-101 (albumin eye drops) in severe dry eye. Its registered primary outcome was ocular adverse events, it is classified not_efficacy, and no results were posted, so the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout. The bundle has no human data on ocular-surface exposure, engagement or a pathway biomarker. The approved and effective systemic uses (cirrhosis, ACLF in NCT03702920, Alzheimer's plasma exchange in NCT01561053) are a different compartment and route, so they cannot support inferred adequacy for a topical ocular product. No other drugs on this target are shown. The trial was not an efficacy test (F9). If it is treated as a failure, engagement is unknown (U).

IVIG (0.2 and 0.4 g/kg) was stopped because the first Phase 3 (NCT00818662) missed both co-primaries (ADAS-Cog, ADCS-ADL). The index trial (NCT01524887) also showed no benefit. The proposed mechanism is anti-amyloid antibodies and immunomodulation (PMID:25186799), but the bundle has no human evidence of brain or CSF penetration, amyloid binding, or Aβ change. The Octagam Phase 2 plasma Aβ1-40 biomarker (NCT00812565) was posted only descriptively, with no comparison. Approvals in CIDP, MMN and ITP act through peripheral immunomodulation, not a CNS amyloid target, so they cannot support inferred engagement. Tolerability was acceptable, so the dose was not capped. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

IVIg (2 g/kg over 4 days) was tested in chronic DCM with endomyocardial B19V persistence (NCT00892112). The intended mechanism is antibody-mediated neutralisation and clearance of cardiac B19V. PMID:33347677 shows circulating B19V antibodies rose after IVIg, so systemic exposure was achieved. However, cardiac B19V load did not fall more than with placebo, so the antiviral effect at the tissue target was not achieved. LVEF improved similarly in both arms (P=0.609), and 6MWT, MLHFQ and LVEDV did not differ. Because the drug did not lower the viral target in the heart, the hypothesis that clearing B19V improves cardiac function was not properly tested. No other drugs share the target, and no dose-limiting toxicity was reported.

In the index trial (NCT00892112), IVIg 2 g/kg over 4 days raised circulating anti-B19V antibodies in DCM patients with cardiac B19V persistence (PMID:33347677). That shows adequate systemic exposure. The intended effect, clearing virus from the myocardium, was not shown: reduction in endomyocardial B19V load did not differ from placebo. Target engagement at the tissue site was therefore not achieved, and LVEF, 6MWT, MLHFQ and LVEDV were all unchanged versus placebo. No human evidence before the trial showed that IVIg clears cardiac B19V, and no other drug on this mechanism succeeded. The mechanism was not properly tested at the site of action. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Confidence is medium because whether antibodies can reach intracellular persistent virus at all is inferred.

Octagam 10% is pooled IVIG with no recorded molecular target. It was tested as a non-specific immunomodulator in severe COVID-19. The index trial (NCT04400058) did not meet its primary endpoint: 89/105 patients stabilized or improved on Octagam vs 82/102 on placebo, and deaths were numerically higher (13/105 vs 6/102). A separate high-dose IVIG trial in ICU patients (NCT04480424) also showed no mortality benefit. My search found no human pharmacodynamic or immunomodulatory biomarker data for COVID-19 patients, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. IVIG's approvals rest on immunological mechanisms in other diseases, which are not the same mechanism or compartment tested here. Because there is no engagement evidence, nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U. F2 is plausible.

No target is recorded for IVIG (Panzyga). The proposed mechanism in PANS, immune modulation of basal ganglia autoimmunity, has no human measure in the bundle: no CSF IgG, no autoantibody lowering and no biomarker. Approvals in CIDP, MMN and ITP cannot support inferred_adequate engagement, because no shared target or compartment is defined. In NCT04508530 (n=71), CY-BOCS improved 31.1% on drug vs 12.1% on placebo, with very wide SDs (one-sided p=0.072). CGI-I was significant (p=0.017). The investigators suggested the OCD-specific primary endpoint missed the broader disease burden (possible F4). The small sample and noisy placebo response point to F7. Nothing separates an untested mechanism from an irrelevant one, so the code is U.

In the index NPC trial (NCT02759250; PMID:34405542, PMC full text), cusatuzumab at 5 mg/kg Q3W gave plasma levels similar to earlier studies (Cmax 123 µg/ml, Ctrough 12.6 µg/ml), so exposure was adequate. No study measured CD70 binding, occupancy or depletion in humans, so engagement is no_human_data. The pathway marker, serum and urine soluble CD27, did not change from baseline to cycle 3 (p=0.56), so pathway is inadequate. Tolerability did not limit the dose; no MTD was reached (PMID:28765328). Patients were enrolled regardless of tumour CD70 status. The investigators suggested tumour CD70 may have been too low in EBV-low patients, which points to patient selection (F3). With only 11 patients, the trial was very small (F7). Nothing here separates a drug that failed to engage CD70 from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Neither the sponsor nor the investigators gave a reason the ESCC program stopped. In the index trial (NCT02013154), DKN-01 was given at 300 mg with paclitaxel. Serum drug levels were measured, so exposure counts as adequate. Engagement was not measured directly: the assay could not tell free DKK1 from drug-bound DKK1. Instead, a target-mediated disposition model estimated that free DKK1 fell with dose. That model used data from NSCLC, myeloma and biliary cancer patients, not ESCC. In the biliary study (NCT02375880), the investigators concluded that 300 mg added no benefit and that a higher dose or intensity was needed. Model results implied lower free DKK1 at higher exposure, so later trials used 600 mg. This points to incomplete engagement at the index-trial dose, so the code is F1a. Confidence is low because the engagement evidence is modeled. No ESCC biomarker data were found.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: In the HNSCC window study (NCT02473731, registered 2015, before the index trial; PMID:31308059), 1,000 mg CDX-3379 reached target trough serum levels in all patients. Tumor pErbB3 fell in 10 of 12 patients and by at least 50% in 58%, meeting the prespecified pharmacodynamic objective, so exposure, engagement and the proximal signaling effect were shown in this disease. In the index phase II with cetuximab (NCT03254927; PMID:35625959), ORR was 6.7%. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related AEs occurred in 53%, mainly diarrhea and acneiform rash, which fit on-target ErbB toxicity, and 70% needed dose modification. The authors say the modest ORR plus excessive dose-limiting toxicity precluded development, so F5 is primary. F2 applies given weak efficacy despite engagement, and F3 for the FAT1-mutant subgroup signal.

The index trial NCT05682170 (Phase 1/2, azenosertib combined with ZN-d5 in AML) had only safety and dose-limiting-toxicity primary endpoints. It was terminated for an unspecified 'Sponsor decision' and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test and no failed efficacy readout is shown. The bundle has no human pillar data in AML. PMID:40231599 reports only preclinical pY15-CDK1 reduction and preliminary solid-tumor activity, which do not count as human engagement or pathway evidence. Because engagement is no_human_data, U applies as a secondary code. The sponsor decision may reflect business reprioritisation (F8), but the bundle does not state this. The toxicity concerns cited in another trial (NCT06351332) are not linked to the AML program.

The index trial NCT02562573 was a small (n=24) Phase 2 study whose primary outcome was safety and tolerability (adverse events and abnormal labs), classified not_efficacy. It was not an efficacy test of fezagepras in metabolic syndrome, and no results were posted. The bundle has no human data on exposure, FFAR1/GPR84 engagement, or pathway biomarkers, so a mechanistic failure cannot be separated from a target that does not matter. Other trials ended for recruitment (NCT02955888) or COVID-19 (NCT03184584). Overall development stopped after initial pharmacokinetic results in a hyperammonemia healthy-volunteer study (NCT05349435), not after an efficacy failure in this disease.

The index trial NCT02562573 was a small (n=24) Phase 2 study whose only primary outcome was safety and tolerability (adverse events, abnormal labs). It was not an efficacy test, and no results were posted. PMID:30477455 describes the completed T2DM study as supportive of anti-inflammatory activity, not as a failure. The bundle has no human PK, FFAR1/GPR84 engagement or pathway data. Development was later dropped after initial PK results in a healthy-volunteer hyperammonemia study (NCT05349435), which was a different indication. Because engagement was never shown, U applies secondarily: nothing in the bundle separates a non-engaging drug from an irrelevant target.

The index trial NCT05349435 was a Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study comparing fezagepras with sodium phenylbutyrate. It was framed for hyperammonemia, and its primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, so it was not an efficacy test. The sponsor stopped development 'based on initial pharmacokinetic results'. Those PK data are not shown, so whether exposure was inadequate cannot be confirmed; F1a is possible only as a secondary code. The bundle has no human target-engagement or pathway data for FFAR1 or GPR84. The Alström Phase 2 trial (NCT02739217) has only a protocol publication (PMID:30477455). The rollover study (NCT03184584) ended because of COVID-19. No efficacy failure is documented.

The index trial NCT02739217 was a single-arm, open-label Phase 2 study of 800 mg/day with a descriptive safety primary outcome (PMID:30477455). No results were posted, so it was not a failed efficacy test of fezagepras. The Alström rollover NCT03184584 was terminated because COVID-19 redeployed site staff. Development ended when the sponsor discontinued fezagepras after initial PK results in an unrelated healthy-volunteer hyperammonemia study (NCT05349435). The bundle has no human data on exposure, FFAR1/GPR84 engagement or pathway biomarkers, so mechanism adequacy cannot be judged. If this were treated as an efficacy failure it would be indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT02538536 was a 12-week open-label study with a safety/tolerability primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. PMID:30578394 reports that 800 mg was well tolerated. FVC was stable with PBI-4050 alone or with nintedanib, and the authors called this encouraging. PK was measured but its adequacy was not judged, and exposure fell with pirfenidone. No human FFAR1/GPR84 engagement or pathway biomarker data appear in the bundle. Development continued in other indications. The sponsor discontinued fezagepras after initial PK results in a healthy-volunteer hyperammonemia study (NCT05349435), not because of an IPF efficacy failure. Since engagement was never shown, a target-level question would be indeterminate (U).

Human plasma PK is characterized (PMID:38329646, PMID:37357226; NCT02837237 in CKD), so exposure is adequate. MR occupancy was never measured directly. Engagement and pathway are inferred because the Phase 2b BLOCK-CKD trial (NCT03574363, PMID:33966452) met its SBP endpoint at 0.25 and 0.5 mg in stage 3b/4 CKD. That is the same population and doses, and the result was published before the index trial started. Small potassium rises are consistent with MR blockade (PMID:37471468). The tolerability cap was not limiting. Despite this, the Phase 3 index trial on the same SBP endpoint stopped at interim futility (NCT04968184), which fits F2 by the rules. The bundle gives no explanation for the discordance with Phase 2b. Trial execution, such as placebo response, remains plausible but unshown, hence the F7 secondary and low confidence.

Engagement was measured directly in humans. In sepsis patients (PMID:30747773, published 2019, before the index start in 2020), BMS-936559 at 900 mg gave full PD-L1 receptor occupancy for 28 days, and monocyte HLA-DR rose at the highest doses. Exposure and pathway activity are also supported indirectly: socazolimab met an overall-survival endpoint in ES-SCLC (NCT04878016), so systemic PD-L1 blockade held there. Engagement was not shown in esophageal cancer. The index trial (NCT04460066) has no posted results and no stop reason. Given adequate engagement and no shown benefit, F2 is the default code. Confidence is low because the bundle does not actually document the failed readout or why the program stopped.

In the index HS trial (NCT04856930), AN count change at Week 16 did not differ from placebo at either dose (p=0.78, p=0.29), and there was no excess of serious AEs, so neither tolerability nor dose capping explains the miss. No human PK, occupancy or biomarker data are in the bundle. However, imsidolimab met its Phase 3 endpoint in generalized pustular psoriasis (NCT05352893) and its Phase 2 GPP endpoint (NCT03619902, started 2019). That is the same IL-36R target in the same skin compartment, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate. The dose comparison is only approximate: 300/750 mg in GPP versus 400/200 mg in HS. The drug also failed in palmoplantar pustulosis (NCT03633396) and acne (NCT04856917). This pattern suggests IL-36 signalling does not drive HS as tested.

In the acne index trial NCT04856917, neither the 400/200 mg nor the 200/100 mg arm beat placebo; placebo numerically did better (p=0.38 and 0.62). The bundle has no direct human PK, IL-36R occupancy or biomarker data. However, imsidolimab met its primary endpoint in GPP (Phase 3 NCT05352893, 300 and 750 mg; Phase 2 NCT03619902). That is the same IL-36R target in the same skin compartment at broadly comparable doses, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Safety was unremarkable, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. Similar null results in PPP (NCT03633396) and HS (NCT04856930) suggest IL-36 signalling does not drive acne. No engagement data in acne patients exist.

The bundle has no direct human PK, occupancy or biomarker data. Imsidolimab met clinical endpoints in generalized pustular psoriasis: single-arm Phase 2 NCT03619902, and Phase 3 NCT05352893 (GPPPGA 0/1 in 8/15 on 750 mg and 8/15 on 300 mg vs 2/15 on placebo). That is the same IL-36R target in the same skin compartment, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. The bundle does not give the index-trial dose, so dose comparability is assumed. In palmoplantar pustulosis, PPPASI change was identical to placebo (p=0.944), with no tolerability limit. No same-target drug succeeded in this disease; spesolimab stopped at Phase 2. So the IL-36 pathway does not appear to drive palmoplantar pustulosis as tested. Phenotypic divergence from GPP (F3) is possible but not stated by the sources.

Reloxaliase is an oral oxalate decarboxylase that degrades dietary oxalate in the GI lumen. Its effect is shown in humans. It significantly lowered urinary oxalate in healthy volunteers on a high-oxalate diet (PMID:27529510), and it met a Phase 3 urinary oxalate surrogate endpoint in enteric hyperoxaluria (NCT03456830, P=0.004). Gut exposure and engagement are therefore inferred adequate, and the pathway effect is adequate. No evidence shows engagement in primary hyperoxaluria patients. In primary hyperoxaluria the oxalate is made by the body, so degrading dietary oxalate plausibly does not drive plasma oxalate there (F2). The index trial mixed enteric and primary patients (F3). The index trial posted no results and the bundle states no reason for stopping, so confidence is low.

Human plasma pharmacokinetics at comparable oral doses (20–60 mg) show systemic exposure of this peripherally restricted D2 antagonist, despite about 22% bioavailability (PMID:2206785, PMID:8799530, PMID:9010988). The bundle has no D2 occupancy or downstream biomarker data in gastroparesis. The 1988 motility study used IV dosing in healthy volunteers and is not a validated D2 readout (PMID:3218950). Index doses of 5–20 mg QID stayed below the tolerated 30 mg x6 level, so the dose was not capped. Metoclopramide, which acts on the same D2 target, is FDA-approved for gastroparesis, yet NG101 has no engagement evidence, which fits F1b. Secondary nausea PGIC improved and trends favoured idiopathic patients (PMID:40367443), suggesting a population effect (F3). Without engagement data, U also applies.

NGM282 did not correct hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes, which the sponsor called unexpected (PMID:30862680, NCT01943045). The bundle has no direct exposure or target-engagement measure in diabetic patients. Engagement is inferred adequate: the same FGFR4/KLB hepatic mechanism produced a rapid, robust liver-fat reduction in NASH (NCT02443116, primary met, p<0.001 at 3 and 6 mg). In healthy volunteers, 7 days of dosing raised HDL-C by 26% (PMID:30679232), so the hepatic pathway responded in humans. The drug therefore engaged its liver target, yet glucose did not improve. FGF19-pathway agonism does not drive glycemic control in human T2D as it did in mice. This engagement evidence came after the index trial started and is not from diabetic patients.

Aldafermin produced clear dose-dependent downstream FGF19-pathway effects in humans. In NASH patients, NCT02443116 (started 2015, before the index trial) showed significant liver-fat reduction at 1, 3 and 6 mg. In healthy volunteers, HDL-C rose 26% (PMID:30679232). The bundle has no direct occupancy or exposure data, so engagement is judged adequate from these pharmacodynamic effects. No tolerability cap is shown: AEs were similar to placebo and the 3 mg dose was used. Yet ALPINE 2/3 (NCT03912532, PMID:35325622) missed the fibrosis-improvement dose response at 24 weeks. ALPINE 4 in cirrhosis also failed its ELF endpoint at 48 weeks (NCT04210245). Engaging the pathway did not translate into an antifibrotic benefit. The short 24-week duration may also have contributed (F4).

In the PSC index trial, aldafermin 1 and 3 mg significantly lowered serum C4, a marker of hepatic CYP7A1 activity (p=0.008 and p<0.001). That shows FGFR4/KLB engagement in patients with this disease (PMID:30414864). Serum bile acids, especially hydrophobic species, fell in a dose-dependent way (PMID:33898959), and ELF and Pro-C3 fibrosis markers improved. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore adequate. GI adverse events were mostly mild, with no dose cap. Even so, ALP was not changed (p=0.434 and p=0.646; NCT02704364). Suppressing bile acid synthesis did not relieve the cholestasis that ALP tracks, which points to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested (F2). The fibrosis-marker gains suggest ALP over 12 weeks may have been an ill-suited endpoint (F4). This engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself, not from before it.

Crenigacestat showed dose-proportional plasma exposure in humans (PMID:30539232, PMID:30060061). At 45-100 mg it inhibited plasma Aβ by about 80% and Notch target genes (HES1, cyclin D1, NRARP) by more than 50% (PMID:30060061), with tumor pharmacodynamic effects (PMID:32915419). In the T-ALL index trial (NCT02518113, PMID:33107983), plasma Aβ fell at the 75 mg MTD, a dose within the engaged range, so engagement was shown in this disease. That evidence was published only after the index trial started in 2015. Even so, only 1 of 36 patients responded, and that was at 50 mg. Despite adequate γ-secretase/Notch engagement, there was no clinical benefit, pointing to the mechanism (F2). On-target Notch gastrointestinal toxicity capped escalation at 125 mg (PMID:34121974), so F5 is secondary.

In NCT05074498, a one-month course of weekly TB006 1000 mg did not reach significance on CDR-SB (p=0.084). The sources show plasma pharmacokinetics only. Galectin-3 acts in the brain, but I found no CSF or brain drug levels, no measure of how much galectin-3 the antibody bound or neutralized, and no galectin-3 biomarker in humans. The sponsor reported that plasma Aβ42 fell, but that is a loosely linked downstream claim and does not show target engagement. The extension study NCT05476783 was terminated for 'Resource Constraints'. The trial was short and small, which limits what it could show. Engagement has no human data, so the sources cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter.

Plasma exposure at 2.5–5 mg was shown in healthy volunteers, with dose-proportional PK (PMID:36734627, PMID:38156730). There is no human receptor occupancy or bladder biomarker data; M3 binding and bladder selectivity are preclinical only (PMID:30502343). The Phase 2 effect was modest: 5 mg gave -1.67 vs -1.01 micturitions/24h for placebo, p=0.04 (PMID:35793990). Higher doses were only moderately tolerated (PMID:36734627), but the bundle does not show a dose cap below the level needed for engagement.
