CHRM3 antagonism is validated in OAB by several approved drugs (solifenacin, darifenacin, fesoterodine, others). A failure of index trial NCT05282069 therefore points to this molecule, not the target (F1b). However, results are unposted and no stop reason is given, so the trial-design explanation (F7) cannot be excluded.

Index trial NCT04465916 showed no HBsAg decline with EYP001a plus nucleos(t)ide versus control at week 16 (-0.029 vs -0.066 log10). It had no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No pharmacodynamic or FXR engagement data in HBV patients are in the bundle, and the Phase 1 HBV pharmacology trial (NCT03272009) posted no results. Engagement is inferred_adequate only because vonafexor met its primary endpoint in NASH (NCT03812029, PMID:36334688) at 100–200 mg/day, with liver fat, enzyme and cT1 improvements through hepatic FXR, the same liver compartment. That NASH result was published after the index trial started. The index dose is not given in the bundle, so the inference is weak and the alternative is U. Hepatic FXR agonism apparently does not lower HBsAg.

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT02454842) in EGFR-mutant, T790M-negative NSCLC stopped for lack of efficacy and posted no results. The bundle has no Phase 1 results and no PubMed abstracts, so there is no human evidence on exposure, EGFR/HER2 engagement or pathway effects. Several other EGFR inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, dacomitinib, osimertinib) are approved in NSCLC, so the target works in this disease. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b), with nothing showing that tarloxotinib engaged adequately. A head-and-neck trial (NCT02449681) also failed for futility, and a later NSCLC trial (NCT03805841) gave low response rates (0–13.6%). Because engagement is unmeasured, U also applies. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The index trial (NCT02449681, PMID:35435625) stopped for lack of efficacy: ORR 3%, median PFS 2.0 months at 150 mg/m2 weekly. The bundle gives no human PK, tumor activation of the hypoxia-activated prodrug, or EGFR/ERBB2 engagement or pathway data. Treatment was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by toxicity. EGFR as a target is validated in a close disease: the bundle lists cetuximab as approved in nasopharyngeal and salivary gland carcinoma. That points to the molecule rather than the target, since prodrug activation and engagement were never shown. Tarloxotinib also failed in EGFR-mutant NSCLC (NCT02454842) and had low ORR in NCT03805841, where other EGFR drugs succeed. The evidence is indirect, so U is a secondary code.

The index single 2 mg/kg SC dose missed week-4 ΔCDAI. It separated by week 12 and in biologic-naive and high-CDAI subgroups (PMID:27489241), which points to timing and subgroup effects. The follow-up TRIDENT trial (NCT02877134, PMID:36939629) showed modest benefit and no dose-response. PopPK/E-R analysis in CD patients found full peripheral NKG2D receptor occupancy at all doses and concluded the inadequate efficacy was unlikely due to exposure or engagement (PMID:37060327). That CD engagement evidence postdates the index trial. The RA Phase 1 measured occupancy earlier (NCT00927927), but no results are shown. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported, and tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement adequate and benefit absent, the target does not appear to drive CD as tested.

The RA index trial (NCT01181050) gave 4.0 mg/kg, the top multiple dose tolerated in the RA first-in-man study (NCT00927927). It showed no DAS28-CRP difference versus placebo (-0.02, p=0.93). NCT00927927 tracked receptor occupancy but posts no values. PopPK and receptor-occupancy analysis in Crohn's disease showed full peripheral NKG2D occupancy at all doses (50–400 mg SC, comparable to 4 mg/kg). The authors concluded the lack of efficacy was not due to insufficient exposure or engagement (PMID:37060327). That evidence comes from another disease and was published after the index trial, and no downstream pathway biomarker is shown. With engagement adequate and no tolerability cap, NKG2D blockade appears not to drive RA activity as tested.

NCT01147458 was stopped early after a serious adverse event. The sponsor said hepatic enzymes rose, that a link to the drug could not be excluded, and that this could change the benefit-risk balance. The program stopped because of a safety signal from this molecule, not because of a completed efficacy failure. Plasma drug levels at 600 mg twice daily were measured in 10 patients. They were roughly 500–1100 ng/mL, which looks above the whole-blood IC80 reported in PMID:20378715, but the sources do not say this level was sufficient. No human evidence shows the drug inhibited 5-LOX: the planned urinary LTE4 test was never run. So engagement is no_human_data. The WOMAC pain result was a non-significant trend (p=0.067) in a trial that was cut short and underpowered. Whether the mechanism works in this disease is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT02279641 was not an efficacy test. It was a 12-subject Phase 1 drug-interaction PK study of RDEA3170 plus allopurinol in gout, with PK/PD primary endpoints. It reported plasma allopurinol and oxypurinol exposure and no efficacy failure. Its link to the tuberculosis program is incidental; the only TB study (NCT02700347) was a healthy-volunteer whole-blood bactericidal assay with no reported outcome. Human pillars are shown in gout before the index trial: oxypurinol exposure, dose-dependent XDH inhibition, and serum urate lowering (PMID:23590252, PMID:26451524, PMID:10583019, PMID:28417592). No engagement was shown in TB patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The readout therefore tells us nothing about efficacy in TB.

In the index trial (NCT02719028), no antroquinonol dose (50–150 mg) lowered triglycerides more than placebo. The only human pharmacology is plasma PK from the NSCLC Phase 1 study (PMID:26807250, NCT01134016). That study found a short half-life of 1.3–4.3 h and recommended at least 600 mg daily, far above the index doses. Tolerability did not limit the dose: there were no DLTs up to 600 mg. The evidence for FTase/GGTase inhibition (the Ras prenylation shift) comes only from cell and animal studies (NCT02047344 protocol, ACS Cent Sci). I found no human measurement of target enzyme inhibition or of a lipid-pathway biomarker, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. No other drug on the same target exists for comparison, so the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter here.

Oral dersimelagon reached plasma exposure that rose roughly with dose. Multiple 150–300 mg doses raised skin melanin density, the expected MC1R pharmacodynamic effect (PMID:37060458). The EPP phase 2 met its endpoint through the same skin MC1R mechanism (NCT03520036), which supports adequate engagement in the skin compartment. That evidence comes from healthy volunteers and EPP, not dcSSc, and was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Despite this, the 52-week ACR CRISS was essentially identical to placebo (0.854 vs 0.850; NCT04440592), suggesting MC1R agonism does not modify dcSSc as tested. The small analysed sample (25 vs 33) is a minor design caveat. Confidence is medium because engagement in dcSSc itself was not shown.

Human PK showed linear plasma exposure and good tolerability up to 1,250 mg (PMID:24337978), but brain penetration and brain APA inhibition were never measured in humans. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate only because firibastat met its BP-lowering primary endpoint in hypertension (NCT03198793) through the same central target at comparable doses (500 mg bid). That inference is weakened by the null pilot (PMID:30882604) and the futility-terminated phase 3 (NCT04857840). In the index trial, LVEF gains were similar to ramipril at both doses, with similar safety (PMID:36757536), so central APA inhibition gave no added benefit post-MI. The lack of a placebo arm limits interpretation (F7). Evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

Phase 1 showed dose-proportional plasma GS-441524 and intracellular active triphosphate in PBMCs, and supported 350 mg BID without tolerability limits (PMID:38940465). In the index BIRCH trial this dose reduced viral RNA and infectious titer versus placebo in COVID-19 patients, so the RdRp mechanism was engaged with a downstream virologic effect (PMID:40694627). However, the trial was stopped because so few events occurred (0% vs 0.5%) that no significant effect was possible. Authors call it underpowered in a changing landscape with 92% seropositive patients (NCT05603143, PMID:40694627). The failure is therefore primarily trial design and execution. The hard endpoint was unanswerable despite the proximal antiviral effect (secondary F4). The symptom endpoint was also narrowly missed in low-risk patients (NCT05715528).

In the index trial (NCT02834247; PMID:38501219), mivavotinib plasma exposure rose roughly in proportion to dose from 60 to 100 mg. The recommended phase 2 dose of 80 mg sits near the single-agent maximum tolerated dose of 100 mg (PMID:32327472), so tolerability did not hold the dose down. Exposure is therefore adequate for a systemic target. The paper says it studied pharmacodynamics, but no human results for SYK or FLT3 engagement (pSYK/pFLT3 inhibition) or for myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) changes appear in any source I could read. The pSYK, pFLT3 and MDSC data come only from mouse models, and the full text was blocked. Nothing reports engagement in ovarian carcinoma (NCT03756818). Single-agent responses in lymphoma do not show engagement of the immunomodulatory mechanism in solid tumours. The expansion stopped for futility with 0% response in TNBC. A drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Exposure is adequate. The phase 1 study (PMID:32327472) shows dose-related plasma exposure at 60–120 mg, with an MTD of 100 mg, the dose used in the index trial. The full text says SYK and FLT3 inhibition in lymphoma patients could not be assessed, and no human SYK engagement or pathway biomarker data exist for DLBCL. FLT3 inhibition (plasma inhibitory assay) was shown only in AML (Haematologica), and FLT3 is not the relevant target in DLBCL. Single-agent ORR of 28–38% in phase 1 (PMID:36702329) hints at activity but does not count as measured engagement. ORR was higher in non-GCB patients than GCB (58% vs 28%), so patient selection (F3) may have played a role. No other SYK drug has succeeded in DLBCL, so F1b does not apply. Engagement is no_human_data, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT02834247, PMID:38501219), plasma exposure was dose-proportional at 60–100 mg, and the RP2D of 80 mg was not limited by tolerability. A plasma inhibitory assay in the AML phase Ib (PMC9973464, published after the index start) showed FLT3 inhibition, which was sustained at ≥90% in some patients, though best with BID dosing. That is engagement shown in another disease. Direct SYK engagement in solid tumors was not measured. In paired TNBC biopsies, macrophages fell, and circulating monocytes also dropped. This matches the immunosuppressive-cell reduction the preclinical rationale predicted, though the authors called it unanticipated. Even so, TNBC ORR was 0% and the expansion stopped for futility. On this evidence the target does not drive disease as tested, but the engagement evidence is indirect, so U remains plausible.

The index trial NCT05579431 is a first-in-human Phase 1 study whose only primary outcome is safety and tolerability (AEs/SAEs to Day 20). It enrolled participants in Parts A and B, with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as the listed condition. It was not an efficacy test of VX-634. The bundle has no posted results, no stated stop reason, no other trials, no PubMed abstracts and no same-target comparators. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. The stop cannot be attributed to an efficacy failure of the drug, so F9 is the primary code. U is a secondary code because engagement is unknown and nothing separates the possible explanations. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

Human exposure is adequate: NYX-2925 crossed the blood-brain barrier, with CSF Cmax about 6-9% of plasma, and was well tolerated up to 1,200 mg (PMID:30242962). In fibromyalgia patients (NCT03249103, started 2017, before the index trial), 20 and 200 mg reduced Glx/tCr in the dACC and posterior insula and altered pain-network connectivity (PMID:42610093). That registry classed this as target engagement, so central NMDAR engagement and a pathway effect are shown in this disease. Engagement was inferred from that functional readout, not measured directly. Yet the 310-patient index trial at 50 and 100 mg showed no pain benefit (p=0.54, p=0.43). Two diabetic neuropathy trials also failed (NCT03219320, NCT04146896). The mechanism does not appear to drive pain as tested. Baseline insular Glx predicted response, which hints at heterogeneity (F3).

Exposure: the first-in-human study showed dose-proportional plasma PK and CSF levels at 6-9% of plasma, with no tolerability limit up to 1,200 mg (PMID:30242962). CNS engagement and pathway effect rest only on the fibromyalgia trial NCT03249103, where 20 mg lowered dACC Glx/tCr (p=0.032; classified as target engagement). That 20 mg dose falls within the index range of 10-200 mg. That evidence comes from fibromyalgia, not DPN, and started after the index trial. Despite this, the index trial showed no dose-response on NRS pain (NCT03219320), a 12-week DPN trial failed (NCT04146896), and a fibromyalgia efficacy trial failed (NCT04147858). This suggests the mechanism does not drive pain as tested. No direct receptor-level engagement data exist, so U remains plausible.

The index trial, NCT03415126, was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study (finding the maximum tolerated dose, plus an expansion arm measuring response rate) and posted no results. I found a 2019 conference abstract on Phase 1 safety and efficacy and an Erasca release with a program update for ERAS-007, but my tool limit ran out before I could read the text of either. So the bundle has no human data on ASN-007 exposure, ERK1/2 engagement (e.g., pERK or pRSK inhibition) or downstream biomarkers. Neither ERK inhibitor in the list, temuterkib or ulixertinib, got past Phase 2, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement is no_human_data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the code is U.

I found no human target-engagement data for ASN007/ERAS-007. The first-in-human abstract (TARG-19-PR09) reports safety and a few responses (a partial response in HRAS-mutant salivary cancer, plus prolonged stable disease), but no pERK, pRSK or DUSP6 pharmacodynamics, no tissue drug levels and no exposure–response data. The only support for ERK engagement is preclinical (PMID:34973117). The index trial NCT03415126 posted no results. Erasca later deprioritized the drug, saying clinical efficacy data 'do not support continued evaluation', and redirected resources to newer assets. That points to a lack of efficacy with a portfolio decision on top. Because engagement was never shown in humans, nothing here separates a drug that failed to engage ERK from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

PM00104 is a DNA-binding alkylating agent. The index trial (NCT00900562, PMID:23771800) gave 2 mg/m² weekly and saw no responses in either cohort. The study closed because of slow recruitment and futility. Phase 1 population PK showed linear, dose-proportional plasma exposure, and neutropenia, an expected cytotoxic effect, tracked dose (PMID:23055348). So systemic exposure was adequate. However, no human measurement of DNA binding or γ-H2AX induction was found. γ-H2AX was only proposed as a biomarker from cell-line work (PMID:19584237). The Ewing trial also had no responses (NCT01222767). With no engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. Small cohorts are a secondary factor.

PM00104 is a DNA-binding alkylator with no recorded protein target. In the index trial (NCT00900562), 2 mg/m² weekly produced 0 responses in either cohort. The published report says the primary efficacy objective was unmet, so stage 2 never opened. The registry's 'slow recruitment' reason is secondary. Human plasma PK has been characterised (PMID:21590449, PMC3326684), and neutropenia tracks exposure (PMID:23055348), so systemic exposure counts as adequate. γ-H2AX was proposed as a pharmacodynamic marker (PMID:19584237), but no human DNA-engagement or tumour biomarker data were found. The dose came from a standard myelosuppression-based dose finding, and the bundle does not show that this capped engagement. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that is ineffective here. The drug also showed no activity in Ewing sarcoma (NCT01222767) or urothelial carcinoma.

PM00104 is a DNA-binding alkaloid. In the index trial (NCT01222767; PMID:24173965), patients got 2 mg/m² weekly and none of 16 responded. Plasma PK in Ewing patients matched other populations, so systemic exposure was shown. γ-H2AX was proposed as a pharmacodynamic marker, but only in cell lines (PMID:19584237). I found no human data on DNA engagement or a pathway biomarker, either in phase 1 trials or in Ewing patients. Neutropenia, the dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:23055348), shows the drug is cytotoxic in humans but is not a measure of engagement in the tumour. No other drug on the same target is listed. Nothing in the sources separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not work here, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT04265456 is a completed Phase 1 study of pregabalin plus acetaminophen in healthy volunteers. Its primary outcomes are treatment-related adverse events and drowsiness/dizziness, so it was not an efficacy test and did not fail on efficacy. Plasma exposure is documented in NCT00493246. Engagement and pathway were never measured directly. They are inferred adequate because acetaminophen met analgesic efficacy endpoints at standard doses: alone in dental pain (NCT01960114) and in combination with pregabalin in later trials (NCT03652818, NCT04495283). It also holds approvals for pain indications. No tolerability cap was shown. The program continued into Phase 2 (NCT04495283, primary met), which is consistent with a safety/PK step rather than a failure.

The PET study NCT02333487, run in schizophrenia patients from 2014, before the index trial, showed high brain occupancy: D1 Emax 81.9%, D2 Emax 102%, 5-HT6 Emax 88%. That supports adequate exposure and engagement, though the bundle does not report occupancy at the 10 mg dose specifically. No dose was capped by tolerability. The pivotal NCT02717195 showed antipsychotic effect but no superiority over risperidone or olanzapine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia (PMID:36115192). This undercuts the D1/D2 synergy hypothesis. The index trial NCT03230864 was terminated early on that external result, with n≈58 randomized and p=0.08 (worse than continued treatment). The index trial was underpowered and stopped early (secondary F7).

The Phase 2 trial in macula-off RRD (NCT05730218, PMID:42894673) missed its primary endpoint, AULCSF at week 24. BCVA did not differ between groups either. The 50 and 200 μg doses were well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. None of the sources gives human data on vitreous drug levels, Fas binding, or a downstream marker such as caspase-8 activity. Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data come only from rabbits, minipigs and mice (PMID:41007616). No other Fas inhibitor has succeeded in RRD. With engagement untested, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged Fas from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U. The sponsor points to post-hoc subgroups (pseudophakic eyes, macula off for more than 8 days), which is a possible F3 secondary.

In the index single-arm trial (NCT03427268), only 20.7% of patients were progression-free at 3 months. The trial set no target rate, but this is low activity. Plasma exposure is shown: the first-in-human study (PMID:30411218) found a half-life of about 4 h and wide diffusion into tissues, and the dose was escalated to the MTD with neuropathy as the dose-limiting toxicity. Dose delays lowered dose intensity, but no source says this kept engagement too low. No human target-engagement or pathway data turned up, such as tubulin or mitotic-arrest biomarkers in tumour biopsies. Only organoid and xenograft data exist (PMID:31752287). Other tubulin drugs, such as docetaxel, reached phase 3 in colorectal cancer but were not approved for it. No source gives a reason the program stopped. Because engagement has no human data, the failure cannot be explained, so the code is U.

Population PK/PD modelling pooled data that included the Phase 2 SLE patients. It characterised exposure and CRP suppression by PF-04236921, showing systemic exposure and an IL-6 pathway effect (PMID:29776017). This analysis was published after the index trial. Direct target binding was not measured. Engagement is inferred adequate because the same 50 mg subcutaneous dose met the primary endpoint in Crohn's disease (NCT01287897, PMID:29247068), and hs-CRP was strongly lowered in CKD (NCT06362759). In SLE, neither 10 nor 50 mg beat placebo on SRI-4, and 50 mg matched placebo (NCT01405196). Benefit appeared only in a post hoc high-activity subgroup at 10 mg (PMID:27672124), supporting F3 as secondary. The 200 mg arm was stopped for safety (F6 secondary), but 50 mg was efficacious elsewhere, so the dose was not capped below adequate engagement.

The index trial, NCT02442414, was a first-in-human dose-escalation study whose primary endpoint was safety. It had no efficacy endpoint. The only result found outside ClinicalTrials.gov is the ASCO 2017 abstract. It says KBP-5209 was well tolerated, with stable disease in 7 patients and tumour shrinkage in 2 of 28, but it reports no pharmacokinetic values, target inhibition or downstream biomarker results. No source gives a reason for stopping the program. No other drug on the same target is in the bundle, so F1b cannot apply. Tolerability is not described as capping the dose, so dose_limited is false. Because there is no human engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

The index solid-tumor trial (NCT03621982) aimed to deplete intratumoral CD25+ Tregs, a mechanism shown only in mice (PMID:32912922). Systemic exposure can be inferred as adequate: the drug met an ORR endpoint in Hodgkin lymphoma at 30–45 µg/kg (NCT04052997, NCT02432235), and the index trial dosed up to 150 µg/kg. That success came from killing CD25+ tumor cells, a different compartment and mechanism. The bundle has no human data on Treg depletion in solid-tumor tissue. The sponsor cited unquantified 'immunomodulatory signals' that were 'insufficiently compelling at the tested dose/schedule'. Nothing here separates inadequate intratumoral Treg depletion from a mechanism that does not drive benefit, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00944697 tested the analgesic efficacy of oxycodone/naloxone PR added to pregabalin. SF-MPQ scores were 47.65 vs 49.56, with no difference between arms. Naloxone is an OPRM1 antagonist included to block gut opioid receptors. It is not the analgesic component, so this trial did not test naloxone's own mechanism in diabetic polyneuropathy. Engagement at gut MOR at the same oral co-formulated dose is inferred adequate: OXN beat oxycodone PR on the Bowel Function Index (NCT01918098). OXN also met pain endpoints elsewhere (NCT01358526, NCT01112644). Human brain MOR occupancy (PMID:30867551) used intranasal doses that are not comparable. The negative pain readout reflects the agonist combination, not a failure of naloxone's antagonist mechanism, hence F9.

Naloxone in OXN PR works by blocking gut mu-opioid receptors to relieve opioid-induced constipation. The same combination met a Bowel Function Index (BFI) superiority endpoint against oxycodone PR in non-cancer pain (NCT01918098) and is FDA-approved for chronic pain, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate in the gut compartment. In the index trial (NCT01885182), BFI at week 4 was 48.3 vs 51.2, with no p-values, and pain was similar. A later cancer-pain RCT (PMID:40866306) found significantly better BFI with OXN PR. That argues against the target failing in cancer and points to trial-specific design or execution, such as short duration, variance and a frail population. The bundle states no reason, so F2 is only a secondary code and confidence is low.

OXN PR met clinical endpoints through the same opioid-receptor mechanism at comparable doses: chronic low back pain (NCT01358526), RLS (NCT01112644) and bowel function from peripheral naloxone antagonism (NCT01918098). It is also approved for chronic pain. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, but there are no direct human pillar data in PD. Tolerability did not cap the dose: adverse events were similar to placebo, apart from more nausea and constipation (PMID:26494524). In the PANDA trial the primary pain score narrowly missed (−0.6, p=0.058), and the authors still suggest potential efficacy. That fits a weak mechanism effect on PD pain as tested (F2). A possibly underpowered trial (F7) and heterogeneous pain types (F3) are plausible contributors, but the sources do not state either.

The index trial NCT02603952 was a Phase 2a safety study. Its primary outcomes were descriptive counts of solicited symptoms and adverse events with no statistical efficacy comparison. Every arm, including the control, received oseltamivir except one MEDI8852-alone arm, so it was not an efficacy test of MEDI8852. PMID:30150460 reports viral shedding declines similar to oseltamivir alone. Because the comparator was an active drug, this cannot isolate MEDI8852's antiviral effect. The authors concluded that safety supported continued development in hospitalized patients. The bundle has no human PK, target-binding or pathway data, and the Phase 1 trial NCT02350751 posted no results. If the program is treated as an efficacy failure, it is indeterminate (U). Animal data do not count.

In the Phase I dose-escalation study in RA patients (PMID:19014836, published 2008, likely after the index trial started), TRU-015 had measurable serum PK (t1/2 12-19 days). It produced dose-dependent CD19+ B-cell depletion, which is target engagement for a CD20 depleter. No neutralizing antibodies were seen and no tolerability ceiling was reported. Downstream pathway markers were not reported. The index trial NCT00634933 missed ACR50 at week 24 (29.3% and 27.4% vs 16.2% placebo; p=0.061 and p=0.120), and the stated stop reason is efficacy, not safety. With engagement shown, the modest clinical effect suggests insufficient benefit as tested (F2). The numerical trend in a trial of about 74 patients per arm leaves possible underpowering as a secondary explanation (F7). The bundle shows no anti-CD20 success in RA, so F1b does not apply.

NVXT (NP213, Novexatin) is a topical antifungal peptide that has no molecular target on record. Its target is effectively the dermatophyte. Human nail drug levels were never measured: nail penetration was shown only ex vivo, and plasma levels were undetectable by design. In patients, NP213 made nail cultures negative: 14/33 vs 2/12 at day 28 in NCT02343627, 56.5% vs 0% at day 360, and 27–36% at day 365 in the index Phase 2b. However, complete cure in the index trial was about zero in every arm (NCT02933879). The investigators blame the endpoint and its timing: dead fungal hyphae stay microscopy-positive until the nail grows out, and treatment lasted only 28–56 days. Small placebo-controlled culture data make this low confidence.

The PD trial NCT04369430 (400 mg twice daily for 12 weeks) missed its primary endpoint: placebo improved slightly more than drug (-5.11 vs -4.21). I found no human evidence of exposure in brain or CSF, CCR3 occupancy, or any blocked eotaxin/CCR3 signal in blood or brain. The Phase 1 trials (NCT01480648 and others) posted no results. The PD SAP only lists plasma PK and flow-cytometry biomarkers as exploratory endpoints, with no reported results. Alzforum's rationale for the drug rests only on mouse data. No other CCR3 drug has succeeded in PD, and the nAMD trials also failed (NCT04331730, NCT02121522). So nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter. Later, 'safety findings in other AKST4290 studies' ended the program (NCT05038020), so F6 is secondary.

In the index trial (NCT02121522), BI 144807 was given for 4 weeks to 14 patients in a single-arm study. Mean central retinal thickness rose by 44 μm (SD 151.5 μm) instead of falling. No human evidence was found for exposure, engagement or pathway effects. The Phase 1 trials (NCT01480648, NCT01651598) posted no results. My searches found no human data on CCR3 occupancy, inhibition of eotaxin-driven eosinophil responses, or drug levels in the eye. The sources give no explanation from the sponsor for why it failed. Later Alkahest trials also missed their endpoints: the aflibercept add-on trial in wet AMD (NCT04331730) and the Parkinson's trial (NCT04369430). Nothing in the evidence separates a drug that never engaged CCR3 from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The small, short, uncontrolled index trial adds F7 as a secondary code.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The index trial NCT03666143 was a Phase 1b basket safety study in advanced solid tumors. Its only primary endpoint was the count of adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of sitravatinib in HNSCC; hence F9. Plasma pharmacokinetics were characterized in humans (half-life 42–51 h; MTD 150 mg; RP2D 120 mg chosen for tolerability) in PMID:35767205. No receptor occupancy, TAM/VEGFR2 inhibition or downstream biomarker data appear in the bundle, so engagement and pathway are no_human_data. The wider program faltered after Phase 3 NSCLC failures (NCT03906071 missed OS; NCT04921358 stopped for safety and unfavorable risk-benefit). However, nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so U is secondary.

In the first-in-human trial (NCT02219711, PMID:35767205), plasma exposure rose roughly in proportion to dose, and VEGF-A and soluble VEGFR2 changed with drug concentration. The authors said the 120 mg dose used in the index trial should give a near-maximal effect on VEGFR2. In the SNOW window study (NCT03575598), sitravatinib alone shifted tumour macrophages from the M2 to the M1 type, as the TAM mechanism predicts. Tolerability did set 120 mg below the 150 mg MTD, but the PD data show that dose still engaged the target. None of this was measured in HCC or gastric patients, and it was published after the index trial started. With the target engaged, ORRs in the index trial were modest (9.5–25%, NCT03941873), and the Phase 3 trials failed (NCT03906071, NCT04921358). Several trials ended for portfolio reasons (NCT05461794).

BOS-589 (GSK3352589) was meant to act on RET in intestinal tissue. The only human data come from the first-in-human study in healthy volunteers (NCT03154086, PMID:33606922). That study measured plasma PK, which showed low bioavailability that rose less than in proportion to dose. It did not measure drug levels in gut tissue, RET inhibition or any downstream biomarker. In the Phase 2a IBS-D trial (NCT03977155), neither dose improved worst abdominal pain. The high dose did no better than the low dose. Tolerability did not cap the dose, and there were no SAEs. The sources found give no human evidence of target engagement and no sponsor explanation for the failure. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged RET cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter in IBS-D, so the code is U.

In the Phase 1 study (NCT04271514, PMID:37984453), multiple daily doses of 50–400 mg, the same range as the index trial, gave about 80% or more CCR4 surface receptor occupancy in healthy volunteers. That supports adequate exposure and engagement. In AD patients, skin transcriptomic profiles changed in the direction the mechanism predicts (pathway). Occupancy was shown only in healthy volunteers, and the paper came out in 2023, after the index trial started. In the Phase 2b trial (NCT05399368), no dose beat placebo on EASI, and 400 mg did worst. So the target was engaged but there was no benefit: F2. The program actually stopped because the FDA placed a clinical hold after a patient had liver failure that may have been drug-related (F6). The very high placebo response (−59.8%) also points to trial-design problems (F7).

In NCT01712204, AC-201 gave only a non-significant 19% flare reduction (RR 0.81, p=0.14, n=82). Exposure: plasma rhein/diacerein pharmacokinetics are documented (PMID:8218958, PMID:8294081). Engagement is not quantified. Serum IL-1β and SAA fell in gout patients, but only in an unblinded combination study published after the index trial (PMID:26035033), with no magnitude given. Engagement is graded inferred_adequate from efficacy in other diseases: knee OA non-inferiority versus celecoxib (NCT02688400) and HbA1c at the top dose (NCT01276106). Canakinumab, a direct IL-1β neutraliser, is approved for gout. That shows the target drives flares, so diacerein, a weak indirect inflammasome/IL-1β modulator, is the likelier cause (F1b). The small, underpowered trial with a favourable trend adds F7.

The index trial NCT01264211 was a 40-patient pilot add-on study in MTX-IR RA. It missed ACR20 at week 24 (65% vs 45%, P=.20) despite a numerical advantage, with baseline imbalances and dropouts. The EULAR secondary endpoint favoured diacerein (75% vs 25%, P=.002), as did ACR20 in completers at weeks 24 and 28 (P=.04). The authors frame the results as preliminary and positive (PMID:31104217), pointing to an underpowered trial rather than a failed mechanism. Human plasma PK at 50 mg is documented (PMID:8218958, PMID:8294081). No human IL-1β engagement data exist in RA. The COVID inflammasome-marker data (PMID:39434905) came later, in another disease, and do not measure IL-1β inhibition directly. Tolerability did not limit dosing.

Venglustat had linear plasma PK and dose-dependent lowering of plasma GL-1 (the enzyme product) and GM3 (a downstream glycosphingolipid) in healthy volunteers (PMID:32851809, NCT01710826). In STAGED-PKD itself it produced a dose-dependent decrease in plasma glucosylceramide in ADPKD patients (PMID:36535535). This is engagement in the disease, but it was shown only in the index trial, not before it. Doses were not tolerability-capped: 15 mg was the highest safe dose. Yet TKV growth was unchanged (p=0.14, p=0.98) and eGFR declined faster on drug (NCT03523728). With engagement adequate, GCS inhibition does not appear to drive ADPKD progression as tested. Confidence is medium because kidney tissue engagement was not directly measured.

In GBA-PD patients (MOVES-PD Part 1, NCT02906020/PMID:34897099), venglustat reached plasma and CSF in a dose-dependent way, and 15 mg lowered CSF GL-1 by about 72-74%, so brain target engagement is adequate. Downstream glycosphingolipids also fell: plasma GL-1 and GM3 in healthy volunteers (PMID:32851809) and CSF GM2 in GM2 gangliosidosis (PMID:41108138). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this engagement, Part 2 at 15 mg missed the MDS-UPDRS II+III endpoint, with a difference of +2.58 favouring placebo (PMID:37479372). The numerical worsening on drug is echoed in mouse data (PMID:37050861, animal only). Lowering glucosylceramide synthesis does not appear to drive GBA-PD progression as tested. The in-disease engagement evidence came from Part 1 of the index trial itself, so it does not predate the index start.

Plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose up to 200 mg and the drug was well tolerated (PMID:38019355), so the dose was not capped. No human study measured direct target engagement: no receptor occupancy, CSF levels or TRPC4/5 channel readout. The only evidence of central action is downstream circuit effects from a single 100 mg dose. It cut CCK-4-induced panic symptoms in healthy men (PMID:38019356) and reduced amygdala BOLD signal in MDD (NCT03854578, p=0.01), both before the index trial. None of this was in BPD. The BPD trial was flat at every dose (NCT04566601). The investigators blamed population, outcome measures and placebo effects (PMID:39832346), not the mechanism. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U, with F7/F3 as secondary codes.

The index decentralized trial (NCT04423757; PMID:39715042) was terminated for deficient enrollment. Only 43 patients were treated, and the result was inconclusive (difference 3.38, CI -1.81 to 8.56), so it could not answer the question. Plasma PK was dose-proportional and doses up to 200 mg were well tolerated, so 125 mg was not dose-limited (PMID:38019355). A single 100 mg dose reduced cortico-limbic BOLD responses in MDD patients (PMID:36343427, NCT03854578) and blunted CCK-4 panic (PMID:38019356), which indicates CNS functional effects. Direct TRPC4/5 engagement was never measured. The larger MDD trial (NCT04521478) was also flat. Without engagement data, a non-engaging molecule cannot be separated from an irrelevant target (U secondary).

In the index trial, 125 mg was no better than placebo on CAPS-5 (difference 0.06, p=0.97; NCT05103657). Exposure: plasma PK was dose-proportional with a long half-life up to 200 mg (PMID:38019355). Tolerability did not cap the dose. No human study measured direct TRPC4/5 engagement such as occupancy or channel inhibition. There were only functional readouts: a single 100 mg dose reduced CCK-4-induced panic symptoms and ACTH/cortisol in healthy men (PMID:38019356), and lowered amygdala BOLD in MDD (NCT03854578). The sponsor calls this central target engagement. Those results are pathway-level evidence, gathered outside PTSD before the index trial. Matching failures in MDD and BPD (PMID:40900110, PMID:39832346) point toward the target not mattering (F2), but under strict criteria engagement is unmeasured, so the code is U.

Bemnifosbuvir is a nucleotide analogue aimed at SARS-CoV-2 RNA polymerase. Exposure: in healthy volunteers at 550 mg BID, lung epithelial lining fluid AT-273 (0.62 µM) only marginally exceeded the in vitro EC90 of 0.5 µM (PMID:38708557). No direct human measure of polymerase engagement exists. The antiviral effect it should produce was absent in outpatients. MOONSONG showed no nasopharyngeal viral RNA reduction at 550 or 1100 mg (NCT04709835, PMID:37338393). The index MORNINGSKY trial also found no viral load reduction and missed its symptom endpoint (PMID:37928891). Only a modest day-2 reduction appeared in hospitalised patients (PMID:38051993). The mechanism was not adequately tested, so F1a applies. The stated business termination (F8) is secondary; SUNRISE-3 also failed (NCT05629962). HCV efficacy is a different viral target and supports no inference here.

Phase 1 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (NCT03309605, PMID:30650260, PMID:33465285). No study in humans measured readthrough directly, for example full-length CFTR protein or transcript levels in patient tissue, so engagement has no human data. In the CF phase 2 trials (NCT04126473/NCT04135495), the only proximal readout was sweat chloride. It fell by just 5.4 mmol/L at 1.5 mg/kg monotherapy, and the CFF summary says the study showed no decrease in sweat chloride and no lung-function gain. That points to weak CFTR rescue, but nothing in the bundle separates too little readthrough from a mechanism that doesn't work. Organoid data (PMID:42728176) suggest that rescue is limited and varies by variant, which also fits F3. So the code is U, with F1a and F3 as secondary.

Tricaprilin has no protein target. Its mechanism is ketogenesis: plasma β-hydroxybutyrate serves as an alternative brain fuel. An earlier AC-1202 trial in AD patients showed serum BHB elevation, published before the index trial (PMID:19664276). In the index NOURISH AD trial (NCT01741194), however, the authors attribute the lack of ADAS-Cog11 benefit partly to lower-than-expected ketone body formation from the AC-1204 formulation (PMID:32310169). Later PBPK modeling identified dispersibility, lipolysis and gastric emptying as limits on ketogenesis (PMID:36470522). So the mechanism was likely under-exposed (F1a). The authors also cite the lack of decline in the placebo arm, a trial-design limitation (F7). No downstream brain-metabolism biomarker was measured, so pathway has no human data. The drug was safe, so the dose was not tolerability-limited.

Trazpiroben, a peripheral D2/D3 antagonist, reached measurable plasma exposure (PMID:34285598, PMID:35218604). Prolactin rose robustly in healthy volunteers across all doses (PMID:33462988, PMID:34967147), showing D2 engagement. It also rose in gastroparesis patients in NCT03268941, registered before the index trial (PMID:34148244). Dosing was well tolerated up to 100-300 mg, so dose was not limited. Pathway evidence was weak: gastric emptying was unchanged, although the metoclopramide control also showed no effect. Volume-to-fullness improved at 25 mg. The index trial showed no symptom benefit at 5, 25 or 50 mg (all p>0.4). Engagement was shown and the drug still failed, which points to F2. The large placebo response raises a possible trial-sensitivity issue (F7).

The first-in-human trial (NCT01765790) took biopsies from mCRC metastases. Imalumab penetrated the tumours, and 10 mg/kg weekly gave more than 100% oxMIF target occupancy in 10 of 15 evaluable patients. An ASCO 2015 abstract, published before the index trial began, reported at least 95% target binding by the end of cycle 1. It also reported that on-treatment biopsies showed changes in PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, but that evidence is qualitative. That dose (10 mg/kg weekly) was named the biologically active dose and was the dose used in the index trial. Tolerability did not cap it: the maximum tolerated dose was 37.5 mg/kg every 2 weeks. Even with this engagement, PFS did not improve with either combination in NCT02448810 (HR 0.8, p=0.246 and p=0.354), so the failure points to the oxMIF target rather than the molecule. The arms were small, which supports F7 as a secondary code.

In the index trial (NCT05042609), TRS01 1% eye drops did worse than the steroid comparator on both primary endpoints. Anterior chamber cell grade reached 0 in 46% of TRS01 patients vs 68% on the steroid, and grade 0 or 1 in 63% vs 89%. The phase 2 trials (NCT04222712, NCT04222725) measured only safety. No human data turned up on drug levels in the eye, NRP1 binding, or downstream biomarkers. The only mechanism evidence is in vitro cytokine suppression in human blood cells, which does not count. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the miss and pointed instead to post hoc benefit-risk and eye-pressure advantages. Since there is no engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged NRP1 can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In the index PBC trial (NCT03394924), about 45-46% of patients on EDP-305 reached the ALP response endpoint versus 11.1% on placebo. The odds ratios were 5.6-7, but p was 0.06-0.11 with extremely wide CIs, because the placebo arm had only 9 patients. The bundle contains no direct FXR engagement markers (FGF19, C4) and no posted Phase 1 PK. A downstream effect is shown in NASH (NCT03421431/PMID:34740705): ALT fell at 2.5 mg (p=0.049) and liver fat fell dose-dependently (p=0.0009), alongside dose-dependent pruritus. Obeticholic acid is approved in PBC, so the target matters here. The miss looks driven by an underpowered design rather than mechanism, though engagement data are absent.

In healthy volunteers, glenzocimab showed dose-proportional plasma exposure up to 2000 mg and dose-dependent inhibition of collagen-induced platelet aggregation (PMID:31017822). PK/PD modelling predicted that 1000 mg, the GARDEN dose, reduces aggregation to 20% in all subjects at 6 h (PMID:32500636). Both were published before the index trial and showed no tolerability cap. Engagement was not measured in COVID-19 ARDS patients. In GARDEN (NCT04659109, PMID:38885234), progression at Day 4 was numerically worse with drug (43.3% vs 29.0%, p=0.245), and the authors concluded clinical impact was not demonstrated. With GPVI inhibition expected to be adequate, the most direct reading is that the target does not drive COVID-19 ARDS outcome. The small exploratory size (n=60) is a secondary limitation.

First-in-human study (PMID:38761014) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and about 90% ex-vivo IL-1β release inhibition over 24h at 100 mg QD or 25 mg BID in healthy volunteers, with no dose-limiting tolerability. Downstream IL-6 and IL-18 reductions were clear in coronary heart disease trials (NCT06031844, NCT06097663). Engagement was not shown in COVID-19 patients, and the bundle neither dates it before 2020 nor states the index-trial dose. DFV890 still missed the APACHE II primary endpoint (8.7 vs 8.6, p=0.467; NCT04382053), consistent with NLRP3 inhibition not driving outcome as tested. Favorable secondary trends (clinical status, viral clearance; PMID:36104613) suggest the endpoint or the small phase 2a size may also have contributed.

IRL201104 is an immunomodulatory peptide derived from a mycobacterial chaperonin, and no molecular target is recorded. The protocol (citing NCT03058458) shows only short-lived plasma exposure: the drug was detectable for just 15–60 minutes after an IV bolus. I found no human data on target binding or pathway effects, and the A20/NF-κB findings in PMID:31845415 come from animals and in vitro work, so they don't count. In the index trial NCT05084963, the 8 mg arm showed a numeric but highly variable drop in eosinophils (n=12 per arm), which the sponsor called positive. The FDA then granted orphan drug designation and the company planned a Phase 2b. With engagement unmeasured, I can't tell whether the drug never engaged a target or the mechanism doesn't matter in EoE, so the code is U. The trial's small size and wide variability (F7) also played a part.

In INDUCE-1 (NCT02723955, PMID:40789742), feladilimab showed linear, dose-proportional PK and maximal ICOS receptor occupancy above 0.1 mg/kg. No MTD was reached across 0.001–10 mg/kg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The 80 mg flat dose (about 1 mg/kg) is within the saturating range. The bundle has no human downstream pathway biomarker data. Occupancy was shown in mixed solid tumors, not specifically NSCLC, and was published in 2025, after the index trial started. Despite robust occupancy, overall survival was not improved with docetaxel (7.8 vs 8.2 months; NCT05553808). The drug also failed in two Phase 3 head and neck trials (NCT04128696, NCT04428333). A review (PMID:41611245) attributes the limited activity to ICOS biology and calls for biomarker-driven patient selection. Together this points to the target not driving benefit.

In the phase 1 INDUCE-1 study (NCT02723955; PMID:40789742), feladilimab showed linear, dose-proportional PK. ICOS receptor occupancy was maximal at doses above 0.1 mg/kg. No MTD was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. PMID:41611245 describes robust receptor occupancy but limited clinical responses with feladilimab and other ICOS agonists, and concludes that receptor engagement was not enough. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported in the bundle. Occupancy was shown in mixed advanced solid tumors, not specifically HNSCC. Despite adequate engagement, adding feladilimab to pembrolizumab worsened OS (HR 1.51; CPS≥20 HR 4.44) in NCT04128696. It also failed with chemotherapy (NCT04428333) and in NSCLC (NCT05553808). ICOS agonism does not drive benefit as tested.

Index trial NCT03907072 was stopped for lack of efficacy after enrolling 6 patients. Its primary endpoint was a target-engagement measure (change in dystrophin level), but no outcome data were posted. NCT03508947 (Phase 1) posted no results, and there are no PubMed abstracts, so exposure, engagement and pathway have no human data in the bundle. Several drugs on the same target (DMD dystrophin restoration) are FDA-approved for DMD: eteplirsen, golodirsen, casimersen, viltolarsen and delandistrogene moxeparvovec. The target is therefore validated, which points to a molecule problem (F1b). Stopping a dystrophin-endpoint trial for lack of efficacy suggests dystrophin was not restored (possible F1a), but the bundle does not show this, so U also applies.

The index Phase 1/2 trial (NCT04210037) of pelcitoclax plus paclitaxel in relapsed SCLC was terminated by 'Sponsor decision'. It posted no results, and its primary endpoint was DLT, so it was not a completed efficacy test. Sibling trials were also stopped for company strategy: NCT03387332 ('The company adjusts strategy') and NCT04893759. This points to a business or portfolio stop rather than a failed readout. The first-in-human study (PMID:37971712) reported good tolerability and modest activity (ORR 6.5%, DCR 30.4%), with platelet reductions consistent with BCL-xL activity. However, it showed no human PK, target-engagement, or tumor pathway data, so all pillars are no_human_data. The efficacy question remains unanswered (U) because no efficacy readout exists.

Mesdopetam's target, the D3 receptor, is in the brain. The only human data are plasma pharmacokinetics: dose-linear in healthy volunteers (PMID:34018344) and about 229 nM in Parkinson's patients (PMID:30534585). My searches found no human measurement of CSF or brain levels, no D3 receptor occupancy by PET (e.g. [11C]PHNO) and no downstream biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the index trial NCT03368170, placebo did numerically better on UDysRS. In the 12-week trial NCT04435431, the primary endpoint (good ON-time) failed but UDysRS, a secondary endpoint, improved, which the sponsor took as a sign of drug activity (PMID:40008823). The approved D3-target drugs listed are agonists, not antagonists, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that did not engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. Code: U.

The first-in-human study (PMID:34018344) showed dose-linear plasma exposure in healthy volunteers. Neither it nor any source found in my searches reports human D3 receptor occupancy (for example by PET) or a pathway biomarker for mesdopetam, so whether the drug engaged its target is unknown. In the index Phase 2a trial (NCT03368170), patients were titrated up to tolerability, with parkinsonism the most common adverse event. Placebo scored numerically better on UDysRS. The Phase 2b trial (NCT04435431) missed its patient-diary primary endpoint (good ON time), although the sponsor reported benefit on secondary UDysRS measures, which points to endpoint or trial-design problems. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive dyskinesia, so the code is U.

JNJ-3989 is a GalNAc siRNA against all HBV RNAs. Population PK models liver uptake via ASGPR (PMID:40375057). In chronic hepatitis B patients it dose-dependently reduced viral antigens (PMID:41362713, REEF-1 NCT03982186). Intrahepatic HBsAg-positive hepatocytes fell by about 78% (NCT04585789). Serum HBsAg fell by 2 log10 or more in about 65% of patients (NCT04667104) and by about 2 log10 at week 24 (PMID:42320551). Target knockdown and antigen lowering were therefore achieved in patients without a tolerability cap. Even so, HBsAg seroclearance at week 72 was 0% versus 0% in the index trial (NCT04129554). Functional cure was also 0% across other regimens (NCT04439539, NCT05275023). Silencing HBV transcripts did not translate into durable seroclearance, which points to a mechanism failure. Secondary F4: the biomarker moved, but the functional-cure endpoint did not.

The index trial (NCT02083289) compared sepetaprost with active Xalatan, not placebo. Sepetaprost lowered diurnal IOP by 7.2 mmHg versus 6.6 mmHg for Xalatan, and post hoc responder analyses favoured it (PMID:27649982). The only miss was formal superiority over an effective active drug, not lack of drug efficacy. Before the index trial, Phase 1 in OHT/OAG patients showed dose-dependent IOP lowering (NCT01670266, PMID:27300645), supporting pathway activity. Exposure and engagement were not measured directly at the receptor; they are inferred from the dose-dependent IOP effect in this disease. The program did not stop: it went on to Phase 3, where ANGEL-J1 met non-inferiority to latanoprost (PMID:42298273), alongside ANGEL-2 and ANGEL-J2. This is not an efficacy failure.

EC-18 (PLAG) has no recorded primary target, and its proposed mechanism, resolving inflammation by controlling neutrophil recruitment, is supported only by animal data (PMC6759802). The healthy-volunteer Phase 1 PK trials (NCT02532712, NCT02496143, NCT02700360) posted no results. My searches found no human data on exposure, target engagement or pharmacodynamic biomarkers, no posted or published results for the index COVID-19 trial (NCT04500132; 2,000 mg once daily, primary endpoint transition to ARDS), and no statement from the sponsor on why the program stopped. No other drug on the same target is listed. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in COVID-19, so the code is indeterminate (U).

Plasma exposure in humans is well characterized (PMID:29134426). The helicase-primase inhibitor met non-inferiority versus valaciclovir in herpes zoster (NCT01959841, skin compartment, 400 mg). That is a related viral helicase-primase rather than the identical HSV target, so engagement is inferred_adequate with a caveat. In the genital herpes Phase 2 (NCT00486200), time above 200 ng/mL related to viral shedding and healing (PMID:27129009), a proximal antiviral effect in this disease. PK/PD modelling (PMID:27461507) found the human effect dose-independent. It attributed lesion healing mainly to the immune response, which masks drug efficacy. This fits the index result: Day-8 healing was 66.4% on drug vs 69.5% on placebo (NCT01959295). The self-limiting healing endpoint appears unable to separate the arms (F4/F7), though a weak mechanism (F2) is possible.

In the RA phase 1 trial (NCT01565408, ACR abstract), plasma exposure rose with dose and total IL-21 went up, which shows the antibody bound IL-21. But total IL-21 varied widely between patients, and nobody measured free IL-21 or how much IL-21 signalling was blocked, so there is no evidence the binding was sufficient. In the T1D trial (NCT02443155, Lancet 2021), total IL-21 was measured but never reported. Immune cell subsets, including follicular helper T cells and B cells, changed only slightly and briefly (under 10%). The antibody alone narrowly missed (ratio 1.23, p=0.093); the combination with liraglutide succeeded. The authors pointed to baseline C-peptide subgroups and gave no reason for stopping. Engagement in T1D was not measured, so a drug that never engaged can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter.

The index trial, NCT01647451, did not fail. Its 2014 ACR abstract reports that 12 mg/kg IV met the primary endpoint, with a DAS28-CRP change of -0.65 vs placebo (p=0.04). The ACR20/50/70 responses were not significant. In RA patients, exposure rose with dose (half-life about 2.5 weeks, NCT01565408). Total IL-21 (free plus antibody-bound) went up, which shows the drug bound its ligand. However, CRP, RF, ESR, IL-21R expression and gene expression did not change in phase 1, so the pathway pillar is rated inadequate. In phase 2, only about a third of patients showed B-cell shifts. The engagement data were published in 2014, after the index trial started. No source gives a reason for stopping. The modest effect points to a portfolio decision, so F8 is a secondary code, but that is inferred, not stated.

Exposure was adequate. The NCT03472326 protocol reports high levels of the active metabolite GS-9148-DP inside PBMCs. In the earlier study GS-US-180-0104, 30 mg cut viral load by a median of about 1 log in treatment-naive HIV patients, so the drug did act on reverse transcriptase in vivo. In the index population, whose virus resisted older nucleoside drugs, the 60 mg sentinel cohort roughly doubled exposure and the virus stayed sensitive in lab tests. Even so, only 2 of 11 patients reached a drop of more than 0.5 log. The 180 mg cohort also missed the target response. No tolerability ceiling was reported. Reverse transcriptase inhibition is a proven HIV mechanism, so this looks like a potency problem with the molecule: it did not inhibit the target enough, rather than the target not mattering. Code F1a, secondary F1b, by inference.

In the index UC phase 2 (NCT02647866, PMID:36776497), colon biopsies showed virtually complete elimination of OX40+ cells at all doses (1–10 mg/kg IV q2w). This shows tissue exposure and depleting engagement in UC patients. The authors state that endoscopic improvement did not correlate with OX40+ T-cell ablation, and no dose group differed from placebo on Mayo endoscopy subscore. Tolerability did not cap the dose, since doses up to 10 mg/kg were well tolerated. The same drug met endpoints in atopic dermatitis (NCT03703102, NCT05651711), so the molecule is active. PMID:40808882 notes no significant clinical response in UC. With the mechanism fully engaged and no benefit, OX40 depletion does not appear to drive UC. Engagement evidence was published only after the index trial.

ALS-L1023 is an oral extract of lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) with no defined molecular target. The only mechanistic evidence comes from in vitro antioxidant and PI3K/Akt work in ARPE-19 cells (PMID:26941573), which does not count as human data. I found no human data on ocular or plasma exposure, target engagement, or a pathway biomarker. In the McEye Phase 2 trial (NCT03725501), mean BCVA gain at 12 months was 11.58 letters at 600 mg, 4.11 at 1200 mg and 7.23 on placebo plus ranibizumab. That inverse dose response is not consistent. Efficacy was analysed in only 95 of 126 patients, and the protocol was amended twice, so trial design issues (F7) may have contributed. Nothing in the sources separates an inactive drug from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT04590599, PMID:39827881), adding IBI310 to sintilimab did not significantly improve response rate (32.3% vs 23.5%, p=0.17), progression-free survival or overall survival, and it raised grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (55% vs 19%). Exposure is adequate: the first-in-human study (NCT03545971; PMC11179243) found linear, dose-proportional plasma levels from 0.3 to 3 mg/kg, and CTLA-4 is a systemic target. None of the sources I found reports human CTLA-4 occupancy or a downstream biomarker, such as ICOS+ CD4 T-cell expansion. Cadonilimab is on the same target in cervical cancer, but the bundle does not show that it met an endpoint. Because engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged CTLA-4 from add-on CTLA-4 blockade not mattering here, so the code is U.

The bundle has no direct human PK, LIGHT-neutralization or biomarker data. Exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate because quisovalimab met its primary endpoint in COVID-19 pneumonia/acute lung injury (NCT04412057; alive and free of respiratory failure 26/31 vs 20/31, p=0.044). That was LIGHT neutralization in a lung inflammatory setting. Comparability of dose is not shown, so this inference is weak. In non-eosinophilic asthma, asthma-related events were 12/45 vs 14/45 on placebo (NCT05288504), with no safety signal and no dose limitation. The likeliest reading is that LIGHT neutralization does not drive poorly controlled non-eosinophilic asthma as tested. The thin bundle, the small trial and the absence of a biomarker in asthma keep confidence low. The Crohn's/UC trial was stopped for strategic reasons (NCT03169894).

Filgotinib 200 mg reached dose-proportional plasma exposure, and IL-6/pSTAT1 whole-blood inhibition was modelled as maximal at 200 mg (PMID:25681059, published 2015, before the index trial). CRP and other PD markers fell in RA patients (PMID:28622463). The same dose met endpoints in RA, Crohn's disease, ankylosing spondylitis and PsA, so the pillars held, though never in CLE patients. Dose was not capped by tolerability. The CLE trial was an exploratory proof-of-concept study with only 8 placebo patients and a large placebo response (-5.5). Filgotinib was numerically better (-8.7; CLASI-50 50% vs 37.5%), with larger differences in select subgroups (PMID:34498056). An underpowered design is the most direct explanation; a mechanism failure (F2) or subgroup effect (F3) are possible alternatives.

Filgotinib 200 mg was the dose in the index trial. PK/PD modelling in healthy volunteers showed maximal IL-6/pSTAT1 inhibition at 200 mg (PMID:25681059), and ex vivo data confirmed JAK1 pathway inhibition equivalent to other JAK inhibitors (PMID:33741556). In RA patients CRP and other PD markers fell (PMID:28622463). The same dose met clinical endpoints in RA, Crohn's, AS and PsA. In Sjogren's, disease-related biomarkers fell (immunoglobulins) and the drug was tolerated, yet the primary endpoint was missed (43.2% vs 26.5%, p=0.17) and neither secondary endpoint was met (PMID:35377447). This supports F2. Secondary codes: F3, because the effect looked larger in the ESSDAI ≥14 and no-DMARD subgroups; F7, because the arms were small (~37 patients) and the confidence intervals wide.

BI 836858 is an Fc-engineered anti-CD33 antibody that was meant to deplete CD33+ myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in lower-risk MDS (PMID:28096534). In the index trial (NCT02240706; PMID:35734924) no MTD was reached up to 320 mg, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The sponsor ended the study before Phase II because the drug produced no haematologic response on its own. Pharmacodynamics in MDS patients suggested the antibody bound CD33, with CD33 masked or internalized on MDSCs. But MDSC numbers did not fall and NK cells were not activated. The intended depletion therefore never happened, so the mechanism (removing MDSCs to restore blood-cell production) was not properly tested. I found no human exposure data in the sources I read.

The index trial NCT03184558 (bemcentinib plus pembrolizumab in TNBC) was stopped at a planned futility analysis with 0% ORR in 29 patients. No source in the bundle shows human AXL engagement at the doses used: no tumour pAXL inhibition, occupancy or target-specific readout. The NSCLC phase 1 (PMID:37423058) reports PK similar to earlier data and broad changes in plasma proteins, including AKT signalling, but nothing that confirms AXL and no measures of whether exposure was enough. The AML protocol and paper list sAXL as a pharmacodynamic endpoint, but the search returned no results. No TNBC engagement data exist. PMID:35022314 notes that bemcentinib hits many off-targets. Response in NSCLC was limited to one cohort (NCT03184571). That hints at patient selection, but nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT03184558), bemcentinib plus pembrolizumab produced an ORR of 0/29 and was stopped at its planned futility analysis. Exposure was adequate: human plasma PK is documented (NCT06469138, PMID:37423058). For engagement, the only human evidence is a qualitative sponsor protocol statement that phospho-AXL, phospho-AKT and phospho-ERK fell in AML blasts. It gives no magnitude and is not from breast cancer, so I treated it as no_human_data. PMID:37423058 reports nonspecific plasma protein changes. In vitro, bemcentinib was a weak pAXL inhibitor (IC50 1.8 µM) with AXL-independent effects, but in vitro data don't count. No tumour engagement or occupancy data exist in TNBC or IBC. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged AXL from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In NCT04890509, median time to sustained clinical improvement was 7.0 days in both arms, so the trial missed its primary endpoint. The trial protocol (Oct 2020) cites human evidence from before the trial: plasma drug levels and complete inhibition of AXL activation (p-AXL) in AML patients' leukaemia cells at the recommended maintenance dose of 200 mg daily (from AML trial NCT02488408). That is human engagement at a comparable dose, but it rests on only two patients and was not shown in COVID-19. The sponsor's ECCMID 2022 poster reported that bemcentinib lowered inflammatory, fibrotic and tissue-damage biomarkers in COVID-19 patients. This is a weak pathway signal from a company source. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. My reading is that the target was engaged but did not drive the outcome (F2). The sponsor pointed to more severe patients and fewer deaths, which suggests a subgroup explanation (F3). The trial was open-label and small (F7). Confidence is low because the engagement evidence is thin.

Serum exposure of the conjugate and payload was characterized in humans, including colorectal cancer patients, over 1.6–8.0 mg/kg (PMID:36053771). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same HER3-directed ADC produced responses in NSCLC and breast cancer at comparable doses, with exposure tracking ORR (PMID:40214010, PMID:37302522, NCT02980341). In the index trial, even the HER3-high colorectal cohort had ORR 2/39, and the interim futility criteria were not met (NCT04479436). Sources describe U3-1402 as ineffective in colorectal cancer despite promising xenograft data (PMID:37302522, PMID:31395690). No tolerability cap or design flaw is cited. HER3-directed payload delivery did not translate into benefit in colorectal cancer. No engagement data exist in colorectal patients.

The index Phase Ib/II trial (NCT01573338) set 5 mg BID on a 3-days-on/4-days-off schedule. The randomized Phase II at that dose (JTO 2019) showed no benefit: PFS was 4.9 vs 5.5 months (HR 1.24) and OS 9.7 vs 10.3 months. Serious adverse events were more common with roniciclib (57.1% vs 38.6%), and the study was stopped early for a negative risk-benefit ratio. Plasma PK was collected, but no human engagement or pathway data were found, such as pRb or RNA Pol II phosphorylation or MCL-1 lowering. The only engagement evidence is in cell lines (PMID:27090615). Trilaciclib is approved in SCLC, but as myeloprotection, not an antitumor effect, so F1b does not fit. Engagement is unknown, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from an irrelevant target (U). Toxicity added to the stop (F6).

In the first-in-human study (NCT02386436, PMID:29900565), modelling estimated target engagement in serum and skin blister fluid in healthy subjects, supporting exposure at the skin target. In the dcSSc proof-of-mechanism trial NCT03041025, PMID:35583273 reports evidence of target engagement. Despite this, no coordinated effect on inflammation or fibrosis biomarkers appeared, so the pathway pillar is inadequate, and no efficacy endpoint differed from placebo. The authors conclude OSM inhibition may not be a useful strategy in SSc, which supports F2. At 300 mg, on-target, dose-dependent falls in haemoglobin and platelets made safety unfavourable (PMID:35583273, PMID:38501358), so F5 applies secondarily. Engagement was shown at 300 mg, so the dose was not capped below engagement.

The index ROBIN trial (NCT03238963) had a descriptive safety primary endpoint (ocular AEs), so it was not a formal efficacy test. Exploratory DRSS ≥2-step improvement (5.7% vs 0%) showed high variability and no clear efficacy signal (PMID:38806700); the small 12-week design limited what it could answer (F7). The same 10 mg dose gave near-complete plasma AOC3 inhibition, about 97% (3.3% residual activity), in NASH patients (NCT03166735, PMID:37932258). ALT and CK-18 also fell dose-dependently there, so systemic exposure, engagement and pathway effect were shown in humans. Engagement was not shown in DR patients or retinal tissue. If the DRSS result is read as an efficacy failure, F2 applies. No dose limitation was shown; 10 mg was well tolerated.

The index trial NCT03166735 was a pharmacodynamic Phase IIa study whose primary endpoint, plasma AOC3 activity, was met. Activity fell dose-dependently to 2–24% of baseline versus about 100% on placebo, so exposure and engagement were adequate in NASH patients. Doses of 3 mg or more also reduced ALT and CK-18 dose-dependently, and all doses were well tolerated (PMID:37932258). The readout was therefore not an efficacy failure of the drug: F9. The bundle states no reason for stopping. Healthy-volunteer studies after the index trial showed off-target brain MAO-B inhibition of about 73% at 10 mg (NCT03927209), and a tyramine interaction study followed (NCT03979820). These hint at a molecule-specific liability (possible F6), but the bundle does not show this as the cause.

Exposure: human PK is dose-proportional (PMID:34700199, PMID:36932300), and REM suppression at plasma ≥100 ng/mL shows a brain effect (PMID:33879769). TAAR1 occupancy was never measured. Engagement is inferred_adequate because the schizophrenia Phase 2 met its endpoint at comparable CNS doses (NCT02969382). Pathway: the drug lowered striatal dopamine synthesis in schizophrenia (NCT04038957, PMID:41130556). No pillar was shown in PD psychosis. The index trial was an exploratory, flexibly dosed pilot of 38 patients (PMID:37273942). It showed a numerical SAPS-PD advantage (p=0.681), 25% vs 0% remission, and a signal in cognitively impaired patients. It was too small to answer the question. Secondary codes: F2 (engaged mechanism, no benefit) and F3 (subgroup signal). Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01972711 was a single-dose BOLD-fMRI mechanistic study in healthy high/low-schizotypy volunteers (PMID:37550314), not an efficacy test, so F9 is primary. The narcolepsy efficacy test was NCT05015673 (PMID:37209427). Exposure: 50 mg gave plasma ≥100 ng/mL with large REM suppression (PMID:33879769). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the drug met PANSS in schizophrenia phase 2 at comparable doses through central TAAR1 (NCT02969382). Pathway: REM was suppressed in narcolepsy patients (less night REM, fewer SOREMPs), and striatal dopamine synthesis fell in schizophrenia (NCT04038957, PMID:41130556). Despite this, cataplexy and sleepiness did not separate from placebo. This suggests REM suppression via this mechanism does not drive narcolepsy outcomes (secondary F2).

The index extension study (NCT03712787) was stopped because its parent study, NCT02880956, showed no efficacy: no dose separated from placebo on CDR-SB at week 96 (PMID:36730056). Exposure: the PSP Phase 1 reported a CSF:plasma ratio typical of antibodies (PMID:29181488). Engagement: in early AD patients, CSF free tau fell significantly at 1000 mg and 2000 mg, and the investigators said the doses were enough to engage CSF tau. That reduction leveled off at higher exposures. These data were published after the index trial started. No downstream pathway biomarker was found. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. With engagement shown and no benefit, extracellular tau binding does not appear to drive AD as tested (F2). QSP modeling (PMID:37658103) suggests very little engagement in the synaptic cleft, which leaves some uncertainty.

Exposure: the Phase 1 trial in PSP (PMID:29181488) found a CSF:plasma ratio typical of humanized antibodies. Engagement: in the PSP Phase 2 trial itself (NCT02985879/PMID:33609476), CSF free tau fell 38% at 2000 mg and 46% at 4000 mg compared with placebo, and plasma total tau rose. Secondary sources describe this as confirmed target engagement. These measurements came from the index trial, so they were not available before it started. Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. I found no downstream pathway biomarker in the sources. The PSPRS showed no benefit and did not improve at the higher dose, so the program fits F2: the target and mechanism, as tested, do not drive PSP. Caveats: the reduction in free tau was only partial, and a modelling study (PMID:37658103) suggests very little engagement in the synaptic cleft. The autopsy case (PMID:36593715) showed no change in tau pathology.

The Phase Ia/b study (NCT02740985, PMID:36044531) reported that plasma exposure at the 75 mg capsule dose used in the index trial was adequate to cover the target. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred at that dose, and index-trial trough levels were similar. In mCRPC patients, intratumoral adenosine signaling fell in 5 of 7 and peripheral-blood immune gene signatures changed. This is pathway evidence in the program's disease. Engagement is graded adequate mainly by inference from PK target coverage plus these downstream changes. No direct occupancy or pCREB data were found, which weakens the call; a strict reading would give U. Despite this, the index trial (NCT04089553) and AARDVARC (NCT04495179, stopped for futility) showed minimal activity, which points to F2. The adenosine-signature subgroup hint supports F3 as secondary.

The index trial NCT00928447 was a 22-person intradermal rHuPH20 vs placebo study in nickel-allergic participants. Its primary outcomes were only counts of positive ICDRG patch reactions (5 vs 9; 3 vs 2), with no statistical comparison, and it was classified as a not_efficacy endpoint with an unassessable primary. It reads as a local tolerability or reactivity test, not an efficacy test of the drug, so F9 applies. Hyaluronan depolymerization in skin tissue is supported in humans. Local injection gives direct exposure. Dispersion and flow rates rose markedly in healthy volunteers (PMID:18095810, 2007), and co-injected insulin absorption accelerated (NCT00705536). Approved subcutaneous co-formulations met efficacy endpoints (NCT00814320), so engagement is inferred adequate. No engagement data come from dermatitis patients, and no stop reason is stated.

Hyaluronidase (rHuPH20) is a dispersion excipient, not the active therapy in this program. The index trial NCT04598477 was an open-label safety extension of efgartigimod PH20 SC. It was stopped because the parent trial ADDRESS (NCT04598451) found no efficacy of efgartigimod in pemphigus. So it was not an efficacy test of hyaluronidase itself. rHuPH20's local action is well shown in humans before the index trial: faster and greater SC absorption of insulin (NCT00705536, NCT00979875), higher SC infusion flow rates (PMID:18095810), and SC efgartigimod IgG lowering non-inferior to IV (NCT04735432). The delivery function therefore held. The failure belongs to the co-formulated efgartigimod/FcRn mechanism in pemphigus (secondary F2), not to the hyaluronidase.

rHuPH20 is a dispersing agent with no recorded pharmacological target. In NCT01756157 it was given with subcutaneous C1-INH in a two-dose crossover with no placebo arm. The higher dose numerically reduced attacks (p=0.0523), and acute-treated attacks were significantly reduced (p=0.0315). The publications state the study was terminated early as a precaution after non-neutralizing anti-rHuPH20 antibodies appeared in 45% of patients (PMID:27931305, PMID:28093999). That is a molecule-specific immunogenicity concern, not lack of efficacy. Its dispersion function is clearly shown elsewhere (insulin exposure doubled to quintupled, NCT00979875, NCT00705536). Its subcutaneous co-administration also succeeded clinically with immunoglobulin (NCT00814320, NCT02549170). Early termination left the trial underpowered (F7), and it was a dose comparison of the co-drug rather than an efficacy test of rHuPH20 (F9).

Exposure in SMA patients was measured, with Cmax quartiles reported (PMID:33624184). In healthy volunteers, reldesemtiv dose- and concentration-dependently amplified the nerve-stimulated muscle force-frequency response (~60% peak force increase), showing troponin activation and its functional effect (PMID:29150952, published 2018, after the index start). In the index SMA trial, MEP improved at both doses and 6MWD improved at the highest exposure, but FVC, MIP, HFMS-E, RULM, mega-score and global assessments did not move (NCT02644668). Both doses were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The same mechanism failed in ALS Phase 2/3, COPD and mobility limitation (NCT03160898, NCT04944784, NCT02662582, NCT03065959), pointing to a mechanism that does not yield clinical benefit. The small, 8-week, hypothesis-generating design adds F7/F4 elements.

In healthy volunteers, reldesemtiv increased tibialis anterior force in response to nerve stimulation in a dose- and plasma-concentration-dependent way (about 60% at 10 Hz) (PMID:29150952). That is direct functional evidence of fast skeletal troponin activation, published before COURAGE-ALS. SMA patients also showed plasma-exposure-linked MEP gains (PMID:33624184). Engagement was not measured in ALS patients. The drug was well tolerated, and no tolerability-imposed dose cap is shown (PMID:32969758). Despite this, phase 2 missed its primary endpoint (NCT03160898). Phase 3 at 300 mg bid was stopped for futility, with the ALSFRS-R difference nominally favoring placebo (PMID:40126464). Tirasemtiv, on the same target, also never succeeded. Amplifying muscle contractility therefore does not alter ALS functional decline as tested.

In healthy volunteers, CK-2127107 raised tibialis anterior force in a dose- and plasma-concentration-dependent way, up to about 60% at 10 Hz (PMID:29150952). This shows exposure, troponin engagement and the expected functional effect, but it was published in 2018, after the index trial started, and not in COPD patients. The SMA trial also showed exposure-related muscle effects (PMID:33624184). Tolerability did not cap the dose: it was well tolerated (PMID:32969758). Even so, constant work rate endurance in COPD did not improve (−12 s vs placebo, p=0.734; NCT02662582). Amplifying fast skeletal muscle contraction therefore did not translate into exercise benefit, which supports F2. Weaker signals: the elderly mobility study was stopped for futility (NCT03065959), and the small 2-week crossover leaves some room for F7.

In healthy volunteers, CK-107 raised the tibialis anterior force-frequency response with rising dose and plasma concentration, peaking near 60% at 10 Hz (PMID:29150952). This shows exposure, troponin engagement and the expected pathway effect of force amplification. In SMA, MEP improved at plasma Cmax above 3.29 µg/mL (PMID:33624184). The index trial in elderly people with mobility limitation (NCT03065959) stopped at interim analysis for lack of efficacy. No results were posted and no dose limit is described. Similar failures in COPD and ALS despite the mechanism being engaged (NCT02662582, NCT03160898, NCT04944784) suggest that amplifying the fast-muscle troponin response does not produce a clinical anti-fatigue benefit. Engagement was not shown in this population, and the evidence was published after the index trial started. The small interim-stopped trial limits certainty.

In healthy humans, CK-2127107 reached plasma levels that raised the force-frequency response of the tibialis anterior.
