Peak force rose about 60% at 10 Hz, with clear dose and concentration dependence (PMID:29150952). This shows exposure, troponin engagement and the expected functional effect. The SMA study confirmed plasma exposure and exposure-related functional effects (PMID:33624184). The drug was well tolerated up to 450 mg bid (PMID:32969758), so the dose was not capped. Even so, the anti-fatigability trial in elderly people with mobility limitation was stopped at interim for lack of efficacy (NCT03065959), consistent with the COPD miss (NCT02662582). Calcium sensitization does not appear to drive fatigability in this population. Caveats: no engagement data in the index population, and the healthy-volunteer evidence was published in 2018, after the index trial started in 2017.

Recifercept is a soluble FGFR3 decoy meant to soak up FGF ligands. In NCT04638153, height growth at all three doses matched the natural-history model's prediction, so there was no treatment effect (PMID:38685585). Pfizer stopped after an interim analysis showed the study would not meet its primary endpoint, not for safety reasons. The only human pharmacology found is in a protocol (NCT05116046): blood levels at 1 mg/kg weekly and 2 mg/kg twice weekly were lower than the model predicted for children. That suggests a possible exposure shortfall, which is why F1a is listed as secondary. However, a daily-dose arm was added and also failed. No human data were found on free-FGF lowering or on downstream growth-plate biomarkers. No other FGFR3 drug in the bundle has met a pivotal endpoint, so F1b does not apply. Because the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, the code is U.

In healthy volunteers (NCT02705989, registered 2016; PMID:32198939), branebrutinib was rapidly absorbed. A single 10 mg dose gave 100% BTK occupancy, and occupancy persisted for days (half-life 115-154 h). It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. No downstream pathway biomarker or patient-population engagement data appear in the bundle, and the index dose is not stated. In NCT04186871, all three cohorts (RA ACR50, SLE mCLASI, pSS composite) numerically favoured placebo with no safety signal. This points to near-complete BTK engagement without clinical benefit, so the mechanism does not drive these diseases as tested (F2). Very small SLE and pSS arms limit inference (F7 secondary). Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers, so confidence is medium.

Phase 1 in healthy participants (NCT02705989, PMID:32198939) showed rapid absorption and 100% BTK occupancy after a single 10 mg dose. Occupancy was sustained, with a decay half-life of about 115-154 h, and the drug was well tolerated. Exposure and engagement were therefore adequate, with no dose limitation. No human downstream pathway biomarker and no engagement data in patients are in the bundle. The index basket trial (NCT04186871) showed no benefit in RA, SLE or pSS; all primary endpoints numerically favoured placebo, with no serious AEs. Near-complete BTK engagement without clinical effect points to the mechanism not driving disease as tested (F2). The SLE and pSS arms were very small, so underpowering is a secondary consideration (F7).

In healthy adults (NCT02255760, PMID:30107283), MEDI3902 showed roughly linear serum PK up to 1500 mg. Ex vivo anticytotoxicity (PcrV) and opsonophagocytic killing (Psl) activity in subjects' serum correlated with drug concentration. This is human functional evidence of target binding at the 1500 mg dose later used in the index trial. That trial was registered before the index start, and tolerability did not cap the dose. No lung or ELF levels and no engagement in ventilated patients are shown, and no downstream pathway effect is reported in disease. At 1500 mg, P. aeruginosa pneumonia was numerically worse than placebo (22.4% vs 18.1%, p=0.49; NCT02696902), suggesting the mechanism does not prevent disease as tested. Confidence is low because lung engagement in patients is unverified; U applies if serum ex vivo data are discounted.

The sponsor terminated NCT04130919 because a new molecular entity achieved greater target coverage. Only 19 participants were enrolled, remission was 0% in every arm, and no formal comparison was made. In healthy participants (PMID:42634341), GS-4875 reached plasma exposure, but inhibition of LPS-stimulated pERK, the TPL2 pathway biomarker, was only 75-80% at 24 h even at 450 mg. The prodrug tilpisertib fosmecarbil reached >90%, and development moved to it (NCT06029972). This partial coverage means the mechanism was not adequately tested with this molecule. No engagement data exist in UC patients, and the PD publication postdates the index start. The creatinine rise was attributed to renal transporter inhibition, not a dose cap. The tiny terminated trial also could not answer the efficacy question (F7).

Human PK was characterized in healthy volunteers (PMID:26904383, PMID:33107218). The same study showed exposure-dependent inhibition of ex vivo LPS-induced TNFα, a standard whole-blood p38 readout, but suppression partly waned despite continuous exposure, which the authors read as inflammation bypassing p38. This evidence comes from healthy volunteers only and was published after the index trial started. Acumapimod was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The index trial missed FEV1 at Day 10 (p=0.082), with only post-hoc or non-prespecified signals at 75 mg repeat dosing (PMID:31682162). The follow-up trial NCT02700919 also missed FEV1. With engagement shown, the most direct reading is that p38 inhibition does not drive FEV1 recovery in AECOPD (F2). The small dose-exploration design (F7) is a secondary factor.

Intranasal AZD8848 engaged TLR7 in allergic rhinitis patients. In the index study (PMID:26342289), CXCL10, TNFα, IL-6 and IFNγ rose. Earlier AR studies (NCT00688779, NCT00770003, PMID:22726593), registered before the index trial, showed raised plasma IL-1RA, lymphocyte reductions and lower nasal tryptase and α2-macroglobulin. Exposure, engagement and pathway were therefore shown in disease. Yet in NCT01185080, TNSS and PNIF differences versus placebo were small and not significant, so the engaged mechanism gave little clinical benefit (F2). The placebo arm was small (n=15), and the publication pooled data with a prior study to show effects, suggesting the trial was underpowered (F7). Dose-dependent flu-like interferon symptoms limited the inhaled program (PMID:26933507), an on-target tolerability issue (F5).

Index trial NCT04179266 (n=23, intranasal ketamine in chronic cluster headache) posted no results and gave no stop reason. The bundle has no human PK, NMDA-receptor occupancy or biomarker data in cluster headache. Engagement of central NMDA receptors is inferred: ketamine met efficacy endpoints in treatment-resistant depression (NCT01627782; PMID:30283029, dose-dependent at 0.5–1 mg/kg IV; PMID:38293803). Ketamine also raised MEG gamma power in MDD (PMID:29487402), so the CNS mechanism holds at subanesthetic doses. Whether intranasal doses in NCT04179266 were comparable is not shown. This leaves a weak F2 reading: a target engaged, yet no evident benefit for cluster headache. The small, unreported trial also supports F7. Confidence is low because the readout itself is absent.

In NCT05155085, SC lirentelimab 300 mg missed EASI-75 (23.0% vs 18.0%, p=0.47), and development stopped. Target depletion is shown directly in humans: near-complete tissue eosinophil depletion in EoG/EoD/EoE trials (NCT03496571, NCT04322604 77/91 vs 4/89, NCT04856891, NCT04322708), all registered before the index trial. That also implies adequate systemic exposure. However, those data come from GI disease and largely IV dosing. The bundle has no engagement or pathway readout in atopic dermatitis and no posted SC pharmacodynamic data, which tempers confidence. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Given adequate Siglec-8 cell depletion with no benefit in AD, and a parallel null result in CSU (NCT05528861), the evidence favours a target that does not drive this disease (F2). U is possible if SC skin engagement is questioned.

In the index EoE trial (NCT04322708), both doses depleted esophageal eosinophils to ≤6/hpf in most patients (86/93 and 80/91 vs 10/92, p<0.0001). That shows exposure, target-cell depletion and the expected tissue effect in EoE patients. However, this EoE-specific evidence came from the index trial itself; earlier depletion data (NCT03496571) were in eosinophilic gastritis/duodenitis. Dysphagia (DSQ) did not improve versus placebo at either dose, and serious AEs were low, so no dose cap. The same pattern repeated in EG/EoD Phase 3 trials (NCT04322604, NCT04856891): histology met, symptoms not. A network meta-analysis notes histologic improvement does not guarantee symptom benefit (PMID:42901296). Eosinophil depletion therefore does not drive symptoms as tested (F2). The choice of endpoint may also contribute (F4).

In the index Phase 3 (NCT04322604), lirentelimab 3 mg/kg depleted tissue eosinophils in EG/EoD patients: 77/91 responders vs 4/89, p<0.0001. This directly shows tissue exposure, target engagement and the expected depleting effect in the disease. The Phase 2 (NCT03496571, started 2018) had already shown the eosinophil reduction (p<0.001) before the index began. Despite near-complete depletion, symptoms did not improve (TSS -10.0 vs -11.5, p=0.34). The same pattern repeated in eosinophilic duodenitis (NCT04856891) and EoE (NCT04322708). Serious AEs were balanced and the dose was not limited. Eosinophil depletion via SIGLEC8 does not drive symptoms as tested, so F2. F4 is possible because the symptom endpoint is where it failed, but no source blames the endpoint.

Siglec-8 engagement is shown in humans: lirentelimab produced near-complete tissue eosinophil depletion in eosinophilic GI disease (NCT03496571, NCT04322604, NCT04856891, NCT04322708), much of it before the index start. Exposure is therefore inferred, though at IV dosing. The SC bioavailability study (NCT04324268) posted no results. Mast-cell inhibition, the mechanism relevant to CSU, was never measured in urticaria patients. The open-label phase 2a looked positive (PMID:34954198, NCT03436797), but the randomized SC trial showed no separation from placebo on UAS7 (-7.9 vs -8.4, p=0.82; NCT05528861). The atopic dermatitis trial also failed (NCT05155085). An engaged target with no benefit fits F2. Untested SC exposure and mast-cell engagement in skin leave F1a possible. The 'business' stop followed a failed readout, so F8 does not apply.

The index CLL trial (NCT02557516) combined monalizumab with ibrutinib. DLTs occurred at 4 mg/kg (2/4 patients), so the RP2D was capped at 2 mg/kg. That is far below the 10 mg/kg q2w regimen used elsewhere, where full NKG2A saturation was reported (PMID:31308062, published after the index trial started) and which modeling treats as the dose needed for tumor receptor occupancy (PMID:33501768). No NKG2A occupancy, PK or pharmacodynamic data exist in CLL patients. CR was 0/9 at the RP2D. The trial was terminated by sponsor decision, and its endpoints were descriptive safety and CR counts with no formal efficacy test, which supports F9 as a secondary code. Overall, the mechanism was likely not adequately tested at the tolerated dose.

Exposure is adequate. The first-in-human study (NCT02122809; PMC6332596) showed linear, dose-dependent plasma levels of the drug and found a maximum tolerated dose of 50 mg/day. The dose-limiting effect was hypertension, a known on-target VEGF effect, so tolerability set the dose ceiling. Plasma VEGF and sVEGFR2 and tumor Aurora B were registered as biomarkers, but no results were found, so engagement and pathway have no human data. I found no published results for the index trial (NCT04830813). The company said the SCLC Phase 3 was finished and it was holding pre-NDA talks, so it is unclear the trial even failed. An ovarian Phase 3 combination trial (NCT04921527) met its PFS endpoint. With several targets and a chemotherapy partner, that result does not show which target worked. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that did not engage from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The phase 1 study in Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID:25887777, NCT01221571; published 2015, before the 2019 index start) measured human PK (half-life up to 19 h), with MTD not reached, so dose was not tolerability-capped. It also showed significant NK-cell activation and soluble CD30 decrease, indicating CD30/CD16A engagement and the expected effector pathway, but only in HL, not T-cell lymphoma. In the index trial (NCT04101331) ORR was 32.4%, narrowly missing significance (p=0.051). Brentuximab vedotin's approvals validate CD30 itself, but it works through payload delivery, not NK-cell recruitment. With engagement shown, the NK-engager mechanism gave insufficient benefit as tested (F2). The near-miss suggests a possible power issue (F7). The bundle is thin, hence low confidence.

In healthy volunteers, CSF exposure was dose-proportional (NCT02362516). CSF glycine rose dose-dependently, by about 50% at 10 mg, which the authors call functional GlyT1 engagement (PMID:30136756). This was registered before the index trial started in 2016. Doses of 2–25 mg were well tolerated (PMID:29846887). The 12-week Alzheimer trial across these doses showed a flat dose-response on ADAS-Cog11 (all p>0.76) despite >97% compliance (NCT02788513, PMID:36709275). No downstream NMDA or pathway marker was shown, and engagement was not measured in Alzheimer patients. The later schizophrenia Phase 3 trials also failed (NCT04846868, NCT04846881, NCT04860830). Adequate engagement without benefit indicates GlyT1 inhibition does not drive cognition in Alzheimer disease as tested.

The index phase 2b trial (NCT03251768) compared rHSA/G-CSF 2400 μg with active rhG-CSF 5 μg/kg. It failed only to meet non-inferiority against that active comparator (PMID:33789616), so it was not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure. Pillars hold in chemotherapy-induced neutropenia patients. The phase 1b (NCT03246009) assessed PK/PD across 1800–2400 μg with acceptable safety. In the phase 2 trial (NCT02465801), 1500 μg gave agranulocytosis duration comparable to rhG-CSF (1.14 vs 1.07 days), showing the expected neutrophil response. The authors judged the drug efficacious and recommended advancing 1500 μg to phase 3. The missed non-inferiority margin fits F9, not a mechanism failure.

The index trial NCT02586233 was a Phase 1/2 ascending-dose safety, PK and PD study in acute ischemic stroke. Its primary outcome was a descriptive count of TEAEs with no efficacy comparison, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). Pillars: in healthy subjects, plasma exposure was dose-proportional, TAFIa activity fell substantially and dose-dependently, and 50% clot lysis time shortened (PMID:28211169, PMID:31243790). In AIS patients (PMID:35061236), exposure rose with dose but there was no clear dose-response for TAFIa activity or D-dimer, so engagement was not shown in disease. That engagement evidence was published in 2017, after the index trial started in 2015. No tolerability cap was seen. The companion PE trial NCT02923115 was also a safety study.

In healthy volunteers, DS-1040 IV (up to 40 mg) gave dose-proportional exposure, a substantial dose-dependent fall in TAFIa activity and shortened 50% clot lysis time (PMID:28211169), and oral dosing gave dose-dependent TAFIa inhibition (PMID:31243790). The PE index trial (NCT02923115) used 20-80 mg. Its primary endpoint was bleeding, a safety measure, so it was not formally an efficacy test (F9). Exploratory thrombus volume and RV/LV ratio did not improve over placebo plus enoxaparin (PMID:37178771). Engagement was not shown in PE patients. In AIS patients at much lower doses, no clear TAFIa or D-dimer dose-response was seen (PMID:35061236). With engagement shown in healthy volunteers and no clinical signal, the best fit is F2. The small exploratory design (F7) tempers confidence.

In the index trial, BI 1026706 100 mg twice daily did not reduce central retinal thickness (CSFT) over 12 weeks (NCT02732951, PMID:32818112). Phase 1 trials report plasma PK (NCT01763333, NCT02513446) but no receptor occupancy, B1 receptor blockade or retinal drug levels, so engagement has no human data. The human pharmacodynamic models were all negative: no effect on laser-evoked potentials in UVB-irradiated skin (NCT02037165), no pain relief after dental surgery (NCT02084511), and no reduction in lung inflammation after LPS challenge at the same 100 mg twice-daily dose (NCT02657408; Gress et al.). None of these shows that the receptor was engaged. The authors suggest the effect may need more than 12 weeks (F4), but nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02126826 was a Phase 1 multiple-rising-dose study in healthy volunteers and knee OA patients. Its primary endpoint was drug-related adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test and no efficacy failure was recorded (F9). Plasma exposure was measured (NCT02513446, Cmax ~206 nmol/L). The bundle has no human B1 receptor occupancy or engagement data. The pathway readout was negative: 100 mg bid did not reduce BAL neutrophils or other biomarkers after LPS challenge in healthy smokers (PMID:37562641). The DME trial also failed (PMID:32818112). Because engagement was never shown, nothing separates a drug that did not engage B1R from a target irrelevant to COPD inflammation, so U is secondary. No tolerability cap is evident (NCT02642614).

The index trial NCT01763333 was a single-rising-dose safety, PK and bioavailability study in healthy volunteers, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). Doses up to 400 mg were tolerated with no serious AEs, so the dose was not limited. Plasma exposure was measured (e.g., NCT02513446 PK), but the bundle has no human BDKRB1 occupancy or engagement data. Later trials showed no benefit: LEP (NCT02037165), dental pain (NCT02084511) and DME CSFT (NCT02732951, PMID:32818112). Without engagement evidence, these misses cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so U is the secondary code.

In the TALLY trial (NCT03745820), neither 0.15 mg nor 0.5 mg BID changed MCCB working memory compared with placebo, and Biogen ended the program in CIAS without giving a mechanistic reason. Plasma pharmacokinetics were measured in schizophrenia patients (NCT02332798), but the sources contain no human CSF levels, brain penetration data or AMPA receptor occupancy. The only brain-uptake data are PET scans in monkeys (PMID:38257338), and that paper notes there are no tools to directly measure AMPA receptor engagement. In healthy volunteers, 5 days of PF-04958242 reduced ketamine-induced memory deficits (PMID:28242871). That is functional evidence of a CNS effect, but the dose relative to the index trial is unclear. With engagement unmeasured, the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so this is U. The secondary code F2 applies only if the ketamine result is taken as a stand-in for engagement.

The index trial NCT02228395 was a single-dose Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study in 12 healthy volunteers. Its primary outcomes were only safety measures (C-SSRS, adverse events, labs, vitals, ECG), so it was not an efficacy test of the drug, which fits F9. Plasma PK is shown (NCT02332798), but the bundle has no human data on drug levels in the cochlea or auditory pathway. The hearing-loss study NCT01518920 posted no results. Target engagement was never measured; PMID:38257338 notes there are no tools to measure AMPA receptor engagement. The ketamine-challenge benefit in PMID:28242871 shows a CNS effect in healthy volunteers, not in hearing loss. With engagement unknown, the hearing-loss question is indeterminate (secondary U).

Bersacapavir is a capsid assembly modulator that targets the HBV core protein. Exposure: plasma PK was dose-proportional, and the chosen regimen was expected to give trough levels above three times the in vitro EC90 (PMID:31267367). Engagement and pathway: in patients, 4 weeks of dosing in NCT02662712 Part II (registered before the index trial) and the JADE trial (NCT03361956) showed marked, dose-related drops in HBV DNA and RNA, the readout expected from blocking encapsidation. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, HBsAg (the primary endpoint) and HBeAg barely moved compared with placebo. The capsid mechanism suppresses replication but does not lower antigen. REEF-1 (PMID:37442152) later used the drug only as an add-on. F4 is listed as secondary because the sponsor said longer treatment might be needed.

AXA1125 is a mix of amino acids, including isoleucine, meant to modulate several metabolic pathways. It has no defined molecular target, and none of the sources report human exposure or engagement data. In the index trial (NCT05152849; PMID:37223439), the primary endpoint was skeletal-muscle τPCr, a downstream marker of mitochondrial function. τPCr and the 6MWT did not change, so the pathway pillar is inadequate in this disease. CFQ-11 fatigue scores did improve. The sponsor said the drug still showed promise, received FDA IND clearance for a Phase 2b/3 trial, then cut 85% of its staff, and no further trial followed. Business reasons may therefore have helped end the program (F8 secondary). Because engagement has no human data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02442778 missed CMAI at both doses (p=0.789, p=0.200). The sister trial NCT02442765 was mixed, and the later Phase 3s were terminated when the program was discontinued. The bundle contains no human exposure, occupancy or biomarker data for AVP-786; no Phase 1 results were posted. Non-deuterated dextromethorphan, which acts on the same NMDA target, is FDA-approved in Alzheimer disease, and PMID:40490784 notes positive AXS-05 trials in AD agitation. That abstract attributes AVP-786's failure to deuteration lowering potency at NMDA receptors (dextrorphan IC50 up 16-fold), but this is in vitro evidence only. So this points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Because human engagement was never measured, U also applies.

The index Phase 2/3 trial (NCT03896945) was stopped for futility at interim analysis. On negative symptoms the drug and placebo differed by only 0.2 points (p=0.768), and an earlier schizophrenia trial (NCT02477670) also missed its primary endpoint. Phase 1 trials (NCT01787747, NCT02336347) studied plasma levels, with deuteration plus quinidine raising exposure, but they posted no results. I found no human CSF levels, NMDA or sigma-1 receptor occupancy data, or biomarker data. No sponsor explanation goes beyond futility. One paper (PMID:40490784) suggests deuteration made the drug weaker at NMDA receptors, raising doubts about adequate engagement, but this rests on lab (in vitro) data only. With no human engagement evidence, the cause of failure can't be determined.

The TBI disinhibition trial NCT03095066 missed its primary endpoint in both stages (p=0.405 and p=0.921). The only human pharmacology found is plasma PK in healthy volunteers (NCT01787747, NCT02336347): Avanir said AVP-786 matched AVP-923's steady-state plasma levels. That does not show the drug reached the brain, which is where its targets (NMDA receptor, sigma-1) are. No human data on brain or CSF levels, receptor occupancy, or a downstream biomarker were found. PMID:40490784 suggests deuteration weakens activity at NMDA receptors, but that comes from in vitro patch-clamp work and does not count as human evidence. No other drug on these targets has succeeded in TBI, so F1b does not apply. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

AVP-786 missed both stages of its TBI disinhibition primary endpoint (NCT03095066, p=0.405 and p=0.921). The bundle has no human PK, NMDA/sigma-1 occupancy or pathway biomarker data, and no Phase 1 results were posted. One AD-agitation trial was mixed (NCT02442765, only the 18 mg dose was significant) and was not replicated (NCT02442778), so it cannot support inferred engagement. PMID:40490784 hypothesizes that deuteration weakened NMDA potency, citing in vitro patch-clamp data and the positive AXS-05 dextromethorphan trials in AD agitation. That points toward a molecule problem (F1b), but the evidence is non-human and comes from a different disease. Engagement is no_human_data, so the failure is indeterminate.

The TBI disinhibition trial NCT03095066 missed its primary endpoint in both stages (p=0.405 and p=0.921). Exposure looks adequate: Phase 1 PK work in healthy volunteers (NCT01787747, NCT02336347) matched the steady-state plasma levels of AVP-923 (dextromethorphan plus quinidine) using less quinidine. I found no human data on NMDA or sigma-1 occupancy, or on any downstream biomarker. PMID:40490784 argues, from patch-clamp (in vitro) data only, that deuteration weakens NMDA antagonism, and notes that non-deuterated dextromethorphan with bupropion (AXS-05) had positive agitation trials. That is a hypothesis about the molecule rather than the target, and it does not concern TBI. Since there is no engagement data, nothing separates non-engagement from target irrelevance, so the code is U. F1b is a weak secondary.

Phase 1 data show the CD47 antigen sink saturated at ≥10 mg/kg, a half-life of about 13 days, strong tumor staining at 30 mg/kg (PMID:30811285), and about 100% CD47 occupancy at 30 mg/kg (PMID:30380386). These were shown before the index trial, but not in TNBC. No MTD was reached, so the dose was not tolerability-capped. Downstream tumor phagocytosis was not measured. The index randomized cohort was tiny (14 per arm): PFS HR 0.456 with a wide CI, p=0.16, which suggests it was underpowered (F7). Magrolimab also failed randomized trials in HNSCC, CRC, MDS and AML, consistent with the mechanism not delivering benefit (F2). Modeling suggests receptor-ligand blockade may lag occupancy (PMID:38790133), leaving some F1a doubt.

Before the index trial, the first-in-human solid-tumor study (PMID:30811285) showed saturation of the CD47 antigen sink at ≥10 mg/kg, a ~13-day half-life, 100% RBC CD47 saturation and strong tumor staining at 30 mg/kg. The NHL study (PMID:30380386) showed ~100% CD47 occupancy on white and red cells at 30 mg/kg. On-target anemia and hemagglutination show the expected phagocytic effect. MTD was not reached, so dose was not limited. CRC-specific engagement was not shown. In ELEVATE CRC, PFS was unchanged (HR 0.956; NCT05330429). The cetuximab combination in CRC was also inactive (PMID:40140179), and randomized failures occurred across other tumors. This suggests the mechanism does not drive benefit. Early closure limits PFS interpretation (PMID:42022129), and modeling suggests ligand blockade may lag occupancy (PMID:38790133).

Magrolimab adding to pembrolizumab/platinum/5-FU gave no PFS benefit in HNSCC (5.5 vs 5.6 mo, HR 1.31; NCT04854499). Human PK showed antigen-sink saturation at ≥10 mg/kg with a ~13-day half-life, and tumor staining at 30 mg/kg (PMID:30811285). About 100% CD47 receptor occupancy on blood cells was shown at 30 mg/kg (PMID:30380386). Both were published before the index trial, but neither was measured in HNSCC. No MTD was reached up to 45 mg/kg, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. A modeling study suggests receptor-ligand blockade may lag occupancy (PMID:38790133), but no human data show it was inadequate. Randomized failures across AML, MDS and CRC (NCT04313881, NCT04778397, NCT05079230, NCT05330429) point to CD47 blockade not driving benefit, which supports F2.

In the first-in-human solid tumor trial (NCT02216409/PMID:30811285), doses of 10 mg/kg or more saturated the CD47 antigen sink, gave a half-life of about 13 days, and one patient at 30 mg/kg showed strong tumor-tissue staining. No MTD was reached up to 45 mg/kg. PMID:30380386 reported about 100% CD47 occupancy on blood cells at 30 mg/kg, with on-target anemia and clinical responses in NHL. The index trial used 45 mg/kg with avelumab without DLTs, yet ORR in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer was 0/21. Occupancy was measured on blood cells, not shown in ovarian tumors. PMID:38790133 models less ligand blockade than occupancy, but this is modeling only. Repeated futility across the program supports a target that does not drive disease as tested.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Phase 1 showed CD47 antigen-sink saturation at ≥10 mg/kg, a ~13-day half-life, no MTD up to 45 mg/kg, and tumor staining at 30 mg/kg (PMID:30811285). The 30 mg/kg dose gave ~100% CD47 occupancy on circulating cells (PMID:30380386). On-target anemia and hemagglutination show the phagocytic effect in humans. All of this predates the index trial, but none of it was measured in HNSCC patients. A modeling paper suggests occupancy may overstate ligand blockade, but it has no human data (PMID:38790133). In ELEVATE HNSCC, adding magrolimab gave no PFS benefit (HR 1.314; NCT04854499, PMID:41785669). Randomized trials in MDS and AML were also futile, supporting a target that does not drive disease as tested (F2). Early closure limited interpretation (F7).

Exposure was adequate: at ≥10 mg/kg the CD47 antigen sink saturated, half-life was about 13 days, and tumor staining was seen at 30 mg/kg (PMID:30811285). Engagement was adequate: 30 mg/kg gave about 100% CD47 occupancy on circulating cells, though in lymphoma and solid-tumor patients, not MDS (PMID:30380386, PMID:30811285). Pathway: on-target anemia and hemagglutination show phagocytic clearance. No MTD was reached, so dose was not limited. Despite full engagement at the 30 mg/kg dose used in MDS (NCT03248479), ENHANCE showed no CR or OS benefit (CR 21.3% vs 23.6%; OS HR 1.20; NCT04313881). Parallel AML phase 3 trials also failed (NCT05079230, NCT04778397), pointing to the target. A model suggests ligand blockade may lag occupancy (PMID:38790133). More serious AEs, a numerically worse OS and a safety pause (PMID:35140129) hint at offsetting toxicity.

Exposure: CD47 antigen sink saturated at ≥10 mg/kg with ~13-day half-life, and no MTD up to 45 mg/kg (PMID:30811285). Engagement: ~100% CD47 occupancy on circulating cells at 30 mg/kg in DLBCL/FL patients (PMID:30380386; NCT02953509, registered before the index trial). Pathway: on-target anemia was seen, and responses occurred with rituximab, but macrophage phagocytosis was not measured in humans. A modeling paper suggests ligand blockade may lag occupancy, but this is not human data (PMID:38790133). The index trial stopped because the ENHANCE phase 3 MDS trial was futile: CR 21.3% vs 23.6%, OS HR 1.20, more serious AEs (NCT04313881). The AML phase 3 trials were also futile (NCT04778397, NCT05079230). The DLBCL work ended with the program (NCT02953509). With engagement adequate and no benefit, the mechanism appears not to drive disease as tested.

PICASSO (NCT03817684) found no difference on RBANS-DMI at 10 or 25 mg twice daily (10.1 and 9.9 vs 9.7 on placebo). Tolerability did not cap the dose. The only human evidence on the target is PET: in a single-dose study in people with depression, BPN14770 blocked PDE4D radioligand uptake in the brain (PMID:32212718; NCT03861000). That shows the drug reaches the brain, but occupancy could not be measured because the radioligand was unstable, and the paper came out after the index trial started. No human pathway biomarker (cAMP, pCREB) was found, and no scopolamine-study results were published. Engagement is therefore unproven, and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Shionogi reported a CDR-SB signal only in the subgroup of 25 mg patients with above-median baseline CDR-SB (secondary F3). Fragile X results are not an approved or pivotal success, so they cannot support inferred_adequate.

Plasma exposure was characterised in healthy subjects and MSA patients (PMID:29873817, 2018), and the same work related exposure to change in MPO-specific activity, so peripheral MPO inhibition was measured in MSA before the index trial started. Its magnitude is not given in the abstract, and brain penetration is not shown. Downstream microglial TSPO-PET fell 13-16% in Parkinson's disease (PMID:26137956), but the MSA Phase 2 PET trial showed no significant change versus placebo (NCT02388295). With the target engaged, the Phase 3 trial still showed no benefit on modified UMSARS (difference 0.35, p=0.47; NCT03952806), pointing to MPO inhibition not modifying MSA. Confidence is medium because the evidence of engagement is indirect.

In the index trial (NCT02151461), adding leucine to low-dose metformin did not beat the control arm on change in 3-hour glucose AUC, and the control arm actually lowered glucose more. In the 12-week extension (NCT02435277), HbA1c also favoured the control arm. The bundle has no human pharmacology for leucine's proposed mechanism, AMPK/SIRT1 activation working with metformin: no plasma or tissue leucine levels, no AMPK or SIRT1 activity and no downstream biomarker change. The other trials (NAFLD NCT02546609, obesity NCT03364335) report only clinical results, and neither the sponsor nor investigators gave a reason for stopping. The bundle does not show whether the drug never engaged its target or the mechanism does not matter in this disease, so the code is U.

NS-0200 combines leucine, metformin and sildenafil. Its proposed mechanism is that leucine allosterically activates Sirt1 and works together with drugs on the AMPK/nitric oxide pathway. No human data were found on Sirt1 or AMPK activation, on drug levels in the liver, or on a pathway biomarker. In the index trial (NCT02546609), neither dose beat placebo on liver fat measured by MRI-PDFF. The investigators pointed instead to a post-hoc high-ALT subgroup, where the high dose cut liver fat by 15.7%. That points weakly to patient selection (F3). Weight loss in the obesity trial (NCT03364335) does not show that Sirt1 was engaged. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Leucine (NS-0200/NS-0300) is described as an allosteric SIRT1 activator that works with metformin and sildenafil on the SIRT1/AMPK/nitric oxide pathway. I found no human data on drug levels, SIRT1 or AMPK activation, or any downstream pathway marker. The obesity trial NCT03364335 actually beat placebo on weight in 3 of 4 arms, but the effects were small, around 1.6–2% versus placebo. Earlier Phase 2 trials in NAFLD and diabetes (NCT02546609, NCT02151461) missed their biomarker endpoints. No source says why the program stopped. Because target engagement is unknown, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U. F9 is a secondary code because the primary endpoint was partly met.

NS-0200 combines leucine, metformin and sildenafil. The sponsor says it works by activating the Sirt1/AMPK/NO pathway. I found no human measurement of Sirt1 or AMPK activation, drug levels in the liver, or a downstream pathway biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the index trial (NCT02546609), neither dose beat placebo on liver fat change at day 112; placebo actually did better. The published report (PMID 29696666, APT) puts the signal in a post hoc subgroup: in patients with high ALT, the high dose cut liver fat by 15.7%. So the sources pin the failure on who was enrolled, which is code F3. Because engagement was never measured, the result is also consistent with code U (indeterminate). The later obesity trial (NCT03364335) showed weight loss but gave no engagement data.

AXA1125 is a mix of amino acids, including leucine, meant to boost mitochondrial bioenergetics, but no molecular target is recorded. The searches found no human data on tissue exposure or target engagement. In the index trial (NCT05152849, PMID:37223439), the mechanistic primary endpoint, muscle phosphocreatine recovery time (τPCr) measured by 31P-MRS, did not change, so the pathway pillar was not shown. The Chalder fatigue score did improve, though. Axcella treated the result as positive and got MHRA and FDA backing to plan a Phase 2b/3 trial. Low capital led the company to drop NASH and later shut down entirely (SEC filings, BioSpace), so business reasons ended the program. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter. Hence U, with F8 and small-pilot F7 as secondary codes.

The bundle has no human PK, receptor occupancy or pathway data for ORP-101, and no Phase 1 results. The index Phase II trial (NCT04129619; PMID:41887552) missed its composite primary endpoint at 100 mg (28.3% vs 21.9%, P=.12), though secondary endpoints favored the drug and it was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Eluxadoline, which acts on the same primary target (OPRM1), is FDA-approved for IBS, which suggests the μ-opioid mechanism can work in this disease. With no evidence that ORP-101 engaged its targets adequately, a molecule-level failure (F1b) is most consistent with the bundle. The pharmacology differs (partial agonism plus κ antagonism), so U also applies. The adaptive design, including dropping the 50 mg arm, and the modest effect size raise possible power issues (F7).

The index PDPN trial (NCT02372578) was stopped for futility. Human pillar data show plasma exposure and strong, long-lasting hepatic HSD-1 inhibition at low doses in healthy adults (PMID:37452998). They also show >90% adipose HSD-1 inhibition in people with type 2 diabetes and obesity (PMID:41240060, NCT05409027). This supports adequate systemic engagement, so F2 is the best fit: the target did not relieve neuropathic pain. Caveats: the index doses are not given. No engagement was shown in PDPN patients. The brain PET occupancy study (NCT02194491) posted no results, so engagement in the CNS or nerve, the likely site of action for pain, is unshown. Pathway evidence is absent. Secondary U, low confidence.

Every ichorcumab dose (0.3–1.8 mg/kg) had a higher total VTE rate (~30%) than apixaban (~12%), with no dose response (NCT03251482). Bleeding was low, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Thrombin is a validated VTE target: dabigatran etexilate and argatroban are FDA-approved for VTE. That points to this molecule, an exosite-1 antibody, rather than the target. Human engagement evidence in the bundle is weak. PMID:30184110 spiked healthy-volunteer blood ex vivo, which is effectively in vitro, and was published after the index trial started. PMID:34008170 mentions a healthy-volunteer PK/PD relationship but gives no occupancy or inhibition levels. Phase 1 results are not posted. No pillar is shown adequate, which fits F1b.

The index trial was stopped after a 14-patient interim analysis that the sponsor framed as a favorable safety result. Strata had only 2 placebo patients each, the confidence intervals were very wide, and the endpoints were MRI measures at 4 weeks. It could not test efficacy (F7). In humans, the drug showed cartilage penetration, and post-hoc transcriptomics found a reversed OA signature with anabolic pathway induction (PMID:36456835, NCT02491281). Integrin α5β1 binding itself was never measured in humans, so engagement is no_human_data and F2 is not supported. A later OA trial gave mixed cartilage-volume results (NCT03275064), and the Phase 2b was stopped for futility (NCT04864392). That leaves it indeterminate whether the mechanism matters (U); the short endpoint timing may also have contributed (F4).

Genta's index melanoma trial (NCT01092585) has no posted results and no stated reason for stopping. I found no published melanoma results for it or for the MD Anderson trial NCT01064713. Phase 1 work, including NCT00077077 and the 2004 ASCO PK abstract, showed the oral drug reached the blood. Reviews say those PK data varied widely between patients and are hard to interpret. I found no human data on microtubule (tubulin) engagement or a downstream biomarker in tumour. Later breast cancer trials ended by sponsor decision (NCT03326674, NCT03858972, NCT03952325), which hints at business factors (F8) but says nothing about melanoma efficacy. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not help melanoma, so the code is U.

KBL697 is an oral Lactobacillus gasseri live biotherapeutic with no defined molecular target. The sponsor has said the Phase 2a trial in 78 patients with moderate plaque psoriasis (NCT04911751) missed its primary endpoint: PASI improvement was not statistically significant versus placebo in the overall population, though some subgroups showed PASI reductions (edaily). I found no human evidence of gut colonization or exposure, of immune engagement such as IL-10 induction, or of IL-17 or IL-23 pathway changes. The mechanistic support (IL-10 induction, lower skin cytokines) comes only from animal and cell studies. No Phase 1 results were posted (NCT04056130). Engagement is no_human_data, so this is U. The subgroup signal weakly points to F3.

SCHUMANN (NCT04614246) was stopped early 'for safety reasons'. It produced fewer than 50% of planned completers and showed no EAPP difference versus placebo (PMID:38890641). A probable drug-induced liver injury at 150 mg BID was the second such case after one in PAGANINI. Bayer said this hepatotoxicity led it to discontinue the entire program in all indications (PMID:37261531), so molecule-specific toxicity ended the program (F6). Human plasma exposure is documented (PMID:35624408, PMID:35437837). The same 25/75/150 mg BID doses met the cough efficacy endpoint (NCT04562155, NCT03310645), which supports inferred peripheral P2X3 engagement. No engagement was shown in endometriosis patients. The truncated, underpowered readout limits interpretation (F7), and the null result at engaged doses suggests F2 as a possible contributor.

Repeated dosing in healthy volunteers reached plasma concentrations predicted to give ≥80% P2X3 occupancy, the level judged needed for efficacy (PMID:35624408). Occupancy was not measured directly. Engagement and pathway are rated inferred_adequate because eliapixant met cough-frequency endpoints in chronic cough (NCT03310645, NCT04562155/PMID:37261531). That benefit runs through peripheral sensory-afferent P2X3 at 25–750 mg doses. Dose-related dysgeusia also supports on-target activity. No tolerability cap below engaging doses is shown. Despite this, the diabetic neuropathic pain trial stopped for lack of efficacy (NCT04641273). Endometriosis pain was also negative (PMID:38890641). Together these point to P2X3 not driving neuropathic pain as tested. Drug-induced liver injury independently led Bayer to end the whole program (PMID:37261531), so F6 is secondary.

In SOLACE (NCT03131154), reproxalap 0.5% performed about the same as vehicle on anterior chamber cell clearance (25/61 vs 24/62; HR 1.13). The sources contain no human measurements of drug levels in the anterior chamber, of lowering of reactive aldehydes (RASP) such as MDA or 4-HNE, or of any downstream biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Reproxalap did succeed in allergic conjunctivitis (NCT03494504) and dry eye (PMID:33529588). Those are ocular-surface diseases, a different tissue compartment from intraocular inflammation, so engagement cannot be inferred from them. Aldeyra blamed the miss on high disease resolution in the vehicle arm, a trial-design and placebo-response problem (F7), and then dropped the program to focus on other indications. Because engagement was never shown, U also applies.

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional in humans (PMID:30151212). Occupancy of α2δ was never measured. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate only because 15 mg BID met endpoints in central and diabetic neuropathic pain (NCT03901352, NCT04094662, NCT01496365). Pregabalin, on the same target, is FDA-approved for fibromyalgia. Within this program it separated from placebo in studies B and C, where mirogabalin did not (PMID:31284771). That points to the molecule, or its dose or kinetics, rather than the target. The index trial itself lacked assay sensitivity: pregabalin also failed there (p=0.187, NCT02146430), so F7 applies secondarily. No tolerability cap is shown. Engagement data come from healthy volunteers and other diseases, not fibromyalgia.

In the index trial (NCT04744207, PMID:38291895), vipoglanstat 120 mg fully inhibited mPGES-1 activity in SSc patients. Urinary PGE2 fell 57% and prostacyclin metabolites rose 50%, which is the expected pathway effect. Phase 1 data (NCT04036227, NCT04617509) show measurable plasma exposure. The drug was safe and well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Despite full target engagement and the predicted pathway shift, Raynaud attacks did not differ from placebo (-3.4 vs -4.2, P=0.628), and neither did cold-challenge blood flow. The authors conclude the drug was ineffective in SSc-related Raynaud's and redirected development to other diseases. This points to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested. Engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, not before it.

The index trial NCT04744207 missed its primary endpoint: change in weekly Raynaud attacks was -3.41 on GS-248 versus -4.22 on placebo. Healthy-volunteer PK (NCT04617509, NCT04036227) shows measurable plasma exposure. Doses up to 180 mg multiple dosing were tolerated without a dose cap. NCT04036227 lists pharmacodynamics in its title, but its posted results in the bundle show only safety data. No human mPGES-1 inhibition or PGE2-lowering data appear. PMID:34372885 is mouse work plus leukocyte assays from healthy volunteers, apparently ex vivo, so it does not count. No other PTGES drug is in the bundle. With engagement and pathway lacking human evidence, the bundle cannot separate inadequate engagement from a target irrelevant to SSc-Raynaud. Code: U.

CJM112 300 mg missed its FEV1 primary endpoint in severe asthma (NCT03299686; difference 0.027 L, CI includes zero), and safety was balanced. Exposure, engagement and pathway were not measured in asthma. They are inferred adequate because the same IL-17A neutralizer gave dose-dependent clinical efficacy in psoriasis at 15–150 mg, comparable to secukinumab (PMID:33617042). It also met its endpoint in hidradenitis suppurativa (NCT02421172), both before the index trial. These are skin diseases, so lung-compartment engagement is assumed for a systemically dosed antibody. Tolerability did not limit the dose. With the target neutralized and no benefit, IL-17A does not appear to drive unselected severe asthma. No anti-IL-17A drug has succeeded in asthma; secukinumab stopped at phase 2. Patient selection could contribute (F3), but no source says so.

The index trial NCT01828086 was a Phase 1 safety and tolerability study in psoriasis, not a failed efficacy test. Its publication (PMID:33617042) reports dose-dependent PASI reductions from 15 mg upward, efficacy similar to secukinumab 150 mg, and acceptable safety. No PK, occupancy or biomarker data are given. The pillars are inferred adequate from clinical efficacy in psoriasis and from the met primary endpoint in hidradenitis suppurativa (NCT02421172). The failures in acne (NCT02998671) and asthma (NCT03299686) are other indications. The bundle states no stop reason. The sources note that adding IL-17AF neutralization gave no advantage over secukinumab, which suggests a lack of differentiation (possibly a business decision, F8). That is not shown explicitly.

No direct PK, target-engagement or biomarker data in acne. The pillars are inferred adequate because CJM112 showed dose-dependent PASI efficacy in psoriasis from 15 mg upward, with 150 mg similar to secukinumab (NCT01828086, PMID:33617042). It also met its responder endpoint in hidradenitis suppurativa (NCT02421172). Both are skin IL-17A indications at doses comparable to or below the 300 mg and 75 mg tested in acne. In acne, neither dose beat placebo, and point estimates favoured placebo (NCT02998671). Futility was met at interim, so only 52 of 75 patients were enrolled (PMID:36305633). The trial was small, but the lack of any trend suggests IL-17A does not drive inflammatory acne. Tolerability did not cap dosing, and no same-target drug has succeeded in acne.

Targacept's exploratory Phase 2 asthma trial of TC-6987 (NCT01296087) first reported success on the FEV1 primary endpoint. A reanalysis then found an error in how the statistical analysis plan had been applied. After the correction, the trial no longer met its protocol-defined success criterion. The program was dropped, along with the failed diabetes study (NCT01293669), and the company restructured. I found no human evidence of alpha7 nicotinic receptor engagement: no receptor occupancy, airway or tissue exposure, or downstream inflammatory biomarker data. No Phase 1 pharmacology was published. The only other drug on this target in the bundle, ASM-024, did not get past Phase 2, so the target has not been validated elsewhere. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot separate a molecule that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter in asthma. A small exploratory trial with a borderline result is a possible secondary factor.

In the exploratory Phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial NCT01293669, TC-6987, an α7 nicotinic receptor (CHRNA7) agonist, did not improve fasting plasma glucose, and Targacept dropped the diabetes indication. My searches found no human data on exposure, receptor engagement or a downstream biomarker. The scientific rationale came only from db/db mice. The parallel asthma trial (NCT01296087) cannot support inferring adequate engagement: it is a different disease and tissue, and a reanalysis reduced its initially reported result. No other drug on this target has succeeded in diabetes. Nothing distinguishes a drug that failed to engage α7 from an α7 mechanism that does not control blood sugar, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

A healthy-volunteer PET study (NCT02716987, 2016) showed brain penetration and dose-dependent DAO occupancy: tracer VT fell sharply 2 h after 100–500 mg. The bundle shows no tolerability cap. INTERACT (NCT03382639) deliberately spanned a range of occupancy and D-serine levels and found no benefit at any dose. In patients, 50 mg gave a nominal mismatch-negativity improvement (PMID:36928351), which counts as a pathway signal. The 50 mg BACS signal from INTERACT (PMID:38943928) did not replicate in ERUDITE at 20 or 50 mg (PMID:42032293). High-occupancy doses also failed, so DAO inhibition does not appear to drive CIAS as tested. The sources describe 50 mg as only partial inhibition, a minor F1a caveat.

Luvadaxistat at 75 or 300 mg BID showed no effect on 9-HPT-1 at week 12 versus placebo in Friedreich ataxia (NCT03214588, PMID:34018342). It was well tolerated, and healthy-volunteer studies went to 1200 mg, so dose was not capped by tolerability (NCT03224325). A cerebellar DAO PET study registered in 2016, before the index trial, showed that 100–500 mg single doses cut [18F]PGM299 VT in cerebellar grey matter by roughly 70–90% at 2 h (NCT02716987). This indicates brain exposure and substantial target occupancy, though only in healthy volunteers, not FRDA patients. INTERACT cites a range of occupancy and d-serine levels (PMID:38943928), but the bundle gives no human d-serine data. With the target engaged and no benefit seen, the evidence points to a mechanism that does not drive FRDA as tested.

AXA1125 is a multi-amino-acid mixture that includes valine. No molecular target is recorded, and I found no human data on exposure or engagement. In NCT05152849 (PMID:37223439), the primary endpoint, muscle τPCr (a mitochondrial bioenergetics measure that serves as the pathway biomarker), did not change, so the pathway pillar is rated inadequate. However, CFQ-11 fatigue fell significantly versus placebo. The sponsor treated the readout as positive and planned a registrational Phase 2b/3. Press coverage shows Axcella cut 85% of its staff, dropped NASH (NCT04880187) and made long COVID a last-ditch focus. The program's uncertain future looks financial, not like a failed readout, so F8. U is listed secondary because engagement was never characterised.

I found no human data on TZP-102's PK, GHSR occupancy, or GH/ghrelin-related pharmacodynamics. A 2020 review lists its pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics as N/A (rco2.9). The one proximal readout, gastric emptying, did not change versus placebo at 10–40 mg in Phase 2a (PMID:23279217), so the pathway pillar looks inadequate. Phase 2b missed its primary endpoint because symptoms improved substantially in every arm, including placebo (NCT01452815, PMID:23848826). The index trial NCT01664637 was stopped at interim for futility. Relamorelin, on the same target, has not been approved, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement is unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged GHSR from a target that does not matter here. That makes the code U, with a high placebo response as a secondary factor.

Exebacase is a lysin that acts on bacteria in the bloodstream. Plasma levels were measured in Phase 1/2 (NCT02439359, NCT03163446), and ContraFect says PK data confirmed drug allocation in DISRUPT (NCT04160468). No source shows target engagement in humans, such as bacterial lysis or faster clearance of bacteria from the blood, and no source shows a pathway biomarker changing. The DSMB stopped DISRUPT for futility: clinical response at Day 14 was 52.7% with exebacase vs 58.6% with standard care. ContraFect said the results could not be interpreted. It pointed to a placebo-arm response about twice the historical rate, an imbalance in APACHE II severity (34.8% vs 13.8% of patients with scores above 15), and the COVID-era conduct of the trial. That points most directly to trial design and execution (F7). Because engagement has no human data, U also applies.

Exebacase is a lysin that breaks down the S. aureus cell wall. No source gives human evidence of exposure at the infection site, bacterial killing or a microbiological biomarker in patients. The only data are in vitro, animal and ex vivo models (PMID:30936103, PMID:34398668), so all three pillars are no_human_data. DISRUPT (NCT04160468) stopped for futility, with responders at 50.0% on exebacase vs 60.6% on antibiotics alone. The authors (CID 2024) blame several possible causes: the Phase 2 MRSA signal (NCT03163446) may have been chance, the control group responded unexpectedly well, the arms were imbalanced in comorbidity, the composite symptom endpoint was problematic, the population was heterogeneous, and COVID-19 may have affected the trial. They also allow that the drug may simply not work. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not help, so the code is U. Design problems (F7) and heterogeneity (F3) are secondary.

The bundle has no PK data. In AVANTI patients, pecavaptan 30 mg raised serum sodium and plasma osmolality at day 7 and day 30 (PMID:42489380). This is the expected aquaretic signature of V2 blockade, so engagement and pathway are judged adequate in this disease. That evidence was published after the index trial started. It also caused early weight loss at day 7 (PMID:42489380). Despite this, Part A showed no 30-day weight or creatinine benefit, and congestion-related serious adverse events were numerically higher (PMID:40788619). So the engaged mechanism did not yield durable decongestive benefit, which fits F2. Secondary codes: the early effect faded by day 30 (F4), and the authors cite suboptimal background diuretic dosing and thiazide interference (F7; PMID:40788619, PMID:42191015).

In UC patients, gut biopsies showed ravagalimab target engagement and pharmacodynamic modulation of the CD40-inducible gene ICAM1 and of CD40-dependent plasma cells (PMID:41920263). Exposure at the tissue site, engagement and pathway effect are therefore shown in this disease. This evidence was published after the index start. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, only 18% reached endoscopic improvement and 9.5% clinical remission (NCT03695185). The result was modest, and UC development did not advance. This suggests CD40 antagonism does not strongly drive UC as tested (F2). The trial was single-arm with no comparator and enrolled a heavily refractory population, so F7 and F3 are secondary.

Index trial NCT05162066 enrolled only 2 participants and was terminated for 'Sponsor Decision'. Primary uPCR results (n=1: -33% at week 12, -9% at week 24) are uninterpretable, so this was not a real efficacy readout. The trial could not answer the question. In healthy volunteers (PMID:40292729, NCT04330534), plasma exposure was dose-proportional and alternative-pathway activity was suppressed by >98% at ≥200 mg Q12h. That shows adequate exposure, engagement and pathway effect, though not in the renal diseases studied here. Every PNH trial was also terminated by sponsor decision despite numerically favorable hemoglobin changes (NCT05116787, NCT05116774). This suggests a program-wide sponsor or business decision rather than a mechanism failure, but the bundle never states the reason.

disease: neuromuscular disease caused by qualitative or quantitative defects of dystrophin
rationale: The index trial NCT06182267 is a Phase 1 maximal-use pharmacokinetic study of COL101 (arginine dentifrice) in dental caries. Its primary outcomes are blood arginine levels only and it posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. That makes F9 the most direct code. The dystrophinopathy trials (NCT01388764, NCT02516085) posted no results in the bundle. No primary target is recorded, and there are no human exposure, engagement or pathway data at the index doses. The related caries efficacy trial NCT04750902 missed its endpoint against fluoride, but it is not the index trial. Because engagement is no_human_data, any efficacy-failure attribution would be indeterminate, so U is listed as secondary.

The index Roche trial NCT02317419 stopped because the benefit:risk ratio did not justify further dosing, and it posted no results. Dose was capped by capillary leak syndrome and creatinine rises at an MTD of 140 µg/kg (PMID:32870522). Anti-drug antibodies reduced LMB-100 blood levels in 38% of patients by cycle 2 and 82% by cycle 3. In pancreatobiliary patients at the MTD, only 33% reached the plasma threshold of 600 ng/mL (NCT04034238). So exposure was inadequate and dosing was tolerability-limited. No target engagement or pathway biomarker data exist in humans. Serious toxicities recurred: pneumonitis deaths, pericardial effusion and tamponade, capillary leak (NCT03436732, NCT04840615). These support secondary toxicity codes. The mechanism was not properly tested.

Phase 1 PK in knee OA patients showed antibody-like, roughly linear serum exposure (PMID:27150261). The same knee OA cohort (NCT01668511, PMID:28964890; started 2012, before the 2014 index trial) showed significant reductions in serum IL-1α/β, hsCRP, neutrophils and MMP-derived collagen. The authors concluded the drug engaged relevant tissue targets. In erosive hand OA, PMID:30552176 states that despite adequate IL-1 blockade there was no benefit on pain or imaging. In the index trial (NCT02087904), WOMAC pain and all MRI synovitis/effusion endpoints were not significant, and safety was comparable to placebo. Engagement was adequate and the mechanism did not drive OA outcomes, so the code is F2. F3 is secondary because the population was selected for inflammatory, synovitis-driven OA.

ExoFlo is a mixture of MSC-derived extracellular vesicles with no recorded molecular target. No source gives human data on exposure at the site of action, target engagement or a mechanistic biomarker. In NCT04493242, 60-day mortality was 10/34 on the 15 mL dose vs 16/34 on placebo (p=0.13), which missed the primary endpoint. The sponsor pointed to a post-hoc subgroup of patients aged 18-65, where mortality was 30.8% vs 72.7% (p=0.059). It also described the trial as positive and took the product into a Phase 3 trial in ARDS (NCT05354141). With no evidence on engagement, nothing separates a product that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease, so the code is U. Subgroup selection (F3) and a small, underpowered trial (F7) are possible secondary explanations.

disease: pneumonia caused by pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
rationale: AR-105 (aerubumab) is an anti-alginate IgG1 against P. aeruginosa. The only human pharmacology is plasma PK from the Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study (NCT02486770): doses up to 20 mg/kg, with a half-life of about 21 days. The index trial used that same 20 mg/kg dose. No source reports lung or epithelial lining fluid levels, binding to bacterial alginate in patients, or any downstream biomarker. Under this task's rules, plasma levels alone do not show the drug reached a lung-site target, so exposure is marked inadequate even though no source shows it was actually insufficient. The trial missed clinical cure (NCT03027609). Mortality and SAEs were higher on drug, but investigators did not consider them drug-related. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason and simply stopped spending on the program. Because there is no engagement data, the outcome is indeterminate (U).

Subcutaneous astegolimab gave dose-proportional systemic exposure in Phase 1 (PMID:41036707), so exposure is adequate. ST2 occupancy and pathway markers are not reported anywhere in the bundle. Engagement is inferred from efficacy elsewhere: the drug cut exacerbations in severe asthma (NCT02918019, PMID:33872652) and in COPD (NCT05595642, NCT05037929). Those diseases involve lung tissue, not skin, and the AD dose is not given, so the inference is weak. In atopic dermatitis the drug was numerically worse than placebo on EASI percent change (-51.5% vs -58.2%; NCT03747575). Tolerability did not limit the dose. Engagement was never shown in AD patients. The likeliest reading is that IL-33/ST2 does not drive AD, but because engagement is only inferred, U is also possible.

Phase 1 studies showed dose-proportional exposure with IV doses up to 700 mg and good tolerability (PMID:41036707). The index COVID-19 trial reported that biomarkers showed astegolimab was pharmacologically active in patients (PMID:36519984). This is direct in-disease evidence of engagement, but it comes from the index trial itself, not before it. The pathway pillar is inferred_adequate: the drug reduced asthma exacerbations through ST2 blockade in lung (NCT02918019, PMID:33872652). Safety was similar to placebo, with no dose limitation. Even so, time to recovery was unchanged (HR 1.01, p=0.93) and all key secondary endpoints were null (NCT04386616). This indicates IL-33/ST2 signalling does not drive recovery in severe COVID-19 pneumonia.

At 54 mg/kg monthly, temelimab missed its fatigue endpoint versus placebo, and its secondary endpoints also failed (NCT05497089, PMID:42409185). Exposure: blood levels rose with dose up to 110 mg/kg and were well tolerated (PMID:31311668), so tolerability did not cap the dose. CSF levels were only about 0.1–0.4% of serum levels (PMID:27030142). No source measured target binding or neutralization of HERV-W ENV in people. The evidence is limited to falling MSRV transcripts in a small open-label MS study (PMID:25392325, 26376649) and the company's general claim of 'target engagement.' The MS phase 2b paper only proposes that engagement happens at lesions. Nothing in long COVID patients separates a drug that did not neutralize W-ENV from a target that does not drive the symptoms. The company reported a near-total failure and gave no mechanistic reason.

In the SLEek trial (NCT03978520, PMID:38923871), the elsubrutinib 60 mg arm was stopped at a planned interim analysis for lack of efficacy, not for safety. The bundle has no human data on BTK occupancy, plasma exposure or pathway biomarkers. BTK occupancy was measured only in animals (PMID:29862859). The RA extension protocol (NCT03823378) says doses were picked from Phase 1 pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data in healthy volunteers, but it gives no numbers. Elsubrutinib monotherapy also failed in RA (NCT03682705). No BTK inhibitor in the bundle has succeeded in SLE, so F1b does not apply. Nothing here can tell apart a drug that never engaged BTK from BTK not mattering in SLE, so the code is U.

The index extension NCT03823378 was stopped because the arms of the feeder study NCT03682705 showed no differentiated clinical benefit. In that study, elsubrutinib alone at 5, 20 and 60 mg barely separated from placebo on DAS28-CRP change (-1.33 to -1.52 vs -1.12, PMID:38293957). The only BTK occupancy data come from animals (PMID:29862859; ACR abstract). The bundle and my searches found no human occupancy, pharmacokinetic or biomarker data, and no sign that tolerability capped the dose. No other BTK inhibitor has succeeded in RA (TAS5315 reached only phase 2), so F1b does not apply. A Lancet Rheumatology editorial suggests the target itself may be failing in RA, but I could not access its text. Without human engagement data, a drug that never engaged BTK cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter in RA, so the code is U.

The index Phase 3 (NCT04985968) was terminated for futility. Biopsies from cobitolimod-treated UC patients showed more IL10+ mononuclear cells and regulatory T cells and fewer IL17+ cells, the mechanism-predicted TLR9 response, published in 2020 before the index start (PMID:31630153). I treat this downstream in-vivo change as evidence of engagement in the disease, though no direct engagement measure exists. Mucosal exposure data are absent; the PK trial NCT05404074 posted nothing. The phase 2b signal was confined to one dose under one-sided exploratory testing (PMID:33031757, NCT03178669). The earlier Phase 3 NCT01493960 also missed its endpoint (44.4% vs 46.5%). Despite the engaged pathway, there was no clinical benefit, which points to F2. The engagement inference is weak, so U remains possible.

In a Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (PMID:30152527), plasma levels rose with dose, the drug was well tolerated, no maximum tolerated dose was reached, and the 100–200 mg doses used in NCT03110458 hit the 100–500 ng/ml range modelled for maximal activity. So exposure was adequate and the dose was not capped. No human data shows the drug actually binding H4 receptors, either as occupancy or as receptor-level effects in the vestibular system. The only functional signal came from a caloric test in healthy volunteers: vertigo latency and duration improved compared with baseline, but nystagmus did not change. I rated pathway adequate, but that evidence is weak. The index trial missed its endpoint, with drug arms numerically worse than placebo, and the sponsor stopped the program without saying why it failed. Because there is no engagement data, the result is indeterminate (U).

drug: human natural killer cell line nk-92 (cd16.158v, er il2) cells
rationale: The index trial NCT03853317 (haNK + N-803 + avelumab in checkpoint-refractory Merkel cell carcinoma) was terminated for 'not meeting recruitment goal' after 9 patients, with 0% ORR. The stated cause is operational: the trial stopped before it could properly answer the efficacy question, though the 0/9 response rate is a negative signal. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic data, persistence data or NK-activity biomarkers for haNK. Phase 1 NCT03027128 reported only safety: 2×10^9 cells with no DLTs, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. With engagement unmeasured, a non-engaging cell product cannot be separated from an ineffective mechanism, so U is a secondary code. Other haNK trials were terminated without stated reasons and add no pillar evidence.

Oral V565 missed its Day-42 response endpoint (35% vs 37% placebo; NCT02976129). The anti-TNF target is validated in Crohn's: infliximab, adalimumab and certolizumab are approved. Luminal exposure was shown in Crohn's patients, with micromolar levels in ileal fluid and stool (PMID:31575982). Tissue engagement was shown only in 5 UC patients (NCT03705117, which started after the index trial). V565 was present in the lamina propria in 4 of 5, and tissue phosphoproteins fell by only about 50%. This partial engagement was never shown in Crohn's tissue, which is often transmural. Because the target succeeds with other molecules, the failure most likely reflects this molecule and its oral, gut-restricted delivery, not the target.

The index trial (NCT02855268, PMID:38829703) was stopped for futility, with no difference in eGFR slope versus placebo. The sponsor's protocol reports kidney biopsy drug levels from Alport patients in phase 1 PDY16327 (NCT03373786). At 1.5 mg/kg every two weeks, levels were 17.8 and 47.8 µg/g, below or at the low end of the 50–140 µg/g that worked in mice. So the sponsor switched to 110 mg weekly, which was only projected to double kidney levels and was never measured. Renal miR-21 data were described as limited and variable with no conclusions possible, so there is no usable human engagement or pathway evidence. Tissue exposure looks marginal, which hints at F1a, but without engagement data I can't tell an unengaged drug from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In the phase 1/2 study NCT02658890 (PMID:39670852), linrodostat exposures exceeded predicted therapeutic target concentrations from 50 mg. Doses of 100–200 mg were used, with an MTD of 200 mg, so dose was not capping engagement. Kynurenine fell with linrodostat plus nivolumab, which the authors say supports IDO1 pathway inhibition, but the fall did not correlate with response. PMID:33298590 also reports a PK/PD relationship in patient samples. These data come from mixed advanced tumors, not specifically gastric cancer. In the index trial NCT02935634, nivolumab plus linrodostat gave a 13.2% ORR in Track 1 and 0% in Track 2, with no control arm. Engaged IDO1 inhibition without benefit points to the mechanism not driving outcomes, so F2. The trial was uncontrolled and descriptive, so F7 also applies.

In the phase 1/2 study NCT02658890 (PMID:39670852), linrodostat exposures exceeded predicted therapeutic concentrations from 50 mg. Kynurenine fell with linrodostat plus nivolumab, which the authors say supports IDO1 pathway inhibition, but the fall did not correlate with response. The MTD was 200 mg, so expansion doses were not tolerability-capped below engagement. These data come from mixed advanced tumors, not shown specifically in RCC, and were published after the index trial started. In the index trial NCT02996110, nivolumab plus linrodostat gave an ORR of 3.2% and a 24-week PFS rate of 0.28, versus 17.4% and 0.43 for nivolumab plus ipilimumab. With engagement adequate and no clinical benefit, the target does not appear to drive benefit as tested. Secondary F7: the arms were small, descriptive and had no prespecified comparison.

The index Phase 3 NCT03329846 enrolled only 20 patients. Its posted primary outcome was a descriptive adverse-event count with no efficacy comparison, so it was not an efficacy test of linrodostat. The bundle gives no stated reason for the truncation. Pillars were shown in humans in the Phase 1/2 NCT02658890 (PMID:39670852), which included melanoma cohorts and was registered in 2016, before the index trial. Exposures exceeded predicted target concentrations from 50 mg upward, the MTD was 200 mg, so dose was not capped below engagement, and kynurenine fell, supporting IDO1 pathway inhibition. Kynurenine lowering did not correlate with response, which hints at F2, but no controlled efficacy readout exists in the bundle.

Index Phase 3 NCT03403205 met its primary endpoint: dNCC AUEC was superior to standard of care in both cohorts (p<0.0001). It was terminated by unspecified sponsor decision, so this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. In Wilson disease patients, the copper-binding mechanism (the relevant one, not SOD1) was shown. Copper mobilized into blood as tripartite complexes. Cu balance became negative through fecal excretion (PMID:42155004). 64Cu PET showed reduced hepatic and cerebral copper uptake (PMID:38081365). NCC normalized in Phase 2 NCT02273596 (PMID:28988934), published before the index trial started. A liver copper biopsy endpoint was not met (NCT04422431), but this does not change the index outcome. The pediatric Phase 3 was also ended by sponsor decision (NCT05047523), suggesting a business stop, though no reason is stated.

Exposure was adequate. In the SLE Phase 1b (NCT02194400, PMID:27852935), serum drug levels and RNase activity rose with dose at 10 mg/kg, the dose used in the index trial, and the half-life was about 19 days. But high RNase activity in serum only shows the enzyme is present. No human source shows that circulating RNA or RNA immune complexes were cleared, or that the interferon signature fell. BAFF dropped in only a subset of patients. In Sjögren's, interferon-inducible genes were not lowered (PMC7839752). So the bundle cannot tell a drug that never cleared its substrate apart from a mechanism that does not matter in lupus. The sponsor blamed patient selection and pointed to trends in high-SLEDAI and high-CLASI subgroups (PMID:38325898, press release), which supports F3 as a secondary code.

RSLV-132 is an RNase-Fc replacement enzyme. Exposure is shown: a serum half-life of about 19 days in SLE (PMID:27852935). In the Sjögren's Phase 2, published in 2020 before the index trial started, steady-state serum drug levels and catalytic RNase activity were about 4–4.6 μg/ml, with clearly higher RNA-digestion activity in whole blood. That counts as engagement of the replaced activity, but not in long COVID. No human evidence shows the downstream effect, such as clearing viral RNA or calming inflammation, in long COVID. In NCT04944121 the investigators blamed the Day-71 miss on a placebo response that grew during the trial (F7). Earlier timepoints were significant, and women seemed to respond better than men (F3).

Plasma exposure at 250 mg QD (spray-dried formulation) was characterized in NCT04682119, at roughly twice the Cmax of the 100 mg dose. PMID:40258136 states this dose maintained exposures shown to engage TRPA1. In healthy volunteers, the cinnamaldehyde-evoked dermal blood flow biomarker fell dose-dependently at 10–100 mg (NCT04183283, PMID:37562824). That trial was registered before the index trial. The authors noted that higher concentrations might give larger effects, and 250 mg delivered them. Engagement was never measured in OA patients. Despite this, OA pain on NRS did not beat placebo (NCT05080660), and the drug also missed in DPNP and CLBP. This points to TRPA1 not driving OA pain as tested. The authors suggest subpopulation heterogeneity (F3) and a hepatotoxicity risk (F6) (PMID:39679712).

At 250 mg the SDD formulation gave robust plasma exposure in healthy volunteers (NCT04682119). PMID:40258136 says this dose maintained plasma exposures shown to engage TRPA1. Engagement was shown in healthy volunteers with a cinnamaldehyde-evoked dermal blood flow biomarker, which fell dose-dependently at 10-100 mg (NCT04183283, PMID:37562824). That trial was registered before the index trial, but no engagement data come from patients. Tolerability was good and did not cap the dose. Even so, the 250 mg dose had no effect on pain versus placebo in diabetic neuropathic pain (NCT05177094), osteoarthritis (NCT05080660) or low back pain (NCT05086289). Peripheral TRPA1 blockade therefore does not appear to drive chronic pain. Confidence is medium: the biomarker effect was partial, and PMID:37562824 suggests higher concentrations might give a larger response, so F1a remains possible.

Index CLBP trial (NCT05086289) missed: posterior difference -0.38, CrI crossing zero. Sister trials in knee OA (NCT05080660) and DPNP (NCT05177094) at the same dose also failed. Exposure is documented: the 250 mg SDD formulation gave high plasma levels (NCT04682119), and the authors say these maintain exposures shown to engage TRPA1 (PMID:40258136). Engagement and pathway rest on dose-dependent inhibition of cinnamaldehyde-evoked dermal blood flow in healthy volunteers (NCT04183283, PMID:37562824). That evidence predates the index trial but was not shown in patients. It was also partial at 100 mg, and the authors suggest higher concentrations might give larger effects. So incomplete engagement (F1a) remains a secondary possibility. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Consistent failure across three pain types points to TRPA1 not driving chronic pain as tested.

In healthy volunteers, 250 mg LY3526318-SDD gave sustained plasma exposure (NCT04682119). The sponsor states this exposure was shown to engage TRPA1, and AEs were mild (PMID:40258136). The cinnamaldehyde dermal blood flow biomarker fell dose-dependently at 10–100 mg in healthy volunteers, registered before the index trial (NCT04183283, PMID:37562824). The 250 mg index dose gave higher exposure than 100 mg. Yet the same parallel master-protocol design showed no benefit in chronic low back pain (NCT05086289), knee osteoarthritis (NCT05080660) or diabetic neuropathic pain (NCT05177094). This points to TRPA1 antagonism not driving chronic pain as tested. Caveats: engagement was never shown in patients, and PMID:37562824 notes a modest human effect that might grow at higher concentrations. Partial engagement (F1a) therefore cannot be excluded.

In BRIGHTER (NCT02178956), adding napabucasin (480 mg twice daily) to paclitaxel did not improve overall survival (HR 1.01). Plasma PK was measured in gastric cancer patients at 480 mg twice daily (PMID:31028219) and in healthy volunteers (PMID:33576192, PMID:34628720), so systemic exposure was shown. No source shows napabucasin inhibiting STAT3 in humans, for example lower pSTAT3 in tumor or reduced STAT3 target genes. pSTAT3 was used only as a baseline selection marker. pSTAT3-positive patients did not benefit either, so pSTAT3 selection did not help in gastric cancer, and it also failed in colorectal cancer (NCT02753127). The drug is also described as an NQO1-activated reactive oxygen species generator. No other STAT3 drug has succeeded in this disease. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that never engaged STAT3 cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT02347917, patients reached measurable plasma levels of napabucasin (Day 23 Cmin about 196 ng/mL, AUC0-24 about 6,100 h·ng/mL) and had no DLTs, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. No source shows in humans that the drug engaged STAT3, such as less pSTAT3 in tumour or a downstream biomarker change. The Phase 1 paper used pSTAT3 IHC on archived tumour only to look for a link to response, not to show engagement. The Phase 2 part was single-arm and descriptive (median PFS 5.59 months, no threshold or comparator), and no stated reason for stopping was found. Phase 3 failures in other cancers (NCT02753127, NCT02178956, NCT02993731) cannot tell a drug that never engaged STAT3 from a target that does not matter. Indeterminate.
