Human plasma PK was measured in patients and volunteers (PMID:32236642, 34291369, 33576192), but I found no human evidence that napabucasin inhibited STAT3: no tumour pSTAT3 reduction, no paired biopsies, and no downstream biomarker. pSTAT3 was used only to select patients at baseline. In the pSTAT3-positive subgroup, OS was no better (HR 0.969, NCT02753127/PMID:36503738), so patient selection does not explain the failure. Later papers describe the drug as an NQO1-activated ROS generator rather than a direct STAT3 inhibitor, which makes the intended mechanism unclear. The sponsor gave no reason beyond missing the endpoints. No other STAT3 drug has succeeded in CRC. The phase 3 trials in refractory CRC, gastric and pancreatic cancer also failed, but none of them separates a drug that never engaged STAT3 from a target that does not matter. So U.

Adding napabucasin to nab-paclitaxel/gemcitabine did not improve overall survival in CanStem111P (11.4 vs 11.7 months, HR 1.07), and the trial was stopped for futility (PMID:36969338). Plasma PK was measured in healthy volunteers (PMID:33576192, PMID:34628720) and in pancreatic cancer patients on the 240 mg BID regimen, with no dose-limiting toxicities (ASCO 2017, NCT02231723). So systemic exposure is documented. I found no human data on STAT3 inhibition, pSTAT3 lowering or a downstream biomarker in pancreatic cancer. The only tissue evidence is an anecdotal post-treatment biopsy from one gastric cancer patient. The drug is also described as an NQO1-activated ROS generator, which muddies the mechanism. There was no survival benefit in the pSTAT3-positive subgroup either, but without engagement data the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged STAT3 apart from a target that doesn't matter here. Code U.

In the Phase II part of NCT02279719, napabucasin 480 mg/day plus sorafenib had a lower response rate than sorafenib alone (ORR 3.6% vs 9.7%; DCR 35.7% vs 48.4%). The dose was not capped: no DLTs occurred, though doses were held or reduced. Human plasma PK exists (PMID:37188895, 33576192, 34628720), but there are no tumour or liver drug levels. I found no human measure of STAT3 inhibition: no tumour pSTAT3 suppression and no downstream biomarker change, in HCC or any other cancer. Protocols mention exploratory biomarkers but report no results. The colorectal Phase 3 (NCT02753127) also failed in pSTAT3-positive patients, but that is patient selection, not proof of engagement. No other STAT3 drug has succeeded in HCC, so F1b does not apply. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. My searches were cut short: the full Phase 1 paper would not load and the search limit was reached.

The index trial NCT02315534 was a single-arm Phase Ib/II study. It found no DLTs at 480 mg BID with temozolomide and reported PFS-6 of 28% only descriptively, with no threshold or comparator, so the trial could not properly test efficacy. Human plasma PK exists (PMID:33576192, PMID:34628720), but brain or tumour penetration was shown only in mice (ASCO abstract). The surgical cohort produced no tissue drug-level or pSTAT3 data. No human measure of STAT3 inhibition or a downstream biomarker was found in any indication. The Phase 3 trials in other cancers (NCT02753127, NCT02993731) failed, so the pillars cannot be inferred from them. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The BRIGHTER trial (NCT02178956) gave napabucasin 480 mg twice daily with paclitaxel. It showed no overall survival benefit (HR 1.01), and the data monitoring board said the trial was unlikely to meet its endpoint. Plasma exposure was documented in Phase 1 and Phase 1b pharmacokinetic studies (NCT01325441, PMC7188713, PMID:33576192, PMID:34628720), but none of the sources found measure STAT3 inhibition in human tumours. The Phase III paper says it performed no pharmacodynamic analyses, and pSTAT3 was used only as a selection marker. The drug's mechanism is also unclear: it is described as a STAT3 inhibitor and also as a NQO1-activated generator of reactive oxygen species (PMID:34107166). Survival endpoints also failed in colorectal and pancreatic cancer (NCT02753127, NCT02993731), including in pSTAT3-positive patients. Without engagement data, the evidence can't tell whether the drug failed to engage STAT3 or STAT3 doesn't matter in this disease, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02352558 was a 15-patient Phase 1 study in refractory hematologic malignancies. Its only primary endpoint was DLT-based safety and tolerability, and no results were posted. It was not an efficacy test of napabucasin, so F9 fits best. Plasma exposure is documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:33576192, PMID:34628720, PMID:34107166), and doses were well tolerated, so the dose was not limited. No human STAT3 engagement or pathway biomarker data appear anywhere in the bundle; the healthy-volunteer papers even describe the drug as an NQO1-bioactivated ROS generator. Phase 3 failures in other cancers (NCT02753127, NCT02178956, NCT02993731) cannot separate a drug that never engaged STAT3 from a target that does not matter, hence the U secondary.

C16G2 is a targeted antimicrobial peptide whose 'target' is S. mutans. The index trial's primary endpoint was itself a target-engagement measure, salivary and plaque S. mutans counts. With the varnish, these did not fall versus placebo: saliva +0.23 vs −0.44; plaque −0.22 vs −0.31 (NCT03196219). The strip study likewise showed no meaningful S. mutans reduction across doses (NCT03052842). An earlier pilot with a rinse reported S. mutans reductions (PMID:21860239), but the formulations taken into the index trial did not reproduce target killing in vivo. Engagement was therefore inadequate, and the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). The arms were tiny (n=6–8), so the trial was underpowered (F7). No tolerability limits were seen.

Cemdisiran's pillars hold in humans. Plasma PK was characterized, with dose-dependent C5 protein reduction of more than 90% (maximum about 99% at 600 mg) in healthy volunteers and PNH patients (PMID:33047216). Complement activity was robustly and durably reduced (PMID:37601837). Engagement was not measured in IgAN patients. The index trial (NCT03841448) randomized only 31 participants (9 on placebo). It showed a 37% placebo-adjusted UPCR reduction that missed significance (p=0.10, CI -61% to +0.5%). The sponsor nonetheless called this a clinically meaningful reduction, met its goal, and stopped early. Ravulizumab, a C5 inhibitor, is approved for IgAN, which supports the target. The miss reflects an underpowered trial rather than a mechanism failure. Discontinuation appears strategic, though no business reason is stated in the bundle.

NCT02988817 was a Phase 1/2 trial with safety as its primary endpoint, so it was not a comparative efficacy test (F9 is a secondary code). Genmab still stopped the drug because expansion cohorts got low response rates (ORR 4.5–12.5%). Plasma levels of the ADC and its MMAE payload rose with dose, so exposure counts as adequate. Doses went up to the maximum tolerated dose (2.2 mg/kg Q3W), but no source says tolerability kept the dose below what engagement needed. Tumour AXL was measured as a predictive marker, not as proof the drug engaged it. No tumour uptake, AXL occupancy or downstream marker data exist, and response did not track AXL expression. No other AXL drug is in the bundle. With no human engagement data, a molecule failure cannot be told apart from a target failure, so the code is U.

Exposure was adequate. Serum, nasopharyngeal and tracheal aspirate drug levels were confirmed in hospitalized patients in the index trial (PMID:32621543). Engagement was adequate in experimental influenza. In the challenge study (NCT01980966, registered before the index trial), 3600 mg cut nasopharyngeal viral AUC by 98% and lowered inflammatory biomarkers (PMID:28807912). Tolerability did not cap the dose; 10,800 mg was tolerated (PMID:27381392). In natural infection, however, the antibody added no viral load reduction over oseltamivir (PMID:32393496). It also failed on viral load and symptoms in outpatients (PMID:35106315). The antiviral mechanism gave no clinical benefit as tested, so F2. Secondary codes: the authors blame variability in the oxygen-removal endpoint (F7/F4).

The index umbrella trial NCT04586244 was terminated for a stated 'Business Decision', with no safety concerns. Only the retifanlimab monotherapy arm (n=6) was analysed for the CD8+ biomarker primary endpoint (p=0.0925). The tuparstobart combination arm enrolled just 4 patients and was never analysed, so this was not a real efficacy test of the drug (F7). Phase 1 (PMID:40631774) showed dose-proportional PK with no MTD reached and 350 mg Q2W selected, so plasma exposure was adequate and the dose was not limited by tolerability. No receptor occupancy or pathway data were reported, so engagement is unknown (U). A separate HNSCC trial (NCT05287113) found no PFS gain from adding tuparstobart, but that is a different disease.

The index trial NCT04312997 missed its primary endpoint, with COVID-19 worsening in 1/49 on PUL-042 vs 1/50 on placebo. The sister trial NCT04313023 was also negative. The bundle has no human exposure, TLR9 engagement or downstream biomarker data. The Phase 1 trials (NCT02124278, NCT02566252) posted no results, and PMID:42063563 is mechanistic, non-human work on lung epithelium. No other TLR9 agonist is shown to have succeeded in COVID-19, so F1b does not apply. With so few events in both arms, the trial could hardly detect a difference, which supports F7 as secondary. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the primary code is U.

The index ADORE platform trial (NCT04097821) was stopped for 'Sponsor Decision'. Its primary endpoints were DLT-focused, and no response data were posted. The sabatolimab arm enrolled only 2 patients with no DLTs, so it was not an efficacy test in myelofibrosis (PMID:40334082). The program ended because Novartis terminated sabatolimab after the MDS Phase II and III trials missed their primary endpoints (NCT03946670, NCT04266301, NCT04878432). In heme malignancy patients, PK was linear and total sTIM-3 plateaued, with modelled bone-marrow TIM-3 occupancy above 95% (PMID:37186155). This supports adequate exposure and engagement, but only in MDS/AML, not myelofibrosis, and it was published after the index trial started. Pathway data are absent. The program-level failure in MDS despite engagement suggests F2 as secondary.

In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT04465955), intravitreal NGM621 dosed Q4W or Q8W did not significantly slow GA lesion growth versus sham (p≈0.43). The Phase 1 study in GA patients (PMID:34509438; NCT04014777) reported only safety and dose-proportional serum exposure. It mentions pharmacodynamic assessments but gives no results. There are no ocular drug levels, no C3 or complement-activity data and no pathway biomarker, so all three pillars lack human data. Another C3 inhibitor, pegcetacoplan, is FDA-approved for dry AMD/GA, which shows the target can work in this disease. With no evidence that NGM621 engaged C3 adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U remains plausible because engagement was never measured. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

The index trial, ASSENT (NCT02809118), was stopped early because of efficacy data from HEALOS (NCT02561091). HEALOS missed its primary endpoint in the overall population. A post-hoc analysis found benefit only in patients with profound hearing loss, and the investigators suggested that JNK activation sets in only after profound damage. That points to patient selection (F3). However, the bundle has no human data on inner-ear (perilymph) drug levels, JNK inhibition, or downstream biomarkers. The only human PK comes from intravenous dosing in healthy volunteers (PMID:25505576), which is not relevant to intratympanic delivery. With engagement not measured, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage JNK from a target that does not drive the disease, so the code is U, with F3 as secondary.

The index trial NCT01029873 was a single-arm phase 1/2 dose escalation of ALT-801 with cisplatin. Its primaries were descriptive (AEs, DLT/MTD, ORR 0-17%), and it stopped on 'sponsor decision', so it was not an efficacy test. The bundle conflates two molecules. The melanoma trial tested ALT-801, an IL-2/p53-TCR fusion protein (PMID:21994418), not the GLP1R/GCGR agonist pemvidutide. GLP1R/GCGR engagement in melanoma has no human data. Pemvidutide's MASH result (NCT05989711) concerns a different disease and compartment. For the fusion protein, serum exposure matched the dose given (PMID:21994418), but target engagement was not measured. No efficacy failure attributable to the stated targets can be determined.

A single oral 200 mg dose of C21 did not significantly improve finger rewarming AUC compared with placebo (NCT04388176; ratio 1.01, p=0.38). None of the sources report human PK at the site of action, AT2R occupancy or a target-engagement biomarker for oral dosing. The only human pharmacodynamic data come from intra-arterial forearm infusion in 5 healthy volunteers, published in 2024 after the index trial (NCT05277922, PMID:38344891). It showed a small, variable rise in forearm blood flow, so it does not establish engagement at the index dose. The investigators blamed the small sample (worsened by COVID-19), testing only one dose, and a 15-minute observation window that cut off rewarming before it finished (F7/F4). They also saw a significant rise in maximum temperature, a secondary measure. With engagement untested, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

The index trial NCT05277922 was an open-label Phase 1 pharmacodynamic study in five healthy volunteers, so it was not an efficacy test in type 2 diabetes. Intra-arterial buloxibutid raised forearm blood flow (27.8–60.5%, largest at 200 µg/min), and the authors read this as a vascular effect supporting endothelial-dysfunction indications (PMID:38344891). That makes the pathway pillar plausibly adequate, though modest beside sodium nitroprusside (230–320%). No human receptor occupancy or exposure data exist. The later T2D endothelial trial NCT05831644 missed its pharmacodynamic endpoint (p=0.19). Without engagement data, a non-engaging drug cannot be separated from an irrelevant target there (U, secondary). The bundle states no stop reason.

In NCT04388176, a single oral 200 mg dose of C21 did not significantly improve finger rewarming after cold challenge (p=0.38). I found no human data on AT2R occupancy or engagement, and none on plasma or digital-tissue drug levels at this dose. Pathway evidence is weak. In healthy volunteers, intra-arterial C21 raised forearm blood flow by only 17–60%, against 230–320% for the nitroprusside positive control (NCT05277922/PMID:38344891), and the endothelial-function trial in type 2 diabetes was null (NCT05831644). The investigators put the miss down to small size (enrolment cut by COVID-19), testing only one dose, a 15-minute window that missed the full effect, and incomplete acclimatisation. That points to trial limits (F7) rather than a failed target. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

ATTRACT-3 (NCT04880642) found no difference in 60-day mortality: 10 deaths in each arm, HR 0.98. None of the sources show AT2R occupancy or a target biomarker in humans. Intra-arterial C21 increased forearm blood flow (NCT05277922, PMID:38344891), but that was local dosing in healthy volunteers, not the oral dose used in the trial. In type 2 diabetes the endothelial effect was not significant (NCT05831644). In the phase 2 COVID trial (NCT04452435), CRP was not reduced; only oxygen need fell. Vicore blamed a change in the patient population: Omicron causes milder upper-airway disease than the wild-type virus seen in phase 2. That points to F3, a population mismatch. Because target engagement was never measured, U also applies.

In NCT04440007, the primary endpoint was missed: 40/48 patients on abivertinib were alive and free of respiratory failure at Day 28, versus 38/48 on placebo. I found no human data showing that abivertinib inhibited BTK in COVID-19 patients. There is no BTK occupancy or cytokine-lowering data, and the cytokine suppression Sorrento cited came only from in vitro work. Human PK and pharmacodynamic data exist only from the NSCLC trials and are about EGFR (PMID:29626621, PMID:28285073). Sorrento's press release blamed patient selection, saying an 'at-risk' subgroup benefited in this trial and in NCT04528667. That is a post hoc claim, so I list F3 as secondary. Because engagement is unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged BTK apart from a target that does not matter here. That makes the answer U.

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional with negligible immunogenicity and no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:38105505, PMID:37768658), so exposure is adequate and the dose was not limited. No direct TIGIT occupancy data appear. Engagement is inferred_adequate: tiragolumab plus atezolizumab beat atezolizumab alone on ORR and PFS in NSCLC (NCT03563716), and a triplet met PFS and OS in esophageal cancer (NCT04540211). Phase 3 trials then failed repeatedly (NCT04294810, NCT04619797, NCT04256421), which points to TIGIT blockade adding little benefit. The TNBC trial (NCT04584112) posted no results or stop reason, so its readout and the cause of stopping are not shown. Confidence is low; U applies if the inference from other diseases is rejected.

Exposure was measured in humans. VIR-2482 had dose-proportional serum levels with a half-life of about 60 days, and it reached the nasal lining at about 2–5% of serum levels (2.1–7.8% in PENINSULA). Uptake into the nose looked saturable (PMID:38376227, PMID:39036981). Engagement means binding to the influenza A hemagglutinin stem. No human measure of it was found, such as in-vivo neutralization or reduced viral load in infected people, so engagement and pathway are no_human_data. The 1200 mg dose cut illness by 15.9%, not significant (NCT05567783), so efficacy did not show engagement either. Investigators suggested flu arrived early, during dosing, before tissue levels peaked after injection into the muscle (secondary F7/F1a). Nothing in these sources separates a drug that did not engage from a mechanism that does not protect. Code: U.

The index trial NCT01353755 is AI0906rP, which tested 120 µg of rPhleum (a recombinant 5-allergen grass mix) given by injection. The symposium review reports it missed: SMS change vs placebo p=0.1124. Phase 3 AI0704rP (80 and 120 µg) and AI0403rP (40 µg) also missed. The immune response was clearly shown in grass-allergic patients before the index trial: in the proof-of-concept study AI0301rP, specific IgG1 rose 60-fold, IgG4 rose 400-fold, and specific IgE fell vs placebo. The review notes no dose-limiting safety problems up to 120 µg, and placebo groups also improved. Exposure is marked inferred_adequate as a judgment call: it was not measured, but the strong antibody response implies the drug reached the immune system. The review blames the failure on patients' differing sensitisation profiles, which a fixed cocktail may not match (F3). Secondary codes: the mechanism was engaged without benefit (F2), and the placebo response was high (F7).

The index trial NCT00744848 compared liposomal bupivacaine (SKY0402) with bupivacaine HCl, an active comparator acting on the same sodium-channel target. It showed no advantage (AUC 396 vs 359). That makes it a formulation-versus-formulation comparison, not a test of whether the drug works. In the same disease, placebo-controlled NCT00890721 met its primary endpoint (AUC 141.8 vs 202.5). Bunionectomy (NCT00890682) and femoral block (NCT01683071) trials were also positive. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate from clinical efficacy. Bupivacaine blocks also reduced post-hemorrhoidectomy pain in earlier studies (PMID:15875295, PMID:22514775). The failure reflects the active-comparator design, not the target or the molecule.

The only human pharmacology I found is a 2012 company press release on the Phase 1 multiple ascending dose study. It says the drug was well tolerated and well absorbed, with predictable plasma PK in young and elderly volunteers, at doses only 'expected' to fall in the therapeutic range. Plasma levels were not shown to reach the nerve and spinal Cav2.2 site, so exposure is no_human_data. Nothing shows the drug blocking Cav2.2 or moving a biomarker in humans. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Neither the PHN crossover trial NCT01848730 (75 mg three times daily) nor the DPN trial NCT01893125 posted results, and I found no sponsor statement explaining the failure. The other Cav2.2 blocker, Z160, also failed in Phase 2, so F1b does not apply. Engagement is unknown, so the code is U.

In the index trial, early AD patients reached median plasma levels of 208–2790 ng/mL. Estimated CSF QC target occupancy was 55% at trough and 94% post-dose (NCT03919162), above the >50% that preclinical work tied to efficacy (PMID:28446518). Phase 1 had already shown CSF exposure and dose-related inhibition of serum and CSF QC (PMID:29854937). SAPHIR assessed occupancy in AD patients (PMID:30309389) and reported EEG connectivity gains (PMID:31759193). Even so, the index trial's ABC, qEEG and CDR-SB endpoints were all null (p=0.23, 0.48, 0.91), and no pGlu-Aβ lowering in humans is shown. With engagement adequate and no benefit, the mechanism appears not to drive disease as tested. Secondary: termination was stated as strategic (F8), and Phase 2B was very small (n=39; F7).

Intratumoral ADU-S100 was rapidly absorbed from the injection site, with a plasma half-life of about 24 minutes (PMID:34716197). This suggests poor tumor retention. Paired tumor biopsies showed no significant on-treatment RNA or immune-infiltrate changes, so the intratumoral pathway effect was not shown. Systemic signals did appear: rising cytokines, T-cell clonal expansion, and 'on-target' pharmacodynamic activity in the Ib study (PMID:36282874). These came from mixed solid-tumor cohorts, not head and neck cancer specifically. The MTD was never reached, so the dose was not tolerability-capped. Inadequate local tumor exposure and pathway effect mean the mechanism was likely not properly tested (F1a). The index trial enrolled only 16, with ORR data for 6 (NCT03937141), limiting interpretation (F7). F2 remains possible given systemic engagement.

In the index single-agent trial (NCT02675439), intratumoral MIW815 left the injection site quickly: it was rapidly absorbed, with a plasma half-life of about 24 minutes (PMID:34716197). Paired tumor biopsies showed no significant on-treatment changes in RNA expression or immune infiltration. So STING activation at the intended site, the tumor, was not shown, although systemic cytokines and T-cell expansion indicated some immune activation. The combination study reported on-target pharmacodynamic activity but minimal responses (PMID:36282874). The MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The engagement evidence was published after the index trial started. The weak tumor-level activity suggests the mechanism was not adequately tested (F1a). F2 remains possible, given the systemic activation and the similar futility in NCT03937141.

Vidutolimod is a TLR9 agonist given by injection directly into the tumour, so it reached its site of action. In the index trial (NCT03438318, 29 patients with NSCLC resistant to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade), the investigators reported fold changes in serum CXCL10, the marker the sponsor uses to show TLR9 activation of plasmacytoid dendritic cells. In melanoma trials (NCT02680184), CXCL10 rose and rose more in responders. Treatment was delivered without a tolerability cap on dose. Activity in NSCLC was minimal. The authors concluded that other cancer immune-evasion pathways may also need targeting, which points to F2: the mechanism was engaged but did not help. Confidence is low because I only saw search snippets, not the full CXCL10 data. That evidence was published after the trial started (2021 and 2023). No stop reason was given; later trials of the drug ended for business or drug-supply reasons.

Phase 1 (NCT01363947, PMID:31540980) showed dose-proportional PK. The MTD was not reached, and 2.4 mg/kg was taken forward, so dose was not limited. Target engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred because all RECIST responses occurred in NaPi2b-high tumors, and 54% of PROC patients had CA-125 declines of 50% or more. In the index trial (PMID:29401246), ORR roughly doubled versus PLD (34% vs 15%, p=0.03), so a proximal antitumor effect was shown in this disease. PFS still missed (HR 0.78, p=0.34). The authors attribute this to short response durations and stress weighing duration as well as response rate. That points to the endpoint/durability rather than non-engagement. The small 95-patient trial may also have been underpowered (F7).

The index trial, NCT01363947, was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study with a safety primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. It showed dose-proportional PK, an acceptable safety profile at the 2.4 mg/kg RP2D, and partial responses plus CA-125 declines in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (PROC). All RECIST responses were in NaPi2b-high tumours, which points to target-dependent activity, but no direct occupancy or engagement measure was found. The program actually stopped after the randomized Phase 2 NCT01991210. There, lifastuzumab vedotin significantly improved objective response rate versus PLD (34% vs 15%), but the PFS gain was modest and not significant. Authors highlighted short response durations, which supports F4. Most benefit was in the highest NaPi2b quartile, which supports F3.

Vebicorvir, a core inhibitor, showed antiviral activity in CHB patients. Phase 1 (NCT02908191, registered before the index trial; PMID:31711752) reported PK and viral responses. At 300 mg it gave added HBV DNA and pgRNA reductions over ETV (NCT03577171, PMID:35697332). In NrtI-suppressed patients it also raised undetectable DNA and lowered pgRNA (PMID:35460726). This proximal core-inhibition effect is evidence of engagement and pathway. Yet HBsAg and HBeAg were unchanged in the index trial (NCT03576066), and the 52-week extension produced no off-treatment response (PMID:38510983). Core inhibition does not drive antigen decline or cure, so F2. The sponsor then ended later trials for strategic reasons (NCT04454567, NCT04781647), giving F8 as a secondary code. No tolerability cap.

Izencitinib is gut-selective by design. In the Phase 1b UC study (NCT02818686, PMID:32161949), colonic tissue concentrations were high, but the only engagement evidence is a qualitative claim of 'local target engagement', with low plasma exposure and no systemic JAK inhibition (PMID:35134999). Clinical, endoscopic and histologic effects were only descriptive trends, so pathway was not shown clearly. The index trial missed its tMS primary endpoint at every dose up to 200 mg, with no tolerability cap. Systemic JAK inhibitors on the same targets (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are FDA-approved for UC, so the target is validated. This points to the molecule and its gut-restricted design rather than the target. Engagement adequacy is unquantified, so F2 remains possible and confidence is low.

Phase 1 data (PMID:34859612) showed consistent plasma exposure at 300 mg in healthy volunteers and OA patients, which counts as exposure. In OA patients (NCT03311009, registered 2017, before the index trial), dosing significantly reduced circulating ARGS-aggrecan neoepitope, the ADAMTS-5 cleavage product, at all doses; this is engagement. Serum versikine, another ADAMTS-5 product, also fell over 52 weeks (PMID:40531968). Pathway is marked inferred_adequate only because no downstream marker beyond these cleavage products was shown. Tolerability did not cap the dose. In ROCCELLA (NCT03595618), which enrolled patients with substantial cartilage loss (PMID:36474770), no dose changed cartilage thickness or symptoms (PMID:37059327). With the target engaged, ADAMTS-5 inhibition does not appear to drive OA structural progression as tested. Cartilage tissue levels were not measured, so confidence is medium.

In the index trial NCT02093221 (Prolastin-C at 90 or 180 mg/kg/wk), C-peptide fell more in every drug arm than with placebo. Exposure is rated adequate because this is an approved augmentation product that raises plasma AAT, though I found no trial-specific drug levels. I found no human measure of target engagement (elastase inhibition or functional anti-protease capacity) in T1D. The investigators (Lagarde 2021, PMID 33244872) reported that the drug lowered IL-6, which is downstream pathway evidence. They called the C-peptide effect inconclusive because results varied and the study was small and not powered. The Glassia T1D trial (NCT02005848) also missed its primary endpoint. With engagement unmeasured, this is coded U; F7 (small, unpowered trial) and F2 are possible alternatives.

The index trial NCT04547140 (IV Alpha1-PI in hospitalized COVID-19, n=57) stopped for futility, with death, ICU and ventilation rates numerically worse on drug. No exposure or elastase-inhibition data in COVID patients are in the bundle. Engagement and exposure are only inferred: the drug is FDA-approved for AAT deficiency, where augmentation raises plasma AAT. NCT02870348 shows trough A1PI levels, and NCT02001688 shows functional AAT in lung lining fluid, so the same SERPINA1/ELANE mechanism works systemically. However, the bundle does not report the COVID dose, which weakens this inference. With plausible engagement and no benefit, the mechanism appears not to drive COVID-19 outcomes (F2). The small, early-terminated trial limits certainty, and if the inference is rejected the case is U.

Exposure is adequate. Tegafur/UFT gave measurable 5-FU in cervical tumour tissue in cervical cancer patients (PMID:7857101, PMID:3933435), and S-1 PK confirmed systemic 5-FU exposure (PMID:21143703, PMID:12114411). TYMS inhibition was never measured, so engagement is inferred_adequate: a tegafur-based regimen (TAS-118) met a pivotal OS endpoint in gastric cancer (NCT02322593), though that trial post-dates the index and its benefit is confounded by its combination partners. In NCT00770874, adding S-1 to cisplatin did not significantly improve OS (HR 0.84, p=0.125) and roughly doubled serious AEs. GOTIC-002 also showed no benefit from tegafur maintenance (PMID:40010135). This suggests fluoropyrimidine/TYMS inhibition adds little in cervical cancer as tested. No source attributes the failure to trial design, so confidence is low.

Human studies published before the 2008 index trial show that gimeracil (CDHP) inhibits DPD. In patients with solid tumours, plasma uracil, a surrogate marker of DPD inhibition, rose in proportion to dose (Springer 2003). In gastric cancer patients, S-1 lowered FBAL and raised uracil compared with infused 5-FU (PMC2394492). 5-FU exposure at standard S-1 doses is established (PMID:21143703). This engagement was not measured in cervical cancer patients. In the index trial NCT00770874, adding S-1 to cisplatin significantly improved PFS but missed the OS primary endpoint (HR 0.84, p=0.125). Because DPD was adequately inhibited, the failure reflects too little benefit from adding the fluoropyrimidine for survival in cervical cancer (F2). The PFS gain without an OS gain partly points to the endpoint (F4).

Oteracil is the part of S-1 that inhibits UMPS (orotate phosphoribosyltransferase), mainly in the gut, to reduce 5-FU toxicity rather than to kill tumour cells. Neither the bundle nor my search found any human measurement of UMPS inhibition, drug levels at the site of action, or a downstream biomarker. In NCT00770874, adding S-1 to cisplatin did not improve overall survival (HR 0.84, p=0.125). Progression-free survival did improve significantly (7.3 vs 4.9 months), so the regimen had some antitumour activity, but that reflects the 5-FU component, not oteracil's target. The published report gives no reason for the overall-survival miss. Because engagement has no human data, the failure cannot be pinned on the drug or the target, so the code is U. F4 is listed as secondary because benefit showed on PFS but not on overall survival.

The index trial, NCT01645709, tested verapamil injected into the knee joint for osteoarthritis pain. The sponsor ended it without giving a reason, and the primary efficacy outcome was posted with no data. No source in the bundle or found by search measures verapamil levels in the joint or synovial fluid, CACNA1C blockade in joint tissue, or a local pathway biomarker. The human pharmacodynamic data (NCT01873950, PMID:10233206, PMID:8181195) show heart effects, such as PR-interval prolongation, after oral or IV dosing. They say nothing about a joint-pain target. The atrial fibrillation approval involves a different tissue and route, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. The bundle does not report an efficacy result, and nothing in it tells a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter here. F7 is a possible secondary code because the trial was stopped early and no data were posted.

In the first-in-human study (NCT01632852; ASH 2014 abstract, published before the index trial started in Aug 2015), patients with CD123+ AML in remission showed saturation of CD123 on monocytes. At doses of 3 mg/kg or more, this saturation lasted through the 14-day dosing interval. The same patients had rapid, complete depletion of CD123-high basophils and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, which shows antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) was working. The protocol picked 9 mg/kg for the index trial because of adequate drug levels and consistent receptor saturation; the dose was not limited by tolerability. Even so, adding talacotuzumab to decitabine did not improve complete response (CR) rate or overall survival (OS) (NCT02472145, PMID:32203138), and an independent data monitoring committee stopped the trial. Because the target was engaged and the mechanism acted, the evidence points to CD123 depletion by ADCC not driving benefit in this population (F2). One caveat: target saturation was shown on blood monocytes, not directly on bone-marrow blasts.

In the index trial NCT03011034, the talacotuzumab arm enrolled only one participant, who did not respond; nearly all 34 patients received daratumumab. The trial therefore could not test talacotuzumab's efficacy in lower-risk MDS. The program appears to have halted after the Phase 3 AML combination trial NCT02472145 missed both its CR and OS endpoints. NCT02992860, in MDS/AML, stopped enrolling on an IDMC/FDA recommendation citing that parallel trial's lack of efficacy. The bundle has no human exposure, CD123 engagement or pathway data: no Phase 1 results are posted for NCT01632852 and there are no abstracts. No other CD123 agent shows success in MDS. Because engagement is untested, the target-versus-molecule question remains indeterminate (U).

Index Phase 3 (NCT03786094) of balixafortide plus eribulin showed no PFS benefit (HR 1.10, p=0.45) and was halted for futility. In healthy volunteers (PMID:28049490, NCT01841476, published 2017), balixafortide at 1500-2500 µg/kg produced robust dose-related HSPC mobilization and leukocytosis. This is a functional readout of CXCR4 blockade, so engagement and pathway are taken as adequate. The phase 1 breast cancer trial (PMID:29706375) characterised PK with eribulin and found no dose-limiting toxicities in the amended design. No tumour-level or in-patient engagement data appear in the bundle. With systemic CXCR4 antagonism demonstrated and no benefit, the CXCR4 mechanism added to eribulin does not appear to drive outcomes in HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer. Confidence is medium because engagement in patients was not shown.

In healthy volunteers (NCT01841476, registered 2012, before the index trial began in 2013; PMID:28049490), balixafortide at 500–2500 µg/kg was well tolerated. It produced dose-dependent CD34+ HSPC mobilization that plateaued at ≥1500 µg/kg, along with leukocytosis. This shows CXCR4 antagonism and the expected mobilization effect without a tolerability cap. Pharmacokinetics were assessed. Engagement was not shown in STEMI patients. The CATCH-AMI index trial (NCT01905475) posted no results and gave no stop reason, so its dose and the size of any LVEF effect are not in the bundle. Because the mobilizing mechanism was engaged yet the program did not advance, the best-supported reading is that the target does not drive LVEF recovery as tested (F2). Confidence is low given the thin bundle.

GSK2798745 had linear, well-tolerated plasma exposure up to 12.5 mg with no dose-limiting safety findings (PMID:30637626). An ex vivo whole-blood endothelial assay showed at least 85% TRPV4 blockade in healthy volunteers and 58-78% in heart failure patients. The authors judged circulating levels sufficient to block TRPV4 largely (PMID:33376150), but this was published in 2021, after the index trial started. In the index LPS proof-of-mechanism trial, BAL protein fell only about 9%, missing the success criterion (NCT03511105, PMID:33189900). This means the expected barrier/pathway effect did not follow. DLco in heart failure, chronic cough, and diabetic macular edema also failed (NCT02497937, NCT03372603, NCT04292912). Engagement was not shown in macular edema patients, and retinal exposure is not shown. Engaged target, no benefit: F2.

Exposure was shown in heart failure patients, with linear PK and no tolerability limits (PMID:30637626, NCT02119260). An ex vivo endothelial impedance assay using blood from HF subjects dosed at 2.4 mg showed at least 78% TRPV4 block after 7 days. The authors judged this sufficient to block lung endothelial TRPV4 to a large extent (PMID:33376150). That evidence was published after the index trial started. Despite this, DLco did not improve versus placebo (NCT02497937, PMID:32227554). In healthy volunteers, the LPS barrier model showed no meaningful change in BAL protein (NCT03511105, PMID:33189900), and the chronic cough trial was futile (NCT03372603). Together these point to TRPV4 blockade not driving the outcome as tested. The index trial was an 11-subject pilot, so underpowering (F7) also applies.

Systemic exposure was characterised in humans, with linear PK and a ~13 h half-life, and the drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped (PMID:30637626). In an ex vivo whole-blood endothelial assay, plasma from dosed healthy volunteers blocked TRPV4 by ≥85%, and plasma from heart-failure patients by ≥58–78%; the authors judged this sufficient. These samples came from trials run before the index trial (PMID:33376150, NCT02119260). Engagement was not measured in chronic cough patients. Downstream effects were absent: BAL protein after LPS challenge was not reduced (NCT03511105, PMID:33189900), and DLco did not improve (NCT02497937). In cough, counts were numerically higher on drug than placebo (NCT03372603). With exposure and engagement adequate but no benefit, TRPV4 blockade does not appear to drive chronic cough.

NEON-NPDR (NCT04722991) found no effect on DRSS: 0% vs 1.9% with ≥2-step improvement. The ARVO abstract gives no reason beyond 'no treatment effect.' The protocol says runcaciguat lowered diastolic blood pressure and raised heart rate in healthy volunteers. That shows the drug reached the bloodstream and caused systemic vasodilation, but not that it reached or acted in the retina. No human retinal or ocular drug levels were found, and no cGMP or sGC activation data. A PK/PD sub-part of the trial was planned, but its results were not found. The UACR fall in CKD (NCT04507061) is a surrogate in another organ, not efficacy through the same tissue. The retinal benefit comes only from rats (PMID:40249725). With no data on engagement in the retina, the failure is indeterminate.

Serum PK was dose-proportional and comparable in AD patients (PMID:39350369). Plasma total tau rose dose-dependently in AD patients, more than in healthy controls, in the Phase 1 trial NCT02820896 (PMID:33980574), and CSF soluble tau fell (PMID:39369294), so engagement counts as shown in disease. The index trial tested doses up to 8100 mg without dose-limiting toxicity. CDR-SB did not differ from placebo, and the tau PET signal was not modulated (NCT03289143, PMID:35696185). Most downstream biomarkers were unchanged (PMID:39513754), so pathway is inadequate. This fits F2: N-terminal tau engagement without benefit. Lauriet in moderate AD met ADAS-Cog only, suggesting a stage effect (F3; NCT03828747). A modelling study predicts minimal synaptic engagement (F1a; PMID:37658103), but this is simulation, not human measurement.

The index 6-week PD trial NCT03256526 met its primary endpoint at 300 mg, with liver fat down 18.7% vs placebo (p=0.0395). Only the 75 mg arm missed. This was a dose-finding biomarker study, not an efficacy failure. Exposure was characterized in phase 1 PK (NCT04427917). Engagement was assessed in healthy volunteers through fructose-metabolism markers in a phase 1 study registered before the index trial (NCT02974374, PMID:33667726), though the abstract is truncated and does not report the size of the effect. The pathway effect replicated: 300 mg cut liver fat in NCT03969719/PMID:36515213, and hepatic insulin sensitivity improved in MASLD (PMID:42844400). HbA1c was unchanged, and the bundle gives no reason for stopping. No tolerability cap was seen.

The index LR-MDS trial (NCT05903274, n=6) stopped for lack of clinical efficacy improvement and posted no results. In MDS/AML patients, briquilimab 0.6 mg/kg showed predictable plasma exposure (PMID:38972509). The same work reported marrow AML/MDS HSPC depletion (mean 62%) and a threefold rise in serum SCF, consistent with CD117 blockade and its downstream effect (NCT04429191, registered 2020; PMID:41785374). That trial was registered before the index trial, but its results were published later. No tolerability cap was shown. Because engagement and pathway were shown in MDS, the failure points to KIT blockade alone not driving clinical benefit in LR-MDS. The tiny enrollment and unknown index dosing limit confidence, so F7 is secondary.

Bamosiran is an siRNA meant to silence ADRB2 in the ciliary body. The bundle has no human evidence of ocular tissue exposure, ADRB2 knockdown or reduced aqueous production. In the phase 1 trial it was undetectable in plasma and gave inconsistent IOP drops in healthy volunteers (PMID:24025752). Uptake into the ciliary body and knockdown were shown only in animals (PMID:24025749). In the index trial (NCT02250612), all four doses produced a flat ~2.4–3.2 mmHg IOP reduction versus 6.1 mmHg with timolol. Timolol, an approved ADRB2 antagonist, worked well in the same trial, and carteolol is also approved. So the target is validated in glaucoma, and the failure points to the molecule (insufficient or plateaued knockdown), not the mechanism. Tolerability did not limit dosing.

The index trial NCT04439071 clearly missed its endpoint: median time to respiratory improvement was 10.0 vs 10.0 days (p=0.949). Exposure was shown in humans. Healthy-volunteer PK reached the target trough plasma concentration tied to preclinical efficacy and was dose-proportional and well tolerated (PMID:27310330). Engagement was shown in cancer patients, not COVID-19 patients, in work published in 2019, before the index trial. Their serum dihydroorotate, the DHODH substrate, rose, indicating enzyme inhibition (PMID:30352802). No human pyrimidine-depletion, antiviral or cytokine biomarker is in the bundle. The antiviral rationale is in vitro only (PMID:33249060). With the target engaged and no benefit, the most likely reading is that DHODH inhibition does not drive recovery in hospitalized COVID-19. Confidence is medium because engagement was not measured in COVID-19 patients and dose comparability is unclear.

In the Phase 1 trial (NCT03750643, PMID:40312358), plasma PK and CD200R target engagement were measured in healthy volunteers. The 500 mg dose was chosen from CD200R receptor-occupancy data, and the same 500 mg dose was used in the CSU index trial. No dose-limiting toxicity was seen. Skin single-cell transcriptomics in AD patients showed gene changes in macrophages after treatment. The CSU index trial failed at interim analysis: UAS7 change was no better than placebo (p=0.38). A later AD Phase 2 (NCT05911841) also stopped for futility. So at a dose picked from occupancy data, agonising CD200R gave no benefit in two diseases, which suggests the mechanism does not drive them. Caveats: the paper does not state the actual occupancy level, engagement was never measured in CSU patients, and the occupancy data were published only in 2025, after the index trial started. Confidence is therefore medium.

In the GAD Phase 3 trial (NCT03829241), troriluzole did no better than placebo on HAM-A at week 8 (difference -0.07, p=0.917), and safety was clean. A Phase 1b oncology study shows troriluzole turns into riluzole in plasma. But no source gives CNS drug levels, EAAT2/SLC1A2 engagement or a glutamate biomarker in humans, so exposure at the brain target, engagement and pathway are all no_human_data. No other drug on this target has succeeded in GAD. The drug also failed in OCD, Alzheimer's disease and SCA. The sponsor (Biohaven) blamed the efficacy results alone and gave no mechanistic reason. Without engagement data, the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in GAD, so the code is U.

T2 Protect AD (NCT03605667) clearly missed both co-primary endpoints: the ADAS-Cog difference was 0.0 and CDR-SB p=0.45. In humans, the only pharmacology I found is from a Phase 1b oncology study, which shows troriluzole turns into riluzole in plasma. I found no human data on brain or CSF levels, no EAAT2/SLC1A2 engagement measure, and no glutamate biomarker for troriluzole in AD. Positive FDG-PET results from a separate riluzole trial in AD (Brain 2021) are a different product and don't show direct engagement. Biohaven pointed to a small, non-significant signal in mild AD (secondary F3), but that was a post hoc subgroup. Because there is no engagement evidence, I can't tell whether the drug failed to engage or the target doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In healthy volunteers, evogliptin 5–20 mg gave dose-proportional plasma exposure, >80% plasma DPP-4 inhibition over 24 h, and a 1.5–2.4-fold rise in active GLP-1 (PMID:25336915, published before the index trial). Efficacy in T2D at 5 mg supports this (NCT02689362, NCT04170998). Engagement was not measured in CAVD patients. The index trial missed its 96-week aortic valve calcium volume endpoint (NCT04055883). However, 48-week 18F-NaF PET active calcification fell significantly at both doses, and AVCV progression appeared suppressed in the second half of the trial (PMID:39260927). The authors call the study exploratory and ask for larger, longer trials. This points to endpoint and duration (F4), with underpowering (F7) and a possibly irrelevant mechanism (F2) as alternatives.

In PANTHEON (NCT02992288; PMID:31523892), HFrEF patients on 5–40 mg showed a dose-dependent fall in heart rate and eGFR and a rise in creatinine and cystatin C. These are recognised A1-receptor effects (sinoatrial node, renal haemodynamics), so systemic exposure, target engagement and immediate A1 signalling are evidenced in the disease population. They are indirect markers, not occupancy measures. Despite this, there was no dose-response on LVEF, NT-proBNP, troponin, volumes or outcomes. PANACHE in HFpEF was also negative (NCT03098979; PMID:31162568). Pre-index pilots (PMID:27624622) showed no heart-rate effect, so engagement evidence postdates the index trial's start. With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, the target appears not to drive HF. The dose-dependent renal decline adds an on-target safety liability (F5).

The index trial NCT04603937 was an active-comparator non-inferiority study against aflibercept. KSI-301 improved BCVA by 6.7 letters but trailed aflibercept (−4.7 letters, NI p>0.9999), so the miss was the non-inferiority margin only, which fits F9. The sister DME trial NCT04611152 failed the same way. The pillars are inferred_adequate rather than measured: the same intravitreal anti-VEGF drug met a sham-controlled endpoint in NPDR (NCT05066230; ≥2-step DRSS 52/128 vs 2/125) and met non-inferiority in RVO (NCT04592419). This shows VEGF engagement in retinal tissue. No direct engagement data in DME exist, and the supporting trials did not predate the index. No dose limitation is shown.

Plasma functional C1-INH rises with dosing in HAE patients (NCT01576523). The same replacement protein met efficacy endpoints in HAE in the same plasma compartment (NCT01912456, NCT02584959, PMID:28328347), so engagement is inferred_adequate. A dose-dependent aPTT prolongation (PMID:22171564) supports the pathway pillar. No engagement or complement biomarker data in AMR patients is in the bundle. In AMR, the pilot trial NCT01147302 showed no histopathology benefit, including unchanged C4d (p=0.65). The Phase 3 trial NCT02547220 stopped for futility: transplant glomerulopathy 50.0% vs 47.4%. No tolerability limit is shown. This points to inhibiting C1-INH-mediated complement not modifying AMR outcomes as tested (F2). The small sample (n=39) and exploratory histologic endpoint add a possible design limitation (F7). A refractory-AMR trial (NCT03221842) ended for enrollment futility.

PROMINENT (NCT03071692) was stopped for futility with a neutral composite CV outcome (HR 1.03). No safety signal was reported. Direct PPARα engagement was not measured. It is inferred adequate because pemafibrate met triglyceride-lowering endpoints in hypertriglyceridemia phase 3 trials (NCT03001817, NCT03011450 registered 2016; NCT04998981). The pathway effect is shown in T2D patients: TG fell and HDL-C, remnant cholesterol and sdLDL-C improved (PMID:36174777, 40747315, 36836015). The bundle shows no dose cap. PMID:37022121 attributes the failure to the mechanism: lowering triglycerides without reducing atherogenic lipoproteins does not reduce CV risk. The target pathway, as tested, does not drive CV outcomes in T2D.

PPARα agonism by pemafibrate was clearly shown in patients with dyslipidemia. Fasting TG fell about 50–59% versus placebo (NCT03001817, NCT03011450, both registered before PROMINENT began), with superiority to fenofibrate (NCT04998981). HDL-C, apoA-I and cholesterol efflux capacity rose, and TRL and sdLDL-C fell (PMID:30077640, PMID:36216531). Human plasma exposure is characterized, including PK-validated models (PMID:31900032). Tolerability did not cap the dose; PROMINENT reported no unexpected safety findings. Despite this robust target and pathway effect, PROMINENT (NCT03071692) was stopped for futility, with a primary composite HR of 1.03 [0.92, 1.16]. PPARα-mediated TG lowering did not translate into cardiovascular event reduction. The mechanism, as tested, does not drive CV outcomes.

The index trial NCT02388347 was a Phase 1 single-dose safety study in healthy adults. Its primary endpoints were adverse events, injection-site reactions, laboratory values, vital signs and ECGs, so it was not an efficacy test and there was no failed efficacy readout. No serious adverse events occurred and AE rates resembled placebo. PMID:33918602 reports measured serum PK across 30–600 mg SC. It also reports a dose-dependent rise in serum IL13 consistent with accumulating drug–IL13 complex, which supports exposure and target binding. That binding was shown only in healthy volunteers and published after the trial started. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Nothing in the bundle explains why the program stopped, so F9 applies.

The index trial NCT04737304 was a first-in-human Phase 1/2 proof-of-concept study of topical BEN2293 in mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis. Its primary outcome was safety and tolerability (adverse events, vital signs, ECG, labs), classified as not_efficacy. No results were posted, no stop reason was given, and the bundle holds no other trials, Phase 1 results or PubMed abstracts. So it does not show an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). Exposure, TRK engagement and pathway effects have no human data, so if an efficacy shortfall occurred it cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter (U, secondary). Other TRK inhibitors (pegcantratinib, lestaurtinib) reached only Phase 2, so F1b does not apply.

HU007 combines 0.02% nanoparticle cyclosporine with 3% trehalose. Trehalose has no recorded target, and no source reports human exposure, engagement or pathway data for it. The index trial NCT03461575 tested non-inferiority to Restasis and superiority to Moisview. Huons reported that the Korean Phase 3 succeeded on non-inferiority and filed for approval. The company later withdrew the filing after the Korean regulator (MFDS) asked it to address the statistical validity of the analysis. That is a regulatory and statistical problem, not a clear efficacy failure. A repeat Phase 3 (NCT05743764) again met non-inferiority to Restasis but was not superior to Moisview (medipana). So the index readout was not a clean efficacy failure (F9). The statistical questions point to F7. Because there is no data on target engagement, the mechanism question is undetermined (U).

HL301 is a standardized extract of seven medicinal plants and has no defined molecular target. The bundle contains no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers, and no Phase 1 PK/PD results. In the Phase 2a trial (PMID:38565405), accrual was poor (63 of 87 planned patients). Grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis was no lower with HL301 than with placebo (55.6% and 52.4% vs 37.5%). The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. With no engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged a target from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease, so the code is U. The underpowered trial caused by under-accrual is a secondary F7 factor. I did not run any web searches, so the bundle is the only source.

The index phase 2 (NCT03177668; PMID:34590026) gave 6 mg/kg weekly and the 6-month disease control rate was 3.2%, below the predefined threshold. Exposure was dose-proportional in both phase 1 studies (PMID:28291776, PMID:31557561). In the first-in-human study, 22 of 33 patients had mesothelioma, and sCD26/DPPIV assays showed CD26 modulation, so engagement was shown in this disease and published in 2017, before the index trial started. Engagement adequacy is graded only on that qualitative statement. The MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no downstream pathway biomarker. With target modulation shown at the recommended dose and little benefit, CD26 blockade does not appear to drive refractory mesothelioma as tested.

In healthy volunteers (NCT04932850, PMID:35477725), a single intramuscular dose was well tolerated, distributed rapidly into serum (exposure) and produced serum neutralizing titers above those of convalescent and vaccinated subjects against alpha through delta (engagement). Potency against omicron was significantly reduced. No engagement or viral-clearance data from COVID-19 patients are in the bundle, so pathway has no human data. The index trial NCT04952805 has unknown status, no stated stop reason and no posted results. Its primary endpoints are safety and time to viral clearance, classified as not efficacy. The bundle does not show a failed efficacy readout, so F9 fits best. Omicron escape is a possible reason for stopping, but the sources do not say so.

Phase 1 (NCT05011812; CROI 2022 poster; mass-balance paper) measured plasma PK and found the drug well tolerated up to 2100 mg/day, so the 1400 mg/day dose was not capped by tolerability. I could not read the poster's numbers to check whether plasma levels stayed above the EC90. No human measure of Mpro inhibition in the respiratory tract was found, so engagement is no_human_data. In the index trial (NCT05543707, PMID:38197702), infectious virus and RNA did not fall faster than on placebo. That shows no antiviral effect, but it does not tell a drug that never engaged apart from a target that doesn't matter. Hence U. The investigators blamed low viral burden, fast natural clearance in vaccinated Omicron patients, and treatment starting up to 5 days after symptoms began (F7/F4).

Rucosopasem (GC4711) is a superoxide dismutase mimetic meant to make SBRT work better against tumours. Its three Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (NCT03194139, NCT03099824, NCT03762031) measured safety and pharmacokinetics but posted no results. I found no human data on drug levels in the tumour, superoxide dismutation or a downstream biomarker such as tumour H2O2. GRECO-2 (NCT04698915) stopped at a futility analysis with 24 vs 20 deaths. Galera said only that the trial was unlikely to succeed as designed, then dropped the NSCLC trial (NCT04476797) and looked at strategic alternatives. Toxicity did not cap the dose, and no other drug works through this mechanism. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Primary code U: I found no human measure of CB2 receptor engagement, so I can't tell whether the drug failed to engage CB2 or CB2 doesn't matter in CF. Exposure: healthy-volunteer dosing studies at 10–40 mg measured systemic drug levels (PMID:34143391). Engagement: no receptor occupancy or other direct CB2 measure in humans. Pathway: in the CF Phase 2a, the 20 mg dose significantly cut sputum IL-8 and IgG; other sputum markers fell only numerically (PMID:33011099). In the Phase 2b index trial, lenabasum did not lower exacerbations at 5 or 20 mg BID and raised no safety concerns (NCT03451045, PMID:40425421). Neither the sponsor nor the trial paper gave a mechanistic reason. Because the sputum markers did move, an irrelevant target (F2) is a possible secondary reading.

RESOLVE-1 (NCT03398837) missed its CRISS primary endpoint, with CRISS 0.888 vs 0.887 and no mRSS benefit (PMID:37098795). Plasma PK is characterised in healthy volunteers (PMID:34143391). No human CB2 occupancy or engagement data exist; the T-cell work is ex vivo (PMID:34543449). Phase 2 skin biopsies in dcSSc showed reduced inflammation and fibrosis gene expression and improved histology (PMID:32336038), which counts as pathway evidence in this disease. The investigators attribute the null result to background immunosuppression, especially mycophenolate, masking any add-on effect, which is a design challenge. Prespecified subgroups differed by mycophenolate use and IST duration (PMID:37098795, PMID:40065521), supporting F3. Without engagement data, U also applies.

Plasma PK at 20 mg doses was characterized in humans (PMID:34143391). The phase 2 in refractory skin-predominant DM (NCT02466243, which ran before the index trial; PMID:35490744) met its CDASI endpoint at 20 mg BID with no tolerability limit. Biopsies from treated patients showed CB2R, IL-31, IFN-γ and IFN-β downregulated in lesional skin (PMID:34983619), so engagement and pathway effects were shown in this disease. The Phase 3 used the composite Total Improvement Score (NCT03813160), and the bundle posts no index results. Sponsor-linked analysis argues TIS is non-specific and CDASI is the more sensitive skin measure (PMID:37331616), pointing to the endpoint. Responder heterogeneity (PMID:40383862) and weaker effects on muscle than skin (PMID:41544891) support patient selection as a secondary explanation.

The Cognite trial (NCT02547818; PMID:42920249) gave oral ibuprofen at 10 mg, less than 5% of the lowest over-the-counter dose (sponsor patent). The trial missed CDR-SB against both monotherapies. Exposure is the only pillar with human data. In healthy elderly volunteers, ibuprofen appeared in CSF (Cmax about 3.9 ng/ml at 10 mg), and the investigators called this level sufficient (PMID:28856569). No source measured COX inhibition, prostaglandin lowering or a downstream inflammatory biomarker in humans at this dose. The bundle therefore cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The very low dose makes inadequate engagement (F1a) plausible but unproven. A non-significant benefit in APOE4 non-carriers points to F3.

The index trial NCT03332524 (SP160412, sunburn) stopped for lack of efficacy and posted no results. COX engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred adequate because ibuprofen met pain endpoints through COX inhibition elsewhere (dental pain, NCT00707057, NCT01098747; multiple approvals). The pathway held in experimental UVB sunburn. Oral ibuprofen cut UVB erythema and skin blood flow by 33-40% (PMID:1558996) and raised heat pain thresholds (PMID:12895189, PMID:22090804). Topical ibuprofen gel lowered UVB erythema versus placebo (NCT02666846). Despite this, earlier data showed ibuprofen had limited value for sunburn symptoms (PMID:3883908), pointing to a mechanism that does not drive the clinical pain endpoint. The index formulation and its dose are not described, and no results were posted, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT04570644 is a Phase 1 plasma/CSF pharmacokinetic study of ALZT-OP1 (cromolyn plus ibuprofen) in Alzheimer's patients and healthy volunteers. Its primary outcomes are PK parameters only, so it was not an efficacy test and cannot be a failed efficacy readout. It also does not concern balanitis, the labelled program disease. Ibuprofen's pillars hold in humans. Exposure: 600 mg gave a plasma Cmax of about 56 µg/mL (PMID:4064467). Engagement: 800 mg tid inhibited COX-2 by about 71% and COX-1 by about 89% in healthy volunteers (PMID:11028250, published before the index trial). Pathway: it reduced UVB-induced erythema (NCT02666846). No engagement data exist in balanitis patients. Many approvals confirm the COX mechanism works clinically.

The index trial tested 5% topical ibuprofen in ankle sprain, and SPID did not separate from placebo (NCT01945034). The bundle has no human tissue exposure or COX-engagement data for this topical dose. COX inhibition was shown only for high-dose oral ibuprofen in healthy volunteers (PMID:11028250), a different compartment and dose, so it cannot be inferred here. The Phase 1 UVB erythema reduction used a 10% gel on skin in healthy volunteers (NCT02666846). Oral ibuprofen 2400 mg/day showed benefit in acute ankle injury (PMID:2512256, PMID:12216965), so COX inhibition matters in this disease. The failure therefore points to the topical formulation, not the target. A topical ibuprofen trial in muscle soreness also failed (NCT01794923). Evidence is thin, so confidence is low.

Lanraplenib 30 mg showed no benefit over placebo on the 12-week CLASI-A score (p=0.75; NCT03134222, PMID:34498056). The protocol says the Phase 1 studies GS-US-379-1372 and -1900 measured PK/PD, but it gives only safety results. The only potency figures (human whole-blood pSYK and CD69 EC50 of 171–301 nM) are ex vivo, and the efficacy-to-pSYK-inhibition link comes from rodents. No skin exposure, in vivo SYK inhibition or downstream biomarker data in humans were found. No other SYK inhibitor has succeeded in CLE. Lanraplenib also failed in RA and Sjögren's (NCT02885181, NCT03100942), but engagement is unverified, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from an irrelevant target. The 8-patient placebo arm and its large response point to a small trial (F7).

In NCT02885181, lanraplenib at 10 mg and 30 mg did no better than placebo on DAS28-CRP change (p=0.30 and p=0.98). The filgotinib control arm did separate (p=0.002), so the trial could detect a real effect, which argues against a design failure (F7). Later protocols mention a first-in-human study in healthy volunteers (GS-US-379-1372) that measured pharmacodynamics, but they say only that no risks were found. I found no human occupancy, SYK-inhibition or biomarker figures, and none in RA patients. My PDF retrieval stopped at the tool-use limit, so the protocol sections on human blood SYK inhibition could not be read. No other SYK inhibitor is approved in RA: fostamatinib reached phase 3 there but is approved only for ITP. Engagement is unknown, so the result is indeterminate (U).

In NCT03100942, lanraplenib 30 mg did not separate from placebo (42.9% vs 26.5%, p=0.16). I found no human data on drug exposure or SYK engagement. Trial protocols mention a first-in-human study in healthy volunteers that measured pharmacodynamics, but they report no occupancy or inhibition results. In the Sjögren's patients, the full paper (PMID:35377447) says disease biomarkers (RF, IgG, IgA, IgM, B-cell and plasma-cell subsets) stayed near baseline on lanraplenib, while filgotinib and tirabrutinib moved them. So the pathway pillar is inadequate. Without engagement data, though, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged SYK apart from a target that does not drive the disease. That makes the code U. Lanraplenib also failed in RA and CLE (NCT02885181, NCT03134222), and the small arms (n≈35) suggest the trial was underpowered (F7).

Index trial NCT05028751 was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation of lanraplenib with gilteritinib. Its primary endpoints were safety, DLT and MTD/RP2D, not efficacy. It was terminated for an unspecified 'sponsor decision', so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. No DLTs occurred and no RP2D was reported. Grade 5 AEs occurred in 4/4 patients at 90 mg, but none were attributed to lanraplenib, so molecule toxicity (F6) is only a possibility. The bundle has no human PK, SYK engagement or pathway data. Lanraplenib missed its primary endpoints in RA, Sjogren's and CLE (NCT02885181, NCT03100942, NCT03134222), so no pillar can be inferred adequate. If treated as a failure, the code would be U.

In humans, MK-7622 reversed scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment and altered qEEG at exposures matching effective preclinical ones, which the authors call target modulation (PMID:29563325). This implies CNS exposure and M1 engagement, though it was likely not measured in AD patients and was published after the 2013 index start. At 45 mg in AD, excess cholinergic AEs (21% vs 8%) also point to on-target activity, yet ADAS-Cog11 and ADCS-ADL were unchanged and the trial stopped for futility (NCT01852110, PMID:29955661). No M1 drug has succeeded in AD in the bundle, so F1b does not apply. Preclinical work suggests ago-PAM overactivation may blunt cognitive benefit and drive AEs (PMID:29581537, PMID:29701957), so F5 is a secondary code.

The index trial NCT02122770 was a CYP3A drug-interaction PK study (Cmax/AUC with fluconazole or itraconazole), not an efficacy test of pevonedistat, so the code is F9. Pillars held in humans. Plasma exposure was dose-proportional. In the melanoma Phase 1 (NCT01011530, registered 2009; PMID:27056178), every post-dose tumor biopsy was positive for the pevonedistat-NEDD8 adduct and NAE-regulated transcripts rose. CDT1 and NRF2 accumulated in solid-tumor biopsies (PMID:26423795). Single-agent activity in melanoma was modest (one partial response), consistent with F2 as a secondary code. Development of the whole drug ended after the Phase 3 MDS failure (NCT03268954), with later trials citing no regulatory path or sponsor discontinuation (NCT04172844, NCT03386214).

Ilixadencel is an allogeneic dendritic-cell immune primer with no recorded molecular target, so classical exposure and engagement pillars are not measured in humans. An immune pathway readout exists only in HCC: 73% of evaluable patients showed more tumor-specific CD8+ T cells (PMID:30719425). The RCC phase 1 (NCT01525017) posted no immunologic data. In the index trial, OS favored the combination numerically (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.42-1.27; median 35.6 vs 25.3 mo) and ORR was 42% vs 24%, but neither was significant. The authors state the study was not adequately powered to detect modest survival differences (PMID:35638086), pointing to a design limitation (F7). Whether the mechanism works in RCC remains indeterminate (U). The later CPI-combination trial was terminated by sponsor decision (NCT03735290).

Ilixadencel is an allogeneic inflammatory dendritic-cell product given into the tumour, and no molecular target is recorded. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data, such as tumour immune infiltration or a pharmacodynamic biomarker. Phase 1b of ILIAD (NCT03735290) finished without safety problems. The sponsor dropped Phase 2 because patients who had never had a checkpoint inhibitor did not respond, and also gave a competitive-positioning reason. Its earlier Phase 2 in kidney cancer (NCT02432846) also missed its overall survival endpoint. With no engagement evidence, nothing in the bundle can tell apart a product that never primed the immune response from a mechanism that does not work here, so the code is U. F8 is listed as secondary because the sponsor partly framed the stop as a strategic choice.

Neurana reported that RESUME-1 (NCT04671082, 50/100/200 mg TID, n=1004) missed its primary and key secondary endpoints at Day 14. Tolperisone was well tolerated, so dose was not limited by tolerability. The only human pharmacology found is plasma PK in healthy volunteers, which varies widely between people with CYP2D6/2C19 genotype (PMID:17323790, PMID:25953735). There are no human data on CNS or spinal exposure, sodium-channel blockade or reflex suppression. Evidence of sodium-channel blockade comes only from in vitro and animal work (PMID:16650844). The Phase 2 STAR signal was weak: 200 mg vs placebo p=0.004, trend test p=0.054, with a large placebo response of -3.5 (PMID:33262641). A high placebo response is therefore a possible contributor. With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The sponsor gave no reason for the failure.

Neurana said RESUME-1 (NCT04671082) missed its primary endpoint, pain on the NRS at day 14, and its key secondary endpoints. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by tolerability, and the company then explored strategic alternatives. Plasma PK in humans is known and varies widely with CYP2D6/2C19 genotype (PMID:17323790, 25953735). But the sodium-channel targets work in the spinal cord, and no source reports CSF levels, channel blockade, or a reflex or pharmacodynamic biomarker in humans. Channel-blocking data come only from oocytes and rats (PMID:16650844). The Phase 2 STAR trial showed a strong placebo response and only a borderline dose trend (p=0.054; PMID:33262641), so trial noise (F7) may also have contributed. With no human evidence of target engagement, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

Plasma exposure at 0.6 mg is documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:32237115, PMID:29786964). Direct AHR engagement was never measured in humans. It is inferred adequate because laquinimod 0.6 mg reduced relapse rate and MRI activity in relapsing MS RCTs (PMID:24228070). In the index PPMS trial the same dose cut new T2 lesions (RR 0.4, p=0.001), showing an anti-inflammatory pathway effect in this disease. Yet it had no effect on the brain-volume primary endpoint (p=0.903; NCT02284568, PMID:32651286). Other RRMS trials also missed on disability (NCT01707992, NCT00605215). So the mechanism engaged but did not modify progressive neurodegeneration. Endpoint or duration may also contribute (F4). The 1.5 mg arm was halted for cardiovascular events (F6).

LEGATO-HD (NCT02215616) missed its UHDRS-TMS primary endpoint at 1.0 mg. I found no human evidence that laquinimod engaged AHR: no CYP1A1 induction measured in patients and no CSF drug levels. AHR activation was shown only in mice and in cultured human hepatocytes (PMID:27671624). The human PK studies (PMID:32237115, 29786964) report plasma levels only. The bundle shows no clinical efficacy through AHR in another disease. The trial did reduce caudate and brain volume loss, a significant secondary result (PMID:38280392). That suggests some biological activity in the CNS, but it is a downstream marker of disease, not proof that AHR was engaged, so F4 is only a possible secondary code. The 1.5 mg arm was stopped because of cardiovascular safety concerns in MS trials, not because of dose-limiting tolerability in HD. Overall the cause is indeterminate.

In the lupus arthritis trial (NCT01085084), swollen joint counts at week 12 were essentially the same on placebo and both laquinimod doses. Tender joint counts improved numerically, but the spread was very wide, there were only about 26 patients per arm, and no statistical test was posted. That points to a trial too small to answer the question (F7). Human data on laquinimod are limited to plasma PK and drug-interaction studies (PMID:32237115). The evidence that it activates AHR, such as Cyp1a1 induction, comes from mice and cells only (PNAS 2016). I found no human measure of AHR engagement or a downstream marker, in lupus or any other disease. The relapsing MS benefit (PMID:24228070) is in the CNS, a different tissue, and lupus nephritis was reported as positive only by press release. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

SY-201 is a topical peptide with no recorded primary target. The sponsor describes it only as having 'multi-modal' immune-modulating mechanisms. In NCT05370495, none of the three doses separated from vehicle on tCFS or eye-dryness VAS at Day 60. The doses were well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap them. I found no human data on ocular tissue exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers. The ARVO abstract reports only post-hoc signals, such as a larger dryness improvement at 0.5% in patients with high tear MMP-9. This hints at a population (F3) explanation but is not confirmatory. Engagement is unknown, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The code is therefore U.

JTA-004 is an enhanced viscosupplement given as a single injection into the knee joint, and clonidine is one of its components. Its Phase III trial (NCT04333160) missed the primary endpoint, WOMAC pain at month 3 versus placebo, and the key secondary comparison with Hylan G-F 20. All arms showed similar pain relief. I found no human data on clonidine levels in the joint, alpha-2 receptor engagement in the joint, or a downstream biomarker at this dose. The systemic data on oral and epidural clonidine in the bundle do not tell us about this local formulation. The sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation. One secondary source mentions a possible different response in patients with more severe baseline pain (F3), and the similar response in every arm points to a trial that could not separate them (F7). Because engagement is unknown, the code is U.

The drug was 0.1% topical clonidine gel aimed at α2 receptors on nociceptors in foot skin. Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up human data on skin drug levels, peripheral α2 engagement, or a nociceptor biomarker. Clonidine's approvals for hypertension and ADHD come from systemic, mostly central action, which is a different compartment, so they don't support inferred adequacy. The index trial NCT02068027 showed no difference (-1.6 vs -1.6), and BDSI called this unexpected after a positive interim look. The follow-up NCT02643251 also failed, and BDSI then dropped the gel at this strength and in this delivery form. Earlier work suggested only capsaicin-responsive or other subsets respond (PMID:22683276, 7596622), which points to heterogeneity. But nothing in the bundle separates a gel that never engaged the receptor from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT03034135, disulfiram plus copper produced 0 responses among 21 patients with recurrent glioblastoma. No target is recorded for copper gluconate, and the proposed mechanism (a disulfiram-copper complex hitting the proteasome or similar targets) was never measured in human brain or tumour. The only human pharmacodynamic data come from a liver-tumour phase 1 (PMID:33957901, NCT00742911): serum protein S-glutathionylation went up, but that is a nonspecific marker, the disease was different, and no objective responses were seen. The glioblastoma trials I found (NCT02715609, the J Neurooncol phase 2) report only safety and efficacy, with no levels of the drug in brain or tumour and no engagement data. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In healthy volunteers, ASC42 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and dose-dependent rises in FGF19 with falls in C4 (NCT04679129; PMID:37919483). That shows FXR engagement and the expected suppression of bile-acid synthesis. The study was registered before the PBC index trial started. Pruritus appeared only at the highest doses, and the bundle does not show the dose was capped. Engagement was never measured in PBC patients. The index trial (NCT05190523, ALP at day 85) posted no results and gave no stop reason. Obeticholic acid is approved for PBC through FXR, which argues against the target being irrelevant. Under the rules, adequate engagement points to F2, but the bundle is thin. A business stop (F8) cannot be excluded.

In NCT04432376, miconazole oil gave a therapeutic cure rate of 14/67 (21%), against 11/64 (17%) for vehicle oil. My search found no human data on how much drug the oil formulation delivers to the ear canal, how strongly it inhibits the fungal target in that tissue, or any biomarker effect. The sponsor also gave no explanation for the failure. Approval for skin use (tinea pedis, a fungal foot infection) uses different formulations. Small otomycosis trials using miconazole cream (PMID:35145933, PMID:25621236) suggest the mechanism can work in this disease, which makes F2 (target does not drive the disease) unlikely. But I can't tell whether this oil delivered too little drug or whether the trial itself was flawed. Low cure rates in both arms point to possible design or execution problems (F7). Because target engagement has no human data, the primary code is U.

First-in-human PET with [11C]-UCB-J (NCT05486195, PMID:36733374) showed brain penetration and dose-proportional SV2A occupancy in healthy volunteers, published before the index trial began. The 1–15 mg doses in the index trial were chosen to cover an estimated 35–80% SV2A occupancy (PMID:41451887). Tolerability did not limit dosing; there were no dose-limiting AEs up to 80 mg. No downstream pathway biomarker result is reported; the fMRI was exploratory with no stated finding. In mild AD (NCT05771428), the 12-week ADAS-Cog 14 change showed no signal at any dose (p=0.98, 0.65, 0.79) and no dose trend. The target was engaged, yet there was no benefit, which points to SV2A modulation not improving cognition in AD as tested. Occupancy was only estimated in patients and the pathway was unmeasured, so confidence is medium.
