In the index trial (NCT03000608), topical EISO (SAN021) missed its primary endpoint: 4 of 45 patients reached PGA clear or almost clear, against 3 of 21 on placebo. No primary target is recorded. The proposed mechanisms, PDE4 inhibition and cytokine suppression, come only from in vitro and reconstituted skin models (PMID:29593534, PMID:28360856). An open-label interim study and a press release reported clinical improvement, but neither measured exposure, engagement or a biomarker in human skin. No source gives a reason the program failed, and no other drug on the same target is listed. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter in psoriasis, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT04508140 (BO-112 plus pembrolizumab, CRC/gastric liver metastases) was terminated for 'Low recruitment rate' after 16 evaluable patients, with 0 responders. The stated reason is operational, so the small trial could not answer the question, which points to F7. The bundle has no human exposure, TLR3/MDA5 engagement or pathway data, and no Phase 1 results or abstracts. The melanoma combination trial NCT04570332 met its ORR endpoint, but it involved a different tumor and lesion compartment and a combination whose effect cannot be attributed to BO-112. It therefore does not establish inferred engagement for liver metastases. The program continued (BCC trial NCT06422936). Without engagement data, a mechanistic failure is indeterminate (U, secondary).

The index trial NCT04508140 (BO-112 plus pembrolizumab, CRC or gastric/GEJ cancer with liver metastases) was terminated for low recruitment after only 16–18 patients, with 0 responders in both cohorts. The stated stop reason is operational, and the truncated trial could not properly answer the question, so F7 is primary. The bundle contains no human exposure, TLR3/MDA5 engagement or pathway biomarker data. The Phase 1 trial NCT02828098 posted no results, and there are no abstracts. The melanoma combination trial NCT04570332 met its ORR endpoint. However, that was a different tumour and injection compartment, and the benefit is confounded by pembrolizumab, so engagement cannot be inferred for liver metastases. With no engagement evidence, target futility cannot be separated from non-engagement, hence U is secondary.

In NCT03837743, topical DUR-928 did no better than vehicle on the IGA. At week 4 vehicle was numerically better (p=0.022). Durect said the drug showed no benefit on any primary or secondary analysis, dropped psoriasis and moved to liver disease. The searches found no human data on skin drug levels, DNMT inhibition, methylation changes in the skin or downstream biomarkers for the topical form. The liver trials, including NCT04563026, also missed their primary endpoints, so they can't support an inferred_adequate rating. No other drug on this target appears in the bundle. The sources give no reason for the failure beyond the lack of efficacy. Without engagement data, there is no way to tell whether the drug failed to engage its target or the target doesn't matter in psoriasis, so the code is U.

In ICONA (NCT04052516), the primary endpoint, NASH resolution, numerically favoured icosabutate but missed significance (p=0.14 at 600 mg). Liver injury and inflammation markers fell (ALT, AST, hsCRP, ELF, PRO-C3; PMID:39938653, sponsor site), and the drug lowered triglycerides in NCT01893515. That points to downstream activity, but these are disease markers rather than a direct readout of FFAR1/FFAR4 signalling. No human receptor occupancy, liver drug levels or other direct FFAR1/4 engagement measure was found. The same-target section of the bundle is empty, so F1b cannot apply. The sponsor frames the trial as positive and points to type 2 diabetes patients as the responsive subgroup, which suggests F3. A modest sample size also limited power (F7). Because engagement is unmeasured, the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT02716194 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study whose primary outcomes were safety, tolerability and immunogenicity. It was not an efficacy test. The posted results show no serious or treatment-related AEs, no FVIII inhibitors, and no AE-driven withdrawals, so toxicity did not visibly end the program and dosing was not limited. The bundle contains no human PK, FVIII activity or half-life data; the only exposure data are from mice and monkeys (PMID:31366602). Many other FVIII replacement products are approved for hemophilia A, so the target is validated. No stop reason is given, and the bundle cannot show why the program halted. F9 is primary, with U as secondary because human exposure and engagement are unmeasured.

The index trial NCT02716194 was a completed Phase 1 dose-escalation study of BAX 826 (PSA-conjugated FVIII) in hemophilia A. Its primary endpoints were safety, tolerability and immunogenicity, not efficacy. Posted results show no SAEs, no deaths, no treatment-related AEs, no withdrawals, and no FVIII inhibitors across three dose cohorts. Tolerability therefore did not cap the dose. The bundle contains no FVIII activity or PK data, so exposure, engagement and pathway have no human evidence. No reason for stopping is stated, and no other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target drugs are in the bundle. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test and did not fail, this is F9. Why the program stopped cannot be determined from the bundle (U secondary).

PMID:27592041 reports PK measurements showing sustained high local knee-joint exposure with low systemic exposure, which reads as coming from the Phase 1 studies (NCT01113333, NCT01463488, NCT01511549). The abstract does not say so explicitly. Target engagement (IKK inhibition) and pathway markers (IL-1β, TNFα, PGE2) were shown only in vitro, so there are no human engagement or pathway data. Dose was not capped, as Phase 1 confirmed safety. The Phase 2a trial (NCT01598415) missed WOMAC pain at day 56 overall. It was statistically significant only in patients with baseline effusion, which suggests an inflammatory subtype may respond. Because engagement was never measured in humans, a target that does not matter cannot be fully excluded, so U is a secondary code.

No human target-engagement or biomarker data in exertional heat stroke appear in the bundle. Pillars are only inferred: dantrolene is FDA-approved (bundle lists multiple sclerosis) through RYR1 blockade in skeletal muscle, so exposure, engagement and pathway held there. PMID:6614536 suggests human dose-response work, but no abstract is given. The index Phase 3 (NCT03600376) enrolled only 17 patients. GCS≥13 recovery at 90 min was 4/9 with Ryanodex vs 2/8 without, a numeric trend favoring drug that was not significant. The Phase 2 (NCT02513095) showed the same pattern: 5/17 vs 2/17, OR 6 with a wide CI, p=0.396. Both trials were too small to answer the question, so trial design (F7) is primary. A mechanism that does not matter (F2) cannot be excluded.

In the Phase 2 trial NCT03927690, LKA651 (an intravitreal anti-EPO antibody fragment) was not superior to Lucentis on visual acuity, given alone or combined with Lucentis. Given alone, it reduced retinal thickness less than Lucentis. Novartis's results summary reports only blood levels of LKA651 and reticulocyte counts. It shows no eye-fluid drug levels, no free or total EPO lowering in the eye, and no downstream eye biomarker. The Phase 1 dose-ranging study NCT02867735 measured pharmacodynamic activity but posted no results. The summary gives no reason for the failure beyond 'failed to demonstrate superiority', and tolerability did not cap the dose. With no human evidence of target engagement, a drug that never engaged EPO cannot be told apart from an EPO target that does not drive DME, so the code is U.

The first-in-human study showed dose-dependent plasma kynurenine lowering, with >80-90% IDO1 inhibition at ≥100 mg BID, the dose used in the index trial (PMID:28053021, PMID:27990653). In urothelial patients, kynurenine fell on epacadostat (PMID:39054491), but this was published after the index trial started. Enrollment in NCT03361865 stopped early because the melanoma Phase 3 (NCT02752074) failed: PFS HR 1.00. That leaves 93 patients, about 64 days of follow-up and no formal comparison (ORR 31.8% vs 24.5%). Since IDO1 was engaged yet adding it to PD-1 gave no benefit, the program stopped on evidence that the mechanism does not drive the disease (F2). The truncated index trial could not answer its own question (F7). ECHO-203 suggested more than 300 mg BID may be needed (PMID:36309837), raising a dose-adequacy doubt (F1a).

EUROCONDOR (NCT01726075) tested topical somatostatin eye drops against an mfERG endpoint. No primary results were posted. The bundle has no human data on retinal drug levels, SSTR engagement or a downstream biomarker; the only exposure and mechanism support is animal work (PMID:32784955). A 2024 review (PMID:38227526) reports that topical somatostatin had neuroprotective effects only in patients with pre-existing retinal neurodysfunction and no impact on DR onset. It calls for identifying the patient subgroups that benefit. Baseline data (PMID:28663190) showed many enrolled patients had normal mfERG and SD-OCT, so neurodegeneration was present in some but not all. This points to benefit confined to a subgroup and to disease heterogeneity (F3). With engagement unmeasured, U also applies.

Index trial NCT02444910 was a 28-day, single-arm study of 9 people. OGTT and insulin sensitivity did not change. KDT501 was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. No PK, tissue levels or PPARγ engagement data exist in humans. Plasma total and HMW adiponectin rose modestly, and TNF-α and post-meal triglycerides fell. Adiponectin is a PPARγ-linked downstream marker, but the sub-study PMID:29033896 traced its rise to a post-transcriptional effect and β-adrenergic potentiation, not clearly PPARγ. 'Inferred_adequate' is a loose label for that pathway signal: it was measured but is weak, and KDT501 met no efficacy endpoint elsewhere. The investigators blame the small sample and short duration, and glitazone glucose effects take longer than 28 days to appear. PPARγ is validated in T2D (rosiglitazone approved), so the molecule itself is a secondary explanation (F1b). Without engagement data the code is close to U.

The index trial NCT03267940 was a Phase 1b study with safety primaries. It was terminated for an unspecified 'Sponsor decision', and the expansion ORR was never posted, so there is no failed efficacy readout. It is not an efficacy test of the drug's mechanism (F9). A business or portfolio stop is plausible (secondary F8): the parallel Morpheus gastric study NCT03281369 closed for portfolio reasons. On the pillars, qMRI in solid-tumor patients (PMID:38773189, PMID:37720027; trials NCT00834704, NCT01170897, NCT01453153) showed day-1 decreases in tumor ADC and T1 and increases in perfusion and permeability. The authors read these as consistent with HA depletion. This evidence is indirect, comes from patients without cholangiocarcinoma, and was published after the index trial started. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

Plasma exposure is characterised in healthy volunteers and gastroparesis patients across 80–600 µg/kg (PMID:19432500, PMID:18199894), covering the 160 and 480 µg/kg index doses. The first-in-human study reports pharmacodynamic receptor activity at doses as low as 40 µg/kg, along with haemodynamic effects at higher doses. This was published in 2008, before the index trial, but only in healthy volunteers, and the PD measure is not specified. No downstream pathway biomarker was shown in ileus patients. Phase 2b suggested benefit (PMID:20087086), but two identical Phase 3 trials, NCT01285570 and NCT01296620, showed no difference from placebo, with no toxicity (PMID:23739196). This points to a mechanism that does not drive recovery from postoperative ileus. The authors cite surgical variance as a limitation (F7). Engagement evidence is thin, hence low confidence.

Exposure is adequate: human PK was characterized in healthy volunteers and gastroparesis patients (PMID:18199894, PMID:19432500). Engagement is inferred_adequate. Phase 1 pharmacodynamics suggested receptor activity at doses of 40 µg/kg and above (PMID:18199894), and a phase 2b postoperative ileus trial met its primary GI motility endpoint at 480 µg/kg (PMID:20087086), the same GHSR/GI compartment. That support is weakened because phase 3 ULISES missed its endpoints with comparable safety (NCT01285570, NCT01296620). No engagement data exist in enteral feeding intolerance, and PROMOTE results are not in the bundle (NCT02784392). The tolerable, engaged drug apparently gave no benefit, so the best-supported code is F2: GHSR agonism does not drive clinical GI recovery as tested. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low and U is listed as secondary.

Phase 1 in HER3-expressing solid tumors had no DLTs up to 30 mg/kg weekly (NCT01966445), so dose was not limited. Exposure was dose-proportional. Immuno-PET showed tumor uptake saturating at 30 mg/kg, with ID90 18 mg/kg (NCT02345174, PMID:30733323). Paired biopsies showed HER3 inhibition (PMID:34132450). Engagement and the pathway effect were therefore shown in patients, though only during or after the index trial. Antitumor activity was nonetheless limited: one partial response in 29 patients. The target, engaged as tested, does not drive these unselected HER3-expressing tumors (F2). The single response came in a CD74-NRG1-fusion NSCLC patient, and the authors propose NRG1-fusion selection, which supports patient selection as a secondary explanation (F3).

Exposure was dose-proportional and comparable in AMI patients (PMID:41222225). In the index trial itself, asundexian 50 mg gave >90% FXIa inhibition in post-MI patients (PMID:36030390), so engagement was adequate in-disease, but this was not shown before the trial started. Healthy-volunteer studies showed dose-dependent aPTT prolongation (PMID:39082898). OCEANIC-STROKE met a hard endpoint through the same systemic target at 50 mg (NCT05686070), so pathway is inferred_adequate. Bleeding was not increased, so the dose was not capped. The index trial was a dose-finding safety study explicitly not powered for efficacy (NCT04304534; PMID:38325992, PMID:40309219). The neutral composite (HR 1.05) therefore cannot separate a futile mechanism (F2) from an underpowered trial, so F7 is primary.

Exposure was dose-proportional and comparable across AF, stroke and MI patients (PMID:41222225). At 50 mg, the dose used in the index trial, asundexian gave >90% FXIa inhibition in acute MI patients, published in 2022 before the index trial started (PMID:36030390). Healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent aPTT prolongation (PMID:39082898). The same dose met its endpoint in OCEANIC-STROKE (NCT05686070), so engagement in plasma holds. In AF, however, it was clearly inferior to apixaban for stroke or systemic embolism (HR 3.79), even though bleeding was lower (NCT05643573, PMID:39225267). This points to FXIa inhibition at this level not protecting against cardioembolic stroke as FXa inhibition does (PMID:40309219). F2 is primary. F1a is secondary because commentary asks whether the pharmacodynamics were insufficient (PMID:38484630). No AF-specific engagement data are in the bundle.

The Phase 1 study (NCT01207323, PMID:26034219) ran 1–30 mg/kg without dose-limiting toxicity and characterized PK, so exposure is treated as adequate and dose was not limiting. However, tumor pharmacodynamic data showed target inhibition in only 25% of evaluable patients, indicating partial engagement and pathway modulation. That evidence is pan-tumor and was published after the index start. In the index trial (PMID:29506988), duligotuzumab gave no PFS or OS benefit versus cetuximab, with a trend to lower ORR and fewer rash events. Rash is an EGFR-inhibition marker, so this hints at weaker EGFR blockade. Cetuximab, on the same EGFR target, is approved in related GI cancers and was the active standard comparator, supporting F1b secondarily. No ERBB3, NRG1 or AREG biomarker relationship was found.

In the phase 1 trial (NCT01207323, PMID:26034219), PK was characterised across 1–30 mg/kg with no DLTs, so exposure was adequate and the dose was not tolerability-capped. However, tumor pharmacodynamics showed downstream EGFR/HER3 target inhibition in only 25% of evaluable patients across mixed epithelial tumors. That is partial engagement and pathway modulation, not shown specifically in SCCHN. The index trial (NCT01577173) compared duligotuzumab with cetuximab and posted no results. A sister trial in colorectal cancer (NCT01652482) showed no PFS or OS benefit over cetuximab. Because cetuximab, on the same EGFR target, is approved in related head and neck cancers, the molecule rather than the target may be at fault (F1b). Overall the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT01207323 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoints were DLTs, MTD, adverse events and anti-drug antibodies. It was not an efficacy test. It completed without DLTs and set a recommended Phase 2 dose (PMID:26034219), so the readout was not an efficacy failure of the drug. PK was sampled, but no exposure values are given in the bundle. Tumor pharmacodynamics showed target and downstream inhibition in only 25% of evaluable patients, which suggests partial engagement. Dose was not tolerability-capped (no DLTs up to 30 mg/kg). The later Phase 2 trial in colorectal cancer (NCT01652482) missed its endpoint against cetuximab. F1a is listed as secondary because engagement looked incomplete.

PMID:32898333 reports that in NCT02378389 pyrotinib was well tolerated but its efficacy was unsatisfactory in HER2+ gastric cancer. It attributes refractoriness to CCND1-CDK4/6-Rb dysregulation, shown only in preclinical models. No human engagement or pathway data exist in gastric cancer. Engagement is inferred from pyrotinib meeting efficacy endpoints in HER2+ breast cancer (NCT03588091) and HER2-mutant NSCLC (NCT02834936) through the same systemic target. Plasma exposure at 400 mg is documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:34873745, PMID:35435627). HER2 is validated in this disease: trastuzumab and trastuzumab deruxtecan are approved in gastric cancer. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). F2 is secondary. No dose limitation was reported.

In NCT02121301, SkQ1 missed both primary endpoints. Inferior corneal staining at Day 29 was 2.40 (low dose) and 2.07 (high dose) vs 2.11 on placebo, and worst-symptom scores were 2.54 and 2.52 vs 2.39. No SAEs were reported, so tolerability did not cap the dose. SkQ1 is meant to scavenge mitochondrial ROS, but none of the sources give human ocular drug levels or oxidative-stress biomarker data, so exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human data. The sponsor called the Phase 2 positive based on secondary or chamber-challenge (CAE) signals and went on to VISTA-1 and VISTA-2 (NCT03764735, NCT04206020). Nothing shows whether SkQ1 failed to engage or whether its mechanism does not matter in dry eye, so U applies. F7 (small single-center trial) is a possible secondary factor.

Adrabetadex has no protein target, so engagement here means mobilizing stored cholesterol. It was given intrathecally, straight into the CNS. In the NIH phase 1–2a trial in NPC1 patients (Ory 2017, published before the index trial started), serum and CSF 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol went up; the investigators called this marker a measure of target engagement, and a single-patient report found the same. CSF total tau fell 19% on treatment (PMID:40064165), though NfL did not (PMID:36470574). Even so, the pivotal trial NCT02534844 showed no NPC-SS difference from sham and had more serious adverse events. Mallinckrodt concluded there was no clear benefit given established risks, such as hearing loss. This fits F2. The secondary codes cover the sponsor's later claim of benefit in infantile-onset patients (F3) and its toxicity burden (F6).

The index trial NCT00903201 had a descriptive safety primary endpoint, so it was not a formal efficacy test (F9 secondary). Its publication (PMID:22995323) states that plasma SB-656933 concentrations in CF patients were lower than predicted and exceeded the IC50 for only about 4 hours at 50 mg, which makes exposure and sustained CXCR2 engagement inadequate. Sputum neutrophils and elastase showed only probabilistic trends, and lung function and symptoms did not change. Healthy-volunteer data (PMID:21426372, NCT00551811) showed CD11b inhibition and less ozone-induced neutrophilia at doses of 50 mg or more, but CF exposure fell short. The mechanism was not properly tested. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

In hypophosphatasia, at 0.8–3.2 mg/kg (bracketing the 1.6 mg/kg used in REVIVAL), the drug gave dose-proportional plasma exposure, raised circulating AP activity and produced dose-dependent falls in its substrates PPi and PLP (PMID:41378916, NCT05890794). This shows exposure and enzymatic engagement in humans, but not in AKI patients, and only after REVIVAL started. No human ATP/adenosine pathway biomarker was reported in AKI. REVIVAL stopped for futility with identical 28-day mortality (NCT04411472, PMID:38172296). The earlier phase 2 creatinine endpoint and the cardiac-surgery phase 2 also failed (NCT02182440, NCT06168799), so the mechanism appears not to drive outcome. Post hoc phenotype analyses suggest benefit confined to severe or inflammatory subgroups (PMID:38373981, PMID:42844256), hence F3 secondary.

No direct human OX2R occupancy or CSF data are in the bundle. However, seltorexant met objective polysomnography endpoints in insomnia, a brain OX2R-mediated effect, at 10–20 mg with a dose-response (NCT02464046, NCT03375203, PMID:40802194). It also met a Phase 3 MADRS endpoint in MDD (NCT04533529) and induced dose-related somnolence in healthy subjects (PMID:30182786). Central exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate, assuming comparable doses; the index dose is not stated. All of this evidence predates the index trial, but none comes from Alzheimer patients. In AD agitation/aggression, NPI-C A+A did not separate from placebo (LS diff -1.5, p≈0.3; NCT05307692). This suggests OX2R antagonism does not drive agitation as tested. The small trial (n≈88) with a numerical trend leaves underpowering (F7) as a secondary explanation.

No direct human OX2R occupancy data are in the bundle. Seltorexant met objective polysomnography efficacy endpoints in insomnia (NCT02464046; NCT03375203/PMID:40802194, dose-dependent LPS reduction at 10–20 mg). It also met a Phase 3 MDD endpoint (NCT04533529), and it induced dose-dependent somnolence in healthy subjects (PMID:30182786). These results establish central exposure, OX2R engagement and the expected sleep-promoting effect at comparable doses, so the three pillars are scored inferred_adequate. That evidence predates the index trial but was not obtained in Alzheimer's patients. In the index trial (NCT05307692), NPI-C agitation/aggression did not separate from placebo (p≈0.3). This suggests OX2R antagonism does not drive AD agitation as tested. The trial was small (n≈73 analyzed) with a large placebo response and a numerical trend favoring the drug, so underpowering (F7) also applies.

NCT00978523 was a first-in-human Phase 1 dose-escalation trial of AR-12 (OSU-03012). Its primary endpoint was safety, so it was not a true efficacy readout. The ASCO 2013 abstract reports that 35 patients were dosed at 100–3200 mg once daily and 800–1600 mg twice daily. There were no dose-limiting toxicities with once-daily dosing, but they did occur with twice-daily dosing. The abstract says PK and PD were measured in platelet-rich plasma and paired tumour biopsies, but the parts I could retrieve show no results for plasma exposure, PDK1/AKT inhibition or downstream biomarkers. I found no statement from the sponsor (Arno) on why the program stopped. No other drug on the same target is in the bundle. Engagement has no human data, so the failure cannot be explained: U.

The sponsor ended the index trial NCT03943446 because it could not recruit enough patients. Only 34 patients were randomized, and endoscopic recurrence was near-universal in every arm (92% placebo, 82% low dose, 91% high dose), so the trial could not answer the efficacy question (F7). Sibofimloc is meant to stay in the gut, and low systemic exposure is consistent with that design (exposure marked adequate). The open-label Phase 1b in 8 active-CD patients (PMID:35266174) is uncontrolled. In it, stool cytokines and calprotectin fell at 1500 mg twice daily, the dose used as the index high dose (pathway marked adequate). No human measure of FimH binding or blockade in the gut was found, so engagement is no_human_data. U applies as secondary because nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

In NCT02542787 (ECTRIMS 2018 abstract), VSN16R 400 mg twice daily did not beat placebo on the spasticity NRS (difference +0.20, p=0.34) or on any secondary endpoint. Plasma PK was taken in a small single-dose group, but nothing shows the drug reached the CNS. There is also no human measure of BKCa channel opening and no human pathway biomarker. Dose was not capped by tolerability: all patients tolerated 800 mg. The investigators point to the drug's short half-life and suggest higher doses or a slow-release formulation. That hints at too little exposure (F1a), but it was never shown. A post-hoc signal in single-dose 800 mg responders is weak. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that did not engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT02542787), VSN16R 400 mg twice daily did not reduce spasticity on the NRS versus placebo (difference +0.20, p=0.34), and the secondary endpoints were also negative. In MS patients, plasma PK matched the earlier healthy-volunteer studies. No human BK channel engagement or downstream biomarker data were found. The investigators linked the failure to dosing and exposure. They said the drug's short half-life was the problem, noted that a single 800 mg dose showed activity, and suggested higher doses or a slow-release formulation. Tolerability did not cap the dose; the drug was well tolerated. Exposure is therefore judged inadequate (F1a), but this rests on the investigators' interpretation rather than a direct measurement. Engagement remains unmeasured, so U also applies.

Exposure was shown in humans: a healthy-volunteer PK study found dose-related plasma levels at 250 and 500 mg/d (PMID:22011694). None of the sources measured ABCA1 inhibition in humans directly; the ABCA1 data come only from cells (AHA paper). Probucol lowers HDL and apoA-I in humans (PMID:10412784, cited in the AHA paper). That is a plausible downstream marker, but the AHA paper ties the HDL lowering partly to a rise in CETP, so it does not cleanly show ABCA1 engagement. The 'inferred_adequate' rating for pathway is my own judgment from that HDL lowering, not the definition given for that category. In the index trial, lipids fell but albuminuria did not (PMID:27493100). The tolerability did not cap the dose, and the investigators gave no reason for the failure. Because engagement has no human data, the result is indeterminate (U).

In the Phase 2 part of NCT04313400, topical AMTX-100 CF3 1.1% failed. The responder rate was 3.8% on drug versus 9.7% on placebo. Part 1 found no dose-limiting toxicity, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The searches found no human data on skin drug levels, importin-α (KPNA1/α5) engagement, or downstream biomarkers. Mechanism data (blocked nuclear transport of NF-κB and STAT, lower cytokines) come only from cell studies and mice (Sci Rep 2022; ACR 2023 abstract). The open-label Phase 1 reported reduced affected body-surface area, but that is a clinical observation, not evidence of target engagement. No other drug on this target exists, and no sponsor explanation for the failure was found. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Topical ASN008 (1.25–5%) showed no separation from vehicle on peak pruritus NRS at week 4, with no dose response (NCT05870865). The bundle has no human data on skin exposure, Nav1.7 engagement or a downstream itch-nerve biomarker. The Phase 1 (NCT03798561) posted no results, and efficacy and duration data come only from a mouse chloroquine model (PMID:32616515). Benzocaine, which acts on the same sodium-channel target, is listed as FDA-approved for atopic eczema. That points to the molecule rather than the target, so F1b. This rests on the bundle's listing of benzocaine, a non-selective local anesthetic, so confidence is low and U also applies. The roughly 50% vehicle response suggests a large placebo effect that limited the trial's ability to detect benefit (F7).

The index trial NCT03267511 compared two experimental KNO3 dentifrices against reference products on stain removal (MLSI). Potassium nitrate is a desensitizing agent, and stain or plaque removal reflects the formulation's abrasive and cleaning properties, not KNO3 pharmacology. So this was not an efficacy test of the drug's mechanism, and the null test-vs-reference differences (p=0.65, 0.57) say nothing about KNO3. The pillars are inferred_adequate from the desensitizing indication rather than measured: KNO3 products met endpoints in dentin hypersensitivity (NCT02226562, PMID:27777061, PMID:29178711). The program also did not stop: later Phase 3 dentifrice trials followed (NCT03296072, NCT06956599).

The index trial NCT03267511 compared two experimental potassium nitrate dentifrices with reference products on extrinsic stain (MLSI). This is a cosmetic formulation property, not a test of potassium nitrate's desensitizing action. Differences were small with narrow CIs (0.06 [-0.19,0.31]; -0.07 [-0.33,0.18]), consistent with comparable stain removal rather than a failed efficacy test of the drug. Potassium nitrate's oral desensitizing activity is shown elsewhere in the bundle: a 3% KNO3 mouthwash met its Schiff-score endpoint in dentin hypersensitivity (NCT02226562, PMID:29178711), and KNO3 dentifrices beat placebo (PMID:27777061). On that basis the pillars are inferred adequate in the oral compartment. The program also continued into Phase 3 (NCT03296072 and later trials). This index readout is therefore not an efficacy failure of the drug.

Optina is an ultra-low-dose oral danazol (0.5 or 1.0 mg/BMI) intended to strengthen the endothelial barrier. Its dosing rationale comes from in vitro permeability work, which does not count as human evidence. In NCT01821677, BCVA at week 12 was worse on danazol than on placebo (0.9 vs 2.5 letters, p=0.03). None of the sources report human evidence at these doses for retinal or plasma exposure, AR/PGR engagement, or a pathway biomarker. The sponsor called the trial positive based on post hoc subgroups (anti-VEGF non-responders, patients unable to receive injections) and a reduction in retinal thickness within those subgroups, so F3 is a secondary code. With no evidence on engagement, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT03135899, was not an efficacy test. It was a methacholine bronchial challenge in asthma, run to check whether the inhaled ENaC blocker made airways more reactive. At 1200 μg, FEV1 fell by about 0.157 L more than placebo. Drug-related adverse events rose with dose in healthy volunteers (67% at 2700–3600 μg; NCT02706925). A later paper from the sponsor's follow-up ENaC program (BI 1265162) says BI 443651 failed Phase 1 because of palatability issues, citing NCT02706925. That is a problem with this particular molecule, not with blocking ENaC. No human data on exposure at the site of action, target engagement (for example, nasal potential difference) or downstream biomarkers was found. So the program ended on molecule-specific tolerability (F6), and the index trial was not an efficacy failure (F9).

G001 is a 4% celecoxib gel (a topical COX-2 inhibitor) from Buzzz Pharmaceuticals. In NCT05007808 it did no better than vehicle on WOMAC pain (p=0.67). The protocol cites only one human study, Phase 1 Study 2019-4679 in healthy volunteers. Plasma celecoxib was about 940-fold lower than after a 200 mg oral dose. Nobody measured human synovial or joint-tissue levels, COX-2 inhibition, or prostaglandin biomarkers; the only synovial data come from dogs. Oral celecoxib, which works on the same target, is approved for OA (stated in the protocol). That points to the delivery or molecule failing rather than the target, which is F1b. Local engagement was never shown, though, so U still applies. PMID:37224227 is about an unrelated HIV vaccine that is also called G001.

The index trial NCT00938353 enrolled only 6 children, posted no results, and was terminated because of doubt about the 'possibility to discriminate the active drug from placebo'. That is a trial-design and feasibility problem, not a measured efficacy failure. GR engagement in airway tissue is inferred_adequate: inhaled BDP met efficacy endpoints in asthma, with AMP challenge, exhaled NO and FEV1 improved (NCT01343745), and in allergic rhinitis (NCT01024608, NCT00988247). These are FDA-approved uses through the same target and topical airway compartment. No engagement biomarker was measured in croup. A small study in croup (PMID:20212395) found inhaled BDP comparable to dexamethasone, so the trial simply could not answer the question. Hence F7.

In the index phase 2a trial (NCT04092582), 1800 mg IV q4w MTPS9579A missed the CompEX primary endpoint (HR 0.90, p=0.68). The phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (PMID:34581002) showed dose-dependent reduction of nasal active tryptase, and modeling predicted ~96% suppression at this dose (PMID:36755366). However, a phase 1c bronchial sampling study in asthma patients (PMID:39250147) found bronchial drug concentrations 6.8-fold lower than nasal levels, and bronchial active tryptase 119-fold higher. The authors conclude the dose was insufficient to inhibit bronchial tryptase (≈3800 mg needed), so lower-airway exposure and engagement were inadequate. The mechanism was not properly tested. Low placebo exacerbation rates were also noted (secondary F7).

drug: human umbilical cord blood derived mesenchymal stem cells
rationale: hUCB-MSCs were delivered intracerebroventricularly via Ommaya reservoir, so they reached the CSF compartment directly. CSF cytokine rises in treated AD patients show the cells were present and biologically active (PMID:35327365). The phase I trial found no dose-limiting toxicities (PMID:34521461). In the phase IIa/follow-up trials (NCT02054208, NCT03172117), MSCs reduced CSF amyloid-beta, p-tau and t-tau versus placebo, matching the proposed Aβ-clearance mechanism (PMID:30224067). Yet there was no significant clinical benefit on ADAS-Cog (PMID:41220869). Engagement is judged adequate only by treating CSF Aβ lowering as the intended effect, since a cell therapy has no defined molecular target; hence medium confidence. The biomarker evidence was published only after the index trial began. The small sample (n=36) adds an underpowering concern (F7).

In DUET-3 (NCT03752398), doses went up to 15 mg/kg with no dose-limiting toxicities and no MTD reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Plasma exposure is documented: the half-life was about 9 days, and the sarcoma protocol (NCT05879185) used a 10 mg/kg phase 2 dose. No source reports human PD-1 or ICOS receptor occupancy, signaling or a downstream biomarker change, and the investigators wrote that data were insufficient to define PD. Single-agent activity was modest: 3 partial responses in escalation, and no responses in the sarcoma trial. Both follow-on trials ended by sponsor or vendor decision with no stated reason. No source separates failure to engage from the mechanism not mattering, so U.

Edivoxetine reached the CNS: CSF levels rose with dose, and 9 mg cut CSF DHPG by 51%, a NET-inhibition biomarker (PMID:25637266; modeled CSF Imax 75%, PMID:26011686). The index trial used higher doses (12–18 mg). In MDD patients, 18 mg raised heart rate as noradrenergic mechanism predicts (NCT01263223), and monotherapy met its MADRS endpoint (NCT00795821, PMID:21511276), so engagement in this disease is supported. Tolerability did not cap dosing (PMID:26005493). Despite this, adjunctive edivoxetine to SSRIs failed in three trials (PMID:27035159), and no responsive subgroup was found (PMID:27685842). Adding NET inhibition did not benefit SSRI partial responders: the mechanism does not drive improvement in this adjunctive setting. Engagement evidence was published after the index trial started.

The Phase 1 trial in healthy volunteers (NCT02603224, MRG201-30-001) gave remlarsen by intradermal injection into incisional wounds. A single dose lowered direct miR-29b target genes, including collagens, in a dose-dependent way and raised downstream targets. Repeat dosing suppressed collagen expression and reduced normal fibroplasia compared with placebo. That counts as human local exposure, target engagement and a pathway effect, all reported in the index protocol before the index trial began. It was shown only in healthy skin, not in keloid patients. In the index trial (NCT03601052), keloids still formed in 92.9% of remlarsen-treated wounds versus 85.7% of placebo wounds. With engagement shown and no benefit, this suggests that miR-29 replacement does not prevent keloids as tested (F2). The trial was very small (n=14), so a design limit is a secondary code (F7). No source gives the sponsor's explanation.

The index trial NCT03445013 is a Phase 1 PK/PD/safety study of topical SB414 (a nitric oxide releaser) in psoriasis. Its primary outcome is plasma hMAP3 concentrations, and no results are posted. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. No primary target is recorded, and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for psoriasis. Efficacy in acne (NCT01844752, NCT02242760) and tinea pedis (PMID:30124729) reflects different, partly antimicrobial, mechanisms, so it cannot support an inferred pillar for psoriasis. If the program were read as an efficacy failure, it would be indeterminate (U). PMID:11041316 concerns an unrelated compound, SB206,553.

The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for relenopride. There are no Phase 1 results, and the index trial NCT02082457 posted no results. The only mechanistic evidence is from dogs (PMID:27418395), where 5-HT4-mediated prokinetic effects were blocked by GR113808, and animal data do not count. Tegaserod, which acts on the same target (HTR4 agonist), is FDA-approved for IBS, so HTR4 agonism is a validated mechanism in IBS-C. The failure therefore points to the molecule (exposure, dose or engagement never shown in humans) rather than the target, which gives F1b. Because no human engagement data exist, U is listed as secondary. The outcome and reason for stopping are not documented, so confidence is low.

The index Phase 2a trial (NCT03045861) was a descriptive dose-ranging proof-of-concept study, not a failed efficacy test. Its publication (PMID:31769793) reports dose-proportional exposure and HIV-1 RNA declines of up to -1.70 log10 over 10 days, with CD4 increases at doses of 50 mg or more. It calls the result a positive proof-of-concept supporting continued development. Healthy-volunteer studies (PMID:29930812) reached the targeted plasma exposure with boosting. Viral load decline in patients shows antiviral engagement and pathway effect, but this evidence came from the index trial itself. An earlier Phase 1 study (NCT02289482) was terminated under a clinical hold, yet tolerability did not cap dosing. The bundle gives no reason for stopping the program, so this is not an efficacy failure.

The index trial NCT02780713 was a healthy-volunteer formulation PK study, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). Plasma exposure was shown there and in the first-in-human study (PMID:29440181), with nonlinear PK (PMID:29921707). The MTD was not reached, so the dose was not capped. In the presurgical window study (NCT03236974, PMID:32234755), which started after the index trial, 250 mg BID gave only a 24% ER H-score reduction. PR and Ki-67 fell less than with fulvestrant, and the drug was not superior. ER degradation in disease was therefore partial (F1a). Other oral SERDs on ESR1 (elacestrant, camizestrant, imlunestrant) were approved, which points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b).

Citrulline has no protein target. It works by supplying substrate: it is converted to arginine, which feeds nitric oxide (NO) synthesis. In children on cardiopulmonary bypass, the same population as the index trial, a 150 mg/kg IV bolus plus infusion kept plasma citrulline near 80–125 µmol/L, against about 13 µmol/L on placebo (NCT01120964). It also prevented the post-bypass fall in plasma arginine and NO metabolites (Barr 2007, PMID 17662768). This was published long before the index trial began. I scored engagement as adequate on the arginine rise, but no assay showed more NO made in the lung. The dose was not capped by tolerability. Even so, the earlier Phase 3 trial missed its endpoint (NCT02891837; p=0.49) and the index trial stopped for futility. Raising this precursor pool does not appear to change ventilation outcomes after bypass, so I coded F2. F3 is a secondary code: the index trial narrowed enrollment to certain heart defects (VSD, AVSD, primum ASD), but no source blames the population for the failure.

In the index trial (NCT00806585), MK-0736 at 0.5–8 mg missed both blood-pressure endpoints, and the results showed no dose response. The earlier hypertension trial (NCT00274716, Shah 2011) also missed its primary endpoint at 7 mg/d, though it reported modest falls in LDL-C and body weight. My searches found no human data on drug levels, 11β-HSD1 inhibition (e.g., liver or fat cortisone-to-cortisol conversion) or a direct downstream biomarker for MK-0736. A review notes that MK-0736/MK-0916 raised circulating adrenal androgens, which only hints indirectly at systemic action. No other drug on this target succeeded in this disease, and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Because engagement was never shown, the bundle cannot separate a drug that did not engage from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

ALTO-100 has no recorded molecular target, and the searched sources contain no human data on exposure at the site of action, engagement or pathway biomarkers. The open-label Phase 2a index trial (NCT05117632) reported better improvement in patients selected by a cognitive biomarker. The placebo-controlled Phase 2b (NCT05712187, about 301 patients) missed its MADRS primary endpoint and all key secondary endpoints, and the earlier signal did not replicate. Commentary pointed to the biomarker-based patient selection and to the high risk of placebo-controlled MDD trials, but the sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation. Without engagement data, the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that doesn't matter in MDD, so the code is U. F3 is secondary because the biomarker-stratification approach failed.

In the index SHELTER trial (NCT00943449, PMID:26952006), HCC patients had typical resminostat PK unaffected by Child-Pugh status or sorafenib. Maximal HDAC inhibition and H4-acetylation rise matched Tmax, so exposure, engagement and pathway effect were all shown in this disease. The first-in-human study (PMID:24065624) showed 100% HDAC inhibition at ≥400 mg, but it was published in 2013, after the index trial began. Despite this, monotherapy gave only 12.5% PFS-rate at 12 weeks. The randomized Asian trial combining resminostat with sorafenib showed no TTP or OS advantage over sorafenib alone (PMID:30198057). Engagement was adequate yet there was no clinical benefit, so HDAC inhibition does not appear to drive HCC as tested. A possible benefit confined to patients with normal-to-high platelet counts (PMID:30198057, PMID:33953226) supports F3 as a secondary code.

NCT03065010 was a small Phase 1 trial of BCD-115 with endocrine therapy (6 patients). Its primary endpoints were PK and safety, and it posted no results. I found no human data on target occupancy, CDK8/19 inhibition or downstream biomarkers. The developers' later paper (PMID:35114084, PMC full text) says senexin B was well tolerated and stabilized metastases in patients, but was 'metabolically labile in humans'. They then made the more stable successor senexin C to give more sustained CDK8/19 inhibition. The paper also notes senexin B was less potent and gave less sustained inhibition than other CDK8/19 inhibitors in cells (PMID:31717492). This points to drug exposure too short or too low to test the mechanism (F1a), though no human PK numbers are given. Because engagement was never measured, the case is partly indeterminate (U). The index trial was a PK/safety study rather than an efficacy test (F9).

No direct receptor-occupancy data, but at the same 25–75 mg doses DS-8500a produced on-mechanism effects in T2DM patients. It raised first- and second-phase insulin secretion and the disposition index (PMID:29624887). It lowered 24-h glucose dose-dependently (NCT02222350, PMID:29607623) and lowered HbA1c in Japanese patients (PMID:29488152, NCT02628392). Exposure and engagement are therefore inferred adequate. The pillars rest on Japanese data, and neither direct GPR119 occupancy nor pathway effects were measured in the index population. In the US metformin add-on index trial (NCT02647320), no dose separated from placebo on HbA1c. Sitagliptin did separate, so the trial had assay sensitivity. Even in successful trials the effect was modest and below sitagliptin, so GPR119 agonism gave insufficient benefit. The failure may also reflect differences in population or background therapy (F3); the sources give no stated reason.

In NCT03760081, ASP1650 produced no responses at either 1000 or 1500 mg/m2 every 2 weeks, and the trial stopped at Simon Stage I for lack of efficacy. Mean plasma Cmax was about 1080–1300 µg/mL, and tolerability did not cap the dose (no dose-limiting toxicities). CLDN6 was expressed in 15 of 16 tumors, so the target was present. However, none of the sources measured tumour binding, occupancy, depletion of CLDN6-positive cells, or a downstream marker in humans. The investigators speculated that antibody binding alone may not be enough to kill tumor cells (a possible F2), but without engagement data the sources cannot tell a drug that failed to engage its target apart from a target that does not matter. That makes the code U. The Phase 1 ovarian trial (NCT02054351) has no posted engagement results.

Engagement was shown in patients with blood cancers enrolled in NCT02587598. In two AML patients taking 100 mg BID, PIM2 expression rose and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation fell, so the PIM pathway responded (PLOS One 2018). The clinical report (PMID:37290996) says the drug 'displayed pharmacodynamic activity'. A review says that despite this target inhibition, the drug alone showed little efficacy. Liver-enzyme rises (ALT/AST) caused dose-limiting toxicities, but the drug was described as generally well tolerated and the sources do not say tolerability capped the dose. With the target hit, the combinations still gave few responses: 2 complete responses in AML and 3 spleen responses in myelofibrosis. That points to PIM inhibition not driving these diseases (F2). The confidence is medium because the human PD data are small and semi-quantitative, and the pBAD inhibition results were not available to check. The engagement evidence came out after the trial started.

The index trial NCT02715882 is a neoadjuvant Phase 2 study whose primary outcome is safety and tolerability (adverse events, vitals, labs, ECG), classified not_efficacy. It has no stated stop reason and no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of entolimod in colorectal cancer. That points to F9. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, TLR5 engagement or pathway biomarker data. Mechanistic evidence comes only from mouse models (PMID:26831100, PMID:37731205). The transaminase elevations in a human safety study (PMID:24500662) are a toxicity finding, not engagement evidence. The pillars are therefore indeterminate (U secondary).

The 6-week, 20 mg trial missed PANSS (diff -5.46, p=0.115). Its authors attribute this to a relatively high placebo effect and the lack of dose-ranging or an active reference, and say secondary endpoints were supportive (PMID:30190165): a design problem (F7). Human PET in healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent striatal occupancy: about 27% at 10 mg and 39% at 30 mg at 3h, falling near zero to 43% at 23h (NCT02370602, PMID:27423256). So 20 mg gave only partial (~30%) peak occupancy. Animal data suggested that level was active (PMID:27725212), but that is not human evidence, hence secondary F1a. Ketamine BOLD/EEG attenuation in healthy subjects supports a pathway effect (PMID:31773211, PMID:32598478). Occupancy was never measured in patients. Doses up to 1000 mg were tolerated, so dose was not limited (PMID:27572830).

SI-613, an intra-articular diclofenac–hyaluronate conjugate, missed WOMAC pain versus placebo in a small trial (n=80; -29.9 vs -27.0, p=0.55; NCT03209362). The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, COX-inhibition or biomarker data. Synovial diclofenac levels were shown only in animals (PMID:29789008), and animal data do not count, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The bundle also shows that COX inhibition works in knee OA: oral diclofenac, other NSAIDs and coxibs are FDA-approved for it. This points to the molecule or local delivery rather than the target, which fits F1b. The large placebo response typical of intra-articular injection and the small sample suggest the trial was also underpowered to detect a difference (F7).

Colloidal oatmeal cream has no defined molecular target, and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. PMID:11867969 shows a different oatmeal extract reduced SLS irritation in healthy skin, which is not pillar evidence for this product. In NCT02120833 the oatmeal arm improved strongly from baseline (EASI p<0.0001). The trial was a small superiority test against an active barrier cream, with arms of 39 vs 12 and only 9 comparator patients evaluable for EASI. The EASI difference favored oatmeal but narrowly missed (p=0.051; CI -2.51 to 0.01) over just 3 days. This looks like an underpowered trial against an active comparator rather than a demonstrated lack of effect (F7). Since no mechanism was ever characterized, U also applies. No toxicity was seen.

Exposure was shown. In the Phase 1b study in adults with CF (NCT02141958), 300 mg/day reached the target plasma concentration of 1–2 µM. That dose went into the index trial, so dose was not limited. Engagement was not shown: no human source measured DEGS1 inhibition, such as dihydroceramide accumulation or a ceramide-ratio shift. The only human readout was a dose-related fall in the plasma AA/DHA ratio and some oxidative-stress markers. That is a broad lipid marker, not a direct DEGS1 readout, the inflammatory markers did not change significantly, and the data were unpublished. The index trial missed its ITT FEV1 endpoint; only the per-protocol analysis reached nominal significance (p=0.049), and the sponsor called the result supportive (PMID:38987119). Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F7 is a possible secondary code because the trial looks underpowered.

Plasma exposure looks adequate. In the sponsor's Phase 1b in cystic fibrosis, the PK met the dose-selection targets, and PMID:20532509 also shows systemic levels in patients. No source shows DEGS1 being engaged in humans, such as a rise in dihydroceramide. Retinol lowering happens through RBP4, so it does not show DEGS1 engagement. The CF Phase 1b reported only pharmacodynamic 'trends', and the CF Phase 2 (NCT03265288) missed its primary endpoint. In vitro work (PMID:34106748) suggests the anti-SARS-CoV-2 effect does not depend on DES1 at all. No COVID-19 biomarker data was found. In NCT04417257, Phase 2 was null (p=0.74) and Phase 3 was stopped for futility because too few aggravation events occurred, which is a power problem (F7). With no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (PMID:25537644), pilaralisib 400 mg QD reached steady-state plasma exposure similar to monotherapy studies (PMID:29593099), so exposure was adequate. Arm 1 (with trastuzumab) had no responses. Arm 2 (adding paclitaxel) had 20% partial responses, not attributable to pilaralisib. Human pharmacodynamics showed only partial PI3K pathway inhibition: about 40-80% reduction of pAKT/pS6 in solid tumors (PMID:24166903), and 'moderate inhibition' in the combination studies (PMID:25669662, PMID:28275119). None of this was in HER2+ breast cancer, and all was published after the index trial started. Other PI3K inhibitors (alpelisib, inavolisib, gedatolisib) are approved in breast cancer. This points to the molecule rather than the target: F1b, with F1a for partial engagement. Efficacy was also limited in the HR+ trial (PMID:26497877).

The index single-arm Phase 2 used 600 mg capsules or 400 mg tablets and gave ORR 6% and PFS>6mo of 11.9% (PMID:25528496). Those doses had dose-proportional PK and matched exposure across formulations (PMID:24166903, 29593099, 27169794). At the MTD, pilaralisib cut phospho-AKT, PRAS40, 4EBP1 and S6 by about 40-80% in tumor and surrogate tissues. The authors call it tolerable at PI3K-inhibiting doses (PMID:24166903). Glucose effects add pharmacodynamic support (PMID:26497877). So the mechanism was engaged, yet activity was minimal: F2. Pathway inhibition was only partial or moderate and the MTD was capped by rash, so F1a remains possible (PMID:28275119, 25669662). Response was unrelated to PI3K pathway alterations in an unselected population, suggesting F3. Engagement was not shown specifically in endometrial patients.

Palucorcel (CNTO 2476) is a cell therapy thought to work by secreting paracrine factors (RTK ligands, bridge molecules, sVEGFR1). It has no recorded molecular target, and its proposed mechanism was shown only in animal and in vitro work (PMID:26523756, 29534722). In the Phase 2b index trial (NCT02659098, PMID:32033908), the cells were delivered to the subretinal space in most patients, but no human study measured cell survival, factor secretion, RPE phagocytosis or any other pharmacodynamic marker. GA area and BCVA did not improve. The Phase 1/2a visual gains (PMID:28435054) came from an uncontrolled, fellow-eye-controlled study, and the index trial was also single-arm. Engagement has no human data, so the evidence cannot separate a mechanism that never engaged from one that does not matter. The program was discontinued.

Azoximer bromide (Polyoxidonium) is described as an immunomodulator, and no molecular target is recorded for it. In index trial NCT03840135, fever duration was 2.04 vs 2.26 days, a mean difference of -0.22 days [-0.6, 0.16]. That falls short of the -0.52-day superiority margin and the interval includes zero. The bundle has no human data on exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker in children with acute respiratory infection. The PubMed abstracts (PMID:32973775, PMID:33147763) cover its use as a vaccine adjuvant, which says nothing about engagement in this disease. No web searches were run, so this rests on the bundle alone. With no evidence on engagement, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

NCT03793712 was stopped for futility at an interim analysis. In the published report (PMID:35704951), neither 1–2 mg nor 3–4 mg/day beat placebo on BNSS or any secondary endpoint. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The Phase 1 studies (NCT02202213, the HRA-listed healthy-volunteer PK/PD study) posted no results. My searches found no human PDE10A PET occupancy, CSF exposure or downstream biomarker data for Lu AF11167; the PDE10A PET radioligand work I found is in monkeys or uses other inhibitors. No other PDE10A inhibitor has succeeded in schizophrenia, which rules out F1b. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter for negative symptoms, so the code is U. F2 is possible if engagement had been adequate.

JTR-161 is an allogeneic dental pulp stem cell product with no defined molecular target. It was given intravenously in the first-in-human phase 1/2 J-REPAIR trial (NCT04608838; protocol PMID:35613802). Teijin and JCR stopped co-development in April 2022 because the trial missed its primary endpoints. I found no human evidence of where the cells went (biodistribution or homing to the brain), no evidence of engagement, and no data on a downstream biomarker such as an inflammation or trophic-factor marker. The sponsors did not explain why it failed. No other drug on the same target is in the bundle. Because there is no engagement data, nothing separates a product that never acted from a mechanism that does not matter in stroke, so the code is U.

DS107 is oral DGLA (dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid), and no primary target is recorded. The NCT02211417 protocol says Phase 1 plasma DGLA pharmacokinetics were linear. That shows the drug was absorbed into the blood, but the actual plasma levels and any skin levels were not found. I labelled exposure inferred_adequate, but strictly that is not the rubric's meaning (no success in another disease), and this pillar is weakly supported. I found no human data on engagement or pathway effects, such as eicosanoid or cytokine changes. Plasma and interleukin samples were planned but no results were found. Three oral Phase 2 trials (NCT02211417, NCT02864498, and NCT03817190 at 2 g) and a topical trial (NCT02925793) all missed. Tolerability was fine (5 SAEs per arm), so the dose was not capped. No other drug on the same target exists. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT00843518), mibampator 3 mg given orally twice daily missed the NPI-4 agitation/aggression endpoint. Placebo improved slightly more than the drug. Exposure is adequate: in a healthy-volunteer study (PMID:16554450), the drug was measurable in CSF at 1 and 5 mg, so it reaches the brain. No human measurement shows the drug engaging the AMPA receptor (no occupancy or electrophysiology readout) or moving a downstream biomarker. The rodent EEG data do not count. The investigators (PMID:23257314) give target engagement as a possible explanation alongside caregiver and design issues, such as both arms improving. The bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U, with trial design (F7) and possible under-engagement (F1a) as secondary codes.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT04434469) posted only adverse-event outcomes across 5 escalation cohorts. It reported no human PK, sBCMA or other target-engagement or pathway data and gave no stop reason. The only engagement evidence is from cynomolgus monkeys (PMID:36127472: a ~100-fold rise in sBCMA), which does not count. That paper's model also predicted that target-mediated disposition could reduce exposure in myeloma patients. Other BCMA-directed agents (belantamab mafodotin, idecabtagene vicleucel) are FDA-approved in plasma cell myeloma, so the target can deliver benefit. With no evidence that this molecule engaged adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The bundle is thin, so U also remains possible.

Exposure: plasma AUC rose in proportion to dose up to 1900 mg in the Phase 1 trial (PMID:32222912, NCT02955420). Engagement: functional GPCR autoantibodies were neutralised in all six autoantibody-positive healthy elderly subjects at 1900 mg, mostly lasting about a month. This was published in 2020, before the index trial, but in healthy volunteers rather than long-COVID patients. No downstream pathway marker was found. The NCT05911009 readout showed no benefit over placebo on FACIT fatigue, and the company then stopped all work for lack of money. The former CEO blamed patient selection that was too broad, since inclusion criteria were widened and the autoantibody test was unreliable. He also said the endpoints were not the best ones (F7). A smaller Erlangen trial in a selected autoantibody-positive subgroup reported benefit.

Brain exposure and GABAA-α5 engagement were shown in humans. PET with [11C]Ro15-4513 confirmed maximum receptor occupancy in healthy volunteers at well-tolerated doses (PMID:33833333, PMID:27466376; imaging studies NCT01667367 and NCT02534207 predate the index trial). EEG showed functional pathway activity in healthy volunteers and in Down syndrome patients (PMID:35123401). No tolerability cap applied: 240 mg BID was well tolerated, with no clinically relevant QT effect (PMID:32572738). Engagement was not measured in schizophrenia patients. Despite this, 24 weeks at 240 mg BID did not improve the MCCB composite (p=0.79), functional measures, or any stratified subgroup, and practice effects were controlled (NCT02953639, PMID:41983730). The drug also failed in Down syndrome (NCT02024789). The evidence points to a mechanism that does not drive the cognitive deficit as tested.

The index pediatric trial NCT02484703 was stopped because the adult/adolescent CLEMATIS trial (NCT02024789) showed no efficacy, with no safety concerns. Phase 1 PET with [11C]Ro15-4513 showed maximal GABAA-α5 occupancy in humans at well-tolerated doses (PMID:33833333). NCT01667367 imaged the brain in Down syndrome subjects before the index trial. In CLEMATIS, EEG spectral changes in Down syndrome adolescents gave evidence of functional target engagement. Even so, responder rates on the primary composite were similar across arms (29% placebo, 20% low dose, 25% high dose) (PMID:35123401). Doses of up to 240 mg BID were safe, so tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:32572738). With engagement adequate and no benefit, α5 negative modulation does not appear to drive cognition in Down syndrome as tested. The index trial was not itself an efficacy readout (F9).

Human plasma exposure is documented: rapid absorption and a 15 mg maximum well-tolerated dose (PMID:22014279, PMID:19763400). ETA engagement was never measured directly in NSCLC. It is inferred adequate because zibotentan at 0.25–1.5 mg, far below the oncology doses, met a UACR endpoint through systemic ETA antagonism (NCT04724837, PMID:38961664). That evidence postdates the index trial and comes from a different tissue. Class-effect adverse events (edema, headache) also fit on-target pharmacology. Tolerability did not cap the dose below what engagement needed. The index trial showed no survival benefit (146 vs 193 days, NCT00745875). Phase 3 prostate and Phase 2 ovarian trials also failed (NCT00617669, NCT00626548, NCT00929162), suggesting ETA does not drive these tumours. The index trial was small (n=66).

Zibotentan is absorbed well into plasma (PMID:22014279, PMID:19763400). A placebo-controlled healthy-volunteer study, published in 2007 before the index trial started, showed that 10 mg and 30 mg blocked ET-1-induced forearm vasoconstriction, which is functional evidence of ETA blockade. 10 mg is the dose used in NCT00929162. Engagement was not shown in ovarian cancer patients or tumour tissue, and no tumour pathway biomarker was found. The 10 mg dose sat below the 15 mg maximum tolerated dose (PMID:19763400), so tolerability did not cap it. Even with ETA blocked, PFS was numerically worse (7.6 vs 10.0 months) and no secondary endpoint improved (PMID:23234805). The same agent also failed across Phase III prostate cancer and NSCLC trials. This fits a target that does not drive the disease as tested (F2). Confidence is medium because engagement was shown only in healthy-volunteer vasculature.

Zibotentan 10 mg plus pemetrexed showed no survival benefit in second-line non-squamous NSCLC (OS HR 1.13; median 146 vs 193 days) (NCT00745875, PMID:21153822). Human systemic exposure is documented: rapid absorption and plasma PK (PMID:22014279, PMID:19763400). The 15 mg maximum tolerated dose was above 10 mg, so the dose was not capped. No receptor occupancy was measured. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because 1.5 mg zibotentan met a UACR endpoint in CKD (NCT04724837). That evidence is later than the index trial and comes from a different tissue. Class adverse effects such as edema and headache also suggest ETA blockade. Repeated failures in prostate and ovarian cancer (NCT00617669, NCT00626548, NCT00929162) suggest ETA does not drive these tumors. The 66-patient trial was small.

AMG 986 reached high plasma exposure in humans. Doses went up to 650 mg/day with no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:35460392, NCT03318809), so exposure was adequate and the dose was not limited by tolerability. None of the sources reports human target engagement: no APJ receptor occupancy, no apelin-pathway biomarker, and no proximal signaling readout. In heart failure patients, LVEF and stroke volume rose only numerically, and the authors say no clinically meaningful pharmacodynamic effects were seen, so I rated the pathway pillar inadequate. The sponsor ended the trial without giving a reason other than ruling out safety (NCT03276728). Because engagement has no human data, nothing here separates a drug that never engaged APJ from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. A business decision (F8) is possible but not documented.

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT03116191) tested SK-1404, a V2 receptor agonist, for nocturnal polyuria and posted no results. The only other trial is a [14C] ADME/microtracer study (NCT02878096), which also posted nothing. I found no human pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic data, such as changes in urine osmolality, urine output or antidiuresis. Kyorin licensed SK-1404 in March 2018, after the Phase 2 finished, which suggests the readout was not plainly negative. Development status is now listed only as 'Pending'. No sponsor explanation for stopping was found, and no other V2 agonist is in the bundle. Engagement has no human data, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter: indeterminate.

Invimestrocel is an allogeneic cell product with no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human data on whether the cells reached the brain, engrafted or survived, and no target-engagement measure. One secondary source says inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β) fell in the earlier phase 2 MASTERS trial (NCT01436487). That suggests some systemic pathway effect, but it is reported only second-hand and is not tied to a defined target. Both MASTERS and TREASURE (NCT02961504, PMID:38227308) missed their efficacy endpoints, with no safety signal and no stated dose limit. Nothing in the bundle separates insufficient delivery or activity of the cells from a mechanism that does not matter in stroke, so the code is U.

Invimestrocel (MultiStem) is an allogeneic cell therapy with no recorded molecular target. The sources contain no human data on whether the cells reached the colon, how long they persisted there, or whether any immunomodulatory biomarker moved. In the index trial NCT01240915, the drug did no better than placebo on the modified Baron endoscopic score or the rectal bleeding subscore, and safety was similar between arms. Athersys said a single dose in refractory patients, while safe, 'was not sufficient to have a meaningful clinical effect.' That statement does not separate inadequate exposure or engagement from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease. The drug also failed in other diseases (NCT01436487, NCT02961504, NCT03807804), so no efficacy can be inferred from elsewhere. Because engagement is no_human_data, the code is U.

Invimestrocel (MultiStem) is an allogeneic cell product with no defined molecular target. TREASURE (NCT02961504; PMID:38227308) gave a single IV dose of 1.2 billion cells 18-36 h after stroke and found no difference in excellent outcome at day 90. Safety was similar between arms, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The earlier phase 2 MASTERS trial (NCT01436487) was also negative, and the sponsor then terminated the MASTERS-2 phase 3 (NCT03545607) without giving a specific reason. Neither the bundle nor my search found human evidence of the cells' biodistribution, of engagement, or of any immunomodulatory biomarker changing in stroke patients. Nothing in the evidence separates a product that failed to act from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

ATIR101 is a donor T-cell product depleted of host-alloreactive cells. It has no recorded molecular target, and the bundle has no human measure of exposure, engagement or pathway effect. The Phase 3 trial NCT02999854 was stopped for insufficient efficacy. At 24 months, GRFS (survival free of graft-versus-host disease and relapse) was 25% with ATIR101 versus 62% with post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy), and deaths were 8/16 versus 6/27. Earlier single-arm trials (NCT01794299, NCT02500550, NCT00967343) gave only descriptive data. The sponsor said it stopped because dropout in the ATIR101 arm was unexpectedly high and real-world PTCy outcomes made success unlikely. That is partly a design or comparator issue (F7). Still, nothing here separates a product that failed to work from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

ATIR101 is a donor T-cell product that has been photodepleted of host-alloreactive cells. It has no molecular target, and the bundle contains no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway effects. The sponsor gave two reasons for stopping the Phase 3 HATCY trial (NCT02999854). First, more patients than expected dropped out before receiving ATIR101. Second, new external data showed that the post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) comparator gave better survival and less severe graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) than the literature used to design the superiority trial. That makes this a trial design and feasibility failure (F7). The sponsor also made a strategic pivot to its NK-cell platform (F8). The posted results still show worse outcomes with ATIR101: GVHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) at 24 months was 25% versus 62% with PTCy, with 8/16 versus 6/27 deaths. Because there is no mechanistic data, U is listed as a secondary code.

ATIR101 is a donor T-cell product depleted of host-alloreactive cells. No molecular target is recorded, and neither the bundle nor the search turned up any human measure of exposure, engagement or pathway effect, such as persistence, immune-reconstitution markers or anti-infective T-cell function tied to a mechanism. In the HATCY Phase 3 trial (NCT02999854), GRFS was 25% with ATIR101 versus 62% with PTCy. Kiadis ended the trial after an unexpectedly high dropout rate in the ATIR101 arm and a review of real-world PTCy outcomes led it to judge that success was unlikely. That also raises comparator and execution issues (F7). The earlier single-arm studies (NCT01794299, NCT02500550) had no control arm. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell an ineffective product apart from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT01116440, n=27, with an oral contraceptive), BGS649 reduced pelvic pain less than placebo (-0.76 vs -2.17). Termination had no stated reason. No direct PK or occupancy data exist, but systemic aromatase inhibition is inferred from human pathway effects. In obese hypogonadal men, testosterone normalised in 59-63 of ~66 per dose versus 7/71 on placebo (NCT02730169; also NCT01200862). In endometriosis patients, follicle development appeared on monotherapy (NCT01190475), but only 6 were enrolled and that trial started after the index trial. Dose comparability is unclear. With engagement inferred, the lack of pain benefit points to the mechanism not driving pain as tested (F2). The tiny, terminated trial and large placebo response also implicate design (F7).

Population PK pooled 330 cancer patients, mostly mCRC, across 0.4–18 mg/kg and characterized serum exposure (PMID:31679083). The phase 1 mCRC trial (NCT01117428, PMID:25962717) confirmed marked Sym004-induced EGFR downmodulation in patients with acquired anti-EGFR resistance. Pathway and activity held there: 44% tumor shrinkage at 9–12 mg/kg, and the index trial showed a decrease in EGFR ECD-mutant ctDNA (PMID:29423521). Skin toxicity and hypomagnesemia were dose-limiting but mechanism-based, and expansion doses were taken forward. Despite engagement, OS was not improved (7.9 and 10.3 vs 9.6 months; NCT02083653). The authors blame high intrapatient genomic heterogeneity and co-occurring resistance mechanisms, with a ctDNA-defined subgroup suggested to benefit. This supports F3, with F2 secondary. The 12 mg/kg arm had worse OS and more SAEs (F5).

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: In the phase 1 mCRC trial (PMID:25962717, NCT01117428), pharmacodynamic studies confirmed marked Sym004-induced EGFR downmodulation at 9–12 mg/kg weekly. This shows tissue exposure and target engagement in humans, but in colorectal cancer, not SCCHN, and published in 2015, after the index start in 2011. Mechanism-based skin toxicity and hypomagnesemia limited escalation, but expansion doses were tolerated, and 18 mg/kg gave no DLTs (NCT01955473). No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. The index single-arm trial in anti-EGFR-refractory SCCHN (NCT01417936) gave a median PFS of only 82 days, with no comparator, suggesting EGFR re-targeting does not drive this refractory disease. The single-arm design (F7) and the refractory population (F3) limit interpretation, and the sources give no stated reason.

Inhaled nemiralisib reached the lung: BAL drug levels were 32-214-fold above plasma in healthy smokers (PMID:30886125). Engagement was only partial. Sputum PIP3 fell by at most 23-36% at 2 mg, double the 1000 µg dose used in the index asthma trial (NCT02567708). In APDS patients there was no convincing lung target engagement (PMID:36841351). Pathway markers did not move: COPD sputum cytokines showed no dose-response (NCT02130635, PMID:28823947). Engagement was never measured in asthma. FEV1 was flat in asthma and in COPD exacerbation trials (PMID:34113095, NCT03345407). With only modest, partial PI3Kδ inhibition and unchanged downstream biomarkers, the mechanism was not adequately tested, which is F1a. Dose-related cough did not clearly cap the dose.

Inhaled nemiralisib reached the lung: BAL drug levels were 32-214-fold above plasma in healthy smokers, and plasma PK was dose-proportional in the index trial (PMID:30886125, PMID:34113095). Target engagement was only partial. Sputum PIP3 fell by at most 23-36% at 2 mg in healthy smokers (PMID:30886125). In APDS patients there was no convincing lung engagement (PMID:36841351). No PIP3 data in COPD patients are in the bundle. The pathway did not move: sputum cytokines were unchanged across 100-2000 µg in stable COPD (NCT02130635). The index trial (≤750 µg) showed no FEV1 or re-exacerbation benefit at any dose (NCT03345407). Cough was dose-related but was not shown to cap the dose. The mechanism was therefore likely never fully tested.

The index trial (NCT02593539, n=5, open-label) had safety primaries, not an efficacy test. Its publication (PMID:36841351) reports no meaningful change in sputum PIP3, the direct PI3Kδ product, and no downstream lung or blood biomarker or lymphocyte changes. The authors conclude there was no convincing evidence of lung target engagement. They speculate poor lung retention, shown by higher systemic exposure, possibly from structural lung damage. Sputum PIP3 lowering had been shown only in healthy smokers (PMID:30886125, published 2019), not in APDS. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Oral leniolisib, on the same target, is approved for APDS, which points to this molecule and its inhaled delivery rather than the target (F1b). The mechanism was not properly tested (F1a).

The index trial NCT03071068 had a primary outcome of acute ocular (serious) adverse events and is classified not_efficacy. It was a safety study, not an efficacy test of THR-317, so F9 applies. No results are posted. The drug was then taken into a ranibizumab combination DME trial (NCT03499223). Human data in the bundle are systemic PK and plasma angiogenic-protein changes in cancer patients and healthy volunteers after IV dosing (PMID:21906811, 25665807, 28314990, 35833850). None show intravitreal exposure or retinal PlGF neutralization in DME, so all pillars are no_human_data in this compartment. Had the readout been treated as an efficacy failure, U would apply. Aflibercept's success is in related diseases and is not specific to PlGF.

In DME, THR-317 was given as an intravitreal injection. Nothing in the bundle measures its levels in the eye or shows it lowered free PlGF in vitreous or aqueous humour. The human pharmacology comes from intravenous cancer studies (PMID:21906811, 25665807, 28314990). These cover a different route, compartment and dose, and the plasma biomarker shifts in glioblastoma happened alongside bevacizumab. No results were posted for the index combination trial (NCT03499223), and my searches found no statement explaining why the program failed. I ran out of search calls before I could confirm the topline result. Aflibercept, which also binds PlGF, is approved for DME. That gives F1b some weight, but its benefit is mainly anti-VEGF, and here ranibizumab already blocked VEGF. Engagement has no human data, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT02866227 randomized women with BV or VVC to two TOL-463 formulations, gel versus insert. It had no placebo or active comparator, no prespecified success threshold and no significance test, so the primary endpoint was not assessable. The publication (PMID:30184181) reports descriptive BV clinical cure rates of 59% (insert) and 50% (gel), says both products were safe and well tolerated, and concludes TOL-463 is effective and recommends further studies. This was not a failed efficacy readout, so F9 applies. No primary target is recorded and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data, so all three pillars are no_human_data. U is listed as secondary for that reason.

In the index trial, NCT02079909, the 224 mg and 448 mg doses missed both co-primary endpoints (ADAS-cog p=0.39, CGIC p=0.76). The drug was tolerated at both doses, so the dose was not capped by side effects. No source shows human brain or CSF drug levels, or any measure that edonerpic bound or engaged CRMP2 (DPYSL2). The target itself is uncertain: a 2019 study (PMID:31680630) found no binding to human CRMP2, and a review calls the specific target underdefined. High-dose patients had lower CSF total tau and p-tau181 (Alzforum, PMID:31282954), but this is a nonspecific marker, not a readout of the mechanism. With no human evidence on engagement, the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter. The code is therefore U.

The index platform trial NCT03555149 (Morpheus-CRC) enrolled only 2 patients in the atezolizumab + LOAd703 arm. Both progressed (ORR 0%).
