The sponsor terminated the study for start-up and recruitment problems caused by limited resources at treating centers, so the trial could not test LOAd703's efficacy in colorectal cancer. That points to a design and execution failure (F7). The bundle contains no human data on CD40L or 4-1BBL transgene expression, target engagement, or pathway effects. Other trials (NCT02705196, NCT03225989, NCT04123470) report only descriptive safety and immune endpoints, with no stated efficacy success criterion. No other drug on the same targets is in the bundle. If the readout were treated as a true efficacy failure, the mechanistic question would remain indeterminate (U).

In the index trial (NCT03466099), intravitreal KVD001 at either dose missed the 16-week BCVA endpoint (high dose +0.8, low dose -0.3, sham -1.8 letters). KalVista also reported no effect on central subfield thickness or DRSS. Patients were anti-VEGF poor responders. I found no human data on vitreous drug levels, plasma kallikrein inhibition, or downstream markers such as bradykinin. The Phase 1 trials (NCT02193113, PMID:31810575) posted no PK/PD results that I could find. A dose cap from tolerability is not evident: the drug was well tolerated. No other plasma kallikrein inhibitor has succeeded in DME (THR-149 is at Phase 2). So nothing separates poor engagement from a target that does not drive DME. Secondary F3 because the trial selected anti-VEGF-refractory patients.

The Phase 1 trial (NCT00816361/PMID:25024259) showed dose-proportional plasma PK. It also showed full suppression of circulating IGF-I and IGF-II at doses above 5 mg/kg, with 30–45 mg/kg q3w named the optimal biologic dose. The MTD was not reached and no DLTs occurred. The index trial used 45 mg/kg q3w, so engagement was adequate and the dose was not tolerability-capped. That evidence came from mixed solid tumors and was published after the index trial started. No downstream human pathway readout was shown: IGF-1R phosphorylation and FDG-PET appear only in mice (PMID:21245093). Despite this, PFS was unchanged (HR 0.991, NCT01446159). The likely conclusion is that IGF ligand neutralization does not drive hormone-sensitive metastatic breast cancer as tested. Xentuzumab on the same targets shows no success, so F1b does not apply.

In the Phase 1 trial in advanced solid tumors (NCT00816361; PMID:25024259), exposure rose with dose, and circulating IGF-I and IGF-II were fully suppressed at doses above 5 mg/kg. That is direct engagement of a systemic ligand target. The MTD was not reached, no DLTs occurred, and 45 mg/kg Q3W was named an optimal biologic dose. The index trial used 45 mg/kg with no DLTs, so the dose was not capped. PMID:25342141 confirms linear PK. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported in humans. Engagement was not shown specifically in HR+ breast cancer and was published after the index trial started. Despite adequate ligand neutralization, PFS was unchanged (HR 0.991, p=0.86; NCT01446159). This points to IGF ligand blockade not driving benefit when added to an aromatase inhibitor.

In NCT04897594, Terns reported that TERN-201 at 10 mg for 12 weeks inhibited plasma VAP-1 by more than 98% in most patients with presumed NASH. This shows that both exposure and engagement were adequate in the program's disease. An earlier healthy-volunteer SAD/MAD study had already shown full suppression of plasma VAP-1 before the index trial (10-K). The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, exploratory serum and imaging NASH biomarkers did not change meaningfully versus placebo. No direct downstream measure of the VAP-1 pathway was reported, so the pathway pillar has no human data. Near-complete target inhibition without benefit points to the target not driving NASH (F2). Part 1 was small (20 drug vs 10 placebo) and safety-focused, so F7 is a secondary code.

The index trial NCT04552197 was a Phase 1 PK/PD and food-effect study in 36 healthy volunteers, not an efficacy test. PMID:38159266 reports dose-proportional plasma and gut tissue exposure, with mucosal concentrations 392- to 1928-fold above plasma, so exposure was adequate. JAK inhibition was confirmed in gut biopsies by reduced pSTAT-3, so engagement and the proximal pathway readout were adequate. The drug was safe and well tolerated, with no dose limitation. Engagement was shown only in healthy participants, and publication came after the index trial started. A later FAP study (NCT05014360) completed without posted results. Because the index trial was not an efficacy readout, the code is F9. The bundle gives no reason why the program stopped.

The bundle has no human data showing that SPI-1620 bound or activated ETB receptors in tumour blood vessels: no receptor or tissue measurements and no posted Phase 1 PK/PD. The planned downstream readout was tumour blood flow. In the Phase 1 trial (NCT00613691, 2011 Endothelin conference abstract), H2-15O PET found no measurable change in blood flow, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. The investigators said this may reflect technical limits of the imaging. The stroke Phase 3 success (NCT04047563) involves a different tissue compartment (brain), so engagement in tumour blood vessels cannot be inferred from it. The index trial (PMID:28632730) missed its PFS ≥5 months goal (median 2.6 months) in an unselected population, and the sources give no reason. Because engagement has no human data, failure of the drug cannot be told apart from failure of the target, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT01741155) stopped after its single-arm lead-in missed its response endpoint, before the randomized phase enrolled. The only human pharmacodynamic data come from the Phase 1 trial in carcinoma patients (NCT00613691), reported at a 2011 endothelin conference. In that study, H2-15O PET scans showed no measurable increase in tumor blood flow, which was the mechanism's intended downstream effect. The investigators suggested PET technical limits as a possible cause, so the pathway pillar is rated inadequate but uncertain. No sources report tumor-site exposure or ETB receptor engagement. The positive stroke trial (NCT04047563) acts in brain tissue, not tumor vasculature, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. With engagement lacking human data, the code is U. F1a is a possible secondary code.

The index trial NCT02001584 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study of baclofen co-administered with memantine in healthy lean and obese adults. Its endpoints were safety only, with no ataxia telangiectasia efficacy readout, so it was not an efficacy test of this drug in the program disease. Pillars are inferred adequate from baclofen's approvals in MS and spastic diplegia, which act through CNS GABA-B. Human CSF exposure is suggested by PMID:4154365. Neurophysiologic engagement (EEG gamma suppression) was shown in fragile X patients (PMID:36167501, NCT02998151), but no engagement data exist in ataxia telangiectasia. The separate AT Phase 1 trial (NCT00640003) has no posted outcome in the bundle.

RESCUE (NCT02652767) missed its primary endpoint. GS010-treated and sham-treated eyes differed by only -0.012 logMAR. REVERSE and REFLECT also failed. No source shows ND4 transgene expression, complex I rescue or any pharmacodynamic biomarker in human retina. The EMA pharmacology section covers only biodissemination and immunogenicity, and calls the clinical pharmacology data 'limited'. All evidence that the vector reaches the other eye comes from nonhuman primates (PMID:34729378), which does not count here. No other drug on this target has succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement has no human data, the code is U. The sponsor argued that bilateral improvement made the sham eye an invalid control, so the trial could not answer the question (F7). EMA found the natural-history external comparison unconvincing, and the application was withdrawn.

In the index COPD study (NCT04032535; PMID:39427187), inhaled CHF6523 reached the lung and plasma, with PK characterised. Target engagement in COPD patients was described as confirmed by a significant ~30% reduction in induced-sputum PIP3 versus placebo (p=0.001). This did not translate into an anti-inflammatory pharmacodynamic effect, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. The authors conclude that PI3Kδ is not a suitable target for COPD, which supports F2. The engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, not from earlier work. A caveat is that PIP3 fell by only ~30%, which could be read as partial engagement, so F1a is listed as secondary. No tolerability cap on the dose was reported.

The Phase 1 study (Clin Cancer Res 2011, related to NCT00597129) gave patients with advanced pancreatic cancer an 111In-labelled hPAM4 imaging dose before treatment. The scans showed normal pharmacokinetics and biodistribution (exposure adequate), and the antibody visibly reached the tumour in 12 of 21 patients. That is direct engagement evidence, in this disease, published before the index trial started in 2013. However, uptake was seen in only about 57% of patients, and the authors called planar imaging suboptimal for pancreatic tumours. So engagement may have been only partial, which is why F1a is listed as secondary. I found no downstream measure such as tumour radiation dose versus response. The DSMB stopped NCT01956812 because overall survival was not improved enough. I found no fuller explanation from the sponsor. Because the drug reached the tumour, F2 is the best-supported code, with low confidence.

LT-02 has no protein target. Its mechanism is replacing the phosphatidylcholine that is depleted in UC rectal mucus (PMID:15513358, PMID:19504612). A 2010 review, published before the index trial, states that delayed-release PC restored mucus PC in UC patients. That is the only tissue exposure/engagement evidence, and it is unquantified (PMID:20926877). No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. Early phase 2 trials looked positive, but phase 3 did not replicate them. The maintenance trial PROTECT-2 showed no difference from placebo (NCT02280629). One induction trial stopped on IDMC advice (NCT02142725), and the index trial stopped for futility (NCT02849951). With the drug delivered but no benefit, F2 fits best. The index trial enrolled only 25 patients and posted no results, so F7 is secondary. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

In the open-label phase 2a study in UDCA-incomplete-responder PBC patients (PMID:29761166, likely the index NCT01430429), NI-0801 was given at 10 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks with PK/PD sampling. The authors report clear pharmacologic responses in blood. They also state that the high production rate of CXCL10 made it difficult to reach drug levels giving sustained neutralization, which limited targetability. No liver function test improved. The dose was not tolerability-capped, as there were no drug-related SAEs. Engagement was therefore partial and not sustained, so the CXCL10 hypothesis in PBC was not adequately tested (F1a). The engagement data come from PBC patients but were published in 2018, after the index trial started in 2011.

FB-401 is a topical live biotherapeutic made of three Roseomonas mucosa strains, and no molecular target is recorded. The index extension trial NCT04936113 was stopped because the parent Phase 2 trial (NCT04504279, PMID:37579728) missed its primary endpoint. EASI-50 at week 16 was about 58% on FB-401 and about 60% on placebo, with no difference at any visit. The bundle has no human data on whether the strains colonized the skin or engraft, and no data on a downstream biomarker such as a change in the skin microbiome or inflammatory markers. Tolerability did not limit the dose. The placebo response was high, but the sources do not blame the trial design (F7 is only secondary). Without engagement data, a drug that never took hold cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U.

Epeleuton, a synthetic n-3 fatty acid derivative (15(S)-HEPE ethyl ester), has no recorded primary target. In humans, the evidence covers only exposure: the first-in-human study NCT02673593 gave a ~2 h half-life with highly variable, non-linear exposure, and NCT02941549 measured trough plasma 15(S)-HEPE. No source found shows receptor or enzyme engagement or a mechanism-specific pathway biomarker. The rationale for the index trial came from post hoc drops in TG and HbA1c in the NAFLD trial (NCT02941549), which missed its own primary endpoints. The index trial NCT04365400 was stopped for futility at interim analysis: neither TG nor HbA1c moved at 2 or 4 g. No tolerability cap was reported. With engagement unknown, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Epeleuton (15-hydroxy-EPA ethyl ester) has no recorded molecular target. No human receptor-occupancy, enzyme-inhibition or target-level data turned up in the bundle or the search. The only earlier signal was a post hoc finding in the NAFLD trial (NCT02941549/PMID:32779505): triglycerides and HbA1c fell at 2 g/day. That is a clinical efficacy signal, not evidence the drug engaged a target. The TRIAGE trial (NCT04365400) was stopped at an interim analysis for lack of efficacy. Triglycerides did not fall at either 2 g or 4 g compared with placebo, and HbA1c did not change. Tolerability was fine, so dose was not the limit. The sources give no explanation beyond lack of efficacy, so nothing shows whether the drug failed to act or the mechanism doesn't matter. Indeterminate.

Epeleuton is a synthetic 15(S)-HEPE ethyl ester (an omega-3 fatty acid derivative) and has no recorded primary target. The published report of the index trial, NCT02941549 (JAHA), measured plasma 15(S)-HEPE levels in NAFLD patients, which shows systemic exposure. It reports no human measurement of engagement of any target, such as the TGF-β receptor mechanism proposed in the patent, and no liver tissue levels. Triglycerides, HbA1c and inflammatory markers fell, but these are not a pathway readout tied to a defined target. The same triglyceride effect was not reproduced in NCT04365400, which stopped for futility. The bundle cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the first-in-human study (PMID:20145186), the maximum tolerated dose was not reached up to 20 mg/kg. Most patients at 10 mg/kg or more kept trough levels above the target concentration taken from mouse xenograft models (PMID:23771513), so plasma exposure counts as adequate and the dose was not limited by tolerability. My searches found no human data on DR5 engagement or on downstream apoptosis markers such as caspase-cleaved CK18 (M30) or caspase-8. Preclinical work shows the antibody's activity depends on cross-linking through Fc gamma receptors (PMID:28506821), and that was never confirmed in patients. No index-trial results or sponsor explanation were found, and no other DR5 drug has succeeded in NHL. With engagement unknown, the failure is indeterminate.

DWC20155 is a Daewoong code with no recorded target. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or pharmacodynamics. NCT03184415 was a Phase 3 trial of the DWC20155/DWC20156 combination against each drug alone. It used endoscopic erosion improvement at 2 weeks as its endpoint. It was terminated for lack of efficacy and posted no results. There are no other trials, no PubMed abstracts and no drugs on the same target. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter. Also, the trial tested whether the combination beat each drug alone, not DWC20155 by itself. So the failure is indeterminate.

DWC20156 is a code-named Daewoong compound with no recorded target. It was tested in combination with DWC20155 in a Phase 3 gastritis trial (NCT03184415), which was terminated for lack of efficacy and posted no results. The search turned up only healthy-volunteer pharmacokinetic and drug-interaction studies (NCT03016494, NCT02947139, NCT03005223), and none of them has published pharmacodynamic data. There is no human evidence on whether the drug engaged a target or moved any pathway marker. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the drug never engaged its target or the mechanism simply doesn't matter in gastritis, so the failure is indeterminate.

The index trial (NCT03368235) was an active-comparator test against prednisolone 20 mg, not a placebo-controlled efficacy test. Both arms improved DAS28-CRP substantially (−1.93 vs −2.40), with a difference of 0.47 (CI −0.49 to 1.43) and no clinically meaningful (>1.0) difference. The authors describe AZD9567's efficacy as similar to prednisolone, 'as anticipated' (PMID:37873558). Human PK came from the SAD/MAD trials (NCT02512575, NCT02760316). Ex vivo whole-blood TNFα inhibition, measured as a PK-PD relationship, set 40 mg AZD9567 as equipotent to 20 mg prednisolone (PMID:32501650), supporting engagement and pathway in humans. The 'not met' classification reflects a small (n=21), 14-day comparator design. The sources call for larger, longer studies, which is why F7 is listed as secondary.

No direct receptor-occupancy data, but AVPR2-mediated renal antidiuresis is established. Desmopressin met efficacy endpoints in nocturia (NCT01223937, NCT01262456, NCT01184859), enuresis (NCT01078753) and CDI (NCT01280188), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. In OAB, a 2009 proof-of-concept study (PMID:18726947) showed fewer voids and urgency episodes. Yet adding desmopressin to tolterodine in women with OAB and nocturia gave only -0.34 extra nocturnal voids (p=0.112). An engaged mechanism adding little benefit in this setting fits F2. The trial of about 50 per arm was likely underpowered for the small effects seen elsewhere (F7). Weaker responses in women (NCT02905682, PMID:23845356) suggest a population factor (F3). The sources do not state the cause.

Ridaforolimus exposure was characterised in humans (PMID:23211938). Phase 1 studies in advanced malignancies showed >90% inhibition of mTOR targets in PBMCs at all doses, plus inhibition in skin and in one tumor (PMID:18202410, PMID:22231376). It also met a PFS endpoint in endometrial cancer (NCT00739830). Engagement was not shown in breast cancer patients. In the index trial (PMID:28324268), mTOR-related stomatitis with dalotuzumab forced ridaforolimus doses down to 20 and 10 mg; PMID:25320355 had already seen DLTs at lower-than-expected doses. Toxicity stayed unacceptable at every dose, PFS did not improve over exemestane, and the combination was dropped. PMID:28681171 suggests the reduced ridaforolimus dose limited efficacy. Everolimus approval in breast cancer argues against the target being irrelevant.

VB-111 delivers a Fas-chimera transgene to angiogenic endothelium, so its target is the tumor blood vessels. In humans, the only engagement signal is transgene expression found in one aspirate from a subcutaneous metastasis in the solid-tumor Phase 1 trial (PMID:23589178), and it was not quantified. Nothing showed endothelial apoptosis or vascular disruption in ovarian cancer patients. The CD8 T-cell infiltrate seen in the Phase I/II trial (PMID:32265057) does not measure the mechanism, and CA-125 response or post-dose fever are only loose surrogates (PMID:33637348). OVAL found no difference in PFS or OS (PMID:37906726), and the glioblastoma trial GLOBE also failed (NCT02511405). The control arm did better than expected, which may have hurt the trial (F7), but nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the Phase 3 Cognite trial (NCT02547818, PMID:42920249), the combination of inhaled cromolyn and ibuprofen did not improve CDR-SB compared with either drug alone. The drug was safe and well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Exposure has human support: a Phase 1 study in healthy elderly volunteers (NCT02482324; Brazier 2017, cited by Alzforum) measured CSF levels that the sponsor judged sufficient to reduce amyloid and inflammation. That judgment rests on preclinical potency, though. No target is recorded, and no human data show target engagement, such as lower Aβ or a change in microglial markers. CSF biomarkers were collected in the trial, but no results were reported. The only lead is a non-significant numerical benefit in APOE4 non-carriers (F3 secondary). Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index AORTA trial (NCT01354184; PMID:25963302) tested CRD007, which was pemirolast, a mast cell inhibitor, rather than cromolyn. It gave 10, 25 or 40 mg or placebo for 52 weeks and found no difference in aneurysm growth. The bundle has no human evidence that pemirolast stabilized aortic-wall mast cells, lowered tryptase or histamine, or changed any downstream inflammatory or protease biomarker in AAA patients. The PK study NCT01723618 posted no results. The cromolyn PK data come from other formulations and diseases, and no tolerability cap was reported. Sources describe the result only as showing that mast cell inhibition did not slow AAA growth. That would fit F2, but because engagement is unmeasured, the failure cannot be pinned on the target rather than the molecule, so the code is U.

The index Phase 2b trial NCT03864328 (inhaled RVT-1601 for cough in IPF) was terminated with the stated reason 'COVID-19 Pandemic' and posted no results, so there was no failed efficacy readout. This is an operational termination: the trial could not answer the question (F7), and it was not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). For the pillars, PMID:32944204 shows adequate systemic exposure with the PA101 eFlow formulation, with comparable PK in patients, but not in IPF. No target is recorded and the bundle has no engagement or pathway biomarker data. The earlier Phase 2 trial NCT02412020 had shown a 31% reduction in daytime cough in IPF, which argues against a mechanistic failure.

PR022 is a topical hypochlorous acid gel with no defined molecular target. In the Phase 2 atopic dermatitis trial (NCT03351777, 122 patients), Realm reported that it showed no difference from vehicle on percent change in EASI. Human data cover only skin irritation (NCT02198963, a 106 mg/L solution in healthy skin) and antimicrobial and wound-healing effects in other settings (PMID:35578822). The bundle has no human evidence of skin penetration, effect on a target or pathway, or a biomarker change in eczema patients. Evidence of an anti-inflammatory mechanism comes only from mouse models (PMC6029395). The sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation for the failure. Because engagement has no human data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Exposure was shown in humans. In NCT05258773, SENS-401 was found in the perilymph of all 15 treated cochlear-implant patients, at levels the sponsor called consistent with a therapeutic effect. That study ran after the index trial began. No human evidence shows that SENS-401 engaged 5-HT3 receptors or calcineurin in the cochlea, and no downstream inner-ear biomarker was measured. The occupancy papers on azasetron (PMID:22993341) are model estimates for the gut in antiemetic use, not measurements in the ear. The index trial NCT03603314 found no dose-response and no difference from placebo. Investigators pointed to a post-hoc subgroup with idiopathic SSNHL treated with corticosteroids (PMID:39173396), which suggests a patient-selection explanation (F3). With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Metoprolol's beta1 blockade is well shown in humans. It produces dose-dependent heart rate reduction at plasma concentrations matching its potency (PMID:3956052, PMID:2312776, PMID:7308277). In the Tesomet T2D trial its primary endpoint was a fall in 24-h heart rate (NCT02737891). In a related setting it abolished the sibutramine-induced rise in heart rate (PMID:12417543). This pattern points to metoprolol as the cardiovascular-safety partner of tesofensine, not the weight-loss agent. The index PWS trial (NCT03149445) tested weight loss of the combination, so it was not an efficacy test of ADRB1 antagonism. The trial was also very small (n=3-6 per arm), and the adult arm missed significance with a -5.4% difference (p=0.10). Engagement was not measured in PWS patients.

The Phase 1 study (NCT03146065, PMID:34369667) shows plasma exposure in healthy volunteers that rose roughly in proportion to dose up to 1000 mg IV, with a half-life of 12–15 days. I rated exposure adequate on that basis, though no glomerular or tissue levels were reported. No human data show the drug engaging its target: no free-SLIT2 lowering and no measure of ROBO2 signalling or podocyte markers. SLIT2 trapping and lower proteinuria were shown only in vitro and in rats. The PODO trial (NCT03448692) was stopped for lack of efficacy at both doses (UPCR −12% at 1000 mg, 0% at 300 mg), not for safety, and the doses were not capped by tolerability. I could not open the interim results abstract. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged SLIT2 apart from a target that does not drive FSGS.

The index trial NCT04433494 is a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of TY-302 in advanced solid tumors and breast cancer, with tamoxifen only as a combination backbone. Its primary outcomes are MTD, RP2D and DLT of TY-302, plus exploratory response measures. It posted no results, stated no stop reason and has unknown status. It is therefore not an efficacy test of tamoxifen in osteosarcoma. The only osteosarcoma-specific trial, NCT00001436, was a completed Phase 1 with no reported outcome. ESR1 pillars are inferred adequate only from tamoxifen's FDA approval in ductal carcinoma in situ (breast) at standard dosing; this is a different disease and tissue. The bundle has no human ESR1 engagement data in osteosarcoma. The bundle shows no efficacy failure attributable to the drug.

In the HORIZON trial (NCT00920946; PMID:23108692), latrepirdine 20 mg three times daily was well tolerated, but it did not separate from placebo on MMSE (P=.39), CIBIC-plus (P=.84) or any secondary endpoint. Medivation and Pfizer then stopped Huntington development. The drug has no defined molecular target. Proposed mechanisms include mitochondrial stabilization, H1/5-HT6 blockade, AMPK activation and autophagy, and the evidence for all of them comes from animal or in vitro work. PMID:21031168 says the mitochondrial mechanism lacks a credible molecular target. No source shows human CNS exposure, occupancy or a downstream biomarker. There is no other drug on the same target to compare against, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Hemay808 is a PDE4B/D inhibitor tested in a 148-patient Phase 2 atopic dermatitis trial (NCT04352595; EASI change at Day 29). No results were posted. The only other trial is a Phase 1 safety study (NCT04100642) with no posted data, and there are no PubMed abstracts, so exposure, engagement and pathway all lack human evidence. Other PDE4 inhibitors (crisaborole, roflumilast, difamilast) are FDA-approved for atopic eczema, which validates the target in this disease. With no evidence that Hemay808 engaged PDE4 adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U is listed as secondary because engagement is unmeasured. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin and does not even document the readout.

Phase 1 in GA patients (NCT03295877, registered 2017, before the 2019 index start; PMID:34214452) showed no DLTs up to 20 mg intravitreal. It also showed a sustained pharmacodynamic effect on the HtrA1-specific substrate DKK3 (cleaved DKK3) in aqueous humor at 20 mg, the dose taken into the index trial. This is direct target engagement in the disease population. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. In the Phase 2 trial (NCT03972709; PMID:40089174), neither Q4W nor Q8W slowed GA growth versus sham, and the numerical trend went against the drug. The authors conclude HtrA1 inhibition did not slow GA progression, so F2 is primary. Intraocular inflammation (7.1%) contributed to the DMC's benefit/risk termination, likely molecule-related, hence secondary F6.

Allantoin (SD-101) has no defined molecular target. The bundle has no human data on how much drug reached wound tissue, on target engagement, or on any pathway biomarker in EB or any other disease, and no approved drug shares its mechanism. In ESSENCE (NCT02384460), 6% allantoin cream did no better than vehicle (HR 1.004). The Phase 2 trial (NCT02014376) also missed its endpoint. Amicus stopped development after the Phase 3 result. The investigators said the vehicle arm healed unexpectedly well, perhaps because the vehicle itself helped or because trial staff gave better wound care (PMID:32693833). That points to a trial-design problem (F7). Because engagement was never measured, nothing separates a drug that never acted from a mechanism that does not matter, so the primary code is U.

Exposure is shown in humans: linear PK, 84-93% SC bioavailability and a 31.5-day half-life (PMID:27129012). Target engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because 64 mg SC olokizumab met pivotal endpoints in rheumatoid arthritis through the same systemic IL-6 neutralization (NCT02760368, NCT02760407, NCT02760433). Pathway is adequate: CRP fell rapidly in volunteers (PMID:27129012), CRP suppression was modeled in RA (PMID:24941311), and an observational COVID-19 report described CRP lowering (PMID:33720587, published after the index trial started). Even so, the 64 mg dose did not beat placebo on day-15 responders (98/124 vs 87/124, p=0.073; NCT04380519). This points to IL-6 neutralization not driving the outcome as tested (F2). The high placebo response rate (about 70%) and borderline p-value suggest limited power (F7).

LFX453 topical TLR7 agonist had no effect in AK in NCT02404389. Complete clearance was 1/20 at both doses versus 1/21 on vehicle, and lesion reduction was about 33% in all arms. The in-trial imiquimod (Aldara) arm, on the same target, cleared 13/21 with 86.7% lesion reduction, and imiquimod is FDA-approved for AK. The target therefore works in this disease. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for LFX453: the phase 1 trial NCT02052687 posted no results. AE counts did not exceed Aldara and no dose cap is shown. LFX453 also failed in genital warts (NCT02482428), another imiquimod-responsive indication. Together this points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U is listed as secondary because engagement was never measured.

LFX453, a topical TLR7 agonist, missed complete clearance of external genital warts at week 14 (1/15 and 0/10 vs vehicle 0/17; NCT02482428). Imiquimod, another TLR7 agonist, is FDA-approved for HPV warts, so the target is validated in this disease. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for LFX453: the Phase 1 trial NCT02052687 posted no results and there are no abstracts. This points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). However, the Aldara (imiquimod) arm also cleared 0/16 in this small trial, so the trial itself may not have been able to detect benefit (F7). LFX453 also failed in actinic keratosis (NCT02404389). The evidence is thin.

In NCT01234402, adding icrucumab to capecitabine did not improve PFS (HR 1.48), and the icrucumab arm actually did worse. No human evidence of VEGFR-1 engagement or a downstream biomarker effect turned up. Receptor occupancy, PlGF or VEGF changes and trough levels against the preclinical threshold of 88 µg/mL (PMID:17085673) were not reported. The Phase 1 trial (NCT00782002) reported only nonlinear PK above 6 mg/kg, and the index paper says no firm conclusions could be drawn about icrucumab's PK. So the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter. Icrucumab also failed in colorectal (NCT01111604) and urothelial (NCT01282463) cancer. Toxicity was heavier on icrucumab: 51% serious AEs vs 12% on capecitabine, 34.7% stopped treatment for AEs, and capecitabine lasted 6.0 weeks vs 18.9 on the control arm. That fits F6 as a secondary code. No other anti-VEGFR-1 drug has succeeded in breast cancer.

In the index trial, NCT01111604, adding icrucumab to mFOLFOX-6 gave a shorter median PFS than chemotherapy alone (15.9 vs 18.4 weeks). Icrucumab also failed in breast cancer (NCT01234402) and urothelial cancer (NCT01282463). The Phase 1 study (NCT00782002; LoRusso, Invest New Drugs) reported only nonlinear PK above 6 mg/kg and stable disease. Neither it nor the Annals paper on the index trial reported human data on VEGFR-1 occupancy, ligand changes (PlGF/VEGF), or whether trough levels reached the preclinical 88 µg/mL threshold (PMID:17085673). The index trial registered Ctrough as an outcome, but no values were found. Approved multikinase inhibitors that also hit VEGFR-1 (regorafenib, fruquintinib) work in CRC, so F1b is possible. Still, engagement is unmeasured, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

Adding icrucumab (12 mg/kg on days 1 and 8) to docetaxel did not improve PFS in second-line urothelial carcinoma (median 1.6 vs 2.8 months, HR 0.863, P=.5053; PMID:26926681). The ramucirumab arm in the same trial did improve PFS. The icrucumab arms of the colorectal and breast trials also failed (NCT01111604, NCT01234402). The Phase 1 study (NCT00782002) looked mainly at safety and the maximum tolerated dose, and the pages I could reach report no human receptor occupancy, VEGFR-1 inhibition or biomarker data. The mouse study set a target trough of 88 µg/mL (PMID:17085673), but no accessible source says whether patients reached it. The colorectal paper only says trough levels matched other studies. No dose limit or stated reason for stopping was found. Engagement is unknown, so the result is indeterminate (U).

Plasma exposure was measured in PN patients and in HD patients, with dose-proportional PK (PMID:36680419, PMID:25885112). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because NAL ER met its primary itch endpoint in uremic pruritus at comparable doses (NCT02143648), and later in PN itself (PRISM, NCT03497975). The index trial was small (n=62), had a high placebo response (36.4%) and dropouts. Completers on 162 mg separated from placebo (66.7% vs 40%, p=0.03; PMID:34780095). PK-PD modeling showed that 81 mg BID was sub-optimal, and these data were used to select the phase 3 dose (PMID:36680419). The adequately powered phase 3 then succeeded. This points to an underpowered, noisy trial rather than a failure of the mechanism.

No direct human exposure or CB1R occupancy data are in the bundle. Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate: at comparable doses (10–50 mg; 25 mg in Phase 1b), monlunabant produced significant weight loss through peripheral CB1R inverse agonism in metabolic syndrome and obesity (PMID:37941317, NCT05891834/PMID:41038215). In the DKD trial, the UACR point estimates favoured the drug (ETR 0.72 at 25 mg) but missed significance with a wide CI. The authors state that greater-than-anticipated variability and a large placebo response (placebo UACR ratio 0.71) affect interpretation (PMID:41866124). This points to a trial unable to answer the question (F7). F2 is possible because the target may simply not drive albuminuria. No pathway biomarker was shown in DKD.

DA-9805 is a botanical extract made from three herbs. It has no defined molecular target. All the pharmacology evidence comes from cell and rodent studies (PMID:30374025, 31387167, 34775235, 35784731). Even in rats, CSF levels of its marker compounds were negligible (PMID:30127277). The bundle and the search found no human data on CSF or brain exposure, target engagement or biomarkers. In the small 12-week Phase 2a trial (NCT03189563, n=61), neither dose separated from placebo on motor MDS-UPDRS (p=0.37 and p=0.31). Serious adverse events were few and did not limit the dose. The sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Engagement is unknown, so the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter in PD. That makes the code U. The trial was also small and possibly underpowered (F7).

Hydromethylthionine missed both co-primary endpoints in the index trial at 150 and 250 mg/day (PMID:27863809). The only human data are plasma concentrations (PMID:31658058). I found no human data on brain levels, on inhibition of tau aggregation (for example tau-PET or CSF tau), or on a downstream tau biomarker. The sponsor's case in later analyses is that the 8 mg/day control arm was itself active: exposure-response plateaued at low plasma levels, and the drug's clearance is non-linear (PMID:31658058, PMID:41917677). That would make this a design problem (F7, secondary). These are post-hoc analyses by the sponsor, though, and they do not show that the target was engaged. The bundle cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged tau from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02245568 was an open-label extension whose only primary outcome was adverse-event counts. It was terminated 'for administrative reasons only', so it was not an efficacy test of LMTM in bvFTD (F9). The randomized bvFTD trial NCT01626378 posted no results. The bundle has plasma PK (PMID:41917677) but no human evidence of brain penetration or tau-aggregation engagement. Post hoc concentration-response claims on cognition and atrophy in AD (PMID:31658058) are not a proximal target or pathway measure. Randomized AD trials missed their primary endpoints (NCT01689246, NCT03446001). Any underlying efficacy failure would therefore be indeterminate, since nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant target (U secondary).

In healthy volunteers, 60 mg BID gave >90% RIPK1 target engagement over 24 h (PMID:29226626, NCT02302404, registered before the index trial). The index Phase 2a (NCT02776033) had safety primaries. It showed modest PLSS and histology gains, with TID results clouded by high placebo response (PMID:32301501). The follow-up NCT04316585 used 960 mg MR, giving troughs >10x higher. It showed near-complete blood RIPK1 engagement in psoriasis patients, reduced circulating cytokines and skin gene-expression changes indicating local exposure and pathway effect. PASI75 was still no better than placebo (PMID:38372938). The RA and UC trials were similarly null (PMID:33726834, PMID:34389633). Engagement and pathway held without clinical benefit, so RIPK1 kinase inhibition does not drive psoriasis as tested.

In the UC phase 2a trial (NCT02903966), GSK2982772 60 mg TID was well distributed into colonic tissue, with higher levels in biopsies than in plasma (PMID:34389633), so exposure was adequate. In healthy volunteers, the first-in-human study (NCT02302404, registered before the index trial) showed >90% RIPK1 target engagement over 24 h at 60–120 mg BID (PMID:29226626). However, no target engagement was reported in UC patients. In UC there were no PD, histological or clinical differences from placebo, so pathway is inadequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Near-complete engagement at much higher exposure also gave no benefit in psoriasis (PMID:38372938), and RA showed none either (PMID:33726834). Together these suggest RIPK1 inhibition does not drive disease as tested.

The RA index trial NCT02858492 (PMID:33726834) tested 60 mg BID/TID. DAS28-CRP and ACR responses matched placebo, and the drug was tolerated without a dose cap. Healthy-volunteer work (NCT02302404, PMID:29226626, before the index) showed linear plasma PK and >90% blood RIPK1 target engagement over 24h at 60 mg BID. RA-specific engagement data are not reported in the bundle. In UC at the same 60 mg TID dose, colonic tissue exposure was good but PD biomarkers did not move (PMID:34389633). At 960 mg MR in psoriasis, near-complete target engagement with tissue PD response still gave no PASI benefit (PMID:38372938). This points to RIPK1 kinase not driving disease. Secondary: the RA authors hedge on exposure level (F1a), and the trial was small and exploratory (F7).

In the index trial (NCT01230749, PMID:24798870), the drug reached the bloodstream in T2DM patients: tmax about 2 h, half-life about 8 h, with exposure rising slightly more than dose-proportionally. So systemic exposure was shown. No human data on target engagement turned up, such as CCR2 receptor occupancy, ex vivo inhibition of MCP-1-driven responses, plasma MCP-1 rising, or changes in monocyte counts. The PD study in healthy volunteers (NCT01106469) posted no results, and no sponsor statement explains the stop. The glucose effect was modest and not dose-dependent: 250 mg reached p=0.038 but 1000 mg did not. HOMA-IR was not significantly lower. Inflammatory markers were listed as outcomes, but none showing the pathway responding were found. No other CCR2 drug has succeeded in T2DM. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged CCR2 cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT01893905 (Roman-Blas 2017), missed its primary endpoint. VAS pain fell by 11.86 mm on CS+GS and by 20.57 mm on placebo, so placebo did better. The drug has no defined molecular target, and no source gives human data on joint exposure, target engagement or a mechanistic biomarker. NCT00604539 reported less cartilage volume loss on MRI, but that is a structural outcome, not proof of engagement. A published comment raised methodologic questions about the trial, and the large placebo response suggests a possible design problem (F7, secondary). The available pages do not say what those questions were. Without engagement data, a drug that never acted cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Uracyst is intravesical 2% chondroitin sulfate, meant to restore the bladder's protective GAG layer. No molecular target is recorded. In the index trial NCT00919113, 19 of 50 patients on Uracyst and 15 of 48 on placebo responded on the GRA (38.0% vs 31.3%), which was not a significant difference. The published report (Nickel 2012) says Uracyst numerically beat control on GRA, ICSI and VAS pain, but none of these differences reached significance. It calls the trial small and suggests only minor improvement. None of the sources show, in humans, that the drug reached or coated the urothelium, or that any GAG-layer or permeability marker changed. Engagement is therefore no_human_data, and the bundle cannot tell an ineffective molecule apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The small sample points to underpowering as a possible secondary cause (F7). No business or toxicity reason was given for stopping.

The index trial (NCT02276209) tested 4 and 6 mg/day. Both missed; 6 mg trended (P=0.074) (PMID:33724251). The earlier adult trial succeeded only at 8 mg/day, but 27.8% of patients on 8 mg discontinued for adverse events (PMID:25948101), which points to tolerability capping the dose. A PET study in healthy volunteers showed only partial DAT occupancy at trough after a single dose (33% at 8 mg, 49% at 16 mg) (PMID:21680689). A model of DHPG in ADHD patients showed exposure-dependent NET inhibition, but it was published in 2016, after the index trial started (PMID:26597180). The paediatric trial showed a clear dose-response (PMID:30694697). Together this suggests the doses in the index trial engaged the target too little. On-target stimulant-type adverse events (F5) and a high placebo response (F7) also contributed.

Single-agent buparlisib 100 mg qd (the MTD) gave 12-week PFS rates of only 23.3% and 20.0% in NCT01297491. Phase 1 data from a trial registered in 2008 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure at this dose. They also showed dose-dependent pharmacodynamic changes (skin pS6, FDG-PET, C-peptide, glucose), described as 'clear evidence of target inhibition' (PMID:22162589, PMID:24652201, PMID:24405565). The same dose met PFS endpoints in breast cancer (NCT01610284, NCT01633060). In NSCLC patients, 100 mg reduced tumour hypoxia (PMID:30991262), but this was a later study and target engagement was not measured directly. Adequate engagement with no clinical benefit points to PI3K not driving NSCLC as tested. One caveat: incomplete tumour pathway blockade at the tolerability-limited dose (PMID:30715997, glioblastoma) supports a secondary F1a.

BELLE-4 (NCT01572727) used buparlisib 100 mg, the MTD. At that dose the first-in-human study (PMID:22162589, 2012, before the index start) reported dose-proportional PK, which supports exposure. The same study reported dose-dependent pS6, C-peptide and FDG-PET changes, called 'clear evidence of target inhibition'; patients included breast cancer. PD inhibition was also shown in HER2+ breast cancer (PMID:24470511). The same dose met PFS endpoints with fulvestrant in HR+ breast cancer (NCT01610284, NCT01633060), so the drug can work in breast cancer. Yet adding PI3K inhibition to paclitaxel in HER2-negative disease gave no PFS benefit (HR 1.18). The mechanism was engaged but does not drive benefit in this setting (F2). The contrast with HR+ endocrine combinations and minimal TNBC activity (PMID:33138866) suggests population or context mattered (F3).

The index trial NCT01468688 was a Phase 1 dose-finding study of imatinib plus buparlisib in third-line GIST. Its primary endpoint was DLTs, and no results were posted, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Pillars held in other solid tumors. At 100 mg/d, plasma exposure was dose-proportional, and pS6, C-peptide and FDG-PET showed dose-dependent pharmacodynamic changes (PMID:22162589, PMID:24652201). Buparlisib also met its PFS endpoint in breast cancer (NCT01610284, NCT01633060). No engagement data exist in GIST patients. Development likely ended through Novartis's program-wide decision not to pursue buparlisib (NCT01633060), which is a commercial reason (secondary F8). The GIST rationale itself is preclinical only (PMID:25316817).

Buparlisib monotherapy produced 2/70 responses in advanced endometrial cancer, with no difference between PI3K-activated and non-activated tumours (NCT01289041). At the 100 mg/d MTD, phase 1 studies showed dose-proportional exposure and dose-dependent falls in skin pS6, C-peptide and FDG-PET uptake, described as clear target inhibition (PMID:22162589, PMID:24652201, PMID:24405565). The drug also met PFS endpoints in breast cancer, so engagement held there (NCT01610284, NCT01633060). This points to PI3K inhibition alone not driving endometrial cancer as tested. However, engagement was never measured in endometrial tumours, and the glioblastoma study blamed incomplete pathway blockade in tumour tissue (PMID:30715997). That leaves F1a as a plausible alternative, so confidence is medium.

In recurrent GBM, buparlisib 100 mg reached tumor tissue (tumor:plasma ratio 1.0), so exposure was adequate. But pAKT fell in only 6/14 patients, and pS6 and proliferation were unchanged. The authors attribute the lack of efficacy to incomplete PI3K pathway blockade (PMID:30715997). In the index trial (NCT01870726, PMID:31776899), buparlisib was capped at 80 mg with capmatinib. No RP2D was declared because of potential drug-drug interactions that may have caused the lack of efficacy. Phase II then tested capmatinib alone, so it was not an efficacy test of buparlisib (F9). The authors also suggest stricter molecular selection (F3). Skin pS6 changes in other cancers (PMID:22162589) do not show adequate engagement in GBM tumor. The mechanism was not properly tested.

The index trial (NCT01911325, buparlisib plus docetaxel in squamous NSCLC) stopped for marginal anti-tumor activity. At 100 mg/day, the first-in-human studies showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and dose-dependent pharmacodynamic changes (FDG-PET, C-peptide, skin pS6), described as clear evidence of target inhibition (PMID:22162589, PMID:24652201). Both were published before the index trial started. The PI3K mechanism was also clinically validated in breast cancer (NCT01610284). Single-agent buparlisib also failed in NSCLC (NCT01297491), which points to the target not driving this disease as tested (F2). Engagement was never shown in mantle cell lymphoma, the program's disease. Incomplete tumor pathway blockade in glioblastoma (PMID:30715997) leaves some possibility of inadequate tumor engagement (F1a).

The index trial (NCT01911325, buparlisib plus docetaxel in squamous NSCLC) stopped for marginal anti-tumor activity. Exposure was dose-proportional at the 100 mg MTD. Engagement and pathway effects were shown in humans before the index trial started: dose-dependent drops in skin pS6 and changes in C-peptide and FDG-PET (PMID:22162589, 24652201). The drug also met a PFS endpoint in breast cancer (NCT01610284). No engagement data exist in DLBCL itself, where single-agent ORR was 11.5% (PMID:28971900). Systemic PI3K inhibition was achieved without benefit, so F2. Incomplete tumor pathway blockade in glioblastoma (PMID:30715997) and the narrow tolerability window (NCT01820325) leave F1a as a secondary possibility.

The index trial (NCT01911325, buparlisib plus docetaxel in squamous NSCLC) stopped for marginal anti-tumor activity. At the 100 mg/d MTD, first-in-human data (PMID:22162589, PMID:24652201) show dose-proportional exposure and dose-dependent pS6, C-peptide and FDG-PET changes, described as clear target inhibition. These were published before the index start. PI3K inhibition also reduced tumour hypoxia in NSCLC (PMID:30991262), and single-agent buparlisib failed in NSCLC (NCT01297491). So the mechanism was engaged without benefit, which fits F2. The glioblastoma study reported incomplete tumour pathway blockade (PMID:30715997), and the 100 mg ceiling is tolerability-bound, so F1a is secondary. No engagement data exist in follicular lymphoma, and the program disease does not match the index trial, so confidence is low.

disease: metastatic malignant neoplasm in the brain
rationale: The index trial (NCT02000882, n=10) of buparlisib plus capecitabine in breast cancer brain metastases gave a CBR of 0.1. Buparlisib reaches the brain: tumor-to-plasma ratio was 1.0 in glioblastoma (PMID:30715997) and the drug was detected in CSF (PMID:37317993). However, at the 100 mg MTD, pAKT fell in only 42.8% of resected brain tumors and pS6 did not change significantly. The authors attribute the lack of efficacy to incomplete PI3K pathway blockade. CSF levels were also below the EC50 (PMID:37317993). Systemic pharmacodynamic effects (PMID:22162589) and the BELLE-2 PFS benefit (NCT01610284) show activity outside the CNS. Tolerability set the 100 mg MTD, so brain-tumor target engagement was inadequate. The 10-patient single-arm trial is too small to say more.

The index trial NCT03300687 is an early-phase safety study of FX-322, a valproate-containing combination, in cochlear-implant patients. Its only primary outcome was adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of valproic acid in SMA (F9). In SMA itself, the VALIANT biomarker study (PMID:27858735, published before the index trial) showed histone H4 hyperacetylation in patients, so HDAC engagement was adequate. However, SMN mRNA and protein were unchanged (pathway inadequate), consistent with negative clinical trials (PMID:21754985, PMID:28833236, PMID:19440247). Exposure is inferred from the systemic engagement seen. The bundle gives no data on the listed target, ALDH5A1. The SMA mechanism failed despite engagement, so F2 is secondary.

The index trial NCT03300687 is an early phase 1, first-in-human study of FX-322, a valproate-containing intratympanic product, in cochlear implant patients with hearing loss. Its only primary outcome was treatment-emergent adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of valproic acid in CLL or any other disease. The bundle has no human data on exposure, ALDH5A1 engagement or pathway effects relevant to CLL. The CLL pretreatment study NCT02144623 posted no results. Approvals in bipolar disorder and migraine are not tied to ALDH5A1 in the bundle, so no pillar can be inferred. The failure is therefore not an efficacy failure (F9). The mechanism itself remains untested (U).

The index trial NCT03300687 is an early-phase, first-in-human safety study of FX-322, a valproate-containing intratympanic product, in 9 adults undergoing cochlear implantation. Its only primary outcome was treatment-emergent adverse events. It neither tested efficacy nor studied acute promyelocytic leukemia, so it cannot be an efficacy failure in the program disease (F9). The bundle has no human data on exposure, ALDH5A1 engagement or a pathway effect in APL. PMID:16294345 measured HDAC2 protein in poor-risk AML, which is a different target and a different population. The bipolar and migraine approvals act in the CNS and cannot support inferred adequacy here. If the program is judged as an efficacy question at all, the mechanism remains indeterminate (U).

FX-322 is CHIR99021 (GSK3 inhibitor) plus valproate (HDAC inhibitor), given by intratympanic injection. The Phase 1b paper reports FX-322 measured in human perilymph, reaching the high-frequency region of the cochlea, so exposure was shown, but only at the cochlear base. No human data show the intended mechanism working: there is no measure of progenitor activation, HDAC or GSK3 engagement in the cochlea, or a downstream biomarker. The listed target, ALDH5A1, was never measured either. In the index trial NCT05086276 the primary and all secondary endpoints missed. The sponsor called the study rigorous and conclusive and gave no mechanistic explanation. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

FX-322 is valproic acid plus CHIR99021, given by injection through the eardrum. It missed its primary endpoint in NCT05086276: 14.7% vs 11.1% word-recognition responders, p=0.525. No secondary endpoint improved. Exposure was shown in humans: perilymph sampling in cochlear-implant patients (Phase 1b paper) found drug in the extended high-frequency region of the cochlea. No human data show the drug engaged its target, whether the listed ALDH5A1, HDAC, or Wnt/progenitor activation. No pathway biomarker or hair-cell regeneration was measured either. No other drug on the same target was available for comparison. The sponsor called the study conclusive and ended all hearing programs without saying why it failed. Because nothing separates non-engagement from a target that does not matter, the code is U.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Human pharmacology is shown in other solid-tumor cohorts. ARTISTRY-1 reported PK and PD at the RP2D (PMID:40759440). ARTISTRY-3 reported dose-proportional exposure, selective expansion of NK and CD8+ T cells with minimal Treg expansion, and tumor infiltration of NK and CD8+ T cells, which it called pharmacodynamic proof of mechanism (PMID:40990800). None of this was in HNSCC, and it was published after the index trial started. Despite this engagement, the HNSCC combination gave 0% and 16.7% ORR in 14 patients (NCT04144517). Across the program, activity was low (single-digit to low-teen ORRs; no responses in ARTISTRY-3), and the phase 3 ovarian trial showed no OS benefit (NCT05092360). Together this suggests the mechanism adds little. The index trial was small and purely descriptive (F7), and related trials ended for business reasons (F8; NCT04830124, NCT05092360).

The Phase 2 index trial NCT04110054 in refractory chronic cough missed its primary endpoint. Cough frequency fell 55–65% across the 50–300 mg arms versus 60% on placebo (p=0.93). There were no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no human PK, P2X3 engagement or pathway data and no Phase 1 results. The only mechanistic evidence is in vitro potency and rat analgesia (PMID:34587541), which does not count. No other P2X3 drug appears in the bundle to separate molecule from target. The very large placebo response suggests the trial may have been unable to detect an effect (F7 secondary), but the sources do not state this. Engagement is unknown, so the failure is indeterminate.

None of the sources I found show human P2X3 occupancy, drug levels at the site of action, or a pathway biomarker for sivopixant. The only evidence is preclinical potency (PMID:34587541) and a borderline Phase 2a cough reduction of about -31% (ERJ 2022). In the Phase 2b index trial (NCT04110054), placebo cut cough frequency by 60.4%, so no dose separated from placebo (p=0.93). A later ERJ Open review blames that large placebo response on poor patient selection, expectation bias and investigator inexperience. That points to trial-design and selection problems (F7/F3), but with no engagement data the sources cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter. Primary code is therefore U. After the readout, sivopixant was dropped from Shionogi's pipeline.

In the index OSCAR trial (NCT04376684, PMID:36229048), a single IV 90 mg dose of otilimab missed the Day 28 alive-and-free-of-respiratory-failure endpoint in both Part 1 and Part 2. Otilimab lowered serum inflammatory markers, including the pharmacodynamic biomarker CCL17, indicating GM-CSF pathway blockade in COVID-19 patients. Engagement was also measured directly in RA (GM-CSF complex ratio, NCT02799472). Exposure is inferred adequate because the drug beat placebo on ACR20 in RA phase 3 (NCT03980483) via the same systemic target. Safety was comparable to placebo, so dose was not limited. The mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, which fits F2. The nominal 70-79 subgroup signal was not confirmed in Part 2, so F3 is only a minor secondary code.

In hand OA, otilimab 180 mg did not separate from placebo on Week 6 hand pain (p=0.442; NCT02683785, PMID:38273625). The same 180 mg regimen showed strong target engagement in RA, with GM-CSF complex ratio vs placebo of 14–56, p<0.001 (NCT02799472, PMID:38279363). Pathway blockade was shown by CCL17 lowering in COVID-19 (PMID:36229048). Otilimab also met ACR20 in RA phase 3 (NCT03980483), so exposure in synovial joints is inferred adequate. Engagement was never measured in OA patients, and that evidence postdates the index start. With the mechanism engaged and no tolerability cap, the failure points to GM-CSF not driving pain in inflammatory hand OA. The small trial (n=44) adds some design uncertainty.

The index trial (contRAst 2, NCT03970837) met its primary endpoint. ACR20 at week 12 was 54.9% and 54.5% on otilimab vs 32.5% on placebo, p<0.0001, and contRAst 1 also met its endpoint (NCT03980483, PMID:37699654). The program stopped because the benefit was modest: otilimab was inferior to tofacitinib and sarilumab, and contRAst 3 missed its primary endpoint (NCT04134728, PMID:37696589). GSK judged the benefit/risk insufficient to file. Target engagement was shown in RA patients before the index trial: a GM-CSF complex ratio increase, p<0.001 (NCT02799472). Pathway blockade was shown by CCL17 lowering, though in COVID-19 (PMID:36229048). The dose was not limited by tolerability. This is not a failed efficacy readout (F9). The weak effect size also points to GM-CSF as only a modest driver of RA (F2).

Target engagement was measured directly in RA patients in NCT02799472 (registered 2016). The GM-CSF complex ratio rose 14–56 fold vs placebo (p<0.001), which supports engagement as adequate, though this was shown in RA, not COVID-19. Otilimab 90 mg also met ACR20 in an RA phase 3 (NCT03980483), so the dose is clinically active. Human PK data exist from NCT03028467. In OSCAR (NCT04376684, PMID:36229048), a single 90 mg IV dose lowered inflammatory markers, including the GM-CSF pathway biomarker CCL17, in severe COVID-19. That shows pathway blockade in the disease itself. Even so, the rate alive and free of respiratory failure at Day 28 did not differ from placebo. A nominal 70–79 years subgroup signal from Part 1 failed in the Part 2 confirmation. The mechanism was engaged and the pathway moved without benefit, so GM-CSF does not drive outcome as tested.

SBI-100 is a topical prodrug of THC that acts on CB1. In the index trial NCT06144918, neither dose lowered IOP at day 14 meaningfully more than placebo (0.5%: -1.99, 1.0%: -1.12, placebo: -0.83 mmHg). Skye then dropped the drug and its whole eye pipeline. The Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers found the prodrug in blood but no THC. It reported a 23% IOP drop only in a subgroup with higher baseline IOP. No source measured drug or THC levels in eye tissue, or CB1 engagement in the eye. The target-level human data are missing, so nothing separates poor delivery or conversion to THC in the eye (F1a) from a target that doesn't matter. Acetazolamide is listed as a same-target drug but acts on carbonic anhydrase, not CB1, so F1b does not apply. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the failure.

SBI-100 is a topical THC prodrug (a CB1 agonist) eye drop. In NCT06144918, IOP change at day 14 was -1.99 mmHg (0.5%) and -1.12 mmHg (1.0%) versus -0.83 mmHg on placebo. Neither dose was statistically significant, and the higher dose did worse, so there was no dose response. The drug was safe: there were no serious AEs and no dropouts, so tolerability did not limit the dose. Skye said only that the results missed its pre-set criteria for continuing, then dropped ophthalmology and moved its resources to metabolic programs. I found no human data on ocular drug levels, CB1 engagement or downstream biomarkers. No other CB1 agonist has succeeded in this disease. Nothing in the sources separates a drug that failed to engage CB1 from a target that does not matter for IOP, so the code is U.

Omiganan is a topical antimicrobial peptide whose intended action is on skin microbiota, chiefly S. aureus. In the index trial, both omiganan doses shifted lesional microbiota toward a non-lesional profile (PMID:32315497). Clinical gains were small and seen only at 2.5%. The follow-up twice-daily AD trial (NCT03091426, PMID:33010325) confirmed the mechanism: dysbiosis recovered, Staphylococcus abundance fell and diversity rose, with a 93.5% S. aureus reduction at 2.5%. Yet there was no clinical improvement. The authors conclude that microbiome-targeted monotherapy is not a successful strategy in mild to moderate AD. Engagement and pathway were adequate in patients, and no tolerability cap was reported, so the mechanism itself does not drive the disease. The engagement data date from the index trial onward, not before it.

Omiganan has no recorded molecular target. No source measured tissue drug levels or target engagement in humans with vulvar HSIL. The only pharmacodynamic readout in the index trial (NCT02596074; PMID:31755993; 12 patients) was high-risk HPV viral load, which did not differ between omiganan and placebo over 12 weeks, so the pathway pillar is inadequate. In genital warts (NCT02849262), low-risk HPV load did fall, but lesions did not improve there either. Dose was not capped by tolerability, because all adverse events were mild. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates poor delivery of the drug or a weak mechanism from a mechanism that is irrelevant to high-risk HPV lesions. The investigators point to the HPV-type difference (relevant to F3), and the very small trial size is relevant to F7.

Omiganan has no recorded molecular target; as a topical antimicrobial peptide its proximal action is on the pathogen. In the index AGW trial, 2.5% gel once daily reduced HPV load by 96.6% versus placebo (P=.045), which counts as engagement in this disease. Lesion count, size and patient-reported outcomes did not differ (PMID:31755993, NCT02849262), and the uVIN sister trial showed nothing (NCT02596074). Exposure at the skin is inferred: drug was applied directly, and a topical rosacea Phase 3 met its endpoint (NCT02547441). A similar pattern in atopic dermatitis, where the microbial target was lowered without clinical gain (PMID:33010325), supports F2: pathogen reduction does not drive lesion clearance. The trial was very small (n=24), and engagement data were published after the index trial started, so confidence is low.

Omiganan has no recorded molecular target. In humans its antimicrobial activity is shown on healthy skin (NCT00608959, -1.91 log10 CFU) and in atopic dermatitis, where it reduced S. aureus and corrected dysbiosis (PMID:33010325, PMID:32315497). No engagement or pathway data exist in rosacea. The parallel, identically designed Phase 3 rosacea trial NCT02547441 met both primary endpoints (lesions -18.1 vs -13.5; IGA 26.3% vs 16.9%), so exposure and engagement are inferred adequate at this dose. The index trial NCT02576860 failed mainly because vehicle response was much higher (-20.9 lesions vs -13.5 in the twin trial), which points to trial variability (F7). The effect size is modest even where positive, so a weak mechanism (F2) may also contribute. No source states why the program stopped.

Omiganan has no recorded molecular target; its intended action is antimicrobial and antifungal. In the index facial seborrheic dermatitis trial (NCT03688971, PMID:37762625), omiganan 1.75% BID was well tolerated but did not improve disease or move any biomarker versus placebo. The authors state its antimicrobial and antifungal properties could not be demonstrated, so the microbial engagement and pathway pillars were measured and inadequate. Ketoconazole, the active comparator, lowered Malassezia, improved barrier function and reduced severity, which supports the anti-Malassezia mechanism; this suggests a molecule failure (secondary F1b by analogy, not the same molecular target). Staphylococcus reduction was shown only in atopic dermatitis (PMID:33010325), not in this disease. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Skin exposure was not reported.

In the index VIDI trial (NCT02302079, PMID:31388454), oral ASP8232 40 mg gave near-complete inhibition of plasma VAP-1 activity in DME patients, confirmed by pooled PK/PD modelling (PMID:32930923). Yet excess CST worsened 11.4% versus -75% with ranibizumab, and adding ASP8232 to ranibizumab gave no extra benefit. The same dose reduced albuminuria in diabetic CKD (NCT02358096), so the drug was pharmacologically active, and no dose limitation is reported. No retinal pathway biomarker was measured in DME. Engagement in this disease came from the index trial itself, so it was not available before the trial started. Engagement was adequate but there was no benefit, so systemic VAP-1 inhibition does not appear to drive macular edema.

The index trial NCT03345485 was a completed single-arm Phase 1/2 study. Its primary outcomes were descriptive: treatment-related AEs, clinical benefit rate and QTcF change, with no prespecified success threshold. It is classified as not an efficacy test, and its clinical benefit rates were 40% in soft tissue sarcoma and 50% in ovarian cancer. The readout therefore does not show an efficacy failure (F9). The bundle has no human PK, HDAC engagement or pathway data, so a failure could not be attributed to the mechanism anyway (U). Notable toxicity appears: mean QTcF increase of 53 ms, frequent serious AEs and deaths. A related myeloma conditioning trial (NCT03687125) was terminated because AEs limited dosing, hinting at molecule-specific toxicity (F6).

In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT04829214), intratympanic OTO-313 failed: 20/77 TFI responders on drug vs 27/76 on placebo (p=0.385). The sources include no human data on drug levels in the cochlea or inner-ear fluid, NMDA receptor occupancy, or any downstream biomarker. The earlier trial (NCT03918109) measured only plasma PK and safety, and plasma is not the site of action. The positive signals come only from animal studies and a small post-hoc subgroup analysis (PMID:34629442). No other drug on this target has succeeded in tinnitus. The investigators partly blamed an unexpectedly high placebo response (PMID:37341760), which makes F7 (trial design) a secondary code. Because nothing shows whether the drug engaged its target, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In NCT05200936, adults with ADHD took LSD 20 µg twice weekly. The JAMA Psychiatry report found plasma PK in line with earlier studies, so exposure was adequate. LSD also produced substantial acute subjective effects versus placebo, a functional psychedelic response; I treat this as the pathway pillar, although the report does not explicitly link those effects to 5-HT2A. No human measure of 5-HT2A occupancy or engagement was found. The GAD success (NCT05407064, PMID:40906494) used single doses of 100–200 µg, while 25–50 µg failed there, so engagement cannot be inferred at 20 µg. Both arms improved a lot (placebo response), and the investigators speculated that other doses or schedules might work. Because engagement has no human data, the code is U; F2 and F7 also apply.

In TOFU (NCT04200248), umedaptanib alone lost 6.1 letters and umedaptanib plus aflibercept lost 1.6, while aflibercept alone gained 2.4. None of the sources report human vitreous or plasma drug levels, FGF2 neutralisation or lowering, or an FGF2-pathway biomarker. The only pharmacokinetic data come from rabbits (PMID:31454678). In the 9-patient Phase 1 SUSHI study (PMID:38040965), central retinal thickness (CST) improved after a single injection. That is a nonspecific clinical sign, not proof the drug engaged FGF2. Tolerability did not limit the dose. The only other anti-FGF2 drug listed, RC28-E, has not been shown to be approved or to have met a pivotal endpoint, so F1b does not apply. The sponsor gave no failure reason and still claims proof of concept (PMID:38036609). With no human engagement data, I cannot tell a drug that never engaged FGF2 from a target that does not matter here.

In healthy volunteers, plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose from 8 to 18 mg, and those doses were tolerated (PMID:32573956). No human study measured whether the drug blocked the noradrenaline transporter (SLC6A2). In the pathway study, a single 18 mg dose in 16 women with stress incontinence did not significantly change maximal urethral closure pressure versus placebo (P=0.80); the proximal urethral change was also not significant (PMC7902327). The index trial (NCT02906683) tested lower doses, 3 and 6 mg, and missed its primary endpoint. A later phase 2 trial (NCT04512053), presumably at a higher dose, met its primary endpoint. That hints the index doses were too low (F1a), but without engagement data the cause cannot be pinned down, so the code is U.

The index TNBC trial (NCT03674242) was terminated by sponsor decision after enrolling only 27 patients. No results were posted, so it never produced an efficacy readout that could answer the question. Exposure was shown in ALL: plasma asparaginase activity stayed above 100 U/L for 18.9 vs 8.5 days and met its primary endpoint (NCT01518517), with prolonged half-life (PMID:35847505). Engagement (asparagine depletion) is inferred from responses in ALL (NCT01523782), not from TNBC patients. Termination came alongside the failed pancreatic phase 3 (NCT03665441), which suggests a portfolio or business decision (F8), but the bundle does not state this. Target irrelevance in solid tumours (F2) is also possible. Confidence is low.

Eryaspase is L-asparaginase encapsulated in red cells. In ALL, the Phase 3 NCT01518517 met its primary endpoint: plasma asparaginase activity stayed above 100 U/L for 18.9 vs 8.5 days. PMID:35847505 reports a prolonged in vivo half-life. Both support exposure and enzyme engagement in humans before the index trial, though not in pancreatic cancer. Asparagine depletion or a downstream tumour effect is not reported in the bundle. In pancreatic cancer, Phase 2 NCT02195180 missed its co-primary endpoints in the low-ASNS subgroup, with benefit only in the whole population, and tolerability was good. The Phase 3 NCT03665441 then missed OS (7.5 vs 6.7 months). With the enzyme active and not dose-limited, the most direct reading is that asparagine depletion does not drive outcome in second-line pancreatic cancer (F2). Patient selection by ASNS level is a possible contributor (F3).

Eryaspase is RBC-encapsulated L-asparaginase that depletes asparagine. In relapsed ALL, phase 3 NCT01518517 met its endpoint of sustained asparaginase activity above 100 U/L (18.9 vs 8.5 days), classified as target engagement. PMID:35847505 confirms a prolonged half-life in humans. Exposure and enzymatic activity, the accepted engagement surrogate, are therefore adequate at comparable doses. However, this was shown only in ALL, not AML, and asparagine depletion itself and downstream effects were not reported. In AML (NCT01810705), median OS was 4.8 months with GRASPA vs 6.4 months with control, with no benefit. With adequate activity and no clinical effect, this suggests asparagine depletion does not drive AML as tested (F2). Engagement in AML is unmeasured, so U remains plausible.

TU-100 (daikenchuto) is a multi-herbal Kampo extract, and no primary target is recorded, so target engagement cannot be judged; no searches were run. Exposure: after 15 g, the same as the index trial's top daily dose, healthy volunteers had herb constituents (hydroxy-α-sanshool, [6]-shogaol, ginsenoside Rb1) in plasma (PMID:20689019). Pathway: single 7.5 g doses in healthy volunteers raised plasma motilin, CGRP, substance P, VIP and 5-HT (PMID:10549871, 15516741, 10726893). At 7.5 g/day it sped emptying of the ascending colon (PMID:20378829). None of this was measured in constipated patients. In the index trial (NCT01139216), transit, rectal compliance and sensation did not change, and the investigators said the drug's mechanisms remain unclear. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease, so the code is U.

I did not run a web search; this judgement uses only the bundle. TU-100 is a multi-herb Kampo extract with no recorded molecular target, so no source can show target engagement. Exposure: at the index dose of 15 g/day, herb constituents (hydroxy-α-sanshool, [6]-shogaol, ginsenoside Rb1) were found in plasma in healthy volunteers (PMID:20689019). Pathway: in healthy volunteers, gut peptides rose (motilin, CGRP, substance P, 5-HT, VIP) and ascending colon emptying sped up at 7.5 g/day (PMID:20378829). In patients, though, the proximal measures did not move: rectal sensation and compliance were unchanged in IBS (index trial, PMID:26486374), and transit, compliance and sensation were unchanged in functional constipation (PMID:23451764). With no target, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter in IBS, so the code is U. F2 is a possible secondary code.

TU-100 (daikenchuto) is a multi-herb Kampo extract with no recorded molecular target, so target engagement cannot be judged. Its marker compounds, such as hydroxy-α-sanshool and [6]-shogaol, appear in human plasma after a 15 g dose (PMID:20689019), so exposure is shown. In healthy volunteers it raised plasma motilin, CGRP and substance P levels (PMID:10549871, PMID:15516741, PMID:10726893). The functional evidence on gut transit is mixed: ascending-colon emptying sped up in healthy volunteers (PMID:20378829), but there was no effect on transit or rectal sensation in patients with constipation or IBS (PMID:23451764, PMID:26486374). The index ERAS trial (NCT04742907) failed at both 7.5 and 15 g/day, and an earlier colectomy trial (NCT02232893) also failed. No source gives the sponsor's reason. With engagement undefined and unmeasured, it is impossible to tell whether the drug never engaged a target or the mechanism simply does not drive postoperative recovery, so the code is U.

No source I found measured direct SREBP engagement in humans, such as suppression of SREBP target genes. PK was collected in the Phase 1 trial (NCT02374047), but no exposure values were reported. In healthy volunteers, median LDL-C fell by up to 20% (10-K). In the index trial (NCT02608697), patients on atorvastatin 40 mg received 250–400 mg once or twice daily, all well tolerated. LDL-C fell by at most 7.1% vs 4.5% on placebo, and TG and non-HDL-C did not change. So the downstream pathway did not move in this disease. The CEO linked the loss of effect to the population, patients already on high-intensity statins (secondary F3). With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage SREBP from SREBP inhibition not adding to statins. Coded U.

Radium-223 has no protein target; it acts by bone uptake at osteoblastic sites. It met an overall survival endpoint in bone-metastatic CRPC at the same 50–55 kBq/kg dose (NCT00699751), so bone exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. The dose-finding study (PMID:23000088) showed dose-dependent bone-ALP declines, an adequate pathway effect. All of this was published before the index trial started. In HR+ bone-predominant breast cancer, the index trial (NCT02258451) missed SSE-FS (HR 0.891, p=0.48) without dose-limiting toxicity. The sister trial NCT02258464 also missed (HR 0.745, terminated for slow recruitment). Breast-specific engagement data are limited to small or uncontrolled reports (PMID:31849202, PMID:25243101). The mechanism seems not to drive benefit in this setting (F2). Heterogeneity of breast bone metastases is plausible as a contributor (F3) but is not stated by the sources.

The index trial NCT01796171 was a single-arm Phase 1/2 dose-finding and response study. Its primary outcomes are classified not_efficacy and not assessable: participant counts with no prespecified threshold or comparator. It did not cleanly fail. Follicular lymphoma patients showed responses (40/15 arm: 7 CR and 5 PR of 18; 100/20 arm: 2 CR and 6 PR of 9). No stated stop reason is given. The bundle has no human dosimetry, CD37 binding or pathway data, and no PubMed abstracts. Phase 1 trials (NCT02658968, NCT03806179) report only DLTs and AEs, and no dose cap below an engagement level is shown. Because the readout was not an efficacy failure, F9 fits best. The reason the program stopped is indeterminate (U).

Adrulipase, a recombinant lipase given as replacement therapy, gave a coefficient of fat absorption (CFA) of 55.6% versus 86.2% for porcine PERT in the index trial (NCT03746483). Pancrelipase, acting on the same lipase-replacement mechanism, is FDA-approved for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. That shows the target is valid and points to this molecule. The bundle has no human data on intraduodenal lipase activity, exposure or engagement. The sponsor's follow-up trials used enteric capsules (NCT04375878) and then enteric microgranules (NCT05719311). This suggests delivery or stability was suspected, but the bundle does not state it. Dose escalation in OPTION 2 did not close the gap: CFA was 66% at 2240 mg/day and 52.8% at 4480 mg/day, against 83–89% for PERT. No dose-limiting toxicity was seen. This fits F1b, with U as a secondary code because engagement was never measured.

Adrulipase is a recombinant lipase replacement. In the index trial NCT03746483 its coefficient of fat absorption was 55.6% versus 86.2% for porcine PERT (pancrelipase) in the same CF population. The same replacement mechanism therefore works with another molecule, and the shortfall points to this molecule, not the target.
