OPTION 2 (NCT04375878) used enteric capsules and was still markedly inferior to PERT; the higher dose gave a lower CFA (52.8% vs 66%). A later microgranule formulation (NCT05719311) suggests delivery or stability was suspected, but the bundle has no human data on intraluminal lipase activity, exposure or engagement. Dosing was not limited by tolerability; there were no serious AEs. F1b is the best fit.

The index trial NCT02433158 is a safety OLE. It was terminated because the parent Phase 3 NCT02187003 failed (HR 0.97 for readiness for discharge). Exposure in SCD patients was well characterized and matched Phase 2 target concentrations (PMID:33993463, PMID:29115052). No selectin occupancy or binding was measured in humans. Phase 1 in stable SCD showed transient falls in sE-/sP-selectin and leukocyte activation markers at some time points (PMID:24988449), which counts as limited pathway evidence. Crizanlizumab, on the same target (P-selectin), is FDA-approved in SCD. Rivipansel's P-selectin affinity is weak (PMID:38728868), so the molecule rather than the target may have failed. Without engagement data, the case remains partly indeterminate.

The index trial NCT03202979 (PMID:32936427) tested very low trazodone doses (30–60 mg/day) added to gabapentin, with no separation from placebo. Plasma exposure is documented in humans (PMID:6688260). Engagement evidence is only a PBPK-modelled brain receptor occupancy in healthy subjects (PMID:35233913), which is not a measurement. Antidepressant-equivalent dosing is about 400 mg/day (PMID:25911132), so the depression approval cannot infer engagement at these doses, especially SERT inhibition. Duloxetine, which shares the SLC6A4 target, is approved for diabetic neuropathy, so the target is validated and this molecule and dose were not shown to engage it. The follow-up fixed-dose trial (NCT03749642, PMID:38914876) also failed. The large placebo/gabapentin background response (-2.5) may have limited sensitivity.

In NCT06383819 (PMID:42261259), bovhyaluronidase azoximer missed its primary endpoint, change in ppFVC at Day 71 (+0.30%, p=0.817). FVC recovered by about 10% in both arms, which suggests spontaneous recovery. I found no human data on drug exposure in lung or plasma, on hyaluronic acid breakdown or lowering, or on any downstream biomarker. The study did not measure hyaluronic acid. The investigators blamed the 71-day treatment period and Day-71 timing of the primary endpoint and pointed to responsive subgroups (earlier virus variants, women, people over 60). Those points support F4 and F3 only as secondary codes, because no proximal effect was shown. Engagement has no human data, so nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here. The code is therefore U.

Bovhyaluronidase azoximer is a hyaluronidase that breaks down hyaluronan. In the index trial in post-COVID lung sequelae (NCT06383819; PMID:42261259), the primary endpoint, change in ppFVC at Day 71, was not met (+0.30%, p=0.817). Two secondary endpoints, exertional desaturation and dyspnea, did improve. My searches found no human data on lung tissue exposure, hyaluronan reduction, or any downstream biomarker. The only hyaluronan-lowering data were from rodent bleomycin models, which do not count. The sponsor's press release attributes the miss to the population: FVC improved only in subgroups (patients with cardiovascular comorbidities and those infected with earlier SARS-CoV-2 variants), which supports F3 as a secondary code. Since engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the primary code is U.

The index Phase 3 trial (NCT06383819, PMID:42261259) missed its primary endpoint: change in percent predicted FVC at Day 71 was +0.30% (p=0.817). No source I found measured the drug's effect on its target in humans. Nobody reported lung or blood drug levels, hyaluronic acid (HA) breakdown, or HA biomarkers in patients. The only evidence that the drug acts on HA comes from mouse bleomycin-fibrosis studies, which do not count here. The investigators blamed a mixed patient population and suggested the 71-day course and Day 71 readout were too short. They pointed to signals in subgroups and at Day 180 (supports F3/F7). But those signals came after the fact, and there is no proof the drug engaged its target. So nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, which makes this U.

The index trial (NCT03899324, PMID:38291616) gave 1.75–3 mg/day bumetanide and missed its primary endpoint, the OFF-state MDS-UPDRS III score. No human data show striatal NKCC1 occupancy or a pathway biomarker. The trial paper itself notes bumetanide's poor brain penetration, and pharmacology reviews report brain:plasma levels below 1%, too low to inhibit NKCC1, though those measurements are mostly from animals. Bumetanide was poorly tolerated in people with PD: side effects caused withdrawals and worse MDS-UPDRS IB scores. The investigators suggested future NKCC1 drugs with better brain penetration or better tolerability. So the mechanism was probably not properly tested (F1a). Because direct human CNS data are missing, U also partly applies.

Sevuparin (18 mg/kg/day IV) did not shorten acute VOC versus placebo (HR 0.89, p=0.55; NCT02515838, PMID:33894169). The bundle has no human P-selectin engagement data and no posted PK. Selectin binding and anti-adhesion were shown only in vitro and in mice (PMID:27549988, PMID:29767405). The 2024 healthy-volunteer hepcidin suppression (PMID:39619244) acts through BMP/SMAD, not SELP, and postdates the index trial. Crizanlizumab, which targets P-selectin, is FDA-approved in sickle cell disease. Without engagement evidence for sevuparin, this points to a molecule problem (F1b). The fit is weak because crizanlizumab's benefit was in VOC prevention, not acute treatment, so the case stays largely indeterminate (U).

The index trial used 380 U/kg/d IV for 14 days. PK at this dose was characterized in DIC patients (PMID:28229162), and modeling places 0.06 mg/kg within the therapeutic range (PMID:27140801). Protein C pathway activation was shown in healthy volunteers, with prothrombinase inhibition of 44-61% to >80% (PMID:9650544, PMID:15456485). Antithrombotic clinical efficacy was shown in hip replacement (PMID:15869592). All of this was published before 2016, but none of it was measured in AE-IPF patients. Despite this pharmacology, 90-day survival was numerically worse on drug (72.5% vs 89.2%, P=0.086) and bleeding was higher (23.8% vs 10.5%) (PMID:31917621). This supports the anticoagulant mechanism not driving AE-IPF outcomes. On-target bleeding may have offset any benefit (F5).

In the Phase 1 study NCT04544813, healthy volunteers received subcutaneous bermekimab, and skin biopsies were then tested ex vivo for their response to injury. The biopsies showed dose-dependent suppression of IL-1α-driven inflammation (IL-6 and IL-8 proteins, plus transcripts), with maximal inhibition above 400 mg (PMID:39214920). That supports drug reaching the skin, functional blockade of IL-1α, and a pathway effect at doses comparable to GENESIS's 700 mg qw. The evidence comes from healthy volunteers, not AD patients, and engagement was read out functionally rather than by measuring free IL-1α. Even so, both GENESIS (NCT04791319) and Study 2 (NCT04021862) failed to separate from placebo, while dupilumab clearly worked in the same trial. The tolerability profile was clean. This points to IL-1α not driving AD as tested (F2). No other IL-1α drug has succeeded in AD.

In NCT01270945 (PMID:26433546), a small open-label phase 2 trial in 43 patients, Xilonix did not reduce 12-month restenosis (24% vs 27%) or MACE (43% vs 36%). The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not the limit. Plasma exposure is supported only weakly: pharmacokinetic studies in type 2 diabetes (NCT01427699) and cancer (PMID:24746841) are known, but no exposure values were retrieved. No source measured free IL-1α neutralization or occupancy in humans, so engagement is no_human_data. A cited IL-6 drop came from cancer patients, not arterial wall tissue, and was too indirect to count as pathway evidence. No vessel-wall biomarker was measured in PAD. Nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U. The trial's small size and its 3-month IV-period trend point to F7 as secondary.

The index phase 3 (NCT01767857) hit futility on overall survival (5.6 vs 5.4 months, p=0.613). The bundle has no direct human measure of IL-1α neutralization; PMID:24746841 gives only a title. A later phase 3 in the same refractory colorectal population (NCT02138422, PMID:28094194), at 7.5 mg/kg q2w, met a composite lean-body-mass and symptom endpoint (33% vs 19%, p=0.0045). That implies exposure, engagement and pathway held in this disease, so all three are inferred_adequate. The sponsor moved to 'a new primary endpoint', which points to OS being the wrong endpoint for an anti-cachexia mechanism (F4). An IL-1Ra-defined responder subgroup (PMID:30723583) supports F3. That evidence came after the index trial started, and the index dose is unstated.

The index trial (NCT04988308) failed outright: HiSCR50 was 37.1% on both bermekimab and placebo. Adalimumab reached 57.1%, so the trial could detect a working drug. The drug reached the blood: mean trough serum bermekimab was about 64 µg/ml (PMID:40865678). In a phase 1 ex vivo assay on skin from dosed healthy volunteers, 800 mg reduced injury-induced inflammation more than 200 or 400 mg (PMID:39214920, NCT04544813). A small HS study saw IL-8 fall (PMID:29129600). No source measured IL-1α binding or neutralization in humans, in skin or in HS patients, and the investigators give no mechanistic reason for the failure. Lutikizumab has not yet succeeded in HS, so F1b does not apply. Engagement has no human data, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01270945 registered a descriptive safety/tolerability primary outcome. That primary was met: AEs were balanced and Xilonix was well tolerated (PMID:26433546). The paper's secondary efficacy endpoints, 12-month restenosis and MACE, showed no difference (24% vs 27%, P=.79), with only a nonsignificant 3-month trend in a 43-patient open study. So the index trial was not a formal efficacy test of the drug. The bundle has no human pillar data: no posted PK, no IL-1α neutralization or downstream biomarker data in vivo; the ex vivo skin explant assay (PMID:39214920) does not count. The drug met no efficacy endpoint elsewhere to infer engagement (NCT01767857, NCT04019041 failed). If the readout is read as an efficacy failure, it is indeterminate (U).

In the R/R AML trial NCT04956042, 0 of 9 evaluable patients had a complete response at the recommended Phase 2 dose (900 mg/m2, MTD from NCT03348514). The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. No human data show γ-secretase engagement or Notch pathway suppression in leukemic blasts or marrow. The only human pharmacodynamic data come from bladder tumor IHC (NCT04608045), a different tissue and disease: Notch and presenilin staining fell, but numbers were small and scatter was wide. The binding evidence is preclinical (PMID:34059639). The sponsors blamed patient selection, saying their PPMP ex vivo assay predicted every enrolled patient would not respond (F3, secondary). That claim comes from the co-developer's own platform. With engagement unmeasured in AML, the data cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so U.

Curcumin (BCM95) has no defined molecular target. Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up human data showing that it reached the CNS, engaged a target, or moved a downstream biomarker at the dose used in MS. In NCT01514370, the primary endpoint was the number of patients with active T2 lesions at month 12: 4/40 on curcumin vs 7/40 on placebo, p=0.271. Event rates were low in both arms, and many patients dropped out (10 by month 12, 27 by month 24). The CONTAIN investigators said this dropout rate was too high to draw firm conclusions, which supports F7 (trial design or execution) as a secondary code. A separate small, open-label Russian study of micellar curcumin reported lower plasma IFN-gamma, but it used a different formulation and did not measure target engagement. Because engagement data are absent, the primary code is U (indeterminate).

Curcumin has no recorded molecular target. The bundle and my search found no human measurement of curcumin levels in the eye, no target engagement data and no human pathway biomarker. The ocular distribution data come only from rabbits (PMID:30013474) and dogs (PMID:32923645), which do not count. In NCT03584724, relapses per patient were numerically lower with curcumin (0.35 vs 0.58) but this was not significant. Relapses fell in both arms compared with the year before, and only a secondary responder analysis favoured the drug (PMID:35353651). That pattern, with about 22 patients per arm, suggests the trial was underpowered and had a placebo/regression effect (F7). Still, nothing separates poor drug exposure from an irrelevant mechanism, so the answer is U.

Oxabact (live O. formigenes) acts by degrading oxalate in the gut. The bundle has no human data on intestinal colonization (exposure) or on oxalate degradation, such as urinary or fecal oxalate or enzyme activity (engagement). The Phase 3 index trial NCT03116685 (n=25) missed its primary endpoint, plasma oxalate change at 52 weeks. Plasma oxalate fell numerically on drug (-0.71 vs +2.35 µmol/L on placebo), but the difference was not significant. No other trials, Phase 1 results, abstracts or same-target drugs are in the bundle. Nothing separates failure to colonize or engage from an ineffective mechanism, so the code is U. The small sample and numerical trend suggest the trial may have been underpowered (secondary F7).

SYNB1020 is a live biotherapeutic with no recorded primary target. The index trial NCT03447730 in cirrhosis was terminated after interim futility analyses found no efficacy. Its posted results cover only safety: TEAEs were mostly grade 1–2, there were no treatment-related serious events, and no treatment-related discontinuations, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The prior Phase 1 trial NCT03179878 (healthy volunteers and urea cycle disorder) posted no results, and the bundle has no PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators. Without human evidence of exposure, engagement or a pathway effect (e.g. ammonia lowering), the bundle cannot separate a molecule that failed to act from a mechanism irrelevant to the disease. Indeterminate.

In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT06796868, PMID:41425080), all three GW117 doses (20–60 mg) beat placebo only numerically on HAMD-17 and MADRS, and none reached significance. The investigators blamed a high placebo response and pointed to a post hoc subgroup (severe illness or insomnia) where the 20 mg dose did better, which supports secondary codes F7 and F3. I found no human evidence that GW117 reached its targets. There is no human brain penetration, MT1/MT2 or 5-HT2C occupancy, or biomarker data. The Phase 1 PK study (NCT06964711) posted no results. The pharmacology evidence is from rodents and dogs only (PMID:38160931, PMID:36268681, Wiley 2021). No drug on the same target has been approved for depression in the bundle. Engagement cannot be judged, so the code is U.

In NCT01011816, a single intradiscal injection of BIOSTAT BIOLOGX fibrin sealant (up to 4 mL) did no better than saline on composite success at 26 weeks (33.5% vs 39.3%, p=0.52), and the trial was stopped for lack of efficacy. I found no human data showing that fibrin formed and stayed inside the disc, sealed the annular fissures, or moved any disc-level biomarker. The approved haemostasis and fibrinogen-deficiency uses work in a different compartment, so they cannot stand in for engagement here. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter. The saline arm's high 39% success rate hints at a placebo or design problem (F7), but no source blames it.

The index trial NCT02891070 was an active-controlled non-inferiority comparison of topical fibrin sealant (Tisseel) against DuraSeal for dural sealing. No CSF leak occurred in 76/89 vs 87/95 patients, with a difference of -9.29% [-21.11, 2.54]. Non-inferiority appears not shown, but this was not a placebo or standard-of-care superiority failure. It is a missed non-inferiority margin against an active product, which is F9. The pillars are inferred from clinical efficacy rather than measured. The same Tisseel formulation met hemostasis superiority endpoints (NCT00892957, NCT01244425). Another fibrin sealant in this drug grouping met CSF-leak endpoints (NCT02457546, NCT02309645). An earlier Tisseel dural phase 2 trial showed no difference versus standard of care (NCT00681824). No direct human engagement measurements exist.

SI-614 is a modified hyaluronate eye drop with no recorded molecular target. In the index Phase 3 trial (NCT05411367), it did not improve corneal fluorescein staining at Day 29 compared with placebo (difference -0.12, p=0.315). The earlier Phase 2 trial (NCT01558999) and Phase 2/3 trial (NCT02205840) posted no usable pharmacodynamic data. My search found only Seikagaku's press release announcing the start of the trial. It found no human data on exposure, engagement or biomarkers, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. Safety was similar between arms. With engagement at no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

TIME-2b (NCT03197870) missed its primary endpoint, a ≥2-step DRSS improvement at 48 weeks. No source gives human data on target engagement, such as VE-PTP inhibition, Tie2 phosphorylation or retinal drug levels. PK was collected but not reported. The sponsor said prespecified secondary biomarkers (urine albumin-creatinine ratio and intraocular pressure) moved favourably, consistent with TIME-2 (NCT02050828). That is weak downstream evidence and cannot stand in for engagement. The eye-drop glaucoma success (NCT04405245) used a different route, tissue compartment and dose, so it cannot support inferred engagement. Doses were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. A review suggested Tie2 activation may need concurrent VEGF suppression, but nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U. The sponsor-reported numeric trend (9.6% vs 3.8%) hints the trial may have been underpowered (F7).

Human plasma PK was shown in Phase 1 (PMID:34108079); CNS penetration and spinal engagement were shown only in rats (PMID:35257579). The pillars are inferred_adequate because the same drug met its primary pain endpoint in diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, a related neuropathic pain with the same CNS target (NCT04455633; LS difference -0.55 to -0.67). In the PHN index trial (NCT04662281), the point estimate of -0.80 was larger than the effect that reached significance in DPNP. However, only 22 drug vs 36 placebo participants were analyzed, so the CI was wide (p=0.12). The trial looks underpowered rather than a clean negative test of the mechanism. F2 is possible but weakly supported. The sources do not state the reason, so confidence is low.

XIRIUS Part 2 (NCT03116113) missed its microperimetry responder endpoint (37.5% low dose, 25% high dose vs 22.2% control). The publication (PMID:38423215) states that COVID-19 cut enrollment short, leaving the trial underpowered with 29 participants. The secondary mean retinal sensitivity change still favored the low dose significantly (P=0.03), and Part 1 post hoc analyses suggested sensitivity gains (PMID:36757689). The bundle has no human measure of RPGR transgene expression, so exposure, engagement and pathway are no_human_data. Dose was not limited: no DLTs occurred across six dose cohorts. Because the sources explicitly blame an underpowered trial, F7 is primary. U is secondary because engagement is unmeasured, so a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter.

The index phase 2a trial (NCT04159831) missed its primary endpoint of treatment failure (OR 1.04, P=0.96). Only 40/43 patients were dosed because of COVID-19 constraints, and the authors attribute the null result to low recruitment (PMID:42310706). The bundle has no human pleural fluid exposure or plasminogen-activation (engagement) data. Stroke efficacy (NCT03541668, NCT05700591) came from intravenous dosing, a different compartment and dose, so engagement cannot be inferred. Still, CT pleural opacification fell significantly in the 400,000 U group and in all treated groups combined, and sensitivity analyses trended toward benefit. That points to biological activity in an underpowered trial, not a disproven mechanism. Bleeding was absent and there was no dose limitation.

Rebamipide has no recorded molecular target, so the bundle holds no human engagement or oral-mucosal exposure data. Gastric tissue levels (PMID:12064818) and a gastric PGE2 readout under naproxen (PMID:27259970) do not apply to the mouthwash setting. The index dose-finding Phase 2 (NCT02085460, about 31 per arm) showed fewer grade ≥3 oral mucositis cases on rebamipide (29.0% at 2%, 25.0% at 4%) than on placebo (38.7%), but posted no statistical analysis. A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled rebamipide mouthwash trials (PMID:31367460) reports an odds ratio of 0.29 for severe mucositis. So this was not a clear efficacy failure: a small, unpowered dose-finding design that could not settle the question. No stop reason is given; U applies by default for the pillars.

No molecular target is recorded. Phase 1 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (Cmax up to ~2000 ng/mL) at 10–200 mg, and the drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited (PMID:31597083). In the index phase 2a trial (NCT03450434, PMID:33095411), the authors report pharmacodynamic engagement in asthma patients: serum CCL2 and CXCL10 fell. That evidence was published after the 2016 start. The primary FEV1 endpoint versus placebo was missed overall. However, patients with high blood eosinophils and/or high IFN-γ on 100 mg improved significantly. The sponsor then ran a follow-up trial restricted to the eosinophilic phenotype (NCT04674137), which points to heterogeneity and patient selection. Small arms (n=30 each) also limited power.

Plasma FTD exposure was measured in humans at the approved dose, and higher AUC tracked neutropenia, a pharmacodynamic marker (PMID:31912801). Direct TYMS engagement was never measured. It is inferred adequate because the same oral regimen met overall-survival endpoints in colorectal and gastric cancer (NCT01607957, NCT01955837, NCT02500043) through the same cytotoxic mechanism in systemic tumors. The bundle has no engagement data in SCLC. That inferred engagement came from trials that read out after the index trial began in 2013. In the index trial (NCT01904253), an ad hoc interim analysis showed PFS imbalanced against topotecan or amrubicin, with no safety signal. This points to insufficient activity of the mechanism in SCLC. The trial was tiny (18 patients) and the analysis ad hoc, so design limits (F7) also apply.

In the MAKO trial (NCT02727881), patients got squalamine 0.2% eye drops twice daily plus monthly Lucentis (ranibizumab), or placebo drops plus Lucentis. The combination added nothing: at 9 months the Lucentis-only arm gained 10.58 letters and the combination arm gained 8.33. This was despite the sponsor using the phase 2 IMPACT trial (NCT01678963) to choose the patients most likely to benefit, so F3 is a possible secondary. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason and moved to evaluate strategic alternatives. The only data on drug reaching the back of the eye (sclera/choroid levels after eye drops, IOVS abstract) came from a preclinical study, not humans. No human evidence was found for drug levels in the choroid, target engagement or a downstream biomarker effect (e.g., on VEGF). Squalamine has no defined primary target, and no comparable drug exists. So a drug that never reached its target cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, which gives U.

In the index trial (NCT04551911), Rayaldee clearly raised serum 25(OH)D in COVID-19 patients: 51/65 reached ≥50 ng/mL vs 10/69 on placebo, so exposure was adequate. Symptom resolution was essentially unchanged (9.8 vs 10.8 days). VDR engagement was not measured in COVID. It is inferred adequate because the drug met its endpoints in SHPT (NCT01219855; iPTH reduction, FDA approval), and the sources show it raises calcitriol and suppresses PTH (PMID:30058895, PMID:37929406). That is systemic VDR agonism at comparable doses, though in parathyroid rather than immune or lung tissue. No COVID pathway biomarker was reported. Robust vitamin D repletion without clinical benefit points to the mechanism not driving mild-moderate COVID-19. The positive signals came only from confounded observational studies (PMID:34097036, PMID:34064175). The modest trial size leaves possible underpowering (F7) as a secondary explanation.

The published report of the Phase 1 trial (PMID:33617672, NCT03298516) followed 18 treated patients with relapsed or refractory AML. Plasma exposure to the conjugate rose with dose. Clearance was rapid, which the authors read as target-mediated clearance and an indirect sign that the drug bound CLL1. Engagement was never measured directly, and the drug did not selectively clear CLL1-positive blasts, so the pathway pillar was not met. No patient had a CR or PR. Dose escalation stopped after liver toxicity at 160 µg/kg, before any maximum tolerated dose was found. The authors attribute this toxicity to the molecule, not to CLL1. They also say they cannot tell whether the doses were high enough, so CLL1 was never adequately tested. Primary code F1a, with F6 as secondary for the molecule-specific toxicity.

In the index trial NCT02427802, the topical gentamicin-collagen sponge given on top of systemic antibiotics produced a 41% clinical cure rate, against 45% with the placebo sponge and 34% with no sponge. The twin trial NCT02447172 also failed. The sponge was well tolerated, so toxicity did not end the program. Neither the bundle nor the search turned up human data on gentamicin levels in the wound or on bacterial killing (for example, bacterial load falling) at the ulcer. Gentamicin's systemic approvals (osteomyelitis, pneumonia, UTI) involve a different route and tissue, so they cannot stand in for those data. The sponsor only said the topical drug added no clinical benefit over standard care, which already included systemic antibiotics. Without engagement data, a delivery failure cannot be told apart from local gentamicin simply being redundant on top of systemic therapy. The add-on design may also have left too little room to show a benefit (secondary F7).

In the index trial NCT01619839 (100–400 mg), knee OA pain change was essentially identical to placebo (-0.06 vs -0.01). Mu-opioid engagement is inferred adequate because the same drug met its Phase 3 primary pain endpoint in chronic low back pain (NCT02362672) through the same central target. Human abuse-potential studies showed CNS mu-opioid effects (pupillary miosis, delayed Drug Liking) at 400–600 mg (PMID:28340145, PMID:31553457). That evidence came from healthy recreational users, not OA patients, and was published after the index trial began. No tolerability cap is shown. The bundle gives no explicit reason for the failure. Under the rules this is F2, with a possible design or placebo issue (F7). Confidence is low because the sources never state why the trial failed.

SM04554 (dalosirvat) is a topical Wnt pathway activator with no defined molecular target. All evidence that it reached the scalp and raised Wnt signalling (β-catenin, Axin2, Lef1 in skin) comes from animals: mice and mini-pigs. No human data on skin drug levels, target engagement or Wnt biomarkers were found. The scalp-biopsy Phase 2 (NCT02503137) missed its terminal-follicle endpoint. The other Phase 2 (NCT02275351) missed its non-vellus hair count endpoint. The Phase 2/3 index trial (NCT03742518) showed no hair-count difference at 48 weeks (p=0.54, p=0.745). No other drug on this target or mechanism has succeeded, and no stated reason for stopping was found. Without human engagement data, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT05406115 is a Phase 1 SAD/MAD study in healthy participants and participants with obesity. Its primary endpoint is treatment-emergent adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test (F9 secondary). It completed with no posted results and no stated stop reason. The bundle records no target, no other trials, no PK, occupancy or biomarker data, no same-target comparators and no publications. Exposure, engagement and pathway therefore have no human data. Nothing distinguishes a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, nor shows toxicity or a business decision, so the outcome is indeterminate (U).

Magnesium sulfate has no recorded molecular target. In the index trial (NCT02145520; PMID:28286262), infants received a single 100 mg/kg IV dose. The full text reports only baseline serum magnesium, about 0.88 vs 0.89 mmol/L. It reports no post-dose levels and no bronchodilator or pathway biomarker. The investigators gave no mechanistic reason for the failure. They said only that IV magnesium did not help and may cause harm: 19.5% vs 6.2% were readmitted. The only approval is for preeclampsia, a different disease and tissue, so adequate engagement cannot be inferred. Asthma efficacy is mentioned only as background, not as an approval or pivotal result in the bundle. Engagement is therefore no_human_data, and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter in bronchiolitis, so the code is U. F2 is a possible alternative.

The index trial NCT06291285 is a Phase 1 capsule-versus-tablet bioavailability study of NDec (decitabine/THU) in healthy volunteers. Its primary outcome is decitabine plasma AUC. It is not an efficacy test in pancreatic adenocarcinoma, so this is not an efficacy failure (F9). Pillars in humans are adequate. Oral THU allowed systemic decitabine exposure, with bioavailability ≥74% of separate dosing (PMID:37417197), which reflects inhibition of CDA. Downstream, DNMT1 protein in blood cells fell by more than 75% and fetal haemoglobin rose in sickle cell patients (PMID:28880867), with DNMT1 downregulation also seen in healthy volunteers (PMID:37417197). These data predate the index trial. No engagement data in pancreatic cancer patients appear in the bundle; the pancreatic trial NCT02847000 reports no results.

No human data show that dusquetide bound SQSTM1/p62 or moved a downstream biomarker. The healthy-volunteer Phase 1 (84 subjects) reported safety only: the maximum tolerated dose was not reached and there were no dose-limiting toxicities, so tolerability did not cap the dose. A Soligenix poster mentions anti-inflammatory responses in Phase 1, but no data appear in the sources. NCT03237325 reduced median severe oral mucositis duration (12.5 vs 20 days in posted results; 8 vs 18 in the topline release) but missed significance (p=0.18). The sponsor blamed variability and pointed to the per-protocol population (p=0.049) and possible patient subsets. The Phase 2 (NCT02013050) dose response did not increase with dose. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U, with F7 and F3 as secondary.

In the OmegaD trial (NCT02980224), neither primary endpoint differed from placebo. TBUT improved by 1.45 vs 1.23 s, and OSDI improved slightly more on placebo. A second Phase 3 trial (NCT04181593) also missed both endpoints, with the arms nearly identical. The drug has no defined molecular target. The bundle and my search found no human data for OmegaD: no omega-3 index or blood EPA/DHA levels, no tear or meibum lipid changes, and no anti-inflammatory biomarkers. The sponsor gave no reason for the failure. Small earlier trials (PMID:24392330, PMID:23642375) reported benefit, but they used different products and measured no pillars. Nothing separates an inadequate exposure from an ineffective mechanism, so the code is U (indeterminate).

The OMEGA-COVID trial (NCT04836052) gave Omacor at 4 g/day, which supplies 3.6 g of EPA plus DHA. Its primary endpoint, ventilator-free days, was not met: 12.4 days with omega-3 versus 11.1 with standard care alone (P=0.48). The published report gives no measurements of blood EPA/DHA levels, Omega-3 Index or eicosanoid shifts during treatment. It also shows no on-treatment biomarker response. CRP and IL-6 appear only as baseline values, and no target is recorded for the drug. The bundle's PubMed papers are observational (PMID:33516093, PMID:34360016) or come from healthy volunteers and other diseases. So human engagement in COVID-19 is unknown. The bundle cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged from an anti-inflammatory mechanism that does not matter here, so the code is U. One exploratory finding, lower mortality in ventilated patients, was not powered and is a weak F3 signal.

Index phase 1 trial NCT04131192 (gemcitabine + larotinib, n=13) stopped for no obvious advantage over standard treatment. Plasma PK in humans was measured at 50-400 mg, with accumulation and no DLTs (PMID:33679419), so systemic exposure was shown and the dose was not capped. No human data on EGFR occupancy, phosphorylation inhibition or a downstream biomarker are in the bundle. Partial responses in NSCLC are not a met efficacy endpoint, and the ESCC phase 2 (NCT03888092) reported only safety. Erlotinib, on the same target, is FDA-approved in pancreatic cancer, so the target is validated in this disease. With no engagement evidence for larotinib, this points to the molecule (F1b), though the small, early, safety-endpoint trial leaves the answer largely indeterminate.

Exposure is adequate. Plasma PK across 100–2400 mg was well characterised (PMID:30612858). In healthy volunteers, an 800 mg dose put cligosiban in the CSF at about 40% of unbound plasma levels (NCT02139826, PMID:30341006). No human measure of target engagement was found: no oxytocin-receptor occupancy and no central oxytocin pharmacodynamic or biomarker readout, in volunteers or in men with PE. The phase 2a trial (NCT02232425, PMID:31351659) showed IELT benefit, but the larger phase 2b trial (NCT03055806, PMID:31351660) showed no effect at any dose, with no dose-response. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects. Two explanations remain open: the 2a result was a false positive, or the target does not drive PE. The commentary (PMID:31542352) asks whether the drug was 'insufficiently tested'. Without engagement data, the failure is indeterminate.

In the first-in-human study (NCT01655225, registered 2012; PMID:29636360), samotolisib exposure rose with dose and gave at least 90% target inhibition at doses of 150 mg or more. That study enrolled mixed solid tumors, not PDAC. The index combination used 150 mg, a dose tolerated in NCT02079636 Part D, so engagement was adequate and the dose was not capped below it. Pathway is inferred_adequate: samotolisib met a PFS endpoint in prostate cancer (NCT02407054), though that was a different disease and combination. In NCT02981342, abemaciclib plus samotolisib did worse than gemcitabine/capecitabine on both DCR (12.1% vs 36.4%) and PFS (1.81 vs 3.25 months). With PI3K/mTOR engaged and no benefit, the mechanism does not appear to drive previously treated PDAC as tested.

The first-in-human study (PMID:29636360, NCT01655225) showed dose-dependent exposure and at least 90% target inhibition at doses of 150 mg or more. The RP2D of 200 mg twice daily sat below the dose-limiting doses, so tolerability did not cap the dose below what engagement needed. These data come from mixed advanced solid tumours, not squamous NSCLC, and were published in 2018, after the index trial started in 2015. Pathway effect is inferred: the drug met a PFS superiority endpoint with enzalutamide in prostate cancer (NCT02407054). Even so, LY3023414 plus necitumumab gave a 6-month disease control rate of only 6.6% and 25%, and the trial stopped for lack of efficacy (NCT02443337). This points to PI3K/mTOR inhibition not driving benefit in this setting. Confidence is medium because the index trial's dose is not shown.

VDA-1102 ointment is meant to detach HK2 from mitochondrial VDAC. In the index trial, neither strength separated from placebo on change in AK lesion count at day 56 (p=0.95 for 5%, p=0.25 for 10%; NCT02844777). The trial included pharmacokinetics, but the sources report no skin or plasma drug levels, no measure of HK2 detachment or engagement, and no downstream biomarker in humans. The sponsor called the result positive, citing a post-hoc benefit in face-treated patients and in Grade 2–3 lesions. That points to a possible subgroup effect (secondary F3). The follow-on open-label Phase 2b (NCT03538951) had no comparator and reported only descriptive results. No other HK2 drug is in the bundle. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

SB623 is a cell therapy with no recorded molecular target. No human biomarker, cell-survival or engagement data appear in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate only because the same cells, implanted stereotactically into peri-lesional brain at comparable doses, met the FMMS primary endpoint in TBI (NCT02416492; p=0.04). That implies the product is biologically active in that compartment. In chronic ischemic stroke, both doses failed against sham on FMMS ≥10-point response (NCT02448641; OR 1.33, p=0.67). Safety did not limit dosing (NCT01287936, PMID:30497166). This suggests the mechanism does not drive motor recovery in chronic stroke as tested (F2). Confidence is low because there is no defined target and the inference across diseases is weak.

The first-in-human study (NCT00881946) and the LCH trial (PMID:27804235) measured dose-proportional plasma exposure at the 125 mg MTD, the dose used in the index trial. No human data on target engagement were found: no pAKT/PRAS40/GSK3 inhibition or tumour pharmacodynamics. In the first-in-human trial, hyperglycaemia, the class surrogate marker, was minimal, and the authors could not link drug levels to glucose or insulin. They recommended further dose exploration with tissue pharmacodynamic biomarkers. In PROFECTA-II, pAKT was a baseline selection marker, not a measure of drug effect. The index trial missed its PFS endpoint (4.3 vs 4.1 months). No other AKT inhibitor has succeeded in ovarian cancer, and capivasertib's approval is in prostate cancer, so F1b does not apply. The evidence can't tell 'never engaged' apart from 'target irrelevant', so the code is U. The secondary code F3 reflects the exploratory benefit in the pAKT-positive subgroup.

In the LCH Phase IIa trial (NCT01395004, PMID:27804235), patients took afuresertib 125 mg, the MTD set in PMID:25075128. Plasma exposures matched those seen in other blood cancers, so exposure counts as adequate for a systemic target. The response rate was 33% in untreated patients and 28% in relapsed or refractory patients, which missed the trial's predefined Bayesian efficacy criteria. Neither the bundle nor my searches turned up any human evidence that the drug engaged AKT, such as reduced phospho-AKT substrates or pathway biomarkers, in LCH or any other disease. Tolerability did not limit the dose. No other AKT inhibitor has succeeded in LCH. Without engagement data, a drug that never hit AKT can't be told apart from an AKT pathway that doesn't drive LCH, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT03222622) tested topical icotinib cream for psoriasis, and it was stopped for missing PASI 50. The Phase 1 cream study (PMID:31187048) measured only plasma levels, which were very low as intended for a topical drug. It did not measure drug levels in the skin, EGFR phosphorylation, or any downstream biomarker in lesions. The only TPSS gain it reported, which was dose-dependent, was a clinical score. The evidence that icotinib blocks EGFR signaling in psoriasis comes from animal and cell studies only (PMID:29276968). Oral icotinib's success in lung cancer works in a different tissue and by a different route, so it does not support engagement in skin. No other EGFR drug has succeeded in psoriasis. With no human engagement data, a drug that failed to engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

Sodium bicarbonate has no recorded molecular target. Its proximal action, raising systemic bicarbonate and pH, is shown in humans in a dose-dependent way: in CKD patients (PMID:23393105), in healthy subjects (PMID:27098290, PMID:29307724) and, before the index trial, in COPD patients (PMID:9219199). Approval for metabolic acidosis supports adequate systemic engagement. No renal or urinary alkalinization or kidney biomarker data appear in AKI patients. The index trial NCT00930436 was terminated with no stated reason and no results, so the failure is inferred, not shown. Indirect support: the 'End of an Era?' commentary on contrast AKI (PMID:34364806) and pediatric cardiac-surgery AKI futility (NCT02046135) suggest alkalinization does not prevent AKI. The unexplained termination leaves F7 possible.

The index trial NCT03680105 was a completed Phase 1 safety and tolerability study of RJX (a sodium bicarbonate-containing product) in 76 healthy participants, listed under critical limb ischemia rather than plasma cell myeloma. Its only primary endpoints were TEAEs, ECGs and neurological exams. Posted results show mostly mild TEAEs, no severe TEAEs, and no ECG or neurological findings. It was not an efficacy test, so there was no failed efficacy readout, and no toxicity signal ended the program. No primary target is recorded, and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data relevant to myeloma. If an efficacy failure were assumed, the evidence would be indeterminate (U).

In Study 1, enerisant at 25–100 mg/day partially improved ESS, but those doses were not tolerated, with many withdrawals for insomnia, headache and nausea. The index trial (Study 2, NCT03267303) therefore used only 5–10 mg/day, chosen by simulating occupancy from a PET study in healthy volunteers (NCT04631276). It was well tolerated but showed no effect on MWT or ESS (PMID:35193545). The bundle does not report the actual H3 occupancy values, so engagement is no_human_data. Tolerability capped the dose below the range that showed signal, so the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). Pitolisant, on the same target, is approved for narcolepsy, which points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The authors also cite large interindividual variability in response (F3).

In the index trial NCT01020799, AZD7268 did not separate from placebo on the 4-week MADRS change (-11.78 vs -11.45). The active control, escitalopram (-11.70), did not separate either, so the trial failed assay sensitivity. That is why F7 (trial design) is a secondary code. The Phase 1 trials (NCT00796965, NCT00861718, NCT00912353, NCT01116011) posted no results. My searches found no human PK, brain penetration, delta-opioid receptor occupancy or pharmacodynamic data. No sponsor statement explains the failure. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a delta-opioid mechanism that does not matter in depression. No other DOR agonist has succeeded in this disease (AZD2327 also failed), so U.

Merlin is a topical mixture of ethanol and glycolic acid. It has no recorded molecular target. In the index trial NCT03192306, lesion duration was the same as with the ethanol vehicle (162.7 h vs 163.6 h). The earlier trial NCT01985321 showed a shorter median healing time (129.6 h vs 154.6 h), but no statistics were posted. Neither the bundle nor the one search I ran gave any human evidence on drug levels in the lesion, antiviral activity such as a drop in viral shedding, or a downstream biomarker. The sponsor gave no explanation for the failure. With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell apart a drug that never acted on the lesion from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the asthma trial NCT01993329, gefapixant 50 and 300 mg did not change methacholine PC20 versus placebo (p=0.616 and p=0.939). Target engagement in human airway sensory nerves was shown directly. A 100 mg dose raised the ATP-evoked cough threshold about 4.7-fold in chronic cough patients (PMID:31023843, NCT02476890, NCT02397460). Chronic cough efficacy trials, including NCT01432730, which predates the index trial, NCT02349425 and NCT02612610, show the expected downstream effect at comparable doses. Exposure is therefore inferred adequate. Engagement was not shown in asthma patients themselves. Doses were not capped by tolerability. With P2X3 engaged, the absent effect on bronchial hyperreactivity indicates that P2X3 signalling does not drive methacholine hyperresponsiveness in asthma.

The index trial of gefapixant 45 mg BID narrowly missed its primary endpoint (difference -0.5, p=0.066) and directionally favoured drug (NCT03654326). The publication calls the result inconclusive because of possible compliance problems: 38 of 94 gefapixant participants had no detectable drug at one or more PK visits (PMID:39260540). So exposure was inadequate in this trial through execution, not tolerability. Engagement is inferred adequate: the same 45 mg BID dose met endpoints in chronic cough, acting on peripheral P2X3 afferents (NCT03449134, NCT03449147). ATP-challenge data also showed peripheral target engagement (PMID:31023843). Neither was shown in endometriosis. The authors attribute the failure to trial conduct, giving F7 primary, with F1a secondary for the inadequate exposure.

The 4-week knee OA trial missed its pain endpoint (NPRS 4.9 vs 5.3 placebo) with no safety signal (NCT01554579). The bundle has no exposure or engagement data in OA patients. Engagement is inferred adequate because gefapixant met efficacy endpoints in chronic cough (NCT01432730, NCT02612610, NCT03449134) through peripheral P2X3 on sensory afferents. A single 100 mg dose also inhibited ATP-evoked cough, which the authors call peripheral target engagement (PMID:31023843, published 2019). That suggests P2X3 antagonism does not meaningfully drive knee OA pain as tested. Confidence is low because the bundle gives neither the OA dose nor joint-afferent engagement, so U is listed as a secondary code.

In OSA, gefapixant 180 mg did not lower AHI versus placebo (GMR 0.92 [0.73, 1.17]; NCT03882801). Peripheral P2X3 engagement was shown directly in humans: 100 mg raised the ATP-evoked cough threshold 4.7-fold in chronic cough patients (PMID:31023843; NCT02476890, registered 2015, before the index trial). Gefapixant also met cough-frequency endpoints at 45-50 mg (NCT02612610, NCT03449134, NCT03449147), well below the 180 mg used here. This supports inferred adequate exposure and pathway activity in peripheral sensory afferents. Engagement was not measured in OSA patients. The likeliest reading is that P2X3 antagonism does not reduce apnea severity. The small 7-day crossover (n≈19 per arm) leaves some design uncertainty.

In the index IC/BPS trial (NCT01569438), gefapixant missed its NPRS pain endpoint (-0.7, p=0.073). No engagement data were collected in IC patients. Engagement is inferred_adequate because gefapixant met efficacy endpoints in chronic cough (NCT01432730, NCT02612610, NCT03449134, NCT03449147) through peripheral P2X3 on sensory afferents with systemic exposure. PMID:31023843 showed ATP-challenge inhibition, i.e. peripheral target engagement, but that was published after the index trial. A similar near-miss in endometriosis pain (NCT03654326) suggests P2X3 antagonism does not meaningfully drive visceral or pelvic pain, which supports F2. The trial was terminated without a stated reason and only 61 participants were analyzed, so it was underpowered (F7). The index dose is not given in the bundle, so confidence is low.

Engagement is directly shown in humans with chronic cough: gefapixant 100 mg raised the ATP cough-challenge threshold about 4.7-fold, described as 'peripheral target engagement' (PMID:31023843, NCT02476890), and lowered Emax (NCT02397460). It met cough-frequency endpoints at 50 mg and 45 mg in refractory chronic cough (NCT02349425, NCT02612610, NCT03449134), so exposure is inferred adequate at the 50 mg BID dose used in IPF. Engagement was never measured in IPF patients. Despite this, the index trial showed no reduction in IPF cough (p=0.90 at day 14). This suggests P2X3 signalling does not drive IPF cough as tested. Secondary codes: a small crossover trial with a protocol amendment and a post hoc log-transformed p=0.07 (F7, PMID:34152585), and variable individual response (F3, PMID:40428850).

The index phase 2 trial (NCT01302600, PMID:28460889) narrowly missed its MFM D1+D2 primary endpoint (p=0.0676). The open-label extension OLEOS (NCT02628743, PMID:33246887) showed motor function declining after 52 weeks and did not support any benefit. Roche stopped the program in 2018, citing disappointing long-term results and difficulties with the liquid formulation. No source gives human data on olesoxime exposure in the CNS or muscle, binding to TSPO or VDAC1, or a downstream mitochondrial biomarker. No other drug on these targets has succeeded in SMA, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage its targets or the mechanism does not matter in SMA, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT00868166, PMID:24447620), 330 mg/day olesoxime did not change 18-month survival (p=0.71). The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Blood levels were measured, but the sources report no CNS or CSF levels. No human data show the drug binding TSPO or VDAC1, or moving a downstream mitochondrial biomarker. The metabolomic differences between arms (PMID:29870556) are not a marker of the mechanism. Binding to the targets was shown only in vitro (PMID:17496168). No other drug on this target has succeeded in ALS. The sponsor blamed disease stage at diagnosis (timing), but without any human evidence of a proximal effect. So the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, and the code is U.

The index trial, NCT00666016, was a small exploratory study (n=22) that looked at whether olesoxime lowers ALT over 30 days in NASH. It posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. My searches found no human data on liver exposure, TSPO/VDAC binding, or a downstream biomarker. The only evidence that olesoxime binds TSPO/VDAC comes from preclinical work. No pillar can be inferred from another disease either, because olesoxime missed its primary endpoints in ALS (NCT00868166) and SMA (NCT01302600). No other drug on this target is in the bundle. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter in NASH, so the code is U.

Exposure: dose-proportional PK with a >100-h half-life in humans (PMID:28449232). Engagement and pathway: dose-dependent lowering of SHBG and HDL, and dose-dependent lean-mass gain in healthy older adults (PMID:28449232, PMID:29982690). In COPD patients in the index trial, lean body mass rose and HDL fell (PMID:36283827), so AR agonism was achieved in this disease. That evidence comes from the index trial itself, so in-disease engagement was not shown beforehand. The drug was well tolerated and the dose was not capped. Despite this, leg strength improved only modestly in men and not significantly in women, with no change in patient-reported outcomes (NCT03359473). AR-driven anabolism did not translate into meaningful functional benefit in COPD. Secondary codes: the sex-confined effect (F3) and an endpoint/duration question (F4).

In NCT05794204, neither dose of RMP-A03 beat placebo on change in hyperemia grade at Day 28 (-0.32 and -0.09 vs -0.30 for placebo). There were no serious adverse events, so toxicity does not explain the failure. No target is recorded, and the trial protocol and drug-database pages found do not name a mechanism. No human data were found on ocular drug levels, target engagement or a biomarker effect. There are no other trials of this drug, no other drugs on the same target and no publications. The sponsor gave no reason for the failure. With engagement unknown, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The index Phase 2 trial of intratumoral BB-401, an EGFR antisense oligonucleotide (NCT03433027, n=16, tumor response endpoint), posted no results and gave no stop reason. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, no other trials of the drug and no PubMed abstracts. So there is no human evidence of tumor exposure, EGFR transcript knockdown or downstream pathway effect. Other EGFR agents are approved, mainly in NSCLC, and afatinib in squamous cell carcinoma. Enlituo reached Phase 3 in HNSCC, but no approval or met pivotal endpoint is shown there. This makes F1b possible but unproven. With engagement as no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02950922 had only safety and PK primary outcomes (adverse events, labs, vitals, ECGs, plasma concentrations), with endpoint class not_efficacy and no posted results. It was not an efficacy test of lotamilast, so F9 applies. Pillars: plasma levels were below quantification (PMID:26581111), and skin tissue levels, PDE4 engagement and pathway biomarkers were not measured in humans. Concentration-dependent lesion improvement in a small 10-day study (PMID:27080209) is a clinical signal, not pillar evidence. Other PDE4 inhibitors (crisaborole, roflumilast, difamilast) are approved for atopic eczema, so if this were judged as an efficacy failure, F1b or U would apply. The bundle gives no explicit reason the program stopped.

EVO100 is a vaginal acidifying gel with no protein target. Its proximal effect, lowering vaginal pH, was shown in healthy women (NCT02693418, 2016, before the index trial): about -0.6 to -0.76 pH units versus about 0 with placebo or no intervention at 6–24 h. Contraceptive efficacy confirms local activity (NCT01306331, NCT03243305). A prior Phase 2b/3 met its chlamydia-prevention endpoint (NCT03107377), so pathway is treated as inferred_adequate. Despite this, the 1,892-patient index trial showed no benefit (684/906 vs 696/913 successes; NCT04553068). This suggests vaginal acidification does not meaningfully prevent chlamydia or gonorrhea. The discordance with the earlier positive trial leaves open a design or chance explanation (F7). The bundle states no reason, so confidence is low.

Izuforant (LEO 152020) is an oral H4R antagonist. A Phase I SAD/MAD study in 64 healthy volunteers (doses 10–600 mg) found linear plasma PK and a long half-life. Ex vivo, the drug fully blocked imetit-induced eosinophil shape change for more than 24 h at high doses, which shows it engaged H4R. All doses were well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, none of the three dose arms in NCT05117060 separated from placebo on EASI (-9.99/-8.83/-8.87 vs -9.11). It also failed in cholinergic urticaria (NCT04853992). Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers and was published in 2024, after the index trial started. No downstream pathway biomarker was measured in AD skin. The most likely explanation is that H4R antagonism does not drive AD.

In a Phase 1 SAD/MAD study in 64 healthy volunteers (10–600 mg), izuforant (LEO 152020) showed measurable plasma exposure. It also inhibited imetit-induced eosinophil shape change, an ex vivo H4R readout, in a dose-dependent way, with full inhibition lasting more than 24 h at high doses. That counts as adequate engagement, but only in healthy volunteers, and it was published in 2024, after the index trial started. I could not confirm the doses used in the index trial or whether H4R was engaged in patients. No downstream biomarker was shown to move in patients. Even so, the drug missed its primary endpoint in cholinergic urticaria (NCT04853992, p=0.277) and also failed in atopic dermatitis (NCT05117060). This points to H4R antagonism not driving these diseases (F2). The small crossover trial (n=19) leaves room for low power (F7).

Phase 1 studies in healthy subjects (NCT01887106, reported in PMID:33960725) showed plasma exposure and GPR84 receptor occupancy versus placebo that the authors say confirmed target engagement. Multiple doses up to 100 mg/day were well tolerated, and nothing in the bundle shows tolerability capping the dose below what engagement needed. The FIH study ran before the UC index trial started. PMID:33267584 states GLPG1205 failed in ulcerative colitis (NCT02337608, Mayo score endpoint; no results posted). It also missed its endpoint in IPF (NCT03725852). With engagement shown and no benefit, the most direct reading is that GPR84 antagonism does not drive UC as tested. Confidence is medium because engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers and no pathway biomarker was measured in colon tissue.

Phase 1 studies in healthy subjects (NCT01887106, PMID:33960725) showed plasma exposure and confirmed GPR84 receptor occupancy versus placebo. The maximum tolerated multiple dose was 100 mg once daily, the dose used in PINTA, so occupancy was shown at the index dose. No human pathway biomarker and no engagement data in IPF patients are in the bundle. PINTA (NCT03725852, PMID:36328358) missed its FVC endpoint (diff 42 mL, p=0.50). Imaging lung volumes trended favourably, but the trial was explicitly not powered (F7). GLPG1205 also had more serious AEs and discontinuations, especially with nintedanib (F6). With engagement shown, the most direct reading is that GPR84 antagonism did not deliver clinical benefit as tested. The small size tempers this.

Zenuzolac (GLS-1027) is described as an oral IL-6/IL-1β inhibitor, but no molecular target is recorded. In the healthy-volunteer Phase 1 studies (NCT00627120, NCT00760396), plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose, with good bioavailability and a half-life of about 7 h. Exposure is rated adequate because the target is assumed to be systemic. However, the protocol reports only PK and safety. No human cytokine or other pharmacodynamic biomarker data were found, so engagement and pathway have no human data. The index trial (NCT04590547) had very few treatment failures: 2 of 44 on placebo, with no difference between arms. Such low event rates suggest the trial was underpowered to answer the question (F7 secondary). Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter here, so the code is U.

Zenuzolac (GLS-1027) is an oral small molecule described as inhibiting IL-6 and IL-1β, with no defined molecular target. Two Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (NCT00627120, NCT00760396; Lee 2016) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure at single doses up to 800 mg and daily doses up to 400 mg. That covers the 120 and 360 mg doses used in the index trial, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. The doses were well tolerated. No human cytokine-inhibition or other engagement or pathway biomarker data were found. The protocol based the dose on mouse data. In NCT04590547 there were very few treatment failures in any arm (1, 3 and 2), so the trial had too few events to show an effect. No sponsor explanation for the failure was found. Engagement is unknown, so the code is U.

Zenuzolac is an oral immunomodulator with no defined target. The protocol says it may inhibit NF-kB, p38 MAPK and cytokines, but that evidence comes only from preclinical work. In healthy volunteers, the sponsor's Phase 1 multiple-dose study (NCT00760396, 40–400 mg/day) showed sustained plasma levels, and the index trial's 120 and 360 mg doses fall within that range. That is the only human evidence on exposure. I found no human data on engagement or pathway effects, such as cytokine suppression, in COVID-19 patients or anyone else. In the index trial (NCT04590547), there were 1, 3 and 2 treatment failures in the 120 mg, 360 mg and placebo arms. With so few events, the trial had very little power (secondary code F7). Because engagement is unknown, the cause of failure can't be determined.

The pillars were measured directly. Exposure: plasma levels matched predictions (PMID:29913894). Engagement: an AstraZeneca slide deck reports 93% ex vivo CCR2 occupancy on blood monocytes. Pathway: CCL2 rose with dose and blood monocytes fell by up to 30% in the pain trials (NCT01201317, NCT01200524). The National Academies document reports the same blood-monocyte drop and CCL2 rise in COPD patients on 100 mg, the index dose. Even so, in the index trial (NCT01153321), lung monocyte recruitment after LPS challenge fell only modestly (398 vs 514; no statistics posted). No benefit followed in COPD or in pain. That fits F2: blocking CCR2 does not drive the disease as tested. Lung-tissue engagement was not measured, and no sponsor statement explains the stop. The COPD engagement data come from trials that ran at the same time, not before the index trial.

The index trial NCT01200524 in posttraumatic neuralgia missed its primary endpoint. NRS pain change was -1.53 at 150 mg and -1.54 at 20 mg versus -1.44 on placebo. The published report of this trial (Kalliomäki 2013, Pain) says plasma drug levels reached the intended range. CCL2 rose in a dose-dependent way, close to maximum in week 1, and mean monocyte counts fell by 30% at 150 mg. The authors read this as interaction with CCR2 in these patients. No dose was limited, since adverse events matched placebo. The sister trial in painful diabetic neuropathy (NCT01201317, PMID:29913894) also failed at the predicted plasma exposures. With engagement shown, the result points to CCR2 not driving neuropathic pain as tested (F2). Caveat: there are no human CNS penetration data, and the NHP PET showed low brain uptake.

The ENTRATA index trial (NCT03163667) prespecified a one-sided alpha below 0.2 for its primary PFS endpoint (PMID:35576438). The observed one-sided p=0.079 (HR 0.64) therefore met that endpoint, and the authors report that telaglenastat plus everolimus improved PFS. So the index trial was not an efficacy failure (F9). The pillars held at the 800 mg twice-daily dose used in the index trial (PMID:34285061): plasma exposure above 300 nM, more than 90% GLS inhibition in platelets, more than 75% GLS inhibition in tumour, and a rise in circulating glutamine. The MTD was not reached, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. Engagement was shown in mixed solid tumours, not specifically RCC, and was published in 2021, after the index trial started. The later pivotal CANTATA trial failed despite this engagement (HR 0.94; NCT03428217, PMID:36048457), which supports F2 as the reason the program stopped.

In the phase 1 solid-tumor study (NCT02071862, PMID:34285061), plasma exposures above 300 nM gave over 90% GLS inhibition in platelets and over 75% inhibition in tumor, with a significant rise in circulating glutamine. MTD was not reached, and the RP2D of 800 mg BID was set without a tolerability cap. PMID:33004309 confirms target binding in patient platelets. These data are not specific to NSCLC, but that trial enrolled NSCLC patients and was registered before the index trial. KEAPSAKE (NCT04265534) was nonetheless terminated for lack of clinical benefit. Other telaglenastat trials also failed despite this engagement: 0% ORR in NSCLC with nivolumab (NCT02771626) and a negative CANTATA (NCT03428217). Adequate GLS inhibition without benefit points to the target not driving KEAP1/NRF2-mutant NSCLC as tested.

In the phase 1 solid-tumor study (PMID:34285061, NCT02071862), all three pillars were shown at the 800 mg BID RP2D. Plasma exposure exceeded 300 nM, with >90% platelet GLS inhibition and >75% tumoral GLS inhibition, and circulating glutamine rose. The MTD was not reached, so the dose was not capped. That evidence was pooled across solid tumors, not shown specifically in TNBC, and published after the index start. In NCT03057600, ORR with paclitaxel met its threshold only in the non-African-ancestry first-line cohort (53.8%), which is plausibly paclitaxel-driven, and failed in the other three cohorts. Across tumor types, adequately engaged GLS inhibition repeatedly failed to add benefit (NCT03428217, NCT02771626, NCT04265534). This points to the target not driving disease (F2). The subgroup-confined signal gives a minor F3 component.

In the phase IIa septic shock trial (NCT01000649, registered 2009; PMID:28807037), selepressin 2.5 ng/kg/min produced dose-dependent pharmacodynamic V1A agonist effects. More patients maintained MAP without norepinephrine, norepinephrine needs fell about threefold, and fluid balance was lower (p<0.01). This functional vasopressor response shows engagement and the immediate pathway effect in patients with the disease before the index trial began. PK was examined there but not reported in the bundle, so exposure is inferred from the pharmacodynamic response. The index trial (NCT02508649) tested 2.5 to 5.25 ng/kg/min without dose limitation and found no benefit on vasopressor- and ventilator-free days (15.00 vs 14.45, p=0.30). Selective V1A agonism, though engaged, did not improve hard outcomes in septic shock.

Serum exposure is documented in Phase 1 PK data (NCT04987333). Engagement of the CD25-biased IL-2 receptor and its pathway effect were shown in humans. Healthy volunteers had robust, selective Treg expansion, and SLE patients in the phase 1b study (NCT03451422) had a dose-dependent rise in CD25-bright Tregs, peaking about 54-fold. The interim results were presented at ACR before the index trial started in Jan 2022. Engagement was never shown in UC patients or in gut tissue. The index trial (NCT04987307) stopped for futility at all three doses (remission 9.6–10.4% vs 7.5%) with no safety problems, and the drug also failed for futility in SLE (NCT04680637). Expanding Tregs systemically did not translate into clinical benefit, which points to the mechanism as tested (F2). Because colonic engagement is unmeasured, some uncertainty remains.

All three pillars were met in SLE patients. The Phase 1b trial in SLE (NCT03451422, interim results at ACR, before the index trial started in May 2021) showed linear, dose-proportional drug levels in blood. It also showed a dose-dependent, selective rise in Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs): a 17.4-fold mean peak at the high dose, and 53.8-fold for CD25-bright Tregs. Other IL-2-responsive immune cells did not change meaningfully, and there were no dose-limiting toxicities. So the drug engaged IL-2 receptor signalling and expanded Tregs as designed, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, the index trial stopped for futility, with SRI-4 response rates on drug at or below placebo (NCT04680637). The ulcerative colitis program also failed futility despite the same mechanism (NCT04987307). Together this points to Treg expansion by this route not driving disease activity: the mechanism does not work as tested.

CE-224,535 at 500 mg twice daily missed ACR20 at week 12 (34.0% vs 36.2% on placebo, p=0.591), with no subgroup effects (NCT00628095, PMID:22382341). The full paper reports a median trough level of about 250 ng/ml in patients. That is about 25 times the IC90 (10 ng/ml) for blocking IL-1β release in an ex vivo whole-blood assay from an earlier human multiple-dose study (Pfizer data on file, not published). Exposure and engagement therefore look adequate, and tolerability did not cap the dose. The authors judged insufficient receptor occupancy unlikely and concluded that blocking P2X7 alone does not work against RA. Engagement was not measured directly in RA patients; it is inferred from plasma levels against the ex vivo assay, so confidence is medium. No other P2X7 drug has succeeded in RA (AZD9056 also stopped in Phase 2), so F1b does not apply.

SCM-AGH is an allogeneic bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cell product given at 1x10^6 cells/kg. No molecular target is recorded. The Phase 1/2a index trial NCT04189419 (n=36) missed both primary endpoints: modified Marshall score change at Day 7 and CTSI at Day 28. The sponsor reported no serious safety signals, so tolerability did not cap the dose. CRP and IL-6 fell significantly versus placebo on Days 1–3. That is an anti-inflammatory signal, which I treated as the pathway pillar, but it comes from a news report, not peer-reviewed data. No source gives cell biodistribution or persistence, or any measure of engagement. Nothing separates inadequate delivery or engagement from an anti-inflammatory mechanism that does not change organ failure. That makes this U. The trial was small and early-phase, so trial design (F7) may also have contributed. The sponsor said it planned a Phase 2b.

In the first-in-human trial (NCT04857138; PMID:42067656), RO7300490 was given at 16-1,100 mg. It showed target-mediated drug disposition with sustained exposure at higher doses, and radiolabeled drug was taken up rapidly and persistently into tumors, so exposure and target binding are adequate. Paired tumor biopsies showed a significant rise in DC-LAMP+ dendritic cell density, more B cells and pre-tertiary lymphoid structures, which is the expected CD40-agonist pathway effect in patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose: grade 3-4 TRAEs were 3.8%. Even so, there were no objective responses and limited clinical activity, which points to the mechanism as tested not driving tumor regression. The trial was primarily a safety and dose-escalation study, hence secondary F9. Engagement data were published only after the trial.

The index crossover trial (NCT04033926, n=25) showed no difference in TIS between zetomipzomib and placebo in either period. In healthy volunteers, KZR-616 selectively inhibited the immunoproteasome and blocked ex vivo cytokine production (PMID:36969170). That supports systemic exposure, engagement and a proximal pathway effect, though the level achieved was not quantified. This evidence was published in 2023, after the index trial started in 2020, and it was not obtained in myositis patients. Muscle-tissue engagement was not shown. Efficacy rests only on a mouse model (PMID:35733374). Tolerability did not limit dosing, given few serious AEs. Engagement apparently held but brought no clinical benefit, which suggests F2. The very small sample means the trial may have been underpowered (F7). Confidence is low.

The index trial NCT05625347 compared plasma PK of inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in subjects with pulmonary dysfunction. Its primary endpoints were PK only, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated because a separate pivotal study, not described in the bundle, failed. Its own readout was not an efficacy failure of aspirin. Plasma exposure is documented (PMID:29540563). Platelet COX-1 engagement and thromboxane suppression are shown directly in humans (PMID:6221533, PMID:2744633). Arachidonic acid-induced aggregation was abolished in NCT01768637. In periodontal disease, topical aspirin lowered salivary PGE2 (PMID:31813866). Oral aspirin did not significantly change gingival crevicular fluid mediators (PMID:17668982). The gingivitis label does not match the index trial's population, and the reason the pivotal study failed is not in the bundle.

The index trial NCT05625347 was a 4-subject Phase 1 PK/PD bridging study comparing inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in people with abnormal pulmonary function. It was not an efficacy test in essential thrombocythemia. It was terminated only because a separate pivotal study, whose content is not shown in the bundle, missed its endpoint, leaving this supportive study without purpose. Human pillars for aspirin are well established, though only in healthy volunteers or other diseases. Exposure is shown in PMID:29540563. Engagement is near-complete platelet COX-1/thromboxane inhibition (PMID:2744633, PMID:6221533, PMID:16172182; NCT01768637, where arachidonic acid aggregation fell to 0). The pathway is shown by suppressed aggregation. No COX engagement is shown in ET patients. PMID:41436639 gives only an associative NET-marker finding.

The index trial NCT05625347 is a supportive Phase 1 PK/PD bridging study. It compared inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in subjects with impaired pulmonary function, and its primary endpoints were Cmax and AUC. It was not an efficacy test. It was terminated only because a separate pivotal study, which is not in the bundle, missed its endpoint. Oral aspirin exposure and COX-1 engagement in healthy humans are well documented. Serum and plasma TXB2 suppression is shown (PMID:2744633, PMID:6221533), and arachidonic acid-induced platelet aggregation is almost abolished (PMID:16172182, NCT01768637). No engagement data exist for the inhaled formulation or in this population. The labelled disease (SCAD deficiency) appears unrelated, and the bundle cannot explain why the pivotal trial failed.

The index trial NCT05625347 was a supportive Phase 1 PK/PD bridging study comparing inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin, with PK primary endpoints. It was terminated only because a separate pivotal study missed its endpoint, so it was not itself an efficacy test. Aspirin's pillars are well shown in humans, all in healthy volunteers or CKD patients, none in polycythemia vera. Exposure is shown by measured plasma ASA (PMID:29540563). Engagement is shown by near-abolished platelet COX and thromboxane activity (PMID:6221533, PMID:2744633, PMID:3925272). Pathway is shown by suppressed arachidonic-acid aggregation (PMID:16172182, NCT01768637, PMID:18277132). The bundle does not identify the failed pivotal trial or explain why it missed, so F9 applies.

The index trial NCT05625347 was a Phase 1 PK/PD bridging study comparing inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in subjects with obstructive or restrictive pulmonary function. Its primary outcomes were Cmax and AUC, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated only because a separate pivotal study (not in the bundle) missed its endpoint, making this supportive study pointless. The obesity label does not match the trial content. For oral aspirin, human pillars are well established in healthy volunteers: plasma exposure (PMID:29540563), suppression of platelet thromboxane/COX-1 (PMID:2744633, PMID:6221533), and abolished arachidonic-acid platelet aggregation (PMID:16172182, NCT01768637). There is no engagement evidence in obesity. The failed pivotal readout's cause cannot be judged from the bundle.

The index trial NCT05625347 was a supportive Phase 1 PK/PD bridging study comparing inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in people with obstructive or restrictive pulmonary function. Its primary outcomes were Cmax and AUC, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated only because a separate pivotal study, which is not in the bundle, missed its endpoint. The bundle gives no information on that pivotal study's indication or data. The 'insomnia' label has no support in the bundle. Oral aspirin's plasma exposure, platelet COX-1 inhibition and thromboxane suppression are well shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:6221533, PMID:2744633, PMID:18277132, PMID:29540563, PMID:16172182). Engagement in the program's disease was not shown. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test of the drug, it is coded F9.

The index trial NCT05625347 compared the PK of inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in people with abnormal pulmonary function. It enrolled 4 and had PK primary endpoints (Cmax, AUC). It was not an efficacy test. It stopped because a separate pivotal study missed its primary endpoint, which left this supportive study without purpose. The bundle does not describe that pivotal study or its endpoint. For oral aspirin, human exposure, COX-1 engagement and pathway effect are well documented: thromboxane suppression (PMID:6221533, PMID:2744633) and near-abolished arachidonic-acid aggregation (PMID:16172182, NCT01768637). Reduced platelet activity in ICH patients taking aspirin is also reported (PMID:19334079). No pillar data exist for the inhaled formulation. The ICH disease label does not match this trial.

The index trial NCT05625347 was a small (n=4) PK/PD bridging study comparing inhaled ASA powder with chewable aspirin in patients with pulmonary function impairment. Its primary endpoints were plasma Cmax and AUC. It was terminated because a separate pivotal study missed its endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of aspirin, and not of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Human data show adequate exposure (PMID:29540563), near-complete platelet COX inhibition (PMID:6221533, PMID:16172182, NCT01768637) and thromboxane/prostaglandin suppression (PMID:2744633, PMID:3241818). All of this was in healthy volunteers or other diseases, not NPC, and was published before the index trial. No tolerability cap is shown. This fits F9.

Grapiprant was tried with pembrolizumab in post-PD-1 lung adenocarcinoma (NCT03696212). The 900 mg q12h dose could not be tolerated: one patient had a dose-limiting toxicity and two others stopped for liver problems. At 300 mg BID, 12 evaluable patients showed no responses, so the sponsor ended the program. No source measured EP4 occupancy or receptor blockade in humans. The only human pharmacodynamic data come from the later RMX1002 trial in mixed solid tumours (PMID:39976872). It showed dose-dependent plasma exposure and a rise in a urinary PGE2 metabolite, which the authors read as a sign of EP4 pathway inhibition. That trial used higher doses (RP2D 500 mg BID), and its signal is indirect. Nothing shows whether 300 mg engaged EP4 enough. So the bundle cannot tell an under-dosed drug apart from a target that does not matter: U. F1a (tolerability cap) and F6 (hepatotoxicity) may also apply.

The index trial (NCT03696212) stopped because of efficacy. A later protocol (NCT05041101) says the 300 mg BID dose was well tolerated but showed no efficacy in 12 evaluable NSCLC patients, so the sponsor did not try lower doses. The only human pharmacology data is PMID:39976872 (2025, mixed solid tumors, published after the index trial, 200–650 mg BID). It showed dose-dependent plasma exposure, and a rise in a urinary PGE2 metabolite was taken to suggest the EP4 pathway was blocked. No study measured EP4 receptor occupancy or direct binding to the target, and nothing was measured in NSCLC patients or at the index trial's dose before it started. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged EP4 apart from a target that doesn't matter here, so the code is U. F2 is a weaker alternative.

In NCT04753164, 100 mg b.i.d. nivasorexant exactly matched placebo on binge-eating days per week (LSM difference 0.00, p=0.9992; PMID:37584285). Healthy-volunteer studies (PMID:32067262, PMID:33159976) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure at doses up to 200 mg b.i.d., and the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose.
