They also reported nonspecific CNS effects and lower cortisol during a CO2 challenge. No human study measured OX1 receptor occupancy, brain levels or a target-specific biomarker. The occupancy figures come only from rat models (PMID:38456603). No other drug on this target is in the bundle, and the investigators did not say why the trial failed beyond calling for more research on OX1R in BED. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the Phase 1 dose escalation NCT03822871 (0.75–9.0 GBq, n=17), no dose-limiting toxicities occurred and there were no RECIST objective responses, only stable or progressive disease. The bundle has no human imaging, dosimetry, tumor uptake or PSA data for CTT1403. Tumor uptake and efficacy were shown only in mice (PMID:28638478, PMID:31321650), and the review PMID:42517398 gives no human details. So exposure, engagement and pathway are all no_human_data. The PSMA target is validated in this disease: lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan is FDA-approved for prostate cancer. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Without any human engagement data, U also applies. Dose was not limited by tolerability.

In FRONTIER (NCT02315443), prehospital nerinetide at 2.6 mg/kg did not improve 90-day mRS (aOR 1.05). The sources contain no human evidence that it disrupted PSD-95 in brain, no brain or CSF levels, and no downstream biomarker. The only human pharmacology found is plasma PK from ESCAPE-NA1: plasma levels fell when patients got alteplase, which cleaves nerinetide via plasmin. That points to inadequate exposure in alteplase-treated patients, but it does not apply cleanly to FRONTIER, where nerinetide was given before hospital arrival. ESCAPE-NEXT (NCT04462536), which excluded thrombolysis, also failed. Because the sources cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the code is U. Secondary F3: 37% of FRONTIER participants did not have ischaemic stroke (PMID:39955120).

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT04388826) enrolled only 39 patients. It favoured sabizabulin numerically: 17/19 vs 14/20 alive without respiratory failure, and 1 vs 5 deaths. No statistical test was posted, and the counts were too small to reach significance, so the trial was underpowered rather than showing an absence of effect. The follow-on Phase 3 (NCT04842747) in hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients met its mortality endpoint (18.7% vs 38.6%) at 9 mg, against 18 mg in the index trial. That supports inferring the pillars held in a closely related setting. No direct human exposure, engagement or biomarker data appear in the bundle. The 'failure' therefore reflects trial size, not the mechanism.

Engagement was not measured directly: the PET occupancy study NCT05666687 started after the index trial and posted no results. Healthy-volunteer data (PMID:37817426) show dose-proportional plasma PK, dose-related EEG changes and dissociative AEs. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same IV dose (0.16 mg/kg) met the 24h MADRS endpoint in TRD (NCT03756129, before the index start), and a later TRD trial showed a high-dose effect (NCT05454410). In the index trial (NCT04722666), every arm, placebo included, improved about 17 MADRS points under comprehensive standard of care in acutely suicidal patients. That points to a placebo and standard-of-care response that swamped any drug signal, or to a population difference, rather than to the target. Termination was unexplained, so confidence is low.

Linvencorvir is an HBV core protein allosteric modulator (CpAM). Phase 1 data show dose-related plasma exposure and good tolerability (NCT02952924, PMID:32839221, PMID:34562067). Modelling predicted adequate liver exposure (PMID:33523474). A 4-week proof-of-mechanism study in CHB patients, registered before the index trial, reports antiviral activity on HBV DNA (PMID:34237271). The abstract is truncated, so the magnitude is not shown. This is direct evidence of engagement and pathway effect in the disease. No dose cap from tolerability appears. Yet in NCT04225715 both CpAM-containing arms achieved 0% HBsAg loss (Combo 1 n=35, Combo 5 n=9). The mechanism, though engaged, did not drive functional cure. The Combo 5 arm was small, which adds some design limitation.

PLX-PAD is an allogeneic placental cell therapy with no defined molecular target. None of the sources give human data on cell persistence or tissue exposure, any engagement marker, or a pathway biomarker such as angiogenic factors. The phase 1 trials reported only small, open-label trends in perfusion and pain (PMID:30686676). In the PACE trial (NCT03006770), amputation-free survival was the same in both arms (HR 0.93, P=0.788), and the trial was stopped after an interim futility analysis by the data monitoring committee. A post hoc subgroup without diabetes or with HbA1c <6.5% did better (HR 0.46, P=0.048), which points to possible patient-selection effects (F3). Because engagement was never measured, the sources cannot tell apart a cell product that did nothing biologically from a mechanism that does not matter in this disease, so the primary code is U.

PLX-PAD is a placental cell therapy with no recorded molecular target, so the sources have no human exposure, occupancy or engagement data. The Phase III hip fracture trial (NCT03451916) missed its primary endpoint, the SPPB functional score at week 26. However, PLX-PAD significantly increased hip abduction strength in the injured leg at week 26 (P=.047) and week 52 (P=.0022). That repeats the muscle-strength signal from the Phase I/II trial (NCT01525667). This is a proximal effect in this disease that fits the intended muscle-regeneration mechanism. The sponsor explicitly framed the failure as a gap between the gain in muscle strength and the functional score, which points to the endpoint (F4). Molecular engagement itself is unmeasured, so U is listed as a secondary code.

PLX-PAD is an allogeneic placental cell therapy, and no molecular target is recorded for it. The bundle contains no human data on cell persistence, paracrine factor secretion, perfusion or other biomarkers, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The index Phase 2 trial in intermittent claudication (NCT01679990, 172 enrolled) posted no results. The sponsor's press coverage frames the readout as positive mobility data, which suggests the primary endpoint was missed and benefit was claimed only in part of the population, but the bundle does not confirm this. F3 is listed as a possible secondary code on that basis. The later Phase 3 in critical limb ischemia (NCT03006770) also missed its endpoint (HR 0.93, P=0.788). Nothing separates a cell therapy that never acted from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

UC-MSCs are a cell therapy with no defined molecular target. The index trial NCT03847844 (single-arm, n=26, front-line aGVHD) posted no results and gives no stop reason. The bundle has no human data on cell persistence or tissue homing, and no in-disease immunomodulatory biomarkers. A healthy-volunteer study showed cytokine shifts (PMID:33061992), but that is not engagement in aGVHD. Related randomized SR-aGVHD data (PMID:39587570) missed ITT ORR but showed benefit per-protocol and in gut involvement. A retrospective study (PMID:41919571) suggests early response benefit. These hint at design or population issues but do not address the index program. Because engagement has no human data, failure cannot be separated from non-engagement, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT04315025, was a small Phase 1/2 safety study of peribulbar UC-MSC or secretome in 18 patients with retinitis pigmentosa. It posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. The drug has no defined molecular target. No human data on exposure (for example, levels in the eye), target engagement or a pathway biomarker appear in the bundle; the only evidence is in vitro (PMID:32514411). No web searches were run, so this rests on the bundle alone. The trial was mainly a safety test, so F9 may also apply. With engagement having no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In NCT01033422, oral CF101 at 1 or 2 mg BID did not lower IOP versus placebo (19.0 and 19.8 vs 18.95 mmHg). PMID:15516022 gives plasma PK in healthy volunteers, but no source measured drug levels in the eye or A3AR engagement in the ciliary body or trabecular outflow tissue. The glaucoma rationale rested on an incidental ~1.1 mmHg IOP drop in a dry-eye trial. The drug met endpoints in RA and psoriasis (NCT01034306, NCT03168256), but those act on immune and skin compartments, not ocular outflow, so they don't support an inferred_adequate rating. Doses were not tolerability-limited (up to 4 mg BID was tolerated). The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the failure, so a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't control IOP.

In the Phase 3 trial NCT01235234, neither oral CF101 dose (0.1 or 1 mg) beat placebo on complete corneal clearing, and placebo did numerically better. Plasma exposure was shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:15516022), and the oral 1 mg BID dose is the same one that met ACR20 in a rheumatoid arthritis Phase 2 (NCT01034306). That supports systemic exposure. It does not show engagement at the ocular surface. A3AR expression in PBMCs (PMID:18050382) measures how much receptor is present, not whether the drug engaged it. No human data on occupancy or downstream pathway effects turned up. The sponsor's filing only says the endpoint was missed and gives no reason. The positive dry-eye Phase 2 (PMID:20304499) could not be repeated. The bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In Sanofi's results summary for NCT00772525, 30 MS patients with past optic neuritis took single 50 mg and 400 mg doses. Neither dose changed VEP P100 latency versus placebo (p=0.97 and p=0.88). Amplitude rose only slightly and was not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and visual function did not change consistently. No human drug levels, Kv1.1/Kv1.2 channel-blocking data or other target-engagement evidence turned up. Only one patient withdrew for side effects, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Sanofi ended the program in 2010 after the walking trial (NCT00811902) and said the data did not support advancing it. Without engagement evidence, there is no way to tell whether the drug failed to block the channels or the mechanism does not matter here, so the answer is U.

The Sanofi results summary for NCT00772525 reports that single 50 mg and 400 mg doses of nerispirdine did not change VEP P100 latency compared with placebo, and that contrast sensitivity and visual acuity showed no consistent change. P100 amplitude rose slightly but not significantly. So the expected pathway effect, faster conduction in demyelinated optic-nerve fibres, did not appear, and the pathway pillar is rated inadequate. My searches found no human data on CNS or optic-nerve drug levels or on Kv1.1/Kv1.2 channel blockade. The Kv1 blockade evidence is in vitro only. Exposure and engagement therefore have no human data, and the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter. Dalfampridine has not succeeded in an optic disease, so F1b does not apply. Tolerability did not limit the 400 mg dose. Code: U.

The bundle holds no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for nerispirdine. No Phase 1 results were posted, and the index trial (NCT00772525, VEP P100 latency) and NCT00811902 posted no results. The only mechanistic evidence is in vitro: Kv1.1/Kv1.2 IC50 about 3.6 µM, plus Na+ channel block at 11.9 µM, which could oppose the conduction-enhancing effect (PMID:19413590). Dalfampridine, a blocker of the same Kv1 targets, is FDA-approved for multiple sclerosis. That shows the target matters in this disease, which points to the molecule rather than the target. With no evidence that nerispirdine engaged adequately in humans, F1b fits best. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin and does not confirm the index readout.

Sanofi's summary of the index trial (NCT00772525) reports that single 50 mg and 400 mg doses of nerispirdine did not change VEP P100 latency in MS patients with past optic neuritis. The differences from placebo were 0.1 and -0.3 ms (p=0.97 and 0.88). Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity did not change consistently, and P100 amplitude rose only by a small numerical amount. So the readout that should move if conduction improved stayed flat (pathway inadequate). No human plasma levels, CNS penetration or Kv1 channel-blockade data were found, and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Another Kv1 blocker, dalfampridine, has not succeeded in optic neuritis, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement is unknown, the data cannot separate a drug that never blocked its channels from a mechanism that does not matter here: U.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The index HNSCC trial (NCT00824343) posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. The Phase 1 abstracts (NCT00407498/NCT00408018; ASCO 2007, AACR-NCI-EORTC 2007) report the MTD (185 mg/m2) and say PK was measured, but they give no plasma levels, tumor drug levels, or human pharmacodynamic data. That means no CDK inhibition, pRb reduction, or Mcl-1/transcription markers in humans. The pRb/E2F and CCND1 effects are preclinical only (PMID:23414419). A secondary source described the HNSCC Phase II as showing 'encouraging' activity, yet the program stopped without a stated reason. No other CDK4/6 inhibitor in the bundle has succeeded in HNSCC, so F1b does not apply. With engagement having no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

Novartis ended NCT03549000 for futility, saying the data showed a low likelihood of efficacy. The phase I NSCLC study of taminadenant (NCT02403193, Clin Cancer Res 2022) found it tolerable, with a maximum tolerated dose of 480 mg twice daily, so dose was not limited. Response rates were low: 9.5% alone and 8.3% with spartalizumab. The study measured pharmacokinetics, but the pages I could read gave no exposure figures. No human A2A receptor occupancy or direct target-engagement measure was found. In tumor biopsies, CD8+ T cells did not change significantly, gene expression showed some increase in immune activity, and an adenosine-pathway signature did not correlate with survival. With engagement unmeasured, I cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage A2A or whether A2A blockade does not matter in NSCLC, so the code is U. No other A2A antagonist has succeeded in NSCLC.

Novartis ended the index trial NCT03549000 early because the data showed a low likelihood of efficacy, and said the decision was not safety-related. No results were posted. The TNBC combination trial NCT03742349 was also stopped by sponsor decision. In the NSCLC Phase I (NCT02403193; Chiappori, Clin Cancer Res 2022), taminadenant was well tolerated at up to 480 mg twice daily. Response rates were low: 9.5% alone and 8.3% with spartalizumab. The follow-up Phase 2 (NCT03207867) found insufficient activity in NSCLC. None of the sources I found report human receptor occupancy, A2AR pathway or adenosine-signature biomarkers, or tissue drug levels. No other A2AR antagonist has succeeded in TNBC. With no human evidence of target engagement, a drug that failed to engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive the disease, so the code is U.

The index trial, PROMIS-II (NCT03460704), showed no difference in exacerbation rate (RR 1.004, p=0.98). The bundle has no direct human target-engagement data in bronchiectasis. Pillars are inferred adequate because the twin trial PROMIS-I (NCT03093974; PMID:39270696) used the same drug, regimen and population and met the same endpoint (RR 0.61, p=0.001). Inhaled CMS also reaches high epithelial lining fluid levels (PMID:22810779). PROMIS-II was terminated early for major COVID-19-related recruitment problems and placebo-exposure concerns, and enrolled during the pandemic. The sponsor's own stated reason points to trial execution and conduct, not to a failed mechanism, given the positive sister trial. Hence F7. Confidence is medium because the attribution is inferred from the stop reason and the discordant twin trial.

The index trial NCT07017114 was a Phase 1 safety, PK and maximum-tolerated-dose study of a PKB171 gel in healthy female volunteers. It was not an efficacy test in Crohn disease, has no stated stop reason and posted no results, so F9 applies. Oral pentoxifylline plasma PK is documented (PMID:3958905), but the bundle has no exposure data for the gel. PDE4 occupancy or inhibition was never measured. Pathway evidence exists: TNF release was blocked in human endotoxaemia (PMID:2574766), and pentoxifylline blunted a serum TNF rise in Crohn disease patients on vedolizumab (PMID:35642747, NCT02953275, after the index start). That pathway rating is weak, because the bundle does not show the TNF effect is mediated by PDE4.

Oral pentoxifylline reaches the systemic circulation in humans (PMID:3958905, PMID:9504437, PMID:3216031). PDE4 engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the drug is FDA-approved for atherosclerosis/claudication through the same systemic mechanism at comparable oral doses. Pathway evidence is mixed. Infusion blocked endotoxin-induced TNF in volunteers (PMID:2574766), but TNF was unchanged in acute pancreatitis (NCT01292005). No engagement data exist in anemia of CKD. In the index trial, the EPO-dose reduction did not differ between arms (p>0.05), and the trial stopped for lack of difference, which supports F2. However, only 17 of 48 enrolled patients were analysed, the variance was large and the numerical trend favoured pentoxifylline (−8700 vs −2988 U), so underpowering (F7) is plausible.

The index trial NCT03082196 met one co-primary endpoint: primary-molar caries increment at 24 months was lower with PVP-I+NaF varnish than NaF alone (p=0.037). The all-teeth endpoint missed narrowly (p=0.062). The publication (PMID:32437626) concludes the varnish is effective, with no harms. This is not a clear efficacy failure of the drug. Release of iodine from the topically applied varnish was shown in a human PK study (PMID:30938600). PVP-I shifted the cariogenic salivary microbiome in caries-active children (PMID:34485763), but that was published after the index trial started and did not use this varnish. Later borderline results (NCT04947527, mixed) and single-site, modest sample sizes suggest limited power rather than a failed mechanism. No stop reason is stated.

Povidone-iodine is a non-specific antiseptic with no recorded molecular target, so the proximal pharmacological effect in bacterial conjunctivitis is bacterial killing. In the index trial (NCT03004924; PMID:32222367), SHP640 (PVP-I 0.6%/dexamethasone 0.1%) failed to improve bacterial eradication at day 5 versus placebo (43.3% vs 46.8%, P=.500). Clinical resolution was also not significantly better (50.5% vs 42.8%, P=.127). The intended antimicrobial action therefore was not demonstrated at this concentration in patients, so the mechanism was not properly tested. Higher-concentration PVP-I (1.25%) matched an antibiotic in PMID:12429243, and IVIEW-1201 was non-inferior to ofloxacin (NCT05816070), consistent with a formulation or dose issue. High placebo resolution in a self-limiting disease (F7) may also have contributed. No ocular exposure data are available.

The index OLE (NCT03917719) was a safety study, terminated only because the pivotal Phase 3 PolarisDMD (NCT03703882) missed its NSAA endpoint with essentially no difference between arms. This makes F9 a secondary code. The underlying program failure is efficacy. Phase 1 adult and pediatric studies assessed PK/PD (PMID:28074489, PMID:30452422). In boys with DMD, MoveDMD at 100 mg/kg reduced NF-κB-regulated gene levels and improved inflammation and muscle-health biomarkers, and it informed the Phase 3 design (PMID:33678513, NCT02439216). Treatment was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited. With engagement and pathway effects shown in the disease, yet no clinical benefit at 52 weeks, NF-κB inhibition does not appear to drive DMD progression as tested. The magnitude of engagement was not quantified, so confidence is medium.

The index trial NCT00999882 was a Phase 1 study in hepatocellular carcinoma. Its primary endpoints were safety, tolerability and PK, so it was not an efficacy test of AZD8055 and no failed efficacy readout is shown. In solid tumours (PMID:22935583), plasma exposure rose with dose, the MTD was 90 mg BID (transaminase DLTs), and some FDG-PET partial metabolic responses were seen. The bundle has no human CSF or brain-tumour levels and no target-engagement data in glioma. Mouse data showing efflux-limited brain penetration (PMID:27553832) do not count as human evidence. The glioma trial NCT01316809 posted no results. Engagement is therefore indeterminate (U) if failure is assumed.

A human PET study showed GSK239512 crosses into the brain and occupies H3 receptors with unexpectedly high affinity (EC50 about 0.0068 ng/mL; PMID:24670146; imaging study NCT00474513 started 2007, before the index trial). At the 80 µg/day maximum in the index trial, occupancy was therefore likely high. That PET data came from healthy volunteers, and no downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Doses up to 80 µg were tolerated (PMID:23521503). In NCT01009255, episodic memory improved only marginally (p=0.0495). Executive function, ADAS-Cog and clinical measures did not change, and the authors conclude no benefit (PMID:24359500). The schizophrenia trial also failed (NCT01009060). Engaging H3 antagonism did not produce meaningful clinical benefit in AD.

A human PET study with [11C]GSK189254 (NCT00474513, registered 2007, before the 2009 index start; published as PMID:24670146) showed brain penetration and H3 receptor occupancy in all regions. Affinity was very high (EC50 about 0.0068 ng/mL), so the microgram doses used would be expected to give substantial occupancy. This was shown only in healthy volunteers, not in schizophrenia patients. No downstream pathway biomarker was measured in humans. Tolerability did not cap dosing: titration up to 80 μg was well tolerated in Alzheimer's disease (PMID:23521503). Despite engagement, the index trial (NCT01009060; PMID:25728831) showed no CSSB cognitive benefit versus placebo at any week. This points to H3 antagonism not improving cognition in schizophrenia as tested. The small sample (n=50) limits certainty.

GSK239512 is brain penetrant. Human PET in healthy volunteers (NCT00474513, PMID:24670146) showed very high-affinity H3 receptor occupancy (EC50 0.0068 ng/mL), so the doses up to 80 µg used in the index trial should give high occupancy. This occupancy evidence was registered before the index trial but was not measured in MS patients. The bundle has no downstream pathway biomarker in humans. Tolerability did not cap the dose: the 80 µg titration was tolerable, with insomnia during titration (PMID:23521503, PMID:27888416). In the index trial, the remyelination effect on MTR was only small (GdE effect size 0.344, 90% CI 0.018–0.671; Delta-MTR not significant), and few patients contributed lesions. With engagement adequate, the modest benefit suggests H3 antagonism does not meaningfully drive remyelination, so the code is F2. Small lesion numbers limit precision (F7).

In NCT01479465, adding simtuzumab to FOLFIRI did not improve PFS at either dose; the 200 mg arm did numerically worse (HR 1.45). Safety did not limit the dose. The Phase 1 trial (NCT01323933) reported pharmacokinetics and tumour shrinkage in some patients, but I found no human data on LOXL2 enzyme inhibition, drug levels in tumour tissue, or a downstream biomarker. Later in vitro and ex vivo work (PMID:39173635, PMC8571951) found that the parent antibody AB0023 does not block LOXL2 catalytic activity. That suggests the antibody may never have inhibited the enzyme, but it is not human evidence, so it cannot count here. No other LOXL2 drug has succeeded in colorectal cancer. With no human engagement data, the evidence cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage LOXL2 or whether LOXL2 does not drive the disease, so the code is U.

Adding simtuzumab at 200 or 700 mg to gemcitabine did not improve PFS or OS in metastatic pancreatic cancer (NCT01472198, PMID:28246206). The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not limit the dose. I found no human evidence of target engagement: no tumor or plasma LOXL2 inhibition, crosslinking marker or stromal biomarker data. The first-in-human trial (NCT01323933) measured only safety and pharmacokinetics, and its results were not posted. Later papers report that the parent antibody, AB0023, does not inhibit LOXL2 catalytic activity in human cell-culture models and in vivo. They also say target engagement was never evaluated in the clinic (PMID:39173635, PMC8571951). This points toward a molecule failure (F1a), but non-human data do not count toward the pillars. No other LOXL2 drug has succeeded in this disease. So the code is U.

In the PSC trial (NCT01672853), neither 75 mg nor 125 mg of simtuzumab changed hepatic collagen content, Ishak stage or clinical events compared with placebo (PMID:30153359). ELF score and ALP also did not differ between arms (PMID:32707342). That is a null clinical result, not evidence about whether the drug hit LOXL2. None of the sources shows human data on exposure in the liver, LOXL2 inhibition or a pathway effect. Two later papers say outright that target engagement was never measured in humans. Lab work suggests the parent antibody AB0023 does not block LOXL2's enzyme activity (PMID:39173635), which points toward F1a. But animal and in vitro data don't count, so engagement stays no_human_data and the code is U. No other LOXL2 drug has succeeded in PSC.

Simtuzumab reached the blood in patients with myelofibrosis: serum trough levels rose in proportion to dose from 200 to 700 mg (PMID:28220932). That supports exposure for this extracellular target. No source measured whether it engaged LOXL2 in humans. Later papers say target engagement in human blood was never measured (PMC8571951, PMID:39173635). Bone marrow fibrosis, the downstream marker, did not fall consistently, so the pathway pillar was not met (NCT01369498). Lab work suggests the parent antibody AB0023 does not block LOXL2's enzyme activity or collagen cross-linking (PMID:39173635). That points to a molecule that may never have engaged its target (F1a), but it is not human evidence. With engagement no_human_data and no LOXL2 drug succeeding in myelofibrosis, the code is U.

The index trial NCT01707472 was an 18-patient descriptive safety study, with treatment-emergent AEs as its only primary outcome. It was not an efficacy test of simtuzumab, so F9 applies. Across the wider program, simtuzumab missed its efficacy endpoints in NASH (NCT01672879, NCT01672866), PSC (NCT01672853) and IPF (NCT01769196). The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data, so those failures cannot be pinned on the molecule versus the target, which is why U is secondary. PMID:39173635 reports that the parent antibody AB0023 did not inhibit LOXL2 catalytic activity or collagen cross-linking, which hints at non-engagement. That evidence is in vitro only and does not count for the human pillars.

The index long-term safety study (NCT01759511) was stopped for lack of efficacy after the companion Phase 2 trial (NCT01769196, PMID:27939076) met its futility criteria, with no benefit in progression-free survival. No human data show simtuzumab's exposure in lung tissue, how much it inhibited LOXL2, or any downstream biomarker change. Later papers say target engagement in humans was never measured. Lab work (PMID:39173635) suggests the parent antibody does not block LOXL2 catalytic activity, which points toward the molecule never engaging the target (F1a). But animal and in vitro data don't count here, and simtuzumab also failed in the liver-fibrosis, PSC and cancer trials. The bundle can't tell a non-engaging drug apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT02580305, neither dose (50 or 100 mg) beat placebo on ADAS-Cog 11 (p=0.41 and p=0.90). The Phase 1 study (PMID:29380267) found plasma exposure that rose more than in proportion to dose, and the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Only animal data show the drug got into the brain (PMID:28212021). The searches found no human evidence of target engagement: no 5-HT6 PET occupancy, no CSF levels and no pharmacodynamic biomarker. Because of that, the bundle can't tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. The sponsor's post hoc analyses blamed concurrent memantine, and benefit was confined to subgroups with agitation (PMID:36168659), which supports F3 as a secondary code. Every other 5-HT6 antagonist also failed, so F1b does not apply.

No web search was run, so this rests on the bundle alone. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, lung-tissue level or receptor-engagement data for ASM-024. In the index crossover trial (PMID:26252534), 50 and 200 mg inhaled doses did not block early or late allergen responses or sputum eosinophils or neutrophils. They did modestly improve methacholine responsiveness (PC20) and FEV1. Cough rose with dose but did not cap it. Within the same trial, ASM-024 lowered allergen-induced basophil CD203c (PMID:25660404). That is a downstream signal, but the drug's mechanism is unclear (nicotinic plus muscarinic activity). No other drug on these targets has succeeded in asthma (tc-6987 stopped at phase 2). A later moderate-asthma trial was terminated for lack of efficacy (NCT01793298). With no data on engagement, a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01703572 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study in lymphoid malignancies whose primary outcome was safety (DLTs). No results were posted, so it was not an efficacy test of brontictuzumab. In the solid-tumor Phase 1 (NCT01778439, PMID:29726923), plasma PK was characterized (nonlinear, half-life 1-4 days) and pharmacodynamic effects were reported in blood and tumor. That evidence comes from solid-tumor patients, not lymphoid disease, and was published after the index start. The MTD of 1.5 mg/kg was set by on-target diarrhea, and an efficacy signal appeared only in Notch1-activated adenoid cystic carcinoma. The bundle gives no stated reason the program stopped, so the code is assigned with low confidence.

The Phase 2b index trial (NCT03517566) found no IGA benefit at any dose from 3 to 50 mg (0.8–7.2% vs 1.9% on placebo), with no dose response, and was stopped for lack of efficacy. The companion trial NCT03948334 was also stopped. The searches turned up no human data on plasma or skin drug levels, H4R occupancy, or any pharmacodynamic biomarker. The Phase 2a trial (PMID:30414855) missed its pruritus primary endpoint; any EASI signal came from the same disease, so it cannot support inferred_adequate. Novartis investigators blame the target, saying H4R antagonism alone is not enough in AD, but with engagement never measured, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a target that doesn't matter. Safety was not limiting.

In NCT02618616, PASI fell 28.0% on adriforant and 37.4% on placebo (p=0.85), so the primary endpoint was missed. I found no human evidence of drug levels, H4 receptor occupancy, or downstream biomarker changes. The Pfizer Phase 1 trials (NCT00992342, NCT00856687) posted no results, and the pages I found give only in vitro or mouse pharmacology. The atopic dermatitis Phase 2a (NCT02424253) missed its primary itch endpoint and showed EASI improvement only as a secondary result, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. Later atopic dermatitis trials stopped for lack of efficacy. No other H4 antagonist has succeeded in psoriasis, so F1b does not apply. Because no source separates a drug that never engaged H4 from a target that does not drive psoriasis, the code is U.

Index trial NCT02880371 (ARRY-382 plus pembrolizumab) stopped for insufficient efficacy, not safety. Phase 2 ORR was 0%, 3.7% and 0% in the PD-1-refractory, pancreatic and ovarian cohorts. Phase 1b found 0-2 DLTs per dose level, and 300 mg was carried forward, so there is no clear evidence that tolerability capped the dose. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, CSF1R occupancy or pathway biomarker data (for example CSF1 levels or monocyte or macrophage depletion). The earlier phase 1 trial NCT01316822 has no posted results. No other CSF1R drug and no PubMed abstracts are in the bundle. Because engagement is no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged CSF1R from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The monotherapy Phase 1 in patients with advanced cancers (NCT01316822; AACR abstract A252, 2013, published before the index trial) found roughly dose-proportional exposure. At doses of 200 mg QD and above, CSF-1-stimulated monocyte pERK fell by more than 80%, with exposures above the IC50, and the investigators concluded that CSF1R was significantly inhibited at tolerated doses. In the index trial (NCT02880371), biomarkers moved as the mechanism predicts: serum CSF-1 rose with dose and circulating nonclassical monocytes were suppressed at the 300 mg MTD/RP2D, a dose not capped below what engagement needed. Even so, ORRs were 0%, 3.7% and 0%, and the study was stopped for insufficient efficacy, not safety. Engagement was shown at the dose tested yet there was no benefit, so the target appears not to drive response as tested (F2). Caveat: tumor macrophage depletion was not documented in these sources.

The index trial NCT01898520 (Sativex for spasticity in children with cerebral palsy, 0-10 NRS) posted no results and gave no stop reason. The same product and mechanism (CNR1 agonism in the CNS) met a spasticity NRS endpoint in multiple sclerosis (NCT00681538, p=0.0002). That supports inferring that exposure, engagement and pathway held in the CNS compartment. Dose-related central effects in humans (PMID:24281276, NCT04130633) support CNS engagement. No engagement data exist in children with cerebral palsy, and pediatric dose comparability is not shown. With engagement inferred adequate and no benefit reported, F2 is the best fit: CB1 agonism may not relieve cerebral palsy spasticity as tested. A small trial (n=72) could also contribute (F7). The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

The Phase 1 trial (NCT01156870, Sanofi summary) showed that plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose across 20–240 mg/m². It did not measure CA6/MUC1 binding in tumors, receptor occupancy or any pathway biomarker. CA15-3 fell only in patients who responded, so it marks response, not target engagement. A PET tracer study (PMID:33104454) used a Fab fragment, not the drug, and saw no significant tumor uptake. Corneal toxicity tracked exposure and forced a lower-intensity schedule (90 mg/m² D1D8 or 120 mg/m² Q2W). The index trial (NCT02984683) stopped for low response (ORR about 9%) plus eye toxicity, which explains the F6 secondary code. Because engagement is no_human_data, the evidence cannot separate a drug that did not engage from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F1a is secondary only because ocular toxicity capped the dose. Whether that cap fell below the level needed for engagement is unknown.

The index trial (NCT01403064) stopped for lack of efficacy. Oral mucositis at 55 Gy was 79.2% on placebo versus 100% (160 mg) and 77.3% (320 mg). The bundle has no direct PK or engagement data in mucositis patients. However, clazakizumab met ACR20 and DAS28 endpoints in RA at 25–200 mg SC monthly (NCT01373151, NCT02015520, PMID:26138593). Those doses are at or below the 160/320 mg used here. The RA paper also reports lab changes consistent with IL-6 blockade, and hs-CRP fell sharply in the dialysis trial (PMID:41178801). Systemic IL-6 neutralisation is therefore inferred adequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With the target neutralised and no benefit seen, IL-6 does not appear to drive radiation-induced mucositis as tested. Deaths and SAEs were numerically higher on drug, but the stated reason for stopping was lack of efficacy.

Clazakizumab met its primary efficacy endpoints in RA (NCT01373151, NCT02015520, PMID:26138593) at 5–200 mg SC, doses at or below the Crohn index arms (100–600 mg). Its target, systemic IL-6 ligand, was the same, so exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate. The RA trial reported lab changes consistent with IL-6 blockade, and dialysis patients showed dose-related hs-CRP suppression (PMID:41178801), so the pathway is adequate, though not shown in Crohn patients. In NCT01545050, 8-week remission showed no dose-response (0–33% vs 17.6% on placebo). This suggests IL-6 neutralization does not drive Crohn activity as tested (F2). However, the trial was terminated by sponsor decision, the arms were small (8–16 patients), and no statistical analysis was posted. The readout is therefore underpowered and not assessable (F7 secondary), which lowers confidence.

NCT02092909 was stopped for lack of efficacy, and its primary endpoint was safety only. In a 2013 Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers (doses up to 0.6 mg/kg), the sponsor reported sustained inhibition of TLR7-, 8- and 9-driven cytokine induction in blood cells stimulated outside the body. That was before the index trial, which tested doses at or above this level (0.6 to 2.4 mg/kg). I therefore rated engagement adequate, though the evidence is a press release, not a measurement of how well the drug blocked MYD88-driven signalling in WM tumour cells. The dose was not capped by tolerability; there was only 1 dose-limiting toxicity. The bundle has no WM biomarker data and no sponsor explanation for the failure. The best-supported reading is that the drug engaged its targets but blocking TLR7/8/9 does not drive WM (F2). Confidence is low, and U is the alternative if the healthy-volunteer evidence is set aside.

Exposure was adequate: linear PK at doses of 400 mg q2w and above indicated saturation of target-mediated disposition, PET showed tumor-specific uptake, no MTD was reached up to 2000 mg, and modelling predicted >95% target saturation (PMID:26463709, PMID:28497320, PMID:28733442). Engagement was adequate: membranous HER3 in tumor biopsies was maximally downregulated at 400 mg and above (PMID:26463709). PET did not show clear tumor saturation, which is a caveat (PMID:28733442). These data came from mixed HER3-positive solid tumors, not squamous NSCLC specifically. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported in the bundle. The index trial NCT02204345 was terminated after enrolling 12, with no stated reason and no results posted. F2 is the default given engagement without benefit, but it is weakly supported. A small, uninformative trial (F7) is also possible.

The index trial NCT04485702 is a Phase 1 bioavailability study of sublingual MELT-100 (midazolam plus ketamine) versus IV drug in 17 healthy volunteers. Its primary outcomes are Cmax, AUC and Tmax, so it was not an efficacy test in acute myocardial infarction and no efficacy readout failed. Plasma exposure to midazolam is well documented in human PK studies (NCT04392011, NCT05526911). GABA-A engagement and the downstream effect are inferred adequate because intranasal midazolam met its primary endpoint in seizure clusters (NCT01390220; approved for epilepsy) through the same CNS target. NCT02515890 also showed a clear amnestic effect. No engagement data exist in MI patients. This is not an efficacy failure of the drug, so F9.

In the index trial (NCT01258153), crying time fell by -119 min on high dose, -97 min on low dose and -91 min on placebo, with no significance test posted. Human NK2 engagement has been shown, but only with intravenous dosing: nepadutant blocked neurokinin A-induced gut motility in healthy volunteers (Lördal 2001) and neurokinin A-induced bronchoconstriction in asthma patients (PMID:19880429). Neither study used oral dosing in colicky infants. In infants, the only evidence is urinary drug recovery (NCT00655083) and population PK (PMID:39327792). The very high apparent oral clearance (68.6 L/h) points to low absorption, but no source tested gut engagement at these doses. A large placebo response and a dose-response trend (PMID:39327792) point to an underpowered trial, but nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

In the index trial (NCT01258153), oral nepadutant at 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg did not reduce crying or fussing in colicky infants any more than placebo. In adults, intravenous doses of 2–8 mg did block NKA effects: NKA-induced bronchoconstriction in asthma (PMID:19880429) and NKA-driven gut motility in healthy volunteers. Those were adult IV doses, not low oral doses of a poorly absorbed peptide in infants (PMID:11561086), so they are not comparable. In infants, drug was found in urine (NCT00655083) and measured in plasma (PMID:39327792), but nothing shows NK2 blockade in the gut at these doses. A modeled dose-response trend (PMID:39327792) hints the doses may have been too low, but this is not proven. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The trial was a small phase 2a with no significance test posted (F7).

Plasma PK was characterised in healthy volunteers (PMID:26249232). A human PET study, registered before the index trial (NCT01613703; PMID:28245513), showed dose-dependent brain TSPO occupancy from 20 to 200 mg, approaching saturation only at 200 mg. The index trial used 20 and 60 mg, so occupancy was likely partial and is not quantified for those doses. No downstream neurosteroid or pathway biomarker was measured in humans. The index trial was an exploratory proof-of-concept study of about 67 subjects per arm. It showed numerical improvements on all co-primary endpoints, largest at 60 mg, without significance. The authors still claimed evidence of efficacy and called for further evaluation (PMID:27910150), which suggests an underpowered design. Sub-saturating doses (F1a) and an ineffective mechanism (F2) remain possible.

Phase 1 studies (NCT01214629, NCT01214642; PMID:28097385) showed dose-dependent plasma exposure. They also showed exposure-dependent increases in phosphohistone H3, a marker of mitotic arrest, in tumor and skin biopsies. Preclinical work (PMID:26304237) validated pHH3 as the target-mediated biomarker, so engagement and pathway effect are treated as shown in humans. These patients had mixed advanced cancers, not specifically breast cancer. Neutropenia was dose-limiting, but pegfilgrastim allowed the higher doses taken into phase 2. Despite this, change in tumor size did not differ from ixabepilone (NCT01416389). Responses were near zero across other tumors (NCT01059643, NCT01025284), so Eg5 inhibition does not appear to drive clinical benefit. The index trial was small and short (F7 secondary).

Phase 1 studies in advanced cancers, which started 2007–2008 before the index trial, showed dose-dependent plasma exposure. They also showed exposure-dependent increases in phosphohistone H3, a mitotic-arrest marker of Eg5 inhibition, in tumor and skin biopsies (PMID:28097385; preclinical validation in PMID:26304237). This supports exposure, engagement and pathway effect, though not in SCLC patients specifically. Neutropenia was managed with pegfilgrastim, allowing the selected Phase 2 doses, so the dose was not shown to be capped below engagement. Despite this, the SCLC index trial gave a 2.6% response rate (NCT01025284). Other tumor cohorts showed 0% responses (NCT01059643), and breast cancer showed no tumor shrinkage (NCT01416389). Eg5 inhibition did not translate into clinical antitumor benefit.

In Phase 1, litronesib plasma exposure rose with dose. There were also exposure-dependent increases in phosphohistone H3 (the marker of mitotic arrest from Eg5 inhibition) in tumor and skin biopsies from patients with advanced solid cancers (PMID:28097385). I read this as adequate engagement and pathway effect, though the evidence came from exploratory analyses published only in 2017. Neutropenia was the dose-limiting toxicity, but pegfilgrastim allowed higher doses, and the Phase 2 regimens were chosen from the pharmacodynamic data, so dose was not shown to be capped below engagement. Even so, the index trial had 0% response in all six solid-tumor cohorts (NCT01059643). Small-cell lung (NCT01025284) and breast (NCT01416389) trials also showed minimal activity. Engaging Eg5 did not translate into tumor response, consistent with F2. On-target myelosuppression is a secondary factor.

In the index trial (NCT03203642), tesevatinib did not slow the growth of height-adjusted total kidney volume (htTKV) at any timepoint. The dose was set by tolerability alone. The ADPKD dose-escalation study (NCT01559363) found an MTD of 100 mg, and the sponsor picked 50 mg for the randomized trial on safety grounds. That is well below the 300 mg MTD in cancer patients (PMID:30030583). No human source measured EGFR/ERBB2 inhibition, receptor occupancy, kidney drug levels or a downstream biomarker at 50 mg. Plasma markers in the Phase 1 cancer studies were inconsistent, and the kidney engagement evidence is from rodents only (PMID:28729967). So the data cannot tell a drug that under-engaged EGFR apart from a target that does not drive ADPKD, which makes the code U. F1a is possible if the low dose fell short, but no source shows that.

The index trial NCT02154529 was a small (n=17) safety-primary phase 1/2 study in HER2+ metastatic breast cancer with brain metastases, closed for lack of response. Human phase 1 data (PMID:30030583) report plasma PK and an MTD of 300 mg, but say pharmacodynamic plasma markers were not consistently changed and no conclusions could be drawn. No human EGFR/HER2 engagement or CNS penetration is shown; brain data are mouse-only (PMID:33785646). Other agents on the same targets (lapatinib, neratinib, pertuzumab) are approved in breast cancer, so the target is validated there. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). U also applies because engagement is unmeasured. The tiny, descriptive trial (F7) limits any inference.

disease: metastatic malignant neoplasm in the brain
rationale: The index trial (NCT02154529) tested tesevatinib plus trastuzumab in HER2+ breast cancer with brain metastases. The sponsor closed it for lack of response after 17 patients. Human data are limited to plasma PK. In Phase 1, plasma pharmacodynamic markers were not consistently changed and no conclusions could be drawn (PMID:30030583). Brain penetration was shown only in mice, where unbound brain levels were low and EGFR inhibition was partial (PMID:33785646). The bundle has no human evidence of HER2/EGFR engagement in brain lesions. Tucatinib, another HER2 inhibitor, is FDA-approved for brain metastases in this setting. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Because engagement has no human data, U also applies. Doses reached the Phase 1 MTD, so the program was not dose-limited.

In the SOLAR trial (NCT02588261), naquotinib was compared with erlotinib or gefitinib in first-line EGFR-mutant NSCLC. PFS was 9.26 vs 9.59 months, with HR 1.611 favouring the comparator. The trial was stopped on the IDMC's recommendation. EGFR inhibition is clearly validated in this disease: erlotinib, gefitinib, osimertinib and others are FDA-approved for NSCLC. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for naquotinib, since the Phase 1 trial NCT02113813 posted no results and the only PubMed abstract is an in silico docking study. The failure therefore points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The ASP8273 arm had more serious AEs (84 vs 67) and deaths (39 vs 35), and NCT02192697 was classified as a safety stop, suggesting molecule-specific toxicity (F6) also contributed.

The index trial NCT02113813 is a Phase 1 dose-escalation study. Its primary endpoints are all safety measures (DLTs, AEs, labs, ECGs) and it posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of naquotinib (F9). The program appears to have ended when Astellas closed enrollment on the SOLAR IDMC recommendation (NCT02192697, NCT02500927). In SOLAR (NCT02588261), PFS favoured erlotinib/gefitinib (HR 1.611) and serious AEs were reported, so toxicity may have contributed (F6 possible). The bundle has no human exposure, EGFR engagement or pathway data. The only PubMed abstract (PMID:33955334) is an in silico docking study. This leaves the mechanism question indeterminate (U).

TMB-001 (topical isotretinoin 0.05%) acts on RARs in the skin. In ASCEND (NCT05295732), 41.4% of patients on TMB-001 responded on IGA versus 44.9% on vehicle (p=0.39). The only human PK found comes from the maximal-use arm and shows minimal systemic absorption. That is a safety measure. It says nothing about drug levels in the epidermis. No source measured RAR engagement in skin or a retinoid-responsive skin biomarker. The phase 2 trials (NCT04154293, PMID:35872261) reported only clinical endpoints. The sponsor blamed an unexpectedly high vehicle response, which points to trial design (F7). But the drug arm did no better than vehicle, and with no engagement data the bundle cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage its target or the mechanism does not matter here. So the primary code is U.

The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, TRPA1 occupancy or pathway biomarker data for ISC 17536. There are no Phase 1 results and no posted results. The index trial NCT01726413 missed its primary 4-week pain endpoint overall. The publication (PMID:34490850) reports significant, clinically meaningful pain improvement in an exploratory subgroup with preserved small nerve fiber function on quantitative sensory testing. It attributes the result to phenotypic heterogeneity and planned a phenotype-selected follow-up study. PMID:36622903 echoes this subgroup efficacy. A subgroup response, if real, implies some target activity, so this points to patient selection (F3). However, the subgroup was post hoc and engagement was never measured, so U remains plausible. No other TRPA1 drug succeeded.

NCT00733980 showed no separation from placebo on the Bech melancholia subscale (p=0.703). No study in the bundle measured brain levels or CRF1 receptor occupancy (receptor binding) in humans. Engagement was shown in other patient groups. In women with 21-hydroxylase deficiency, single doses lowered ACTH by about 41–43% (PMID:26751191). In anxious alcohol-dependent women, 350 mg daily strongly blocked the hormonal stress (HPA-axis) response on the dex-CRF test and dampened amygdala responses (npp201661). None of this was in MDD, and all of it was published after the index trial began. The tolerability data gave no sign that dosing was limited. Verucerfont also failed in PTSD and alcohol craving, and other CRF1 antagonists failed in MDD and anxiety. The investigators concluded that CRF1 antagonists do not work as monotherapy (PMID:28793974). Together this points to the target, not the molecule (F2). Confidence is medium because engagement in the brain was never measured directly.

The index trial, NCT01279083, was a Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study of topical DE-112 eye drops. Its primary endpoint was intraocular pressure (IOP) at day 29, and no results were posted. I found no human data on drug levels in the eye, A2A receptor engagement, or a downstream biomarker. I also found no statement from the sponsor (Santen) about why the program stopped. Patsnap lists evodenoson only as discontinued, and a 2019 Frontiers review mentions it only in passing, without glaucoma results. The other A2A agonist in glaucoma, OPA-6566, stopped at Phase 2 and has no shown success, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In NCT01603277, 400 mg IV KB003 missed its primary endpoint, FEV1 change at week 24 (118 vs 54 mL, p=0.224), and KaloBios stopped the asthma program. The full paper (PMID:26739717, PMC4716197) says PK samples were collected but gives no drug levels. GM-CSF was not measured in blood or sputum, the study did not test a range of doses, and no downstream biomarker was reported. The only PK data are in healthy Korean volunteers (PMID:41104395) and do not show the drug engaged its target. The authors suggest the dose may have been too low to neutralise GM-CSF in neutrophilic asthma and point to benefit in eosinophilic and other subgroups, so the cause could be low dose or the wrong patients. Because no human engagement data exist, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter: U, with F3 as secondary.

The index trial NCT04351152 (LIVE-AIR) did not fail. The bundle reports that lenzilumab increased its primary endpoint, ventilator-free survival, in hospitalised COVID-19 patients (PMID:35377717, PMID:34863332, PMID:33972949). That makes this F9, not an efficacy failure. Later analyses emphasise greater benefit in patients with CRP <150 mg/L (PMID:35793833, PMID:35037816), so a population or subgroup element (F3) is secondary. Dose-proportional systemic exposure was shown in healthy volunteers (PMID:41104395). In a COVID case series, CRP, IL-6 and inflammatory myeloid cells fell after dosing, a pathway signal (PMID:32587983). Direct GM-CSF neutralisation or engagement was never measured. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, so the business or regulatory cause is unconfirmed.

The index trial NCT01361555 was a long-term safety extension with a blood-pressure primary endpoint. It was terminated for 'failure to meet primary endpoint', most plausibly because the unselected TRD efficacy studies NCT01309945 and NCT01369095 failed; this reading is an inference. Healthy-volunteer PET in NCT00892840 (PMID:25116481, PMID:24337079), done before the index trial started, showed about 80% SERT occupancy at 0.5 mg and 14-35% DAT occupancy, levels the authors call therapeutic. No dose cap was evident, since 2-4 mg was tolerated (PMID:25904041). No downstream biomarker was measured. Later, the biomarker-guided trial NCT05113771 met its primary endpoint, suggesting benefit is confined to a selected subgroup, so wrong population (F3). F2 applies secondarily for the unselected population, and F9 because the index trial itself was not an efficacy test.

The index trial NCT01361555 was a long-term safety study with a blood-pressure primary outcome. It was terminated for 'failure to meet primary endpoint', most plausibly reflecting the parallel TRD efficacy trials (NCT01309945, NCT01369095), which completed without a met endpoint. Engagement was shown in healthy volunteers only: PET found about 80% striatal SERT occupancy at 0.5 mg multiple doses and 14–35% DAT occupancy, which the authors judged in the antidepressant-efficacy range (PMID:25116481, PMID:24337079). Doses up to 4 mg were tolerated (PMID:25904041), so the dose was not capped. A later biomarker-guided TRD trial at 1–2 mg met its primary endpoint (NCT05113771). This suggests benefit confined to a selected subgroup, so the code is F3. F2 also applies, and F9 because the index trial was not itself an efficacy test.

Exposure is supported by human PK showing a long half-life with steady state at about 36 weeks (PMID:30128316). Dystrophin was detected in all week 68–72 biopsies from DMD patients (PMID:27588424). That is evidence of exon skipping, but it was not quantified, and the bundle first shows it after the index trial started. Pathway is graded inferred_adequate on dystrophin production, although serum MMP-9 was not predictive of response (PMID:29263366). The index trial missed its primary endpoint (+10.3 m, p=0.415). The authors attribute this to greater variability and subgroup heterogeneity: power fell from 90% to 53% under looser inclusion criteria, and a post-hoc 300–400 m subgroup gained 35.4 m (p=0.039) (PMID:29203355). Earlier phase 2 trials gave mixed signals (NCT01153932, NCT01462292). Eteplirsen, an approved exon 51 drug, makes F1b plausible.

Code F9: the index trial NCT01963598 met its primary endpoint. Regeneron's patent reports that all three doses raised total lean mass at week 12 more than placebo (+1.7%, +1.8% and +2.3%; p≤0.008). Exposure and engagement: in healthy-volunteer Phase 1 studies (NCT01507402, NCT01720576), drug levels and total-GDF8 (myostatin) measurements pointed to saturating target engagement at 400 mg; the index trial used 300 mg. These were not patient data, and the patent carrying them appeared only later. Pathway: lean mass rose in sarcopenia patients. Strength and function improved only directionally, and a review says the lean mass gains came without better strength or function. So bigger muscle did not become a functional benefit. That fits F4 (wrong endpoint) or F2 (mechanism doesn't drive the outcome) as secondary codes. No stop reason was stated.

Roxadustat's human PK is well characterised (PMID:32603526). At 1–2 mg/kg it raised endogenous EPO and lowered hepcidin, a direct pathway readout of HIF-PH inhibition (PMID:26238121, PMID:26846333). It also met Hb endpoints in many CKD-anemia Phase 3 trials at comparable doses (NCT01750190, NCT01887600, NCT02652819), so engagement is inferred adequate. No engagement or EPO data in MDS patients appear in the bundle. In MATTERHORN, the 2.5 mg/kg dose was chosen from the lead-in (PMID:34724251) and was well tolerated. Transfusion independence was 47.5% vs 33.3% (p=0.217) (NCT03263091, PMID:38884137), so the mechanism did not deliver benefit in lower-risk MDS. Secondary codes: a possible subgroup benefit at higher transfusion burden (F3) and a high placebo TI rate (F7).

The Phase 1 trial (NCT02061865) tested rinucumab with aflibercept up to 3 mg:2 mg and reported only safety and tolerability. I found no human ocular pharmacokinetics, PDGFR-beta occupancy or other engagement data. In CAPELLA (NCT02418754), adding rinucumab gave no gain in BCVA over aflibercept alone. It also did no better on retinal thickness or on clearing subretinal hyper-reflective material, the fibrosis-related change that blocking PDGF is expected to produce, so I scored pathway inadequate. Tolerability did not limit the dose. No other drug on this target has succeeded in wet AMD; the same-target drugs listed reached Phase 2 or 3 without approval. Without engagement evidence, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged PDGFR-beta from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U. F2 would apply if engagement were assumed.

The index HCVerso2 trial (NCT01728324) met its primary SVR12-versus-historical-control endpoint for both regimens (p<0.0001; p=0.0020). Only the 24- versus 16-week duration comparison was non-significant (p=0.0532), so this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. Plasma exposure was characterised in HCV patients and healthy volunteers (NCT01525628, NCT01737996, PMID:25313217). Dose-dependent viral load reduction in HCV patients, registered in 2007–2009 before the index trial (NCT02176525, NCT00905632), supports adequate NS5B polymerase engagement and antiviral effect in the disease. The SOUND-C2 trial (NCT01132313, PMID:25512403) showed SVR with the interferon-free regimen. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping the program, so a commercial cause (F8) cannot be confirmed.

Engagement looks adequate, but the anti-myeloma benefit did not follow. In the Phase 1b relapsed/refractory myeloma study (NCT00741377, BJH 2014), the 10 mg/kg dose was chosen because the drug saturated its target, DKK1, through the whole dosing interval. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In the index smoldering myeloma trial (NCT01302886, ASH 2012 abstract), 10 mg/kg reached maximal, plateaued capture of total DKK1 by day 8. That shows engagement in this disease, but the data were published after the trial started. The downstream bone effect was only a trend: rising bone density in the Phase 1b and 'early evidence of anabolic bone activity' in this trial, so I rated pathway inferred_adequate rather than measured. The abstract stresses bone effects, not myeloma response. That points to F2: DKK1 neutralization does not drive tumor response in smoldering myeloma. No posted results or sponsor statement confirm the missed response endpoint, so confidence is medium.

Exposure was measured in humans. NCT01007032 reported dose-proportional Cmax up to about 1390 µg/mL with no DLTs through 20 mg/kg. PMID:22184397 reported troughs above the target concentration. Serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 rose consistently, the expected feedback from IGF1R blockade (PMID:22184397, 23956055, 23605083, 21750201). Biopsies showed pERK/pS6 suppression, though only in combination with selumetinib (PMID:25268371). These data come from other tumours and were published after the index trial began. Even so, the drug engaged its target without a dose cap. Adding cixutumumab did not improve response rate (20% vs 31%; NCT00870870), and other NSCLC trials were also negative (NCT01232452, NCT00955305). No other IGF1R agent succeeded in NSCLC. This points to a target that does not drive the disease.

Exposure was adequate. Dose-proportional Cmax was reached up to 20 mg/kg with no DLTs (NCT01007032, NCT00785538), and the 9 mg/kg trough exceeded the xenograft-effective level (PMID:22184397). Receptor occupancy was never measured directly. The engagement call rests on a surrogate: a consistent compensatory rise in serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 after dosing, which indicates systemic IGF-1R blockade. This was seen in metastatic breast cancer patients (PMID:23605083) and other cohorts (PMID:21750201, PMID:23956055), but published after the index trial started. At 10 mg/kg q2w, alone or with antiestrogen, there was no meaningful efficacy (PFS 2.0-3.1 months; PMID:26324738). Adding cixutumumab in HER2+ disease also failed (PMID:33852121). No IGF-1R agent succeeded in breast cancer, so the target likely does not drive the disease (F2). IR-expression heterogeneity and the lack of a non-IGF-1R control are secondary.

The Phase 2a Crohn's study (NCT03155945, PMC9802051) measured olorinab's plasma pharmacokinetics at 25 and 100 mg three times daily (TID). That shows systemic exposure for a peripherally acting drug. The study was open-label and uncontrolled, so its pain improvement cannot show that the target was engaged. No human data on CB2 receptor occupancy, receptor engagement or a downstream biomarker were found; the only mechanistic evidence is from rodents (PMID:33863856). In CAPTIVATE (NCT04043455, PMID:36740814), no dose (10–50 mg TID) separated from placebo on the primary endpoint. Only a prespecified subgroup with moderate-to-severe baseline pain responded to 50 mg (F3). The trial was terminated as a 'Business Decision' (F8), but the readout itself failed. Because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that failed to engage CB2 apart from a target that does not matter in IBS, so the code is U.

Plasma exposure and brain penetration are documented, so exposure is adequate. In healthy volunteers, PET with [11C]-RO5011232 (NCT01483469, which started after the index trial) linked plasma levels to mGlu5 occupancy. Applying that link to drug levels measured in the MDD patients, the JAMA Psychiatry paper (PMID:27304433) estimated only about 25% occupancy at 0.5 mg and 53% at 1.5 mg. That is partial engagement. By comparison, mavoglurant reached 85% occupancy at its top PET dose. So the mechanism may not have been fully tested. Dizziness rose with Cmax (PMID:29877614), and a modified-release formulation was developed to improve tolerability, which suggests a limit on higher doses, but no source says the dose was capped. No downstream biomarker data were found. Patient-rated scales favoured 1.5 mg while the clinician-rated MADRS did not, which points to a possible measurement or trial-design issue (F7). No source says what level of occupancy depression requires, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01015430 had safety, tolerability and PK as its primary outcomes, so it was not an efficacy test of basimglurant (F9). The program's actual efficacy failure was FragXis (NCT01517698; PMID:28816242): neither 0.5 mg nor 1.5 mg beat placebo on the ADAMS score, and the placebo response was marked. Human plasma PK exists (PMID:27123695). A healthy-volunteer mGlu5 PET occupancy study was registered (NCT01483469), and PMID:33541889 cites clinical exposure-occupancy data, but the bundle reports no occupancy levels and no data from FXS patients. Brain engagement is therefore not shown. That leaves no way to separate a drug that never engaged from an irrelevant target for the efficacy failure (U). Mavoglurant reached Phase 3 but no success is shown, so F1b does not apply.

Belimumab, which hits the same target (BAFF), is FDA-approved for SLE, so the target is validated in this disease. In SLE patients, blisibimod showed dose-proportional PK (PMID:26290435). Downstream markers moved as expected: B-cell reduction, lower anti-dsDNA, higher C3/C4, and less proteinuria (PMID:24748629, PMID:29563108). However, no direct BAFF binding or free-BAFF suppression is reported, so engagement adequacy is not shown. The phase 3 trial (NCT01395745) missed SRI-6 at the 200 mg weekly dose despite a steroid-sparing effect. A network meta-analysis ranked blisibimod weakest among BAFF agents (PMID:31777515), which supports a molecule-level shortfall. Secondary: the steroid taper confounded the SRI endpoint, and reviews cite flaws in patient selection, response criteria and glucocorticoid use (PMID:27663753).

In photosensitive epilepsy patients (NCT00784212, registered before the index trial; PMID:25963722), single selurampanel doses of 15–100 mg abolished or reduced the photoparoxysmal response dose-dependently, with a clear PK/PD relationship. This shows brain exposure and functional AMPA antagonism in humans at doses below the 250 mg used in migraine. Receptor occupancy was not measured, so engagement is judged from this functional CNS effect. Despite this, the migraine proof-of-concept trial missed its criterion: primary response 58% vs 40% on placebo, P=0.2 (PMID:23963355). That points to acute AMPA blockade not driving migraine pain relief as tested. The trial was small (n=75), with numerical trends such as pain-free 25% vs 16%, so F7 (underpowered) is secondary. No engagement data exist in migraine patients.

CNS pharmacodynamic activity at 50–100 mg was shown in humans: dose-dependent PPR suppression with a clear PK/PD relationship in photosensitive epilepsy (NCT00784212, PMID:25963722). This supports exposure and pathway, with engagement inferred, though not in tinnitus patients. In the index trial (NCT01302873, PMID:33637230), the TBF-12 responder endpoint met the proof-of-concept criteria and single-dose VAS loudness and annoyance fell, but 2-week VAS loudness did not separate from placebo. Dizziness affected 50% at 100 mg TID versus 9.6% on placebo. The 100 mg dose was more effective but less tolerated, and the authors called for AMPA antagonists with an improved benefit/risk ratio. Dizziness was also dose-related in epilepsy (PMID:28500678). Efficacy offset by on-target CNS adverse effects best explains the stop; the partially positive readout supports F9.

Exposure: 300 mg/day (150 mg BID) gave plasma exposures within the PK/PD-defined therapeutic window, with no DLTs (PMID:24868575, PMID:26526984, PMID:33811482). Engagement: exposure-related pSMAD2 reduction in PBMCs was shown in the first-in-human study in glioma and solid-tumour patients, not HCC (NCT01682187, PMID:25529192). Pathway: in second-line HCC, circulating TGF-β1 fell in about half of patients, and responders lived longer (PMID:30963691, PMID:32210440). The dose was not capped by tolerability. Despite engagement at the tested dose, the index trial showed no OS benefit for galunisertib alone or with sorafenib (NCT02178358). TGF-βRI inhibition does not appear to drive HCC outcome as tested. Biomarker-defined responder subgroups suggest possible heterogeneity (F3).

Lomustine plus galunisertib did not improve overall survival in recurrent GBM, and galunisertib alone did no better (NCT01582269; PMID 26902851). At the 300 mg/day intermittent dose, plasma exposure was in the predicted therapeutic window, and the drug was not capped by side effects (PMID:24868575). In first-in-human glioma patients, PBMC pSMAD2 fell in 64% of patients, by about 40% on average. That is above the 30% level set in advance as biologically effective (PMID:25529192, PMC4387272). However, the effect varied widely, and it was published after the index trial began. Brain or tumour drug levels were never measured; only one re-resected patient had lower ID1 and CD44. Peripheral engagement looks adequate, so this points to F2 (target doesn't drive the disease as tested), but weakly. Engagement at the tumour is unproven, hence the U secondary. Tissue-biomarker subgroup signals (IDH, pSMAD2) add F3.

Praliciguat showed dose-proportional PK and dose-related increases in plasma cGMP (direct sGC engagement) with sustained BP lowering at 15-40 mg in healthy volunteers (PMID:30422390). It also produced BP and lipid effects in T2D/hypertension (PMID:31858186). In the DKD index trial, 24-h SBP fell 4 mmHg, along with HbA1c and cholesterol, showing pathway activity at the tested 20/40 mg doses. UACR still did not differ significantly from placebo (-15%, p=0.17) (NCT03217591, PMID:33328269). No cGMP was measured in DKD patients themselves. Engagement was adequate, yet there was no significant renal benefit, consistent with F2. The modest point estimate in a 12-week, 156-patient trial suggests possible underpowering (F7 secondary). The 40 mg dose had more SAEs, but 20 mg was equally effective, so the dose was not limited.

In healthy volunteers (NCT02616861, PMID:30422390), praliciguat showed dose-proportional PK and dose-related plasma cGMP increases, the direct product of sGC stimulation, at doses including 40 mg, all tolerated. Sustained BP lowering confirmed the downstream vasodilatory pathway. In type 2 diabetes with hypertension, 40 mg lowered mean arterial pressure (PMID:31858186). The index trial (NCT03254485) used 40 mg and was not tolerability-capped, yet peak VO2 did not improve (-0.30, p=0.37). No HFpEF-specific engagement data are in the bundle. Vericiguat reached phase 3 in HFpEF but no success is shown, so F1b does not apply. With engagement adequate and no benefit, sGC stimulation does not appear to drive exercise capacity in HFpEF as tested.

ARMOR1/2 (PMID:26527750) assessed PK and reported a well-tolerated 2,550 mg/d dose. Pharmacodynamic changes were consistent with AR-signaling inhibition, with PSA50 of 54.5% in CRPC patients. So exposure, engagement (indirect, via AR-axis PD) and the PSA pathway effect held in this disease, and the dose was not tolerability-capped. That publication dates from 2016, after the index trial started in 2015. In the AR-V7+ index trial (PMID:31542304), the DMC closed the study early on interim evidence that rPFS would not be met, and galeterone's PSA50 was 13% versus 42% for enzalutamide. This suggests the AR/CYP17 mechanism of galeterone did not deliver the hypothesized advantage in AR-V7+ disease. Secondary: small sample, high censoring and dropout (F7); population-specific hypothesis (F3).

In Phase I patients with mixed advanced solid tumours (NCT00909740, NCT01075464), parsatuzumab showed typical IgG1 plasma PK and no MTD was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. A circulating marker of EGFL7 inhibition (CPCs, an EGFL7-expressing blood progenitor cell) fell in a dose-dependent way: 40–60% in 67% of patients at 5 mg/kg every 2 weeks. That result set the Phase II dose (7.5 mg/kg every 3 weeks, about 600 mg as used in the index trial). Engagement is rated adequate only through this indirect marker. No direct binding or ligand-lowering data exist, and the investigators later said validated PD biomarkers were lacking (PMID:28275117). Despite this activity, PFS was worse in NSCLC (PMID:29438092) and benefit was also absent in colorectal cancer (NCT01399684). That points to the mechanism not adding to bevacizumab. The authors also mention unselected populations (F3).

Plasma exposure was adequate: PK in the colorectal trial NCT01399684 matched population-model predictions from Phase 1a (Oncologist full text). No study measured target engagement directly, such as EGFL7 binding or neutralization in tumor. As a surrogate pharmacodynamic marker in the Phase 1 trials (NCT00909740, NCT01075464; JCI), circulating progenitor cells fell 40–60% in a dose-dependent way, sustained in 4 of 6 patients at 5 mg/kg with bevacizumab. These patients had mixed solid tumors, not only colorectal cancer. The marker did not track tumor response. Investigators blamed the lack of validated pharmacodynamic or predictive biomarkers (PMID:28275117, PMID:29438092). The CRC trial ran no pharmacodynamic analyses, and the NSCLC trial was also negative. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from an irrelevant target, so the code is U, with F2 possible.

No direct NGF-engagement or biomarker data exist for sciatica. Engagement is inferred: fasinumab met pain endpoints in OA through the same peripheral NGF mechanism (NCT02447276, NCT03304379, NCT02683239). Those OA doses (1–9 mg) were comparable to or lower than the sciatica doses of 0.1–0.3 mg/kg SC (about 7–21 mg). PopPK characterized systemic exposure across these doses (PMID:38323727). In acute sciatica, neither dose separated from placebo on the primary or any secondary pain/function endpoint, and both arms were numerically worse (PMID:25210473). Tolerability did not cap the dose. The OA engagement evidence postdates the 2009 index start. Other anti-NGF drugs show no success in neuropathic pain. NGF blockade appears not to drive acute radicular pain as tested.

In the Phase 1 trial in mycosis fungoides (NCT02580552), cobomarsen was measured in skin-lesion biopsies after systemic dosing. Those lesions showed de-repression of miR-155 target genes, the same pattern seen in directly injected lesions. The sponsor's protocol and 10-K describe this as pharmacodynamically relevant exposure, so the evidence was in this disease and predates the 2019 SOLAR start. Exploratory analyses also linked lower T-cell clonality and gene changes to the mechanism. This evidence is small and exploratory. Even so, in SOLAR (NCT03713320) the 4-month objective skin response rate (ORR4) was 15.8% vs 16.7% for vorinostat, with no superiority. That points to miR-155 inhibition giving no meaningful benefit (F2). The registry gives business reasons for stopping, and the small interim analysis (n=37) limits interpretation (F8, F7).

A population PK/PD model built from phase I/II data in geographic atrophy patients (PMID:26535160) described ocular and serum lampalizumab and CFD kinetics. It predicted near-complete vitreous target engagement at the 10 mg Q4W/Q6W phase 3 regimens. Exposure and engagement are therefore supported in this disease, though engagement is model-derived and was published in 2015, after the index trial started. No human downstream complement biomarker was reported, so pathway is no_human_data. Both phase 3 trials (NCT02247479, NCT02247531) and NCT02288559, which included a more frequent Q2W arm, showed no reduction in GA growth. The prespecified CFI-positive subgroup also showed no benefit, which argues against a selection explanation. Failure is best explained as a target that does not drive disease as tested.

The index cIAI trial (NCT01381562) had safety-only primary outcomes with 4-5 patients per arm, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated because microbiological resistance emerged on therapy in a separate cUTI trial (NCT01381549), not because of its own readout. NCT01702350 was stopped for the same reason. Human plasma and lung PK were shown at 1500 mg (PMID:23650164), so systemic exposure is documented. Intra-abdominal tissue levels and bacterial LeuRS engagement were never measured in humans. No human pathway data exist. Doses up to 1500 mg were tolerated, so the dose was not limited. Because engagement is no_human_data, the resistance finding cannot be attributed to the molecule or to the target, so U is a secondary code.

Human plasma PK of IV GSK2251052 was characterised (CL 22 L/h, t1/2 10.7 h, ~30% urinary excretion; PMID:23650164), and doses up to 4000 mg/day were tolerated (PMID:41125659), so tolerability did not cap the dose. The cUTI trial (NCT01381549) and its sister cIAI trial (NCT01381562, NCT01702350) were stopped because resistance emerged on therapy, which PMID:29437618 attributes to rapid microbiological failure. That study's animal comparison suggests GSK2251052 urinary exposure stayed below the mutant prevention concentration, a successor compound avoided resistance when it stayed above. Target engagement was therefore not sustained against the pathogen. No direct human engagement or biomarker data exist, and the MPC argument rests only on animal data. Confidence is low.

PANDA-1 (NCT03577899) and PANDA-2 (NCT03630952) were stopped because the primary endpoint, BCVA change at week 36, was not met. Intravitreal conbercept met its BCVA endpoint in BRVO (NCT03108352), which acts through the same retinal VEGF compartment. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. Serum VEGF also fell after injection in ROP infants (PMID:33836990). No direct engagement evidence exists in wet AMD. Many anti-VEGF drugs are approved for wet AMD (aflibercept, ranibizumab, brolucizumab, faricimab), so the target clearly matters. That points to a molecule- or comparison-level shortfall rather than a target failure. The bundle does not show the comparator design, so a missed active-control margin (F9) cannot be confirmed. Confidence is low.

The index first-in-human trial (NCT01115751, PMID:25902900) was a dose-finding study. Plasma exposures exceeded predicted efficacious levels, but rose less than dose-proportionally. Target engagement was weak. At 500 mg, just over half of patients showed reduced S6 in skin biopsies at Day 8, the effect was not maintained, and plasma levels did not correlate with S6. Avatar models showed minimal pharmacodynamic effect and antitumor activity was minimal. So the mechanism was not adequately tested (F1a). The trial nominally met its RP2D endpoint, so it was not a true efficacy test (F9). Capivasertib, on the same target, is approved in prostate cancer, which points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Combination studies (PMID:28750271, PMID:34781168) added no pharmacodynamic evidence.

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation trial (NCT00887926, 5–30 mg/kg) was terminated for lack of efficacy. The MTD was reported as NA. No deaths occurred, and serious AEs did not cap escalation, so dose_limited is false. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, FLT3 occupancy or downstream signalling data, so all pillars are no_human_data.
