Several FLT3-targeted drugs (gilteritinib, midostaurin, quizartinib) are FDA-approved in AML, which shows the target matters in myeloid leukemia. That points to the molecule, a neutralizing antibody rather than a kinase inhibitor, as the likely failure (F1b) rather than the target. The modality difference and the thin bundle leave this partly indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT01983683 was a non-inferiority comparison against vancomycin. Clinical cure was 81% vs 85.7%, difference -4.7 [-10.7, 1.3]. It missed only the presumed -10% non-inferiority margin, with no safety excess. The twin Phase 3 NCT01987895 met non-inferiority (-1.4 [-7.2, 4.3]). This is not a clear efficacy failure of the drug, so F9. Exposure at the site of action was adequate: faecal levels were thousands of times the C. difficile MIC90 in patients with severe CDI and in healthy subjects (PMID:26419191, PMID:24106141; NCT02053181). The bundle has no direct target-engagement or pathway measures. Development was later discontinued, and the pediatric trial NCT03105479 was terminated for business/portfolio reasons (F8 secondary).

The index trial, NCT01543451 (Phase IIa proof of concept, 138 patients), does not look like a failed readout. In May 2013, Helsinn and Zealand said it ended with positive results and moved elsiglutide into Phase IIb. I could not confirm whether its primary endpoint reached statistical significance, so this F9 call is tentative. The program stopped after the larger Phase IIb (ASCO 2017, 480 patients). A third-party protocol describes that trial's results as numerically positive but not statistically significant. No human evidence on target engagement turned up: no data on GLP-2 receptor activation or citrulline as a marker of gut mass. The ASCO abstract shows citrulline was measured, but I could not retrieve the results. If the later Phase IIb is treated as the failure, the code would be U. My search budget ran out before I could check further.

The index Phase Ib/II trial (NCT01495247) stopped because it could not establish an MTD or recommended dose with paclitaxel. It was a dose-finding failure, not an efficacy readout. Across the program, tolerability capped dosing: DLTs occurred at the lowest dose with abiraterone (NCT01717898, PMID:28282611), RCC was closed for toxicity (NCT01453595), and stomatitis and GI toxicity limited 400 mg bid (PMID:32993794). PD analyses were planned (PMID:30446785, PMID:32993794), but the bundle shows no human exposure, engagement or pathway results. Other drugs on the same targets (everolimus, alpelisib, inavolisib) are approved in breast cancer. This points to a molecule-specific failure (tolerability preventing adequate dosing) rather than an invalid target. Novartis later halted the drug entirely (NCT01856101).

The index trial NCT01482156 was a Phase 1 dose-finding study of BEZ235 plus everolimus in solid tumors. Its primary endpoints were DLT and adverse events, not efficacy, and it has no posted results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug in CML (F9). The only leukemia trial (NCT01756118/PMID:32993794) enrolled a single CML-BP patient. It measured PK and phospho-AKT/S6/4EBP1, but the bundle reports no pharmacodynamic results, so exposure, engagement and pathway lack human evidence. Tolerability was a recurring problem: stomatitis and GI toxicity at 400 mg BID, and DLTs at 200 mg BID with abiraterone (NCT01717898, PMID:28282611, NCT01453595). Novartis also halted marketing of BEZ235 (NCT01856101). Whether the target matters in CML stays indeterminate.

The index trial NCT01482156 was a Phase 1 dose-finding study of everolimus plus BEZ235 in solid tumors. Its primary outcomes were DLTs and adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test in AML (F9). In leukemia, the Phase 1 study (NCT01756118, PMID:32993794) set an RP2D of 300 mg BID because stomatitis and GI toxicity at 400 mg BID were incompatible with prolonged treatment. Only 4 of 24 patients showed clinical benefit. Pharmacodynamic markers (pAKT, pS6, p4EBP1) were collected, but the bundle reports no results for them, so the pillars are no_human_data. Toxicity recurred across the program (NCT01717898, NCT01453595), and Novartis stopped BEZ235 development (NCT01856101), so F6 and F8 are secondary.

In the index trial, BEZ235 failed to beat everolimus on PFS in pNET (8.2 vs 10.8 months) and was stopped for futility (NCT01628913). Everolimus, which acts on the same target (MTOR), is FDA-approved in pNET. The bundle has no human PK/PD data showing BEZ235 adequately inhibited PI3K/mTOR in vivo. Phase 1 reports mention PK/PD sampling but no results (PMID:32993794, PMID:30446785). PMID:40956674 shows pathway loss only in ex vivo tumor slices, which do not count. Tolerability was a recurring problem: DLTs at 200 mg bid with abiraterone, stomatitis at 400 mg bid, and an RCC trial closed for toxicity (NCT01717898, PMID:32993794, NCT01453595). This points to a molecule-specific failure rather than an invalid target. It is not proven that the dose was capped below what engagement needed.

Serelaxin's systemic exposure in humans is well characterized and dose-proportional (PMID:25408331, PMID:30014598, NCT02002702). There is no direct RXFP1 occupancy measure. Engagement is inferred from two lines of evidence. First, mechanism-consistent human PD effects: eGFR rose in healthy volunteers (PMID:25408331), renal plasma flow rose in CHF (NCT01546532), and PCWP fell in AHF (NCT01543854), the latter two registered before the index trial. Second, the AHF trial NCT02007720 met its primary endpoint. However, none of this was shown in coronary artery disease patients. Despite this, myocardial perfusion reserve did not improve versus placebo (p=0.438, NCT01979614), suggesting RXFP1 agonism does not improve coronary perfusion as tested. The index trial was small and exploratory (n=58), so F7 is a secondary code.

In the index trial NCT05401565 (10 mg, n=29), balovaptan showed no separation from placebo on CAPS-5 or on any secondary endpoint, and it was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Human data show only plasma pharmacokinetics (PMID:34176392). Brain V1a receptor occupancy was only predicted: it was modelled from in vitro and ex vivo data (PMID:38308741; the protocol says about 89% predicted). I found no measured human occupancy, CSF level or pathway biomarker. The results of the healthy-volunteer proof-of-mechanism study (NCT02205073) were not found. No AVPR1A drug has succeeded in PTSD, and balovaptan also failed in autism (NCT02901431, NCT03504917), so inferred_adequate does not apply. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F7 is secondary because the very small trial was underpowered. The publication gives no reason for the failure.

The phase 3 trial NCT03504917 was stopped for futility. The 10 mg dose was well tolerated, and plasma pharmacokinetics in humans are well described (PMID:34176392). However, V1a occupancy in the brain was only predicted, at about 89% at trough, from plasma levels plus ex vivo platelet binding and preclinical brain penetration (PMID:38308741; PTSD protocol). There was no PET tracer, so no human CSF level, occupancy or pathway biomarker was measured. The healthy-volunteer proof-of-mechanism study NCT02205073 posted no results. No other V1a drug has succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Placebo response was large across the trials (PMID:35690870, PMID:37045991), which suggests a design problem. Even so, because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that did not engage from a target that does not matter. That makes the code U.

Oral emixustat had dose-proportional plasma PK (PMID:21519291, PMID:24056528). In GA patients (NCT01002950, registered 2009 as a PK/PD study, before the 2013 index start), 2–10 mg produced dose-dependent suppression of rod recovery after photobleach (PMID:25932553). This ERG readout is an indirect measure of RPE65 inhibition and slowing of the visual cycle. The 10 mg dose gave near-complete suppression in Stargardt patients (PMID:33214244). The index trial used the same 2.5–10 mg doses, and mechanism-related ocular AEs were frequent but did not cap the dose. GA growth was unchanged at every dose (PMID:29716784). The same null result occurred in Stargardt (NCT03772665). With the target engaged and the visual cycle slowed, RPE65 inhibition does not appear to drive GA progression.

Oral emixustat had dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:21519291, PMID:24056528). In Stargardt patients, 10 mg gave near-complete (median 96.7%) suppression of rod b-wave recovery, an indirect measure of RPE65 inhibition (NCT03033108, PMID:33214244). That study was published before SeaSTAR (NCT03772665, started 2019) and was used to select its dose. Ocular adverse events were mild and did not cap the dose. Downstream bisretinoid lowering was never measured in humans. Despite this engagement, macular atrophy growth was unchanged (1.280 vs 1.309 mm²/yr). Geographic atrophy growth was also unchanged in the related disease (NCT01802866). Preclinical data suggest retinal sequestration rather than RPE65 inhibition drives protection (PMID:26075817). Together this points to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested.

Volixibat is a minimally absorbed, gut-restricted ileal ASBT inhibitor (PMID:29548345). Its action at the site was shown in Phase 1 trials registered before the index trial (NCT02287779, NCT02475317). Fecal bile acid excretion rose about 4-fold, maximal at ≥20 mg/day, with large dose-related C4 increases and LDL reductions (PMID:29548345, PMID:29304731). In NASH patients in the index trial, C4 rose and total/LDL cholesterol fell dose-dependently. The authors state this is evidence of target engagement, yet the trial was terminated for lack of efficacy. Interim MRI-PDFF and ALT endpoints were missed, and at week 48 histology responders were 9/30 on drug vs 5/13 on placebo (PMID:32234329, NCT02787304). Tolerability (mild diarrhoea) did not cap dosing. The mechanism was engaged but did not drive benefit in NASH.

In the phase 2/3 trial (NCT01110720, PMID:24873720), intranasal davunetide 30 mg twice daily had no effect on PSPRS or SEADL. My searches found no human data showing that the drug reached the CNS (no CSF or brain levels), bound microtubules or tau, or reliably moved a downstream marker. A schizophrenia MRS study found only a trend in brain NAA (npp201323), which is not evidence of engagement. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Later post hoc work by the investigators blames the 4R-tau population (PMID:30865715) and claims a benefit in women (PMID:37845254, PMID:42399413). That supports F3 as a secondary code. These are exploratory analyses. Their claim of 'target engagement' rests on CSF p-tau correlations, not on any direct measure.

Verubecestat reduced CSF Aβ40, Aβ42 and sAPPβ (a direct BACE1 product) in healthy volunteers and in AD patients (PMID:27807285, PMID:30347431). The AD patient data came from NCT01496170, which started in 2011, before the index trial. In the EPOCH PET substudy, amyloid load fell dose-dependently, about 22% at 40 mg (PMID:35794343), so the pathway moved. EPOCH (NCT01739348, PMID:29719179) still showed no ADAS-Cog or ADCS-ADL benefit. The prodromal trial NCT01953601 failed too, with 40 mg worse than placebo (PMID:30970186). Reviews conclude that robust BACE inhibition gives no clinical benefit (PMID:30277096). Disease stage and slow plaque turnover are offered as explanations (F4). Adverse events increased and may be on-target (PMID:31387606, F5). Tolerability did not cap the dose.

Plasma PK supported 9–20 mg/kg dosing with no MTD reached (PMID:23591447), so exposure looks adequate and the dose was not tolerability-capped. The only human engagement measure, a [64Cu]-patritumab PET study, found apparent tumor receptor occupancy of only ~42% after 9 mg/kg. That study had 3 evaluable patients with mixed solid tumors, not NSCLC specifically, and was published in 2016, after the index trial started (PMID:26567113). This suggests partial engagement. The bundle has no pathway biomarker data. The index trial enriched for heregulin-high patients on the strength of a phase 2 subgroup signal (NCT01211483), but PFS was worse with patritumab in both strata (NCT02134015). The subgroup selection hypothesis failed (F3 secondary). Overall, the mechanism was likely not adequately tested. The evidence is thin.

Index trial NCT02633800 showed no PFS benefit in heregulin-high SCCHN (HR 0.93, p=0.83). Plasma exposure was adequate: no MTD was reached and PK supported 9–20 mg/kg dosing (PMID:23591447). The only human engagement data is a PET study in mixed advanced solid tumors (n=3 evaluable). At 9 mg/kg, apparent tumor HER3 receptor occupancy was only about 42% (PMID:26567113). That is partial occupancy, not shown in head and neck cancer, and published after the index trial started. No pathway biomarker data exist. The mechanism therefore appears incompletely tested (F1a), though the evidence is thin. The heregulin-high selection strategy, prompted by a subgroup signal in NSCLC (NCT01211483), also failed in NCT02134015, so patient selection is a secondary consideration (F3).

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Patritumab plus cetuximab/platinum gave identical PFS to placebo in HRG-high HNSCC (5.56 vs 5.56 months, HR 0.93; NCT02633800). Plasma PK supported 9-20 mg/kg dosing with no MTD reached, so exposure was adequate and the dose was not tolerability-capped (PMID:23591447). The only engagement measure, a PET study in mixed solid tumors (n=3) published after the index trial started, showed only about 42% apparent tumor HER3 occupancy at 9 mg/kg (PMID:26567113). That is partial engagement, not shown in HNSCC. No pathway biomarker data exist. The HRG-high enrichment rested on an NSCLC subgroup (NCT01211483) that failed to replicate (NCT02134015). Partial occupancy suggests the mechanism was not fully tested, but the evidence is thin.

In NCT05592418, rintatolimod missed the primary endpoint, change in PROMIS Fatigue at week 13. The difference from placebo was 0.03 (p=0.985), and both arms improved by about 25 points. I found no human data on TLR3 engagement or on downstream markers such as interferon, 2'-5' oligoadenylate synthetase or RNase L, either in long COVID or at the doses used. The pathway evidence I found comes from cell experiments (PMC8227153) or describes the mechanism without human measurements (the CFS review). The rintatolimod COVID trial in cancer patients (NCT04379518) enrolled only 4 people and produced no usable data. The sponsor blamed patient selection: it named a moderate-to-severe subgroup for a follow-up trial and pointed to a secondary 6-minute walk test result, which is consistent with F3. Because engagement is unknown, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Exposure was adequate. In Phase 1 (PMID:36717298), the 192 and 384 mg doses later used in PROSEEK gave CSF levels above the in vitro c-Abl IC50 for the whole dosing interval, with similar levels in PD patients. No dose cap from tolerability was reported. Target engagement in humans was never measured: there is no c-Abl inhibition or phospho-substrate marker. The authors only inferred 'potential' inhibition from CSF concentrations. CSF biomarkers in the DLB trial (PMID:40939527) did not change, including homovanillic acid, but none of them directly reads out c-Abl. PROSEEK (NCT03655236; PMID:41634026) favored placebo, and neurofilament light rose. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F2 is possible if CSF exposure is taken to mean engagement.

Index trial NCT03827655: IV TAK-954 0.1 and 0.5 mg did not shorten GI recovery after surgery (HR 0.92, p=0.649). Phase 1 trials showed plasma exposure (NCT03173170, NCT03870555). Receptor engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate: velusetrag met its clinical endpoint in chronic idiopathic constipation through the same GI 5-HT4 target (NCT00391820/PMID:21039672). Pathway effects were clear: faster GI and colonic transit in healthy volunteers (PMID:19691492) and shorter gastric emptying at all IV TAK-954 doses up to 1 mg in gastroparesis (NCT03281577). None of this was shown in postoperative patients. No tolerability cap is evident. With the mechanism engaged and the expected motility effect shown, the lack of benefit points to 5-HT4 agonism not driving recovery in postoperative GI dysfunction as tested.

Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional PK was shown in healthy volunteers and constipation patients (PMID:19691492). Receptor occupancy was never measured. Engagement is inferred_adequate because velusetrag met a clinical endpoint in chronic constipation at 15–50 mg, the same 5-HT4 target in GI tissue (NCT00391820, PMID:21039672). The pathway was clearly engaged in gastroparesis: gastric emptying accelerated before the index trial (NCT01718938, PMID:33811761). In the index trial, emptying improved at all doses and normalized in >70% at 30 mg. Yet the symptom endpoint missed after multiplicity adjustment, and only the lowest dose showed a nominal signal (PMID:36624727). Faster emptying did not translate into symptom relief, so the mechanism does not drive symptoms as tested. Secondary: endpoint/proximal dissociation (F4) and a possible idiopathic subgroup signal (F3). Dose was not tolerability-limited.

Velusetrag 15 mg showed dose-proportional plasma PK in healthy volunteers and constipation patients (PMID:19691492). It accelerated colonic transit and gastric emptying at 15-50 mg in humans (PMID:19691492) and in gastroparesis (NCT01718938, NCT03281577), so the pathway pillar held. Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same 15 mg dose met the efficacy endpoint in chronic idiopathic constipation through the same GI 5-HT4 target (PMID:21039672, NCT00391820). None of this was shown in CIPO patients. In CIPO, the WGGSAIS change was not significant (p=0.13, NCT05724069), with no tolerability cap on dose. The mechanism engaged without benefit, so F2. The crossover trial was very small (n=15), so underpowering (F7) is plausible.

The index trial (NCT00991796, PMID:24148258) found no PFS or OS benefit when tigatuzumab was added to carboplatin/paclitaxel in unselected NSCLC. It was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. The only human target-binding evidence is the 111In-CS-1008 imaging study in colorectal cancer (NCT01220999, PMID:26124477). It started after the index trial and was not done in NSCLC. Serum PK and tumor localization were shown, but tumor uptake occurred in only 63% of patients, was not dose-dependent, and was heterogeneous within patients. Lack of uptake tracked with lack of clinical benefit. No human apoptosis or pathway biomarker was reported. Engagement therefore looks incomplete. A prespecified FcγR-genotype subset showed a non-significant PFS trend, suggesting patient selection may also matter (F3). The bundle is thin.

The index trial (NCT01033240, PMID:26071796) missed its time-to-progression endpoint at both tigatuzumab doses. Weekly dosing was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The only human target data come from colorectal cancer (NCT01220999, PMID:26124477, started after the index trial). In that study, imaging found the drug in tumours of only 63% of patients, uptake did not rise with dose, and DR5 expression did not predict uptake. This counts as plasma and tumour exposure. It does not measure DR5 activation or downstream apoptosis signalling, and nothing was measured in liver cancer. The HCC sensitisation work (PMID:22978563) is preclinical only. No source explains why the program failed. Engagement in liver cancer therefore has no human data, so the code is U. Patchy tumour uptake hints at F1a.

The index trial (NCT00945191) had one arm and no success threshold. 12 of 24 patients had confirmed partial responses with carboplatin/paclitaxel, so the result is descriptive and cannot be judged a pass or fail. Serum drug levels are documented, so exposure counts as adequate. The only human target evidence is a 111In-tigatuzumab imaging study in colorectal cancer (NCT01220999/PMID:26124477), published in 2015, after the index trial began. It showed the antibody reached tumour in only 63% of patients, and this did not depend on dose. Uptake only shows binding, not activation of the receptor (receptor occupancy was validated only in mice, PMID:24045184), and no ovarian data exist. No apoptosis or pathway biomarker was found. A randomised lung cancer trial (NCT00991796) showed no added benefit. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter. The patchy tumour uptake points weakly to F1a.

Sucampo stopped the Phase 2a oral-spray trial of cobiprostone in oral mucositis (NCT02542215) after a futility analysis. The company said the clinical benefit was too small to justify continuing, reported no safety concerns, and ended development of the drug. That rules out toxicity (F5/F6) and business reasons (F8) as the cause. I found no human data showing that the drug reached the oral mucosa, activated the CLCN2 chloride channel there, or moved any downstream biomarker. No other drug on the same target has succeeded in this disease, so F1b does not apply. The other cobiprostone trials did not produce usable efficacy data: NCT00597818 posted no results, and NCT00737594 stopped because it could not enrol enough patients. With no human evidence on whether the target was engaged, the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged CLCN2 from a target that does not matter in this disease, so the code is U.

Evacetrapib reached robust plasma exposure (NCT02168803, PMID:24452615). It inhibited CETP activity 83–95% at 100–500 mg in dyslipidemic patients (PMID:24786356; NCT01375075 registered 2011) and 84–91% in healthy volunteers (PMID:24961753). The expected pathway effects followed: HDL-C rose about 80–130% and LDL-C fell 15–48% (NCT01105975, 2010, before the 2012 index start). The 130 mg dose used was well tolerated (PMID:25736283), and the index trial showed no excess of serious AEs, so dose was not limited. Despite full engagement and lipid effects, the 12,092-patient outcomes trial showed no benefit (HR 1.006, p=0.91; NCT01687998). No other CETP inhibitor in the bundle succeeded. CETP inhibition does not reduce cardiovascular events as tested.

The index trial NCT02260635 met its primary endpoint: LDL-C fell 34.3% versus 0% on placebo, with no serious adverse events. Its 'insufficient efficacy' termination therefore reflects the program-wide stop, not a failure of this trial; the sister Japanese trial NCT02260648 and NCT02227784 also met their endpoints. The pillars were measured directly in dyslipidemic patients before the index trial started. Plasma exposure was shown (NCT02168803, PMID:24452615). CETP activity was inhibited 83–95% in Japanese dyslipidemia patients (PMID:24786356, 2014), with large rises in HDL-C and falls in LDL-C (PMID:24961753, NCT01375075). The underlying failure was the outcome trial NCT01687998, where events were neutral (HR 1.006) despite full engagement. That points to CETP inhibition not reducing cardiovascular risk (secondary F2).

MK-6913 is a selective ERβ agonist. In the Phase 2a hot-flash trial NCT01015677, 75 mg did not beat placebo (−40.7% vs −34.4%; p=0.488). Merck stopped development after an interim analysis showed the compound missed its pre-set efficacy criteria. No human data turned up on exposure, ERβ engagement or a downstream biomarker: no Phase 1 results, papers or PK/PD reports. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from an ERβ mechanism that does not matter here, so the code is U. Secondary F7: the active control, estradiol 1 mg, also failed to reach significance against placebo (p=0.069). With a high placebo response (−34%) and about 33 women per arm, the trial had limited power to show any effect.

The index trial NCT01020006 was a Phase 2 safety and tolerability study. Its primary outcome was a descriptive count of treatment-emergent AEs (8/8, 18/18, 16/16), so it was not an efficacy test of PCI-27483 plus gemcitabine. Serious AEs were numerically higher in the drug arm (12/18 vs 7/16), but the counts are small and no clear toxicity signal is shown. The bundle has no human exposure, factor VIIa engagement or pathway data, such as coagulation markers, and no Phase 1 results or publications. With no efficacy failure shown, F9 applies. If an efficacy failure were assumed, the absence of engagement data would make it indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT00948259 was a 30-patient escalating-dose safety pilot. Its primary endpoint was adverse events, and PMID:22936007 states it could neither support nor reject benefit, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). The program's real efficacy failure was ARGO (NCT01350362/PMID:25537011), which showed no benefit. There, engagement is unresolved: human PK is plasma only (PMID:40871085), with no CSF levels or GSK3 inhibition measured. CSF signals were scattered: BACE1 fell in a small subgroup, and the placebo rise in AChE activity did not occur on drug (PMID:32955735). So a non-engaging drug cannot be separated from an irrelevant target (U). The sources point to a benefit confined to mild patients at 500 mg (F3).

The index trial NCT02091362 was a 6-week ambulatory blood-pressure safety/PD study, not an efficacy test. Its 'unmet' primary was a significant SBP rise (+2.26 mmHg). Efficacy was shown earlier: HbA1c fell versus placebo in NCT01241448 and partly in NCT00871572. Pillars held in T2DM before 2014. Plasma exposure was documented (NCT01836198, NCT02217618). Compensatory glucagon rises indicated receptor blockade, and fasting/postprandial glucose fell with hepatic glycogen increasing (PMID:25656305, NCT01588366). The program ended on benefit-risk grounds: hepatic fat rose (NCT02111096, NCT01588366), along with dose-dependent aminotransferase elevations and the BP increase. These mechanism-plausible liver and BP effects offsetting glycemic benefit support secondary F5.

Intravitreal nesvacumab plus aflibercept was not superior to aflibercept on BCVA at weeks 12 or 36 (NCT02712008, PMID:35234673). The same result occurred in wet AMD (NCT02713204). The bundle has no ocular exposure, Ang2 neutralization or Tie2 pathway data in humans. The intravitreal Phase 1 (NCT01997164) posted nothing. Systemic PK in oncology (PMID:26490310) is not the relevant compartment. The nominal week-36 thickness gains are confounded by the combination and dosing schedules, so they do not show engagement. Faricimab, another ANGPT2 drug, is FDA-approved for DME, which points to the molecule or regimen rather than the target. However, the index trial demanded superiority over aflibercept, so the case for F1b is weak and U also applies. Dose was not limited and safety was comparable.

Intravitreal REGN910-3 (nesvacumab plus aflibercept) showed no BCVA superiority over aflibercept at weeks 12 or 36 (NCT02713204), echoing the DME trial NCT02712008. The bundle has no human ocular exposure, Ang2 engagement or pathway data. The intravitreal Phase 1 (NCT01997164) posted no results. The IV oncology Phase 1 (PMID:26490310) gave only plasma PK, and its angiogenesis biomarkers were uninformative, which is not relevant to the eye. Faricimab, which also hits ANGPT2, is FDA-approved for AMD. That points to the molecule rather than the target, given no evidence this drug engaged adequately. However, faricimab's benefit is not shown here as superiority over anti-VEGF, so an indeterminate reading (U) also fits.

In healthy volunteers, JNJ-42165279 reached plasma and CSF, raised plasma and CSF fatty acid amides, and saturated brain FAAH occupancy (PET, [11C]MK3168) at doses ≥10 mg (PMID:29575526; PET trial NCT02169973 registered before the index trial). The index trial used 25 mg. In the MDD patients of that trial, the drug produced substantial plasma fatty acid amide increases that correlated with drug levels (PMID:41616640). HDRS17 change still did not separate from placebo (difference -0.2, p=0.416). This points to FAAH inhibition not driving antidepressant benefit as tested (F2). One caveat: the SAD study suggested 25 mg trough levels may not fully inhibit FAAH (PMID:33070154), so incomplete engagement (F1a) remains a secondary possibility. Tolerability did not limit the dose.

In healthy volunteers, JNJ-42165279 reached plasma and CSF, raised plasma and CSF fatty acid amides, and PET (NCT02169973, PMID:29575526) showed brain FAAH occupancy saturating at doses of 10 mg or more. In the index SAD trial at 25 mg daily, LSAS change missed significance, though responder rates and CGI-I favoured the drug. The authors state that trough concentrations at 25 mg were insufficient to completely inhibit FAAH activity, which may have led to suboptimal efficacy (PMID:33070154). Engagement is therefore judged inadequate (partial at trough) in patients, so the mechanism was not fully tested. Tolerability did not cap the dose; the drug was well tolerated. Positive secondary responder endpoints suggest a possible endpoint sensitivity issue (F4).

In healthy volunteers, PET showed brain FAAH occupancy saturated at doses ≥10 mg. The same study showed raised CSF and plasma fatty acid amides (FAA) (PMID:29575526, NCT02169973; published before the index trial began). The index trial dosed 25 mg BID, above the saturating dose and twice daily, which addresses the trough shortfall reported with 25 mg QD in social anxiety (PMID:33070154). In ASD patients, FAA concentrations rose throughout treatment (PMID:39414987), so engagement and pathway were confirmed in the disease. Tolerability was acceptable and the dose was not capped. All primary ABI endpoints still missed (NCT03664232), so FAAH inhibition did not drive core ASD symptoms as tested. Some secondary endpoints were nominally positive (RBS-R) and the sample was small (61 analysed), so endpoint choice and power may have contributed.

In healthy volunteers, JNJ-42165279 raised plasma and CSF fatty acid amides and saturated brain FAAH occupancy on PET at doses of 10 mg or more (PMID:29575526, NCT02169973). In the index MDD-with-anxious-distress trial, 25 mg produced substantial plasma FAA increases that correlated strongly with drug levels, yet HDRS17 did not separate from placebo (PMID:41616640, NCT02498392). The disease-population evidence came from the index trial itself. The SAD trial suggested trough levels at 25 mg once daily did not fully inhibit FAAH (PMID:33070154), so partial engagement remains a secondary explanation (F1a). However, 25 mg twice daily also failed in PTSD and ASD despite raised anandamide (PMID:40382500, PMID:39414987). This supports a mechanism that does not drive the disease (F2). Tolerability did not cap the dose.

Exposure was measured in humans. Phase 1 serum and CSF PK showed that doses of 10 mg/kg or more (AFFINITY used 750 mg, about 10 mg/kg) reached concentrations at or above the level linked to 90% of maximal remyelination in rats (PMID:25340070). No human source measured LINGO-1 binding, occupancy or downstream signalling. The best available remyelination readout, VEP latency in optic neuritis, did not differ from placebo in the ITT populations of RENEW and RENEWED (NCT01721161, NCT02657915). SYNERGY showed no dose-response trend (NCT01864148). AFFINITY missed its primary endpoint, with only numerically larger effects in older, longer-duration and higher-EDSS subgroups (PMID:41454463). That suggests a possible population problem (F3). Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug never engaged LINGO-1 or whether LINGO-1 blockade does not matter, so the code is U.

Exposure: the Phase 1 trials (PMID:25340070) measured opicinumab in serum and CSF. At doses of 10 mg/kg or more, levels matched or exceeded the level linked to 90% of the maximal remyelination effect in rats, and the index trial gave 100 mg/kg. That benchmark comes from rats, so 'adequate' rests on cross-species extrapolation. Engagement: no human evidence found of LINGO-1 occupancy, LINGO-1 neutralization or LINGO-1 internalization; the secondary-site mechanism (PMID:31928294) was shown only in vitro. Pathway: no remyelination biomarker was shown in humans, and phase 1 blood and CSF transcript profiling found no significant changes. The ITT primary endpoint was missed, with only per-protocol and older-age subgroup signals (PMID:30349850, which points to F3). The MS trials also failed (NCT01864148, NCT03222973). Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

NCT02957617 was the extension study. It was terminated because the parent Phase 2b trial in lumbosacral radiculopathy (NCT02935608) missed its primary and secondary endpoints, and Biogen then stopped development in this indication. The human data in the bundle are healthy-volunteer pharmacokinetics only (PMID:33278330, 31650711, 36045316): plasma exposure rose with dose, and doses up to 450 mg twice daily were tolerated. No source reports human Nav1.7 occupancy or channel block at nerve sites, or a pharmacodynamic biomarker change. The electrical hyperalgesia PD study (NCT00964288) ended on a safety event without results. The trigeminal neuralgia trial also missed its primary endpoint. No other drug on the same target succeeded. The sources give no mechanistic explanation, so a drug that never engaged Nav1.7 cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter here: U.

Plasma exposure was measured, which counts for this peripheral target: Phase 1 studies (PMID:33278330) and a population PK analysis that included erythromelalgia patients. No source shows human Nav1.7 engagement, such as channel block in patients' nociceptors or a pharmacodynamic biomarker. The index trial (NCT02917187, n=8) posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. A positive Phase 2 readout in small fiber neuropathy (NCT03339336, 200 mg) does not settle engagement. It was not a pivotal result, and molecular pharmacology work describes vixotrigine as a broad-spectrum sodium channel blocker, so any benefit there may not come through Nav1.7. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from an irrelevant target, so the code is U. The tiny trial size also points to F7.

In the index randomized-withdrawal trial (NCT01540630, PMID:28216232), BIIB074 150 mg TID gave fewer treatment failures than placebo (33% vs 64%), but the difference was not significant (p=0.097). Only 29 patients were randomized. Plasma PK and tolerability up to 450 mg BID are documented in healthy volunteers (PMID:33278330), so systemic exposure was achieved. No human Nav1.7 engagement or pathway biomarker is in the bundle: the electrical hyperalgesia study NCT00964288 was terminated without results. The same-target drugs listed (lidocaine etc.) are not approved in trigeminal neuralgia, so F1b does not apply. Recruitment difficulties and a small sample (PMID:30587219) suggest the trial was underpowered (F7). Without engagement data, the cause is indeterminate.

Rodatristat ethyl produced robust, dose-dependent reductions of plasma and urinary 5-HIAA, the main serotonin metabolite, in healthy subjects (PMID:35795492; likely from Phase 1 NCT02746237, which predates the index trial). This indicates systemic exposure and TPH1 engagement in humans. The bundle does not show engagement in PAH patients. In ELEVATE-2 (NCT04712669), both doses significantly worsened PVR (+63% and +64% vs +6% on placebo). Activity measures also declined (PMID:41973984), and serious AEs were more frequent on drug. No downstream pathway effect (e.g., vascular remodeling) is shown in humans. With engagement adequate and no benefit, or even harm, peripheral serotonin-synthesis inhibition does not appear to drive PAH as tested (PMID:39307144). The harm may be on-target (F5).

The index asthma allergen-challenge trial (NCT04673591) posted no results. Human evidence of target engagement exists. A PK-PD model built on clinical data from healthy volunteers and RA patients used cell-surface CD4 downmodulation as the activity marker (PMID:28090323, 2016, before the index trial). This shows exposure and engagement in humans, but it was strongest in healthy volunteers and diminished in RA, possibly because of thioredoxin-1. No engagement data exist in asthma patients, and no downstream Treg-activation pathway biomarker is shown. The drug also failed in RA (NCT01999192). With engagement shown in humans and no benefit, the default is target/mechanism failure (F2). Reduced engagement in inflamed disease is plausible, so F1a is secondary. The bundle is thin.

Index phase IIb (NCT01999192) missed ACR20 at week 12 at all three doses (42–47% vs 35% placebo). The dose cap was not tolerability: dosing went up to 200 mg weekly, was well tolerated, and adverse events were comparable to placebo. PMID:29343509 reports dose-dependent CD4 downmodulation in RA patients, calling it 'the expected biological effect'. A PK-PD model built on clinical data (PMID:28090323) shows plasma exposure was measured. No human readout of downstream Treg activation is given, so the pathway pillar is no_human_data. PMID:28090323 notes weaker CD4 downmodulation in RA than in healthy volunteers, possibly because thioredoxin-1 impairs binding. That leaves open partial engagement (F1a secondary). Overall, engagement was achieved without benefit (F2). Engagement data were published after the index trial started.

Buspirone is FDA-approved for anxiety, a CNS indication acting via 5-HT1A partial agonism, so brain exposure and HTR1A engagement are inferred_adequate at clinical doses. This assumes the anxiety and JM-010 doses are comparable, which the bundle does not confirm. Human healthy-volunteer data show linear PK (PMID:2860931) and central monoaminergic effects (PMID:9826102). There is no direct occupancy or biomarker evidence in dyskinesia patients. The index trial NCT02439203 posted no results, and the bundle does not show the readout. With engagement presumed adequate and no demonstrated benefit, F2 is the closest fit. Later JM-010 trials (NCT04377945, NCT05516875) were terminated for business reasons, so F8 also applies. The bundle is thin, hence low confidence.

APD405 is Acacia Pharma's IV buspirone. In the index trial (NCT00895830), no dose from 0.3 to 3 mg reduced 24-hour PONV compared with placebo, and the results showed no dose-response. Neither the bundle nor my search found human evidence that these low IV doses produced 5-HT1A occupancy, central exposure or a pathway biomarker. Human data cover only oral doses of 10–40 mg (PMID:2860931, PMID:9826102), and no source links those to the IV doses. The anxiety approval is for a different route and dose, and no source shows the exposure is comparable, so inferring engagement from it is not justified. No sponsor explanation was found; Acacia went on to develop APD421 (amisulpride) for PONV instead. Since engagement is unknown, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not drive PONV.

Plasma exposure was shown in humans (PMID:27999038). No direct miR-124 or target-engagement data exist in COVID-19 patients. However, the same 50 mg once-daily dose met clinical efficacy endpoints in ulcerative colitis, in Phase 2b (NCT03760003) and Phase 3 (NCT05507203, NCT05507216). That indication works through the same systemic anti-inflammatory miR-124 mechanism in immune cells, so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. In the miR-AGE trial (NCT04393038, PMID:37781656), 50 mg gave no benefit over placebo on the hard respiratory-failure outcome and was stopped for futility. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The most consistent reading is that this anti-inflammatory mechanism does not drive progression of COVID-19 as tested. Confidence is moderate because engagement in COVID-19 was inferred rather than measured.

The index trial NCT01597505 compared surotomycin with active vancomycin on a non-inferiority basis. Clinical cure was 79.0% vs 83.6% (difference -4.6, 95% CI -11.0 to 1.9). It missed only the -10% margin and was not a superiority failure. The twin Phase 3 trial NCT01598311 met non-inferiority (83.4% vs 82.1%), and Phase 2 cure rates were comparable to vancomycin (NCT01085591). On exposure, healthy volunteers reached very high stool concentrations (6394 μg/g) with minimal systemic absorption (PMID:28347318). On engagement, clostridial gut counts fell in healthy volunteers (PMID:26787687). Both sources were published after the index trial started. There was a numerical death imbalance (18 vs 9), but the bundle does not attribute discontinuation to it.

In GLACIER (NCT01258907), orticumab, an anti-oxLDL (MDA-p45 ApoB) IgG1, missed its FDG-PET target-to-background ratio primary endpoint. Reviews say there were no major effects on imaging or on circulating inflammatory markers, so I rated the pathway pillar inadequate. I found no human data on drug levels in plaque or on engagement, such as oxLDL binding, immune-complex formation or free oxLDL lowering. The only mechanistic evidence comes from primates and mice (PMID:24049738, PMID:33857652), which does not count. No other drug on this target is in the bundle. Because engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. One review cites methodological weaknesses in the trial (F7 secondary).

The index CRPC trial (NCT03690141) gave tomivosertib 200 mg BID, presumably the RP2D from NCT02605083. It produced 0/16 responses and was terminated for lack of efficacy. The only human pharmacodynamic evidence is from metastatic breast cancer (PMID:39576211). There, serum levels were measured and tumour biopsies showed a clear reduction in eIF4E S209 phosphorylation (target engagement), with proteome and translatome perturbations (pathway effect). No toxicity cap was reported. However, that engagement was shown in another tumour type, not prostate cancer, and was published in 2025, after the index trial started. Comparability of dose and tissue is uncertain. Taken together, this most supports F2: MNK1/2 inhibition does not drive response in CRPC. Confidence is low.

The index CRPC trial (NCT03690141, 200 mg BID) produced 0/16 responses and was stopped for lack of efficacy. No tolerability cap is described. Human target engagement comes only from a metastatic breast cancer phase 1b (PMID:39576211, NCT04261218). There, serum drug levels were measured and tumour biopsies showed a clear reduction in eIF4E S209 phosphorylation, the main MNK1/2 substrate, plus proteome and translatome perturbations. This supports adequate exposure, engagement and pathway effect, but the dose is not stated in the bundle. Engagement was not shown in CRPC patients, and this evidence appeared after the index trial began (2020 registration, 2025 publication). F2 is the most supported code, with low confidence because the evidence comes from another disease.

The index trial NCT04495621 was a small single-arm Phase 1b/2 with descriptive outcomes only: RP2D 48 mg, no DLTs, Phase 2 ORR 14.2%. It had no prespecified success threshold or hypothesis test and was classified not_efficacy and not_assessable, so it was not a formal efficacy test. Exposure at the 48 mg MTD matched preclinical efficacious levels, and FDG-PET SUVmax fell in 5/7 patients with mixed solid tumors (PMID:25231405). That is a downstream pathway signal, not direct target-engagement data, and no CRC-specific pharmacodynamics appear in the bundle. PMID:36793223 is model-based extrapolation only and does not count as human evidence. Dose was not capped by tolerability. Why the program stopped is not shown, so U is a secondary code.

Aldoxorubicin, a doxorubicin prodrug, did worse than topotecan in second-line metastatic SCLC (median PFS 1.5 vs 2.7 months; NCT02200757). The bundle has no direct human PK, TOP2A engagement or biomarker data. The pillars are inferred_adequate only because the drug met a PFS endpoint in soft tissue sarcoma (NCT01514188, 2012, before the index trial) and response rates in Kaposi sarcoma (NCT02029430). This is systemic tumour exposure, but the dose comparability is not shown. Doxorubicin, which hits the same target, is FDA-approved in SCLC, so TOP2A inhibition is a valid mechanism there. The failure therefore points to this molecule or its delivery rather than the target, though nothing shows engagement in SCLC patients. The evidence is thin, hence low confidence.

Aldoxorubicin's plasma pharmacokinetics were measured in patients with solid tumours at 230–350 mg/m2 (PMID:25388939). However, no human data show drug levels in brain or glioblastoma tissue, TOP2A engagement, or a downstream biomarker. The claim that it crosses the blood-brain barrier comes only from mouse data (PMID:25379024) and from the sponsor and ASCO 2016 abstract reading tumour responses as a sign of penetration. Neither is a measurement. The drug's efficacy signals in soft tissue sarcoma and Kaposi's sarcoma (NCT01514188, NCT02029430) involve a different tissue compartment, so they cannot stand in for engagement in the brain. Doxorubicin is not approved for glioblastoma, so F1b does not apply. The index trial (NCT02014844) produced 1 response in 28 patients. The bundle cannot separate a drug that never reached its target from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT01018875; PMID:25024314) tested 1 and 3 mg doses and stopped for futility. ADAS-Cog scores were numerically worse than placebo, while donepezil worked, so the trial could detect a drug effect. The Phase 1 paper says no human receptor occupancy study was done for ABT-288. The 1 and 3 mg doses were chosen within healthy-volunteer and elderly tolerability limits, using occupancy predicted from Ki, about 25-40% at 1 mg and 50-70% at 3 mg. Only plasma levels were measured in humans; brain levels, occupancy and biomarkers were not. Histamine-type side effects such as insomnia and abnormal dreams hint at central activity but are not measured engagement. The schizophrenia trial (NCT01077700) also failed, at higher doses. Nothing separates a drug that did not engage enough from an H3 target that does not matter, so the code is U. F1a is possible because tolerability capped the doses.

Exposure was shown in people with schizophrenia. In the Phase 1 trial NCT00888693 (PMID:24215171), patients tolerated doses up to 60 mg, and trough CSF levels were about 40% of plasma, so the drug reached the brain and the dose was not limited by tolerability at 10–25 mg. No human H3 receptor occupancy was ever measured. Occupancy and neurotransmitter-release data come only from rats (PMID:22815533), and there is no human biomarker showing the pathway responded. More psychosis-related and sleep-related side effects on ABT-288 hint at CNS activity but are not formal engagement evidence. The index trial (PMID:24516190) and the Alzheimer's trial (PMID:25024314) both failed. No H3 antagonist has succeeded in schizophrenia, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement is unmeasured, it is not possible to tell whether the drug failed to engage the target or the target does not matter, so the code is U.

The index Phase 3 trial (NCT02956486) of 50 mg elenbecestat missed CDR-SB (diff -0.17, p=0.385). It was stopped for no evidence of efficacy plus an AE profile worse than placebo. PMID:33569570 states elenbecestat reduced CSF Aβ, and PMID:30277096 says BACE inhibitors robustly and dose-dependently lowered CSF Aβ in AD patients, so engagement is treated as adequate. Exposure is inferred from that CNS effect. Both papers postdate the index start, and the Phase 1 trial in AD patients (NCT01600859) posted no results. No BACE1 inhibitor in the bundle succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Target lowering without benefit points to F2. PMID:33938131 suggests plaque turnover is too slow for BACE inhibition to work. The worse AE profile adds a possible F5.

The index Phase 2 trial (NCT02544633) missed its ORR endpoint in all MET-altered NSCLC cohorts (ORR 0–25%). The Phase 2 publication (PMID:38417277) attributes the modest activity to suboptimal drug bioavailability, already seen in Phase I. Formulations were repeatedly changed for poor exposure (PMID:36459255; NCT00975767 was terminated for reformulation). That publication also reports lower than anticipated rises in soluble shed MET, a pharmacodynamic marker, in NSCLC patients. Phase I reported only exploratory, unquantified engagement. Other MET inhibitors (capmatinib, tepotinib) are FDA-approved in this disease, which points to a molecule problem rather than the target. Exposure and engagement were inadequate, so the mechanism was not properly tested: F1a, with F1b secondary.

Tanezumab neutralizes systemic NGF. It met pain endpoints in osteoarthritis (NCT00733902, NCT00744471, NCT00830063) and in interstitial cystitis bladder pain (NCT00601484), so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. Modeled free-NGF suppression in OA (PMID:37470295) supports this. Engagement was not measured in endometriosis. In the index trial (NCT00784693) there was no benefit: the point estimate favoured placebo (LS diff 0.41 [-0.87, 1.69]). Dose was not capped by tolerability; serious AEs were 0/22 on tanezumab. This points to NGF blockade not driving endometriosis pain as tested (F2). Recruitment stopped early, leaving only 35 patients analysed, so the trial was underpowered (F7 secondary). The bundle gives no stated rationale for stopping.

Index SC trial (1–20 mg) showed no pain benefit at any dose (NCT00999518). No pillar was measured in IC. Engagement is inferred adequate because tanezumab met pivotal OA endpoints at 5–10 mg through the same peripheral NGF target (NCT00733902, NCT00830063). Modelled free-NGF suppression in OA (PMID:37470295) supports this but was published after the index trial. An earlier IC trial at 200 μg/kg IV met its primary endpoint (NCT00601484, PMID:21420111). The sponsor's pooled analysis attributes benefit to women and to patients with non-urological somatic syndromes, not pelvic-pain-only patients (PMID:26576710), which points to patient heterogeneity. Early termination during the 2010 FDA clinical hold (PMID:29386912) may have limited power, but the bundle does not state the index trial's stop reason.

Engagement was not measured in CP/CPPS. It is inferred_adequate because tanezumab at comparable IV doses (10–20 mg) met pain endpoints through systemic NGF neutralization in OA, interstitial cystitis, chronic low back pain and diabetic neuropathy (NCT00733902, NCT00601484, NCT00876187, NCT01087203). Modeled free-NGF suppression in OA patients (PMID:37470295) is consistent with this. The single 20 mg IV dose in the index trial gave only a marginal pain effect (−0.47, 90% CI crossing zero; NCT00826514). The authors call for stricter phenotype-based selection (PMID:23010344). A pooled analysis found benefit confined to women with IC/BPS and to patients with nonurological somatic syndromes, with no effect in men with CP/CPPS alone (PMID:26576710). The sources therefore attribute failure to population heterogeneity. The trial was a small proof-of-concept study (F7), and the target may not drive pelvic-only pain (F2).

BFH772 is a potent VEGFR2 inhibitor in vitro (Cayman). It was tested as a 1% ointment in a small proof-of-concept trial (n=36, three arms) in erythemato-telangiectatic rosacea (NCT01449591). The trial measured blood drug levels but posted no results. The Cochrane review of unpublished data found BFH772 no better than vehicle. We found no human data on skin drug levels, VEGFR2 inhibition in skin, or any downstream vascular biomarker, from either this trial or the psoriasis trial (NCT00987870). No other VEGFR2 drug in the bundle succeeded in rosacea. The evidence cannot tell apart a topical drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The very small sample size adds a possible F7 (trial design) element.

The index trial (ONYX-3, NCT00902928) was a phase IIb dose-confirmation study comparing darexaban regimens with enoxaparin. Its 'miss' was no difference between qd and bid dosing or between 30 and 60 mg/day. VTE rates were similar to enoxaparin, and the authors concluded darexaban appears effective (PMID:24136153). So this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. Darexaban beat placebo in Asian orthopaedic trials (PMID:22952213) and showed a dose response in ONYX-2 (PMID:20088935). In healthy volunteers, exposure and engagement were dose-dependent, with FXa activity lowered and PT/aPTT prolonged (PMID:23929659, PMID:27121937; NCT01655056 registered 2006). D-dimer fell in AF patients (PMID:26052866). The bundle gives no reason the program stopped.

The index trial RUBY-1 (NCT00994292, PMID:21878434) was a safety and tolerability dose-finding study. Its primary endpoint was bleeding, not efficacy. Bleeding rose two- to four-fold with dose, as expected for anticoagulation on top of dual antiplatelet therapy. Efficacy showed no signal, but the authors state the study was underpowered and call for a phase III trial. So it was not an efficacy test (F9), with on-target bleeding (F5) and power limits (F7) as secondary codes. In healthy volunteers, plasma exposure and FXa activity inhibition were dose-dependent, and PT/aPTT tracked exposure (PMID:23929659, PMID:27121937; NCT01655056 registered 2006). Pathway effects appeared in patients: D-dimer fell in AF (PMID:26052866) and VTE fell dose-dependently after hip arthroplasty (PMID:20088935). No engagement was measured in ACS patients.

Bococizumab clearly engaged PCSK9 in hypercholesterolemic patients before the index trial began, cutting LDL-C by 43-84% in Phase 1 and about 50-57% in Phase 2/3 (PMID:29078037, NCT01592240, NCT01968967). So exposure, engagement and pathway were adequate. The target is validated: the sister outcomes trial NCT01975389 met MACE (HR 0.79), and evolocumab is approved. The index trial (HR 0.99) was terminated early when the whole program was discontinued. The sources attribute that to a molecule-specific problem: a high rate of anti-drug antibodies that reduced exposure, giving attenuated and highly variable LDL lowering (PMID:37658997, PMID:37994400). Early termination with short follow-up left the index trial unable to show benefit, so F7 and F4 are secondary.

Phase 1 showed dose-related plasma exposure, near-complete urinary LTE4 inhibition at ≥50 mg and 24 h blood LTB4 inhibition at ≥150 mg (PMID:22803688). In asthmatics, 100 mg suppressed sputum LTB4 by >90% (PMID:23331559) and sputum LTB4 and urine LTE4 by >90% (PMID:24333186). The pathway effect followed: the allergen early and late responses and sputum eosinophils were attenuated (NCT00748306). The drug was well tolerated up to 200–300 mg, so dose was not limiting. Yet the index exercise-challenge trial showed no dose separating from placebo, up to 200 mg (NCT00812929). Trough FEV1 also missed in the dose-ranging and add-on trials (NCT01147744, NCT01156792, NCT01248975) and in neutrophilic asthma (NCT01471665). FLAP inhibition was achieved but did not drive clinical benefit in asthma as tested.

The index trial NCT03001219 was terminated for lack of efficacy: ACR50 at Week 12 was 11.1% on 810 mg versus 16.2% on placebo. The only other trial, Phase 1 healthy-volunteer study NCT02742779, posted no PK or engagement results, and the bundle has no PubMed abstracts. There is no human evidence of exposure, Nav1.7 engagement or pathway effect at the doses used. Other SCN9A blockers (bupivacaine, lidocaine) are local anesthetics used in osteoarthritis pain, not RA, so F1b does not apply. The index trial also measured anti-drug antibodies, which suggests the drug identity mapping is uncertain. Nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT00656097 was a Phase 2 safety and neutralizing-activity study of CL184 plus vaccine in healthy adults. Its primary outcome was safety and tolerability, and its endpoint class is not_efficacy, so it was not an efficacy test against rabies. In Phase 1 work in healthy volunteers (PMID:18804136), serum rabies virus neutralizing activity was detectable after 20–40 IU/kg. All subjects reached adequate RVNA (>0.5 IU/mL) with vaccine, supporting exposure and functional engagement, though not in patients with the disease. A validated RFFIT assay supported this pharmacodynamic measure (PMID:22547629). No human data address downstream effects in infection. The bundle gives no reason for stopping and no failed efficacy readout, so F9 applies.

The index trial NCT01134120 was a Phase 1 3+3 dose-escalation study whose primary objectives were safety and a recommended dose, not efficacy. It met them: MTD 120 mg, with plasma PK characterized (Cmax at 4 h, t1/2 about 6 h). Spleen and symptom responses at that dose supported further testing (PMID:28934680), and the program advanced to Phase 2 (NCT01594723). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred from the 120 mg Phase 2 response rates of 95% in JAK2 V617F PV and 90.5% in ET (PMID:30025280), but MF response was only 9.1%. That suggests benefit concentrated in other MPN subtypes, so F3 is secondary. The primary code is F9 because the index trial was not an efficacy test.

The index trial NCT05647343 is a Phase 1 healthy-volunteer safety/PK study with an adverse-event primary endpoint and no posted results. It was not an efficacy test of ciclopirox in NSCLC, so F9 applies. The NSCLC Phase 2 (NCT04032847) was terminated by sponsor decision with only descriptive TEAE endpoints. No human data show UROS engagement or a pathway effect in NSCLC. Oral ciclopirox plasma PK and survivin repression were shown in hematologic malignancy (PMID:24273151), but that is not UROS target engagement. Other sources describe poor oral bioavailability and GI toxicity (PMID:34059639, PMID:31113837). Mechanistically, it remains indeterminate whether the drug never engaged its target or the target does not matter (U as secondary).

The index trial NCT01953081 was a 13-patient Phase 1/2 safety and pharmacodynamics comparison against metoclopramide in enteral feeding intolerance. It reported only participant counts for adverse events and gastric retention, with no statistical test, so it was not an efficacy test of felcisetrag (F9). Its small size and descriptive design also mean it could not answer an efficacy question (F7). Plasma exposure was characterised in healthy volunteers (NCT01644240), a trial that was terminated for business reasons. Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred from a dose-dependent acceleration of gastric, small bowel and colonic transit in gastroparesis patients (PMID:33711180), which supports the pathway pillar. That evidence comes from a different disease and was generated after the index trial.

FORT-1 (NCT03410693) showed rogaratinib ORR 19.5% vs 21.6% for chemotherapy, with no superiority. Plasma exposure was robust at 800 mg BID in bladder cancer patients, and the MTD was reached without DLTs (NCT01976741), so the dose was not limited. Engagement is inferred: hyperphosphatemia consistent with FGFR1 engagement and a 41.7% ORR in SDH-deficient GIST (PMID:42191879), but this is another disease and was published after the index trial. No PD biomarker was shown in urothelial cancer. Erdafitinib is approved in urothelial carcinoma, so the target matters there. Rogaratinib enrolled by FGFR mRNA expression, whereas PMID:31405822 notes FGFR inhibitor activity seems restricted to genetic aberrations. This points to patient selection, with a molecule-specific explanation (F1b) also possible.

The index trial, NCT01322594, was a Phase 1 safety study in COPD. It reported only adverse events at doses from 10 to 1000 mg, with no serious adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test (F9 secondary). The myeloma program stopped after the Phase 1b study NCT04671251 tested 4, 9 and 14 mg/kg every 4 weeks. Avalo said the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose, but there was no efficacy signal and the program was dropped. I found no human data on free IL-18 lowering, drug levels in bone marrow, or downstream biomarkers for camoteskimab, in myeloma or in any other disease. Without engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that failed to neutralize IL-18 from IL-18 not mattering in myeloma, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT02096666, n=11, Asian Phase 1/2) has no posted results. The program ended after the parallel Phase 2 (NCT02016534; PMID:30366938) showed lower-than-expected efficacy: ORR 18% in MET-amplified gastric/GEJ cancer and no responses in other tumors. Phase 1 (PMID:30425090) gave plasma PK at the 300 mg MTD. Headache from off-target adenosine-transport inhibition set that MTD (PMID:31330495), but no source shows the cap fell below the dose needed to engage MET. No human evidence of MET phosphorylation inhibition, receptor engagement or a pathway biomarker turned up. The >90% inhibition threshold comes only from xenografts (PMID:27196782). Partial responses suggest some activity, but nothing separates incomplete engagement from limited MET dependence. The index trial itself was not a clear efficacy test, so F9 is secondary.

Plasma exposure is documented at the 300 mg QD RP2D (PMID:30425090). Headache from off-target adenosine transporter inhibition set the MTD (PMID:31330495), but that dose was still active. No human pMET or occupancy data appear in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate only loosely: at the same dose, AMG 337 produced responses in MET-amplified tumors (29.6% ORR, PMID:30425090; 18% in gastric cancer, PMID:30366938). The drug is highly MET-selective (PMID:27196782). However, the gastric trial stopped early for lower-than-expected efficacy, so no endpoint was formally met. In clear cell sarcoma, 1 of 8 patients responded (NCT03132155), suggesting MET inhibition does not drive this disease. No MET drug has succeeded in clear cell sarcoma, so F1b does not apply. U remains plausible.

The program stopped because of efficacy concerns. The phase II gastric trial (NCT02016534, PMID:30366938) stopped enrolling after a protocol-permitted review showed lower-than-expected activity, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 18%. The index trial (NCT02096666) was a small Asian phase 1/2 study and was not mainly an efficacy test. Plasma pharmacokinetics were measured at the 300 mg maximum tolerated dose (PMID:30425090), so systemic exposure is documented. No human data on MET phosphorylation, tumor pharmacodynamics or downstream biomarkers were found; all pathway data come from animal or cell studies (PMID:27196782). Headache from off-target adenosine-transporter inhibition limited the dose (PMID:31330495), but nothing shows this kept MET engagement too low. Responses clustered in tumors with high MET amplification, which suggests patient selection mattered (secondary F3). Engagement is no_human_data, so the code is U.

In DMD boys, serum domagrozumab rose with dose (PMID:32522498). PK/PD modelling of measured total myostatin predicted >90% myostatin coverage throughout the phase 2 trial (PMID:36104012), so engagement was shown in the disease, although it was published after the index trial started. In healthy volunteers, engagement plateaued at 20 mg/kg and lean mass and muscle volume increased (PMID:28881472). The downstream effect followed in DMD: lean mass rose significantly in the arms and appendicular skeleton, with a non-significant rise in muscle volume (PMID:36335191, PMID:32522498). Despite this, the 4-stair climb change was null (p=0.94) and no secondary endpoint differed. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limiting. Myostatin blockade did not translate into function: F2. Exploratory NSAA signals (PMID:35998119) hint at endpoint or duration issues (F4).

In the Phase 1 trial in advanced solid tumours (PMID:28972963, published before the index start), PK was linear and dose-proportional at the 300 mg QD RP2D. Phosphate and FGF19 changes reached significance and were described as target-engagement markers. Engagement was never shown in gastric cancer patients. Hyperphosphataemia occurred in only 5% of patients, so engagement may have been modest, which leaves F1a open. Derazantinib produced responses in FGFR2-fusion iCCA (22% ORR, NCT03230318), but that trial had no prespecified threshold. In the index trial (NCT04604132), ORR was 0% at 300 mg QD and PFS4 was 7.7% at 200 mg BID. With engagement read as adequate, the failure fits FGFR inhibition not driving benefit in this gastric population (F2). Small cohorts and administrative termination limit certainty (F7).

Derazantinib had low ORR in FGFR-altered mUC (8.2% monotherapy, 0–14% elsewhere; NCT04045613, PMID:38627238), and the authors judged efficacy insufficient. Erdafitinib, which hits the same FGFR target, is FDA-approved in urothelial carcinoma, so the target is validated in this disease. The Phase 1 (PMID:28972963) showed linear, dose-proportional PK up to 300 mg, supporting exposure. Changes in phosphate and FGF19 were statistically significant. However, only 5% of patients had hyperphosphataemia, all grade 1, which suggests partial FGFR pathway engagement. This was measured in mixed solid tumours, not in UC specifically. The dose was capped by AST elevation, but nothing shows that cap fell below the dose engagement needed. The likeliest explanation is a molecule-specific shortfall rather than a failure of the target.

The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, GR-engagement or pathway data for mapracorat, and no PubMed abstracts. In the index trial (NCT01230125), both primary endpoints moved numerically in the drug's favour but neither was significant. Glucocorticoid-receptor agonism is a validated mechanism in ocular inflammation: clobetasol and hydrocortisone are FDA-approved for eye disorders, and several steroids reached phase 3 after cataract surgery. That points to the molecule (potency, ocular exposure or formulation), not the target. Later 3% trials showed partial effects: pain was significant in NCT01591161 and favourable counts appeared in NCT01591655, so a modest effect size and an underpowered trial (F7) may also explain the miss. With no engagement data, the evidence stays thin.

In the index trial NCT01163643, vehicle was numerically better than every mapracorat dose (0.3–2%) on corneal staining and worst VAS symptom at 12 weeks. No serious AEs occurred, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no human PK, ocular tissue exposure, GR engagement or biomarker data for mapracorat. Its post-cataract inflammation trials were mixed or not significant and posted no p-values (NCT01230125, NCT01591161, NCT01591655), so no pillar can be inferred adequate. Another GR agonist, loteprednol etabonate, is FDA-approved for dry eye syndrome, which shows the target can work in this disease. A molecule-level failure (F1b) is therefore the best-supported code. Because engagement was never measured, U also applies.

The index trial NCT02304198 was a 48-week long-term safety study. Its primary outcome was adverse events, classified not_efficacy, so it was not an efficacy test of udenafil (F9). Plasma exposure in humans is documented by PK studies (PMID:18318773). PDE5 engagement is inferred_adequate: udenafil met primary endpoints in erectile dysfunction Phase 3 trials through the same systemic PDE5 target (NCT01037218, NCT01037244). It also lowered PASP in COPD patients in an uncontrolled study (PMID:22946546). The related PAH Phase 2 trial (NCT01553721) missed overall 6MWD but was significant in ERA-pretreated patients, suggesting subgroup-confined benefit (secondary F3). The bundle states no stop reason.

The index trial NCT02304198 is a 48-week long-term safety study with safety-only primary outcomes. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Human PK shows systemic exposure (PMID:18318773). Engagement is inferred_adequate: udenafil met pivotal ED endpoints through PDE5 inhibition at comparable systemic doses (NCT01037218, NCT01037244). In PAH patients, single 50 mg doses lowered mPAP and PVRI (PMID:30808080), so the pathway effect held. The related Phase IIb efficacy trial, with 63 patients, narrowly missed on 6MWD (+25 m, p=0.087). Benefit reached significance only in ERA-pretreated patients (PMID:31202506). That suggests an underpowered trial (F7) and a subgroup signal (F3) rather than a failed mechanism. Approved sildenafil and tadalafil validate PDE5 as a target in this disease.

PET in humans (PMID:24239329, published 2014, before the 2017 index start) showed dose-dependent striatal DAT occupancy of 18–77% across 0.125–1 mg, with a maximum near 80%. That is brain exposure and engagement, though not measured in Prader-Willi patients; plasma PK is also shown (PMID:19705923). The index trial NCT03149445 was tiny: 6 vs 3 adults on 0.5 mg and 5 vs 4 adolescents on 0.125 mg. The adult arm showed a -5.4% weight difference with a wide CI (-12.3 to 1.5, p=0.10), a trend the trial was too underpowered to confirm. The adolescent dose of 0.125 mg sits at the low end of occupancy (well below the ~0.25 mg estimated to give half-maximal occupancy), so engagement there was likely partial. Serious AEs occurred in 3/6 adults on the high dose. The trial could not answer the efficacy question.

The bundle has no human pillar data for DE-104. There are no posted results from the index trial NCT00650338 or the other Phase 2 IOP trials (NCT00656240, NCT00657579, NCT00868894). There are no Phase 1 results and no PubMed abstracts. Exposure, ROCK engagement and pathway effect therefore cannot be judged. Another ROCK inhibitor, netarsudil, is FDA-approved for open-angle glaucoma, so ROCK inhibition can lower IOP in this disease. That points to the molecule, not the target, which fits F1b. However, the bundle does not state why the program stopped, and it does not show the efficacy readout itself. It is possible the reason was non-efficacy, such as commercial or tolerability. Confidence is low, and U remains plausible as a secondary code.

A 2014 review reports that Santen dropped DE-104, a topical ROCK inhibitor, in late 2010 after a Phase II trial missed its primary IOP endpoint (NCT00650338 and related trials; no results were posted). I found no human data on DE-104 for any of the three pillars: no ocular exposure, no ROCK inhibition, and no biomarker. Other ROCK inhibitors did lower IOP in the same disease. K-115 (ripasudil) did so in Phase II, and netarsudil, also a ROCK inhibitor, was FDA-approved in 2017 for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. That shows the target works for this condition, so the failure points to the molecule rather than the mechanism (F1b). Because DE-104's own engagement was never measured, U also applies. The review says ROCK candidates usually failed from insufficient efficacy or hyperemia.

Exposure was shown in humans: dose-proportional plasma PK (PMID:31654487), and CSF concentrations similar to plasma in MS patients (PMID:38436271). Engagement was shown in healthy volunteers, with full PBMC BTK occupancy after repeat 25 mg dosing (PMID:31654487, PMID:36165192). The bundle has no occupancy data from MS patients. Pathway: in the phase 2 RMS trial, Gd+ lesions fell (rate ratio 0.30 at 75 mg; NCT02975349, PMID:31075187) and serum NfL decreased (PMID:38436271). Even so, both phase 3 trials showed ARR no better than teriflunomide (0.14 vs 0.13; 0.11 vs 0.11; NCT04338022, NCT04338061). With the target engaged and a biomarker effect shown, BTK inhibition at these doses did not add clinical benefit over an active comparator. The active-comparator design, chosen after the phase 2 extension, is a secondary consideration (F7).

Exposure: dose-proportional plasma PK, and CSF levels in RMS patients similar to plasma (PMID:38436271). Engagement: in healthy volunteers BTK occupancy was dose-dependent and full after repeat dosing at 25 mg, published in 2020 before the index trial (PMID:31654487, PMID:36165192). Occupancy was not shown in MS patients. Pathway: the phase 2 RMS trial met its Gd+ lesion endpoint at 75 mg (NCT02975349), and NfL fell (PMID:38436271). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, both phase 3 trials showed no ARR advantage over teriflunomide (0.14 vs 0.13; 0.11 vs 0.11; NCT04338022, NCT04338061). BTK inhibition, though engaged, did not drive greater clinical benefit than the comparator. F4 is secondary because the lesion effect did not translate to relapses.

Healthy-volunteer data show dose-proportional plasma PK and near-full BTK occupancy with repeated 25 mg dosing (PMID:31654487; PMID:36165192). That covers the index doses of 25 mg QD, 75 mg QD and 50 mg BID. Tolerability did not cap dosing: TEAEs were similar to placebo with no dose effect. Evobrutinib also met a Phase 2 MS imaging endpoint (NCT02975349), supporting functional BTK engagement. Even so, SRI-4 and SRI-6 showed no benefit at any dose (NCT02975336), and the authors conclude BTK inhibition is not effective in SLE (PMID:36530019). RA trials also failed (NCT02784106, NCT03233230). Engagement was not shown in SLE patients: the Phase 1b (NCT02537028) posted no results. Index Ig and B-cell biomarker results are truncated in the bundle, so the pathway pillar is unknown.

In healthy volunteers, evobrutinib showed dose-proportional plasma PK. BTK occupancy was full with repeated 25 mg dosing and >90% after single doses of 200 mg or more (PMID:31654487, PMID:36165192), so exposure and engagement were adequate. That evidence is from healthy volunteers, not RA patients, and was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:36418156). The bundle has no human pathway biomarker data. Despite adequate occupancy, the small index trial missed ACR20 (NCT02784106). The larger Phase IIb also failed at 25 mg QD, 75 mg QD and 50 mg BID (NCT03233230). Evobrutinib also failed in SLE (NCT02975336, PMID:36530019), while it was active on MS lesions (NCT02975349). This pattern implicates BTK as a target in RA rather than the molecule. The 65-patient index trial was underpowered (F7, secondary).

Phase 1 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure with good tolerability (PMID:29663420). In the 2012 RSV challenge study (NCT01756482), which predates the index trial, presatovir clearly lowered viral load (P<0.001), showing the fusion-inhibitor mechanism works in human RSV infection. It also reduced viral load in HCT recipients with upper-tract infection (NCT02254408). However, it failed to lower viral load in hospitalized adults (NCT02135614), in HCT lower-tract disease (NCT02254421) and in lung transplant recipients (NCT02534350). The pattern points to treatment given at a later or more established disease stage, or to the wrong population, rather than to an untested mechanism. The bundle does not explicitly state the cause, so confidence is low.

The cause is indeterminate (U). STEADFAST (NCT02080364) missed both primary endpoints, ADAS-cog and CDR-sb, at 5 mg. I found no human data showing that azeliragon bound RAGE: no receptor occupancy, no ligand–RAGE blockade, and no brain or CSF drug levels. Plasma levels at 5 mg are known (PMID:24423155), but brain exposure for this CNS target is not. The phase 2 studies found no consistent effect on plasma Aβ, inflammatory markers or CSF/MRI biomarkers (PMID:21192237, PMID:24696507), so the pathway pillar is inadequate. Because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged RAGE from a target that does not matter. A post-hoc subgroup idea (diabetes, NCT03980730) also failed, which only weakly supports F3. No other RAGE drug is in the bundle.

Plasma PK was characterized in ALS patients (PMID:22591195). Early ALS studies showed proximal pharmacodynamic effects: improved maximum voluntary ventilation and handgrip endurance, and slower SVC decline in phase 2b (PMID:22591195, PMID:26982815). In VITALITY-ALS, however, 34.2% of tirasemtiv patients discontinued versus 12.2% on placebo, driven by dizziness, fatigue and nausea. SVC did not differ from placebo at any dose (NCT02496767). The authors state that poor tolerability may have contributed (PMID:31081694). Patients who tolerated their intended dose showed a dose-related trend toward benefit (p=0.11). The mechanism was therefore not adequately tested at effective exposure. The sponsor moved to a more potent, better-tolerated activator, reldesemtiv (PMID:29150952), consistent with a molecule-specific tolerability limit (F6 secondary).

In the index PAD trial (NCT01131013; PMID:24872402), claudicating calf-muscle performance rose with dose and plasma concentration of tirasemtiv. That shows exposure and functional engagement of the fast skeletal troponin mechanism in PAD patients; the authors state the mechanism improved muscle function. However, the 750 mg dose had to be cut to 500 mg for adverse events. Six-minute walk distance fell with dose and concentration, which the authors attribute to dose-related adverse events, especially dizziness, impeding walking. Dizziness looks like a molecule-specific rather than troponin-mediated effect, so molecule-specific tolerability offset the clinical benefit (F6). A proximal effect was shown while the walking endpoint failed (secondary F4). The next-generation activator CK-107 was more potent (PMID:29150952), consistent with a molecule-level limitation.

Lanabecestat reached the brain and engaged BACE1 in humans. In mild-moderate AD patients (NCT01795339, PMID:27767991), CSF Aβ fell by at least 76% at 50 mg and at least 51% at 15 mg, and CSF sAPPβ also fell (PMID:28618005). This was shown before the index trial started. The pathway effect followed: amyloid plaque burden fell on PET in AMARANTH and DAYBREAK (PMID:33614894). Doses were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, ADAS-Cog13 did not separate from placebo at either dose (NCT02245737, NCT02783573), tau, FDG and perfusion were unchanged, and some cognitive measures worsened (PMID:33049114). No BACE1 inhibitor succeeded (PMID:30277096). Lowering Aβ production by BACE1 inhibition did not deliver clinical benefit, pointing to the mechanism as tested.

In schizophrenia patients, the index proof-of-mechanism crossover trial (NCT01137799, PMID:22766391) found no effect on P50 sensory gating, MMN, P300 or EEG. These are the downstream markers the mechanism predicts should move, so I rated pathway inadequate. No analysis identified a responsive subgroup. A study measured drug levels in the cerebrospinal fluid of healthy volunteers (NCT01556217), but it started after the index trial, and I found no published results from it. My searches turned up no human data on brain exposure, receptor occupancy, or any other measure of α7 engagement. Repeated failures in depression and smoking cessation (PMID:34023797, 29185480) also lack engagement data. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged α7 from an α7 mechanism that does not matter in schizophrenia, so the code is U.

In NCT00824408, volasertib alone did worse than pemetrexed on PFS (1.4 vs 5.3 months, HR 2.05). Adding it to pemetrexed gave no benefit (HR 1.14). The 300 mg dose was the MTD from Phase 1 (NCT00969553, NCT01348347). Plasma levels at that dose were measured (Cmax about 1150 nmol/L, NCT01145885).
