The bundle has no human data on drug levels in tumour, PLK1 inhibition or a downstream marker in solid tumours or NSCLC. The only PD sampling found was in AML marrow (NCT00804856). The AML Phase 3 response win (NCT01721876) was in blood and marrow, a different compartment, so it cannot support inferred adequacy for lung tumours. No other PLK1 drug has succeeded in NSCLC, so F1b does not apply. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. My searches stopped early at a tool limit, so the evidence trail is incomplete.

In the index trial (NCT01121406, PMID:26755507), volasertib 300 mg every 3 weeks missed its 24-week disease control endpoint (30.6% vs 43.1% for chemotherapy). The 300 mg dose was the single-agent maximum tolerated dose (NCT00969553), and Phase 1 studies (NCT01145885, BJC 2014) show substantial plasma exposure. No source shows PLK1 engagement in human tumours, such as mitotic arrest or phospho-histone H3 changes in biopsies. The only such evidence I found came from cell lines. The tested tissue biomarkers did not predict response. Volasertib met its response endpoint in AML (NCT01721876), but that is a blood cancer, not the same tissue compartment, so engagement in ovarian tumours cannot be inferred from it. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage PLK1 in solid tumours from a target that does not drive this disease, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT01121406), volasertib was given at 300 mg every 3 weeks, the single-agent MTD (NCT00969553). It did worse than chemotherapy on 24-week disease control (30.6% vs 43.1%). Human data are limited to plasma pharmacokinetics (NCT01145885) and dose-limiting neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. I found no measurement of drug levels in tumour, PLK1 inhibition or mitotic-arrest biomarkers in solid tumours, including ovarian cancer. The AML results (NCT00804856, NCT01721876) concern a different disease and tissue, so they do not support inferring engagement in ovarian cancer. The trial reports and the review attribute the solid-tumour shortfall to no specific cause; the review notes benefit was clearest in AML. Because there are no engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter here.

The index trial (NCT01023958) treated 50 patients after platinum failure. 14% responded and there was no prespecified threshold for success. Plasma levels were measured and look adequate at the 300 mg MTD carried forward: long half-life, dose-linear PK and Cmax around 1150 nmol/L (NCT01145885, NCT00969553). However, no source shows PLK1 engagement in humans. There are no human measurements of PLK1 inhibition or downstream markers such as phospho-histone H3 or mitotic arrest in tumour or surrogate tissue, in patients with this disease or anyone else; the review cites only preclinical mechanism data. Myelosuppression set the MTD, but nothing shows the dose was capped below what engagement needed. No other PLK1 drug succeeded in urothelial cancer, and no source gives a reason for stopping. Engagement is unknown, so this is U.

Setipiprant 1000 mg BID did not change hair count or self-assessment versus placebo in male AGA (NCT02781311, PMID:34703265). It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Human plasma PK and CRTH2-internalization PK/PD on eosinophils were modelled before the index trial (PMID:26692193), but that abstract gives no occupancy level for this dose. Engagement is therefore inferred_adequate from the Phase 2 allergic rhinitis trial, which met a dose-related endpoint at the same 1000 mg BID dose (NCT01241214), though the Phase 3 failed (NCT01484119). No engagement or downstream PGD2/CRTH2 biomarker was measured in scalp or in AGA patients. Systemic CRTH2 antagonism appears not to drive hair loss. Low confidence: the inference rests on a different tissue and a non-replicated result, so U is plausible.

Human plasma exposure is well characterised up to 1000 mg b.i.d. with good tolerability, so the dose was not limited (PMID:24734908). Engagement is inferred_adequate: 1000 mg b.i.d. met the primary endpoint in seasonal allergic rhinitis via CRTH2 (NCT01241214), though the Phase 3 replication failed (NCT01484119). A PK/PD model of CRTH2 internalization blockade exists (PMID:26692193), but the abstract reports no occupancy level for setipiprant. Pathway: in allergic asthmatics, 1000 mg b.i.d. cut the late asthmatic response by 25.6% and protected against airway hyperresponsiveness, but did not change eNO (PMID:24964348). That evidence was published after the index trial started. No FEV1 benefit drove further development, and no CRTH2 antagonist in the bundle is approved for asthma. This suggests the mechanism contributes little to FEV1. Index results were not posted and engagement evidence is indirect, so confidence is low.

Setipiprant 1000 mg b.i.d. was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. In the Phase 2 SAR trial (NCT01241214) the same dose gave a statistically significant, dose-related DNSS improvement. That result supports systemic exposure and CRTH2 engagement, though only as an inference: it comes from the same disease and the effect was small. Human PK/PD modelling of blockade of PGD2-induced CRTH2 internalization (PMID:26692193, published 2016, after the index trial) exists. However, its abstract does not report the level of blockade setipiprant achieved. The Phase 3 trial (NCT01484119) showed no effect on any symptom score (PMID:28392807). This fits a CRTH2 mechanism with marginal impact on SAR symptoms, or a false-positive Phase 2 (F7). Engagement was never directly quantified, so U remains possible.

NTRA-2112 is enteral insulin meant to act on insulin receptors in the gut. No source in the bundle gives human data on gut exposure, intestinal INSR activation or a gut-maturation biomarker, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The registry record for NCT02510560 shows the primary endpoint was missed (p=0.115 and p=0.243). However, the sponsor's 2022 release, citing a JAMA Pediatrics paper, says the endpoint was met in a different analysis set. It highlights the infants born before 28 weeks and says the program went on to a confirmatory Phase 3 with Chiesi. Nothing in the bundle shows whether the drug engaged its target or whether the target matters, so the code is U. The conflicting reports and the program's continuation keep confidence low.

The index trial NCT00957918 (oral NC001 nicotine, 4–24 mg/day, for levodopa-induced dyskinesia) had safety and impulse-control (rMIDI) primary endpoints, so it was not designed as an efficacy test. PMID:31133957 reports the drug was safe and well tolerated, with no dose cap. Dyskinesia reduction showed a nonsignificant trend (30% vs 19%, p=0.09) in a small trial of 65 patients, which suggests limited power. Falls and freezing of gait improved on reanalysis. No pillar was measured in Parkinson patients. Brain uptake and occupancy were shown only in smokers (PMID:35962133, PMID:10657031). Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate from approved efficacy in nicotine dependence through central α4β2 receptors at similar doses (NCT02355665).

The index trial NCT00957918 registered only safety primary outcomes (adverse events, rMIDI impulse control) with no success criterion, so it was not an efficacy test of nicotine. The reanalysis (PMID:31133957) reports NC001 at up to 24 mg/day was safe and well tolerated. Dyskinesia reduction on UDysRS was a non-significant trend (30% vs 19%, p=0.09), while falls and freezing of gait improved. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate, not measured: nicotine met efficacy endpoints in nicotine dependence through central nAChRs (NCT02355665, NCT00715871). Brain uptake and nAChR occupancy are documented in humans (PMID:35962133, PMID:10657031), though not in PD patients. Small size suggests the trial was underpowered for dyskinesia.

There is no direct human occupancy or CNS data for filorexant. However, the same 10 mg dose met polysomnography endpoints in primary insomnia (NCT01021852, PMID:26979830), which acts through central orexin receptor antagonism. Brain exposure, engagement and the pathway effect are therefore inferred adequate. That insomnia evidence predates the index trial, but engagement was not shown in MDD patients. In the MDD trial (NCT01554176), 10 mg adjunctive filorexant gave no separation on MADRS (−11 vs −10.3, p=0.679), with a confidence interval excluding a meaningful benefit. Tolerability did not cap the dose. This suggests orexin antagonism does not drive depression as tested. The review notes ORA trials in MDD have been largely negative (PMID:36436175). The trial ended early for low enrollment, so underpowering (F7) is secondary.

No direct human PK, receptor occupancy or biomarker data are in the bundle. However, filorexant met its primary polysomnography endpoint in primary insomnia at 2.5–20 mg, with dose-related sleep improvements (NCT01021852, PMID:26979830). That is the same orexin receptor target in the same CNS compartment, so central exposure, engagement and pathway effect are inferred adequate. The insomnia trial was registered in 2009, before the index trial. The migraine dose is not stated in the bundle, which limits confidence. The index trial was well tolerated, with AE discontinuation 6.7% vs 4.3% and no SAEs, so the dose was not tolerability-capped. Monthly migraine days were unchanged versus placebo (-0.4, p=0.33), indicating orexin antagonism does not drive migraine prevention as tested. Adjunctive use in MDD was also negative (NCT01554176).

The bundle has no direct human PK, receptor occupancy or biomarker data. However, filorexant 10 mg, the same dose used in the PDN index trial, met its polysomnography primary endpoint in primary insomnia (NCT01021852, PMID:26979830). That benefit acts through the same orexin receptors in the CNS, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. This insomnia evidence predates the index trial. Dosing was not tolerability-limited (0/88 serious AEs). The enriched randomized-withdrawal trial showed no difference from placebo on efficacy failure or pain scores (PMID:28448426), and the authors conclude there is no evidence of efficacy. Filorexant also failed in migraine and MDD. Orexin antagonism does not appear to drive PDN pain as tested.

The index phase 2 trial (NCT01762033) in 40 VEGF-pretreated clear cell mRCC patients missed its 2-month PFS primary endpoint (PMID:27727447). Sonepcizumab is an anti-S1P ligand antibody. Biomarker studies in these patients showed S1P concentrations rising on therapy, which fits antibody binding and sequestration of the ligand. I took this as evidence of engagement in the disease, though it was published only after the trial. No PK, tissue exposure or downstream pathway data are in the bundle. Toxicity was mild and did not cap the dose. With engagement apparent and no benefit, S1P antagonism did not drive outcome as tested. Durable benefit in VHL/PBRM1-altered patients hints at subgroup effects (F3). Confidence is low because adequacy of engagement is not quantified.

Intravitreal iSONEP (anti-S1P antibody) given with anti-VEGF did no better than anti-VEGF alone on BCVA at Day 120 (4.22 and 3.63 vs 4.34 letters), and iSONEP alone made vision worse (NCT01414153). I found no human data on drug levels in the eye, on S1P neutralisation in vitreous or aqueous humour, or on a downstream biomarker. The ocular Phase 1 (NCT00767949) posted no results. The only engagement-related evidence I found is preclinical binding affinity. The systemic tumour Phase 1 (NCT00661414) does not show ocular engagement. Lpath's 10-K says only that the trial missed its endpoints, so Pfizer let its option lapse, and it describes post-hoc 'signals'. It gives no mechanistic explanation. Nothing here separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Exposure was shown: the phase 1 trials posted dose-proportional serum levels (NCT02009449, NCT03267732). The Cancer Cell paper from the phase 1 trial shows the drug acted on its target in patients. Serum IFN-γ, IL-18, FasL and granzyme B rose in a lasting way, PD-1+LAG-3+ CD8 T cells expanded, and phospho-STAT3+ CD8 T cells (the direct IL-10 receptor signal) and granzyme B+ CD8 T cells increased inside tumours. Those data came mostly from melanoma and kidney cancer patients, not NSCLC, and were published in late 2018, after the index trial began. Even so, adding the drug to PD-1 blockade gave no benefit in either NSCLC trial (ORR 47.1% vs 44.0% in NCT03382899; 14.8% vs 12.0% in NCT03382912), and it also failed in pancreatic cancer (PMID:33555926). With the mechanism engaged, the failure points to the target not driving the disease (F2). The 'unfavourable risk-benefit' stop reflects that lack of benefit plus more deaths, not a dose cap.

Phase 1 PK (NCT02009449, NCT03267732) shows dose-proportional systemic exposure, which fits a target on circulating immune cells. In the phase 1 study published before the index trial (PMC4649279; Cancer Cell/PMC8098754), patients across tumor types showed dose-related rises in IFN-γ, IL-18 and granzyme B and expansion of activated CD8+ T cells. That counts as IL-10R engagement plus a pathway effect, though no direct receptor-occupancy measure exists. In SEQUOIA itself (pancreatic patients, PMID:33555926), the same markers rose and TGF-β fell in the pegilodecakin arm only, yet overall survival did not improve (HR 1.045). The authors noted on-target blood-count toxicity and the dose reached, and did not claim tolerability capped the dose. Because the mechanism was engaged without clinical benefit, the code is F2. F3 is secondary because the authors say better patient selection is needed.

The index trial compared CVC with active efavirenz. Virologic success at week 24 was 76% and 73% for CVC versus 71% for EFV, with numerically higher rates at week 48. 'Not met' reflects no significant superiority in a trial apparently not powered for it. The authors concluded CVC 'showed efficacy and favorable safety' and selected CVC200 for phase 3 (PMID:26636929), so this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. Pillars hold in HIV patients before the index trial: plasma PK with a steep exposure-response for HIV RNA (PMID:21486960), and a dose-dependent MCP-1 rise indicating CCR2 blockade alongside significant viral-load reductions (PMID:21317794, NCT01092104). No dose limitation was seen. The bundle gives no explicit business reason for stopping.

Cenicriviroc was well absorbed with a long half-life (PMID:21486960). At the 150 mg dose later used in AURORA it suppressed HIV-1 RNA, showing functional CCR5 blockade, and raised plasma MCP-1, which the authors read as strong CCR2 blockade (PMID:21317794, NCT01092104, NCT01338883). This evidence predates the index trial but comes from HIV patients, not NASH, and the bundle has no hepatic antifibrotic pathway data. The 150 mg dose was well tolerated long term (PMID:38285756), so tolerability did not cap it. Despite adequate exposure and engagement, fibrosis improvement was 22.3% vs 25.5% on placebo in AURORA (NCT03028740), consistent with the earlier CENTAUR miss (NCT02217475). This points to CCR2/CCR5 blockade not driving NASH fibrosis as tested.

Cenicriviroc was well absorbed with long half-life (PMID:21486960). At the same 150 mg dose used in PERSEUS, it raised MCP-1 significantly, which the authors read as strong CCR2 blockade (PMID:21317794). It also met HIV viral-load endpoints through CCR5, so the CCR5 pathway held (NCT01092104, NCT01338883). This engagement was shown in HIV patients before the index trial, not in PSC. Dosing was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. In PSC, ALP fell only modestly (median 18%, mean -4.5%), with no normalization or 50% responses (NCT02653625, PMID:33681680). The liver-fibrosis failures in NASH (NCT03028740, NCT02217475) are consistent with CCR2/5 blockade not driving the disease. Secondary F7: the trial was single-arm, small and descriptive, with no prespecified test.

The index trial (NCT01033396, PMID:25024716) tested 5 mg PF-03654764 plus fexofenadine against pseudoephedrine plus fexofenadine. It was not superior. In post-hoc analysis it lowered TNSS versus placebo, but there was no fexofenadine-alone arm, so the H3 drug's own contribution cannot be separated out. The 5 mg dose was chosen to give a plasma Cmax about 10 times Ki, based on earlier dosing in healthy volunteers. That supports plasma exposure, though the PK values were not reported in the paper. No human receptor occupancy or H3 pathway biomarker was found. CNS side effects (insomnia, hallucinations, jitteriness), which the paper puts down to a fully brain-penetrant H3 antagonist, offset any benefit (secondary F5). The follow-on study NCT01298505 stopped for lack of efficacy. Because engagement is unknown, the code is U.

THN102 combined modafinil with very low-dose flecainide (3 or 27 mg), meant to block astroglial connexins (Cx43/Cx30) in the brain. The connexin evidence comes only from rodents (PMID:27091533, 29635319). No source shows in humans that flecainide reached the brain at these doses, blocked connexins or moved a downstream biomarker. In NCT02821715, both doses scored the same as modafinil alone on the ESS (15.34 vs 14.68). The positive Parkinson's trial (NCT03624920) compared THN102 with placebo, so modafinil alone could explain the benefit. It does not show that flecainide added anything or engaged the target. The sponsor suggested that too many poorly responding narcolepsy patients were enrolled (F3), but this was a guess. Because engagement is untested, the cause is indeterminate.

The index trial NCT01884285 was a first-in-patient dose-escalation study with a safety and tolerability primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. The publication (PMID:35247924) reports that the drug was well tolerated, with DLTs mainly rash, and that an RP2D was identified (60 mg BID 5:2 and 120 mg BID). PK was dose proportional, and target inhibition was observed in plasma and tumour tissue of patients. However, this was published in 2022, after the trial started. The abstract does not quantify a downstream pathway biomarker. Only limited antitumour activity was seen, with some PSA reductions. The trial met its stated objectives, and the bundle gives no stated reason for stopping. F2 is secondary because engagement occurred but benefit was limited.

Exposure was measured in psoriasis patients: serum Cmax and AUC rose more than dose-proportionally at 0.1-3 mg/kg (PMID:29679478). Engagement was adequate in humans. In healthy volunteers, B-cell CD40 occupancy was maximal above 0.01 mg/kg, well below the psoriasis doses (PMID:23356210, NCT01565681, run before the index trial). In kidney transplant recipients, maximal occupancy was reached at all doses (PMID:31397943). Occupancy was a primary endpoint of the index trial but is not reported in the bundle, so engagement in psoriasis is not shown. Tolerability did not cap dosing; only transient liver enzyme rises were seen. Despite this, PASI, PSGA and %BSA did not improve versus placebo, pointing to CD40 blockade not driving psoriasis. Caveat: the index trial was a small PK/safety study rather than a powered efficacy test (F9/F7).

Exposure and engagement were measured directly in humans. In de novo kidney transplant recipients (NCT01279538, PMID:31397943), maximal B-cell CD40 receptor occupancy was reached at every dose from 50 to 500 mg, with dose-dependent PK and good tolerability. Healthy-volunteer data (PMID:23356210) agree, and all of this predates the 2017 index trial. Engagement was not shown specifically in FSGS patients, and the bundle has no human downstream pathway biomarker. In the index trial, bleselumab only numerically reduced the composite rFSGS endpoint (18.5% vs 31.3%, p=0.37). Biopsy-proven recurrence differences were small (3.9–7.5%) (PMID:39042770). With the target saturated, this supports CD40 blockade not driving recurrence (F2). The small open-label trial was underpowered, and the meta-analysis calls the evidence inconclusive (PMID:42421428), so F7 is secondary.

In de novo kidney transplant recipients, bleselumab 50–500 mg reached maximal B-cell CD40 receptor occupancy at all doses, prolonged with dose, and was well tolerated (PMID:31397943, NCT01279538, started 2010, before the index trial). Healthy-volunteer data agree (PMID:23356210). The index trial used 200 mg, so exposure and engagement were adequate and the dose was not capped. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported. In the index trial, bleselumab with reduced tacrolimus was noninferior to standard care. But bleselumab replacing tacrolimus (with MMF) clearly failed: BPAR was 30.7% higher. Full CD40 blockade did not adequately prevent rejection without a calcineurin inhibitor, so the mechanism is insufficient as tested (F2). F9 is secondary because one arm met noninferiority (PMID:31509331).

The index trial NCT02640755 was a 4-patient [14C] absorption/metabolism/excretion PK study in solid malignancies with only PK endpoints. It was not an efficacy test, so F9. Across the program, exposure at the 50 mg BID MTD was judged consistent with preclinical activity, and tumour p-S6 fell in 8/8 paired biopsies (PMID:25805799, published before the index trial). Later sources report only variable p4EBP1 inhibition without pAKT (mTORC2) modulation (PMID:34269152). They also state 'insufficient target engagement of vistusertib observed in adult trials' (PMID:34543871), and tolerability capped dosing (fatigue, mucositis; NCT01026402). This supports F1a as the underlying reason the program waned. No prostate-specific engagement data are shown; NCT02064608 posted no results.

Index trial NCT03291067 missed both co-primary VMS endpoints. At week 12, frequency fell -2.91 to -3.38 on MT-8554 versus -2.78 on placebo, and severity was unchanged. There was a large placebo response, and only modest week-4 separation at 5 and 10 mg. A healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic study (NCT02536209) and a multiple-dose study in women with VMS (NCT02803268) exist, but neither posted results. The bundle therefore has no human exposure, TRPM8 engagement or pathway data. No other TRPM8 drug is listed for comparison. Later trials (migraine Phase 2b NCT06848075, primary endpoint not met) show no adequacy either, and dose was not capped by tolerability. A drug that never engaged TRPM8 cannot be separated from a target that does not drive the disease, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT03291067, none of the three MT-8554 doses (1, 5 or 10 mg) beat placebo on VMS frequency or severity at week 12. A pharmacodynamic study in healthy men using the cold pressor test was run (NCT02536209, per its HRA summary), but no results were posted or published. I found no human data on drug levels, TRPM8 blockade or a downstream biomarker. The later migraine Phase 2b (NCT06848075) missed 2-hour pain freedom at every dose in the registry, though Kallyope's press release calls it positive. It also involves a different tissue (trigeminal nerves), so it cannot support an inferred engagement. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With no engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't drive VMS, so the code is U.

Verinurad showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:28744099, PMID:35593744). URAT1 engagement was shown by increased urinary urate excretion and dose-dependent serum urate lowering. This held in renal impairment (PMID:29949102, 2018) and in albuminuric T2DM patients (PMID:33130235), both before the index trial. In SAPPHIRE (NCT03990363, PMID:38564654), verinurad plus allopurinol lowered serum urate dose-dependently in CKD patients. Yet UACR did not improve versus allopurinol alone or placebo (high dose p=0.065; combined vs allopurinol p=0.63). Tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement and urate lowering confirmed in this disease and no albuminuria benefit, the evidence indicates that intensive URAT1-mediated urate lowering does not drive albuminuria in CKD. The earlier small phase 2a signal was not reproduced.

Verinurad's plasma exposure was dose-proportional in humans (PMID:28744099, PMID:35593744). URAT1 inhibition was shown directly by increased urinary urate excretion, and dose-dependent serum urate lowering of up to about 74-82% with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (PMID:29531784, PMID:29733447, PMID:29657831). This was well tolerated with no dose cap, and was published before 2020. Urate lowering also reduced albuminuria in T2D (NCT03118739). In HFpEF, verinurad plus allopurinol did not change peak VO2 versus placebo (difference -0.10, p=0.862; NCT04327024). The target was engaged and the pathway moved, yet there was no functional benefit, so urate lowering via URAT1 does not appear to drive HFpEF exercise capacity. Engagement was not documented in HFpEF patients themselves, hence medium confidence.

In Phase 1 (NCT00677105, PMID:23741066), exposure rose in proportion to dose. Acetylated H3 increased in skin, tumour and PBMCs, and Ki67 fell, supporting the recommended 12 mg MWF dose. In the index CTCL trial (NCT01486277, PMID:26836950), serial tumour biopsies showed increased acetylated tubulin, so target engagement was shown in this disease. Confirmed cutaneous response rate was 24%, and the authors concluded quisinostat is active with acceptable safety and suggested combinations. The readout was therefore not an efficacy failure, and the bundle gives no clinical reason for stopping. Approved HDAC inhibitors in CTCL (vorinostat, romidepsin) suggest a crowded market, so a commercial reason is plausible but is not stated in the bundle.

In the first-in-human study in ALS patients (NCT00875446, PMID:24841795), ozanezumab was well tolerated up to 15 mg/kg. PK was typical of a monoclonal antibody, and the drug showed dose-dependent co-localization with Nogo-A in skeletal muscle, the target tissue. PKPD modelling of that co-localization was used to choose a regimen of 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks for sustained engagement (PMID:25706882). Muscle biomarkers did not change, however, so the pathway pillar was not shown. The index phase 2 trial at that regimen missed its joint function-survival endpoint, with a numerical trend favouring placebo (NCT01753076, PMID:28139349). No dose limitation was reported. With exposure and engagement adequate but no benefit, Nogo-A blockade appears not to drive ALS progression. Confidence is medium because co-localization is only a surrogate for engagement.

In the 2016 interim poster from NCT02482441, the drug showed linear, slow-clearing antibody PK in patients with solid tumors. Serum bone-turnover markers (B-CTX, P1NP) changed in step with dose, and SOST and DKK1 shifted, both expected effects of blocking Wnt signalling. Investigators read this as target engagement and chose 15 mg/kg Q2W as the top dose on that basis. The MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, OncoMed said the trial, which enrolled RSPO3-fusion and RSPO3-high patients, 'failed to provide compelling evidence of clinical benefit', and Celgene declined its option. With systemic engagement shown at the chosen dose and no benefit, this points to F2. Caveats: RSPO3 binding was never measured directly, tumour penetration was only modest, and the evidence came after the trial started.

In the adjunctive Phase 2 trial in MDD (NCT01457677, PMID:32663909), none of the three decoglurant doses beat placebo on MADRS change. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Plasma levels were measured but did not track with any endpoint, and there are no CSF levels. No human receptor occupancy, target-engagement or pathway biomarker data exist for decoglurant. The investigators state that, without this data, they cannot rule out that central exposure was too low. Secondary sources agree that whether the doses were adequate is unclear. The authors also cite a high placebo response (F7). No other mGlu2/3 drug has succeeded in MDD. So the bundle cannot separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, which makes the code U.

Engagement was measured directly in humans. In healthy-volunteer PET, PF-04457845 at 1–20 mg reduced brain FAAH activity by ≥91% (>95% at 1 mg), showing brain penetration (PMID:26082009). Leukocyte FAAH was >97% inhibited at ≥0.5 mg daily, and plasma fatty acid amides rose 3.5- to 10-fold, a pathway effect. Doses up to 8 mg daily were well tolerated (PMID:22044402). Both studies were published before the index trial began in 2021. The 4 mg arm therefore gave near-complete engagement without a tolerability cap, yet CAPS-5 change matched placebo (LSM difference -0.74, p=0.68; NCT05178316). No engagement data in PTSD patients are in the bundle; the PTSD fMRI study ended for portfolio reasons (NCT02216097). FAAH inhibition does not appear to drive PTSD symptoms as tested.

All three pillars were measured directly in humans. In healthy volunteers, PF-04457845 gave dose-proportional plasma exposure and near-complete (>97%) leukocyte FAAH inhibition at ≥0.5 mg QD. Fatty acid amides (the substrates, including anandamide) rose 3.5–10-fold and plateaued, and doses well above saturation were well tolerated (PMID:22044402; PD study NCT00836082 started before the index trial). PET showed >95% inhibition of brain FAAH at 1 mg (PMID:26082009). Although engagement was not shown in OA patients, the target was maximally engaged with the expected pathway effect, yet the knee OA pain trial NCT00981357 failed. FAAH inhibition therefore does not appear to drive OA pain as tested (PMID:24429592). No tolerability cap applied.

The index Phase 2 CAP trial (NCT00797108) enrolled only 35 patients, with 8–10 evaluable per arm. Sulopenem arms had numerically higher clinical cure than ceftriaxone/amoxicillin-clavulanate (90.0% and 87.5% vs 62.5%). The wide confidence intervals crossed zero (27.5 [-4.0, 55.3]; 25.0 [-13.1, 57.9]), so 'not met' reflects a trial too small to answer the question rather than a demonstrated lack of efficacy. The bundle has no human PK, lung exposure or target-engagement data. The uUTI efficacy cited in PMID:39907459 involves a different oral regimen and tissue compartment, so it cannot support an inferred_adequate rating for pneumonia. No stop reason is stated. Later Phase 3 cUTI and cIAI misses (NCT03357614, NCT03358576) are outside pneumonia. Because engagement is unmeasured, U is listed as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT03358576 compared sulopenem with active ertapenem in cIAI. Clinical success was 85.5% vs 90.2%, so the primary endpoint was not met. This was an active-comparator design, so the miss was a failure to show non-inferiority to an effective antibiotic, not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure (F9). The bundle does not state the margin, which lowers confidence. Serious AEs were higher with sulopenem (25 vs 12). The bundle has no human PK or tissue exposure data. Oral sulopenem efficacy in uUTI (PMID:39907459) involves a different formulation and compartment, so pillars cannot be inferred. The cUTI trial NCT03357614 also missed against ertapenem. Because the pillars are unmeasured, U is a secondary code.

The index cUTI trial was a non-inferiority comparison against ertapenem followed by oral step-down. Sulopenem missed the margin: 67.8% vs 73.9%, difference -6.1% (95% CI -12.0 to -0.1). The authors attribute the gap to a lower rate of asymptomatic bacteriuria in comparator patients stepped down to ciprofloxacin, with no substantial difference at other time points (PMID:36068705). This is a missed NI margin against an active drug, not a clear efficacy failure (F9). The endpoint's sensitivity to asymptomatic bacteriuria is also implicated (F4). No PK or target data appear in the bundle, so the pillars are inferred. The same oral regimen was superior to ciprofloxacin against resistant uUTI and non-inferior to amoxicillin/clavulanate (PMID:36069202, PMID:40552968), and was later approved for uUTI (PMID:40555323).

The index single-arm Phase II in bladder cancer had an ORR of 2.6% (NCT00661609). Plasma exposure rose with dose in Phase 1 (PMID:22615058, PMID:21494838). Monoaster formation in PBMCs, a direct mitotic readout of Eg5 inhibition, was shown at doses up to the MTD. The sources call this proof of mechanism and evidence of target inhibition. This was shown in solid tumor/lymphoma and AML patients, not bladder cancer, and was published after the index trial started. Tolerability set the MTD (neutropenia, stomatitis), but nothing indicates engagement fell short at that dose. AML efficacy also failed (NCT00486265). This points to Eg5 inhibition not driving clinical benefit as tested (F2). Intratumoral exposure was never shown, so F1a remains possible.

The index trial NCT00979251 tested oral triple-combination antivirals, including ribavirin, in immunocompromised influenza patients. It enrolled only 2 subjects and posted no results, so it could not answer the efficacy question; this is an execution failure. Plasma ribavirin PK exists in healthy volunteers (NCT00982553), but nothing in the bundle shows that exposure is sufficient against influenza. PMID:31271195's title states that oral ribavirin for respiratory viruses needs PK-PD dose optimization, but no data are given. There is no human evidence of antiviral engagement or a viral load effect in influenza. The HCV and RSV approvals involve different viral targets, so they cannot support inferred adequacy. Had the trial been informative, U would apply, since engagement has no human data.

Exposure was adequate: plasma levels were measured and PK was dose-proportional (PMID:27214145, PMID:28212463). Engagement was adequate: dose-related 24-h cortisol suppression in healthy volunteers, then in COPD patients within the index trial itself, so the in-disease evidence postdates the index start. Pathway is inferred_adequate: the same doses attenuated the allergen-induced FEV1 fall in asthma (NCT01225549), same lung compartment, though COPD inflammatory markers did not move. In COPD, neither AZD5423 nor a reference GR agonist at double the approved dose improved FEV1. The authors attribute this to the selected COPD population not responding and note a different COPD population might respond (PMID:28212463). The inactive reference arm also raises target-relevance (F2) and assay-sensitivity (F7) concerns. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

The index trial (NCT01582815, PMID:26804646) dosed 50–150 mg twice daily and missed its primary endpoint (HAM-A6, p=0.51). Only weak signals showed up on secondary measures, and the drug was well tolerated, so dose was not capped by tolerability. In healthy volunteers, plasma exposure rose with dose (PMID:25735992), but no human CSF or brain levels were found, and mGlu2 occupancy was measured only in rats (PMID:25692015). The human functional data are not specific: at a single 500 mg dose the drug blunted ketamine effects and increased deep sleep, but it left REM sleep unchanged, which was the predicted translational marker (PMID:26686390). Those effects come from doses or settings that don't match the index regimen. With no human evidence of engagement, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged mGlu2 from a target that doesn't matter here. The small, flexibly dosed proof-of-concept design (F7) may also have contributed.

The index trial NCT04836559 missed its primary endpoint in both cohorts (HR 0.75 and 0.83, not significant), and J&J then stopped the program. Exposure: plasma levels rose with dose in healthy volunteers (PMID:25735992). Pathway: in healthy elderly subjects, 500 mg increased deep sleep but did not change REM sleep (PMID:26686390). The drug also blunted ketamine-induced effects in humans (PMID:25735992). These central effects support some CNS activity but do not measure the target directly. Engagement: no human mGlu2 occupancy or other direct engagement measure was found; the only occupancy data are from rats (PMID:25692015). There is no human data at all in focal epilepsy patients. The sponsors gave no reason for the failure beyond the missed endpoint. Nothing separates poor engagement from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

F598 is an anti-PNAG antibody. A patent describes a Phase 1 dose-escalation study in healthy volunteers that measured serum half-life and ex vivo opsonophagocytic activity. These are plasma levels and an ex vivo functional readout, not proof of exposure or engagement at the urethral mucosa. A later review says the gonorrhoea challenge model (NCT03222401) showed no protection. It also says whether F598 reaches or equilibrates in urogenital tissue was never studied, and suggests circulating antibody alone may be insufficient. The sponsor stopped the trial after an interim analysis judged it underpowered (F7). With no evidence of engagement at the site of action, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so U.

The index trial (NCT05027997, PMID:38310362) gave single 50 or 100 mg doses for 2 days and saw no trend toward benefit. A human PET study in healthy volunteers (NCT02447640, released in 2016, before the index trial) showed the drug reached the brain. Its mGlu5 occupancy rose with dose: 27% at 100 mg, 44% at 200 mg and 54% at 300 mg. The sponsor itself named 50–70% occupancy as the range needed for a robust effect, so both index doses fell well short and the mechanism was not properly tested. There was no tolerability cap: 300 mg was well tolerated. No downstream biomarker was measured in humans. The sponsor called the readout inconclusive, and the trial was a tiny, very short feasibility study (secondary code F7).

Dipraglurant reached the brain. In the healthy-volunteer PET study (NCT02447640, 2016), mGlu5 occupancy rose with dose: 27% at 100 mg, 44% at 200 mg and 54% at 300 mg. The sponsor defined 50–70% occupancy as the target range for efficacy. The blepharospasm trial (NCT05027997, PMID:38310362) used only 50 and 100 mg, which by that study gives about 27% occupancy or less, well below target. Engagement was therefore inadequate, so the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). Tolerability did not force the low doses: 300 mg caused only mild adverse events. No pathway biomarker was measured in patients. As a secondary factor (F7), the trial was a tiny 2-day feasibility study that the sponsor called inconclusive.

The published phase I paper for NCT00775502 shows plasma PK that rose with dose from 0.03 to 3 mg/kg. Trough levels were in the range that preclinical models suggested would kill myeloma cells, so plasma exposure is rated adequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose: no MTD was found. However, the study stopped before reaching 10 mg/kg, and no human measure of GM2 binding, ADCC or a downstream marker was reported. The investigators could not determine the GM2 status of patients' tumour cells and said the reason for the lack of activity is unknown. The lung cancer trial NCT01898156 also stopped for futility. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged GM2 from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Possible patient selection (unknown GM2 status) is listed as a secondary code.

BIW-8962 is a non-fucosylated anti-GM2 IgG1 antibody. In the lung cancer Phase 1/2 trial (NCT01898156), patients got 1–10 mg/kg every 3 weeks. The maximum tolerated dose was never reached and only rare partial responses were seen, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The myeloma Phase 1 (NCT00775502) gave no responses. Its authors said the reason for the lack of activity is unknown and suggested the preclinical activity may not carry over to patients. Only plasma drug levels were reported. I found no human data on drug levels in tumor, binding to GM2 on tumor cells, or downstream ADCC/CDC (antibody- or complement-mediated killing) markers. No other anti-GM2 drug has succeeded. Nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged GM2 from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

A receptor-occupancy study in healthy subjects (NCT01404091) was registered but posted no results, so no direct engagement data appear in the bundle. PMID:30701317 reports that BTRX-246040 (40 mg) met efficacy in an alcohol-dependence proof of concept (NCT01798303). It also reports a reduction in facial-recognition negative bias and in depression symptoms in an earlier MDD trial (NCT01724112). Same CNS target and comparable dose, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. The index trial nonetheless missed on MADRS (-1.3, p=0.59) with no tolerability limit. This suggests NOP antagonism does not drive benefit in MDD as tested. A large placebo response (-13.6) and the failure to replicate the earlier signal raise a possible trial-design contribution (F7). No source states a reason.

A [11C]NOP-1A PET study in healthy subjects (NCT01404091; DMD 2016, published before the 2018 index start) found that LY2940094 readily enters the human brain. Receptor occupancy rose with plasma concentration and approached complete occupancy over the 4–40 mg range, and the drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited by side effects. Exposure and engagement therefore count as adequate, but they were shown only in healthy volunteers, not in Parkinson's patients. No human biomarker of downstream pathway effect was found. In NCT03608371, the maximal change in UPDRS-III was no better on drug than on placebo (−15.2 vs −17.0), so NOP antagonism did not improve PD motor symptoms when tested (F2). With 6 patients per arm and a large placebo response, the trial was underpowered (F7). The sponsor gave no stated reason.

No direct human pillar data appear in the bundle. A healthy-volunteer NOP receptor occupancy study (NCT01404091) is registered, but its results are not shown. PMID:30701317 reports a positive MDD proof-of-concept at 40 mg p.o. (NCT01724112), a CNS effect through the same target. On that basis exposure, engagement and pathway are taken as inferred_adequate. The same review says the alcohol trial (NCT01798303, n=88) reduced heavy drinking, raised the probability of abstinence and lowered GGT. The registered primary endpoint, drinks per day, is not reported as met and no results were posted. So signals on other drinking measures in this disease came alongside a missed primary, which points to the endpoint (F4). The small trial size (F7) and a failed later MDD trial (NCT03193398) also leave doubt.

In a phase 1 prostate cancer study (PMID:16145049, 2005), custirsen plasma and tumor tissue levels rose with dose and tumor clusterin expression fell by more than 90%. This occurred dose-dependently at doses up to 640 mg, the dose also tested in healthy subjects (PMID:25782535). Exposure and engagement were therefore shown in humans before the NSCLC index trial began, but in prostate tumors, not NSCLC. No downstream pathway biomarker is reported in the bundle. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite adequate knockdown, adding custirsen to docetaxel did not improve overall survival in NSCLC (NCT01630733). It also failed on OS in two prostate cancer phase 3 trials (NCT01188187, NCT01578655). Together this suggests clusterin suppression does not drive chemotherapy outcome as tested.

In a phase 1 study in prostate cancer patients (PMID:16145049, 2005, NCT00054106), 40–640 mg custirsen gave dose-proportional plasma exposure and dose-dependent drug levels in prostate tissue. At 640 mg it cut clusterin expression in tumor and lymph nodes by more than 90%. That is the dose used in SYNERGY. Serum clusterin also fell in mCRPC patients on custirsen (PMID:24156019, PMID:21788353). This is a lowered target protein, so it counts as engagement; no separate downstream pathway marker beyond clusterin was measured, so pathway is only weakly supported. The drug was tolerated at 640 mg, so the dose was not limited. Even so, SYNERGY showed no overall survival benefit (HR 0.93; PMID:28283282). The cabazitaxel trial NCT01578655 was also negative, including in its poor-prognosis subgroup. With the target engaged, clusterin knockdown does not appear to improve chemotherapy outcomes in mCRPC.

The index Phase 1 dose-escalation trial NCT00733031 of the pan-Trk inhibitor AZD6918 in advanced solid tumours was terminated. The stated reason is that PK showed low and variable plasma concentrations, so reaching therapeutic concentrations was unlikely. Exposure is therefore directly shown to be inadequate in humans. No engagement or pathway data are in the bundle. The bundle gives no tolerability-driven dose cap, no other drugs on the same target and no publications. The mechanism was never properly tested because systemic exposure was insufficient, which makes this F1a. Confidence is high because the sponsor explicitly states the PK reason.

LTX-109 is a topical antimicrobial peptide that disrupts bacterial membranes. No human target is recorded. The bundle and my searches found no human measure of skin drug levels, bacterial killing or microbiological eradication at the 1–2% doses used. The only pharmacodynamic data are in vitro (PMID:28802058), and the nasal study NCT01158235 reported safety only. Lytix said the 210-child impetigo trial (NCT01803035) showed LTX-109 was safe and had a strong trend over placebo, but did not reach statistical significance. The company then sought a partner instead of running another trial. That points to a possibly underpowered trial (F7) and a business decision (F8), but with no engagement data the result is indeterminate (U).

CSF penetration was confirmed at 25 and 75 mg (PMID:33029934). There is no direct receptor-occupancy measure for this D1 PAM. Engagement is instead judged adequate from dose-dependent central D1 pharmacodynamics. These include increased sleep latency in volunteers, a stated translational biomarker (PMID:34893551), and motor improvement in PD (PMID:34664427), all from trials registered before the index trial. In LBD itself, MDS-UPDRS, ADCS-CGIC and daytime sleep improved dose-dependently (PMID:34859493, PMID:35694933). Despite this, the primary attention composite and the secondary cognition endpoints were not met (NCT03305809). D1 potentiation therefore did not improve cognition as tested (F2). Benefit appeared on motor and global endpoints rather than the chosen cognitive endpoint, so F4 is secondary. Blood-pressure effects at 75 mg did not cap the dose below active levels.

In the index RCD-II trial (NCT02633020, n=28, 10 weeks of dosing), AMG 714 missed its primary endpoint, the change in aberrant IELs (p=0.75). Histology endpoints were also null, but diarrhoea improved on a nominal basis. The sources found give no human data on IL-15 neutralisation, drug levels in the gut, or downstream IL-15 pathway markers at the doses used. The protocol cites only mouse and ex vivo data. The related celiac trials (NCT02637141, NCT04424927) also failed and likewise report no engagement data. No other anti-IL-15 drug has succeeded in this disease. Investigators did not say why it failed and suggested further study. The trial was small and short (F7 possible), but nothing separates a drug that never engaged IL-15 from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02637141 missed its primary endpoint: AMG 714 at 150 mg and 300 mg did not stop gluten from damaging the gut lining, measured as villous height to crypt depth ratio. Its only downstream signal was partial. Growth of the gut-lining immune cells (CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes) that IL-15 drives was smaller at 300 mg, with a nominal p of 0.03, but not at 150 mg. Symptoms also improved somewhat. The searches found no human data on drug levels, IL-15 neutralization or NK-cell lowering. The only pharmacodynamic data come from a surrogate antibody in monkeys, which does not count. The later trials in type 2 refractory disease (NCT02633020) and in diet-non-responsive disease (NCT04424927) also failed. No pillar shows whether the drug engaged IL-15 in the gut. That leaves a drug that never engaged indistinguishable from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the RCD-II trial (NCT02633020), AMG 714 did not reduce aberrant IELs compared with placebo (p=0.75, n=22 analysed). The published report says the investigators saw some improvement on secondary measures. None of the sources I found shows IL-15 neutralisation in humans: no free IL-15 levels, no receptor or pathway-signalling readout, and no tissue drug levels. The protocol cites only mouse and ex vivo explant pharmacology. A Celimmune patent mentions vague 'signals' in serum IL-15 and a fall in IELs at 300 mg in the gluten-challenge trial (NCT02637141), but no numbers are given and it was not this disease. The later trial (NCT04424927) also failed. No other IL-15 drug has succeeded in this disease. With engagement unmeasured, I can't tell whether the drug failed to engage or the target doesn't matter, so the code is U. The small sample makes F7 a possible secondary code.

The phase I/IIa study (PMID:25193991) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure. Its dose-limiting toxicities appeared only at 30 mg, so the 10 mg index dose was not tolerability-capped. No direct human target-engagement or pathway biomarker data appear in the bundle. Frequent hypertension and proteinuria are consistent with VEGFR inhibition but do not count as measured engagement. The index trial (NCT07824505; PMID:42928801) randomized only 68 patients and missed IRC-assessed PFS (HR 0.60, p=0.105). The authors attribute the miss to non-proportional hazards that the prespecified log-rank test underestimated. Restricted mean survival time analysis and investigator-assessed PFS (HR 0.53, p=0.03) were significant. The sources therefore present a small trial with an analysis that could not capture the effect, not an absence of drug activity, pointing to a design or power failure (F7).

In the CASPAR Phase 2b trial (NCT03194217), none of the three bavisant doses (0.5, 1 and 3 mg/day) improved Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores over placebo after 6 weeks. The dose response was flat, and the 1 mg arm did slightly worse than placebo. My searches found no human data on brain H3 receptor occupancy, central exposure or a downstream biomarker (such as EEG or wakefulness measures) for bavisant at any dose. The only brain-penetration claims come from vendor pages, which are preclinical. The earlier ADHD trial (NCT00880217) used higher doses (up to 10 mg/day), which were poorly tolerated, and also failed. That suggests the PD doses were low, but it does not show inadequate engagement. No other H3 drug appears in the bundle, and the sponsor gave no explanation. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell apart a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT03194217, no dose of bavisant (0.5, 1 or 3 mg/day) beat placebo on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale in Parkinson's patients with daytime sleepiness. I found no human evidence of brain H3 receptor occupancy, CSF exposure or a pharmacodynamic marker (such as sleep EEG or wakefulness measures), whether in Parkinson's patients or in healthy volunteers. The only other efficacy data, the adult ADHD trial (NCT00880217, Weisler 2012), also failed. There, 10 mg/day was poorly tolerated (19.2% stopped due to side effects vs 2.7% on placebo), and the Parkinson's trial used lower doses. That hints that the doses may have been limited, but no source ties this to engagement. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged H3 from a target that does not matter, so the answer is U. F1a is listed as a possible secondary code.

Serabelisib 200 mg QD with sapanisertib failed to beat everolimus on PFS in ccRCC (NCT02724020). In the phase 1 (NCT01449370, PMID:28490463), plasma exposure was dose-proportional and skin pS6 was suppressed at ≥200 mg. That supports engagement and pathway at the index dose, but only in surrogate tissue of mixed solid-tumour patients, not in ccRCC tumours. The engagement call rests on a downstream marker, which is why U is a secondary code. QD dosing had a narrow tolerable window because of ALT/AST elevations, and food and PPI use made exposure variable (PMID:30168905), so under-exposure is possible (F1a secondary). The sapanisertib-only arm also failed, and other serabelisib combinations failed (NCT02393209, NCT02725268). This points to PI3Kα/mTOR inhibition adding no benefit over everolimus in ccRCC.

The index trial (NCT02393209), docetaxel plus TAK-117 in unselected NSCLC, enrolled only 14 patients in phase 1b. RP2D was 200 mg, and the trial stopped for 'lack of efficacy in combination' with no PFS data posted. In the first-in-human study (PMID:28490463, NCT01449370), plasma exposure rose roughly dose-proportionally. Skin pS6 was suppressed at ≥200 mg, a downstream PD marker that we take as evidence of PI3Kα engagement and pathway inhibition at the RP2D. That data came from mixed solid tumors, not NSCLC, and was published after the index trial started. Single-agent activity was limited and confined to PIK3CA-mutant patients. Combination trials in other cancers also failed (NCT02725268, NCT02724020). This points toward the mechanism not driving benefit in unselected NSCLC (F2). Lack of PIK3CA selection (F3) and the tiny, uninformative trial (F7) are alternative explanations.

Index Phase 3 NCT01004315 posted no results and gave no stop reason. Phase 1 PK studies and a pharmacodynamic study in neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NCT02259751) exist but posted no results, so the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. Two drugs on the same target, mirabegron and vibegron, are FDA-approved for overactive bladder, which points to the molecule rather than the target. In vitro data (PMID:37656760) show ritobegron's intrinsic activity falls at lower β3 receptor density and that it is less selective than vibegron. This is consistent with weaker engagement, but it is not human evidence. Animal efficacy (PMID:22511202, PMID:22552730) does not count. Because engagement is no_human_data, U also applies.

Sustained plasma SN-38 exposure is reported to have translated to cancer patients (PMID:25228368), so exposure is adequate. The bundle has no direct human TOP1 engagement or pathway biomarker data. The index trial (NCT00856375) compared EP 145 mg/m2 with active irinotecan and was terminated before completing accrual 'due to evolving standards of care' (PMID:29043412). With only 83 patients, PFS still favoured EP (4.0 vs 2.8 months, HR 0.65, p=0.07), with longer duration of response and tolerable toxicity; the authors call EP active. The miss reflects an underpowered, prematurely closed trial rather than a demonstrated mechanism or molecule failure. The non-efficacy termination reason adds F8 as secondary.

BEACON missed its OS primary endpoint against active physician's-choice chemotherapy (HR 0.87, p=0.084; NCT01492101, PMID:26482278). Sustained plasma SN38 exposure in patients at 145 mg/m2 is reported (PMID:25228368, PMID:26463521), and dose intensity was high with fewer grade ≥3 toxicities, so dose was not limited (PMID:27441152). No direct human TOP1 engagement or pathway data are in the bundle. Phase 2 objective responses of 29% (PMID:24095299) suggest the drug was active, but that is clinical efficacy, not a pillar measurement. The sources attribute residual signal to a prespecified subgroup with stable brain metastases. That subgroup benefit then failed to confirm in ATTAIN (NCT02915744, PMID:35552364). Because engagement is unmeasured, U also applies.

In the index RA trial (NCT02884635, PMID:32075475), ASP1707 30 mg BID cut plasma LH by more than 90% in over 90% of patients. LH fell rapidly below 1 IU/L by week 1 and stayed suppressed. This shows direct GnRH receptor antagonism and the expected downstream pathway effect in RA patients. Pharmacokinetics were also evaluated. The same drug met its endpoint in endometriosis through the same target at lower doses (NCT01767090, PMID:31067329), confirming it is pharmacologically active. Despite robust engagement, ACR20/50/70 and all secondary endpoints were unchanged. GnRH/LH suppression therefore does not drive RA activity as tested. The engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, so it was not available before the index trial started.

Human PET (NCT00829907, registered 2008, before the index trial; PMID:33296042) showed brain penetration and dose-related α2C-AR occupancy, framed by the authors as validated target engagement. Modelled maximum occupancy was only 52–63%, so the partial engagement still leaves F1a open. Occupancy was measured only in healthy volunteers, and the bundle has no human pathway biomarker. The 12-week exploratory phase 2a in AD (NCT01324518; PMID:29067315) was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Only one of four CDR primary endpoints improved (episodic memory, P=.030, unadjusted); speed and attention did not. That looks like engagement without robust cognitive benefit (F2). The small, multi-endpoint design (F7) also limits interpretation. The program then shifted to agitation (NCT02471196).

In the index trial (NCT01315899; ACR 2012 abstract), patients with Raynaud's secondary to systemic sclerosis took single 30 or 100 mg doses. Finger blood flow recovered more slowly after a cold challenge on drug than on placebo, the trial stopped on DSMC advice, and the drug was well tolerated. The only human engagement data are brain PET in healthy volunteers (NCT00829907, PMID:33296042). That study shows plasma exposure and dose-related α2C occupancy, with modelled maximum occupancy of only 52–63%. No study measured occupancy of the relevant peripheral (digital vascular) α2C receptors or a vascular biomarker in patients. A 2016 review calls the paradoxical result unexplained. Nothing separates a drug that did not engage the target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F1a (partial occupancy) and F2 are possible alternatives.

MERU (NCT03033511) missed OS in DLL3-high ES-SCLC (HR 1.07), with more serious AEs on Rova-T. TAHOE (NCT03061812) was worse than topotecan, and TRINITY (NCT02674568) gave only about 15% ORR. The bundle has no human PK, DLL3 occupancy or pathway biomarker data; phase 1 (PMID:27932068) reports only toxicity-defined dosing and responses. Another DLL3 agent, tarlatamab, is FDA-approved in SCLC, so DLL3 is a valid target in this disease. That points to the molecule (the PBD-payload ADC) rather than the target, with no pillar evidence that Rova-T engaged adequately. Molecule-specific toxicity also contributed: excess serious AEs and deaths in MERU and TAHOE, and Grade 5 events in combination trials (NCT03026166). A tolerability cap below the engagement needed is not shown, so dose_limited is false.

In SLE patients, AMG 557 at doses up to 210 mg SC (the index dose) showed dose-dependent PK, maximal target occupancy of ICOSL, and a selective reduction in anti-KLH IgG consistent with ICOS pathway blockade, with acceptable safety (PMID:27099766; NCT02391259 and NCT00774943 were registered before the index start). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore adequate, though shown in SLE rather than Sjögren's. The index Phase 2a in primary Sjögren's (NCT02334306) missed its ESSDAI endpoint at day 99 (difference -1.4, p=0.262) without dose-limiting toxicity. This points to ICOSL blockade not driving clinical disease activity as tested (F2). The small trial (n=32) leaves possible underpowering (F7).

The index trial (NCT01161615) tested a topical etodolac-lidocaine patch for shoulder tendonitis and bursitis. It posted no results and gives no stop reason. The bundle does show COX-2 inhibition works in this disease: oral etodolac at 200–300 mg b.i.d. was efficacious in tendinitis and bursitis, comparable to naproxen and diclofenac (PMID:1699764, PMID:17694363). That points to the patch product rather than the target. However, no human data show tissue exposure or COX-2 engagement from the patch. Only plasma detection after a topical gel is reported (PMID:7812122), so all three pillars are no_human_data for the index formulation. A follow-on shoulder Phase 3 (NCT01506154) suggests the program continued. The bundle is thin, so U is a plausible alternative.

The index trial NCT01198834 tested a topical etodolac-lidocaine patch for ankle sprain. It posted no results and gave no stop reason, so the bundle does not even document the efficacy failure. Oral etodolac produced dose-dependent analgesia, and modeling ties pain relief to COX-2 inhibition (PMID:6212554, PMID:2948162, PMID:28875479, PMID:10392328). That is systemic oral dosing, not transdermal delivery to ankle tissue, so it cannot support an inferred-adequate rating for the patch. The bundle has no human tissue-exposure or COX-2 engagement data for the patch. Other COX inhibitors, such as topical methyl salicylate, are approved for injury, which hints at F1b, but the patch's engagement is unknown. The code is therefore U.

Quilizumab depletes membrane-IgE B cells rather than neutralizing circulating IgE. In asthma patients (SOLARIO NCT01196039, registered before COSTA) and in COSTA itself, it lowered serum total and allergen-specific IgE by only 30-40% (PMID:26993628, PMID:24990880). That is partial lowering of the target ligand, so engagement and pathway are inadequate. Omalizumab, on the same target (IgE), is FDA-approved in asthma, so the target is validated and this molecule's partial IgE lowering is the more direct explanation (F1b). Tolerability did not limit dose. The authors conclude that depleting IgE-switched B cells was not sufficient, which also fits F1a: the mechanism was not adequately tested. Subgroup analyses by biomarker showed no benefit, which argues against F3.

AMBLED (NCT03162874; PMID:35218231) did not reduce OFF time or dyskinesia at 10 or 30 mg. Safety was clean and off time fell numerically with dose, so tolerability did not cap the dose. All evidence of brain penetration and mGlu4 engagement comes from macaques (PMID:30216534, PMID:30066121). The human PET occupancy study of foliglurax in healthy volunteers and PD patients (NCT04175132) started after the index trial and was ended once AMBLED failed, as was the PD pharmacodynamic study (NCT04322227). The human [11C]PXT012253 paper only reports test-retest of the tracer. No other mGlu4 drug has been tested clinically. Because there is no human data on engagement, a drug that never engaged mGlu4 cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. Lundbeck gave lack of efficacy as the reason.

The index Phase 1-2 CRPC trial (NCT02049190) had DLT and response as primary endpoints, status unknown, and posted no results. It is classified not_efficacy, and the bundle shows no failed efficacy readout. Later trials were terminated for sponsor decisions: 'Sponsor decision to discontinue onapristone development' (NCT05618613) and funding (NCT04738292), which points to business reasons. Earlier hepatotoxicity concerns were largely adjudicated as unrelated for the extended-release formulation (PMID:32594454). The only human pharmacodynamic data are endometrial PR-antagonism effects in healthy women at 400 mg of the old formulation (PMID:9176442). There are no exposure or engagement data in prostate cancer or at the index doses. If this were treated as an efficacy failure, it would be indeterminate (U).

In the index trial in relapsed/refractory cHL (NCT01572519; PMID:25628399), exposure rose near dose-proportionally from 150 to 450 mg QD and plateaued at 600 mg. Target engagement was confirmed in these patients (>80% inhibition of CSF-1R phosphorylation). No dose-limiting toxicities occurred and no MTD was reached, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Despite this, monotherapy produced 1 complete remission and mostly stable disease, which the authors called limited activity. No downstream pathway biomarker in cHL is reported, so pathway is no_human_data. In RA (PMID:26233509), the drug also showed adequate exposure and peripheral engagement (raised CSF-1, fewer CD16+ monocytes) without efficacy. Engagement was adequate, so CSF1R inhibition alone does not appear to drive cHL.

Before the Crohn's index trial (NCT03854305, no results posted), human data showed adequate systemic pharmacology. In RA (PMID:26233509, NCT01597739; 100 mg BID), exposure exceeded the projected active concentration. Target engagement and pathway activity were also shown: CSF-1 rose and CD16+ monocytes fell, yet there was no efficacy. In Hodgkin lymphoma (PMID:25628399), CSF-1R phosphorylation was inhibited by more than 80%, with no dose-limiting toxicities and no MTD reached, so dose was not capped. Mucosal CSF-1R engagement in Crohn's patients is not shown; the colitis data are murine only (PMID:31710624). Peripheral engagement was nonetheless adequate, so the failed readout is best read as CSF-1R/macrophage inhibition not driving clinical activity. Confidence is medium because the index results and the index dose are absent from the bundle.

In the index RA trial (NCT01597739; PMID:26233509), edicotinib 100 mg BID gave exposure above the projected pharmacologically active concentration. Target engagement and proof of activity were shown in RA patients: CSF-1 rose and CD16+ monocytes fell with drug but not placebo. In Hodgkin lymphoma, >80% inhibition of CSF-1R phosphorylation was reported (PMID:25628399), with no dose-limiting toxicities. Despite adequate exposure and peripheral engagement, DAS28-CRP improvement did not exceed placebo (1.15 vs 1.42, p=0.30), and the authors conclude efficacy was absent. This points to CSF1R inhibition not driving DMARD-refractory RA as tested. The engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself, so it was not available before the trial started. Synovial tissue engagement was not measured.

The index trial of azacitidine with or without birinapant in MDS/CMML (NCT02147873) was terminated for lack of efficacy. In humans, birinapant had a 30–35 h plasma half-life and accumulated in tumor tissue. It suppressed cIAP1 and increased apoptosis in PBMCs and tumor at doses up to an MTD of 47 mg/m2 (PMID:26333381, NCT00993239). The ovarian phase 2 at 47 mg/m2 also showed consistent cIAP1 downregulation and procaspase-3 decrease in tumors and PBMCs, yet no clinical benefit (PMID:26566079, NCT01681368). So the target was engaged and the apoptotic pathway moved. Engagement was not shown in MDS patients, and the MDS dose is not given in the bundle, so the classification is inferred: an engaged IAP target that does not drive benefit as tested. No other IAP antagonist has succeeded in this disease.

Index trial NCT02147873 (azacitidine ± birinapant in MDS/CMML) was terminated for lack of efficacy, with no results posted. Human pillars come from solid-tumor patients. Phase 1 (PMID:26333381) showed a 30–35 h plasma half-life and accumulation in tumor tissue. The drug suppressed cIAP1 and increased apoptosis in PBMCs and tumor, with an MTD of 47 mg/m2 and good tolerability. The ovarian phase 2 (PMID:26566079) confirmed consistent cIAP1 downregulation and procaspase-3 decrease in tumor and PBMCs, again without clinical benefit. Engagement was therefore adequate, but it was never shown in MDS/CMML patients, and those reports were published after the index trial started. Repeated futility despite engagement (NCT01681368, NCT02587962) points to the mechanism not driving the disease.

In severe sepsis patients, the Phase IIa trial (NCT00615017, registered 2008, before the index trial; PMID:22340283) showed dose-proportional PK. At the same multiple-dose regimens used in the index trial (250/50 and 500/100 U/kg), serum TNF-α fell to near-undetectable levels within 2 hours and stayed suppressed. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. In Japanese sepsis patients (PMID:23681364), TNF-α decreased with a similar fall in IL-6 and IL-8, supporting a pathway effect, although placebo values also declined. PK/PD modelling guided dose selection for the index trial (PMID:23001587). Despite adequate engagement, NCT01145560 showed no ventilator-free-day benefit and no dose response. This points to TNF neutralization not driving outcome in sepsis as tested.

The index maintenance trial NCT01316939 was stopped because the induction trial NCT01277666 / PMID:26400458 failed at 500 mg once and twice daily. Plasma exposure was shown in humans (PMID:27121943). The Phase 2 paper (PMID:23527300 / PMC3603920) modeled plasma levels in patients. It estimated that 500 mg once daily stayed above the in vitro serum IC90 for at least 8 hours, and that 250 mg twice daily was probably too low. That is an inference from potency in the lab, not a measured CCR9 occupancy or chemotaxis blockade, and the sources report no downstream biomarker. PMID:27926729 notes that very high doses were needed to block the receptor, which hints that engagement was incomplete but does not show it. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged CCR9 can't be separated from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Exposure: LY2787106 had dose-proportional PK in cancer-anemia patients (PMID:28327200). Engagement was not measured as free hepcidin, but neutralization is supported by consistent dose-dependent rises in serum iron and transferrin saturation at 3 and 10 mg/kg. These were shown in the target disease, though published after the trial started. The iron effect was transient, returning to baseline by day 8. At 10 mg/kg weekly, with or without oral iron, hemoglobin fell (-0.5 and -0.2 g/dL; NCT01340976). The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Hepcidin neutralization mobilized iron but did not improve anemia, which fits F2. The short 4-week exposure and the transient effect leave room for a duration or timing explanation (F4).

Pillars were measured directly. Omarigliptin gave about 90% trough DPP-4 inhibition with raised active GLP-1 in obese T2D patients (NCT01088711, started 2010; PMID:26869191) and in healthy subjects (PMID:27225334). Multiple Phase 2/3 trials met their A1C endpoints at 25 mg weekly (NCT01217073, NCT01717313, NCT01755156, NCT01704261, NCT01703221), and the drug is approved in Japan. The index trial in young adults (18-45) missed largely because of an unusually large placebo response (-0.45 vs -0.33), which points to a trial or population artifact rather than mechanism failure. The US program ended through a business decision not to file, and the CV outcomes trial was terminated for business reasons (PMID:28893244, NCT01703208). The program-level stop is therefore commercial, not an efficacy failure.

TPX-114 is an autologous fibroblast cell therapy made by Tego Science, even though the bundle lists it as a peptide. It has no recorded molecular target. No human source measures exposure, engagement or a pathway effect. The 6-patient Phase 1 reported only MRI tendon healing. In the Phase 3 part of NCT03668028, the 24-week retear rate was 21.88% with TPX-114, and the difference from repair alone was not significant (p=0.4184). The sponsor blamed little prior research to base the design on and high pandemic-related dropout (F7). It planned a follow-up trial with a more specific patient population and an adequate sample size (F3). Because engagement is no_human_data, nothing separates a drug that failed to engage from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In metastatic non-squamous NSCLC patients (phase 1b NCT01189968, registered 2010; PMID:29188408), demcizumab with carboplatin/pemetrexed reached concentrations exceeding those saturating DLL4 binding. It also modulated Notch-signaling and angiogenesis genes in peripheral blood, so exposure, engagement and pathway were shown. Cardiopulmonary toxicity forced a truncated regimen in duration, but the 5 mg/kg dose kept saturating levels, so the dose was not capped below engagement. In the index trial NCT02259582, response was numerically lower with demcizumab (6/29 and 10/28 vs 13/25), with more serious AEs. The pancreatic trial NCT02289898 also failed. This points to DLL4 blockade not adding benefit. Mechanism-related cardiovascular toxicity (PMID:25324140) may also have offset efficacy.

The index trial NCT01189942 was a Phase 1 MTD study of demcizumab plus FOLFIRI in mCRC. It had no efficacy primary endpoint and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). Pillars held in humans outside CRC. In NSCLC, PMID:29188408 reports concentrations exceeding DLL4-saturating levels and modulation of Notch and angiogenesis genes in blood, published after the index start. Elsewhere, randomized Phase 2 trials with saturating truncated regimens failed: NCT02259582 (lower response with demcizumab) and NCT02289898 (PFS HR 0.93). That pattern suggests the mechanism adds little benefit (F2). Cumulative cardiopulmonary toxicity forced truncated dosing (PMID:25324140), though not below engagement (F5 secondary).

Demcizumab reached plasma concentrations exceeding those saturating DLL4 binding at the 5 mg/kg q3w truncated regimen, and peripheral-blood expression of Notch and angiogenesis genes shifted (PMID:29188408). This supports exposure, engagement and pathway in humans, though only in NSCLC, and was published after the index trial began. In pancreatic cancer, adding truncated demcizumab to gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel did not improve PFS (HR 0.93, p=0.72; NCT02289898). The parallel NSCLC phase 2 also failed (NCT02259582), so the target does not appear to drive benefit as tested (F2). The regimen was shortened because of on-target cardiopulmonary toxicity: pulmonary hypertension and heart failure with prolonged dosing (PMID:25324140, PMID:29188408). That limited how long the drug was given rather than how fully it engaged DLL4, so F5 is secondary.

Plasma exposure was dose-linear (PMID:25105516, PMID:33043969). In CHB patients, 1–4 mg weekly gave dose-dependent ISG15 induction, but it was transient and returned to baseline within a week. No patient had serum IFN-α (PMID:25733157, PMID:29104121). The HIV study saw consistent immune stimulation only above 4 mg (PMID:33043969). Doses were deliberately kept low because flu-like, IFN-α-linked AEs rose with dose at 8–12 mg (PMID:23416308, PMID:39278975). Chimpanzee efficacy came with IFN-α induction (PMID:23415804), but animal data do not count. HBsAg was unchanged in both phase 2 trials (NCT02166047, NCT02579382). Immune activation at tolerable doses was likely insufficient. F2 is possible because ISG15 did not track HBsAg (PMID:29851204).

PMID:20662070 reports single- and multiple-dose PK in healthy volunteers, so exposure was measured. It also reports ex vivo inhibition of MIP-1β-stimulated CCR5 internalization across the 20-150 mg range used in NCT00713544, which is target engagement, apparently not measured in RA patients. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. No AZD5672 dose separated from placebo on ACR20 at 12 weeks, while etanercept did (NCT00713544). The review PMID:22494450 notes that maraviroc and SCH351125 also failed in RA and concludes CCR5 is not a desirable RA target, citing chemokine redundancy. That supports F2: the mechanism does not drive RA as tested. The review also mentions patient selection, a minor F3 consideration.

The data monitoring committee stopped NCT00770354 early because the AS1402 + letrozole arm trended toward worse response and more early progression, and the final analysis showed no efficacy difference. FcγR and MUC1 polymorphisms did not pick out any subgroup that benefited. Exposure counts as adequate: in the Phase 1 breast cancer study (PMC2790853), plasma levels at the 9 mg/kg dose reached concentrations that elicited ADCC in vitro. No human measure of engagement was found: no MUC1 binding or occupancy in tumour, no ADCC in patients, no downstream biomarker. In vitro work (PMID:17692456) suggests shed serum MUC1 may block the antibody, but that is not human evidence. No other anti-MUC1 drug has succeeded in breast cancer. So the bundle cannot tell a molecule that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter: U.

In the 2-week knee OA trial NCT00689273, the drug did not beat placebo on WOMAC pain (difference -0.49, p=0.39). The search found human evidence that it engaged CCR2. The NCT02732938 protocol says healthy-volunteer studies (single doses 1-1000 mg; 5-500 mg twice daily for 14 days) were well tolerated. In those studies the drug maximally suppressed CCL2-induced pERK in blood monocytes at ≥150 mg twice daily, suggesting near-complete CCR2 saturation. Pancreatic cancer studies also showed fewer CCR2+ monocytes in blood and fewer tumor macrophages. No tolerability cap was reported. Caveats: the dose used in the OA trial is not known, nothing was measured in OA patients or joints, and the engagement data appeared only after the index trial. This most likely means CCR2 blockade does not drive OA pain over this time frame. Medium confidence.

Human PK was dose-proportional, and α4β7 receptor occupancy had an EC50 of 0.01 µg/mL in healthy and UC subjects (PMID:24803302; trial NCT01164904 registered 2010, before the index trial). Index doses of 21–210 mg should give near-saturating occupancy. The same doses met week-8 remission in UC (NCT01694485), so the gut pathway is inferred adequate. No engagement was measured in Crohn disease. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Despite this, week-8 remission was not significant at any dose (NCT01696396). Approvals of vedolizumab and natalizumab in Crohn disease argue the target matters. The small, unbalanced arms with ~10-point numerical gains (F7) and a short 8-week endpoint (F4) are plausible contributors, but the bundle does not state a cause.

The bundle has no direct target-engagement measure, such as myostatin binding or free-ligand levels. In older fallers with muscle weakness (NCT01604408, started after the index trial), the drug met its aLBM endpoint (difference 0.426 kg, p<0.001). That trial's doses are not shown, so treating engagement and the lean-mass pathway effect as inferred adequate assumes comparable dosing. In the index trial (NCT01369511), aLBM rose with dose (0.30% placebo, then 0.74%, 1.02% and 1.36%), but standard errors were wide (about 0.5%) and roughly 30% of participants were missing from the analysis. No dose was significant. Phase 1 data showed no tolerability cap (NCT01341470, NCT01524224). This pattern points to an underpowered, noisy post-surgical setting rather than an inactive mechanism. The sources do not state a reason, so confidence is low.

No PK, myostatin-binding or muscle biomarker data are posted for pancreatic cancer patients. Engagement is inferred: landogrozumab met its appendicular lean body mass endpoint in older fallers (NCT01604408, p<0.001). That shows anti-myostatin activity in human muscle, though the bundle does not give that trial's dose. The hip-replacement trial at 35–315 mg missed aLBM (NCT01369511), so the inference is shaky. Doses were not capped by tolerability: phase 1 escalated to 700 mg without dose-limiting signals (NCT01524224, NCT01341470). Both index arms (100/300 mg) had numerically worse OS than placebo (NCT01505530). This suggests myostatin blockade does not improve survival here. OS is also distal to an anti-cachexia mechanism (F4). U is possible given no direct engagement data.

Olumacostat glasaretil is a topical ACC inhibitor meant to cut sebum production. ACC inhibition and sebum suppression were only shown in human sebocytes in vitro and in hamster and pig skin (PMID:28259683). I found no human data on skin drug levels, ACC inhibition or sebum output. A 2017 review notes that none of the trials measured sebum directly.
