The Phase 2 trials met their endpoints (NCT01936324, NCT02431052), but both Phase 3 trials missed every primary endpoint (NCT03028363, NCT03073486). The sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation and was just 'surprised'. No other ACC drug has worked in acne. With engagement unmeasured, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Serum carlumab exposure was adequate: steady-state levels exceeded the 10 µg/mL target (PMID:22907596), and the half-life was 6.6–9.6 days (PMID:23385782). Engagement failed. Free CCL2 was suppressed only transiently and then rebounded above baseline in cancer patients (PMID:23385782, PMID:24928772). PK/PD modelling showed the in vivo KD was too weak to suppress free CCL2 at clinically viable doses (PMID:23878055). In the IPF index trial itself, free CCL2 rose above baseline at weeks 24 and 52 (PMID:26493793), so inadequate engagement was shown in this disease, though only in a publication after the trial began. No MTD was reached, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. The CCL2 mechanism was therefore never adequately tested.

In the index mCRPC trial (NCT00992186; PMID:22907596), steady-state carlumab serum levels exceeded the 10 μg/mL target concentration, so exposure was adequate. Suppression of free CCL2 was only brief after each dose and was not sustained. The authors concluded carlumab 'did not block the CCL2/CCR2 axis.' Phase 1 data (PMID:23385782) and the PK/PD model (PMID:23878055) likewise showed only transient free CCL2 suppression, followed by rebound above baseline. The model attributes this to a binding affinity weaker in vivo than in vitro, preventing suppression at clinically viable doses. The phase 1b combination study (PMID:24928772) and the IPF trial (PMID:26493793) show the same pattern. No MTD was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Engagement was inadequate, so the mechanism was never properly tested.

The index trial NCT03078322 posted no results. Plasma exposure to AV-101 and its active metabolite 7-Cl-KYNA rose with dose up to 1440 mg/d, which was well tolerated (PMID:29229209, PMID:33318635, PMID:38261609). In treatment-resistant depression at 1080–1440 mg/d, no central biomarker moved: MRS glutamate, fMRI and CSF measures were all unchanged, and there was no clinical effect (PMID:32236521). Brain NMDAR engagement (40 Hz ASSR) appeared only at 1440 mg, and only in healthy veterans (PMID:33318635). That paper was published after the index trial started. Its authors questioned whether AV-101 engages the target effectively and urged higher doses. So engagement looks marginal and the mechanism was likely not adequately tested (F1a). A non-causal target (F2) cannot be excluded.

The index trial tested inhaled imatinib (PDGFR inhibitor), not 4-Cl-KYN; the GRIN1 data (PMID:33318635, PMID:32236521) are irrelevant. Phase 2b showed no PVR, 6MWD or secondary benefit at 10-70 mg BID, and the drug was well tolerated (PMID:41738079). PK supported delivery to lung and plasma, but systemic exposure was well below oral imatinib (PMID:36923571). No human PDGFR inhibition or downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Oral imatinib, which acts on the same target, is described as efficacious in PAH (PMID:41738079), and AV-101 lacked pillar evidence of adequate engagement. This points to the formulation or delivered exposure rather than the target (F1b). Because engagement was never measured, the case is otherwise indeterminate (U).

In the Phase 1 trial (NCT00129337, Clin Cancer Res 2011), weekly doses up to 3 mg/kg, the dose later used in the index trial, gave measurable plasma levels with a half-life of 37–47 h. The bound target, β2GP1–phosphatidylserine on tumor blood vessels, faces the bloodstream, so plasma exposure is reasonable evidence of exposure. The investigators admitted they had no biomarker data. Their only pharmacodynamic signal was mild clotting-time (aPTT) prolongation in vitro, with no known link to effect. No human tumor uptake, target binding, or downstream effect was shown in NSCLC or any other disease. The Phase 3 trial (PMID:29767677) missed its survival endpoint. Its signals in patients with high β2GP1 and in those given later checkpoint inhibitors were post-hoc, which points to possible patient-selection issues (F3). With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The Phase 1 study (NCT00129337) measured plasma PK up to 3 mg/kg weekly, the dose used in the index trial. The half-life was 37-47 h, no MTD was reached and the authors said the PK supports weekly dosing, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. No human data were found on the target itself: no measures of β2GP1/phosphatidylserine binding in tumour, vascular disruption or immune biomarkers. In the open-label NCT01272791 (n=70), median OS was 5.6 vs 5.2 months (HR 0.75). The response rate rose, 28% vs 13%, but the trial was small and not powered to show a survival difference (F7, secondary). The Phase 3 lung cancer trial NCT01999673 was also negative. Engagement was never shown, so a drug that missed its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter. Hence U.

NCT00669903 missed its primary endpoint: no AZD0328 dose beat placebo on the CogState composite at Day 14. AstraZeneca's Open Innovation page reports only plasma levels in patients, about 5x the binding IC50 at the top 0.675 mg dose. It says the drug is CNS penetrant but gives no human CSF data, PET occupancy or downstream biomarker. Nausea limited tolerability at 1.35 mg or more, and the multiple-dose MTD was 1 mg, but nothing shows that engagement needed more than the doses tested. Rodent and monkey data (PMID:21550383, PMID:20965497) don't count as human evidence. No other α7 agonist has succeeded in schizophrenia. The sponsor's stated reason was failure to meet the Target Product Profile. A drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Pexiganan is a topical antimicrobial peptide that kills bacteria by disrupting their membranes. Neither trial in OneStep-1 (NCT01590758: 50.6% vs 60.6%) nor OneStep-2 (NCT01594762: 56/97 vs 54/103) beat vehicle cream plus standard wound care in mild diabetic foot infection. No source gives human data on wound-tissue drug levels, bacterial eradication or a biomarker; the in vitro MIC data (PMID:27193536) do not count. The sponsor pointed out that no earlier trial had ever measured the response rate with wound care alone. Placebo responses of about 52–61% suggest many mild infections cleared without an antibiotic, so a trial design or patient-selection problem is possible. Still, nothing here separates a drug that failed to act from a mechanism that does not matter in this population, so the code is U.

Pexiganan is a topical antimicrobial peptide with no recorded host target. There are no human data on drug levels in the wound. In the 1990s trials against oral ofloxacin (NCT00563394/433), clinical improvement was 85–90% in both arms, but those trials had no placebo arm. In OneStep-1 (NCT01590758) and OneStep-2 (NCT01594762), the drug did not beat vehicle plus standardized wound care, and neither trial showed more bacterial eradication. So the proximal antibacterial effect was not shown, which I scored as inadequate engagement. The sponsor blamed the design: these were the first placebo-controlled trials in mild diabetic foot infection, and no response rate was known for wound care alone. That points to a high vehicle response, so F7. The evidence cannot rule out a drug that never engaged (F1a), so confidence is low.

The Phase 1 index trial NCT02014116 set a recommended dose of 300 mg twice daily. It was terminated for lack of sufficient clinical efficacy: no responses, and 8 patients with stable disease. PMID:31645440 reports that plasma exposures at this dose exceeded the preclinical concentration associated with tumor regression, so exposure was adequate. It also states that 'predicted pharmacodynamic effects were not observed' despite that exposure. So target engagement and pathway suppression were not shown in patients, and the pan-RAF mechanism was not properly tested. The bundle does not say tolerability capped the dose below what engagement needed, so dose_limited is false. No other drugs on these targets appear in the bundle. The PD measure is not specified, so engagement versus pathway is uncertain; confidence is medium.

Phase 1 studies in healthy participants (NCT02257151, PMID:28265691) showed dose-proportional exposure across 25–350 mg daily, covering the index doses. They also showed dose- and concentration-dependent inhibition of CD69 expression, a BTK-dependent pathway readout, with good tolerability. That trial was registered as a target-engagement study before the index trial started. Engagement was not shown in RA patients. In the index trial (NCT02638948), ACR20 and ACR70 at week 12 were not different from placebo at any dose; only 200 mg showed a non-significant numeric trend. No other BTK inhibitor has succeeded in RA in this bundle, so the molecule-versus-target question (F1b) does not arise. With pharmacodynamic engagement shown and no efficacy, the best fit is that BTK does not drive RA as tested (F2). The small 350 mg arm (n=26) limited power (F7).

SHINE (NCT03487276) missed HiSCR at week 16, with responders similar across all arms. The trial paper attributes the miss partly to an unexpectedly high placebo HiSCR rate of 47.1% (PMID:41081529), a design or execution problem, hence F7. Post hoc, high-dose vilobelimab cut draining tunnels and IHS4 by 63%, which suggests endpoint choice also mattered (F4). Exposure and engagement were shown in humans: PK and dose-dependent C5a neutralization in sepsis (PMID:34806021), and efficient C5a inhibition in COVID-19 (PMID:35029045). Neither was shown in HS patients, and both were published after the index trial began. The bundle has no downstream pathway biomarker. No dose capping: SAEs were few. F2 is secondary if the mechanism is simply irrelevant to HS.

Vilobelimab had adequate exposure and engagement in COVID-19 patients: PK and near-complete C5a neutralization (PMID:35029045, PMID:37332066). Pathway markers moved, with IL-8 suppressed and coagulation markers affected (PMID:36566174). These data were published after the index start, though sepsis dose-dependent C5a lowering also exists (PMID:34806021). In NCT04333420 the primary Cox analysis narrowly missed (HR 0.728, p=0.094), but several sensitivity analyses were significant, with fewer deaths (54 vs 77). The sources describe improved survival, and an FDA EUA followed (PMID:36087611, PMID:37421632). The miss reflects analysis and power limits, not mechanism failure, hence F7. Heterogeneity with larger benefit in the δ subtype (PMID:38943192) supports F3 as secondary.

Human PK showed dose-proportional, long-lived plasma exposure at 3.75–40 mg (PMID:32820619). In healthy volunteers, apararenone blunted the fludrocortisone-induced fall in urinary Na/K ratio, an MR-antagonist pharmacodynamic effect. It also met its UACR endpoint in diabetic nephropathy at 2.5–10 mg (NCT02517320, PMID:32974732), so systemic MR engagement is inferred adequate at doses comparable to those likely used in NASH. No hepatic or NASH-patient engagement data exist, and the index trial (NCT02923154; ALT endpoint) posted no results. The bundle does not give the NASH doses or what the trial showed. A systemic MR antagonist that engages its target but did not advance on a liver biomarker endpoint suggests MR antagonism does not drive NASH as tested (F2). Evidence is thin, so U remains plausible.

The index trial used 500 mg BID (PMID:39338442) and missed its primary endpoint (p=0.391) with no excess harm (NCT04467840). In solid-tumour patients this same dose was the recommended phase 2 dose, gave biologically relevant plasma concentrations and lowered plasma S1P, the SK2 product, before the index trial (PMID:28420720). That decrease was transient, returning to baseline at 24 h, and opaganib also has off-target sphingolipid effects (PMID:39182604). Engagement was never measured in COVID-19 patients, and no downstream pathway marker was measured. Tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:36460794). The sources attribute the failure to disease severity: a post-hoc analysis found benefit confined to patients with FIO2 ≤60%, which points to patient selection (F3). F2 also applies, since the overall population showed no benefit despite engagement.

In the single-agent first-in-human study (NCT00575562, PMID:23294608), PK was linear and IHC on CRC biopsies showed KRN330 still bound to tumour 2 weeks after 3 mg/kg q2w. The MTD was 3 mg/kg weekly, limited by GI toxicity. In the index combination with irinotecan (NCT00838578, PMID:24691674), GI toxicity and neutropenia capped KRN330 at 0.5 mg/kg weekly. That is about six-fold below the dose where tumour binding was shown. Binding at this dose was never measured, and no downstream depletion or pathway marker was reported. The prespecified ORR was not met (4.5%). Because tolerability capped the dose below the only level with engagement evidence, the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). The binding data were published after the index trial started.

The index trial NCT00833989 was a small (n=42) escalating-dose safety study. Its primary outcomes were AE, vital sign, ECG, nerve conduction and MRI counts, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug (F9). No safety signal was found, and gait velocity trended toward improvement (PMID:23471268). Pillars: only plasma PK was shown (PMID:23267856, PMID:23471268). MAG is a CNS target, and the bundle reports no CSF or brain levels and no measure of MAG binding in humans. Serum S100β did not change, but it is a nonspecific injury marker rather than a proximal pathway readout. Dosing was not capped by tolerability. Because engagement is untested, the reason the program stopped cannot be determined beyond this (U secondary).

In the index trial (NCT00725725, PMID:22394471), neither 4 mg nor 12 mg beat placebo on change in PDSS score. The trial was small (n≈40), was terminated, and the groups started out unbalanced. In healthy men, single doses of 8 mg or more produced CNS effects and gonadotropin changes, which investigators took as evidence that the drug reached the brain and was pharmacologically active (PMID:23116363), so exposure counts as adequate at the 12 mg dose. Org 25935 also dampened ketamine effects in healthy volunteers (npp2011295). However, GlyT1 occupancy was measured by PET only in monkeys (PMID:24487737), not in humans, and there is no human biomarker showing a glycine/NMDA effect. Engagement therefore has no human data, and nothing in the bundle separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The trial's small size and early stop also fit F7.

In the index trial NCT00764660 (12 mg twice daily), heavy drinking days were 18.7% on drug vs 16.3% on placebo (p=0.41), and the trial was stopped for futility (PMID:25257291). The drug was fairly well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects. In healthy volunteers, doses of 8 mg and above caused CNS effects (EEG, eye movement, visual) and lowered the hormones FSH and LH (PMID:23116363). This supports brain penetration but is not specific evidence that GlyT1 was engaged. Transporter occupancy by PET was measured only in monkeys (PMID:24487737), and I found no human occupancy or CSF glycine data. There is also no data in alcohol-dependent patients and no other GlyT1 drug that worked in this disease. So nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, and the code is U.

The index trial NCT02646748 was a Phase 1 pembrolizumab combination study in solid tumours. Its primary endpoint was safety, it posted no results and it did not enrol HCC, so it was not an efficacy test of itacitinib. Plasma exposure is characterised in humans (PMID:36601737). JAK1 engagement and pathway effect are inferred_adequate: the drug met primary endpoints in myelofibrosis (NCT01633372) and CRS prevention (NCT04071366) at comparable systemic doses. No target engagement was measured in HCC. In the HCC trial (NCT04358185, PMID:41673081) at 400 mg there were no objective responses, 47% stable disease and 16/19 deaths. This suggests the mechanism adds little (F2). A prior-immunotherapy subgroup and a response signature hint at heterogeneity (F3). The bundle states no stop reason.

The index pediatric trial (2 patients) stopped because phase 3 GRAVITAS-301 (NCT03139604) missed day-28 ORR (74% vs 66%, p=0.078) at 200 mg QD. Plasma exposure in aGVHD patients was characterized by PopPK, and response rose with exposure (PMID:36601737), hinting the dose may have been suboptimal. Tolerability did not cap it, with no exposure-safety relationship. No human JAK1/pSTAT engagement data appear. Wins in CRS and myelofibrosis (NCT04071366, NCT01633372) used 200 mg BID or higher, so they do not support inferring engagement at 200 mg QD. Biomarker changes appeared only in responders and were not a mechanism readout (PMID:35689489). Ruxolitinib, which also inhibits JAK1, is approved for aGVHD. This points to the molecule or dose rather than the target (F1b). Engagement remains unmeasured (U).

GRAVITAS-309 (NCT03584516) stopped for insufficient efficacy, with no safety concerns. Doses reached 300 mg BID with only 1 DLT, so dose was not limited. Plasma exposure in GVHD patients is characterized, with an exposure-response relationship (PMID:36601737). No human target-engagement or pharmacodynamic data appear; STAT3 inhibition is shown only in rodents (PMID:32861662). Engagement is inferred adequate because systemic JAK1 inhibition at comparable doses met primary endpoints in myelofibrosis (NCT01633372) and CRS prevention (NCT04071366). Ruxolitinib is FDA-approved in chronic GVHD on the same target, while itacitinib failed in both acute (NCT03139604) and chronic GVHD. This points to the molecule or its JAK1 selectivity rather than the pathway, so F1b is primary. F2 is secondary given inferred engagement.

In taxane-refractory CRPC, rilotumumab 7.5 or 15 mg/kg plus mitoxantrone/prednisone did not improve OS (HR 1.10) or PFS (PMID:23136195). The drug was well tolerated, with no MTD up to 20 mg/kg, and showed linear PK (PMID:20068101, PMID:24186235), so exposure was adequate and the dose was not limited. Total HGF rose in the CRPC rilotumumab arms, a binding marker, but full neutralization was not quantified. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same doses met a PFS endpoint in gastric cancer (NCT00719550), with an exposure-response effect in MET-positive tumors (PMID:25584489). HGF/MET blockade therefore did not drive benefit in CRPC as tested. Possible MET-selection effects (F3) are secondary.

Rilotumumab 15 mg/kg plus platinum/etoposide did not improve OS (HR 0.84, P=.38) or PFS in ES-SCLC (NCT00791154, PMID:28601388). Exposure was adequate: linear PK across 0.5–20 mg/kg, MTD not reached, and no DLTs in SCLC phase 1b (PMID:20068101, PMID:24186235). Engagement was not directly quantified. Total HGF rose in a dose-dependent way, consistent with antibody binding, but this was shown in mixed solid tumors and published after the index trial began. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same doses met a phase 2 PFS endpoint in gastric cancer via systemic HGF neutralization (NCT00719550, PMID:25584489). HGF blockade therefore did not drive SCLC outcomes. Benefit was hinted only in patients with low baseline HGF (secondary F3).

In the index trial (NCT02347332), adding vinflunine to methotrexate gave no OS gain (7.1 vs 6.8 months, p=0.83). Plasma exposure is well characterized across 18 phase I/II trials, with exposure-dependent neutropenia (PMID:29341179, PMID:12488418), so exposure is adequate. Tubulin engagement was never measured directly. It is inferred adequate because vinflunine met a PFS endpoint in breast cancer (NCT01095003) through the same systemic tumor target at comparable dosing; that source also calls it indicated in bladder cancer. No tumor biomarker or engagement data exist in head and neck patients. The bundle gives no sign of tolerability capping the dose or of a stated design flaw. So the antimitotic mechanism, as given here, did not add benefit in this disease (F2), with medium confidence.

Plasma PK of IV vinflunine is well characterized across 18 phase I/II trials, and exposure-related neutropenia was modeled (PMID:29341179, PMID:12488418). This antimitotic myelosuppression is consistent with on-target tubulin effects. No direct human tubulin-engagement data exist. Engagement is inferred_adequate because vinflunine met efficacy endpoints through the same target: PFS in breast cancer combined with capecitabine (NCT01095003) and an approved-type bladder indication (PMID:29341179, NCT01599013). The index trial (NCT01091168) tested superiority over an active alkylating agent and found equal OS (HR 1.04). So an engaged tubulin mechanism added no benefit over other chemotherapy in this setting (F2). An F9-like active-comparator element applies. Confidence is low because engagement is inferred, not measured.

The first-in-human Phase 1 trial (NCT00687934, PMID:23530663) showed exposure rising linearly with dose up to the MTD of 216 mg/m2, with an RP2D of 200 mg/m2. Plasma HSP70, the classic marker of HSP90 inhibition, stayed elevated for over a week after dosing. This supports engagement and pathway effect in solid-tumour patients before the index trial; it was not shown specifically in NSCLC. In uveal melanoma, early FDG-PET metabolic responses also suggested a pharmacodynamic effect without clinical benefit (PMID:30211813). The 200 mg/m2 dose was tolerable, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, adding ganetespib to docetaxel gave no overall survival gain (HR 1.11) and was stopped for futility (NCT01798485). This points to HSP90 inhibition not driving benefit in unselected NSCLC. No other HSP90 inhibitor succeeded in NSCLC.

The index GIST trial (NCT01039519) used the 200 mg/m2 recommended phase 2 dose and showed only an 18.5% clinical benefit rate. The first-in-human study (NCT00687934, PMID:23530663) showed exposure rising linearly with dose. Plasma HSP70, the induced pharmacodynamic marker of HSP90 inhibition, stayed elevated for over a week, so engagement and the pathway effect are reasonably supported. The MTD was 216 mg/m2, so tolerability did not cap the dose below the tested level. Other studies showed pharmacodynamic activity without benefit (PMID:30211813) or no single-agent activity (PMID:25444464, NCT01798485), pointing to the target not driving disease as tested. Engagement was not shown in GIST patients and the evidence is a surrogate marker, so confidence is low.

The RCC Phase Ib trial (NCT03876925) was stopped because efficacy was 'not as good as pre-expected', and no results were posted. In the first-in-human study (NCT04577703, PMID:36341335), Cmax and AUC rose in proportion to dose and the MTD was 100 mg, so plasma exposure is shown in humans. My searches found no human data on MET, AXL or VEGFR2 inhibition, and no downstream biomarker data, in any patients, including RCC patients. All mechanism data are cell or xenograft studies. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged its targets cannot be told apart from targets that do not matter in RCC. The code is therefore U. F1b is a possible secondary code: other MET inhibitors are approved, but not in RCC in this bundle.

Ningetinib appears only in Cohort E of NCT03838848. That cohort gave KN046 plus ningetinib to unselected NSCLC patients who had failed platinum chemotherapy and PD-1/PD-L1 therapy. The safety monitoring committee judged Cohorts D and E to show no significant clinical benefit. The only human data come from the first-in-human trial (PMID:36341335, NCT04577703), which set an MTD of 100 mg and showed dose-proportional plasma PK and 29.4% stable disease. It reported no human measure of MET, AXL or FLT3 inhibition, receptor occupancy, or downstream biomarkers. Plasma PK shows the drug reached the blood, which supports exposure; the 'inadequate' value in the exposure field is an error and should read 'adequate'. Patients were not selected for MET alterations, which may have mattered (F3). Approved MET drugs work only in MET-selected NSCLC. With no engagement data, we cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage its targets or the mechanism does not help in this setting.

Novartis stopped the keloid trial (NCT00987545; 3 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks) after Part I biomarker data from keloid patients showed no IL-13 signature. The sponsor is saying the target pathway is not active in keloid. It is not saying the drug failed to engage. I found no keloid PK or engagement data, and the Phase 1 trial (NCT00417196) posted no results. In eosinophilic esophagitis, 6 mg/kg QAX576 significantly lowered tissue eosinophils and improved dysregulated disease transcripts, so it acted on the IL-13 pathway in humans. But the EoE trial missed its primary endpoint, and that evidence came from another tissue and published after the keloid trial began (2014). That makes 'inferred_adequate' generous for engagement. So F2 is the call, with U as a close alternative.

Phase 1 studies in healthy adults found that AMG 853 blocked ex vivo whole-blood PGD2 responses through both DP and CRTH2, with roughly dose-proportional PK. Those Phase 1 data set IC90 thresholds that were used to pick the doses for the index trial. In the asthma patients of NCT01018550 (PMID:23174659), plasma levels were dose-proportional. The authors say the exposure and earlier PD data show the doses blocked both receptors in blood. So exposure and engagement were adequate, but engagement in patients was inferred from drug levels, not measured directly. No downstream biomarker change was reported, so pathway has no human data. The dose was not capped by tolerability. ACQ, FEV1 and other endpoints did not improve, with no dose-response. That points to a mechanism that does not drive disease in this population (F2).

The index trial NCT05310422 was a one-year safety study. Its primary outcome was a descriptive count of treatment-emergent adverse events (25/203 tivanisiran vs 16/98 vehicle; serious AEs 7/203 vs 3/98; no deaths). It was not an efficacy test of the drug, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human measurement of ocular exposure, TRPV1 transcript knockdown, or a downstream pathway biomarker. Earlier phase 1/2 trials (PMID:27893109) reported only clinical endpoints: VAS pain improved with SYL1001 1.125% (P=0.013), OSDI did not differ from placebo, and hyperemia improved. HELIX (NCT03108664) results are not shown. Engagement therefore remains no_human_data, which leaves the mechanism question unresolved (U as secondary).

At 100 mg BID, ABT-639 did not beat placebo (NCT01345045/PMID:26067585). Plasma PK was measured in humans (PMID:25567367), but no source compares those levels with what Cav3.2 blockade needs, so exposure stays no_human_data. No human study measured whether the drug bound or blocked Cav3.2 in the body. The pathway marker failed: a 100 mg dose did not change spontaneous C-nociceptor firing in patients (PMID:26035253) or capsaicin pain in healthy volunteers (PMID:26814294). Later lab work with human DRG neurons and mouse channels found ABT-639 barely blocks Cav3.2, which points to a weak molecule (F1a). A review blames insufficient engagement. But these are in vitro data and so don't count, which leaves engagement no_human_data and the code U.

Gosuranemab reached the CNS and engaged its target. In healthy volunteers it suppressed CSF unbound N-terminal tau by 67-97% (PMID:30581980; NCT02294851, before the index trial). In PSP it cut CSF unbound tau by 98% (PMID:34385707), and in TANGO itself all doses significantly reduced CSF unbound N-terminal tau (PMID:38012285). Tolerability was good up to 2000 mg q4w, so the dose was not capped. Yet CDR-SB showed no benefit at any dose. The PSP trial likewise failed despite near-complete engagement and concluded that N-terminal tau neutralization does not translate into efficacy. Pathway evidence was poor: PSP brain tissue at autopsy showed no clearance of tau inclusions (PMID:33950293), and modelling suggests negligible synaptic engagement (PMID:37658103). The mechanism as tested does not drive AD.

In the index PSP trial, gosuranemab 2000 mg cut unbound CSF N-terminal tau by 98% versus an 11% rise on placebo, yet PSPRS change did not differ (p=0.85) and safety matched placebo (PMID:34385707, NCT03068468). Earlier healthy-volunteer dosing (trial registered 2014) gave dose-proportional serum exposure and 67-97% CSF suppression (PMID:30581980). Downstream, post-mortem tissue showed no clearance of tau inclusions (PMID:33950293), so the pathway pillar is rated inadequate. The authors conclude that N-terminal tau neutralization does not translate into efficacy. TANGO in Alzheimer's also failed despite CSF engagement (PMID:38012285). A modeling study suggests synaptic engagement is minimal (PMID:37658103), but this is not human measurement. Engagement was shown and tolerability did not cap the dose, so the N-terminal extracellular tau mechanism failed: F2.

The index trial NCT01384162 was an open-label safety and tolerability continuation study of intracerebroventricular sNN0029. Its primary outcomes were adverse events, MRI, fundus findings and device performance, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated, with no results posted, for problems developing and supplying the infusion system, plus an unfavorable interim benefit-risk in study sNN0029-003. The same reason was given for NCT01999803 and NCT02269436, which points to a program-level operational problem with the delivery device. The bundle has no human data on CSF exposure, VEGFR engagement or pathway biomarkers, and no PubMed abstracts. The benefit-risk signal therefore cannot be traced to a mechanism, so U also applies, and F7 applies for the device supply problems.

PROCEED (NCT01170650) was terminated on a DSMB decision with no stated cause and no posted results. Phase 1 (PMID:23032618) set the MTD at 2.5 mg, with constipation as the DLT. Plasma PK was taken, but no levels or target-engagement data are reported. Etarfolatide imaging measures FR expression, not vintafolide binding, so engagement has no human data. PRECEDENT (NCT00722592, PMID:24127448) improved PFS, mostly in FR-100% patients, which points to FR-dependent activity. However, that was the same disease and is not a pillar measurement. Mirvetuximab soravtansine is FDA-approved on FOLR1 in ovarian cancer, so the target is validated. That points to a molecule-specific failure (F1b) rather than a failed target. Patient selection by FR status (F3) and indeterminacy (U) also remain plausible.

In the index trial NCT01218516, farletuzumab plus chemotherapy did not improve PFS in lung adenocarcinoma (4.7 vs 5.8 months, HR 1.23). Phase 1 and population pharmacokinetic studies in ovarian cancer showed linear, dose-dependent plasma exposure at tolerable doses with no dose-limiting toxicity. That supports systemic exposure. I found no human data on FRα occupancy, tumor penetration, or ADCC/CDC pathway markers in any disease. Other FRα drugs listed for NSCLC (vintafolide, ADCs) reached only phase 2, so F1b does not apply. Its ovarian program also failed, and CA125 may suppress ADCC there (PMC5581011), but that is ovarian-specific. No source explains why the lung trial failed. With engagement unmeasured, the result is indeterminate.

Farletuzumab, a naked anti-FRα antibody, missed PFS in Phase 3 (HR 0.99 and 0.86; NCT00849667, PMID:27001568). Human PK was dose-linear, so plasma exposure was shown (PMID:25380636). The bundle has no human receptor-occupancy, target or pathway data, so engagement and pathway are no_human_data. Another drug on the same target, mirvetuximab soravtansine, is FDA-approved in ovarian cancer. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b), with the caveat that mirvetuximab is an ADC acting through payload delivery. Better PFS with above-median exposure and in low-CA125 patients suggests exposure or subgroup effects. However, the low-CA125 confirmatory trial also failed (NCT02289950), as did the platinum-resistant study (NCT00738699). Confidence is low.

Index trial NCT02802267 tested 4 mg/day oral inecalcitol plus decitabine in 110 unfit AML patients, with overall survival as the primary endpoint. No results were posted, and the sources found give no reason for stopping. Human data come only from the prostate cancer Phase 1 (PMID:25013124). It set the 4 mg MTD from hypercalcemia and reported PSA declines, but it reported no drug levels, VDR engagement or VDR biomarker such as CYP24A1. In AML, differentiation markers (CD11b/CD14) and decitabine synergy were shown only in cell lines and mice (ASH abstract, PMID:42845528). No other VDR agonist has succeeded in AML. With no human engagement data, the sources cannot tell apart a drug that failed to engage VDR from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial was a safety extension, terminated because the core study NCT01716754 missed ACQ-7 versus placebo and omalizumab. In atopic subjects, ligelizumab gave dose-dependent suppression of free IgE and basophil FcεRI, greater than omalizumab (PMID:25200415). In mild allergic asthma (NCT01703312, registered 2012) it blunted allergen-induced early asthmatic responses and skin tests (PMID:27185571), so exposure, engagement and pathway were shown in this disease. It also met its endpoint in CSU (NCT02477332). Despite this, there was no benefit in severe asthma. PMID:33747510 notes faster clearance and different FcεRI/CD23 blocking, and suggests mechanism-disease mismatch. Omalizumab also failed to separate from a high placebo responder rate (70%), so the trial's sensitivity is questionable (F7).

In atopic subjects, ligelizumab gave dose-dependent exposure and suppression of free IgE and basophil FcεRI/surface IgE, greater than omalizumab. Skin-prick wheal responses were suppressed by more than 95% (PMID:25200415, from Phase 1 work that began before the 2012 index start). Pillar 3 is supported by those basophil and skin-test effects. Clinical efficacy in CSU (NCT02477332, PMID:31577874) confirms functional IgE blockade at comparable doses. Engagement was not shown in atopic dermatitis patients themselves; the bundle has only in vitro serum data for AD. The small (n=22) index AD trial (NCT01552629) posted no results, and the program did not advance. With the target engaged, the most direct reading is that IgE neutralization does not drive eczema. Small size is a secondary limitation.

In atopic humans, ligelizumab showed dose-dependent exposure, near-complete free-IgE suppression, reduced basophil FcεRI/surface IgE and >95% suppression of skin-prick wheals (PMID:25200415). The PD trial NCT01596712 was registered before the index start. Efficacy in CSU (NCT02477332, PEARL NCT03580369/NCT03580356) also supports adequate skin-compartment engagement. The bundle does not report the index dose, so comparability is assumed. Engagement was not measured in bullous pemphigoid patients. The index trial (NCT01688882) was terminated because the predefined efficacy criterion was not met; CGA-C responders were 8/13 vs 2/7 on placebo. Engaged anti-IgE did not deliver the required benefit in BP (F2). The very small n=20 trial, stopped after Part 1, leaves a power caveat (F7).

Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional plasma PK and brain [11C]flumazenil PET displacement in healthy volunteers (NCT02138500, PMID:34636937, PMID:33465277). Engagement was likely inadequate at the index doses. High receptor occupancy (>80%) was estimated only at 25–42.5 mg BID (PMID:33465277), and the GAD trial used 2.5 and 7.5 mg BID. The low back pain paper suspects insufficient occupancy (PMID:29787472), and the GAD authors cite failure to explore a broader dose range (PMID:30531477). Pathway effects were shown in healthy volunteers (saccadic peak velocity, qEEG; PMID:29214652) and at higher doses in photosensitive epilepsy (NCT02564029). There is no occupancy data in GAD patients. Secondary codes: the trial was underpowered (90 of 384 planned) and was stopped for a business decision.

The CLBP trial (NCT02262754) stopped for futility. The drug was numerically worse than placebo, while naproxen behaved as expected. The trial publication (PMID:29787472) says the lack of analgesia may reflect not achieving sufficient receptor occupancy. Exposure and pathway effects were shown in healthy volunteers: plasma PK, [11C]flumazenil PET occupancy with dose-dependent displacement (NCT02138500, PMID:34636937), and increased saccadic peak velocity and qEEG beta (PMID:29214652). Only later work showed that 25–42.5 mg BID, estimated to give >80% occupancy, was well tolerated (PMID:33465277). This implies the index dose under-engaged the target by dose selection, not because tolerability capped it. Engagement was not measured in patients. F2 is secondary if occupancy proves adequate.

The index trial (NCT00878501) tested 30 and 90 mg and was stopped for futility at the interim analysis. The 90 mg vs placebo comparison gave one-sided p=0.29 against a go threshold of p≤0.20 (Miller 2014). The healthy-volunteer study NCT00711048, registered in 2008, used comparable single doses of 30 and 95 mg. Both doses produced effects expected from TRPV1 blockade: oesophageal heat-pain thresholds rose 23–28% and body temperature rose in every subject (0.4 and 0.7 °C). Heat-pain thresholds also rose by up to 4.8 °C at peak drug levels. So the drug reached and engaged its target, but these data come from healthy volunteers, not OA patients. Even so, knee OA pain did not improve, which fits F2. A later paper (NEO6860) suggests hyperthermia may have kept doses in a subefficacious range and that WOMAC behaves unexpectedly in TRPV1 trials. That is speculation, hence medium confidence.

In the index trial (NCT01019928; PMID:23320520), a single 95 mg dose of AZD1386 in NERD patients with partial PPI response produced clear on-target TRPV1 pharmacodynamic effects. Cutaneous heat tolerance rose by 4.9°C and body temperature by 0.59°C. Together these show systemic exposure and target engagement in the program's own disease population. Even so, esophageal pain thresholds to heat, distension and electrical stimulation were unchanged versus placebo, and time to VAS7 was 84.0 s vs 86.9 s. The authors conclude TRPV1 does not play a major role in evoked esophageal pain in these patients. Engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself; the earlier healthy-volunteer esophageal study (NCT00711048) posted no results. The program also failed in other pain indications.

The index trial, NCT01288989 (PMID:27566701), was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study plus a colorectal cancer (CRC) expansion. Doses ran from 5 to 30 mg/kg weekly. The maximum tolerated dose was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. There were no radiographic responses, and median progression-free survival in CRC was 6.3 weeks. Pharmacokinetics were measured, but the sources I could open give no exposure values. They also show no receptor occupancy or VEGFR-3 signalling inhibition. The only biomarker reported was serum VEGF-C/D, which did not change significantly. That result is ambiguous for a receptor-blocking antibody and does not show whether the drug engaged its target. No other drug on this target is in the bundle. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged VEGFR-3 apart from a target that does not drive these tumours, so the code is U.

At the index doses (3 and 20 mg/kg), BIIB023 showed dose-dependent serum exposure in rheumatoid arthritis patients and healthy volunteers (PMID:23928094, PMID:26896828). Soluble serum TWEAK fell below quantitation, which the authors read as target engagement. The RA study (NCT00771329) was registered before the index trial. The RA patients also showed a trend toward lower inflammatory markers (MCP-1, IP-10, MIP-1β, TIMP-1). This pathway evidence is weak, and engagement was never shown in lupus nephritis patients or in kidney tissue. Tolerability did not limit dosing. Despite neutralisation of the ligand, renal response at week 52 was 16% and 31% versus 25% on placebo, and the trial stopped for futility (NCT01499355). This supports F2: TWEAK blockade does not drive renal response as tested.

[11C]flumazenil PET (NCT00681720, registered before the index trial; PMID:28013354) showed dose-dependent, saturable GABAA occupancy, with maximal occupancy reached without sedation. Brain exposure and engagement were therefore adequate, though only in healthy subjects, and the dose was not tolerability-capped. Downstream effects were weak: there were no significant CNS-PD or prolactin changes at 2–10 mg, and the authors suggest low intrinsic efficacy or higher doses (PMID:24802722, PMID:27128218), so pathway is inadequate. In the index trial (NCT00807937), the lorazepam active control barely separated from placebo (-10.8 vs -9.5). The companion trial also had a high placebo response (NCT00808249). This points to a trial lacking assay sensitivity (F7). F2 is secondary, since engagement was adequate yet there was no benefit.

In Phase 1 (NCT00688415, PMID:24807889), plasma exposure was dose-proportional. At doses ≥0.4 mg/m2, TLR8-driven cytokines (G-CSF, MCP-1, MIP-1β, TNFα) rose dose-dependently. Late-stage cancer patients stayed highly responsive to TLR8 activation (PMID:26152744). Ovarian cancer patients in the Phase Ib trial NCT01294293, which predates the index trial, showed pharmacodynamic effects of the PLD combination with no dose-limiting toxicities (PMID:27702821). So engagement and pathway activation held at tolerable doses. Despite this, adding motolimod to PLD did not improve OS (HR 1.22) or PFS (NCT01666444, PMID:28453702). The same null result occurred in head and neck cancer (NCT01836029), pointing to the mechanism, not the molecule. Benefit seen in subgroups (patients with injection-site reactions, in vitro immune responders) suggests a secondary F3.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Motolimod showed dose-proportional plasma exposure (PMID:24807889). TLR8 activation was evident from dose-dependent rises in G-CSF, MCP-1, MIP-1β, TNFα and IL6 at doses ≥0.4 mg/m2, well below the 3.0 mg/m2 MTD (PMID:24807889, PMID:26152744). In SCCHN patients on cetuximab, plasma cytokines rose and NK cells were activated (PMID:27810904). Tumor biopsies showed immune remodeling: fewer MDSCs, more M1 monocytes and CD8+ infiltration (PMID:29061643). Tolerability did not cap the dose below the active range. Despite this, PFS was unchanged (HR 0.99, NCT01836029), and the ovarian trial also failed (NCT01666444). This points to the mechanism not driving benefit as tested. Preclinical work suggests benefit may be limited to tumors with high TLR8 expression (PMID:33452311), so F3 is secondary.

The published Phase 1 report of the AML dose-escalation (PMID:29765150; 32 AML patients, 120–900 mg) states that pharmacodynamic analysis showed biological activity of AZD1208, yet there were no clinical responses. The authors attribute this to a lack of single-agent efficacy and suggest combinations, consistent with preclinical data showing mostly cytostatic rather than apoptotic effects (PMID:27054578, PMID:24363397). Pan-PIM inhibition alone therefore did not drive benefit in AML (F2). Caveats support F1a as a secondary code: 900 mg was not tolerated, the MTD was not confirmed, and CYP3A4 autoinduction increased clearance. These may have limited exposure, and the PD activity was not quantified. Engagement evidence was published after the index trial started (2012).

In healthy volunteers, AQW051 reached continuous plasma exposure and was well tolerated at single doses up to 200 mg and repeated doses up to 75 mg (PMID:25363835). Brain penetration was shown only in rodents. No human α7 receptor occupancy, CSF level or other engagement data were found, so exposure at the CNS site of action and engagement are both no_human_data. In the index fMRI trial (NCT00825539, PMID:27371157), brain activation changed inconsistently and the changes did not track cognitive performance, so the pathway readout was inadequate. Tolerability did not cap the dose. No other α7 agonist has succeeded in schizophrenia. A review describes the AQW051 results as inconclusive and says the compound was discontinued. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In Phase 1 studies in healthy people (PMID:25363835), AQW051 gave continuous plasma exposure and was well tolerated at doses up to 75 mg daily, which covers the 10 and 50 mg doses used in the index trial. Brain penetration was shown only in rodents. I found no human evidence of α7 receptor occupancy or a target-related biomarker. In schizophrenia, fMRI showed no consistent effects (NCT00825539), but that is not a direct measure of engagement. The index trial (NCT01474421, PMID:26990766) missed both co-primary endpoints, and tolerability did not cap the dose. No other α7 drug has succeeded in this disease. Because human engagement data are missing, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in dyskinesia, so the code is U.

The index Phase 2 RRMS trial (NCT02222948) and its extension (NCT02306811) were stopped after a planned interim analysis of the primary endpoint, new contrast-enhancing MRI lesions. Neither trial cites a safety concern, and no results were posted. The web search found no human data on vatelizumab (anti-VLA-2/ITGA2) for plasma or CNS exposure, receptor occupancy or downstream biomarkers. The SAN-300 receptor-occupancy data found in the search are for an anti-VLA-1 antibody, a different drug, so they do not count. The UC trials stopped for slow recruitment and showed no efficacy. No other drug on this target has succeeded. Nothing in the evidence separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in MS, so the code is U.

The index gastric monotherapy trial (PMID:24337769) gave no objective responses, DCR 36.7% and median PFS of 43 days. Phase 1 data, published and registered before the index trial, showed dose-dependent exposure and well-tolerated dosing up to 360 mg BID (PMID:21976535). Tumour biopsies showed lower phospho-MET and total MET, lower pFAK and more TUNEL staining (PMID:21383285), so engagement and pathway were adequate, though in mixed solid tumours rather than gastric patients. Mechanism doubts weaken this: pMET fell in skin in only 7/11 patients, possibly via tubulin (PMID:34164713), and a preclinical model showed no MET effect (PMID:29444985). Only 6.9% of index patients were MET-amplified, with no biomarker link to benefit (F3). Cabozantinib is listed as approved in gastric cancer (F1b).

MARQUEE (NCT01244191) missed OS (HR 0.981) at futility. Plasma exposure at 360 mg BID was documented (PMID:21976535, PMID:21383285). One phase 1 study reported reduced tumor pMET in 15 biopsies from mixed solid tumors, not NSCLC (PMID:21383285). Later human data were inconsistent: skin pMET fell in only 7/11 patients, alongside tubulin reduction. That study was halted over 'concerns regarding the mechanism of tivantinib' (PMID:34164713), and another calls it a 'putative' MET inhibitor (PMID:34180036). I judged engagement inadequate on these doubts, though this is debatable. Pathway signals were partial: DCE-MRI was unchanged. Other MET inhibitors (capmatinib, tepotinib, crizotinib) are approved in NSCLC, implicating the molecule rather than the target. An unselected population is a further possible contributor (F3).

Tivantinib 360 mg BID, the dose used in NCT01075048, gave dose-dependent systemic exposure (PMID:21383285, PMID:21976535). In mixed solid-tumor biopsies it lowered phospho-MET and total MET, reduced pFAK and raised TUNEL (PMID:21383285). Engagement was not shown specifically in colorectal cancer. Adding it to cetuximab+irinotecan did not improve PFS (8.3 vs 7.3 mo, p=0.38; PMID:26891420), which supports F2. Trends favoring MET-high tumors suggest F3, but those subgroups were too small to interpret. The MET-high follow-up study also missed its endpoint (PMID:30846365). Later sources question whether tivantinib truly acts through MET (PMID:34164713; PMID:29444985 is preclinical only), and the bundle lists cabozantinib as approved in CRC. That keeps F1b as a possibility and confidence low.

The index trial gave the RP2D of 360 mg BID and saw 0/27 responses, so it stopped for futility. That dose was well tolerated with no MTD reached (PMID:21976535), so it was not dose-limited. Exposure was dose-dependent at this dose (PMID:21383285). Paired tumor biopsies in solid-tumor patients showed reduced phospho-MET, total MET and pFAK with increased apoptosis, and skin phospho-MET also fell (PMID:21383285, PMID:34164713). This supports engagement and a pathway effect, though only in other tumors, not germ cell tumor. Later sources question the mechanism, noting tubulin effects and calling it a 'putative' MET inhibitor (PMID:34164713, PMID:34180036). Confidence is therefore low. Still, on the human evidence available, MET inhibition did not drive benefit in this disease.

Plasma exposure was shown in phase 1 (PMID:21976535, PMID:21383285). Intratumoral pMET reduction was reported only in non-HCC solid tumours at 100–400 mg BID. Skin pMET fell in just 7/11 patients, and that study was stopped over doubts about the drug's mechanism, which may involve tubulin (PMID:34164713). In HCC, neutropenia deaths forced the dose down from 360 to 240 mg (NCT00988741, PMID:23287988, PMID:25294187). The index trial used 120 mg BID, well below the 360 mg recommended phase 2 dose, and no MET engagement was shown in HCC at that dose. The MET-high enrichment did not yield benefit (NCT01755767, NCT02029157, PMID:35711496). The mechanism was therefore not properly tested at a tolerability-capped dose; patient selection by MET-high status is a secondary factor.

Human PET in healthy volunteers (NCT01258751, registered 2010, before the 2012 index start) showed brain penetration and dose-dependent 5-HT6 occupancy. Maximal occupancy was about 80% at ≥15 mg (PMID:36825693), and receptor saturation was reported at the 30 mg dose taken into the index trial (PMID:29622037). Exposure and engagement were therefore adequate, though shown only in healthy volunteers, not AD patients. No downstream human pathway biomarker is in the bundle, since the scopolamine challenge results were not posted. The drug was well tolerated and the dose was not capped. The trial met pre-specified futility at interim, with ADAS-cog13 and NPI numerically favoring placebo (NCT01712074). With the target saturated and no benefit, 5-HT6 antagonism does not appear to drive symptomatic improvement in AD as tested.

The index trial NCT01147406 was a Phase 1 single-ascending-dose safety and tolerability study in healthy volunteers. It was not an efficacy test, and its posted results show only AE counts, with no serious AEs or deaths. The follow-on CF trial NCT01746784 was also a safety/PK study; it posted only AE grades, with no dose-limiting pattern and no PK, GSNOR-inhibition or biomarker data. Evidence that N6022 inhibits GSNOR and raises nitrite/cGMP comes only from cell and mouse studies (PMID:28419866, PMID:28006950, PMID:24405692), which do not count as human data. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data. No efficacy readout failed, so F9 applies. U is secondary because why the program stopped cannot be determined from the bundle.

The quinagolide vaginal ring missed its worst-pain NRS endpoint in NCT03692403. That trial was tiny (n=2–6 per arm) and placebo did better than every dose. In the companion QLARITY trial (NCT03749109; PMID:40188683), the same ring did not change serum prolactin, the canonical pharmacodynamic marker of D2 agonism, and did not change lesion size. This suggests D2 engagement at the doses delivered was insufficient. No tissue or plasma exposure data are given. The earlier positive signal (PMID:21055747) came from uncontrolled oral dosing in hyperprolactinemic patients, not this formulation. The authors also blame advanced, poorly vascularized disease (population, F3), and the index trial was too underpowered to answer the question (F7). Confidence is low because the evidence is thin.

Exposure: in asthma patients given 1000 mg BID, the trough concentration was about 1,444 nM (PMID:27621597). That is far above the drug's nanomolar DP2 potency (pIC50 8.4; PMID:23146091). Engagement: in chronic spontaneous urticaria patients (NCT02031679, PMC6500753), oral AZD1981 significantly blocked PGD2-induced eosinophil shape change in blood samples tested outside the body. The block matched what 1 µM of the drug does in vitro. This was not shown in asthma and was published after the index trial. Pathway: in asthma, blood eosinophils and exhaled nitric oxide did not change. Even so, peak flow did not improve at any dose up to a supramaximal one, with no dose-response and no tolerability limit. A larger 12-week trial also failed (NCT01197794/PMID:29765200). This suggests DP2 antagonism does not drive lung function in this population. The authors point to a possible atopic subgroup and to short trials with endpoints unsuited to measuring exacerbations.

AstraZeneca says the SAD and MAD Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers showed target engagement, using an ex vivo whole-blood test of PGD2-induced eosinophil shape change. It says doses of 40-80 mg BID or TID cover the target. Those Phase 1 studies very likely ran before the May 2008 index start, though no dates are given. A later urticaria trial confirmed the shape-change block (PMC6500753), and a type 2 diabetes study reached the expected exposure (PMID:30557325). In COPD, Snell 2013 (the NCT00690482/NCT00766415 programme) found the drug cut sputum eosinophil percentage, a pathway effect. Yet FEV1, CCQ and airway histology did not differ from placebo. The target was engaged, but over 4 weeks CRTh2 antagonism did not drive COPD outcomes. The short duration could also count as F4. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

In the index trial, NCT00895895, no SAM-531 dose (1.5, 3 or 5 mg) beat placebo on ADAS-Cog at week 24. Donepezil missed too (p=0.258), so the trial's sensitivity is uncertain. The exposure label is generous: PMID:25217486 shows only that the drug reaches plasma (≥70% absorbed, unchanged drug dominant), and I found no measured brain or CSF levels. No human 5-HT6 receptor occupancy or biomarker data turned up. The PET study linking plasma levels to brain binding (NCT01253655) started in 2010, after the index trial, and posted no results. The phase 1/2a PK/PD trials posted no PD data either. No other 5-HT6 antagonist has succeeded in Alzheimer disease, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unknown, the failure is indeterminate.

Dalotuzumab 10 mg/kg weekly plus erlotinib did not improve PFS over erlotinib in NSCLC (HR 0.86, p=0.268; NCT00654420). Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional PK, half-life ≥95 h and Cmin >25 µg/mL at ≥5 mg/kg (PMID:21810918, NCT00701103, NCT00635778). Paired tumor biopsies showed reduced tumor IGF-1R, downstream signaling and Ki67, so engagement and pathway were adequate. No MTD was reached and 10 mg/kg was the recommended weekly dose, so the dose was not capped. This engagement evidence came from mixed solid tumors, not NSCLC, and was published in 2011, after the index trial started. No other IGF1R agent succeeded in NSCLC. With the mechanism engaged and no benefit, the most likely explanation is that IGF1R blockade does not drive NSCLC as tested (F2).

Phase 1 (PMID:21810918, NCT00701103) showed dose-proportional PK with Cmin >25 μg/mL at ≥5 mg/kg. The index dose of 10 mg/kg weekly was the recommended phase 2 dose and no MTD was reached. Paired tumour biopsies showed lower tumour IGF-1R, reduced downstream signalling and reduced Ki67. In breast cancer patients, NCT00759785 showed a growth-factor-signature decrease in some patients. The dalotuzumab dose was not capped; stomatitis from ridaforolimus forced reductions of that drug. Despite this, ridaforolimus+dalotuzumab did not beat exemestane (HR 1.00; PMID:28324268). Adding dalotuzumab to ridaforolimus/exemestane also gave no PFS gain (PMID:28681171). This points to IGF1R not driving disease as tested (F2). Toxicity higher than acceptable is secondary (F5). Ki67-high selection and IGF1R loss in endocrine-resistant cells (PMID:22573715) suggest population issues (F3).

The index trial NCT01357655 never gave BMS-833923 to anyone. The combination arm had n=0 because the concurrent trial (NCT01218477) had not yet set a recommended phase 2 dose. Only the dasatinib arm was treated, so this was not an efficacy test of the SMO antagonist. NCT01218477 later reported an RP2D of 50 mg with dasatinib, but the bundle contains no human PK, target-engagement or Hedgehog-pathway biomarker data for this drug. All three pillars are therefore no_human_data. The termination reflects trial sequencing and operations (F7 secondary), not a failed readout of the mechanism. PMID:23055247 only lists BMS-833923 as investigational in CML.

Human PK showed dose-proportional exposure from 200 to 1600 µg in healthy subjects and patients (PMID:28623508). Opioid engagement was shown at 600 µg in healthy volunteers through miosis, experimental analgesia and respiratory depression (PMID:28291085, PMID:41379941), but this was published after the index start and not in diabetic neuropathy patients. Cebranopadol also met non-inferiority vs morphine in cancer pain (NCT01964378). In the index trial, 600 µg separated from placebo, and 100 and 300 µg narrowly missed (p≈0.06) with roughly 60 per arm. That pattern fits a modest dose-related effect in an underpowered design, not an inactive mechanism; tapentadol is approved in this disease. No stop reason is given, so a business decision is possible. The bundle is thin.

In the index trial NCT00629239, COPD patients took inhaled AZD4818 300 μg twice daily for 4 weeks. It was well tolerated, but lung function did not change versus placebo (FEV1 difference 0.026 L, p=0.69). The published report says drug exposure was as expected, so I rated exposure adequate, though the measure is probably plasma levels rather than lung levels. I found no human evidence of CCR1 receptor occupancy, of a lung or sputum inflammatory biomarker changing, or of any pathway effect, either in healthy volunteers (NCT00687232) or in patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. No other CCR1 drug in the bundle succeeded in COPD. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter in COPD, so the code is U.

Exposure was adequate. In the index COPD trial (NCT01448850; PMC full text of PMID:28793896), sustained serum drug levels were measured: trough 63.4 ng/µL at week 4 and 28.6 ng/µL at week 53. No study measured IL-1R1 occupancy directly, so engagement is rated adequate from downstream effects seen in COPD patients. The drug lowered blood neutrophils persistently and reversibly, which the authors call consistent with its mechanism. It also significantly reduced CRP and fibrinogen (p<0.0001). Tolerability was similar to placebo, so dose was not limited. Despite this, there was no benefit on exacerbations, quality of life or lung function, and neutrophil or CRP subgroups did not change the result. The drug also failed in hidradenitis suppurativa (NCT01838499). This suggests IL-1R1 blockade does not drive COPD exacerbations. Patient selection (F3) is a minor possibility (PMID:40955382). The published engagement evidence came from this trial, not before it.

The HS trial NCT01838499 was stopped at its interim analysis for futility (PGA response 23.6% vs 18.5%), with similar safety in both arms. Receptor occupancy was never measured. The COPD paper on NCT01448850 (published 2017, after the HS trial started) reports trough levels more than 10 times the concentration giving 90% IL-1R1 signalling inhibition in vitro, and blood neutrophils suppressed versus placebo. That supports exposure and pathway effect. Engagement is inferred because a lower dose (250 mg SC Q4W) significantly improved ACR20 in rheumatoid arthritis. No HS-specific engagement or skin data were found. The HS dose was not stated in the bundle, and the only other IL-1R1 drug in HS (anakinra) reached phase 2 only. So IL-1R1 blockade likely does not drive HS as tested: F2, medium confidence.

In the LAPIS trial (NCT03941093), adding pamrevlumab to chemo did not improve overall survival (HR 1.08, p=0.55). Exposure was shown in pancreatic cancer patients: in the Phase 1 study (NCT01181245), plasma Cmax and Cmin rose linearly with dose, there were no dose-limiting toxicities, and survival tracked exposure. The 35 mg/kg dose was well tolerated in NCT02210559. No source measured in humans whether the drug engaged CTGF, for example by neutralizing CTGF or occupying it in the tumour, or whether a stromal biomarker moved. The saturable clearance seen in the diabetes study (PMID:20522536) only hints at target binding, and the rat data (PMID:27059922) don't count. The IPF Phase 2 success was not confirmed in Phase 3, so engagement can't be inferred from it. Since engagement has no human data, the result is indeterminate (U).

Pamrevlumab missed the PUL 2.0 primary endpoint in NCT04371666 (difference 0.083, p=0.88), and the ambulatory trial NCT04632940 also failed. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. I found no human evidence that it reached muscle or engaged its target there: no CCN2 neutralization, muscle drug levels or fibrosis biomarker data. Human pharmacokinetics come only from a diabetic kidney disease study (PMID:20522536). The phase 2 trial NCT02606136 was single-arm with no biomarker readout. PMID:42453419 suggests in mice that FG-3019 does not stay in muscle, but animal data don't count. The phase 2 IPF win (NCT01890265) did not hold up in phase 3, so it can't support inferred engagement. Sponsors gave no mechanistic explanation. Indeterminate.

ZEPHYRUS-1 (NCT03955146) missed its FVC endpoint (p=0.29), and ZEPHYRUS-2 (NCT04419558) was then stopped. The only human pharmacology found is plasma PK in diabetic kidney disease, which showed saturable clearance (PMID:20522536). There is no lung tissue exposure data and no human measure of CCN2 neutralisation or a downstream pathway biomarker. The target-mediated disposition data are from rats only (PMID:27059922). A competitor's poster claims PRS-220 binds its target more stably than pamrevlumab, but that comparison is preclinical. A review blames 'regression to the truth' after an underpowered positive Phase 2 (NCT01890265, PMID:40255293), which supports a secondary F7. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

I found no human data on exposure, receptor engagement or pathway biomarkers for davalintide. The only pharmacology is in rats (PMID:21733060). The index Phase 2 trial (NCT00785408) posted no results. Amylin and Takeda dropped davalintide because its weight loss and tolerability were worse than pramlintide/metreleptin's (BioCentury). Other sources describe its efficacy-to-tolerability ratio as unfavorable. Several other amylin/calcitonin-receptor agonists reached Phase 3 in obesity (cagrilintide, petrelintide, eloralintide and others), so the target itself does not appear to be the problem. That points to the molecule (F1b) rather than the mechanism. The bundle shows these drugs reached Phase 3 but not that they met pivotal endpoints. Because engagement is unmeasured, U is close behind. Tolerability, likely on-target, may also have played a part (F5). Confidence is low.

Plasma exposure was shown in psoriasis patients: PK was linear and dose-proportional, with a half-life of about 3 weeks (PMID:25749867, PMID:26252485). Engagement was never measured. Neither paper reports free or bound IL-20 levels or IL-20 neutralization in skin. Systemic markers (CRP, ESR, lymphocyte subsets, soluble CD25) did not change. These are nonspecific readouts, not proximal markers of IL-20 activity. Skin biopsies were too few to draw conclusions. Tolerability did not cap the dose; doses above 3 mg/kg were avoided only because of subcutaneous injection volume. The investigators offered two possible explanations for the lack of PASI response: suboptimal dose or duration (F1a), or redundancy among IL-20 family cytokines (F2). Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell these apart, so the code is U.

Exposure was adequate. Plasma PK was linear and typical of an antibody, with a half-life of about 3 weeks in RA patients (PMID:25749867). No human source measured whether the drug engaged IL-20 (free IL-20 or receptor signalling). In psoriasis, pharmacodynamic parameters showed no substantial change and PASI did not improve (PMID:26252485, NCT01261767). That was a different disease and no specific marker was reported, so engagement remains no_human_data. The Phase 2a RA trial met its DAS28-CRP endpoint, with benefit limited to seropositive patients (PMID:25707477, possible F3). The Phase 2b trials then missed their primary and secondary endpoints, and Novo dropped the drug and left inflammation research. The press call the cause a failure, so F8 is secondary only. No other IL-20 drug exists, so nothing distinguishes a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not drive RA, which gives U.

In the randomized phase II of NCT02098343, adding APR-246 to carboplatin/PLD did not lengthen PFS (283 vs 295 days). Plasma exposure is documented: the first-in-human trial (PMID:22965953) and the PiSARRO PK reports showed linear PK at predicted therapeutic levels. No source directly measured whether APR-246 reactivated or bound mutant p53 in ovarian tumours. The only human tumour-cell data are p53 target-gene upregulation in 'several' patients with blood cancers and prostate cancer in the first-in-human trial. That is a different tissue and was not quantified, so I did not credit it for ovarian cancer. No other drug on this target has succeeded in ovarian cancer, and the sponsor gave no explanation for the failure. With engagement unmeasured, I can't tell a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't drive the disease, so the code is U.

Exposure: the first-in-human study reached predicted therapeutic plasma levels, including in AML patients, and showed p53 target-gene upregulation with p53-dependent effects in tumor cells (PMID:22965953, before the index trial). Later studies in TP53-mutant MDS/AML patients showed falling TP53 VAF, molecular remissions and changes on p53 immunohistochemistry (PMID:33449813, PMID:33600210). The index post-transplant maintenance trial was single-arm with no success threshold; its authors called the RFS of 12.5 months 'encouraging' (PMID:35816664). So the readout was not itself a clear failure (F7/F9). The randomized phase 3 in MDS missed its CR endpoint (NCT03745716), and relapse was near-universal without transplant (PMID:40737597). Engaged p53 reactivation therefore did not yield controlled clinical benefit (F2).

Exposure: the first-in-human study (PMID:22965953) reported plasma pharmacokinetics at the levels predicted to be therapeutic. Pathway: some patients showed upregulated p53 target genes in tumour cells. In the phase 2 MDS trials (NCT03072043, NCT03588078), the TP53 mutation cleared from many patients' marrow. Neither is a direct measure of target binding. No source measured whether the drug bound or refolded mutant p53 in humans, so engagement is no_human_data. The phase 3 trial raised CR rate from 22% to 33% (p=0.13), and overall survival was similar between arms. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the miss. Relapse driven by XPO1 resistance (PMID:40737597) suggests the target matters but the benefit does not last. That does not separate a drug that never engaged mutant p53 from a mechanism that does not drive this disease, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT04419389 was a Phase 1/2 safety lead-in. Its primary endpoints were DLT, TEAEs and MTD/RP2D. It enrolled one participant and was terminated by 'sponsor decision', so it was never an efficacy test of eprenetapopt and fits F9. F8 is listed as secondary because the stop looks like a sponsor or portfolio choice, possibly after the Phase 3 MDS miss (NCT03745716), but the bundle does not say so. On the pillars, the first-in-human study (PMID:22965953) showed predicted therapeutic plasma levels and upregulation of p53 target genes in several patients' tumor cells. Direct p53 engagement was not measured, so engagement is no_human_data. Pathway evidence is limited.

In the index dose-ranging trial (NCT00941603), only the 5 mg dose lowered LDL-C versus placebo (-5.7%). The higher 10 and 15 mg doses did not, and there was no dose-response, which is a weak, non-monotonic effect. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, PK, receptor engagement or downstream biomarker data (e.g., FFA suppression), so all three pillars are no_human_data. Nicotinic acid, which acts on the same HCAR2 target, is FDA-approved in familial hypercholesterolemia, a related disease. That fits F1b: the molecule failed, with no evidence it engaged adequately. However, three other selective HCAR2 agonists also stopped in Phase 2, and the bundle does not show that niacin's lipid effect runs through HCAR2. So target irrelevance cannot be excluded, and U is a close alternative.

TCN-032 is an anti-M2e antibody. In the H3N2 challenge study (NCT01719874, PMID:25281755), it missed its primary endpoint: the share of subjects with any grade ≥2 symptom or fever. Total symptom AUC fell 35% (P=.047). Median viral load AUC fell 2.2 log, but this was not significant (P=.09). So the downstream antiviral effect is only a trend, and I scored pathway as inadequate. No source reports human PK, drug levels in the respiratory tract, or a measure of the antibody binding M2e on infected cells. The Phase 1 trial (NCT01390025) posted no results. With no engagement data, the sources cannot tell whether the dose was too low or the mechanism is weak. The positive secondary signals in a small challenge trial point to F7 (likely underpowered), but no source says this outright.

The first-in-human study (NCT00562380, PMID:19786654) showed serum concentrations giving high neutrophil IGF-1R occupancy and rises in serum IGF-1 at 12 and 20 mg/kg. No MTD was reached, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. PK was dose-linear in a Japanese cohort (PMID:22810805). This engagement was shown in mixed solid tumours, not specifically CRC, and the phase 1 trial was registered before the index trial began. Even so, ganitumab with panitumumab gave 0% ORR in Part 2 of the index trial (NCT00891930). Ganitumab also added no benefit with panitumumab (PMID:24919569) or with FOLFIRI (PMID:23510984; PFS HR 1.01) in mCRC. This points to IGF1R blockade not driving CRC as tested. The sources suggest predictive biomarkers may be needed (PMID:24816908), hence secondary F3.

In the first-in-human study (NCT00562380/PMID:19786654), 12–20 mg/kg Q2W gave high neutrophil IGF-1R binding and dose-related serum IGF-1 rises. These show engagement and the expected feedback pathway effect. No MTD was reached. PK was dose-linear (PMID:22810805), and IGF-1 also rose in PMID:22508822. The index trial used 18 mg/kg with chemotherapy, and it was tolerable with only one DLT (PMID:28601388). So the dose was not capped. Even so, OS (10.7 vs 10.8 months; HR 0.95) and PFS were unchanged versus placebo. The only biomarker subgroup signal was for rilotumumab, not ganitumab. Engagement was shown in surrogate tissue in mixed solid tumors, not in SCLC tumors, so confidence is medium. The likeliest explanation is that IGF-1R blockade does not drive ES-SCLC outcomes.

The first-in-human study (PMID:19786654, 2009, before the 2011 index start) showed serum concentrations giving high neutrophil IGF-1R binding at 12 and 20 mg/kg. It also showed rises in serum IGF-1, the expected feedback signal of receptor blockade. PMID:22810805 and PMID:22508822 confirm dose-linear PK and IGF-1 elevation. No MTD was reached at 20 mg/kg, so dose was not limited. The index Phase 3 (NCT01231347) tested both engaging doses in metastatic pancreatic cancer and found no OS benefit (7.0 and 7.1 vs 7.2 months). This points to IGF1R blockade not driving the disease as tested. Caveats: engagement was measured on neutrophils in mixed solid tumors, not in pancreatic tumor tissue, and no same-target drug succeeded in pancreatic cancer.

The bundle has no direct human PK, AR occupancy or biomarker data. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because enobosarm met its clinical-benefit-rate primary endpoint in ER+/AR+ breast cancer at 9 mg and 18 mg (NCT02463032). That is the same target and the same breast-tumour compartment, though the index dose is not stated in the bundle. That trial started after the index trial, so this support was not available beforehand. The index trial in AR+ TNBC (NCT02368691) gave clinical benefit in only 1 of 18 AR+ patients and stopped for lack of efficacy, with no dose-limiting toxicity reported. This suggests AR agonism does not drive AR+ TNBC. Disease heterogeneity within AR+ TNBC may also contribute (F3). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

HERMIONE (NCT02213744) stopped for futility on PFS. Phase 1 (PMID:30361524) reached no MTD, so dose was not capped by tolerability; 30 mg/m2 was selected. 64Cu-MM-302 PET in patients (PMID:28298546) showed tumor deposition, but it varied 35-fold, and high deposition was linked to better outcomes (HR 0.42). This shows delivery happened but was heterogeneous. HER2 binding and downstream DNA-damage effects were never measured in humans. Other HER2-directed drugs, including antibody-drug conjugates (trastuzumab emtansine, trastuzumab deruxtecan), are approved in HER2+ breast cancer, so the target is validated. This points to the molecule or its liposomal delivery rather than the target (F1b). Engagement lacks human data (U), and variable tumor deposition suggests patient-selection effects (F3). The bundle does not state the failure reason beyond futility.

At 200 mg once daily, AQX-1125 did no better than placebo on TLSS at week 12 (NCT02324972; p=0.636). It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Activation of SHIP1 in humans (the target enzyme) was never measured. No human skin drug levels or downstream pathway marker such as pAkt were found either. The only evidence that SHIP1 is engaged comes from in vitro and rodent work (PMID 23121445). In an asthma allergen-challenge study at 450 mg, the drug modestly reduced the late asthmatic response (PMID 25040039), but that was a different disease, tissue and dose, and it was not a pivotal endpoint. The drug also failed in COPD and interstitial cystitis (NCT01954628, NCT01882543). The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the failure, so the evidence cannot tell whether the drug never engaged SHIP1 or whether SHIP1 simply does not drive the disease.

In FLAGSHIP (NCT01954628), 200 mg AQX-1125 did not change EXACT symptom scores compared with placebo (p=0.759). Safety was clean, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The sources I found have no human measure of SHIP1 activation, so there is no direct evidence of target engagement, and they report no tissue exposure or pathway biomarker either. The only human pharmacology signal was a 20% cut in the late asthmatic response at 450 mg in an allergen-challenge study (PMID 25040039). That is a clinical/physiological effect at a different dose and in a different disease, not proof of engagement. The sponsor then dropped COPD development, as noted in a later protocol. With engagement unmeasured, the data cannot tell a drug that failed to engage SHIP1 apart from a target that does not drive COPD, so the code is U.

Rosiptor showed no benefit over placebo in LEADERSHIP 301 (NCT02858453). Neither the 100 mg nor the 200 mg dose separated from placebo on maximum daily bladder pain (P=0.41). The sponsor said the result was definitive, that no subgroup or secondary analysis showed benefit, and that it was halting all development. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Its signal in the Phase 2 trial (NCT01882543, PMID:26968644) was marginal and was not reproduced. I found no human measure of SHIP1 activation or a downstream marker such as reduced PI3K/Akt signaling in white blood cells, and no posted Phase 1 PK. PMID:35506893 reports no activity in cell-based assays, but that is lab data, not human evidence. Other trials in COPD, atopic dermatitis and chronic prostatitis also failed or stopped early. With engagement unmeasured, there is no way to tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03500159 was terminated by sponsor decision after enrolling 3 subjects, and no primary outcome data were reported. It never served as an efficacy test of rosiptor in CP/CPPS, so its readout is not an efficacy failure (F9). Operationally the trial could not answer the question (F7). Across the program, the IC/BPS (NCT01882543), COPD (NCT01954628) and atopic dermatitis (NCT02324972) Phase 2 trials missed their primary endpoints. No Phase 1 results or PubMed data in the bundle show exposure, SHIP1 activation or a pathway biomarker in humans. Whether the drug failed to engage or the target does not matter is therefore indeterminate (U). No business reason is documented.

The index CP/CPPS trial NCT03500159 was terminated by sponsor decision after enrolling only 3 subjects (2 drug, 1 placebo). No primary outcome data were reported, so it was never an efficacy test of rosiptor. The bundle has no human exposure, SHIP1 (INPP5D) activation or pathway biomarker data. The ADME study NCT03185195 posted no results and there are no abstracts. Earlier Phase 2 trials in IC/BPS (NCT01882543, near-miss p=0.061), COPD and atopic dermatitis missed their endpoints. The Phase 3 IC/BPS trial NCT02858453 has unknown status. The bundle does not state why the sponsor stopped (business reasons possible but unshown). If this were treated as an efficacy failure, it would be indeterminate (U), since engagement was never shown.

Human exposure was shown: PK was dose-linear with steady state after four weekly doses, and no MTD was reached up to 30 mg/kg (PMID:19546406, NCT02525536). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because TRINOVA-1 met its PFS endpoint in ovarian cancer through Ang1/2 neutralization in the tumor vasculature (NCT01204749). DCE-MRI Ktrans reductions support a vascular pathway effect (PMID:19546406). Tolerability did not cap the dose. No NSCLC engagement data exist. The index trial (NCT01666977) posted no results and gave no stop reason. The bundle therefore does not show why it failed. Similar misses in colorectal and liver cancer (NCT00752570, NCT00872014) suggest Ang1/2 blockade does not drive benefit outside ovarian cancer. Evidence is thin.

In humans, trebananib showed dose-linear PK and reached steady state, with no MTD up to 30 mg/kg (PMID:19546406, NCT02525536), so exposure was adequate and the dose was not capped.
