DCE-MRI Ktrans fell in treated tumors, consistent with the expected anti-vascular effect (PMID:19546406). No direct angiopoietin-binding data appear in the bundle. Engagement is inferred adequate because TRINOVA-1 met its PFS endpoint in ovarian cancer through the same Ang1/2–Tie2 vascular mechanism (NCT01204749). The ovarian phase 2 at 10 mg/kg, the index dose, also suggested a dose-response (PMID:22184370). Yet at 10 mg/kg plus FOLFIRI in second-line CRC, PFS was not improved (HR 1.23) (PMID:23361051). This points to Ang1/2 blockade not driving benefit in this setting. No engagement data come from CRC patients.

First-in-human data showed dose-linear PK, no MTD up to 30 mg/kg, and Ktrans reductions on DCE-MRI (PMID:19546406). This supports systemic exposure and a vascular effect, so the dose was not tolerability-capped. Ang1/2 neutralization was not measured directly. Engagement is inferred_adequate because trebananib met its PFS endpoint in ovarian cancer (TRINOVA-1, NCT01204749; dose-response in PMID:22184370) through the same target in the tumor vasculature, at doses comparable to 10–15 mg/kg weekly. In HCC, adding trebananib to sorafenib did not improve 4-month PFS over historical control (PMID:28592620), suggesting Ang1/2 blockade does not add benefit there. Secondary: possible low-baseline Ang-2 subgroup (F3); small single-arm design against a historical control (F7).

Exposure was adequate: dose-linear PK and no MTD reached up to 30 mg/kg (PMID:19546406, NCT02525536). Pathway was adequate: DCE-MRI Ktrans fell in treated lesions (PMID:19546406). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred adequate because the same 15 mg/kg weekly dose met its PFS endpoint in recurrent ovarian cancer in TRINOVA-1 (NCT01204749, PMID:24950985), but that evidence was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose (PMID:25037684). TRINOVA-3 (PMID:31076365) tested the same engaged dose with first-line carboplatin/paclitaxel and the program stopped without benefit. This points to the angiopoietin mechanism not driving outcome in that setting. Benefit was confined to the recurrent setting and the ascites subgroup (PMID:27546885), so F3 is secondary.

In the index trial, trebananib 10 mg/kg QW plus FOLFIRI did not prolong PFS in second-line mCRC (HR 1.23; PMID:23361051). Exposure was adequate: PK was dose-linear with steady state reached, and no MTD was found up to 30 mg/kg (PMID:19546406, NCT02525536), so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred_adequate because trebananib met its PFS endpoint in ovarian cancer (TRINOVA-1, NCT01204749) through the same systemic tumor-vasculature mechanism, with dose-response at 10 mg/kg (PMID:22184370). Phase 1 Ktrans reductions support a vascular pathway effect. That evidence came from other diseases, and the engagement evidence postdates the index start. With the mechanism engaged, the lack of benefit in colorectal cancer points to angiopoietin/Tie2 blockade not driving this disease as tested.

In healthy volunteers, a D4-cortisol tracer study with CSF sampling (NCT01009216, PMID:23982627) found no CNS HSD-1 product at ABT-384 doses of 2 mg or more, indicating full brain inhibition. That trial was registered before the index trial. Hepatic inhibition was complete from 1 mg. ACTH, cortisol production and androgens rose as the mechanism predicts, though this pathway evidence is peripheral (PMID:27121668). No maximum tolerated dose was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The index trial (NCT01137526) used 10 and 50 mg, well above the fully inhibiting dose, and was stopped for futility, while donepezil was active (PMID:24418055). The authors conclude that complete brain HSD-1 inhibition gave no symptomatic benefit. The target does not drive cognition in AD as tested. Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers, not AD patients.

Exposure and engagement: according to the sponsor's 015 protocol, Phase 1 human studies tied MK-1029 plasma levels to ex-vivo inhibition of PGD2-induced CD11b on eosinophils, a marker of CRTH2 blockade. The 150 mg dose was chosen as being at or near the plateau. Pathway: in allergen-challenged asthmatics (NCT01343407, 2011, before the index trial), 60 mg and 500 mg reduced sputum eosinophils and the late asthmatic response. No dose was capped by tolerability. In the index trial, FEV1 improved by only 47 mL (p=0.282). The sponsor attributed the miss to a genotype subgroup, with a 268 mL effect in carriers of one SNP, and to a baseline imbalance between crossover sequences. The follow-up trial NCT02720081 enrolled genotype-selected patients and met its endpoint. This points to patient selection (F3) as the main reason, with trial execution (F7) and the target not driving disease as tested (F2) as secondary codes.

The index trial NCT01364844 was a first-in-human Phase 1 dose-finding study with an adverse-event primary endpoint. It completed and was not an efficacy test of DS-7423, so it fits F9. PMID:29795308 reports that PK and PD were measured in the US and Japanese cohorts and that the RP2D was 240 mg/day, with no regional differences. That shows plasma exposure in humans. However, no target-engagement or pathway magnitudes are given, so engagement and pathway lack usable human evidence. The bundle gives no reason for discontinuation, so why the program stopped beyond this trial is indeterminate (U as secondary).

Uprifosbuvir, an NS5B nucleotide polymerase inhibitor (PMID:33934558), lowered HCV RNA by up to 4.50 log10 vs 0.42 on placebo in HCV-infected patients at Day 8 (NCT01974687, 2013). This is direct antiviral engagement in the disease, shown before the index trial. Grazoprevir-containing triple regimens reached high SVR12 across genotypes (NCT02332707, NCT02332720, NCT02613403). In the index uprifosbuvir+ruzasvir trial, SVR12 was 97–100% in GT1/GT2 and 90% in GT4, but only 76.9% in GT3 and 66.7% in GT6 (NCT02759315). NCT02956629 gave a similar pattern. The shortfall is confined to genotype subgroups, consistent with insufficient pangenotypic potency of this two-drug regimen. Hence F3, with F2 secondary. No tolerability limit was seen.

At 230 mg, plasma exposure targets predicted (from nonclinical models) for maximal pharmacodynamic response were reached in the index pancreatic trial (PMID:28202004, PMID:27598338), so exposure was adequate. No direct human CHK1 engagement or pathway biomarker was measured. Engagement is inferred_adequate only because the same drug met a randomized PFS endpoint in NSCLC with pemetrexed/cisplatin at a comparable dose of 275 mg (NCT01139775). That trial started after the index trial. Tolerability did not cap the dose below the exposure targets. Despite this, OS was not improved (7.8 vs 8.3 months; posterior probability 0.333) (NCT00839332). This points to CHK1 inhibition plus gemcitabine not driving benefit in pancreatic cancer. Confidence is low: engagement is inferred, and tumor penetration in pancreas is unmeasured, so U remains plausible.

Exposure counts as adequate. At the 230 mg dose used in the Phase 2 pancreatic trial, plasma exposure met the AUC and Cmax targets that predicted maximal pharmacodynamic effect in preclinical models (PMID:28202004, PMID:27598338). Those targets come from animal models, though. None of the sources reports direct human evidence of CHK1 inhibition, such as reduced CHK1 autophosphorylation or a gamma-H2AX change in tumour or surrogate tissue. The only biomarker reported is circulating plasma DNA in partial responders, which is not specific to CHK1 (PMID:26288133). Tolerability did not cap the dose, since 230 mg was tolerable. The trial was negative on overall survival (7.8 vs 8.3 months; posterior probability 0.33). Because engagement is unmeasured, a drug that never engaged CHK1 cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. A CHK1 combination did meet a PFS endpoint in lung cancer (NCT01139775), which hints that the target was engaged (F2).

In healthy volunteers, XEN-D0501 at 1–5 mg BID was rapidly absorbed and well tolerated (PMID:21676011, 2011). It caused a dose-related rise in core body temperature, an on-target TRPV1 effect, which is human engagement evidence predating the 2014 index trial. In refractory chronic cough, 4 mg BID markedly reduced capsaicin-evoked maximal cough (P<0.0001) but did not reduce spontaneous cough frequency (PMID:28650204, NCT02233699). The authors concluded TRPV1 is ruled out as an effective target. Dosing was not capped by tolerability. Engagement was not shown in COPD patients, and the COPD index trial (NCT02233686) posted no results. With adequate engagement and pathway effect but no clinical benefit, the most direct reading is that the target does not drive cough. Confidence is medium because the COPD data are absent.

Healthy-volunteer PK showed rapid absorption and good tolerability up to 5 mg BID. A dose-related rise in body temperature, an on-target TRPV1 effect, was published in 2011, before the index trial started (PMID:21676011). In refractory chronic cough patients, 4 mg BID markedly reduced capsaicin-evoked maximal cough (P<0.0001), showing engagement and pathway effect, yet spontaneous cough frequency did not fall. The authors conclude TRPV1 is ruled out as an effective target for cough (PMID:28650204). The COPD index trial (NCT02233686) posted no results, and engagement was not measured in COPD patients specifically. Its failure is therefore inferred to share the same cause: the target engaged at a tolerable dose but does not drive spontaneous cough. Confidence is medium because the COPD readout itself is absent from the bundle.

Masitinib 9 mg/kg/day plus gemcitabine did not improve OS overall in advanced PDAC (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.70-1.13; NCT00789633, PMID:25858497). No human PK, target-engagement or biomarker data in pancreatic cancer appear in the bundle. Exposure and engagement are inferred adequate because masitinib at lower doses met KIT-driven endpoints in systemic mastocytosis (NCT00814073) and imatinib-resistant GIST (NCT01506336). These are a different tissue compartment, and both trials started after the index trial, so the inference is tenuous. The authors attribute the result to heterogeneity: benefit was confined to prespecified subgroups (ACOX1 overexpression HR 0.23; pain VAS>20 HR 0.62). A confirmatory subgroup trial followed (NCT03766295). This fits F3. F2 applies if the inferred engagement holds; U applies if engagement is treated as unmeasured.

Sanofi's neuropathic pain trial of ataciguat (NCT00799656) posted no results and gave no reason for stopping. The only human pharmacology found is a warfarin interaction study (PMID:17192504), which shows plasma exposure and CYP2C9 inhibition but says nothing about sGC activation. No human data were found for cGMP rise, blood pressure change or drug levels in nerve or CNS tissue. Mayo/Kardigan aortic valve trials later reported slower valve calcification (NCT02481258), but that is a different tissue and mostly a structural or biomarker endpoint, so it can't be used to infer engagement for pain. TCTMD notes earlier angina and PAD studies were negative, again without engagement data. With engagement unmeasured, I can't tell whether the drug failed to engage or the target doesn't matter in pain, so the code is U.

The 2014 EULAR abstract reports results of the index trial (NCT01404585). In RA patients, steady-state trough levels were about 17 and 46 times the ex vivo IC90 for MIP-1α at 200 and 400 mg BID, so exposure was high. CCR1 ligands rose only in the two treated arms, which the investigators called confirmation of biologically effective CCR1 inhibition in vivo. I counted that ligand rise as the pathway marker too, though it overlaps with the engagement evidence. The drug was safe and well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Even so, DAS28-CRP, ACR responses and MRI synovitis/osteitis did not improve. With engagement shown in this disease, the failure points to CCR1 not driving RA as tested (F2). The engagement data were published only after the trial, which started in 2011.

Inclacumab showed dose-dependent plasma exposure, soluble P-selectin occupancy and inhibition of platelet-leukocyte aggregates in healthy volunteers up to 20 mg/kg without tolerability limits (PMID:25714598, PMID:26363899), with >90% P-selectin inhibition at 20 mg/kg (PMID:37436495). It also reduced circulating PLAs in PAD patients (PMID:23522853; NCT00760565, started before the index trial), but not in coronary or CABG patients. With engagement and pathway adequate and no dose cap, a failed SELECT-CABG (NCT01245634) readout points to P-selectin blockade not driving vein-graft disease (F2). SELECT-ACS (NCT01327183) gave only a marginal troponin signal. The bundle gives only the index publication title (PMID:26796402), with no results, so confidence is low.

disease: idiopathic malabsorption due to bile acid synthesis defects
rationale: The index trial (NCT02078856, n=19, A3384 250 mg or 1 g twice daily vs placebo for 2 weeks in BAD) is reported in PMID:28507750, where A3384 improved diarrhoeal symptoms versus placebo (median 2.2-point Likert reduction, p<0.05) and the authors conclude it produced symptomatic benefit. The readout therefore does not look like an efficacy failure, though the abstract does not report the registered bowel-movement primary endpoint. FGF19 and C4 were unchanged, consistent with colonic release rather than showing a lack of engagement. Colonic bile acid binding was never measured directly. No business reason for stopping appears in the bundle. The later short bowel syndrome trial (NCT04046328) ended because of difficult recruitment. The evidence is thin and the trial was small.

The index Morpheus-CRC platform (NCT03555149) was terminated for start-up and recruitment problems. Only 6 patients entered the selicrelumab arm (0% ORR, 50% SD), so the trial could not answer the efficacy question. CD40 engagement and pathway activation in humans were shown before the index trial: B-cell costimulatory upregulation and depletion, cytokine release, and Ki67+ CD8 T-cell activation (PMID:20855968, PMID:23983255, PMID:33097612). This evidence comes from solid-tumour and pancreatic patients, not colorectal cancer. Despite this, clinical activity was minimal across indications, including the failed pancreatic platform (NCT03193190), which supports F2. Development later ended for portfolio and drug-supply reasons (NCT03892525, PMID:41502913). Tolerability (an MTD set by cytokine release syndrome) did not clearly cap the dose below engagement.

In boys with DMD, plasma exposure was low and highly variable, below healthy-volunteer levels (PMID:27055247, PMID:30650257). Cohort 1 had a trough of only 17 ng/mL (NCT02858362). In the open-label index trial, muscle biopsies at week 24 showed more utrophin and less developmental myosin. By week 48 the developmental myosin and MR T2 effects were gone, the biopsy secondary endpoints were missed, and fat fraction kept rising. The only engagement evidence is this transient, uncontrolled signal from the index trial itself. Later papers blame ezutromid's poor ADME properties and limited in vivo exposure (PMID:33915371, PMID:32551645). That points to engagement that was not sustained (F1a). A target that does not drive disease (F2) cannot be ruled out. Tolerability did not cap the dose.

In UC patients at 1.2 mg daily, KRP203 markedly lowered total peripheral lymphocytes and naive and central memory T-cell and B-cell subsets. This is the expected S1PR1-mediated sequestration, so exposure, engagement and pathway are shown in the disease (PMID:33313070). That evidence was published in 2020, after the index trial started. The drug was well tolerated, with no dose cap. Remission was 2/14 on drug versus 0/8 on placebo. The authors call the difference insignificant in a small population and recommend a larger study with improved design. The trial was terminated at 27 enrolled (NCT01375179). Ozanimod and etrasimod are approved for UC on the same target, so the target is valid. The bundle points to an underpowered trial that could not answer the question.

In mild AD/MCI patients, IV GSK933776 at 0.001–6 mg/kg gave dose-dependent plasma exposure (t1/2 10–15 days). Free plasma Aβ fell dose-dependently while total Aβ rose, and CSF Aβ species shifted (PMID:25789616, PMID:24716469). This shows systemic target engagement at doses spanning the index trial's 3–6 mg/kg; the index also tested 15 mg/kg. NCT00459550 was registered in 2007, before the index trial began. No ocular or retinal exposure or pathway data exist, and engagement was never shown in geographic atrophy patients. In the index trial (NCT01342926), GA growth at 18 months was no better than placebo at any dose, with numerically more growth, and no tolerability cap. With adequate systemic engagement and no benefit, the evidence points to Aβ neutralization not driving GA progression. Confidence is medium because retinal penetration is unmeasured.

Zimlovisertib 400 mg QD gave no HiSCR benefit over placebo in HS (34.0% vs 33.3%, RD 0.7; NCT04092452, PMID:38335032). Phase 1 studies showed dose-proportional plasma exposure with no MTD reached, so dose was not tolerability-capped. hsCRP fell in a sustained way at ≥250 mg, and whole-blood interferon gene signature dropped in healthy volunteers (PMID:31805989, PMID:34423919), supporting the pathway pillar. Engagement is inferred adequate: the same 400 mg dose met the SDAI endpoint in RA (NCT02996500) through systemic IRAK4 inhibition. Engagement was not shown in HS patients. The authors conclude the results did not confirm a role for selective IRAK4 inhibition in HS, so the target does not drive the disease as tested. A minor F7 caveat applies: 28% of participants were lost to follow-up in a small phase 2a trial.

The index trial (NCT01940887) found no benefit from adding Fovista to anti-VEGF treatment (9.42 vs 9.04 letters). The two Lucentis-combination Phase 3 trials (NCT01940900, NCT01944839) also failed. I found no human measurements of vitreous drug levels, PDGF-B neutralization, or pericyte stripping. The Phase 1 trial (PMID:26499921) reported shrinking CNV lesions on FA and OCT, but every patient also got ranibizumab and there was no control arm, so the effect cannot be credited to PDGF blockade. Tolerability did not limit the dose. The Phase 2b gain (PMID:28029445) did not replicate, and no sponsor statement explains why. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a pericyte-stripping idea that does not matter clinically. F2 is a plausible secondary code.

Phase 1 studies in type 2 diabetes patients measured gevokizumab pharmacokinetics and found that CRP fell in a dose-dependent way (Cavelti-Weder, Diabetes Care 2012). These results were presented at ADA in June 2009, before the index trial began in January 2010. In the index trial NCT01066715 (421 patients on metformin, four monthly doses for 6 months), every gevokizumab arm lowered CRP and two arms raised HDL, which shows IL-1β neutralization and the expected anti-inflammatory effect. HbA1c still did not improve versus placebo, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Free IL-1β was never measured directly, so I rated engagement adequate based on the CRP drop. Given that, the most likely reason for failure is that IL-1β does not drive blood sugar control in this population (F2).

XOMA ended the erosive hand OA program because the Phase 2 trials (NCT01683396/NCT01882491, which enrolled only patients with CRP ≥2.5 mg/L) showed no drug-related benefit at 6 months. It gave no mechanistic explanation. The only human pharmacology I found comes from type 2 diabetes (NCT01066715, PMID 22699287, published 2012). There gevokizumab reduced inflammatory markers and modestly improved glycemia, a downstream pathway effect, but outside OA. I found no measurement of IL-1β neutralization or drug levels in synovial fluid or joint tissue, and no biomarker data from OA patients. I could only read search snippets because the fetch limit ran out. Because engagement at the joint is no_human_data, the evidence can't separate inadequate engagement from IL-1β not driving hand OA pain, so the code is U (F2 possible).

The index trial, EYEGUARD-US (NCT02258867), enrolled 4 patients and was terminated after the sister trial EYEGUARD-B (NCT01965145, PMID:29370572) missed its primary endpoint of time to first ocular exacerbation at 60 mg SC every 4 weeks. Exposure is shown by human PK (half-life 22 days; PK also measured in Behçet patients, PMID:22084392). No direct binding or occupancy assay was found. Engagement is graded adequate on functional grounds only: in a published T2D dose-escalation study (PMID 22699287), doses of 0.03 to 1 mg/kg lowered CRP and spontaneous and inducible cytokines. That study was in T2D, not Behçet's, and predates the index trial. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The sponsor reported activity signals on secondary endpoints (visual acuity, macular edema), but they did not prevent exacerbations. That suggests IL-1β modulation does not drive exacerbation risk as tested. F4 is secondary, given those secondary-endpoint signals. Confidence is medium.

The index trial NCT01684345 (EYEGUARD-A) was terminated with no stated reason and no posted results. The related phase 3 EYEGUARD-B trial (NCT01965145, PMID:29370572) missed its primary endpoint of ocular exacerbations. The investigators still called IL-1β a possibly relevant target. None of the sources measured direct target engagement in humans, such as IL-1β binding or lowering of free IL-1β. None reported drug levels in the eye. The only pathway evidence comes from type 2 diabetes (NCT01066715, PMC3402269), where CRP fell in a dose-dependent, U-shaped pattern and ex vivo cytokine production dropped. Nothing measured engagement in uveitis. The open-label uveitis studies (PMID:22084392, PMID:26829647) were uncontrolled. Because engagement has no human data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

NCT00804973 was stopped after an interim efficacy analysis. At 2 hours, 6 of 40 patients on LY2590443 were pain free, the same as placebo (6/40). Sumatriptan reached 12/40, so the trial was able to detect a real treatment effect. The bundle has no Phase 1 results and no PubMed abstracts. My searches turned up only database listings and patents, with no human data on drug levels, 5-HT7 receptor occupancy or downstream biomarkers. No other drug on this target has succeeded in migraine, and no toxicity was reported. Without any engagement data, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage 5-HT7 or whether 5-HT7 does not drive acute migraine. That makes this indeterminate (U).

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional in T2DM patients and in Japanese subjects, with no ethnic PK differences (PMID:22775976, PMID:22943931). No direct glucokinase activity measure exists, so engagement is inferred. Dose-dependent insulin secretion and glucose lowering in patients before the index start support it (pathway adequate). The drug also met its HbA1c endpoint as metformin add-on (NCT01020123/PMID:23464532). No tolerability cap limited dosing. In the index Japanese monotherapy trial, HbA1c fell 0.3-0.8% over 2 months, then the effect declined; the 4-month result was not significant (p=0.30; PMID:23522182). Efficacy also waned in the add-on extension. The mechanism engaged but did not durably control glycaemia: F2, with loss of durability (F4) secondary.

Exposure was shown in humans: rhAT-gamma raised plasma antithrombin activity to levels bioequivalent to plasma-derived AT in healthy volunteers (PMID:31493216). Engagement is inferred_adequate: in DIC, a systemic plasma compartment, the drug achieved DIC recovery similar to pAT (NCT01384903). Engagement was not measured in preeclampsia patients. The excess of hemorrhage-related events and anemia in the index trial is consistent with on-target anticoagulant activity. Even so, pregnancy prolongation was not significantly improved (16.9 vs 13 days, P=0.07) (NCT04182373, PMID:41789451). This points to AT replacement not driving benefit in early-onset severe preeclampsia as tested (F2). Increased bleeding adds a secondary F5 element. No coagulation pathway biomarkers were reported.

The index trial NCT01988558 was a Phase 1/2 study of DL-lactic acid syrup in children with recurrent tonsillitis. Its only primary outcome was safety (adverse events at 90 days), it is classified not_efficacy, and no results or stop reason were posted. It was therefore not an efficacy test of the drug. No primary target is recorded, and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data in the oropharynx. Vaginal pH lowering (NCT02693418) and the vaginal-gel efficacy in chlamydia (NCT03107377) are a different formulation and tissue compartment, so they do not support inferred adequacy here. If the program is read as an efficacy failure, it is indeterminate (U) because engagement has no human data. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

STA363 is lactic acid injected straight into the disc. It has no molecular target; it is meant to turn the nucleus pulposus into connective tissue. Because it is injected into the disc, exposure is assured. The published phase 2b paper on the index trial (NCT04673461; PMID 41056050; 109 patients given 90 or 180 mg) reports MRI changes consistent with fibrosis of the nucleus pulposus. That shows the intended tissue effect happened in patients with this disease, so engagement and pathway count as adequate. Still, back pain did not differ from placebo at any time point. The mechanism worked but did not relieve discogenic pain, which fits F2. All arms, including placebo, improved markedly, so placebo response (F7) may also have played a part. The engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself.

No molecular target is recorded. The mechanism is vaginal acidification. In healthy women, the Phase 1 NCT02693418 (2016) showed that the topical gel lowered vaginal pH versus placebo for at least 12 to 24 hours. That counts as direct local exposure and engagement, though not in an at-risk or infected population. The pathway pillar is inferred adequate because the same intravaginal acidifying gel was contraceptively effective (NCT01306331, NCT03243305). It also met the chlamydia-prevention endpoint in the Phase 2b/3 NCT03107377. Even so, the Phase 3 NCT04553068 showed no benefit (75.5% vs 76.2% study success), with no tolerability limit. With engagement shown, the likely reading is that acidification does not reliably prevent CT/NG. Trial-related explanations for the discordance with the Phase 2b/3 (F7) cannot be excluded, and the bundle gives no stated reason.

Phase 1 studies showed dose-proportional serum exposure (PMID:21037025, PMID:25502863). In mesothelioma patients, amatuximab caused a marked, reversible rise in serum CA-125 consistent with blocking mesothelin–CA-125 binding, which is evidence of engagement and a functional effect. It was published in 2010, after the index trial started (PMID:19744744). The single-arm index trial missed its 6-month PFS target against historical controls (NCT00738582, PMID:25231400). Population PK showed patients above the median Cmin had longer OS and PFS, and the authors recommended more frequent dosing to raise exposure (PMID:26898299). A mouse study suggests shed mesothelin acts as a decoy (PMID:29720923). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Underexposure is the stated lead; F2 is also possible, and the uncontrolled design (F7) limits interpretation.

The index trial NCT01283373 was a Phase 1 3+3 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoint was DLT incidence, so it was not an efficacy test. PMID:31689155 reports acceptable safety at an RP2D of 2.4 mg/kg q3w and antitumor activity: 18% had a ≥50% PSA decline, 59% had CTC conversions and there were some partial responses. Plasma PK was linear and matched model predictions (PMID:27679517), so exposure is adequate. No STEAP1 binding or occupancy data in humans appear in the bundle. Payload-type toxicities such as neuropathy and transaminitis forced dose reductions from 2.8 mg/kg, but the bundle states no reason for stopping. This leaves the discontinuation unexplained by an efficacy failure.

The index trial NCT00911963 was a phase 1b antiviral-activity study in genotype 1 HCV patients. It posted no results, but PMID:24982088 reports substantial plasma HCV RNA reductions with VX-222. Its NS5B resistance variants selected during 3-day monotherapy are direct evidence of on-target engagement in patients. Exposure is not measured directly; it is taken as adequate from these antiviral effects at the site of action. In the phase 2a ZENITH study (PMID:24901821), TRIPLE and QUAD regimens reached 67–90% SVR24, comparable to telaprevir-based therapy. Only the DUAL arm failed, from viral breakthrough. The bundle does not show an efficacy failure of the index trial. Discontinuation was likely strategic: PMID:25384989 says most HCV drug discontinuations were corporate decisions, though it does not name this drug.

Exposure: in phase 1 (NCT02459886, PMID:31211448) serum exposure was dose-proportional and the CSF/serum ratio was 0.13–0.56%, typical for an antibody. Engagement: plasma BIIB054/α-syn complexes were almost completely saturated in PD participants, and CSF complexes rose with dose (PMID:39892989). Phase 2 doses were modelled to give ≥90% target binding in brain interstitial fluid (PMID:32613752), and dosing was not limited by tolerability. Pathway: in SPARK, α-syn seeding stayed positive in 99% of patients and CSF/plasma biomarkers and DaT-SPECT were unchanged (PMID:38315945). The MDS-UPDRS was flat at every dose (NCT03318523, PMID:35921450). This points to F2. F1a is secondary because engagement in the synaptic compartment is uncertain (PMID:37658103).

The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for methylsamidorphan (ALKS 37). There are no posted results from the index trial NCT01100151 or the later Phase 2 trials (NCT01382797, NCT01418092), no Phase 1 results and no PubMed abstracts. The target itself is validated in this exact disease: peripheral mu-opioid antagonists methylnaltrexone, naloxegol and naldemedine are FDA-approved for opioid-induced constipation, and alvimopan is approved for bowel dysfunction. That rules out 'the target does not matter'. With no evidence that this molecule engaged adequately, the failure is best attributed to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin and does not even document the readout or the reason the program stopped.

In healthy volunteers, BI 409306 entered CSF (CSF/plasma ratio about 28%) and raised CSF cGMP dose-dependently (NCT01493570, PMID:28120486). That study was registered in 2011, before the index trial, and its authors call it proof of mechanism. The index trial and its twin (NCT02240693, NCT02337907; PMID:30755255) tested 10–50 mg daily for 12 weeks and showed no NTB benefit at any dose. The schizophrenia trial with doses up to 100 mg also failed (NCT02281773). This supports a target that does not drive cognition as tested (F2). One caveat: at 25–50 mg the CSF cGMP rise was modest (about 1.2–1.3x, with wide variability) compared with 100–200 mg. Engagement was never measured in AD patients. So partial engagement at the index doses (F1a) cannot be excluded.

In healthy volunteers (NCT01493570, PMID:28120486, registered 2011, before the 2014 index start), BI 409306 25–200 mg crossed into CSF (CSF/plasma ratio about 28%). It produced dose-dependent CSF cGMP increases, about 2.2-fold at 100 mg versus 0.9 on placebo; the authors called this proof of mechanism. Engagement was never measured in schizophrenia patients; the patient study PMID:29177699 gave PK only. Doses up to 100 mg were well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, no dose improved MCCB or SCoRS over 12 weeks (NCT02281773, PMID:29718385). Relapse prevention (NCT03351244) and two Alzheimer trials also failed. Together these suggest PDE9A-driven cGMP elevation does not improve cognition in schizophrenia. The short half-life with once-daily dosing leaves some uncertainty.

The index trial NCT02478866 was a first-in-human dose-escalation study whose primary outcome was adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test. PMID:31948451 reports no DLTs up to 800 mg, MTD not reached, plasma exposure saturating near 600 mg, and 1 PR with 10 SD among 19 evaluable patients. The authors say this supports further development, so the readout was not an efficacy failure (F9). Plasma PK was measured (PMID:29028616), but the bundle shows no MET/AXL target engagement or pathway biomarker data in humans. The later trial NCT02929290 has unknown status. Why development stopped therefore cannot be separated into a drug or target cause (U as secondary).

In the first-in-human index trial NCT01673737, PMID:28976556 reports that SAR260301 was cleared rapidly. Exposures linked to preclinical antitumor activity were not sustained even at the highest dose, and food lowered exposure further. The authors conclude that exposure sufficient to inhibit the PI3K pathway was unachievable and that development was terminated for this reason. Target engagement was assessed in platelets, but the abstract gives no adequacy result, and sustained engagement could not have been reached without adequate exposure. The MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose; pharmacokinetics did. The mechanism was never properly tested, which fits F1a. Confidence is high because the source states the reason directly.

The index OCD trial (NCT01813019) was stopped at interim analysis for futility, with no separation from placebo on Y-BOCS (-6.9 vs -8.0, p=0.671). Human PET in healthy volunteers (PMID:33545349) showed brain penetration and dose-dependent mGluR5 occupancy (59-85% at 100-400 mg). That study was published in 2021, after the index trial started, and was not done in patients. Mavoglurant met clinical endpoints at about 200 mg/day in a CNS indication (levodopa-induced dyskinesia, NCT00986414/PMID:23853029) and in cocaine use disorder (NCT03242928), so the pathway pillar is inferred adequate. Tolerability limits are mentioned (PMID:27823869), but nothing shows they capped engagement. The index dose is not given in the bundle. The likeliest reading is that mGluR5 antagonism does not drive SSRI-resistant OCD; the small trial ended early at interim (F7 secondary).

In the HD chorea trial (NCT01019473, PMID:25689146), AFQ056 25–150 mg bid did not improve chorea at day 28 and was well tolerated, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. In healthy volunteers, PET showed brain penetration and dose-dependent mGluR5 occupancy of 59% at 100 mg and 74% at 200 mg (PMID:33545349). This was published after the index trial and was not measured in HD patients. Pathway function in basal ganglia motor circuits is inferred from efficacy at comparable doses against Parkinson's levodopa-induced dyskinesia (NCT00986414, PMID:23853029; NCT00888004). With the target engaged at tolerated doses and no chorea benefit, mGluR5 antagonism does not appear to drive HD chorea as tested.

In healthy volunteers, PET showed mavoglurant crossed the blood-brain barrier with dose-dependent mGluR5 occupancy: 74% at 200 mg and 85% at 400 mg (PMID:33545349). This was published in 2021, after the index trial, and was not measured in OCD patients. Pathway is inferred_adequate: 200 mg/day met the primary dyskinesia endpoint in Parkinson's levodopa-induced dyskinesia via the same brain target (NCT00986414, PMID:23853029). The bundle does not state the OCD dose, which limits confidence. Tolerability did not clearly cap dosing. The index trial showed no Y-BOCS benefit (-6.9 vs -8.0 placebo, p=0.671). The authors concluded the results do not support mGluR5 antagonism for OCD (PMID:28044255), so target irrelevance (F2) is primary. The small interim analysis (n=38 completers) is a secondary design limitation (F7).

The index trial is an open-label safety extension, terminated because both core Phase 2b FXS trials (NCT01253629, NCT01357239; PMID:26764156) missed the ABC-CFX endpoint at up to 100 mg bid. In healthy-volunteer PET (PMID:33545349, published 2021, after the index), mavoglurant crossed the blood-brain barrier with dose-dependent mGluR5 occupancy (59% at 100 mg, 74% at 200 mg). Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same 200 mg/day dose met the primary endpoint in levodopa-induced dyskinesia (NCT00986414, PMID:23853029), the same CNS target. The extensions showed no new safety signal, so tolerability did not cap dosing (PMID:30451888). The paediatric FXLEARN trial also failed and concluded the mechanism does not translate to humans (PMID:37651202). Secondary codes: the sources also raise age and treatment duration (PMID:26764156).

The phase 1 trial (NCT00721266, registered 2008; PMID:21900113) reached 1,400 mg with no MTD. Clearance plateaued above 400 mg, consistent with saturated target-mediated disposition. On-target EGFR rash occurred in 80% of patients, and circulating NK cells fell. In HNSCC (PMID:28950289), EGFR-expressing tumor cells fell by 35-42%, with immune effector infiltration, so engagement and pathway effects were shown in humans, though not in NSCLC. Despite this, the non-squamous NSCLC chemotherapy-combination trial (NCT01185847) did not lead to further development, suggesting EGFR/ADCC targeting adds little in this setting. Necitumumab's approval only in squamous NSCLC hints at subtype dependence (F3). No index results are posted, so confidence is low.

The index trial posted no results and gave no stop reason, so the cause is inferred. Exposure: the Phase 1 trial (PMID:21900113) showed clearance plateauing above 400 mg, consistent with target-mediated clearance being saturated at the chosen 1400 mg dose. No MTD was reached, so the dose was not limited by tolerability. Engagement: on-target rash and hypomagnesemia were frequent, and EGFR-expressing tumour cells fell by about 42% in head and neck cancer biopsies (PMID:28950289). In CRC biopsies, immune infiltration rose after one cycle (PMID:24262587, published 2014, after the 2011 index start). With the target engaged and ADCC effects shown, the lack of benefit on FOLFIRI points to the enhanced-ADCC EGFR mechanism adding nothing in this setting (F2). Patient selection (KRAS status) may also have contributed (F3).

In healthy subjects (PMID:27402064), lulizumab showed dose-proportional PK with 68% SC bioavailability. CD28 receptor occupancy stayed at roughly ≥80% throughout the dosing interval in the MAD study (SC 6.25 mg q2w and 12.5 mg weekly), matching the top index doses. IV doses ≥9 mg suppressed the T-cell-dependent anti-KLH antibody response, a functional pathway readout. Safety was acceptable, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In the index SLE trial (NCT02265744), BICLA response was flat across all arms (57–63% vs 59% placebo, all p>0.6), with no dose-response. Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers, not in SLE patients, and was published after the index trial started (2017). Hence F2 at medium confidence.

In healthy subjects (PMID:27402064), lulizumab showed dose-proportional plasma exposure. CD28 receptor occupancy stayed at roughly 80% or more throughout the dosing interval at SC doses including 12.5 mg weekly, the top dose in the index trial. IV doses of 9 mg or more inhibited the antibody response to KLH, a downstream T-cell-dependent effect. No dose limitation from tolerability was reported. Despite this, every dose arm in NCT02265744 had a BICLA response matching placebo (57-63% vs 59%, all p>0.6), with no dose-response. Adequate engagement with no benefit points to CD28 blockade not driving SLE as tested. Engagement was shown only in healthy volunteers, and the 2017 publication came after the index trial started, so confidence is medium.

Ponezumab bound circulating Aβ in AD patients: plasma Aβ1-40 and Aβ1-x rose dose-dependently from Phase 1 onward (NCT00455000, PMID:23334070, PMID:24131736). The target is central, though. CSF penetration was about 0.5% of plasma and is repeatedly described as low. One single-dose CSF Aβ rise at 10 mg/kg was not reproduced. In the index trial, CSF biomarkers showed no dose response, and cognition and brain volume were unchanged (PMID:29067341). In the 1-year PET study, CSF biomarkers and brain amyloid were unaffected (PMID:29067345). Central exposure, engagement and pathway were therefore inadequate, and the mechanism was not properly tested. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Other anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab, aducanumab) are approved in AD, which points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b).

Ponezumab gave dose-dependent plasma exposure and robust plasma Aβ1-40 rises, so it bound Aβ peripherally (PMID:23334069, PMID:29067341). But CSF penetration was low, below 0.5% of plasma (PMID:23334070, PMID:24131736). CSF biomarkers showed no dose response and brain amyloid burden was unchanged in AD (PMID:29067345, PMID:29067341). So central or vascular engagement and the downstream pathway effect were not shown. No engagement data were collected in CAA patients. The small (n=36) index trial missed its exploratory fMRI cerebrovascular-reactivity endpoint, trending opposite to the hypothesis (NCT01821118, PMID:31020004). With poor brain-compartment exposure and no central pillar evidence, the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). The trial's small size adds an F7 element.

In the phase 1 lymphoma study (NCT01742988; PMID:27049457, PMID:28860342), patients took the 60 mg 5/2 dose later used in the index trial. Their blood cells showed more acetylated histone H3, a sign of HDAC inhibition, and less AKT phosphorylation, a sign of PI3K pathway inhibition. This was reported before the index trial started in July 2016. The evidence is qualitative western blots of blood cells, not tumor tissue. The dose was set by MTD and was not cut below what engagement needed. Even so, the phase 2 trial got only a 15% response rate in MYC-IHC≥40% DLBCL (PMID:34341990). So engaging the targets did not give enough single-agent benefit (F2). The investigators point to combinations and better biomarker-based selection, such as VIPER, which supports F3 as a secondary code.

NCT04378075 (MIT-E) missed its seizure endpoint (p=0.173), and PTC said the results do not support further development. Plasma PK is reported only in healthy volunteers and Friedreich ataxia patients (PMID:41011210, 36166059). No human brain or CSF levels were found. No human 15-LO inhibition or occupancy data were found: the protocol cites only a cell-free IC50 of 1.9 µM. The open-label glutathione change in 10 Leigh patients (PMID:23583222) is an uncontrolled redox marker, not a measure of target engagement. Vatiquinone was also negative in Ndufs4 mice (PMID:38883711). With engagement no_human_data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from an irrelevant target, so the code is U. The sponsor claimed a signal in the Leigh syndrome subgroup, which supports F3 as a secondary code.

The index trial (NCT02104336) enrolled 2 patients and was stopped because other studies did not support continuing it. No human data in the bundle show that vatiquinone engaged 15-lipoxygenase, such as enzyme inhibition or a fall in lipid peroxidation products. The PK papers are in healthy volunteers and FA patients and give only plasma levels; none measures exposure at the site of action. Two open-label reports describe redox signals: glutathione rose in Leigh syndrome patients (PMID:23583222) and HMPAO uptake tracked clinical change (PMID:23084792). Neither shows 15-LO engagement, and neither involves Pearson syndrome. No other drug on this target is in the bundle, and the drug also missed its endpoints in the Phase 3 trials in mitochondrial epilepsy and FA. Nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

Voxtalisib 50 mg BID (the MTD) plus letrozole gave a 6-month PFS rate of only 8% in AI-refractory HR+/HER2- breast cancer (PMID:26497877). Plasma exposure at the MTD is characterized, though the half-life is short (PMID:24583798). Pathway inhibition in skin, hair and tumor was reported but not quantified (PMID:24583798) and was only 'moderate' in skin elsewhere (PMID:26019185). In the index patients voxtalisib had less pharmacodynamic impact (glucose homeostasis) than pilaralisib (PMID:26497877). Other drugs on the same target (everolimus, alpelisib, inavolisib, gedatolisib) are approved in breast cancer, so the target is valid there. The weak engagement points to the molecule rather than the target. Lymphoma activity (NCT01403636) is a different tissue.

Voxtalisib reached plasma exposure and reduced PI3K/mTOR signalling in hair, skin and tumour at single-agent MTDs of 90 mg QD and 50 mg BID (PMID:24583798). In combination, inhibition was only moderate (PMID:26019185), and its pharmacodynamic impact was weaker than pilaralisib's (PMID:26497877). With pimasertib, poor tolerability capped voxtalisib at 70 mg QD, below its single-agent MTD; 73% of patients needed dose interruptions (PMID:30425349, NCT01390818). No engagement data exist in ovarian cancer. In NCT01936363, adding voxtalisib did not improve ORR in low-grade serous ovarian cancer (9.4–12.5% vs 12.1%). The trial ended early for low ORR and high discontinuation, and the authors note it was limited by small numbers (PMID:31870556). The mechanism was therefore likely not tested at adequate engagement; design limits are secondary.

The index trial compared lambda against active peginterferon alfa (both with RBV and telaprevir). It missed only the non-inferiority margin: SVR12 was 76.2% vs 82%, p=0.0855 (NCT01598090). That is an F9 outcome, not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure. Exposure was characterized by population PK, and exposure–response modeling supported the 180 μg dose (PMID:25043197, PMID:25042797). Engagement was not measured directly and is inferred, within HCV itself rather than another disease, from the clear antiviral activity. HCV-RNA decline was dose-related and early responses beat alfa in phase 2b (PMID:25064437), and lambda-based regimens met SVR12 endpoints in other phase 3s (NCT01718158, NCT01741545). A sister trial was terminated by sponsor decision, explicitly not for safety or efficacy (NCT01866930), suggesting a business stop.

The index LIRA-B trial (NCT01204762, PMID:26739688) missed only a non-inferiority margin against active peginterferon alfa: week-24 post-treatment HBeAg seroconversion was 13.8% vs 30.1%. Lambda was not shown to be inactive. Exposure is adequate: population PK at 180 μg is characterised (PMID:25043197, PMID:25042797). Engagement is inferred_adequate because 180 μg lambda met SVR12 endpoints in HCV, acting on the same hepatic receptor (NCT01718158, NCT01741545, PMID:25064437). In HBV patients, lambda produced greater early HBV-DNA and qHBsAg declines than alfa and immune activation (PMID:26739688, PMID:28611778), so the pathway is adequate. The ALT/bilirubin limit applied at 240 μg, not 180 μg. Secondary F2: post-treatment durability favored alfa despite engagement.

In the index Phase 1 (NCT00827138; PMID:27927766), rebastinib was rapidly absorbed. Dose escalation was capped by neurologic DLTs (dysarthria, muscle weakness, neuropathy), giving an MTD of 150 mg BID. Pharmacodynamics showed some inhibition of BCR-ABL1 substrate phosphorylation in CML patients, but no level was reported as sufficient. Only 8 of 40 evaluable patients had a complete hematologic response. The authors judged benefit insufficient and pointed to TIE2 as the more relevant target, implying ABL1 inhibition was inadequate at tolerable doses. ABL1 is a validated CML target: imatinib, ponatinib, asciminib and others are approved. This points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b), with tolerability-limited engagement (F1a). The preclinical T315I activity is animal and in vitro data only.

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional (PMID:27162173, PMID:32274653). Healthy-volunteer studies registered before the index trial (NCT01364974, NCT01225224) showed dose-dependent JAK/pSTAT5 inhibition, with peak inhibition >85% at 100-200 mg. These are adequate engagement data, but not from UC patients. Pathway is inferred adequate from Phase 3 RA efficacy at 100-150 mg QD, a range comparable to the UC doses (NCT02305849, NCT02308163). In UC the dose-response primary endpoint failed, with only numerical benefit and biomarker normalisation at ≥75 mg (PMID:29917064). By the coding rules this is F2. However, tofacitinib's UC approval argues against JAK irrelevance. A modest dose-ranging design (F7) or molecule-specific gut pharmacology may explain the miss, but the bundle does not show either. Confidence is low.

In the index trial NCT02067156, only 1 of 21 patients was progression-free at 6 months, so the primary endpoint was missed. Mipsagargin is a prodrug that PSMA activates to release a thapsigargin analog (12ADT), which inhibits SERCA pumps. The trial listed CSF and blood pharmacokinetics and blood-flow metrics as secondary outcomes, but none of the pages I found reported those results. I found no human evidence of 12ADT release in tumor, SERCA inhibition or a downstream biomarker change in glioblastoma or elsewhere. No other drug on this target succeeded, and the sponsor gave no reason for the failure. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. My web searches hit their limit before I could open the full-text papers.

T-CALM (NCT03101241) missed its video-rated TETRAS-PS primary endpoint at 10 mg BID, although investigator-rated TETRAS-PS and ADL improved (PMID:33764619). That gap between raters points to measurement or design problems (F7, secondary). There was a 2018 healthy-volunteer pharmaco-EEG proof-of-principle study, but the results I retrieved did not include occupancy, channel-inhibition or biomarker data, and the phase 1 MAD abstract reports only PK and safety. I found no human target-engagement evidence in ET patients. No other T-type drug has succeeded in ET. Later trials at higher doses also failed: EveresT (NCT05122650) and the PD tremor study (NCT05642442). Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

MK-8998 (12/16 mg) did not separate from placebo on PANSS at week 4 (diff -0.6, p=0.86; NCT00827918). The active comparator olanzapine also failed to separate (diff -4.3, p=0.25), so the trial lacked assay sensitivity. The authors state that, given the limited efficacy of the active comparator, they cannot exclude that T-type calcium channel antagonists could work in schizophrenia (PMID:23532746). The trial therefore could not answer the question (F7). The bundle has no human data on exposure, CNS penetration, channel engagement or a pathway biomarker. The later tremor trials also failed without any engagement data (NCT03101241, NCT05122650, NCT05642442). Molecule versus target therefore remains indeterminate (U secondary).

In pancreatic and gastric cancer (NCT01166490, PMID:26994014), dose escalation hit the MTD at 1.2 mg/kg. A grade 4 GI haemorrhage was dose-limiting at 1.5 mg/kg, and there was only 1 PR per cohort. Plasma PK was measured in both phase 1 trials. Every biopsy expressed SLC44A4, but no paper measured tumour drug delivery, target engagement or a downstream biomarker, so engagement is no_human_data. In the prostate trial (NCT01228760), the investigators said development stopped because of a narrow therapeutic index. They linked some toxicities to on-target effects in normal tissue that expresses SLC44A4. Tolerability capped the dose while activity was limited, so I coded efficacy offset by on-target toxicity (F5). Off-target MMAE toxicity is possible (F6), and engagement itself is still unknown (U).

The index trial NCT01154634 was a Phase IIa test in healthy men. Reflux episodes after a meal did not clearly fall versus placebo at 5, 16 or 40 mg, and no statistical test was posted. Before the trial, AstraZeneca registered a PET study of central mGluR5 receptor occupancy (NCT00892944), but neither its results nor any published occupancy, pharmacokinetic or biomarker data could be found. No serious adverse events were reported, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No other mGluR5 drug in the bundle succeeded, and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping. Because there is no human engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter for reflux.

Index NCT01715896 was a head-to-head comparison against active golimumab, and PMID:28941039 says it was not powered to formally compare the two. Mavrilimumab ACR20 (62%) was similar to golimumab (65.6%), so this was not an efficacy test against placebo. Placebo-controlled RA trials met their primary endpoints (NCT01706926, NCT01050998, PMID:23234647). In RA patients, PK and modelled >90% receptor occupancy were shown, with SOCS3 suppression (PMID:21613310, PMID:21947370), all published before 2013. Pathway markers also moved: dose-dependent VICM suppression and IL-6/CRP lowering (PMID:30418117, PMID:30358109). The extension NCT01712399 was terminated for development plans, which suggests a business stop.

Exposure: in the Phase 1 trial (NCT01357759), plasma exposure rose roughly in proportion to dose and the half-life was 9–13 days, and GM-CSF is a systemic target. Engagement: in BREATHE (NCT04351243, PMID:35290169), COVID-19 patients given gimsilumab had rising GM-CSF levels, which the authors attributed to the antibody binding GM-CSF. This is evidence of ligand capture in the disease, but free GM-CSF was not measured and it was published after the trial. Pathway: most cytokines did not differ between arms; MCP-1 fell only numerically more. Day-43 mortality was numerically worse on drug (32/113 vs 26/112). The investigators said GM-CSF was not elevated in most patients and that cytokine release is not a major feature of many COVID-19 cases, which points to the target not driving this disease (F2), with population selection as a secondary factor (F3). No dose limitation was reported.

The index trial of omipalisib plus trametinib in advanced solid tumors (NCT01248858) was terminated for 'lack of tolerability and efficacy of the combination'. Monotherapy phase 1 (PMID:26603258) showed plasma exposure above target level and dose-dependent rises in insulin and glucose, an on-target PI3K pathway marker. Its MTD was capped by diarrhea and rash. Human target engagement (pAKT and PIP3 inhibition in blood and lung) was shown only in IPF (PMID:30765508, NCT01725139), after the index trial started, not in cancer. Pan-PI3K inhibitors have narrow therapeutic windows (PMID:28537878). The combination's toxicities (diarrhea, rash, hyperglycemia) are consistent with on-target PI3K/MEK effects that prevented an efficacious regimen. Dose capping (F1a) also applies. The bundle is thin on combination doses.

Elacytarabine is a lipid prodrug of cytarabine. Its intended effect is ara-CTP formation and DNA synthesis inhibition. A solid-tumour Phase 1 trial measured plasma PK, and an AML population-PK model measured ara-CTP in blood. Neither gives tumour drug levels, ara-CTP inside tumour cells, or a DNA-synthesis biomarker in ovarian cancer. The index trial (NCT00831636/PMID:21909644) found myelosuppressive DLTs at 125 mg/m², so the recommended dose was 100 mg/m². The best response was stable disease in 3 patients, and the investigators said further study in ovarian cancer was not warranted, without giving a reason. Nothing shows the dose was too low for engagement, and no other drug on this target is in the bundle. So it is unclear whether the drug never engaged its target or the mechanism does not matter here: U.

Elacytarabine is a lipid-ester prodrug of cytarabine. It is meant to become intracellular ara-C and then ara-CTP, which inhibits DNA synthesis. Phase 1 studies in solid tumours and refractory leukaemia measured plasma pharmacokinetics, so systemic exposure was shown. However, no source reports intracellular ara-CTP levels or DNA-synthesis inhibition in human blasts, so there is no direct human evidence of target engagement. The drug did show anti-leukaemic activity: about 11% complete remissions in Phase 1 and a 41% response rate with idarubicin (PMID:24255981). In the index trial (PMID:24841975), overall survival and response were no better than with investigator's-choice salvage regimens, and the sources give no specific reason. Because engagement has no human data, the code is U. F2 is a possible secondary code, since activity was seen but gave no survival benefit.

The bundle has no human measurement of A1 receptor engagement or of downstream pathway effects in the eye, such as trabecular outflow facility or MMP activity. It also has no drug levels in eye tissue, only plasma PK in healthy volunteers (PMID:27046445). Phase 2 showed modest, dose-related IOP lowering (PMID:27002298), but IOP is the clinical surrogate endpoint, not engagement evidence. Inotek blamed the MATrX-1 miss (NCT02565173) on a larger-than-expected placebo/vehicle response, which supports F7 as a secondary code. However, the later fixed-dose combination trial (NCT02829996) found trabodenoson added nothing to latanoprost, and that trial had no placebo arm to blame. With no human engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The sources have no human data on target engagement for this drug. No one measured drug levels in the eye, binding to the A1 receptor, or any downstream biomarker. The only human pharmacokinetic data are plasma levels from topical dosing (PMID:27046445). Intraocular pressure (IOP) lowering in Phase 2 was dose-dependent but modest (-4.1 vs -1.6 mmHg at 500 mcg; PMID:27002298). IOP is the clinical surrogate endpoint itself, so it cannot stand in for proof of engagement. In the index trial (MATrX-1, NCT02565173), the drug was not superior to placebo at all 12 time points. The 2000 µg dose was superior to placebo at some time points. Inotek blamed an unexpectedly high placebo response (F7). The later fixed-dose combinations with latanoprost added no benefit over latanoprost alone (NCT02829996). With engagement unmeasured, the sources cannot tell a weak molecule apart from a target that does not matter, so the primary code is U.

The index trial NCT01897519 was stopped after the topline readout of the sister Phase 2b, NCT01777165 / PMID:27543797, which showed no effect at any dose (800–2100 μg/kg) on AKI incidence, novel kidney biomarkers or 90-day outcomes. There were no safety problems and no dose cap. A PK study (NCT00903604) exists but posted no results. I found no human measurement of MC1R/MC3R occupancy or activation. The only downstream signal is a sponsor press-release claim from an earlier Phase 2 (NCT01256372) of a 40% IL-6 reduction. It was not confirmed, and the 2b biomarkers did not move. No other drug on this target succeeded in AKI. With no human engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter in AKI, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01897519 was stopped after topline results from the sister trial M13-796 (NCT01777165) showed no efficacy and no safety concerns. In the Phase 2b study (PMID 27543797), AKI rates were the same on cumulative doses of 800, 1600 and 2100 µg/kg as on placebo, and the drug did not move urine or plasma kidney-injury markers. Those markers measure disease, not the MC1R/MC3R pathway. A PK study was run (NCT00903604) and a pharmacodynamics study was planned (NCT00628264), but neither posted results. My searches found no human data on drug levels, melanocortin receptor engagement or anti-inflammatory biomarkers (for example cytokines). The supporting evidence is animal-only (PMID:18354376, which showed a bell-shaped dose response). Because nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, the code is U.

The index trial NCT02511886 was an 18-patient inpatient dose-escalation study. Its primary outcomes were the maximum tolerated dose and plasma pharmacokinetics (Cmax, AUC, half-life), and it is classified not_efficacy. It was not an efficacy test of arbaclofen placarbil in alcohol use disorder, so F9 applies. No results were posted, so human exposure, engagement and pathway evidence in this disease are absent. In GERD, PMID:23721547 mentions prior reduction of reflux episodes. However, the GERD trial NCT00978016 missed its primary endpoint, so no pillar can be inferred adequate. Baclofen reached phase 3 in alcohol dependence, but the bundle shows no success. Why the program stopped is otherwise indeterminate (U).

The index extension study NCT02641392 stopped for futility after the pivotal NCT02596893 missed remission (about 25% vs 25%). Phase 2 had shown strong benefit (PMID:25785968). An earlier phase 1 is said to show SMAD7 targeting in gut, but the bundle gives no human data. Later sources state that many phase 3 batches were chemically different, with uncontrolled phosphorothioate chirality, and could not knock down SMAD7 (PMID:35263186, 33871807, 35841457, 36678723). In open-label use an active batch restored efficacy and lowered CCR9+ cells (PMID:33871807). The engagement evidence for the phase 3 batches is in vitro only, and the pharmacodynamic trial NCT02685683 posted no results. So the mechanism was likely not tested properly, but human proof is lacking (U secondary).

Index trial NCT02601300 was a single-arm UC study with 17.1% remission at week 8 and no comparator. I found no human data on mucosal drug levels, SMAD7 knockdown in tissue, or a downstream TGF-β/p-Smad3 biomarker, in UC or in Crohn's disease. The only human marker reported was a drop in CCR9+ cells in an open-label Crohn's study. In Crohn's disease the phase 3 trial (NCT02596893) was stopped for futility. Investigators later blamed manufacturing batches with different chemistry, some of which could not knock down SMAD7 in cultured cells (PMID:36678723). That points to a molecule or engagement problem, but the evidence is only in vitro. Without human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be separated from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for sapitinib. No phase 1 results are posted, and PMID:25149507 only describes PET tracer radiosynthesis. In the index trial NCT01579578, adding AZD8931 to paclitaxel did not change 8-week tumour size versus paclitaxel alone (p=0.688), but only 11 patients per arm were analysed. The trial was terminated when AstraZeneca halted all AZD8931 trials, after futile breast cancer trials NCT00900627 and NCT01151215. HER2 itself is a validated target in this disease, since trastuzumab and zanidatamab are approved for gastric or gastroesophageal cancer. That points to the molecule (F1b) rather than the target. The small, early-terminated trial (F7) and the absence of engagement data (U) also apply.

In the phase 1 solid-tumor trial (NCT01277146, PMID:30591982), biomarker analysis showed regulation of Notch and stem-cell gene signaling, and the authors state that Notch pathway inhibition was demonstrated at tolerated doses. That supports engagement and pathway effect in humans, though not in SCLC patients, and it was published after the index trial started. PK was assessed but no values are reported, so exposure is no_human_data. The index phase 2 used 15 mg/kg with chemotherapy without excess DLTs, so dose was not capped. PFS and response were similar to placebo (NCT01859741), and the pancreatic phase 2 also failed (NCT01647828). This points to Notch2/3 blockade not adding benefit to chemotherapy in SCLC. Engagement evidence is indirect and not in SCLC, so U remains a possibility.

In the phase 1 solid-tumor study (NCT01277146, PMID:30591982), biomarker analysis showed regulation of Notch and stem-cell gene signaling. The authors state Notch pathway inhibition was demonstrated at tolerated doses, which supports engagement and pathway effect in humans. PK results are not given, and pancreatic-specific engagement and pre-2012 publication are not shown. The index phase 2 dose of 15 mg/kg was tolerated in phase 1b (1/10 DLT), so the dose was not capped. Survival was not improved: 71/89 vs 60/88 deaths. Notch3-high subgroups showed no consistent benefit, so selection does not explain the failure. The SCLC trial also failed (NCT01859741). Together this points to Notch2/3 blockade not driving outcome (F2). The excess of deaths in the drug arm raises possible toxicity offsetting benefit (F5).

In healthy subjects given oral axomadol 66–225 mg (PMID:26924818), plasma levels of parent and O-demethyl metabolite were measured. The metabolite produced a concentration-dependent decrease in pupil diameter, an opioid-engagement biomarker that the abstract itself names as such. Cold-pressor analgesia was also reduced in proportion to the pupil effect. Together these support exposure, mu-opioid engagement and a pathway effect at doses plausibly comparable to the index trial. That evidence comes only from healthy volunteers and was published in 2016, after the chronic low back pain trial started (NCT01043263). The index trial posted no results and no reason for stopping. With engagement apparently shown but no benefit inferred, F2 fits best. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin and the index dose and readout are not shown.

The index Phase 3 (NCT05470387) was terminated by 'company decision' after enrolling only 23 patients. Time to GI recovery was numerically shorter on LB1148 (81.7 vs 90.6 h), with no statistical analysis, so the trial could not answer the efficacy question; this is not a demonstrated failure. Systemic plasmin/fibrinolysis inhibition by TXA is well shown in humans (PMID:33443933, PMID:33576009). However, LB1148 is given enterally and acts in the gut lumen in ileus. The bundle has no human luminal exposure, engagement, or pathway data, and the systemic menstrual-disorder approval is a different compartment. The Phase 2 (NCT02836470) was descriptive only. The unspecified business decision (F8) and the missing engagement evidence (U) also apply.

The index trial (NCT00679588, PMID:24374549) was a non-inferiority comparison of postoperative semuloparin 20 mg against active preoperative enoxaparin. It missed the 1.25 NI margin (OR 1.16, CI 0.84-1.59), with less major bleeding. It was not a placebo-controlled efficacy failure. At the same 20 mg dose, semuloparin beat placebo in VTE prevention in cancer patients on chemotherapy (NCT00694382, PMID:22335737) and in extended hip-fracture prophylaxis (NCT00709904, PMID:23539696). It also beat enoxaparin in SAVE-HIP1 (PMID:22429800), and TREK showed a dose-response (PMID:19187076). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. The program ended when Sanofi withdrew its marketing applications worldwide (NCT01567904, business), so F8 is secondary.

Plasma PK of SAR3419 was characterised in humans: a long half-life and low clearance, with no dose effect (PMID:24132920). The phase 2 single-agent DLBCL trial met its ORR endpoint at a comparable dose (NCT01472887), so CD19 engagement in malignant B cells is inferred adequate. It was never measured directly in ALL, and there are no pathway biomarker data. In ALL, 70 mg/m2 was tolerated, with the DLT occurring only at 90 mg/m2. ORR was low (~25%) and responses were brief (PMID:26775883). The trial stopped for 'very modest activity compared to competitors' (NCT01440179). CD19 is validated in ALL by approved CD19 CAR-Ts (brexucabtagene, obecabtagene), which points to the molecule, not the target. Payload potency is a plausible limitation (PMID:30733273, preclinical).

The index trial, NCT05551598, randomized 46 Chinese patients to placebo or to 8 or 12 mg/m2 of CSPC's liposomal mitoxantrone. An ECTRIMS 2026 abstract reported only a trend in relapse risk versus placebo: 52.5% lower at 8 mg/m2 and 11.7% lower at 12 mg/m2. The trend did not rise with dose, and the authors made no efficacy claim. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, TOP2A-inhibition or immune-cell biomarker data for the liposomal formulation in NMOSD or anywhere else. Conventional mitoxantrone's approval in MS cannot be carried over, because the liposome changes how the drug is distributed. Other NMOSD evidence is mixed: one observational study suggests benefit (PMID:23138769), another shows no benefit (PMID:28572277). With engagement unmeasured, the code is U. A small, possibly underpowered trial (F7) may also apply.

NCT01113801 (Voelker, JASN 2017) was stopped early for futility. None of the doses (2, 10 or 50 mg a month) slowed the rise in serum creatinine or changed eGFR or UPCR, and the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. A population PK analysis was done, but no kidney-tissue drug levels or free or active TGF-β1 lowering were reported, so exposure at the site of action and target engagement have no human data. Downstream pharmacodynamic biomarkers did not move with treatment: urinary fibronectin, type IV collagen, MCP-1 and MMP-7, and plasma KIM-1, NGAL and sTNFR2. That flat result fits a drug that never neutralised TGF-β1 in the kidney just as well as a target that does not drive progression. Later reviews raise both possibilities, insufficient intrarenal engagement and pathway redundancy. The evidence cannot tell these apart, so the code is U.

In NCT01319929, 80 mg of LY2828360 for 4 weeks did no better than placebo on knee OA pain (change of -0.90 vs -1.20). There were no serious AEs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The only human report is the Pereira 2013 CPT abstract, and the sources that cite it mention only safety and lack of efficacy. My searches found no human PK at the site of action, no CB2 occupancy data and no pathway biomarker. Other CB2 agonists in OA (GW842166, cannabinol) also stopped at Phase 2, with no approval or pivotal success, so F1b does not apply. Engagement has no human data, so the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged CB2 apart from a target that does not drive OA pain. The code is U.

Plasma exposure was shown: in cancer patients, Cmax and AUC rose with dose across 250–1500 mg (NCT00958477, NCT01327313; PMID:24242902). No DLTs occurred up to 1000 mg in POSEIDON, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No source reports human αv-integrin occupancy, saturation or tumour-tissue target inhibition. The only pharmacodynamic readout was DCE-MRI Ktrans in CRC liver metastases (NCT00848510), which changed little across doses and is not a direct measure of target binding. PFS was unchanged at 500 and 1000 mg (HR 1.13 and 1.11). The investigators pointed to a possible benefit in patients with high αvβ6 tumour expression (an exploratory OS signal, PMID:25319061), which suggests patient selection (F3). Because engagement is unmeasured, the evidence cannot separate a drug that did not engage its target from a target that does not matter.

Exposure is adequate. Phase 1 PK in mCRPC (NCT00958477, PMID:23791392) showed dose-dependent serum levels with no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs). According to the PERSEUS paper, PK modelling predicted that troughs at 750 mg every 3 weeks would stay above the IC95. However, no study measured αv integrin occupancy or inhibition in humans, including in prostate tumours or bone lesions, so engagement is no_human_data. Downstream markers did not move: bone-turnover markers, PSA and CTCs did not change with abituzumab, so pathway is inadequate. PFS was not improved (NCT01360840). Bone-lesion progression was lower but soft-tissue progression was not. The authors suggest low αv expression or pathway redundancy in soft-tissue metastases, which hints at F3 (heterogeneity). Because engagement was never measured, the bundle cannot tell an unengaged drug from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT01432353), 39 relapsed/refractory myeloma patients received 0.3–2.4 mg/kg every 3 weeks or 0.8–1.1 mg/kg weekly. Plasma exposure rose linearly with dose and the MTD was not reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Flow cytometry on blood plasma cells from 8 patients showed only partial receptor occupancy (about 63%), and these data were published in 2019, after the trial began. No pathway marker was measured, such as payload getting inside the cells or cell killing. The investigators say intracellular MMAE may have been too low and that an MMAE ADC may be a poor fit for slowly dividing myeloma cells, while FcRH5 'may be a valid myeloma target'. Cevostamab's response rate supports the target but has not met a pivotal endpoint, so F1b does not apply. This points to F1a, with F2 as a secondary code.

The bundle contains only the index trial NCT01098240, a terminated Phase 2 augmentation study. Its stated stop reason is not available. The MADRS change was -10.3 on drug vs -8.8 on placebo, with no statistical test reported. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, PubMed abstracts or other trials of this drug, so there is no human evidence of CNS exposure, α4β2 receptor occupancy or a pathway biomarker. No other drug on the same target is approved or met a pivotal endpoint in MDD, so F1b does not apply. Safety looked unremarkable (1/77 vs 1/85 serious AEs), so toxicity is not shown. Because engagement is no_human_data and nothing separates non-engagement from an irrelevant target, the code is indeterminate (U).

The index trial (NCT01001195) did not show a failure to lower intraocular pressure. Simenepag reduced IOP by 5.7–7.65 mmHg from baseline at Day 29, and NCT00809848 showed reduction beyond vehicle (-5.8 vs -2.4 mmHg). The 'not met' classification reflects smaller reductions than the active comparator bimatoprost (-8.57), not inactivity. NCT01291108 shows the same pattern (-7.57 vs -10.28). This is closest to F9: the drug only underperformed an active drug. No PK or target-engagement data are in the bundle, but the IOP effect in patients indicates the pathway was engaged, so U does not apply. Omidenepag, on the same EP2 target, is approved for glaucoma, suggesting a molecule-specific potency shortfall (secondary F1b). No safety signal was seen.

The index trial NCT01001195 compared three AGN-210669 doses with bimatoprost. Every dose lowered IOP (-5.7 to -7.7 mmHg) but less than bimatoprost (-8.6). An earlier trial showed IOP lowering beyond vehicle (NCT00809848), and the drug again underperformed bimatoprost in NCT01291108. There are no human exposure, EP2 engagement or pathway biomarker data, and no dose-limiting toxicity was reported (few serious AEs). The same target is validated in glaucoma by FDA-approved omidenepag isopropyl. So the shortfall points to this molecule's competitive efficacy rather than the target: F1b. Because the drug was active and missed mainly against an active comparator, F9 also partly applies. The bundle is thin and gives no stated reason, so confidence is low.

In the Phase 1 study, exposure at the 105 mg/m2 MTD matched the exposure that gave maximal xenograft responses (PMID:27044938). The MTD was set by transient hematologic toxicity, and no source shows it fell below what engagement needed. In ovarian cancer patients, γ-H2AX rose in blood after treatment (PMID:32709712). Paired HGSOC biopsies showed reduced RAD51 foci and increased γ-H2AX, pKAP1 and pRPA, though with olaparib (PMID:34131002). These are downstream markers of CHK1 inhibition; engagement is inferred from them, not measured directly. Despite this, the index trial (NCT03414047) gave only about 7–13% ORR, below the earlier pilot's 29–33% (PMID:29361470, PMID:38555285). That pattern points to the mechanism lacking monotherapy benefit. Sources also invoke biomarker or subtype heterogeneity (POLA1, HRP subtypes; PMID:38555285, PMID:40736012), so F3 is secondary.

Index SCLC trial used the 105 mg/m2 q14d MTD/RP2D and got ORR 5.2% in platinum-sensitive and 0% in platinum-resistant disease (NCT02735980). Exposure at the MTD matched the exposure that gave maximal xenograft responses (PMID:27044938). Pharmacodynamic DNA damage was seen in peripheral immune cells at 105 mg/m2 (PMID:32510664). In combination with olaparib, paired tumor biopsies showed increased γ-H2AX, pKAP1 and pRPA and reduced RAD51 foci (PMID:34131002). This is mechanism-consistent pathway evidence, read here as implying engagement, so F2: CHK1/2 inhibition alone does not drive SCLC response. Caveats: direct engagement was not measured, no evidence comes from SCLC patients, and the PD was published after the index trial started. The hematologic MTD may have limited the dose. Confidence is low.

The first-in-human study (NCT01618136, PMID:32523090) reported significant concentration-dependent PARP inhibition across 50-800 mg in patients with mixed solid tumours. The MTD was 600 mg, the same dose used in the index trial, so exposure and engagement appear adequate and the dose was not capped below engagement. Engagement was not shown specifically in breast cancer, and no downstream pathway marker was reported. PARP1/2 is a validated breast cancer target, with olaparib and talazoparib approved. The index trial (NCT03562832, n=20, no posted results) enrolled patients selected by the experimental 2X-121 DRP rather than by BRCA/HRD status. The likely explanation is therefore patient selection rather than an invalid target. The bundle states no failure reason, and the trial was small, so confidence is low.

The first-in-human study (NCT01458067, PMID:28645941) found that 400 mg once daily gave sufficient exposure and target inhibition, with phospho/total AKT reduced in tumor and surrogate tissue. Results were not reported separately for prostate cancer. In the index enzalutamide combination (NCT02215096, PMID:34281912), DLTs at 300 mg (2/12) and 400 mg (2/2) capped the recommended dose at 200 mg, half the monotherapy dose judged sufficient. No engagement or pathway data were reported at 200 mg. Exposure was not reduced by a drug interaction, but tolerability held the dose below the level shown to engage the target, so the mechanism was not properly tested. Activity was limited (12-week non-PD 50%, PSA50 12%). Benefit clustered in PIK3CB-altered tumors (PMID:28645941), which suggests a selection issue (F3).

Phase 1 (PMID:29707140) showed dose-linear PK and full (>95%) KIR occupancy at all doses from 0.015–10 mg/kg, with no dose-limiting toxicity. Both index doses (0.1 and 1 mg/kg) therefore engaged KIR. The cohort included hematologic malignancies, but AML patients are not specifically shown. This was published in 2018, after the index trial started. No downstream NK-activation biomarker was reported; lymphocyte subsets were unchanged, which is not a pathway readout. Despite this, EFFIKIR maintenance (NCT01687387) showed no leukemia-free survival benefit, and the 1 mg/kg arm did worse than placebo. Lirilumab plus azacitidine in relapsed AML stopped for futility (NCT02399917). The sponsor then dropped myeloid indications (NCT02599649). KIR blockade appears not to drive benefit in AML as tested.

In the 2017 first-in-human study, healthy volunteers took 10–40 mg/day, the same range as the index trial's 20–40 mg. Plasma levels rose with dose, and MGLL inhibition in blood cells was time- and dose-related, at levels the sponsor matched to preclinical efficacy.
