A PET study showed dose-dependent brain penetration and MGLL engagement. A vendor page reports that plasma 2-AG, the enzyme's substrate, rose with dose; this pathway evidence comes from a weak source. All engagement data predate the index trial but come from healthy volunteers, not Tourette patients. In NCT03625453 (PMID:34117788) tics did not improve and the result numerically favoured placebo, with no tolerability cap on dose. The single-dose signal in PMID:34847610 did not replicate. With the target engaged and no benefit, MGLL inhibition does not appear to reduce tics (F2). The small sample and strong placebo response are minor contributors (F7).

The first-in-human study (PMID:27449137, PMC5238716) measured plasma pharmacokinetics (Cmax, AUC, half-life) and set the maximum tolerated dose at 3 mg/kg, so there is human evidence that the drug reached the blood. It has no human data on the drug binding its target in tumours, such as imaging uptake or occupancy, and no measured human ADCC or other downstream effect. Cytokines were mostly unchanged, and that is not a mechanism readout. The DSMB stopped the index trial NCT01834235 for futility, with median overall survival of 6.6 vs 5 months. No source explains why it failed. Clivatuzumab, another antibody on this target, did not succeed, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, the failure is indeterminate (U).

Pradigastat reached plasma exposure (PMID:25854859, PMID:25963481). It engaged intestinal DGAT1, shown by dose-dependent suppression of postprandial triglycerides in overweight subjects (PMID:25854859). It lowered fasting TG by 41–70% in severe hypertriglyceridemia (NCT01146522, registered before the index trial) and met a fasting-TG endpoint at 40 mg in FCS (NCT01514461). Pathway effects were also seen: GLP-1 rose and glucose and insulin fell. No engagement was measured in CAD patients within the index trial. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The index trial (NCT01474434) stopped at interim for futility: MPRi and exercise duration trended worse than placebo. The target, engaged, did not improve myocardial perfusion as tested. Secondary: the 5-day treatment periods and small cohorts (n≈13 per arm) limited the test.

The index HCV trial (NCT01387958) was terminated for futility on viral load, with no results posted. Plasma exposure is well characterised (PMID:25854859, PMID:25627776). DGAT1 inhibition in humans is shown by dose-dependent suppression of postprandial triglycerides (PMID:25854859). There were 41–70% fasting TG reductions in NCT01146522 (registered before the index trial) and the fasting-TG endpoint was met at 40 mg in FCS (NCT01514461). Liver-fat reduction in NAFLD (NCT01811472) hints at hepatic activity. Engagement was never shown in HCV patients or directly in hepatocytes, the compartment relevant to viral assembly, and the HCV dose is unknown. The best-supported reading is that DGAT1 inhibition does not suppress HCV clinically (F2). Hepatic engagement remains uncertain, hence low confidence and U as secondary.

Pradigastat showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and dose-dependent suppression of postprandial TG in healthy obese subjects (PMID:25854859). In hypertriglyceridemic/FCS patients it cut fasting TG 41–70%, mostly chylomicron TG, and lowered apoB48 (NCT01146522, started 2010, before the index trial; PMID:25889044). These are functional markers of intestinal DGAT1 inhibition in the disease. It was well tolerated with only mild GI events, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, the index trial in CAD/hypertriglyceridemia showed no benefit at interim on myocardial perfusion reserve (-0.22 vs 0.32) or exercise duration (NCT01474434). DGAT1-mediated TG lowering did not improve these short-term cardiovascular physiological endpoints. The 5-day duration may also be a factor (F4), but the sources do not say so.

Exposure is well characterized in humans (PMID:25854859, PMID:25963481). DGAT1 engagement was shown functionally: dose-dependent suppression of postprandial TG in healthy subjects (PMID:25854859). In FCS patients, an open-label study (NCT01146522, PMID:25889044) reported 41% and 70% fasting TG falls at 20 and 40 mg, plus lower chylomicron TG and apoB48, at well-tolerated doses. That study was registered before the index trial started. In the pivotal FCS study (NCT01514461), 40 mg met the fasting TG endpoint and 20 mg was borderline. The extension (NCT01589237) was stopped because interim analysis showed the anticipated benefit too small. So the mechanism was engaged without enough clinical benefit (F2). The index trial's primary endpoint was safety, not efficacy, hence F9 as secondary.

In the Phase 1 solid-tumour study (NCT01688206, registered 2012; PMID:29217526), PK was dose-linear. The 2,000 mg flat dose matched 30 mg/kg, no MTD was reached, and all patients had reduced free plasma VEGF-A and Ang-2 (exposure and engagement adequate). Pathway effects followed: reduced KTRANS, and tumour microvessel density fell 32% with Ang-2+ vessels down 62% (PMID:33338877). These data came from mixed solid tumours, not a CRC population. Despite this, McCAVE (NCT02141295) at 2,000 mg showed no PFS gain over bevacizumab (HR 0.91 posted; 1.00 stratified, PMID:32162804) and more antiangiogenic toxicity. So adding Ang-2 blockade did not add benefit. An exploratory benefit in KRAS-wt/high-Ang-2 patients (PMID:37207143) supports F3 as secondary, although baseline Ang-2 was not predictive in the primary analysis.

The index trial NCT02665416 is a Phase 1 dose-finding study of selicrelumab combined with vanucizumab. Its primary endpoints are DLT, MTD and RP2D, and its efficacy part tests selicrelumab with bevacizumab, so it is not an efficacy test of vanucizumab (F9). Pillars were shown in solid-tumour patients. PK was dose-linear and the MTD was not reached (PMID:29217526). All patients had reduced free VEGF-A and Ang-2, and KTRANS fell. Microvessel density dropped in tumour biopsies (PMID:33338877). This engagement evidence was published after the index trial started. The program's actual efficacy failure was McCAVE (NCT02141295, PMID:32162804): no PFS gain over bevacizumab despite engagement, and more antiangiogenic toxicity. That supports F2 as a secondary code: added Ang-2 blockade did not drive benefit.

Plasma exposure to the active nucleoside ALS-8112/JNJ-63549109 was measured and dose-proportional in the index trial (NCT02935673). In the RSV-A challenge study (NCT02094365, PMID:30376079), which predates the index trial, lumicitabine gave large, dose-dependent viral load AUC reductions, with more than 99% viral inhibition. This shows antiviral engagement in human RSV infection. In hospitalized adults, however, viral load AUC(1-7) did not differ from placebo, and placebo viral load was already falling. Infants likewise showed no antiviral effect, along with dose-related neutropenia (PMID:37467213), which that paper contrasts with the challenge results. The challenge model treated early, controlled infection, whereas the index trial enrolled naturally infected hospitalized patients. This points to disease stage or timing, and the population, as the likely gap. The sources do not state the reason, so confidence is low.

In the first-in-human study (NCT02503774, PMID:37016126), oleclumab up to 40 mg/kg Q2W produced sustained decreases in free soluble CD73 and in CD73 on peripheral T cells and tumor cells, with reduced tumor CD73 enzymatic activity. There were no DLTs, so the dose was not capped. Engagement is therefore adequate, though it was shown in CRC, PDAC and NSCLC, not prostate cancer. Downstream adenosine or immune pathway effects were not shown in humans. In the index trial (NCT04089553, PMID:38430405), oleclumab 1500 mg plus AZD4635 gave 0% ORR and 3.3% PSA response in mCRPC. CD73 blockade does not appear to drive disease control here. The authors note a heavily pretreated population (median 4 prior lines), so patient selection is a possible secondary factor.

Exposure was dose-dependent, and engagement was measured directly in T2DM patients. In the 14-day MRD study (NCT01874483, started 2013, before the index trial), adipose 11β-HSD1 inhibition was ≥80% at doses ≥40 mg, and the urinary THF/THE ratio fell, indicating hepatic inhibition (PMID:36343645). In the index trial (PMID:36478142), hepatic 11β-HSD1 inhibition was near-complete and the expected pathway effect followed: HPA axis activation with increased urinary corticosteroids. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Despite complete inhibition, there was no clinically relevant effect on glucose, lipids or bodyweight, and weighted mean glucose even rose. The authors conclude that complete target inhibition produced no benefit, so the target does not drive glycaemia as tested. No other HSD11B1 drug progressed beyond Phase 2.

Pimodivir PK was characterised in healthy volunteers and hospitalized influenza A patients (PMID:30098042, NCT02532283). Before the index trial, the drug reduced viral load in challenge (PMID:29244026, NCT01561807) and uncomplicated influenza A (TOPAZ NCT02342249, primary met). Emergent PB2 resistance mutations (PMID:37226302) also support engagement. The sister outpatient Phase 3 met its symptom-resolution endpoint (NCT03381196), yet the index trial in hospitalized patients on standard of care showed no Day-6 recovery-scale benefit and was stopped for futility (NCT03376321). The antiviral mechanism works early but did not translate at the hospitalized stage or on this clinical endpoint. The sources do not state the cause, so stage/population (F4/F3) is inferred, with F2 for severe disease as an alternative.

The index trial NCT04880863 was single-arm. It reported an ORR of 15.6% (n=32) with no prespecified threshold or comparator, so the primary endpoint was classified not assessable. The trial could not establish efficacy failure, and no stop reason is given. Phase 1 data (PMID:19636016) in NSCLC patients showed the expected immune effects of the superantigen fusion: systemic cytokine rise, selective expansion of SEA/E-120-reactive T cells, and tumor T-cell infiltration. That supports the pathway pillar. Binding to 5T4 itself and plasma exposure values are not reported in the bundle. MTDs were defined, but nothing shows dosing was capped below what engagement needed. With no human engagement data and an uninterpretable readout, the trial design is the most direct explanation; U also applies.

Entospletinib added to first-line corticosteroids gave an identical best overall response rate to placebo (72.7% vs 72.7%, p=0.99; NCT02701634), and no stop reason was stated. In healthy volunteers, plasma exposure was dose-proportional up to a solubility plateau. SYK engagement was shown as >70% pSYK inhibition at peak and >50% at trough, with >90%/>60% inhibition of the functional basophil CD63 readout (PMID:27785737). In CLL patients, downstream pSTAT3/MCL1 downmodulation was seen (PMID:34196037). However, engagement was never measured in cGVHD, and the evidence was published after the index trial started. With engagement adequate and no benefit, SYK inhibition did not add to steroids in cGVHD (F2). The high steroid response in both arms may have limited the trial's ability to detect an add-on effect (F7).

Exposure and engagement were adequate, but only in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In the earlier RA Phase I/II trial (NCT01284569), the protocol for NCT02287922 reports trough levels near 10 µg/mL and rapid, lasting rises in sIL-6R, which the sponsor treats as a target-engagement marker. At doses matching the SLE trial, sIL-6R rose about 10-fold (from about 33 to 376–460 ng/mL), and RA ACR20 rates were similar to tocilizumab. No downstream marker such as CRP was found for any population, and no SLE engagement data were found. The SLE index trial (NCT02437890) showed no dose response and no arm beat placebo. Tolerability was good across all doses up to 225 mg q2w, so dose was not capped. Ablynx gave no reason beyond the missed endpoint. Drug engaged, no benefit: IL-6R blockade does not appear to drive SLE as tested (F2).

The bundle has no human PK, sIL-6R or CRP data, and no Phase 1 results. PMID:25994180 is preclinical only, so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the index trial NCT02309359, every dose arm had numerically higher ACR20 than placebo (72–83% vs 62%), but the primary analysis was a dose-response trend test (p=0.172). That test fails when the doses sit on a flat plateau, and the placebo response was high. In the monotherapy trial NCT02287922, ACR20 was similar to tocilizumab (73–81% vs 78%), though only descriptively. The trial design, not an absence of effect, seems to explain the miss. No source states this, and engagement is unmeasured, so U also applies.

The index trial NCT00880048 was terminated 'to allow assessment of isolated events of seizure during program', a molecule-specific safety signal that ended the MDD program. Efficacy was not clearly absent. HAM-D separated from placebo at weeks 1–4 at both doses. Week 6 missed significance (p=0.11 and p=0.47) as dropout reduced the sample, which points to trial execution (F7) as a contributor. The sister trial NCT00880399 met its week-6 primary endpoint. Engagement is judged adequate only from the title of PMID:23539641, which reports full central NK1 blockade from orvepitant clinical studies. That source has no abstract, appeared after the index trial started, and does not show engagement in patients. The NT-0796 abstracts concern a different drug (an NLRP3 inhibitor) and were ignored.

Index trial NCT00880048 was terminated 'to allow assessment of isolated events of seizure during program'. The same reason ended the sister trial NCT00880399, which met its Week 6 HAM-D endpoint (30 mg p=0.0245, 60 mg p=0.0082). In the index trial, orvepitant beat placebo at Weeks 1–4, but Week 6 was not significant with shrinking sample sizes. So the readout is not a clean efficacy failure; molecule-specific safety (seizures) stopped the MDD program. PMID:23539641's title indicates orvepitant clinical studies achieved full central NK1 blockade. This supports adequate exposure and engagement, though only the title is available and it was published after the index trial started. No engagement data in patients and no pathway biomarker data appear in the bundle.

Orvepitant 60 mg met its HAM-D primary endpoint in MDD (NCT00880399, 30 and 60 mg). That is the same central NK1 target and CNS compartment at the same dose used in the PTSD index trial, so exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. PMID:23539641 is titled as reporting full central NK1 blockade from orvepitant clinical studies; only the title is available. No engagement was shown in PTSD patients, and none was shown before the index trial. Despite this, CAPS change at week 12 was not different from placebo (diff -5.62, p=0.36), pointing to NK1 antagonism not driving PTSD as tested. Only 35 patients contributed to the week-12 analysis out of 132 enrolled, and the program had a seizure-related pause (NCT00880048). The trial was likely underpowered (F7).

Orvepitant met its primary HAM-D endpoint at 30 and 60 mg in major depression (NCT00880399). The title of PMID:23539641 (2013) says full central NK1 blockade was shown in orvepitant studies, but no abstract is given. Engagement is therefore inferred_adequate at doses comparable to the index 30 mg arm, though not shown in IPF patients. Despite this, IPF cough severity did not improve: 10 mg p=0.989, 30 mg p=0.054 (NCT05185089). This matches the earlier failure in chronic refractory cough (NCT02993822), pointing to NK1 antagonism not driving cough as tested. The near-significant 30 mg result in 39 patients per arm suggests possible underpowering (F7). The NT-0796 abstracts concern an unrelated NLRP3 inhibitor and were disregarded.

Orvepitant, an NK1 antagonist, was tested at 10, 20 and 30 mg in chronic refractory cough (NCT02993822). No dose beat placebo on objective awake cough frequency, and placebo improvement was substantial. PMID:23539641 (title only) reports human evidence of full central NK1 receptor blockade, tied to depression efficacy at 30–60 mg. NCT00880399 met its HAM-D endpoint at 30 mg. So exposure, engagement and pathway effect are supported at comparable doses, but only in depression, not in cough. With engagement in hand and a flat dose-response, the NK1 mechanism does not appear to drive refractory cough as tested. A later IPF-cough trial was also negative, borderline at 30 mg (NCT05185089). The NT-0796 abstracts describe a different NLRP3 drug and were disregarded.

In the index cough trial (NCT02993822), no orvepitant dose (10–30 mg) beat placebo on objective cough frequency. The 30 mg arm was numerically no better than placebo. Engagement was not measured in cough patients. It is inferred adequate because orvepitant met its primary HAM-D endpoint in major depression at 30 and 60 mg (NCT00880399). That is a central NK1 mechanism at doses comparable to the index top dose. The 2013 publication title (PMID:23539641) indicates its clinical studies achieved full central NK1 receptor blockade. The program was not dose-capped in cough, and serious adverse events were rare. The failure in cough, repeated in IPF cough (NCT05185089), therefore points to NK1 antagonism not driving refractory cough as tested.

In the index TNBC trial, lacnotuzumab at 10 mg/kg showed a typical IgG PK profile and engaged circulating CSF1 ligand in patients (PMID:34615719). Healthy-volunteer data showed target-mediated disposition and dose-dependent on-target downstream biomarker effects, including CK elevation linked to CSF1 pathway inhibition (PMID:30894455). The same 10 mg/kg dose shrank PVNS tumors (NCT01643850). Despite this, PFS was 5.6 vs 5.5 months (NCT02435680), and the authors conclude that engagement did not translate into antitumor benefit. This fits F2: the mechanism does not drive TNBC as tested. Secondary F7: enrollment was halted for recruitment reasons and no formal hypothesis testing was done. Engagement evidence was published after the index trial started (2019, 2022), and tumor macrophage depletion was not shown.

NCT04705597 was stopped early because enrollment was no longer feasible. It still missed its primary endpoint, and the result went the wrong way: 31/94 patients on asapiprant died or progressed to respiratory failure vs 26/97 on placebo (OR 1.37, p=0.33). The bundle and searches contain no human evidence for any pillar. There are no exposure data in COVID-19 patients, no DP1 receptor occupancy or PGD2-cAMP inhibition data in humans, and no downstream biomarker data. The case for the mechanism rests only on mouse studies (PMID:35314834, 33907749) and in vitro or animal pharmacology. No other DP1 antagonist succeeded in COVID-19, and the earlier allergic rhinitis trial (NCT01651871) has no classified outcome. The early stop for enrollment (F7) limited power, but the observed trend does not favor the drug. Code U, because engagement is unknown.

Exposure and engagement are adequate. The first-in-human study (PMID:22767667, published before the index trial started in 2013) showed CD105-saturating serum concentrations at 10 mg/kg weekly, the dose used in the index trial, with mechanism-based telangiectasia and anemia. Pathway effects were shown: plasma CD105 reduction with VEGF induction (PMID:25407442), a soluble endoglin increase (PMID:29997150), and angiogenic biomarker modulation in RCC patients (PMID:30190302). The dose reached the MTD with no DLTs at 10 mg/kg in RCC. Despite this, adding the drug to axitinib worsened median PFS (6.7 vs 11.4 months; NCT01806064, PMID:33829609). A randomized bevacizumab combination in RCC also failed (PMID:28832978). Endoglin blockade does not drive benefit in VEGF-refractory RCC. An exploratory low-VEGF subgroup signal suggests possible selection issues (F3).

In the AVANTE trial (NCT03211234), adding intravitreal DE-122 to Lucentis did not improve BCVA; the DE-122 arms did numerically worse. Santen and TRACON stopped development without giving a mechanistic reason. In the eye, the bundle has no human evidence for any pillar: no drug levels in the eye, no measure of endoglin binding, and no biomarker change. The SAP planned aqueous angiogenesis biomarkers, but no results were found. In the Phase 1 eye study (PMID:34935908), the only signal was a CST reduction in 4 of 12 patients, with rescue anti-VEGF allowed and no control arm. IV doses in cancer trials saturated CD105 and lowered plasma CD105 (PMID:22767667, PMID:25407442). But those data come from a different route and compartment, and the drug never succeeded clinically, so no pillar can be inferred adequate. No other ENG drug exists for comparison. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01326481 was a dose-finding study whose primary outcome was the MTD of TRC105 plus capecitabine. It reported 0 DLTs at 7.5 and 10 mg/kg and had no efficacy test, so it was not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). Pillars: first-in-human data showed CD105-saturating serum levels at 10 mg/kg weekly and 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks (PMID:22767667, published after the index trial started). Plasma CD105 fell and VEGF rose in mCRPC (PMID:25407442), and soluble endoglin rose with bevacizumab (PMID:29997150). In breast cancer patients, on-target telangiectasia in 92% plus PK/PD data appeared only in 2023 (PMID:36735117). The doses tested were at or near the MTD, so the dose was not tolerability-limited.

The index trial NCT02560779 was a small phase 1/2 study. Its primary endpoints (DLTs; ORR 2/14 and 1/11) were posted descriptively, with no comparison or efficacy threshold, so it was not a formal efficacy test (F9). Pillars at the index doses were supported before the trial. Serum concentrations saturating CD105 were maintained at 10 mg/kg weekly and 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks (PMID:22767667). Plasma CD105 fell and VEGF rose in mCRPC (PMID:25407442), and soluble endoglin increased (PMID:29997150). None of this was in HCC; the HCC soluble endoglin data are not reported (PMID:28465443). Despite engagement, monotherapy failed in post-sorafenib HCC (PMID:26535124), and combinations failed in RCC and angiosarcoma (NCT01806064, NCT02979899). This suggests the target does not drive the disease (F2, secondary).

Single-agent TRC105 in recurrent ovarian cancer gave 0 of 23 patients progression-free at 6 months and 0 of 22 responses (NCT01381861). In the first-in-human study (NCT00582985, registered 2007; PMID:22767667), exposure rose with dose. Serum concentrations that saturate CD105 were maintained at 10 mg/kg weekly and 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks, without dose capping. Mechanism-related toxicities (anemia, telangiectasia) appeared. Pathway effects followed: plasma CD105 fell and VEGF rose (PMID:25407442), and soluble endoglin increased (PMID:29997150). This engagement evidence comes from other solid tumors, not ovarian cancer. Monotherapy also failed in urothelial cancer (PMID:27328856) and in combination trials (NCT02979899). With the mechanism engaged, the lack of any activity points to endoglin blockade not driving this disease.

At 10 mg/kg weekly, the index-trial dose, the first-in-human study reports continuous serum concentrations that saturate CD105 (PMID:22767667). In other cancers, pharmacodynamic markers moved: plasma CD105 fell and VEGF rose (PMID:25407442), soluble endoglin rose (PMID:29997150), and mechanism-based telangiectasias were common (PMID:36735117). The MTD matched the saturating dose, so tolerability did not cap engagement. This engagement evidence predates the index trial but was not shown in angiosarcoma patients. Despite engagement, TAPPAS found no PFS benefit (4.2 vs 4.3 months) and more serious AEs (NCT02979899, PMID:35357396). A randomized renal cancer trial was similarly negative (NCT01806064). This points to endoglin blockade added to VEGFR inhibition not driving benefit.

Exposure was adequate in GBM patients: serum TRC105 stayed above the 25 ug/mL target concentration in all evaluable patients at 10 mg/kg (PMID:37684373). Engagement was adequate, though shown outside GBM. The 10 mg/kg weekly dose maintained CD105-saturating concentrations (PMID:22767667, 2012, before the index trial), and soluble endoglin and plasma CD105 changed (PMID:29997150, PMID:25407442). Pathway was adequate: VEGF-A rose after treatment, including in GBM patients (PMID:25407442, PMID:37684373). The dose was the tolerated MTD, not capped below engagement (NCT01332721). The index trial was small and single-arm, so it could not answer the question (NCT01564914). However, the randomized N1174 trial in recurrent GBM showed no PFS benefit (HR 1.16; PMID:35664553). The mechanism was engaged and did not deliver clinical benefit.

The index trial NCT02968563 was a small, uncontrolled combination study (tirabrutinib+idelalisib±obinutuzumab, n=35). Its CR rates were descriptive with no prespecified test, so it was not an efficacy test of tirabrutinib itself. Plasma exposure was shown in patients (PMID:30815927). BTK occupancy above 90% was shown at doses of 40 mg/day or more, but only in healthy volunteers and RA patients (PMID:34623640), published after the index trial started. Pathway effect is inferred from monotherapy responses in CLL/NHL (PMID:30815927) and the Japanese approval for WM (PMID:36058857). The MTD was not reached, so the dose was not capped. BTK is validated in CLL by approved inhibitors. The combination study NCT02457598 noted only 'no efficacy advantage' over expectations, so the trial could not answer whether the drug worked.

Tirabrutinib 40 mg missed the week-12 composite endpoint in Sjögren's (35.1% vs 26.5% placebo, p=0.33), and neither secondary endpoint was met (NCT03100942, PMID:35377447). Plasma PK was linear and well characterized (NCT02626026, PMID:30815927). A PK/PD model built on BTK occupancy data from healthy volunteers and RA patients (NCT02626026, which predates the index trial) showed that ≥40 mg/day gives >90% occupancy (PMID:34623640). Engagement was therefore adequate at the index dose, though it was not measured in Sjögren's patients. Pathway is inferred from clinical responses in B-cell malignancies (PMID:30815927); index-trial biomarker reductions were reported only pooled across arms. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Small arms (about 37 per arm) and the authors' 'hypothesis-generating' framing suggest the trial was underpowered (F7).

In the index MDD trial (NCT01145755), the active comparator duloxetine (-14.03) did not separate from placebo (-14.16), and neither did AZD2066 (-13.17). This failed assay sensitivity points to a trial that could not answer the question, plausibly from high placebo response. The bundle states no stop reason. Brain penetration and concentration-dependent mGluR5 occupancy were shown by PET in healthy volunteers before the index trial (NCT00686504, PMID:23668965; Ki ~1170 nM). However, occupancy at the MDD dose is not reported, so 'adequate' is a loose call. A dose-dependent functional effect on TLESRs (PMID:22469098) supports engagement, but there are no CNS pathway data in depression. If the trial was informative, F2 would apply.

In healthy volunteers, a human PET study (NCT00686504, registered 2008 before the index trial; PMID:23668965) showed concentration-dependent displacement of an mGluR5 radioligand across brain regions (Kipl 1170 nM). This shows brain exposure and target engagement. A functional effect also followed: AZD2066 reduced TLESRs and reflux episodes dose-dependently, with CNS adverse events at 13 mg (PMID:22469098). Despite this, the index trial in painful diabetic neuropathy showed no benefit over placebo (NRS -2.33 vs -2.52), and the MDD trial also failed (NCT01145755). The bundle does not report occupancy at the index dose, and engagement was not measured in neuropathy patients, so confidence is medium. On balance, mGluR5 antagonism appears not to drive neuropathic pain as tested.

A healthy-volunteer PET study (NCT00686504, PMID:23668965) showed brain mGluR5 occupancy rising with AZD2066 plasma concentration (Kipl 1170 nM), which supports brain exposure and engagement. Occupancy at the pain-trial doses is not stated, so calling engagement adequate is a judgement. Dose-dependent TLESR and reflux reduction plus CNS adverse events (PMID:22469098) indicate a functional mGluR5 effect in humans. Even so, the related diabetic neuropathy pain trial (NCT00857623) and the MDD trial (NCT01145755) showed no benefit over placebo. This suggests the mechanism does not drive neuropathic pain as tested. The index trial was terminated without a stated reason or statistical comparison; its numerical trend favoured the drug (NCT00939094), which limits interpretation (F7). The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

The index trial (NCT00743938) compared BMS-690514 with erlotinib on PFS in previously treated NSCLC. It posted no results and gave no stop reason. In the phase I-IIa study (NCT00329004, registered 2006; PMID:23490650), the 200 mg MTD gave measurable plasma exposure and modulated EGFR- and VEGFR-pathway pharmacodynamic biomarkers, including in NSCLC cohorts. The dose was the MTD, with expected EGFR-class toxicities (diarrhoea, rash), and was not shown to be capped below engagement. Activity was modest: objective response about 3%, and disease control was higher in EGFR-mutant (70%) than wild-type (29%) patients, which hints at a selection issue. With engagement shown, failure to beat erlotinib suggests the added pan-HER/VEGFR mechanism gives no benefit as tested. The bundle is thin, so confidence is low.

CREAD (NCT02670083) was stopped for futility at 60 mg/kg; CDR-SB difference was -0.17. In AD patients, crenezumab raised plasma and CSF Aβ and lowered CSF oligomeric Aβ by about 45% (PMID:31969177, PMID:31168802). However, its CSF:serum ratio was only about 0.3%, and modeling identifies brain ISF delivery as the limiting step (PMID:32116192). Amyloid PET did not decline (NCT01397578, PMID:30231896), and tau PET was unchanged (NCT03977584). So central engagement and the pathway effect were at best partial. Dosing was not tolerability-limited: 120 mg/kg was tolerated (PMID:32568196). Other anti-Aβ antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab, aducanumab) are approved for AD. This points to a molecule-level failure to engage brain amyloid adequately, rather than an irrelevant target.

The index trial NCT00920257 was a first-in-human dose-finding study. Its primary objective was the recommended Phase II dose, not efficacy. It completed and met that objective: RP2D 75 mg daily, well tolerated, favorable PK, and partial responses in PIK3CA/PTEN-altered tumors (PMID:29611022). So it was not an efficacy failure. In gynecologic (mostly ovarian) patients, PMID:26429956 showed AKT inhibition confirmed by biopsy phospho-AKT changes and an exposure-related decrease in tumor FDG uptake. That evidence was published in 2015, after the index start, and was not specific to uterine corpus cancer. The bundle gives no efficacy readout or stated reason for stopping the endometrial program (NCT01935973 shows no outcome).

INTELLANCE-1 (NCT02573324) showed no overall survival benefit (HR 1.02), although PFS improved slightly. Human data show only dose-proportional plasma PK and corneal accumulation (PMID:29982805, PMID:33201054). They do not show drug levels or EGFR engagement inside glioblastoma. The 111In-ABT-806 SPECT study used the parent antibody in other tumors, not glioblastoma. Explanations for the failure are proposed but not measured in patients: heterogeneous blood–brain-barrier delivery (orthotopic PDX work in Neuro-Oncology) and spatial EGFR heterogeneity relative to tumor vessels, which may point to patient selection (PMC13043081). No other EGFR agent has succeeded in glioblastoma. Corneal toxicity was frequent but managed; the dose was not capped. Because engagement is no_human_data, the bundle cannot separate poor delivery from an irrelevant target, so the code is U, with F1a and F3 as plausible alternatives.

In the first-in-human index trial (NCT01248949; PMID:29559563), MEDI3617 showed linear pharmacokinetics and maximal accumulation of peripheral Ang2 binding at doses above 300 mg Q3W in patients with advanced solid tumors. Doses up to 1,500 mg Q3W were given with no MTD reached, so neither exposure nor engagement was dose-limited. This engagement evidence came from the index trial itself, not from before it. No downstream pathway biomarker result is reported in the bundle. Response rates were 6% in the ovarian expansion and 0% in glioma, and the authors state development was discontinued for limited clinical activity. That supports F2: target engaged, no benefit. Prolonged grade 3 edema in ovarian cancer, a class-related effect of Ang2 inhibitors, is a secondary F5 signal.

The index OPAL trial (NCT00780598, PMID:23453583) is classified as having met its primary endpoint: authors reported 10% CR/CRp and concluded that tosedostat has activity in older relapsed/refractory AML. This was not a clear efficacy failure, so F9 applies. Aminopeptidase inhibition in AML blasts was shown only in vitro (PMID:21145592), and the bundle has no human PK, engagement or pathway data, so U is secondary. Toxicity may have contributed: five treatment-related deaths occurred, and an FDA clinical hold in 2013 cancelled a phase II portion (NCT01636609). Later trials stopped for funding and drug-supply reasons (NCT02352831). The bundle gives no explicit reason the program ended.

The index trial NCT00603668 was a small Phase I/II dose and schedule study whose primary outcome was safety over 12 weeks, classified not_efficacy, with no posted results. It was not an efficacy test of milatuzumab in CLL, so F9 is the primary code. The only human PK/PD evidence comes from multiple myeloma (PMID:24112026, published 2013, after the index trial started). There, milatuzumab was rapidly cleared, with little serum accumulation and low trough levels. B cells fell only moderately (median 34%), suggesting partial engagement. No dose-limiting toxicity occurred. No CLL engagement data appear in the bundle. The weak exposure and partial depletion suggest the mechanism may not have been adequately tested (F1a secondary).

The index trial, NCT01663766, was a 12-patient Phase 1 safety study. It was stopped because the investigators judged that milatuzumab did not appear to reduce GVHD risk. They reported no safety signals and no dose limit from tolerability. The ASH abstract from this trial describes dosing on days -7, -4, -1 and +7 but reports no measurements of drug levels, CD74 binding or antigen-presenting-cell effects. In the myeloma trial (PMID:24112026), the drug was cleared quickly and trough levels were low, with B cells falling a moderate median of 34%. That was in another disease, and no direct CD74 occupancy was measured. The protective effect against GVHD comes only from mouse data (PMID:23025988). No other CD74 drug has data in GVHD. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged CD74 apart from a target that does not matter for GVHD, so the code is U.

The Phase 1 trials (NCT02013388; PMID:28209466) showed that cavosonstat was absorbed with linear, dose-proportional plasma levels and that tolerability did not cap the dose. No source measured GSNOR (ADH5) inhibition or S-nitrosoglutathione levels in humans, so engagement is no_human_data. The pathway readout was weak. Sweat chloride fell only 4.1 mmol/L at the top Phase 1 dose. In the index trial (200/400 mg twice daily, on Orkambi), sweat chloride and FEV1 did not differ from placebo at 12 weeks, and the add-on-to-ivacaftor trial (NCT02724527) gave the same result. Tolerability did not limit the dose. The sponsor did not say why the drug failed. Without engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged GSNOR from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The asthma trial (NCT01823016, PMID:30102965) tested one dose, 30 mg/day, and missed its primary endpoint. In healthy-volunteer Phase 1 studies, the drug reached plasma levels, but the sponsor's ex vivo test of target blockade (histamine-induced eosinophil shape change) showed no effect at 15 mg. An effect appeared only at 50–300 mg. The sponsor's authors conclude that doses of 30 mg or less gave little or no inhibition, and say the 3–30 mg rheumatoid arthritis study (NCT01679951) 'should not have worked'. A synovial biopsy study at 30 mg (PMID:30739130) found no clear signs of the drug's pharmacology. There was no tolerability ceiling: the drug was well tolerated up to 150–300 mg. So the mechanism was likely not tested at an engaging dose. These data come from healthy volunteers, not asthma patients, and were published after the trial started.

In Phase 1 studies, toreforant had good oral pharmacokinetics suitable for once-daily dosing. It also produced dose-dependent inhibition of histamine-induced eosinophil shape change, which the investigators took as evidence that H4R was inhibited in vivo. This was shown only in healthy volunteers, and the paper was published in 2017, after the index trial started. QT prolongation was seen only at the highest Phase 1 dose, and the 30 and 60 mg doses were well tolerated. A synovial biopsy study in RA found no clear pharmacology biomarker signal (PMID:30739130). Toreforant also failed in RA (NCT01679951) and asthma (NCT01823016). In psoriasis, PASI75 effects were modest and missed the Bayesian success threshold (PMID:30124726), which points to H4R antagonism not driving disease. The trial was small, with only 6 placebo patients, and narrowly missed the threshold (posterior probability 97.4% against 97.5% required), so F7 is a secondary code.

The Phase 1 report (Thurmond 2017) shows plasma exposure was adequate and rose with dose. Target engagement was measured with an ex vivo assay of histamine-induced eosinophil shape change in healthy volunteers. At trough there was no inhibition at 15 mg and only partial inhibition at 50–300 mg (about 30–75%). The index Phase IIb trial (NCT01679951; PMID:27422891) tested only 3, 10 and 30 mg. The authors themselves conclude these doses should have given little or no blood H4R inhibition, so the mechanism was not properly tested. At 30 mg, the synovial biopsy study (NCT01862224; PMID:30739130) found no clear pharmacology biomarker signal. The earlier 100 mg Phase IIa trial (NCT00941707) hinted at benefit but was stopped after a death and analysed post hoc. Engagement was measured only in healthy volunteers and was published after the index trial started. The authors also question whether blood engagement reflects engagement in tissue.

Eldelumab was given IV at 10 or 20 mg/kg, and plasma exposure was measured in Crohn's (PMID:28333187) and UC (PMID:23461895). Exposure was the primary objective in the Crohn's trial, but no exposure-remission relationship was found, and remission did not differ significantly from placebo (29.3% and 22.5% vs 20.0%). The bundle and my searches had no human data on target engagement: no free or bound CXCL10 measurements, no evidence of CXCL10 neutralization in gut tissue, and no downstream marker such as chemokine-receptor (CXCR3+) immune-cell movement into the gut. The rheumatoid arthritis trial met its endpoint (NCT01017367), but that is joint tissue, not gut, so engagement in the gut cannot be inferred from it. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged CXCL10 in the gut from a target that does not drive Crohn's, so the code is U.

In the index trial (NCT00656890; 10 mg/kg IV q2w), the primary endpoint was missed (52.7% vs 35.2%, p=0.083). A post hoc analysis linked higher trough concentrations to response (87.5% vs 37.0%) and to histological improvement, and the authors called for dose-response studies, suggesting under-exposure at the tested dose (PMID:23461895). No free IP-10 suppression or other engagement or pathway marker appears in the bundle. The RA success (NCT01017367) involves a different tissue, so it cannot support inferred engagement here. Higher doses (15 and 25 mg/kg) also failed in UC (PMID:26721935), with signals mainly in anti-TNF-naive patients, and the Crohn's exposure-remission link was not significant (NCT01466374). This weakens the exposure explanation, so U and F3 remain plausible.

No direct human target-engagement measure (corneal TRPV1 occupancy or biomarker) appears in the bundle. The FIH study (PMID:36394843) showed tolerability up to 2.5% with low systemic exposure, so the dose was not capped. The same topical eye drop met its primary pain endpoint in acute post-PRK ocular pain (NCT02961062), acting on the same target in the same corneal compartment. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore inferred adequate. The index trial in chronic post-operative corneal pain (NCT04630158) showed no separation at 5 or 15 mg/mL (p=0.70, p=0.93). This suggests TRPV1 antagonism does not drive chronic ocular pain as tested. The large placebo response (-25 VAS) may also have contributed (F7), but the sources do not state it.

EMERGE (NCT01156753) missed its ORR primary endpoint (6% vs 7%, PMID:25847941). Only plasma PK was measured in humans: serum ADC, total antibody and MMAE (PMID:25267761; METRIC, NCT01997333). Nothing measured drug delivery to the tumor, gpNMB binding or internalization, or any downstream effect in tumor tissue. The [89Zr]-CR011 PET work was done only in mice (PMID:35027482). Dose escalation stopped at 1.88 mg/kg because of neuropathy, but no source ties that to falling short of engagement. The sources blame patient selection and heterogeneity: the gpNMB-overexpressing TNBC signal did not hold up in METRIC, and gpNMB IHC did not predict response. There is no human engagement evidence and no other gpNMB drug for comparison, so this is U, with F3 as secondary.

The index AML/ALL trial (NCT00798213), reported in PMID:23949430, gave 50 mg/m2 as a 2-h infusion every 21 days. Plasma peaks came quickly, but the half-life was short. In patients' blood cells, Mcl-1 suppression and PARP cleavage were seen at 4 h but lost by 24 h, and did not track outcome. Blasts fell dramatically but only transiently, with no remissions. The authors attribute the lack of durable activity to the bolus schedule: in vitro, longer exposure at clinically attainable concentrations killed more leukemia cells, so they proposed prolonged infusions. Engagement and pathway effects in AML were therefore too brief, and the mechanism was not adequately tested. Phase 1 pharmacodynamic data in solid tumors (PMID:28859059, PMID:24131779) showed engagement only in other diseases.

In the index trial NCT01512160, PF-04531083 at 1000 and 2000 mg did no better than placebo on TOTPAR 0–6h, while ibuprofen did separate from placebo. That makes it a sensitive assay, not a failed trial. No dose was limited by tolerability. No human PK at the site of action, Nav1.8 engagement, or biomarker data were found: the Phase 1 trials posted no results, and the UV-burn heat-pain study NCT01127906 has no published outcome. Suzetrigine, another selective Nav1.8 blocker, was FDA-approved in 2025 for acute pain, which includes post-surgical pain. So Nav1.8 blockade can work in acute post-surgical pain, and the failure points to this molecule (for example, inadequate exposure or potency) rather than the target. Engagement was never measured, so U is a reasonable alternative.

The index trial NCT01394003 was a Phase 1 dose escalation, not an efficacy test. It stopped because 'pharmacokinetic properties do not allow further dose escalation.' PMID:24440085 reports Grade 3 DLTs (vomiting, pancreatitis, lipase rise) that capped the dose at 75 mg BID or 100 mg QD. It also reports highly variable, non-dose-proportional exposure and no responses. Skin phospho-S6 was sampled, but no result is given, so engagement in humans is not shown. The mechanism was therefore never adequately tested (F1a). PMID:29178617 says the program was terminated for hepatotoxicity risk, possibly from the 4-APP metabolite, which supports F6. Its LDL lowering was seen in dyslipidemic volunteers, not in cancer. F9 applies secondarily because no efficacy readout failed.

No human PK or receptor-binding data were posted; Phase 1 trials (NCT02217839, NCT02217826) report no results. In untreated acromegalics, veldoreotide produced a dose-dependent but partial GH suppression: 1, 2 and 3 of 8 patients reached trough hGH <2.5 versus 4/8 on octreotide (NCT02217800). The earlier single-dose study also showed fewer responders than octreotide (4-8 vs 8; NCT02235987). No statistics were reported and no safety signal was seen. Octreotide, lanreotide and pasireotide act on the same SSTR2/5 targets and are approved for acromegaly, so the target is validated. The weaker effect therefore points to the molecule or dose, not the target. The in vitro promise (PMID:22065857) does not count. The index trial was a small descriptive PD study, so the evidence is thin.

The bundle and my searches turned up no human evidence for any of the three pillars. There are no CSF levels, no occupancy data for the NMDA receptor glycine-site modulator, and no pharmacodynamic EEG or biomarker results. The one human imaging study, NCT01844726, missed its BOLD endpoint (p=.10) and was terminated. Healthy volunteers tolerated doses up to 1800 mg without any measurable CNS effect (PMID:34423904), so tolerability did not cap the dose. The phase 2 benefit (PMID:25782764) was confined to the middle doses and did not replicate in any of the phase 3 trials (NCT02932943, NCT02943564, NCT02943577, NCT02951988, NCT03560518). Allergan gave no mechanistic explanation. Esketamine and dextromethorphan are approved for this disease, but both block the receptor rather than enhance it, so F1b does not apply. Nothing shows whether the drug never engaged its target or the mechanism simply doesn't matter, so the code is U.

Sapacitabine is an oral prodrug of CNDAC, a nucleoside analogue that breaks DNA strands. It has no recorded protein target. The Phase 1 trial in leukemia and MDS (NCT00380653; Kantarjian, J Clin Oncol 2010) was a pharmacokinetic study, so it supports adequate plasma exposure to CNDAC. I found no human data on target engagement or downstream effects: no measures of CNDAC-triphosphate in leukemic blasts, DNA strand breaks or pathway markers. Earlier response rates of 15–45% (PMID:26523431) show some activity but no pivotal efficacy. SEAMLESS (NCT01303796) found no overall survival benefit (HR 1.01). The investigators pointed only to a possible benefit in patients with WBC <10×10^9/L (PMID:34424530), which suggests F3 as a secondary code. Because engagement is not documented, I can't tell whether the drug was underdosed or the mechanism doesn't add benefit, so the code is U.

Human plasma PK is documented (PMID:27128838, PMID:22634319). KEAP1/Nrf2 engagement was shown by NQO1 mRNA induction in PBMCs, and the drug was tolerated at doses showing target engagement (PMID:22634319, PMID:25897966); the MTD of 900 mg/d is far above CKD doses, so the dose was not capped. The expected pathway effect, an on-treatment eGFR rise, occurred in an ADPKD cohort (NCT03366337) and across CKD (NCT00811889, NCT03019185). That engagement evidence came from cancer patients, not ADPKD. In FALCON (NCT03918447) the off-treatment eGFR change at week 108 did not differ from placebo (p=0.39). This suggests the acute eGFR effect did not translate into disease modification. The termination was for business reasons, but the readout itself failed, so F8 is secondary only.

Plasma PK was characterised in humans (PMID:27128838, PMID:22634319). Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 was shown by increased PBMC NQO1 mRNA, but only in cancer patients (PMID:22634319, 2012), before the index trial. In DKD, the mechanism's proximal effect was reproduced: dose-dependent eGFR rises (BEAM, PMID:21699484) and inulin-measured GFR gains with titrated low doses in TSUBAKI (PMID:32518870), which match AYAME's 5–15 mg scheme (PMID:36002026). Despite this, BEACON showed no reduction in ESRD or cardiovascular death (PMID:24206459). AYAME's hard renal endpoint was likewise insufficient for filing (NCT03550443). So the mechanism was engaged but did not translate into outcome benefit (F2). F4 is secondary: a surrogate eGFR effect was seen in this disease, but the hard endpoint failed.

Plasma exposure is characterised in humans (PMID:27128838, PMID:22634319). Direct KEAP1 binding was never measured, and there is no PH-specific biomarker data. Nrf2 target NQO1 mRNA rose in PBMCs of cancer patients (PMID:22634319). The same systemic mechanism met eGFR endpoints in CKD and Alport syndrome (NCT00811889, NCT03019185, NCT04702997), so engagement and pathway are inferred adequate. In PH, both LARIAT (NCT02036970) and CATALYST (NCT02657356) missed 6MWD, with CATALYST trending in favour of placebo (-12.86 m, p=0.068). That points to Nrf2 activation not improving exercise capacity in PAH. COVID-related early termination (F7) cut the trial short, but the direction of effect argues against a hidden benefit.

Human plasma PK is documented (PMID:27128838; PMID:22634319). In PMID:22634319, cancer patients showed PBMC NQO1 induction, a sign of Nrf2 activation, but at oncology doses. Engagement is inferred: bardoxolone repeatedly moved eGFR through systemic KEAP1/Nrf2 activation in CKD and Alport (PMID:21699484, NCT03019185, NCT04702997). This is a different tissue, and no engagement or biomarker was measured in PAH patients. Despite that, two PAH trials missed the 6MWD endpoint: LARIAT (NCT02036970) and CATALYST (NCT02657356), whose 202 enrolled patients showed a trend favouring placebo (-12.86 m). This suggests KEAP1/Nrf2 activation does not drive PAH outcomes as tested. The COVID-related termination is a minor design or execution factor (F7). Confidence is low because there is no in-disease engagement data.

Exposure was confirmed by plasma and sputum drug levels in the bronchiectasis trial (PMID:23433769). Ex vivo zymosan-stimulated NE inhibition was dose-dependent and maximal at 60 mg, the index dose, in healthy volunteers and COPD patients (PMID:23391369). That engagement evidence was published in 2013 and was not shown in bronchiectasis. Sputum neutrophils were unchanged and the sputum NE activity result is not reported, so the pathway evidence is weak, with only trend-level changes in IL-8, IL-6 and RANTES. FEV1 improved by 100 mL (p=0.006), but this was a small 4-week signal-searching study (F7). The same 60 mg dose failed in larger COPD trials (NCT01023516, NCT01054170) and in cystic fibrosis (NCT00757848). Taken together, adequate inhibition did not translate into clinical benefit.

Plasma PK was dose-linear and similar in healthy volunteers and COPD patients. Ex vivo whole-blood NE inhibition was maximal at 60 mg, the dose used in the index trial (PMID:23391369), so systemic exposure and blood engagement were adequate. In CF patients, however, AZD9668 60 mg twice daily had no effect on sputum neutrophil elastase activity, the direct engagement measure at the airway site of action (PMID:22267768). Sputum neutrophils, lung function and QoL were also unchanged (NCT00757848). Only modest IL-6, RANTES and urinary desmosine reductions were seen, which is partial pathway evidence. Tolerability did not cap the dose. Because airway NE was not shown to be inhibited, the mechanism was not adequately tested (F1a). The short 28-day duration with some biomarker signal makes F4 a possible secondary.

Exposure: plasma PK in schizophrenia patients rose with dose (NCT01556763, PMID:25438724). No human study measured receptor occupancy. The only occupancy data come from pigs (PMID:38601007), which showed limited occupancy, and animal data cannot count. Pathway: in a proof-of-concept trial in patients with schizophrenia, the drug normalised brain responses to sound (mismatch negativity and P300) (PMID:24419307, PMID:30397594). The Phase 2 trial improved cognition scores (PMID:26089183). In both Phase 3 trials, every arm improved strongly on the cognition and functional scales, including placebo, and the drug did not separate from placebo. The sponsor said the placebo groups improved more than expected. That points to a trial that could not answer the question (F7). Because engagement was never measured in humans, failure of the mechanism itself cannot be ruled out (U).

Exposure in mCRC patients is characterised by pooled population PK (PMID:31679083). In the phase 1 trial in anti-EGFR-refractory mCRC, pharmacodynamic studies confirmed marked EGFR downmodulation, and 44% of patients had tumor shrinkage (PMID:25962717, published 2015, after the index trial started). In the index trial, EGFR ECD-mutant ctDNA fell on Sym004, so the pathway effect occurred, yet OS was not improved (HR 1.31 and 0.97; NCT02083653). The authors attribute this to high intrapatient genomic heterogeneity and co-occurring resistance mechanisms after anti-EGFR therapy, and define a ctDNA-selected subgroup (PMID:29423521). That supports F3, wrong population. F2 also applies because the target was engaged without overall benefit. F5 is secondary: the 12 mg/kg arm had more serious AEs and worse OS, with skin toxicity and hypomagnesemia as mechanism-based toxicities.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: Index trial NCT01417936 was a single-arm study in anti-EGFR-refractory SCCHN (n=26), reporting a median PFS of 82 days with no comparator. Human pillar evidence comes from colorectal cancer, not SCCHN. In PMID:25962717 (NCT01117428), pharmacodynamic studies confirmed marked Sym004-induced EGFR downmodulation at 9–12 mg/kg. That study also reported mechanism-based skin toxicity and hypomagnesemia plus tumor shrinkage, supporting exposure, engagement and pathway effects. Dose expansion proceeded at engaging doses, so dose was not limited. This evidence was published in 2015, after the index trial started. With EGFR engaged yet only modest PFS, the most likely explanation is that anti-EGFR-resistant SCCHN is not EGFR-driven. The single-arm design (F7) and the resistant population (F3) weaken this inference.

Plasma exposure was dose-proportional with about 28-31% pulmonary bioavailability (NCT02648438, PMID:35264846, PMID:34853068). In asthma patients, FENO fell at all doses, a pathway marker (PMID:30777086). Glucocorticoid receptor engagement, however, looked weak or partial. Healthy Japanese volunteers showed only 25% cortisol suppression, and only at the top dose (PMID:31814707); asthma patients showed no significant cortisol change. In the index trial, the fluticasone furoate comparator on the same target separated from placebo (p=0.014). Velsecorat's best doses fell short (720 µg p=0.060). Tolerability did not cap the dose. Many ICS on this target are approved, so the shortfall points to this selective modulator's insufficient agonist activity, not the target. The borderline p-values also leave a possible power or dose-selection issue.

No efficacy failure is documented. The index trial NCT00882063 was a small Phase 1/2 study (n=19) whose primary endpoint was the maximum tolerated dose, and it posted no results or stop reason. A solid-tumour Phase 1 abstract (AACR) reported plasma Cmax of about 0.7–1 µM at low doses, above the enzyme IC50s (20–79 nM), so systemic exposure looks adequate. Evidence of target engagement was only anecdotal: lower cyclin D1/Ki67 in one patient's skin biopsy. No occupancy, Rb-phosphorylation or Mcl-1 data were found in myeloma patients; the myeloma pathway data are preclinical only (leu2008378). The mantle cell lymphoma trial NCT00843050 was stopped for futility, but that does not separate a drug that failed to engage from a target that does not matter. Indeterminate.

The index trial (NCT00843050, PMID:25816934) dosed 185 mg/m2/day, the MTD. Of 13 relapsed MCL patients, none responded: 11 progressed and median time to progression was 43 days. Tolerability did not cap the dose. A phase 1 abstract in solid tumours (AACR/MCT A112) reports that plasma Cmax at 9–12.6 mg/m2 was already about 10–14 times the CDK4 IC50, so I rated plasma exposure adequate. No direct target measure exists (CDK kinase inhibition, Rb phosphorylation or Mcl-1 lowering). The only human biomarker is lower cyclin D1/Ki67 in one skin biopsy from a single solid-tumour patient, which is anecdotal and was not in MCL. So nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter. The investigators suggested testing earlier in the disease or in combinations (F3 secondary).

Endo reported that the index trial NCT00830154 (IP456-041) missed its pre-specified criteria for success. It then closed the open-label study NCT00216255 and dropped pagoclone in December 2011 (AdisInsight). None of the sources we found reports human data on pagoclone exposure, brain levels, GABA-A receptor occupancy (e.g., by PET), or a pharmacodynamic biomarker such as EEG or sedation at 0.3–0.6 mg BID. The only engagement evidence is rodent binding and behaviour (PMID:8103792), which doesn't count. No GABA-A modulator has succeeded in stuttering, so F1b doesn't apply. The later business-focus statement came after the efficacy miss, so this isn't F8. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

VISTA-16 (NCT01130246) tested varespladib methyl 500 mg daily in ACS and was terminated for lack of efficacy. In the earlier FRANCIS-ACS phase 2 trial (NCT00743925, PMID:20863951, PMID:21989792), the same 500 mg dose in ACS patients lowered sPLA2-IIA by about 82% versus 16% on placebo. This shows adequate systemic exposure and target engagement in the program's disease, before the index trial started. Downstream pathway markers also moved: LDL-C fell further and hsCRP and IL-6 were reduced. Major cardiovascular events were not different in FRANCIS. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. Robust engagement with no clinical benefit indicates sPLA2 inhibition does not drive ACS outcomes as tested.

A human PET study in healthy volunteers (NCT00886067, 2009, before the index trial; Jucaite et al.) found that AZD1446 gets into the brain. The in vivo plasma concentration giving 50% receptor occupancy was about 128 nM. At 80 mg, the dose used in the index trial, α4β2 occupancy was above 80%. Plasma exposure was well characterized and the drug was well tolerated (PMID:27128232). So the dose was not limited by side effects. In NCT01012375 (PMID:23640072), no dose or schedule improved CAARS or other clinical scores, in nicotine users or non-users. There was one isolated Groton Maze gain. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. Since occupancy was high and still gave no benefit, the most likely explanation is that α4β2 agonism does not drive adult ADHD symptoms as tested. Occupancy was measured only in healthy volunteers, not in ADHD patients.

The index trial NCT03976648 was a long-term safety extension with a TEAE endpoint, not an efficacy test. It was terminated alongside the IPF ISABELA program (NCT03733444, NCT03711162) for 'benefit-risk'. Those IPF trials showed no FVC benefit and more deaths on drug than placebo. In SSc itself, NOVESA (NCT03798366, PMID:36787101) met its week-24 mRSS endpoint at 600 mg. It also showed reduced plasma LPA C18:2 (target engagement in SSc patients) and lower blood fibrosis biomarkers. Exposure and engagement were established earlier in healthy volunteers and IPF (PMID:31012984, PMID:29792287). ISABELA analyses say exposure and engagement do not explain the IPF failure (PMID:38071462). The SSc stop was therefore not an SSc efficacy failure. A safety or mortality signal from IPF plausibly contributed.

The phase 2a FLORA trial in IPF (NCT02738801, PMID:29792287, 2018) and the population PK/PD analysis in IPF patients (PMID:30953319) assessed pharmacodynamics before the index trial began. The bundle gives only their titles, so the strength of engagement there rests on the follow-up analysis. That analysis (PMID:38071462) states that plasma exposure and target engagement in the ISABELA trials do not explain the lack of efficacy. The trial was not dose-limited. In SSc, LPA was lowered (PMID:36787101). No downstream lung pathway marker is shown in IPF, so pathway is no_human_data. FVC decline did not differ from placebo at either dose (NCT03711162, NCT03733444). With engagement shown, the ATX/LPA mechanism did not drive IPF progression as tested. A mortality imbalance on drug in NCT03733444 contributed to the benefit-risk stop (secondary F6).

The index trial NCT01014975 was a Phase 1/2 safety and dose-finding study. Its primary outcome was symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, and there were 0 cases at 20, 40 and 80 mg, with no deaths. It was not an efficacy test, and it met its safety objective, so this was not an efficacy failure of the drug. Target engagement (fibrin clot lysis) was shown in humans before the index trial, but not in stroke patients. Locally delivered plasmin produced dose-dependent thrombolysis in occluded hemodialysis grafts, with all subjects at 24 mg achieving more than 75% lysis and no systemic fibrinogen depletion (PMID:18384651, PMID:18760830). Thrombolysis was also seen in peripheral arterial occlusion (NCT01222117). The bundle gives no reason why the stroke program did not continue.

Molibresib plus fulvestrant at 60–80 mg QD gave an ORR of 13%, below the 25% threshold, and the trial stopped for protocol-defined futility (NCT02964507, PMID:37992310). Plasma exposure was measured in the index trial and in the first-in-human study (PMID:32328561). That study, registered as NCT01587703 in 2012 and so before the index trial, showed dose-dependent reductions in circulating MCP-1 in solid-tumour patients. Its authors state the drug was tolerated at doses demonstrating target engagement, which supports engagement and pathway effect. Engagement was not shown specifically in HR+ breast cancer. Thrombocytopenia required dose reductions, but the doses used matched the engaging range. Engagement was adequate with no clinical benefit, so F2. A ctDNA copy-number association with poor PFS hints at heterogeneity (F3).

Plasma exposure was measured in the index trial (NCT02964507) and in the first-in-human study. That study (PMID:32328561) showed dose-dependent reductions in circulating MCP-1 and concluded molibresib was 'tolerated at doses demonstrating target engagement' at 60–100 mg, matching the index doses of 60/80 mg. This evidence came from mixed solid tumours rather than specifically HR+ breast cancer, and was published after the index trial started. Despite this, molibresib plus fulvestrant gave an ORR of 13%, below the 25% threshold, and the trial stopped for protocol-defined futility (PMID:37992310). The CRPC combination was also futile (NCT03150056). The mechanism appears not to drive endocrine-resistant disease as tested. ctDNA copy-number amplification predicted poor PFS, suggesting a heterogeneity contribution (F3).

Human plasma PK was characterized in the first-in-human study (PMID:32328561, PMID:34724226). That study reported dose-dependent reductions in circulating MCP-1, a BET pharmacodynamic biomarker, and concluded the drug was 'tolerated at doses demonstrating target engagement' (60–100 mg). This was published from NCT01587703, which predates the index trial. Part 2 included a CRPC cohort, but GSEA changes varied by patient and tumour type, so engagement specific to prostate cancer is not clearly shown. The index trial used 40–80 mg, comparable to engaging doses, with abiraterone or enzalutamide; PSA50 was 0% in every arm and the trial stopped for futility (NCT03150056). This supports F2: target engaged, no benefit. On-target thrombocytopenia and GI toxicity forced frequent dose reductions and delays, a secondary factor.

In NCT01587703, molibresib showed measured plasma PK. Dose-dependent reductions in circulating MCP-1 were seen in cancer patients, and the authors state it 'was tolerated at doses demonstrating target engagement' (PMID:32328561). Thrombocytopenia and GI toxicity drove frequent dose interruptions (83%) and reductions (PMID:34724226), but the sources do not say dosing was capped below engagement. At the RP2D, predefined response rates were not met in any tumor type, with only isolated partial responses in NUT carcinoma and CRPC. Combination trials stopped for futility (NCT03150056, NCT02964507, PMID:37992310). Engagement held, yet there was no benefit, which points to F2. Activity limited to NUT carcinoma suggests F3. Dose-limiting thrombocytopenia is a possible F5 contributor. The engagement data were published after the trial started.

In the index UC trial (NCT01284062/PMID:25567115), serum total IL-13 rose in all anrukinzumab arms but not placebo. The authors read this as significant IL-13 binding and concluded efficacy failed despite binding. So engagement is adequate and was shown in UC patients, but only within the index trial itself. Plasma PK was characterised in UC (PMID:25614144). No IL-13 pathway biomarker was reported. Fecal calprotectin, Mayo score, remission and mucosal healing were not improved, which points to F2. Caveats: UC patients cleared the drug 72% faster and the PK authors suggest higher doses may be needed (possible F1a). The trial also had high dropout and a placebo arm of only 7 evaluable patients (F7).

The index trial NCT01003379 (185 patients, 12-week ascending dose 1→5→25 mg) met its primary endpoint: GMLT favored TC-5619 (P=0.036), and SANS also improved (PMID:23303043). The index readout was therefore not an efficacy failure, so F9 applies. The program later stopped after the larger 24-week trial NCT01488929 failed on SANS, CSB and UPSA-B at 5 and 50 mg (PMID:26071208). The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not limited. The bundle has no human exposure, CSF, occupancy or biomarker data; the only engagement evidence is pig PET showing about 40% α7 occupancy (PMID:38601007), which does not count as human evidence. Had the later failure been the index, the code would be U. No α7 agonist has succeeded in schizophrenia.

In NCT01472991, TC-5619 missed its primary endpoint, the CAARS-INV inattention subscale at 4 weeks. Its safety profile was placebo-like, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Targacept then dropped ADHD with no further explanation. I found no human evidence of exposure, α7 receptor occupancy or a biomarker effect. The only occupancy data are from pigs (PMID:38601007: about 40% occupancy), and animal data do not count. The earlier 'positive' CDS trial (NCT01003379) was a proof-of-concept study using a lenient one-sided p<0.10. The Phase 2b schizophrenia trial (NCT01488929) failed, so engagement cannot be inferred from another indication. No α7 agonist has succeeded in ADHD. With engagement unknown, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter.

In the index crossover trial NCT03622216, bradanicline was raised to 150 mg. It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose, but it did not lower awake cough frequency or patient-reported outcomes compared with placebo (ERS 2020 abstract). None of the sources I found report human evidence of exposure, α7 receptor occupancy or a downstream biomarker effect, in cough patients or anyone else. The only occupancy data come from pigs, about 40% (PMID:38601007), and animal data do not count. No other α7 agonist has succeeded in cough, so F1b does not apply. The sources give no reason for the failure beyond the null result. Because engagement has no human data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter: U.

NCT01588678 was a first-in-human dose-escalation study. Its only primary endpoint was the maximum tolerated dose, so it did not test efficacy (F9). The 2013 AACR abstract reported measurable plasma exposure at 450 mg once daily (mean Cmax 542 ng/ml). In patients with advanced solid tumors, platelet phospho-AKT, a readout of the mTOR target, fell by up to 89%, and up to 60% inhibition remained at 24 h at doses of 320 mg or more. The investigators called the drug pharmacodynamically active. No tumor biopsy data on phospho-S6 or other downstream markers were reported, so the pathway pillar has no human data. The 640 mg dose exceeded the MTD because of vomiting and nausea, but 450 mg was tolerated and still showed engagement. The best response was stable disease. No source says why the program stopped, which is why confidence is low.

Index trial NCT02473289 tested sirukumab 50 mg and missed HDRS-17 at week 12 (-11.4 vs -10.6, p=0.31), with tolerable safety. No IL-6 engagement or biomarker data were measured in MDD. Pillars are inferred: 50 mg met pivotal RA endpoints (NCT01604343, NCT01606761), and exposure-response modeling showed near-maximal efficacy at 50 mg q4w (PMID:29901815). Linear PK appears in healthy subjects (PMID:21392075). This implies adequate systemic IL-6 neutralization at the index dose. Post hoc RA data suggested mood benefit (PMID:28676350). Peripheral IL-6 blockade therefore appears not to drive depressive symptoms in an unselected MDD population (F2). Caveat: CNS penetration was never shown. If the relevant compartment is central, engagement is unproven (U).

No IL-6 engagement or biomarker data in lupus nephritis are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate because systemic soluble IL-6 neutralization by sirukumab met pivotal RA endpoints (NCT01604343, NCT01606761; earlier phase 2 NCT00718718). Those RA trials used SC 50 mg q4w, which E-R modeling calls near-maximal (PMID:29901815). The index trial used a much higher 10 mg/kg IV q4w, and PK was dose-proportional up to that dose (PMID:21392075). Yet median proteinuria change was 0% at week 24 (PMID:27110697), suggesting IL-6 does not drive LN proteinuria as tested. Infection-related serious AEs in 47.6% of patients, plausibly on-target, also made safety unacceptable (F5). The tiny trial (21 vs 4) limits inference (F7).

Index trial NCT04380961 gave a single 5 mg/kg IV dose. It missed time to sustained improvement in critical COVID-19 (HR 1.1, p>0.05). The publication (PMID:39182655) reports objective sequestration of circulating IL-6 in these patients and concludes the result questions IL-6 as a key therapeutic target. Engagement was therefore shown in disease, but only within the index trial itself. Exposure is supported by dose-proportional PK up to 10 mg/kg (PMID:21392075). Pathway is inferred adequate because lower SC doses met RA endpoints (NCT01604343, NCT01606761; PMID:29901815). No tolerability cap: grade ≥3 AEs and deaths were not higher on drug. A biomarker-defined responder subgroup (PMID:39362933) supports a secondary population/heterogeneity code (F3).

CARRIE (NCT02399137) gave istiratumab 2.8 g IV every 2 weeks with gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel to patients selected for high IGF-1. PFS was worse than control (HR 1.88), and the HRG+ subgroup did not benefit either (PMID:31912800). The first-in-human study (NCT01733004) measured PK and PD and set the dosing schedule, so plasma exposure is reasonably supported. However, none of the sources found reports human IGF-1R/ErbB3 occupancy, receptor degradation, or any downstream signalling (pAKT) result; the only target-lowering data come from xenografts. The investigators said only that the drug failed to add benefit and gave no mechanistic reason. Dose was not limited by tolerability. Other IGF-1R antibodies (ganitumab, cixutumumab, dalotuzumab) also did not succeed in pancreatic cancer, but without engagement data this drug's failure remains indeterminate.

The index trial NCT02538627 was a Phase 1 dose-finding combination study whose primary endpoint was the MTD of MM-151, not istiratumab. It enrolled 5 patients, was terminated for an unspecified 'sponsor decision', and posted no results. It therefore was not an efficacy test of istiratumab, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human exposure, ERBB3/IGF1R engagement or pathway data. The Phase 1 trial NCT01733004 posted no results, and there are no abstracts. The separate Phase 2 pancreatic trial NCT02399137 missed PFS (worse in the high IGF-1 cohort) but does not show engagement. Engagement is no_human_data, so U is secondary. The unspecified sponsor decision may also have been a business call (F8).

At the 750 mg dose used in phase 2, PET and biopsies showed the ASO reached tumor tissue (PMID:21772926, PMID:21041181), so exposure was adequate. Target knockdown was only partial. Median survivin mRNA and protein fell about 20% with very wide variability (±34–63%), whereas the PK/PD model predicted that these tumor concentrations would give 50–90% inhibition (PMID:21284701). In AML, survivin fell only in high expressers (PMID:23397500). The authors did report restored apoptotic signaling, which supports pathway at a modest level. No engagement data exist in NSCLC patients. The index trial showed no effect on tumor size (NCT01107444), and the prostate trial also failed (NCT00642018). Weak knockdown means the mechanism was likely not tested properly. F2 remains possible because the authors called the inhibition pharmacologically relevant.

The index CRPC trial showed no PFS benefit with LY2181308 plus docetaxel (8.64 vs 9.00 mo; PMID:24246407). At the 750 mg dose used, PET imaging and biopsies showed the drug reached tumor tissue (PMID:21772926, PMID:21041181), so exposure was adequate. Engagement was partial: median survivin mRNA and protein knockdown was only about 20% (SD 34–63%), against a predicted 50–90% (PMID:21284701). In AML, knockdown occurred only in high-expressers (PMID:23397500). Engagement was shown in mixed solid tumors, not prostate cancer, and was published after the index trial started. Downstream apoptosis evidence was anecdotal. The same null result in NSCLC (NCT01107444) fits weak knockdown, so the mechanism was likely not adequately tested. F2 cannot be excluded.

In RA patients, the phase 1 study (PMID:22225620) showed linear, dose-independent PK, no dose-limiting toxicities, and reduced serum CXCL13, which the authors call biologic activity on the LTα pathway. In the index ALTARA trial (NCT01225393; PMID:25359150), 360 mg SC every 2 weeks again lowered CXCL13 significantly, which the authors describe as demonstrating pharmacological target engagement. Despite this, the DAS28-ESR change (-1.89) did not differ from placebo (-1.54), while adalimumab separated clearly. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With exposure and engagement shown, the failure points to LTα blockade not driving RA meaningfully beyond TNF. Engagement evidence is indirect (a CXCL13 pathway marker, not free LTα) and was published after the index trial started.

The index trial NCT00888745 was a Phase 1 safety and PK study in RA, with adverse events as its primary outcome. It was not an efficacy test, and its publication (PMID:22225620) reported good tolerability, linear PK, no dose-limiting toxicities, serum CXCL13 reductions and preliminary clinical activity. All of this pillar evidence came from the index trial itself, so none predates it. The program's real efficacy failure came later in Phase 2 ALTARA (NCT01225393, PMID:25359150). At 360 mg every 2 weeks in RA, pateclizumab significantly lowered CXCL13, which the authors call target engagement, yet DAS28 did not separate from placebo while adalimumab did. Engagement was adequate without benefit, which points to F2 (LTα blockade does not drive RA as tested) as the substantive reason.

I found no human evidence that ABT-126 engaged α7 nAChR. A Phase 1 study measured CSF pharmacokinetics and biomarkers in healthy volunteers (NCT00912431), but it posted no results and I found no publication of them. There are no PET occupancy data in humans or P50 gating results for ABT-126. The only PET occupancy study was done in pigs (PMID:38601007), and animal data do not count. The index trial missed its primary endpoint at 25 mg. Its exposure-response analysis found no plateau, so the investigators thought higher doses might work (PMID:29854928). But 50–75 mg also failed, and tolerability did not limit those doses (PMID:27756421, PMID:26967214). That argues against a simple dose problem, but without engagement data I can't tell whether the drug never engaged its target or the target doesn't matter in this disease.

The extension study NCT01834638 was terminated after its parent trial NCT01655680 missed the MCCB endpoint (PMID:27319970). The smokers trial NCT01678755 also failed (PMID:28922590). A Phase 1 study, NCT00912431, measured CSF levels and exploratory biomarkers, but it posted no results and I found none published. No human receptor occupancy, P50 gating or other pathway biomarker data turned up. The only occupancy data, for TC-5619, come from pigs (PMID:38601007), and animal data don't count. Tolerability was placebo-like, so the dose wasn't capped by side effects. No α7 agonist has succeeded in schizophrenia. With no human engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't drive the disease, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03657095 was a safety extension. It was terminated because the pivotal BEAT trial (NCT01908699) missed its clinical-worsening primary endpoint, with no meaningful separation from placebo. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for esuberaprost. PMID:31158340 shows potent IP agonism only in cells and isolated arteries, which does not count. Other IP-receptor agonists (selexipag, treprostinil, iloprost) are FDA-approved for PAH, so the target is validated in this disease. That points to the molecule, or how it was tested, rather than the target: F1b. BEAT added esuberaprost on top of Tyvaso, itself an IP agonist, so incremental benefit may have been limited. This design concern is inferred, not stated in the sources (secondary F7).

The 240 mg alicaforsen enema missed both co-primary endpoints in NCT02525523: endoscopic remission was 3/65 vs 3/61 on placebo. On exposure, a ResearchGate abstract page (from a search snippet; the page itself could not be opened) says intact drug levels in human colonic mucosal biopsies were far higher than plasma levels, so I rated exposure adequate. I found no human measurement of ICAM-1 knockdown in mucosa or of a downstream biomarker, so engagement and pathway have no human data. The open-label pouchitis and ulcerative colitis studies (PMID:14984374, 16669956, 16669955) only report clinical outcomes, and their main results were negative or uncontrolled. The sponsor said an encouraging stool-frequency signal was seen and that re-scoring the endoscopy data with new methods gave a significant result. That points to the endpoint or how it was measured (F7/F4), but with no engagement data the main code is U.

Human PK modelling, confirmed against single-ascending-dose data, predicted a 1 g oral dose was needed to reach about 12x Nav1.7 IC50 at Cmax and about 3x at a BID trough (PMID:26895021). The index DPN trial used only 150 mg BID (NCT02215252), which implies trough exposure well below IC50. No tolerability limit is shown, so dose_limited is false. No human target-engagement or pathway biomarker was measured in any population. Higher single doses (1600 mg) also failed in dental pain (NCT01529346), and evoked-pain models in healthy volunteers were negative (PMID:31642607). That leaves open whether the target itself matters. Underexposure at the index dose is the most direct explanation, with U as an alternative.
