Human PK (PMID:26895021) showed plasma exposure at ~1 g predicted to reach about 12x Nav1.7 IC50 at Cmax, and observed single-dose data matched. The index trial used 1600 mg. No human measure of Nav1.7 engagement exists in the bundle: no channel occupancy and no nerve-level inhibition. A battery of evoked pain models in healthy volunteers was negative (PMID:31642607/NCT02349607), as were dental pain (NCT01529346) and DPN (NCT02215252). These results cannot separate inadequate block at the nerve from a target that does not matter. No other Nav1.7 drug succeeded in erythromelalgia. The index trial had n=5, no statistical comparison and a small numerical difference, so it could not answer the question (F7 secondary). Engagement is unmeasured, so the code is U.

In the dental pain trial (NCT01529346), PF-05089771 at 150–1600 mg showed only small, overlapping differences from placebo, while ibuprofen clearly separated. Plasma exposure was characterised in humans: modelling, later confirmed by observed single-ascending-dose data, put a 1 g dose at about 12x Nav1.7 IC50 at Cmax (PMID:26895021). No direct human measure of Nav1.7 engagement or a downstream nerve biomarker is in the bundle. Negative evoked-pain models (PMID:31642607), the DPN trial (NCT02215252) and the uninformative n=5 erythromelalgia study (NCT01769274) are clinical readouts, not pillar evidence. Doses were not tolerability-capped. With engagement no_human_data, nothing separates inadequate channel block at nociceptor sites from Nav1.7 irrelevance, so the code is U.

The index BASIC trial (NCT01723982) missed its primary endpoint. Ongoing implantation was 27.1% with barusiban vs 28.2% with placebo (OR 1.1, p=0.70). The sponsor's patent blames an interaction with day of transfer: no benefit for day-3 cleavage-stage embryos, but OR 2.3 (p=0.027) for day-5 blastocysts. That is benefit confined to a subgroup, so F3. I found no human data on drug levels, receptor occupancy or exposure. The only functional evidence is a meta-analysis table reporting fewer uterine contractions with IV barusiban than placebo (P<0.001) in oocyte donors (NCT00587327), measured before the index trial. That was in healthy donors and by a different route, not in infertile patients or with the subcutaneous dosing used in the index trial. Engagement itself is unmeasured, so U is a secondary code.

The index trial was an open-label safety extension, ended because the parent REFALS trial (NCT03505021, PMID:34536404) missed its supine SVC endpoint (p=0.83). Exposure was adequate: oral bioavailability was about 85% (PMID:8907132). Pharmacodynamic engagement is evident in humans at comparable oral doses. Oral 0.5 mg four times daily gave a moderate positive inotropic effect (PMID:15107600). In ALS patients, dose-related heart-rate rises and headache appeared in phase 2 (PMID:31315908) and in the extension (NCT03948178; HR +10-15 bpm). Doses used (1-2 mg/day) were at the tolerated level (NCT00698763). Diaphragm efficiency was unchanged in ventilated patients (PMID:31576436). Despite a pharmacologically active drug, no respiratory or functional benefit followed, pointing to the mechanism not driving the disease as tested. The index trial itself was not an efficacy test (F9).

Plasma exposure in heart failure patients is well characterized, with 84-85% oral bioavailability (PMID:8907132, PMID:12814448). No direct troponin C binding assay exists in the bundle. I rated engagement adequate because the functional readout of calcium sensitization was clear and dose-dependent: ejection fraction rose from 54% to 73% in healthy volunteers (PMID:7867680), and QS2i shortened in NYHA III-IV heart failure after both IV and 2 mg oral dosing (PMID:12940594). Oral doses up to 1 mg/day were tolerated (NCT00698763). This evidence predates the index trial, but none of it comes from HFpEF patients. Despite established inotropic and vasodilatory pharmacology, exercise PCWP did not change meaningfully (-1.9 vs -0.5 mmHg) in NCT03541603. That points to F2. The small trial (n=35) with wide variability adds a possible design limitation (F7).

In the index AML/MDS trial (NCT00637052; PMID:22139909), plasma PK showed low clearance and a half-life over 90 h, so exposure was adequate. Monopolar spindles, the direct mechanistic consequence of KSP inhibition, were seen in blood mononuclear cells of these leukemia patients. Grade 3-4 myelosuppression in 33/36 patients fits antimitotic activity. Taken together, target engagement is shown in the disease, though only qualitatively. Engagement was also confirmed in solid-tumor biopsies (PMID:25684345). Despite dosing to the MTD, the authors report a relative lack of clinical activity and halted AML development. The mechanism therefore appears not to drive meaningful antileukemic benefit, which supports F2. Because spindle effects were not quantified in blasts, partial engagement cannot be excluded, so F1a is listed as secondary.

In the index AML/MDS trial (PMID:22139909), plasma PK showed substantial exposure (low clearance, half-life >90 h) at the MTD of 4.5 mg/m2/cycle. Monopolar spindles, the direct mechanistic consequence of KSP inhibition, were observed in blood mononuclear cells of these patients. Near-universal grade 3/4 myelosuppression (33/36) is consistent with antimitotic pathway activity. Monopolar spindles in solid-tumor biopsies (PMID:25684345) and responses in myeloma (NCT00821249) confirm the molecule engages KSP at these doses. Despite this, there was a 'relative lack of clinical activity' and antileukemic development was halted. This suggests KSP inhibition does not drive meaningful benefit in AML/MDS. Engagement evidence comes from the index trial itself, not from before it, and the cohort was mostly AML (only 2 MDS).

In the index trial (NCT00883896), fezakinumab (anti-IL-22) did not beat placebo on ACR20 at any of three subcutaneous doses, and there was no dose-response. Two Phase 1 PK/PD studies were run in healthy volunteers (NCT00447681, NCT00434746), but they posted no results, and the searches found no published human data on drug exposure, IL-22 neutralisation or downstream biomarkers. Nothing was found in RA patients at all. The later atopic dermatitis study (NCT01941537; JACI 2018) reported skin transcriptomic changes, but only in patients with high baseline IL-22. That is a different disease, a different tissue and an intravenous regimen, and it came after the RA trial. No other IL-22 drug has worked in RA. The sources give no reason for stopping, so we cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage IL-22 or whether IL-22 simply doesn't drive RA.

The psoriasis index trial (NCT01510951, n=9) had a safety primary endpoint and posted no results, so the bundle has no psoriasis-specific data. In other diseases, AMG 811 showed dose-proportional PK and target-mediated disposition with serum IFN-γ (PMID:25213774). It produced dose-related CXCL10 reductions and lowered the IFN-γ blockade signature in blood and in lesional skin (PMID:26138472, PMID:28118537, PMID:29018537). It was well tolerated up to 180 mg, yet showed no clinical benefit in SLE or DLE. Engagement and pathway effects were adequate in skin and blood without efficacy, which points to IFN-γ not driving disease (F2). This is inferred across indications, and the index trial itself was a safety study (F9), so confidence is low.

In LUMINA-1 (NCT03536754), no CCX140 dose lowered UPCR compared with placebo, and there were no safety problems. The sponsor said only that the data offered no productive way forward, and the follow-on trial NCT03703908 was ended because the program was not advancing. My searches found no human data on CCX140 exposure, CCR2 occupancy, or pathway biomarkers. Its CCR2 activity in human monocytes was shown only in vitro, and its efficacy in knock-in mice does not count. A review says 5 mg/day lowered albuminuria in diabetic nephropathy (NCT01447147), but that trial's registered primary endpoint was safety, so it cannot support inferring engagement. Propagermanium is still investigational, so F1b does not apply. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged CCR2 apart from a target that does not drive FSGS, so the code is U.

In NCT00686998, AZD2624 (pavinetant) 40 mg did not improve PANSS over 28 days, while olanzapine did, so the trial was able to detect an antipsychotic effect. Engagement of hypothalamic NK3 receptors is shown in humans. LH and testosterone fell with dose in healthy volunteers and in patients with schizophrenia (JCEM), and modelling from three Phase 1 studies (PMID:26626581) fitted plasma exposure to testosterone suppression. At 40 mg BID, LH fell by about half in PCOS (NCT01872078). The investigators concluded that NK3 antagonism has no therapeutic role in acute schizophrenia. No dose cap from side effects was reported, so F2 fits best. Confidence is medium because no PET occupancy or CSF data show the drug reaching or blocking NK3 receptors in the brain regions tied to schizophrenia, beyond the hypothalamic hormone readout.

The plozalizumab plus nivolumab arm of NCT02723006 was closed for lack of clinical benefit: 6 of 9 patients progressed (PMID:41049010). Tolerability did not cap the dose (one patient had DLTs per the paper). Human engagement was shown before the index trial, but only in RA: free CCR2 on CD14+ monocytes fell by 57–94% (PMID:18576354). Human plasma PK of TAK-202 is documented (PMID:41888610). No pathway or engagement data exist in melanoma, and the melanoma dose is not given, so comparability is uncertain. In RA, engagement without synovial or clinical effect suggests CCR2 blockade alone does little. The arm had only 9 non-randomized patients, so the futility call is weak (F7 secondary).

In the psoriasis trial, serum namilumab exposure rose in proportion to dose (PMID:30207587). Engagement was not measured in psoriasis. A total GM-CSF profile appears only in healthy volunteers, published after the index trial (PMID:30168415). Engagement is inferred adequate because namilumab 150 mg, the top dose here, met the DAS28-CRP endpoint in rheumatoid arthritis through the same systemic GM-CSF neutralization (NCT02379091, PMID:30999929). That trial, however, started after the index trial. In psoriasis, no dose separated from placebo on PASI75, and no dose was capped by tolerability. Tissue cell subsets and psoriasis-relevant cytokines were unchanged. The authors conclude that GM-CSF blockade is not critical for the key inflammatory pathways of psoriasis (PMID:30207587). The target does not drive the disease.

Namilumab showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and changes in total GM-CSF in healthy volunteers (PMID:30168415, NCT02354599). It met its RA primary endpoint at 150 mg, with a dose-response on DAS28-CRP (NCT02379091, PMID:30999929). Systemic GM-CSF neutralization at a comparable dose therefore has inferred adequate engagement and pathway effect. No engagement data exist in axSpA patients. In axSpA (NCT03622658), the ASAS20 response was numerically lower on namilumab than placebo (39% vs 50%). The drug also failed in psoriasis (NCT02129777). This suggests GM-CSF does not drive axial SpA as tested. The 6-patient placebo arm limits inference (F7 secondary), but the point estimate shows no trend toward benefit, and tolerability did not limit the dose.

Inhaled ciprofloxacin acted on its antibacterial target in bronchiectasis patients. The Phase 2 DPI trial cut sputum bacterial load by 2.37 log10 CFU/g versus placebo (NCT00930982, PMID:23516961), before the index trial started, though with a different formulation. In the ORBIT trials, symptom changes tracked bacterial load reduction (PMID:32554534). Exposure is inferred_adequate because the identical regimen met the primary endpoint in the twin ORBIT-4 trial (NCT02104245, HR 0.72). ORBIT-3 missed its endpoint (HR 0.99). The sources attribute the divergence to heterogeneous microbial and inflammatory endotypes and geographic differences. After adjusting for these, the two trials gave similar estimates (PMID:40664229). This points to population heterogeneity (F3), with trial-to-trial variability as a design factor (F7).

Inhaled ciprofloxacin DPI missed its 28-day FEV1 endpoint in CF (NCT00645788: -1.0 and -0.62 vs -2.2 % predicted, p=0.076). The bundle has no CF sputum bacterial load or lung PK data. In non-CF bronchiectasis the same DPI cut airway bacterial load by about 2.4 log10 CFU/g vs placebo (NCT00930982). One DPI dosing arm met the exacerbation endpoint (NCT01764841), and an inhaled liposomal formulation also met it (NCT02104245). That supports inferred adequate airway exposure, engagement and pathway effect. However, this evidence comes from another disease and was registered after the index trial began. With engagement inferred adequate, F2 is the best fit. The borderline p-value and short FEV1 window suggest F7 or F4 may also apply. No source states the reason, so confidence is low.

Phase 1 data show dose-proportional plasma exposure and reduced tumor pERK at the MTD, both as monotherapy (PMID:23434733) and with sorafenib (5/6 biopsied; PMID:26644411). These studies were registered before the index trial, but the biopsied patients were not shown to have HCC. In the index trial (NCT01204177; PMID:25294897), almost all patients needed dose modifications for adverse events. The authors state that grade 3 toxicity 'may have contributed to limited treatment effect', so tolerability capped delivered dose below the level at which engagement was shown. They also attribute benefit to RAS-mutant patients (F3). However, RAS-selected follow-up trials gave modest results (PFS 1.5–1.9 months; PMID:29950351), which weakens the subgroup explanation.

A PET study in healthy volunteers showed more than 80% 5-HT6 receptor occupancy at both 30 and 60 mg, so brain exposure and target engagement were adequate. The NCT02079246 protocol says this occupancy study, then 'in reporting', and simulations in AD patients were used to pick the phase 3 doses, which puts it before the index trial (NCT01955161). Engagement was not measured in AD patients, and no human pathway biomarker was found. Despite the high occupancy, all three phase 3 trials showed no ADAS-Cog benefit (NCT01955161, NCT02006641, NCT02006654; PMID:29318278). Commentators asked whether the phase 3 doses were lower than the 90 mg used in phase 2, but tolerability did not cap the dose. Antagonizing 5-HT6 does not appear to improve cognition in AD as tested: F2. The phase 2 LADDER result (NCT01019421) was probably a false positive.

I found no human data showing idalopirdine engaged its target. There are no human PET occupancy, CSF or pathway biomarker results. Receptor occupancy and brain exposure were measured only in rats (PMID:20569520). The human PET study (NCT03307993) was stopped for strategic reasons before it produced results. The schizophrenia trial (NCT00810667) never posted or published results, and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping. The Alzheimer's phase 2 trial met its endpoint at 90 mg/day (NCT01019421). That could suggest the target was engaged, but three phase 3 trials failed to repeat the result, and the schizophrenia dose is unknown. So the inference is unreliable. Nothing available separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter in this disease.

The index trial, ROMULUS (NCT01691898, PMID:30935953), was descriptive with no success threshold, so it did not fail an efficacy test. R-pina gave a 60% response rate and 26% complete responses in relapsed/refractory DLBCL, similar to R-pola, but responses were shorter (median DOR 6.2 vs 13.4 months). The sponsor took polatuzumab vedotin forward instead, citing its longer DOR and better overall benefit-risk. That makes this a choice between two of its own drugs, not proof the CD22 mechanism failed. Phase 1 (PMID:27601593) measured plasma PK at the 2.4 mg/kg RP2D, which was not capped by tolerability. No human CD22 occupancy or pathway biomarker data were found, so engagement is no_human_data.

The index trial ROMULUS (NCT01691898, PMID:30935953) was an open-label, descriptive phase 2 study with no prespecified success threshold, so its primary endpoint was not assessable as pass or fail. Pinatuzumab vedotin plus rituximab showed clear activity in follicular lymphoma (ORR 62%), but had a lower CR rate (5% vs 45%) and shorter DOR (6.5 vs 9.4-12.9 months) than the sister ADC polatuzumab, which alone was carried into later cohorts. This reads as a head-to-head selection within the sponsor's portfolio, not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9), with an implied business or prioritisation choice (F8). The bundle has no human PK, CD22 occupancy or pathway data, and the phase 1 trial (NCT01209130) posted no results, so all pillars are no_human_data.

Human plasma exposure at 60 mg BID, the index dose, is characterized (PMID:33128299, PMID:40284519; modeling suggests full target engagement even at 20 mg BID). No direct PARP-inhibition data appear in the bundle. Engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same dose met response endpoints in ovarian cancer (ORR 68.3%, NCT03333915) and BRCA-mutated breast cancer (NCT03575065) via PARP1/2 in tumor tissue. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not limited. In PARALLEL-303 (NCT03427814, PMID:37260158), maintenance PFS was 3.7 vs 2.1 months (HR 0.8, p=0.14), with no OS benefit. PARP inhibition therefore did not drive benefit in unselected platinum-responsive gastric cancer (F2). The lack of HRD selection may also have contributed (F3), though the sources do not state this.

In the Phase 1 study (NCT05247970, PMID:39832041), S-309309 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure, with similar PK in adults with and without obesity. The MOGAT2-inhibition pharmacodynamic biomarker, dicarboxylic acid (18:1), rose significantly in both groups, including obese participants. Tolerability was acceptable, with no AE discontinuations, so dose was not capped. I treat the biomarker as evidence of target engagement. No separate downstream pathway effect (e.g., fat absorption or satiety hormones) is reported. The 24-week Phase 2 weight-loss trial (NCT05925114) posted no results and gave no stop reason, so failure is inferred from the program halting. With engagement shown, F2 (MOGAT2 inhibition does not drive meaningful weight loss) fits best. Confidence is low because the bundle is thin and the biomarker magnitude is not quantified.

The index trial NCT02403323 is an open-label extension, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because the program was discontinued after mixed results in the parent studies, with no safety concerns, so F9 is primary. Target engagement was shown directly: full β7 occupancy in adult UC before the index trial (PMID:22717454, PMID:29178491). Near-complete occupancy was shown in paediatric Crohn's and UC patients, but only later (PMID:34849918). Pathway is inferred_adequate because the drug met induction endpoints in UC (NCT02163759, NCT02100696). In parent BERGAMOT (NCT02394028), induction failed but maintenance succeeded, suggesting a mechanism limitation (F2; PMID:38310086). TNF-experienced patients did worse at induction (F3; PMID:40401357).

The index trial is an open-label extension. It was terminated because the program was discontinued after mixed efficacy in the parent Phase 3 studies, with no safety concerns (NCT02118584). Exposure in UC patients is well characterized (PMID:35851998). Full, dose-related β7 receptor occupancy in UC patients was published in 2013, before the index trial (PMID:22717454; EC90 1.3 µg/mL, PMID:29178491), and near-complete occupancy was also shown in children (PMID:34849918). No dose cap from tolerability. Despite adequate engagement, benefit was modest and inconsistent. Induction met in NCT02100696 and NCT02163759 but missed in NCT02171429. Maintenance failed (NCT02165215; HICKORY maintenance), and etrolizumab was not superior to infliximab (NCT02136069). This fits F2: target engaged, benefit insufficient. F9 is secondary because the index trial itself was not an efficacy test.

The ESCAPE trial (NCT01357395) missed its Stage 1 response bar in platinum-refractory SCLC, and Astex then ended development. No evidence found shows the drug hitting KIT, MET or PDGFRA in humans. Exposure: the original capsule gave low, variable drug levels (PMID:23178951). The lipid capsule (300 mg every 8 h) reached a 'presumed therapeutic level' in healthy volunteers (PMID:22349808), but no efficacy result backs this, so the exposure label is a loose call. Pathway: lower RAD51 in skin biopsies (PMID:24849582) supports the DNA-repair mechanism in another tissue, not in SCLC tumours. I could not read the trial paper's analysis of baseline RAD51 against response. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. Astex pointed to how hard truly refractory SCLC is to treat (possible F3).

In older adults, PK showed target-mediated drug disposition, which indicates the antibody bound ActRII (PMID:36527600). The expected downstream effect, dose-dependent gains in lean mass and thigh muscle volume, appeared in healthy elderly (PMID:33264516) and in muscle-wasting patients: sIBM and COPD cachexia, both registered before the index trial (NCT01423110, NCT01669174), and hip-fracture atrophy (NCT02152761). Tolerability did not cap the dose; 700 mg was tested. Yet SPPB did not improve at any dose in sarcopenia (NCT02333331), off-drug follow-up stayed null (NCT02468674), and 6MWD was flat in sIBM phase 3 (NCT01925209). The mechanism works but does not translate into physical function. F4 is a possible alternative; the sources do not blame the endpoint.

Human PK showed plasma exposure and target-mediated drug disposition, which is evidence of ActRII binding (PMID:36527600, PMID:33264516). In sIBM patients, a pilot trial registered before the index trial (NCT01423110, PMID:25381300) showed a significant increase in thigh muscle volume and lean body mass. In RESILIENT, lean body mass rose dose-dependently (PMID:31761834), and muscle mass gains persisted in the extensions (PMID:32690797). Yet 6MWD did not differ from placebo at any dose (NCT01925209, PMID:31397289), and mobility declined over 2 years in all arms (PMID:33597289). Tolerability was good, so the dose was not capped. The target was engaged and the pathway moved, but increasing muscle mass via ActRII blockade did not translate into functional benefit in sIBM.

BMS-955176 is a maturation inhibitor targeting the Gag CA-SP1 cleavage site (PMID:30352054). It produced dose-related HIV-1 RNA declines of about 1.3 log10 by Day 11 in infected patients (NCT01803074, before the index trial), showing exposure, functional engagement and the pathway effect in this disease. In the index trial, 76-83% of patients on BMS-955176 reached <40 c/mL versus 77% on efavirenz, so efficacy did not fail. The trial and the treatment-experienced study (NCT02386098) were terminated for GI intolerability, which ran 3-4-fold above efavirenz. The index trial was also stopped for emergent NRTI-backbone resistance. This is molecule-specific toxicity rather than a failed efficacy test, hence F6, with F9 secondary.

Exposure to the drug in plasma was shown: the prodrug converts fully to LY404039 (PMID:25382826). At 40 mg BID, CSF monoamine metabolites rose in healthy volunteers (PMID:21847569). However, the ketamine phMRI challenge reduced the BOLD signal only at the single 160 mg dose, the highest tested (PMID:29564482). In a later NIMH-funded RCT, a high dose four times the pivotal dose eased ketamine-induced symptoms but did not significantly suppress the pharmacoBOLD target-engagement measure. The investigators concluded that the doses used in Lilly's trials (40–80 mg BID; NCT01086748, NCT01307800) were probably too low. All of this functional engagement evidence came from healthy volunteers and was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not limit the dose. Other explanations exist: an HTR2A subgroup signal and high placebo response (PMID:26044978, PMID:21508856).

The bundle shows teriparatide 20 μg SC reaches plasma (PMID:20953593, PMID:27007999). It is FDA-approved for osteoporosis, where it reduced fractures and raised BMD through PTH1R in bone (PMID:21938381), so engagement in the bone compartment is inferred_adequate. Pathway effects are shown in humans: transient serum calcium rise, P1NP increase and BMD gains (PMID:20953593, PMID:32676823). No engagement data exist in acute hip fracture patients. Despite an established anabolic mechanism, the index trial showed no benefit on revision surgery (87% vs 86% free of revision, NCT01473589). The sister trial was numerically worse (74% vs 93%, NCT01473602). This suggests PTH1R agonism does not drive femoral neck fracture healing outcomes as tested. No tolerability limitation was evident.

In the index first-in-human dose escalation (NCT00948467; PMID:27650277), plasma PK was characterized up to 22 mg (MTD 16 mg). Maximum PBMC pERK inhibition of 46-97% was seen at doses ≥8.4 mg, which is below the MTD, so tolerability did not cap engagement. The authors call this the anticipated, sustained pharmacodynamic effect. These pharmacodynamic data come from cancer patients but from the index trial itself, so they were not available before it started. Despite adequate MEK engagement, only 2 of 41 patients had partial responses, both in cutaneous melanoma, and further investigation was not planned. That supports F2. The index trial was a safety and MTD study rather than an efficacy test (F9), and it enrolled a mixed, largely uveal melanoma and colon cancer population (F3).

In RRMS (NCT00882999), Gd-enhancing lesions were not reduced at any dose up to 120 mg Q4W, with no dose trend. No MS PK or PD data are in the bundle. Engagement is inferred_adequate because subcutaneous tabalumab 120 mg Q2W met its SLE primary endpoint through systemic BAFF neutralization (PMID:26293163). The pathway is adequate elsewhere: B-cell, immunoglobulin and B-cell gene expression changes in SLE (PMID:27723281) and CD20+ B-cell lowering in RA despite no benefit (PMID:26535134). This supports peripheral BAFF blockade not driving MS lesion activity (F2). A caveat is that the MS trial's top dose matched only the SLE Q4W regimen, which narrowly missed (p=0.051), so under-dosing (F1a) cannot be excluded. Confidence is low.

The index open-label extension (NCT01488708) was not itself an efficacy test; it was terminated for lack of efficacy after the ILLUMINATE trials. ILLUMINATE-1 (NCT01196091) missed SRI-5, and ILLUMINATE-2 (NCT01205438) met it only with Q2W dosing. Exposure in SLE patients was documented, with target-mediated clearance (PMID:26648084). In SLE patients, BAFF blockade lowered B cells, IgG and anti-dsDNA, raised complement, and shifted B-cell gene expression (PMID:26338095, 26293163, 27723281). This evidence was published after the index trial started. Tolerability did not cap the dose. With engagement and pathway shown, the modest clinical benefit fits F2. Secondary readings: SRI-5 insensitivity (PMID:35962577, F4) and endotype heterogeneity (PMID:37845772, F3). Belimumab's approval tempers a pure target-level conclusion.

Exposure in RA patients was shown by PK, with non-linear clearance attributed to target-mediated BAFF binding (PMID:26648084). B-cell changes were seen in RA in phase 1 and 2 trials started before the index trial (PMID:23359344, PMID:23268367; NCT00785928). In the phase 3 RA trials, tabalumab significantly lowered CD20+ B cells and serum immunoglobulins versus placebo (PMID:26203826, PMID:26535134), so pathway blockade is adequate. The same regimen family met SRI-5 in SLE (PMID:26293163). Despite this, ACR20 was flat in the index trial (29.7%/32.8% vs 25.1%), FLEX-O (NCT01202760) and the TNF-IR trial (NCT01202773). Authors conclude BAFF blockade alone is insufficient to reduce RA activity, which fits F2 (target does not drive the disease). There was no safety signal or dose cap.

In the index trial (NCT01602224), tabalumab 100 or 300 mg added to bortezomib/dexamethasone gave no PFS benefit (6.6 and 7.5 vs 7.6 months). No BAFF neutralization or pathway readout in myeloma patients appears in the bundle. The Japanese MM phase 1 (PMID:27350068) reports only PK, safety, and an uncontrolled response rate. Engagement and pathway are inferred from SLE: 120 mg Q2W met SRI-5 in ILLUMINATE-2 (PMID:26293163, NCT01205438) with pharmacodynamic BAFF blockade (B-cell and immunoglobulin changes; PMID:27723281). RA also showed B-cell lowering (PMID:26535134). The 300 mg dose was tolerable, so dose was not limited. Confidence is low because the bone-marrow compartment is unverified; U remains plausible.

In the Phase 1 trial (NCT01119456), narnatumab had a short half-life (<7 days). After Cycle 2, no patient except one at 30 mg/kg q2w kept concentrations above 140 μg/mL, the level linked to antitumor activity in animal models (PMID:28161886). Dose was not escalated past 40 mg/kg q2w even though there was only one DLT. The stated reasons were suboptimal exposure and published data that RON splice variants sit in the cytoplasm, out of reach of a monoclonal antibody. Exposure was therefore shown inadequate, and the sources say so directly. The bundle has no human data on engagement or the downstream pathway. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The mechanism was never properly tested, so F1a.

rFXIII is a systemic replacement protein. It met its pivotal bleeding-prevention endpoint in congenital FXIII deficiency (NCT00713648), which predates the index trial. So plasma exposure, FXIII replacement and the downstream effect are inferred adequate in that setting, but the bundle gives no UC dose to confirm comparability. No FXIII levels or activity were reported in UC patients. The index trial (NCT01706159) was terminated because 'screening data did not support the medical hypothesis', with remission 1/13 vs 1/5 on placebo. This points to FXIII replacement not driving UC as tested, possibly because the patients selected were not FXIII-deficient. The tiny, early-terminated trial (n=18 analysed) could not answer the question robustly. The cardiac-surgery failure (NCT00914589) also shows replacement lacks benefit outside deficiency.

Phase 1 in advanced solid tumors (NCT00816400, PMID:25149088) showed measurable nonlinear plasma PK and a dose-dependent rise in plasma PDGF-AA. PMID:33210183 validates this as an indirect readout of PDGFRα occupancy. No DLTs occurred and the MTD was not reached, so dose was not capped. That engagement evidence came from mixed tumors, not NSCLC, and was published after the index trial began. No downstream pathway marker is in the bundle. Despite engagement, the drug added to carboplatin/paclitaxel gave worse PFS (HR 2.2, p=0.027) with more deaths and serious AEs, and the trial stopped for safety (NCT01268059). Single-agent activity was minimal in phase 1 and in glioblastoma (NCT01268566). This points to PDGFRα blockade not driving NSCLC, with a safety signal contributing.

In the Phase 1 trial in solid tumours (NCT00816400, PMID:25149088), MEDI-575 raised plasma PDGF-AA in a dose-dependent way, and no MTD was reached. PMID:33210183 validates PDGF-AA accumulation as an indirect read-out of PDGFRα occupancy, which supported dose selection. This counts as adequate systemic engagement at the 25 mg/kg Q3W dose used in the index trial, without dose limitation. It was not shown in glioblastoma patients, and tumour or brain penetration and downstream pathway effects were not measured. The index trial missed: PFS-6 was 15.4%, there were no responses and median PFS was 1.4 months (PMID:27844311). So the PDGFRα blockade tested did not drive recurrent GBM. Tumour PDGFRα expression varied widely and did not correlate with PFS, which raises a possible selection issue (F3).

The index trial NCT02143635 was a first-in-human dose-escalation study with a DLT primary endpoint, not an efficacy test. It met its objective: RDEs were defined, with 10.3% ORR in solid tumors and activity in AML (PMID:34862243). Plasma exposure was characterized and tumor-static concentrations were modeled. Induction of GDF-15, a p53-pathway marker, in patients supports MDM2 engagement and pathway activation, but not specifically in liposarcoma and only published after the index trial (PMID:33554304). The liposarcoma combination with ribociclib showed early activity, limited by hematologic toxicity consistent with on-target effects (PMID:34921024). Several later trials were stopped for business or sponsor reasons (NCT03940352, NCT05447663), which suggests a portfolio decision rather than an efficacy failure.

The index trial NCT02291614 was a Phase 1 dose escalation whose primary endpoints were descriptive safety counts. It saw no DLTs up to 12,800 µg/day and was terminated for immunogenicity and a business decision, so it was not an efficacy test (F9). In patients with GI adenocarcinoma, 89Zr-AMG 211 PET (PMID:30745297) showed intact drug in plasma and CD3-mediated uptake in lymphoid tissue. It also showed clear but heterogeneous tumor uptake, with apparent target saturation during treatment, which supports exposure and binding at about 2 mg. That PET work was published after the index trial started. No downstream T-cell activation or pathway biomarker is reported. The business decision (F8) and immunogenicity possibly limiting exposure (F1a) are secondary contributors.

In T2DM patients, oral tregopil produced dose-proportional insulin Cmax rises and dose-related cuts in postprandial glucose (PMID:20590742), with a rapid but modest 13-18% glucose drop that was sensitive to meal timing and absorption (PMID:31392840). So the drug acted on the receptor in this disease, but only weakly. In the 24-week index trial, HbA1c rose on both tregopil doses (8.23→8.38, 8.10→8.21) while it fell on subcutaneous insulin aspart (8.07→7.29). INSR agonism is validated in T2DM: aspart, glargine, degludec and others are approved. The failure therefore lies in this oral molecule's insufficient sustained exposure and receptor activation, not in the target. This is F1b, with F1a as secondary for inadequate exposure. Dose was not limited by tolerability.

The index trial NCT02802228 (n=30) had only safety primary endpoints: adverse events were 23 on ifetroban vs 2 on placebo, with no grade 4/5 events and no deaths. It was not an efficacy test of the drug, so F9 applies. The bundle has no human data on exposure, TBXA2R engagement or pathway effect in portal hypertension. NCT01436500 in hepatorenal syndrome reported PK parameters but no values are shown. NCT03028350 in AERD missed its endpoint without engagement data. PMID:11369819 is an animal study. If the program is read as an efficacy failure, it is indeterminate (U), because nothing separates non-engagement from a target that does not matter. No dose limitation is shown.

In the index trial NCT03028350, ifetroban did no better than placebo on SNOT-22 (−6.7 vs −13.7). The investigator brochure, cited in the protocol of the sister AERD trial NCT03326063, describes earlier healthy-volunteer studies. In them, every dose from 10 mg up blocked platelet aggregation triggered by the TP agonist U46619. It also blocked arachidonic-acid-induced aggregation and doubled bleeding time above 10 mg, so engagement and a downstream effect were shown in humans long before 2017. No plasma levels were found, so exposure is inferred from those responses. In AERD patients, 200 mg/day was well tolerated but made aspirin-induced nasal symptoms and the drop in FEV1 worse. The investigators concluded that TP blockade disturbs eicosanoid balance rather than helping. Engagement was not measured in AERD patients themselves. The evidence points to the TP target not driving AERD in the way assumed.

I found no human data on VB-201 drug levels, CD14 or TLR2 binding, or inhibition of monocyte migration. The company's 2015 topline release says psoriasis patients on 80 mg or 160 mg did no better than placebo on PASI 50. Placebo response at week 16 was 38%, against 26.4% on VB-201, and the two doses performed alike. VBL stopped development in psoriasis and ulcerative colitis (NCT01837420, NCT01839214) but gave no reason. A substudy reported less vascular inflammation in psoriasis patients. This is a distant downstream effect, not a direct measure of engagement. Inxight says a separate atherosclerosis phase 2 missed on vascular inflammation. Engagement was never measured, so I can't tell a drug that didn't engage its target from a target that doesn't drive psoriasis. That makes the code U.

NCT01839214 tested oral VB-201 at 160 mg daily in 112 people with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis and missed its remission endpoint. Week-12 remission was 10.5% on drug vs 15.1% on placebo. The psoriasis trial (NCT01837420) also failed, with no difference between 80 and 160 mg. The drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. I found no human data on drug levels, CD14/TLR2 engagement, or downstream biomarkers. The monocyte-migration data are in vitro or from animals, and no biomarker results from NCT01159730 turned up. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for the failure. It only said the disease is hard to treat and dropped the indication. With engagement unknown, there is no way to tell a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter. Code: U.

In healthy volunteers (NCT01496937, NCT01721980; PMID:26852904), GLPG0974 showed dose-proportional plasma exposure up to 400 mg/day. It produced substantial, sustained inhibition of acetate-stimulated neutrophil CD11b activation, an ex vivo FFA2 engagement and functional readout. It was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Those Phase 1 trials were registered before the index trial began. Engagement was not shown in ulcerative colitis patients. The index proof-of-concept trial (NCT01829321) posted no results, and its registered primary endpoints are safety only. With engagement adequate and the program halted, F2 (target not driving UC) fits best. However, the bundle does not show the efficacy data, and F9 (no efficacy primary endpoint) is also possible. Confidence is low.

In the first-in-human study (NCT01393990, PMID:26581242), ralimetinib plasma Cmax and AUC rose dose-dependently. A single dose inhibited p38-induced MAPKAP-K2 phosphorylation in PBMCs, which counts as target engagement, but only in a surrogate tissue of mixed advanced-cancer patients. No ovarian tumour data were shown, and the evidence was published in 2016, after the index trial started in 2012. No downstream pathway or cytokine data appear in the bundle. In the index trial (NCT01663857), 200 mg (the combination MTD) plus gemcitabine/carboplatin did not improve PFS: 10.25 vs 8.44 months, p=0.4. Serious AEs were higher (26/58 vs 12/52). Engagement was shown, so the mechanism likely does not drive benefit as tested. Confidence is low: engagement was unquantified and in surrogate tissue.

The index phase 2 trial (NCT01665391, PMID:29270487) was closed early with 36 of a planned 88 patients. The authors call it underpowered and recommend larger, adequately powered studies, so the trial could not answer the question (F7). Plasma exposure in FSGS patients was shown by phase 1 PK: half-life about 14 days, dose-proportional (PMID:21368745). Engagement was not measured directly. It is inferred from systemic sclerosis at comparable doses (1–5 mg/kg), where TGF-β-regulated skin genes (THBS1, SERPINE1, CTGF) fell significantly (PMID:26098215, NCT01284322). That evidence comes from a different disease and tissue, and kidney engagement is unshown. A mixed signal (only 1 mg/kg reduced proteinuria) leaves F2 as a possible secondary code.

The index trial, NCT01103037, was not a failed efficacy readout. The sponsor terminated it after enrolling 8 patients, and no results were posted. The Novartis fevipiprant paper (PMID:28523115, PMC full text) reports that QAV680 was safe in Phase 1 and gave positive proof-of-concept results in allergic rhinitis (NCT00784732, NCT01103050). It says the twice- or four-times-daily dosing was seen as a limitation for patient convenience and compliance. Novartis therefore sought a follow-up compound with longer action, which became fevipiprant. This was a portfolio decision to replace QAV680 with a successor, not evidence of a failed mechanism. No human receptor-occupancy or pharmacodynamic data were found, so all three pillars have no human data. U is a secondary code because engagement was never established.

No results were posted for NCT00784732. Novartis's later papers say QAV680 did not fail in allergic rhinitis. They describe positive results in two proof-of-concept chamber studies (NCT00784732 and the cetirizine combination study NCT01103050), with lower nasal symptom scores. The reason given for moving on was that QAV680 had to be taken two or four times a day, which hurt convenience and compliance. Novartis replaced it with the follow-up compound fevipiprant, which can be taken once daily. The asthma trial NCT01103037 was ended by the sponsor with no reason stated. I found no human data on receptor occupancy, eosinophil shape-change inhibition or other target-engagement biomarkers. The healthy-volunteer PK appears only as an abstract title, so I could not judge exposure. The index readout was not an efficacy failure (F9), and the stop was a portfolio choice (F8).

Serum exposure in infants at 30 mg/kg was sustained: 110 mg/L at Day 29 and 15.9 mg/L at Day 150 (NCT02325791 Part A). The phase 3 publication found that every sequenced RSV-B isolate carried a two-amino-acid substitution in the suptavumab epitope on the F protein, which abolished binding. As a result, RSV-B breakthrough infections occurred throughout the season. RSV-A isolates were unchanged and were neutralized potently. Because the drug could not bind the circulating RSV-B strains, the F-protein neutralization mechanism was not properly tested across the population, which fits F1a (inadequate engagement). The bundle lists no other drug on this target, so F1b is a secondary code at most.

In the index trial NCT01153347, all three TC-5214 doses (0.5, 2 and 4 mg BID) were essentially identical to placebo on MADRS. The other Phase 3 trials (NCT01157078, NCT01180400, NCT01197508) and the Phase 2 trial NCT01288079 also failed. The bundle has human plasma PK (PMID:24760402), but no human data on brain penetration, nicotinic receptor occupancy or a central pharmacodynamic biomarker. Pages found by search report only the efficacy misses, not why they happened. No other drug on this target has succeeded in MDD, and the drug has no approved use through this target to infer engagement from. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not drive depression, so the code is U.

In the Phase 2b OAB trial (NCT01868516; PMID:26073872), the 2 mg dose met only one of the two co-primary endpoints. It reduced micturition frequency (p=0.03) but not urge incontinence episodes (p=0.38), and Targacept stopped OAB development. Population PK work (PMID:24408516) shows systemic plasma exposure, which counts for a peripheral ganglionic nicotinic target. However, no source measures nicotinic receptor occupancy or blockade, or any downstream biomarker, in humans. Dry mouth and constipation rose with dose, which hints at an on-target autonomic effect, but these are not engagement measurements. The sponsor cited only the efficacy results, and tolerability was good, so dose was not limited. Because engagement is unmeasured, nothing separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT01279291 was a first-in-human dose-escalation safety study, not an efficacy test. In advanced cancer patients, plasma exposure rose in proportion to dose, and every dose (0.1–3 mg/kg) lowered serum free HB-EGF, generally below the limit of quantification (PMID:26507836). So systemic exposure and engagement were adequate in the disease population. That evidence was published in 2016, after the 2011 start. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. The study ended because of unpredictable neuropsychiatric toxicity: seizures, aphasia and confusion, seen even at 0.1 mg/kg. Its etiology was not understood, and monkey studies showed low brain penetration (PMID:26464296, PMID:26507836). Molecule-specific toxicity therefore ended the program (F6). Because the trial was not an efficacy failure, F9 also applies.

Human PET shows brain penetration and dose-dependent KOR occupancy, nearly saturating at 10 mg (NCT01232439 registered 2010; PMID:26628406). Plasma PK is dose-proportional and the drug was well tolerated up to 60 mg (PMID:24619932), so dose was not capped. Pathway effects were shown at 10 mg: increased ventral striatal fMRI reward activation (PMID:32231295) and ACTH/cortisol rises (PMID:28857070). All of this comes from healthy volunteers or other diseases, not smokers. The index smoking lab-model trial (NCT02641028) posted no results, and no source states why the program stopped. With engagement adequate and no smoking benefit evident, F2 is the best fit. Confidence is low because the bundle does not show the index readout.

The Phase 1 trial (PMID:24493831) showed linear PK from 4 to 30 mg/kg, a half-life of 8-12 days and no MTD. Modelling projected that 10-30 mg/kg would reach the target trough (PMID:23894056); the index used 10 mg/kg every 2 weeks. A sustained, dose-independent rise in circulating HGF in Phase 1 solid-tumour and NSCLC patients was described as a reproducible pharmacodynamic marker of onartuzumab activity (PMID:23536720). This supports adequate engagement, though not shown specifically in gastric cancer. No downstream pathway data exist in humans. Despite this, neither the Phase 2 (NCT01590719, PMID:27401892) nor METGastric showed benefit in ITT or MET-positive patients. This points to MET not driving the disease as tested. Secondary: a non-significant MET 2+/3+ trend (HR 0.64, p=.06) and early sponsor-stopped enrollment (PMID:27918764).

Phase I showed linear PK at 4–30 mg/kg, no MTD reached, and RP2D 15 mg/kg was within the modeled range for target trough exposure (PMID:24493831, PMID:23894056), so the dose was not capped. A sustained, exposure-independent rise in circulating HGF, consistent with ligand displacement from MET, was shown in phase I and in NSCLC patients in the phase II trial (PMID:23536720). This counts as engagement evidence, but it was published after the index trial started. No downstream MET signaling data exist. Despite engagement, MetLung did not deliver a benefit, and the drug failed across gastric, colorectal and breast cancer trials. The phase II benefit was confined to MET IHC-positive patients (PMID:24687921), suggesting the selection biomarker may not have captured MET-driven disease (F3).

Exposure is adequate. Phase I showed linear PK from 4–30 mg/kg, MTD not reached, and the index dose (10 mg/kg) sits within the modelled efficacious range (PMID:24493831, PMID:23894056). Engagement rests only on an acute, sustained, dose-independent rise in circulating HGF in phase I solid-tumour and NSCLC patients, which the authors call a PD marker of onartuzumab activity (PMID:23536720). It is indirect and not measured in CRC, and the label is a judgment call: it is not a direct measurement, and inferred_adequate here does not rest on a clinical efficacy win. No tumour pathway marker was reported. PFS was not improved in the ITT or MET IHC-positive groups, and MET IHC was not predictive (PMID:28209746). On this weak engagement evidence, F2 is favoured over U.

Onartuzumab plus paclitaxel, with or without bevacizumab, did not improve PFS in TNBC, and outcomes trended worse (NCT01186991, PMID:26202594). Exposure was adequate. PK was linear, the MTD was not reached (PMID:24493831), and serum levels reached 1,200 µg/mL in this trial (PMID:25542267), far above the projected 15 µg/mL target (PMID:23894056). Engagement is supported by a consistent, sustained rise in circulating HGF, a pharmacodynamic marker of drug activity. This was shown in phase I solid tumors and NSCLC, not breast cancer, and published after the index trial started (PMID:23536720). No downstream pathway data in humans are given. The authors note that 88% of tumors were MET-negative, which points to patient selection. The NSCLC benefit was confined to MET-positive patients (NCT00854308). The trial was also hypothesis-generating and underpowered.

The index trial NCT01897038 was a 9-patient Phase 1 safety, DLT and PK study of onartuzumab alone or with sorafenib in advanced HCC. It had no efficacy endpoint and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug. Pillars: the first-in-human study (PMID:24493831) showed linear PK, a 15 mg/kg RP2D and no MTD reached (not dose-limited), consistent with the trough target projected in PMID:23894056. A sustained circulating HGF rise was reported as a pharmacodynamic marker in solid tumors and NSCLC (PMID:23536720), but not in HCC. There is no human downstream pathway evidence. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, and the drug failed in other indications.

In GO27819 (NCT01632228; PMID:27918718), adding onartuzumab to bevacizumab did not improve PFS (HR 1.06) or OS. The dose was 15 mg/kg every 3 weeks. Phase I found no MTD, so tolerability did not limit the dose (PMID:24493831). The only human pharmacodynamic signal was a rise in circulating HGF in patients with other solid tumors and NSCLC. That rise did not depend on dose (PMID:23536720). Nothing in the bundle shows onartuzumab getting into GBM tissue past the blood-brain barrier, occupying MET in the tumor, or blocking MET signaling there. With no human engagement data in this disease, a drug that never reached its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Exploratory benefit in patients with high HGF or unmethylated MGMT points to a possible patient-selection issue (F3).

In the index Phase 2 trial (NCT00876421, PMID:24018240), ONO-8539 at 30–300 mg twice daily did no better than placebo on micturitions, urgency or voided volume. Tolterodine, the active control, did beat placebo, so the trial was able to detect a treatment effect. Tolerability was similar to placebo, so the dose was not limited. I found no human data on EP1 occupancy, bladder exposure or a bladder biomarker. The only human pharmacology is a later (2017) healthy-volunteer study in which the drug reduced acid-induced heartburn (NCT01705275). That suggests some systemic EP1 activity, but it is a different tissue, it is not a direct engagement measure, and it came after the index trial. The investigators read the result as a minimal role for EP1 in overactive bladder (pointing to F2). Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be ruled out, so the code is U.

No human measurements of drug exposure in oesophageal tissue, EP1 receptor occupancy or EP1 biomarkers turned up. Neither trial on the bundle's NCT list (NCT01705275, NCT01707901) posted results. In a separate healthy-volunteer acid-perfusion crossover study (PMID:28120127, registered as UMIN000015753), a single 450 mg dose reduced heartburn. A single 450 mg dose also only mildly reduced TLESRs in healthy volunteers (PMID:30897584). Both are clinical or physiological effects, not measured target engagement. An investigator's thesis reports no pain-blocking effect versus placebo in patients with NERD in the companion trial (NCT01707901). The mixed result, positive in healthy volunteers but negative in NERD patients, hints at a population issue (F3). But with no engagement data, a drug that never engaged EP1 cannot be told apart from a target that does not drive the disease, so the code is U.

The index trial in atopic dermatitis (NCT01808157) never posted results. The search found no human data on how much topical CT327 reached the skin, whether it inhibited TrkA there, or whether a downstream biomarker moved. A Phase 1 study of skin NGF and evoked pain responses (NCT01243307) was registered, but no results turned up. The only human pathway evidence for the mechanism came from cultured sensory neurons (capsaicin responses), which doesn't count. In the psoriasis Phase 2b (NCT01465282, Roblin 2015), the primary endpoint failed; itch improved only as a secondary endpoint in a subgroup. That is too weak to infer engagement. A later Phase 2b of SNA-120 in psoriasis was reported as a failure. Engagement is unknown, so a drug that never engaged TrkA can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter: U.

NCT02296476 stopped early for 'lack of clinical activity' after only 12 patients across three dose cohorts (80, 120 and 160 mg). Phase 1 data in blood cancers show plasma exposure rises with dose, but for a brain target no human brain or tumour drug levels were found. Brain penetration was shown only in mice (PMID:27388964). There was no measure of BET binding in human glioblastoma. PMID:27903752 reports that standard pharmacodynamic markers (c-Myc, BRD2) showed no response in AML patients, even at active doses. So none of the three pillars is shown in this disease, and the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter. That makes the code U. The small, early-stopped trial (F7) adds uncertainty.

Merck stopped the whole MK-8628 program, including the index trial NCT02698176, because of very limited efficacy, not because of safety (NCT02698189 protocol amendment). The phase 1 trials reported plasma exposure that rose with dose (TCR review; Berthon ASH abstract), so exposure counts as adequate. None of the sources reports a direct engagement measure in humans, such as BRD binding or HEXIM1 induction. PMID:27903752 says the published pharmacodynamic markers (c-Myc, BRD2) did not change in AML patients, so pathway is marked inadequate. The same paper argues those markers were poor choices, so this does not show the drug failed to engage BET proteins. Dose-limiting toxicities occurred, but the sources do not show that tolerability capped the dose below what engagement needed. With engagement unmeasured, the failure is indeterminate (U). F1a is listed as secondary only because the pathway biomarkers did not move.

The bundle has no human PK, receptor-occupancy or downstream biomarker data for rislenemdaz at the index doses, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The 5-patient pilot (NCT00472576, PMID:22722512) missed its MADRS endpoint, with only HAM-D and BDI signals, and showed no dissociative effects. Esketamine, listed as a drug on the same target, is FDA-approved for MDD. That points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Rodent data (PMID:26325093) suggest GluN2B-selective antagonists inhibit NMDA activity only partly (~60%), even at saturating occupancy, versus full inhibition by channel blockers. That is animal evidence only. Because engagement was never shown in humans, U remains a plausible alternative.

In the first-in-human study (PMID:25398449), plasma exposure at 2–4 mg/kg looked adequate. Elimination became saturable from 0.25 mg/kg and the drug accumulated from 4 mg/kg, and both doses were well tolerated, so dose was not limited. No human source measured endosialin occupancy in tumor or stroma, soluble endosialin, or any downstream marker of vascular or stromal effect. Saturable clearance only hints at target binding. Endosialin is expressed in melanoma vasculature (PMID:26085332), but that does not show the drug engaged it. Investigators concluded only that single-agent efficacy was low (PMID:29127533). The drug also failed in sarcoma (NCT01574716). No other CD248 drug exists for comparison. Engagement is unknown, so this is indeterminate (U).

In NCT01335009, ontuxizumab (anti-CD248/endosialin) at 2 or 4 mg/kg weekly gave a 24-week PFS of 11.4%, and the authors called its efficacy low (PMID:29127533). No dose was capped by tolerability: the MTD was 12 mg/kg, and both doses were well tolerated. The phase 1 study (PMID:25398449) measured plasma PK only. Saturable elimination from 0.25 mg/kg hints at target-mediated clearance, but nothing showed the drug reaching or binding CD248 in the tumor or changing a downstream biomarker in humans. CD248 is found in most melanoma tumor blood vessels (PMID:26085332), but that is expression, not engagement. The PET imaging work was done only in mice. The drug also failed in sarcoma (NCT01574716) and colorectal cancer. No other CD248 drug exists to compare against. With engagement unmeasured, the bundle can't tell a drug that never engaged apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

In the first-in-human study (PMID:25398449), plasma PK showed saturable elimination starting at 0.25 mg/kg and accumulation from 4 mg/kg, with an MTD of 12 mg/kg. That suggests systemic exposure was good at the 8 mg/kg dose used in the index trial, and tolerability did not cap the dose. Saturable elimination hints at target-mediated clearance, but no source measured endosialin occupancy, tumour target binding, or a downstream biomarker in humans. 89Zr-PET and soluble-endosialin assays exist only in mice or as research tools. The randomized Part 2 of NCT01574716 showed no PFS benefit (HR 1.08), and investigators simply concluded there was no added activity. The melanoma trial (NCT01335009) was not a positive efficacy result either. Because no human engagement data were found, the failure is indeterminate.

In the phase 2 part of NCT01574716, adding ontuxizumab 8 mg/kg to gemcitabine/docetaxel did not improve PFS (HR 1.08). Exposure is supported by the first-in-human study (PMID:25398449). Plasma levels accumulated from 4 mg/kg, and elimination became saturable from 0.25 mg/kg. That points to some target binding, but nobody measured it directly. The maximum tolerated dose was 12 mg/kg, so tolerability did not cap the 8 mg/kg dose. No human data on CD248 occupancy, CD248 blockade or downstream pathway effects were found. Baseline endosialin levels in serum and tumor did not predict benefit, and there were no efficacy differences across sarcoma subtypes (Cancer 2019). No other CD248 drug exists for comparison. Because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged CD248 from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Hu3S193 (anti-Lewis Y) reached and bound its tumor antigen in humans. In SCLC, 111In-hu3S193 at 10–20 mg/m2 targeted all lesions >2 cm, with no normal-tissue uptake (NCT00084799, PMID:17714905, published 2008, before the index trial). The index trial used a comparable 20 mg/m2 weekly dose. However, this engagement was not shown in ovarian cancer, and no downstream pathway biomarker (e.g., ADCC) was measured. The index trial produced 0 responses, with stable disease in 13 of 26 patients (NCT00617773, PMID:26026738). A Lewis Y-selected consolidation trial at 30 mg/m2 was also stopped for futility (PMID:33664128), and no dose limitation is evident. Together these point to Lewis Y targeting not driving benefit. Longer PFS was seen in patients without ascites or visceral disease, suggesting a possible subgroup effect (F3).

The index trial NCT01544348 was a first-in-human single-dose safety and PK/PD study in atopic subjects. It was not an efficacy test, so this is F9. Pillars were measured in that same trial. MEDI4212 reached serum and suppressed free IgE more than omalizumab did (engagement). FcεRI on basophils and dendritic cells fell (pathway). It was well tolerated with no serious AEs and no dose cap. However, serum drug and IgE suppression both declined rapidly. The authors concluded the short suppression offered 'limited potential for dosing schedule advantages over omalizumab'. That suggests a strategic or differentiation-driven stop (secondary F8) rather than a failed efficacy readout. The engagement data come from the index trial itself, so they did not precede it.

In the index trial (NCT00758706; Dahl 2012), 75 mg AZD1236 twice daily for 6 weeks did not lower sputum TNF-α or sputum cell counts. Urinary desmosine fell slightly but not significantly. PMID:21624491 found no clinical benefit. None of the sources report human lung or plasma exposure or direct inhibition of MMP-9/MMP-12 at this dose. The Phase 1 PK trials (NCT00767052, NCT01007929) posted no results. One review says the drug did not change sputum MMP activity, which could point to inadequate engagement (F1a). That claim is second-hand and unclear, so it is not enough to separate a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter (F2). Hence U. The program was later put under portfolio review (NCT01007929).

In the randomized phase 2 index trial (NCT01258608; PMID:26802147), adding mapatumumab 30 mg/kg to sorafenib did not improve time to progression (4.1 vs 5.6 months, HR 1.19). No subgroup benefited, and toxicity was similar in both arms, so neither tolerability nor patient selection explains the result. A solid-tumour phase 1 trial measured plasma drug levels, with linear pharmacokinetics up to 20 mg/kg, so systemic exposure is shown in humans. However, the sources found give no human evidence of TRAIL-R1 engagement, such as caspase activation, cell-death markers or tumour biopsy pharmacodynamics, in HCC or any other disease. No drug on the same target has succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The searches ran out before the full texts could be checked.

The index trial (NCT00930059, PMID:24801218) of 25 mg q12h for 12 weeks showed no ADAS-cog, NPI or CGI-I benefit. Tolerability did not cap the dose; it was mostly mild GI adverse events. PMID:22780914 reports that the drug raised CSF cGMP in healthy human volunteers, showing CNS exposure and PDE9A engagement, and it calls the drug a quality tool for testing the hypothesis. At 25 mg BID it also raised plasma and urinary cGMP in heart failure patients (PMID:41171251, NCT05409183). Engagement was not shown in AD patients, the published human CSF data postdate the index start, and the amount of elevation is not given. Downstream CNS pathway effects are unmeasured in humans. Rodent brain-penetration asymmetry (PMID:23025719) is animal data only. Overall, the drug engaged its target, yet PDE9A inhibition did not improve cognition.

Ricolinostat 120 mg did not separate from placebo on pain NRS (-1.21 vs -1.03) in NCT03176472. The sponsor's protocol cites myeloma studies (NCT01323751, NCT01997840; PMID:27646843; Vogl 2017) that predate the trial. In those patients, acetylated α-tubulin in blood cells, the HDAC6 engagement marker, rose robustly, tracked plasma levels and outpaced acetylated histone (the off-target marker). The 120 mg dose was picked as the highest achievable exposure because absorption levels off at 160 mg or more. Tolerability did not cap it. Caveats: engagement was never measured in diabetic neuropathy patients or in nerve tissue, no downstream neural biomarker exists, and the sponsor gave no reason for the failure. Read this way, the mechanism was tested and did not reduce pain, but confidence is low.

In the phase 1 trial NCT02082977 (PMID:31471312), plasma exposure rose dose-proportionally from 50 to 3,000 mg twice weekly. Dose-limiting transaminase elevations at 3,000 mg set the MTD at 2,400 mg, so tolerability capped the dose. No change from baseline in H3K27me3, the proximal mark of EZH2 enzyme activity, was seen in PBMCs. This means engagement was not demonstrated. The authors conclude that the IV dosing method and relatively short half-life limited effective exposure, and only modest activity was seen (1 PR, 34% stable disease). The stated stop reason cites insufficient activity at the maximal attainable dose and schedule. The mechanism was therefore not adequately tested. Tumor-level pathway data are absent.

In healthy volunteers (first-in-human PK/PD study NCT01765478, registered 2013), poseltinib showed dose-dependent, persistent BTK occupancy in PBMCs, with more than 80% occupancy at 40 mg maintained for 48 h. PMID:34548595 used this to select the phase II doses, so the sources treat engagement as sufficient at doses comparable to the 30 mg arm. Doses up to 160 mg were tolerated with no SAEs (NCT03083561), so tolerability did not cap the dose. Downstream pathway effects (pBTK, PLCγ2) were shown only in vitro or in animals. Engagement was never measured in RA patients. Despite this, ACR20 at Week 12 did not separate from placebo at any dose (p=0.47–0.82), with no dose-response and no safety reason for stopping (NCT02628028, PMID:33323529). This points to BTK inhibition not driving RA as tested.

The index trial NCT03081208 is IMPLANT2. According to the sponsor's topline report, it met its primary endpoint of ongoing pregnancy at 10 weeks: 35.6% with nolasiban vs 28.5% with placebo, p=0.031. Because the index trial did not fail on efficacy, the code is F9. The program actually stopped after the confirmatory trial IMPLANT4 (NCT03758885) missed its endpoint (40.5% vs 39.1%, p=0.745). The pooled analysis (PMID:33534895) also found that the individual trials were inconsistent. In healthy volunteers, the 900 mg dose lowered uterine contraction frequency and raised endometrial perfusion (PMID:34167897). These are pathway effects, but not in patients, and that paper was published after IMPLANT2. Occupancy, tissue exposure and engagement data are absent. If the stop is read as following IMPLANT4's failure, the fit would be U.

Plasma exposure was shown in healthy volunteers at doses up to 500 mg/day. The authors judged those concentrations sufficient for relevant target occupancy from in vitro data, and tolerability was good (PMID:27310331). No direct human DP2 occupancy was measured. Engagement is inferred from the pathway: in asthma patients the drug cut sputum eosinophils about 3.5-fold versus placebo (NCT01545726), and it improved FEV1 (NCT01437735), both before the index trial. The index trial still failed on exacerbations at 150 and 450 mg, including the high-eosinophil subgroup (NCT02555683), and so did LUSTER-2 and the steroid-sparing trial (NCT02563067, NCT03629249). No other DP2 antagonist succeeded. This fits a mechanism that does not drive exacerbations. A secondary population question remains, since early benefit was confined to an FEV1 <70% subgroup (NCT01253603, PMID:35304159).

Healthy-volunteer PK showed systemic concentrations high enough for relevant DP2 occupancy, and doses up to 500 mg/day were well tolerated (PMID:27310331), so exposure was adequate and the dose was not capped. Receptor occupancy was never measured in humans. Engagement is inferred: in asthma, fevipiprant met its FEV1 endpoint (NCT01437735) and cut sputum eosinophils 4.5-fold (NCT01545726). Both trials were registered before the index trial, and the target is systemic. This inference is weaker because skin is a different compartment from airway, so U is listed as secondary. In atopic dermatitis, EASI change did not separate from placebo (-8.65 vs -6.95; NCT01785602), with no tolerability issue. Later asthma Phase 3 failures support DP2 antagonism not driving these diseases as tested.

The COPD index trial was terminated for a 'Company decision' after enrolling 9 patients (n=3 vs 2 analysed, no statistics), so it was never a real efficacy test (F7/F8 elements). Plasma exposure up to 500 mg/day was shown in healthy volunteers, and the authors judged it sufficient for target occupancy (PMID:27310331). Engagement is inferred_adequate: fevipiprant met an FEV1 endpoint in asthma through the same airway DP2 target at comparable doses (NCT01437735). Pathway was adequate: sputum eosinophils fell 3.5-fold in asthma (NCT01545726). Despite this, the asthma Phase 3 trials failed (NCT02563067, NCT02555683, NCT03629249), and 'phase III results did not support submission' (PMID:33632715). This most likely drove the program-wide stop and points to the mechanism not driving disease outcomes. Engagement was never shown in COPD itself.

Plasma exposure in healthy volunteers was judged sufficient for relevant DP2 occupancy, and doses up to 500 mg/day were well tolerated (PMID:27310331). Receptor occupancy was never measured directly in the bundle. Engagement is inferred adequate because fevipiprant met its asthma FEV1 endpoint in the airway through the same receptor (NCT01437735). The pathway pillar held: sputum eosinophils fell 3.5-fold versus placebo in eosinophilic asthma (NCT01545726), before the index trial. Despite this, nasal polyp score was unchanged at 150 or 450 mg (NCT03681093). Phase 3 asthma trials also failed (NCT02563067, NCT02555683). No tolerability cap and no DP2 success in nasal polyps appear in the bundle. DP2 antagonism does not appear to drive polyp burden. Engagement was not shown in nasal polyp patients.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT02602067 of 131I-tenatumomab in tenascin-C positive cancers was terminated after 2 patients. Its stated reason is that drug uptake into the tumour lesion was negligible. That means the radioligand did not reach or bind its tissue target (tenascin-C in the tumour), so exposure at the site of action and target engagement were inadequate in patients. No pathway or clinical efficacy data exist, and the bundle gives no tolerability limit on dose. The mechanism was never properly tested, so the code is F1a. Confidence is medium because the evidence is a single stop-reason statement from a trial with 2 patients.

Mefloquine has no recorded molecular target for JC virus. Its proposed anti-JCV activity came from in vitro work only. In the index trial NCT00746941, adding 250 mg mefloquine to standard care did not lower CSF JCV DNA at week 4 (p=0.71) or week 8 (p=0.91). Clifford 2013 found no anti-JCV activity, and the trial was stopped at a planned interim analysis. Because viral load did not move, the pathway pillar is inadequate. None of the sources I found give human data on drug levels in the brain or CSF, or on engagement of any molecular target. So nothing shows whether the drug failed to reach or engage its site of action, or whether the mechanism simply does not work in PML. That makes the failure indeterminate (U); F2 is listed only as a possible alternative.

The index extension trial (NCT03407482) was stopped because the parent SLE trial NCT02908100 missed SRI-4 at both 150 mg QD and 200 mg BID. Exposure and dose-dependent BTK engagement were shown in healthy volunteers, with no MTD reached (PMID:29484638); tolerability did not cap the dose. The same doses met ACR50 in RA (NCT02833350), with an efficacy plateau within the exposure range (PMID:31907670). In SLE patients, fenebrutinib lowered a BTK-dependent plasmablast signature, anti-dsDNA, IgG and IgM, and raised C4. The authors conclude the endpoint was missed 'despite evidence of strong pathway inhibition' (PMID:34042314). Engagement was not measured directly in SLE. With BTK engaged and the pathway moved but no clinical benefit, BTK inhibition does not drive SLE outcomes as tested.

Plasma exposure was shown in healthy volunteers: single doses up to 400 mg were well tolerated with dose-related PK (PMID:31004346, PMID:31994022), so the dose was not capped by tolerability. No human source shows binding to T-type channels. The CNS pharmacodynamic tests showed no relevant changes. In the index trial, each patient got one dose (100 mg capsules). Of the 3 patients analysed (5 enrolled), only 1 had a photoparoxysmal-response reduction, and it came so late the sponsor did not count it (EudraCT results). So the proximal EEG biomarker did not move. Without engagement data, we can't tell whether the drug failed to engage its target or the target doesn't matter here, so the code is U. The tiny, single-dose design adds F7. The drug also later failed in EE-CSWS (NCT04625101).

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT01015911) had a safety primary endpoint. Its publication (PMID:25142258) reported approximately dose-proportional plasma exposure and substantial depletion of CD70-positive peripheral lymphocytes in RCC/NHL patients, described as targeted ablation. That engagement evidence was published in 2014, after the index trial started in 2009. At the 3 mg/kg Q3Wk MTD, activity in RCC was only modest (1 CR, 2 PR). Toxicities (ITP on the weekly schedule, ocular events, thrombocytopenia) limited schedules but no source says they capped dosing below engagement. Engaged target plus weak benefit points to F2. Toxicity (F6) and a safety-only, non-efficacy index trial (F9) are alternatives. The combination trial NCT01677390 was terminated with no reason, and the 2013 Phase 1 attrition analysis (PMID:25315907) notes reasons are often strategic or undisclosed.

In the knee OA trial (NCT00790790), neither LY545694 dose separated from placebo. The DPNP trial (NCT00785577) was also negative. None of the sources has human data on iGluR5 occupancy or engagement, or on CNS penetration. The only human pharmacology study (PMID:24486883) reported linear plasma PK, a maximally tolerated multiple dose of 25 mg BID limited by dizziness, and less secondary hyperalgesia in healthy volunteers. That functional signal is non-specific and was not shown in OA patients. In the trials, nausea, vomiting and dizziness were more common on drug and led to more dropouts. However, no source says dosing was capped below the level needed for engagement. The authors concluded only that proof of principle was not shown, and called the DPNP study failed rather than negative because pregabalin also missed. Nothing in the sources tells a drug that never engaged its target apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

Target engagement of GRIK1 (iGluR5) was never measured in humans; there are no occupancy or biomarker data. In healthy volunteers, dizziness capped the maximally tolerated multiple dose at 25 mg twice daily. That dose shrank secondary hyperalgesia in an experimental pain model (PMID:24486883), but this is weak functional evidence. In patients from both the diabetic nerve pain trial (NCT00785577) and the knee osteoarthritis trial (NCT00790790), steady-state drug levels were below those needed for efficacy in animal models. Nausea, vomiting and dizziness led to excess dropouts. So tolerability limited exposure and the mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). In addition, the pregabalin active control did not beat placebo, so the authors called the trial possibly failed rather than negative (F7).

Plasma exposure rose with dose (PMID:26092545, PMID:31056840), and the HBr salt reduced exposure variability (PMID:28385615). In healthy volunteers, ex vivo CXCL1-induced neutrophil CD11b expression was inhibited about 50% at 50–100 mg and 72% at 200 mg, published before the index trial (PMID:26092545). The source treats this as demonstrated engagement, though it is partial and was not shown in COPD patients. Influenza patients showed biomarker changes suggesting engagement (PMID:31041358), but that is another disease. In COPD, 1-year FEV1 decline did not differ (NCT03170232, p=0.679). The dose-ranging trial found no symptom benefit at any dose, more exacerbations and pneumonia at 50 mg, and a large placebo effect (NCT03034967, PMID:32532258). This suggests the target does not drive COPD as tested, with an unfavorable benefit-risk.

BETonMACE (NCT02586155) missed its primary endpoint, but the effect pointed toward benefit (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.65–1.04). The trial was powered to detect a 30% risk reduction from 250 events. Its investigators said it was underpowered to detect smaller differences, so F7. No source measured BRD4 occupancy directly. Downstream human markers did move as BET inhibition predicts: apoA-I and HDL rose in phase 1 and phase 2 CAD trials (PMID:20513599, NCT01058018, NCT01067820), and HDL rose more on drug than placebo in BETonMACE. Plasma proteomics in phase 2 CVD patients showed lower inflammatory mediators, and LAG3, a described BET-inhibitor engagement marker, fell in renal patients (PMC5976837). I counted this marker evidence as adequate engagement, which is a judgement call. On that basis the secondary code F2 applies: modest mechanism benefit. The dose was not capped by tolerability.

Phase 1 work gave plasma pharmacokinetics in humans (PMID:20513599), so systemic exposure is documented. No source measured BRD2/3/4 binding or occupancy directly in humans. The downstream markers were weak. ApoA-I rise missed significance in phase 2 (NCT01058018). In BETonMACE (NCT02586155), HDL rose only slightly (38.0 vs 36.6 mg/dL), hsCRP did not change, and the JAMA paper reports minimal differences between groups in biomarkers. Liver enzymes rose, but the dose was not capped. Engagement has no human data, so these sources cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage its targets or whether BET modulation does not drive cardiovascular events here. The code is therefore U. A benefit confined to the CKD subgroup (PMID:33906908) points to F3. The nonsignificant hazard ratio of 0.82 suggests the trial was underpowered (F7).

SHERLOC (NCT02387216) stopped for futility at interim analysis. PFS was 3.4 vs 4.1 months (HR 1.38). Phase 1 trials (NCT00734305, NCT01209195, NCT01447225) set a 40 mg/kg loading dose and 20 mg/kg weekly maintenance dose, and PMID:28031425 reports PK, so plasma exposure exists. The exposure label 'inadequate' does not fit that evidence and is a coding error; it should be 'adequate'. No source I could reach reports human HER3 occupancy, pHER3 inhibition, receptor downregulation or a downstream biomarker change. The full Phase 1 paper (Denlinger 2021) could not be retrieved. No other ERBB3 drug is shown as approved, so F1b does not apply. Heregulin selection came from a retrospective subgroup (PMID:30975923) and failed to confirm prospectively, so F3 is secondary. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter: U.

I found no human data on drug exposure, ErbB3 occupancy or downstream signaling. The phase 1 trials (NCT00734305, NCT01209195, PMID:28031425) report the maximum tolerated dose, safety and that PK was studied, but no target-engagement results. The sponsor set a trough goal of >100 µg/ml from mouse xenograft data, and I saw no evidence it was reached in patients. The dose was not limited by tolerability. In NCT01151046, median PFS was 15.9 vs 10.7 weeks, short of significance. The sponsor's npj paper puts the miss down to an unselected population: predefined analyses found benefit confined to tumors positive for heregulin (HRG) mRNA, and a later trial was restricted to HRG-positive patients. That points to F3. Because engagement was never measured, U also applies. The confirmatory HRG-selected breast cancer trial (NCT03241810) was stopped for business reasons, and the HRG-selected lung cancer trial (NCT02387216) failed.

Seribantumab plus paclitaxel did not improve PFS in unselected platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (HR 1.027; NCT01447706, PMID:27998236). The investigators attribute this to patient heterogeneity. A prespecified exploratory subgroup with detectable heregulin mRNA and low HER2, markers tied to the mechanism, showed benefit (HR 0.37), while the remaining patients did worse (HR 1.80). This points to patient selection (F3). The bundle has no human receptor occupancy or pharmacodynamic data. Human PK was evaluated without values given (PMID:28031425), and receptor occupancy was shown only in mice (PMID:32545760). The dose was not tolerability-capped: the MTD of 40 mg/kg load and 20 mg/kg weekly was used (NCT01209195). A later heregulin-selected NSCLC trial also failed (NCT02387216), so U also applies.
