The bundle has no direct human occupancy or HER3-phosphorylation data. PMID:28031425 mentions pharmacodynamics but reports no results. Engagement is inferred from CRESTONE (PMID:41428976, NCT04383210): 3,000 mg weekly gave a 34.5% ORR in NRG1-fusion tumours, including 36.4% in NSCLC. This must have required HER3 blockade in tumour. Phase 1 trials reached 40/20 mg/kg without a tolerability cap. That single-arm evidence came after the index trial started. The PMID:30975923 subgroup signal for HRG-positive tumours was not confirmed prospectively: in NCT02387216 PFS was 3.4 vs 4.1 months (HR 1.38). This suggests ligand-dependent ErbB3 blockade does not drive HRG-expressing NSCLC, with benefit confined to NRG1-fusion disease (F3).

The index trial NCT02305563 (ulocuplumab plus LDAC in newly diagnosed AML) was terminated for changed business objectives, slow accrual and a shift in standard of care that halted enrollment. Its small Phase 2 arms showed numerically lower best overall response with ulocuplumab (15.4% and 7.1%) than with LDAC alone (25.0%). Doses were not capped: there were no DLTs at 600/800 mg, and the MTD was 1600 mg in NCT03225716. The bundle has no human PK, CXCR4 occupancy or mobilization data, only in vitro and xenograft work (PMID:23213054, PMID:26646452). Per the sources, operational and business factors kept the trial from answering the question. Mechanistically the failure is indeterminate (U).

The Phase 1 study (NCT01803282, PMID:29691300) found linear PK and no DLT. It chose 800 mg q2w on the basis of target engagement and showed maximal target binding, meaning undetectable free MMP9 in plasma, in gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma patients. The index trial used this dose. That study was registered in 2013, before the index trial, but its results were only published in 2018, so the before-index call is uncertain. PK in Japanese GEJ patients was similar (PMID:34992093). Despite full plasma engagement, adding andecaliximab to nivolumab gave no response or survival benefit (ORR 10% vs 7%, p=0.8; PMID:34893523). The Phase 3 with mFOLFOX6 also missed OS (NCT02545504). No downstream pathway marker was shown, and tumor-tissue engagement was not measured. Overall, MMP9 inhibition does not appear to drive this disease as tested.

At week 8, none of the three andecaliximab doses separated from placebo on clinical or endoscopic response (NCT02405442, PMID:29846530). Plasma exposure was shown in UC patients, with target-mediated disposition at doses including 150 mg SC (NCT01831427, PMID:27218676). The Crohn's paper says its doses were chosen for target saturation in healthy volunteers and UC patients, so engagement counts as adequate, though it was not shown in Crohn's patients. Free MMP9 in plasma became undetectable at higher IV doses in cancer patients (PMID:29691300). Tissue MMP9 fell only in UC responders, so the pathway pillar is unproven. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not the limit. The UC Phase 3 also failed (NCT02520284). A commentary argues MMP9 is a marker of IBD, not a cause. Together this points to a target that does not drive the disease (F2).

In the Phase 1 trial NCT01803282 (PMID:29691300), andecaliximab showed linear PK and target-mediated disposition, with no dose-limiting toxicity up to 1800 mg. Maximal target binding (undetectable free MMP9 in plasma) was shown in the gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma cohort at 800 mg q2w, the dose chosen 'based on target engagement' for Phase 3. That engagement evidence came from patients with this disease and the trial started in 2013, before the index trial (2015). No downstream tumor pathway biomarker in gastric cancer is reported in the bundle. Despite adequate engagement, the index trial NCT02545504 showed no OS benefit (HR 0.93, p=0.56). The randomized Phase 2 NCT02864381 (PMID:34893523) also showed no benefit from adding andecaliximab. Together this indicates MMP9 inhibition does not drive outcomes in this disease. The sponsor then stopped oncology development (NCT02862535).

Andecaliximab 150 mg SC weekly or Q2W gave no remission benefit over placebo, and histological healing was also unchanged (NCT02520284, PMID:29767728). Exposure was shown in UC patients (NCT01831427). However, PK showed target-mediated disposition and more than dose-proportional AUC across the UC dose range, suggesting MMP9 was not saturated (PMID:27218676). Tissue MMP9 fell only about 49%, and only in responders. In oncology, maximal engagement (undetectable free plasma MMP9) required 800 mg IV q2w, roughly five-fold the UC dose (PMID:29691300). Tolerability did not cap the dose. The weak human evidence points to under-dosing rather than a disproven target. No other MMP9 drug in the bundle helps separate the two, so confidence is low.

The index trial NCT01803282 was a Phase 1 safety and tolerability study with only adverse-event and lab endpoints. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Exposure was adequate: linear PK and no DLT up to 1800 mg. Engagement was adequate: plasma andecaliximab-free MMP9 was undetectable in gastric/GEJ patients at 800 mg q2w (PMID:29691300). This was published in 2018, after the index trial started. No downstream pathway biomarker was shown. The oncology program then failed on efficacy despite engagement: the Phase 3 OS hazard ratio was 0.93 (NCT02545504), and adding the drug to nivolumab gave no ORR benefit (NCT02864381, PMID:34893523). This supports F2 as a secondary code. The sponsor ended oncology development (NCT02862535).

Direct BMP9/BMP10 binding or ligand lowering is not reported. Engagement is judged adequate from on-target ALK1-blockade effects in humans. In first-in-human dosing (PMID:24173543), tumor blood flow fell in 82% of evaluable patients and HHT-like telangiectasia appeared. In RCC patients (DART, PMID:28031424), telangiectasia and epistaxis occurred, PK/PD were assessed, there were no DLTs, and 0.9 mg/kg was chosen. The dose was not capped by tolerability, and the drug was well tolerated in the randomized part. Even so, adding dalantercept to axitinib gave no PFS benefit (6.8 vs 5.6 months, HR 1.11, p=0.67) and no ORR benefit (PMID:30951193). The same pattern of no added activity appeared in HCC and SCCHN (PMID:30352941, PMID:27648727). This suggests ALK1 ligand trapping does not drive RCC outcomes as tested. Confidence is medium because engagement rests on downstream effects; if direct binding data are required, U also applies.

The index trial (NCT02024087) was a Phase 1b safety study. Toxicity forced the dalantercept dose down to 0.4 mg/kg in HCC, below the 0.9–1.2 mg/kg used in other cancers (PMID:28031424, 27648727). No responses were seen, and the sponsor stopped the HCC program (PMID:30352941). The first-in-human study measured plasma PK and found falls in tumor blood flow and metabolism plus telangiectasia, which is consistent with ALK1-pathway blockade (PMID:24173543). These are downstream signs only. No source measures binding of BMP9 or BMP10 directly, and nothing was measured in HCC or at 0.4 mg/kg. Because the dose was capped, F1a is possible, but no source shows that 0.4 mg/kg gave too little engagement. Without that, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

disease: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
rationale: The bundle has no direct BMP9/BMP10 ligand-binding assay, so engagement is judged from downstream effects. In the first-in-human study (NCT00996957, PMID:24173543), tumor blood flow fell in 82% and tumor metabolic activity in 63% of evaluable patients. Telangiectasia also appeared, an on-target ALK1-blockade phenotype. Doses up to 1.6 mg/kg were tolerated, and the index trial used up to 1.2 mg/kg, so the dose was not capped. Exposure is not reported numerically; it is assumed from these effects. Despite this, monotherapy in recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma gave a 5% response rate and median PFS of 1.4 months, missing the primary endpoint (PMID:27648727). The randomized renal cell carcinoma combination trial was also futile (NCT01727336), suggesting ALK1 ligand trapping does not drive tumor control. The authors note the population was unselected and heavily pretreated (F3 secondary).

Index NCT02024087 was a phase 1b/2 trial with a descriptive safety primary endpoint, not an efficacy test (F9). The sponsor still stopped HCC development after it showed no additive antitumor activity and no responses (PMID:30352941). In HCC, 0.6 mg/kg was poorly tolerated (5/5 deaths) and the dose was de-escalated to an MTD of 0.4 mg/kg, below doses used in RCC (0.9) and SCCHN (1.2). That suggests dose limitation (F1a). No BMP9/BMP10 ligand-lowering or engagement data are in the bundle. The pathway entry is only partly supported: the first-in-human study in other solid tumors showed lower tumor blood flow and telangiectasia (PMID:24173543), not efficacy-based inference. Failures in RCC and SCCHN (NCT01727336, NCT01458392) leave target relevance indeterminate (U).

EGb 761 is a multi-component plant extract with no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human evidence that it engaged any mechanism relevant to Friedreich ataxia, such as a mitochondrial or antioxidant marker. PMID:12002672 shows only that ginkgolide B reaches the plasma in healthy volunteers. In the index trial (NCT00824512, n=22), the primary endpoint, post-exercise creatine rephosphorylation rate, did not change versus placebo (p=0.91). That endpoint is itself a proximal mitochondrial readout, so the pathway pillar arguably did not move, but with no defined target this cannot be read as a test of the target. The sponsor gave no explanation for the failure, and the trial was small. Because engagement is no_human_data, the failure is indeterminate.

In the 12-week RA trial (NCT02919475), all four JTE-051 doses (50–200 mg) gave ACR20 rates similar to placebo (27–31 of about 51 patients vs 29/52; p≥0.84). The response was flat across the dose range, and the drug was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The sources I found contain no human PK, ITK inhibition, or downstream T-cell biomarker data (such as IL-2 suppression). The psoriasis protocol (NCT03358290) mentions Phase 1 studies only in general terms and reports no numbers. The other trial (NCT03358290, psoriasis) was terminated for poor enrollment. No ITK inhibitor has succeeded in RA. With no engagement data, the evidence cannot tell whether the drug failed to inhibit ITK or ITK does not drive RA, so the failure is indeterminate.

In healthy volunteers (NCT02468908, PMID:40973220), inhaled molgramostim reached measurable serum levels and caused the expected dose-related rise in white blood cells. That is a pathway effect showing the GM-CSF receptor was engaged. The same 300 µg daily inhaled dose met the efficacy endpoint in aPAP, where it acts on lung alveolar macrophages (per a review abstract listed on ResearchGate). So lung exposure and engagement are inferred adequate. NTM patients in OPTIMA developed eosinophilia, but no engagement biomarker was measured in NTM. Only 5 of 32 patients achieved the strict sputum culture conversion, and 54% of MAC patients showed no microbiological response. This suggests the mechanism does not clear refractory NTM, hence F2. The trial was a small, uncontrolled pilot (F7). The authors noted the NTM dose-response may differ, and response was worse in M. abscessus (F3).

No one measured target engagement in the lungs of NTM patients. The healthy-volunteer study (PMID:40973220) found picogram serum levels and a rise in white blood cells, but those results came out after the index trial. All three pillars are inferred_adequate because inhaled molgramostim met its primary endpoint (DLCO) in the Phase 3 IMPALA-2 trial in aPAP. That trial acts through the same GM-CSF receptor in the same compartment, the alveolar macrophage, and the index trial used inhaled 300 µg daily. My sources did not state IMPALA-2's dose, so 'comparable' is assumed. Even so, only 5 of 32 participants converted at 48 weeks (NCT03421743). That points to F2. The OPTIMA authors saw some benefit in MAC but not MABS (F3). The trial was uncontrolled, and the CF trial NCT03597347 ended early because of COVID (F7). Confidence is low.

The index Pentasa trial (NCT00862121) was terminated for poor recruitment. Only 18 patients were analysed (43% vs 55% CDAI response, p=0.231, wide CI), so it could not answer the efficacy question. A sister Crohn's trial (NCT00245505) also stopped for lack of eligible patients. No direct human PPARG engagement data exist. The pillars are inferred adequate because mesalamine is approved for, and met endpoints in, ulcerative colitis via the same mucosal compartment (NCT01016262, PMID:9589293). About 80% of the dose remains for colonic activity (PMID:1981363). That inference is weaker for ileal Crohn's. A meta-analysis showing only marginal benefit of mesalamine in Crohn's (PMID:17031095) suggests the mechanism contributes little to this disease, supporting F2 as secondary.

In the open-label phase 2a pilot (NCT05488405; PMID:41448478), 5 adults with EoE took mesalamine oral suspension 1 g twice daily for 4 weeks. None reached histologic remission or response. The sources found contain no human data on esophageal mucosal drug levels, PPARG engagement, or a downstream biomarker in EoE. The UC efficacy cannot support inferred_adequate here because it involves a different tissue compartment (colon) and a different formulation. No other PPARG agonist has succeeded in EoE, so F1b does not apply. With only 5 patients and 4 weeks of treatment, the trial is too small and short to be decisive (F7 secondary). Nothing in the sources separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

CSL112 is apoA-I replacement. Infusions raised plasma apoA-I dose-proportionally, up to about 3-fold (PMID:24122814, PMID:24969776), so exposure and engagement were adequate. The pathway effect also held: total and ABCA1-dependent cholesterol efflux capacity, pre-β1-HDL and HDL-C rose strongly. This was shown in stable atherosclerosis (PMID:26307570, PMID:29437574) and in post-AMI patients in AEGIS-I (NCT02108262; PMID:27881559, published 2016, before the 2018 index start; PMID:36282079). Modeling confirmed that 6 g, the dose used in the index trial, gave the desired efflux elevation (PMID:33217027). The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. Despite this, AEGIS-II missed MACE (HR 0.925, p=0.121; NCT03473223). Only exploratory signals for type 1 MI appeared (PMID:38588930). Raising efflux via apoA-I did not drive outcomes as tested.

CD10367 is a topical Galderma compound with no target recorded. In the exploratory psoriasis plaque test (NCT03025282), the 1% and 3% solutions did no better than placebo on the AUC of the summed erythema, scaling and induration score: 118.6 and 116.6 vs 118.0. Pretreating the plaques with a keratolytic did not help either (101.7 vs 103.4). The Betneval 0.1% steroid control clearly worked (75.3), so the test itself was sensitive. The bundle and the search show no human data on skin penetration, target binding or biomarkers, and no sponsor explanation for the failure. A drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is indeterminate.

GB001 is an oral small-molecule DP2 antagonist, not a peptide. In a Phase 2 trial in asthma patients (NCT01448954, registered before the index trial; published as PMC7027764), 30 mg once daily gave good plasma exposure (t1/2 14.5 h). It also blocked PGD2-induced eosinophil shape change ex vivo by about 97%, with more than 85% in every treated patient. That is near-complete receptor blockade at a dose close to the 40 mg used in the index trial. Downstream markers barely moved: FeNO fell only modestly and not significantly, and blood eosinophils did not drop. Even so, the index trial NCT03956862 showed no difference on SNOT-22 (difference -0.2, p=0.95). The asthma trial NCT03683576 also failed, and the sponsor dropped CRS. With the target blocked and no benefit, DP2 does not appear to drive CRS as tested. Engagement was never measured in CRS patients themselves.

ATH3G10 is an anti-phosphorylcholine antibody tested in STEMI patients in NCT03991143. That trial's primary endpoint was left ventricular remodelling on MRI, and no results have been posted. The Dutch trial registry says the 250 mg dose was chosen from pharmacokinetic data in healthy volunteers and patients, but I found no published human exposure numbers. I also found no human data on target binding, such as how much oxidized phospholipid or phosphorylcholine epitope the antibody captured, and no downstream inflammatory biomarker data. The only pharmacology evidence is from mouse studies (JIM 2021). The related Lp(a) trial NCT03320265 was terminated without a stated reason. No other drug on this target is listed and the sponsor gave no explanation, so a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter.

The index trial (NCT04551352) was a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of safety and tolerability, not a formal efficacy test. Its publication (PMID:38577337) found that active-drug PK showed rapid loss of active exposure in all participants on 0.4 mg flat dosing for 3 or more cycles. This loss came with anti-drug antibodies against both the TYRP1 and CD3 domains. Drug-ADA immune complexes were present and showed no drug activity. Early CRS and IL-6/TNF rises point to transient CD3 engagement, but sustained exposure and engagement were not achieved. The dose was not capped by toxicity, since toxicities were mostly grade 1-2. The mechanism was not properly tested, so F1a. F9 is secondary because this was not an efficacy test of the drug.

The index first-in-human trial (NCT04551352) was a dose-escalation safety study with DLT/AE primary endpoints in 20 patients with TYRP1-positive melanoma. PMID:38577337 reports that active-drug PK showed loss of active (dual-binding) drug exposure in all participants dosed at 0.4 mg flat for ≥3 cycles. This loss was linked to anti-drug antibodies against both the TYRP1 and CD3 domains, which formed immune complexes without drug activity. CRS and IL-6/TNF rises show some initial CD3 engagement in patients. However, sustained exposure and engagement were neutralized, so the mechanism was not properly tested. Tolerability (grade 1-2 CRS, mitigated by fractionated dosing) did not cap the dose. The trial was not a formal efficacy test, so F9 is secondary.

The index first-in-human trial (NCT04551352) was a dose-escalation safety study in TYRP1-positive cutaneous, uveal and mucosal melanoma. PMID:38577337 reports that active-drug PK showed loss of active (dual-binding) drug exposure in all participants given 0.4 mg flat dosing for ≥3 cycles. This loss was linked to anti-drug antibodies against both the TYRP1 and CD3 domains, and the ADA-bound complexes had no drug activity. Grade 1-2 CRS suggests transient CD3 engagement, but sustained exposure and engagement were not achieved, so the mechanism was not properly tested. Tebentafusp, another CD3-engaging drug, is approved in uveal melanoma, which points to a molecule-specific problem (F1b secondary). Toxicity was manageable and did not cap the dose. No pathway or efficacy data are reported.

GAIN (NCT03823404) missed both co-primary endpoints (ADAS-Cog11 and ADCS-ADL). The engagement evidence comes from the sponsor: at AD/PD 2022, Cortexyme reported that an activity-based probe showed lysine-gingipain (Kgp) inhibition in GAIN patients. This was presented only after the trial ended. Downstream CSF p-tau/total-tau and MRI volume changes were only numerical trends, so pathway is rated inadequate. No human data on CSF or brain exposure turned up in my searches. The sponsor blamed patient selection: in the prespecified subgroup with P. gingivalis DNA in saliva, the 80 mg dose slowed ADAS-Cog decline by 57% (significant). Even so, the program ended after dose-dependent liver toxicity led the FDA to a full clinical hold in January 2022 (F6). With engagement shown, F2 also applies for the all-comer population.

The index trial NCT02798978 was a first-in-human safety, PK and PD study in healthy volunteers. It was not an efficacy test, and it met its aims. PMID:32739049 reports dose-proportional exposure and transient, dose-dependent cytokine, chemokine and immune-cell changes, described as evidence of target engagement and downstream pharmacology. No SAEs occurred, so the dose was not capped. In the later patient study NCT03447314, a manufacturing change to the formulation abolished the cytokine PD response despite higher exposure (PMID:36097345), and anti-tumor activity could not be assessed. That points to a secondary F1a: engagement was lost with the modified molecule formulation. The patient engagement evidence (original formulation) was published after the index trial started.

CKD-497 is a botanical drug with no recorded molecular target. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or biomarkers. Its proposed NF-κB anti-inflammatory mechanism comes only from animal studies (Frontiers 2024). In the published Phase 2 index trial (NCT03726853; PMC7867795), neither CKD-497 nor the active positive control significantly improved the Bronchitis Severity Score (BSS). Because even the comparator failed, the trial lacked assay sensitivity, meaning it could not tell whether any drug worked. This points to a trial-design problem (F7) rather than a test of the mechanism. A mild, significant benefit at 300 mg in early, more severe bronchitis patients was a post-hoc subgroup finding, which supports F3 as a secondary code. Since engagement is unknown, U also applies.

The index trial, NCT02668588, tested one 30 mg intramuscular injection of LF-PB, a new extended-release octreotide formulation, against placebo for seroma after axillary lymph node dissection. It enrolled 48 patients, stopped in 2016, posted no results and gave no stated reason. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, SSTR2 engagement or lymphatic-flow biomarker data for LF-PB. Other octreotide products are approved for systemic indications, but those results cannot be carried over to this formulation at the surgical site. Separate randomized trials of other octreotide regimens report mixed effects on drainage volume after mastectomy. Nothing in the bundle separates a formulation that never engaged the target from a mechanism that does not matter for seroma, so the code is U.

BMS-241027 was tested at very low doses (0.003 to 0.03 mg/kg weekly) in mild AD patients in NCT01492374. That trial measured CSF tau fragments, but no results were posted or published. Alzforum says only that the program was discontinued after the trial. The only human engagement evidence is microtubule bundle formation in blood cells (PBMCs) at oncology doses of 100 mg/m2 (PMID:22072399). That dose is about 100 times higher than the AD doses and says nothing about brain levels. Brain penetration and the benefit of low doses were shown only in mice (PMID:22623658). A secondary review says the drug failed to meet clinical endpoints but gives no data. Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore unknown in humans at the AD doses, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

SA001 is an oral mofetil-ester prodrug of rebamipide. Phase 1 trials (NCT02470286, NCT05303961; PMID:36678630) showed rebamipide plasma exposure up to about 12-fold higher than conventional tablets, with good tolerability, so dose was not capped. The site of action is ocular and glandular tissue, and no tear or tissue drug levels, target engagement data or pathway biomarker were found in humans. Topical 2% rebamipide works in dry eye, but that is a different route and compartment, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. The Sjögren's Phase 2a (NCT05269810; PMID:41599786) also failed despite high systemic exposure. Its authors suggest future trials measure target engagement near the glands, which implies it was never measured. No results were posted for the index trial. Engagement is unknown, so the failure cannot be explained.

SA001 is a prodrug of rebamipide, and no target is recorded for it. Phase 1 showed much higher plasma rebamipide than with conventional rebamipide (PMID:36678630). Plasma is not the site of action here, though. No one measured drug levels in the lacrimal or salivary glands, so exposure is rated inadequate (not shown at the tissue). The authors say systemic exposure alone may not be enough and call for strategies driven by tissue exposure. I found no human data on target engagement. Anti-SSA levels, the only downstream biomarker measured, did not change, so pathway is rated inadequate (PMID:41599786). Without engagement data, there is no way to tell a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The trial was small (n=28), exploratory and not powered (F7). The authors also point to patient selection (F3).

NCT02978755 was a first-in-human dose-escalation study, with safety (DLTs and AEs) as its primary endpoint. Among 68 patients, the drug was well tolerated with no DLTs and showed only hints of antitumor activity (one partial response). PK was collected, but no exposure values were reported. No study measured AMHR2 binding or occupancy on tumor cells, or depletion of AMHR2+ cells, in humans. The only pharmacodynamic data were blood changes (more classical monocytes, activated T cells and neutrophils) in 25 patients, and these are not specific to the target. The pathway field is set to 'inadequate' only because the schema has no 'not specific' option; these signals do not show that the pathway failed. No source gives a reason for stopping. Because engagement has no human data, the code is U. F9 is secondary because the index trial was a safety study, not a failed efficacy test.

None of the sources I found report human AMHRII occupancy or tumor drug levels. The first-in-human trial (NCT02978755) dosed 1–20 mg/kg with no dose-limiting toxicities, but it reported no target-engagement data. In the index Phase 2 colorectal trial (NCT03799731; ESMO-GI 2019 LBA-004), the sponsor reported immune-cascade activation in the tumor microenvironment, which I count as pathway evidence; this is the sponsor's claim and the numbers are not shown. The sponsor described PFS with FTD/TPI as longer than expected, especially in patients with medium/high AMHRII expression. That makes patient selection by target-expression level (F3) the explanation the sources point to. Because engagement was never measured, U is a secondary code. I could only see snippets of the full abstracts and could not open the pages, so confidence is low.

NCT02978755 was a first-in-human dose-escalation trial whose primary endpoints were DLTs and safety. Murlentamab was well tolerated at every dose with no DLTs, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The sources found report a slower tumor growth rate in 8 of 17 ovarian patients. None of them gives human AMHR2 occupancy, binding to tumor or depletion of AMHR2-positive cells, and none reports PK values. The Cancers 2021 paper describes only qualitative immune-cell activation in patient samples, which is not enough to count as pathway evidence. The sponsor then took the drug into colorectal cancer (NCT03799731) and did not state a reason for stopping the gynecologic program. With engagement unmeasured, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. F9 is also possible because the index trial was not an efficacy test.

The index Phase 2b/3 trial (NCT04382924) missed its primary endpoint, the WHO ordinal score at Day 15. The sponsor said mean scores were similar across all arms and secondary endpoints did not change. I found no human evidence of ifenprodil exposure at the site of action, GluN2B occupancy, or NMDA receptor inhibition at the trial doses. The only biomarker reported was a fall in IL-6 at day 5 in the 20 mg arm (p=0.029). That is a nonspecific inflammatory marker, not a validated readout of the mechanism, so it does not establish engagement or the pathway pillar. Because engagement is no_human_data, the evidence cannot separate a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. Algernon also cited the global vaccination rate and other available COVID-19 drugs when it dropped Phase 3 (F8). It estimated that about 1,900 patients would be needed to confirm a possible secondary signal (F7).

The index trial NCT03466320 (DEPLETHINK, Phase 1/2, AML/MDS) had a single primary outcome, dose-limiting toxicity. It is classified not_efficacy, was completed, and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of CYAD-01. The bundle has no human data on CAR-T expansion or persistence, on engagement of the MICA/MICB NKG2D ligands, or on downstream effects. There are no PubMed abstracts and no posted Phase 1 results. The related trial NCT03370198 was terminated for recruitment difficulties and a change in clinical strategy, which hints at a portfolio shift, perhaps toward next-generation CYAD-02, but nothing shows a failed efficacy readout. If an efficacy failure were assumed, it would be indeterminate (U) because engagement data are absent.

The index trial NCT00796211 was a small (n=20), single-center exploratory study of CRx-197. Its primary outcome was safety and tolerability (adverse events, vitals, subject-assessed pruritus), classified not_efficacy, and no results were posted. So it was not an efficacy test that failed (F9). CRx-197 appears to be a topical formulation (NCT00721331, topical Phase 1 in healthy volunteers). The bundle has no human skin exposure, H1 engagement or pathway data for that formulation. Oral loratadine suppresses histamine wheals (PMID:10564333, PMID:1680760) and is effective in urticaria (PMID:42887704), but this does not establish engagement for topical CRx-197 in psoriasis. If the readout were treated as an efficacy failure, it would be indeterminate (U).

Loratadine 10 mg QD failed to reduce pegfilgrastim-associated bone pain versus no prophylaxis (42.5% vs 46.6%; CI includes zero; NCT01712009). The same 10 mg dose was used. Exposure at this dose is documented in human PK (PMID:17620221). Peripheral H1 blockade is shown as histamine wheal suppression (PMID:1977782, PMID:10564333, PMID:1680760). Engagement is rated inferred adequate because loratadine is FDA-approved for allergic rhinitis at 10 mg through the same systemic H1 mechanism. However, PMID:1977782 reports only about 50% wheal inhibition, weaker than cetirizine. Partial peripheral engagement therefore remains possible, so F1a is listed as secondary. No H1 engagement was measured in G-CSF-treated patients. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The most direct reading is that H1 antagonism does not meaningfully drive G-CSF bone pain.

Exposure: in the first-in-human study, plasma PK rose in proportion to dose with a 23–30 day half-life (PMID:38996969). No human measure of VP1 binding or neutralization exists, so engagement has no human data. The downstream marker did move in patients. At week 12, median viral load fell 1.14 log on drug versus a 0.37 rise on placebo (p=0.051), and 55% vs 13% had a ≥1-log drop (p=0.040), so pathway is adequate. NCT04294472 had only 28 patients, and its time-to-event primaries gave p≈0.05–0.19. The sponsor called the data positive and said they warranted more study. The trial looks underpowered rather than showing a true null (F7). The search found no stated reason for stopping, so a business decision (F8) is possible but unconfirmed.

TNX-601 ER 39.4 mg showed no separation from placebo on MADRS change at week 6 (−12.7 vs −12.8; NCT05686408), and Tonix stopped development on that efficacy result without giving a mechanistic explanation. Exposure: human studies show near-complete oral bioavailability (PMID:3180120, PMID:2341111). Healthy-volunteer EEG changes tracked plasma levels, which suggests the drug acts in the brain (PMID:9026373), and the sponsor says the ER tablet is bioequivalent to the IR form. Engagement: mu-opioid agonism is shown only in vitro and in rodents (Gassaway 2014). No human occupancy or opioid-specific pharmacodynamic marker (e.g., pupil size) was found. Because nothing separates a drug that did not engage its target from a target that does not matter, the code is U.

In the UPLIFT trial (NCT05686408), MADRS change at week 6 was identical for drug and placebo (-12.7 vs -12.8). Tonix stopped development because of this efficacy result and gave no mechanistic explanation. The tolerability was good, so dose was not capped. The only human data are plasma PK (half-life about 5-7 h for the ER form; PMID:3180120) and nonspecific EEG and neurotransmitter changes (PMID:9026373). None of it measures brain mu-opioid receptor occupancy or a downstream opioid biomarker. Tonix also said the S-isomer mainly acts on PPAR-β/δ, not mu-opioid. No same-target drug has succeeded in MDD. With engagement at no_human_data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT01711801, was a Phase 1 safety, pharmacokinetic and food-effect study in healthy volunteers. Its primary outcome was adverse events, it posted no results, and it did not test efficacy, so F9 also applies. Roche did run a PET study measuring how much PDE10A the drug occupied in the brain, using [11C]IMA107 (NCT01923025; HRA summary), but I found no published occupancy results. I also found no exposure or biomarker data in humans, and no results for the negative-symptom study NCT02824055. The searches gave no sponsor explanation for stopping. No other PDE10A inhibitor has succeeded in schizophrenia, so F1b does not apply. With no human evidence on whether the drug engaged its target, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter.

In the index trial (NCT02734849), the anti-Siglec-8 antibody AK001 at 25 mg and 250 mg did not reduce Total Polyp Score meaningfully more than placebo (-0.5 and -0.3 vs -0.2). The trial randomized 40 patients, below the roughly 70 planned in the SAP, so it may have been underpowered (possible F7). The Phase 1 trial NCT02563938 listed pharmacodynamics as an objective but posted no results. My searches found no human data for AK001 on exposure, Siglec-8 binding, eosinophil or mast-cell depletion, or tissue biomarkers. Published human data on eosinophil depletion concern the different molecule AK002 (lirentelimab). The bundle has no other Siglec-8 drug in nasal polyps and no sponsor statement on why the program failed. Engagement is unknown, so a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter: U.

The Phase 1b part of ProSTAR (NCT03480646), in mCRPC patients, reported significant target engagement with both regimens: H3K27me3 fell in PBMCs and circulating tumor cells, and the drug was well tolerated at full doses. The sponsor reported PK/PD data and saw no added PD or efficacy benefit when cobicistat boosted exposure, so the dose was not capped by tolerability. Engagement in this disease was published in 2019, after the trial started in 2017. The earlier lymphoma data (NCT02395601) also appeared in 2018. In the randomized Phase 2, adding the drug gave only small gains over enzalutamide alone (ORR 7.9% vs 5.7%; composite 31.4% vs 17.1%), with no formal comparison and a small sample. That points to a target that does not drive the disease as tested (F2), with the trial's limited power as a secondary factor. No downstream pathway marker was reported.

In the lymphoma Phase 1 (NCT02395601), CPI-1205 lowered H3K27me3 in skin and tumor tissue. That abstract appears to date from about 2016, but I could not confirm the date. In mCRPC, the ProSTAR Phase Ib abstract (AACR 2019) reports that both CPI-1205 regimens produced significant target engagement (reduced H3K27me3) at the dose taken forward to Phase 2. Tolerability did not cap the dose. In the randomized Phase 2 of NCT03480646, adding CPI-1205 to enzalutamide gave similar objective response rates (7.9% vs 5.7%). The composite response rate was higher (31% vs 17%), but no statistical comparison was reported. A later review says EZH2 inhibitors combined with AR pathway inhibitors failed to show efficacy and development stopped. With engagement shown, the best fit is that EZH2 inhibition does not drive this disease as tested (F2). The small randomized phase with descriptive endpoints also points to F7. I found no human data on exposure or downstream pathway effects.

Exposure was adequate: in this first-in-human T2D trial (NCT02524782; PMID:30593607), PK supported weekly dosing. The PCSK9 arm worked: free PCSK9 and LDL-C fell in a dose-dependent way. The GLP-1 arm did not: glucose AUC after a mixed meal did not drop at any dose up to 400 mg weekly. The authors blamed this on a lack of sufficient GLP-1 activity, and the preclinical paper says the GLP-1 peptide was deliberately engineered with reduced potency. So the GLP-1R mechanism was never properly tested, which fits F1a; the dose was not capped by tolerability. The engagement and pathway ratings reflect the failed GLP-1 component. The evidence comes from the index trial itself, so it does not predate it.

AUT00063 is a Kv3.1/Kv3.3 positive modulator. The evidence that it suppresses auditory hyperactivity and improves gap detection comes only from rodent and in vitro work (PMID 33348192; Hear Res papers). The sources show it was safe at doses up to 800 mg/day. In the QUIET-1 tinnitus trial (NCT02315508) and the QuicKfire age-related hearing loss trial (NCT02832128), it had no significant effect on tinnitus or speech perception. None of the sources give human data on brain or auditory-system exposure, Kv3 channel engagement, or a downstream biomarker such as an ABR or EEG change. No other Kv3.1 drug has succeeded. Without that evidence, a drug that never engaged its target can't be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the failure is indeterminate (U).

QUIET-1 (NCT02315508, PMID:30939361) was stopped early for futility. The 800 mg/day dose was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Plasma PK was 'within the expected therapeutic range', but the target sits in central auditory neurons. No human data in the bundle show brain or CSF levels, Kv3.1 engagement, or a downstream effect such as EEG or auditory evoked responses. The first-in-human study reported only safety and PK. The evidence of mechanism comes from rodents only (PMID:29453003, 29773471). The investigators questioned whether the rodent models predict human response. No other Kv3.1 drug has succeeded in tinnitus. Nothing here separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT02947854 was a Phase 1 study in 96 healthy volunteers. It tested fimaporfin photochemical internalisation, with Hiltonol used only as the vaccine adjuvant in every arm. Its primary endpoints were safety and local tolerability, so it was not an efficacy test of hiltonol in HIV. The publication (PMID:33488576) reports that doses below 17.5 µg fimaporfin were safe, and that PCI raised T-cell responses about 10-fold over antigen plus Hiltonol alone. It describes no failure. The bundle has no direct human measurement of TLR3 engagement, exposure or a pathway biomarker. Antigen-specific immunity (PMID:24739759) is confounded by the vaccine components. The stop therefore reflects a completed safety study, not a drug efficacy failure.

The index trial NCT02947854 was a completed Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers. Its primary endpoints were safety and local tolerability of fimaporfin photochemical internalisation (PCI) vaccination, with Hiltonol given as adjuvant to both arms. It was not an efficacy test of hiltonol in acute promyelocytic leukemia (PMID:33488576). The paper reports acceptable safety and roughly 10-fold more T-cell responders with PCI. The comparison concerned fimaporfin, not poly-ICLC. The bundle has no human measure of TLR3/MDA5 engagement, such as interferon-stimulated gene induction. Antigen-specific T-cell responses in vaccine trials (PMID:24739759, NCT02924038) are confounded by co-administered antigens. Engagement is therefore unshown, and U applies secondarily. No efficacy readout failed in this disease.

This was the only human trial of topical PF-06763809, a RORC2 inverse agonist, in a psoriasis plaque test (NCT03469336, PMID:32767679). None of the three doses (0.23% to 2.3%) reduced skin infiltrate thickness compared with vehicle. Betamethasone did, so the test could detect an effect. Gene expression in lesion biopsies did not change versus vehicle, so the pathway pillar was inadequate. No source reports skin or plasma drug levels, receptor occupancy or direct target inhibition, so exposure and engagement have no human data. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The anti-IL-17 antibodies mentioned in the paper support the IL-17 pathway in psoriasis, and the flat biomarkers hint that the drug never reached or engaged RORC2 in the skin (F1a). But without exposure or engagement data, the sources cannot tell poor delivery apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

SPX-101 is an inhaled peptide that mimics SPLUNC1 and causes ENaC to be internalized. ENaC internalization, lower amiloride-sensitive current and better mucus transport were shown only in vitro and in animals (PMID:28481660, PMID:30190268), which do not count here. In humans (NCT03056989, PMID:31302339), the studies measured plasma PK (little or no systemic exposure) and safety. No lung or airway drug levels, nasal potential difference, ENaC activity or mucociliary clearance were reported. In the final HOPE-1 results (NCT03229252), ppFEV1 did not improve over placebo at 60 or 120 mg BID, even though the sponsor had described the first cohort as positive. No other ENaC drug has succeeded in CF, so F1b does not apply. Because human engagement data are absent, a molecule that never engaged ENaC cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial (NCT01602068), a single preoperative iontophoretic dose of EGP-437, showed no separation on day-7 zero AC cells (3/23 vs 2/22). The bundle has no ocular exposure, GR engagement or pathway data for this delivery in cataract patients. PMID:22115712 reports only low systemic exposure and uncontrolled cell reduction in uveitis. The target is validated in this disease: conventional dexamethasone phosphate drops given repeatedly beat placebo on postoperative flare (PMID:12446370) and matched prednisolone (PMID:11760033). The failure therefore points to the formulation and delivery regimen, not GR agonism (F1b). The small trial and the stringent endpoint, with low response in both arms, may also have contributed (F7).

The index Phase 3 (NCT01505088, reported in PMID:31726034) was a non-inferiority trial of iontophoretic EGP-437 against active prednisolone acetate 1%. Day-14 anterior chamber cell clearance was essentially identical (33.3% vs 33.0%). The trial failed only because the 95% CI lower bound (-12.94) crossed the -10% margin. That is a missed non-inferiority margin, not a lack of efficacy. The Phase 1/2 (PMID:22115712) showed ACC clearance in anterior uveitis and low systemic exposure. Ocular target engagement was never measured directly; it is inferred from the drug's clinical activity matching the active comparator and from approved corticosteroids on NR3C1 in uveitis. A CI too wide for the margin suggests limited power (F7). No dose-limiting toxicity was reported.

CNM-ZnAg is a zinc-silver ionic solution with no defined molecular target. The index trial, NCT04610138, randomized 296 outpatients in Brazil to low dose, high dose or placebo. Clene reported that it missed its primary endpoint, time to substantial symptom alleviation, in 288 PCR-confirmed patients, with no benefit over placebo. The drug was safe and well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. Clene stopped COVID development without giving a mechanistic reason. The bundle has no human data on drug levels, target engagement or downstream biomarkers such as viral load. No other drug on the same target is listed. Nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In relapsed/refractory myeloma patients, the index trial NCT03340883 measured free APRIL and posted a dose-dependent fall in its AUEC (median 1000 at 50 mg down to 72 at 2700 mg Q2W). This indicates target neutralization at the higher doses. Escalation reached 2700 mg with only one participant counted under the safety endpoint, so tolerability did not cap the dose. In healthy volunteers and IgAN patients (PMID:40482854, NCT03945318), exposure was dose-proportional, free APRIL fell durably, and IgA and IgM dropped, so exposure and the pathway held; that engagement evidence postdates the index start. Despite this, no objective myeloma responses occurred and the trial was terminated for futility. APRIL neutralization alone appears not to drive myeloma control as tested.

The bundle contains no human pharmacokinetic data and no measure of GHR transcript or protein knockdown, so exposure and engagement are no_human_data. The downstream pathway biomarker did not move: IGF-1 did not fall meaningfully versus placebo (-2.8% low dose, -7.5% high dose vs +8.9% placebo; p=0.306) in NCT03548415. A later single-arm study showed only about -7% IGF-1 at week 27 (NCT04522180). Pegvisomant, which acts on the same GHR target, is FDA-approved for acromegaly, so the target can drive benefit in this disease. With no evidence that cimdelirsen engaged GHR adequately, the failure points to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). Doses up to 160 mg showed no tolerability cap. No source states the reason, so confidence is medium.

The index Phase 1 trial NCT05306444 tested dose-escalation safety (DLT) and posted no results. In August 2024 Cullinan stopped CLN-418 after reviewing the Phase 1 data, citing 'initial clinical observations' and a wish to focus resources, and ended the Harbour BioMed licence. Two searches found no human data on exposure, 4-1BB/B7-H4 engagement, or downstream pharmacodynamic biomarkers. No other drug on this target appears in the bundle. Because engagement is no_human_data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, the code is U. F8 is a possible secondary code because the stated reason was resource prioritisation, though that statement points back to the clinical observations.

Per PMID:38190001, taldefgrobep alfa produced robust dose-dependent suppression of free myostatin in healthy volunteers (NCT02145234), which counts as direct engagement. It also significantly increased thigh muscle volume there. In DMD boys, the phase 1b/2 trial (NCT02515669, registered before the 2017 index start) showed myostatin suppression with a positive lean body mass effect, though muscle mass gains were modest. The drug was well tolerated, with no dose cap. Despite engagement in the disease, the index trial NCT03039686 showed no NSAA benefit at either dose (CIs spanning zero) and failed futility; the program was terminated for lack of clinical benefit (PMID:38640165). No other myostatin-targeting drug in the bundle succeeded in DMD. Myostatin inhibition does not translate into functional benefit in DMD as tested.

Amiselimod 0.4 mg failed to beat placebo on CDAI-100 at week 12 (48.7% vs 54.1%) and was well tolerated (PMID:34758080), so dose was not capped. Plasma exposure was dose-dependent (PMID:36708138, PMID:33115374). Lymphocyte counts fell, the expected S1P1-mediated sequestration effect, in healthy volunteers and SLE patients (PMID:27714763, PMID:33115374). Engagement is inferred adequate because the same 0.4 mg dose met the MRI lesion endpoint in relapsing MS (NCT01742052). No engagement data in Crohn's patients are in the bundle; the Crohn's PK/PD study NCT02148185 posted no results. No S1PR1 drug has succeeded in Crohn's itself, only in UC, so F1b does not apply. This points to F2. The high placebo response in a small trial (78 patients) suggests F7 as a secondary code.

PLC has no defined molecular target. In healthy volunteers, the MMX formulation released PLC mainly in the colon and raised plasma PLC, so exposure is shown (PMID:21810044). No human data show the drug engaging a target. A small biopsy study (PMID:24646507, published 2014, after the index trial began) found fewer ICAM-1+/iNOS+ microvessels and fewer inflammatory cells with PLC. Those are anti-inflammatory readouts, not a clear pathway effect predicted by a specific target, so the pathway pillar is not shown to be adequate and remains unconfirmed. The Phase 2 trial was positive at 1 g/day (PMID:21929562), but both Phase 3 trials stopped for futility with no stated cause and no safety issues. Nothing in the sources separates poor engagement from an irrelevant mechanism, so the code is U.

Heptex® is a herbal combination of Phyllanthus niruri and Silybum marianum extracts. It has no recorded molecular target. Its primary endpoint, 'anti-oxidant activity', was not reported with any oxidative-stress marker. No source reports human exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker. The index trial (NCT05343780, PMID:39789561) found no difference from placebo in the change in ALT, AST or FIB-4. Because there is no engagement data, nothing separates a product that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The authors called for 'more accurate investigation tools, a larger sample size, and/or higher doses', which suggests a design or power problem (secondary F7). The product was well tolerated, so tolerability did not limit the dose.

Silymarin has no defined molecular target. The Phase 1 trial NCT00389376 (Hawke 2010; Schrieber) measured plasma flavonolignans in NAFLD and HCV patients. Exposure rose with dose but did not rise proportionally, and in NAFLD it was lower than in HCV. Plasma exposure was therefore shown, but its adequacy is uncertain. No human engagement or pathway biomarker data exist. In the index trial NCT00680407, ≥2-point NAS improvement occurred in 5/26 (420 mg), 4/27 (700 mg) and 3/25 (placebo). The investigators called the result inconclusive: 63% of participants failed central histological entry criteria, and the placebo effect was unexpected. Those are trial-execution reasons, so F7 is primary. Because engagement was never measured, a mechanism-level cause cannot be separated out (U as secondary).

In the index trial (NCT00680407, Navarro 2019), silymarin (Legalon 420 or 700 mg three times daily) did not improve the NAS score over placebo (p=0.79). It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The Phase 1 trial (NCT00389376) measured plasma flavonolignan levels in patients with NAFLD and HCV. Silybin A and B reached the plasma, but parent levels stopped rising in proportion to dose above 560 mg (shown in HCV). No liver drug levels were found. Silymarin has no defined molecular target; the candidate mechanisms are antioxidant activity and, from in vitro work only, LXR antagonism (PMID:42246628). No human study measured target engagement or a mechanism-specific biomarker. The evidence cannot tell a drug that never engaged apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

MIB-626 (oral βNMN) raised blood NMN and NAD+ in a dose-related way in older adults (PMID:35182418). In the index trial it substantially raised blood NAD+ and NAD+ metabolites in COVID-19 AKI patients (PMID:40746868), so exposure and engagement were shown in this disease, though only in the index trial itself. Downstream markers did not move: cystatin C, creatinine, AKI markers, CRP, IL-6 and TNFα were all unchanged (NCT05038488). The authors blame the slow rise in NAD+, which peaked at days 5–14, too late for an acute injury, and propose rapid parenteral dosing. That points to timing (F4). Engagement inadequate during the acute window (F1a) or an irrelevant mechanism (F2) remain possible. Kidney tissue NAD+ was not measured, and the trial was small (n=42).

MP1032 is described as a ROS scavenger and macrophage modulator, and no molecular target is recorded. The only human data found are plasma PK. In the Phase 2a (NCT02908347, 100 mg twice daily), just 16 of the treated patients exceeded an exposure threshold of 120 ng·h/ml, so the dose was raised. No exposure figures turned up for the 150/300 mg doses used in the index trial. No study measured target engagement or a pathway biomarker. The index trial (NCT03706209) missed PASI75 and PGA, with responders at about 8% vs 2% on placebo. MetrioPharm blamed the small sample size, which points to F7 as a secondary code, but nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in psoriasis. Hence U. Tolerability did not limit the dose.

No primary target is recorded for MP1032. It is described as a multi-target ROS scavenger and PARP-1 modulator with in vitro antiviral activity (PMID:33233817), which is preclinical evidence only. The index trial measured plasma PK and ran an exposure-response model linked to D-dimer and eGFR (PMID:38076629, PMC10704330), so systemic exposure is documented. No source shows human target engagement, such as PARP inhibition or ROS lowering. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. It also missed its efficacy endpoints in psoriasis (NCT03706209), so there is no inferred engagement from success in another disease. With no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter in COVID-19.

The index trial compared oral I338 with subcutaneous insulin glargine in insulin-naive type 2 diabetes. Its primary endpoint was the treatment difference in fasting plasma glucose (FPG) at 8 weeks (NCT02470039, PMID:30679095). FPG fell from 9.7 to 7.1 mmol/L with I338 versus 6.8 mmol/L with glargine, a non-significant difference (p=0.46), and both were well tolerated. The 'not met' label reflects finding no difference from an active comparator, not a lack of effect. I338 achieved glucose lowering comparable to glargine, so systemic exposure, insulin-receptor engagement and the downstream glycaemic effect held in patients. This was not an efficacy failure of the drug. The bundle gives no stated reason for stopping, so a commercial or formulation cause cannot be confirmed.

The sponsor's ASCO GU 2023 poster for NCT03437941 reports that exicorilant 240–320 mg once daily with food, given with enzalutamide, changed 8 validated GR target genes in mCRPC patients. Four were suppressed and four increased; enzalutamide alone did not alter them. This shows functional GR antagonism in the disease, so engagement and pathway are rated adequate. No tissue drug levels were found, so exposure is inferred from the pharmacodynamic effect. 240 mg once daily was called a pharmacodynamically active regimen, and the DLTs did not stop dosing below that level. Even so, there were no meaningful PSA or radiographic responses, and further study was dropped. That points to GR antagonism not driving disease as tested (F2). Possible secondary factors: the patients were heavily pretreated, and PSA doubling-time gains clustered in those with high urinary free cortisol (F3). This evidence was published after the index trial started.

In the first-in-human trial (PMID:33755924), vafidemstat showed dose-proportional plasma exposure and CNS penetration by the CSF-to-plasma unbound ratio. It also bound KDM1A in PBMCs in a dose-dependent way in healthy volunteers. This evidence was published before the index trial and supported phase II dose selection. Engagement was not measured in BPD patients or in brain tissue, and no downstream pathway biomarker is shown. At 1.2 mg/day, a tolerated dose with no dose-limiting toxicity, the randomized trial NCT04932291 missed both primary endpoints (CGI-S A/A p=0.23; BPDCL p=0.38). The positive signal came from an open-label, single-arm basket study (PMID:39936839). The large placebo improvement suggests trial-sensitivity issues as a secondary factor (F7).

The index trial NCT00700687 was a Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers comparing gastroduodenal mucosal injury (Lanza scores) with PA32540 (aspirin plus omeprazole) ± celecoxib versus aspirin plus celecoxib. It was not an efficacy test of omeprazole in Barrett esophagus, and it posted no results and no failure. Human pillars are well documented. Plasma exposure is characterized (PMID:38541153, PMID:35522794). In Barrett patients, omeprazole 20 mg twice daily normalized acid reflux (PMID:8076761, 1994, before the index trial), showing proton-pump engagement and the downstream acid effect in this disease. Omeprazole is FDA-approved for acid-related diseases, and PA32540 met its gastric-ulcer endpoints (NCT00960869, NCT00961350). The program stopping at Phase 1 does not reflect an efficacy failure of the drug.

Two earlier Phase 2 trials in hypertensive patients (NCT03714776, 2019; NCT04083222, 2019) met their target-engagement primaries: plasma AGT fell 54% and 67% vs placebo (p<0.001). Engagement was therefore shown in this disease before the index trial. Hepatic exposure is implied by the AGT lowering. No downstream pathway marker (angiotensin II, renin) or blood-pressure effect appears in the bundle. In index trial NCT04714320, the Day 85 change in office SBP did not separate from placebo at either dose (-13 at 80 mg, p=0.135; -9 at 120 mg, p=0.867). This fits F2: AGT lowering at this magnitude did not lower BP as tested. A large placebo response (-9 mmHg) and about 45 patients per arm suggest a possible design contribution (F7). Zilebesiran has reached Phase 3 but is not approved, so F1b does not apply.

In the first-in-human study (NCT03915379; PMID:38494922), 68 r/r AML/MDS patients were treated across 10 escalation cohorts. Cytokine release syndrome, infusion reactions and hepatotoxicity limited dosing, and a prolonged step-up schedule did not prevent the liver toxicity. The authors state that the projected efficacious exposure was never safely reached, so no MTD or RP2D was set. T-cell activation in AML patients suggested some target engagement but did not correlate with activity, and there were no responses. Because the dose was capped by tolerability below the projected exposure, the CD33xCD3 mechanism was not adequately tested (F1a). Toxicity also contributed to termination (F6). Preclinical activity (PMID:32150609) does not count as human evidence.

In the first-in-human study (NCT03915379, PMID:38494922) of r/r AML/MDS patients, 11 of 68 had dose-limiting toxicities. Cytokine release syndrome, infusion reactions and hepatotoxicity occurred, and a prolonged step-up strategy did not prevent the liver toxicity. The authors state that the projected efficacious exposure was never safely reached, so no MTD or RP2D was set. T-cell activation 'suggested target engagement' in patients, but it did not correlate with clinical activity. There were only transient reductions in disease burden and no responses. The dose was capped by tolerability below adequate exposure, so the CD33xCD3 mechanism was not properly tested (F1a). The toxicity appears largely mechanism-related (cytokine-driven), which supports F5 as secondary. The engagement evidence was published in 2024, after the trial began in 2019.

In the index trial NCT04064242, CMK389 at 10 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks did not improve ppFVC at week 16 (difference -1.49, p=0.18). Tolerability was fine, with 2/31 serious AEs, so dose was not the limit. The protocol chose 10 mg/kg as the maximum feasible dose and says it would give more than 90% IFN-γ inhibition and troughs about 50-fold above EC80. Those figures come from nonclinical modelling, not from human measurements. The bundle has no human data on free IL-18, IFN-γ or CXCL9, and no Phase 1 PK/PD results. A 2026 review calls the sarcoidosis results negative and unpublished. No other IL-18 drug has succeeded in sarcoidosis. Without human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged IL-18 from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT04836858, IGA response at week 16 was 5/34 with 10 mg/kg IV and 2/17 with 300 mg SC, against 0/16 on placebo. The record posts no statistical test, and the study was small. The sarcoidosis trial NCT04064242 also missed its endpoint. I found no human evidence of target engagement for CMK389: no free IL-18 suppression, no measure of IL-18 neutralisation, and no PK/PD data. The dose-rationale section of the protocol is blacked out as commercially confidential. No other IL-18 drug has succeeded in atopic dermatitis, so F1b does not apply. Nothing in the sources separates a drug that failed to engage IL-18 from a target that does not drive atopic dermatitis. F7 is a minor secondary code because of the small trial size.

In THEIA-1 (NCT03833388), 202 patients received TOP1630 0.1% eye drops or placebo for 4 weeks. The drug missed both co-primary endpoints, ocular grittiness and total ocular surface staining at day 29. It did show nominal improvements in some secondary endpoints (discomfort, dryness, OSDI) and was well tolerated, so tolerability did not limit the dose. No source found shows human ocular-tissue drug levels or inhibition of p38, SRC or SYK by TOP1630, and none shows a downstream inflammatory biomarker moving. The sponsor said it chose the primary endpoints based on a small single-centre earlier study (NCT03088605) and noted that the gap versus placebo was growing over time. That points to endpoint choice and trial length (F7/F4). Without any engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U.

The bundle lists KCNQ2/3 as the target, but the papers describe ASP0819 as a KCa3.1 opener (PMID:33469353). ASP0819 at 15 mg/day missed its week-8 pain endpoint (p=0.086) in NCT03056690. It did separate from placebo at weeks 2, 6 and 7 and improved some sleep items (PMID:33328761). No human data on exposure, KCa3.1 engagement or any downstream biomarker was found. The pharmacology evidence comes only from rats (PMID:33469353). The dose was not limited by tolerability. No other drug on this target has succeeded in fibromyalgia. Without engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged its target from a target that doesn't matter, so the code is U. A small trial with a borderline result may also have played a part (F7).

The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, target-engagement or viral-load data. RNA polymerase inhibition by the metabolite VR17-04 is shown only in vitro and in cell culture (PMID:32511388, PMID:34572438), so all three pillars are no_human_data. In the index trial, no significant difference was seen in all patients (PMID:33469600). After an interim analysis, enrollment was restricted to patients on supplementary oxygen (SR 4). The sources then attribute apparent benefit to that subgroup and to patients treated early after symptom onset (PMID:38804439). This points to failure attributed to patient selection or timing (F3). Because engagement was never shown, U also applies. The mid-study redesign suggests a trial-design contribution (F7).

Plasma LCAT levels rose in proportion to dose (PMID:26628614). Enzyme activity was shown by dose-dependent rises in its product, cholesteryl ester (HDL-CE, total CE), and in HDL-C: up to +178% IV and +144% at Day 19 with multiple doses (PMID:34121413, PMID:33493256, NCT02601560, NCT03004638). The downstream pathway also moved: apoA1 and non-ABCA1 efflux capacity rose and apoB and small LDL fell. This was shown in stable CAD patients, not STEMI, and before the index trial started. Tolerability was acceptable, so the dose was not capped. In REAL-TIMI 63B (NCT03578809, PMID:36039762), infarct size was not reduced in either regimen. With the mechanism engaged, the failure points to HDL raising via LCAT not limiting infarct size.

The index trial NCT02718911 was a Phase 1 combination dose-finding study. Its primary endpoint was the MTD/RP2D, and it met that endpoint (100 mg QW with durvalumab). It was not an efficacy test of the drug. In the monotherapy Phase 1 (PMID:33624233; NCT01346358, registered 2011), PK was dose-dependent. Serum CSF-1 and IL-34 rose, consistent with receptor blockade. TAMs and CD14dimCD16bright monocytes fell in solid-tumor patients, showing engagement and the expected pathway effect. The drug was well tolerated and the RP2D was not capped by toxicity. Monotherapy produced no responses, which suggests limited benefit from CSF1R blockade in heterogeneous solid tumors (secondary F2).

In MANGROVE (NCT04578548), 150 mg once daily had no effect on htTKV or eGFR. Plasma PK was measured, so exposure is adequate. Engagement evidence in ADPKD patients came only from the trial itself: a modest drop in the granulocyte MPO index, used as a peripheral marker of CFTR inhibition, plus more dry mouth. Neither was quantified in the kidney, and the evidence was not available before the trial. The dose was picked from in vitro potency and plasma levels, not kidney engagement. The sold CF data (NCT03474042) reflect corrector activity, not inhibition. The authors call the cause unclear but name too low a dose as a possible reason, citing an htTKV exposure-response trend. So this was probably undertested engagement (F1a). The alternative is that the mechanism is not relevant (F2). Confidence is low.

CHF5633 is a synthetic surfactant given intratracheally, so it is delivered directly to its site of action. In the first-in-human study in preterm infants with RDS (NCT01651637/PMID:28465315, published before the 2016 index start), 98% of infants showed rapid, sustained FiO2 improvement at 100–200 mg/kg, and both doses were well tolerated. That is the expected immediate functional effect of surfactant replacement, though uncontrolled. The index trial (NCT02452476) tested superiority against an active, effective surfactant (poractant alfa). Oxygenation, FiO2 and BPD/mortality were nearly identical between arms (SAEs 20/59 vs 20/58). Missing superiority over an effective comparator is not evidence the drug or mechanism failed. The trial could not show inefficacy, so F9 applies, with design (F7) secondary.

IMCY-0098 is a proinsulin peptide meant to induce cytolytic CD4 T cells. There is no human PK data, so exposure is no_human_data. The human evidence that the mechanism worked is exploratory but specific to the drug, and comes from new-onset T1D patients. In phase 1b, doses B and C raised immune markers consistent with the mechanism (PMID:38902652). An interim IMPACT analysis of 17 patients found Granzyme B+ CD4 T cells expanded and antigen-specific pathogenic CD4 cells did not expand versus placebo. All of this was published after IMPACT started in December 2020. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped (PMID:37226224). Yet the phase 2 showed no C-peptide benefit at 1 year (NCT04524949), even though it enrolled mainly HLA-DR4+ patients. This points to F2. Confidence is low because the biomarker data are small, exploratory and from a press release. If those markers are not accepted as engagement, the answer is U.

I could not determine why the program failed. TOP1288 is a gut-restricted kinase inhibitor (p38α, Src family, Syk) given rectally in the Phase 2a index trial NCT02888379, which posted no results. I found no published efficacy readout or sponsor statement explaining the failure. The ECCO 2017 abstract describes rectal dosing in UC patients (NCT02463045). The ECCO 2018 abstract describes an oral Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (NCT03071081) that included pharmacokinetics and target engagement in serial colon biopsies, and TopiVert called the results 'positive' in January 2018. That study began after the index trial, and the snippets I saw gave no numbers for colon tissue levels, kinase inhibition or biomarkers. No other drug on these targets has succeeded in UC. With no human engagement data, the outcome is indeterminate.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT02876510) had a safety primary endpoint, and the publication reports IMA101 was feasible and well tolerated (PMID:37172100), so F9 also applies. Exposure was adequate: target-specific T cells reached up to 78.7% of CD8+ cells, persisted for over a year, and were found in post-treatment tumor tissue. Still, there were no objective responses. The authors point to TCR avidity: most TCRs in the products were low-avidity. They call for future work with potent high-avidity TCRs, which implies the target-pHLA engagement was not potent enough. This engagement evidence was published in 2023, after the index trial began. No pathway or killing biomarker was reported. The program reads as an inadequately tested mechanism, not a disproven target.

MC2-25 cream showed no advantage over vehicle on the weekly WI-NRS at 12 weeks in CKD-associated pruritus (-3.70 vs -3.87; NCT05482698). It also failed in vulvar lichen sclerosus (NCT06132919). The bundle records no primary target and contains no human data on skin exposure, target engagement or pathway biomarkers, no Phase 1 results, and no PubMed abstracts. No other drug on the same target is listed. A large vehicle response is evident, but no source attributes the failure to trial design. Nothing distinguishes a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the failure is indeterminate.

MC2-25 is a topical cream containing 30 mg/g of the dipeptide Ala-Gln. It is meant to mop up isocyanate and so reduce carbamylation of skin proteins. The only evidence that it blocks carbamylation is >90% inhibition in an in vitro uremic skin model, which does not count as human data. The CSR synopsis says skin tape-strip biomarkers were collected in the index trial but never analysed, so no human exposure, engagement or pathway data exist. Both NCT05482698 (CKD-associated itch) and NCT06132919 (vulvar lichen sclerosus) found no difference from vehicle, and both arms improved a lot. A large vehicle effect may point to a design problem (F7). Still, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index ITP trial (NCT04056195), platelet response was numerically higher on cevidoplenib (200 mg 12/26, 400 mg 14/22) than placebo (4/12), but the difference was not significant. The placebo arm had only 12 patients, so the trial was likely underpowered (F7). The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, SYK-occupancy or pathway data: the Phase 1 trials (NCT02717988, NCT03315494, NCT05042986) posted no results and there are no abstracts. The RA trial (NCT04057118) also failed, so it cannot support inferred engagement. Fostamatinib, which acts on the same SYK target, is FDA-approved for ITP. With engagement of this molecule unshown, F1b (the molecule, not the target) fits best.

In NCT04057118, no dose of cevidoplenib separated from placebo on DAS28 at week 12 (400 mg -1.15 vs placebo -0.95). The Phase 1 PK trials (NCT02717988, NCT03315494) posted no results, and I found no human data on SYK inhibition, occupancy or a downstream biomarker. PMID:36346114 is mouse-only. Inferred adequacy can't be borrowed from ITP because NCT04056195 is classified as missing its primary endpoint. The sponsor blamed the population (many patients had severe RA) and said a higher dose might improve efficacy. That suggests possible underdosing, but neither explanation is backed by engagement data. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence can't separate a drug that never engaged SYK from a target that doesn't drive RA, so this is U, with F3 as secondary.

Index trial NCT04056195 missed its primary platelet-response endpoint (200 mg 12/26, 400 mg 14/22 vs placebo 4/12; not significant). The bundle has no human PK, SYK engagement or pathway biomarker data: the Phase 1 trials (NCT02717988, NCT03315494) posted no results and there are no abstracts. The RA trial NCT04057118 also failed, so engagement cannot be inferred from it. Fostamatinib, another SYK inhibitor, is FDA-approved for ITP, which supports the target in this disease and points to the molecule (F1b). The response rates numerically favoured the drug, but the placebo arm had only 12 patients, so underpowering (F7) may also have contributed. With no pillar data, U also applies.

The extension study NCT01622088 was stopped because EMPOWER (NCT01281189, PMID:24067398) missed its primary endpoint: CAFS, ALSFRS-R and survival were all flat at 150 mg BID. No primary target is recorded. The proposed mechanism, mitochondrial F1Fo ATP synthase modulation, rests only on animal and in vitro work (PMID:28320070). The sources I found give plasma PK in healthy volunteers and in renal impairment (PMID:24965504, PMID 20959524). Neither reports CSF levels in ALS patients, any human measure of target engagement, or a mitochondrial biomarker. The eosinophil lowering seen in humans is off-mechanism for ALS. Mouse SOD1 data were negative at human-equivalent exposures (PMID:25526593). Without human engagement evidence, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

No molecular target is recorded, so the intended mechanism is eosinophil depletion. In the index trial (NCT02217332; PMID:30284267), 150 mg BID in CRSwNP patients cut blood eosinophils by 94% (p<0.001) and nasal polyp tissue eosinophils by 97% (p=0.001). That shows systemic exposure, tissue-level effect and the expected pathway change. The dose was well tolerated, with no drug-related serious AEs, so it was not capped. Despite near-elimination of polyp eosinophils, total polyp score and symptoms did not change. This points to eosinophils not driving polyp size as tested. Secondary F7: the study was small (n=16), single-arm and open-label. The disease-specific engagement evidence came from the index trial itself.

ALH-L1005 is a horse chestnut leaf extract from AngioLab that is proposed to work by inhibiting MMPs (MMP-9 and MMP-13). The only evidence for that mechanism is a canine ligature-periodontitis study (PMC5489472), and animal data don't count here. No human source was found on drug exposure, MMP inhibition in gum tissue or crevicular fluid, or downstream biomarkers. The index trial NCT04503746 compared 600 mg and 1200 mg over 12 weeks and posted no results. No sponsor statement explains why the program stopped, and no other drug on this target is in the bundle. Because engagement has no human data and nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a target that doesn't matter, the code is U.

In the index trial NCT03832738, efficacy was weak and dose-dependent. PASI-75 was 22% at 400 mg BID (p=0.035 vs 7.8% placebo) and 11.8% at 200 mg (not significant). That is far below the benchmarks of approved psoriasis drugs. The Phase 1 PK/PD study in psoriasis patients (NCT03018509) posted no results. My searches found no human data on exposure, RORγt engagement or downstream markers such as ex vivo IL-17 inhibition. They also found no sponsor statement on why development stopped. The 400 mg dose doing better than 200 mg hints that engagement was incomplete, but this was never measured. No other RORγt antagonist has succeeded in psoriasis, so F1b does not apply. With no engagement data, a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

ProTmune is a donor graft treated ex vivo before transplant, and no molecular target is recorded for it. In the Phase 2 part of NCT02743351, the primary endpoint was missed: grade II-IV aGvHD by Day 100 was 44.4% with ProTmune versus 24.9% with control, and there were more deaths (12/40 vs 6/41). No subgroup favoured ProTmune (HRA summary). Fate gave no mechanistic explanation. It said only that the study missed its endpoint and that it would turn to its iPSC programs. The sources I found contain no human data showing the treated cells were pharmacologically changed as intended or that a downstream immune biomarker moved. They do not have Phase 1 pharmacodynamic results either. With no engagement data, an ineffective product cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT05307978 is a Phase 1 single-dose safety, PK and PD study in 48 healthy participants, with doses from 5 to 135 mg given SC or IV. Its only primary outcome was the count of TEAEs. It was not an efficacy test of ALXN1910. Safety was unremarkable: one serious TEAE at 135 mg, no deaths and no AE-related withdrawals. No PK, pharmacodynamic or target-engagement data are posted. No target, disease, other trials, approvals or publications appear in the bundle. So none of the three pillars can be judged, and the reason the program stopped is not shown. F9 is primary because there was no efficacy readout to fail. U is secondary because engagement is unknown.

The index trial NCT04781816 missed its primary endpoint: CLASI-A change was -42.8% on drug versus -37.1% on placebo (difference -5.7, CI crosses zero). Safety was clean, so the dose was not tolerability-limited. The healthy-volunteer Phase 1 (PMID:40536759) showed plasma PK and well-tolerated dosing up to 800 mg single and 600 mg daily. It measured pS166-RIPK1 reduction, and the abstract (truncated) indicates high inhibition at doses of 100 mg and above. That supports peripheral engagement, but it is not shown in CLE skin, and it was published after the index trial started. No human pathway biomarker is in the bundle; the CLE skin data (PMID:41713617) are ex vivo or preclinical only. Taking engagement as adequate, the target does not drive CLE as tested. Confidence is low because the engagement figure is truncated and the index dose is not shown.

The index Phase 1b COVID-19 trial (NCT04469621; CRP change at Day 7) posted no results and gave no stop reason, so the bundle does not show why the program ended. In healthy volunteers (PMID:40536759), eclitasertib had dose-related exposure, was well tolerated up to 600 mg/day and reduced pS166-RIPK1 at doses of 100 mg and above. The truncated abstract suggests high inhibition, so engagement is treated as adequate. That evidence comes from healthy volunteers, was published after the index trial started, and the COVID trial dose is not shown. No downstream pathway data exist in patients. Adequate engagement with no evident clinical continuation points weakly to F2. The bundle is thin, and indeterminacy (U) remains plausible. No tolerability cap was shown.

In healthy volunteers (PMID:40536759), eclitasertib up to 600 mg/day was well tolerated with measurable plasma PK. The abstract says reduction of phosphorylated RIPK1 (S166) occurred at ≥100 mg, but the text is truncated, so the size of the effect is uncertain. That engagement evidence was published in 2025, after the index trial, and was not shown in COVID patients. In severe COVID-19 (NCT04469621, PMID:38419035), 600 mg/day did not significantly lower CRP versus placebo (GMR 0.85, p=0.30), and clinical trends were only numerical. With exposure and apparent engagement adequate but no meaningful pathway or clinical effect, F2 fits best. The small Phase 1b size (n=68) makes F7 a secondary code. The cutaneous lupus trial with the same drug also missed its endpoint (NCT04781816).

Randomized trials in people with a history of resected colon polyps, published in 1998, showed that oral DFMO reached the colorectal mucosa and inhibited ODC.
