Its product, putrescine, fell in a dose-dependent way, and the spermidine/spermine ratio dropped at 0.2–0.4 g/m2 with few side effects. The index trial's 750 mg dose is comparable, so tolerability did not cap engagement. That evidence comes from sporadic adenoma patients, not FAP patients, but it predates the index trial. The index trial NCT01483144 still missed its primary endpoint: progression was 32% on the combination vs 38% on sulindac and 40% on eflornithine. With the pathway engaged and no benefit on the composite endpoint, F2 fits. The benefit seen only in lower-GI events across the mixed anatomical strata supports F3, and possibly a heterogeneous, underpowered composite endpoint (F7).

In the EASE trial (NCT06144424, PMID:42629547), 150 mg EP262 was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped. The paper says predicted plasma concentrations were reached by Week 1 (data not shown), and the Phase 1 press release reports exposures several fold above preclinical efficacious levels, so systemic exposure counts as adequate. The skin biomarkers did not move: gene expression and epidermal thickness were unchanged, and EASI, vIGA-AD and itch scores showed no benefit. No human evidence of MRGPRX2 engagement in skin was found, such as an icatibant wheal challenge or occupancy data. The investigators raise both explanations: MRGPRX2 may not drive AD, or EP262 may not have engaged the target in skin. The parallel urticaria trial (NCT06077773) also missed its primary endpoint. With engagement unmeasured, the outcome is indeterminate (U).

Pyronaridine has no defined human antiviral target. Its proposed mechanism, PLpro inhibition, comes only from in vitro and mouse work (PMID:35609344). Plasma exposure at the malaria dose is well documented (PMID:38734217), but no source measured lung levels or engagement of a SARS-CoV-2 target in humans. The expected downstream effect, faster viral clearance, did not appear. The Korean Phase 2 (NCT04475107) missed its RT-PCR clearance endpoint. PMID:36332361 found no difference from standard care, and MALCOV (PMID:41552003) found slower clearance with pyronaridine-artesunate. Without engagement data, the evidence cannot show whether the drug never engaged a target or the mechanism does not matter, so the code is U. Secondary F7: the monitoring committee changed the Phase 3 endpoint because Omicron and vaccination made severe cases rarer. No Phase 3 results were found.

Ridinilazole is a non-absorbable antibiotic. At 200 mg BID, faecal levels were about 1,400 μg/g, far above the C. difficile MIC, and total clostridia fell below detection in healthy volunteers (PMID:25880933). Exposure, engagement and pathway are therefore adequate, though shown in volunteers rather than patients, and published before the index trial. Phase 2 showed sustained clinical response versus vancomycin in CDI (NCT02092935). The index Phase 3 tested superiority against active vancomycin. Ridinilazole was numerically better (64.3% vs 60.0%) but missed superiority (NCT03595553). This is not a failure of the drug to treat CDI, so F9 is the closest fit, though not a strict one. Development then stopped for a corporate or partnering decision (NCT04802837), supporting F8. A demanding superiority design (F7) also contributed.

AZD1981 is a GPR44/DP2 (CRTh2) antagonist. In NCT02367066, 20 T2DM patients took 100 mg twice daily for 3 days. Insulin secretion did not change: C-peptide was flat (p=0.41), and the glucose effect was small and not clinically significant. The PLoS One paper (PMC6296667) says plasma exposure reached the expected antagonist level and the drug was well tolerated, so exposure was adequate and the dose was not limited. No human receptor occupancy or target-inhibition data were found. PGD2 metabolite biomarkers were measured but did not correlate with response. The authors put the failure down to biology: there may be no PGD2 tone in T2DM islets, or too few GPR44 receptors. That points to F2, but because engagement was never measured, the rules require U.

The index trial NCT06278493 was a single-arm phase I/IIa dose-escalation study whose primary endpoints were DLT and MTD, not efficacy. The MTD was not reached and safety was tolerable. Efficacy was only a secondary readout (ORR 6%, mPFS 3.7 mo, mOS 5.6 mo), and the authors note no improvement over standard treatment (PMID:39760815). The bundle has no human PK, MET engagement or pathway biomarker data; the phase 1 trial NCT02779699 posted no results. So if the weak signal is read as an efficacy failure, it cannot be separated into non-engagement versus target irrelevance (U). Cabozantinib, another MET-active TKI, is listed as approved in pancreatic neoplasm, likely a neuroendocrine subtype, so F1b is a weak secondary.

BTD-001 (pentetrazol) is a GABA-A antagonist. It was tested in idiopathic hypersomnia (IH) and narcolepsy type 2 in NCT02512588, a Phase 2 trial whose primary endpoint was the Epworth Sleepiness Scale. No results were posted, and the Phase 1 PK studies (NCT03107013, NCT03150498) posted no data either. I found no human evidence of brain exposure, GABA-A receptor engagement, or a pathway biomarker such as an EEG change. The follow-up trial NCT03542851 (Arise2) was described as inconclusive. After it, Balance Therapeutics stopped IH development, wound down operations and put the company up for sale. The sponsor stated no mechanistic reason for the failure. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

RDX013 is Ardelyx's potassium secretagogue, and no molecular target is recorded. I found no human data on exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker. In NCT04780841, serum potassium fell significantly versus placebo after 8 days in Part A, which Ardelyx called proof of concept. However, the trial missed its 4-week primary endpoint in Part B. Ardelyx's planned next step was a new formulation that could improve patient compliance and efficacy. That suggests the company traced the 4-week miss to adherence and formulation, an execution and delivery problem, rather than a failed mechanism. The program was then deprioritized for resource reasons. With no engagement data, it remains uncertain whether drug exposure dropped off over 4 weeks (U/F1a are secondary codes).

The index trial (NCT03434353) showed no HBsAg decline over TAF alone at 50–400 mg, so the expected immune-mediated antigen effect did not appear. ACHIEVE (NCT02751996) reported dose-dependent drops in HBV DNA and RNA, but these could come from the drug's direct polymerase interference. The bundle has no human measure of RIG-I/NOD2 engagement, such as interferon-stimulated gene induction; the ISG data are from woodchucks only. The program ended because of safety. In the Phase 2b CATALYST 2 trial at 400 mg, patients had hepatocellular dysfunction with ALT rises consistent with liver injury, and one patient died. Spring Bank then stopped HBV development, and the other trials (NCT03932513, NCT04023721, NCT04059198) were terminated for liver injury. The toxicity was not shown to be on-target, so F6 is primary. Because engagement is unmeasured, the efficacy failure itself is indeterminate (U).

The index trial NCT04402060 was a Phase 1/2 study whose primary endpoint was descriptive safety (TEAEs and serious TEAEs), not an efficacy test of APL-9. Part 2 showed numerically more deaths with APL-9 (13/33) than control (8/32), but no stated stop reason or source attributes the program's end to toxicity or lack of efficacy. The bundle has no human pharmacokinetic, C3 inhibition or downstream complement biomarker data, no Phase 1 results and no abstracts, so all three pillars are no_human_data. Other C3 inhibitors in COVID-19 (AMY-101, NGM-621) reached only Phase 2, so there is no benchmark success. With engagement unmeasured, the mechanism remains untested (U as secondary).

In the full population of the index UC trial (NCT03861143), omilancor missed its primary endpoint: week-12 remission was 30-32% on drug vs 22.7% on placebo. The sponsor's own papers from that trial (izad258, PMID:35104848) report that the gut-restricted drug reached colonic tissue at both doses with no dose-limiting toxicity. They say 'target engagement was confirmed', based on more mucosal Tregs and IL-10-producing cells, fewer TNF-expressing myeloid cells and fecal calprotectin normalization. No direct LANCL2 binding was measured, so calling engagement adequate leans on these downstream markers. This evidence came from the index trial itself, not before it. The sponsor credits benefit only to a post-hoc subgroup of patients with confirmed inflammation (30.4% vs 3.7%), which points to patient selection or heterogeneity (F3). A high placebo response in the full population (F7) and a weakly acting mechanism (F2) are also plausible. The Crohn's trial (NCT03870334) was ended by sponsor decision.

In the PREVAIL-1 multiple-dose study in healthy volunteers (NCT03955666, ACR 2020), the same 10 mg/kg dose used in the index trial gave dose-dependent PK. It also gave sustained binding to more than 90% of available B cells (engagement) and a sustained 44% drop in IgM without depleting B cells (pathway). This was published before PREVAIL-2 started in 2022. Engagement in SLE patients was shown only in lab tests on their cells (about 63% inhibition of B-cell proliferation), not in treated patients. Even so, the index trial NCT05087628 showed no benefit: 53.8% vs 50.0% maintained improvement, p=0.761, with no safety signal. So the mechanism was engaged but did not prevent SLE flares (F2). With only 27 patients and a termination 'for strategic reasons', the trial was small and stopped early (F7).

The index trial NCT02648269 is a Phase 1 safety and pharmacodynamics study of SEL-212, which combines pegsiticase with SEL-110 (ImmTOR, nanoparticle sirolimus), in subjects with elevated uric acid or gout. Its primary outcome is drug-related adverse events, it completed, and it posted no results and no stop reason. It was not an efficacy test of sirolimus in coronary artery disorder, so no efficacy failure is shown. The pillars are inferred adequate because sirolimus is FDA-approved through mTOR inhibition in transplant, lymphangioleiomyomatosis and tuberous sclerosis. Human blood exposure is documented (PMID:9156373), and sirolimus-eluting coronary scaffolds met a noninferiority endpoint for late lumen loss (PMID:41670556). There is no disease-specific engagement data for the index trial.

Santen and MacuSight stopped the index trial (NCT00712491; subconjunctival 1320 µg or intravitreal 352 µg sirolimus) without giving a reason or posting results. Their companion trial combining sirolimus with Lucentis (NCT00766337) also ended with no results. The human data found are phase 1 safety results and retinal-thickness changes in AMD and diabetic macular edema patients. The DME study measured blood levels and found them low, but no study measured drug levels in the eye or showed mTOR inhibition (for example, a change in phospho-S6K) in eye tissue. Later AMD trials (PMID:29806044, PMID:33593448) were also clinical or anatomic only. With no human engagement data, the bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged mTOR apart from a target that doesn't matter in AMD.

The CODY trial (NCT04893486) tested topical QTORIN 3.9% sirolimus gel in 73 Gorlin syndrome patients. Fewer new facial BCCs appeared at 24 weeks on drug than on vehicle, but the difference was not statistically significant. A prespecified secondary endpoint, shrinkage of existing BCCs, was nominally significant. My searches found no human skin or BCC drug levels and no mTOR pathway markers (such as pS6) for this formulation. NCT02152007 shows only that a different topical cream was barely absorbed into blood. Topical sirolimus approved for TSC used a different formulation and strength, so it does not establish engagement here. The sponsor did not say why the trial failed. Nothing separates a drug that did not engage mTOR in BCCs from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

In gemcitabine-resistant pancreatic cancer patients, sirolimus 5 mg daily was well tolerated, showed predictable PK and inhibited mTOR signalling (p70S6K) in post-treatment PBMCs (PMID:20664591, 2010, before the 2018 index start). PMID:29948021 likewise shows PBMC pp70S6K modulation in solid tumours. Despite this, activity was marginal (6-month survival 26%), and tumour p70S6K did not predict benefit. That points to mTOR inhibition not driving pancreatic adenocarcinoma outcomes. The index trial (NCT03512756) tested SM-88, a regimen in which sirolimus is only one component at an unstated dose. OS favoured physician's choice (14.0 vs 24.1 weeks). So this is not a clean efficacy test of sirolimus (F9 secondary), and dose comparability is uncertain, which keeps confidence low. Everolimus approval relates mainly to neuroendocrine subtypes.

Santen stopped LUMINA (NCT03711929) as a 'business decision'. The posted primary result was 15.7% for DE-109 440 µg vs 12.2% for sham on VH-zero, with no significance reported. Human PK data for intravitreal DE-109 cover whole blood only, where levels stayed below those linked to systemic immunosuppression. Vitreous and retinal levels were measured only in rabbits, so drug level at the site of action is unknown in humans. No human data show mTOR inhibition or pathway biomarkers in the eye. SAKURA found 440 µg beat a 44 µg control on vitreous haze, but that was the same disease, so it cannot support an inferred_adequate rating. Without engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the answer is U. The early stop for business reasons with a small, uninterpretable difference also points to F8 and F7.

In the BRADiNP crossover trial (NCT05219812, PMID:40334047), fulmetibant 450 mg once daily did not lower pain scores compared with placebo. The treatment difference was 0.07 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.31). The drug was mostly well tolerated, so there is no sign that side effects capped the dose. The two Phase 1 trials (NCT05517746, NCT05563454) posted no results. My searches found no human data on drug levels in plasma or tissue, B1 receptor occupancy, or any downstream marker such as blocking the response to a B1 agonist. The authors say only that the preclinical efficacy did not carry over to patients. No other B1 antagonist has succeeded in this disease. Because engagement was never measured, the evidence cannot tell a drug that missed its target apart from a target that doesn't matter here.

In the BRADiNP crossover trial (NCT05219812, PMID:40334047), fulmetibant (BAY2395840) at 450 mg once daily did not reduce diabetic neuropathic pain: the difference from placebo at week 4 was 0.07. Tolerability was acceptable, so the dose was not capped. The Phase 1 trials (NCT05517746, NCT05563454) posted no results. My searches found no human PK, B1 receptor occupancy or downstream biomarker data, for example blocking responses to a B1 agonist challenge. The investigators said only that preclinical efficacy did not translate and did not give a mechanistic reason. The only other B1 antagonist listed (MK-0686) never succeeded, so F1b does not apply. Because engagement has no human data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter for this pain, so the code is U.

The index trial, NCT03045887, was GSK2292767A's first-in-human study, in healthy smokers. It measured safety plus PK/PD, not efficacy, so F9 also applies. The JPET paper reports a linear rise in plasma exposure with dose, and BAL found drug in the lung at 24 hours, so exposure at the site of action was adequate. Target engagement fell short: sputum PIP3, the direct product of PI3Kδ, dropped only 27% at 3 hours after a single dose and was not reduced at 24 hours after single or repeat 2 mg doses. That is too brief for once-daily dosing, which the sister compound nemiralisib achieved. The drug was well tolerated, so the dose was not capped by side effects. Engagement was not tested in asthma patients. The authors call this an exposure-response disconnect. The mechanism was never properly tested, which is F1a.

The index trial NCT01005966 was an in situ enamel remineralization model. Its primary analysis compared two active fluoride toothpastes (NaF 1426 ppm vs AmF 1400 ppm) for superiority, and found no difference (p=0.21). It was not a test of fluoride against placebo, so it is not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). In a similar in situ model, every fluoride toothpaste beat placebo on SMH recovery (NCT01607411, p<0.0001), showing fluoride engages enamel and drives remineralization in humans. However, that trial started after the index trial. Salivary fluoride bioavailability after brushing is shown in humans (PMID:35222673). Neither study enrolled caries patients specifically, and no tolerability limit appeared.

The first-in-human study in healthy volunteers (PMID:33503289, published Jan 2021, before the index trial began) showed exposure rising with dose. It also showed dose-dependent, complete or near-complete target saturation. Pathway effects matched the mechanism: SEB-stimulated cytokines and anti-KLH antibody responses were both suppressed. Doses went up to 10 mg/kg single and 1 mg/kg weekly, which is comparable to the 3 mg/kg every-two-weeks dose used in Synergy. No dose limit from tolerability was seen. Engagement was not shown in SLE patients. Even with engagement shown, the drug did numerically worse than placebo in NCT04835441 (SRI-4 27% vs 46%, BICLA 22% vs 32%). That points to dual CD28/ICOS blockade not driving SLE as tested (F2). Secondary F7: enrollment was stopped early under the AbbVie amendment, so only 76 patients were randomized.

The index trial NCT03770689 was a dose-escalation study with a DLT endpoint. DLTs reached 3/6 at 250 mg, and only ≤150 mg once daily was tolerable with capecitabine-CRT. Authors state peposertib 'did not improve complete response rates at tolerable dose levels' and closed the study without an MTD/RP2D (PMID:38051750). PBMC p-DNA-PK reduction was shown only in advanced solid tumours on monotherapy, where the RP2D was 400 mg BID (PMID:33230210). With CRT in head and neck, the tolerable dose gave 'insufficient exposure' (PMID:37751793). So tolerability capped the dose far below the monotherapy level, and engagement in rectal cancer was never measured. Severe late rectal toxicity (PMID:41693813) suggests on-target normal-tissue radiosensitization (F5). The index trial was not formally an efficacy test (F9).

In NCT03064438, topical ACU-D1 missed its primary endpoint. At week 12 the total lesion count fell by 10.2 on drug and by 12.0 on vehicle (p=0.366). This small pilot was described as first-in-human (PMID:34076401). My searches found no human data on skin drug levels, proteasome inhibition in skin, or any downstream biomarker such as NF-κB signalling. No other PSMB5 drug has been tested in rosacea. Without evidence of engagement, nothing separates a drug that never engaged its target from a target that does not matter, so the code is U. The investigators called the results positive based on uncontrolled within-arm responses and did not explain the miss. The small trial with a 2:1 split (only 13 on vehicle) and a large vehicle response suggests possible design limits (F7). ACU-D1 later moved to HPV-related lesions instead.

The index trial NCT05328297 enrolled genotype-selected bipolar depression patients on 50 mg daily. It missed MADRS at week 6 (-16.0 vs -15.4, p=0.438). The publication (PMID:42181295) explicitly calls the study inconclusive because a high placebo response obscured any effect, so the primary code is F7. The P2X7 PET occupancy study (NCT03437590) and the Phase 1 PK study (NCT03151486) were in healthy volunteers and posted no results. Brain penetration and occupancy are shown only in rodents (PMID:30026598). All three pillars are therefore no_human_data, which keeps U as a secondary code. A non-significant trend in the homozygous gain-of-function subgroup and a secondary social-function signal suggest F3 as a possibility.

The index trial NCT03815916 was a single-arm, 13-patient exploratory 31P-MRS study. The brain NAD+/NADH ratio rose by about 0.39 units in PD (p=0.11). PMID:38087362 reports concordant increases in the PD and MS cohorts, with significance in the prespecified pooled analysis (10.4%, p=0.037) plus β-ATP effects, and frames this as brain target engagement. The miss in PD therefore reflects a tiny, uncontrolled, underpowered biomarker study rather than clear absence of drug effect. No brain exposure data and no defined molecular target are in the bundle. No dose-limiting toxicity was seen (0 serious AEs). The ALS efficacy miss (NCT04098406) hints that the mechanism may not deliver clinical benefit, which supports F2 as a secondary code. Overall evidence is thin.

The index trial NCT01275248 tested low-dose adjunctive ondansetron (about 0.5–1 mg/day in the prior pilot, PMID:19958042) against a CNS target and stopped for lack of efficacy, with no results posted. In humans, CSF levels were about 7-fold lower than plasma even after 16 mg IV, and the authors say this low penetration may explain limited CNS efficacy (PMID:32495990). In healthy volunteers, fMRI effects were robust only at 24 mg and weak at 8 mg (PMID:30116006). Both suggest a low-dose regimen gives inadequate brain exposure. No receptor occupancy or OCD-specific biomarker data exist. The antiemetic approvals act largely peripherally, so engagement cannot be inferred for the brain. The mechanism was likely not properly tested; U is also plausible.

Index trial NCT04368507 was a Phase 1b/2a combination study with irinotecan. Its primary endpoints were DLT/MTD safety and ORR framed as safety and tolerability, and it is classified not_efficacy. No results were posted and no failure is documented, so the bundle does not show an efficacy failure of the drug. In the first-in-human trial (NCT02499224, PMID:32536979), PK was dose-proportional up to 30 mg/kg with no MTD reached, so plasma exposure was adequate and the dose was not capped. Target engagement was not quantified. Serum HGF fell only in responders, and HGF, MET and ERK did not predict response, so engagement and pathway lack adequate human evidence. If this were treated as a failure, the code would be U.

The index trial NCT05890950 is a Phase 1 safety/PK/PD study in obese T2D patients. Its only primary outcomes are adverse events and discontinuations, no results are posted, and no stop reason is given. It was not an efficacy test, so this is F9. Human pharmacology for the gut-targeted GPR40 agonist exists. PK was characterized in humans (PMID:40708100). K-757 120 mg BID with K-833 robustly raised GLP-1, PYY, CCK and oxyntomodulin (PMID:40954563). Engagement is inferred from this functional readout rather than measured directly. That evidence comes from obese subjects without T2D and was published in 2025, after the index trial started. The Phase 2a obesity trial NCT06019559 found K-757 alone produced non-significant weight loss (p=0.0756).

K-757 is a gut-restricted GPR40 agonist. In Phase 1 studies in overweight/obese volunteers (NCT05900531, NCT05890950), the drug's PK and PD were characterized (PMID:40708100). The Cell Metabolism report says satiety hormones (GLP-1, PYY, CCK) rose in humans, to levels above those seen after bariatric surgery. Rising hormones is functional evidence of engagement and of the pathway effect. Even so, in the index trial (NCT06019559) K-757 alone at 120 mg BID cut weight by only 1.57% versus 0.15% on placebo (p=0.076), and no arm had serious AEs. Engaging this mechanism does not produce meaningful weight loss. The combination's 2.9% was significant but not competitive, and K-833 was then dropped from the pipeline, which points to a commercial element (F8). The human PD data were published only after the index trial began.

In the topical EVO101 cream Phase 2a trial (NCT05579899), EASI change at week 8 was worse than vehicle (-43.5% vs -62.0%), and Evommune then dropped the drug. No human data were found on skin drug levels, IRAK4 inhibition, or downstream biomarkers such as IL-1/TLR cytokines, and no Phase 1 results were posted. The sponsor gave no mechanistic reason for stopping, only that it made 'an efficient decision based on the data'. The other IRAK4 drugs in atopic dermatitis (zabedosertib, tipasertideg) reached only Phase 2, with no success shown, so F1b does not apply. Nothing separates a cream that failed to engage IRAK4 in skin from IRAK4 not mattering in AD, so the code is U. F2 is a possible alternative.

The index trial NCT03565068 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study whose primary outcomes were AE counts. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. The Alzheimer study NCT05227118 was also safety-only, with no efficacy readout. Human data are limited to plasma PK (NCT02181803). The bundle has no human striatal PDE10A occupancy or CSF data. Occupancy in the Phase 2b paper was only 'predicted' at up to 80% (PMID:41724750), and the measured PET occupancy comes from monkeys (PMID:39893013). The schizophrenia Phase 2 trials missed their primary endpoints (NCT03055338, NCT04624243), but engagement remains unmeasured in humans. If the program's stop is read as an efficacy failure, U applies as a secondary code.

Exposure was adequate: plasma exposure rose with dose in schizophrenia patients (NCT02181803). A Phase 1 human PET study with [11C]MK-8193 (Smith 2022 abstract, cited in PMID:41724750) set the occupancy–exposure relationship that guided dose choice. Sources report high trough occupancy in Phase 1, about 63% sustained occupancy at the 12 mg index dose, and about 80% predicted at 24 mg. Doses were not capped by tolerability: up to 80 mg was tolerated in patients. The index trial (NCT03055338) showed a trend only (p=0.074), while risperidone separated from placebo. The larger Phase 2b trial at higher occupancy (NCT04624243) clearly failed, and investigators concluded PDE10A inhibition has no antipsychotic effect at the doses tested. So the target, not engagement, is what failed. No human downstream biomarker was found, and the PET data seem to come from Phase 1 rather than specifically from patients with the disease.

The index trial NCT05953740 was a small (n=17) Phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study in schizophrenia participants, and it was not an efficacy test. Its primary outcomes were adverse events and the PK of MK-5720 and MK-8189. Plasma PK was measured: low-nM MK-5720 Cmax, with MK-8189 AUC0-28d rising with dose. No target is recorded, though, and no brain-penetration, occupancy or biomarker data are given, so the pillars cannot be judged adequate. Tolerability did not limit the dose: there were no AE discontinuations in Period 2. Because there was no failed efficacy readout, F9 applies. U is secondary because engagement evidence is absent and no stop reason is given.

Blautix is a single-strain live biotherapeutic (Blautia hydrogenotrophica) with no recorded molecular target. Its proposed mechanism is consuming gut hydrogen. In a Phase 1 trial in IBS patients that predates the index trial, lactulose breath H2 fell significantly after about 2 weeks on drug but not on placebo (a sponsor patent). In the index trial, stool microbiome changes seen only on Blautix show the strain reached the gut and acted there. Still, overall response missed in both cohorts: IBS-C 25.0% vs 17.1% (p=0.152) and IBS-D 23.4% vs 17.8% (p=0.216) (NCT03721107). This fits F2, a mechanism that was engaged without clinical benefit. The sponsor called the pooled IBS-C+IBS-D result significant, which hints that each cohort was underpowered (F7). The engagement data are small and come from a patent, so confidence is low.

PDC-1421 is a Polygala tenuifolia extract. The sponsor's protocols say it inhibits the norepinephrine transporter (NET), but that claim rests only on in vitro radioligand binding and animal studies. In the Phase 2 ADHD index trial NCT05202327, neither dose separated from placebo on ≥40% ADHD-RS-IV response: 9/23 low dose and 10/24 high dose vs 11/22 placebo. The placebo response of 50% was high, and the trial was small. The Phase 1 trial NCT01774045 reported only safety results, with no dose-limiting toxicities, and no pharmacokinetic, NET occupancy or noradrenergic biomarker data. The earlier positive ADHD trial NCT02699086 had only 6 patients and no control arm. Without human evidence on exposure or engagement, the bundle cannot tell whether the drug never engaged NET or whether the mechanism doesn't work in ADHD. Code U, with F7 secondary because of the small trial and high placebo response.

The index trial NCT05890950 was a 24-patient Phase 1 study whose primary outcomes were adverse events and discontinuations. It was not an efficacy test and has no posted failure, so this is not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). K-833 is a gut-targeted GPR119 agonist. In obese non-diabetic participants, K-833 combined with K-757 raised GLP-1, PYY, oxyntomodulin and other gut hormones (pathway adequate). In Phase 2a (NCT06019559) the combination met its weight-loss endpoint, outperforming K-757 alone. Exposure and engagement are therefore inferred adequate in the same gut compartment, though only in obesity, not T2D, and published after the index trial started (PMID:40954563, PMID:40708100). Nothing in the bundle explains why the T2D program stopped.

In the index trial NCT06019559, the K-833-containing arm (K-757+K-833) met its primary endpoint: -2.94% body weight vs -0.15% on placebo at 13 weeks (p=0.0008), with no serious AEs. The 'mixed' result reflects only K-757 monotherapy (p=0.0756). There was no K-833-alone arm, so this was not a failed efficacy test of K-833. PMID:40708100 reports human PK/PD characterized, with circulating gut-hormone effects that largely recapitulated preclinical findings (exposure and pathway supported). Direct receptor-engagement data are absent. The bundle gives no stated stop reason. Discontinuation after a positive but modest readout suggests a strategic or commercial decision, though this is not documented.

RP-G28, an oral GOS prebiotic, acts by shifting colonic microbiota. In lactose-intolerant patients it produced a bifidogenic response in 90% of subjects (PMID:28049818, Phase 2 NCT01113619, published 2017, after the index start). In the index trial it increased Bifidobacterium and downstream fermenters (PMID:32290344, PMID:34365905). This supports adequate colonic exposure, engagement and pathway effect in the disease. The registered primary endpoint (abdominal pain change at Day 31) is not reported. The publication instead reports a composite-symptom responder endpoint as met (40% vs 26%, p=0.016). Phase 2 symptom and breath-hydrogen primaries only trended. A proximal effect was clearly shown, but the clinical endpoint choice appears to be the problem. The program went on to another Phase 3 (NCT03597516) with no results, so the bundle is thin.

The index trial NCT03170193 was a first-in-human Phase 1 safety study. Its only primary endpoint was adverse-event counts, so it was not an efficacy test of AMG 529. AEs were few, none were grade 3 or higher, none were serious, and none led to discontinuation, even at 700 mg SC, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no pharmacokinetic, ASGR1 engagement or downstream biomarker data (e.g. LDL or non-HDL cholesterol). It has no other trials, no same-target comparators, no publications and no stated stop reason. The failure is therefore not an efficacy failure of the drug (F9). Why the program ended cannot be determined from the bundle, and engagement is no_human_data, so U applies as secondary.

The index trial NCT02719990 was an open-label safety extension in adult GHD with an adverse-event primary endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test. It was terminated because the pediatric Phase 3 NCT02339090 missed non-inferiority against daily rhGH. In that trial somavaratan still produced substantial height velocity (9.43 vs 10.70 cm/yr). In GH-deficient adults, PMID:23585663 (2013, before the index trial) showed dose-proportional exposure, a long half-life and dose-dependent IGF-I increases into the normal range. That IGF-I response is direct evidence of GHR activation and its pathway effect. PMID:26672637 confirmed the IGF-1 and height-velocity responses in children. The drug was active; the program ended over a missed non-inferiority margin against an active comparator, not a failed efficacy test of this drug.

The index trial NCT03145831 was a long-term safety study with an adverse-event primary outcome, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because the pivotal pediatric trial NCT02339090 missed non-inferiority against daily rhGH: height velocity was 9.43 vs 10.70 cm/yr, with the lower CI bound of -2.32. That trial still showed robust growth. The pillars held in GH-deficient patients before 2017. Exposure was dose-proportional with a long half-life, and IGF-1 rose dose-dependently into the normal range in GHD adults and children (PMID:23585663, PMID:26672637), indicating GHR engagement and pathway activation. Tolerability did not cap the dose. The program stopped over a missed non-inferiority margin against an active comparator, not a lack of drug effect, so this is F9.

The index trial NCT02068521 was a long-term safety study, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because the pivotal pediatric Phase 3 (NCT02339090) missed non-inferiority against daily rhGH. Somavaratan still produced robust height velocity there (9.43 vs 10.70 cm/yr). Exposure, GHR activation and pathway effects were shown in humans: linear PK with a long half-life and dose-dependent IGF-1 increases in GH-deficient adults (PMID:23585663) and in prepubertal children with GHD. The pediatric study (NCT01718041, registered 2012, before the index start; PMID:26672637) showed clinically meaningful height velocity gains. The drug engaged the target and worked; it only fell short of a non-inferiority margin versus an active comparator, which fits F9. Inferior dosing or IGF-1 targeting could explain the gap, but the bundle does not say so.

The index trial NCT02445794 was a 28-day Phase 1/2 study with a descriptive safety primary endpoint (adverse events), so it was not an efficacy test. It reported an early signal in peak workload (PMID:29624723). Exposure was adequate: plasma and RBC-membrane D2-LA and D2-AA reached steady state, near the 20% therapeutic target (PMID:32871154, PMID:36462055). That membrane incorporation is the drug's mechanism, so engagement counts as shown in FA patients, though only after the index trial started. No downstream lipid-peroxidation biomarker was reported, so pathway has no human data. The program's real efficacy failure was the later 11-month trial, which found no benefit on MVO2 despite steady-state levels and good tolerability (PMID:36462055). That points to F2 as a secondary code.

RT001 has no protein target. It is meant to work by building deuterated linoleic acid (D2-LA) into cell membranes so that they resist lipid peroxidation. Exposure was adequate: in the Phase 1/2 trial in FA patients (NCT02445794, PMID:29624723), the 9 g/day dose put about 25.8% D2-LA into red-cell membranes, above the 20% therapeutic target. In the index trial, plasma and red-cell levels reached steady state (PMID:36462055, PMID:32871154). I counted this membrane incorporation as engagement, shown in FA patients before the index trial began. No human marker of lipid peroxidation, the pathway pillar, appears in the sources. Peak VO2 and all secondary measures showed no effect. Likely reading: the mechanism does not drive FA, or not at this dose (F2). Confidence is low because no lipid-peroxidation readout was available, so U also applies.

The index trial NCT01124565 (RT001 for lateral canthal lines, 2010) had a safety-only primary outcome: treatment-emergent adverse events. It was classified not_efficacy and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug, which supports F9. The RT001 code appears to cover different molecules across programs: a topical product for wrinkles, a deuterated compound in Friedreich's ataxia (NCT04102501 missed peak VO2) and an mRNA vaccine. No target is recorded, and the bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data. U is listed as secondary because engagement has no human data and the mechanism was never tested.

The index trial NCT02316509 was a Phase 1 dose-escalation safety and PK study, not an efficacy test. The MTD was not reached, the drug was well tolerated, and PK supported once-daily dosing (PMID:37261814). Target engagement in ER+ patients was shown by >90% reduction in FES-PET uptake, with ~40% ER reduction. This was published in 2023, after the index trial started in 2015. No downstream pathway biomarker was reported. There were no objective responses, but the clinical benefit rate was 29%. PMID:37102506 states development was halted because of high pill burden due to poor absorption and metabolism, and the follow-on molecule giredestrant replaced it. That is a molecule-property/portfolio decision, not an efficacy failure of the mechanism.

The index Phase 1 trial (NCT03008161) had a safety primary endpoint and was not powered for efficacy. NPT088 was generally safe, with infusion reactions in a minority of patients. Exploratory amyloid and tau PET in mild-to-moderate AD patients showed no reduction in plaque or tau aggregates and no symptomatic effect at any of 4 doses (PMID:31686093). Target-lowering therefore was not achieved in humans, and the plaque and tau reductions were seen only in mice (PMID:29067301). No brain exposure data are given. Other amyloid-targeting antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab, aducanumab) are FDA-approved in AD and do clear plaque. That points to a failure of this molecule, not of the target (F1b), with inadequate engagement (F1a). Because the index trial was a safety study, F9 is secondary.

The index trial NCT02458677 was a single ascending dose study in healthy subjects. Its primary outcomes were only safety and pharmacokinetics, so it was not an efficacy test of imaprelimab. No results were posted for it. The follow-on multiple ascending dose study in psoriasis patients (NCT02630901) completed with no classified outcome or posted results. The bundle has no PubMed abstracts, no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for MCAM blockade, and no other drugs on this target. The readout cannot be counted as an efficacy failure (F9). Why the program stopped cannot be determined from the bundle, and with engagement unmeasured, U also applies.

The index trial NCT02758392 was a single-dose first-in-human safety study in 54 healthy volunteers with an adverse-event primary endpoint. It was not an efficacy test, so F9 applies. Exposure was shown in humans, with dose-proportional Cmax and AUC (PMID:30776134). Total TNF and IL-17A rose dose-dependently, and human target-complex profiles matched predictions (PMID:32544369). Apparent in vivo affinity was lower than the parental antibodies, and all treated subjects developed antidrug antibodies, which raised clearance; these are possible molecule-specific liabilities. No downstream pathway biomarker or patient data exist, and the publications postdate the 2016 trial start. The bundle gives no stated reason why the program stopped.

In healthy volunteers given 5–480 mg (PMID:38204407, NCT04622111), CPL207280 reached the bloodstream, and plasma exposure is the right measure for a pancreatic beta-cell target. So exposure was adequate, though exposure rose less than proportionally with dose. No human study measured target engagement. The pathway readouts (glucose, insulin, C-peptide, glucagon) showed no clear relationship with dose. No pharmacodynamic data in people with type 2 diabetes were found. The index trial (NCT05248776) posted no results and the sponsor gave no reason for stopping, so even the failure itself is unconfirmed. Fasiglifam, which works on the same target, met glucose-lowering endpoints in Phase 2 and 3 (PMC8459971). That suggests GPR40 is a valid target, which points to the molecule (F1b), but the evidence is thin. U also applies because engagement was never measured.

TSC has no recorded molecular target. Its proposed mechanism is better oxygen diffusion into hypoxic tissue. The index Phase 1/2 trial in claudication (NCT00725881; PMID:22003000) was a small dose-ranging study with only 65% power. Its primary endpoints were safety and PK, and it showed only a borderline cubic trend in peak walking time (p=0.07). No one measured tissue oxygenation or a pharmacodynamic marker in PAD patients. The only human PD data come from a 2021 tcpO2 study in healthy volunteers (NCT04808622), long after the index trial. There, TSC shifts overlapped with placebo except possibly at 2.0–2.5 mg/kg. Development turned to glioblastoma and other indications, and no failure reason is given. Engagement therefore has no human data, so the code is U. The underpowered design is a secondary factor (F7).

In CANBERRA (NCT04265261, PMID:39802207), plasma exposure rose with dose, and both doses were well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No human data show the drug reached the eye: the investigators say they are unsure whether plasma levels gave enough ocular exposure. That leaves exposure at the retinal site of action unshown, so I rated it inadequate. The doses were only 'expected' to engage CB2R by half to fully, based on modelling. No receptor occupancy or downstream biomarker was measured in humans, so engagement and pathway have no human data (animal data in PMID:39070793 do not count). The authors list several possible causes: the target may not matter in humans, ocular exposure may have been too low, the DRSS endpoint may be unsuitable, or 36 weeks may have been too short. Nothing in the sources separates poor engagement from an irrelevant target, so the code is U, with F4 as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT03959189 was a 12-patient single-dose Phase 1 study in DM1. Its only primary outcome was safety and tolerability. It was not an efficacy test, and there was no failed efficacy readout. ERX-963 at 1 mg and 2 mg was well tolerated, with no serious AEs and no drug-related AEs in the active periods. No PK, receptor occupancy or biomarker data were posted. Exposure and engagement are inferred_adequate from flumazenil's approved use reversing benzodiazepines at similar sub-milligram to milligram doses. Case reports also show reversal in DM patients (PMID:33432421, PMID:33625620), but these were published after the index trial started. The DM1 rationale rests on mouse data (PMID:36150891). No reason for stopping is given in the bundle.

FURESTEM-AD is a cell therapy made from umbilical cord blood stem cells (hUCB-MSCs) and has no defined molecular target, so the bundle has no human data on exposure or target engagement. In the index Phase 3 (NCT03269773), a single high dose missed the week-12 EASI-50 endpoint: 31.82% of treated patients responded versus 27.16% on placebo. The sponsor said EASI improved significantly at week 4, and that TARC, a disease-severity biomarker, fell almost 10-fold versus placebo. So there was a pathway-level effect in atopic dermatitis patients, but it faded before week 12. The sponsor blamed the single-dose regimen and timing, and switched to repeated dosing (NCT04725136, NCT05004324). That fits F4 (endpoint or timing) best. Because there is no engagement data, U also applies. Confidence is low: all evidence comes from press reports.

In NCT05305599 (CEC-11/NAS, EASL 2024), ZED1227 at 20, 50 and 100 mg did not lower PRO-C3 significantly compared with placebo: -6.5% and -8.1% at 20 mg and 100 mg, with no effect at 50 mg. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not the limit. The only human engagement evidence comes from coeliac disease (NEJM; drug accumulation in enterocytes). There the capsule is built to release in the duodenum, a different compartment, so it cannot be used to infer that the drug reached or inhibited TG2 in the liver. No liver TG2 occupancy or activity data were found. With no way to tell a drug that never engaged from a target that does not matter, the code is U. Investigators saw a dose-dependent PRO-C3 drop in patients with above-median baseline PRO-C3, which supports F3 as a secondary code.

The index Phase 2a trial (NCT05305599) missed its primary endpoint, the change in PRO-C3 (a blood marker of fibrosis) over 12 weeks. At EASL 2024 the investigators reported lower PRO-C3 and PRO-C6 only in a subgroup with high disease activity and significant fibrosis, and they framed the drug's potential around that subgroup. That points to patient selection (F3). No human source shows liver exposure, liver TG2 inhibition, or liver engagement. The drug met its endpoint in celiac disease, but that capsule is built for duodenal targeting and gut drug levels were measured in enterocytes. That is a different tissue, so engagement cannot be inferred for the liver. Since engagement has no human data, U also applies. No dose-limiting toxicity was reported.

T89 is a botanical extract of Danshen and Sanqi with borneol, and no molecular target is recorded. The index Phase 3 trial (NCT04993729) has no posted results, and none of the sources give a reason for stopping. Human data cover safety (NCT01679028) and the lack of a warfarin PK/PD interaction (PMID:24142885). No source shows tissue exposure, target engagement or a pathway biomarker relevant to acute mountain sickness. A related Phase 2 trial of AR36, another plant extract described much like T89 (PMID:37923683), did not improve LLSS score or AMS incidence at either dose. Because there is no target and no engagement data, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT03038113 was a Phase 1 safety/PK/PD study with no failed efficacy endpoint, so the code is partly inferred. In virologically suppressed CHB patients, RO7062931 lowered HBsAg in a dose- and time-dependent way, which the authors call target engagement (PMID:34037271). The best regimen (3.0 mg/kg QW) reached only a ~0.5 log10 IU/mL mean nadir, a partial knockdown. Supradose-proportional plasma exposure and higher urinary excretion at ≥2–3 mg/kg indicate ASGPR liver-uptake saturation (PMID:34037271, PMID:37147890). That caps hepatic delivery whatever the dose. Tolerability was not limiting. The likeliest explanation is insufficient hepatic exposure and engagement; the bundle gives no explicit stop reason.

Plasma bryostatin levels rose roughly in proportion to dose between 20 and 40 µg. Brain exposure and brain PKCε engagement were never measured in humans, so all three pillars are no_human_data at the CNS site. The only human signal is a brief rise in blood-cell (PBMC) PKCε after a single dose in 6 AD patients (PMID:28482641). That is peripheral, small and published after the index trial began. Investigators suggested the 40 µg dose may have downregulated PKC rather than activated it, and that arm also had more adverse events and dropouts (F7 and F1a are possible). Neither idea was tested with biomarkers. The 20 µg dose then failed in the confirmatory trial (NCT03560245). With no CNS engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT00942825, adding CBP501 to cisplatin/pemetrexed did not improve PFS (median 140 vs 165 days). Toxicity was similar between arms, and no sponsor explanation for the failure was found. The Phase 1 studies (NCT00551512; Clin Cancer Res 2011) set the dose at the MTD of 25 mg/m², which hypersensitivity reactions capped at higher doses. They describe PK but no human measure of calmodulin engagement or a downstream marker such as increased tumor platinum uptake or G2 checkpoint abrogation; the full text could not be fetched to check. The evidence for engagement comes from animal and in vitro studies. The mesothelioma signal (NCT00700336) had no formal test, so it cannot support inferred engagement. No other drug on this target appears in the bundle. Engagement is therefore no_human_data, giving U.

The index trial NCT03126097 was a Phase 1 oral-contraceptive drug-interaction study in healthy females, not an efficacy test. It was terminated because 'study stopping rules were met', probably safety-related, so this is F9. Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional PK up to 150 mg, reaching exposures expected to be efficacious (PMID:29927386). In the influenza challenge study (NCT02588521, PMID:30053042), 150 mg twice daily gave dose-dependent reductions in viral load, symptoms and mucus weight. This supports endonuclease engagement and a pathway effect in infected humans before the index trial; I counted that viral-load drop as engagement because no direct binding measure exists. A repeat-dosing study (NCT03411421) was also halted because 'data did not support continuation', suggesting molecule-specific safety concerns (F6 secondary).

HDIT101 is an antibody against HSV glycoprotein B. In the first-in-human study (PMID:35869929), serum exposure rose linearly with dose up to 12,150 mg and there was no dose-limiting toxicity. Systemic exposure was therefore adequate, and the 2 g dose was not capped by tolerability. However, no human source shows the drug engaging its target: there is no data on neutralizing titres in patients or on lower HSV DNA shedding from the daily swabs. The MATCH-2 index trial (NCT04165122, PMID:41109488) missed its primary endpoint of lesion days, although the recurrence rate was lower. The HSV-1 trial (NCT04539483) stopped for futility. The sponsors give no reason for the failure beyond suggesting an immune-modulation effect. With no engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a mechanism that does not work, so the code is U.

HDIT101 is an anti-HSV glycoprotein B mAb. The index trial (NCT04539483) gave it topically for herpes labialis and was stopped for futility at an interim analysis. The only human PK data are serum levels after IV dosing in healthy volunteers (PMID:35869929, PMID:33015449). No source measured drug levels in lip skin or lesions after topical use, binding to the target, or a virologic effect in herpes labialis patients. The IV genital herpes trial (NCT04165122, MATCH-2) missed its primary endpoint against valacyclovir, though some secondary recurrence measures favoured HDIT101. It reported no measure of target engagement either. Without engagement data, the sources cannot tell whether the drug failed to engage its target or whether neutralising gB does not prevent recurrences, so the code is U.

In the index trial NCT03446846, neither 2.5 mg nor 5.0 mg MIN-117 separated from placebo on the week-6 MADRS. All arms changed by -12, which also points to a large placebo response. The bundle has no Phase 1 results, PK, PET occupancy or biomarker data, so exposure, engagement and pathway are all no_human_data. The same targets are clearly validated in MDD: drugs acting on SLC6A4 or HTR1A (amitriptyline, aripiprazole, brexpiprazole) are FDA-approved for depression. That makes 'target does not drive disease' unlikely and points to the molecule or its dose (F1b). Because engagement was never shown, U also applies. The uniform placebo response suggests a possible trial-sensitivity issue (F7). The bundle is thin.

NCX 4251, a topical fluticasone propionate nanosuspension for the eyelid, missed its Phase 2 primary endpoint. Complete cure at Day 15 occurred in 4/109 eyes on drug vs 2/111 on placebo (p=0.44, NCT04675242). It was well tolerated, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The bundle has no human evidence of eyelid or lid-margin tissue exposure, GR engagement, or an anti-inflammatory biomarker for this formulation. Airway and nasal pharmacology data come from different compartments. Meanwhile, loteprednol etabonate, another NR3C1 agonist, is FDA-approved for blepharitis. That points to the molecule or formulation and its delivery rather than the target, which fits F1b. U also applies because engagement is unmeasured. The stringent complete-cure endpoint at only 15 days may have limited sensitivity (F7).

Bayer's full-text paper (PMID:31647607, PMC7383986) says development of BAY1003803 stopped for inadequate efficacy. The dose-escalation trial NCT02936492 was ended early because of results from a parallel psoriasis plaque test, which is the index trial NCT02940002. Healthy volunteers showed only plasma exposure, and skin delivery was measured only in vitro. No human data show glucocorticoid receptor engagement in skin or a biomarker change, such as cortisol suppression or reduced skin inflammation. Topical GR agonists like clobetasol and betamethasone are approved for psoriasis, so the target clearly works. That points to this molecule (its potency, skin delivery or SEGRA profile), not the target. With no engagement data, F1b is the best fit and U also applies. There was no tolerability limit: no safety signals were seen.

The index trial NCT03406364 is a Phase 1 dose-finding study of MG005 (GW5074) combined with sorafenib in solid tumors. Its primary outcomes are MTD and DLTs, so it was a safety and tolerability study, not an efficacy test of the drug. No results were posted, no stop reason is given, and the bundle has no other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target comparators. There is no human evidence on exposure, RAF1 engagement or pathway effects, so all pillars are no_human_data. Nothing shows an efficacy failure or a dose cap from tolerability. F9 is primary; U is secondary because engagement is untested. Confidence is low because the bundle is very thin.

The ASH 2019 abstract reports results from the index trial NCT02543879 (84 AML/MDS and 10 NHL patients). Exposure rose in proportion to dose from 10 to 600 mg, with a half-life of about 52 hours. In patients, whole-blood BET markers changed with drug concentration: CCR1 fell and HEXIM1 rose, more robustly at doses above 180 mg. HEXIM1 is a standard proxy for BET engagement, so engagement and pathway effect were both shown in the program's diseases. Tolerability did not cap the dose: an MTD of 400 mg every other week was reached inside the range where the markers moved. Even so, efficacy was modest: 1 CRi among 30 evaluable AML/MDS patients, and 1 stable disease among 3 NHL patients. This pattern supports F2 (target engaged, little single-agent benefit). The sponsor gave no stated reason for stopping, and these data appeared only after the trial began.

The index trial NCT02625636 was a Phase 1 safety, PK and PD dose-escalation study of the glucagon receptor agonist SAR438544 versus placebo and glucagon, in healthy subjects and type 1 diabetes patients. Its primary outcome was adverse events. No results were posted, and there are no other trials, PubMed abstracts or same-target comparator drugs in the bundle. There is therefore no human evidence on exposure, engagement or pathway, and no stated reason for stopping. Because engagement is no_human_data, the primary code is U. F9 is a secondary possibility, since the index trial was a safety study rather than an efficacy test.

The index trial NCT01723241 is a Phase 1 topical XAF5 gel study in 32 healthy volunteers. It lists no primary outcome and posted no results, so it was not an efficacy test of salmeterol in obesity (F9). The bundle has no human data on salmeterol levels in adipose tissue or on ADRB2 engagement in fat after topical or subcutaneous dosing. Systemic beta2 effects (heart rate, glucose, potassium) appear only after inhaled doses in healthy subjects (PMID:1349491, PMID:10899240). The asthma/COPD approvals act through lung, a different tissue compartment. A related XAF5 eyelid-fat trial met its endpoint (NCT02230761), while the LIPO-202 Phase 3 failed (NCT02398188). Nothing separates non-engagement from target irrelevance, so U is secondary.

The bundle records no target and no human data on exposure, engagement or pathway, and no PubMed abstracts or posted results. The index trial NCT03239223 was a Phase 1 maximum-tolerated-dose study with no posted results, so it was not a clear efficacy test (F9). The only stated reason for stopping in the program is that the sibling anal HSIL trial NCT03677960 was terminated for 'Pre-Clinical Toxicology Findings'. That points to molecule-specific toxicity ending the program (F6). The other trials, NCT03202992 and NCT03697226, completed without results. Engagement is no_human_data, so if this were treated as an efficacy failure it would be indeterminate (U). Confidence is low because the bundle is thin.

Echinacea has no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human exposure or engagement data. The index trial (NCT03812900) compared high-dose new formulations with a lower-dose conventional Echinacea control, not placebo. It missed its 10-day time-to-remission endpoint (median 10 vs 11 days, p=0.10 ITT). PMID:37138742 reports a proximal antiviral effect in this disease: higher viral clearance by PCR (70 vs 53%, p=0.046). An extrapolated analysis beyond day 10 was significant (9.6 vs 11.0 days, p<0.001). This points to the 10-day observation window as the limiting factor (F4). The active same-drug comparator also limited the trial's ability to show benefit (F7/F9). A separate prevention trial was positive (NCT02971384).

Echinacea purpurea whole extract has no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human data on drug levels at the site of action, target binding or a biomarker linked to a mechanism, so all three pillars are no_human_data. The index trial (NCT03812900, PMID:37138742) had no placebo arm. It compared high-dose new formulations against lower-dose standard echinacea. Time to remission favoured the new formulations but missed significance (ITT p=0.10, per-protocol p=0.07). An extrapolated sensitivity analysis and viral clearance (70% vs 53%, p=0.046) also favoured them. A dose comparison like this, possibly underpowered, cannot show whether the drug engages a target or whether that target matters. This supports U, with F7 and F9 (not a test against placebo) as secondary codes. NCT02971384 met its endpoint against vitamin C. No web searches were run, so this rests on the bundle alone.

The index trial NCT02612844 is a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK/PD study in T1D. Its only primary outcome is the number of treatment-emergent adverse events, so it was not an efficacy test of NNC0143-0406. No results were posted for it or for the follow-on proof-of-principle trial NCT02938572. There are no PubMed abstracts and no stated stop reason. All three pillars therefore lack human data. Many insulin receptor agonists are approved in T1D, but nothing in the bundle shows this molecule failed, nor any toxicity or business reason. The program halt is best classed as not an efficacy failure (F9). The underlying reason is indeterminate (U), and the evidence is thin.

The index trial NCT01010737 was a Phase 1/2 study of Multimeric-001 influenza vaccine in elderly volunteers, with Montanide ISA 51 VG as the adjuvant. It completed, and its primary endpoint was safety, tolerability and reactogenicity. No efficacy endpoint was tested and no results were posted. The companion trial NCT00877448 likewise measured only descriptive adverse-event counts and was classed as not an efficacy test. The drug is an adjuvant with no recorded molecular target, so the exposure, engagement and pathway pillars cannot be assessed from human data in the bundle. The PubMed abstracts on influenza are animal studies only. Because the index trial was not an efficacy test of this drug, the failure is coded F9.

In the Phase 1 trial (PMID:40586764/NCT05905614), plasma exposure rose with dose from 50 to 600 mg, with a plateau at 600 mg, and steady state at 400 mg, the dose used in the index trial. No DLT or MTD was reached, so tolerability did not cap the dose. No human data on target engagement were found: no pRb phosphorylation, Ki-67 or TK1 measurements, and no tumor drug levels. Neutropenia, a class effect, is indirect evidence at best. The index trial (NCT05580588) stopped because efficacy was 'less than anticipated' (12-week PFS in 2 of 14), and the sponsor gave no mechanistic explanation. Other CDK4/6 inhibitors reached Phase 3 in liposarcoma, but the bundle shows none approved or meeting a pivotal endpoint. A drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In NCT03598699, AXR-159 50 mg/mL topical failed to separate from vehicle on either primary endpoint: inferior corneal staining -0.08 vs -0.03, and eye dryness -12.5 vs -14.9. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data for AXR-159: no Phase 1 results, no other trials and no abstracts. Another LFA-1 (ITGAL) antagonist, lifitegrast, is FDA-approved for dry eye syndrome, so the target is validated in this disease. With no pillar evidence that AXR-159 engaged LFA-1 adequately, the failure is best attributed to the molecule rather than the target (F1b). The safety data show no toxicity signal, with 0/54 serious adverse events on drug. Because engagement is entirely undocumented, U also applies as a secondary code.

MK-8583 is a tenofovir prodrug that inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase. After one 100 mg dose in HIV-infected people (NCT03552536), the active metabolite TFV-DP in PBMCs stayed above the 100 nM trough that works for marketed tenofovir prodrugs, so exposure was adequate. Inhibition of reverse transcriptase itself was never measured. The pathway result was inadequate: viral load fell only 0.6 log10 at day 7, the drop was modest and transient, some participants had no consistent fall, and viral load did not track TFV-DP levels. Marketed tenofovir prodrugs work through the same target, so the target matters; the problem lies with this molecule and its weekly single-dose regimen. The investigators questioned whether extended-interval dosing of tenofovir prodrugs is feasible and suggested daily dosing might do better (secondary code F4). Tolerability did not limit the dose.

Human plasma PK was measured in Phase 1 and in sickle cell disease. In the SCD protocol (NCT03401112), the 50 mg dose fell below target exposure, so the program moved to 200–400 mg, the doses used in the index trial. I found no human measure of PDE9 inhibition or cGMP rise in any source, so engagement is no_human_data. On the pathway, F-cells rose modestly in SCD Phase 2a and tracked exposure. However, in the beta-thalassemia trial (Forte, NCT04411082), most disease biomarkers did not improve, and in the SCD Phase 2b (Ardent, NCT04474314) HbF response did not differ from placebo. So the pathway effect looks inadequate. The drug was well tolerated, so dose was not capped by tolerability. Because engagement was never measured, a drug that did not engage cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter here, so the code is U.

The index trial NCT04590430 was a Phase 1 safety, tolerability and PK study in healthy adults. It had no efficacy endpoint, so it was not an efficacy test of the drug, which makes F9 the code. Exposure was adequate: dose-proportional serum Cmax and AUC, with a long half-life of 89-107 days (PMID:37332355). Engagement was shown ex vivo as dose-dependent pseudovirus neutralization titres in serum from healthy subjects (PMID:39793935). That evidence comes only from healthy volunteers, not COVID-19 patients, and was published after the index trial started. No pathway or clinical antiviral data appear in the bundle. All adverse events were grade 1-2, so there was no dose limitation. The bundle gives no reason for the program stopping.

The index trial NCT03752242 was not an efficacy test of the drug. Enrollment was stopped for chemistry work on the investigational product. Only 2 subjects enrolled, and outcomes were reported descriptively with no comparison, so the primary endpoint is not assessable. A parallel rosacea trial (NCT03756389) was suspended for re-formulation, which points to a product/formulation issue rather than an efficacy failure. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data, and no primary target is recorded. Because the stop was not due to a failed efficacy readout, F9 fits best. F7 is secondary because operational problems and the 2-patient enrollment meant the trial could not answer the question.

In NCT04299464, neither 20 mg nor 60 mg alogabat beat placebo on the Vineland-3 ABC (p≈0.76 for both), and there were no serious AEs. The target is in the brain, so plasma Cmax from NCT03774576 does not show that the drug reached its site of action. Roche ran a human [11C]Ro15-4513 PET occupancy study in healthy volunteers (NCT03507569), but no occupancy values were posted. The sponsor's 2025 paper (PMID:40761395) shows occupancy and EEG effects only in rodents and says the human PET and EEG results are still unpublished. No human biomarker data in ASD were found. The sources do not say why the program failed, and the Angelman program (NCT05630066) was also stopped. With no human engagement data, a drug that never engaged cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter, so the code is U.

In the single-ascending-dose study (5–40 mg/kg) in healthy volunteers and stable CAD patients, MDCO-216 raised plasma ApoA-I dose-dependently. ApoA-I Milano was incorporated into large HDL particles and pre-β1 HDL rose. ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux increased profoundly, and the drug was well tolerated (PMID:27418968, 26916733, 27816804, 28844118). The index trial used 20 mg/kg weekly, within the engaged range, and showed the expected HDL-C fall (PMID:30046837). Yet PAV showed no regression versus placebo on statins and trended unfavourably (0.73%, p=0.07; NCT02678923). Other ApoA-I infusions were also non-significant in a meta-analysis (PMID:40539788). This points to the mechanism not driving plaque regression as tested. Engagement was not measured in ACS patients, and the engagement papers postdate the index start.

In RA patients on MTX, the index phase 2a trial (NCT03257852) of ASP5094 10 mg/kg IV q4w missed ACR50 at week 12 (6.3% vs 18.2% placebo). There were no subgroup trends and no safety signals. PMID:33087159 measured PK and PD of downstream α9 effectors. It reports no difference in secondary efficacy or PD endpoints 'despite achiev[ing]…'. That truncated phrase implies the expected exposure or target saturation was reached, though the bundle does not show the measurement itself. Dose was not limited by tolerability. Taking engagement as adequate, the lack of any clinical signal points to α9 not driving RA as tested (F2). The engagement evidence is truncated, published after the index trial, and the phase 1 trial (NCT02698657) posted no results, so confidence is low and U is a fallback.

The first-in-human study (NCT01098838, PMID:25113756) showed dose-proportional exposure and cIAP1 protein degradation in blood, skin and tumor at tolerable doses up to 1,800 mg, with increased circulating cytokines. That covers exposure, engagement and a pathway effect in patients with mixed advanced solid tumors, not specifically TNBC. The trial was registered before the index trial began, though the data were published in 2014. In the index TNBC trial (NCT01617668), adding LCL161 to paclitaxel gave no pCR gain in gene-signature-positive patients (24.9% vs 23.4%) or signature-negative patients. Serious AEs rose (45/106 vs 7/103). With engagement shown, the lack of benefit points to the IAP mechanism not driving response. The failed predictive-signature selection is a possible secondary factor.

No direct human PK, occupancy or PD data are in the bundle. Exposure, engagement and pathway are inferred adequate because the same oral doses (20–40 mg BID) of this systemic PDE4B/D inhibitor met the PASI primary endpoint in psoriasis (NCT05190419, PMID:37951245). That evidence was published after the index trial started. In ADESOS (NCT05469464), orismilast arms reduced EASI by 52–61%, but placebo reduced it by 50.4%, so no dose separated (p>0.1). IGA 0/1 and early itch secondary endpoints favoured orismilast (PMID:39847538). PDE4 inhibitors are approved in atopic eczema, so the target is relevant. An unusually high placebo response most directly explains the miss (F7). A mechanism-level shortfall in this disease (F2) remains possible.

The bundle has no human evidence that the drug engaged EGFR, so the failure is coded U. In the first-in-human trial (NCT03234712, PMID:36814898), Ser-T was tolerable up to the recommended phase 2 dose of a 50 µg/kg loading dose then 25 µg/kg every 4 weeks. Only one dose-limiting toxicity occurred, so tolerability did not cap the dose. The glioblastoma expansion cohort closed for lack of efficacy: 1 partial response among 24 patients. Plasma PK was a trial endpoint, but the bundle reports no tumor or CSF drug levels, EGFR occupancy, or downstream biomarkers. Preclinical work (PMID:36071925) suggests EGFR ADCs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly when given systemically. That makes inadequate exposure (F1a) possible, but it is not shown in humans. The bundle cannot tell a drug that never engaged EGFR from a target that does not matter.

Perindopril reaches plasma at standard doses (perindoprilat PK, PMID:1327596, PMID:1576057). It inhibits plasma ACE strongly and dose-dependently, about 87.5% maximum, in hypertensive and cirrhotic patients (PMID:1576057, PMID:1327596), all published well before the 2016 index start. Pathway effects followed: renin and aldosterone changed and blood pressure fell (PMID:2550045), and the drug is approved for hypertension (NCT01556997). Engagement was never measured in obese subjects, and no tolerability cap is shown. The index trial (NCT02777489) tested a CPD-genotype hypothesis for weight and fat loss and was terminated as an 'unproven hypothesis' with no results posted. With engagement adequate, this points to ACE inhibition not driving weight loss as tested (F2). Genotype-based selection makes F3 a secondary possibility.

DMT310 is a topical with no recorded molecular target. The bundle has no human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects. Dermata's December 2022 topline release says the rosacea Phase 2 (NCT05108025) missed its primary endpoints: 36% of DMT310 patients were IGA responders vs 23% on placebo, which was not statistically significant. The company suggested the high 23% dropout rate and the waxing-and-waning course of rosacea could explain the weaker effect. That points to trial execution (F7), but the company offered it as a possible explanation, not a finding. Because engagement was never measured, nothing separates a drug that failed to act from a mechanism that doesn't matter in rosacea, so the primary code is U. There are no safety issues: the release reports no treatment-related serious adverse events.

Baxter, the sponsor, stopped RENEW (NCT01508910) early in December 2013 for financial or strategic reasons. By then only 112 of the planned 444 patients were enrolled. The investigators called the trial an incomplete experiment, so the missed exercise-time endpoint (108.7 vs 90.0 s) reflects a trial too small to answer the question. CLBS16 is an autologous CD34+ cell therapy with no defined molecular target, and I found no human data on cell retention, engagement or a pathway biomarker. The CFR improvement in coronary microvascular dysfunction (NCT03508609) was in another disease and was not a pivotal efficacy result. F7 is primary; the business-driven stop (F8) and the absence of engagement data (U) also apply.

BTA585 (BTA-C585) is an oral drug designed to block the RSV fusion (F) protein. Healthy-volunteer SAD and MAD studies (IDWeek abstract) showed dose-proportional plasma exposure at levels described as enough to kill the virus, and the drug was detectable in nasal wash. So exposure is adequate. No human study measured binding to the F protein or a pathway biomarker separately from viral load. In the RSV challenge trial NCT02718937, viral load did not fall significantly. The sponsor blamed large variability in viral load between cohorts and the small number of infected subjects, saying these limited the trial's ability to detect a difference. That points to F7, trial design. Because engagement was never shown in humans, U also applies.

LYC-30937-EC is an enteric-coated allosteric modulator of F1F0-ATPase. It was designed to act in the gut lumen and is barely absorbed into the blood. In the index psoriasis trial (NCT02872285), 25 mg once daily missed its PASI endpoint (p=0.22, with only 27 patients analysed). The protocol mentions Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers up to 300 mg, but they reported only safety and low systemic exposure. I found no human data on gut-tissue drug levels, ATP synthase inhibition, apoptosis of activated lymphocytes, or any downstream biomarker. The drug also failed in ulcerative colitis (NCT02762500), where it would have acted locally, and no other drug on this target has succeeded. Without engagement evidence, nothing separates a drug that never engaged from a mechanism that does not matter, so the code is U. The trial's small size may also have limited its power.

The open-label extension (NCT02764229) was stopped for lack of efficacy after the parent Phase 2 trial, NCT02762500, missed its primary endpoint: 25 mg gave 7/62 remissions vs 12/62 on placebo. The same drug also failed in psoriasis (NCT02872285). The only human data are low plasma levels in healthy volunteers and UC patients (NCT02818543), which the protocol cites for safety and for evidence of delivery to the colon. The drug targets the colon, and colon tissue levels and pharmacodynamic biomarkers were only exploratory objectives, with no results found. There is no human measure of F1F0-ATPase modulation or lymphocyte apoptosis. Tolerability did not limit the dose, and no other drug on this target exists. So a drug that never engaged its target cannot be told apart from a target that does not matter.

XEN-101 is an oral small molecule that Xeno says is modeled on how gastric bypass surgery works. No molecular target is recorded. The Phase 1b trial NCT06417697 was stopped for futility, not safety: in the first 23 patients there was no sign of weight loss. The earlier dose-ranging study in healthy volunteers (NCT05667129) posted no results. The company's press releases mention only that the drug was safe and well tolerated. The Phase 1b planned to measure pharmacodynamic effects (microbiome, serum ketones, metabolic biomarkers), but none were reported. No human data on exposure, target engagement or pathway effects were found. Nothing separates a drug that failed to engage its target from a mechanism that does not matter in obesity, so the code is U.

No molecular target is recorded. Systemic exposure at 4 g/day is documented: plasma EPA and DHA rose dose-proportionally, with EPA exposure similar to icosapent ethyl (PMID:28116646, PMID:32567203). Engagement is inferred adequate because the drug met its regulatory efficacy endpoint, triglyceride lowering, in hypertriglyceridemia, leading to FDA approval (NCT01242527, NCT02009865). The expected lipid-pathway effect, lower triglycerides and non-HDL-C, was shown in statin-treated patients with hypertriglyceridemia and high CV risk (NCT01408303), before the index trial began. Despite this, STRENGTH showed no effect on MACE (HR 0.99, p=0.837; NCT02104817). This indicates that triglyceride lowering by this mechanism does not reduce cardiovascular events as tested. Dose was not limited by tolerability.

No primary target is recorded. Phase 1 PK studies show dose-proportional plasma EPA/DHA exposure at 2–4 g/day (PMID:28116646, PMID:32567203, NCT01208961), so exposure is adequate. Engagement and pathway are inferred_adequate because the drug met triglyceride-lowering endpoints, a hepatic lipid-metabolism effect, in hypertriglyceridemia at 2–4 g (NCT01242527, NCT02009865, NCT01408303), leading to approval. The bundle does not state the index-trial dose, so comparability is assumed. Despite this, Epanova did not reduce MRI liver fat versus placebo at 12 weeks (GMR 0.92, 95% CI 0.76–1.12; NCT02354976). This points to the mechanism not driving liver fat as tested (F2). The trial was small (about 22 per arm) and exploratory, with a wide CI (F7). A combination with dapagliflozin did lower liver fat (NCT02279407).

In this 4-week trial, NCT01280695, fasting glucose was not significantly lower than placebo at any dose, though 250 mg (p=0.08) and 500 mg (p=0.06) came close. The NASH protocol (NCT02784444) reports dose-related steady-state plasma exposure, so exposure is adequate. At 500 mg, fasting insulin and HOMA-IR fell significantly, along with a small HbA1c drop; I count that as the downstream insulin-sensitizing effect, so pathway is adequate. No human measure of MPC binding or inhibition was found, so engagement is no_human_data. The sponsor called the glucose reductions 'clinically meaningful' and moved the drug into NASH rather than further T2D work. With engagement unmeasured, the evidence is indeterminate (U). A small, short, near-miss trial points to F7 as a secondary code.

The index trial NCT02690519 was a 7-patient open-label Phase 2 study in S1251N CF whose primary outcomes were all safety measures (AEs, labs, vitals, ECG). It is classified not_efficacy, and no results are posted, so it was not an efficacy test of GLPG1837. The sister G551D study NCT02707562 also had a descriptive safety primary endpoint. The bundle has no human exposure, engagement or pathway data: Phase 1 trials (e.g. NCT02325037) posted no results, and no sweat chloride or other biomarker results are shown. CFTR binding and potentiation are shown only in vitro and structurally (PMID:31221859, PMID:29079713). Approved potentiators such as ivacaftor show the target is valid, but the readout was not an efficacy failure.

TERPSIS (NCT05165394, PMID:40719142) missed its DARS primary endpoint (p=0.87) and the MADRS and CGI-S secondaries, with the drug well tolerated. Phase 1 showed linear plasma PK with a long half-life and no dose-limiting toxicity (PMID:35277995). No GPR139 PET ligand existed, so occupancy was never measured directly. Instead, [11C]PHNO PET in healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent attenuation of amphetamine-induced striatal dopamine release, which the authors read as brain entry and GPR139 interaction (NCT02959892, PMID:34675381). That evidence predates the index trial but comes only from healthy volunteers, not MDD patients. Treating this functional central effect as engagement, the mechanism appears tested and did not improve anhedonia, so F2. Because engagement is indirect, U is a fallback.

Plasma PK was linear with a long half-life and good tolerability up to 160 mg (PMID:35277995). No GPR139 occupancy ligand exists, but a [11C]PHNO PET study in healthy volunteers showed dose-dependent attenuation of amphetamine-induced dopamine release at 20–40 mg (NCT02959892, PMID:34675381); the authors read this as brain entry and GPR139 interaction, before the index trial. In schizophrenia patients the drug altered CBF and day-14 reward BOLD (PMID:40817174). Despite this functional engagement, BACS and day-1 VS BOLD primaries were not met (NCT03319953), and the MDD anhedonia trial also failed (NCT05165394), suggesting the mechanism does not deliver benefit. Time-dependent effects (F4) and a tiny single-dose crossover (F7) are secondary contributors. Engagement rests on indirect pharmacodynamic evidence, hence medium confidence.
